lessons.title: Nationalism in India
yt: class 10 history nationalism in india

blocks.x: Indian nationalism became a mass movement after the First World War, when high prices, taxes, forced recruitment and the influenza epidemic caused hardship. Mahatma Gandhi returned in 1915 and tried satyagraha at Champaran (1917), Kheda (1917) and Ahmedabad (1918). The Rowlatt Act (1919) and the Jallianwala Bagh massacre led to the Non-Cooperation and Khilafat Movement (1920-22), which was called off after Chauri Chaura. The Simon Commission (1927), the Lahore Congress (Purna Swaraj, 1929) and the Salt March (March 1930) began the Civil Disobedience Movement, followed by the Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931), the Round Table Conferences and the Poona Pact (1932). Peasants, business groups, workers, women and Dalits joined in different ways, and symbols such as Bharat Mata, the tricolour and folklore built a sense of belonging.
Deep dive: the First World War and Gandhi's early satyagrahas

The war created a new economic and political situation. Defence expenditure was financed by war loans and high taxes: customs duties were raised and income tax introduced. Prices doubled between 1913 and 1918. Villages were forced to supply soldiers. Crop failures of 1918-19 and 1920-21 and an influenza epidemic killed millions, so people were in distress. Gandhi came back from South Africa in January 1915 with the idea of satyagraha, the power of truth and non-violence. He organised satyagraha at Champaran in Bihar (1917) against the oppressive plantation system, at Kheda in Gujarat (1917) for peasants who could not pay revenue after crop failure, and at Ahmedabad (1918) among cotton mill workers.
Deep dive: Rowlatt Act, Jallianwala Bagh and the Khilafat

The Rowlatt Act of 1919 allowed detention without trial for two years, and Gandhi launched a nationwide satyagraha, with a hartal on 6 April 1919. On 13 April 1919, the Baisakhi day, General Dyer fired on a peaceful crowd in the enclosed Jallianwala Bagh at Amritsar. Hundreds were killed. The Khilafat issue concerned the Ottoman Caliph after the Treaty of Sevres, and the Khilafat Committee led by Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali joined with Gandhi to build Hindu-Muslim unity in a broader movement.
Deep dive: Non-Cooperation Movement 1920-22

At Calcutta (September 1920) and Nagpur (December 1920) the Congress adopted the programme of non-cooperation: surrender of titles, boycott of civil services, army, police, courts, legislative councils, schools and foreign goods. The movement began in January 1921. Students left government schools, lawyers gave up practice, council elections were boycotted (except by the Justice Party in Madras), foreign cloth was burnt and khadi popularised. In the countryside Baba Ramchandra led peasants in Awadh against talukdars and begar; in the Gudem Hills of Andhra, Alluri Sitaram Raju led a militant guerrilla movement; Assam plantation workers left the gardens, defying the Inland Emigration Act of 1859. After a violent clash at Chauri Chaura in February 1922 Gandhi called off the movement.
Deep dive: Civil Disobedience Movement

The Simon Commission of 1927 had no Indian members and was met with Go Back Simon slogans. In 1929 Lord Irwin announced a vague offer of dominion status, and at Lahore (December 1929) the Congress under Jawaharlal Nehru demanded Purna Swaraj; 26 January 1930 was observed as Independence Day. Gandhi sent an eleven-point list of demands to the Viceroy and began the Salt March from Sabarmati on 12 March 1930 with 78 volunteers, walking about 240 miles to Dandi where he broke the salt law on 6 April. Across India people violated salt laws, boycotted foreign cloth, refused to pay revenue and chaukidari tax and broke forest laws. The Gandhi-Irwin Pact of 5 March 1931 released political prisoners and Gandhi attended the Second Round Table Conference in London, but the movement was relaunched and faded by 1934.
Hindi saransh

Pehle vishwa yuddh ke baad mehangai, kar aur mahamari se janta pareshan thi. Gandhi ji ne Champaran, Kheda aur Ahmedabad mein satyagraha kiya. Rowlatt Act, Jallianwala Bagh aur Khilafat ke baad Asahyog Andolan (1920-22) aur phir Namak Satyagraha (1930) se Civil Disobedience shuru hua. Poona Pact 1932 mein hua.
Learn the chain: war distress, Champaran 1917, Rowlatt 1919, Non-Cooperation 1920, Chauri Chaura 1922, Simon 1928, Purna Swaraj 1929, Dandi 1930, Pact 1931, Poona 1932.

How did the First World War create hardships for Indians?
qa.a: The government raised defence spending by war loans and higher taxes. Customs duties went up and income tax was introduced. Prices doubled between 1913 and 1918, villagers were forced to supply soldiers, and crop failures and an influenza epidemic added to the misery.

qa.q: What was satyagraha according to Gandhi?
qa.a: Satyagraha was a method of mass agitation that emphasised the power of truth and the need to search for truth. It held that if the cause was true, physical force was not necessary to fight the oppressor, and it relied on non-violence.

qa.q: Why did the Khilafat Movement matter to nationalism?
qa.a: It was a protest by Muslims against the harsh treatment of the Ottoman Caliph after the war. Gandhi saw a chance to unite Hindus and Muslims under a common national movement against British rule.

qa.q: Why did some Congress leaders hesitate about non-cooperation in 1920?
qa.a: They feared that boycotting the councils would give a free hand to other groups and that the movement might turn violent. A compromise at the Nagpur session accepted the programme.

qa.q: How did the Non-Cooperation Movement spread in the cities?
qa.a: Middle-class students left government schools, lawyers gave up practice, councils were boycotted and foreign cloth was burnt. But khadi was costlier than mill cloth, so poor people could not boycott it for long.

qa.q: Why did the movement slow down in the cities?
qa.a: Khadi cloth was more expensive than mass-produced mill cloth and Indian institutions to replace British ones were few, so students and teachers drifted back to government schools and lawyers to courts.

qa.q: What was the peasant movement in Awadh?
qa.a: Peasants led by Baba Ramchandra protested against talukdars and landlords who demanded high rents and forced labour, begar. The Oudh Kisan Sabha was formed and Nehru helped. Peasants thought Gandhi would help.

qa.q: What happened in the Gudem Hills?
qa.a: Tribal peasants resented restrictions on grazing and shifting cultivation. Alluri Sitaram Raju led a guerrilla war, claiming special powers and rejecting non-violence, and was captured and executed in 1924.

qa.q: How did plantation workers in Assam interpret swaraj?
qa.a: They believed swaraj meant freedom to leave the confines of the plantation and to retain a link with their villages. They left the plantations, defying the Inland Emigration Act of 1859, expecting Gandhi Raj.

qa.q: Why was the Simon Commission opposed?
qa.a: It was a British-only commission to suggest constitutional changes. Indians were excluded, so all parties welcomed it with black flags and slogans of Go Back Simon.

qa.q: What was the significance of the Lahore Congress of 1929?
qa.a: The Congress, under Nehru, formally demanded Purna Swaraj, complete independence, and decided to observe 26 January 1930 as Independence Day.

qa.q: Why did Gandhi choose salt as a symbol?
qa.a: Salt was consumed by the rich and the poor alike and was one of the most essential items of food. The tax on salt and the government monopoly over its production was an oppressive burden.

qa.q: Describe the Salt March.
qa.a: Gandhi and 78 volunteers walked about 240 miles in 24 days from Sabarmati to Dandi on the Gujarat coast. On 6 April 1930 he picked up salt and violated the salt law, which started civil disobedience.

qa.q: What forms did civil disobedience take?
qa.a: People broke salt law, boycotted foreign cloth and liquor shops, peasants refused to pay revenue and chaukidari tax, village officials resigned and forest people violated forest laws.

qa.q: Why did business groups support civil disobedience?
qa.a: They wanted protection against imports of foreign goods and a favourable exchange rate. They formed the Indian Industrial and Commercial Congress in 1920 and FICCI in 1927 and funded the movement.

qa.q: Why did the industrial workers not participate much?
qa.a: Industrialists were close to the Congress, so workers kept away from the movement. Some workers in Nagpur adopted Gandhian symbols and demands against low wages and poor working conditions.

qa.q: What role did women play in civil disobedience?
qa.a: Thousands of women, many from high-caste families in urban areas and rich peasant households in rural areas, took part in protest marches, manufactured salt and picketed foreign cloth and liquor shops, and some went to jail.

qa.q: Why did Dalits not initially join the Congress movement?
qa.a: The Congress had ignored the Dalits for fear of offending the sanatanis, so many Dalit leaders asked for separate electorates and their own political solutions. Ambedkar led this demand.

qa.q: What was the Poona Pact?
qa.a: After Gandhi's fast unto death against separate electorates, Ambedkar and Gandhi signed the pact in September 1932. It gave Depressed Classes reserved seats in provincial and central councils but voted by the general electorate.

qa.q: Why did the Muslim League and Hindu Mahasabha grow after 1922?
qa.a: After the Khilafat Movement collapsed, relations between Hindus and Muslims soured. Communal riots broke out and the two organisations expanded.

qa.q: How did images help build nationalism?
qa.a: The image of Bharat Mata, first painted by Abanindranath Tagore as an ascetic figure, gave the nation a visible form. Later versions showed her as a mother figure which people could worship.

qa.q: How did folklore and history strengthen nationalism?
qa.a: Nationalists collected folk tales, ballads and songs to rediscover an authentic culture, and Indians wrote histories showing past glories to take pride and oppose colonial claims.

qa.q: What were the limits of the Civil Disobedience Movement?
qa.a: It lacked wide Dalit and Muslim participation. Many Muslims were alienated by the Congress's close links with Hindu religious symbols, and the movement faded by 1934.

problems.q: Why did Gandhi launch a nationwide satyagraha against the Rowlatt Act in 1919?
problems.a: The Rowlatt Act gave the government power to repress political activities and allowed detention of political prisoners without trial for two years. Gandhi saw it as an unjust law passed against the unanimous opposition of Indian members, so he organised a hartal on 6 April 1919 and a non-violent civil disobedience campaign against it.

rubric.t: Act allowed detention without trial for two years

problems.q: Explain why the Non-Cooperation Movement began and why Gandhi called it off in 1922.
problems.a: It began because of the Jallianwala Bagh massacre, the Rowlatt Act and the Khilafat issue; Gandhi felt Indians cooperated with British rule and could end it by withdrawing cooperation: boycotting schools, courts, councils and foreign goods. In February 1922 a crowd at Chauri Chaura set a police station on fire, killing policemen. Gandhi feared violence and called off the movement because satyagraha had to be non-violent and masses were not yet disciplined.

rubric.t: Causes: Rowlatt Act, Jallianwala Bagh and Khilafat
Programme: boycott of institutions and foreign goods

problems.q: Discuss the participation of different social groups in the Civil Disobedience Movement and how the Poona Pact tried to settle the Dalit question.
problems.a: Rich peasants such as Patidars and Jats, hit by falling prices, supported it and wanted revenue reduced. Business groups, including FICCI leaders like Birla and Purshottamdas Thakurdas, backed it to end colonial restrictions on trade. Workers in Nagpur joined in some places. Women marched, picketed and went to jail. Many Dalits stayed away until Ambedkar organised the Depressed Classes Association in 1930 and demanded separate electorates. Gandhi began a fast unto death against this and under the Poona Pact of September 1932 the Depressed Classes got reserved seats in provincial and central councils, to be voted by the general electorate.

rubric.t: Peasants and business groups and their reasons
Poona Pact reserved seats voted by general electorate

Visual lesson

Nationalism in India

Indian nationalism became a mass movement after the First World War, when high prices, taxes, forced recruitment and the influenza epidemic caused hardship

🔑

Big idea

  • Indian nationalism became a mass movement after the First World War, when high prices, taxes, forced recruitment and the influenza epidemic caused…
  • Mahatma Gandhi returned in 1915 and tried satyagraha at Champaran (1917), Kheda (1917) and Ahmedabad (1918)
  • The Rowlatt Act (1919) and the Jallianwala Bagh massacre led to the Non-Cooperation and Khilafat Movement (1920-22), which was called off after…
  • The Simon Commission (1927), the Lahore Congress (Purna Swaraj, 1929) and the Salt March (March 1930) began the Civil Disobedience Movement, followed…
Read the full explanation

Indian nationalism became a mass movement after the First World War, when high prices, taxes, forced recruitment and the influenza epidemic caused hardship. Mahatma Gandhi returned in 1915 and tried satyagraha at Champaran (1917), Kheda (1917) and Ahmedabad (1918). The Rowlatt Act (1919) and the Jallianwala Bagh massacre led to the Non-Cooperation and Khilafat Movement (1920-22), which was called off after Chauri Chaura. The Simon Commission (1927), the Lahore Congress (Purna Swaraj, 1929) and the Salt March (March 1930) began the Civil Disobedience Movement, followed by the Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931), the Round Table Conferences and the Poona Pact (1932). Peasants, business groups, workers, women and Dalits joined in different ways, and symbols such as Bharat Mata, the tricolour and folklore built a sense of belonging.

🕰️

The First World War and Gandhi's early satyagrahas

  • The war created a new economic and political situation
  • Defence expenditure was financed by war loans and high taxes: customs duties were raised and income tax introduced
  • Prices doubled between 1913 and 1918
  • Villages were forced to supply soldiers
Read the full explanation

The war created a new economic and political situation. Defence expenditure was financed by war loans and high taxes: customs duties were raised and income tax introduced. Prices doubled between 1913 and 1918. Villages were forced to supply soldiers. Crop failures of 1918-19 and 1920-21 and an influenza epidemic killed millions, so people were in distress. Gandhi came back from South Africa in January 1915 with the idea of satyagraha, the power of truth and non-violence. He organised satyagraha at Champaran in Bihar (1917) against the oppressive plantation system, at Kheda in Gujarat (1917) for peasants who could not pay revenue after crop failure, and at Ahmedabad (1918) among cotton mill workers.

🧠

Rowlatt Act, Jallianwala Bagh and the Khilafat

  • The Rowlatt Act of 1919 allowed detention without trial for two years, and Gandhi launched a nationwide satyagraha, with a hartal on 6 April 1919
  • On 13 April 1919, the Baisakhi day, General Dyer fired on a peaceful crowd in the enclosed Jallianwala Bagh at Amritsar
  • Hundreds were killed
  • The Khilafat issue concerned the Ottoman Caliph after the Treaty of Sevres, and the Khilafat Committee led by Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali joined…
Read the full explanation

The Rowlatt Act of 1919 allowed detention without trial for two years, and Gandhi launched a nationwide satyagraha, with a hartal on 6 April 1919. On 13 April 1919, the Baisakhi day, General Dyer fired on a peaceful crowd in the enclosed Jallianwala Bagh at Amritsar. Hundreds were killed. The Khilafat issue concerned the Ottoman Caliph after the Treaty of Sevres, and the Khilafat Committee led by Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali joined with Gandhi to build Hindu-Muslim unity in a broader movement.

🕰️

Non-Cooperation Movement 1920-22

  • At Calcutta (September 1920) and Nagpur (December 1920) the Congress adopted the programme of non-cooperation: surrender of titles, boycott of civil…
  • The movement began in January 1921
  • Students left government schools, lawyers gave up practice, council elections were boycotted (except by the Justice Party in Madras), foreign cloth…
  • In the countryside Baba Ramchandra led peasants in Awadh against talukdars and begar
Read the full explanation

At Calcutta (September 1920) and Nagpur (December 1920) the Congress adopted the programme of non-cooperation: surrender of titles, boycott of civil services, army, police, courts, legislative councils, schools and foreign goods. The movement began in January 1921. Students left government schools, lawyers gave up practice, council elections were boycotted (except by the Justice Party in Madras), foreign cloth was burnt and khadi popularised. In the countryside Baba Ramchandra led peasants in Awadh against talukdars and begar; in the Gudem Hills of Andhra, Alluri Sitaram Raju led a militant guerrilla movement; Assam plantation workers left the gardens, defying the Inland Emigration Act of 1859. After a violent clash at Chauri Chaura in February 1922 Gandhi called off the movement.

🕰️

Civil Disobedience Movement

  • The Simon Commission of 1927 had no Indian members and was met with Go Back Simon slogans
  • In 1929 Lord Irwin announced a vague offer of dominion status, and at Lahore (December 1929) the Congress under Jawaharlal Nehru demanded Purna Swaraj
  • 26 January 1930 was observed as Independence Day
  • Gandhi sent an eleven-point list of demands to the Viceroy and began the Salt March from Sabarmati on 12 March 1930 with 78 volunteers, walking about…
Read the full explanation

The Simon Commission of 1927 had no Indian members and was met with Go Back Simon slogans. In 1929 Lord Irwin announced a vague offer of dominion status, and at Lahore (December 1929) the Congress under Jawaharlal Nehru demanded Purna Swaraj; 26 January 1930 was observed as Independence Day. Gandhi sent an eleven-point list of demands to the Viceroy and began the Salt March from Sabarmati on 12 March 1930 with 78 volunteers, walking about 240 miles to Dandi where he broke the salt law on 6 April. Across India people violated salt laws, boycotted foreign cloth, refused to pay revenue and chaukidari tax and broke forest laws. The Gandhi-Irwin Pact of 5 March 1931 released political prisoners and Gandhi attended the Second Round Table Conference in London, but the movement was relaunched and faded by 1934.

lessons.title: The Making of a Global World
yt: class 10 history the making of a global world

blocks.x: The global world grew from ancient silk routes and the exchange of food, goods and ideas. After 1492 the Americas joined the world economy and silver, disease and slavery changed the world. In the nineteenth century trade, migration and capital flows expanded under the influence of the abolition of the Corn Laws, railways, steamships and colonial rule, and Indians were sent as indentured labour. The First World War, the 1920s boom and the Great Depression (1929) wrecked this economy. After the Second World War the Bretton Woods Conference (1944) created the IMF and World Bank, decolonisation brought new nations, and from the 1970s multinational companies, floating exchange rates and a shift of industry to Asia led to a new phase of globalisation.
Deep dive: the pre-modern world

The silk routes linked Asia with Europe and North Africa, carrying Chinese pottery, textiles from India and spices from Southeast Asia, while Christian missionaries, Muslim preachers and Buddhist monks travelled the same roads. Food also travelled: noodles are believed to have gone from China to the West, and potatoes, soya, groundnuts, maize, tomatoes, chillies and sweet potatoes reached the rest of the world after the Americas were discovered in 1492. The potato became the staple of poor Europeans; the Irish potato famine of the 1840s killed about a million people. After the conquest by the Portuguese and Spanish in the sixteenth century, smallpox and other diseases killed native Americans, and silver from Potosi in Peru and Mexico financed trade with Asia. African slaves were forced to work on cotton and sugar plantations.
Deep dive: the nineteenth century world economy

Britain abolished the Corn Laws in 1846 under pressure from industrialists and urban people, which opened the country to cheap food imports and led farmers to fall back. Railways, steamships and the telegraph speeded the movement of goods and people, and refrigerated ships allowed the shipment of meat. In Africa, the cattle plague rinderpest of the 1890s killed about 90 percent of cattle, which forced Africans to take wage work. Indentured labourers from India, who signed contracts for five years, went to plantations in the Caribbean, Fiji, Mauritius and Trinidad, and the system was abolished in 1921. India supplied raw cotton, jute and wheat, and paid Britain home charges while its exports earned a surplus that balanced Britain's deficits with other countries.
Deep dive: war, boom and depression

The First World War of 1914-18 was fought between the Allies (Britain, France, Russia) and the Central Powers (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Ottoman Turkey), caused about 9 million deaths and turned the USA from a debtor into a creditor. In the 1920s the American economy boomed with Ford's assembly line, mass production and consumer goods bought on credit, but agriculture suffered overproduction. The Great Depression started in 1929 after the Wall Street Crash, when banks recalled loans, farm prices collapsed, thousands of banks failed and unemployment reached about one third of the US workforce by 1933. Indian exports and prices of farm goods fell sharply, so peasants fell into debt.
Deep dive: the post-war order

In July 1944 delegates from 44 countries met at Bretton Woods in New Hampshire, USA. They set up the International Monetary Fund to deal with external surpluses and deficits and the World Bank (IBRD) to finance post-war reconstruction, with fixed exchange rates linked to the dollar and gold. Many former colonies became independent but remained poor, so the G-77 demanded a New International Economic Order in the 1960s. From the 1970s exchange rates were floated, multinational companies (MNCs) moved production to low-wage Asian countries and industrial unemployment rose in the West. The 1990s saw China, India and Brazil among the fast-growing economies.

How did the silk routes link the world?
qa.a: Merchants carried Chinese pottery, Indian textiles and Southeast Asian spices across Asia to Europe and Africa. Travellers also spread religions such as Buddhism, Christianity and Islam along these routes.

qa.q: Why did the potato become important in Europe?
qa.a: It gave poor people a cheap, filling food that grew well in poor soil, improving diet and life expectancy, but heavy dependence led to the Irish famine when blight destroyed the crop in the 1840s.

qa.q: How did disease help the conquest of the Americas?
qa.a: The native Americans had no immunity to smallpox brought by Europeans. Millions died, which weakened resistance and helped the Spanish and Portuguese conquer them.

qa.q: Why did Britain abolish the Corn Laws?
qa.a: Industrial growth raised food demand. Industrialists and city dwellers wanted cheaper food, and under their pressure the government abolished the laws, allowing food imports that undercut British farmers.

qa.q: What were the effects of rinderpest in Africa?
qa.a: It killed about 90 percent of cattle, destroying livelihoods. Africans had to work for wages on mines and plantations, which helped colonisers conquer and control the continent.

qa.q: Why did people migrate in the nineteenth century?
qa.a: People left for jobs and better lives. Industry and farms in the Americas and Australia needed workers, and cheaper ships and railways made travel easier, while many Indians went under indenture.

qa.q: Describe the life of Indian indentured labourers.
qa.a: They signed contracts, often under false promises, and worked on plantations in the Caribbean, Fiji and Mauritius. Conditions were harsh, and many could not return after the contract ended.

qa.q: How did indentured labourers create new cultures?
qa.a: They developed cultural forms such as the Hosay festival, chutney music in Trinidad and Guyana, and the Rastafarian movement.

qa.q: What was India's role in the nineteenth-century world economy?
qa.a: India exported raw cotton, jute and wheat and imported British manufactures. Its trade surplus with Britain helped pay Britain's deficits with other countries and home charges.

qa.q: How did the First World War change the global economy?
qa.a: War debts made the US a creditor and Britain a debtor. Industries in Europe were shifted to war production and trade was disrupted, hurting economies for years.

qa.q: What was the effect of mass production in the USA?
qa.a: Ford's assembly line lowered costs and raised sales of cars, refrigerators and washing machines. Credit financed consumers, but demand finally slowed and left overproduction.

qa.q: Why did the Great Depression spread across the world?
qa.a: US banks stopped lending and recalled loans, and countries raised tariffs. Falling demand and prices cut trade and production and spread unemployment.

qa.q: How did the Great Depression affect India?
qa.a: Exports fell, prices of farm goods dropped by half while revenue stayed fixed, peasants went into debt, and gold flowed out of India, benefiting Britain.

qa.q: What decisions were taken at Bretton Woods?
qa.a: The IMF was set up to handle external deficits and surpluses, the World Bank to finance reconstruction, and exchange rates were fixed relative to the dollar and gold.

qa.q: Why were the IMF and World Bank called Bretton Woods twins?
qa.a: Both were created at the 1944 conference and were meant to work together to stabilise the post-war international economic system.

qa.q: What was the NIEO?
qa.a: The New International Economic Order was a demand of developing countries, organised as the G-77, for control over their natural resources and fairer trade terms.

qa.q: How did MNCs change the world economy after 1970?
qa.a: They moved production to low-wage countries in Asia to cut costs, which created jobs there but caused industrial unemployment in the West.

qa.q: Why did fixed exchange rates end?
qa.a: US finances and competition from Europe and Japan weakened the dollar, so by the 1970s the system of fixed rates broke and floating rates came in.

qa.q: What is globalisation according to the chapter?
qa.a: It is the growing integration of the world through the flow of trade, people, capital and ideas, a process with several phases.

qa.q: How did the Depression show the danger of a connected economy?
qa.a: A crash in one country spread to others through trade and credit, so problems in the US banking system affected farmers in India and workers in Europe.

problems.q: Explain how the discovery of the Americas changed the world economy.
problems.a: After 1492 food crops such as potato, maize and tomato spread across the world, improving diets and population. The conquest by Spain and Portugal and the use of silver from Potosi and Mexico financed trade with Asia, and the demand for labour on plantations led to the slave trade, while diseases like smallpox destroyed the native population.

problems.q: Describe how the Great Depression began and how it affected India.
problems.a: The depression began in 1929 with overproduction in agriculture, falling prices and the Wall Street Crash. US banks recalled loans from Europe, causing bank failures, collapse of trade and mass unemployment. In India exports of jute and cotton fell, prices of wheat and jute dropped, and peasants were hit by rigid revenue demands and debt.

rubric.t: Fall in Indian exports and prices

problems.q: Discuss the role of the Bretton Woods institutions and why their system changed after 1970.
problems.a: Bretton Woods in 1944 created the IMF to handle balance of payments and the World Bank to finance reconstruction, with fixed exchange rates linked to the dollar and gold. It supported growth in the West in the 1950s and 1960s. By the 1970s US finances weakened, fixed rates collapsed and floating exchange rates were introduced. Developing countries could not rely on the IMF and World Bank alone and demanded a New International Economic Order, while MNCs shifted production to low-wage countries in Asia, ending an era of Western industrial dominance.

Big idea

  • The global world grew from ancient silk routes and the exchange of food, goods and ideas
  • After 1492 the Americas joined the world economy and silver, disease and slavery changed the world
  • In the nineteenth century trade, migration and capital flows expanded under the influence of the abolition of the Corn Laws, railways, steamships and…

Read the full explanation

The global world grew from ancient silk routes and the exchange of food, goods and ideas. After 1492 the Americas joined the world economy and silver, disease and slavery changed the world. In the nineteenth century trade, migration and capital flows expanded under the influence of the abolition of the Corn Laws, railways, steamships and colonial rule, and Indians were sent as indentured labour. The First World War, the 1920s boom and the Great Depression (1929) wrecked this economy. After the Second World War the Bretton Woods Conference (1944) created the IMF and World Bank, decolonisation brought new nations, and from the 1970s multinational companies, floating exchange rates and a shift of industry to Asia led to a new phase of globalisation.

📌

The pre-modern world

  • The silk routes linked Asia with Europe and North Africa, carrying Chinese pottery, textiles from India and spices from Southeast Asia, while…
  • Food also travelled: noodles are believed to have gone from China to the West, and potatoes, soya, groundnuts, maize, tomatoes, chillies and sweet…
  • The potato became the staple of poor Europeans
  • The Irish potato famine of the 1840s killed about a million people
Read the full explanation

The silk routes linked Asia with Europe and North Africa, carrying Chinese pottery, textiles from India and spices from Southeast Asia, while Christian missionaries, Muslim preachers and Buddhist monks travelled the same roads. Food also travelled: noodles are believed to have gone from China to the West, and potatoes, soya, groundnuts, maize, tomatoes, chillies and sweet potatoes reached the rest of the world after the Americas were discovered in 1492. The potato became the staple of poor Europeans; the Irish potato famine of the 1840s killed about a million people. After the conquest by the Portuguese and Spanish in the sixteenth century, smallpox and other diseases killed native Americans, and silver from Potosi in Peru and Mexico financed trade with Asia. African slaves were forced to work on cotton and sugar plantations.

🏛️

The nineteenth century world economy

  • Britain abolished the Corn Laws in 1846 under pressure from industrialists and urban people, which opened the country to cheap food imports and led…
  • Railways, steamships and the telegraph speeded the movement of goods and people, and refrigerated ships allowed the shipment of meat
  • In Africa, the cattle plague rinderpest of the 1890s killed about 90 percent of cattle, which forced Africans to take wage work
  • Indentured labourers from India, who signed contracts for five years, went to plantations in the Caribbean, Fiji, Mauritius and Trinidad, and the…
Read the full explanation

Britain abolished the Corn Laws in 1846 under pressure from industrialists and urban people, which opened the country to cheap food imports and led farmers to fall back. Railways, steamships and the telegraph speeded the movement of goods and people, and refrigerated ships allowed the shipment of meat. In Africa, the cattle plague rinderpest of the 1890s killed about 90 percent of cattle, which forced Africans to take wage work. Indentured labourers from India, who signed contracts for five years, went to plantations in the Caribbean, Fiji, Mauritius and Trinidad, and the system was abolished in 1921. India supplied raw cotton, jute and wheat, and paid Britain home charges while its exports earned a surplus that balanced Britain's deficits with other countries.

🕰️

War, boom and depression

  • The First World War of 1914-18 was fought between the Allies (Britain, France, Russia) and the Central Powers (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Ottoman…
  • In the 1920s the American economy boomed with Ford's assembly line, mass production and consumer goods bought on credit, but agriculture suffered…
  • The Great Depression started in 1929 after the Wall Street Crash, when banks recalled loans, farm prices collapsed, thousands of banks failed and…
  • Indian exports and prices of farm goods fell sharply, so peasants fell into debt
Read the full explanation

The First World War of 1914-18 was fought between the Allies (Britain, France, Russia) and the Central Powers (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Ottoman Turkey), caused about 9 million deaths and turned the USA from a debtor into a creditor. In the 1920s the American economy boomed with Ford's assembly line, mass production and consumer goods bought on credit, but agriculture suffered overproduction. The Great Depression started in 1929 after the Wall Street Crash, when banks recalled loans, farm prices collapsed, thousands of banks failed and unemployment reached about one third of the US workforce by 1933. Indian exports and prices of farm goods fell sharply, so peasants fell into debt.

🕰️

The post-war order

  • In July 1944 delegates from 44 countries met at Bretton Woods in New Hampshire, USA
  • They set up the International Monetary Fund to deal with external surpluses and deficits and the World Bank (IBRD) to finance post-war…
  • Many former colonies became independent but remained poor, so the G-77 demanded a New International Economic Order in the 1960s
  • From the 1970s exchange rates were floated, multinational companies (MNCs) moved production to low-wage Asian countries and industrial unemployment…
Read the full explanation

In July 1944 delegates from 44 countries met at Bretton Woods in New Hampshire, USA. They set up the International Monetary Fund to deal with external surpluses and deficits and the World Bank (IBRD) to finance post-war reconstruction, with fixed exchange rates linked to the dollar and gold. Many former colonies became independent but remained poor, so the G-77 demanded a New International Economic Order in the 1960s. From the 1970s exchange rates were floated, multinational companies (MNCs) moved production to low-wage Asian countries and industrial unemployment rose in the West. The 1990s saw China, India and Brazil among the fast-growing economies.

lessons.title: The Age of Industrialisation
yt: class 10 history the age of industrialisation

blocks.x: Industrialisation did not begin with factories alone. Before them, merchants used proto-industrialisation, giving work to peasants and artisans in the countryside. In Britain, cotton mills, Arkwright, Watt's steam engine and the railways drove the Industrial Revolution, yet hand labour remained important because it was cheap and seasonal. In India, textiles were exported from Surat, Masulipatam and Hooghly until the East India Company's gomasthas, monopoly and the flood of Manchester goods ruined many weavers. From 1854 Indian entrepreneurs such as Dwarkanath Tagore, the Tatas, Birla and Hukumchand set up cotton, jute and steel firms, helped by the First World War and Swadeshi. Advertisements and labels created a market, and labour was recruited through jobbers.
Deep dive: before the factory: proto-industrialisation

From the seventeenth century merchants from towns moved to the countryside, supplying money to peasants and artisans to produce goods for an international market. Poor peasants and cottagers welcomed this, as it gave extra income. Producers worked at home, while the clothier bought wool from the stapler, then gave it to spinners, carders and fullers before it reached the weavers. This was called proto-industrialisation because it was a phase before and alongside the factory. It was also more profitable for the merchants because they escaped the restrictions of urban guilds.
Deep dive: the coming of the factory

The first factories in England came up by the 1730s, and the cotton mill became the symbol of the new era. Richard Arkwright created the cotton mill, and new machines raised output: the spinning jenny of James Hargreaves (1764), steam engines improved by James Watt, and rail. Raw cotton imports rose from 2.5 million pounds in 1760 to 22 million pounds in 1787. Yet hand labour did not vanish. Many industries, such as Victorian tailoring, bookbinding and the London season trades, relied on seasonal demand and cheap labour. Workers feared machines, and women attacked spinning jennies in the woollen industry.
Deep dive: Indian textiles and colonial rule

Before the 1760s Indian silk and cotton goods dominated trade in Asia. Surat, Masulipatam and Hooghly were major ports; with colonial control, Bombay and Calcutta rose. The East India Company wanted a monopoly, eliminated competition, appointed paid gomasthas to supervise weavers, checked the quality of cloth and prevented weavers from selling to others. Weavers rebelled in places. By the 1850s Manchester cloth flooded Indian markets, raw cotton exports rose and weavers lost both markets and raw materials. In the 1860s the American Civil War cut the cotton supply to Britain, so Indian cotton prices rose and weavers were starved of supply.
Deep dive: Indian factories, workers and markets

The first cotton mill in Bombay started in 1854 and the first jute mill in Bengal in 1855. Dwarkanath Tagore invested in shipping, mining and plantations, while the Parsis Dinshaw Petit and Jamsetji Tata, the Marwari Seth Hukumchand and the Birla family built industries. Tata Iron and Steel at Jamshedpur began producing steel in 1912. The First World War cut British imports and created demand for jute bags, cloth and steel. Mill workers were hired through jobbers who also controlled them. New markets were built with advertisements, calendars and labels, and Indian firms used nationalist messages. Small handloom units survived by using fly-shuttle looms.

qa.q: Why did some producers in Europe prefer hand labour to machines?
qa.a: In Victorian Britain labour was cheap and the supply plentiful, so owners saw no need for costly machines. Many goods needed seasonal work, detailed design or small batches that machines could not handle, such as fashion goods and bespoke clothes.

qa.q: What was the impact of the spinning jenny on workers?
qa.a: It spun many threads at once so fewer workers were needed. Women dependent on spinning for income feared unemployment, so they attacked machines, and the protests continued in the 1790s.

qa.q: Why did industrialisation start with cotton in Britain?
qa.a: Cotton was a growing consumer market with cheap imports of raw cotton from colonies. New machines made mass production possible and the cotton mills, power looms and later railways formed a base for more growth.

qa.q: How did colonial rule hurt Indian weavers?
qa.a: Gomasthas controlled prices, supplies and sales. Raw cotton was exported to Britain so weavers faced a shortage, and Manchester cloth was cheaper than hand-made cloth.

qa.q: Why did Indian textiles decline in the nineteenth century?
qa.a: British machine-made cloth flooded the Indian market, India's exports of cloth to Britain fell as duties rose, and cotton was shipped to England as raw material.

qa.q: How did the American Civil War affect Indian weavers?
qa.a: The war stopped cotton shipments from the US, so Britain bought Indian raw cotton in large quantities. Prices rose and Indian weavers could not get cotton at a price they could afford.

qa.q: Who were the early Indian industrialists?
qa.a: They included Dwarkanath Tagore, Dinshaw Petit, Jamsetji Tata, Seth Hukumchand and G. D. Birla, many of whom made fortunes in the China trade and invested in mills and steel.

qa.q: Why could Indian business grow after the Swadeshi movement?
qa.a: The movement encouraged boycott of British goods and preference for Indian goods, increasing the demand for Indian cloth and other products.

qa.q: What was a jobber's role in Indian mills?
qa.a: A jobber recruited villagers, helped them get a place and settle in the city, and also demanded money and favours. He gained influence by controlling the workers.

qa.q: Why were workers in Indian mills mostly from nearby districts?
qa.a: Industrial workers came from villages around the factory. Many remained connected to their villages and went back at harvest time, so the workforce moved with seasons.

qa.q: How did the First World War help Indian industry?
qa.a: British imports fell as mills made war goods, while Indian mills supplied jute bags, cloth and steel to the army. Demand and profits rose and more workers were employed.

qa.q: Why did handloom weavers survive in India?
qa.a: They concentrated on finer varieties and fancy designs that mills could not copy easily. Adoption of fly-shuttle looms increased output, so handlooms continued despite mill competition.

qa.q: How did advertisements help sell goods?
qa.a: Labels, calendars and newspapers made goods familiar and trusted. Pictures of gods and rulers appealed to many people, so even those who could not read recognised the brands.

qa.q: How did Indian manufacturers use advertisements for nationalism?
qa.a: Their ads carried nationalist messages: if you care for the nation, buy products that Indians make, linking buying to patriotism.

qa.q: What were the effects of the abolition of the East India Company's monopoly?
qa.a: After 1813 more British traders could trade with India, adding to competition and cheap imports that hurt local weavers.

qa.q: What is the significance of Manchester labels?
qa.a: Labels carrying the place of manufacture conveyed quality and helped sell British cloth. Indian companies copied them to build trust.

qa.q: Why are Indian handloom clusters such as Sholapur and Madras known?
qa.a: They survived by making coarse cloth for local use and through the use of the fly shuttle, serving poorer consumers.

qa.q: Why did industries use jobbers instead of direct hiring?
qa.a: Recruiting workers from villages was hard, and jobbers knew them and could organise them quickly. They controlled workers on behalf of the factory owners.

qa.q: How did colonial government attitudes shape Indian industry?
qa.a: British officials favoured British goods and exporters, and policies like low tariffs on imports favoured Manchester while limiting Indian industry.

qa.q: What kinds of Indian industries were mostly set up by the 1900s?
qa.a: Cotton and jute mills dominated, with coal mining, indigo and iron and steel following. Tata Steel started in 1912 in Jamshedpur.

problems.q: What was proto-industrialisation and why did merchants prefer it?
problems.a: It was the phase of industrial production for an international market that was not based on factories. Merchants moved to the countryside, gave advances to peasants and artisans and avoided the restrictions of town guilds, while poor peasants gained extra income.

rubric.t: Definition: production for the market before factories

problems.q: Explain how the East India Company controlled Indian weavers.
problems.a: The Company wanted a monopoly over cotton and silk. It eliminated competition by merchants, appointed paid gomasthas to supervise weavers, collect supplies and examine the quality of cloth, gave advances so weavers could not sell to others, and punished delays. This reduced the weavers' bargaining power, and conflicts rose between weavers and gomasthas.

rubric.t: Advances and ban on selling to others
Conflict and loss of bargaining power

problems.q: Discuss how the First World War and the Swadeshi movement helped Indian industry grow.
problems.a: In the war British mills were busy producing for the army, so Manchester imports to India fell. Indian mills got a huge demand for jute bags, cloth, uniforms and steel and ran multiple shifts, hiring more workers and making large profits. The Swadeshi and boycott movements encouraged Indians to buy Indian goods. After the war Manchester could not recover its old Indian market, so factory production in India expanded and industrialists like Tata and Birla grew in importance.

rubric.t: Fall in imports from Manchester during the war
Army demand for jute, cloth and steel and more shifts

The Age of Industrialisation

Industrialisation did not begin with factories alone

🔑

Big idea

  • Industrialisation did not begin with factories alone
  • Before them, merchants used proto-industrialisation, giving work to peasants and artisans in the countryside
  • In Britain, cotton mills, Arkwright, Watt's steam engine and the railways drove the Industrial Revolution, yet hand labour remained important because…
  • In India, textiles were exported from Surat, Masulipatam and Hooghly until the East India Company's gomasthas, monopoly and the flood of Manchester…
Read the full explanation

Industrialisation did not begin with factories alone. Before them, merchants used proto-industrialisation, giving work to peasants and artisans in the countryside. In Britain, cotton mills, Arkwright, Watt's steam engine and the railways drove the Industrial Revolution, yet hand labour remained important because it was cheap and seasonal. In India, textiles were exported from Surat, Masulipatam and Hooghly until the East India Company's gomasthas, monopoly and the flood of Manchester goods ruined many weavers. From 1854 Indian entrepreneurs such as Dwarkanath Tagore, the Tatas, Birla and Hukumchand set up cotton, jute and steel firms, helped by the First World War and Swadeshi. Advertisements and labels created a market, and labour was recruited through jobbers.

📌

Before the factory: proto-industrialisation

  • From the seventeenth century merchants from towns moved to the countryside, supplying money to peasants and artisans to produce goods for an…
  • Poor peasants and cottagers welcomed this, as it gave extra income
  • Producers worked at home, while the clothier bought wool from the stapler, then gave it to spinners, carders and fullers before it reached the weavers
  • This was called proto-industrialisation because it was a phase before and alongside the factory
Read the full explanation

From the seventeenth century merchants from towns moved to the countryside, supplying money to peasants and artisans to produce goods for an international market. Poor peasants and cottagers welcomed this, as it gave extra income. Producers worked at home, while the clothier bought wool from the stapler, then gave it to spinners, carders and fullers before it reached the weavers. This was called proto-industrialisation because it was a phase before and alongside the factory. It was also more profitable for the merchants because they escaped the restrictions of urban guilds.

🧠

The coming of the factory

  • The first factories in England came up by the 1730s, and the cotton mill became the symbol of the new era
  • Richard Arkwright created the cotton mill, and new machines raised output: the spinning jenny of James Hargreaves (1764), steam engines improved by…
  • Raw cotton imports rose from 2.5 million pounds in 1760 to 22 million pounds in 1787
  • Yet hand labour did not vanish
Read the full explanation

The first factories in England came up by the 1730s, and the cotton mill became the symbol of the new era. Richard Arkwright created the cotton mill, and new machines raised output: the spinning jenny of James Hargreaves (1764), steam engines improved by James Watt, and rail. Raw cotton imports rose from 2.5 million pounds in 1760 to 22 million pounds in 1787. Yet hand labour did not vanish. Many industries, such as Victorian tailoring, bookbinding and the London season trades, relied on seasonal demand and cheap labour. Workers feared machines, and women attacked spinning jennies in the woollen industry.

⚖️

Indian textiles and colonial rule

  • Before the 1760s Indian silk and cotton goods dominated trade in Asia
  • Surat, Masulipatam and Hooghly were major ports
  • With colonial control, Bombay and Calcutta rose
  • The East India Company wanted a monopoly, eliminated competition, appointed paid gomasthas to supervise weavers, checked the quality of cloth and…
Read the full explanation

Before the 1760s Indian silk and cotton goods dominated trade in Asia. Surat, Masulipatam and Hooghly were major ports; with colonial control, Bombay and Calcutta rose. The East India Company wanted a monopoly, eliminated competition, appointed paid gomasthas to supervise weavers, checked the quality of cloth and prevented weavers from selling to others. Weavers rebelled in places. By the 1850s Manchester cloth flooded Indian markets, raw cotton exports rose and weavers lost both markets and raw materials. In the 1860s the American Civil War cut the cotton supply to Britain, so Indian cotton prices rose and weavers were starved of supply.

🚀

Indian factories, workers and markets

  • The first cotton mill in Bombay started in 1854 and the first jute mill in Bengal in 1855
  • Dwarkanath Tagore invested in shipping, mining and plantations, while the Parsis Dinshaw Petit and Jamsetji Tata, the Marwari Seth Hukumchand and the…
  • Tata Iron and Steel at Jamshedpur began producing steel in 1912
  • The First World War cut British imports and created demand for jute bags, cloth and steel
Read the full explanation

The first cotton mill in Bombay started in 1854 and the first jute mill in Bengal in 1855. Dwarkanath Tagore invested in shipping, mining and plantations, while the Parsis Dinshaw Petit and Jamsetji Tata, the Marwari Seth Hukumchand and the Birla family built industries. Tata Iron and Steel at Jamshedpur began producing steel in 1912. The First World War cut British imports and created demand for jute bags, cloth and steel. Mill workers were hired through jobbers who also controlled them. New markets were built with advertisements, calendars and labels, and Indian firms used nationalist messages. Small handloom units survived by using fly-shuttle looms.

lessons.title: Print Culture and the Modern World
yt: class 10 history print culture and the modern world

blocks.x: Printing began in China, Japan and Korea with hand-printing from woodblocks. Marco Polo brought the technique to Europe, and in the 1430s Johann Gutenberg built the printing press in Strasbourg, producing the Bible. Print spread ideas: Martin Luther's Ninety-Five Theses (1517) fuelled the Reformation, the Church created the Index of Prohibited Books, and reading culture helped the Enlightenment and the French Revolution. New presses, cheap books, novels and magazines created new readers including women and workers. In India print came with the Portuguese in Goa, and newspapers, social reform, religious debate and women's writing grew in the nineteenth century, while the colonial government answered with the Vernacular Press Act of 1878.
Deep dive: the first printed books

Printing technology developed in China, Japan and Korea where books were printed by hand with woodblocks. China had a large number of educated officials and the state was the major producer of printed material. Buddhist missionaries brought printing to Japan around AD 768-770, and the oldest Japanese book, the Buddhist Diamond Sutra, was printed in AD 868. In Japan Kitagawa Utamaro produced ukiyo pictures of the floating world. Marco Polo brought woodblock printing from China to Italy in 1295, and soon books were printed in Europe on woodblocks, mainly for the rich and for Church use.
Deep dive: Gutenberg and the print revolution

Johann Gutenberg, the son of a merchant, grew up on a large agricultural estate and saw wine and olive presses. He adapted that technology to design a printing press with metal moulds for the alphabet in the 1430s at Strasbourg. The first book he printed was the Bible, and about 180 copies were printed in three years. Presses spread across Europe and between 1450 and 1550 printing presses were set up in most countries. The new technology changed how people read and thought: they could read cheap books, and there was an explosion of reading. Martin Luther wrote Ninety-Five Theses in 1517 criticising the practices of the Roman Catholic Church, and his translation of the New Testament sold 5,000 copies in a few weeks, which helped begin the Protestant Reformation. In 1558 the Church began to maintain an Index of Prohibited Books, and Menocchio, an Italian miller, was executed for his reading of the Bible and other books.
Deep dive: the print and the modern world

Print popularised ideas of the Enlightenment through writers such as Voltaire and Rousseau, created a public debate and prepared the ground for the French Revolution. Louis-Sebastien Mercier said the printing press was the powerful engine of progress and public opinion would sweep despotism away. In the nineteenth century the steam-powered cylindrical press of Richard M. Hoe printed 8,000 sheets per hour, the offset press and electrically operated presses followed, and publishers produced penny magazines, novels, almanacs and cheap series. Women became readers and writers, including Jane Austen, the Bronte sisters and George Eliot; children's books such as the Grimm brothers' fairy tales were published.
Deep dive: print in India

Printing came to India with the Portuguese missionaries in Goa in the mid-sixteenth century. Catholic priests printed the first Tamil book in 1579 at Cochin and the first Malayalam book in 1713, and Dutch Protestant missionaries printed Tamil texts. James Augustus Hicky began the Bengal Gazette in 1780, and Gangadhar Bhattacharya started the first Indian weekly in 1816. Raja Rammohan Roy's Sambad Kaumudi appeared in 1821 and the Bombay Samachar in 1822. Printing fed religious debate through tracts and newspapers, helped social reform through writers like Jyotiba Phule (Gulamgiri, 1871), allowed women such as Rashsundari Debi (Amar Jiban, 1876) and Tarabai Shinde (Stripurushtulna, 1882) to publish, and raised nationalism. The Vernacular Press Act of 1878 gave the government the right to censor reports and editorials.

qa.q: How did printing develop in China?
qa.a: Printing in China began as hand-printing from woodblocks. Because of civil service examinations the state produced many printed books. In the late nineteenth century Shanghai became the new print centre as western methods of mechanical printing arrived.

qa.q: How did printing reach Japan?
qa.a: Buddhist missionaries from China introduced hand-printing technology to Japan around AD 768-770, and the oldest Japanese book, the Diamond Sutra, was printed in AD 868.

qa.q: How did Gutenberg invent his press?
qa.a: Gutenberg knew the olive and wine presses. He adapted the screw-press, and made metal moulds of the alphabet so that pages could be set and printed many times.

qa.q: Why did print help the Reformation?
qa.a: Luther's ideas were printed and spread widely in a short time. The translated New Testament was sold in thousands of copies, so ordinary people could read the Bible and question the Church.

qa.q: What was the Church's reaction to the spread of print?
qa.a: It feared that heretical ideas would spread so it controlled publishers and booksellers and in 1558 maintained an Index of Prohibited Books.

qa.q: Why were new readers created by print?
qa.a: Books became cheaper and could be read aloud to the illiterate. Libraries and reading groups grew and popular ballads and stories were printed for farmers and artisans.

qa.q: How did print help the Enlightenment?
qa.a: Works of thinkers such as Voltaire and Rousseau were printed and discussed widely. They urged people to question custom and rely on reason, forming a public opinion that challenged absolute monarchies.

qa.q: How did print prepare for the French Revolution?
qa.a: Books and cartoons criticised the monarchy and Church, and ideas of liberty and reason spread. People read and debated the new ideas in public, which made revolution thinkable.

qa.q: What changes in printing happened in the nineteenth century?
qa.a: Hoe's steam-powered cylindrical press printed 8,000 sheets an hour, offset printing and electric presses followed, and automatic paper reels increased speed and cut the cost of newspapers and books.

qa.q: How did women become part of the reading public?
qa.a: Novels, penny magazines and serials attracted women. Writers like Jane Austen and the Bronte sisters wrote about women's lives and women became both readers and authors.

qa.q: How did print reach India?
qa.a: The Portuguese missionaries brought the press to Goa in the mid-sixteenth century. Priests printed Konkani and Tamil books, and in the eighteenth century English presses started in Bengal.

qa.q: What was Hicky's Bengal Gazette?
qa.a: It was a commercial weekly started by James Augustus Hicky in 1780, proud of being independent of colonial influence, and it attacked the Company officials.

qa.q: How did the print revive religious debate in India?
qa.a: Newspapers and tracts carried discussions among Hindu and Muslim reformers and Christian missionaries about customs and beliefs, and religious texts such as the Ramcharitmanas reached many homes in print.

qa.q: How did the print help social reform?
qa.a: Reformers like Rammohan Roy and Phule wrote against sati, child marriage and caste. Newspapers spread their ideas and let people discuss reform.

qa.q: Why were women's writings important in India?
qa.a: They showed women's views and experiences, such as Rashsundari Debi's Amar Jiban, and encouraged women to read and write despite social restrictions.

qa.q: How did the print help nationalism in India?
qa.a: Newspapers criticised colonial rule and reported the activities of nationalists. Printed songs and pamphlets spread a common identity.

qa.q: Why did the British pass the Vernacular Press Act in 1878?
qa.a: The government worried about the growing criticism in Indian language newspapers. The Act, modelled on Irish press laws, let it censor reports and seize press equipment.

qa.q: How did Indians respond to the Vernacular Press Act?
qa.a: Nationalist papers protested and continued to publish. The Act strengthened the demand for freedom of the press and nationalism.

qa.q: What is the significance of Mercier's statement about the press?
qa.a: It shows the Enlightenment faith that print could spread reason, build public opinion and end despotism.

qa.q: How did the print reduce the cost of books?
qa.a: Mechanised presses printed many copies faster and cheaply, and cheaper paper and distribution made books affordable to the middle class and workers.

qa.q: What was Tilak's Kesari and why was he jailed?
qa.a: Kesari was a Marathi newspaper of Bal Gangadhar Tilak that wrote strongly against colonial rule. He was jailed in 1908 for sedition after his writings.

problems.q: How did Gutenberg's printing press change the way books were produced?
problems.a: Gutenberg adapted wine and olive presses and used metal moulds for the alphabet to print a page quickly. About 180 copies of the Bible were printed in three years, far faster than hand copying, so books became cheaper and spread among common people.

rubric.t: Use of press technology and metal type

problems.q: Explain how print helped Martin Luther and the Reformation, and how the Catholic Church reacted.
problems.a: Luther wrote the Ninety-Five Theses in 1517 criticising Church practices. Printed copies spread widely, and his New Testament translation sold thousands of copies in weeks, so reformers reached large audiences. The Church feared the new ideas, began to censor publishers and booksellers, and from 1558 kept an Index of Prohibited Books. The Italian miller Menocchio was executed for his reading.

rubric.t: Translation of the New Testament sold quickly
Church censorship and the Index of 1558

problems.q: Discuss the role of print in nineteenth-century India in religion, social reform and nationalism, and how the government responded.
problems.a: Printed tracts and newspapers carried religious debate among Hindu and Muslim reformers and Christian missionaries. Social reformers like Rammohan Roy and Jyotiba Phule used print for reform and to attack caste; women like Rashsundari Debi and Tarabai Shinde wrote and published. Newspapers, including Bengal Gazette and Kesari, criticised colonial rule and spread nationalism. The colonial government feared this and passed the Vernacular Press Act of 1878 which allowed it to censor reports and editorials and later used sedition laws.

rubric.t: Religious debates through tracts and newspapers

🔑

Big idea

  • Printing began in China, Japan and Korea with hand-printing from woodblocks
  • Marco Polo brought the technique to Europe, and in the 1430s Johann Gutenberg built the printing press in Strasbourg, producing the Bible
  • Print spread ideas: Martin Luther's Ninety-Five Theses (1517) fuelled the Reformation, the Church created the Index of Prohibited Books, and reading…
  • New presses, cheap books, novels and magazines created new readers including women and workers
Read the full explanation

Printing began in China, Japan and Korea with hand-printing from woodblocks. Marco Polo brought the technique to Europe, and in the 1430s Johann Gutenberg built the printing press in Strasbourg, producing the Bible. Print spread ideas: Martin Luther's Ninety-Five Theses (1517) fuelled the Reformation, the Church created the Index of Prohibited Books, and reading culture helped the Enlightenment and the French Revolution. New presses, cheap books, novels and magazines created new readers including women and workers. In India print came with the Portuguese in Goa, and newspapers, social reform, religious debate and women's writing grew in the nineteenth century, while the colonial government answered with the Vernacular Press Act of 1878.

📌

The first printed books

  • Printing technology developed in China, Japan and Korea where books were printed by hand with woodblocks
  • China had a large number of educated officials and the state was the major producer of printed material
  • Buddhist missionaries brought printing to Japan around AD 768-770, and the oldest Japanese book, the Buddhist Diamond Sutra, was printed in AD 868
  • In Japan Kitagawa Utamaro produced ukiyo pictures of the floating world
Read the full explanation

Printing technology developed in China, Japan and Korea where books were printed by hand with woodblocks. China had a large number of educated officials and the state was the major producer of printed material. Buddhist missionaries brought printing to Japan around AD 768-770, and the oldest Japanese book, the Buddhist Diamond Sutra, was printed in AD 868. In Japan Kitagawa Utamaro produced ukiyo pictures of the floating world. Marco Polo brought woodblock printing from China to Italy in 1295, and soon books were printed in Europe on woodblocks, mainly for the rich and for Church use.

🕰️

Gutenberg and the print revolution

  • Johann Gutenberg, the son of a merchant, grew up on a large agricultural estate and saw wine and olive presses
  • He adapted that technology to design a printing press with metal moulds for the alphabet in the 1430s at Strasbourg
  • The first book he printed was the Bible, and about 180 copies were printed in three years
  • Presses spread across Europe and between 1450 and 1550 printing presses were set up in most countries
Read the full explanation

Johann Gutenberg, the son of a merchant, grew up on a large agricultural estate and saw wine and olive presses. He adapted that technology to design a printing press with metal moulds for the alphabet in the 1430s at Strasbourg. The first book he printed was the Bible, and about 180 copies were printed in three years. Presses spread across Europe and between 1450 and 1550 printing presses were set up in most countries. The new technology changed how people read and thought: they could read cheap books, and there was an explosion of reading. Martin Luther wrote Ninety-Five Theses in 1517 criticising the practices of the Roman Catholic Church, and his translation of the New Testament sold 5,000 copies in a few weeks, which helped begin the Protestant Reformation. In 1558 the Church began to maintain an Index of Prohibited Books, and Menocchio, an Italian miller, was executed for his reading of the Bible and other books.

🌟

The print and the modern world

  • Print popularised ideas of the Enlightenment through writers such as Voltaire and Rousseau, created a public debate and prepared the ground for the…
  • Louis-Sebastien Mercier said the printing press was the powerful engine of progress and public opinion would sweep despotism away
  • In the nineteenth century the steam-powered cylindrical press of Richard M
  • Hoe printed 8,000 sheets per hour, the offset press and electrically operated presses followed, and publishers produced penny magazines, novels…
Read the full explanation

Print popularised ideas of the Enlightenment through writers such as Voltaire and Rousseau, created a public debate and prepared the ground for the French Revolution. Louis-Sebastien Mercier said the printing press was the powerful engine of progress and public opinion would sweep despotism away. In the nineteenth century the steam-powered cylindrical press of Richard M. Hoe printed 8,000 sheets per hour, the offset press and electrically operated presses followed, and publishers produced penny magazines, novels, almanacs and cheap series. Women became readers and writers, including Jane Austen, the Bronte sisters and George Eliot; children's books such as the Grimm brothers' fairy tales were published.

🔬

Print in India

  • Printing came to India with the Portuguese missionaries in Goa in the mid-sixteenth century
  • Catholic priests printed the first Tamil book in 1579 at Cochin and the first Malayalam book in 1713, and Dutch Protestant missionaries printed Tamil…
  • James Augustus Hicky began the Bengal Gazette in 1780, and Gangadhar Bhattacharya started the first Indian weekly in 1816
  • Raja Rammohan Roy's Sambad Kaumudi appeared in 1821 and the Bombay Samachar in 1822
Read the full explanation

Printing came to India with the Portuguese missionaries in Goa in the mid-sixteenth century. Catholic priests printed the first Tamil book in 1579 at Cochin and the first Malayalam book in 1713, and Dutch Protestant missionaries printed Tamil texts. James Augustus Hicky began the Bengal Gazette in 1780, and Gangadhar Bhattacharya started the first Indian weekly in 1816. Raja Rammohan Roy's Sambad Kaumudi appeared in 1821 and the Bombay Samachar in 1822. Printing fed religious debate through tracts and newspapers, helped social reform through writers like Jyotiba Phule (Gulamgiri, 1871), allowed women such as Rashsundari Debi (Amar Jiban, 1876) and Tarabai Shinde (Stripurushtulna, 1882) to publish, and raised nationalism. The Vernacular Press Act of 1878 gave the government the right to censor reports and editorials.

yt: class 10 quadratic equations ap

blocks.x: **Quadratic equation** a x^2 + b x + c = 0 has roots x = (-b +/- sqrt(D)) / 2a with discriminant D = b^2 - 4ac. D > 0 two distinct real roots; D = 0 equal roots; D < 0 no real roots. Example: 2x^2 - 7x + 3 = 0: D = 49 - 24 = 25, roots **3** and **0.5**. Sum of roots = -b/a; product = c/a. **AP:** a_n = a + (n - 1) d; S_n = n/2 [2a + (n - 1) d]. For 2, 5, 8, ...: S_20 = 10 (4 + 57) = **610**.
Deep dive: quadratic equations

**What it is.** An equation that can be written as a x^2 + b x + c = 0 with a not equal to 0. The highest power of x is 2, so there are at most two roots. If a = 0 the x^2 term vanishes and it is only linear. **Method 1: factorisation (splitting the middle term).** To solve a x^2 + b x + c = 0, find two numbers whose product is a x c and whose sum is b. Split b x into those two terms, group, and use the zero product rule: if P x Q = 0 then P = 0 or Q = 0. Example: 6x^2 - x - 2 = 0. a x c = -12; the numbers 3 and -4 give sum -1. So 6x^2 + 3x - 4x - 2 = 3x(2x + 1) - 2(2x + 1) = (3x - 2)(2x + 1) = 0, so x = 2/3 or x = -1/2. **Method 2: completing the square.** Divide by a, move the constant, add (b/2a)^2 to both sides: (x + b/2a)^2 = (b^2 - 4ac)/4a^2. Taking the square root gives the quadratic formula, so the formula is simply this method done once for all equations. **Method 3: the quadratic formula.** x = (-b +/- sqrt(b^2 - 4ac)) / 2a. It always works, even when factorising is hard. Put brackets round negative values of b when substituting. **Discriminant D = b^2 - 4ac** tells the nature of the roots before you solve: D > 0 two distinct real roots; D = 0 two equal real roots x = -b/2a; D < 0 no real roots (the parabola does not touch the x-axis). If a, b, c are integers and D is a perfect square the roots are rational. **Sum and product of roots.** If the roots are p and q then p + q = -b/a and p q = c/a. A quadratic with given roots is x^2 - (p + q) x + p q = 0. Useful identities: p^2 + q^2 = (p + q)^2 - 2 p q and |p - q| = sqrt(D)/|a|. **Word problems.** Define the unknown, write one equation, reduce it to standard form, solve, and reject answers that cannot be real quantities (a negative length, age or number of people). Typical types: two numbers with a given sum of squares; a rectangle with given area and perimeter relation; speed, distance and time (time = distance / speed); two taps filling a tank; consecutive integers. **Common mistakes.** Forgetting that a x^2 + b x + c must equal 0 before factorising; dividing both sides by x and losing the root x = 0; dropping the minus sign of b; reading D = b^2 - 4ac as b^2 - 4 a c with the wrong sign when c is negative (then D is a sum: b^2 + 4|a c|).
Deep dive: arithmetic progressions

**Definition.** A list in which every term after the first is got by adding the same number d (the common difference). d can be positive, negative or zero. Check with d = a_(k+1) - a_k for any two neighbouring terms. **nth term.** a_n = a + (n - 1) d. The 10th term of 7, 11, 15, ... is 7 + 9 x 4 = 43. To check whether a number belongs to the AP solve a + (n - 1) d = that number: n must be a positive whole number. **Sum of n terms.** S_n = n/2 [2a + (n - 1) d] = n/2 (a + l) where l is the last term. Also a_n = S_n - S_(n-1). The sum of the first n natural numbers is n(n + 1)/2, of the first n odd numbers is n^2, of the first n even numbers is n(n + 1). **Useful facts.** Three numbers a - d, a, a + d are in AP; four numbers a - 3d, a - d, a + d, a + 3d are in AP. If a, b, c are in AP then 2b = a + c (b is the arithmetic mean). The kth term from the end of an AP with last term l is l - (k - 1) d. Equal gaps mean the sum of terms equidistant from the ends is constant. **Word problems.** Savings that grow by a fixed amount, seats in rows of a hall, instalments of a loan, and the number of logs in a stack are all APs. Write a, d and what is asked (a_n or S_n or n), then substitute. If the equation for n has two solutions, check which are whole and positive.

What is a quadratic equation?
qa.a: An equation that can be written as a x^2 + b x + c = 0 with a not equal to 0.

qa.q: Why must a not be zero in a x^2 + b x + c = 0?
qa.a: If a = 0 the x^2 term disappears and the equation becomes linear, not quadratic.

qa.q: How many roots can a quadratic equation have?
qa.a: At most two real roots: two distinct, two equal, or none real.

qa.q: What is the zero product rule?
qa.a: If P x Q = 0 then P = 0 or Q = 0 (or both).

qa.q: What is a root of an equation?
qa.a: A value of the variable that makes both sides equal, that is, it satisfies the equation.

qa.q: State the quadratic formula.
What is the discriminant?
qa.a: D = b^2 - 4ac. It tells the nature of the roots without solving.

qa.q: What does D > 0 tell us?
qa.a: The equation has two distinct real roots.

qa.q: What does D = 0 tell us?
qa.a: The equation has two equal real roots, each equal to -b / 2a.

qa.q: What does D < 0 tell us?
qa.a: The equation has no real roots.

qa.q: When are the roots of a quadratic with integer coefficients rational?
qa.a: When D is a perfect square (and D is not negative).

qa.q: How does completing the square work?
qa.a: Divide by a, move the constant, add (b/2a)^2 to both sides, then take square roots.

qa.q: How is the quadratic formula derived?
qa.a: By completing the square on a x^2 + b x + c = 0 once for general a, b, c.

qa.q: What is the sum of the roots of a x^2 + b x + c = 0?
What is the product of the roots of a x^2 + b x + c = 0?
How do you form a quadratic equation with roots p and q?
How can you find p^2 + q^2 without finding p and q?
qa.a: Use (p + q)^2 - 2 p q with the sum and product from the coefficients.

qa.q: Why is dividing both sides by x dangerous when solving x^2 = 5x?
qa.a: It loses the root x = 0. Write x^2 - 5x = 0 and factorise x (x - 5) = 0.

qa.q: Why do we reject a negative answer in a problem about length?
qa.a: A length cannot be negative, so only the positive root is meaningful.

qa.q: What is meant by splitting the middle term?
qa.a: Writing b x as the sum of two terms whose coefficients multiply to a x c, so the quadratic can be grouped and factorised.

qa.q: What is the shape of the graph of y = a x^2 + b x + c?
qa.a: A parabola, opening upward if a > 0 and downward if a < 0.

qa.q: What does the discriminant tell about the graph?
qa.a: D > 0: cuts the x-axis twice; D = 0: touches it once; D < 0: does not meet it.

qa.q: Where is the vertex of y = a x^2 + b x + c?
qa.a: At x = -b / 2a, which is also the midpoint of the two roots.

qa.q: Is x = 0 a root of x^2 + 3x = 0?
qa.a: Yes. The equation factorises as x (x + 3) = 0, so x = 0 or x = -3.

qa.q: Can a quadratic have exactly one real root that is repeated?
qa.a: Yes, when D = 0 the two roots coincide.

qa.q: What is an arithmetic progression?
qa.a: A list of numbers in which each term after the first is got by adding a fixed number d, the common difference.

qa.q: How do you find the common difference of an AP?
qa.a: Subtract any term from the term that follows it: d = a_(k+1) - a_k.

qa.q: State the formula for the nth term of an AP.
State two forms of the sum of n terms of an AP.
qa.a: S_n = n/2 [2a + (n - 1) d] and S_n = n/2 (a + l).

qa.q: How is a_n related to S_n?
qa.a: a_n = S_n - S_(n-1) for n greater than 1.

What is the sum of the first n odd numbers?
What is the sum of the first n even numbers?
If a, b, c are in AP, what is the relation between them?
qa.a: 2b = a + c, so b is the average of a and c.

qa.q: How should three numbers in AP be taken in a problem?
qa.a: As a - d, a, a + d, so the sum is simply 3a.

qa.q: Is 2, 4, 8, 16 an AP?
qa.a: No. The differences are 2, 4, 8, so d is not constant. It is a geometric progression.

qa.q: Can the common difference of an AP be negative?
qa.a: Yes. A negative d gives a decreasing AP such as 20, 17, 14, ...

qa.q: What AP has d = 0?
qa.a: A constant list such as 5, 5, 5, ... Each term equals the first.

qa.q: How do you test if a number is a term of an AP?
qa.a: Solve a + (n - 1) d = number; it is a term only if n is a positive whole number.

qa.q: How do you find the kth term from the end of an AP?
qa.a: l - (k - 1) d where l is the last term.

qa.q: Why is the sum of terms equidistant from the ends of an AP constant?
qa.a: Because moving one step in from each end adds d to one term and subtracts d from the other.

Is a finite AP's sum always defined?
qa.a: Yes. Any finite list can be added; the formula needs a, d and n (or a and l).

Quadratic equations and arithmetic progressions

Quadratic equation a x^2 + b x + c = 0 has roots x = (-b +/- sqrt(D)) / 2a with discriminant D = b^2 - 4ac
