lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Electricity and light (Class 10)

Ohm's law V = IR

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Electricity›3Light
🔑

Big idea

  • Ohm's law V = IR
  • Power P = VI = I2 R
  • For V = 5 V and R = 10 ohm: I = 0.5 A, P = 2.5 W
  • Resistors in series add
Read the full explanation

Ohm's law V = IR; power P = VI = I^2 R. For V = 5 V and R = 10 ohm: I = 0.5 A, P = 2.5 W. Resistors in series add; in parallel 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2: 2 ohm and 3 ohm give 1.2 ohm. Heating effect H = I^2 R t. Light: mirror formula 1/v + 1/u = 1/f; magnification m = -v/u. Concave mirror f = -15 cm, object at u = -30 cm: v = -30 cm, m = -1 (real, inverted, same size). Refraction: Snell's law; refractive index n = c / v: if light travels at 2 x 10^8 m/s in glass, n = 1.5. Lens power P = 1/f (metres), in dioptres. Magnetic effects: field around a current carrying wire; motor, generator, electromagnetic induction.

⚡

Electricity

  • Charge and current
  • Current I is the rate of flow of charge: I = Q / t
  • One ampere is one coulomb per second
  • The charge of one electron is 1.6 x 10-19 C, so 1 C is about 6.25 x 1018 electrons
Read the full explanation

Charge and current. Current I is the rate of flow of charge: I = Q / t. One ampere is one coulomb per second. The charge of one electron is 1.6 x 10^-19 C, so 1 C is about 6.25 x 10^18 electrons. Conventional current flows from the positive to the negative terminal, opposite to the electron flow. Potential difference. V = W / Q: the work done to move one coulomb between two points. Unit: volt (1 V = 1 J/C). A voltmeter is connected in parallel across a component; an ammeter is connected in series. Ohm's law. At constant temperature V is proportional to I, so V = I R. The graph of V against I is a straight line through the origin whose slope is R. Resistance depends on length, area and material: R = rho L / A. Doubling the length doubles R; doubling the area halves R. Resistivity rho depends only on the material and temperature (metals: low, alloys: higher, insulators: very high). Series and parallel. Series: the same current passes through every resistor, R = R1 + R2 + ... and the voltages add. Parallel: every resistor has the same voltage, 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ... and the currents add; the combined resistance is smaller than the smallest. Household appliances are in parallel so each gets 220 V and works independently. Heating effect. H = I^2 R t = V I t = V^2 t / R (Joule's law). Used in heaters, geysers, irons and fuses. A fuse is a thin wire of low melting point in series with the appliance that melts when the current is too high. Electric power and energy. P = V I = I^2 R = V^2 / R, in watts. Energy E = P t. The commercial unit is the kilowatt hour: 1 kWh = 3.6 x 10^6 J = 1 unit of electricity.

🔦

Light

  • The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection
  • The incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in one plane
  • A plane mirror forms a virtual, erect image the same size as the object, as far behind the mirror as the object is in front
  • Spherical mirrors
Read the full explanation

Reflection. The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection; the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in one plane. A plane mirror forms a virtual, erect image the same size as the object, as far behind the mirror as the object is in front. Spherical mirrors. Focal length f = R / 2. Sign convention (Cartesian): distances measured from the pole; in the direction of the incident light is positive, against it is negative. For a concave mirror f is negative; for a convex mirror f is positive. Mirror formula: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f. Magnification m = h'/h = -v/u. A concave mirror gives a real inverted image when the object is beyond f; with the object between pole and f it gives a virtual, erect, enlarged image (shaving mirror, dentist's mirror). A convex mirror always gives a virtual, erect, diminished image (rear-view mirrors). Refraction. Light bends when it passes from one medium to another because its speed changes. Snell's law: sin i / sin r = n21 = constant. Absolute refractive index n = c / v with c = 3 x 10^8 m/s. Going into a denser medium the ray bends towards the normal. Glass slab: the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray but shifted sideways. Lenses. Lens formula: 1/v - 1/u = 1/f. Magnification m = v/u. Power P = 1/f with f in metres; the unit is the dioptre. Convex lens: f positive, converging, P positive. Concave lens: f negative, diverging, P negative. Lenses placed in contact add their powers: P = P1 + P2. Human eye. Myopia (short sight) is corrected by a concave lens; hypermetropia (long sight) by a convex lens. Presbyopia comes with age and needs bifocal lenses. Dispersion by a prism splits white light into VIBGYOR; a rainbow is dispersion plus internal reflection in raindrops; the sky is blue because shorter wavelengths scatter most.

🧮

lessons.title: Chemical reactions, acids and bases, and heredity
yt: class 10 chemical reactions acids heredity

blocks.x: **Balanced equation:** atoms of each element equal on both sides. Example: 2 Mg + O2 -> 2 MgO; Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu (displacement). Types: combination, decomposition, displacement, double displacement, redox. **Acids and bases:** acids turn blue litmus red; pH below 7 acidic, 7 neutral, above 7 basic. Neutralisation: acid + base -> salt + water; e.g. HCl + NaOH -> NaCl + H2O. Common salt, baking soda (NaHCO3) and washing soda (Na2CO3.10H2O). **Heredity:** Mendel's monohybrid cross gives a 3:1 phenotypic ratio in the F2 generation; human sex is determined by XY (male) and XX (female); the sex of the child depends on the father's chromosome.
Deep dive: chemical reactions and equations

**Equations.** A chemical equation uses formulae for reactants and products. It must be balanced so each element has the same number of atoms on both sides (law of conservation of mass). Balance by trial: balance elements that appear once first, hydrogen and oxygen last. State symbols: (s), (l), (g), (aq). Conditions such as heat or catalyst are written over the arrow. Example: 2 H2 + O2 -> 2 H2O; Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu. **Types.** Combination: A + B -> AB (CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2, exothermic). Decomposition: AB -> A + B, by heat (CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2), light (2 AgCl -> 2 Ag + Cl2) or electricity (electrolysis of water). Displacement: a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one (Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu). Double displacement: ions exchange and often a precipitate forms (Na2SO4 + BaCl2 -> BaSO4 + 2 NaCl). Redox: oxidation is gain of oxygen or loss of electrons; reduction is loss of oxygen or gain of electrons; they occur together (CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O). **Everyday changes.** Corrosion is slow oxidation of metals (rusting of iron needs air and water; prevent by painting, galvanising). Rancidity is oxidation of fats and oils; prevent with antioxidants, airtight containers, nitrogen flushing. Exothermic reactions release heat (burning, respiration); endothermic reactions absorb heat (photosynthesis, thermal decomposition).
Deep dive: acids, bases and salts

**Acids** taste sour, turn blue litmus red, give H+ ions in water (HCl, H2SO4, HNO3, CH3COOH). **Bases** are bitter, soapy, turn red litmus blue and give OH- in water (NaOH, KOH, Ca(OH)2); a water-soluble base is an alkali. Indicators: litmus, phenolphthalein (pink in base), methyl orange (red in acid, yellow in base), turmeric (red in base). **Reactions.** Acid + metal -> salt + hydrogen (Zn + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + H2; the gas burns with a pop). Acid + metal carbonate -> salt + water + carbon dioxide (which turns lime water milky). Acid + base -> salt + water (neutralisation). Acid + metal oxide -> salt + water. Non-metal oxides are acidic; metal oxides are basic. **pH scale.** pH = -log [H+]. 0 to 7 acidic, 7 neutral, 7 to 14 basic. Each unit is a tenfold change. Gastric juice about 1.5-3, lemon juice 2.2, milk 6.5, pure water 7, blood 7.4, baking soda solution 8.3, milk of magnesia 10, NaOH 14. Uses: antacids for acidity, tooth enamel decays below pH 5.5, soil pH, acid rain below 5.6. **Salts.** Common salt NaCl (from brine; chlor-alkali process gives NaOH, Cl2 and H2). Bleaching powder CaOCl2 (Cl2 + Ca(OH)2). Baking soda NaHCO3 (NaCl + H2O + CO2 + NH3 -> NaHCO3 + NH4Cl); on heating gives Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2; used in antacids and baking powder. Washing soda Na2CO3.10H2O. Plaster of Paris CaSO4.1/2 H2O (gypsum heated at 373 K) sets as CaSO4.2H2O. Water of crystallisation is the fixed number of water molecules in one formula unit of a salt (CuSO4.5H2O is blue and turns white when heated).
Deep dive: heredity

**Basics.** Heredity is the transmission of characters from parents to offspring; variation is the difference between individuals. Variations arise from DNA copying errors and sexual reproduction and are the raw material of evolution. Genes on chromosomes are the units of heredity. A gene has alleles (dominant and recessive). **Mendel.** Worked on garden pea (Pisum sativum) with seven contrasting pairs of traits. Monohybrid cross: tall (TT) x dwarf (tt) gives all tall Tt in F1; selfing F1 gives F2 with phenotypic ratio 3 tall : 1 dwarf and genotypic ratio 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt. Dihybrid cross (round yellow RRYY x wrinkled green rryy): F2 phenotypic ratio 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 shows independent assortment. Laws: dominance, segregation of alleles, independent assortment. **Sex determination.** Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes: 22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes (XX female, XY male). The mother always gives X; the father gives X or Y, so the sex of the child depends on the father. The chance of a boy or a girl is 50% each. **Evolution points.** Acquired traits are not inherited. Speciation arises from variation, natural selection and isolation. Homologous organs (forelimb of man, bat, whale) show common ancestry; analogous organs (wing of bird and insect) have the same function with different origin. Fossils and carbon dating give evidence of evolution.

🔑

Big idea

  • Balanced equation: atoms of each element equal on both sides
  • Example: 2 Mg + O2 -> 2 MgO
  • Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu (displacement)
  • Types: combination, decomposition, displacement, double displacement, redox
Read the full explanation

Balanced equation: atoms of each element equal on both sides. Example: 2 Mg + O2 -> 2 MgO; Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu (displacement). Types: combination, decomposition, displacement, double displacement, redox. Acids and bases: acids turn blue litmus red; pH below 7 acidic, 7 neutral, above 7 basic. Neutralisation: acid + base -> salt + water; e.g. HCl + NaOH -> NaCl + H2O. Common salt, baking soda (NaHCO3) and washing soda (Na2CO3.10H2O). Heredity: Mendel's monohybrid cross gives a 3:1 phenotypic ratio in the F2 generation; human sex is determined by XY (male) and XX (female); the sex of the child depends on the father's chromosome.

🧮

Chemical reactions and equations

  • A chemical equation uses formulae for reactants and products
  • It must be balanced so each element has the same number of atoms on both sides (law of conservation of mass)
  • Balance by trial: balance elements that appear once first, hydrogen and oxygen last
  • State symbols: (s), (l), (g), (aq)
Read the full explanation

Equations. A chemical equation uses formulae for reactants and products. It must be balanced so each element has the same number of atoms on both sides (law of conservation of mass). Balance by trial: balance elements that appear once first, hydrogen and oxygen last. State symbols: (s), (l), (g), (aq). Conditions such as heat or catalyst are written over the arrow. Example: 2 H2 + O2 -> 2 H2O; Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu. Types. Combination: A + B -> AB (CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2, exothermic). Decomposition: AB -> A + B, by heat (CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2), light (2 AgCl -> 2 Ag + Cl2) or electricity (electrolysis of water). Displacement: a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one (Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu). Double displacement: ions exchange and often a precipitate forms (Na2SO4 + BaCl2 -> BaSO4 + 2 NaCl). Redox: oxidation is gain of oxygen or loss of electrons; reduction is loss of oxygen or gain of electrons; they occur together (CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O). Everyday changes. Corrosion is slow oxidation of metals (rusting of iron needs air and water; prevent by painting, galvanising). Rancidity is oxidation of fats and oils; prevent with antioxidants, airtight containers, nitrogen flushing. Exothermic reactions release heat (burning, respiration); endothermic reactions absorb heat (photosynthesis, thermal decomposition).

⚗️

Acids, bases and salts

  • Acids taste sour, turn blue litmus red, give H+ ions in water (HCl, H2SO4, HNO3, CH3COOH)
  • Bases are bitter, soapy, turn red litmus blue and give OH- in water (NaOH, KOH, Ca(OH)2)
  • A water-soluble base is an alkali
  • Indicators: litmus, phenolphthalein (pink in base), methyl orange (red in acid, yellow in base), turmeric (red in base)
Read the full explanation

Acids taste sour, turn blue litmus red, give H+ ions in water (HCl, H2SO4, HNO3, CH3COOH). Bases are bitter, soapy, turn red litmus blue and give OH- in water (NaOH, KOH, Ca(OH)2); a water-soluble base is an alkali. Indicators: litmus, phenolphthalein (pink in base), methyl orange (red in acid, yellow in base), turmeric (red in base). Reactions. Acid + metal -> salt + hydrogen (Zn + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + H2; the gas burns with a pop). Acid + metal carbonate -> salt + water + carbon dioxide (which turns lime water milky). Acid + base -> salt + water (neutralisation). Acid + metal oxide -> salt + water. Non-metal oxides are acidic; metal oxides are basic. pH scale. pH = -log [H+]. 0 to 7 acidic, 7 neutral, 7 to 14 basic. Each unit is a tenfold change. Gastric juice about 1.5-3, lemon juice 2.2, milk 6.5, pure water 7, blood 7.4, baking soda solution 8.3, milk of magnesia 10, NaOH 14. Uses: antacids for acidity, tooth enamel decays below pH 5.5, soil pH, acid rain below 5.6. Salts. Common salt NaCl (from brine; chlor-alkali process gives NaOH, Cl2 and H2). Bleaching powder CaOCl2 (Cl2 + Ca(OH)2). Baking soda NaHCO3 (NaCl + H2O + CO2 + NH3 -> NaHCO3 + NH4Cl); on heating gives Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2; used in antacids and baking powder. Washing soda Na2CO3.10H2O. Plaster of Paris CaSO4.1/2 H2O (gypsum heated at 373 K) sets as CaSO4.2H2O. Water of crystallisation is the fixed number of water molecules in one formula unit of a salt (CuSO4.5H2O is blue and turns white when heated).

🌟

Heredity

  • Heredity is the transmission of characters from parents to offspring
  • Variation is the difference between individuals
  • Variations arise from DNA copying errors and sexual reproduction and are the raw material of evolution
  • Genes on chromosomes are the units of heredity
Read the full explanation

Basics. Heredity is the transmission of characters from parents to offspring; variation is the difference between individuals. Variations arise from DNA copying errors and sexual reproduction and are the raw material of evolution. Genes on chromosomes are the units of heredity. A gene has alleles (dominant and recessive). Mendel. Worked on garden pea (Pisum sativum) with seven contrasting pairs of traits. Monohybrid cross: tall (TT) x dwarf (tt) gives all tall Tt in F1; selfing F1 gives F2 with phenotypic ratio 3 tall : 1 dwarf and genotypic ratio 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt. Dihybrid cross (round yellow RRYY x wrinkled green rryy): F2 phenotypic ratio 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 shows independent assortment. Laws: dominance, segregation of alleles, independent assortment. Sex determination. Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes: 22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes (XX female, XY male). The mother always gives X; the father gives X or Y, so the sex of the child depends on the father. The chance of a boy or a girl is 50% each. Evolution points. Acquired traits are not inherited. Speciation arises from variation, natural selection and isolation. Homologous organs (forelimb of man, bat, whale) show common ancestry; analogous organs (wing of bird and insect) have the same function with different origin. Fossils and carbon dating give evidence of evolution.

lessons.title: Chemical Reactions and Equations
yt: class 10 science chemical reactions and equations

blocks.x: A chemical reaction changes reactants into products with new properties. Signs are change in state, colour, evolution of gas, or temperature. A chemical equation must be balanced to obey the law of conservation of mass. Types: combination, decomposition (thermal, electrolytic, photolytic), displacement, double displacement (precipitation, neutralisation), and redox reactions. Oxidation is gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen; reduction is loss of oxygen or gain of hydrogen. Corrosion and rancidity are everyday oxidation effects, prevented by painting, galvanising, or adding antioxidants and nitrogen flushing.
Deep dive: Balancing equations

Count atoms of each element on both sides. Start with the compound with most atoms or the most complex formula, balance metals, then non-metals, then hydrogen and oxygen. Use only coefficients, never change subscripts. Add state symbols (s), (l), (g), (aq). Example: Fe + H2O -> Fe3O4 + H2 balances as 3Fe + 4H2O -> Fe3O4 + 4H2. The law of conservation of mass (Lavoisier) says mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.
Deep dive: Types of reactions

Combination: CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2 (slaked lime, exothermic); 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO. Decomposition: 2FeSO4 -> Fe2O3 + SO2 + SO3 (thermal); 2H2O -> 2H2 + O2 (electrolytic); 2AgCl -> 2Ag + Cl2 (photolytic, used in black and white photography). Displacement: Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu, more reactive metal displaces less reactive. Double displacement: Na2SO4 + BaCl2 -> BaSO4 (white ppt) + 2NaCl. Neutralisation is acid + base -> salt + water.
Deep dive: Oxidation and reduction

Oxidation is addition of oxygen or removal of hydrogen; reduction is removal of oxygen or addition of hydrogen. In CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O, CuO is reduced and H2 is oxidised. Both occur together, so it is a redox reaction. The substance oxidised is the reducing agent; the substance reduced is the oxidising agent.
Deep dive: Corrosion and rancidity

Corrosion is the slow eating away of metals by air, moisture or acids: iron rusts (Fe2O3.xH2O) and silver turns black (Ag2S), copper turns green (basic copper carbonate). Prevention: painting, oiling, galvanisation (zinc coating), alloying. Rancidity is the oxidation of fats and oils in food giving bad smell and taste; prevented by antioxidants, airtight containers, refrigeration, or flushing with nitrogen as in chips packets.

problems.q: Balance Fe + H2O -> Fe3O4 + H2 and state the type of reaction.
problems.a: 3Fe + 4H2O -> Fe3O4 + 4H2; it is a displacement and redox reaction.

problems.q: Distinguish between displacement and double displacement reactions with an example each.
problems.a: Displacement: a more reactive element displaces a less reactive from its compound, Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu. Double displacement: two compounds exchange ions, Na2SO4 + BaCl2 -> BaSO4 + 2NaCl, forming a precipitate.

problems.a: Corrosion is the slow attack on metals by oxygen and moisture (rusting of iron, black silver, green copper); it damages structures costing billions. Rancidity is oxidation of fats giving bad smell and taste. Prevention: paint, oil, galvanising, alloying for corrosion; antioxidants, nitrogen flushing, airtight containers, cool storage for rancidity.

Visual lesson

Chemical Reactions and Equations

A chemical reaction changes reactants into products with new properties

minutes
formulas
Q&A

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Balancing equations›3Types of reactions›4Oxidation and reduction›5Corrosion and rancidity
🔑

Big idea

  • A chemical reaction changes reactants into products with new properties
  • Signs are change in state, colour, evolution of gas, or temperature
  • A chemical equation must be balanced to obey the law of conservation of mass
  • Types: combination, decomposition (thermal, electrolytic, photolytic), displacement, double displacement (precipitation, neutralisation), and redox…
Read the full explanation

A chemical reaction changes reactants into products with new properties. Signs are change in state, colour, evolution of gas, or temperature. A chemical equation must be balanced to obey the law of conservation of mass. Types: combination, decomposition (thermal, electrolytic, photolytic), displacement, double displacement (precipitation, neutralisation), and redox reactions. Oxidation is gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen; reduction is loss of oxygen or gain of hydrogen. Corrosion and rancidity are everyday oxidation effects, prevented by painting, galvanising, or adding antioxidants and nitrogen flushing.

🧮

Balancing equations

  • Count atoms of each element on both sides
  • Start with the compound with most atoms or the most complex formula, balance metals, then non-metals, then hydrogen and oxygen
  • Use only coefficients, never change subscripts
  • Add state symbols (s), (l), (g), (aq)
Read the full explanation

Count atoms of each element on both sides. Start with the compound with most atoms or the most complex formula, balance metals, then non-metals, then hydrogen and oxygen. Use only coefficients, never change subscripts. Add state symbols (s), (l), (g), (aq). Example: Fe + H2O -> Fe3O4 + H2 balances as 3Fe + 4H2O -> Fe3O4 + 4H2. The law of conservation of mass (Lavoisier) says mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.

⚗️

Types of reactions

  • Combination: CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2 (slaked lime, exothermic)
  • 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO
  • Decomposition: 2FeSO4 -> Fe2O3 + SO2 + SO3 (thermal)
  • 2H2O -> 2H2 + O2 (electrolytic)
Read the full explanation

Combination: CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2 (slaked lime, exothermic); 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO. Decomposition: 2FeSO4 -> Fe2O3 + SO2 + SO3 (thermal); 2H2O -> 2H2 + O2 (electrolytic); 2AgCl -> 2Ag + Cl2 (photolytic, used in black and white photography). Displacement: Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu, more reactive metal displaces less reactive. Double displacement: Na2SO4 + BaCl2 -> BaSO4 (white ppt) + 2NaCl. Neutralisation is acid + base -> salt + water.

🌟

Oxidation and reduction

  • Oxidation is addition of oxygen or removal of hydrogen
  • Reduction is removal of oxygen or addition of hydrogen
  • In CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O, CuO is reduced and H2 is oxidised
  • Both occur together, so it is a redox reaction
Read the full explanation

Oxidation is addition of oxygen or removal of hydrogen; reduction is removal of oxygen or addition of hydrogen. In CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O, CuO is reduced and H2 is oxidised. Both occur together, so it is a redox reaction. The substance oxidised is the reducing agent; the substance reduced is the oxidising agent.

🔬

Corrosion and rancidity

  • Corrosion is the slow eating away of metals by air, moisture or acids: iron rusts (Fe2O3.xH2O) and silver turns black (Ag2S), copper turns green…
  • Prevention: painting, oiling, galvanisation (zinc coating), alloying
  • Rancidity is the oxidation of fats and oils in food giving bad smell and taste
  • Prevented by antioxidants, airtight containers, refrigeration, or flushing with nitrogen as in chips packets
Read the full explanation

Corrosion is the slow eating away of metals by air, moisture or acids: iron rusts (Fe2O3.xH2O) and silver turns black (Ag2S), copper turns green (basic copper carbonate). Prevention: painting, oiling, galvanisation (zinc coating), alloying. Rancidity is the oxidation of fats and oils in food giving bad smell and taste; prevented by antioxidants, airtight containers, refrigeration, or flushing with nitrogen as in chips packets.

lessons.title: Acids, Bases and Salts
yt: class 10 science acids bases and salts

blocks.x: Acids turn blue litmus red, taste sour and release H+ ions in water; bases turn red litmus blue, are bitter and slippery, and give OH- ions; those soluble in water are alkalis. The pH scale from 0 to 14 measures H+ concentration: acids below 7, neutral 7, bases above 7. Acid + metal gives salt + hydrogen; acid + base gives salt + water; acid + metal carbonate/hydrogencarbonate gives salt + CO2 + water. Common salts: NaCl, NaOH from chlor-alkali process, bleaching powder CaOCl2, baking soda NaHCO3, washing soda Na2CO3.10H2O, and Plaster of Paris CaSO4.1/2H2O.
Deep dive: Properties and indicators

Natural indicators: litmus, turmeric, red cabbage, China rose. Synthetic: phenolphthalein (colourless in acid, pink in base), methyl orange (red in acid, yellow in base). Olfactory indicators like onion, vanilla and clove lose smell in a base. Acids need water to release H+ (H3O+); dry HCl gas does not change dry litmus. Diluting an acid is exothermic: always add acid to water slowly with stirring, never water to acid.
Deep dive: Reactions of acids and bases

Acid + metal: Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2 (pop test). Base + metal: 2NaOH + Zn -> Na2ZnO2 + H2. Metal carbonate + acid: Na2CO3 + 2HCl -> 2NaCl + H2O + CO2, CO2 turns lime water milky (Ca(OH)2 + CO2 -> CaCO3 + H2O) and the milkiness disappears on excess CO2 forming calcium hydrogencarbonate. Neutralisation: NaOH + HCl -> NaCl + H2O. Metal oxides are basic; non-metal oxides are acidic.
Deep dive: pH and its importance

pH is the negative logarithm of hydrogen ion concentration. Stomach acid pH about 1.5-3; lemon juice 2.2; tomato 4.2; milk 6.4; pure water 7; blood 7.4; baking soda solution 8.4; milk of magnesia 10; NaOH 14. Importance: tooth decay begins below pH 5.5, so use basic toothpaste; acid rain pH below 5.6 harms aquatic life; indigestion treated with antacids (Mg(OH)2); bee sting (methanoic acid) and nettle sting treated by baking soda or dock leaf; soil pH for crops.
Deep dive: Important salts

Common salt NaCl from sea water; rock salt. Chlor-alkali: 2NaCl + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + Cl2 + H2. Bleaching powder CaOCl2 (Ca(OH)2 + Cl2) for bleaching and disinfecting water. Baking soda NaHCO3 (NaCl + H2O + CO2 + NH3 -> NH4Cl + NaHCO3) used in antacids and baking powder, 2NaHCO3 -> Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2 on heating. Washing soda Na2CO3.10H2O from recrystallising sodium carbonate, used in glass, soap, paper. Plaster of Paris CaSO4.1/2H2O made by heating gypsum CaSO4.2H2O at 373 K; it sets into gypsum on mixing with water, used for supporting fractured bones. Water of crystallisation: CuSO4.5H2O is blue, anhydrous white.

problems.q: What happens when an acid reacts with a metal carbonate? Write the equation for HCl and Na2CO3.
problems.a: Salt, water and carbon dioxide are formed. Na2CO3 + 2HCl -> 2NaCl + H2O + CO2. CO2 turns lime water milky.

problems.q: Why is pH important in daily life? Give three examples.
problems.a: Tooth decay starts when mouth pH falls below 5.5, so basic toothpaste neutralises acids; acid rain pH below 5.6 harms rivers and life; antacids neutralise stomach acid; bee sting is treated with baking soda; soil pH decides crops.

problems.q: How is Plaster of Paris prepared? Why must it be stored in a moisture-proof container? Give uses.
problems.a: POP is made by heating gypsum CaSO4.2H2O at 373 K: CaSO4.2H2O -> CaSO4.1/2H2O + 1.5 H2O. It absorbs water and sets to hard gypsum, so moisture would spoil it. Uses: plaster for fractures, toys, decoration, smoothing surfaces.

Visual lesson

Acids, Bases and Salts

Acids turn blue litmus red, taste sour and release H+ ions in water

🔑

Big idea

  • Acids turn blue litmus red, taste sour and release H+ ions in water
  • Bases turn red litmus blue, are bitter and slippery, and give OH- ions
  • Those soluble in water are alkalis
  • The pH scale from 0 to 14 measures H+ concentration: acids below 7, neutral 7, bases above 7
Read the full explanation

Acids turn blue litmus red, taste sour and release H+ ions in water; bases turn red litmus blue, are bitter and slippery, and give OH- ions; those soluble in water are alkalis. The pH scale from 0 to 14 measures H+ concentration: acids below 7, neutral 7, bases above 7. Acid + metal gives salt + hydrogen; acid + base gives salt + water; acid + metal carbonate/hydrogencarbonate gives salt + CO2 + water. Common salts: NaCl, NaOH from chlor-alkali process, bleaching powder CaOCl2, baking soda NaHCO3, washing soda Na2CO3.10H2O, and Plaster of Paris CaSO4.1/2H2O.

📌

Properties and indicators

  • Natural indicators: litmus, turmeric, red cabbage, China rose
  • Synthetic: phenolphthalein (colourless in acid, pink in base), methyl orange (red in acid, yellow in base)
  • Olfactory indicators like onion, vanilla and clove lose smell in a base
  • Acids need water to release H+ (H3O+)
Read the full explanation

Natural indicators: litmus, turmeric, red cabbage, China rose. Synthetic: phenolphthalein (colourless in acid, pink in base), methyl orange (red in acid, yellow in base). Olfactory indicators like onion, vanilla and clove lose smell in a base. Acids need water to release H+ (H3O+); dry HCl gas does not change dry litmus. Diluting an acid is exothermic: always add acid to water slowly with stirring, never water to acid.

⚗️

Reactions of acids and bases

  • Acid + metal: Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2 (pop test)
  • Base + metal: 2NaOH + Zn -> Na2ZnO2 + H2
  • Metal carbonate + acid: Na2CO3 + 2HCl -> 2NaCl + H2O + CO2, CO2 turns lime water milky (Ca(OH)2 + CO2 -> CaCO3 + H2O) and the milkiness disappears on…
  • Neutralisation: NaOH + HCl -> NaCl + H2O
Read the full explanation

Acid + metal: Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2 (pop test). Base + metal: 2NaOH + Zn -> Na2ZnO2 + H2. Metal carbonate + acid: Na2CO3 + 2HCl -> 2NaCl + H2O + CO2, CO2 turns lime water milky (Ca(OH)2 + CO2 -> CaCO3 + H2O) and the milkiness disappears on excess CO2 forming calcium hydrogencarbonate. Neutralisation: NaOH + HCl -> NaCl + H2O. Metal oxides are basic; non-metal oxides are acidic.

🌟

PH and its importance

  • PH is the negative logarithm of hydrogen ion concentration
  • Stomach acid pH about 1.5-3
  • Lemon juice 2.2
  • Baking soda solution 8.4
Read the full explanation

pH is the negative logarithm of hydrogen ion concentration. Stomach acid pH about 1.5-3; lemon juice 2.2; tomato 4.2; milk 6.4; pure water 7; blood 7.4; baking soda solution 8.4; milk of magnesia 10; NaOH 14. Importance: tooth decay begins below pH 5.5, so use basic toothpaste; acid rain pH below 5.6 harms aquatic life; indigestion treated with antacids (Mg(OH)2); bee sting (methanoic acid) and nettle sting treated by baking soda or dock leaf; soil pH for crops.

⚗️

Important salts

  • Common salt NaCl from sea water
  • Chlor-alkali: 2NaCl + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + Cl2 + H2
  • Bleaching powder CaOCl2 (Ca(OH)2 + Cl2) for bleaching and disinfecting water
  • Baking soda NaHCO3 (NaCl + H2O + CO2 + NH3 -> NH4Cl + NaHCO3) used in antacids and baking powder, 2NaHCO3 -> Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2 on heating
Read the full explanation

Common salt NaCl from sea water; rock salt. Chlor-alkali: 2NaCl + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + Cl2 + H2. Bleaching powder CaOCl2 (Ca(OH)2 + Cl2) for bleaching and disinfecting water. Baking soda NaHCO3 (NaCl + H2O + CO2 + NH3 -> NH4Cl + NaHCO3) used in antacids and baking powder, 2NaHCO3 -> Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2 on heating. Washing soda Na2CO3.10H2O from recrystallising sodium carbonate, used in glass, soap, paper. Plaster of Paris CaSO4.1/2H2O made by heating gypsum CaSO4.2H2O at 373 K; it sets into gypsum on mixing with water, used for supporting fractured bones. Water of crystallisation: CuSO4.5H2O is blue, anhydrous white.

lessons.title: Metals and Non-metals
yt: class 10 science metals and non metals

blocks.x: Metals are lustrous, malleable, ductile, good conductors of heat and electricity, and form basic oxides by losing electrons to become cations. Non-metals are brittle, non-lustrous (except iodine, graphite), poor conductors (except graphite) and form acidic oxides. Amphoteric oxides such as Al2O3 and ZnO react with both acids and bases. The reactivity series is K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Pb, H, Cu, Hg, Ag, Au. Ionic compounds have high melting points, conduct in molten state and in solution. Extraction depends on reactivity: electrolytic reduction for top metals, carbon reduction for the middle, and heating for the least reactive. Corrosion is prevented by galvanisation and alloying.
Deep dive: Physical and chemical properties

Metals: sonorous, hard (except Na, K soft), solid (except mercury liquid), high melting points (except Ga, Cs low). Gold and silver are the most malleable; copper and silver the best conductors; lead and mercury poor conductors. Chemically: metal + oxygen -> metal oxide (4Na + O2; 2Cu + O2 -> 2CuO black); Na and K are stored in kerosene; Mg burns brilliantly; Al2O3 and ZnO are amphoteric. Metal + water: Na and K react violently; Ca less; Mg with hot water/steam; Al, Fe, Zn with steam giving oxide and hydrogen. Metal + acid gives salt and hydrogen (not with nitric acid). Aqua regia (3 HCl : 1 HNO3) dissolves gold and platinum.
Deep dive: Reactivity series and ionic compounds

More reactive metals displace less reactive from solutions: Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu. Ionic compounds like NaCl form by transfer of electrons: Na loses an electron to Cl making Na+ and Cl-. They are solids, hard and brittle, have high melting and boiling points due to strong electrostatic forces, are soluble in water and conduct electricity in molten and aqueous states but not in solid.
Deep dive: Occurrence and extraction

Minerals contain metals and ores are minerals from which metals can be extracted profitably. Steps: concentration (enrichment) of ore by gravity separation, magnetic separation or froth flotation; extraction; refining. Metals at the top (K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al) by electrolysis of molten chlorides, e.g. NaCl -> Na + Cl2; Al2O3 is reduced electrolytically. Middle metals (Zn, Fe, Pb) are found as sulphides or carbonates; ores are roasted (sulphides heated in air to oxide) or calcined (carbonates heated in limited air) and then reduced by carbon: ZnO + C -> Zn + CO. Thermite reaction: Fe2O3 + 2Al -> 2Fe + Al2O3 used for welding rail tracks. Least reactive Cu, Hg: HgS heated gives Hg. Electrolytic refining of copper: impure copper is anode, pure copper cathode, acidified copper sulphate electrolyte, impurities settle as anode mud.
Deep dive: Corrosion and alloys

Rusting of iron needs both air and water. Prevention: painting, oiling, galvanising (zinc), chrome plating, anodising (aluminium), alloying. Alloys are homogeneous mixtures of metals, or metal with non-metal: brass (Cu + Zn), bronze (Cu + Sn), solder (Pb + Sn), stainless steel (Fe, Ni, Cr), and amalgam has mercury. Pure gold is 24 carat; 22 carat gold is alloyed with copper or silver to make it hard. Iron is made hard by adding carbon.

problems.q: Why are sodium and potassium kept immersed in kerosene oil?
problems.a: They are highly reactive and catch fire in air or react violently with moisture; kerosene keeps air and water away.

problems.q: Explain the extraction of a metal of medium reactivity such as zinc from its ore.
problems.a: Zinc sulphide is roasted: 2ZnS + 3O2 -> 2ZnO + 2SO2; zinc carbonate is calcined: ZnCO3 -> ZnO + CO2. ZnO is reduced with carbon: ZnO + C -> Zn + CO. Then refined electrolytically.

problems.q: Describe the formation of NaCl and MgCl2 by electron transfer and list the properties of ionic compounds.
problems.a: Na (2,8,1) loses 1 electron to become Na+ and Cl (2,8,7) gains it becoming Cl-; Mg (2,8,2) loses two electrons and two Cl atoms each gain one. Properties: solid, hard and brittle; high melting and boiling points; soluble in water; conduct in molten and aqueous states only.

Visual lesson

Metals and Non-metals

Metals are lustrous, malleable, ductile, good conductors of heat and electricity, and form basic oxides by losing electrons to become cations

ThermiteFe2O3 + 2Al
🔑

Big idea

  • Metals are lustrous, malleable, ductile, good conductors of heat and electricity, and form basic oxides by losing electrons to become cations
  • Non-metals are brittle, non-lustrous (except iodine, graphite), poor conductors (except graphite) and form acidic oxides
  • Amphoteric oxides such as Al2O3 and ZnO react with both acids and bases
  • The reactivity series is K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Pb, H, Cu, Hg, Ag, Au
Read the full explanation

Metals are lustrous, malleable, ductile, good conductors of heat and electricity, and form basic oxides by losing electrons to become cations. Non-metals are brittle, non-lustrous (except iodine, graphite), poor conductors (except graphite) and form acidic oxides. Amphoteric oxides such as Al2O3 and ZnO react with both acids and bases. The reactivity series is K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Pb, H, Cu, Hg, Ag, Au. Ionic compounds have high melting points, conduct in molten state and in solution. Extraction depends on reactivity: electrolytic reduction for top metals, carbon reduction for the middle, and heating for the least reactive. Corrosion is prevented by galvanisation and alloying.

⚗️

Physical and chemical properties

  • Metals: sonorous, hard (except Na, K soft), solid (except mercury liquid), high melting points (except Ga, Cs low)
  • Gold and silver are the most malleable
  • Copper and silver the best conductors
  • Lead and mercury poor conductors
Read the full explanation

Metals: sonorous, hard (except Na, K soft), solid (except mercury liquid), high melting points (except Ga, Cs low). Gold and silver are the most malleable; copper and silver the best conductors; lead and mercury poor conductors. Chemically: metal + oxygen -> metal oxide (4Na + O2; 2Cu + O2 -> 2CuO black); Na and K are stored in kerosene; Mg burns brilliantly; Al2O3 and ZnO are amphoteric. Metal + water: Na and K react violently; Ca less; Mg with hot water/steam; Al, Fe, Zn with steam giving oxide and hydrogen. Metal + acid gives salt and hydrogen (not with nitric acid). Aqua regia (3 HCl : 1 HNO3) dissolves gold and platinum.

🧠

Reactivity series and ionic compounds

  • More reactive metals displace less reactive from solutions: Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu
  • Ionic compounds like NaCl form by transfer of electrons: Na loses an electron to Cl making Na+ and Cl-
  • They are solids, hard and brittle, have high melting and boiling points due to strong electrostatic forces, are soluble in water and conduct…
Read the full explanation

More reactive metals displace less reactive from solutions: Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu. Ionic compounds like NaCl form by transfer of electrons: Na loses an electron to Cl making Na+ and Cl-. They are solids, hard and brittle, have high melting and boiling points due to strong electrostatic forces, are soluble in water and conduct electricity in molten and aqueous states but not in solid.

🌟

Occurrence and extraction

  • Minerals contain metals and ores are minerals from which metals can be extracted profitably
  • Steps: concentration (enrichment) of ore by gravity separation, magnetic separation or froth flotation
  • Metals at the top (K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al) by electrolysis of molten chlorides, e.g. NaCl -> Na + Cl2
  • Al2O3 is reduced electrolytically
Read the full explanation

Minerals contain metals and ores are minerals from which metals can be extracted profitably. Steps: concentration (enrichment) of ore by gravity separation, magnetic separation or froth flotation; extraction; refining. Metals at the top (K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al) by electrolysis of molten chlorides, e.g. NaCl -> Na + Cl2; Al2O3 is reduced electrolytically. Middle metals (Zn, Fe, Pb) are found as sulphides or carbonates; ores are roasted (sulphides heated in air to oxide) or calcined (carbonates heated in limited air) and then reduced by carbon: ZnO + C -> Zn + CO. Thermite reaction: Fe2O3 + 2Al -> 2Fe + Al2O3 used for welding rail tracks. Least reactive Cu, Hg: HgS heated gives Hg. Electrolytic refining of copper: impure copper is anode, pure copper cathode, acidified copper sulphate electrolyte, impurities settle as anode mud.

🔬

Corrosion and alloys

  • Rusting of iron needs both air and water
  • Prevention: painting, oiling, galvanising (zinc), chrome plating, anodising (aluminium), alloying
  • Alloys are homogeneous mixtures of metals, or metal with non-metal: brass (Cu + Zn), bronze (Cu + Sn), solder (Pb + Sn), stainless steel (Fe, Ni…
  • Pure gold is 24 carat
Read the full explanation

Rusting of iron needs both air and water. Prevention: painting, oiling, galvanising (zinc), chrome plating, anodising (aluminium), alloying. Alloys are homogeneous mixtures of metals, or metal with non-metal: brass (Cu + Zn), bronze (Cu + Sn), solder (Pb + Sn), stainless steel (Fe, Ni, Cr), and amalgam has mercury. Pure gold is 24 carat; 22 carat gold is alloyed with copper or silver to make it hard. Iron is made hard by adding carbon.

lessons.title: Carbon and its Compounds
yt: class 10 science carbon and its compounds

blocks.x: Carbon forms covalent bonds by sharing electrons, due to tetravalency and catenation. It occurs as diamond, graphite and fullerene (C-60). Hydrocarbons are saturated (alkanes, CnH2n+2) or unsaturated (alkenes CnH2n, alkynes CnH2n-2). A functional group decides properties: alcohol -OH, aldehyde -CHO, ketone C=O, carboxylic acid -COOH, halo -Cl/-Br. Homologous series differ by CH2 (14 u). IUPAC naming uses prefix, word root and suffix. Ethanol and ethanoic acid are important; reactions include combustion, oxidation, addition (hydrogenation), substitution, esterification and saponification. Soaps are sodium or potassium salts of long-chain fatty acids and act by micelle formation; detergents work in hard water.
Deep dive: Bonding and allotropes

Carbon (2,4) neither gains nor loses four electrons easily so it shares electrons forming covalent bonds with low melting and boiling points and poor conductivity. Tetravalency lets carbon bond with four atoms. Catenation is self-linking into chains, branches and rings. Diamond: each carbon bonded to four others in a rigid 3D lattice, the hardest natural substance, non-conductor. Graphite: each carbon bonded to three, hexagonal layers, slippery, conducts electricity, used as lubricant. Fullerene C-60 has 60 carbon atoms like a football. Isomers have the same molecular formula but different structures: butane and isobutane.
Deep dive: Hydrocarbons and nomenclature

Alkanes (single bonds): methane CH4, ethane C2H6, propane C3H8, butane C4H10, pentane C5H12. Alkenes (double bond): ethene C2H4, propene C3H6. Alkynes (triple bond): ethyne C2H2. Count carbon atoms in the longest chain for the word root (meth, eth, prop, but, pent, hex), suffix -ane, -ene, -yne, and prefixes like chloro-, bromo-. Functional groups: alcohol -ol, aldehyde -al, ketone -one, carboxylic acid -oic acid. Homologous series: same functional group and similar chemical properties, with physical properties changing gradually.
Deep dive: Chemical properties

Combustion: CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O; saturated hydrocarbons burn with a clean blue flame, unsaturated with a yellow sooty flame. Oxidation: alcohols are oxidised to carboxylic acids with alkaline KMnO4 or acidified potassium dichromate. Addition: unsaturated hydrocarbon + H2 -> saturated in the presence of nickel (hydrogenation of vegetable oils to make ghee). Substitution: CH4 + Cl2 -> CH3Cl + HCl in sunlight. Ethanol: reacts with sodium giving H2; dehydrated with conc. H2SO4 at 443 K to ethene. Ethanoic acid: vinegar is 5-8% acetic acid; freezes at 290 K as glacial acetic acid; reacts with NaHCO3 giving CO2; esterification with ethanol (conc. H2SO4 catalyst) gives ethyl ethanoate with fruity smell; ester + NaOH gives alcohol + soap (saponification).
Deep dive: Soaps and detergents

Soap is the sodium or potassium salt of a long-chain carboxylic acid. Its molecule has an ionic hydrophilic head and a long hydrophobic hydrocarbon tail. In water the tails dissolve in oil and the heads face water forming a micelle that traps dirt and gets rinsed. Soaps form scum with calcium and magnesium salts of hard water; detergents are ammonium or sulphonate salts that do not form scum and clean in hard water as well. Ethanol is consumed as alcoholic drinks but is toxic; methanol causes blindness; denatured alcohol is made unfit for drinking.

Visual lesson

Carbon and its Compounds

Carbon forms covalent bonds by sharing electrons, due to tetravalency and catenation

AlkeneCnH2n
AlkyneCnH2n-2
🔑

Big idea

  • Carbon forms covalent bonds by sharing electrons, due to tetravalency and catenation
  • It occurs as diamond, graphite and fullerene (C-60)
  • Hydrocarbons are saturated (alkanes, CnH2n+2) or unsaturated (alkenes CnH2n, alkynes CnH2n-2)
  • A functional group decides properties: alcohol -OH, aldehyde -CHO, ketone C=O, carboxylic acid -COOH, halo -Cl/-Br
Read the full explanation

Carbon forms covalent bonds by sharing electrons, due to tetravalency and catenation. It occurs as diamond, graphite and fullerene (C-60). Hydrocarbons are saturated (alkanes, CnH2n+2) or unsaturated (alkenes CnH2n, alkynes CnH2n-2). A functional group decides properties: alcohol -OH, aldehyde -CHO, ketone C=O, carboxylic acid -COOH, halo -Cl/-Br. Homologous series differ by CH2 (14 u). IUPAC naming uses prefix, word root and suffix. Ethanol and ethanoic acid are important; reactions include combustion, oxidation, addition (hydrogenation), substitution, esterification and saponification. Soaps are sodium or potassium salts of long-chain fatty acids and act by micelle formation; detergents work in hard water.

⚗️

Bonding and allotropes

  • Carbon (2,4) neither gains nor loses four electrons easily so it shares electrons forming covalent bonds with low melting and boiling points and poor…
  • Tetravalency lets carbon bond with four atoms
  • Catenation is self-linking into chains, branches and rings
  • Diamond: each carbon bonded to four others in a rigid 3D lattice, the hardest natural substance, non-conductor
Read the full explanation

Carbon (2,4) neither gains nor loses four electrons easily so it shares electrons forming covalent bonds with low melting and boiling points and poor conductivity. Tetravalency lets carbon bond with four atoms. Catenation is self-linking into chains, branches and rings. Diamond: each carbon bonded to four others in a rigid 3D lattice, the hardest natural substance, non-conductor. Graphite: each carbon bonded to three, hexagonal layers, slippery, conducts electricity, used as lubricant. Fullerene C-60 has 60 carbon atoms like a football. Isomers have the same molecular formula but different structures: butane and isobutane.

🧠

Hydrocarbons and nomenclature

  • Alkanes (single bonds): methane CH4, ethane C2H6, propane C3H8, butane C4H10, pentane C5H12
  • Alkenes (double bond): ethene C2H4, propene C3H6
  • Alkynes (triple bond): ethyne C2H2
  • Count carbon atoms in the longest chain for the word root (meth, eth, prop, but, pent, hex), suffix -ane, -ene, -yne, and prefixes like chloro-…
Read the full explanation

Alkanes (single bonds): methane CH4, ethane C2H6, propane C3H8, butane C4H10, pentane C5H12. Alkenes (double bond): ethene C2H4, propene C3H6. Alkynes (triple bond): ethyne C2H2. Count carbon atoms in the longest chain for the word root (meth, eth, prop, but, pent, hex), suffix -ane, -ene, -yne, and prefixes like chloro-, bromo-. Functional groups: alcohol -ol, aldehyde -al, ketone -one, carboxylic acid -oic acid. Homologous series: same functional group and similar chemical properties, with physical properties changing gradually.

⚗️

Chemical properties

  • Combustion: CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O
  • Saturated hydrocarbons burn with a clean blue flame, unsaturated with a yellow sooty flame
  • Oxidation: alcohols are oxidised to carboxylic acids with alkaline KMnO4 or acidified potassium dichromate
  • Addition: unsaturated hydrocarbon + H2 -> saturated in the presence of nickel (hydrogenation of vegetable oils to make ghee)
Read the full explanation

Combustion: CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O; saturated hydrocarbons burn with a clean blue flame, unsaturated with a yellow sooty flame. Oxidation: alcohols are oxidised to carboxylic acids with alkaline KMnO4 or acidified potassium dichromate. Addition: unsaturated hydrocarbon + H2 -> saturated in the presence of nickel (hydrogenation of vegetable oils to make ghee). Substitution: CH4 + Cl2 -> CH3Cl + HCl in sunlight. Ethanol: reacts with sodium giving H2; dehydrated with conc. H2SO4 at 443 K to ethene. Ethanoic acid: vinegar is 5-8% acetic acid; freezes at 290 K as glacial acetic acid; reacts with NaHCO3 giving CO2; esterification with ethanol (conc. H2SO4 catalyst) gives ethyl ethanoate with fruity smell; ester + NaOH gives alcohol + soap (saponification).

🔬

Soaps and detergents

  • Soap is the sodium or potassium salt of a long-chain carboxylic acid
  • Its molecule has an ionic hydrophilic head and a long hydrophobic hydrocarbon tail
  • In water the tails dissolve in oil and the heads face water forming a micelle that traps dirt and gets rinsed
  • Soaps form scum with calcium and magnesium salts of hard water
Read the full explanation

Soap is the sodium or potassium salt of a long-chain carboxylic acid. Its molecule has an ionic hydrophilic head and a long hydrophobic hydrocarbon tail. In water the tails dissolve in oil and the heads face water forming a micelle that traps dirt and gets rinsed. Soaps form scum with calcium and magnesium salts of hard water; detergents are ammonium or sulphonate salts that do not form scum and clean in hard water as well. Ethanol is consumed as alcoholic drinks but is toxic; methanol causes blindness; denatured alcohol is made unfit for drinking.

lessons.title: Life Processes
yt: class 10 science life processes

blocks.x: Life processes are the basic functions that maintain life: nutrition, respiration, transportation and excretion. Autotrophs make food by photosynthesis (6CO2 + 12H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2 + 6H2O) in chloroplasts using stomata for gas exchange. Heterotrophs take food in holozoic, saprophytic or parasitic ways. Human digestion: mouth (salivary amylase), oesophagus, stomach (HCl, pepsin, mucus), small intestine (bile, pancreatic juice, intestinal juice; villi absorb), large intestine absorbs water. Respiration is aerobic (glucose to CO2, water and 38 ATP) or anaerobic (ethanol or lactic acid). Humans have a double circulation by a four-chambered heart. Blood has plasma, RBC, WBC, platelets; plants transport water by xylem and food by phloem (translocation). Excretion in humans is by nephrons of kidneys forming urine; plants release waste in leaves, bark and gum.
Deep dive: Nutrition

Autotrophic nutrition: chlorophyll absorbs light, light energy converts to chemical, water splits to release oxygen and CO2 reduced to carbohydrates. Stomata open and close by guard cells. Heterotrophs: Amoeba engulfs food with pseudopodia in a food vacuole; Paramecium uses cilia; saprophytes like fungi (bread mould) use extracellular digestion; parasites like Cuscuta. Human alimentary canal: saliva with salivary amylase digests starch to maltose; peristalsis moves food; stomach has gastric glands that secrete HCl (kills bacteria, activates pepsin), pepsin (proteins) and mucus (protects); the pyloric sphincter regulates exit; liver bile emulsifies fats (alkaline), pancreas gives trypsin (proteins), amylase (starch) and lipase (fats); intestinal juice completes digestion; villi increase surface area for absorption; large intestine absorbs water.
Deep dive: Respiration

Glucose is broken in the cytoplasm to pyruvate (glycolysis). In the absence of oxygen yeast gives ethanol + CO2; muscle cells give lactic acid (cramps); in oxygen mitochondria complete oxidation giving CO2 + H2O + energy. ATP is the energy currency: ADP + Pi + energy -> ATP. Human respiratory path: nostrils, pharynx, larynx, trachea (cartilage rings), bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli (gas exchange), with diaphragm and rib muscles in breathing. Haemoglobin carries oxygen. Aquatic organisms breathe dissolved oxygen through gills; terrestrial have lungs; fish breathe faster as water has less oxygen.
Deep dive: Transportation

Human heart has four chambers (two atria, two ventricles) preventing mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood, which is needed because we are warm-blooded with high energy needs. Double circulation: pulmonary (heart to lungs) and systemic (heart to body). Arteries thick-walled carry blood from heart; veins thin with valves carry blood to heart. Capillaries are one-cell thick for exchange. Blood pressure: about 120/80 mm Hg. Lymph carries digested fats and drains tissue fluid. In plants, xylem (tracheids, vessels) carries water by root pressure and transpiration pull; phloem (sieve tubes, companion cells) translocates sugar using energy ATP.
Deep dive: Excretion

Excretion is removal of metabolic wastes. In humans, a pair of kidneys filter blood; each has nephrons: Bowman's capsule with glomerulus filters, the tubule reabsorbs glucose, amino acids, salts and water, and urine collects in the ureter, bladder and out through the urethra. Artificial kidney is dialysis for failure. Plants excrete oxygen, store waste in old leaves, fall of leaves, bark, resins and gums.

problems.q: Differentiate between aerobic and anaerobic respiration.
problems.a: Aerobic uses oxygen, occurs in mitochondria, gives CO2, water and about 38 ATP. Anaerobic occurs in cytoplasm without oxygen giving ethanol + CO2 (yeast) or lactic acid (muscles) and little energy.

problems.q: Describe the double circulation of blood in humans and why it is necessary.
problems.a: Blood passes twice through the heart in one cycle: right ventricle to lungs (pulmonary) and returns oxygenated to the left atrium, then left ventricle pumps to the body (systemic) and returns to the right atrium. It keeps oxygenated and deoxygenated blood separate, supplying high energy needs of warm-blooded animals.

problems.q: Explain the structure of a nephron and the formation of urine.
problems.a: A nephron has Bowman's capsule with glomerulus, a long tubule and collecting duct. Blood is filtered in the glomerulus; the tubule reabsorbs glucose, amino acids, salts and water; the remaining nitrogenous waste (urea) is urine, which passes ureter to bladder to urethra. Water reabsorption depends on how much excess water there is and the amount of dissolved waste.

Visual lesson

Life Processes

Life processes are the basic functions that maintain life: nutrition, respiration, transportation and excretion

Big idea

  • Life processes are the basic functions that maintain life: nutrition, respiration, transportation and excretion
  • Autotrophs make food by photosynthesis (6CO2 + 12H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2 + 6H2O) in chloroplasts using stomata for gas exchange

Read the full explanation

Life processes are the basic functions that maintain life: nutrition, respiration, transportation and excretion. Autotrophs make food by photosynthesis (6CO2 + 12H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2 + 6H2O) in chloroplasts using stomata for gas exchange. Heterotrophs take food in holozoic, saprophytic or parasitic ways. Human digestion: mouth (salivary amylase), oesophagus, stomach (HCl, pepsin, mucus), small intestine (bile, pancreatic juice, intestinal juice; villi absorb), large intestine absorbs water. Respiration is aerobic (glucose to CO2, water and 38 ATP) or anaerobic (ethanol or lactic acid). Humans have a double circulation by a four-chambered heart. Blood has plasma, RBC, WBC, platelets; plants transport water by xylem and food by phloem (translocation). Excretion in humans is by nephrons of kidneys forming urine; plants release waste in leaves, bark and gum.

📌

Nutrition

  • Autotrophic nutrition: chlorophyll absorbs light, light energy converts to chemical, water splits to release oxygen and CO2 reduced to carbohydrates
  • Stomata open and close by guard cells
  • Heterotrophs: Amoeba engulfs food with pseudopodia in a food vacuole
  • Paramecium uses cilia
Read the full explanation

Autotrophic nutrition: chlorophyll absorbs light, light energy converts to chemical, water splits to release oxygen and CO2 reduced to carbohydrates. Stomata open and close by guard cells. Heterotrophs: Amoeba engulfs food with pseudopodia in a food vacuole; Paramecium uses cilia; saprophytes like fungi (bread mould) use extracellular digestion; parasites like Cuscuta. Human alimentary canal: saliva with salivary amylase digests starch to maltose; peristalsis moves food; stomach has gastric glands that secrete HCl (kills bacteria, activates pepsin), pepsin (proteins) and mucus (protects); the pyloric sphincter regulates exit; liver bile emulsifies fats (alkaline), pancreas gives trypsin (proteins), amylase (starch) and lipase (fats); intestinal juice completes digestion; villi increase surface area for absorption; large intestine absorbs water.

🧠

Respiration

  • Glucose is broken in the cytoplasm to pyruvate (glycolysis)
  • In the absence of oxygen yeast gives ethanol + CO2
  • Muscle cells give lactic acid (cramps)
  • In oxygen mitochondria complete oxidation giving CO2 + H2O + energy
Read the full explanation

Glucose is broken in the cytoplasm to pyruvate (glycolysis). In the absence of oxygen yeast gives ethanol + CO2; muscle cells give lactic acid (cramps); in oxygen mitochondria complete oxidation giving CO2 + H2O + energy. ATP is the energy currency: ADP + Pi + energy -> ATP. Human respiratory path: nostrils, pharynx, larynx, trachea (cartilage rings), bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli (gas exchange), with diaphragm and rib muscles in breathing. Haemoglobin carries oxygen. Aquatic organisms breathe dissolved oxygen through gills; terrestrial have lungs; fish breathe faster as water has less oxygen.

🌟

Transportation

  • Human heart has four chambers (two atria, two ventricles) preventing mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood, which is needed because we are…
  • Double circulation: pulmonary (heart to lungs) and systemic (heart to body)
  • Arteries thick-walled carry blood from heart
  • Veins thin with valves carry blood to heart
Read the full explanation

Human heart has four chambers (two atria, two ventricles) preventing mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood, which is needed because we are warm-blooded with high energy needs. Double circulation: pulmonary (heart to lungs) and systemic (heart to body). Arteries thick-walled carry blood from heart; veins thin with valves carry blood to heart. Capillaries are one-cell thick for exchange. Blood pressure: about 120/80 mm Hg. Lymph carries digested fats and drains tissue fluid. In plants, xylem (tracheids, vessels) carries water by root pressure and transpiration pull; phloem (sieve tubes, companion cells) translocates sugar using energy ATP.

🔬

Excretion

  • Excretion is removal of metabolic wastes
  • In humans, a pair of kidneys filter blood
  • Each has nephrons: Bowman's capsule with glomerulus filters, the tubule reabsorbs glucose, amino acids, salts and water, and urine collects in the…
  • Artificial kidney is dialysis for failure
Read the full explanation

Excretion is removal of metabolic wastes. In humans, a pair of kidneys filter blood; each has nephrons: Bowman's capsule with glomerulus filters, the tubule reabsorbs glucose, amino acids, salts and water, and urine collects in the ureter, bladder and out through the urethra. Artificial kidney is dialysis for failure. Plants excrete oxygen, store waste in old leaves, fall of leaves, bark, resins and gums.

lessons.title: Control and Coordination
yt: class 10 science control and coordination

blocks.x: Animals respond to stimuli through the nervous system and hormones; plants use hormones and tropisms. A neuron has dendrites, cell body, axon and nerve endings, passing impulses via synapses. The reflex arc (receptor, sensory neuron, spinal cord, motor neuron, effector) gives rapid involuntary response. The brain has forebrain (cerebrum), midbrain and hindbrain (cerebellum, pons, medulla). The brain is protected by the cranium and cerebrospinal fluid. Plant hormones: auxin, gibberellin, cytokinin (growth promoters), abscisic acid (inhibitor), ethylene (ripening). Animal hormones: thyroxine, insulin, growth hormone, adrenaline and sex hormones, controlled by feedback.
Deep dive: Nervous system

Receptors in sense organs (eye, ear, nose, tongue, skin) detect stimuli; the information travels from the dendrite tip to cell body, as an electrical impulse to the axon end where a chemical is released to cross the gap (synapse) to the next neuron. Muscle cells respond by contraction, as effectors; glands respond by secretion. Reflex action: touching a hot object; spinal cord handles the response without the brain thinking, so it is quick. Reflex arc: receptor -> sensory neuron -> relay neuron in spinal cord -> motor neuron -> muscle. Brain: forebrain (cerebrum) for thinking, memory and voluntary action; hypothalamus for hunger; midbrain; hindbrain: cerebellum for posture and balance, medulla for involuntary actions like blood pressure and salivation, pons.
Deep dive: Plant movement and hormones

Plants move without muscles: sensitive plant Mimosa pudica droops on touch because of changes in turgor. Tropisms: phototropism (towards light, shoot positive), geotropism (root positive), hydrotropism, chemotropism (pollen tube growth). Auxin accumulates on the shady side of the shoot making it longer so the shoot bends towards light. Gibberellins help stem growth; cytokinins promote cell division in fruits and seeds; abscisic acid inhibits growth and causes wilting of leaves; ethylene ripens fruits.
Deep dive: Hormones in animals

Endocrine glands release hormones directly into blood: pituitary (master gland, growth hormone), thyroid (thyroxine regulates metabolism; needs iodine; deficiency causes goitre), pancreas (insulin lowers blood sugar; deficiency causes diabetes), adrenal (adrenaline for fight or flight), testes (testosterone), ovaries (oestrogen). Feedback: if sugar rises, insulin is released; when sugar is normal, secretion stops. Iodised salt prevents goitre. Dwarfism arises from too little growth hormone and gigantism from too much.
Deep dive: Comparing systems

Nervous coordination is rapid, short-lived, uses electrical impulses and chemicals, and acts through nerves on specific organs. Hormonal coordination is slow, long-lasting, carried in blood and reaches every cell. Both together make a flexible and efficient control system.

problems.q: What is a reflex action? Trace the path of a reflex arc.
problems.a: A reflex action is a rapid, involuntary response to a stimulus. Path: receptor -> sensory neuron -> spinal cord (relay neuron) -> motor neuron -> effector (muscle).

problems.q: How does auxin make a shoot bend towards light?
problems.a: Light makes auxin move to the shady side of the shoot tip. Auxin stimulates cell elongation there so the shady side grows more and the shoot bends towards light (positive phototropism).

problems.q: Compare nervous and hormonal control and explain feedback regulation of blood sugar.
problems.a: Nervous: nerves, electrical impulses, fast, short-lived, specific. Hormonal: blood, chemical, slow, long-lasting, widespread. Blood sugar: rise stimulates pancreas to release insulin which lets cells and liver take up sugar; when level falls insulin secretion decreases.

Visual lesson

Control and Coordination

Animals respond to stimuli through the nervous system and hormones

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Nervous system›3Plant movement and hormones›4Hormones in animals›5Comparing systems
🔑

Big idea

  • Animals respond to stimuli through the nervous system and hormones
  • Plants use hormones and tropisms
  • A neuron has dendrites, cell body, axon and nerve endings, passing impulses via synapses
  • The reflex arc (receptor, sensory neuron, spinal cord, motor neuron, effector) gives rapid involuntary response
Read the full explanation

Animals respond to stimuli through the nervous system and hormones; plants use hormones and tropisms. A neuron has dendrites, cell body, axon and nerve endings, passing impulses via synapses. The reflex arc (receptor, sensory neuron, spinal cord, motor neuron, effector) gives rapid involuntary response. The brain has forebrain (cerebrum), midbrain and hindbrain (cerebellum, pons, medulla). The brain is protected by the cranium and cerebrospinal fluid. Plant hormones: auxin, gibberellin, cytokinin (growth promoters), abscisic acid (inhibitor), ethylene (ripening). Animal hormones: thyroxine, insulin, growth hormone, adrenaline and sex hormones, controlled by feedback.

📌

Nervous system

  • Receptors in sense organs (eye, ear, nose, tongue, skin) detect stimuli
  • The information travels from the dendrite tip to cell body, as an electrical impulse to the axon end where a chemical is released to cross the gap…
  • Muscle cells respond by contraction, as effectors
  • Glands respond by secretion
Read the full explanation

Receptors in sense organs (eye, ear, nose, tongue, skin) detect stimuli; the information travels from the dendrite tip to cell body, as an electrical impulse to the axon end where a chemical is released to cross the gap (synapse) to the next neuron. Muscle cells respond by contraction, as effectors; glands respond by secretion. Reflex action: touching a hot object; spinal cord handles the response without the brain thinking, so it is quick. Reflex arc: receptor -> sensory neuron -> relay neuron in spinal cord -> motor neuron -> muscle. Brain: forebrain (cerebrum) for thinking, memory and voluntary action; hypothalamus for hunger; midbrain; hindbrain: cerebellum for posture and balance, medulla for involuntary actions like blood pressure and salivation, pons.

🕰️

Plant movement and hormones

  • Plants move without muscles: sensitive plant Mimosa pudica droops on touch because of changes in turgor
  • Tropisms: phototropism (towards light, shoot positive), geotropism (root positive), hydrotropism, chemotropism (pollen tube growth)
  • Auxin accumulates on the shady side of the shoot making it longer so the shoot bends towards light
  • Gibberellins help stem growth
Read the full explanation

Plants move without muscles: sensitive plant Mimosa pudica droops on touch because of changes in turgor. Tropisms: phototropism (towards light, shoot positive), geotropism (root positive), hydrotropism, chemotropism (pollen tube growth). Auxin accumulates on the shady side of the shoot making it longer so the shoot bends towards light. Gibberellins help stem growth; cytokinins promote cell division in fruits and seeds; abscisic acid inhibits growth and causes wilting of leaves; ethylene ripens fruits.

🧬

Hormones in animals

  • Endocrine glands release hormones directly into blood: pituitary (master gland, growth hormone), thyroid (thyroxine regulates metabolism
  • Deficiency causes goitre), pancreas (insulin lowers blood sugar
  • Deficiency causes diabetes), adrenal (adrenaline for fight or flight), testes (testosterone), ovaries (oestrogen)
  • Feedback: if sugar rises, insulin is released
Read the full explanation

Endocrine glands release hormones directly into blood: pituitary (master gland, growth hormone), thyroid (thyroxine regulates metabolism; needs iodine; deficiency causes goitre), pancreas (insulin lowers blood sugar; deficiency causes diabetes), adrenal (adrenaline for fight or flight), testes (testosterone), ovaries (oestrogen). Feedback: if sugar rises, insulin is released; when sugar is normal, secretion stops. Iodised salt prevents goitre. Dwarfism arises from too little growth hormone and gigantism from too much.

🔬

Comparing systems

  • Nervous coordination is rapid, short-lived, uses electrical impulses and chemicals, and acts through nerves on specific organs
  • Hormonal coordination is slow, long-lasting, carried in blood and reaches every cell
  • Both together make a flexible and efficient control system

lessons.title: How do Organisms Reproduce?
yt: class 10 science how do organisms reproduce

blocks.x: Reproduction produces new individuals and maintains continuity of species through DNA copying with variation. Asexual methods: fission (binary in Amoeba, multiple in Plasmodium), fragmentation (Spirogyra), regeneration (Hydra, Planaria), budding (Hydra, yeast), vegetative propagation (cutting, layering, grafting, tissue culture) and spore formation (Rhizopus). Sexual reproduction in flowering plants involves pollination, fertilisation, seed and fruit formation. In humans, the male system has testes, vas deferens, urethra; the female system has ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus. Fertilisation forms a zygote that implants in the uterus; menstruation occurs if no fertilisation. Contraceptive methods (barrier, hormonal, IUCD, surgical) control pregnancy; STDs include AIDS, gonorrhoea, syphilis and HPV.
Deep dive: Asexual reproduction

Binary fission: Amoeba divides into two after nuclear division; Leishmania has a whip-like structure at one end. Multiple fission: Plasmodium divides into many daughter cells. Fragmentation: Spirogyra breaks into pieces that grow. Regeneration: Hydra and Planaria grow from cut pieces using specialised cells. Budding: a bud develops on parent Hydra and detaches. Vegetative propagation: roots, stems and leaves produce new plants as in Bryophyllum leaf buds, potato eyes, rose cutting, mango grafting; advantages: fruit and flower early, genetically identical, seedless plants like banana and orange grown. Spore formation: Rhizopus hyphae form sporangia with spores that germinate in moisture. Tissue culture grows plantlets from a small tissue in nutrient medium, e.g. orchids.
Deep dive: Sexual reproduction in plants

Flower: sepals, petals, stamens (anther with pollen, filament) and carpel (stigma, style, ovary with ovules). Pollination transfers pollen from anther to stigma (self or cross, by wind, water, insects). Pollen germinates to form a pollen tube that carries male gametes to the ovule; fertilisation produces a zygote; ovule becomes seed; ovary becomes fruit. Unisexual flowers: papaya, watermelon; bisexual: Hibiscus, mustard.
Deep dive: Reproduction in humans

Male: testes produce sperms and testosterone in the scrotum (lower temperature), vas deferens, seminal vesicle and prostate add fluid forming semen; urethra. Female: ovaries produce one egg every month, fallopian tube (fertilisation site), uterus (implantation and growth), cervix, vagina. Puberty: sex hormones; menarche at about 10-12 years in girls. Fertilisation forms a zygote that divides into an embryo; the placenta provides nutrition, oxygen and removes wastes. If no fertilisation, the thickened uterine lining breaks about every 28 days: menstruation.
Deep dive: Reproductive health

Contraception: barrier methods (condom, diaphragm), chemical (oral pills changing hormonal balance), IUCD (copper-T), and surgical methods (vasectomy, tubectomy). Abortion and sex determination misuse reduce the female ratio. STDs: bacterial gonorrhoea and syphilis; viral warts and HIV-AIDS; condoms offer protection. Population growth matters because of resources.

problems.q: Distinguish between binary fission and multiple fission.
problems.a: Binary fission: parent divides into two (Amoeba). Multiple fission: parent divides into many daughter cells (Plasmodium) under unfavourable conditions by forming a cyst.

problems.q: Describe the process of pollination and fertilisation in flowering plants.
problems.a: Pollen transfer from anther to stigma by wind, water or insects; pollen grain germinates forming a pollen tube through style to the ovule; male gamete fuses with the egg to form a zygote; ovule becomes seed and ovary a fruit.

problems.q: Explain the roles of the placenta and the menstrual cycle, and compare contraceptive methods.
problems.a: Placenta, embedded in the uterus wall, supplies oxygen and nutrients to the embryo and removes wastes. If no zygote implants the uterine lining is shed about every 28 days. Barrier methods prevent sperm meeting egg and protect against STDs; pills change hormones; IUCD prevents implantation; surgery blocks the tubes.

Visual lesson

How do Organisms Reproduce?

Reproduction produces new individuals and maintains continuity of species through DNA copying with variation

formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Asexual reproduction›3Sexual reproduction in…›4Reproduction in humans›5Reproductive health
Menstrual cycleAbout 28 days
GestationAbout 9 months
🔑

Big idea

  • Reproduction produces new individuals and maintains continuity of species through DNA copying with variation
  • Asexual methods: fission (binary in Amoeba, multiple in Plasmodium), fragmentation (Spirogyra), regeneration (Hydra, Planaria), budding (Hydra…
  • Sexual reproduction in flowering plants involves pollination, fertilisation, seed and fruit formation
  • In humans, the male system has testes, vas deferens, urethra
Read the full explanation

Reproduction produces new individuals and maintains continuity of species through DNA copying with variation. Asexual methods: fission (binary in Amoeba, multiple in Plasmodium), fragmentation (Spirogyra), regeneration (Hydra, Planaria), budding (Hydra, yeast), vegetative propagation (cutting, layering, grafting, tissue culture) and spore formation (Rhizopus). Sexual reproduction in flowering plants involves pollination, fertilisation, seed and fruit formation. In humans, the male system has testes, vas deferens, urethra; the female system has ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus. Fertilisation forms a zygote that implants in the uterus; menstruation occurs if no fertilisation. Contraceptive methods (barrier, hormonal, IUCD, surgical) control pregnancy; STDs include AIDS, gonorrhoea, syphilis and HPV.

📌

Asexual reproduction

  • Binary fission: Amoeba divides into two after nuclear division
  • Leishmania has a whip-like structure at one end
  • Multiple fission: Plasmodium divides into many daughter cells
  • Fragmentation: Spirogyra breaks into pieces that grow
Read the full explanation

Binary fission: Amoeba divides into two after nuclear division; Leishmania has a whip-like structure at one end. Multiple fission: Plasmodium divides into many daughter cells. Fragmentation: Spirogyra breaks into pieces that grow. Regeneration: Hydra and Planaria grow from cut pieces using specialised cells. Budding: a bud develops on parent Hydra and detaches. Vegetative propagation: roots, stems and leaves produce new plants as in Bryophyllum leaf buds, potato eyes, rose cutting, mango grafting; advantages: fruit and flower early, genetically identical, seedless plants like banana and orange grown. Spore formation: Rhizopus hyphae form sporangia with spores that germinate in moisture. Tissue culture grows plantlets from a small tissue in nutrient medium, e.g. orchids.

🧬

Sexual reproduction in plants

  • Flower: sepals, petals, stamens (anther with pollen, filament) and carpel (stigma, style, ovary with ovules)
  • Pollination transfers pollen from anther to stigma (self or cross, by wind, water, insects)
  • Pollen germinates to form a pollen tube that carries male gametes to the ovule
  • Fertilisation produces a zygote
Read the full explanation

Flower: sepals, petals, stamens (anther with pollen, filament) and carpel (stigma, style, ovary with ovules). Pollination transfers pollen from anther to stigma (self or cross, by wind, water, insects). Pollen germinates to form a pollen tube that carries male gametes to the ovule; fertilisation produces a zygote; ovule becomes seed; ovary becomes fruit. Unisexual flowers: papaya, watermelon; bisexual: Hibiscus, mustard.

🧬

Reproduction in humans

  • Male: testes produce sperms and testosterone in the scrotum (lower temperature), vas deferens, seminal vesicle and prostate add fluid forming semen
  • Female: ovaries produce one egg every month, fallopian tube (fertilisation site), uterus (implantation and growth), cervix, vagina
  • Puberty: sex hormones
  • Menarche at about 10-12 years in girls
Read the full explanation

Male: testes produce sperms and testosterone in the scrotum (lower temperature), vas deferens, seminal vesicle and prostate add fluid forming semen; urethra. Female: ovaries produce one egg every month, fallopian tube (fertilisation site), uterus (implantation and growth), cervix, vagina. Puberty: sex hormones; menarche at about 10-12 years in girls. Fertilisation forms a zygote that divides into an embryo; the placenta provides nutrition, oxygen and removes wastes. If no fertilisation, the thickened uterine lining breaks about every 28 days: menstruation.

🔬

Reproductive health

  • Contraception: barrier methods (condom, diaphragm), chemical (oral pills changing hormonal balance), IUCD (copper-T), and surgical methods…
  • Abortion and sex determination misuse reduce the female ratio
  • STDs: bacterial gonorrhoea and syphilis
  • Viral warts and HIV-AIDS
Read the full explanation

Contraception: barrier methods (condom, diaphragm), chemical (oral pills changing hormonal balance), IUCD (copper-T), and surgical methods (vasectomy, tubectomy). Abortion and sex determination misuse reduce the female ratio. STDs: bacterial gonorrhoea and syphilis; viral warts and HIV-AIDS; condoms offer protection. Population growth matters because of resources.
