lessons.title: Heredity
yt: class 10 science heredity

blocks.x: Heredity is the transmission of characters from parents to offspring and variation is difference between individuals. Gregor Mendel experimented on the garden pea (Pisum sativum) and found the laws: a monohybrid cross of tall (TT) and dwarf (tt) gives all tall F1 (Tt) and 3 tall : 1 dwarf in F2, with genotype ratio 1:2:1. Dihybrid cross of round yellow and wrinkled green seeds gives 9:3:3:1 in F2, showing independent assortment. Traits are controlled by genes on chromosomes; dominant traits show in F1. In humans there are 23 pairs of chromosomes, 22 pairs autosomes and one pair sex chromosomes (XX female, XY male); the father decides the sex of the child. Variation arises by errors in DNA copying and sexual reproduction, and speciation results from natural selection and genetic drift; evolution is shown by fossils, homologous and analogous organs.
Deep dive: Mendel's experiments

Mendel chose pea for contrasting characters such as tall/dwarf, round/wrinkled seeds, yellow/green seeds, violet/white flowers. He took pure lines, cross-pollinated them and counted the offspring. In a monohybrid cross (TT x tt): F1 all Tt tall; F1 self gives F2 tall:dwarf = 3:1 and genotype TT:Tt:tt = 1:2:1. This showed that traits are inherited independently, with each having two factors; dominant factors express in the presence of recessive ones, and the recessive reappear in F2. In a dihybrid cross (RRYY x rryy): F1 all RrYy round yellow; F2: 9 round yellow : 3 round green : 3 wrinkled yellow : 1 wrinkled green, showing that characters are inherited independently (law of independent assortment).
Deep dive: Genes and sex determination

A gene is a segment of DNA that codes for a protein. Each cell has genes in pairs, one from each parent. Sexual reproduction: half of the chromosomes come from each parent, restoring the number in the zygote. Sex chromosomes: women have XX, men XY. All eggs carry X; sperm carry X or Y. If an X sperm fertilises the egg: XX girl; if a Y sperm: XY boy. So the probability of a boy or girl is 50 per cent and the father's chromosome decides the sex.
Deep dive: Variation and inheritance of acquired traits

Variation helps survival (e.g. green beetles on green bushes are eaten by crows; a red beetle variant gets eaten more). Acquired traits (such as a weight loss or cutting tails of mice) are not inherited because they do not change the DNA in germ cells. Only inherited traits in germ cells pass to offspring.
Deep dive: Evolution

Evolution is gradual change in organisms over generations. Homologous organs have the same structure and origin but different functions (forelimbs of human, bat, whale); analogous organs have different origin but same function (wings of birds and insects). Fossils are preserved remains (Archaeopteryx links reptiles and birds). Fossil dating uses relative position or radioactive carbon-14. Darwin proposed natural selection. Speciation arises by geographical isolation, genetic drift and natural selection. Acquired and inherited traits are different. Human evolution: Africa is the origin; Homo sapiens migrated across the earth.

Mendel ne matar ke paudhon par prayog kiye. Ekasankar sankar mein F2 mein 3:1, dwisankar mein 9:3:3:1. Linga nirdharan mein pita ka kromosom nirnayak hai. Arjit gun anuvanshik nahi hote.
Monohybrid 3:1 (genotype 1:2:1); dihybrid 9:3:3:1. Father decides the sex.

problems.a: F1 all tall (Tt), showing tall is dominant. F2 gives 3 tall : 1 dwarf; genotype ratio 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt. Recessive trait reappears in F2.

problems.q: Explain how sex of a child is determined in humans.
problems.a: Females have XX, males XY. All eggs carry X; sperm carry either X or Y. X sperm + egg gives XX girl; Y sperm + egg gives XY boy; the father's chromosome decides the sex and the chance is 50:50.

problems.q: Distinguish between acquired and inherited traits, and explain how variation and natural selection lead to speciation.
problems.a: Inherited traits are in germ-cell DNA and pass to offspring; acquired traits arise in body cells in a lifetime and are not inherited. Variations arise from DNA copying errors and sexual reproduction; those suited to the environment survive and reproduce (natural selection); geographical isolation and genetic drift accumulate differences until populations cannot interbreed, forming a new species.

🔑

Big idea

  • Heredity is the transmission of characters from parents to offspring and variation is difference between individuals
  • Gregor Mendel experimented on the garden pea (Pisum sativum) and found the laws: a monohybrid cross of tall (TT) and dwarf (tt) gives all tall F1…
  • Dihybrid cross of round yellow and wrinkled green seeds gives 9:3:3:1 in F2, showing independent assortment
  • Traits are controlled by genes on chromosomes
Read the full explanation

Heredity is the transmission of characters from parents to offspring and variation is difference between individuals. Gregor Mendel experimented on the garden pea (Pisum sativum) and found the laws: a monohybrid cross of tall (TT) and dwarf (tt) gives all tall F1 (Tt) and 3 tall : 1 dwarf in F2, with genotype ratio 1:2:1. Dihybrid cross of round yellow and wrinkled green seeds gives 9:3:3:1 in F2, showing independent assortment. Traits are controlled by genes on chromosomes; dominant traits show in F1. In humans there are 23 pairs of chromosomes, 22 pairs autosomes and one pair sex chromosomes (XX female, XY male); the father decides the sex of the child. Variation arises by errors in DNA copying and sexual reproduction, and speciation results from natural selection and genetic drift; evolution is shown by fossils, homologous and analogous organs.

📌

Mendel's experiments

  • Mendel chose pea for contrasting characters such as tall/dwarf, round/wrinkled seeds, yellow/green seeds, violet/white flowers
  • He took pure lines, cross-pollinated them and counted the offspring
  • In a monohybrid cross (TT x tt): F1 all Tt tall
  • F1 self gives F2 tall:dwarf = 3:1 and genotype TT:Tt:tt = 1:2:1
Read the full explanation

Mendel chose pea for contrasting characters such as tall/dwarf, round/wrinkled seeds, yellow/green seeds, violet/white flowers. He took pure lines, cross-pollinated them and counted the offspring. In a monohybrid cross (TT x tt): F1 all Tt tall; F1 self gives F2 tall:dwarf = 3:1 and genotype TT:Tt:tt = 1:2:1. This showed that traits are inherited independently, with each having two factors; dominant factors express in the presence of recessive ones, and the recessive reappear in F2. In a dihybrid cross (RRYY x rryy): F1 all RrYy round yellow; F2: 9 round yellow : 3 round green : 3 wrinkled yellow : 1 wrinkled green, showing that characters are inherited independently (law of independent assortment).

🧬

Genes and sex determination

  • A gene is a segment of DNA that codes for a protein
  • Each cell has genes in pairs, one from each parent
  • Sexual reproduction: half of the chromosomes come from each parent, restoring the number in the zygote
  • Sex chromosomes: women have XX, men XY
Read the full explanation

A gene is a segment of DNA that codes for a protein. Each cell has genes in pairs, one from each parent. Sexual reproduction: half of the chromosomes come from each parent, restoring the number in the zygote. Sex chromosomes: women have XX, men XY. All eggs carry X; sperm carry X or Y. If an X sperm fertilises the egg: XX girl; if a Y sperm: XY boy. So the probability of a boy or girl is 50 per cent and the father's chromosome decides the sex.

🌟

Variation and inheritance of acquired traits

  • Variation helps survival (e.g. green beetles on green bushes are eaten by crows
  • A red beetle variant gets eaten more)
  • Acquired traits (such as a weight loss or cutting tails of mice) are not inherited because they do not change the DNA in germ cells
  • Only inherited traits in germ cells pass to offspring
🔬

Evolution

  • Evolution is gradual change in organisms over generations
  • Homologous organs have the same structure and origin but different functions (forelimbs of human, bat, whale)
  • Analogous organs have different origin but same function (wings of birds and insects)
  • Fossils are preserved remains (Archaeopteryx links reptiles and birds)
Read the full explanation

Evolution is gradual change in organisms over generations. Homologous organs have the same structure and origin but different functions (forelimbs of human, bat, whale); analogous organs have different origin but same function (wings of birds and insects). Fossils are preserved remains (Archaeopteryx links reptiles and birds). Fossil dating uses relative position or radioactive carbon-14. Darwin proposed natural selection. Speciation arises by geographical isolation, genetic drift and natural selection. Acquired and inherited traits are different. Human evolution: Africa is the origin; Homo sapiens migrated across the earth.

lessons.title: Light: Reflection and Refraction
yt: class 10 science light reflection and refraction

blocks.x: Light travels in straight lines at 3 x 10^8 m/s in vacuum. Reflection follows two laws: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in one plane. Spherical mirrors: concave converges, convex diverges. Focal length f = R/2. Mirror formula 1/v + 1/u = 1/f; magnification m = -v/u = h2/h1. Refraction is bending of light as it passes between media; Snell's law n = sin i / sin r; refractive index n = c/v. Lens formula 1/v - 1/u = 1/f, magnification m = v/u, power P = 1/f in metres (dioptre). Convex lens converges (f positive) and concave diverges (f negative). Sign convention: distances measured from the pole or optical centre; those in the direction of the incident light are positive.
Deep dive: Spherical mirrors

Terms: pole P, centre of curvature C, radius of curvature R, principal focus F, aperture. Concave mirror images: object at infinity -> real, at F, very small; beyond C -> between F and C, real, inverted, diminished; at C -> at C, real, inverted, same size; between C and F -> beyond C, real, inverted, enlarged; at F -> at infinity, highly enlarged; between P and F -> virtual, erect, enlarged behind mirror. Convex mirror always forms virtual, erect, diminished images between P and F; used as rear view mirror for wide field of view. Concave mirrors are used in shaving mirrors, headlights, solar furnaces, torches and by dentists.
Deep dive: Refraction

Light going from rarer to denser bends towards the normal; denser to rarer bends away. Rectangular glass slab: emergent ray parallel to incident ray, with lateral displacement. n = c/v: refractive index of water 1.33, glass 1.5, diamond 2.42; higher n means optically denser and slower light. Absolute n of medium; relative n of 2 w.r.t. 1 = v1/v2 = n2/n1. Apparent depth, twinkling, advanced sunrise arise from refraction.
Deep dive: Lenses

Convex lens images: object at infinity -> at F2, real, point sized; beyond 2F1 -> between F2 and 2F2, real, inverted, diminished; at 2F1 -> at 2F2, same size; between F1 and 2F1 -> beyond 2F2, enlarged; at F1 -> infinity; between F1 and O -> virtual, erect, enlarged on the same side (magnifying glass). Concave lens: always virtual, erect, diminished between O and F1. Power P = 1/f(m); +ve for convex, -ve for concave; combination P = P1 + P2. 1 dioptre is the power of a lens of focal length 1 m.
Deep dive: Sign convention and ray diagrams

Cartesian convention: pole as origin, principal axis as x-axis, incident light from left. Object distance u is negative. Concave mirror f negative, convex mirror f positive; convex lens f positive, concave lens f negative. Ray diagrams: ray parallel to axis passes through the focus; ray through the focus goes parallel; ray through the centre of curvature retraces; ray to the pole reflects with equal angle; for lenses a ray through the optical centre goes undeviated.

Praakash ka parawartan: kon i = kon r. Darpan sutra 1/v+1/u=1/f. Apavartan mein Snell ka niyam n = sin i / sin r. Lens sutra 1/v-1/u=1/f. Shakti P=1/f (dioptre). Avatal darpan abhisari, uttal darpan apasari.

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Light: Reflection and Refraction

Light travels in straight lines at 3 x 10^8 m/s in vacuum

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Spherical mirrors›3Refraction›4Lenses›5Sign convention and ray…
Speed of light3 x 10^8 m/s
Water n1.33
Glass n1.5
Diamond n2.42
🔑

Big idea

  • Light travels in straight lines at 3 x 108 m/s in vacuum
  • Reflection follows two laws: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in one plane
  • Spherical mirrors: concave converges, convex diverges
  • Focal length f = R/2
Read the full explanation

Light travels in straight lines at 3 x 10^8 m/s in vacuum. Reflection follows two laws: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in one plane. Spherical mirrors: concave converges, convex diverges. Focal length f = R/2. Mirror formula 1/v + 1/u = 1/f; magnification m = -v/u = h2/h1. Refraction is bending of light as it passes between media; Snell's law n = sin i / sin r; refractive index n = c/v. Lens formula 1/v - 1/u = 1/f, magnification m = v/u, power P = 1/f in metres (dioptre). Convex lens converges (f positive) and concave diverges (f negative). Sign convention: distances measured from the pole or optical centre; those in the direction of the incident light are positive.

🔦

Spherical mirrors

  • Terms: pole P, centre of curvature C, radius of curvature R, principal focus F, aperture
  • Concave mirror images: object at infinity -> real, at F, very small
  • Beyond C -> between F and C, real, inverted, diminished
  • At C -> at C, real, inverted, same size
Read the full explanation

Terms: pole P, centre of curvature C, radius of curvature R, principal focus F, aperture. Concave mirror images: object at infinity -> real, at F, very small; beyond C -> between F and C, real, inverted, diminished; at C -> at C, real, inverted, same size; between C and F -> beyond C, real, inverted, enlarged; at F -> at infinity, highly enlarged; between P and F -> virtual, erect, enlarged behind mirror. Convex mirror always forms virtual, erect, diminished images between P and F; used as rear view mirror for wide field of view. Concave mirrors are used in shaving mirrors, headlights, solar furnaces, torches and by dentists.

🧠

Refraction

  • Light going from rarer to denser bends towards the normal
  • Denser to rarer bends away
  • Rectangular glass slab: emergent ray parallel to incident ray, with lateral displacement
  • N = c/v: refractive index of water 1.33, glass 1.5, diamond 2.42
Read the full explanation

Light going from rarer to denser bends towards the normal; denser to rarer bends away. Rectangular glass slab: emergent ray parallel to incident ray, with lateral displacement. n = c/v: refractive index of water 1.33, glass 1.5, diamond 2.42; higher n means optically denser and slower light. Absolute n of medium; relative n of 2 w.r.t. 1 = v1/v2 = n2/n1. Apparent depth, twinkling, advanced sunrise arise from refraction.

🔦

Lenses

  • Convex lens images: object at infinity -> at F2, real, point sized
  • Beyond 2F1 -> between F2 and 2F2, real, inverted, diminished
  • At 2F1 -> at 2F2, same size
  • Between F1 and 2F1 -> beyond 2F2, enlarged
Read the full explanation

Convex lens images: object at infinity -> at F2, real, point sized; beyond 2F1 -> between F2 and 2F2, real, inverted, diminished; at 2F1 -> at 2F2, same size; between F1 and 2F1 -> beyond 2F2, enlarged; at F1 -> infinity; between F1 and O -> virtual, erect, enlarged on the same side (magnifying glass). Concave lens: always virtual, erect, diminished between O and F1. Power P = 1/f(m); +ve for convex, -ve for concave; combination P = P1 + P2. 1 dioptre is the power of a lens of focal length 1 m.

🔦

Sign convention and ray diagrams

  • Cartesian convention: pole as origin, principal axis as x-axis, incident light from left
  • Object distance u is negative
  • Concave mirror f negative, convex mirror f positive
  • Convex lens f positive, concave lens f negative
Read the full explanation

Cartesian convention: pole as origin, principal axis as x-axis, incident light from left. Object distance u is negative. Concave mirror f negative, convex mirror f positive; convex lens f positive, concave lens f negative. Ray diagrams: ray parallel to axis passes through the focus; ray through the focus goes parallel; ray through the centre of curvature retraces; ray to the pole reflects with equal angle; for lenses a ray through the optical centre goes undeviated.

🧮

Formula tiles

Mirror formula1/v + 1/u = 1/fMirrors
Lens formula1/v - 1/u = 1/fLenses
Mirror magnificationm = -v/u = h2/h1Mirrors
Lens magnificationm = v/uLenses
Focal lengthf = R/2Mirrors
Snell lawn = sin i / sin rRefraction
Refractive indexn = c/vMedium
PowerP = 1/f (m)Dioptre
🎯 Remember Concave mirror and convex lens f positive in lens, negative mirror; u always negative. m = -v/u for mirror, v/u for lens.
🇮🇳

lessons.title: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
yt: class 10 science human eye and colourful world

blocks.x: The human eye forms real, inverted images on the retina, with the cornea and lens refracting light; the iris controls the pupil size; ciliary muscles change the focal length of the lens (accommodation). The near point is 25 cm and the far point is infinity. Defects: myopia (far point nearer; corrected by concave lens), hypermetropia (near point farther; convex lens), presbyopia (old age; bifocal) and cataract (cloudy lens; surgery). Dispersion splits white light into VIBGYOR through a prism. Atmospheric refraction causes twinkling, advance sunrise and delayed sunset. Scattering explains blue sky, red sun at sunrise and sunset (Rayleigh scattering) and the Tyndall effect. A rainbow combines refraction, dispersion and total internal reflection in water drops.
Deep dive: Structure and function

Light enters through the cornea, passes the aqueous humour, pupil and lens and forms an image on the retina with rods (dim light) and cones (colour). The optic nerve carries electrical signals to the brain. The iris controls pupil size. Ciliary muscles relax to flatten the lens for distant objects and contract to thicken it for near objects: this is accommodation. A normal eye sees objects between 25 cm (near point) and infinity (far point). Persistence of vision is about 1/16 s. Two eyes give a wider field of view and detect faint objects. Eye donation: cornea transplant helps blind people.
Deep dive: Defects and correction

Myopia: distant objects blurred because the image forms in front of the retina due to too long an eyeball or too much curvature; correct with a concave lens. Hypermetropia: near objects blurred; image forms behind the retina; correct with a convex lens. Presbyopia: weakening of ciliary muscles in old age, requires bifocal lens (concave upper, convex lower). Cataract: cloudy lens, treated by surgery. Power of corrective lens P = 1/f, where f equals the far point distance (negative) for myopia.
Deep dive: Dispersion and the atmosphere

Newton showed a glass prism splits white light into VIBGYOR (violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, red); red deviates least and violet most. A second inverted prism recombines the spectrum. Rainbow: sunlight enters water droplets, undergoes refraction and dispersion, internal reflection, and refraction again; seen with the Sun behind the observer. Twinkling of stars is due to atmospheric refraction; planets do not twinkle since they are extended sources. Advance sunrise and delayed sunset by about 2 minutes.
Deep dive: Scattering of light

Tyndall effect is scattering of light by colloidal particles, as sunlight through a canopy of trees or a beam in a dusty room. Rayleigh scattering is inversely proportional to the fourth power of wavelength, so blue scatters more; the sky looks blue. At sunrise and sunset the light travels through a thicker atmosphere so most of the blue is scattered and red reaches us. The sky is dark to astronauts as there is no atmosphere. Danger signals use red since it is scattered least.

problems.q: What is myopia? Explain how it is corrected.
problems.a: Myopia is short-sightedness where distant objects look blurred because the image forms in front of the retina. It is corrected by a concave lens of suitable power which diverges rays so the image forms on the retina.

problems.q: Why is the sky blue and the sun red at sunrise?
problems.a: Blue light has a shorter wavelength and is scattered more by atmospheric particles (Rayleigh), so we see a blue sky. At sunrise and sunset light travels a longer path, blue is scattered away and red reaches the eye.

problems.q: A myopic person has a far point at 80 cm. Find the power of the lens needed.
problems.a: The lens must form a virtual image of infinity-object at 80 cm: u = infinity, v = -80 cm, so f = -80 cm = -0.8 m and P = 1/f = -1.25 D (concave lens).

Visual lesson

The Human Eye and the Colourful World

The human eye forms real, inverted images on the retina, with the cornea and lens refracting light

Near point25 cm
Persistence1/16 s
RayleighScattering ∝ 1/λ^4
🔑

Big idea

  • The human eye forms real, inverted images on the retina, with the cornea and lens refracting light
  • The iris controls the pupil size
  • Ciliary muscles change the focal length of the lens (accommodation)
  • The near point is 25 cm and the far point is infinity
Read the full explanation

The human eye forms real, inverted images on the retina, with the cornea and lens refracting light; the iris controls the pupil size; ciliary muscles change the focal length of the lens (accommodation). The near point is 25 cm and the far point is infinity. Defects: myopia (far point nearer; corrected by concave lens), hypermetropia (near point farther; convex lens), presbyopia (old age; bifocal) and cataract (cloudy lens; surgery). Dispersion splits white light into VIBGYOR through a prism. Atmospheric refraction causes twinkling, advance sunrise and delayed sunset. Scattering explains blue sky, red sun at sunrise and sunset (Rayleigh scattering) and the Tyndall effect. A rainbow combines refraction, dispersion and total internal reflection in water drops.

📌

Structure and function

  • Light enters through the cornea, passes the aqueous humour, pupil and lens and forms an image on the retina with rods (dim light) and cones (colour)
  • The optic nerve carries electrical signals to the brain
  • The iris controls pupil size
  • Ciliary muscles relax to flatten the lens for distant objects and contract to thicken it for near objects: this is accommodation
Read the full explanation

Light enters through the cornea, passes the aqueous humour, pupil and lens and forms an image on the retina with rods (dim light) and cones (colour). The optic nerve carries electrical signals to the brain. The iris controls pupil size. Ciliary muscles relax to flatten the lens for distant objects and contract to thicken it for near objects: this is accommodation. A normal eye sees objects between 25 cm (near point) and infinity (far point). Persistence of vision is about 1/16 s. Two eyes give a wider field of view and detect faint objects. Eye donation: cornea transplant helps blind people.

🧠

Defects and correction

  • Myopia: distant objects blurred because the image forms in front of the retina due to too long an eyeball or too much curvature
  • Correct with a concave lens
  • Hypermetropia: near objects blurred
  • Image forms behind the retina
Read the full explanation

Myopia: distant objects blurred because the image forms in front of the retina due to too long an eyeball or too much curvature; correct with a concave lens. Hypermetropia: near objects blurred; image forms behind the retina; correct with a convex lens. Presbyopia: weakening of ciliary muscles in old age, requires bifocal lens (concave upper, convex lower). Cataract: cloudy lens, treated by surgery. Power of corrective lens P = 1/f, where f equals the far point distance (negative) for myopia.

🌟

Dispersion and the atmosphere

  • Newton showed a glass prism splits white light into VIBGYOR (violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, red)
  • Red deviates least and violet most
  • A second inverted prism recombines the spectrum
  • Rainbow: sunlight enters water droplets, undergoes refraction and dispersion, internal reflection, and refraction again
Read the full explanation

Newton showed a glass prism splits white light into VIBGYOR (violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, red); red deviates least and violet most. A second inverted prism recombines the spectrum. Rainbow: sunlight enters water droplets, undergoes refraction and dispersion, internal reflection, and refraction again; seen with the Sun behind the observer. Twinkling of stars is due to atmospheric refraction; planets do not twinkle since they are extended sources. Advance sunrise and delayed sunset by about 2 minutes.

🔦

Scattering of light

  • Tyndall effect is scattering of light by colloidal particles, as sunlight through a canopy of trees or a beam in a dusty room
  • Rayleigh scattering is inversely proportional to the fourth power of wavelength, so blue scatters more
  • The sky looks blue
  • At sunrise and sunset the light travels through a thicker atmosphere so most of the blue is scattered and red reaches us
Read the full explanation

Tyndall effect is scattering of light by colloidal particles, as sunlight through a canopy of trees or a beam in a dusty room. Rayleigh scattering is inversely proportional to the fourth power of wavelength, so blue scatters more; the sky looks blue. At sunrise and sunset the light travels through a thicker atmosphere so most of the blue is scattered and red reaches us. The sky is dark to astronauts as there is no atmosphere. Danger signals use red since it is scattered least.

🧮

lessons.title: Electricity
yt: class 10 science electricity

blocks.x: Electric current I = Q/t in ampere (A); potential difference V = W/Q in volt (V); resistance R = V/I in ohm. Ohm's law: V = IR at constant temperature. Resistance R = rho x l/A; resistivity depends on the material and temperature. In series: Rs = R1 + R2 + R3, same current; in parallel: 1/Rp = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ..., same voltage. Heating effect H = I^2 R t (Joule's law). Electric power P = VI = I^2R = V^2/R in watt; energy in kWh (1 kWh = 3.6 x 10^6 J). Ammeter in series and voltmeter in parallel. Fuse protects circuits, and alloys like nichrome are used for heaters because of high resistivity and melting point.
Deep dive: Current, potential difference and Ohm's law

Charge of one electron is 1.6 x 10^-19 C; 1 A is 1 C flowing per second, so number of electrons in 1 C is about 6.25 x 10^18. Conventional current flows from positive to negative while electrons move the other way. V = IR, giving a straight V-I graph; the slope is resistance. Ohmic conductors obey the law; filament lamps do not at high temperatures. Rheostat is a variable resistor; a key controls the circuit; the battery (cell combination) provides the potential difference.
Deep dive: Resistance and combinations

R = rho l/A: resistance increases with length and decreases with area of cross-section. Resistivity of metals and alloys is low (silver 1.6 x 10^-8 ohm m, copper 1.62 x 10^-8) while insulators like rubber have 10^12-10^17. Alloys are used in heating devices since resistivity is high and they do not oxidise easily. Series: the same current flows, total resistance increases, voltage divides; the failure of one stops the whole circuit. Parallel: the potential difference is the same, total resistance is less than the smallest; if one fails the others work; household circuits are parallel.
Deep dive: Heating effect and power

Heat produced H = I^2 R t = VIt = V^2 t/R. Applications: heaters, toasters, irons, electric bulb (tungsten with high melting point filled with inert gas nitrogen and argon), and fuse (low melting point wire of tin-lead alloy). Power P = VI. 1 watt = 1 volt x 1 ampere. Commercial unit: 1 kWh = 1 unit = 3.6 x 10^6 J. Energy = power x time. For example a 100 W bulb in 10 h uses 1 kWh.
Deep dive: Circuits and safety

Household supply is 220 V, 50 Hz AC. Live wire (red), neutral wire (black), earth (green) in three-pin plug; earthing prevents shocks. Overloading and short-circuiting cause too much current; MCBs and fuses protect. Measurements: ammeter is connected in series with low resistance; voltmeter in parallel with high resistance. Internal resistance and EMF are beyond the Class 10 scope.

🔑

Big idea

  • Electric current I = Q/t in ampere (A)
  • Potential difference V = W/Q in volt (V)
  • Resistance R = V/I in ohm
  • Ohm's law: V = IR at constant temperature
Read the full explanation

Electric current I = Q/t in ampere (A); potential difference V = W/Q in volt (V); resistance R = V/I in ohm. Ohm's law: V = IR at constant temperature. Resistance R = rho x l/A; resistivity depends on the material and temperature. In series: Rs = R1 + R2 + R3, same current; in parallel: 1/Rp = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ..., same voltage. Heating effect H = I^2 R t (Joule's law). Electric power P = VI = I^2R = V^2/R in watt; energy in kWh (1 kWh = 3.6 x 10^6 J). Ammeter in series and voltmeter in parallel. Fuse protects circuits, and alloys like nichrome are used for heaters because of high resistivity and melting point.

⚖️

Current, potential difference and Ohm's law

  • Charge of one electron is 1.6 x 10-19 C
  • 1 A is 1 C flowing per second, so number of electrons in 1 C is about 6.25 x 1018
  • Conventional current flows from positive to negative while electrons move the other way
  • V = IR, giving a straight V-I graph
Read the full explanation

Charge of one electron is 1.6 x 10^-19 C; 1 A is 1 C flowing per second, so number of electrons in 1 C is about 6.25 x 10^18. Conventional current flows from positive to negative while electrons move the other way. V = IR, giving a straight V-I graph; the slope is resistance. Ohmic conductors obey the law; filament lamps do not at high temperatures. Rheostat is a variable resistor; a key controls the circuit; the battery (cell combination) provides the potential difference.

🧠

Resistance and combinations

  • R = rho l/A: resistance increases with length and decreases with area of cross-section
  • Resistivity of metals and alloys is low (silver 1.6 x 10-8 ohm m, copper 1.62 x 10-8) while insulators like rubber have 1012-1017
  • Alloys are used in heating devices since resistivity is high and they do not oxidise easily
  • Series: the same current flows, total resistance increases, voltage divides
Read the full explanation

R = rho l/A: resistance increases with length and decreases with area of cross-section. Resistivity of metals and alloys is low (silver 1.6 x 10^-8 ohm m, copper 1.62 x 10^-8) while insulators like rubber have 10^12-10^17. Alloys are used in heating devices since resistivity is high and they do not oxidise easily. Series: the same current flows, total resistance increases, voltage divides; the failure of one stops the whole circuit. Parallel: the potential difference is the same, total resistance is less than the smallest; if one fails the others work; household circuits are parallel.

🌡️

Heating effect and power

  • Heat produced H = I2 R t = VIt = V2 t/R
  • Applications: heaters, toasters, irons, electric bulb (tungsten with high melting point filled with inert gas nitrogen and argon), and fuse (low…
  • 1 watt = 1 volt x 1 ampere
  • Commercial unit: 1 kWh = 1 unit = 3.6 x 106 J
Read the full explanation

Heat produced H = I^2 R t = VIt = V^2 t/R. Applications: heaters, toasters, irons, electric bulb (tungsten with high melting point filled with inert gas nitrogen and argon), and fuse (low melting point wire of tin-lead alloy). Power P = VI. 1 watt = 1 volt x 1 ampere. Commercial unit: 1 kWh = 1 unit = 3.6 x 10^6 J. Energy = power x time. For example a 100 W bulb in 10 h uses 1 kWh.

⚡

Circuits and safety

  • Household supply is 220 V, 50 Hz AC
  • Live wire (red), neutral wire (black), earth (green) in three-pin plug
  • Earthing prevents shocks
  • Overloading and short-circuiting cause too much current
Read the full explanation

Household supply is 220 V, 50 Hz AC. Live wire (red), neutral wire (black), earth (green) in three-pin plug; earthing prevents shocks. Overloading and short-circuiting cause too much current; MCBs and fuses protect. Measurements: ammeter is connected in series with low resistance; voltmeter in parallel with high resistance. Internal resistance and EMF are beyond the Class 10 scope.

lessons.title: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current
yt: class 10 science magnetic effects of electric current

blocks.x: Oersted found that a current-carrying conductor deflects a compass needle. Magnetic field lines emerge from the north pole and enter the south pole, never intersect, and are closer where the field is stronger. A straight wire has concentric circular fields given by the right-hand thumb rule; a solenoid has a field like a bar magnet; the strength depends on current, number of turns and core (iron). A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field feels force, with direction by Fleming's left-hand rule (force, field, current). An electric motor converts electrical energy to mechanical energy using a split ring commutator. Electromagnetic induction (Faraday) produces induced current when flux changes; Fleming's right-hand rule gives its direction. A generator converts mechanical energy to electrical energy; AC reverses every half rotation (50 Hz in India, so reverses every 1/100 s); DC flows one way. Domestic circuits use live, neutral and earth wires with fuses and earthing.
Deep dive: Magnetic field and field lines

A compass needle is a small magnet. Field strength is greater where lines are close. Properties: lines are closed curves; direction north to south outside the magnet; tangent gives direction; never cross. Right-hand thumb rule: curl fingers; thumb along current gives field direction on the fingers (or: grasp the wire with the right thumb in direction of current, fingers show field). A circular loop produces a field at the centre perpendicular to the plane; for N turns the field is N times stronger. Solenoid: coil of many circular turns; one end acts as north pole, other south; inside the field is uniform. An electromagnet is a soft iron core in a solenoid; a permanent magnet uses steel.
Deep dive: Force on a conductor and motor

A conductor perpendicular to the field experiences maximum force F; reverses if current or field is reversed. Fleming's left-hand rule: stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger mutually perpendicular: forefinger = field, middle = current, thumb = force. Motor: a rectangular coil between magnets with split-ring commutator that reverses current direction every half rotation, brushes and an armature; uses: fans, mixers, washing machines. The commercial motor has electromagnet, a large number of turns of soft iron core.
Deep dive: Electromagnetic induction

Faraday: moving a magnet in a coil or changing the field induces current in the coil; galvanometer deflects. Induced current is greater with fast motion, more turns and stronger magnet. Fleming's right-hand rule: forefinger = field, thumb = motion, middle = induced current. AC generator: a rotating coil in a magnetic field with slip rings and brushes; produces alternating current; DC generator uses a split ring commutator. AC advantages: easy to transmit over long distances without much loss by transformers.
Deep dive: Domestic electric circuits

Mains: live wire (red, 220 V), neutral (black), earth (green). Earth wire connects the metal body to the ground. A fuse of the right rating protects against overloading; MCB trips. Short-circuiting happens when live and neutral touch. Overloading when too many appliances are connected to one socket. Safety: earthing, fuse, insulated wires, not touching switches with wet hands.
Hindi saransh

Oersted ne dikhaya ki dhara chumbakiya prabhav deti hai. Dakshin hasth angutha niyam. Fleming ka baayen haath ka niyam bal ki dishaa batata hai; motor vidyut ko yantrik urja mein badalti hai. Vidyut chumbakiya prerana se generator banta hai.
Left hand for motors (force). Right hand for generators (induced current).

qa.q: Why is the commutator needed in a DC motor?

qa.q: What is induced current?

qa.q: How does a generator differ from a motor?
qa.a: A generator produces electricity from motion; a motor produces motion from electricity.

qa.q: Why does AC have an advantage over DC?

qa.q: How often does AC at 50 Hz reverse?
qa.a: 100 times each second, i.e. every 1/100 s.

qa.a: To disconnect the supply from the appliance when overloaded.

qa.q: What causes overloading?

qa.a: To pass any leakage current to the ground and prevent shock.

problems.q: State Fleming's left-hand rule and one use of it.
problems.a: Stretch thumb, forefinger and middle finger perpendicular: forefinger = magnetic field, middle finger = current, thumb = force on the conductor. It is used for finding the direction of rotation in an electric motor.

problems.q: Explain the working of an electric motor with the role of the split ring commutator.
problems.a: A rectangular coil is placed in a field; current flows, and forces act in opposite directions on the two arms making it rotate. After half a turn the split ring commutator reverses the current so that the force keeps the same direction of rotation.

problems.q: Describe electromagnetic induction and an AC generator. How does it differ from a DC generator?
problems.a: Changing flux through a coil induces an EMF. In an AC generator a coil rotates in the field; slip rings and brushes give an alternating current reversing every half rotation (50 Hz). In a DC generator split rings convert it to a unidirectional current.

Visual lesson

Magnetic Effects of Electric Current

Oersted found that a current-carrying conductor deflects a compass needle

Flat concept map (2D)

AC frequency50 Hz
🔑

Big idea

  • Oersted found that a current-carrying conductor deflects a compass needle
  • Magnetic field lines emerge from the north pole and enter the south pole, never intersect, and are closer where the field is stronger
  • A straight wire has concentric circular fields given by the right-hand thumb rule
  • A solenoid has a field like a bar magnet
Read the full explanation

Oersted found that a current-carrying conductor deflects a compass needle. Magnetic field lines emerge from the north pole and enter the south pole, never intersect, and are closer where the field is stronger. A straight wire has concentric circular fields given by the right-hand thumb rule; a solenoid has a field like a bar magnet; the strength depends on current, number of turns and core (iron). A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field feels force, with direction by Fleming's left-hand rule (force, field, current). An electric motor converts electrical energy to mechanical energy using a split ring commutator. Electromagnetic induction (Faraday) produces induced current when flux changes; Fleming's right-hand rule gives its direction. A generator converts mechanical energy to electrical energy; AC reverses every half rotation (50 Hz in India, so reverses every 1/100 s); DC flows one way. Domestic circuits use live, neutral and earth wires with fuses and earthing.

⚡

Magnetic field and field lines

  • A compass needle is a small magnet
  • Field strength is greater where lines are close
  • Properties: lines are closed curves
  • Direction north to south outside the magnet
Read the full explanation

A compass needle is a small magnet. Field strength is greater where lines are close. Properties: lines are closed curves; direction north to south outside the magnet; tangent gives direction; never cross. Right-hand thumb rule: curl fingers; thumb along current gives field direction on the fingers (or: grasp the wire with the right thumb in direction of current, fingers show field). A circular loop produces a field at the centre perpendicular to the plane; for N turns the field is N times stronger. Solenoid: coil of many circular turns; one end acts as north pole, other south; inside the field is uniform. An electromagnet is a soft iron core in a solenoid; a permanent magnet uses steel.

🚀

Force on a conductor and motor

  • A conductor perpendicular to the field experiences maximum force F
  • Reverses if current or field is reversed
  • Fleming's left-hand rule: stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger mutually perpendicular: forefinger = field, middle = current, thumb = force
  • Motor: a rectangular coil between magnets with split-ring commutator that reverses current direction every half rotation, brushes and an armature
Read the full explanation

A conductor perpendicular to the field experiences maximum force F; reverses if current or field is reversed. Fleming's left-hand rule: stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger mutually perpendicular: forefinger = field, middle = current, thumb = force. Motor: a rectangular coil between magnets with split-ring commutator that reverses current direction every half rotation, brushes and an armature; uses: fans, mixers, washing machines. The commercial motor has electromagnet, a large number of turns of soft iron core.

⚡

Electromagnetic induction

  • Faraday: moving a magnet in a coil or changing the field induces current in the coil
  • Galvanometer deflects
  • Induced current is greater with fast motion, more turns and stronger magnet
  • Fleming's right-hand rule: forefinger = field, thumb = motion, middle = induced current
Read the full explanation

Faraday: moving a magnet in a coil or changing the field induces current in the coil; galvanometer deflects. Induced current is greater with fast motion, more turns and stronger magnet. Fleming's right-hand rule: forefinger = field, thumb = motion, middle = induced current. AC generator: a rotating coil in a magnetic field with slip rings and brushes; produces alternating current; DC generator uses a split ring commutator. AC advantages: easy to transmit over long distances without much loss by transformers.

⚡

Domestic electric circuits

  • Mains: live wire (red, 220 V), neutral (black), earth (green)
  • Earth wire connects the metal body to the ground
  • A fuse of the right rating protects against overloading
  • Short-circuiting happens when live and neutral touch
Read the full explanation

Mains: live wire (red, 220 V), neutral (black), earth (green). Earth wire connects the metal body to the ground. A fuse of the right rating protects against overloading; MCB trips. Short-circuiting happens when live and neutral touch. Overloading when too many appliances are connected to one socket. Safety: earthing, fuse, insulated wires, not touching switches with wet hands.

lessons.title: Our Environment
yt: class 10 science our environment

blocks.x: An ecosystem consists of biotic (producers, consumers, decomposers) and abiotic components. Food chains link organisms by who eats whom: grass -> grasshopper -> frog -> snake -> eagle. Energy flows in one direction and only about 10 per cent passes to the next trophic level (10 per cent law). Biomagnification increases the concentration of non-biodegradable chemicals such as DDT with each level, highest in the top carnivores. The ozone layer (O3) in the stratosphere absorbs harmful UV; chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) deplete it, and the 1987 Montreal Protocol limited CFC use. Waste is biodegradable or non-biodegradable; Reduce, Reuse, Recycle; managing waste protects the environment.
Deep dive: Ecosystem and food chain

Producers (green plants, algae) make food by photosynthesis; primary consumers (herbivores) eat plants; secondary consumers (carnivores) eat herbivores; tertiary consumers (top carnivores). Decomposers (bacteria, fungi) break down dead remains and return nutrients. Food chains usually have three or four trophic levels because energy loss at each step is large. A food web is a network of interconnected food chains. Artificial ecosystems include gardens, crop fields and aquarium; natural ecosystems include forest, pond and lake.
Deep dive: Energy flow

Plants capture about 1 per cent of solar energy; at each trophic level only 10 per cent of energy is available to the next (Lindeman's 10 per cent law). So 1000 J in producers gives 100 J to herbivores, 10 J to carnivores and 1 J to top carnivores. Energy flows unidirectionally, whereas nutrients cycle. Pesticides like DDT accumulate in the food chain (biomagnification), appearing in the highest concentration in humans and other top carnivores.
Deep dive: Ozone and human impact

Ozone is formed when UV splits O2 into free atoms, which join O2: O2 -> O + O; O + O2 -> O3. It shields life from UV rays. CFCs from refrigerators, aerosol sprays and fire extinguishers release chlorine radicals that destroy ozone, leading to a hole over the Antarctic in the 1980s. UNEP agreed in 1987 to freeze CFC production at 1986 levels (Montreal Protocol). UV exposure causes skin cancer, cataract and plant damage.
Deep dive: Waste management

Biodegradable wastes (vegetable peels, paper, cotton, dung) are broken by bacteria and fungi; non-biodegradable (plastics, DDT, glass, metals) persist. Effects: pollution of soil and water, harm to animals and humans. Waste is managed by composting, vermicomposting, recycling, landfills and incineration. Principles: refuse, reduce, reuse, recycle and rethink. Ban on plastic bags, use of cloth bags and the Swachh Bharat campaign help.

problems.q: What is the 10 per cent law? If producers have 5000 J of energy, find the energy at the tertiary consumer level.
problems.a: Only 10 per cent of energy passes to the next level. Producers 5000 J -> herbivores 500 J -> carnivores 50 J -> tertiary 5 J.

problems.q: What is biomagnification? Why is it high in top carnivores?
problems.a: Biomagnification is the increase in concentration of non-biodegradable chemicals like DDT at each higher trophic level, because they are not excreted but accumulate in tissues. A top carnivore feeds on many contaminated animals so it has the highest concentration.

problems.q: Explain the depletion of the ozone layer and the steps taken to protect it.
problems.a: UV splits O2 into atoms forming O3. CFCs release chlorine which breaks ozone molecules, forming a hole over Antarctica. UV causes skin cancer and cataract. The Montreal Protocol (1987) froze CFC production; alternatives like hydrofluorocarbons are used in refrigerators.

Visual lesson

Our Environment

An ecosystem consists of biotic (producers, consumers, decomposers) and abiotic components

🔑

Big idea

  • An ecosystem consists of biotic (producers, consumers, decomposers) and abiotic components
  • Food chains link organisms by who eats whom: grass -> grasshopper -> frog -> snake -> eagle
  • Energy flows in one direction and only about 10 per cent passes to the next trophic level (10 per cent law)
  • Biomagnification increases the concentration of non-biodegradable chemicals such as DDT with each level, highest in the top carnivores
Read the full explanation

An ecosystem consists of biotic (producers, consumers, decomposers) and abiotic components. Food chains link organisms by who eats whom: grass -> grasshopper -> frog -> snake -> eagle. Energy flows in one direction and only about 10 per cent passes to the next trophic level (10 per cent law). Biomagnification increases the concentration of non-biodegradable chemicals such as DDT with each level, highest in the top carnivores. The ozone layer (O3) in the stratosphere absorbs harmful UV; chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) deplete it, and the 1987 Montreal Protocol limited CFC use. Waste is biodegradable or non-biodegradable; Reduce, Reuse, Recycle; managing waste protects the environment.

📌

Ecosystem and food chain

  • Producers (green plants, algae) make food by photosynthesis
  • Primary consumers (herbivores) eat plants
  • Secondary consumers (carnivores) eat herbivores
  • Tertiary consumers (top carnivores)
Read the full explanation

Producers (green plants, algae) make food by photosynthesis; primary consumers (herbivores) eat plants; secondary consumers (carnivores) eat herbivores; tertiary consumers (top carnivores). Decomposers (bacteria, fungi) break down dead remains and return nutrients. Food chains usually have three or four trophic levels because energy loss at each step is large. A food web is a network of interconnected food chains. Artificial ecosystems include gardens, crop fields and aquarium; natural ecosystems include forest, pond and lake.

🔄

Energy flow

  • Plants capture about 1 per cent of solar energy
  • At each trophic level only 10 per cent of energy is available to the next (Lindeman's 10 per cent law)
  • So 1000 J in producers gives 100 J to herbivores, 10 J to carnivores and 1 J to top carnivores
  • Energy flows unidirectionally, whereas nutrients cycle
Read the full explanation

Plants capture about 1 per cent of solar energy; at each trophic level only 10 per cent of energy is available to the next (Lindeman's 10 per cent law). So 1000 J in producers gives 100 J to herbivores, 10 J to carnivores and 1 J to top carnivores. Energy flows unidirectionally, whereas nutrients cycle. Pesticides like DDT accumulate in the food chain (biomagnification), appearing in the highest concentration in humans and other top carnivores.

🧬

Ozone and human impact

  • Ozone is formed when UV splits O2 into free atoms, which join O2: O2 -> O + O
  • It shields life from UV rays
  • CFCs from refrigerators, aerosol sprays and fire extinguishers release chlorine radicals that destroy ozone, leading to a hole over the Antarctic in…
  • UNEP agreed in 1987 to freeze CFC production at 1986 levels (Montreal Protocol)
Read the full explanation

Ozone is formed when UV splits O2 into free atoms, which join O2: O2 -> O + O; O + O2 -> O3. It shields life from UV rays. CFCs from refrigerators, aerosol sprays and fire extinguishers release chlorine radicals that destroy ozone, leading to a hole over the Antarctic in the 1980s. UNEP agreed in 1987 to freeze CFC production at 1986 levels (Montreal Protocol). UV exposure causes skin cancer, cataract and plant damage.

🔬

Waste management

  • Biodegradable wastes (vegetable peels, paper, cotton, dung) are broken by bacteria and fungi
  • Non-biodegradable (plastics, DDT, glass, metals) persist
  • Effects: pollution of soil and water, harm to animals and humans
  • Waste is managed by composting, vermicomposting, recycling, landfills and incineration
Read the full explanation

Biodegradable wastes (vegetable peels, paper, cotton, dung) are broken by bacteria and fungi; non-biodegradable (plastics, DDT, glass, metals) persist. Effects: pollution of soil and water, harm to animals and humans. Waste is managed by composting, vermicomposting, recycling, landfills and incineration. Principles: refuse, reduce, reuse, recycle and rethink. Ban on plastic bags, use of cloth bags and the Swachh Bharat campaign help.

lessons.title: Introduction to Accounting
yt: class 11 accountancy introduction to accounting

blocks.x: Accounting is the process of identifying, measuring, recording, classifying, summarising, analysing and communicating financial information. Book-keeping is the recording part; accounting includes summarising and interpretation. The users of accounting information are internal (owners, managers, employees) and external (investors, creditors, banks, government, customers, researchers). Basic terms: assets, liabilities, capital, drawings, revenue, expenses, income, gain, profit, loss, debtors, creditors, goods, purchases, sales, stock, discount and bad debts. The accounting equation is Assets = Liabilities + Capital. Branches: financial, cost and management accounting. Limitations include historical cost basis and the exclusion of non-monetary information.
Deep dive: Meaning and objectives

Accounting maintains systematic records, ascertains profit or loss, ascertains financial position, provides information to users and helps in assessing tax liability. Book-keeping is the art of recording transactions in the books; accounting is the process of summarising and interpreting. Accountancy is the body of principles and rules. The accounting cycle is the sequence: transactions, journal, ledger, trial balance, adjustments, final accounts.
Deep dive: Basic terms

Asset: a resource owned with future economic benefit (fixed, current, tangible, intangible). Liability: obligation to be paid (long-term, current, contingent). Capital: amount invested by the owner. Drawings: money or goods taken by the owner for personal use, reducing capital. Revenue is the amount earned from business activity; expenditure is amount spent; capital expenditure benefits many years while revenue expenditure benefits the current period. Debtor owes money to the business; creditor is owed money. Discount: trade discount is on list price and not recorded; cash discount is for prompt payment and recorded.
Deep dive: Accounting equation

Assets = Liabilities + Capital (A = L + C). Capital = Assets - Liabilities. Each transaction has two aspects (dual aspect) and the equation stays balanced. Example: purchase of goods for cash increases stock and decreases cash; no change in total. Starting business with Rs 1,00,000 gives assets Rs 1,00,000 and capital Rs 1,00,000. Borrowing Rs 20,000 raises assets and liabilities to Rs 1,20,000 each side. Profit increases capital; drawings decrease it.
Deep dive: Users and branches

Internal users: owners, managers, employees. External users: investors, creditors, lenders, government, customers, researchers. Financial accounting records and reports financial position. Cost accounting finds the cost of products. Management accounting helps in decision making. Accounting information qualities: reliability, relevance, understandability, comparability. Advantages: systematic records, tax assessment, legal evidence, comparison; limitations: historical cost, personal judgement, ignores price level changes.

🔑

Big idea

  • Book-keeping is the recording part

Read the full explanation

Accounting is the process of identifying, measuring, recording, classifying, summarising, analysing and communicating financial information. Book-keeping is the recording part; accounting includes summarising and interpretation. The users of accounting information are internal (owners, managers, employees) and external (investors, creditors, banks, government, customers, researchers). Basic terms: assets, liabilities, capital, drawings, revenue, expenses, income, gain, profit, loss, debtors, creditors, goods, purchases, sales, stock, discount and bad debts. The accounting equation is Assets = Liabilities + Capital. Branches: financial, cost and management accounting. Limitations include historical cost basis and the exclusion of non-monetary information.

📘

Meaning and objectives

  • Accounting maintains systematic records, ascertains profit or loss, ascertains financial position, provides information to users and helps in…
  • Book-keeping is the art of recording transactions in the books
  • Accounting is the process of summarising and interpreting
  • Accountancy is the body of principles and rules
Read the full explanation

Accounting maintains systematic records, ascertains profit or loss, ascertains financial position, provides information to users and helps in assessing tax liability. Book-keeping is the art of recording transactions in the books; accounting is the process of summarising and interpreting. Accountancy is the body of principles and rules. The accounting cycle is the sequence: transactions, journal, ledger, trial balance, adjustments, final accounts.

📘

Basic terms

  • Asset: a resource owned with future economic benefit (fixed, current, tangible, intangible)
  • Liability: obligation to be paid (long-term, current, contingent)
  • Capital: amount invested by the owner
  • Drawings: money or goods taken by the owner for personal use, reducing capital
Read the full explanation

Asset: a resource owned with future economic benefit (fixed, current, tangible, intangible). Liability: obligation to be paid (long-term, current, contingent). Capital: amount invested by the owner. Drawings: money or goods taken by the owner for personal use, reducing capital. Revenue is the amount earned from business activity; expenditure is amount spent; capital expenditure benefits many years while revenue expenditure benefits the current period. Debtor owes money to the business; creditor is owed money. Discount: trade discount is on list price and not recorded; cash discount is for prompt payment and recorded.

🧮

Accounting equation

  • Assets = Liabilities + Capital (A = L + C)
  • Capital = Assets - Liabilities
  • Each transaction has two aspects (dual aspect) and the equation stays balanced
  • Example: purchase of goods for cash increases stock and decreases cash
Read the full explanation

Assets = Liabilities + Capital (A = L + C). Capital = Assets - Liabilities. Each transaction has two aspects (dual aspect) and the equation stays balanced. Example: purchase of goods for cash increases stock and decreases cash; no change in total. Starting business with Rs 1,00,000 gives assets Rs 1,00,000 and capital Rs 1,00,000. Borrowing Rs 20,000 raises assets and liabilities to Rs 1,20,000 each side. Profit increases capital; drawings decrease it.

💡

Users and branches

  • Internal users: owners, managers, employees
  • External users: investors, creditors, lenders, government, customers, researchers
  • Financial accounting records and reports financial position
  • Cost accounting finds the cost of products
Read the full explanation

Internal users: owners, managers, employees. External users: investors, creditors, lenders, government, customers, researchers. Financial accounting records and reports financial position. Cost accounting finds the cost of products. Management accounting helps in decision making. Accounting information qualities: reliability, relevance, understandability, comparability. Advantages: systematic records, tax assessment, legal evidence, comparison; limitations: historical cost, personal judgement, ignores price level changes.

yt: class 11 accountancy theory base of accounting concepts

blocks.x: Accounting is based on generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP): concepts, principles and conventions. The basic accounting concepts are business entity, money measurement, going concern, accounting period, cost, dual aspect, revenue recognition, matching, full disclosure, consistency, conservatism, materiality, and objectivity. Accounting standards (AS in India, Ind AS converged with IFRS) are issued by ICAI. Systems of accounting are cash basis and accrual basis; the books can be kept on the double entry system, which uses debit and credit. Accounting basis, bases of measurement and the accounting equation under Indian GAAP apply to all entities.
Deep dive: Accounting concepts

Business entity: the business is separate from the owner, so drawings are not expenses. Money measurement: only transactions in money are recorded. Going concern: the business will continue indefinitely, so assets are valued at cost, not sale value. Accounting period: usually 12 months (1 April to 31 March). Cost: assets are recorded at purchase cost. Dual aspect: each transaction has two aspects. Revenue recognition: revenue is recorded when earned. Matching: expenses are matched with revenue of the same period. Full disclosure: all material facts are reported. Consistency: same methods used year to year. Conservatism: anticipate no profits but provide for all possible losses. Materiality: only significant items need to be reported separately. Objectivity: records are based on verifiable evidence.
Deep dive: Accounting standards and IFRS

Accounting standards are written policy documents issued by ICAI (the Accounting Standards Board) to harmonise practices. Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS) converge with IFRS (International Financial Reporting Standards) of the IASB; they are applicable to companies as notified under the Companies Act. IFRS provide global comparability.
Deep dive: Bases of accounting

Cash basis: transactions are recorded only when cash is received or paid. Accrual basis: revenue is recorded when earned and expenses when incurred whether or not cash is exchanged; required by the Companies Act. Accrual basis follows matching. Double entry: every transaction affects at least two accounts, with equal debit and credit.
Deep dive: Rules of debit and credit

Accounts classify into personal (natural, artificial, representative), real (tangible, intangible) and nominal accounts. Personal: debit the receiver, credit the giver. Real: debit what comes in, credit what goes out. Nominal: debit expenses and losses, credit incomes and gains. Modern approach: assets and expenses increase by debit; liabilities, capital and income increase by credit.

problems.q: State the going concern concept and its implication.
problems.a: The business is assumed to continue for the foreseeable future, so fixed assets are recorded at cost, not at sale value, and depreciation is charged.

problems.q: Differentiate between cash basis and accrual basis of accounting.
problems.a: Cash basis records only cash receipts and payments; accrual basis records revenue when earned and expenses when incurred irrespective of cash. Accrual follows the matching concept and is compulsory for companies.

problems.q: Explain conservatism, consistency and materiality with examples.
problems.a: Conservatism: provide for probable losses and ignore unrealised gains (stock at cost or market, whichever is lower). Consistency: use the same method (like straight line depreciation) every year. Materiality: only significant items are shown separately (a small stationery is expensed at once).

Visual lesson

Theory Base of Accounting

Accounting is based on generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP): concepts, principles and conventions

🔑

Big idea

  • Accounting is based on generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP): concepts, principles and conventions
  • The basic accounting concepts are business entity, money measurement, going concern, accounting period, cost, dual aspect, revenue recognition…
  • Accounting standards (AS in India, Ind AS converged with IFRS) are issued by ICAI
  • Systems of accounting are cash basis and accrual basis
Read the full explanation

Accounting is based on generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP): concepts, principles and conventions. The basic accounting concepts are business entity, money measurement, going concern, accounting period, cost, dual aspect, revenue recognition, matching, full disclosure, consistency, conservatism, materiality, and objectivity. Accounting standards (AS in India, Ind AS converged with IFRS) are issued by ICAI. Systems of accounting are cash basis and accrual basis; the books can be kept on the double entry system, which uses debit and credit. Accounting basis, bases of measurement and the accounting equation under Indian GAAP apply to all entities.

📘

Accounting concepts

  • Business entity: the business is separate from the owner, so drawings are not expenses
  • Money measurement: only transactions in money are recorded
  • Going concern: the business will continue indefinitely, so assets are valued at cost, not sale value
  • Accounting period: usually 12 months (1 April to 31 March)
Read the full explanation

Business entity: the business is separate from the owner, so drawings are not expenses. Money measurement: only transactions in money are recorded. Going concern: the business will continue indefinitely, so assets are valued at cost, not sale value. Accounting period: usually 12 months (1 April to 31 March). Cost: assets are recorded at purchase cost. Dual aspect: each transaction has two aspects. Revenue recognition: revenue is recorded when earned. Matching: expenses are matched with revenue of the same period. Full disclosure: all material facts are reported. Consistency: same methods used year to year. Conservatism: anticipate no profits but provide for all possible losses. Materiality: only significant items need to be reported separately. Objectivity: records are based on verifiable evidence.

🧠

Accounting standards and IFRS

  • Accounting standards are written policy documents issued by ICAI (the Accounting Standards Board) to harmonise practices
  • Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS) converge with IFRS (International Financial Reporting Standards) of the IASB
  • They are applicable to companies as notified under the Companies Act
  • IFRS provide global comparability
⚗️

Bases of accounting

  • Cash basis: transactions are recorded only when cash is received or paid
  • Accrual basis: revenue is recorded when earned and expenses when incurred whether or not cash is exchanged
  • Required by the Companies Act
  • Accrual basis follows matching
Read the full explanation

Cash basis: transactions are recorded only when cash is received or paid. Accrual basis: revenue is recorded when earned and expenses when incurred whether or not cash is exchanged; required by the Companies Act. Accrual basis follows matching. Double entry: every transaction affects at least two accounts, with equal debit and credit.

⚖️

Rules of debit and credit

  • Accounts classify into personal (natural, artificial, representative), real (tangible, intangible) and nominal accounts
  • Personal: debit the receiver, credit the giver
  • Real: debit what comes in, credit what goes out
  • Nominal: debit expenses and losses, credit incomes and gains
Read the full explanation

Accounts classify into personal (natural, artificial, representative), real (tangible, intangible) and nominal accounts. Personal: debit the receiver, credit the giver. Real: debit what comes in, credit what goes out. Nominal: debit expenses and losses, credit incomes and gains. Modern approach: assets and expenses increase by debit; liabilities, capital and income increase by credit.

lessons.title: Recording of Transactions I
yt: class 11 accountancy journal ledger recording of transactions

blocks.x: Recording begins with the source documents: cash memo, invoice, vouchers, debit note, credit note. Transactions are first recorded in the journal (book of original entry) in chronological order with date, particulars (Dr and Cr accounts), ledger folio (L.F.), debit and credit amount and a narration. Then they are posted to the ledger (book of final entry): each account has a debit and credit side, balanced at the end of the period. Compound journal entries have more than two accounts. Opening entry brings forward balances. Journal proper is for transactions that do not fit special books. Posting from journal to ledger completes the cycle, and the balance of each account is carried down. Capital and revenue items are distinguished; GST is shown as input tax credit and output tax liability.
Deep dive: Journal

Format: Date | Particulars | L.F. | Dr (Rs) | Cr (Rs). Debit account is written first with Dr, the credit account next with To. Narration explains. Rules: Personal (receiver Dr, giver Cr); Real (comes in Dr, goes out Cr); Nominal (expenses/losses Dr, incomes/gains Cr). Opening entry: Assets A/c Dr. To Liabilities A/c; To Capital A/c. Closing entries transfer nominal accounts to Profit and Loss.
Deep dive: Ledger and posting

Ledger folio L.F. cross-references the journal and ledger. For the debit account, write the credit account on the debit side as "To" in the particulars, and vice versa with "By". Balance: if debit total exceeds credit, the balance is a debit balance (carried down on the credit side as By balance c/d and brought down on the debit side as To balance b/d). Real and personal accounts are balanced; nominal accounts are closed by transfer.
Deep dive: Documents and vouchers

Cash memo is the basis for cash sale; invoice is issued by the seller and the same is bill for the buyer; debit note is sent by the buyer to the seller on return of goods; credit note is sent by the seller to the buyer; voucher is the written evidence of cash payment and receipt. Receipts, pay-in slips, cheque counterfoils are also source documents.
Deep dive: Goods and Services Tax

GST replaced several indirect taxes. CGST and SGST are levied on intra-state supplies; IGST on inter-state supplies. Input tax credit is deducted from output tax. Purchases are recorded net of GST and input GST is a debit to an asset account (Input CGST, Input SGST); sales are credited net with Output GST as a liability. The net amount is paid to the government.

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Recording of Transactions I

Recording begins with the source documents: cash memo, invoice, vouchers, debit note, credit note

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Journal›3Ledger and posting›4Documents and vouchers›5Goods and Services Tax
🔑

Big idea

  • Recording begins with the source documents: cash memo, invoice, vouchers, debit note, credit note
  • Transactions are first recorded in the journal (book of original entry) in chronological order with date, particulars (Dr and Cr accounts), ledger…
  • Then they are posted to the ledger (book of final entry): each account has a debit and credit side, balanced at the end of the period
  • Compound journal entries have more than two accounts
Read the full explanation

Recording begins with the source documents: cash memo, invoice, vouchers, debit note, credit note. Transactions are first recorded in the journal (book of original entry) in chronological order with date, particulars (Dr and Cr accounts), ledger folio (L.F.), debit and credit amount and a narration. Then they are posted to the ledger (book of final entry): each account has a debit and credit side, balanced at the end of the period. Compound journal entries have more than two accounts. Opening entry brings forward balances. Journal proper is for transactions that do not fit special books. Posting from journal to ledger completes the cycle, and the balance of each account is carried down. Capital and revenue items are distinguished; GST is shown as input tax credit and output tax liability.

📌

Journal

  • Format: Date | Particulars | L.F
  • | Dr (Rs) | Cr (Rs)
  • Debit account is written first with Dr, the credit account next with To
  • Narration explains
Read the full explanation

Format: Date | Particulars | L.F. | Dr (Rs) | Cr (Rs). Debit account is written first with Dr, the credit account next with To. Narration explains. Rules: Personal (receiver Dr, giver Cr); Real (comes in Dr, goes out Cr); Nominal (expenses/losses Dr, incomes/gains Cr). Opening entry: Assets A/c Dr. To Liabilities A/c; To Capital A/c. Closing entries transfer nominal accounts to Profit and Loss.

🧠

Ledger and posting

  • Ledger folio L.F
  • Cross-references the journal and ledger
  • For the debit account, write the credit account on the debit side as "To" in the particulars, and vice versa with "By"
  • Balance: if debit total exceeds credit, the balance is a debit balance (carried down on the credit side as By balance c/d and brought down on the…
Read the full explanation

Ledger folio L.F. cross-references the journal and ledger. For the debit account, write the credit account on the debit side as "To" in the particulars, and vice versa with "By". Balance: if debit total exceeds credit, the balance is a debit balance (carried down on the credit side as By balance c/d and brought down on the debit side as To balance b/d). Real and personal accounts are balanced; nominal accounts are closed by transfer.

🌟

Documents and vouchers

  • Cash memo is the basis for cash sale
  • Invoice is issued by the seller and the same is bill for the buyer
  • Debit note is sent by the buyer to the seller on return of goods
  • Credit note is sent by the seller to the buyer
Read the full explanation

Cash memo is the basis for cash sale; invoice is issued by the seller and the same is bill for the buyer; debit note is sent by the buyer to the seller on return of goods; credit note is sent by the seller to the buyer; voucher is the written evidence of cash payment and receipt. Receipts, pay-in slips, cheque counterfoils are also source documents.

🔬

Goods and Services Tax

  • GST replaced several indirect taxes
  • CGST and SGST are levied on intra-state supplies
  • IGST on inter-state supplies
  • Input tax credit is deducted from output tax
Read the full explanation

GST replaced several indirect taxes. CGST and SGST are levied on intra-state supplies; IGST on inter-state supplies. Input tax credit is deducted from output tax. Purchases are recorded net of GST and input GST is a debit to an asset account (Input CGST, Input SGST); sales are credited net with Output GST as a liability. The net amount is paid to the government.

lessons.title: Recording of Transactions II
yt: class 11 accountancy cash book subsidiary books petty cash

blocks.x: To save time, a business uses special journals (subsidiary books): purchases book (credit purchases of goods), sales book (credit sales), purchases return book, sales return book, bills receivable and payable books, cash book and journal proper. The cash book is both a journal and a ledger. Types: single column, double column (cash and discount / cash and bank), triple column (cash, bank, discount). Contra entries affect both cash and bank. Petty cash book records small expenses under the imprest system; the analytical petty cash book has columns for each expense. Accounts of purchases and sales book are posted periodically to Purchases A/c and Sales A/c; totals are credited/debited.
Deep dive: Subsidiary books

Purchases book records credit purchases of goods only (not assets): posted to Purchases A/c Dr on total and to each supplier Cr. Sales book similarly. Returns books record returns; debit note to purchases return; credit note to sales return. GST columns show input and output taxes. Journal proper handles opening entries, closing entries, adjustment entries, rectifications and credit purchase or sale of assets.
Deep dive: Cash book

A single column cash book has one amount column on each side: receipts on debit, payments on credit; balance is always debit or nil. In a double column cash book with discount, the discount allowed column on debit and discount received on credit are totals posted separately. A triple column cash book has cash, bank and discount columns. Contra entry: cash deposited in bank (Bank Dr, Cash Cr) shown on both sides with C in LF. Bank column can show a credit balance as an overdraft.
Deep dive: Petty cash book

The chief cashier gives an advance (imprest) to the petty cashier who spends on small items such as postage, stationery, carriage and refreshments. The petty cashier records expenses in an analytical way and at the end of the period submits the totals; the head cashier reimburses the amount spent to restore the imprest. Advantage: saves time, controls petty expenses.
Deep dive: Advantages and posting

Special journals divide work among staff, allow quick posting of totals and reduce errors. Totals of sales book posted to Sales A/c credit; each customer debited individually. The cash book is balanced like an account.

problems.q: Explain the imprest system of petty cash and its advantages.
problems.a: A fixed amount is given to the petty cashier at the start of a period; he spends on small items; at the end the head cashier reimburses the amount spent so the imprest is restored. Advantages: control on small expenses, saving of time of the chief cashier, less risk, analysis of expenses.

Visual lesson

Recording of Transactions II

To save time, a business uses special journals (subsidiary books): purchases book (credit purchases of goods), sales book (credit sales), purchases return book, sales…

🔑

Big idea

  • To save time, a business uses special journals (subsidiary books): purchases book (credit purchases of goods), sales book (credit sales), purchases…
  • The cash book is both a journal and a ledger
  • Types: single column, double column (cash and discount / cash and bank), triple column (cash, bank, discount)
