Read the full explanation

To save time, a business uses special journals (subsidiary books): purchases book (credit purchases of goods), sales book (credit sales), purchases return book, sales return book, bills receivable and payable books, cash book and journal proper. The cash book is both a journal and a ledger. Types: single column, double column (cash and discount / cash and bank), triple column (cash, bank, discount). Contra entries affect both cash and bank. Petty cash book records small expenses under the imprest system; the analytical petty cash book has columns for each expense. Accounts of purchases and sales book are posted periodically to Purchases A/c and Sales A/c; totals are credited/debited.

📌

Subsidiary books

  • Purchases book records credit purchases of goods only (not assets): posted to Purchases A/c Dr on total and to each supplier Cr
  • Sales book similarly
  • Returns books record returns
  • Debit note to purchases return
Read the full explanation

Purchases book records credit purchases of goods only (not assets): posted to Purchases A/c Dr on total and to each supplier Cr. Sales book similarly. Returns books record returns; debit note to purchases return; credit note to sales return. GST columns show input and output taxes. Journal proper handles opening entries, closing entries, adjustment entries, rectifications and credit purchase or sale of assets.

🧠

Cash book

  • A single column cash book has one amount column on each side: receipts on debit, payments on credit
  • Balance is always debit or nil
  • In a double column cash book with discount, the discount allowed column on debit and discount received on credit are totals posted separately
  • A triple column cash book has cash, bank and discount columns
Read the full explanation

A single column cash book has one amount column on each side: receipts on debit, payments on credit; balance is always debit or nil. In a double column cash book with discount, the discount allowed column on debit and discount received on credit are totals posted separately. A triple column cash book has cash, bank and discount columns. Contra entry: cash deposited in bank (Bank Dr, Cash Cr) shown on both sides with C in LF. Bank column can show a credit balance as an overdraft.

🌟

Petty cash book

  • The chief cashier gives an advance (imprest) to the petty cashier who spends on small items such as postage, stationery, carriage and refreshments
  • The petty cashier records expenses in an analytical way and at the end of the period submits the totals
  • The head cashier reimburses the amount spent to restore the imprest
  • Advantage: saves time, controls petty expenses
Read the full explanation

The chief cashier gives an advance (imprest) to the petty cashier who spends on small items such as postage, stationery, carriage and refreshments. The petty cashier records expenses in an analytical way and at the end of the period submits the totals; the head cashier reimburses the amount spent to restore the imprest. Advantage: saves time, controls petty expenses.

🔬

Advantages and posting

  • Special journals divide work among staff, allow quick posting of totals and reduce errors
  • Totals of sales book posted to Sales A/c credit
  • Each customer debited individually
  • The cash book is balanced like an account

lessons.title: Bank Reconciliation Statement
yt: class 11 accountancy bank reconciliation statement

blocks.x: A bank reconciliation statement (BRS) reconciles the balance as per the cash book (bank column) with the balance as per the pass book (bank statement) on a given date. Differences arise from items recorded in one but not in the other. Causes: cheques issued but not yet presented for payment, cheques deposited but not yet collected, direct deposits by customers, direct payments by bank (standing instructions, insurance premium), interest and bank charges, dishonour of cheques, and errors. Start from the favourable or overdraft balance and add/subtract each item to get the other. The BRS is prepared periodically to detect errors and frauds and is not a part of the ledger.
Deep dive: Reasons for difference

Timing differences: cheques issued but not presented (cash book credit, not in the pass book); cheques deposited but not yet credited by the bank; bank charges, interest on overdraft, collection charges; direct credits like dividend and interest; direct debits like insurance or loan instalments; cheques dishonoured (bank debits the account); errors by the bank or business.
Deep dive: Preparing the statement

Starting with balance as per cash book (debit balance): Add: cheques issued but not presented; interest credited by bank. Less: cheques deposited but not collected; bank charges; direct payments. Result: balance as per pass book. If starting from an overdraft as per cash book (credit balance), reverse the adding and subtracting. When starting from the pass book, the signs are opposite to those starting from the cash book.
Deep dive: Adjusted cash book

Items already known to the bank but not recorded in the cash book (interest, charges, dishonour, direct payments) require corrections in the cash book first (Adjusted cash book) and then the remaining items form the BRS. The balance of the adjusted cash book reconciles with the passbook after timing items.
Deep dive: Why BRS is needed
Detects errors, frauds, delays and bank charges, and ensures the correct bank balance; it is internal control and gives true cash position. It is not a ledger account and does not alter the books.
Hindi saransh
Cash book aur pass book ke balance mein antar ko BRS se samjhaya jata hai. Jaari kiye par pesh nahi hue cheque jodte hain; jama kiye par vasool nahi hue ghatate hain.
From cash book debit balance: add issued not presented, less deposited not collected.

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Bank Reconciliation Statement

A bank reconciliation statement (BRS) reconciles the balance as per the cash book (bank column) with the balance as per the pass book (bank statement) on a given date

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Reasons for difference›3Preparing the statement›4Adjusted cash book›5Why BRS is needed
🔑

Big idea

  • A bank reconciliation statement (BRS) reconciles the balance as per the cash book (bank column) with the balance as per the pass book (bank…
  • Differences arise from items recorded in one but not in the other
  • Causes: cheques issued but not yet presented for payment, cheques deposited but not yet collected, direct deposits by customers, direct payments by…
  • Start from the favourable or overdraft balance and add/subtract each item to get the other
Read the full explanation

A bank reconciliation statement (BRS) reconciles the balance as per the cash book (bank column) with the balance as per the pass book (bank statement) on a given date. Differences arise from items recorded in one but not in the other. Causes: cheques issued but not yet presented for payment, cheques deposited but not yet collected, direct deposits by customers, direct payments by bank (standing instructions, insurance premium), interest and bank charges, dishonour of cheques, and errors. Start from the favourable or overdraft balance and add/subtract each item to get the other. The BRS is prepared periodically to detect errors and frauds and is not a part of the ledger.

📌

Reasons for difference

  • Timing differences: cheques issued but not presented (cash book credit, not in the pass book)
  • Cheques deposited but not yet credited by the bank
  • Bank charges, interest on overdraft, collection charges
  • Direct credits like dividend and interest
Read the full explanation

Timing differences: cheques issued but not presented (cash book credit, not in the pass book); cheques deposited but not yet credited by the bank; bank charges, interest on overdraft, collection charges; direct credits like dividend and interest; direct debits like insurance or loan instalments; cheques dishonoured (bank debits the account); errors by the bank or business.

🧠

Preparing the statement

  • Starting with balance as per cash book (debit balance): Add: cheques issued but not presented
  • Interest credited by bank
  • Less: cheques deposited but not collected
  • Direct payments
Read the full explanation

Starting with balance as per cash book (debit balance): Add: cheques issued but not presented; interest credited by bank. Less: cheques deposited but not collected; bank charges; direct payments. Result: balance as per pass book. If starting from an overdraft as per cash book (credit balance), reverse the adding and subtracting. When starting from the pass book, the signs are opposite to those starting from the cash book.

🌟

Adjusted cash book

  • Items already known to the bank but not recorded in the cash book (interest, charges, dishonour, direct payments) require corrections in the cash…
  • The balance of the adjusted cash book reconciles with the passbook after timing items
🔬

Why BRS is needed

  • Detects errors, frauds, delays and bank charges, and ensures the correct bank balance
  • It is internal control and gives true cash position
  • It is not a ledger account and does not alter the books
🧮

lessons.title: Trial Balance and Rectification of Errors
yt: class 11 accountancy trial balance rectification errors

blocks.x: A trial balance is a statement of debit and credit balances of ledger accounts at a date to check arithmetical accuracy. Total debits equal total credits. Accounts with debit balances: assets, expenses, losses, drawings. Credit balances: liabilities, capital, incomes, gains. Prepared by the total method, balance method or total-cum-balance. Errors not disclosed by the trial balance: errors of omission, commission (same account type), principle, compensating errors. Disclosed errors: one-sided errors, wrong totals, wrong balances. A suspense account holds the difference until errors are found. Rectification is done by one-day or journal entries.
Deep dive: Preparing a trial balance

Take the balances from the ledger; place debit balances in the debit column and credit in the credit column; total each. Items: Capital, Drawings, Sales, Purchases, Returns, Debtors, Creditors, Stock (opening), Expenses and incomes, Loans, Fixed assets, Cash and bank. Closing stock is not shown in the trial balance since it appears in the adjustments.
Deep dive: Types of errors

Errors of omission (complete or partial), commission (wrong posting, wrong total), principle (capital/revenue confusion), compensating (offsetting errors). Errors affecting the trial balance: one-sided posting, wrong balancing, wrong totalling, mismatch between debit and credit amounts. These are disclosed. Errors not affecting the agreement: omission, principle, commission with correct double entry, compensating.
Deep dive: Suspense account

If the trial balance does not tally, the difference is put in the suspense account on the shorter side. After finding errors, rectify through suspense: for one-sided errors an entry with Suspense A/c; for two-sided errors a single journal entry that corrects the accounts. When all are found, the suspense account is closed.
Deep dive: Rectification of errors

Before preparing final accounts: rectify with Suspense as needed. After the final accounts are prepared: affect profit, so use Profit and Loss Adjustment A/c. Steps: find the wrong entry, the correct entry, and pass the corrective entry. Example: Furniture purchased Rs 5,000 debited to purchases: Furniture A/c Dr 5,000 To Purchases A/c 5,000.
Hindi saransh
Saaranshpatra (trial balance) mein debit aur credit shesh ka milan hota hai. Ashuddhiyan: chhoot, kamishan, siddhant, pratikarak. Antar hone par suspense khata. Shodhan prvishti dwara.
Errors of principle and omission do not affect the trial balance agreement.

Read the full explanation

A trial balance is a statement of debit and credit balances of ledger accounts at a date to check arithmetical accuracy. Total debits equal total credits. Accounts with debit balances: assets, expenses, losses, drawings. Credit balances: liabilities, capital, incomes, gains. Prepared by the total method, balance method or total-cum-balance. Errors not disclosed by the trial balance: errors of omission, commission (same account type), principle, compensating errors. Disclosed errors: one-sided errors, wrong totals, wrong balances. A suspense account holds the difference until errors are found. Rectification is done by one-day or journal entries.

📌

Preparing a trial balance

  • Take the balances from the ledger
  • Place debit balances in the debit column and credit in the credit column
  • Items: Capital, Drawings, Sales, Purchases, Returns, Debtors, Creditors, Stock (opening), Expenses and incomes, Loans, Fixed assets, Cash and bank
  • Closing stock is not shown in the trial balance since it appears in the adjustments
🧠

Types of errors

  • Errors of omission (complete or partial), commission (wrong posting, wrong total), principle (capital/revenue confusion), compensating (offsetting…
  • Errors affecting the trial balance: one-sided posting, wrong balancing, wrong totalling, mismatch between debit and credit amounts
  • These are disclosed
  • Errors not affecting the agreement: omission, principle, commission with correct double entry, compensating
Read the full explanation

Errors of omission (complete or partial), commission (wrong posting, wrong total), principle (capital/revenue confusion), compensating (offsetting errors). Errors affecting the trial balance: one-sided posting, wrong balancing, wrong totalling, mismatch between debit and credit amounts. These are disclosed. Errors not affecting the agreement: omission, principle, commission with correct double entry, compensating.

🌟

Suspense account

  • If the trial balance does not tally, the difference is put in the suspense account on the shorter side
  • After finding errors, rectify through suspense: for one-sided errors an entry with Suspense A/c
  • For two-sided errors a single journal entry that corrects the accounts
  • When all are found, the suspense account is closed
🔬

Rectification of errors

  • Before preparing final accounts: rectify with Suspense as needed
  • After the final accounts are prepared: affect profit, so use Profit and Loss Adjustment A/c
  • Steps: find the wrong entry, the correct entry, and pass the corrective entry
  • Example: Furniture purchased Rs 5,000 debited to purchases: Furniture A/c Dr 5,000 To Purchases A/c 5,000
🧮

Formula tiles

Debit sideAssets, expenses, losses, drawingsDr balance
Credit sideLiabilities, capital, income, gainsCr balance
SuspenseDifferencePlaced on shorter side
Errors disclosedOne-sided, totalsAffect TB
Errors not disclosedOmission, principle, commission, compensatingDo not affect TB
🎯 Remember Errors of principle and omission do not affect the trial balance agreement.
🇮🇳

हिंदी सार

Saaranshpatra (trial balance) mein debit aur credit shesh ka milan hota hai. Ashuddhiyan: chhoot, kamishan, siddhant, pratikarak. Antar hone par suspense khata. Shodhan prvishti dwara.

lessons.title: Depreciation, Provisions and Reserves
yt: class 11 accountancy depreciation provisions reserves

blocks.x: Depreciation is the decrease in the value of a fixed asset due to use, passage of time or obsolescence. Causes: wear and tear, expiry of legal rights, obsolescence, abnormal factors. Methods: straight line method (SLM) — fixed amount each year: (Cost - Scrap)/Life; written down value method (WDV) — a fixed percentage on the reducing balance. Depreciation is a non-cash expense debited to Profit and Loss and credited to the asset account (or provision for depreciation account). Provision is a charge against profit for a known liability whose amount is uncertain (bad debts, discount, depreciation). Reserves are appropriations of profit for general or specific purposes: general reserve, capital reserve, revenue reserve, secret reserve, specific reserve.
Deep dive: Straight line and WDV

SLM: annual depreciation = (Cost - Residual value)/Useful life; rate = depreciation/cost x 100. Book value falls evenly. WDV: depreciation each year = rate x opening book value; it declines year to year; scrap value is not deducted. Example: machinery Rs 1,00,000, scrap Rs 10,000, life 5 years: SLM = 18,000 a year. WDV at 10 per cent: year 1: 10,000; year 2: 9,000; book value year 2 = 81,000. Change in method requires adjustments with prospective effect (AS-6).
Deep dive: Accounting treatment

Method 1 (charge to asset): Depreciation A/c Dr To Machinery A/c; asset appears at reduced value. Method 2 (provision for depreciation): Depreciation A/c Dr To Provision for Depreciation A/c; the asset stays at cost. At year end, Depreciation A/c is closed by transfer to Profit and Loss A/c. On sale of an asset: calculate profit or loss as sale price - book value. Profit on sale credited to P and L; loss debited. Transfer from the asset account or sale account appears via Asset Disposal A/c.
Deep dive: Provisions

Provision for doubtful debts: P&L Dr; Provision A/c Cr; presented as a deduction from debtors. Provision for discount on debtors is made on (debtors - bad debts - provision for doubtful debts). Provision for depreciation, repairs, taxation, and discounts. A provision is a charge against profit, whereas a reserve is an appropriation of profit. Provisions are created for known liabilities; reserves are for strengthening the financial position.
Deep dive: Reserves

General reserve strengthens finances; specific reserves have a purpose (dividend equalisation, workmen compensation). Capital reserve comes from capital profits (not distributable as dividend); revenue reserve comes from revenue profits. Secret reserve is not shown on the balance sheet. Reserve fund and sinking fund. Creating reserve: Profit and Loss Appropriation A/c Dr To Reserve A/c.

Hras (depreciation) sthayi sampatti ke mulya mein kami hai. SLM: (Laagat - avashesh)/Aayu. WDV: ghatti hui shesh rashi par dar. Prabandh dayitva ke liye, arakshit labh ka vitaran.

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Depreciation, Provisions and Reserves

Depreciation is the decrease in the value of a fixed asset due to use, passage of time or obsolescence

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Straight line and WDV›3Accounting treatment›4Provisions›5Reserves
🔑

Big idea

  • Depreciation is the decrease in the value of a fixed asset due to use, passage of time or obsolescence
  • Causes: wear and tear, expiry of legal rights, obsolescence, abnormal factors
  • Methods: straight line method (SLM) — fixed amount each year: (Cost - Scrap)/Life
  • Written down value method (WDV) — a fixed percentage on the reducing balance
Read the full explanation

Depreciation is the decrease in the value of a fixed asset due to use, passage of time or obsolescence. Causes: wear and tear, expiry of legal rights, obsolescence, abnormal factors. Methods: straight line method (SLM) — fixed amount each year: (Cost - Scrap)/Life; written down value method (WDV) — a fixed percentage on the reducing balance. Depreciation is a non-cash expense debited to Profit and Loss and credited to the asset account (or provision for depreciation account). Provision is a charge against profit for a known liability whose amount is uncertain (bad debts, discount, depreciation). Reserves are appropriations of profit for general or specific purposes: general reserve, capital reserve, revenue reserve, secret reserve, specific reserve.

📌

Straight line and WDV

  • SLM: annual depreciation = (Cost - Residual value)/Useful life
  • Rate = depreciation/cost x 100
  • Book value falls evenly
  • WDV: depreciation each year = rate x opening book value
Read the full explanation

SLM: annual depreciation = (Cost - Residual value)/Useful life; rate = depreciation/cost x 100. Book value falls evenly. WDV: depreciation each year = rate x opening book value; it declines year to year; scrap value is not deducted. Example: machinery Rs 1,00,000, scrap Rs 10,000, life 5 years: SLM = 18,000 a year. WDV at 10 per cent: year 1: 10,000; year 2: 9,000; book value year 2 = 81,000. Change in method requires adjustments with prospective effect (AS-6).

🧠

Accounting treatment

  • Method 1 (charge to asset): Depreciation A/c Dr To Machinery A/c
  • Asset appears at reduced value
  • Method 2 (provision for depreciation): Depreciation A/c Dr To Provision for Depreciation A/c
  • The asset stays at cost
Read the full explanation

Method 1 (charge to asset): Depreciation A/c Dr To Machinery A/c; asset appears at reduced value. Method 2 (provision for depreciation): Depreciation A/c Dr To Provision for Depreciation A/c; the asset stays at cost. At year end, Depreciation A/c is closed by transfer to Profit and Loss A/c. On sale of an asset: calculate profit or loss as sale price - book value. Profit on sale credited to P and L; loss debited. Transfer from the asset account or sale account appears via Asset Disposal A/c.

🌟

Provisions

  • Provision for doubtful debts: P&L Dr
  • Provision A/c Cr
  • Presented as a deduction from debtors
  • Provision for discount on debtors is made on (debtors - bad debts - provision for doubtful debts)
Read the full explanation

Provision for doubtful debts: P&L Dr; Provision A/c Cr; presented as a deduction from debtors. Provision for discount on debtors is made on (debtors - bad debts - provision for doubtful debts). lessons.title: Bills of Exchange
yt: class 11 accountancy bills of exchange

blocks.x: A bill of exchange is a written, signed, unconditional order from the drawer to the drawee to pay a fixed sum on demand or at a fixed future date to the payee. It has three parties: drawer, drawee, payee; the drawer and payee can be the same. A promissory note is an unconditional promise by the maker to pay; it has two parties. Terms: acceptance, term, maturity date (due date plus three days of grace), endorsement, discounting, retirement, dishonour, noting, renewal. Accounting: the drawer records Bills Receivable (asset); the drawee records Bills Payable (liability). A bill may be retained until maturity, discounted, endorsed, or sent for collection. If dishonoured, the drawee remains liable and the drawer debits the drawee, together with noting charges.
Deep dive: Features and parties

Bill of exchange: in writing, signed by the drawer, unconditional order, certain sum, to a certain person, stamped. Parties: drawer (creditor who draws), drawee (debtor who accepts), payee. Promissory note: made by the debtor, two parties (maker and payee), no acceptance needed. Difference: promissory note is a promise, a bill is an order; in a note the maker is liable primarily; the note cannot be drawn payable to bearer on demand.
Deep dive: Maturity and discounting

The due date is the date of maturity plus 3 days of grace. For a bill drawn on 1 January for 3 months, the term ends on 1 April, and the maturity is 4 April. The discount charged by the bank is calculated on the face value for the unexpired period at the bank's rate: Discount = Face value x rate x time. Cash received = face value - discount. A bill can be endorsed to a creditor in settlement of a debt.
Deep dive: Accounting treatment

In the books of the drawer: Bills Receivable A/c Dr To Debtor on receipt; Bank Dr To Bills Receivable on maturity; if discounted: Bank Dr, Discount Dr To Bills Receivable. In the books of the drawee: Creditor Dr To Bills Payable on acceptance; Bills Payable Dr To Bank on payment. On dishonour, the drawer debits the drawee with the bill amount and noting charges; the drawee reverses the entry. On renewal, interest is added and a new bill is accepted.
Deep dive: Dishonour, noting and renewal

When the drawee fails to pay on maturity, the bill is dishonoured. Noting by a notary public records the fact and protests the bill. A dishonoured bill can be renewed by cancellation of the old bill and acceptance of a new bill with interest, often after part payment. Retirement: payment before the due date with rebate.

Visual lesson

Bills of Exchange

A bill of exchange is a written, signed, unconditional order from the drawer to the drawee to pay a fixed sum on demand or at a fixed future date to the payee

🔑

Big idea

  • A bill of exchange is a written, signed, unconditional order from the drawer to the drawee to pay a fixed sum on demand or at a fixed future date to…
  • It has three parties: drawer, drawee, payee
  • The drawer and payee can be the same
  • A promissory note is an unconditional promise by the maker to pay
Read the full explanation

A bill of exchange is a written, signed, unconditional order from the drawer to the drawee to pay a fixed sum on demand or at a fixed future date to the payee. It has three parties: drawer, drawee, payee; the drawer and payee can be the same. A promissory note is an unconditional promise by the maker to pay; it has two parties. Terms: acceptance, term, maturity date (due date plus three days of grace), endorsement, discounting, retirement, dishonour, noting, renewal. Accounting: the drawer records Bills Receivable (asset); the drawee records Bills Payable (liability). A bill may be retained until maturity, discounted, endorsed, or sent for collection. If dishonoured, the drawee remains liable and the drawer debits the drawee, together with noting charges.

📌

Features and parties

  • Bill of exchange: in writing, signed by the drawer, unconditional order, certain sum, to a certain person, stamped
  • Parties: drawer (creditor who draws), drawee (debtor who accepts), payee
  • Promissory note: made by the debtor, two parties (maker and payee), no acceptance needed
  • Difference: promissory note is a promise, a bill is an order
Read the full explanation

Bill of exchange: in writing, signed by the drawer, unconditional order, certain sum, to a certain person, stamped. Parties: drawer (creditor who draws), drawee (debtor who accepts), payee. Promissory note: made by the debtor, two parties (maker and payee), no acceptance needed. Difference: promissory note is a promise, a bill is an order; in a note the maker is liable primarily; the note cannot be drawn payable to bearer on demand.

🧠

Maturity and discounting

  • The due date is the date of maturity plus 3 days of grace
  • For a bill drawn on 1 January for 3 months, the term ends on 1 April, and the maturity is 4 April
  • The discount charged by the bank is calculated on the face value for the unexpired period at the bank's rate: Discount = Face value x rate x time
  • Cash received = face value - discount
Read the full explanation

The due date is the date of maturity plus 3 days of grace. For a bill drawn on 1 January for 3 months, the term ends on 1 April, and the maturity is 4 April. The discount charged by the bank is calculated on the face value for the unexpired period at the bank's rate: Discount = Face value x rate x time. Cash received = face value - discount. A bill can be endorsed to a creditor in settlement of a debt.

🌟

Accounting treatment

  • In the books of the drawer: Bills Receivable A/c Dr To Debtor on receipt
  • Bank Dr To Bills Receivable on maturity
  • If discounted: Bank Dr, Discount Dr To Bills Receivable
  • In the books of the drawee: Creditor Dr To Bills Payable on acceptance
Read the full explanation

In the books of the drawer: Bills Receivable A/c Dr To Debtor on receipt; Bank Dr To Bills Receivable on maturity; if discounted: Bank Dr, Discount Dr To Bills Receivable. In the books of the drawee: Creditor Dr To Bills Payable on acceptance; Bills Payable Dr To Bank on payment. On dishonour, the drawer debits the drawee with the bill amount and noting charges; the drawee reverses the entry. On renewal, interest is added and a new bill is accepted.

🔬

Dishonour, noting and renewal

  • When the drawee fails to pay on maturity, the bill is dishonoured
  • Noting by a notary public records the fact and protests the bill
  • A dishonoured bill can be renewed by cancellation of the old bill and acceptance of a new bill with interest, often after part payment
  • Retirement: payment before the due date with rebate

lessons.title: Financial Statements I
yt: class 11 accountancy financial statements trading profit and loss account

blocks.x: Financial statements are the final accounts prepared at the end of the accounting period: trading account, profit and loss account and balance sheet. The trading account finds gross profit (net sales - cost of goods sold). Cost of goods sold = opening stock + net purchases + direct expenses - closing stock. The profit and loss account finds net profit = gross profit + other incomes - indirect expenses. Operating profit and net profit are important. Capital and revenue items are separated. Closing entries transfer nominal accounts. Adjustments: closing stock, outstanding and prepaid expenses, accrued and received in advance incomes, depreciation, bad debts, provision for doubtful debts, interest on capital and drawings, and manager commission.
Deep dive: Trading account

Debit side: opening stock, purchases (less returns), direct expenses (wages, carriage inwards, freight, fuel, power), gross loss. Credit side: sales (less returns), closing stock, gross profit. Gross profit = sales - cost of goods sold. Gross profit ratio = GP/net sales x 100. Closing stock is valued at cost or net realisable value, whichever is lower.
Deep dive: Profit and loss account

Debit side: indirect expenses (salaries, rent, advertising, depreciation, bad debts, interest paid, carriage outwards, discount allowed, loss on sale of assets). Credit side: gross profit, other incomes (rent received, interest received, commission, discount received). Net profit goes to capital. Operating profit = gross profit - operating expenses; excludes non-operating items.
Deep dive: Adjustments

Outstanding expenses are added to the expense and shown as a liability. Prepaid expenses are deducted from the expense and shown as an asset. Accrued income is added to income and shown as an asset. Income received in advance is deducted from income and shown as a liability. Depreciation is debited to P and L. Bad debts are deducted from debtors; provision is made on remaining debtors. Interest on capital is an expense for the business and income for the owner; interest on drawings is an income for the business.
Deep dive: Closing entries

Transfer purchases and expenses to trading account: Trading A/c Dr To Purchases A/c. Sales are transferred: Sales A/c Dr To Trading A/c. Gross profit is transferred to P and L: Trading A/c Dr To P and L A/c. Net profit goes to Capital: P and L A/c Dr To Capital A/c. Drawings are closed to capital.

Visual lesson

Financial Statements I

Financial statements are the final accounts prepared at the end of the accounting period: trading account, profit and loss account and balance sheet

Q&A

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Trading account›3Profit and loss account›4Adjustments›5Closing entries
Gross profit ratioGP / Net sales x 100
Net profit ratioNP / Net sales x 100
🔑

Big idea

  • Financial statements are the final accounts prepared at the end of the accounting period: trading account, profit and loss account and balance sheet
  • The trading account finds gross profit (net sales - cost of goods sold)
  • Cost of goods sold = opening stock + net purchases + direct expenses - closing stock
  • The profit and loss account finds net profit = gross profit + other incomes - indirect expenses
Read the full explanation

Financial statements are the final accounts prepared at the end of the accounting period: trading account, profit and loss account and balance sheet. The trading account finds gross profit (net sales - cost of goods sold). Cost of goods sold = opening stock + net purchases + direct expenses - closing stock. The profit and loss account finds net profit = gross profit + other incomes - indirect expenses. Operating profit and net profit are important. Capital and revenue items are separated. Closing entries transfer nominal accounts. Adjustments: closing stock, outstanding and prepaid expenses, accrued and received in advance incomes, depreciation, bad debts, provision for doubtful debts, interest on capital and drawings, and manager commission.

📌

Trading account

  • Debit side: opening stock, purchases (less returns), direct expenses (wages, carriage inwards, freight, fuel, power), gross loss
  • Credit side: sales (less returns), closing stock, gross profit
  • Gross profit = sales - cost of goods sold
  • Gross profit ratio = GP/net sales x 100
Read the full explanation

Debit side: opening stock, purchases (less returns), direct expenses (wages, carriage inwards, freight, fuel, power), gross loss. Credit side: sales (less returns), closing stock, gross profit. Gross profit = sales - cost of goods sold. Gross profit ratio = GP/net sales x 100. Closing stock is valued at cost or net realisable value, whichever is lower.

🧠

Profit and loss account

  • Debit side: indirect expenses (salaries, rent, advertising, depreciation, bad debts, interest paid, carriage outwards, discount allowed, loss on sale…
  • Credit side: gross profit, other incomes (rent received, interest received, commission, discount received)
  • Net profit goes to capital
  • Operating profit = gross profit - operating expenses
Read the full explanation

Debit side: indirect expenses (salaries, rent, advertising, depreciation, bad debts, interest paid, carriage outwards, discount allowed, loss on sale of assets). Credit side: gross profit, other incomes (rent received, interest received, commission, discount received). Net profit goes to capital. Operating profit = gross profit - operating expenses; excludes non-operating items.

🌟

Adjustments

  • Outstanding expenses are added to the expense and shown as a liability
  • Prepaid expenses are deducted from the expense and shown as an asset
  • Accrued income is added to income and shown as an asset
  • Income received in advance is deducted from income and shown as a liability
Read the full explanation

Outstanding expenses are added to the expense and shown as a liability. Prepaid expenses are deducted from the expense and shown as an asset. Accrued income is added to income and shown as an asset. Income received in advance is deducted from income and shown as a liability. Depreciation is debited to P and L. Bad debts are deducted from debtors; provision is made on remaining debtors. Interest on capital is an expense for the business and income for the owner; interest on drawings is an income for the business.

🔬

Closing entries

  • Transfer purchases and expenses to trading account: Trading A/c Dr To Purchases A/c
  • Sales are transferred: Sales A/c Dr To Trading A/c
  • Gross profit is transferred to P and L: Trading A/c Dr To P and L A/c
  • Net profit goes to Capital: P and L A/c Dr To Capital A/c
Read the full explanation

Transfer purchases and expenses to trading account: Trading A/c Dr To Purchases A/c. Sales are transferred: Sales A/c Dr To Trading A/c. Gross profit is transferred to P and L: Trading A/c Dr To P and L A/c. Net profit goes to Capital: P and L A/c Dr To Capital A/c. Drawings are closed to capital.

🧮

yt: class 11 accountancy balance sheet financial statements

blocks.x: The balance sheet is a statement of assets and liabilities (including capital) at a given date. Assets = Liabilities + Capital. Assets are classified as fixed (tangible, intangible), investments, current assets (cash, bank, debtors, stock, bills receivable, prepaid expenses), and fictitious assets. Liabilities are long-term (loans, debentures) and current (creditors, bills payable, outstanding expenses, bank overdraft). Assets can be arranged in the order of liquidity or permanence. A balance sheet in vertical format shows capital and liabilities first in order of permanence. Capital = opening capital + net profit - drawings (+ additional capital). The balance sheet is prepared after the trading and profit and loss accounts. Adjustments affect both final accounts and the balance sheet.
Deep dive: Classification

Assets: current assets (cash, bank, stock, debtors, bills receivable, prepaid expenses, accrued income, short-term investments); non-current assets (fixed assets, long-term investments). Fixed assets: tangible (land, building, machinery, furniture) and intangible (goodwill, patents, trademarks). Liabilities: current (creditors, bills payable, outstanding expenses, bank overdraft, income received in advance) and long-term (loans, debentures). Capital is the owner's equity.
Deep dive: Marshalling

Order of liquidity: assets arranged from the most liquid (cash) to the least liquid (land); liabilities from the most urgent. Order of permanence: assets arranged from fixed to current (land first, cash last); liabilities from capital to current liabilities. Banks follow liquidity; companies follow permanence under the Companies Act (Schedule III).
Deep dive: Preparing the balance sheet

Steps: calculate capital (opening + profit - drawings + additional capital). Show closing stock, debtors less bad debts and provision, outstanding expenses (liability) and prepaid (asset), fixed assets less depreciation, bills and investments. Check that assets equal liabilities plus capital. The balance sheet is a statement, not an account; it does not use Dr and Cr, and it is prepared as on a date.
Deep dive: Significance and limits

The balance sheet shows financial position, solvency, liquidity, and capital structure; it helps compare with previous years. Limitations: valued at historical cost, ignores non-monetary assets (employee skill), window dressing may distort, and it only shows position on a given date.

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Financial Statements II

The balance sheet is a statement of assets and liabilities (including capital) at a given date

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Classification›3Marshalling›4Preparing the balance sheet›5Significance and limits
🔑

Big idea

  • The balance sheet is a statement of assets and liabilities (including capital) at a given date
  • Assets = Liabilities + Capital
  • Assets are classified as fixed (tangible, intangible), investments, current assets (cash, bank, debtors, stock, bills receivable, prepaid expenses)…
  • Liabilities are long-term (loans, debentures) and current (creditors, bills payable, outstanding expenses, bank overdraft)
Read the full explanation

The balance sheet is a statement of assets and liabilities (including capital) at a given date. Assets = Liabilities + Capital. Assets are classified as fixed (tangible, intangible), investments, current assets (cash, bank, debtors, stock, bills receivable, prepaid expenses), and fictitious assets. Liabilities are long-term (loans, debentures) and current (creditors, bills payable, outstanding expenses, bank overdraft). Assets can be arranged in the order of liquidity or permanence. A balance sheet in vertical format shows capital and liabilities first in order of permanence. Capital = opening capital + net profit - drawings (+ additional capital). The balance sheet is prepared after the trading and profit and loss accounts. Adjustments affect both final accounts and the balance sheet.

📌

Classification

  • Assets: current assets (cash, bank, stock, debtors, bills receivable, prepaid expenses, accrued income, short-term investments)
  • Non-current assets (fixed assets, long-term investments)
  • Fixed assets: tangible (land, building, machinery, furniture) and intangible (goodwill, patents, trademarks)
  • Liabilities: current (creditors, bills payable, outstanding expenses, bank overdraft, income received in advance) and long-term (loans, debentures)
Read the full explanation

Assets: current assets (cash, bank, stock, debtors, bills receivable, prepaid expenses, accrued income, short-term investments); non-current assets (fixed assets, long-term investments). Fixed assets: tangible (land, building, machinery, furniture) and intangible (goodwill, patents, trademarks). Liabilities: current (creditors, bills payable, outstanding expenses, bank overdraft, income received in advance) and long-term (loans, debentures). Capital is the owner's equity.

🧠

Marshalling

  • Order of liquidity: assets arranged from the most liquid (cash) to the least liquid (land)
  • Liabilities from the most urgent
  • Order of permanence: assets arranged from fixed to current (land first, cash last)
  • Liabilities from capital to current liabilities
Read the full explanation

Order of liquidity: assets arranged from the most liquid (cash) to the least liquid (land); liabilities from the most urgent. Order of permanence: assets arranged from fixed to current (land first, cash last); liabilities from capital to current liabilities. Banks follow liquidity; companies follow permanence under the Companies Act (Schedule III).

🌟

Preparing the balance sheet

  • Steps: calculate capital (opening + profit - drawings + additional capital)
  • Show closing stock, debtors less bad debts and provision, outstanding expenses (liability) and prepaid (asset), fixed assets less depreciation, bills…
  • Check that assets equal liabilities plus capital
  • The balance sheet is a statement, not an account
Read the full explanation

Steps: calculate capital (opening + profit - drawings + additional capital). Show closing stock, debtors less bad debts and provision, outstanding expenses (liability) and prepaid (asset), fixed assets less depreciation, bills and investments. Check that assets equal liabilities plus capital. The balance sheet is a statement, not an account; it does not use Dr and Cr, and it is prepared as on a date.

  • It helps compare with previous years
  • Limitations: valued at historical cost, ignores non-monetary assets (employee skill), window dressing may distort, and it only shows position on a…

lessons.title: Accounts from Incomplete Records
yt: class 11 accountancy incomplete records single entry statement of affairs

blocks.x: Accounts from incomplete records (single entry system) are kept by small traders who do not maintain full double entry. The profit is ascertained by the statement of affairs (net worth) method or by the conversion method. Statement of affairs lists assets and liabilities at a date; capital = assets - liabilities. Profit = closing capital - opening capital + drawings - additional capital. In the conversion method, books are converted into double entry: cash book summary, total debtors account, total creditors account, bills accounts, then trading and profit and loss account and balance sheet. Credit purchases = payments to creditors + closing creditors - opening creditors. Credit sales = receipts from debtors + closing debtors - opening debtors. Margin and mark-up: cost + mark-up = selling price; gross profit on sales is margin.
Deep dive: Features and limitations

Single entry system is a hybrid: personal accounts maintained, real and nominal accounts partly or not at all. Features: no uniform record, cash book usually kept, personal accounts maintained. Limitations: no trial balance, true profit not known, difficult to detect errors and frauds, not accepted by tax authorities. Statement of affairs is not a balance sheet since it is prepared from incomplete records and may include estimates.
Deep dive: Net worth method

Opening capital = opening assets - opening liabilities. Closing capital = closing assets - closing liabilities. Profit = (closing capital - opening capital) + drawings - fresh capital introduced. Adjust for interest on drawings and any other adjustments after this. Example: opening capital 2,00,000; closing capital 2,60,000; drawings 30,000; additional capital 10,000: profit = 60,000 + 30,000 - 10,000 = 80,000.
Deep dive: Conversion method

Prepare a summary cash book to find missing figures (cash sales, cash purchases or expenses). Prepare total debtors account: opening debtors + credit sales - cash received - discount - bad debts - returns = closing debtors. Total creditors account: opening creditors + credit purchases - payments - discount - returns = closing creditors. Find credit sales and purchases as balancing figures. Then prepare trading and P and L and the balance sheet.
Deep dive: Ratios and margin

Mark-up = profit as percentage of cost: selling price = cost x (1 + mark-up). Margin = profit as percentage of sales. If margin is 20% then mark-up is 25%. Using these, find missing sales or cost of goods sold. Stock destroyed or missing can be computed by trading account approach.

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Accounts from Incomplete Records

Accounts from incomplete records (single entry system) are kept by small traders who do not maintain full double entry

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Features and limitations›3Net worth method›4Conversion method›5Ratios and margin
🔑

Big idea

  • Accounts from incomplete records (single entry system) are kept by small traders who do not maintain full double entry
  • The profit is ascertained by the statement of affairs (net worth) method or by the conversion method
  • Statement of affairs lists assets and liabilities at a date
  • Capital = assets - liabilities
Read the full explanation

Accounts from incomplete records (single entry system) are kept by small traders who do not maintain full double entry. The profit is ascertained by the statement of affairs (net worth) method or by the conversion method. Statement of affairs lists assets and liabilities at a date; capital = assets - liabilities. Profit = closing capital - opening capital + drawings - additional capital. In the conversion method, books are converted into double entry: cash book summary, total debtors account, total creditors account, bills accounts, then trading and profit and loss account and balance sheet. Credit purchases = payments to creditors + closing creditors - opening creditors. Credit sales = receipts from debtors + closing debtors - opening debtors. Margin and mark-up: cost + mark-up = selling price; gross profit on sales is margin.

📌

Features and limitations

  • Single entry system is a hybrid: personal accounts maintained, real and nominal accounts partly or not at all
  • Features: no uniform record, cash book usually kept, personal accounts maintained
  • Limitations: no trial balance, true profit not known, difficult to detect errors and frauds, not accepted by tax authorities
  • Statement of affairs is not a balance sheet since it is prepared from incomplete records and may include estimates
Read the full explanation

Single entry system is a hybrid: personal accounts maintained, real and nominal accounts partly or not at all. Features: no uniform record, cash book usually kept, personal accounts maintained. Limitations: no trial balance, true profit not known, difficult to detect errors and frauds, not accepted by tax authorities. Statement of affairs is not a balance sheet since it is prepared from incomplete records and may include estimates.

🔄

Net worth method

  • Opening capital = opening assets - opening liabilities
  • Closing capital = closing assets - closing liabilities
  • Profit = (closing capital - opening capital) + drawings - fresh capital introduced
  • Adjust for interest on drawings and any other adjustments after this
Read the full explanation

Opening capital = opening assets - opening liabilities. Closing capital = closing assets - closing liabilities. Profit = (closing capital - opening capital) + drawings - fresh capital introduced. Adjust for interest on drawings and any other adjustments after this. Example: opening capital 2,00,000; closing capital 2,60,000; drawings 30,000; additional capital 10,000: profit = 60,000 + 30,000 - 10,000 = 80,000.

🔄

Conversion method

  • Prepare a summary cash book to find missing figures (cash sales, cash purchases or expenses)
  • Prepare total debtors account: opening debtors + credit sales - cash received - discount - bad debts - returns = closing debtors
  • Total creditors account: opening creditors + credit purchases - payments - discount - returns = closing creditors
  • Find credit sales and purchases as balancing figures
Read the full explanation

Prepare a summary cash book to find missing figures (cash sales, cash purchases or expenses). Prepare total debtors account: opening debtors + credit sales - cash received - discount - bad debts - returns = closing debtors. Total creditors account: opening creditors + credit purchases - payments - discount - returns = closing creditors. Find credit sales and purchases as balancing figures. Then prepare trading and P and L and the balance sheet.

🔬

Ratios and margin

  • Mark-up = profit as percentage of cost: selling price = cost x (1 + mark-up)
  • Margin = profit as percentage of sales
  • If margin is 20% then mark-up is 25%
  • Using these, find missing sales or cost of goods sold
Read the full explanation

Mark-up = profit as percentage of cost: selling price = cost x (1 + mark-up). Margin = profit as percentage of sales. If margin is 20% then mark-up is 25%. Using these, find missing sales or cost of goods sold. Stock destroyed or missing can be computed by trading account approach.

🧮

lessons.title: Applications of Computers in Accounting
yt: class 11 accountancy computers in accounting spreadsheet database

blocks.x: Computerised accounting uses software to record, store and report accounting information. Features: speed, accuracy, automation, security, reports and integration. Components: hardware, software, data, procedures, people. Types: accounting software ready-made (Tally, QuickBooks), customised, tailored and ERP. The process: create company, create ledgers, record vouchers, generate trial balance and final accounts. A spreadsheet helps to analyse data using formulas, functions (SUM, AVERAGE, IF, VLOOKUP), charts and pivot tables. A database stores records in tables with primary keys; queries retrieve data. Advantages: speed, accuracy, savings, reports, security. Limitations: cost, training, virus and data loss risk. Security through passwords, backup, firewall, encryption.
Deep dive: Computerised accounting

Features: accuracy, speed, up-to-date reports, instant trial balance, voucher entry, GST integration, and secure access. Master data includes ledgers and stock items; transaction data includes vouchers. Steps: install and create company, set features, create account groups and ledgers, record vouchers (receipt, payment, contra, journal, sales, purchase), generate reports (trial balance, P and L, balance sheet).
Deep dive: Spreadsheet and database

Spreadsheet: workbook, worksheet, cell address (A1), formula (=A1+B1), functions SUM, AVERAGE, MAX, MIN, IF, charts. Used for depreciation schedules, ratio analysis, payroll and budgets. Database: data stored in tables of fields and records; primary key identifies each record; DBMS software like MS Access, MySQL; SQL queries retrieve data.
Deep dive: Security and controls

Threats: unauthorised access, virus, accidental deletion, hardware failure. Controls: user ID and password, access rights, regular backup, antivirus, firewall, encryption, audit trail. Cloud accounting gives remote access but needs internet security.
Deep dive: Advantages and limits

Advantages: speed, accuracy, saving of space and effort, easy corrections, better reports, wide access. Limitations: initial cost, need for trained staff, risk of virus and data loss, dependence on electricity and hardware, security risk.
Hindi saransh
Computer se lekhankan tez, shuddh aur surakshit hota hai. Spreadsheet mein sutra aur function, database mein table aur primary key. Backup aur password se suraksha.
Backup + password + antivirus = data safety.

Computerised accounting uses software to record, store and report accounting information. Features: speed, accuracy, automation, security, reports and integration. Components: hardware, software, data, procedures, people. Types: accounting software ready-made (Tally, QuickBooks), customised, tailored and ERP. The process: create company, create ledgers, record vouchers, generate trial balance and final accounts. A spreadsheet helps to analyse data using formulas, functions (SUM, AVERAGE, IF, VLOOKUP), charts and pivot tables. A database stores records in tables with primary keys; queries retrieve data. Advantages: speed, accuracy, savings, reports, security. Limitations: cost, training, virus and data loss risk. Security through passwords, backup, firewall, encryption.

Database: data stored in tables of fields and records; primary key identifies each record; DBMS software like MS Access, MySQL; SQL queries retrieve data.

Security and controls

  • Threats: unauthorised access, virus, accidental deletion, hardware failure
  • Controls: user ID and password, access rights, regular backup, antivirus, firewall, encryption, audit trail

lessons.title: The Living World and Biological Classification
yt: class 11 biology living world biological classification five kingdoms

blocks.x: Living organisms show growth, reproduction, metabolism, cellular organisation, consciousness (response to environment) and self-regulation. Taxonomy identifies, names and classifies organisms. Taxonomic hierarchy: Species, Genus, Family, Order, Class, Phylum/Division, Kingdom. Binomial nomenclature (Linnaeus) gives each organism a generic and a specific name (Homo sapiens). Whittaker proposed five kingdoms in 1969: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia. Monera are prokaryotes (bacteria, archaebacteria, cyanobacteria, mycoplasma). Protista include chrysophytes, dinoflagellates, euglenoids, slime moulds, protozoans. Fungi have chitin cell walls and are heterotrophic. Viruses, viroids and prions are non-cellular. Lichens are symbiotic associations of algae and fungi.
Deep dive: What is living

Growth is an increase in mass and size; non-living objects grow by accumulation from outside, living ones from inside. Reproduction is not a defining characteristic (mules are sterile). Metabolism is the sum of all chemical reactions and is the defining feature of life. Consciousness: all organisms respond to stimuli. Cellular organisation is a characteristic. Biodiversity: about 1.7 to 1.8 million species described. Nomenclature rules: biological names are in Latin, written in italics, genus first with capital letter, species second in lower case (Mangifera indica). Author citation follows.
Deep dive: Taxonomic categories

Species is the lowest category (a group of organisms that can interbreed). Genus (Panthera) includes related species; Family (Felidae); Order (Carnivora); Class (Mammalia); Phylum (Chordata); Kingdom (Animalia). Man: Homo sapiens, Hominidae, Primata, Mammalia, Chordata, Animalia. Mango: Mangifera indica, Anacardiaceae, Sapindales, Dicotyledonae, Angiospermae, Plantae. Taxonomic aids: herbarium (preserved plants), botanical gardens, museums, zoological parks, keys.
Deep dive: Five kingdom classification

Monera: bacteria are the most abundant; shapes: coccus, bacillus, vibrio, spirillum; some are autotrophs; archaebacteria live in harsh habitats (methanogens, halophiles, thermoacidophiles); cyanobacteria (Nostoc, Anabaena) fix nitrogen; mycoplasma lack cell wall. Protista: unicellular eukaryotes; chrysophytes (diatoms), dinoflagellates (red tide), euglenoids (Euglena), slime moulds, protozoans (Amoeba, Paramecium, Plasmodium). Fungi: Phycomycetes (Rhizopus), Ascomycetes (Penicillium, yeast), Basidiomycetes (mushrooms), Deuteromycetes. Plantae: eukaryotic, chlorophyll, cellulose cell wall; Animalia: heterotrophic, no cell wall.
Deep dive: Viruses, viroids, lichens

Viruses were studied by D. J. Ivanowsky (1892) in tobacco mosaic and M. W. Beijerinck called the fluid contagium vivum fluidum; W. M. Stanley crystallised them. Viruses have nucleic acid and protein coat (capsid); they are obligate parasites. Viroids (T. O. Diener) are free RNA without a protein coat. Prions are infectious proteins causing BSE (mad cow disease). Lichens are symbiotic associations of algae (phycobiont) and fungi (mycobiont) and are pollution indicators.

Visual lesson

The Living World and Biological Classification

Living organisms show growth, reproduction, metabolism, cellular organisation, consciousness (response to environment) and self-regulation

Five kingdomsWhittaker 1969
🔑

Big idea

  • Living organisms show growth, reproduction, metabolism, cellular organisation, consciousness (response to environment) and self-regulation
  • Taxonomy identifies, names and classifies organisms
  • Taxonomic hierarchy: Species, Genus, Family, Order, Class, Phylum/Division, Kingdom
  • Binomial nomenclature (Linnaeus) gives each organism a generic and a specific name (Homo sapiens)
Read the full explanation

Living organisms show growth, reproduction, metabolism, cellular organisation, consciousness (response to environment) and self-regulation. Taxonomy identifies, names and classifies organisms. Taxonomic hierarchy: Species, Genus, Family, Order, Class, Phylum/Division, Kingdom. Binomial nomenclature (Linnaeus) gives each organism a generic and a specific name (Homo sapiens). Whittaker proposed five kingdoms in 1969: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia. Monera are prokaryotes (bacteria, archaebacteria, cyanobacteria, mycoplasma). Protista include chrysophytes, dinoflagellates, euglenoids, slime moulds, protozoans. Fungi have chitin cell walls and are heterotrophic. Viruses, viroids and prions are non-cellular. Lichens are symbiotic associations of algae and fungi.

📘

What is living

  • Growth is an increase in mass and size
  • Non-living objects grow by accumulation from outside, living ones from inside
  • Reproduction is not a defining characteristic (mules are sterile)
  • Metabolism is the sum of all chemical reactions and is the defining feature of life
Read the full explanation

Growth is an increase in mass and size; non-living objects grow by accumulation from outside, living ones from inside. Reproduction is not a defining characteristic (mules are sterile). Metabolism is the sum of all chemical reactions and is the defining feature of life. Consciousness: all organisms respond to stimuli. Cellular organisation is a characteristic. Biodiversity: about 1.7 to 1.8 million species described. Nomenclature rules: biological names are in Latin, written in italics, genus first with capital letter, species second in lower case (Mangifera indica). Author citation follows.

🧠

Taxonomic categories

  • Species is the lowest category (a group of organisms that can interbreed)
  • Genus (Panthera) includes related species
  • Family (Felidae)
  • Order (Carnivora)
Read the full explanation

Species is the lowest category (a group of organisms that can interbreed). Genus (Panthera) includes related species; Family (Felidae); Order (Carnivora); Class (Mammalia); Phylum (Chordata); Kingdom (Animalia). Man: Homo sapiens, Hominidae, Primata, Mammalia, Chordata, Animalia. Mango: Mangifera indica, Anacardiaceae, Sapindales, Dicotyledonae, Angiospermae, Plantae. Taxonomic aids: herbarium (preserved plants), botanical gardens, museums, zoological parks, keys.

🌟

Five kingdom classification

  • Monera: bacteria are the most abundant
  • Shapes: coccus, bacillus, vibrio, spirillum
  • Some are autotrophs
  • Archaebacteria live in harsh habitats (methanogens, halophiles, thermoacidophiles)
Read the full explanation

Monera: bacteria are the most abundant; shapes: coccus, bacillus, vibrio, spirillum; some are autotrophs; archaebacteria live in harsh habitats (methanogens, halophiles, thermoacidophiles); cyanobacteria (Nostoc, Anabaena) fix nitrogen; mycoplasma lack cell wall. Protista: unicellular eukaryotes; chrysophytes (diatoms), dinoflagellates (red tide), euglenoids (Euglena), slime moulds, protozoans (Amoeba, Paramecium, Plasmodium). Fungi: Phycomycetes (Rhizopus), Ascomycetes (Penicillium, yeast), Basidiomycetes (mushrooms), Deuteromycetes. Plantae: eukaryotic, chlorophyll, cellulose cell wall; Animalia: heterotrophic, no cell wall.

💡

Viruses, viroids, lichens

  • Viruses were studied by D
  • Ivanowsky (1892) in tobacco mosaic and M
  • Beijerinck called the fluid contagium vivum fluidum
  • Stanley crystallised them
Read the full explanation

Viruses were studied by D. J. Ivanowsky (1892) in tobacco mosaic and M. W. Beijerinck called the fluid contagium vivum fluidum; W. M. Stanley crystallised them. Viruses have nucleic acid and protein coat (capsid); they are obligate parasites. Viroids (T. O. Diener) are free RNA without a protein coat. Prions are infectious proteins causing BSE (mad cow disease). Lichens are symbiotic associations of algae (phycobiont) and fungi (mycobiont) and are pollution indicators.

lessons.title: Plant Kingdom
yt: class 11 biology plant kingdom algae bryophytes pteridophytes gymnosperms angiosperms

blocks.x: Plant classification uses artificial, natural and phylogenetic systems. Plants include Algae (thallophytes: green, brown, red), Bryophytes (liverworts and mosses; amphibians of the plant kingdom), Pteridophytes (first vascular plants), Gymnosperms (naked seeds) and Angiosperms (flowering plants, monocots and dicots). Life cycles show alternation of generations: haplontic (algae), diplontic (gymnosperms, angiosperms), haplo-diplontic (bryophytes, pteridophytes). Algae: Chlorophyceae (chlorophyll a, b), Phaeophyceae (fucoxanthin, laminarin), Rhodophyceae (phycoerythrin, floridean starch). Bryophyte sporophyte depends on the gametophyte. Pteridophytes have well-developed vascular tissues. Gymnosperms bear naked ovules; angiosperms show double fertilisation and a triploid endosperm.
Deep dive: Algae

Chlorophyceae (green algae): pigments chlorophyll a and b, cellulose wall, food reserve starch; Chlamydomonas, Volvox, Spirogyra, Chara. Phaeophyceae (brown algae): fucoxanthin, food reserve laminarin and mannitol; Ectocarpus, Dictyota, Laminaria, Sargassum, Fucus. Rhodophyceae (red algae): phycoerythrin, floridean starch; Polysiphonia, Porphyra, Gracilaria, Gelidium. Algae are used for food (Porphyra, Laminaria), agar (Gelidium, Gracilaria), carrageen, hydrocolloids (algin) and as primary producers.
Deep dive: Bryophytes and Pteridophytes

Bryophytes: liverworts (Marchantia) and mosses (Funaria, Sphagnum); thalloid or leafy; rhizoids; antheridia and archegonia; sporophyte (foot, seta, capsule) is attached to the gametophyte. Sphagnum gives peat; mosses prevent soil erosion and initiate ecological succession. Pteridophytes: Psilopsida, Lycopsida (Selaginella, Lycopodium), Sphenopsida (Equisetum), Pteropsida (Dryopteris, Pteris, Adiantum); dominant sporophyte, independent gametophyte (prothallus); heterospory in Selaginella is a step towards the seed habit.
Deep dive: Gymnosperms and angiosperms

Gymnosperms: Cycas, Pinus, Cedrus, Ginkgo, Gnetum; tap roots; coralloid roots (Cycas) with cyanobacteria; male cones with microsporophylls and female cones with megasporophylls; no fruit. Angiosperms: flowering plants with seed in fruit; two classes: Dicotyledons and Monocotyledons. Male gametophyte is pollen grain; female gametophyte is embryo sac (7-celled, 8-nucleate). Double fertilisation: one male gamete fuses with the egg (zygote, 2n), the other with two polar nuclei (primary endosperm nucleus, 3n).
Deep dive: Alternation of generations

Haplontic: dominant gametophyte, zygote only diploid (Volvox, Spirogyra). Diplontic: dominant sporophyte, gametophyte reduced (gymnosperms, angiosperms, Fucus). Haplo-diplontic: both multicellular (bryophytes, pteridophytes, Ectocarpus, Polysiphonia, kelps). In bryophytes the gametophyte dominates; in pteridophytes the sporophyte dominates.

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Plant Kingdom

Plant classification uses artificial, natural and phylogenetic systems

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Algae›3Bryophytes and Pteridophytes›4Gymnosperms and angiosperms›5Alternation of generations
🔑

Big idea

  • Plant classification uses artificial, natural and phylogenetic systems
  • Plants include Algae (thallophytes: green, brown, red), Bryophytes (liverworts and mosses
  • Amphibians of the plant kingdom), Pteridophytes (first vascular plants), Gymnosperms (naked seeds) and Angiosperms (flowering plants, monocots and…
  • Life cycles show alternation of generations: haplontic (algae), diplontic (gymnosperms, angiosperms), haplo-diplontic (bryophytes, pteridophytes)
Read the full explanation

Plant classification uses artificial, natural and phylogenetic systems. Plants include Algae (thallophytes: green, brown, red), Bryophytes (liverworts and mosses; amphibians of the plant kingdom), Pteridophytes (first vascular plants), Gymnosperms (naked seeds) and Angiosperms (flowering plants, monocots and dicots). Life cycles show alternation of generations: haplontic (algae), diplontic (gymnosperms, angiosperms), haplo-diplontic (bryophytes, pteridophytes). Algae: Chlorophyceae (chlorophyll a, b), Phaeophyceae (fucoxanthin, laminarin), Rhodophyceae (phycoerythrin, floridean starch). Bryophyte sporophyte depends on the gametophyte. Pteridophytes have well-developed vascular tissues. Gymnosperms bear naked ovules; angiosperms show double fertilisation and a triploid endosperm.

📌

Algae

  • Chlorophyceae (green algae): pigments chlorophyll a and b, cellulose wall, food reserve starch
  • Chlamydomonas, Volvox, Spirogyra, Chara
  • Phaeophyceae (brown algae): fucoxanthin, food reserve laminarin and mannitol
  • Ectocarpus, Dictyota, Laminaria, Sargassum, Fucus
Read the full explanation

Chlorophyceae (green algae): pigments chlorophyll a and b, cellulose wall, food reserve starch; Chlamydomonas, Volvox, Spirogyra, Chara. Phaeophyceae (brown algae): fucoxanthin, food reserve laminarin and mannitol; Ectocarpus, Dictyota, Laminaria, Sargassum, Fucus. Rhodophyceae (red algae): phycoerythrin, floridean starch; Polysiphonia, Porphyra, Gracilaria, Gelidium. Algae are used for food (Porphyra, Laminaria), agar (Gelidium, Gracilaria), carrageen, hydrocolloids (algin) and as primary producers.

🧠

Bryophytes and Pteridophytes

  • Bryophytes: liverworts (Marchantia) and mosses (Funaria, Sphagnum)
  • Thalloid or leafy
  • Antheridia and archegonia
  • Sporophyte (foot, seta, capsule) is attached to the gametophyte
Read the full explanation

Bryophytes: liverworts (Marchantia) and mosses (Funaria, Sphagnum); thalloid or leafy; rhizoids; antheridia and archegonia; sporophyte (foot, seta, capsule) is attached to the gametophyte. Sphagnum gives peat; mosses prevent soil erosion and initiate ecological succession. Pteridophytes: Psilopsida, Lycopsida (Selaginella, Lycopodium), Sphenopsida (Equisetum), Pteropsida (Dryopteris, Pteris, Adiantum); dominant sporophyte, independent gametophyte (prothallus); heterospory in Selaginella is a step towards the seed habit.

🌟

Gymnosperms and angiosperms

  • Gymnosperms: Cycas, Pinus, Cedrus, Ginkgo, Gnetum
  • Coralloid roots (Cycas) with cyanobacteria
  • Male cones with microsporophylls and female cones with megasporophylls
  • Angiosperms: flowering plants with seed in fruit
Read the full explanation

Gymnosperms: Cycas, Pinus, Cedrus, Ginkgo, Gnetum; tap roots; coralloid roots (Cycas) with cyanobacteria; male cones with microsporophylls and female cones with megasporophylls; no fruit. Angiosperms: flowering plants with seed in fruit; two classes: Dicotyledons and Monocotyledons. Male gametophyte is pollen grain; female gametophyte is embryo sac (7-celled, 8-nucleate). Double fertilisation: one male gamete fuses with the egg (zygote, 2n), the other with two polar nuclei (primary endosperm nucleus, 3n).

🧬

Alternation of generations

  • Haplontic: dominant gametophyte, zygote only diploid (Volvox, Spirogyra)
  • Diplontic: dominant sporophyte, gametophyte reduced (gymnosperms, angiosperms, Fucus)
  • Haplo-diplontic: both multicellular (bryophytes, pteridophytes, Ectocarpus, Polysiphonia, kelps)
  • In bryophytes the gametophyte dominates
Read the full explanation

Haplontic: dominant gametophyte, zygote only diploid (Volvox, Spirogyra). Diplontic: dominant sporophyte, gametophyte reduced (gymnosperms, angiosperms, Fucus). Haplo-diplontic: both multicellular (bryophytes, pteridophytes, Ectocarpus, Polysiphonia, kelps). In bryophytes the gametophyte dominates; in pteridophytes the sporophyte dominates.

🧮

lessons.title: Animal Kingdom
yt: class 11 biology animal kingdom phyla classification

blocks.x: Animals are classified on levels of organisation (cellular, tissue, organ, organ system), symmetry (asymmetrical, radial, bilateral), germ layers (diploblastic, triploblastic), coelom (acoelomate, pseudocoelomate, coelomate), segmentation and notochord. Phyla: Porifera, Coelenterata (Cnidaria), Ctenophora, Platyhelminthes, Aschelminthes, Annelida, Arthropoda, Mollusca, Echinodermata, Hemichordata, Chordata. Chordata has Urochordata, Cephalochordata and Vertebrata (Cyclostomata, Gnathostomata: Pisces and Tetrapoda). Chondrichthyes have cartilaginous skeleton; Osteichthyes bony. Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves, Mammalia.
Deep dive: Basis of classification

Levels of organisation: cellular (sponges), tissue (coelenterates), organ (flatworms), organ system (higher). Symmetry: asymmetrical (sponges), radial (coelenterates, echinoderm adults), bilateral (annelids to chordates). Diploblastic have ectoderm and endoderm with mesoglea; triploblastic add mesoderm. Coelom is the body cavity lined by mesoderm: acoelomate (flatworms), pseudocoelomate (roundworms), coelomate (annelids onwards). Notochord is a mesodermal rod; animals are non-chordates or chordates.
Deep dive: Non-chordate phyla

Porifera: pores, canal system, choanocytes, spicules, spongin (Sycon, Spongilla, Euspongia). Coelenterata: cnidoblasts, polyp and medusa (Hydra, Aurelia, Physalia, Adamsia, Pennatula). Ctenophora: comb plates, bioluminescence (Pleurobrachia). Platyhelminthes: flame cells, hooks and suckers (Taenia, Fasciola, Planaria). Aschelminthes: roundworms, sexes separate (Ascaris, Wuchereria, Ancylostoma). Annelida: metameric segmentation (Nereis, Pheretima, Hirudinaria). Arthropoda: jointed appendages, chitinous exoskeleton, largest phylum (Apis, Bombyx, Laccifer, Anopheles, Locusta). Mollusca: soft body, mantle, radula, shell (Pila, Octopus, Pinctada). Echinodermata: water vascular system, spiny skin (Asterias, Echinus). Hemichordata: Balanoglossus.
Deep dive: Chordates

Three features: notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, paired pharyngeal gill slits. Urochordata (Ascidia, Salpa), Cephalochordata (Branchiostoma), Vertebrata with vertebral column. Cyclostomata: jawless (Petromyzon, Myxine). Chondrichthyes: Scoliodon, Pristis, Trygon, Torpedo. Osteichthyes: Exocoetus, Hippocampus, Labeo, Catla. Amphibia: Rana, Bufo, Hyla, Salamandra. Reptilia: Chelone, Testudo, Chameleon, Calotes, Crocodilus, Naja. Aves: Corvus, Columba, Psittacula, Pavo. Mammalia: mammary glands, hair; Ornithorhynchus, Macropus, Pteropus, Panthera.
Deep dive: Comparison of vertebrates

Fishes: two-chambered heart, cold-blooded, gills. Amphibians: three-chambered heart, moist skin. Reptiles: scales, mostly three-chambered heart (crocodile four). Birds and mammals: four-chambered heart, warm-blooded (homeotherms). Birds: feathers, pneumatic bones. Mammals: viviparous mostly, mammary glands, diaphragm.

Visual lesson

Animal Kingdom

Animals are classified on levels of organisation (cellular, tissue, organ, organ system), symmetry (asymmetrical, radial, bilateral), germ layers (diploblastic…

🔑

Big idea

  • Animals are classified on levels of organisation (cellular, tissue, organ, organ system), symmetry (asymmetrical, radial, bilateral), germ layers…
  • Phyla: Porifera, Coelenterata (Cnidaria), Ctenophora, Platyhelminthes, Aschelminthes, Annelida, Arthropoda, Mollusca, Echinodermata, Hemichordata…
  • Chordata has Urochordata, Cephalochordata and Vertebrata (Cyclostomata, Gnathostomata: Pisces and Tetrapoda)
  • Chondrichthyes have cartilaginous skeleton
Read the full explanation

Animals are classified on levels of organisation (cellular, tissue, organ, organ system), symmetry (asymmetrical, radial, bilateral), germ layers (diploblastic, triploblastic), coelom (acoelomate, pseudocoelomate, coelomate), segmentation and notochord. Phyla: Porifera, Coelenterata (Cnidaria), Ctenophora, Platyhelminthes, Aschelminthes, Annelida, Arthropoda, Mollusca, Echinodermata, Hemichordata, Chordata. Chordata has Urochordata, Cephalochordata and Vertebrata (Cyclostomata, Gnathostomata: Pisces and Tetrapoda). Chondrichthyes have cartilaginous skeleton; Osteichthyes bony. Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves, Mammalia.

📌

Basis of classification

  • Levels of organisation: cellular (sponges), tissue (coelenterates), organ (flatworms), organ system (higher)
  • Symmetry: asymmetrical (sponges), radial (coelenterates, echinoderm adults), bilateral (annelids to chordates)
  • Diploblastic have ectoderm and endoderm with mesoglea
  • Triploblastic add mesoderm
Read the full explanation

Levels of organisation: cellular (sponges), tissue (coelenterates), organ (flatworms), organ system (higher). Symmetry: asymmetrical (sponges), radial (coelenterates, echinoderm adults), bilateral (annelids to chordates). Diploblastic have ectoderm and endoderm with mesoglea; triploblastic add mesoderm. Coelom is the body cavity lined by mesoderm: acoelomate (flatworms), pseudocoelomate (roundworms), coelomate (annelids onwards). Notochord is a mesodermal rod; animals are non-chordates or chordates.

🧠

Non-chordate phyla

  • Porifera: pores, canal system, choanocytes, spicules, spongin (Sycon, Spongilla, Euspongia)
  • Coelenterata: cnidoblasts, polyp and medusa (Hydra, Aurelia, Physalia, Adamsia, Pennatula)
  • Ctenophora: comb plates, bioluminescence (Pleurobrachia)
  • Platyhelminthes: flame cells, hooks and suckers (Taenia, Fasciola, Planaria)
Read the full explanation

Porifera: pores, canal system, choanocytes, spicules, spongin (Sycon, Spongilla, Euspongia). Coelenterata: cnidoblasts, polyp and medusa (Hydra, Aurelia, Physalia, Adamsia, Pennatula). Ctenophora: comb plates, bioluminescence (Pleurobrachia). Platyhelminthes: flame cells, hooks and suckers (Taenia, Fasciola, Planaria). Aschelminthes: roundworms, sexes separate (Ascaris, Wuchereria, Ancylostoma). Annelida: metameric segmentation (Nereis, Pheretima, Hirudinaria). Arthropoda: jointed appendages, chitinous exoskeleton, largest phylum (Apis, Bombyx, Laccifer, Anopheles, Locusta). Mollusca: soft body, mantle, radula, shell (Pila, Octopus, Pinctada). Echinodermata: water vascular system, spiny skin (Asterias, Echinus). Hemichordata: Balanoglossus.

🌟

Chordates

  • Three features: notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, paired pharyngeal gill slits
  • Urochordata (Ascidia, Salpa), Cephalochordata (Branchiostoma), Vertebrata with vertebral column
  • Cyclostomata: jawless (Petromyzon, Myxine)
  • Chondrichthyes: Scoliodon, Pristis, Trygon, Torpedo
Read the full explanation

Three features: notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, paired pharyngeal gill slits. Urochordata (Ascidia, Salpa), Cephalochordata (Branchiostoma), Vertebrata with vertebral column. Cyclostomata: jawless (Petromyzon, Myxine). Chondrichthyes: Scoliodon, Pristis, Trygon, Torpedo. Osteichthyes: Exocoetus, Hippocampus, Labeo, Catla. Amphibia: Rana, Bufo, Hyla, Salamandra. Reptilia: Chelone, Testudo, Chameleon, Calotes, Crocodilus, Naja. Aves: Corvus, Columba, Psittacula, Pavo. Mammalia: mammary glands, hair; Ornithorhynchus, Macropus, Pteropus, Panthera.

🔬

Comparison of vertebrates

  • Fishes: two-chambered heart, cold-blooded, gills
  • Amphibians: three-chambered heart, moist skin
  • Reptiles: scales, mostly three-chambered heart (crocodile four)
  • Birds and mammals: four-chambered heart, warm-blooded (homeotherms)
Read the full explanation

Fishes: two-chambered heart, cold-blooded, gills. Amphibians: three-chambered heart, moist skin. Reptiles: scales, mostly three-chambered heart (crocodile four). Birds and mammals: four-chambered heart, warm-blooded (homeotherms). Birds: feathers, pneumatic bones. Mammals: viviparous mostly, mammary glands, diaphragm.

Root: tap root and fibrous root; regions: root cap, meristematic, elongation, maturation zones; modifications (carrot, radish, prop, stilt, pneumatophores). Stem: nodes, internodes, buds; modifications (tuber, rhizome, tendrils, thorns, runners). Leaf: lamina, petiole, leaf base; venation (reticulate, parallel); phyllotaxy (alternate, opposite, whorled); simple and compound leaves. Inflorescence: racemose and cymose. Flower: calyx, corolla, androecium, gynoecium; aestivation; placentation; ovary position (hypogynous, perigynous, epigynous). Fruit develops from the ovary; seed has seed coat, embryo; dicot and monocot seeds. Families: Fabaceae, Solanaceae, Liliaceae.
Deep dive: Root, stem and leaf

Tap root (dicots), fibrous (monocots), adventitious (grass, Monstera, banyan). Root hairs absorb water. Modified roots: storage (carrot, turnip, sweet potato), prop roots (banyan), stilt roots (maize, sugarcane), pneumatophores (Rhizophora). Stem modifications: underground (potato tuber, ginger rhizome, colocasia corm), tendrils (cucumber, pumpkin), thorns (Citrus, Bougainvillea), flattened (Opuntia), runners (grass). Leaf: venation reticulate in dicots, parallel in monocots; modifications: tendrils (pea), spines (cacti), pitcher (Nepenthes).
Deep dive: Inflorescence and flower

Racemose: main axis grows continuously; cymose: main axis ends in a flower. Flower is bisexual or unisexual; actinomorphic (radial) or zygomorphic (bilateral). Calyx has sepals, corolla petals; aestivation: valvate, twisted, imbricate, vexillary. Androecium: stamens (anther and filament); gynoecium: carpels (stigma, style, ovary); apocarpous or syncarpous. Placentation: marginal, axile, parietal, free central, basal. Ovary position: superior (hypogynous), half-inferior (perigynous), inferior (epigynous).
Deep dive: Fruit, seed and families

Fruit is the mature ovary; parthenocarpic fruit (banana) develops without fertilisation. Pericarp has epicarp, mesocarp, endocarp. Dicot seed (bean, gram): seed coat (testa and tegmen), two cotyledons, plumule, radicle; monocot (maize): single scutellum, endosperm, coleoptile, coleorhiza. Fabaceae: papilionaceous corolla, diadelphous stamens, legume. Solanaceae: bicarpellary superior ovary, berry or capsule. Liliaceae: perigonium, trimerous flowers, 6 stamens, capsule.
Deep dive: Floral formula

Floral formula uses K for calyx, C for corolla, A for androecium, G for gynoecium; the underline of G shows a superior ovary; % zygomorphic; ⊕ actinomorphic. Fabaceae: % K(5) C1+2+(2) A(9)+1 G1. Solanaceae: ⊕ K(5) C(5) A5 G(2). Liliaceae: ⊕ P(3+3) A3+3 G(3).
