Big idea

  • Morphology studies external form
  • Root: tap root and fibrous root
  • Regions: root cap, meristematic, elongation, maturation zones
  • Modifications (carrot, radish, prop, stilt, pneumatophores)
Read the full explanation

Morphology studies external form. Root: tap root and fibrous root; regions: root cap, meristematic, elongation, maturation zones; modifications (carrot, radish, prop, stilt, pneumatophores). Stem: nodes, internodes, buds; modifications (tuber, rhizome, tendrils, thorns, runners). Leaf: lamina, petiole, leaf base; venation (reticulate, parallel); phyllotaxy (alternate, opposite, whorled); simple and compound leaves. Inflorescence: racemose and cymose. Flower: calyx, corolla, androecium, gynoecium; aestivation; placentation; ovary position (hypogynous, perigynous, epigynous). Fruit develops from the ovary; seed has seed coat, embryo; dicot and monocot seeds. Families: Fabaceae, Solanaceae, Liliaceae.

📌

Root, stem and leaf

  • Tap root (dicots), fibrous (monocots), adventitious (grass, Monstera, banyan)
  • Root hairs absorb water
  • Modified roots: storage (carrot, turnip, sweet potato), prop roots (banyan), stilt roots (maize, sugarcane), pneumatophores (Rhizophora)
  • Stem modifications: underground (potato tuber, ginger rhizome, colocasia corm), tendrils (cucumber, pumpkin), thorns (Citrus, Bougainvillea)…
Read the full explanation

Tap root (dicots), fibrous (monocots), adventitious (grass, Monstera, banyan). Root hairs absorb water. Modified roots: storage (carrot, turnip, sweet potato), prop roots (banyan), stilt roots (maize, sugarcane), pneumatophores (Rhizophora). Stem modifications: underground (potato tuber, ginger rhizome, colocasia corm), tendrils (cucumber, pumpkin), thorns (Citrus, Bougainvillea), flattened (Opuntia), runners (grass). Leaf: venation reticulate in dicots, parallel in monocots; modifications: tendrils (pea), spines (cacti), pitcher (Nepenthes).

🔄

Inflorescence and flower

  • Racemose: main axis grows continuously
  • Cymose: main axis ends in a flower
  • Flower is bisexual or unisexual
  • Actinomorphic (radial) or zygomorphic (bilateral)
Read the full explanation

Racemose: main axis grows continuously; cymose: main axis ends in a flower. Flower is bisexual or unisexual; actinomorphic (radial) or zygomorphic (bilateral). Calyx has sepals, corolla petals; aestivation: valvate, twisted, imbricate, vexillary. Androecium: stamens (anther and filament); gynoecium: carpels (stigma, style, ovary); apocarpous or syncarpous. Placentation: marginal, axile, parietal, free central, basal. Ovary position: superior (hypogynous), half-inferior (perigynous), inferior (epigynous).

🌟

Fruit, seed and families

  • Fruit is the mature ovary
  • Parthenocarpic fruit (banana) develops without fertilisation
  • Pericarp has epicarp, mesocarp, endocarp
  • Dicot seed (bean, gram): seed coat (testa and tegmen), two cotyledons, plumule, radicle
Read the full explanation

Fruit is the mature ovary; parthenocarpic fruit (banana) develops without fertilisation. Pericarp has epicarp, mesocarp, endocarp. Dicot seed (bean, gram): seed coat (testa and tegmen), two cotyledons, plumule, radicle; monocot (maize): single scutellum, endosperm, coleoptile, coleorhiza. Fabaceae: papilionaceous corolla, diadelphous stamens, legume. Solanaceae: bicarpellary superior ovary, berry or capsule. Liliaceae: perigonium, trimerous flowers, 6 stamens, capsule.

🧮

Floral formula

  • Floral formula uses K for calyx, C for corolla, A for androecium, G for gynoecium
  • The underline of G shows a superior ovary
  • % zygomorphic
  • ⊕ actinomorphic
Read the full explanation

Floral formula uses K for calyx, C for corolla, A for androecium, G for gynoecium; the underline of G shows a superior ovary; % zygomorphic; ⊕ actinomorphic. Fabaceae: % K(5) C1+2+(2) A(9)+1 G1. Solanaceae: ⊕ K(5) C(5) A5 G(2). Liliaceae: ⊕ P(3+3) A3+3 G(3).

lessons.title: Anatomy of Flowering Plants
yt: class 11 biology anatomy of flowering plants tissues secondary growth

blocks.x: Plant tissues: meristematic (apical, intercalary, lateral) and permanent (simple: parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma; complex: xylem, phloem). Tissue systems: epidermal, ground and vascular. Dicot root has radial vascular bundles with exarch xylem, 2-4 xylem bundles (di- to tetrarch). Monocot root has polyarch. Dicot stem: vascular bundles in a ring, conjoint, collateral, open. Monocot stem: scattered, closed. Dorsiventral and isobilateral leaves. Secondary growth by vascular cambium and cork cambium: annual rings, heartwood, sapwood, bark, lenticels.
Deep dive: Tissues

Meristematic: apical (root and shoot tip), intercalary (grasses), lateral (cambium). Parenchyma: living, thin walled, photosynthesis and storage. Collenchyma: pectin and cellulose thickening at corners, support in young stems. Sclerenchyma: dead, lignified (fibres, sclereids). Xylem: tracheids, vessels, xylem fibres, xylem parenchyma; conducts water. Phloem: sieve tube elements, companion cells, phloem parenchyma, phloem fibres; conducts food. Protoxylem is towards the centre in stems (endarch) and towards the periphery in roots (exarch).
Deep dive: Tissue systems

Epidermal: epidermis, cuticle, stomata (guard cells and subsidiary cells), root hairs, trichomes. Ground: all tissues except epidermis and vascular bundles (cortex, pericycle, pith). Vascular: xylem and phloem; conjoint (same radius), radial (different radii); open (cambium present, dicots), closed (monocots). Guard cells of dumb-bell shape in grasses and kidney shape in dicots.
Deep dive: Primary structure

Dicot root: epidermis with root hairs, cortex, endodermis with Casparian strips, pericycle, vascular bundles 2-4, conjunctive tissue, small pith. Monocot root: more than 6 xylem bundles, large pith. Dicot stem: epidermis, hypodermis (collenchyma), cortex, endodermis, pericycle, bundles in ring, pith. Monocot stem: sclerenchymatous hypodermis, scattered bundles with sclerenchymatous sheaths, no differentiated ground tissue. Dorsiventral leaf: palisade and spongy mesophyll; isobilateral leaf (monocot): bulliform cells.
Deep dive: Secondary growth

Vascular cambium forms secondary xylem inward and secondary phloem outward. Cork cambium (phellogen) forms cork (phellem) outward and secondary cortex (phelloderm) inward; periderm = phellogen + phellem + phelloderm. Spring wood (light, wide vessels) and autumn wood (dark, narrow) form an annual ring; dendrochronology counts rings. Heartwood is dark with tannins and resins; sapwood conducts water. Lenticels allow gas exchange. Monocots lack secondary growth.

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Anatomy of Flowering Plants

Plant tissues: meristematic (apical, intercalary, lateral) and permanent (simple: parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Tissues›3Tissue systems›4Primary structure›5Secondary growth
🔑

Big idea

  • Plant tissues: meristematic (apical, intercalary, lateral) and permanent (simple: parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma
  • Complex: xylem, phloem)
  • Tissue systems: epidermal, ground and vascular
  • Dicot root has radial vascular bundles with exarch xylem, 2-4 xylem bundles (di- to tetrarch)
Read the full explanation

Plant tissues: meristematic (apical, intercalary, lateral) and permanent (simple: parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma; complex: xylem, phloem). Tissue systems: epidermal, ground and vascular. Dicot root has radial vascular bundles with exarch xylem, 2-4 xylem bundles (di- to tetrarch). Monocot root has polyarch. Dicot stem: vascular bundles in a ring, conjoint, collateral, open. Monocot stem: scattered, closed. Dorsiventral and isobilateral leaves. Secondary growth by vascular cambium and cork cambium: annual rings, heartwood, sapwood, bark, lenticels.

🧬

Tissues

  • Meristematic: apical (root and shoot tip), intercalary (grasses), lateral (cambium)
  • Parenchyma: living, thin walled, photosynthesis and storage
  • Collenchyma: pectin and cellulose thickening at corners, support in young stems
  • Sclerenchyma: dead, lignified (fibres, sclereids)
Read the full explanation

Meristematic: apical (root and shoot tip), intercalary (grasses), lateral (cambium). Parenchyma: living, thin walled, photosynthesis and storage. Collenchyma: pectin and cellulose thickening at corners, support in young stems. Sclerenchyma: dead, lignified (fibres, sclereids). Xylem: tracheids, vessels, xylem fibres, xylem parenchyma; conducts water. Phloem: sieve tube elements, companion cells, phloem parenchyma, phloem fibres; conducts food. Protoxylem is towards the centre in stems (endarch) and towards the periphery in roots (exarch).

🧬

Tissue systems

  • Epidermal: epidermis, cuticle, stomata (guard cells and subsidiary cells), root hairs, trichomes
  • Ground: all tissues except epidermis and vascular bundles (cortex, pericycle, pith)
  • Vascular: xylem and phloem
  • Conjoint (same radius), radial (different radii)
Read the full explanation

Epidermal: epidermis, cuticle, stomata (guard cells and subsidiary cells), root hairs, trichomes. Ground: all tissues except epidermis and vascular bundles (cortex, pericycle, pith). Vascular: xylem and phloem; conjoint (same radius), radial (different radii); open (cambium present, dicots), closed (monocots). Guard cells of dumb-bell shape in grasses and kidney shape in dicots.

🌟

Primary structure

  • Dicot root: epidermis with root hairs, cortex, endodermis with Casparian strips, pericycle, vascular bundles 2-4, conjunctive tissue, small pith
  • Monocot root: more than 6 xylem bundles, large pith
  • Dicot stem: epidermis, hypodermis (collenchyma), cortex, endodermis, pericycle, bundles in ring, pith
  • Monocot stem: sclerenchymatous hypodermis, scattered bundles with sclerenchymatous sheaths, no differentiated ground tissue
Read the full explanation

Dicot root: epidermis with root hairs, cortex, endodermis with Casparian strips, pericycle, vascular bundles 2-4, conjunctive tissue, small pith. Monocot root: more than 6 xylem bundles, large pith. Dicot stem: epidermis, hypodermis (collenchyma), cortex, endodermis, pericycle, bundles in ring, pith. Monocot stem: sclerenchymatous hypodermis, scattered bundles with sclerenchymatous sheaths, no differentiated ground tissue. Dorsiventral leaf: palisade and spongy mesophyll; isobilateral leaf (monocot): bulliform cells.

🔬

Secondary growth

  • Vascular cambium forms secondary xylem inward and secondary phloem outward
  • Cork cambium (phellogen) forms cork (phellem) outward and secondary cortex (phelloderm) inward
  • Periderm = phellogen + phellem + phelloderm
  • Spring wood (light, wide vessels) and autumn wood (dark, narrow) form an annual ring
Read the full explanation

Vascular cambium forms secondary xylem inward and secondary phloem outward. Cork cambium (phellogen) forms cork (phellem) outward and secondary cortex (phelloderm) inward; periderm = phellogen + phellem + phelloderm. Spring wood (light, wide vessels) and autumn wood (dark, narrow) form an annual ring; dendrochronology counts rings. Heartwood is dark with tannins and resins; sapwood conducts water. Lenticels allow gas exchange. Monocots lack secondary growth.

🧮

lessons.title: Structural Organisation in Animals
yt: class 11 biology structural organisation in animals tissues earthworm cockroach frog

blocks.x: Animal tissues: epithelial, connective, muscular, neural. Epithelium: simple (squamous, cuboidal, columnar, ciliated) and compound; junctions: tight, adhering, gap. Connective: loose (areolar, adipose), dense (regular, irregular), specialised (cartilage, bone, blood). Muscle: skeletal, smooth, cardiac. Neural: neurons and neuroglia. Earthworm (Pheretima): 100-120 segments, clitellum on 14-16, setae, nephridia, 4 pairs of spermathecae. Cockroach (Periplaneta): head, thorax, abdomen, mosaic vision, Malpighian tubules, open circulation, 10 pairs of spiracles. Frog (Rana tigrina): three-chambered heart, tadpole metamorphosis.
Deep dive: Epithelial and connective tissue

Squamous epithelium: lining of blood vessels and alveoli; cuboidal: ducts of glands, tubules of nephrons; columnar: stomach and intestine lining; ciliated: trachea, oviducts. Glandular: unicellular (goblet cells) or multicellular (salivary glands). Tight junctions prevent leakage, adhering junctions cement cells, gap junctions allow communication. Areolar tissue has fibroblasts, macrophages and mast cells; adipose stores fat; tendons join muscle to bone, ligaments join bone to bone. Cartilage has chondrocytes in lacunae; bone has osteocytes with Haversian canals; blood is a fluid connective tissue.
Deep dive: Muscle, neural and organ systems

Skeletal muscle is striated and voluntary; smooth muscle is non-striated, involuntary and spindle-shaped; cardiac muscle is striated, involuntary and branched with intercalated discs. A neuron has dendrites, cell body (cyton) and axon; neuroglia support neurons. Earthworm: digestive tract with pharynx, oesophagus, gizzard, stomach, intestine with typhlosole; closed circulation; hermaphrodite; fertilisation external to the body in cocoon. Cockroach: crop, gizzard with chitinous teeth, hepatic caecae, tracheal respiration, nocturnal; males have anal styles.
Deep dive: Frog

Rana tigrina: smooth moist skin, buccal cavity, cloaca, 3-chambered heart (2 atria, 1 ventricle), sinus venosus, renal portal system, hepatic portal system, kidneys (mesonephric), male has vocal sacs and nuptial pads, fertilisation external, tadpole with gills develops into adult by metamorphosis. Respiration: cutaneous, buccopharyngeal and pulmonary.
Hindi saransh
Jantuon mein sanrachnatmak sangathan: epithelial, sanyojee, peshi, tantrika utak. Kenchua, tilchatta aur mendhak ke tantra.
Cockroach has an open circulatory system; earthworm has a closed system.

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Structural Organisation in Animals

Animal tissues: epithelial, connective, muscular, neural

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Epithelial and connective…›3Muscle, neural and organ…›4Frog
🔑

Big idea

  • Animal tissues: epithelial, connective, muscular, neural
  • Epithelium: simple (squamous, cuboidal, columnar, ciliated) and compound
  • Junctions: tight, adhering, gap
  • Connective: loose (areolar, adipose), dense (regular, irregular), specialised (cartilage, bone, blood)
Read the full explanation

Animal tissues: epithelial, connective, muscular, neural. Epithelium: simple (squamous, cuboidal, columnar, ciliated) and compound; junctions: tight, adhering, gap. Connective: loose (areolar, adipose), dense (regular, irregular), specialised (cartilage, bone, blood). Muscle: skeletal, smooth, cardiac. Neural: neurons and neuroglia. Earthworm (Pheretima): 100-120 segments, clitellum on 14-16, setae, nephridia, 4 pairs of spermathecae. Cockroach (Periplaneta): head, thorax, abdomen, mosaic vision, Malpighian tubules, open circulation, 10 pairs of spiracles. Frog (Rana tigrina): three-chambered heart, tadpole metamorphosis.

🧬

Epithelial and connective tissue

  • Squamous epithelium: lining of blood vessels and alveoli
  • Cuboidal: ducts of glands, tubules of nephrons
  • Columnar: stomach and intestine lining
  • Ciliated: trachea, oviducts
Read the full explanation

Squamous epithelium: lining of blood vessels and alveoli; cuboidal: ducts of glands, tubules of nephrons; columnar: stomach and intestine lining; ciliated: trachea, oviducts. Glandular: unicellular (goblet cells) or multicellular (salivary glands). Tight junctions prevent leakage, adhering junctions cement cells, gap junctions allow communication. Areolar tissue has fibroblasts, macrophages and mast cells; adipose stores fat; tendons join muscle to bone, ligaments join bone to bone. Cartilage has chondrocytes in lacunae; bone has osteocytes with Haversian canals; blood is a fluid connective tissue.

🧬

Muscle, neural and organ systems

  • Skeletal muscle is striated and voluntary
  • Smooth muscle is non-striated, involuntary and spindle-shaped
  • Cardiac muscle is striated, involuntary and branched with intercalated discs
  • A neuron has dendrites, cell body (cyton) and axon
Read the full explanation

Skeletal muscle is striated and voluntary; smooth muscle is non-striated, involuntary and spindle-shaped; cardiac muscle is striated, involuntary and branched with intercalated discs. A neuron has dendrites, cell body (cyton) and axon; neuroglia support neurons. Earthworm: digestive tract with pharynx, oesophagus, gizzard, stomach, intestine with typhlosole; closed circulation; hermaphrodite; fertilisation external to the body in cocoon. Cockroach: crop, gizzard with chitinous teeth, hepatic caecae, tracheal respiration, nocturnal; males have anal styles.

🌟

Frog

  • Rana tigrina: smooth moist skin, buccal cavity, cloaca, 3-chambered heart (2 atria, 1 ventricle), sinus venosus, renal portal system, hepatic portal…
  • Respiration: cutaneous, buccopharyngeal and pulmonary

Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells
Prokaryotes (bacteria) lack a membrane-bound nucleus and organelles; DNA lies in a nucleoid; ribosomes are 70S. Eukaryotes have a nucleus, membrane-bound organelles and 80S ribosomes.
Organelles

x: **Mitochondria:** ATP production, own DNA. **Chloroplast:** photosynthesis. **ER:** protein/lipid synthesis. **Golgi:** packaging and secretion. **Lysosomes:** digestion. **Ribosomes:** protein synthesis. **Nucleus:** DNA, controls cell.

blocks.x: Cell cycle

Interphase (G1, S, G2) then M phase. **Mitosis** phases: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase; gives two identical diploid daughter cells. **Meiosis** has two divisions and produces four haploid cells with crossing over in prophase I.

visuals.data: Prophase; Metaphase; Anaphase; Telophase and cytokinesis

visuals.data: Mitosis=1 division~2 identical diploid cells~growth and repair; Meiosis=2 divisions~4 haploid cells~gametes and variation

problems.q: List four differences between mitosis and meiosis.
problems.a: Divisions (1 vs 2), daughter cells (2 vs 4), ploidy (diploid vs haploid), crossing over (absent vs present).

problems.q: Describe the stages of mitosis.
problems.a: Prophase: chromosomes condense; metaphase: line up at equator; anaphase: sister chromatids separate; telophase: nuclei re-form and cytokinesis follows.

problems.q: If a cell with 2n = 46 undergoes meiosis, state chromosome numbers at the end of meiosis I and II.
problems.a: After meiosis I: two cells with 23 chromosomes (each with two chromatids). After meiosis II: four cells with 23 single chromatids.

lessons.title: Cell: The Unit of Life
yt: class 11 biology cell the unit of life organelles

blocks.x: Cell theory (Schleiden and Schwann, Virchow): all organisms are made of cells, cells are the basic units, and all cells arise from pre-existing cells. Prokaryotic cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus (bacteria, 70S ribosomes, nucleoid, plasmids, mesosomes). Eukaryotic cells have membrane-bound organelles. Fluid mosaic model (Singer and Nicolson, 1972). Cell wall: cellulose in plants, peptidoglycan in bacteria. Endomembrane system: ER, Golgi, lysosomes, vacuoles. Mitochondria (cristae, F1 particles), plastids (chloroplast with grana and stroma), ribosomes (80S), cytoskeleton, cilia, flagella, centrosome, nucleus (nuclear envelope, nucleolus, chromatin).
Deep dive: Cell theory and types

Robert Hooke discovered cells (1665) in cork. Leeuwenhoek saw living cells. Robert Brown discovered the nucleus. Schleiden (plants) and Schwann (animals) proposed cell theory; Virchow added Omnis cellula e cellula. Prokaryotes: size 0.1-0.5 µm for mycoplasma; bacteria 3-5 µm. Cell envelope: glycocalyx, cell wall, plasma membrane. Flagella of bacteria, pili, fimbriae. Ribosomes 70S (50S + 30S). Eukaryotic ribosomes 80S (60S + 40S).
Deep dive: Membrane and organelles

Plasma membrane: phospholipid bilayer with proteins; integral and peripheral; cholesterol in animals. Transport: passive (simple diffusion, facilitated), active (against gradient with ATP, Na+-K+ pump), osmosis. ER: RER with ribosomes, SER makes lipids. Golgi (Camillo Golgi): packaging and secretion. Lysosomes: hydrolytic enzymes, suicide bags. Vacuoles: tonoplast in plants. Mitochondria: double membrane, matrix, own DNA and 70S ribosomes, ATP synthesis. Plastids: chloroplast, chromoplast, leucoplast (amyloplast, elaioplast, aleuroplast).
Deep dive: Nucleus and cytoskeleton

Nucleus: double membrane with pores, nucleoplasm, nucleolus (rRNA synthesis), chromatin. Chromosomes classified by centromere position: metacentric, sub-metacentric, acrocentric, telocentric. Microbodies: peroxisomes and glyoxysomes. Cytoskeleton: microtubules, microfilaments, intermediate filaments. Cilia and flagella have 9+2 axoneme structure; centrioles have 9+0 triplet structure. Centrosome forms spindle.

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Cell: The Unit of Life

Cell theory (Schleiden and Schwann, Virchow): all organisms are made of cells, cells are the basic units, and all cells arise from pre-existing cells

Q&A

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Cell theory and types›3Membrane and organelles›4Nucleus and cytoskeleton
🔑

Big idea

  • Cell theory (Schleiden and Schwann, Virchow): all organisms are made of cells, cells are the basic units, and all cells arise from pre-existing cells
  • Prokaryotic cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus (bacteria, 70S ribosomes, nucleoid, plasmids, mesosomes)
  • Eukaryotic cells have membrane-bound organelles
  • Fluid mosaic model (Singer and Nicolson, 1972)
Read the full explanation

Cell theory (Schleiden and Schwann, Virchow): all organisms are made of cells, cells are the basic units, and all cells arise from pre-existing cells. Prokaryotic cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus (bacteria, 70S ribosomes, nucleoid, plasmids, mesosomes). Eukaryotic cells have membrane-bound organelles. Fluid mosaic model (Singer and Nicolson, 1972). Cell wall: cellulose in plants, peptidoglycan in bacteria. Endomembrane system: ER, Golgi, lysosomes, vacuoles. Mitochondria (cristae, F1 particles), plastids (chloroplast with grana and stroma), ribosomes (80S), cytoskeleton, cilia, flagella, centrosome, nucleus (nuclear envelope, nucleolus, chromatin).

🧬

Cell theory and types

  • Robert Hooke discovered cells (1665) in cork
  • Leeuwenhoek saw living cells
  • Robert Brown discovered the nucleus
  • Schleiden (plants) and Schwann (animals) proposed cell theory
Read the full explanation

Robert Hooke discovered cells (1665) in cork. Leeuwenhoek saw living cells. Robert Brown discovered the nucleus. Schleiden (plants) and Schwann (animals) proposed cell theory; Virchow added Omnis cellula e cellula. Prokaryotes: size 0.1-0.5 µm for mycoplasma; bacteria 3-5 µm. Cell envelope: glycocalyx, cell wall, plasma membrane. Flagella of bacteria, pili, fimbriae. Ribosomes 70S (50S + 30S). Eukaryotic ribosomes 80S (60S + 40S).

🧬

Membrane and organelles

  • Plasma membrane: phospholipid bilayer with proteins
  • Integral and peripheral
  • Cholesterol in animals
  • Transport: passive (simple diffusion, facilitated), active (against gradient with ATP, Na+-K+ pump), osmosis
Read the full explanation

Plasma membrane: phospholipid bilayer with proteins; integral and peripheral; cholesterol in animals. Transport: passive (simple diffusion, facilitated), active (against gradient with ATP, Na+-K+ pump), osmosis. ER: RER with ribosomes, SER makes lipids. Golgi (Camillo Golgi): packaging and secretion. Lysosomes: hydrolytic enzymes, suicide bags. Vacuoles: tonoplast in plants. Mitochondria: double membrane, matrix, own DNA and 70S ribosomes, ATP synthesis. Plastids: chloroplast, chromoplast, leucoplast (amyloplast, elaioplast, aleuroplast).

⚛️

Nucleus and cytoskeleton

  • Nucleus: double membrane with pores, nucleoplasm, nucleolus (rRNA synthesis), chromatin
  • Chromosomes classified by centromere position: metacentric, sub-metacentric, acrocentric, telocentric
  • Microbodies: peroxisomes and glyoxysomes
  • Cytoskeleton: microtubules, microfilaments, intermediate filaments
Read the full explanation

Nucleus: double membrane with pores, nucleoplasm, nucleolus (rRNA synthesis), chromatin. Chromosomes classified by centromere position: metacentric, sub-metacentric, acrocentric, telocentric. Microbodies: peroxisomes and glyoxysomes. Cytoskeleton: microtubules, microfilaments, intermediate filaments. Cilia and flagella have 9+2 axoneme structure; centrioles have 9+0 triplet structure. Centrosome forms spindle.

lessons.title: Biomolecules
yt: class 11 biology biomolecules enzymes proteins carbohydrates lipids nucleic acids

blocks.x: Biomolecules include carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, vitamins and enzymes. Amino acids have an amino group, carboxyl group and R group; peptide bond links them. Protein structure: primary, secondary (alpha helix, beta sheet), tertiary, quaternary (haemoglobin). Monosaccharides (glucose), disaccharides (sucrose, maltose, lactose), polysaccharides (starch, glycogen, cellulose, chitin) linked by glycosidic bonds. Lipids: fats with glycerol and fatty acids; phospholipids. Nucleic acids: nucleotide = sugar + base + phosphate; DNA and RNA. Enzymes lower activation energy; Michaelis-Menten constant Km; factors: temperature, pH, substrate concentration; inhibitors competitive and non-competitive.
Deep dive: Carbohydrates, lipids, amino acids

Glucose is an aldohexose (C6H12O6); fructose a ketohexose. Sucrose = glucose + fructose; maltose = glucose + glucose; lactose = glucose + galactose. Starch has amylose and amylopectin; glycogen is highly branched; cellulose is beta-1,4 linked. Fatty acids may be saturated or unsaturated; triglycerides contain glycerol and 3 fatty acids; phospholipids contain phosphate and are amphipathic (lecithin). Essential amino acids cannot be made by the body; zwitterion has both charges at isoelectric pH.
Deep dive: Proteins and nucleic acids

Primary structure is the linear sequence of amino acids; secondary has alpha helix stabilised by hydrogen bonds; tertiary is 3D folding; quaternary has multiple chains (haemoglobin: 2 alpha + 2 beta). Collagen is the most abundant protein in animals; RuBisCO is the most abundant protein in the biosphere. Nucleotides: adenine, guanine (purines), cytosine, thymine, uracil (pyrimidines); nucleoside = sugar + base. DNA is a double helix with A=T and G≡C (Chargaff).
Deep dive: Enzymes

Enzymes are mostly proteins (ribozymes are RNA). Active site binds substrate (lock and key; induced fit). Classes: oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases, ligases. Cofactors: prosthetic group, coenzyme (NAD, NADP from vitamins), metal ions. Rate rises with temperature up to the optimum then falls by denaturation. Optimum pH differs. Km is the substrate concentration at half Vmax. Competitive inhibitors resemble the substrate (e.g., malonate on succinate dehydrogenase). Feedback inhibition regulates pathways.

Visual lesson

Biomolecules

Biomolecules include carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, vitamins and enzymes

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Carbohydrates, lipids…›3Proteins and nucleic acids›4Enzymes
🔑

Big idea

  • Biomolecules include carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, vitamins and enzymes
  • Amino acids have an amino group, carboxyl group and R group
  • Peptide bond links them
  • Protein structure: primary, secondary (alpha helix, beta sheet), tertiary, quaternary (haemoglobin)
Read the full explanation

Biomolecules include carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, vitamins and enzymes. Amino acids have an amino group, carboxyl group and R group; peptide bond links them. Protein structure: primary, secondary (alpha helix, beta sheet), tertiary, quaternary (haemoglobin). Monosaccharides (glucose), disaccharides (sucrose, maltose, lactose), polysaccharides (starch, glycogen, cellulose, chitin) linked by glycosidic bonds. Lipids: fats with glycerol and fatty acids; phospholipids. Nucleic acids: nucleotide = sugar + base + phosphate; DNA and RNA. Enzymes lower activation energy; Michaelis-Menten constant Km; factors: temperature, pH, substrate concentration; inhibitors competitive and non-competitive.

⚗️

Carbohydrates, lipids, amino acids

  • Glucose is an aldohexose (C6H12O6)
  • Fructose a ketohexose
  • Sucrose = glucose + fructose
  • Maltose = glucose + glucose
Read the full explanation

Glucose is an aldohexose (C6H12O6); fructose a ketohexose. Sucrose = glucose + fructose; maltose = glucose + glucose; lactose = glucose + galactose. Starch has amylose and amylopectin; glycogen is highly branched; cellulose is beta-1,4 linked. Fatty acids may be saturated or unsaturated; triglycerides contain glycerol and 3 fatty acids; phospholipids contain phosphate and are amphipathic (lecithin). Essential amino acids cannot be made by the body; zwitterion has both charges at isoelectric pH.

⚗️

Proteins and nucleic acids

  • Primary structure is the linear sequence of amino acids
  • Secondary has alpha helix stabilised by hydrogen bonds
  • Tertiary is 3D folding
  • Quaternary has multiple chains (haemoglobin: 2 alpha + 2 beta)
Read the full explanation

Primary structure is the linear sequence of amino acids; secondary has alpha helix stabilised by hydrogen bonds; tertiary is 3D folding; quaternary has multiple chains (haemoglobin: 2 alpha + 2 beta). Collagen is the most abundant protein in animals; RuBisCO is the most abundant protein in the biosphere. Nucleotides: adenine, guanine (purines), cytosine, thymine, uracil (pyrimidines); nucleoside = sugar + base. DNA is a double helix with A=T and G≡C (Chargaff).

🌟

Enzymes

  • Enzymes are mostly proteins (ribozymes are RNA)
  • Active site binds substrate (lock and key
  • Classes: oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases, ligases
  • Cofactors: prosthetic group, coenzyme (NAD, NADP from vitamins), metal ions
Read the full explanation

Enzymes are mostly proteins (ribozymes are RNA). Active site binds substrate (lock and key; induced fit). Classes: oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases, ligases. Cofactors: prosthetic group, coenzyme (NAD, NADP from vitamins), metal ions. Rate rises with temperature up to the optimum then falls by denaturation. Optimum pH differs. Km is the substrate concentration at half Vmax. Competitive inhibitors resemble the substrate (e.g., malonate on succinate dehydrogenase). Feedback inhibition regulates pathways.

lessons.title: Cell Cycle and Cell Division
yt: class 11 biology cell cycle mitosis meiosis

blocks.x: The cell cycle has interphase (G1, S, G2) and M phase. Mitosis (equational division) has prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase and cytokinesis; it produces two identical diploid daughter cells. Meiosis (reductional) has two divisions: meiosis I (prophase I with leptotene, zygotene, pachytene, diplotene, diakinesis) and meiosis II; it produces four haploid cells. Crossing over occurs at pachytene with recombination nodules; chiasmata are seen at diplotene. G0 is the quiescent stage. Significance: growth, repair, gamete formation and genetic variation.
Deep dive: Cell cycle phases

Interphase is the longest. G1: cell grows and prepares; S: DNA replicates (amount doubles from 2C to 4C, chromosome number unchanged); G2: protein synthesis for mitosis. Human cell cycle about 24 hours with M phase about 1 hour. Cells exiting the cycle enter G0 (heart cells). Checkpoints (G1/S, G2/M, spindle) are regulated by cyclins and CDKs.
Deep dive: Mitosis

Prophase: chromatin condenses, centrioles move to poles, nucleolus and nuclear envelope disappear. Metaphase: chromosomes align at the equatorial plate, spindle fibres attach at kinetochores. Anaphase: centromeres split and chromatids move to opposite poles. Telophase: chromosomes decondense, nuclear envelope reforms. Cytokinesis: furrow in animals, cell plate in plants. Karyokinesis is nuclear division.
Deep dive: Meiosis

Meiosis I prophase I: leptotene (condensation), zygotene (synapsis, synaptonemal complex, bivalents), pachytene (crossing over), diplotene (chiasmata, dictyotene in oocytes), diakinesis (terminalisation). Metaphase I bivalents on plate; anaphase I homologous chromosomes separate (no centromere division); telophase I gives dyad. Meiosis II resembles mitosis. Result: four haploid cells. Significance: constancy of chromosome number, variation through crossing over and independent assortment.

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Cell Cycle and Cell Division

The cell cycle has interphase (G1, S, G2) and M phase

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Cell cycle phases›3Mitosis›4Meiosis
🔑

Big idea

  • The cell cycle has interphase (G1, S, G2) and M phase
  • Mitosis (equational division) has prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase and cytokinesis
  • It produces two identical diploid daughter cells
  • Meiosis (reductional) has two divisions: meiosis I (prophase I with leptotene, zygotene, pachytene, diplotene, diakinesis) and meiosis II
Read the full explanation

The cell cycle has interphase (G1, S, G2) and M phase. Mitosis (equational division) has prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase and cytokinesis; it produces two identical diploid daughter cells. Meiosis (reductional) has two divisions: meiosis I (prophase I with leptotene, zygotene, pachytene, diplotene, diakinesis) and meiosis II; it produces four haploid cells. Crossing over occurs at pachytene with recombination nodules; chiasmata are seen at diplotene. G0 is the quiescent stage. Significance: growth, repair, gamete formation and genetic variation.

🔄

Cell cycle phases

  • Interphase is the longest
  • G1: cell grows and prepares
  • S: DNA replicates (amount doubles from 2C to 4C, chromosome number unchanged)
  • G2: protein synthesis for mitosis
Read the full explanation

Interphase is the longest. G1: cell grows and prepares; S: DNA replicates (amount doubles from 2C to 4C, chromosome number unchanged); G2: protein synthesis for mitosis. Human cell cycle about 24 hours with M phase about 1 hour. Cells exiting the cycle enter G0 (heart cells). Checkpoints (G1/S, G2/M, spindle) are regulated by cyclins and CDKs.

🧠

Mitosis

  • Prophase: chromatin condenses, centrioles move to poles, nucleolus and nuclear envelope disappear
  • Metaphase: chromosomes align at the equatorial plate, spindle fibres attach at kinetochores
  • Anaphase: centromeres split and chromatids move to opposite poles
  • Telophase: chromosomes decondense, nuclear envelope reforms
Read the full explanation

Prophase: chromatin condenses, centrioles move to poles, nucleolus and nuclear envelope disappear. Metaphase: chromosomes align at the equatorial plate, spindle fibres attach at kinetochores. Anaphase: centromeres split and chromatids move to opposite poles. Telophase: chromosomes decondense, nuclear envelope reforms. Cytokinesis: furrow in animals, cell plate in plants. Karyokinesis is nuclear division.

🌟

Meiosis

  • Meiosis I prophase I: leptotene (condensation), zygotene (synapsis, synaptonemal complex, bivalents), pachytene (crossing over), diplotene…
  • Metaphase I bivalents on plate
  • Anaphase I homologous chromosomes separate (no centromere division)
  • Telophase I gives dyad
Read the full explanation

Meiosis I prophase I: leptotene (condensation), zygotene (synapsis, synaptonemal complex, bivalents), pachytene (crossing over), diplotene (chiasmata, dictyotene in oocytes), diakinesis (terminalisation). Metaphase I bivalents on plate; anaphase I homologous chromosomes separate (no centromere division); telophase I gives dyad. Meiosis II resembles mitosis. Result: four haploid cells. Significance: constancy of chromosome number, variation through crossing over and independent assortment.

blocks.x: **Photosynthesis:** 6 CO2 + 6 H2O + light -> C6H12O6 + 6 O2. Light reaction (thylakoid membranes): water splits, O2 released, ATP and NADPH made. Calvin cycle (stroma): CO2 fixed by RuBisCO into 3-PGA and then sugars. C4 plants (maize, sugarcane) use PEP carboxylase and show Kranz anatomy. **Respiration:** C6H12O6 + 6 O2 -> 6 CO2 + 6 H2O + energy. Glycolysis (cytoplasm) gives 2 ATP, 2 NADH and 2 pyruvate; Krebs cycle (mitochondrial matrix); electron transport chain (inner membrane) makes most ATP. Net about **30-32 ATP** per glucose in eukaryotes (older textbooks say 36-38).

problems.q: Write the overall equation of photosynthesis.

problems.q: Compare the light reaction and the Calvin cycle.
problems.a: Light reaction: thylakoid, needs light, makes ATP, NADPH and O2. Calvin cycle: stroma, uses ATP and NADPH to fix CO2 into sugar.

problems.q: Explain why C4 plants are efficient in hot dry climates.
problems.a: PEP carboxylase fixes CO2 in mesophyll and delivers it to bundle sheath cells, concentrating CO2 around RuBisCO and reducing photorespiration.

Visual lesson

Photosynthesis and respiration

Photosynthesis: 6 CO2 + 6 H2O + light -> C6H12O6 + 6 O2

minutes
formulas
Q&A

🔑

Big idea

  • Photosynthesis: 6 CO2 + 6 H2O + light -> C6H12O6 + 6 O2
  • Light reaction (thylakoid membranes): water splits, O2 released, ATP and NADPH made
  • Calvin cycle (stroma): CO2 fixed by RuBisCO into 3-PGA and then sugars
  • C4 plants (maize, sugarcane) use PEP carboxylase and show Kranz anatomy
Read the full explanation

Photosynthesis: 6 CO2 + 6 H2O + light -> C6H12O6 + 6 O2. Light reaction (thylakoid membranes): water splits, O2 released, ATP and NADPH made. Calvin cycle (stroma): CO2 fixed by RuBisCO into 3-PGA and then sugars. C4 plants (maize, sugarcane) use PEP carboxylase and show Kranz anatomy. Respiration: C6H12O6 + 6 O2 -> 6 CO2 + 6 H2O + energy. Glycolysis (cytoplasm) gives 2 ATP, 2 NADH and 2 pyruvate; Krebs cycle (mitochondrial matrix); electron transport chain (inner membrane) makes most ATP. Net about 30-32 ATP per glucose in eukaryotes (older textbooks say 36-38).

🎯 Remember Light reaction makes ATP and NADPH; Calvin cycle uses them.

lessons.title: Photosynthesis in Higher Plants
yt: class 11 biology photosynthesis in higher plants light reaction calvin cycle C4

blocks.x: Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy: 6CO2 + 12H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6H2O + 6O2. Early experiments: Priestley, Ingenhousz, Sachs, Engelmann, Van Niel, Hill, Calvin. Chloroplast pigments: chlorophyll a (bright blue-green), chlorophyll b, xanthophylls, carotenoids. Photosystem I (P700) and II (P680). Light reaction: photolysis of water, Z scheme, photophosphorylation (non-cyclic and cyclic), chemiosmotic hypothesis. Dark reaction (Calvin cycle): carboxylation by RuBisCO, reduction, regeneration of RuBP; C3 plants give 3-PGA. C4 pathway (Hatch and Slack): PEP carboxylase, Kranz anatomy, OAA. Photorespiration. Limiting factors (Blackman).
Deep dive: Light reaction

Photosystems: PS II has P680 reaction centre and splits water to give O2, protons and electrons. PS I has P700. Electrons from PS II pass via pheophytin, plastoquinone, cytochrome b6f, plastocyanin to PS I, then ferredoxin and NADP reductase to NADPH. Non-cyclic photophosphorylation produces ATP and NADPH; cyclic involves only PS I and gives ATP only. Chemiosmosis: protons accumulate in the lumen, ATP synthase CF0-CF1 makes ATP in stroma.
Deep dive: Calvin cycle and C4

Calvin cycle in stroma: carboxylation (CO2 + RuBP -> 2 PGA by RuBisCO), reduction (using 2 ATP and 2 NADPH per CO2 to give G3P), regeneration (1 ATP). For one glucose, 6 turns need 18 ATP and 12 NADPH. C4 plants (maize, sugarcane): mesophyll PEP carboxylase fixes CO2 into OAA, converted to malate or aspartate, transported to bundle sheath where decarboxylation releases CO2 for the Calvin cycle; no photorespiration; optimum temperature 30-45 C.
Deep dive: Photorespiration and factors

RuBisCO has oxygenase activity at high O2; the process occurs in chloroplast, peroxisome, mitochondria and wastes energy. Blackman law of limiting factors: light, CO2 concentration (0.03-0.04% atmospheric), temperature, water. C3 plants respond to rising CO2 up to 450 ppm, C4 saturate about 360 ppm. Red and blue wavelengths are most effective (action spectrum, Engelmann).

Photosynthesis in Higher Plants

Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy: 6CO2 + 12H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6H2O + 6O2

🔑

Big idea

  • Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy: 6CO2 + 12H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6H2O + 6O2
  • Early experiments: Priestley, Ingenhousz, Sachs, Engelmann, Van Niel, Hill, Calvin

Read the full explanation

Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy: 6CO2 + 12H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6H2O + 6O2. Early experiments: Priestley, Ingenhousz, Sachs, Engelmann, Van Niel, Hill, Calvin. Chloroplast pigments: chlorophyll a (bright blue-green), chlorophyll b, xanthophylls, carotenoids. Photosystem I (P700) and II (P680). Light reaction: photolysis of water, Z scheme, photophosphorylation (non-cyclic and cyclic), chemiosmotic hypothesis. Dark reaction (Calvin cycle): carboxylation by RuBisCO, reduction, regeneration of RuBP; C3 plants give 3-PGA. C4 pathway (Hatch and Slack): PEP carboxylase, Kranz anatomy, OAA. Photorespiration. Limiting factors (Blackman).

⚗️

Light reaction

  • Photosystems: PS II has P680 reaction centre and splits water to give O2, protons and electrons
  • PS I has P700
  • Electrons from PS II pass via pheophytin, plastoquinone, cytochrome b6f, plastocyanin to PS I, then ferredoxin and NADP reductase to NADPH
  • Non-cyclic photophosphorylation produces ATP and NADPH
Read the full explanation

Photosystems: PS II has P680 reaction centre and splits water to give O2, protons and electrons. PS I has P700. Electrons from PS II pass via pheophytin, plastoquinone, cytochrome b6f, plastocyanin to PS I, then ferredoxin and NADP reductase to NADPH. Non-cyclic photophosphorylation produces ATP and NADPH; cyclic involves only PS I and gives ATP only. Chemiosmosis: protons accumulate in the lumen, ATP synthase CF0-CF1 makes ATP in stroma.

🔄

Calvin cycle and C4

  • Calvin cycle in stroma: carboxylation (CO2 + RuBP -> 2 PGA by RuBisCO), reduction (using 2 ATP and 2 NADPH per CO2 to give G3P), regeneration (1 ATP)
  • For one glucose, 6 turns need 18 ATP and 12 NADPH
  • C4 plants (maize, sugarcane): mesophyll PEP carboxylase fixes CO2 into OAA, converted to malate or aspartate, transported to bundle sheath where…
  • No photorespiration
Read the full explanation

Calvin cycle in stroma: carboxylation (CO2 + RuBP -> 2 PGA by RuBisCO), reduction (using 2 ATP and 2 NADPH per CO2 to give G3P), regeneration (1 ATP). For one glucose, 6 turns need 18 ATP and 12 NADPH. C4 plants (maize, sugarcane): mesophyll PEP carboxylase fixes CO2 into OAA, converted to malate or aspartate, transported to bundle sheath where decarboxylation releases CO2 for the Calvin cycle; no photorespiration; optimum temperature 30-45 C.

🌟

Photorespiration and factors

  • RuBisCO has oxygenase activity at high O2
  • The process occurs in chloroplast, peroxisome, mitochondria and wastes energy
  • Blackman law of limiting factors: light, CO2 concentration (0.03-0.04% atmospheric), temperature, water
  • C3 plants respond to rising CO2 up to 450 ppm, C4 saturate about 360 ppm
Read the full explanation

RuBisCO has oxygenase activity at high O2; the process occurs in chloroplast, peroxisome, mitochondria and wastes energy. Blackman law of limiting factors: light, CO2 concentration (0.03-0.04% atmospheric), temperature, water. C3 plants respond to rising CO2 up to 450 ppm, C4 saturate about 360 ppm. Red and blue wavelengths are most effective (action spectrum, Engelmann).

lessons.title: Respiration in Plants
yt: class 11 biology respiration in plants glycolysis krebs cycle ETS

blocks.x: Cellular respiration oxidises organic food to release energy stored as ATP. Glycolysis (EMP pathway) in cytoplasm: glucose to 2 pyruvate, net 2 ATP and 2 NADH. Aerobic: pyruvate to acetyl CoA (link reaction), Krebs cycle in the matrix (3 NADH, 1 FADH2, 1 GTP per turn), electron transport system on the inner mitochondrial membrane with oxidative phosphorylation. Anaerobic: fermentation (alcohol by yeast, lactic acid in muscles). Respiratory quotient RQ = CO2 released / O2 consumed; 1 for carbohydrates, <1 for fats, >1 for organic acids. Net gain from glucose about 30-38 ATP.
Deep dive: Glycolysis and fermentation

Glycolysis occurs in all living cells. Steps: phosphorylation to glucose-6-phosphate, fructose 1,6-bisphosphate, splitting into DHAP and PGAL, oxidation to 1,3-BPGA with NADH, substrate level phosphorylation making ATP, finally pyruvate. Net 2 ATP, 2 NADH. Fermentation in yeast gives ethanol and CO2 (pyruvate decarboxylase, alcohol dehydrogenase), 2 ATP only; in muscles lactic acid (lactate dehydrogenase). Fermentation releases less than 7% of energy of glucose.
Deep dive: Krebs cycle and ETS

Pyruvate enters mitochondria; pyruvate dehydrogenase gives acetyl CoA, NADH and CO2. Krebs cycle: acetyl CoA + oxaloacetic acid -> citric acid; steps release 2 CO2, 3 NADH, 1 FADH2 and 1 ATP/GTP per turn. ETS: complexes I to IV, ubiquinone, cytochrome c; oxygen is the final acceptor forming water; ATP synthase (F0F1) by chemiosmosis. NADH gives about 2.5 ATP, FADH2 about 1.5 ATP.
Deep dive: Respiratory balance sheet and RQ

Per glucose: glycolysis 2 ATP (+2 NADH), link 2 NADH, Krebs 2 ATP + 6 NADH + 2 FADH2; total about 30 ATP (modern) or 38 (older). Amphibolic pathway: respiration involves both catabolism and anabolism (fatty acid breakdown and synthesis). RQ: glucose 1.0; fats about 0.7; proteins about 0.9; tripalmitin 0.7; oxalic acid 4.0.

🔑

Big idea

  • Cellular respiration oxidises organic food to release energy stored as ATP
  • Glycolysis (EMP pathway) in cytoplasm: glucose to 2 pyruvate, net 2 ATP and 2 NADH
  • Aerobic: pyruvate to acetyl CoA (link reaction), Krebs cycle in the matrix (3 NADH, 1 FADH2, 1 GTP per turn), electron transport system on the inner…
  • Anaerobic: fermentation (alcohol by yeast, lactic acid in muscles)
Read the full explanation

Cellular respiration oxidises organic food to release energy stored as ATP. Glycolysis (EMP pathway) in cytoplasm: glucose to 2 pyruvate, net 2 ATP and 2 NADH. Aerobic: pyruvate to acetyl CoA (link reaction), Krebs cycle in the matrix (3 NADH, 1 FADH2, 1 GTP per turn), electron transport system on the inner mitochondrial membrane with oxidative phosphorylation. Anaerobic: fermentation (alcohol by yeast, lactic acid in muscles). Respiratory quotient RQ = CO2 released / O2 consumed; 1 for carbohydrates, <1 for fats, >1 for organic acids. Net gain from glucose about 30-38 ATP.

📌

Glycolysis and fermentation

  • Glycolysis occurs in all living cells
  • Steps: phosphorylation to glucose-6-phosphate, fructose 1,6-bisphosphate, splitting into DHAP and PGAL, oxidation to 1,3-BPGA with NADH, substrate…
  • Net 2 ATP, 2 NADH
  • Fermentation in yeast gives ethanol and CO2 (pyruvate decarboxylase, alcohol dehydrogenase), 2 ATP only
Read the full explanation

Glycolysis occurs in all living cells. Steps: phosphorylation to glucose-6-phosphate, fructose 1,6-bisphosphate, splitting into DHAP and PGAL, oxidation to 1,3-BPGA with NADH, substrate level phosphorylation making ATP, finally pyruvate. Net 2 ATP, 2 NADH. Fermentation in yeast gives ethanol and CO2 (pyruvate decarboxylase, alcohol dehydrogenase), 2 ATP only; in muscles lactic acid (lactate dehydrogenase). Fermentation releases less than 7% of energy of glucose.

🔄

Krebs cycle and ETS

  • Pyruvate enters mitochondria
  • Pyruvate dehydrogenase gives acetyl CoA, NADH and CO2
  • Krebs cycle: acetyl CoA + oxaloacetic acid -> citric acid
  • Steps release 2 CO2, 3 NADH, 1 FADH2 and 1 ATP/GTP per turn
Read the full explanation

Pyruvate enters mitochondria; pyruvate dehydrogenase gives acetyl CoA, NADH and CO2. Krebs cycle: acetyl CoA + oxaloacetic acid -> citric acid; steps release 2 CO2, 3 NADH, 1 FADH2 and 1 ATP/GTP per turn. ETS: complexes I to IV, ubiquinone, cytochrome c; oxygen is the final acceptor forming water; ATP synthase (F0F1) by chemiosmosis. NADH gives about 2.5 ATP, FADH2 about 1.5 ATP.

🌟

Respiratory balance sheet and RQ

  • Per glucose: glycolysis 2 ATP (+2 NADH), link 2 NADH, Krebs 2 ATP + 6 NADH + 2 FADH2
  • Total about 30 ATP (modern) or 38 (older)
  • Amphibolic pathway: respiration involves both catabolism and anabolism (fatty acid breakdown and synthesis)
  • RQ: glucose 1.0
Read the full explanation

Per glucose: glycolysis 2 ATP (+2 NADH), link 2 NADH, Krebs 2 ATP + 6 NADH + 2 FADH2; total about 30 ATP (modern) or 38 (older). Amphibolic pathway: respiration involves both catabolism and anabolism (fatty acid breakdown and synthesis). RQ: glucose 1.0; fats about 0.7; proteins about 0.9; tripalmitin 0.7; oxalic acid 4.0.

lessons.title: Plant Growth and Development
yt: class 11 biology plant growth and development hormones auxin gibberellin

blocks.x: Growth is an irreversible permanent increase in size. Phases: meristematic, elongation, maturation; sigmoid curve; arithmetic and geometric growth. Differentiation, dedifferentiation, redifferentiation. Plant growth regulators: auxins (IAA, IBA, NAA, 2,4-D), gibberellins (GA3), cytokinins (zeatin, kinetin), ethylene, abscisic acid (ABA). Photoperiodism: short-day, long-day, day-neutral plants; phytochrome. Vernalisation. Seed dormancy and germination.
Deep dive: Growth and development

Growth rate: arithmetic (linear), geometric (exponential, Wt = W0 e^rt). Relative growth rate. Conditions: water, oxygen, nutrients, temperature. Development includes growth and differentiation. Plasticity: heterophylly (cotton, coriander, larkspur). Open form of growth: meristems throughout life.
Deep dive: Plant growth regulators

Auxin: discovered by Darwin and Went; apical dominance, root initiation, parthenocarpy, weed killer (2,4-D). Gibberellins: bolting in cabbage, elongation of sugarcane stem, seedless grapes, malting. Cytokinins: cell division, delay senescence, overcome apical dominance, Skoog and Miller. Ethylene: fruit ripening, abscission, in Cranberry; ethephon. ABA: stress hormone, stomatal closure, seed dormancy.
Deep dive: Photoperiodism and vernalisation

Short day plants: Xanthium, rice, chrysanthemum flower when night exceeds a critical length; long day plants: wheat, spinach. Phytochrome Pr and Pfr senses red/far-red light. Vernalisation: low temperature promotes flowering (winter wheat, barley). Florigen was proposed as a flowering hormone. Seed dormancy broken by scarification, stratification, GA.
Hindi saransh
Paudha vriddhi niyamak: auxin, gibberelin, saitokinin, ethylene, ABA. Prakashkalavadhi: chhote din, lambe din. Vasantikaran.
Auxin causes apical dominance; cytokinin overcomes it.

Visual lesson

Plant Growth and Development

Growth is an irreversible permanent increase in size

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Growth and development›3Plant growth regulators›4Photoperiodism and…
🔑

Big idea

  • Growth is an irreversible permanent increase in size
  • Phases: meristematic, elongation, maturation
  • Sigmoid curve
  • Arithmetic and geometric growth
Read the full explanation

Growth is an irreversible permanent increase in size. Phases: meristematic, elongation, maturation; sigmoid curve; arithmetic and geometric growth. Differentiation, dedifferentiation, redifferentiation. Plant growth regulators: auxins (IAA, IBA, NAA, 2,4-D), gibberellins (GA3), cytokinins (zeatin, kinetin), ethylene, abscisic acid (ABA). Photoperiodism: short-day, long-day, day-neutral plants; phytochrome. Vernalisation. Seed dormancy and germination.

📌

Growth and development

  • Growth rate: arithmetic (linear), geometric (exponential, Wt = W0 e^rt)
  • Relative growth rate
  • Conditions: water, oxygen, nutrients, temperature
  • Development includes growth and differentiation
Read the full explanation

Growth rate: arithmetic (linear), geometric (exponential, Wt = W0 e^rt). Relative growth rate. Conditions: water, oxygen, nutrients, temperature. Development includes growth and differentiation. Plasticity: heterophylly (cotton, coriander, larkspur). Open form of growth: meristems throughout life.

🧬

Plant growth regulators

  • Auxin: discovered by Darwin and Went
  • Apical dominance, root initiation, parthenocarpy, weed killer (2,4-D)
  • Gibberellins: bolting in cabbage, elongation of sugarcane stem, seedless grapes, malting
  • Cytokinins: cell division, delay senescence, overcome apical dominance, Skoog and Miller
Read the full explanation

Auxin: discovered by Darwin and Went; apical dominance, root initiation, parthenocarpy, weed killer (2,4-D). Gibberellins: bolting in cabbage, elongation of sugarcane stem, seedless grapes, malting. Cytokinins: cell division, delay senescence, overcome apical dominance, Skoog and Miller. Ethylene: fruit ripening, abscission, in Cranberry; ethephon. ABA: stress hormone, stomatal closure, seed dormancy.

🌟

Photoperiodism and vernalisation

  • Short day plants: Xanthium, rice, chrysanthemum flower when night exceeds a critical length
  • Long day plants: wheat, spinach
  • Phytochrome Pr and Pfr senses red/far-red light
  • Vernalisation: low temperature promotes flowering (winter wheat, barley)
Read the full explanation

Short day plants: Xanthium, rice, chrysanthemum flower when night exceeds a critical length; long day plants: wheat, spinach. Phytochrome Pr and Pfr senses red/far-red light. Vernalisation: low temperature promotes flowering (winter wheat, barley). Florigen was proposed as a flowering hormone. Seed dormancy broken by scarification, stratification, GA.

🧮

lessons.title: Human circulation and breathing
yt: human heart circulation class 11

blocks.x: The heart has four chambers: two atria and two ventricles. Blood flows right atrium -> right ventricle -> lungs (pulmonary circulation) -> left atrium -> left ventricle -> body (systemic circulation). The **SA node** is the pacemaker. Normal heart rate about 72 beats/min; cardiac output = heart rate x stroke volume = 72 x 70 mL = about **5 L/min**. **ECG:** P wave (atrial depolarisation), QRS complex (ventricular depolarisation), T wave (ventricular repolarisation). **Breathing:** inspiration uses the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles; tidal volume 500 mL; vital capacity about 3.5 to 4.5 L. O2 is carried by haemoglobin; most CO2 is carried as bicarbonate.
Hindi saransh
Dil ke 4 chambers hote hain. SA node pacemaker hai. Cardiac output = heart rate x stroke volume.
The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood and the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood: the opposite of the usual artery/vein rule.

lessons.title: Breathing and Exchange of Gases
yt: class 11 biology breathing and exchange of gases lungs oxygen transport

blocks.x: Respiratory system: nostrils, nasal chamber, pharynx, larynx (sound box), trachea with C-shaped cartilage rings, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli. Lungs enclosed in double pleura. Inspiration: diaphragm contracts and external intercostals contract, thoracic volume increases and pressure falls. Expiration reverses. Volumes: TV 500 mL, IRV 2500-3000 mL, ERV 1000-1100 mL, RV 1100-1200 mL; VC = IRV + TV + ERV about 3500-4500 mL; TLC about 5800-6000 mL. Gas exchange by diffusion across the alveolar membrane; pO2 alveoli 104 mm Hg, pCO2 40. Oxygen carried as oxyhaemoglobin (97%); CO2 as bicarbonate (70%), carbamino-haemoglobin (20-25%), dissolved (7%). Bohr effect. Respiratory regulation by the medulla rhythm centre, pneumotaxic centre. Disorders: asthma, emphysema, occupational lung disease.
Deep dive: Mechanism of breathing

Boyle law: volume and pressure are inversely related. Inspiration: diaphragm flattens, ribs and sternum move up and out, lung volume increases, intra-pulmonary pressure falls below atmosphere and air enters. Expiration: relaxation of muscles; pressure rises. About 12-16 breaths per minute. Pulmonary ventilation = TV x rate = about 6000-8000 mL/min. Spirometer measures volumes. Functional residual capacity = ERV + RV. Inspiratory capacity = TV + IRV. Expiratory capacity = TV + ERV.
Deep dive: Gas exchange and transport

Partial pressures: atmosphere pO2 159, alveoli 104, deoxygenated blood 40, oxygenated 95; pCO2: alveoli 40, deoxygenated blood 45, tissues 45. CO2 solubility is 20-25 times that of O2. Diffusion membrane: squamous epithelium of alveoli, endothelium of capillaries and basement substance; thickness less than 1 mm. Oxygen dissociation curve is sigmoid; low pCO2, high pH, lower temperature, fewer 2,3-BPG shift curve left; opposite shifts right (Bohr effect). Carbonic anhydrase makes CO2 + H2O -> H2CO3 -> H+ + HCO3-; chloride shift.
Deep dive: Regulation and disorders

Rhythm centre in medulla; pneumotaxic centre in pons moderates; chemosensitive area adjacent to rhythm centre is sensitive to CO2 and H+; receptors in aortic arch and carotid artery. Asthma: inflammation of bronchi; emphysema: damaged alveolar walls, major cause cigarette smoking; occupational lung disease from dust (silicosis, asbestosis). Hypoxia and carbon monoxide poisoning (CO binds Hb 200 times more strongly).
Hindi saransh
Shwasan aur gaison ka vinimay: fephde, alveoli, aaytan shwasan ka maapan. Oxyhaemoglobin 97%, CO2 bicarbonate roop mein 70%.
Vital capacity is IRV + ERV + TV.

Big idea

  • Respiratory system: nostrils, nasal chamber, pharynx, larynx (sound box), trachea with C-shaped cartilage rings, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli
  • Lungs enclosed in double pleura
  • Inspiration: diaphragm contracts and external intercostals contract, thoracic volume increases and pressure falls
  • Expiration reverses
Read the full explanation

Respiratory system: nostrils, nasal chamber, pharynx, larynx (sound box), trachea with C-shaped cartilage rings, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli. Lungs enclosed in double pleura. Inspiration: diaphragm contracts and external intercostals contract, thoracic volume increases and pressure falls. Expiration reverses. Volumes: TV 500 mL, IRV 2500-3000 mL, ERV 1000-1100 mL, RV 1100-1200 mL; VC = IRV + TV + ERV about 3500-4500 mL; TLC about 5800-6000 mL. Gas exchange by diffusion across the alveolar membrane; pO2 alveoli 104 mm Hg, pCO2 40.   • Boyle law: volume and pressure are inversely related
  • Inspiration: diaphragm flattens, ribs and sternum move up and out, lung volume increases, intra-pulmonary pressure falls below atmosphere and air…
  • Expiration: relaxation of muscles

Inspiration: diaphragm flattens, ribs and sternum move up and out, lung volume increases, intra-pulmonary pressure falls below atmosphere and air enters. Expiration: relaxation of muscles; pressure rises. About 12-16 breaths per minute. Pulmonary ventilation = TV x rate = about 6000-8000 mL/min. Spirometer measures volumes. Functional residual capacity = ERV + RV. Inspiratory capacity = TV + IRV. Expiratory capacity = TV + ERV.

lessons.title: Body Fluids and Circulation
yt: class 11 biology body fluids and circulation blood heart ECG lymph

blocks.x: Blood is a fluid connective tissue: plasma (55%, water 90-92%, proteins fibrinogen, globulin, albumin) and formed elements (RBC, WBC, platelets). RBC (5-5.5 million/mm3) lack nucleus and contain Hb (12-16 g/100 mL). WBC: granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils) and agranulocytes (lymphocytes, monocytes). Blood groups ABO and Rh; Landsteiner. Coagulation: thromboplastin, prothrombin to thrombin, fibrinogen to fibrin. Lymph. Heart: four chambers, SA node (pacemaker), AV node, bundle of His, Purkinje fibres. Cardiac output = stroke volume x heart rate (5 L/min). ECG waves P, QRS, T. Double circulation. Disorders: hypertension (120/80 normal), coronary artery disease, angina, heart failure.
Deep dive: Blood and groups

Plasma without clotting factors is serum. Albumin maintains osmotic balance; globulins defence; fibrinogen clotting. Neutrophils (60-65%) are phagocytic; lymphocytes (20-25%) are B and T cells. Platelets 1.5-3.5 lakh/mm3. ABO: A antigen/anti-B, B/anti-A, AB universal recipient, O universal donor. Rh factor: Rh-positive 80%; erythroblastosis foetalis when Rh-negative mother carries Rh-positive foetus. Coagulation cascade involves calcium ions and factors.
Deep dive: Heart and cardiac cycle

Heart is mesodermal, in the thoracic cavity, enclosed in the pericardium. Right atrium receives deoxygenated blood via superior and inferior vena cava; tricuspid valve; right ventricle to pulmonary artery. Left atrium receives pulmonary veins; bicuspid (mitral) valve; left ventricle to aorta. Nodal tissue: SA node generates 70-75 impulses/min; AV node; AV bundle; Purkinje fibres. Cardiac cycle about 0.8 s: atrial systole 0.1 s, ventricular systole 0.3 s, joint diastole 0.4 s. Heart sounds: lub (closure of AV valves) and dub (closure of semilunar valves). ECG: P wave atrial depolarisation, QRS ventricular depolarisation, T ventricular repolarisation.
Deep dive: Circulation and disorders

Double circulation: pulmonary and systemic; hepatic portal circulation; coronary circulation. Open circulation in arthropods, closed in annelids and vertebrates. Fish have single circulation. Lymph: colourless, lymphocytes, drains tissue fluid, carries fats absorbed (lacteals). Regulation: neural (medulla cardiac centres, sympathetic increases rate, parasympathetic decreases) and hormonal (adrenaline). Disorders: hypertension above 140/90; atherosclerosis; angina; heart failure (congestive); cardiac arrest.

Visual lesson

Body Fluids and Circulation

Blood is a fluid connective tissue: plasma (55%, water 90-92%, proteins fibrinogen, globulin, albumin) and formed elements (RBC, WBC, platelets)

Q&A

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Blood and groups›3Heart and cardiac cycle›4Circulation and disorders
Atrial systole0.1 s
Ventricular systole0.3 s
Joint diastole0.4 s
🔑

Big idea

  • Blood is a fluid connective tissue: plasma (55%, water 90-92%, proteins fibrinogen, globulin, albumin) and formed elements (RBC, WBC, platelets)
  • RBC (5-5.5 million/mm3) lack nucleus and contain Hb (12-16 g/100 mL)
  • WBC: granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils) and agranulocytes (lymphocytes, monocytes)
  • Blood groups ABO and Rh
Read the full explanation

Blood is a fluid connective tissue: plasma (55%, water 90-92%, proteins fibrinogen, globulin, albumin) and formed elements (RBC, WBC, platelets). RBC (5-5.5 million/mm3) lack nucleus and contain Hb (12-16 g/100 mL). WBC: granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils) and agranulocytes (lymphocytes, monocytes). Blood groups ABO and Rh; Landsteiner. Coagulation: thromboplastin, prothrombin to thrombin, fibrinogen to fibrin. Lymph. Heart: four chambers, SA node (pacemaker), AV node, bundle of His, Purkinje fibres. Cardiac output = stroke volume x heart rate (5 L/min). ECG waves P, QRS, T. Double circulation. Disorders: hypertension (120/80 normal), coronary artery disease, angina, heart failure.

📌

Blood and groups

  • Plasma without clotting factors is serum
  • Albumin maintains osmotic balance
  • Globulins defence
  • Fibrinogen clotting
Read the full explanation

Plasma without clotting factors is serum. Albumin maintains osmotic balance; globulins defence; fibrinogen clotting. Neutrophils (60-65%) are phagocytic; lymphocytes (20-25%) are B and T cells. Platelets 1.5-3.5 lakh/mm3. ABO: A antigen/anti-B, B/anti-A, AB universal recipient, O universal donor. Rh factor: Rh-positive 80%; erythroblastosis foetalis when Rh-negative mother carries Rh-positive foetus. Coagulation cascade involves calcium ions and factors.

🔄

Heart and cardiac cycle

  • Heart is mesodermal, in the thoracic cavity, enclosed in the pericardium
  • Right atrium receives deoxygenated blood via superior and inferior vena cava
  • Tricuspid valve
  • Right ventricle to pulmonary artery
Read the full explanation

Heart is mesodermal, in the thoracic cavity, enclosed in the pericardium. Right atrium receives deoxygenated blood via superior and inferior vena cava; tricuspid valve; right ventricle to pulmonary artery. Left atrium receives pulmonary veins; bicuspid (mitral) valve; left ventricle to aorta. Nodal tissue: SA node generates 70-75 impulses/min; AV node; AV bundle; Purkinje fibres. Cardiac cycle about 0.8 s: atrial systole 0.1 s, ventricular systole 0.3 s, joint diastole 0.4 s. Heart sounds: lub (closure of AV valves) and dub (closure of semilunar valves). ECG: P wave atrial depolarisation, QRS ventricular depolarisation, T ventricular repolarisation.

🌟

Circulation and disorders

  • Double circulation: pulmonary and systemic
  • Hepatic portal circulation
  • Coronary circulation
  • Open circulation in arthropods, closed in annelids and vertebrates
Read the full explanation

Double circulation: pulmonary and systemic; hepatic portal circulation; coronary circulation. Open circulation in arthropods, closed in annelids and vertebrates. Fish have single circulation. Lymph: colourless, lymphocytes, drains tissue fluid, carries fats absorbed (lacteals). Regulation: neural (medulla cardiac centres, sympathetic increases rate, parasympathetic decreases) and hormonal (adrenaline). Disorders: hypertension above 140/90; atherosclerosis; angina; heart failure (congestive); cardiac arrest.

lessons.title: Excretory Products and their Elimination
yt: class 11 biology excretory products kidney nephron urine formation

blocks.x: Ammonotelic (aquatic animals), ureotelic (mammals) and uricotelic (birds, reptiles, insects) excretion. Human excretory system: kidneys, ureters, bladder, urethra. Nephron: Malpighian body (glomerulus + Bowman capsule) and renal tubule (PCT, loop of Henle, DCT, collecting duct). Cortical (85%) and juxtamedullary nephrons. Urine formation: glomerular filtration (GFR 125 mL/min, 180 L/day), reabsorption, secretion. Counter-current mechanism concentrates urine (osmolarity 1200 mOsm/L). Regulation: ADH, RAAS (JGA, renin, angiotensin II, aldosterone), ANF. Micturition. Disorders: uremia, renal calculi, glomerulonephritis; haemodialysis; kidney transplant.
Deep dive: Nephron and urine formation

Each kidney has about one million nephrons. Podocytes in Bowman capsule form filtration slits; filtration is ultrafiltration through three layers: endothelium, basement membrane, podocytes. PCT reabsorbs nearly all glucose, amino acids, 70-80% of electrolytes and water, and secretes H+, K+ and ammonia. Descending limb permeable to water; ascending limb impermeable to water but transports electrolytes. DCT conditionally reabsorbs Na+ and water, reabsorbs HCO3-. Collecting duct reabsorbs water, urea. Urine is 1-1.5 L/day, pH 6.0, with urea 25-30 g/day.
Deep dive: Concentration and regulation

Counter-current mechanism: loop of Henle (counter-current flow) and vasa recta; NaCl and urea create the osmotic gradient in medullary interstitium up to 1200 mOsm/L. ADH from the neurohypophysis increases water permeability; low ADH gives diabetes insipidus. JG cells release renin when GFR falls: renin converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I and then II, which constricts vessels, stimulates aldosterone and Na+ reabsorption. ANF from the atria causes vasodilation and decreases RAAS.
Deep dive: Other organs and disorders

Lungs remove CO2 (200 mL/min) and water; liver secretes bilirubin, cholesterol, degraded steroid hormones; skin sweat glands remove NaCl, urea, lactic acid; sebaceous glands sterols. Micturition is a reflex: stretch receptors send signals to the CNS, smooth muscle contraction. Uremia (urea accumulation) may cause kidney failure; haemodialysis removes urea using cellophane tubing, heparin as an anticoagulant. Glomerulonephritis inflames glomeruli. Renal calculi are stone masses of crystallised oxalates. Kidney transplant is the best long-term remedy.

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Excretory Products and their Elimination

Ammonotelic (aquatic animals), ureotelic (mammals) and uricotelic (birds, reptiles, insects) excretion

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Nephron and urine formation›3Concentration and regulation›4Other organs and disorders
🔑

Big idea

  • Ammonotelic (aquatic animals), ureotelic (mammals) and uricotelic (birds, reptiles, insects) excretion
  • Human excretory system: kidneys, ureters, bladder, urethra
  • Nephron: Malpighian body (glomerulus + Bowman capsule) and renal tubule (PCT, loop of Henle, DCT, collecting duct)
  • Cortical (85%) and juxtamedullary nephrons
Read the full explanation

Ammonotelic (aquatic animals), ureotelic (mammals) and uricotelic (birds, reptiles, insects) excretion. Human excretory system: kidneys, ureters, bladder, urethra. Nephron: Malpighian body (glomerulus + Bowman capsule) and renal tubule (PCT, loop of Henle, DCT, collecting duct). Cortical (85%) and juxtamedullary nephrons. Urine formation: glomerular filtration (GFR 125 mL/min, 180 L/day), reabsorption, secretion. Counter-current mechanism concentrates urine (osmolarity 1200 mOsm/L). Regulation: ADH, RAAS (JGA, renin, angiotensin II, aldosterone), ANF. Micturition. Disorders: uremia, renal calculi, glomerulonephritis; haemodialysis; kidney transplant.

📌

Nephron and urine formation

  • Each kidney has about one million nephrons
  • Podocytes in Bowman capsule form filtration slits
  • Filtration is ultrafiltration through three layers: endothelium, basement membrane, podocytes
  • PCT reabsorbs nearly all glucose, amino acids, 70-80% of electrolytes and water, and secretes H+, K+ and ammonia
Read the full explanation

Each kidney has about one million nephrons. Podocytes in Bowman capsule form filtration slits; filtration is ultrafiltration through three layers: endothelium, basement membrane, podocytes. PCT reabsorbs nearly all glucose, amino acids, 70-80% of electrolytes and water, and secretes H+, K+ and ammonia. Descending limb permeable to water; ascending limb impermeable to water but transports electrolytes. DCT conditionally reabsorbs Na+ and water, reabsorbs HCO3-. Collecting duct reabsorbs water, urea. Urine is 1-1.5 L/day, pH 6.0, with urea 25-30 g/day.

🧠

Concentration and regulation

  • Counter-current mechanism: loop of Henle (counter-current flow) and vasa recta
  • NaCl and urea create the osmotic gradient in medullary interstitium up to 1200 mOsm/L
  • ADH from the neurohypophysis increases water permeability
  • Low ADH gives diabetes insipidus
Read the full explanation

Counter-current mechanism: loop of Henle (counter-current flow) and vasa recta; NaCl and urea create the osmotic gradient in medullary interstitium up to 1200 mOsm/L. ADH from the neurohypophysis increases water permeability; low ADH gives diabetes insipidus. JG cells release renin when GFR falls: renin converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I and then II, which constricts vessels, stimulates aldosterone and Na+ reabsorption. ANF from the atria causes vasodilation and decreases RAAS.

🧬

Other organs and disorders

  • Lungs remove CO2 (200 mL/min) and water
  • Liver secretes bilirubin, cholesterol, degraded steroid hormones
  • Skin sweat glands remove NaCl, urea, lactic acid
  • Sebaceous glands sterols
Read the full explanation

Lungs remove CO2 (200 mL/min) and water; liver secretes bilirubin, cholesterol, degraded steroid hormones; skin sweat glands remove NaCl, urea, lactic acid; sebaceous glands sterols. Micturition is a reflex: stretch receptors send signals to the CNS, smooth muscle contraction. Uremia (urea accumulation) may cause kidney failure; haemodialysis removes urea using cellophane tubing, heparin as an anticoagulant. Glomerulonephritis inflames glomeruli. Renal calculi are stone masses of crystallised oxalates. Kidney transplant is the best long-term remedy.

🧮

lessons.title: Locomotion and Movement
yt: class 11 biology locomotion and movement muscle skeleton joints

blocks.x: Types of movement: amoeboid, ciliary, muscular. Muscle: skeletal (striated, voluntary), visceral (smooth), cardiac. Skeletal muscle ultrastructure: sarcomere (between two Z lines), A band (myosin), I band (actin), H zone, M line. Sliding filament theory (Huxley): actin slides over myosin; cross-bridges; ATP and Ca2+; troponin, tropomyosin. Neuromuscular junction, acetylcholine. Red fibres (myoglobin) and white fibres. Human skeleton: 206 bones; axial 80, appendicular 126; skull 29, vertebral column 26, ribs 12 pairs, sternum, girdles. Joints: fibrous, cartilaginous, synovial (ball and socket, hinge, pivot, gliding, saddle). Disorders: myasthenia gravis, tetany, muscular dystrophy, arthritis, osteoporosis, gout.
Deep dive: Muscle structure and contraction

Muscle fibre has sarcolemma, sarcoplasm, sarcoplasmic reticulum (stores Ca2+), myofibrils. Thick filaments of myosin with head and tail (meromyosins, ATPase); thin filaments of actin with tropomyosin and troponin. Contraction: signal from CNS releases ACh at the motor end plate, action potential, Ca2+ release, binds troponin, exposes myosin binding sites, cross-bridge forms, ATP hydrolysed, actin pulled to centre, I bands shorten, A band stays same. Relaxation: Ca2+ pumped back. Rigor mortis, muscle fatigue due to lactic acid. Red fibres have more mitochondria and myoglobin.
Deep dive: Skeletal system

Axial skeleton 80 bones: skull (cranial 8 and facial 14, hyoid 1, ear ossicles 6), vertebral column (7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral fused, 4 coccygeal fused), sternum 1, ribs 24. Appendicular 126: pectoral girdle (clavicle and scapula), upper limb 30 each, pelvic girdle, lower limb 30 each. Ribs: true (7 pairs), false (3 pairs), floating (2 pairs). Glenoid cavity and acetabulum articulate with humerus and femur. Patella is the knee cap.
Deep dive: Joints and disorders

Fibrous joints: sutures of skull. Cartilaginous: between vertebrae. Synovial: synovial fluid; ball and socket (shoulder, hip), hinge (knee, elbow), pivot (atlas-axis), gliding (carpals), saddle (carpo-metacarpal of thumb). Myasthenia gravis: autoimmune, neuromuscular junction; tetany: low Ca2+; muscular dystrophy: genetic progressive degeneration; arthritis: joint inflammation; osteoporosis: reduced bone mass with age and oestrogen decline; gout: uric acid crystals in joints.

Chalan aur gati: peshi, kankal tantra, sandhiyan. Sarkomiyar mein actin aur myosin; sliding filament sidhant.

Locomotion and Movement

Types of movement: amoeboid, ciliary, muscular

🔑

Big idea

  • Types of movement: amoeboid, ciliary, muscular
  • Muscle: skeletal (striated, voluntary), visceral (smooth), cardiac
  • Skeletal muscle ultrastructure: sarcomere (between two Z lines), A band (myosin), I band (actin), H zone, M line
  • Sliding filament theory (Huxley): actin slides over myosin
Read the full explanation

Types of movement: amoeboid, ciliary, muscular. Muscle: skeletal (striated, voluntary), visceral (smooth), cardiac. Skeletal muscle ultrastructure: sarcomere (between two Z lines), A band (myosin), I band (actin), H zone, M line. Sliding filament theory (Huxley): actin slides over myosin; cross-bridges; ATP and Ca2+; troponin, tropomyosin. Neuromuscular junction, acetylcholine. Red fibres (myoglobin) and white fibres. Human skeleton: 206 bones; axial 80, appendicular 126; skull 29, vertebral column 26, ribs 12 pairs, sternum, girdles. Joints: fibrous, cartilaginous, synovial (ball and socket, hinge, pivot, gliding, saddle). Disorders: myasthenia gravis, tetany, muscular dystrophy, arthritis, osteoporosis, gout.

📌

Muscle structure and contraction

  • Muscle fibre has sarcolemma, sarcoplasm, sarcoplasmic reticulum (stores Ca2+), myofibrils
  • Thick filaments of myosin with head and tail (meromyosins, ATPase)
  • Thin filaments of actin with tropomyosin and troponin
  • Contraction: signal from CNS releases ACh at the motor end plate, action potential, Ca2+ release, binds troponin, exposes myosin binding sites…
Read the full explanation

Muscle fibre has sarcolemma, sarcoplasm, sarcoplasmic reticulum (stores Ca2+), myofibrils. Thick filaments of myosin with head and tail (meromyosins, ATPase); thin filaments of actin with tropomyosin and troponin. Contraction: signal from CNS releases ACh at the motor end plate, action potential, Ca2+ release, binds troponin, exposes myosin binding sites, cross-bridge forms, ATP hydrolysed, actin pulled to centre, I bands shorten, A band stays same. Relaxation: Ca2+ pumped back. Rigor mortis, muscle fatigue due to lactic acid. Red fibres have more mitochondria and myoglobin.

🧠

Skeletal system

  • Axial skeleton 80 bones: skull (cranial 8 and facial 14, hyoid 1, ear ossicles 6), vertebral column (7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral…
  • Appendicular 126: pectoral girdle (clavicle and scapula), upper limb 30 each, pelvic girdle, lower limb 30 each
  • Ribs: true (7 pairs), false (3 pairs), floating (2 pairs)
  • Glenoid cavity and acetabulum articulate with humerus and femur
Read the full explanation

Axial skeleton 80 bones: skull (cranial 8 and facial 14, hyoid 1, ear ossicles 6), vertebral column (7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral fused, 4 coccygeal fused), sternum 1, ribs 24. Appendicular 126: pectoral girdle (clavicle and scapula), upper limb 30 each, pelvic girdle, lower limb 30 each. Ribs: true (7 pairs), false (3 pairs), floating (2 pairs). Glenoid cavity and acetabulum articulate with humerus and femur. Patella is the knee cap.

🌟

Joints and disorders

  • Fibrous joints: sutures of skull
  • Cartilaginous: between vertebrae
  • Synovial: synovial fluid
  • Ball and socket (shoulder, hip), hinge (knee, elbow), pivot (atlas-axis), gliding (carpals), saddle (carpo-metacarpal of thumb)
Read the full explanation

Fibrous joints: sutures of skull. Cartilaginous: between vertebrae. Synovial: synovial fluid; ball and socket (shoulder, hip), hinge (knee, elbow), pivot (atlas-axis), gliding (carpals), saddle (carpo-metacarpal of thumb). Myasthenia gravis: autoimmune, neuromuscular junction; tetany: low Ca2+; muscular dystrophy: genetic progressive degeneration; arthritis: joint inflammation; osteoporosis: reduced bone mass with age and oestrogen decline; gout: uric acid crystals in joints.
