lessons.title: Neural Control and Coordination
yt: class 11 biology neural control and coordination neuron brain reflex action potential

blocks.x: Neuron: dendrites, cell body, axon; myelinated and non-myelinated; unipolar, bipolar, multipolar. Resting potential -70 mV maintained by Na+-K+ pump. Action potential: depolarisation, repolarisation, hyperpolarisation; all-or-none. Synapse: electrical and chemical; neurotransmitters acetylcholine, dopamine. Human brain: forebrain (cerebrum, thalamus, hypothalamus), midbrain, hindbrain (pons, cerebellum, medulla). Spinal cord. Reflex arc: receptor, afferent, CNS, efferent, effector. Sensory organs: eye (retina, rods and cones, rhodopsin), ear (cochlea, organ of Corti, semicircular canals for balance). Cerebrospinal fluid.
Deep dive: Neuron and impulse

Resting membrane: K+ leak channels, Na+-K+ ATPase pumps 3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in. Stimulus opens Na+ channels; Na+ influx reverses polarity (depolarisation) to +30 mV; K+ efflux repolarises. Conduction in myelinated fibres is saltatory (Nodes of Ranvier) and faster. Chemical synapse: presynaptic neuron releases neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft; binds receptors on the postsynaptic membrane generating EPSP or IPSP. Electrical synapses have gap junctions and faster transmission.
Deep dive: Brain and spinal cord

Meninges: dura mater, arachnoid, pia mater. Cerebrum divided by a longitudinal fissure into hemispheres connected by the corpus callosum; cerebral cortex (grey matter) has sensory, motor and association areas; Broca and Wernicke areas for speech. Thalamus: relay centre; hypothalamus: body temperature, hunger, thirst, hormones; limbic system for emotions. Midbrain: corpora quadrigemina. Pons: respiration regulation. Cerebellum: balance and coordination. Medulla: cardiovascular and respiratory reflexes, vomiting. Reflex action: involuntary, rapid, via spinal cord (knee jerk).
Deep dive: Sensory organs

Eye: sclera, cornea, choroid, iris, pupil, lens, retina; fovea (cones highest), blind spot (no photoreceptors); aqueous humor, vitreous humor. Rods are for dim light with rhodopsin (opsin + retinal from vitamin A); cones for colour and bright vision (red, green, blue). Ear: outer (pinna, canal, tympanum), middle (malleus, incus, stapes, Eustachian tube), inner (cochlea with organ of Corti, vestibular apparatus: semicircular canals and otolith organs). Hearing: sound waves move tympanum, ossicles, oval window, cochlear fluid, hair cells, nerve impulses.

Visual lesson

Neural Control and Coordination

Neuron: dendrites, cell body, axon

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Neuron and impulse›3Brain and spinal cord›4Sensory organs
Resting-70 mV
Peak+30 mV
🔑

Big idea

  • Neuron: dendrites, cell body, axon
  • Myelinated and non-myelinated
  • Unipolar, bipolar, multipolar
  • Resting potential -70 mV maintained by Na+-K+ pump
Read the full explanation

Neuron: dendrites, cell body, axon; myelinated and non-myelinated; unipolar, bipolar, multipolar. Resting potential -70 mV maintained by Na+-K+ pump. Action potential: depolarisation, repolarisation, hyperpolarisation; all-or-none. Synapse: electrical and chemical; neurotransmitters acetylcholine, dopamine. Human brain: forebrain (cerebrum, thalamus, hypothalamus), midbrain, hindbrain (pons, cerebellum, medulla). Spinal cord. Reflex arc: receptor, afferent, CNS, efferent, effector. Sensory organs: eye (retina, rods and cones, rhodopsin), ear (cochlea, organ of Corti, semicircular canals for balance). Cerebrospinal fluid.

📌

Neuron and impulse

  • Resting membrane: K+ leak channels, Na+-K+ ATPase pumps 3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in
  • Stimulus opens Na+ channels
  • Na+ influx reverses polarity (depolarisation) to +30 mV
  • K+ efflux repolarises
Read the full explanation

Resting membrane: K+ leak channels, Na+-K+ ATPase pumps 3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in. Stimulus opens Na+ channels; Na+ influx reverses polarity (depolarisation) to +30 mV; K+ efflux repolarises. Conduction in myelinated fibres is saltatory (Nodes of Ranvier) and faster. Chemical synapse: presynaptic neuron releases neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft; binds receptors on the postsynaptic membrane generating EPSP or IPSP. Electrical synapses have gap junctions and faster transmission.

🧠

Brain and spinal cord

  • Meninges: dura mater, arachnoid, pia mater
  • Cerebrum divided by a longitudinal fissure into hemispheres connected by the corpus callosum
  • Cerebral cortex (grey matter) has sensory, motor and association areas
  • Broca and Wernicke areas for speech
Read the full explanation

Meninges: dura mater, arachnoid, pia mater. Cerebrum divided by a longitudinal fissure into hemispheres connected by the corpus callosum; cerebral cortex (grey matter) has sensory, motor and association areas; Broca and Wernicke areas for speech. Thalamus: relay centre; hypothalamus: body temperature, hunger, thirst, hormones; limbic system for emotions. Midbrain: corpora quadrigemina. Pons: respiration regulation. Cerebellum: balance and coordination. Medulla: cardiovascular and respiratory reflexes, vomiting. Reflex action: involuntary, rapid, via spinal cord (knee jerk).

🧬

Sensory organs

  • Eye: sclera, cornea, choroid, iris, pupil, lens, retina
  • Fovea (cones highest), blind spot (no photoreceptors)
  • Aqueous humor, vitreous humor
  • Rods are for dim light with rhodopsin (opsin + retinal from vitamin A)

yt: class 11 biology chemical coordination and integration hormones endocrine glands

blocks.x: Endocrine glands: hypothalamus, pituitary, pineal, thyroid, parathyroid, thymus, adrenal, pancreas, gonads. Hormones are non-nutrient chemicals acting as intercellular messengers. Hypothalamic releasing and inhibiting hormones. Pituitary: adenohypophysis (GH, PRL, TSH, ACTH, LH, FSH, MSH) and neurohypophysis (oxytocin, vasopressin). Thyroid: T3, T4, calcitonin; parathyroid: PTH. Adrenal medulla: adrenaline and noradrenaline; cortex: glucocorticoids (cortisol), mineralocorticoids (aldosterone), sex steroids. Pancreas: insulin, glucagon. Testis: testosterone; ovary: oestrogen, progesterone. Heart: ANF; kidney: erythropoietin. Mechanism: membrane receptors (cAMP) and intracellular receptors. Disorders: dwarfism, gigantism, acromegaly, goitre, cretinism, Graves, Addison, Cushing, diabetes mellitus.
Deep dive: Pituitary and hypothalamus

Hypothalamus produces GnRH, TRH, somatostatin. GH deficiency in childhood causes pituitary dwarfism; excess causes gigantism (children) and acromegaly (adults). Prolactin regulates milk production. TSH stimulates thyroid; ACTH stimulates adrenal cortex; LH and FSH regulate gonads. MSH acts on melanocytes. Oxytocin causes contraction of uterus at childbirth and milk ejection; vasopressin (ADH) promotes water reabsorption in the kidney.
Deep dive: Thyroid, parathyroid, adrenal, pancreas

Thyroid hormones regulate BMR; iodine deficiency causes simple goitre; hypothyroidism in infants gives cretinism; hyperthyroidism gives exophthalmic goitre (Graves disease). Calcitonin lowers blood calcium. PTH raises blood Ca2+ (hypercalcemic), acts on bones and kidneys; vitamin D is also involved. Adrenaline is the emergency hormone (fight or flight). Cortisol: gluconeogenesis, anti-inflammatory. Aldosterone: Na+ reabsorption. Addison disease: hypocortisolism; Cushing: excess cortisol. Insulin (beta cells) reduces blood glucose; glucagon (alpha cells) raises; diabetes mellitus causes glycosuria and ketonuria.
Deep dive: Gonads, others and mechanism

Testosterone: male secondary sexual characters and spermatogenesis. Oestrogen: development of female characters; progesterone: maintains pregnancy. Pineal: melatonin (circadian rhythm). Thymus: thymosin (T-cell differentiation). GI hormones: gastrin, secretin, CCK, GIP. Hormone action: water soluble (peptide) via membrane receptors, second messengers cAMP, IP3, Ca2+; steroids via intracellular receptors regulating gene expression. Feedback regulation: negative feedback.
Hindi saransh
Rasayanik samanvay: antahsravi granthiyan, harmon. Insulin glucose ghatata hai, glucagon badhata hai. Thyroxine BMR niyantrit karta hai.
Insulin lowers blood glucose and glucagon raises it.

Calcitonin lowers blood calcium. PTH raises blood Ca2+ (hypercalcemic), acts on bones and kidneys; vitamin D is also involved. Adrenaline is the emergency hormone (fight or flight). Cortisol: gluconeogenesis, anti-inflammatory. Aldosterone: Na+ reabsorption. Addison disease: hypocortisolism; Cushing: excess cortisol. Insulin (beta cells) reduces blood glucose; glucagon (alpha cells) raises; diabetes mellitus causes glycosuria and ketonuria.

lessons.title: Business, Trade and Commerce
yt: class 11 business studies business trade and commerce

blocks.x: Business is an economic activity involving regular production or purchase and sale of goods and services to earn profit. Features: economic activity, production or procurement, sale or exchange, dealings in goods and services, profit earning, recurring transactions, uncertainty of return, risk. Business, profession and employment differ in qualification, reward, risk, capital and transfer of interest. Industry: primary (extractive, genetic), secondary (manufacturing, construction), tertiary. Commerce = trade + auxiliaries to trade (transport, banking, insurance, warehousing, communication, advertising). Trade: internal (wholesale, retail) and external (import, export, entrepot). Objectives: profit, market standing, innovation, productivity, social responsibility. Business risks arise from natural, human, economic causes.
Deep dive: Business, profession, employment

Business: no minimum qualification, profit as reward, risk, capital needed, transfer of interest with consent. Profession: specialised knowledge, professional fees, code of conduct, membership of an association (doctors, lawyers, chartered accountants). Employment: contract of service, wages or salary, little risk, no or little capital. Objectives of business: profit is necessary but not the only one; market standing, innovation, productivity, social responsibility.
Deep dive: Industry and commerce

Primary: extractive (farming, mining, fishing, hunting) and genetic (nurseries, cattle breeding). Secondary: manufacturing (analytic, synthetic, processing, assembling) and construction. Tertiary: banking, transport, insurance, communication. Auxiliaries to trade: transport removes hindrance of place, banking of finance, insurance of risk, warehousing of time, advertising of knowledge. Trade: wholesale and retail. Hindrances to trade: person (trade), place, time, finance, risk, knowledge.
Deep dive: Business risk

Risk is the possibility of loss. Causes: natural (flood, fire, earthquake), human (dishonest employees, strikes), economic (price fluctuations, competition), other (government policy, technological change). Nature: uncertainty, essential part of business, degree depends on nature and size, profit is the reward for risk. Insurable and uninsurable risks. Business is a part of the larger concept of economic activities including non-economic activities done for love and sentiments.
Hindi saransh
Vyavsay, vyapar aur vanijya. Vyavsay mein laabh, jokhim aur punji. Udyog prathmik, dwitiyak, tritiyak. Vanijya = vyapar + vyapar sahayak.
Commerce includes trade and auxiliaries to trade; business includes industry and commerce.

Big idea

Read the full explanation

Business is an economic activity involving regular production or purchase and sale of goods and services to earn profit. Features: economic activity, production or procurement, sale or exchange, dealings in goods and services, profit earning, recurring transactions, uncertainty of return, risk. Business, profession and employment differ in qualification, reward, risk, capital and transfer of interest. Industry: primary (extractive, genetic), secondary (manufacturing, construction), tertiary. Commerce = trade + auxiliaries to trade (transport, banking, insurance, warehousing, communication, advertising). Trade: internal (wholesale, retail) and external (import, export, entrepot). Objectives: profit, market standing, innovation, productivity, social responsibility. Business risks arise from natural, human, economic causes.

📌

Business, profession, employment

  • Business: no minimum qualification, profit as reward, risk, capital needed, transfer of interest with consent
  • Profession: specialised knowledge, professional fees, code of conduct, membership of an association (doctors, lawyers, chartered accountants)
  • Employment: contract of service, wages or salary, little risk, no or little capital
  • Objectives of business: profit is necessary but not the only one

Business: no minimum qualification, profit as reward, risk, capital needed, transfer of interest with consent. Profession: specialised knowledge, professional fees, code of conduct, membership of an association (doctors, lawyers, chartered accountants). Employment: contract of service, wages or salary, little risk, no or little capital. Objectives of business: profit is necessary but not the only one; market standing, innovation, productivity, social responsibility.

🧠

Industry and commerce

  • Primary: extractive (farming, mining, fishing, hunting) and genetic (nurseries, cattle breeding)
  • Secondary: manufacturing (analytic, synthetic, processing, assembling) and construction
  • Tertiary: banking, transport, insurance, communication
  • Auxiliaries to trade: transport removes hindrance of place, banking of finance, insurance of risk, warehousing of time, advertising of knowledge
Read the full explanation

Primary: extractive (farming, mining, fishing, hunting) and genetic (nurseries, cattle breeding). Secondary: manufacturing (analytic, synthetic, processing, assembling) and construction. Tertiary: banking, transport, insurance, communication. Auxiliaries to trade: transport removes hindrance of place, banking of finance, insurance of risk, warehousing of time, advertising of knowledge. Trade: wholesale and retail. Hindrances to trade: person (trade), place, time, finance, risk, knowledge.

🌟

Business risk

  • Risk is the possibility of loss
  • Causes: natural (flood, fire, earthquake), human (dishonest employees, strikes), economic (price fluctuations, competition), other (government…
  • Nature: uncertainty, essential part of business, degree depends on nature and size, profit is the reward for risk
  • Insurable and uninsurable risks

Risk is the possibility of loss. Causes: natural (flood, fire, earthquake), human (dishonest employees, strikes), economic (price fluctuations, competition), other (government policy, technological change). Nature: uncertainty, essential part of business, degree depends on nature and size, profit is the reward for risk. Insurable and uninsurable risks. Business is a part of the larger concept of economic activities including non-economic activities done for love and sentiments.

lessons.title: Forms of Business Organisation
yt: class 11 business studies forms of business organisation sole proprietorship partnership HUF cooperative company

blocks.x: Forms: sole proprietorship, joint Hindu family business (HUF), partnership (Indian Partnership Act 1932), cooperative society (Cooperative Societies Act 1912), joint stock company (Companies Act 2013). Sole proprietor: single owner, unlimited liability, no separate legal entity. HUF: karta, coparceners, Hindu Law, unlimited liability of karta. Partnership: minimum 2, maximum 50 (Companies Act), partnership deed, kinds of partners (active, sleeping, secret, nominal, partner by estoppel), unlimited joint liability. LLP: limited liability, separate legal entity. Cooperative society: minimum 10 members, one member one vote. Company: private (min 2, max 200 members) and public (min 7, no limit), separate legal entity, perpetual succession, limited liability. Choice depends on cost, liability, continuity, control, capital, legal formalities.
Deep dive: Sole proprietorship, HUF, partnership

Sole proprietorship merits: quick decisions, secrecy, direct incentive, easy formation; limits: limited resources, limited life, unlimited liability. HUF: formation by birth in the family, minor coparceners, continuity unaffected by the death of karta. Partnership: agreement oral or written; profit-sharing; mutual agency; types by duration (at will, particular), liability (general, limited). Registration optional. Merits: easy formation, balanced judgement, more funds, sharing of risks. Limits: unlimited liability, instability, lack of public confidence, limited resources.
Deep dive: Cooperative society and company

Cooperative: voluntary association, democratic management, service motive, limited liability; types: consumer, producer, marketing, farmers, credit, cooperative housing. Company: formation by incorporation; features: artificial legal person, separate legal entity, formation, perpetual succession, control, liability, common seal, risk bearing, ownership and management separation. Private company: restrictions on transfer of shares, minimum paid-up capital not mandatory, cannot invite public. Public company: free transfer, invites public subscription. One Person Company (OPC) permitted by the 2013 Act.
Deep dive: Choice of form

Factors: cost and ease of formation, liability, continuity, management and control, capital considerations, nature of business. Sole proprietorship suits small retail; partnership suits professions; company suits large capital. Comparative merits: company has the largest funds and stability, but most legal formalities and least secrecy.

Visual lesson

Forms of Business Organisation

Big idea

  • Forms: sole proprietorship, joint Hindu family business (HUF), partnership (Indian Partnership Act 1932), cooperative society (Cooperative Societies…
  • Sole proprietor: single owner, unlimited liability, no separate legal entity
  • HUF: karta, coparceners, Hindu Law, unlimited liability of karta
  • Partnership: minimum 2, maximum 50 (Companies Act), partnership deed, kinds of partners (active, sleeping, secret, nominal, partner by estoppel)…
Read the full explanation

Forms: sole proprietorship, joint Hindu family business (HUF), partnership (Indian Partnership Act 1932), cooperative society (Cooperative Societies Act 1912), joint stock company (Companies Act 2013). Sole proprietor: single owner, unlimited liability, no separate legal entity. HUF: karta, coparceners, Hindu Law, unlimited liability of karta. Partnership: minimum 2, maximum 50 (Companies Act), partnership deed, kinds of partners (active, sleeping, secret, nominal, partner by estoppel), unlimited joint liability. LLP: limited liability, separate legal entity. Cooperative society: minimum 10 members, one member one vote. Company: private (min 2, max 200 members) and public (min 7, no limit), separate legal entity, perpetual succession, limited liability. Choice depends on cost, liability, continuity, control, capital, legal formalities.

📌

Sole proprietorship, HUF, partnership

  • Sole proprietorship merits: quick decisions, secrecy, direct incentive, easy formation
  • Limits: limited resources, limited life, unlimited liability
  • HUF: formation by birth in the family, minor coparceners, continuity unaffected by the death of karta
  • Partnership: agreement oral or written
Read the full explanation

Sole proprietorship merits: quick decisions, secrecy, direct incentive, easy formation; limits: limited resources, limited life, unlimited liability. HUF: formation by birth in the family, minor coparceners, continuity unaffected by the death of karta. Partnership: agreement oral or written; profit-sharing; mutual agency; types by duration (at will, particular), liability (general, limited). Registration optional. Merits: easy formation, balanced judgement, more funds, sharing of risks. Limits: unlimited liability, instability, lack of public confidence, limited resources.

🧠

Cooperative society and company

  • Cooperative: voluntary association, democratic management, service motive, limited liability
  • Types: consumer, producer, marketing, farmers, credit, cooperative housing
  • Company: formation by incorporation
  • Features: artificial legal person, separate legal entity, formation, perpetual succession, control, liability, common seal, risk bearing, ownership…
Read the full explanation

Cooperative: voluntary association, democratic management, service motive, limited liability; types: consumer, producer, marketing, farmers, credit, cooperative housing. Company: formation by incorporation; features: artificial legal person, separate legal entity, formation, perpetual succession, control, liability, common seal, risk bearing, ownership and management separation. Private company: restrictions on transfer of shares, minimum paid-up capital not mandatory, cannot invite public. Public company: free transfer, invites public subscription. One Person Company (OPC) permitted by the 2013 Act.

🌟

Choice of form

  • Factors: cost and ease of formation, liability, continuity, management and control, capital considerations, nature of business
  • Sole proprietorship suits small retail
  • Partnership suits professions
  • Company suits large capital
Read the full explanation

Factors: cost and ease of formation, liability, continuity, management and control, capital considerations, nature of business. Sole proprietorship suits small retail; partnership suits professions; company suits large capital. Comparative merits: company has the largest funds and stability, but most legal formalities and least secrecy.

🎯 Remember A company is a separate legal entity with perpetual succession and limited liability.

lessons.title: Private, Public and Global Enterprises
yt: class 11 business studies private public and global enterprises PSU MNC joint venture

blocks.x: Private sector: owned by private individuals. Public sector: owned by government; forms: departmental undertakings (railways, post and telegraph), statutory corporations (LIC, ONGC, Air India earlier), government companies (BHEL, SAIL, HAL). Features of public enterprise: ownership, finance, management, public welfare. Changing role: liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation (LPG, 1991); disinvestment, navratna and maharatna status, MOU. Global enterprises: multinational corporations (MNCs) with branches in many countries, large size, foreign collaborations, advanced technology. Joint ventures: equity-based and contractual. Public private partnership (PPP): BOT and build-own-operate-transfer.
Deep dive: Public sector forms

Departmental undertaking: part of a ministry, financed through the budget, audited by the CAG, no separate legal entity. Statutory corporation: set up by Act of Parliament (LIC, RBI, FCI), separate legal entity, autonomous, own funds. Government company: at least 51% paid-up capital with government under Companies Act (BHEL, SAIL, GAIL). Merits: financial resources, social benefit, balanced regional development. Limits: bureaucracy, delayed decisions, political interference, lack of accountability.
Deep dive: Changing role and PSU reforms

New industrial policy 1991: reduced reserved industries (from 17 to 3), disinvestment, restructuring of sick units, MOU between government and PSU for performance targets. Navratna (nine) and Maharatna (larger) PSUs given greater autonomy. Privatisation: denationalisation, franchising, contracting out. Disinvestment of shares to improve efficiency and revenue.
Deep dive: Global enterprises and PPP

MNCs features: huge capital and assets, foreign collaboration, advanced technology, product innovation and marketing strategies, expansion of markets, centralised control. Examples: Coca-Cola, Unilever, Nestle. Joint venture: Maruti Suzuki. Benefits to India: technology, capital, employment, exports. Public private partnership: BOT (Build-Operate-Transfer), BOOT; applied in roads and airports.

Private, Public and Global Enterprises

Private sector: owned by private individuals

🔑

Big idea

  • Private sector: owned by private individuals
  • Public sector: owned by government
  • Forms: departmental undertakings (railways, post and telegraph), statutory corporations (LIC, ONGC, Air India earlier), government companies (BHEL…
  • Features of public enterprise: ownership, finance, management, public welfare
Read the full explanation

Private sector: owned by private individuals. Public sector: owned by government; forms: departmental undertakings (railways, post and telegraph), statutory corporations (LIC, ONGC, Air India earlier), government companies (BHEL, SAIL, HAL). Features of public enterprise: ownership, finance, management, public welfare. Changing role: liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation (LPG, 1991); disinvestment, navratna and maharatna status, MOU. Global enterprises: multinational corporations (MNCs) with branches in many countries, large size, foreign collaborations, advanced technology. Joint ventures: equity-based and contractual. Public private partnership (PPP): BOT and build-own-operate-transfer.

📌

Public sector forms

  • Departmental undertaking: part of a ministry, financed through the budget, audited by the CAG, no separate legal entity
  • Statutory corporation: set up by Act of Parliament (LIC, RBI, FCI), separate legal entity, autonomous, own funds
  • Government company: at least 51% paid-up capital with government under Companies Act (BHEL, SAIL, GAIL)
  • Merits: financial resources, social benefit, balanced regional development
Read the full explanation

Departmental undertaking: part of a ministry, financed through the budget, audited by the CAG, no separate legal entity. Statutory corporation: set up by Act of Parliament (LIC, RBI, FCI), separate legal entity, autonomous, own funds. Government company: at least 51% paid-up capital with government under Companies Act (BHEL, SAIL, GAIL). Merits: financial resources, social benefit, balanced regional development. Limits: bureaucracy, delayed decisions, political interference, lack of accountability.

🧠

Changing role and PSU reforms

  • New industrial policy 1991: reduced reserved industries (from 17 to 3), disinvestment, restructuring of sick units, MOU between government and PSU…
  • Navratna (nine) and Maharatna (larger) PSUs given greater autonomy
  • Privatisation: denationalisation, franchising, contracting out
  • Disinvestment of shares to improve efficiency and revenue
Read the full explanation

New industrial policy 1991: reduced reserved industries (from 17 to 3), disinvestment, restructuring of sick units, MOU between government and PSU for performance targets. Navratna (nine) and Maharatna (larger) PSUs given greater autonomy. Privatisation: denationalisation, franchising, contracting out. Disinvestment of shares to improve efficiency and revenue.

🌟

Global enterprises and PPP

  • MNCs features: huge capital and assets, foreign collaboration, advanced technology, product innovation and marketing strategies, expansion of…
  • Examples: Coca-Cola, Unilever, Nestle
  • Joint venture: Maruti Suzuki
  • Benefits to India: technology, capital, employment, exports
Read the full explanation

MNCs features: huge capital and assets, foreign collaboration, advanced technology, product innovation and marketing strategies, expansion of markets, centralised control. Examples: Coca-Cola, Unilever, Nestle. Joint venture: Maruti Suzuki. Benefits to India: technology, capital, employment, exports. Public private partnership: BOT (Build-Operate-Transfer), BOOT; applied in roads and airports.

lessons.title: Business Services
yt: class 11 business studies business services banking insurance communication transport warehousing

blocks.x: Services are intangible, inseparable, perishable, involve the consumer, lack ownership and are heterogeneous. Types: business services (banking, insurance, transportation, warehousing, communication), social services, personal services. Banking: commercial banks (public, private, foreign, regional rural), cooperative banks, specialised banks, central bank (RBI). Services: ATM, debit card, credit card, internet banking, RTGS, NEFT, UPI. Insurance: principles (utmost good faith, insurable interest, indemnity, contribution, subrogation, causa proxima); types: life, health, fire, marine, motor. Postal services (speed post, e-post) and telecom (cellular, broadband). Transport modes, warehousing types (private, public, bonded, cooperative, government), functions (consolidation, break-bulk, stock holding, pricing).
Deep dive: Banking and insurance

Bank accounts: savings, current, fixed deposit, recurring. E-banking: ATM, debit and credit cards, RTGS (above Rs 2 lakh), NEFT, UPI, mobile banking. Insurance: contract in which insurer promises to indemnify insured for loss against premium. Principles: utmost good faith (uberrimae fidei), insurable interest, indemnity (not for life), contribution, subrogation, causa proxima. Types: life (whole life, endowment, term, money-back), health, fire, marine (hull, cargo, freight), motor.
Deep dive: Communication and transport

Postal: mail (letters), parcel, money order, speed post, e-post, banking and insurance via post offices, PIN. Telecommunication: cellular, radio paging, fixed line, cable, VSAT, DTH, internet. Transport: road, rail, air, water. Advantages of rail: heavy goods, long distances; air: speed; road: door-to-door; water: low cost. Freight and passenger types.
Deep dive: Warehousing

Warehouse is a building to store goods. Types: private, public, bonded, cooperative, government (FCI, CWC, SWC). Functions: consolidation, break-bulk, stock holding, value addition, price stabilisation, transit, financing (warehouse receipt as collateral), risk bearing. Importance: removes hindrance of time; helps price stability; supports exports.
Hindi saransh
Vyavsayik sevayen: banking, bima, sanchar, parivahan, bhandaran. Bima ke siddhant: param vishwas, bimit hit, kshatipurti.

Business Services

🔑

Big idea

  • Services are intangible, inseparable, perishable, involve the consumer, lack ownership and are heterogeneous
  • Types: business services (banking, insurance, transportation, warehousing, communication), social services, personal services
  • Banking: commercial banks (public, private, foreign, regional rural), cooperative banks, specialised banks, central bank (RBI)
  • Services: ATM, debit card, credit card, internet banking, RTGS, NEFT, UPI
Read the full explanation

Services are intangible, inseparable, perishable, involve the consumer, lack ownership and are heterogeneous. Types: business services (banking, insurance, transportation, warehousing, communication), social services, personal services. Banking: commercial banks (public, private, foreign, regional rural), cooperative banks, specialised banks, central bank (RBI). Services: ATM, debit card, credit card, internet banking, RTGS, NEFT, UPI. Insurance: principles (utmost good faith, insurable interest, indemnity, contribution, subrogation, causa proxima); types: life, health, fire, marine, motor. Postal services (speed post, e-post) and telecom (cellular, broadband). Transport modes, warehousing types (private, public, bonded, cooperative, government), functions (consolidation, break-bulk, stock holding, pricing).

📌

Banking and insurance

  • Bank accounts: savings, current, fixed deposit, recurring
  • E-banking: ATM, debit and credit cards, RTGS (above Rs 2 lakh), NEFT, UPI, mobile banking
  • Insurance: contract in which insurer promises to indemnify insured for loss against premium
  • Principles: utmost good faith (uberrimae fidei), insurable interest, indemnity (not for life), contribution, subrogation, causa proxima
Read the full explanation

Bank accounts: savings, current, fixed deposit, recurring. E-banking: ATM, debit and credit cards, RTGS (above Rs 2 lakh), NEFT, UPI, mobile banking. Insurance: contract in which insurer promises to indemnify insured for loss against premium. Principles: utmost good faith (uberrimae fidei), insurable interest, indemnity (not for life), contribution, subrogation, causa proxima. Types: life (whole life, endowment, term, money-back), health, fire, marine (hull, cargo, freight), motor.

🧠

Communication and transport

  • Postal: mail (letters), parcel, money order, speed post, e-post, banking and insurance via post offices, PIN
  • Telecommunication: cellular, radio paging, fixed line, cable, VSAT, DTH, internet
  • Transport: road, rail, air, water
  • Advantages of rail: heavy goods, long distances
Read the full explanation

Postal: mail (letters), parcel, money order, speed post, e-post, banking and insurance via post offices, PIN. Telecommunication: cellular, radio paging, fixed line, cable, VSAT, DTH, internet. Transport: road, rail, air, water. Advantages of rail: heavy goods, long distances; air: speed; road: door-to-door; water: low cost. Freight and passenger types.

🕰️

Warehousing

  • Warehouse is a building to store goods
  • Types: private, public, bonded, cooperative, government (FCI, CWC, SWC)
  • Functions: consolidation, break-bulk, stock holding, value addition, price stabilisation, transit, financing (warehouse receipt as collateral), risk…
  • Importance: removes hindrance of time
Read the full explanation

Warehouse is a building to store goods. Types: private, public, bonded, cooperative, government (FCI, CWC, SWC). Functions: consolidation, break-bulk, stock holding, value addition, price stabilisation, transit, financing (warehouse receipt as collateral), risk bearing. Importance: removes hindrance of time; helps price stability; supports exports.

lessons.title: Emerging Modes of Business
yt: class 11 business studies emerging modes of business e-business outsourcing

blocks.x: E-business covers all business activities through electronic means; e-commerce is online buying and selling. Scope: B2B, B2C, C2C, intra-B, P2P. Benefits: speed, low costs, wider access, convenience. Limitations: low personal touch, security, system failure. Online transactions: registration, placing order, payment (cash on delivery, cheque, credit/debit card, net banking, digital cash). Security and safety concerns: privacy, phishing, hacking. Outsourcing: contracting out non-core activities (BPO, KPO). Scope: contract manufacturing, contract research, contract sales. Need: focus on core, cost, skill, speed. Concerns: loss of confidentiality, lack of control, ethical concerns.
Deep dive: E-business and e-commerce

E-business has wider scope than e-commerce: includes buying, selling, customer service, logistics, supply chain and collaborating with partners. Types: B2B (suppliers and manufacturers), B2C (retailers to customers), C2C (OLX), B2G, intra-B. Differences with traditional business: ease of formation, low investment, convenience, speed, global reach, impersonal nature, resource requirements. Online transactions steps: register, place order, make payment, delivery, post-sale service.
Deep dive: Payment and security

Payment: cash on delivery, cheque, net banking, credit or debit cards, digital cash (e-wallet), UPI. Security: encryption, firewalls, passwords, digital signatures, SSL. Risks: transaction risks (non-delivery), data storage and transmission risk, risk of threat to intellectual property, privacy risks. Safeguards: secure websites, digital certificates, authentication. IT Act 2000 provides legal recognition.
Deep dive: Outsourcing

Outsourcing means entrusting non-core activities to outside agencies. Features: long-term contract, reduces cost, focus on core competence. Forms: BPO (call centres, data entry), KPO (research, analytics), contract manufacturing. Need: focus on core, reduce costs, access to skills, speed. Concerns: lack of confidentiality, dependence on vendor, ethical considerations, loss of jobs in developed countries.
Hindi saransh
Vyavsay ke ubharte swaroop: e-vyapar, bahyasrotan. E-vyapar mein B2B, B2C, C2C. Bahyasrotan se mool gatividhiyon par dhyan.
E-commerce is part of e-business; outsourcing contracts non-core activities.

Emerging Modes of Business

E-business covers all business activities through electronic means

🔑

Big idea

  • E-business covers all business activities through electronic means
  • E-commerce is online buying and selling
  • Scope: B2B, B2C, C2C, intra-B, P2P
  • Benefits: speed, low costs, wider access, convenience
Read the full explanation

E-business covers all business activities through electronic means; e-commerce is online buying and selling. Scope: B2B, B2C, C2C, intra-B, P2P. Benefits: speed, low costs, wider access, convenience. Limitations: low personal touch, security, system failure. Online transactions: registration, placing order, payment (cash on delivery, cheque, credit/debit card, net banking, digital cash). Security and safety concerns: privacy, phishing, hacking. Outsourcing: contracting out non-core activities (BPO, KPO). Scope: contract manufacturing, contract research, contract sales. Need: focus on core, cost, skill, speed. Concerns: loss of confidentiality, lack of control, ethical concerns.

📌

E-business and e-commerce

  • E-business has wider scope than e-commerce: includes buying, selling, customer service, logistics, supply chain and collaborating with partners
  • Types: B2B (suppliers and manufacturers), B2C (retailers to customers), C2C (OLX), B2G, intra-B
  • Differences with traditional business: ease of formation, low investment, convenience, speed, global reach, impersonal nature, resource requirements
  • Online transactions steps: register, place order, make payment, delivery, post-sale service
Read the full explanation

E-business has wider scope than e-commerce: includes buying, selling, customer service, logistics, supply chain and collaborating with partners. Types: B2B (suppliers and manufacturers), B2C (retailers to customers), C2C (OLX), B2G, intra-B. Differences with traditional business: ease of formation, low investment, convenience, speed, global reach, impersonal nature, resource requirements. Online transactions steps: register, place order, make payment, delivery, post-sale service.

🧠

Payment and security

  • Payment: cash on delivery, cheque, net banking, credit or debit cards, digital cash (e-wallet), UPI
  • Security: encryption, firewalls, passwords, digital signatures, SSL
  • Risks: transaction risks (non-delivery), data storage and transmission risk, risk of threat to intellectual property, privacy risks
  • Safeguards: secure websites, digital certificates, authentication
Read the full explanation

Payment: cash on delivery, cheque, net banking, credit or debit cards, digital cash (e-wallet), UPI. Security: encryption, firewalls, passwords, digital signatures, SSL. Risks: transaction risks (non-delivery), data storage and transmission risk, risk of threat to intellectual property, privacy risks. Safeguards: secure websites, digital certificates, authentication. IT Act 2000 provides legal recognition.

🌟

Outsourcing

  • Outsourcing means entrusting non-core activities to outside agencies
  • Features: long-term contract, reduces cost, focus on core competence
  • Forms: BPO (call centres, data entry), KPO (research, analytics), contract manufacturing
  • Need: focus on core, reduce costs, access to skills, speed
Read the full explanation

Outsourcing means entrusting non-core activities to outside agencies. Features: long-term contract, reduces cost, focus on core competence. Forms: BPO (call centres, data entry), KPO (research, analytics), contract manufacturing. Need: focus on core, reduce costs, access to skills, speed. Concerns: lack of confidentiality, dependence on vendor, ethical considerations, loss of jobs in developed countries.

lessons.title: Social Responsibilities of Business and Business Ethics
yt: class 11 business studies social responsibilities of business and business ethics

blocks.x: Social responsibility is the obligation of businessmen to pursue policies and make decisions that are desirable in terms of the values and objectives of society. Arguments for: justification for existence, long-term interest of the firm, avoidance of government regulation, maintenance of society, availability of resources, better environment. Against: violation of profit maximisation, burden on consumers, lack of social skills, lack of broad public support. Social responsibility towards shareholders, workers, consumers, government and community. Business and environmental protection: pollution (air, water, land, noise); causes, need for protection. Business ethics: values and principles guiding conduct; elements: top management commitment, publication of a code, establishment of compliance mechanisms, involving everyone, measuring results.
Deep dive: Social responsibility

Concept: obligation to society; Bowen and Davis defined it. Levels of responsibility: economic, legal, ethical, discretionary (Carroll). Towards shareholders (fair return), workers (fair wages, safety), consumers (quality, fair price), government (taxes), community (health, education, environment). Kinds: economic, legal, ethical, discretionary responsibilities. Reasons: justification for existence, long-term interest, avoidance of government regulation, maintenance of society, availability of resources.
Deep dive: Environmental protection

Pollution: air (industries, vehicles), water (effluents, sewage), land (solid waste, pesticides), noise. Need: reduction of health hazards, lower costs, avoid legal action, public image, ecological balance. Role of business: Central Pollution Control Board, Environment Protection Act 1986, polluter pays principle, corporate social responsibility (CSR) under Companies Act 2013 (2% of average net profit for companies with net worth Rs 500 crore, turnover Rs 1000 crore or profit Rs 5 crore).
Deep dive: Business ethics

Ethics deal with right and wrong. Elements: top management commitment, publication of code, compliance mechanism, involving everyone at all levels, measuring results. Concept: honesty, fairness, respect. Ethics pay in the long run: goodwill, customer loyalty, employee morale. Unethical practices: adulteration, hoarding, misleading advertisement, pollution, child labour.
Hindi saransh
Vyavsay ke samajik dayitva aur naitikta. CSR: kuch laabh samaj ke liye. Pradushan aur paryavaran sanrakshan.
Under the Companies Act 2013, qualifying companies must spend 2 percent of average net profit on CSR.

Social responsibility is the obligation of businessmen to pursue policies and make decisions that are desirable in terms of the values and objectives of society. Arguments for: justification for existence, long-term interest of the firm, avoidance of government regulation, maintenance of society, availability of resources, better environment. Against: violation of profit maximisation, burden on consumers, lack of social skills, lack of broad public support. Social responsibility towards shareholders, workers, consumers, government and community. Business and environmental protection: pollution (air, water, land, noise); causes, need for protection. Business ethics: values and principles guiding conduct; elements: top management commitment, publication of a code, establishment of compliance mechanisms, involving everyone, measuring results.

lessons.title: Formation of a Company
yt: class 11 business studies formation of a company promotion incorporation prospectus

blocks.x: Stages of company formation: promotion, incorporation, subscription of capital (public company), commencement of business (earlier certificate of commencement). Promotion: identification of business opportunity, feasibility studies, name approval, fixing of signatories to the memorandum, appointment of professionals, preparation of documents. Incorporation: documents to Registrar of Companies: memorandum of association (name, registered office, objects, liability, capital clauses), articles of association, consent of directors, agreement, declaration, address proof, fee payment. Certificate of incorporation is conclusive evidence. Subscription of capital: SEBI approval, prospectus, application, allotment, minimum subscription (90%), share certificates. Prospectus content and statement in lieu of prospectus. Private company does not issue a prospectus.
Deep dive: Promotion and incorporation

Promoter conducts promotional functions: opportunity, feasibility (technical, financial, economic), name (reserved with Registrar), signatories, professionals (mercantile bankers, auditors), documents. Memorandum clauses: name, registered office, objects, liability, capital, association (subscription). Articles: internal rules about directors, shares, meetings, dividends. Incorporation documents: memorandum, articles, agreement, declaration, address proof. Registrar issues certificate of incorporation, and Corporate Identity Number (CIN).
Deep dive: Capital subscription

Public company: SEBI guidelines; prospectus invites public; contents: name of company, issue details, capital, objects, directors; Letter of allotment, application money, allotment, calls. Minimum subscription is 90% of issue. Allotment within 60 days. Money received kept in escrow with a scheduled bank. Private company can start after incorporation; public company after complying subscription rules.
Deep dive: Documents

Memorandum of association: charter, defines relationship with the outside world, can be altered only per the Act. Articles of association: internal rules. Prospectus: document inviting the public (any notice, circular). Statement in lieu of prospectus: filed by a public company not issuing a prospectus. Red herring prospectus. Differences: memorandum is subordinate to the Act and articles to the memorandum. Doctrine of ultra vires and constructive notice.
Hindi saransh
Company ka gathan: pravartan, nigamit, poonji sabhi, vyavsay prarambh. Gyapan patra, antarniyam, vivaran patrika.
The certificate of incorporation is conclusive evidence that a company is legally formed.

Big idea

Read the full explanation

Stages of company formation: promotion, incorporation, subscription of capital (public company), commencement of business (earlier certificate of commencement). Promotion: identification of business opportunity, feasibility studies, name approval, fixing of signatories to the memorandum, appointment of professionals, preparation of documents. Incorporation: documents to Registrar of Companies: memorandum of association (name, registered office, objects, liability, capital clauses), articles of association, consent of directors, agreement, declaration, address proof, fee payment. Certificate of incorporation is conclusive evidence. Subscription of capital: SEBI approval, prospectus, application, allotment, minimum subscription (90%), share certificates. Prospectus content and statement in lieu of prospectus. Private company does not issue a prospectus.

🚀

Promotion and incorporation

  • Promoter conducts promotional functions: opportunity, feasibility (technical, financial, economic), name (reserved with Registrar), signatories…
  • Memorandum clauses: name, registered office, objects, liability, capital, association (subscription)
  • Articles: internal rules about directors, shares, meetings, dividends
  • Incorporation documents: memorandum, articles, agreement, declaration, address proof
Read the full explanation

Promoter conducts promotional functions: opportunity, feasibility (technical, financial, economic), name (reserved with Registrar), signatories, professionals (mercantile bankers, auditors), documents. Memorandum clauses: name, registered office, objects, liability, capital, association (subscription). Articles: internal rules about directors, shares, meetings, dividends. Incorporation documents: memorandum, articles, agreement, declaration, address proof. Registrar issues certificate of incorporation, and Corporate Identity Number (CIN).

🧠

Capital subscription

  • Public company: SEBI guidelines
  • Prospectus invites public
  • Contents: name of company, issue details, capital, objects, directors
  • Letter of allotment, application money, allotment, calls
Read the full explanation

Public company: SEBI guidelines; prospectus invites public; contents: name of company, issue details, capital, objects, directors; Letter of allotment, application money, allotment, calls. Minimum subscription is 90% of issue. Allotment within 60 days. Money received kept in escrow with a scheduled bank. Private company can start after incorporation; public company after complying subscription rules.

🌟

Documents

  • Memorandum of association: charter, defines relationship with the outside world, can be altered only per the Act
  • Articles of association: internal rules
  • Prospectus: document inviting the public (any notice, circular)
  • Statement in lieu of prospectus: filed by a public company not issuing a prospectus
Read the full explanation

Memorandum of association: charter, defines relationship with the outside world, can be altered only per the Act. Articles of association: internal rules. Prospectus: document inviting the public (any notice, circular). Statement in lieu of prospectus: filed by a public company not issuing a prospectus. Red herring prospectus. Differences: memorandum is subordinate to the Act and articles to the memorandum. Doctrine of ultra vires and constructive notice.

lessons.title: Sources of Business Finance
yt: class 11 business studies sources of business finance equity shares debentures bank loan

blocks.x: Business finance is the money required for carrying out business activities. Classification: by period (long-term, medium-term, short-term), by ownership (owner funds, borrowed funds), by source of generation (internal, external). Sources: retained earnings, trade credit, factoring, lease financing, public deposits, commercial paper, issue of shares (equity and preference), debentures, loans from commercial banks, financial institutions, international financing (commercial banks, ADR, GDR, FCCB, FDI). Equity shares: ownership, voting rights, dividends. Preference shares: preferential dividend and repayment; types cumulative, non-cumulative, participating, convertible, redeemable. Debentures: creditorship, interest, types secured, unsecured, convertible, non-convertible, registered, bearer. Factoring: bills receivable sold at discount. Trade credit and bank overdraft for working capital.
Deep dive: Classification and owner funds

Owner funds: equity share capital, preference share capital, retained earnings (ploughing back of profits), ordinary shares. Equity shares: permanent capital, residual claim, voting rights, no fixed dividend, more risk but potential gains. Preference shares: fixed rate, priority over equity at winding up, no voting rights (except in certain cases). Retained earnings: no cost of floatation, no dilution, may cause dissatisfaction among shareholders.
Deep dive: Borrowed funds

Loans from commercial banks: short-term (cash credit, overdraft), term loans. Public deposits (companies invite deposits from the public for 1 to 3 years, RBI regulations). Trade credit: credit by suppliers (credit period 30-60 days). Commercial paper: unsecured promissory note by large firms, 15 days to 1 year, discounted. Factoring: sale of receivables (factor pays 80%), with or without recourse. Lease: lessor and lessee; operating and finance lease. Debentures: interest fixed, credit risk; redemption.
Deep dive: Choice of source

Factors: cost (interest vs dividend), financial strength, tax benefits (interest is deductible), flexibility, risk profile, control (equity dilutes), nature of the enterprise, purpose and time period. Global sources: ADR (American Depository Receipts), GDR, FCCB, ECB, FDI, FII. Long-term finance should match long-term assets (matching principle). Trading on equity: borrowing at lower cost than return on capital.
Hindi saransh
Vyavsayik vitt ke strot: sva-swamitva aur udhaar. Anshdhari swami, rinpatra rin deta hai. Vyapar udhaar, factoring, pattaa.

Visual lesson

Sources of Business Finance

Business finance is the money required for carrying out business activities

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Classification and owner…›3Borrowed funds›4Choice of source
Commercial paper15 days to 1 year
🔑

Big idea

  • Business finance is the money required for carrying out business activities
  • Classification: by period (long-term, medium-term, short-term), by ownership (owner funds, borrowed funds), by source of generation (internal…
  • Sources: retained earnings, trade credit, factoring, lease financing, public deposits, commercial paper, issue of shares (equity and preference)…
  • Equity shares: ownership, voting rights, dividends
Read the full explanation

Business finance is the money required for carrying out business activities. Classification: by period (long-term, medium-term, short-term), by ownership (owner funds, borrowed funds), by source of generation (internal, external). Sources: retained earnings, trade credit, factoring, lease financing, public deposits, commercial paper, issue of shares (equity and preference), debentures, loans from commercial banks, financial institutions, international financing (commercial banks, ADR, GDR, FCCB, FDI). Equity shares: ownership, voting rights, dividends. Preference shares: preferential dividend and repayment; types cumulative, non-cumulative, participating, convertible, redeemable. Debentures: creditorship, interest, types secured, unsecured, convertible, non-convertible, registered, bearer. Factoring: bills receivable sold at discount. Trade credit and bank overdraft for working capital.

📌

Classification and owner funds

  • Owner funds: equity share capital, preference share capital, retained earnings (ploughing back of profits), ordinary shares
  • Equity shares: permanent capital, residual claim, voting rights, no fixed dividend, more risk but potential gains
  • Preference shares: fixed rate, priority over equity at winding up, no voting rights (except in certain cases)
  • Retained earnings: no cost of floatation, no dilution, may cause dissatisfaction among shareholders
Read the full explanation

Owner funds: equity share capital, preference share capital, retained earnings (ploughing back of profits), ordinary shares. Equity shares: permanent capital, residual claim, voting rights, no fixed dividend, more risk but potential gains. Preference shares: fixed rate, priority over equity at winding up, no voting rights (except in certain cases). Retained earnings: no cost of floatation, no dilution, may cause dissatisfaction among shareholders.

🧠

Borrowed funds

  • Loans from commercial banks: short-term (cash credit, overdraft), term loans
  • Public deposits (companies invite deposits from the public for 1 to 3 years, RBI regulations)
  • Trade credit: credit by suppliers (credit period 30-60 days)
  • Commercial paper: unsecured promissory note by large firms, 15 days to 1 year, discounted
Read the full explanation

Loans from commercial banks: short-term (cash credit, overdraft), term loans. Public deposits (companies invite deposits from the public for 1 to 3 years, RBI regulations). Trade credit: credit by suppliers (credit period 30-60 days). Commercial paper: unsecured promissory note by large firms, 15 days to 1 year, discounted. Factoring: sale of receivables (factor pays 80%), with or without recourse. Lease: lessor and lessee; operating and finance lease. Debentures: interest fixed, credit risk; redemption.

🌟

Choice of source

  • Factors: cost (interest vs dividend), financial strength, tax benefits (interest is deductible), flexibility, risk profile, control (equity dilutes)…
  • Global sources: ADR (American Depository Receipts), GDR, FCCB, ECB, FDI, FII
  • Long-term finance should match long-term assets (matching principle)
  • Trading on equity: borrowing at lower cost than return on capital
Read the full explanation

Factors: cost (interest vs dividend), financial strength, tax benefits (interest is deductible), flexibility, risk profile, control (equity dilutes), nature of the enterprise, purpose and time period. Global sources: ADR (American Depository Receipts), GDR, FCCB, ECB, FDI, FII. Long-term finance should match long-term assets (matching principle). Trading on equity: borrowing at lower cost than return on capital.

lessons.title: Small Business and Entrepreneurship
yt: class 11 business studies small business and entrepreneurship MSME start-up

blocks.x: MSMED Act 2006 classified enterprises by investment in plant and machinery; revised in 2020 with composite criteria: micro (investment up to Rs 1 crore, turnover up to Rs 5 crore), small (up to Rs 10 crore, Rs 50 crore), medium (up to Rs 50 crore, Rs 250 crore). Role: employment, balanced regional development, equitable distribution, mobilisation of resources, export, self-reliance. Problems: finance, raw material, managerial skills, labour, marketing, infrastructure, technology, competition. Government assistance: Entrepreneurship Development Programme, NSIC, SIDBI, DIC, Khadi and Village Industries Commission, Mudra, Start-up India, Stand-up India. Entrepreneurship: process of seeking opportunities, taking risks, managing resources. Entrepreneur vs manager; characteristics: initiative, risk taking, innovation, vision; process of entrepreneurial development.
Deep dive: Small business

Cottage industries (household), village industries, small-scale industries. Enterprises can be manufacturing or service. Role: employment generation (second to agriculture), contribution to GDP and exports, dispersal of industries, use of local resources. Problems: lack of funds, raw materials, finding labour, marketing, outdated technology.
Deep dive: Government support

Schemes: Credit Guarantee Fund, Mudra loans (Shishu, Kishor, Tarun), Prime Minister Employment Generation Programme, Start-up India (tax relief, simplified compliance), Make in India. Institutions: NSIC (marketing support, raw material), SIDBI (finance), KVIC, DICs (district level), technology development centres, export promotion councils, SISI. Policies: reservation of items, tax holidays, subsidised power, priority sector lending.
Deep dive: Entrepreneurship

Entrepreneur: initiative, risk taking, innovation, vision, hardworking. Entrepreneurship is a process; entrepreneurs vs managers: motive, status, risk, rewards. Steps: idea, opportunity, resources, plan, launch. Entrepreneurial development process: identification of opportunity, project report, resource mobilisation, implementation. Theories: Schumpeter innovation theory. Women entrepreneurs: SHGs, Mahila Udyam. Intrapreneurship.
Hindi saransh
Chhote vyavsay aur udyamita: MSME, sarkari sahayata, udyamita ke gun. Mudra yojana, Start-up India.
Entrepreneurs innovate and bear risk; managers direct existing resources.

Read the full explanation

MSMED Act 2006 classified enterprises by investment in plant and machinery; revised in 2020 with composite criteria: micro (investment up to Rs 1 crore, turnover up to Rs 5 crore), small (up to Rs 10 crore, Rs 50 crore), medium (up to Rs 50 crore, Rs 250 crore). Role: employment, balanced regional development, equitable distribution, mobilisation of resources, export, self-reliance. Problems: finance, raw material, managerial skills, labour, marketing, infrastructure, technology, competition. Government assistance: Entrepreneurship Development Programme, NSIC, SIDBI, DIC, Khadi and Village Industries Commission, Mudra, Start-up India, Stand-up India. Entrepreneurship: process of seeking opportunities, taking risks, managing resources. Entrepreneur vs manager; characteristics: initiative, risk taking, innovation, vision; process of entrepreneurial development.

📌

Small business

  • Cottage industries (household), village industries, small-scale industries
  • Enterprises can be manufacturing or service
  • Role: employment generation (second to agriculture), contribution to GDP and exports, dispersal of industries, use of local resources
  • Problems: lack of funds, raw materials, finding labour, marketing, outdated technology
🏛️

Government support

  • Schemes: Credit Guarantee Fund, Mudra loans (Shishu, Kishor, Tarun), Prime Minister Employment Generation Programme, Start-up India (tax relief…
  • Institutions: NSIC (marketing support, raw material), SIDBI (finance), KVIC, DICs (district level), technology development centres, export promotion…
  • Policies: reservation of items, tax holidays, subsidised power, priority sector lending

Schemes: Credit Guarantee Fund, Mudra loans (Shishu, Kishor, Tarun), Prime Minister Employment Generation Programme, Start-up India (tax relief, simplified compliance), Make in India. Institutions: NSIC (marketing support, raw material), SIDBI (finance), KVIC, DICs (district level), technology development centres, export promotion councils, SISI. Policies: reservation of items, tax holidays, subsidised power, priority sector lending.

🌟

Entrepreneurship

  • Entrepreneurship is a process
  • Entrepreneurs vs managers: motive, status, risk, rewards
  • Steps: idea, opportunity, resources, plan, launch

Entrepreneur: initiative, risk taking, innovation, vision, hardworking. Entrepreneurship is a process; entrepreneurs vs managers: motive, status, risk, rewards. Steps: idea, opportunity, resources, plan, launch. Entrepreneurial development process: identification of opportunity, project report, resource mobilisation, implementation. lessons.title: Internal Trade
yt: class 11 business studies internal trade wholesale retail GST

blocks.x: Internal trade is the buying and selling of goods and services within the boundaries of a country. Wholesale trade: purchase in bulk from producers and sale to retailers; services to producers (risk bearing, financing, storage, grading, market information) and retailers (credit, goods availability, small lots, specialised knowledge, transport). Retail trade: sale to ultimate consumers. Types: itinerant (hawkers, peddlers, street traders), fixed shop (general stores, speciality stores, supermarkets, department stores, chain stores, mail order houses, consumer cooperative stores, vending machines, online). Chambers of commerce (FICCI, CII, ASSOCHAM). Goods and Services Tax (GST) 2017 replaced multiple indirect taxes; components CGST, SGST, IGST, UTGST. Documents: invoice, debit and credit note, lorry receipt, railway receipt, bill of lading. Terms of trade: cash on delivery, FOB, C.I.F., E.O.E., and 3 other terms.
Deep dive: Wholesale and retail

Services of wholesaler to manufacturer: bulk purchase, risk bearing, financing, warehousing, expert advice, marketing. To retailers: availability, marketing support, credit, specialised knowledge. Retailer to consumer: availability of goods, new products, after-sales service, credit. Retailer to wholesaler/manufacturer: distribution, personal selling, enabling large-scale operations, market information, risk. Large-scale retailers: department stores (one roof), chain stores (multiple shops), supermarkets (self-service), mail order, vending machine, hypermarket.
Deep dive: Types of retailers and GST

Itinerant: hawkers, cheap jacks, peddlers, market traders. Fixed shop: general stores, speciality shops, street stalls, second-hand goods shops, consumer cooperative stores. GST: destination-based tax on supply of goods and services; one nation one tax; input tax credit; slabs 5, 12, 18 and 28 percent; GSTN; registration for turnover above the threshold. Benefits: removes cascading effect, simpler compliance, uniform prices.
Deep dive: Documents and terms

Documents: invoice, debit note, credit note, lorry receipt (LR), railway receipt (RR), way bill (e-way bill), bill of lading. Terms: Cash on delivery (COD), cash discount, trade discount, quantity discount, FOB (free on board), CIF (cost, insurance, freight), E and O.E. (errors and omissions excepted), payment, delivery, return, advice. Chambers: FICCI, CII, ASSOCHAM represent business interests.
Hindi saransh
Aantarik vyapar: thok vyapar, khudra vyapar, GST. Thok vyapari utpadak aur khudra vyapari ke beech kadi hota hai.
GST replaced several indirect taxes with one destination-based tax on supply.

Visual lesson

Internal Trade

Internal trade is the buying and selling of goods and services within the boundaries of a country

minutes

Q&A

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Wholesale and retail›3Types of retailers and GST›4Documents and terms
🔑

Big idea

  • Internal trade is the buying and selling of goods and services within the boundaries of a country
  • Wholesale trade: purchase in bulk from producers and sale to retailers
  • Services to producers (risk bearing, financing, storage, grading, market information) and retailers (credit, goods availability, small lots…
  • Retail trade: sale to ultimate consumers
Read the full explanation

Internal trade is the buying and selling of goods and services within the boundaries of a country. Wholesale trade: purchase in bulk from producers and sale to retailers; services to producers (risk bearing, financing, storage, grading, market information) and retailers (credit, goods availability, small lots, specialised knowledge, transport). Retail trade: sale to ultimate consumers. Types: itinerant (hawkers, peddlers, street traders), fixed shop (general stores, speciality stores, supermarkets, department stores, chain stores, mail order houses, consumer cooperative stores, vending machines, online). Chambers of commerce (FICCI, CII, ASSOCHAM). Goods and Services Tax (GST) 2017 replaced multiple indirect taxes; components CGST, SGST, IGST, UTGST. Documents: invoice, debit and credit note, lorry receipt, railway receipt, bill of lading. Terms of trade: cash on delivery, FOB, C.I.F., E.O.E., and 3 other terms.

📌

Wholesale and retail

  • Services of wholesaler to manufacturer: bulk purchase, risk bearing, financing, warehousing, expert advice, marketing
  • To retailers: availability, marketing support, credit, specialised knowledge
  • Retailer to consumer: availability of goods, new products, after-sales service, credit
  • Retailer to wholesaler/manufacturer: distribution, personal selling, enabling large-scale operations, market information, risk
Read the full explanation

Services of wholesaler to manufacturer: bulk purchase, risk bearing, financing, warehousing, expert advice, marketing. To retailers: availability, marketing support, credit, specialised knowledge. Retailer to consumer: availability of goods, new products, after-sales service, credit. Retailer to wholesaler/manufacturer: distribution, personal selling, enabling large-scale operations, market information, risk. Large-scale retailers: department stores (one roof), chain stores (multiple shops), supermarkets (self-service), mail order, vending machine, hypermarket.

🧠

Types of retailers and GST

  • Itinerant: hawkers, cheap jacks, peddlers, market traders
  • Fixed shop: general stores, speciality shops, street stalls, second-hand goods shops, consumer cooperative stores
  • GST: destination-based tax on supply of goods and services
  • One nation one tax
Read the full explanation

Itinerant: hawkers, cheap jacks, peddlers, market traders. Fixed shop: general stores, speciality shops, street stalls, second-hand goods shops, consumer cooperative stores. GST: destination-based tax on supply of goods and services; one nation one tax; input tax credit; slabs 5, 12, 18 and 28 percent; GSTN; registration for turnover above the threshold. Benefits: removes cascading effect, simpler compliance, uniform prices.

🌟

Documents and terms

  • Documents: invoice, debit note, credit note, lorry receipt (LR), railway receipt (RR), way bill (e-way bill), bill of lading
  • Terms: Cash on delivery (COD), cash discount, trade discount, quantity discount, FOB (free on board), CIF (cost, insurance, freight), E and O.E
  • (errors and omissions excepted), payment, delivery, return, advice
  • Chambers: FICCI, CII, ASSOCHAM represent business interests

lessons.title: International Business
yt: class 11 business studies international business export import WTO documents

blocks.x: International business covers commercial transactions across national borders: exports, imports, FDI, licensing, franchising, joint ventures. Differences from domestic business: nationality of buyers and sellers, mobility of factors, customer heterogeneity, differences in business practices, political factors, currency, trade regulations. Benefits to nations: earning foreign exchange, more efficient use of resources, improving growth prospects, increased standard of living. Benefits to firms: higher profits, increased capacity utilisation, prospects for growth, way out to intense domestic competition, improved business vision. Modes of entry: exporting and importing, contract manufacturing, licensing and franchising, joint ventures, wholly owned subsidiaries. Export-import procedure: export (enquiry, quotation, order, letter of credit, production, pre-shipment inspection, excise clearance, insurance, customs, bill of lading, invoice, payment); import (trade enquiry, procurement of licence, obtaining foreign exchange, placing order, shipment, customs clearance, payment). Documents: commercial invoice, certificate of origin, bill of lading, mate’s receipt, packing list. WTO: formed 1995, principles of non-discrimination.
Deep dive: Nature and benefits

International business includes merchandise exports and imports, service exports and imports, licensing and franchising, foreign investments. Differences: nationalities, factor mobility, markets, business systems, political and legal environment, currency, documentation. Reasons: availability of resources, comparative advantage, trade surplus. Barriers: tariffs, quotas, subsidies, non-tariff barriers.
Deep dive: Export and import procedure

Export: enquiry, receipt of order, assessing importer’s creditworthiness, obtaining export licence, obtaining pre-shipment finance, production, pre-shipment inspection, excise clearance, obtaining certificate of origin, reservation of shipping space, packing and forwarding, insurance, customs clearance, mate’s receipt, payment of freight, issue of invoice, preparing of bill of exchange and presentation to bank. Import: trade enquiry, procurement of import licence, obtaining foreign exchange, placing order, letter of credit, arrangement of finance, receipt of shipment advice, retirement of import documents, arrival of goods, customs clearance, payment of customs duty, warehousing and release of goods.
Deep dive: Documents and WTO

Export documents: invoice, packing list, bill of lading, certificate of origin, certificate of inspection, mate’s receipt, shipping bill, airway bill. Import: bill of entry, import licence, letter of credit. Letter of credit: bank’s guarantee of payment. WTO: replaced GATT in 1995, headquartered in Geneva, objectives: trade liberalisation, dispute settlement; principles: non-discrimination, MFN, national treatment. Trade policy bodies and export promotion: EXIM Bank, Export Promotion Councils, Special Economic Zones (SEZ), EPZ, 100% EOUs.
Hindi saransh
Antarrashtriya vyavsay: niryat, aayat, WTO, dastavej. Niryat prakriya: poochhtaach se bhugtan tak.

International Business

International business covers commercial transactions across national borders: exports, imports, FDI, licensing, franchising, joint ventures

🔑

Big idea

  • International business covers commercial transactions across national borders: exports, imports, FDI, licensing, franchising, joint ventures
  • Differences from domestic business: nationality of buyers and sellers, mobility of factors, customer heterogeneity, differences in business…
  • Benefits to nations: earning foreign exchange, more efficient use of resources, improving growth prospects, increased standard of living

Read the full explanation

International business covers commercial transactions across national borders: exports, imports, FDI, licensing, franchising, joint ventures. Differences from domestic business: nationality of buyers and sellers, mobility of factors, customer heterogeneity, differences in business practices, political factors, currency, trade regulations. Benefits to nations: earning foreign exchange, more efficient use of resources, improving growth prospects, increased standard of living. Benefits to firms: higher profits, increased capacity utilisation, prospects for growth, way out to intense domestic competition, improved business vision. Modes of entry: exporting and importing, contract manufacturing, licensing and franchising, joint ventures, wholly owned subsidiaries. Export-import procedure: export (enquiry, quotation, order, letter of credit, production, pre-shipment inspection, excise clearance, insurance, customs, bill of lading, invoice, payment); import (trade enquiry, procurement of licence, obtaining foreign exchange, placing order, shipment, customs clearance, payment). Documents: commercial invoice, certificate of origin, bill of lading, mate’s receipt, packing list. WTO: formed 1995, principles of non-discrimination.

📌

Nature and benefits

  • International business includes merchandise exports and imports, service exports and imports, licensing and franchising, foreign investments
  • Differences: nationalities, factor mobility, markets, business systems, political and legal environment, currency, documentation
  • Reasons: availability of resources, comparative advantage, trade surplus
  • Barriers: tariffs, quotas, subsidies, non-tariff barriers
Read the full explanation

International business includes merchandise exports and imports, service exports and imports, licensing and franchising, foreign investments. Differences: nationalities, factor mobility, markets, business systems, political and legal environment, currency, documentation. Reasons: availability of resources, comparative advantage, trade surplus. Barriers: tariffs, quotas, subsidies, non-tariff barriers.

🔄

Export and import procedure

  • Export: enquiry, receipt of order, assessing importer’s creditworthiness, obtaining export licence, obtaining pre-shipment finance, production…
  • Import: trade enquiry, procurement of import licence, obtaining foreign exchange, placing order, letter of credit, arrangement of finance, receipt of…
Read the full explanation

Export: enquiry, receipt of order, assessing importer’s creditworthiness, obtaining export licence, obtaining pre-shipment finance, production, pre-shipment inspection, excise clearance, obtaining certificate of origin, reservation of shipping space, packing and forwarding, insurance, customs clearance, mate’s receipt, payment of freight, issue of invoice, preparing of bill of exchange and presentation to bank. Import: trade enquiry, procurement of import licence, obtaining foreign exchange, placing order, letter of credit, arrangement of finance, receipt of shipment advice, retirement of import documents, arrival of goods, customs clearance, payment of customs duty, warehousing and release of goods.

🌟

Documents and WTO

  • Export documents: invoice, packing list, bill of lading, certificate of origin, certificate of inspection, mate’s receipt, shipping bill, airway bill
  • Import: bill of entry, import licence, letter of credit
  • Letter of credit: bank’s guarantee of payment
  • WTO: replaced GATT in 1995, headquartered in Geneva, objectives: trade liberalisation, dispute settlement
Read the full explanation

Export documents: invoice, packing list, bill of lading, certificate of origin, certificate of inspection, mate’s receipt, shipping bill, airway bill. Import: bill of entry, import licence, letter of credit. Letter of credit: bank’s guarantee of payment. WTO: replaced GATT in 1995, headquartered in Geneva, objectives: trade liberalisation, dispute settlement; principles: non-discrimination, MFN, national treatment. Trade policy bodies and export promotion: EXIM Bank, Export Promotion Councils, Special Economic Zones (SEZ), EPZ, 100% EOUs.

lessons.title: Some basic concepts: mole and stoichiometry
yt: mole concept class 11 chemistry

blocks.x: **Mole:** the amount of substance containing 6.022 x 10^23 particles (Avogadro number N_A). Molar mass in g/mol equals the relative atomic/molecular mass: water (18 g/mol), 18 g = 1 mol.
Concentration terms

x: **Molarity** (M) = moles of solute / litres of solution. 5.85 g NaCl (58.5 g/mol) in 500 mL: moles = 0.1; M = 0.1 / 0.5 = **0.2 M**.
Molality = moles / kg of solvent; mole fraction x_A = n_A / (n_A + n_B); mass percent.

blocks.x: Percentage composition and empirical formula

H2SO4: M = 98.08 g/mol; H 2.06%, S 32.69%, O 65.26%. Empirical formula example: C 40%, H 6.7%, O 53.3%. Moles: C 40/12 = 3.33, H 6.7/1 = 6.7, O 53.3/16 = 3.33. Ratio 1 : 2 : 1, so empirical formula **CH2O**.
Limiting reagent
In 2 H2 + O2 -> 2 H2O, with 4 g H2 (2 mol) and 16 g O2 (0.5 mol), O2 needs 1 mol H2 so O2 is limiting; it forms 1 mol (18 g) of water.
Gas laws
At STP (0 C, 1 atm) 1 mol of ideal gas occupies about 22.4 L. PV = nRT with R = 0.0821 L atm/(mol K): 2 mol at 300 K and 1 atm occupies 49.3 L.
Hindi saransh
1 mol = 6.022 x 10^23 kan. Molarity = mol / L. Empirical formula mole ratio se. Limiting reagent product decide karta hai.
Always convert to moles first.

lessons.title: Structure of the atom and the Bohr model
yt: bohr model class 11

blocks.x: **Subatomic particles:** electron (-1), proton (+1), neutron (0). **Atomic number Z** = protons; **mass number A** = protons + neutrons.
Bohr model (hydrogen-like)

Electrons move in fixed orbits; energy E_n = -13.6 Z^2 / n^2 eV. Radius r_n = 0.529 n^2 / Z angstrom. Transition energy dE = 13.6 Z^2 (1/n1^2 - 1/n2^2) eV. Wavelength lambda (nm) = 1240 / dE (eV). Example: n = 3 to n = 2 in hydrogen: dE = 13.6 (1/4 - 1/9) = 1.889 eV, lambda = **656 nm** (red H-alpha line of the Balmer series).
Quantum numbers
n (shell), l (subshell: 0 s, 1 p, 2 d, 3 f), m_l (-l to +l), m_s (+/- 1/2). Each shell holds 2n^2 electrons.
Electron configuration rules

**Aufbau** (fill lowest energy first), **Pauli exclusion** (no two electrons share all four quantum numbers), **Hund's rule** (fill degenerate orbitals singly first). Exceptions: Cr is [Ar] 3d5 4s1, Cu is [Ar] 3d10 4s1.
de Broglie and uncertainty
lambda = h / (m v). Heisenberg: dx x dp >= h / 4 pi.
