lessons.title: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry
yt: class 11 chemistry some basic concepts mole concept stoichiometry limiting reagent

blocks.x: Matter: elements, compounds, mixtures. Laws of chemical combination: conservation of mass (Lavoisier), definite proportions (Proust), multiple proportions (Dalton), Gay-Lussac law of gaseous volumes, Avogadro law. Dalton atomic theory. Atomic mass unit = 1/12 of C-12 mass = 1.66 x 10^-24 g. Mole = 6.022 x 10^23 entities; molar mass in g/mol; molar volume 22.4 L at STP (22.7 L at 1 bar, 273 K). Percentage composition, empirical and molecular formula (n = molecular mass / empirical mass). Stoichiometry, limiting reagent. Concentration: mass %, mole fraction, molarity (mol/L), molality (mol/kg), normality. Significant figures, scientific notation, SI units, dimensional analysis. Precision and accuracy.
Deep dive: Laws and the mole

Lavoisier: mass of reactants equals mass of products. Proust: a compound always has the same elements in a fixed ratio by mass. Dalton: if two elements form more than one compound, masses of one combining with a fixed mass of the other are in simple whole-number ratio (CO and CO2). Gay-Lussac: gases react in simple volume ratios. Avogadro: equal volumes of gases at the same T and P contain equal numbers of molecules. Mole: 1 mol contains 6.022 x 10^23 particles; number of moles = mass / molar mass = particles / NA = volume at STP / 22.4 L. Molar mass of H2O = 18 g/mol, CO2 = 44 g/mol.
Deep dive: Formulae and stoichiometry

Empirical formula: simplest whole-number ratio; molecular formula = n x empirical formula. Steps: percentage to mass, divide by atomic mass, divide by smallest, convert to whole numbers. Stoichiometric coefficients give mole ratios, not mass. Limiting reagent: the reactant that is completely consumed and fixes the amount of product; the other is in excess. Example: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O. Percent yield = actual / theoretical x 100. Combustion analysis for C and H.
Deep dive: Concentration terms

Mass % = mass of solute / mass of solution x 100. Mole fraction x_A = n_A / (n_A + n_B); sum of mole fractions is 1. Molarity M = moles of solute / volume of solution in L, changes with temperature. Molality m = moles of solute / kg of solvent, independent of temperature. Dilution: M1V1 = M2V2. Relation: M = (density x 1000 x mass % ) / (100 x molar mass). Significant figures: rules for zeros; calculations. Dimensional analysis uses unit factors.

Rasayan ki mool dharnayen: mole, sutra, moolanupaat. Ek mole mein 6.022 x 10^23 kan. Seemit abhikarak se utpaad nirdharit.

Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry

🔑

Big idea

  • Matter: elements, compounds, mixtures
  • Laws of chemical combination: conservation of mass (Lavoisier), definite proportions (Proust), multiple proportions (Dalton), Gay-Lussac law of…
  • Dalton atomic theory
  • Atomic mass unit = 1/12 of C-12 mass = 1.66 x 10-24 g
Read the full explanation

Matter: elements, compounds, mixtures. Laws of chemical combination: conservation of mass (Lavoisier), definite proportions (Proust), multiple proportions (Dalton), Gay-Lussac law of gaseous volumes, Avogadro law. Dalton atomic theory. Atomic mass unit = 1/12 of C-12 mass = 1.66 x 10^-24 g. Mole = 6.022 x 10^23 entities; molar mass in g/mol; molar volume 22.4 L at STP (22.7 L at 1 bar, 273 K). Percentage composition, empirical and molecular formula (n = molecular mass / empirical mass). Stoichiometry, limiting reagent. Concentration: mass %, mole fraction, molarity (mol/L), molality (mol/kg), normality. Significant figures, scientific notation, SI units, dimensional analysis. Precision and accuracy.

⚖️

Laws and the mole

  • Lavoisier: mass of reactants equals mass of products
  • Proust: a compound always has the same elements in a fixed ratio by mass
  • Dalton: if two elements form more than one compound, masses of one combining with a fixed mass of the other are in simple whole-number ratio (CO and…
  • Gay-Lussac: gases react in simple volume ratios
Read the full explanation

Lavoisier: mass of reactants equals mass of products. Proust: a compound always has the same elements in a fixed ratio by mass. Dalton: if two elements form more than one compound, masses of one combining with a fixed mass of the other are in simple whole-number ratio (CO and CO2). Gay-Lussac: gases react in simple volume ratios. Avogadro: equal volumes of gases at the same T and P contain equal numbers of molecules. Mole: 1 mol contains 6.022 x 10^23 particles; number of moles = mass / molar mass = particles / NA = volume at STP / 22.4 L. Molar mass of H2O = 18 g/mol, CO2 = 44 g/mol.

🧮

Formulae and stoichiometry

  • Empirical formula: simplest whole-number ratio
  • Molecular formula = n x empirical formula
  • Steps: percentage to mass, divide by atomic mass, divide by smallest, convert to whole numbers
  • Stoichiometric coefficients give mole ratios, not mass
Read the full explanation

Empirical formula: simplest whole-number ratio; molecular formula = n x empirical formula. Steps: percentage to mass, divide by atomic mass, divide by smallest, convert to whole numbers. Stoichiometric coefficients give mole ratios, not mass. Limiting reagent: the reactant that is completely consumed and fixes the amount of product; the other is in excess. Example: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O. Percent yield = actual / theoretical x 100. Combustion analysis for C and H.

🌟

Concentration terms

  • Mass % = mass of solute / mass of solution x 100
  • Mole fraction x_A = n_A / (n_A + n_B)
  • Sum of mole fractions is 1
  • Molarity M = moles of solute / volume of solution in L, changes with temperature
Read the full explanation

Mass % = mass of solute / mass of solution x 100. Mole fraction x_A = n_A / (n_A + n_B); sum of mole fractions is 1. Molarity M = moles of solute / volume of solution in L, changes with temperature. Molality m = moles of solute / kg of solvent, independent of temperature. Dilution: M1V1 = M2V2. Relation: M = (density x 1000 x mass % ) / (100 x molar mass). Significant figures: rules for zeros; calculations. Dimensional analysis uses unit factors.

lessons.title: Structure of Atom
yt: class 11 chemistry structure of atom quantum numbers orbitals Bohr model

blocks.x: Discovery of electron (Thomson, e/m = 1.76 x 10^8 C/g), proton (Goldstein), neutron (Chadwick). Thomson plum pudding. Rutherford nuclear model from alpha scattering. Atomic number Z, mass number A. Isotopes, isobars, isotones. Electromagnetic radiation: wavelength, frequency, wave number, c = nu x lambda; Planck E = h nu (h = 6.626 x 10^-34 J s); photoelectric effect; hydrogen spectrum (Lyman, Balmer, Paschen, Brackett, Pfund). Bohr model: En = -2.18 x 10^-18 / n^2 J = -13.6/n^2 eV, r_n = 52.9 n^2/Z pm. de Broglie lambda = h/mv; Heisenberg uncertainty principle. Quantum numbers n, l, m_l, m_s. Shapes of orbitals. Aufbau principle, Pauli exclusion, Hund rule; electronic configuration; stability of half-filled and fully filled orbitals (Cr, Cu).
Deep dive: Early models and radiation

Cathode rays are electrons. Rutherford: most alpha particles pass through; few deflect at large angles; nucleus is small, dense, positive. Limitations: stability and line spectra. Planck quantum theory: energy emitted in quanta. Photoelectric effect (Einstein): h nu = W0 + KE; threshold frequency. Hydrogen spectrum: 1/lambda = R_H (1/n1^2 - 1/n2^2), R_H = 1.097 x 10^7 m^-1; Lyman (UV, n1=1), Balmer (visible, n1=2), Paschen (IR, n1=3).
Deep dive: Bohr and quantum mechanics

Bohr postulates: stationary orbits, L = n h / 2 pi, energy change on jumping. Limitations: fails for multi-electron atoms, Zeeman and Stark effects. de Broglie: matter waves. Heisenberg: delta x . delta p >= h / 4 pi. Schrodinger equation, psi, psi^2 as probability density. Radial nodes = n - l - 1; angular nodes = l; total nodes = n - 1.
Deep dive: Quantum numbers and configuration

Principal n = 1, 2, 3 (shell size); azimuthal l = 0 to n-1 (s, p, d, f shapes); magnetic m_l = -l to +l (orientation); spin m_s = +1/2 or -1/2. Number of orbitals in a shell is n^2; electrons 2n^2. Aufbau: filling in order of increasing (n + l), 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p 5s. Pauli: no two electrons have the same four quantum numbers. Hund: pairing after each orbital is singly occupied. Cr is [Ar] 3d5 4s1; Cu is [Ar] 3d10 4s1.

Visual lesson

Structure of Atom

Discovery of electron (Thomson, e/m = 1.76 x 10^8 C/g), proton (Goldstein), neutron (Chadwick)

🔑

Big idea

  • Discovery of electron (Thomson, e/m = 1.76 x 108 C/g), proton (Goldstein), neutron (Chadwick)
  • Thomson plum pudding
  • Rutherford nuclear model from alpha scattering
  • Atomic number Z, mass number A
Read the full explanation

Discovery of electron (Thomson, e/m = 1.76 x 10^8 C/g), proton (Goldstein), neutron (Chadwick). Thomson plum pudding. Rutherford nuclear model from alpha scattering. Atomic number Z, mass number A. Isotopes, isobars, isotones. Electromagnetic radiation: wavelength, frequency, wave number, c = nu x lambda; Planck E = h nu (h = 6.626 x 10^-34 J s); photoelectric effect; hydrogen spectrum (Lyman, Balmer, Paschen, Brackett, Pfund). Bohr model: En = -2.18 x 10^-18 / n^2 J = -13.6/n^2 eV, r_n = 52.9 n^2/Z pm. de Broglie lambda = h/mv; Heisenberg uncertainty principle. Quantum numbers n, l, m_l, m_s. Shapes of orbitals. Aufbau principle, Pauli exclusion, Hund rule; electronic configuration; stability of half-filled and fully filled orbitals (Cr, Cu).

📌

Early models and radiation

  • Cathode rays are electrons
  • Rutherford: most alpha particles pass through
  • Few deflect at large angles
  • Nucleus is small, dense, positive
Read the full explanation

Cathode rays are electrons. Rutherford: most alpha particles pass through; few deflect at large angles; nucleus is small, dense, positive. Limitations: stability and line spectra. Planck quantum theory: energy emitted in quanta. Photoelectric effect (Einstein): h nu = W0 + KE; threshold frequency. Hydrogen spectrum: 1/lambda = R_H (1/n1^2 - 1/n2^2), R_H = 1.097 x 10^7 m^-1; Lyman (UV, n1=1), Balmer (visible, n1=2), Paschen (IR, n1=3).

🧠

Bohr and quantum mechanics

  • Bohr postulates: stationary orbits, L = n h / 2 pi, energy change on jumping
  • Limitations: fails for multi-electron atoms, Zeeman and Stark effects
  • De Broglie: matter waves
  • Heisenberg: delta x
Read the full explanation

Bohr postulates: stationary orbits, L = n h / 2 pi, energy change on jumping. Limitations: fails for multi-electron atoms, Zeeman and Stark effects. de Broglie: matter waves. Heisenberg: delta x . delta p >= h / 4 pi. Schrodinger equation, psi, psi^2 as probability density. Radial nodes = n - l - 1; angular nodes = l; total nodes = n - 1.

🌟

Quantum numbers and configuration

  • Principal n = 1, 2, 3 (shell size)
  • Azimuthal l = 0 to n-1 (s, p, d, f shapes)
  • Magnetic m_l = -l to +l (orientation)
  • Spin m_s = +1/2 or -1/2
Read the full explanation

Principal n = 1, 2, 3 (shell size); azimuthal l = 0 to n-1 (s, p, d, f shapes); magnetic m_l = -l to +l (orientation); spin m_s = +1/2 or -1/2. Number of orbitals in a shell is n^2; electrons 2n^2. Aufbau: filling in order of increasing (n + l), 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p 5s. Pauli: no two electrons have the same four quantum numbers. Hund: pairing after each orbital is singly occupied. Cr is [Ar] 3d5 4s1; Cu is [Ar] 3d10 4s1.

lessons.title: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
yt: class 11 chemistry periodic table periodicity ionisation enthalpy electronegativity

blocks.x: Dobereiner triads, Newlands octaves, Mendeleev periodic law (atomic mass), Moseley (atomic number); modern periodic law. Long form: 18 groups, 7 periods; s, p, d, f blocks. IUPAC names for Z above 100 (unnilunium etc.; now Nh, Mc, Ts, Og). Periodic trends: atomic radius (decreases across a period, increases down a group), ionic radius, isoelectronic species, ionisation enthalpy (increases across, decreases down, with exceptions Be/B, N/O), electron gain enthalpy (Cl highest), electronegativity (Pauling, F = 4.0), valence, oxidation states. Diagonal relationship. Anomalous properties of the second period elements.
Deep dive: Development and structure

Mendeleev left gaps and predicted eka-aluminium (gallium) and eka-silicon (germanium). Modern table: periods 1 (2 elements), 2 (8), 3 (8), 4 (18), 5 (18), 6 (32), 7 (incomplete). s-block: group 1 and 2; p-block: groups 13 to 18; d-block: groups 3 to 12 (transition); f-block: lanthanoids and actinoids. Representative elements; noble gases; halogens; chalcogens (group 16); pnictogens (15).
Deep dive: Periodic trends

Atomic radius: covalent, metallic, van der Waals; decreases across a period due to increasing effective nuclear charge; increases down due to extra shells. Cation smaller than parent atom; anion larger. Isoelectronic ions: size decreases with increasing nuclear charge (N3- > O2- > F- > Na+ > Mg2+). Ionisation enthalpy: first IE of Mg > Al (s vs p), P > S (half-filled). Electron gain enthalpy more negative for Cl than F (small size of F). Electronegativity: Pauling scale; increases across period; decreases down. Metallic character decreases across a period.
Deep dive: Oxidation states and anomalies

Group valence; transition metals show multiple oxidation states. Anomalous behaviour of Li, Be, B, C, N, O, F due to small size, high electronegativity and absence of d orbitals. Diagonal relationships: Li-Mg, Be-Al, B-Si. Basic oxides on left, acidic on right, amphoteric Al2O3. Reactivity of metals decreases across; nonmetals increases.

Visual lesson

Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties

Dobereiner triads, Newlands octaves, Mendeleev periodic law (atomic mass), Moseley (atomic number)

🔑

Big idea

  • Dobereiner triads, Newlands octaves, Mendeleev periodic law (atomic mass), Moseley (atomic number)
  • Modern periodic law
  • Long form: 18 groups, 7 periods
  • S, p, d, f blocks
Read the full explanation

Dobereiner triads, Newlands octaves, Mendeleev periodic law (atomic mass), Moseley (atomic number); modern periodic law. Long form: 18 groups, 7 periods; s, p, d, f blocks. IUPAC names for Z above 100 (unnilunium etc.; now Nh, Mc, Ts, Og). Periodic trends: atomic radius (decreases across a period, increases down a group), ionic radius, isoelectronic species, ionisation enthalpy (increases across, decreases down, with exceptions Be/B, N/O), electron gain enthalpy (Cl highest), electronegativity (Pauling, F = 4.0), valence, oxidation states. Diagonal relationship. Anomalous properties of the second period elements.

📌

Development and structure

  • Mendeleev left gaps and predicted eka-aluminium (gallium) and eka-silicon (germanium)
  • Modern table: periods 1 (2 elements), 2 (8), 3 (8), 4 (18), 5 (18), 6 (32), 7 (incomplete)
  • S-block: group 1 and 2
  • P-block: groups 13 to 18
Read the full explanation

Mendeleev left gaps and predicted eka-aluminium (gallium) and eka-silicon (germanium). Modern table: periods 1 (2 elements), 2 (8), 3 (8), 4 (18), 5 (18), 6 (32), 7 (incomplete). s-block: group 1 and 2; p-block: groups 13 to 18; d-block: groups 3 to 12 (transition); f-block: lanthanoids and actinoids. Representative elements; noble gases; halogens; chalcogens (group 16); pnictogens (15).

🧠

Periodic trends

  • Atomic radius: covalent, metallic, van der Waals
  • Decreases across a period due to increasing effective nuclear charge
  • Increases down due to extra shells
  • Cation smaller than parent atom
Read the full explanation

Atomic radius: covalent, metallic, van der Waals; decreases across a period due to increasing effective nuclear charge; increases down due to extra shells. Cation smaller than parent atom; anion larger. Isoelectronic ions: size decreases with increasing nuclear charge (N3- > O2- > F- > Na+ > Mg2+). Ionisation enthalpy: first IE of Mg > Al (s vs p), P > S (half-filled). Electron gain enthalpy more negative for Cl than F (small size of F). Electronegativity: Pauling scale; increases across period; decreases down. Metallic character decreases across a period.

🌟

Oxidation states and anomalies

  • Group valence
  • Transition metals show multiple oxidation states
  • Anomalous behaviour of Li, Be, B, C, N, O, F due to small size, high electronegativity and absence of d orbitals
  • Diagonal relationships: Li-Mg, Be-Al, B-Si
Read the full explanation

Group valence; transition metals show multiple oxidation states. Anomalous behaviour of Li, Be, B, C, N, O, F due to small size, high electronegativity and absence of d orbitals. Diagonal relationships: Li-Mg, Be-Al, B-Si. Basic oxides on left, acidic on right, amphoteric Al2O3. Reactivity of metals decreases across; nonmetals increases.

blocks.x: At equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal; concentrations stay constant. For a A + b B <=> c C + d D, **K_c = [C]^c [D]^d / ([A]^a [B]^b)**. lessons.title: Thermodynamics and enthalpy
yt: thermodynamics class 11 chemistry

blocks.x: **First law:** dU = q + w (internal energy). **Enthalpy** H = U + PV; at constant pressure q_p = dH. Exothermic: dH < 0. **Hess's law:** total enthalpy change is independent of the path. **Standard enthalpy of reaction** = sum of formation enthalpies of products minus reactants. Example (methane combustion): CH4 + 2 O2 -> CO2 + 2 H2O(l). dH = (-393.5) + 2 (-285.8) - (-74.8) = **-890.3 kJ/mol**. **Entropy** S measures disorder. **Gibbs free energy** dG = dH - T dS; reaction is spontaneous if dG < 0. At equilibrium dG = 0.
Hindi saransh
dU = q + w. Hess ka niyam: path se koi fark nahi. dG = dH - T dS < 0 to spontaneous.
Spontaneous means dG is negative, not that the reaction is fast.

lessons.title: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure
yt: class 11 chemistry chemical bonding VSEPR hybridisation molecular orbital theory

blocks.x: Kossel-Lewis approach: octet rule, Lewis dot structures, formal charge. Ionic bond: lattice enthalpy, Born-Haber cycle. Covalent bond: bond parameters (length, angle, enthalpy, order), resonance, polarity, dipole moment (mu = q x d), Fajans rules. VSEPR theory predicts shapes: linear (BeCl2), trigonal planar (BF3), tetrahedral (CH4), trigonal bipyramidal (PCl5), octahedral (SF6), bent (H2O), pyramidal (NH3), see-saw (SF4), T-shaped (ClF3), square planar (XeF4). Valence bond theory, hybridisation sp, sp2, sp3, sp3d, sp3d2; sigma and pi bonds. Molecular orbital theory: bonding and antibonding MOs, bond order = (Nb - Na)/2; O2 is paramagnetic; N2 bond order 3. Hydrogen bonding (intramolecular, intermolecular).
Deep dive: Ionic and covalent bonding

Octet rule exceptions: incomplete octet (BeCl2, BF3), expanded octet (PCl5, SF6), odd electron (NO). Formal charge = V - L - B/2. Lattice enthalpy increases with higher charge and smaller size; NaCl 788 kJ/mol. Born-Haber cycle: sublimation, ionisation, dissociation, electron gain, lattice. Resonance: CO3^2- with bond order 1.33; benzene. Fajans: small cation, large anion, high charge gives more covalent character (LiCl vs NaCl). Dipole moment: NH3 > NF3; CO2 zero; CH4 zero; H2O 1.85 D.
Deep dive: VSEPR and hybridisation

Lone pair-lone pair repulsion > lone pair-bond pair > bond pair-bond pair. Bond angles: CH4 109.5, NH3 107, H2O 104.5. sp: linear (BeCl2, C2H2); sp2: trigonal planar 120 (BF3, C2H4); sp3: tetrahedral (CH4); sp3d: PCl5; sp3d2: SF6. A sigma bond is formed by head-on overlap, pi by sideways overlap; single bond one sigma, double one sigma + one pi, triple one sigma + two pi.
Deep dive: MO theory and hydrogen bond

LCAO: bonding MO lower energy; antibonding higher. Order for O2, F2: sigma1s < sigma*1s < sigma2s < sigma*2s < sigma2pz < pi2px = pi2py < pi*2px = pi*2py < sigma*2pz; for B2, C2, N2: pi before sigma2pz. Bond order: H2 1, He2 0, N2 3, O2 2, O2^+ 2.5, O2^- 1.5. Hydrogen bond: H bonded to F, O, N; explains the high boiling point of water and the lower density of ice; intramolecular in o-nitrophenol (lower boiling point than p-isomer).
Hindi saransh
Rasayanik bandhan: Lewis, VSEPR, sankarn, MO sidhant. Bandh kram = (Nb - Na)/2. O2 anuchumbakiya.
Bond order = (bonding electrons - antibonding electrons) / 2.

🔑

Big idea

  • Kossel-Lewis approach: octet rule, Lewis dot structures, formal charge
  • Ionic bond: lattice enthalpy, Born-Haber cycle
  • Covalent bond: bond parameters (length, angle, enthalpy, order), resonance, polarity, dipole moment (mu = q x d), Fajans rules
  • VSEPR theory predicts shapes: linear (BeCl2), trigonal planar (BF3), tetrahedral (CH4), trigonal bipyramidal (PCl5), octahedral (SF6), bent (H2O)…
Read the full explanation

Kossel-Lewis approach: octet rule, Lewis dot structures, formal charge. Ionic bond: lattice enthalpy, Born-Haber cycle. Covalent bond: bond parameters (length, angle, enthalpy, order), resonance, polarity, dipole moment (mu = q x d), Fajans rules. VSEPR theory predicts shapes: linear (BeCl2), trigonal planar (BF3), tetrahedral (CH4), trigonal bipyramidal (PCl5), octahedral (SF6), bent (H2O), pyramidal (NH3), see-saw (SF4), T-shaped (ClF3), square planar (XeF4). Valence bond theory, hybridisation sp, sp2, sp3, sp3d, sp3d2; sigma and pi bonds. Molecular orbital theory: bonding and antibonding MOs, bond order = (Nb - Na)/2; O2 is paramagnetic; N2 bond order 3. Hydrogen bonding (intramolecular, intermolecular).

⚗️

Ionic and covalent bonding

  • Octet rule exceptions: incomplete octet (BeCl2, BF3), expanded octet (PCl5, SF6), odd electron (NO)
  • Formal charge = V - L - B/2
  • Lattice enthalpy increases with higher charge and smaller size
  • NaCl 788 kJ/mol
Read the full explanation

Octet rule exceptions: incomplete octet (BeCl2, BF3), expanded octet (PCl5, SF6), odd electron (NO). Formal charge = V - L - B/2. Lattice enthalpy increases with higher charge and smaller size; NaCl 788 kJ/mol. Born-Haber cycle: sublimation, ionisation, dissociation, electron gain, lattice. Resonance: CO3^2- with bond order 1.33; benzene. Fajans: small cation, large anion, high charge gives more covalent character (LiCl vs NaCl). Dipole moment: NH3 > NF3; CO2 zero; CH4 zero; H2O 1.85 D.

🧠

VSEPR and hybridisation

  • Lone pair-lone pair repulsion > lone pair-bond pair > bond pair-bond pair
  • Bond angles: CH4 109.5, NH3 107, H2O 104.5
  • Sp: linear (BeCl2, C2H2)
  • Sp2: trigonal planar 120 (BF3, C2H4)
Read the full explanation

Lone pair-lone pair repulsion > lone pair-bond pair > bond pair-bond pair. Bond angles: CH4 109.5, NH3 107, H2O 104.5. sp: linear (BeCl2, C2H2); sp2: trigonal planar 120 (BF3, C2H4); sp3: tetrahedral (CH4); sp3d: PCl5; sp3d2: SF6. A sigma bond is formed by head-on overlap, pi by sideways overlap; single bond one sigma, double one sigma + one pi, triple one sigma + two pi.

⚗️

MO theory and hydrogen bond

  • LCAO: bonding MO lower energy
  • Antibonding higher
  • Order for O2, F2: sigma1s < sigma*1s < sigma2s < sigma*2s < sigma2pz < pi2px = pi2py < pi*2px = pi*2py < sigma*2pz
  • For B2, C2, N2: pi before sigma2pz
Read the full explanation

LCAO: bonding MO lower energy; antibonding higher. Order for O2, F2: sigma1s < sigma*1s < sigma2s < sigma*2s < sigma2pz < pi2px = pi2py < pi*2px = pi*2py < sigma*2pz; for B2, C2, N2: pi before sigma2pz. Bond order: H2 1, He2 0, N2 3, O2 2, O2^+ 2.5, O2^- 1.5. Hydrogen bond: H bonded to F, O, N; explains the high boiling point of water and the lower density of ice; intramolecular in o-nitrophenol (lower boiling point than p-isomer).

lessons.title: Thermodynamics
yt: class 11 chemistry thermodynamics enthalpy entropy Gibbs energy Hess law

blocks.x: System, surroundings, boundary; open, closed, isolated systems. State functions (U, H, S, G, P, V, T) and path functions (q, w). First law: delta U = q + w; work of expansion w = -P_ext delta V; isothermal reversible w = -2.303 nRT log(V2/V1). Enthalpy H = U + PV; delta H = delta U + delta n_g RT. Heat capacity Cp - Cv = R. Enthalpies of formation, combustion, neutralisation (-57.1 kJ/mol), atomisation, bond, lattice, solution. Hess law. Spontaneity: entropy S (second law), delta S_universe > 0; Gibbs energy delta G = delta H - T delta S; delta G < 0 spontaneous; delta G standard = -RT ln K = -2.303 RT log K. Third law: entropy of a perfect crystal at 0 K is zero. Calorimetry: bomb calorimeter (delta U), constant pressure (delta H).
Deep dive: First law and enthalpy

Internal energy changes via heat and work. Sign convention: work done on system positive, heat absorbed positive. Free expansion: w = 0. Adiabatic: q = 0. Isochoric: w = 0, delta U = q_v. Isobaric: delta H = q_p. For ideal gas delta U depends only on T. Enthalpy of formation of elements in their standard state is zero. delta_r H = sum delta_f H(products) - sum delta_f H(reactants). Bond enthalpy: delta_r H = sum bonds broken - sum bonds formed.
Deep dive: Hess law and enthalpy types

Hess law: total enthalpy change is independent of the path. Combustion: complete oxidation. Neutralisation of strong acid with strong base: -57.1 kJ/mol. Lattice enthalpy via Born-Haber cycle. Enthalpy of solution. Enthalpy of fusion of ice 6.01 kJ/mol; vaporisation of water 40.7 kJ/mol. Phase transitions: delta S = delta H / T.
Deep dive: Entropy and Gibbs energy

Entropy S is a measure of randomness; units J/K/mol; S(gas) > S(liquid) > S(solid). delta S_system + delta S_surroundings > 0 for spontaneous process; delta S_surr = -delta H / T. delta G = delta H - T delta S; four cases: exothermic and entropy increase always spontaneous; endothermic and entropy decrease never; others depend on T. At equilibrium delta G = 0 and T = delta H / delta S. delta G standard = -RT ln K.

Visual lesson

Thermodynamics

System, surroundings, boundary

minutes

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2First law and enthalpy›3Hess law and enthalpy types›4Entropy and Gibbs energy
🔑

Big idea

  • System, surroundings, boundary
  • Open, closed, isolated systems
  • State functions (U, H, S, G, P, V, T) and path functions (q, w)
  • First law: delta U = q + w
Read the full explanation

System, surroundings, boundary; open, closed, isolated systems. State functions (U, H, S, G, P, V, T) and path functions (q, w). First law: delta U = q + w; work of expansion w = -P_ext delta V; isothermal reversible w = -2.303 nRT log(V2/V1). Enthalpy H = U + PV; delta H = delta U + delta n_g RT. Heat capacity Cp - Cv = R. Enthalpies of formation, combustion, neutralisation (-57.1 kJ/mol), atomisation, bond, lattice, solution. Hess law. Spontaneity: entropy S (second law), delta S_universe > 0; Gibbs energy delta G = delta H - T delta S; delta G < 0 spontaneous; delta G standard = -RT ln K = -2.303 RT log K. Third law: entropy of a perfect crystal at 0 K is zero. Calorimetry: bomb calorimeter (delta U), constant pressure (delta H).

⚖️

First law and enthalpy

  • Internal energy changes via heat and work
  • Sign convention: work done on system positive, heat absorbed positive
  • Free expansion: w = 0
  • Adiabatic: q = 0
Read the full explanation

Internal energy changes via heat and work. Sign convention: work done on system positive, heat absorbed positive. Free expansion: w = 0. Adiabatic: q = 0. Isochoric: w = 0, delta U = q_v. Isobaric: delta H = q_p. For ideal gas delta U depends only on T. Enthalpy of formation of elements in their standard state is zero. delta_r H = sum delta_f H(products) - sum delta_f H(reactants). Bond enthalpy: delta_r H = sum bonds broken - sum bonds formed.

⚖️

Hess law and enthalpy types

  • Hess law: total enthalpy change is independent of the path
  • Combustion: complete oxidation
  • Neutralisation of strong acid with strong base: -57.1 kJ/mol
  • Lattice enthalpy via Born-Haber cycle
Read the full explanation

Hess law: total enthalpy change is independent of the path. Combustion: complete oxidation. Neutralisation of strong acid with strong base: -57.1 kJ/mol. Lattice enthalpy via Born-Haber cycle. Enthalpy of solution. Enthalpy of fusion of ice 6.01 kJ/mol; vaporisation of water 40.7 kJ/mol. Phase transitions: delta S = delta H / T.

🚀

Entropy and Gibbs energy

  • Entropy S is a measure of randomness
  • Units J/K/mol
  • S(gas) > S(liquid) > S(solid)
  • Delta S_system + delta S_surroundings > 0 for spontaneous process
Read the full explanation

Entropy S is a measure of randomness; units J/K/mol; S(gas) > S(liquid) > S(solid). delta S_system + delta S_surroundings > 0 for spontaneous process; delta S_surr = -delta H / T. delta G = delta H - T delta S; four cases: exothermic and entropy increase always spontaneous; endothermic and entropy decrease never; others depend on T. At equilibrium delta G = 0 and T = delta H / delta S. delta G standard = -RT ln K.

lessons.title: Equilibrium
yt: class 11 chemistry equilibrium Le Chatelier Kc Kp ionic equilibrium pH buffer Ksp

blocks.x: Physical equilibrium (solid-liquid, liquid-vapour, solid-vapour, dissolution) and chemical equilibrium. Law of mass action: for aA + bB <-> cC + dD, Kc = [C]^c [D]^d / [A]^a [B]^b. Kp = Kc (RT)^delta n. Reaction quotient Q. Le Chatelier principle: concentration, pressure, temperature, catalyst (no effect on position). Ionic equilibrium: strong and weak electrolytes; Arrhenius, Bronsted-Lowry, Lewis acids and bases; conjugate pairs. Ionisation: Ka, Kb, Ka x Kb = Kw = 10^-14 at 298 K. pH = -log[H+]; pH + pOH = 14. Degree of dissociation alpha = sqrt(Ka/C). Buffer: Henderson-Hasselbalch pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]). Salt hydrolysis. Solubility product Ksp. Common ion effect.
Deep dive: Chemical equilibrium

Equilibrium is dynamic; rates of forward and reverse reactions are equal. Characteristics: constant concentrations, attained from either side, catalyst does not change Kc. Kc units depend on delta n. If Q < K reaction goes forward; Q > K reverse. Examples: N2 + 3H2 <-> 2NH3 (delta n = -2), PCl5 <-> PCl3 + Cl2, H2 + I2 <-> 2HI (Kc independent of volume). Le Chatelier: increasing pressure shifts to fewer moles of gas; exothermic reaction favoured by low temperature; Haber process 450 C, 200 atm, Fe catalyst. K changes only with temperature.
Deep dive: Acids, bases, pH

Arrhenius: acid gives H+, base gives OH-. Bronsted-Lowry: acid is a proton donor, base a proton acceptor; strong acid has weak conjugate base. Lewis: acid accepts an electron pair. Water autoprotolysis Kw = 1 x 10^-14. pH of 0.01 M HCl = 2. Weak acid: [H+] = sqrt(Ka C). Weak base: [OH-] = sqrt(Kb C). Polyprotic acids ionise stepwise (Ka1 > Ka2). Ostwald dilution law: alpha increases with dilution.
Deep dive: Buffers, hydrolysis, solubility

Buffer resists pH change: acidic buffer (CH3COOH + CH3COONa), basic buffer (NH4OH + NH4Cl). pH = pKa + log [salt]/[acid]; buffer capacity highest when ratio is 1. Salt hydrolysis: salt of strong acid and weak base is acidic; weak acid and strong base basic; weak acid and weak base depends. Solubility product: for AxBy, Ksp = (xs)^x (ys)^y; ionic product Q > Ksp precipitates. Common ion effect lowers solubility. Examples: AgCl, BaSO4.

Visual lesson

Equilibrium

Physical equilibrium (solid-liquid, liquid-vapour, solid-vapour, dissolution) and chemical equilibrium

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Chemical equilibrium›3Acids, bases, pH›4Buffers, hydrolysis…
Kw10^-14
Ksp AgCls^2
🔑

Big idea

  • Physical equilibrium (solid-liquid, liquid-vapour, solid-vapour, dissolution) and chemical equilibrium
  • Law of mass action: for aA + bB <-> cC + dD, Kc = [C]^c [D]^d / [A]^a [B]^b
  • Kp = Kc (RT)^delta n
  • Reaction quotient Q
Read the full explanation

Physical equilibrium (solid-liquid, liquid-vapour, solid-vapour, dissolution) and chemical equilibrium. Law of mass action: for aA + bB <-> cC + dD, Kc = [C]^c [D]^d / [A]^a [B]^b. Kp = Kc (RT)^delta n. Reaction quotient Q. Le Chatelier principle: concentration, pressure, temperature, catalyst (no effect on position). Ionic equilibrium: strong and weak electrolytes; Arrhenius, Bronsted-Lowry, Lewis acids and bases; conjugate pairs. Ionisation: Ka, Kb, Ka x Kb = Kw = 10^-14 at 298 K. pH = -log[H+]; pH + pOH = 14. Degree of dissociation alpha = sqrt(Ka/C). Buffer: Henderson-Hasselbalch pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]). Salt hydrolysis. Solubility product Ksp. Common ion effect.

⚗️

Chemical equilibrium

  • Equilibrium is dynamic
  • Rates of forward and reverse reactions are equal
  • Characteristics: constant concentrations, attained from either side, catalyst does not change Kc
  • Kc units depend on delta n
Read the full explanation

Equilibrium is dynamic; rates of forward and reverse reactions are equal. Characteristics: constant concentrations, attained from either side, catalyst does not change Kc. Kc units depend on delta n. If Q < K reaction goes forward; Q > K reverse. Examples: N2 + 3H2 <-> 2NH3 (delta n = -2), PCl5 <-> PCl3 + Cl2, H2 + I2 <-> 2HI (Kc independent of volume). Le Chatelier: increasing pressure shifts to fewer moles of gas; exothermic reaction favoured by low temperature; Haber process 450 C, 200 atm, Fe catalyst. K changes only with temperature.

⚗️

Acids, bases, pH

  • Arrhenius: acid gives H+, base gives OH-
  • Bronsted-Lowry: acid is a proton donor, base a proton acceptor
  • Strong acid has weak conjugate base
  • Lewis: acid accepts an electron pair
Read the full explanation

Arrhenius: acid gives H+, base gives OH-. Bronsted-Lowry: acid is a proton donor, base a proton acceptor; strong acid has weak conjugate base. Lewis: acid accepts an electron pair. Water autoprotolysis Kw = 1 x 10^-14. pH of 0.01 M HCl = 2. Weak acid: [H+] = sqrt(Ka C). Weak base: [OH-] = sqrt(Kb C). Polyprotic acids ionise stepwise (Ka1 > Ka2). Ostwald dilution law: alpha increases with dilution.

🌟

Buffers, hydrolysis, solubility

  • Buffer resists pH change: acidic buffer (CH3COOH + CH3COONa), basic buffer (NH4OH + NH4Cl)
  • PH = pKa + log [salt]/[acid]
  • Buffer capacity highest when ratio is 1
  • Salt hydrolysis: salt of strong acid and weak base is acidic
Read the full explanation

Buffer resists pH change: acidic buffer (CH3COOH + CH3COONa), basic buffer (NH4OH + NH4Cl). pH = pKa + log [salt]/[acid]; buffer capacity highest when ratio is 1. Salt hydrolysis: salt of strong acid and weak base is acidic; weak acid and strong base basic; weak acid and weak base depends. Solubility product: for AxBy, Ksp = (xs)^x (ys)^y; ionic product Q > Ksp precipitates. Common ion effect lowers solubility. Examples: AgCl, BaSO4.

yt: class 11 chemistry states of matter

blocks.x: Boyle: P V = constant (T, n fixed); Charles: V/T = constant; Gay-Lussac: P/T = constant; Avogadro: V proportional to n. Combined: PV = nRT with R = 0.0821 L atm/(mol K) = 8.314 J/(mol K). Dalton: P_total = sum of partial pressures; Graham: r1/r2 = sqrt(M2/M1). Real gases follow (P + a n^2/V^2)(V - n b) = nRT.
Deep dive: gas laws

Boyle law: at constant temperature P1 V1 = P2 V2. Charles law: at constant pressure V1/T1 = V2/T2 (T in kelvin). Gay-Lussac law: at constant volume P1/T1 = P2/T2. Avogadro law: equal volumes of gases at the same T and P contain equal numbers of molecules; molar volume at STP (0 C, 1 atm) is 22.4 L and at 1 bar 22.7 L. Combined gas law P1 V1/T1 = P2 V2/T2 and the ideal gas equation PV = nRT = (m/M) RT, giving density d = PM/(RT). R = 0.0821 L atm K^-1 mol^-1 = 8.314 J K^-1 mol^-1 = 0.0831 L bar K^-1 mol^-1.
Deep dive: mixtures, diffusion and kinetic energy

Dalton law of partial pressures: P_total = P1 + P2 + ...; the partial pressure P_i = x_i P_total where x_i is the mole fraction. Graham law of diffusion: r1/r2 = sqrt (M2/M1) = sqrt (d2/d1) (at equal pressure). Kinetic molecular theory: pressure arises from molecular collisions; average kinetic energy is (3/2) k T, so it depends only on temperature. Speeds: u_rms = sqrt (3RT/M), u_avg = sqrt (8RT/(pi M)), u_mp = sqrt (2RT/M), with u_mp < u_avg < u_rms.
Deep dive: real gases and liquids

Real gases deviate from ideality at high pressure and low temperature. The compressibility factor Z = PV/(nRT) is 1 for an ideal gas, below 1 where attractions dominate and above 1 where repulsion dominates. van der Waals equation (P + a n^2/V^2)(V - n b) = nRT, where a measures attraction and b is the excluded volume. Boyle temperature T_B = a/(R b). Critical constants: T_c = 8a/(27 R b), P_c = a/(27 b^2), V_c = 3 b. Liquids: vapour pressure rises with temperature (boiling when it equals external pressure); surface tension and viscosity decrease with temperature; intermolecular forces include London dispersion, dipole-dipole and hydrogen bonding.

Read the full explanation

Boyle: P V = constant (T, n fixed); Charles: V/T = constant; Gay-Lussac: P/T = constant; Avogadro: V proportional to n. Combined: PV = nRT with R = 0.0821 L atm/(mol K) = 8.314 J/(mol K). Dalton: P_total = sum of partial pressures; Graham: r1/r2 = sqrt(M2/M1). Real gases follow (P + a n^2/V^2)(V - n b) = nRT.

⚖️

Gas laws

  • Boyle law: at constant temperature P1 V1 = P2 V2
  • Charles law: at constant pressure V1/T1 = V2/T2 (T in kelvin)
  • Gay-Lussac law: at constant volume P1/T1 = P2/T2
  • Avogadro law: equal volumes of gases at the same T and P contain equal numbers of molecules
Read the full explanation

Boyle law: at constant temperature P1 V1 = P2 V2. Charles law: at constant pressure V1/T1 = V2/T2 (T in kelvin). Gay-Lussac law: at constant volume P1/T1 = P2/T2. Avogadro law: equal volumes of gases at the same T and P contain equal numbers of molecules; molar volume at STP (0 C, 1 atm) is 22.4 L and at 1 bar 22.7 L. Combined gas law P1 V1/T1 = P2 V2/T2 and the ideal gas equation PV = nRT = (m/M) RT, giving density d = PM/(RT). R = 0.0821 L atm K^-1 mol^-1 = 8.314 J K^-1 mol^-1 = 0.0831 L bar K^-1 mol^-1.

🚀

Mixtures, diffusion and kinetic energy

  • Dalton law of partial pressures: P_total = P1 + P2 +
  • The partial pressure P_i = x_i P_total where x_i is the mole fraction
  • Graham law of diffusion: r1/r2 = sqrt (M2/M1) = sqrt (d2/d1) (at equal pressure)
  • Kinetic molecular theory: pressure arises from molecular collisions
Read the full explanation

Dalton law of partial pressures: P_total = P1 + P2 + ...; the partial pressure P_i = x_i P_total where x_i is the mole fraction. Graham law of diffusion: r1/r2 = sqrt (M2/M1) = sqrt (d2/d1) (at equal pressure). Kinetic molecular theory: pressure arises from molecular collisions; average kinetic energy is (3/2) k T, so it depends only on temperature. Speeds: u_rms = sqrt (3RT/M), u_avg = sqrt (8RT/(pi M)), u_mp = sqrt (2RT/M), with u_mp < u_avg < u_rms.

🌟

Real gases and liquids

  • Real gases deviate from ideality at high pressure and low temperature
  • The compressibility factor Z = PV/(nRT) is 1 for an ideal gas, below 1 where attractions dominate and above 1 where repulsion dominates
  • Van der Waals equation (P + a n2/V2)(V - n b) = nRT, where a measures attraction and b is the excluded volume
  • Boyle temperature T_B = a/(R b)
Read the full explanation

Real gases deviate from ideality at high pressure and low temperature. The compressibility factor Z = PV/(nRT) is 1 for an ideal gas, below 1 where attractions dominate and above 1 where repulsion dominates. van der Waals equation (P + a n^2/V^2)(V - n b) = nRT, where a measures attraction and b is the excluded volume. Boyle temperature T_B = a/(R b). Critical constants: T_c = 8a/(27 R b), P_c = a/(27 b^2), V_c = 3 b. Liquids: vapour pressure rises with temperature (boiling when it equals external pressure); surface tension and viscosity decrease with temperature; intermolecular forces include London dispersion, dipole-dipole and hydrogen bonding.

lessons.title: Redox Reactions
yt: class 11 chemistry redox reactions oxidation number balancing

blocks.x: Classical idea: oxidation is addition of oxygen/electronegative element or removal of hydrogen; reduction is the reverse. Electron concept: oxidation is loss of electrons, reduction is gain (OIL RIG). Oxidation number rules: free element 0; monoatomic ion equals charge; H is +1 (except metal hydrides -1); O is -2 (peroxides -1, OF2 +2, superoxides -1/2); F always -1; sum equals charge. Oxidising agent gets reduced; reducing agent gets oxidised. Types: combination, decomposition, displacement, disproportionation (2H2O2 -> 2H2O + O2; Cl2 in alkali), comproportionation. Balancing: oxidation number method and half-reaction (ion-electron) method in acidic and basic media. Redox couples; electrode potential; electrochemical series; Daniell cell. Corrosion; Fe2+/Fe3+.
Deep dive: Oxidation numbers

Examples: S in H2SO4 is +6; Cr in K2Cr2O7 is +6; Mn in KMnO4 is +7; N in HNO3 is +5; C in glucose 0; Cl in HClO4 +7; S in Na2S2O3 average +2; fractional oxidation number in Fe3O4 (+8/3), Na2S4O6 (+2.5). Maximum oxidation state equals group number (up to 8), minimum equals group number minus 8 for non-metals. A species in an intermediate state can act as both oxidant and reductant (H2O2, SO2).
Deep dive: Balancing redox equations

Oxidation number method: identify changes, balance electrons, balance O with H2O, H with H+ (acidic) or OH- (basic). Half-reaction method: split into oxidation and reduction half-reactions, balance atoms other than H and O, balance O with water, H with H+, charge with electrons, equalise electrons, add. MnO4- + 5Fe2+ + 8H+ -> Mn2+ + 5Fe3+ + 4H2O. Cr2O7^2- + 14H+ + 6e- -> 2Cr3+ + 7H2O. In basic medium add OH- to neutralise H+. Disproportionation: P4 + 3NaOH + 3H2O -> PH3 + 3NaH2PO2.
Deep dive: Electrode processes

Redox couple: oxidised and reduced forms. Electrode potential, standard hydrogen electrode (0 V). Higher reduction potential means better oxidising agent (F2 +2.87 V, Li -3.05 V). Daniell cell: Zn anode, Cu cathode, E cell = 1.1 V. Metals above hydrogen displace H2 from acids. Corrosion of iron as an electrochemical process. Redox in titrations: permanganate, dichromate, iodometric.

Big idea

Read the full explanation

Classical idea: oxidation is addition of oxygen/electronegative element or removal of hydrogen; reduction is the reverse. Electron concept: oxidation is loss of electrons, reduction is gain (OIL RIG). Oxidation number rules: free element 0; monoatomic ion equals charge; H is +1 (except metal hydrides -1); O is -2 (peroxides -1, OF2 +2, superoxides -1/2); F always -1; sum equals charge. Oxidising agent gets reduced; reducing agent gets oxidised. Types: combination, decomposition, displacement, disproportionation (2H2O2 -> 2H2O + O2; Cl2 in alkali), comproportionation. Balancing: oxidation number method and half-reaction (ion-electron) method in acidic and basic media. Redox couples; electrode potential; electrochemical series; Daniell cell. Corrosion; Fe2+/Fe3+.

📌

Oxidation numbers

  • Examples: S in H2SO4 is +6
  • Cr in K2Cr2O7 is +6
  • Mn in KMnO4 is +7
  • N in HNO3 is +5
Read the full explanation

Examples: S in H2SO4 is +6; Cr in K2Cr2O7 is +6; Mn in KMnO4 is +7; N in HNO3 is +5; C in glucose 0; Cl in HClO4 +7; S in Na2S2O3 average +2; fractional oxidation number in Fe3O4 (+8/3), Na2S4O6 (+2.5). Maximum oxidation state equals group number (up to 8), minimum equals group number minus 8 for non-metals. A species in an intermediate state can act as both oxidant and reductant (H2O2, SO2).

🧮

Balancing redox equations

  • Oxidation number method: identify changes, balance electrons, balance O with H2O, H with H+ (acidic) or OH- (basic)
  • Half-reaction method: split into oxidation and reduction half-reactions, balance atoms other than H and O, balance O with water, H with H+, charge…
  • MnO4- + 5Fe2+ + 8H+ -> Mn2+ + 5Fe3+ + 4H2O
  • Cr2O72- + 14H+ + 6e- -> 2Cr3+ + 7H2O
Read the full explanation

Oxidation number method: identify changes, balance electrons, balance O with H2O, H with H+ (acidic) or OH- (basic). Half-reaction method: split into oxidation and reduction half-reactions, balance atoms other than H and O, balance O with water, H with H+, charge with electrons, equalise electrons, add. MnO4- + 5Fe2+ + 8H+ -> Mn2+ + 5Fe3+ + 4H2O. Cr2O7^2- + 14H+ + 6e- -> 2Cr3+ + 7H2O. In basic medium add OH- to neutralise H+. Disproportionation: P4 + 3NaOH + 3H2O -> PH3 + 3NaH2PO2.

🔄

Electrode processes

  • Redox couple: oxidised and reduced forms
  • Electrode potential, standard hydrogen electrode (0 V)
  • Higher reduction potential means better oxidising agent (F2 +2.87 V, Li -3.05 V)
  • Daniell cell: Zn anode, Cu cathode, E cell = 1.1 V
Read the full explanation

Redox couple: oxidised and reduced forms. Electrode potential, standard hydrogen electrode (0 V). Higher reduction potential means better oxidising agent (F2 +2.87 V, Li -3.05 V). Daniell cell: Zn anode, Cu cathode, E cell = 1.1 V. Metals above hydrogen displace H2 from acids. Corrosion of iron as an electrochemical process. Redox in titrations: permanganate, dichromate, iodometric.

lessons.title: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
yt: class 11 chemistry organic chemistry basic principles inductive effect resonance IUPAC

blocks.x: Tetravalence of carbon, shapes of organic molecules (sp3 tetrahedral, sp2 planar, sp linear). Structural representations: Lewis, condensed, bond-line. Classification: acyclic, alicyclic, aromatic; functional groups; homologous series. IUPAC nomenclature: longest chain, lowest locants, alphabetical order, prefixes and suffixes. Isomerism: structural (chain, position, functional group, metamerism, tautomerism) and stereoisomerism (geometrical, optical). Fundamental concepts: fission (homolytic gives free radicals, heterolytic gives carbocations and carbanions), electrophiles and nucleophiles, electron displacement effects (inductive, electromeric, resonance, hyperconjugation). Types of reactions: substitution, addition, elimination, rearrangement. Purification: crystallisation, sublimation, distillation (simple, fractional, steam, reduced pressure), differential extraction, chromatography (column, TLC, paper). Qualitative analysis: Lassaigne test (Na fusion), Duma and Kjeldahl method for nitrogen, Carius method for halogens and sulphur. Quantitative estimation of C and H by combustion.
Deep dive: Nomenclature and isomerism

IUPAC rules: choose the longest chain with the principal functional group, number to give the lowest locant, name substituents alphabetically. Priority: acid > ester > amide > aldehyde > ketone > alcohol > amine. Examples: CH3CH(CH3)CH2CH3 is 2-methylbutane; CH3COCH2CH3 is butan-2-one. Chain isomers: butane/isobutane; position: 1- and 2-propanol; functional: ethanol/dimethyl ether; metamerism: diethyl ether/methyl propyl ether; tautomerism: keto-enol.
Deep dive: Electronic effects and reaction intermediates

Inductive effect: permanent polarisation of sigma bonds; -I groups: NO2 > CN > COOH > F > Cl > Br > I; +I: alkyl groups. Resonance (mesomeric) effect: +R (OH, NH2, halogens) and -R (NO2, C=O). Hyperconjugation: sigma-pi delocalisation; more alpha H means more stability (CH3+ < 1 < 2 < 3 carbocation). Carbocation stability: 3 > 2 > 1 > methyl; benzyl and allyl are stable. Carbanion stability: methyl > 1 > 2 > 3. Free radicals stability 3 > 2 > 1. Electrophiles: H+, NO2+, carbocations, AlCl3; nucleophiles: OH-, CN-, NH3, H2O.
Deep dive: Purification and analysis

Crystallisation separates solid mixtures by solubility; sublimation for camphor, naphthalene; distillation for liquids with different bp; fractional for close bp; steam for liquids immiscible with water (aniline); distillation under reduced pressure (glycerol). Chromatography: adsorption (silica or alumina stationary phase), Rf = distance moved by substance / solvent front. Lassaigne extract: N gives Prussian blue, S gives violet with nitroprusside or black PbS, halogens give AgX precipitate. Kjeldahl: percentage N = 1.4 x M x V / mass. Duma: N2 volume at STP. Carius: AgX and BaSO4.

Visual lesson

Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques

Tetravalence of carbon, shapes of organic molecules (sp3 tetrahedral, sp2 planar, sp linear)

formulas
Q&A

CarbanionCH3- > 1 > 2 > 3

🔑

Big idea

  • Tetravalence of carbon, shapes of organic molecules (sp3 tetrahedral, sp2 planar, sp linear)
  • Structural representations: Lewis, condensed, bond-line
  • Classification: acyclic, alicyclic, aromatic
  • Functional groups
Read the full explanation

Tetravalence of carbon, shapes of organic molecules (sp3 tetrahedral, sp2 planar, sp linear). Structural representations: Lewis, condensed, bond-line. Classification: acyclic, alicyclic, aromatic; functional groups; homologous series. IUPAC nomenclature: longest chain, lowest locants, alphabetical order, prefixes and suffixes. Isomerism: structural (chain, position, functional group, metamerism, tautomerism) and stereoisomerism (geometrical, optical). Fundamental concepts: fission (homolytic gives free radicals, heterolytic gives carbocations and carbanions), electrophiles and nucleophiles, electron displacement effects (inductive, electromeric, resonance, hyperconjugation). Types of reactions: substitution, addition, elimination, rearrangement. Purification: crystallisation, sublimation, distillation (simple, fractional, steam, reduced pressure), differential extraction, chromatography (column, TLC, paper). Qualitative analysis: Lassaigne test (Na fusion), Duma and Kjeldahl method for nitrogen, Carius method for halogens and sulphur. Quantitative estimation of C and H by combustion.

📌

Nomenclature and isomerism

  • IUPAC rules: choose the longest chain with the principal functional group, number to give the lowest locant, name substituents alphabetically
  • Priority: acid > ester > amide > aldehyde > ketone > alcohol > amine
  • Examples: CH3CH(CH3)CH2CH3 is 2-methylbutane
  • CH3COCH2CH3 is butan-2-one
Read the full explanation

IUPAC rules: choose the longest chain with the principal functional group, number to give the lowest locant, name substituents alphabetically. Priority: acid > ester > amide > aldehyde > ketone > alcohol > amine. Examples: CH3CH(CH3)CH2CH3 is 2-methylbutane; CH3COCH2CH3 is butan-2-one. Chain isomers: butane/isobutane; position: 1- and 2-propanol; functional: ethanol/dimethyl ether; metamerism: diethyl ether/methyl propyl ether; tautomerism: keto-enol.

⚗️

Electronic effects and reaction intermediates

  • Inductive effect: permanent polarisation of sigma bonds
  • -I groups: NO2 > CN > COOH > F > Cl > Br > I
  • +I: alkyl groups
  • Resonance (mesomeric) effect: +R (OH, NH2, halogens) and -R (NO2, C=O)
Read the full explanation

Inductive effect: permanent polarisation of sigma bonds; -I groups: NO2 > CN > COOH > F > Cl > Br > I; +I: alkyl groups. Resonance (mesomeric) effect: +R (OH, NH2, halogens) and -R (NO2, C=O). Hyperconjugation: sigma-pi delocalisation; more alpha H means more stability (CH3+ < 1 < 2 < 3 carbocation). Carbocation stability: 3 > 2 > 1 > methyl; benzyl and allyl are stable. Carbanion stability: methyl > 1 > 2 > 3. Free radicals stability 3 > 2 > 1. Electrophiles: H+, NO2+, carbocations, AlCl3; nucleophiles: OH-, CN-, NH3, H2O.

🌟

Purification and analysis

  • Crystallisation separates solid mixtures by solubility
  • Sublimation for camphor, naphthalene
  • Distillation for liquids with different bp
  • Fractional for close bp
Read the full explanation

Crystallisation separates solid mixtures by solubility; sublimation for camphor, naphthalene; distillation for liquids with different bp; fractional for close bp; steam for liquids immiscible with water (aniline); distillation under reduced pressure (glycerol). Chromatography: adsorption (silica or alumina stationary phase), Rf = distance moved by substance / solvent front. Lassaigne extract: N gives Prussian blue, S gives violet with nitroprusside or black PbS, halogens give AgX precipitate. Kjeldahl: percentage N = 1.4 x M x V / mass. Duma: N2 volume at STP. Carius: AgX and BaSO4.

lessons.title: Hydrocarbons
yt: class 11 chemistry hydrocarbons alkanes alkenes alkynes benzene aromaticity

blocks.x: Alkanes (CnH2n+2): preparation (Wurtz reaction, Kolbe electrolysis, hydrogenation, decarboxylation of sodium salts with soda lime), properties (substitution by halogenation - free radical mechanism: initiation, propagation, termination; combustion; isomerisation; aromatisation; pyrolysis), conformations of ethane (staggered more stable than eclipsed; torsional strain). Alkenes (CnH2n): preparation (dehydrohalogenation, dehydration of alcohols, partial hydrogenation of alkynes), properties (electrophilic addition, Markovnikov rule, anti-Markovnikov (Kharasch, peroxide effect), ozonolysis, oxidation with KMnO4 (Baeyer test), polymerisation), geometrical isomerism (cis-trans). Alkynes (CnH2n-2): preparation (CaC2 + H2O, dehydrohalogenation), acidic nature of terminal alkynes, addition reactions, hydration to ketone/aldehyde, polymerisation to benzene. Aromatic hydrocarbons: benzene, Kekule structure, resonance, Huckel rule (4n+2) pi electrons, electrophilic substitution (nitration, halogenation, sulphonation, Friedel-Crafts), directing groups (o,p-activating: -OH, -NH2, -CH3; m-directing: -NO2, -COOH, -CN), carcinogenicity.
Deep dive: Alkanes

Wurtz: 2R-X + 2Na -> R-R + 2NaX (dry ether). Kolbe: 2RCOONa + 2H2O -> R-R + 2CO2 + H2 + 2NaOH. Decarboxylation: RCOONa + NaOH -> RH + Na2CO3 (CaO). Halogenation reactivity: F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2; hydrogen order 3 > 2 > 1. Combustion: CnH2n+2 + (3n+1)/2 O2 -> n CO2 + (n+1) H2O. Conformations: staggered (60 degrees dihedral, minimum energy), eclipsed (0, maximum, energy difference 12.5 kJ/mol).
Deep dive: Alkenes and alkynes

Markovnikov: the negative part adds to the carbon with fewer hydrogens. Peroxide effect: HBr adds anti-Markovnikov. Ozonolysis gives carbonyl compounds (propene gives CH3CHO + HCHO). Cold dilute KMnO4 gives diols (Baeyer), hot gives acids/ketones. Geometrical isomers cis and trans (but-2-ene). Alkynes: acetylene has sp carbons, 180 degrees, bond length 120 pm; terminal H acidic (sodium, ammoniacal AgNO3, Cu2Cl2 give precipitates); hydration with HgSO4/H2SO4 gives acetaldehyde from ethyne, acetone from propyne; trimerisation to benzene via red-hot iron tube at 873 K.
Deep dive: Aromatic hydrocarbons

Benzene C6H6: planar, all C-C bonds 139 pm, sp2, resonance energy 150 kJ/mol; aromatic if cyclic, planar, conjugated with 4n+2 pi electrons (benzene 6, naphthalene 10, cyclopentadienyl anion 6). Electrophilic substitution mechanism: electrophile generation, sigma complex (arenium ion), loss of H+. Nitration: HNO3 + H2SO4 gives NO2+. Friedel-Crafts alkylation and acylation with AlCl3. Activating groups direct o/p; deactivating (except halogens) direct meta. Addition to benzene under drastic conditions: hydrogenation (cyclohexane), chlorination (BHC).

Big idea

Read the full explanation

Alkanes (CnH2n+2): preparation (Wurtz reaction, Kolbe electrolysis, hydrogenation, decarboxylation of sodium salts with soda lime), properties (substitution by halogenation - free radical mechanism: initiation, propagation, termination; combustion; isomerisation; aromatisation; pyrolysis), conformations of ethane (staggered more stable than eclipsed; torsional strain). Alkenes (CnH2n): preparation (dehydrohalogenation, dehydration of alcohols, partial hydrogenation of alkynes), properties (electrophilic addition, Markovnikov rule, anti-Markovnikov (Kharasch, peroxide effect), ozonolysis, oxidation with KMnO4 (Baeyer test), polymerisation), geometrical isomerism (cis-trans). Alkynes (CnH2n-2): preparation (CaC2 + H2O, dehydrohalogenation), acidic nature of terminal alkynes, addition reactions, hydration to ketone/aldehyde, polymerisation to benzene. Aromatic hydrocarbons: benzene, Kekule structure, resonance, Huckel rule (4n+2) pi electrons, electrophilic substitution (nitration, halogenation, sulphonation, Friedel-Crafts), directing groups (o,p-activating: -OH, -NH2, -CH3; m-directing: -NO2, -COOH, -CN), carcinogenicity.

📌

Alkanes

  • Wurtz: 2R-X + 2Na -> R-R + 2NaX (dry ether)
  • Kolbe: 2RCOONa + 2H2O -> R-R + 2CO2 + H2 + 2NaOH
  • Decarboxylation: RCOONa + NaOH -> RH + Na2CO3 (CaO)
  • Halogenation reactivity: F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2
Read the full explanation

Wurtz: 2R-X + 2Na -> R-R + 2NaX (dry ether). Kolbe: 2RCOONa + 2H2O -> R-R + 2CO2 + H2 + 2NaOH. Decarboxylation: RCOONa + NaOH -> RH + Na2CO3 (CaO). Halogenation reactivity: F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2; hydrogen order 3 > 2 > 1. Combustion: CnH2n+2 + (3n+1)/2 O2 -> n CO2 + (n+1) H2O. Conformations: staggered (60 degrees dihedral, minimum energy), eclipsed (0, maximum, energy difference 12.5 kJ/mol).

🧠

Alkenes and alkynes

  • Markovnikov: the negative part adds to the carbon with fewer hydrogens
  • Peroxide effect: HBr adds anti-Markovnikov
  • Ozonolysis gives carbonyl compounds (propene gives CH3CHO + HCHO)
  • Cold dilute KMnO4 gives diols (Baeyer), hot gives acids/ketones
Read the full explanation

Markovnikov: the negative part adds to the carbon with fewer hydrogens. Peroxide effect: HBr adds anti-Markovnikov. Ozonolysis gives carbonyl compounds (propene gives CH3CHO + HCHO). Cold dilute KMnO4 gives diols (Baeyer), hot gives acids/ketones. Geometrical isomers cis and trans (but-2-ene). Alkynes: acetylene has sp carbons, 180 degrees, bond length 120 pm; terminal H acidic (sodium, ammoniacal AgNO3, Cu2Cl2 give precipitates); hydration with HgSO4/H2SO4 gives acetaldehyde from ethyne, acetone from propyne; trimerisation to benzene via red-hot iron tube at 873 K.

🌟

Aromatic hydrocarbons

  • Benzene C6H6: planar, all C-C bonds 139 pm, sp2, resonance energy 150 kJ/mol
  • Aromatic if cyclic, planar, conjugated with 4n+2 pi electrons (benzene 6, naphthalene 10, cyclopentadienyl anion 6)
  • Electrophilic substitution mechanism: electrophile generation, sigma complex (arenium ion), loss of H+
  • Nitration: HNO3 + H2SO4 gives NO2+
Read the full explanation

Benzene C6H6: planar, all C-C bonds 139 pm, sp2, resonance energy 150 kJ/mol; aromatic if cyclic, planar, conjugated with 4n+2 pi electrons (benzene 6, naphthalene 10, cyclopentadienyl anion 6). Electrophilic substitution mechanism: electrophile generation, sigma complex (arenium ion), loss of H+. Nitration: HNO3 + H2SO4 gives NO2+. Friedel-Crafts alkylation and acylation with AlCl3. Activating groups direct o/p; deactivating (except halogens) direct meta. Addition to benzene under drastic conditions: hydrogenation (cyclohexane), chlorination (BHC).

lessons.title: Computer System
yt: class 11 computer science computer system CPU memory software

blocks.x: A computer system has hardware and software. Input unit, CPU (ALU, CU, registers), output unit, memory. Von Neumann architecture: stored program. Memory hierarchy: registers, cache, RAM (primary, volatile), ROM, secondary storage (HDD, SSD, optical, USB flash). Units: bit, nibble, byte, KB (1024 B), MB, GB, TB. Interface and ports: USB, HDMI, VGA, Ethernet. Software: system software (operating system, language processors, device drivers, utilities), application software (general purpose, customised, utility). Language processors: assembler, compiler, interpreter. Operating system functions: process management, memory management, file management, device management, user interface. Boolean logic: AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR, XOR; truth tables; De Morgan laws; logic gates.
Deep dive: Hardware organisation

Microprocessor with clock speed in GHz; instruction cycle fetch-decode-execute; registers hold data temporarily; ALU does arithmetic and logic; CU controls. Primary memory: RAM is volatile and holds running programs; ROM is non-volatile (BIOS). Cache is fast memory between CPU and RAM. Secondary: magnetic (HDD), optical (CD, DVD, Blu-ray), flash (SSD, pen drive, SD card). Input devices: keyboard, mouse, scanner, microphone, touch screen, sensors. Output devices: monitor, printer (impact and non-impact), plotter, speakers, projector.
Deep dive: Software and OS

System software manages hardware; compilers translate the whole program to machine code and report errors together; interpreters translate and execute line by line; assemblers convert assembly to machine code. Operating system provides interface (CLI, GUI), schedules processes, manages memory, files and devices. Examples: Windows, Linux, macOS, Android. Utility software: antivirus, disk defragmenter, backup. Application software: word processors, spreadsheets, presentations, databases. Free and open source (FOSS), proprietary, freeware, shareware.
Deep dive: Boolean logic

Logic gates: AND outputs 1 only if both inputs are 1; OR outputs 1 if either is 1; NOT inverts; NAND and NOR are universal gates; XOR outputs 1 when inputs differ. De Morgan: (A.B)' = A' + B'; (A+B)' = A'.B'. Truth table for n inputs has 2^n rows. Uses: circuits, search conditions, decision making. Boolean identities: A + 0 = A; A . 1 = A; A + A' = 1; A . A' = 0.
Hindi saransh
Computer pranali: hardware, software, CPU, smriti, OS. Boolean tark: AND, OR, NOT. De Morgan niyam.

A computer system has hardware and software. Input unit, CPU (ALU, CU, registers), output unit, memory. Von Neumann architecture: stored program. Memory hierarchy: registers, cache, RAM (primary, volatile), ROM, secondary storage (HDD, SSD, optical, USB flash). Units: bit, nibble, byte, KB (1024 B), MB, GB, TB. Interface and ports: USB, HDMI, VGA, Ethernet. Software: system software (operating system, language processors, device drivers, utilities), application software (general purpose, customised, utility). Language processors: assembler, compiler, interpreter. Operating system functions: process management, memory management, file management, device management, user interface. Boolean logic: AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR, XOR; truth tables; De Morgan laws; logic gates.

🕰️

Hardware organisation

  • Microprocessor with clock speed in GHz
  • Instruction cycle fetch-decode-execute
  • Registers hold data temporarily
  • ALU does arithmetic and logic
Read the full explanation

Microprocessor with clock speed in GHz; instruction cycle fetch-decode-execute; registers hold data temporarily; ALU does arithmetic and logic; CU controls. Primary memory: RAM is volatile and holds running programs; ROM is non-volatile (BIOS). Cache is fast memory between CPU and RAM. Secondary: magnetic (HDD), optical (CD, DVD, Blu-ray), flash (SSD, pen drive, SD card). Input devices: keyboard, mouse, scanner, microphone, touch screen, sensors. Output devices: monitor, printer (impact and non-impact), plotter, speakers, projector.

🕰️

Software and OS

  • System software manages hardware
  • Compilers translate the whole program to machine code and report errors together
  • Interpreters translate and execute line by line
  • Assemblers convert assembly to machine code
Read the full explanation

System software manages hardware; compilers translate the whole program to machine code and report errors together; interpreters translate and execute line by line; assemblers convert assembly to machine code. Operating system provides interface (CLI, GUI), schedules processes, manages memory, files and devices. Examples: Windows, Linux, macOS, Android. Utility software: antivirus, disk defragmenter, backup. Application software: word processors, spreadsheets, presentations, databases. Free and open source (FOSS), proprietary, freeware, shareware.

🌟

Boolean logic

  • Logic gates: AND outputs 1 only if both inputs are 1
  • OR outputs 1 if either is 1
  • NAND and NOR are universal gates
  • XOR outputs 1 when inputs differ
Read the full explanation

Logic gates: AND outputs 1 only if both inputs are 1; OR outputs 1 if either is 1; NOT inverts; NAND and NOR are universal gates; XOR outputs 1 when inputs differ. De Morgan: (A.B)' = A' + B'; (A+B)' = A'.B'. Truth table for n inputs has 2^n rows. Uses: circuits, search conditions, decision making. Boolean identities: A + 0 = A; A . 1 = A; A + A' = 1; A . lessons.title: Encoding Schemes and Number System
yt: class 11 computer science encoding schemes number system binary ASCII Unicode

blocks.x: Encoding: converting data into a format for storage. ASCII (7-bit, 128 characters; extended 8-bit 256), ISCII (Indian), Unicode (UTF-8, UTF-16, UTF-32), supports all languages. Number systems: decimal (base 10), binary (base 2), octal (base 8), hexadecimal (base 16, digits 0-9 and A-F). Conversions: decimal to binary (repeated division by 2), binary to decimal (positional weights), binary to octal (group 3 bits), binary to hexadecimal (group 4 bits), decimal fractions (repeated multiplication). Binary addition; two’s complement. Examples: ASCII A = 65, a = 97, 0 = 48. Hex FF = 255. Data representation of integers, characters, images (pixels), audio, video.
Deep dive: Encoding schemes

ASCII uses 7 bits per character: 128 characters (control codes 0-31, printable 32-126). A = 65, Z = 90, a = 97, z = 122, 0 = 48, 9 = 57, space = 32. ISCII 8-bit supports Indian scripts. Unicode assigns a code point to every character; UTF-8 variable length 1 to 4 bytes backward compatible with ASCII. Emojis are Unicode characters. Parity bit for error detection.
Deep dive: Number conversions

Decimal to binary: 25 -> 11001. Binary to decimal: 1011 = 8 + 2 + 1 = 11. Binary to octal: 101110 = 56 (101 = 5, 110 = 6). Binary to hex: 11111111 = FF = 255. Hex to decimal: 2F = 2 x 16 + 15 = 47. Octal to decimal: 17 = 15. Fractions: 0.625 = 0.101. Binary addition: 1 + 1 = 10; 1011 + 0110 = 10001. Subtraction by 1 s and 2 s complement.
Deep dive: Data representation

Integers stored as binary; negative numbers in 2 s complement; n-bit unsigned range 0 to 2^n - 1. An 8-bit number holds 0 to 255. Image: pixel matrix, RGB colours with 8 bits per channel (24-bit colour = 16.7 million colours). Sound: sampling rate and bit depth. Compression: lossless (ZIP, PNG) and lossy (JPEG, MP3). Floating point representation uses mantissa and exponent.

Sankhya paddhatiyan aur kootlekhan: binary, octal, hex. ASCII A = 65, a = 97. Unicode sabhi bhashaon ke liye.
An n-bit unsigned number can store values from 0 to 2^n minus 1.

Number systems: decimal (base 10), binary (base 2), octal (base 8), hexadecimal (base 16, digits 0-9 and A-F). Conversions: decimal to binary (repeated division by 2), binary to decimal (positional weights), binary to octal (group 3 bits), binary to hexadecimal (group 4 bits), decimal fractions (repeated multiplication). Binary addition; two’s complement. Examples: ASCII A = 65, a = 97, 0 = 48. Hex FF = 255. Data representation of integers, characters, images (pixels), audio, video.

📌

Encoding schemes

  • ASCII uses 7 bits per character: 128 characters (control codes 0-31, printable 32-126)
  • A = 65, Z = 90, a = 97, z = 122, 0 = 48, 9 = 57, space = 32
  • ISCII 8-bit supports Indian scripts
  • Unicode assigns a code point to every character
Read the full explanation

ASCII uses 7 bits per character: 128 characters (control codes 0-31, printable 32-126). A = 65, Z = 90, a = 97, z = 122, 0 = 48, 9 = 57, space = 32. ISCII 8-bit supports Indian scripts. Unicode assigns a code point to every character; UTF-8 variable length 1 to 4 bytes backward compatible with ASCII. Emojis are Unicode characters. Parity bit for error detection.

🧠

Number conversions

  • Decimal to binary: 25 -> 11001
  • Binary to decimal: 1011 = 8 + 2 + 1 = 11
  • Binary to octal: 101110 = 56 (101 = 5, 110 = 6)
  • Binary to hex: 11111111 = FF = 255
Read the full explanation

Decimal to binary: 25 -> 11001. Binary to decimal: 1011 = 8 + 2 + 1 = 11. Binary to octal: 101110 = 56 (101 = 5, 110 = 6). Binary to hex: 11111111 = FF = 255. Hex to decimal: 2F = 2 x 16 + 15 = 47. Octal to decimal: 17 = 15. Fractions: 0.625 = 0.101. Binary addition: 1 + 1 = 10; 1011 + 0110 = 10001. Subtraction by 1 s and 2 s complement.

🌟

Data representation

  • Integers stored as binary
  • Negative numbers in 2 s complement
  • N-bit unsigned range 0 to 2^n - 1
  • An 8-bit number holds 0 to 255
Read the full explanation

Integers stored as binary; negative numbers in 2 s complement; n-bit unsigned range 0 to 2^n - 1. An 8-bit number holds 0 to 255. Image: pixel matrix, RGB colours with 8 bits per channel (24-bit colour = 16.7 million colours). Sound: sampling rate and bit depth. Compression: lossless (ZIP, PNG) and lossy (JPEG, MP3). Floating point representation uses mantissa and exponent.

🎯 Remember An n-bit unsigned number can store values from 0 to 2^n minus 1.
🇮🇳

हिंदी सार

Sankhya paddhatiyan aur kootlekhan: binary, octal, hex. ASCII A = 65, a = 97. Unicode sabhi bhashaon ke liye.

blocks.x: Emerging technologies: artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), natural language processing (NLP), immersive experience (augmented reality AR, virtual reality VR), robotics, big data (volume, velocity, variety, veracity, value), data analytics, internet of things (IoT), cloud computing (SaaS, PaaS, IaaS; public, private, hybrid), grid computing, blockchain, sensors and smart cities, smart homes, wearables, 3D printing, cyber security. Machine learning: supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement. Deep learning uses neural networks. Digital footprint. Applications: chatbots, recommendation systems, self-driving cars, voice assistants. Issues: privacy, bias, job loss, ethics.
Deep dive: AI, ML and NLP

AI is the ability of machines to mimic intelligent behaviour. ML learns from data; types: supervised (labelled data), unsupervised (clustering), reinforcement (rewards). NLP lets computers understand human language (translation, speech recognition, sentiment analysis). Computer vision, expert systems, chatbots, deep learning with neural networks. Turing test. Ethical concerns: bias, transparency, accountability, deepfakes.
Deep dive: IoT, cloud and big data

IoT connects physical objects with sensors and networks (smart home, smart agriculture, wearables). Cloud computing delivers services over the Internet: IaaS (infrastructure), PaaS (platform), SaaS (software); benefits: scalability, cost saving, accessibility. Big data: 5 Vs; tools Hadoop, Spark. Blockchain: distributed ledger of linked blocks with hash, tamper resistance, used in cryptocurrency (Bitcoin), supply chain. Edge and grid computing.
Deep dive: AR, VR, robotics and society

AR overlays digital information on the real world (Pokemon Go); VR creates a fully simulated environment. Robotics: machines performing tasks automatically (industrial robots, drones). 3D printing builds objects layer by layer. Cyber security threats: malware, phishing, ransomware. Issues: digital divide, e-waste, privacy, data protection laws.
Hindi saransh
Ubharti takneekein: AI, ML, IoT, cloud, big data, blockchain. Cloud sevaayen: SaaS, PaaS, IaaS.
The 5 Vs of big data are volume, velocity, variety, veracity and value.

lessons.title: Introduction to Problem Solving
yt: class 11 computer science problem solving algorithm flowchart pseudocode

blocks.x: Steps in problem solving: analysing the problem, developing an algorithm, coding, testing and debugging. Algorithm: finite step-by-step procedure; characteristics: precision, uniqueness, finiteness, input, output. Representation: flowchart (oval start/stop, parallelogram input/output, rectangle process, diamond decision, arrows) and pseudocode. Decomposition: breaking a problem into subproblems. Control structures: sequence, selection, iteration. Verifying algorithms by dry run. Comparison of algorithms by efficiency (time and space). Examples: largest of three numbers, sum of n numbers, factorial, prime test, Fibonacci, GCD, linear search. Types of errors: syntax, logical, runtime.
Deep dive: Algorithm and flowchart

Algorithm to find the sum of two numbers: START, read A and B, SUM = A + B, print SUM, STOP. Flowchart symbols: terminal (oval), input/output (parallelogram), process (rectangle), decision (diamond), connector (circle), flow lines (arrows). Pseudocode uses keywords like INPUT, IF, THEN, ELSE, WHILE, FOR, PRINT. Dry run uses sample data and a trace table to check.
Deep dive: Control structures and examples

Sequence: statements in order. Selection: IF-THEN-ELSE. Iteration: loops. Examples: Even or odd: if N mod 2 = 0. Largest of three: compare. Factorial: product of 1 to n. Prime: no divisor from 2 to sqrt(n). Fibonacci: next = previous two. GCD by Euclid. Linear search: compare each element until found. Decomposition simplifies complex tasks, for example building a calculator from add, subtract, multiply.
Deep dive: Testing and debugging

Syntax errors violate language rules; runtime errors occur during execution (division by zero); logical errors give wrong output. Debugging: tracing, print statements, debuggers. Testing with boundary and typical cases. Documentation and maintenance. Efficiency: number of steps grows with input (linear, quadratic). Pseudocode versus flowchart.

problems.q: Draw the flowchart steps to find the factorial of N.
problems.a: Start; read N; F=1, I=1; while I<=N: F=F*I, I=I+1; print F; stop.

problems.q: Write pseudocode for a prime test and do a dry run for 7.
problems.a: For I from 2 to sqrt(N): if N mod I = 0 not prime; for 7 no divisor so prime.

Sequence: statements in order. Selection: IF-THEN-ELSE. Iteration: loops. Examples: Even or odd: if N mod 2 = 0. Largest of three: compare. Factorial: product of 1 to n. Prime: no divisor from 2 to sqrt(n). Fibonacci: next = previous two. GCD by Euclid. Linear search: compare each element until found. Decomposition simplifies complex tasks, for example building a calculator from add, subtract, multiply.

Testing and debugging

  • Syntax errors violate language rules
  • Runtime errors occur during execution (division by zero)
  • Logical errors give wrong output
  • Debugging: tracing, print statements, debuggers

Syntax errors violate language rules; runtime errors occur during execution (division by zero); logical errors give wrong output. Debugging: tracing, print statements, debuggers. Testing with boundary and typical cases. Documentation and maintenance. Efficiency: number of steps grows with input (linear, quadratic). Pseudocode versus flowchart.

lessons.title: Getting Started with Python
yt: class 11 computer science getting started with python data types operators

blocks.x: Python is an interpreted, high-level, general-purpose, open-source language created by Guido van Rossum. Modes: interactive and script. Tokens: keywords, identifiers, literals, operators, punctuators. Variables and dynamic typing. Data types: int, float, complex, bool, str, list, tuple, dict, set, NoneType. Operators: arithmetic (+, -, *, /, //, %, **), relational, logical (and, or, not), assignment (+=), identity (is), membership (in). Operator precedence. Expressions, statements, comments (#), input() returns a string, print(), type conversion int(), float(), str(). Indentation defines blocks. Debugging: syntax, logical, runtime errors. Mutable and immutable. Modules: math, random, statistics.
Deep dive: Basics

Python identifiers: letters, digits, underscore, not starting with a digit, case sensitive. Keywords: if, else, while, for, def, True, False, None, and, or, not. Literals: numeric, string, Boolean, None. Statements: print("Hello"). Variables: x = 5; id(x). Dynamic typing: the type is determined at run time. Multiple assignment a, b = 1, 2. Comments for readability.
Deep dive: Operators and expressions

Arithmetic: 7 // 2 = 3; 7 % 2 = 1; 2 ** 3 = 8; 7 / 2 = 3.5. Relational: == != > < >= <=. Logical: and or not with short-circuit evaluation. Precedence: ** then unary, then * / // %, then + -, then comparisons, then not, and, or. Type conversion: implicit (int to float) and explicit. input() returns str: n = int(input()). Mutability: int, float, str, tuple immutable; list, dict, set mutable.
Deep dive: Using functions and modules

import math: math.sqrt(16), math.pi, math.ceil, math.floor, math.pow. import random: random.randint(1, 6), random.random(). statistics: mean, median, mode. Built-ins: len(), type(), abs(), round(), max(), min(), sum(). Escape sequences: \n, \t. Formatted output. Errors: NameError, TypeError, ZeroDivisionError, SyntaxError, IndentationError.

lessons.title: Conditional and Iterative Statements
yt: class 11 computer science python if else for while loops break continue

blocks.x: Selection: if, if-else, if-elif-else with indentation. Nested conditions. Iteration: for loop with range(start, stop, step), while loop. Jump statements: break (exits the loop), continue (skips current iteration), pass (does nothing). Loop else clause. Nested loops for patterns. range generates integers up to stop minus 1. Common programs: even/odd, largest of three, leap year, factorial, sum of digits, Fibonacci, prime, palindrome, reverse a number, table, patterns. Sentinel loops. Infinite loops. Operators used in conditions. Truthiness of values.
Deep dive: Selection

if x > 0: ... elif x == 0: ... else: .... Leap year: year % 4 == 0 and (year % 100 != 0 or year % 400 == 0). Grade calculation using elif. Nested if inside if. Boolean expressions with and, or, not. Conditional values: 0, empty string, None are False; others True.
Deep dive: Iteration

for i in range(1, 6) prints 1 to 5; range(10, 0, -2) gives 10, 8, 6, 4, 2. while loop repeats while a condition is true; must update the control variable to avoid an infinite loop. Sum 1 to n; factorial; digits: while n > 0: d = n % 10; n //= 10. Break exits; continue skips. for-else runs when the loop finishes without break. Nested loops: triangle pattern with for i in range(1, 6): print("*" * i).
Deep dive: Programs

Prime test: for i in range(2, n): if n % i == 0: break; else prime. Fibonacci: a, b = 0, 1; for loop updates a, b = b, a + b. Palindrome number: reverse and compare. Armstrong numbers: sum of cubes of digits. GCD by loop. Multiplication table with range(1, 11). Counting vowels. Menu-driven programs with while True and break.
