🔑

Big idea

  • Selection: if, if-else, if-elif-else with indentation
  • Nested conditions
  • Iteration: for loop with range(start, stop, step), while loop
  • Jump statements: break (exits the loop), continue (skips current iteration), pass (does nothing)
Read the full explanation

Selection: if, if-else, if-elif-else with indentation. Nested conditions. Iteration: for loop with range(start, stop, step), while loop. Jump statements: break (exits the loop), continue (skips current iteration), pass (does nothing). Loop else clause. Nested loops for patterns. range generates integers up to stop minus 1. Common programs: even/odd, largest of three, leap year, factorial, sum of digits, Fibonacci, prime, palindrome, reverse a number, table, patterns. Sentinel loops. Infinite loops. Operators used in conditions. Truthiness of values.

📌

Selection

  • Leap year: year % 4 == 0 and (year % 100 != 0 or year % 400 == 0)
  • Grade calculation using elif
  • Nested if inside if
  • Boolean expressions with and, or, not
Read the full explanation

if x > 0: ... elif x == 0: ... else: .... Leap year: year % 4 == 0 and (year % 100 != 0 or year % 400 == 0). Grade calculation using elif. Nested if inside if. Boolean expressions with and, or, not. Conditional values: 0, empty string, None are False; others True.

🧠

Iteration

  • For i in range(1, 6) prints 1 to 5
  • Range(10, 0, -2) gives 10, 8, 6, 4, 2
  • While loop repeats while a condition is true
  • Must update the control variable to avoid an infinite loop
Read the full explanation

for i in range(1, 6) prints 1 to 5; range(10, 0, -2) gives 10, 8, 6, 4, 2. while loop repeats while a condition is true; must update the control variable to avoid an infinite loop. Sum 1 to n; factorial; digits: while n > 0: d = n % 10; n //= 10. Break exits; continue skips. for-else runs when the loop finishes without break. Nested loops: triangle pattern with for i in range(1, 6): print("*" * i).

🌟

Programs

  • Prime test: for i in range(2, n): if n % i == 0: break
  • Fibonacci: a, b = 0, 1
  • For loop updates a, b = b, a + b
  • Palindrome number: reverse and compare
Read the full explanation

Prime test: for i in range(2, n): if n % i == 0: break; else prime. Fibonacci: a, b = 0, 1; for loop updates a, b = b, a + b. Palindrome number: reverse and compare. Armstrong numbers: sum of cubes of digits. GCD by loop. Multiplication table with range(1, 11). Counting vowels. Menu-driven programs with while True and break.

blocks.x: A function is a named block of reusable code. Definition: def name(parameters): body; return. Call by name with arguments. Types: built-in, module, user-defined. Parameters (formal) and arguments (actual). Positional, keyword, default and variable arguments. Returning values and multiple values (tuple). Functions without return give None. Scope: local, global; the global keyword; LEGB rule. Mutable arguments are modified in place. Recursion: a function calling itself with a base case (factorial, Fibonacci). Docstrings. Modules and importing. Flow of execution. Advantages: reusability, modularity, readability, easy debugging.
Deep dive: Defining and calling

def add(a, b): return a + b. Call add(3, 4) gives 7. Default arguments must come after non-default ones: def greet(name, msg="Hello"). Keyword arguments: greet(msg="Hi", name="Ram"). Returning multiple values: return a, b. A function without return returns None. Functions may call other functions. Docstring in triple quotes describes the function.
Deep dive: Scope and mutability

A variable defined inside a function is local; one defined outside is global. A local variable hides a global of the same name; to modify global use the global keyword. Lists passed to functions can be changed in place; integers cannot. Order of search: Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in.
Deep dive: Recursion and modules

Recursive factorial: def fact(n): if n == 0: return 1; return n * fact(n-1). Fibonacci recursion. Each call adds a frame to the stack; missing base case causes RecursionError. Modules: math, random, statistics; user modules. from math import sqrt. Built-in functions: abs, round, max, min, sum, sorted, len, type, int, str.
Hindi saransh
Phalan: def, return, argument, sthaniya aur vaishvik paridhi, punaravriti. Default tark ant mein.

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Functions

A function is a named block of reusable code

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Defining and calling›3Scope and mutability›4Recursion and modules
🔑

Big idea

  • A function is a named block of reusable code
  • Definition: def name(parameters): body
  • Call by name with arguments
  • Types: built-in, module, user-defined
Read the full explanation

A function is a named block of reusable code. Definition: def name(parameters): body; return. Call by name with arguments. Types: built-in, module, user-defined. Parameters (formal) and arguments (actual). Positional, keyword, default and variable arguments. Returning values and multiple values (tuple). Functions without return give None. Scope: local, global; the global keyword; LEGB rule. Mutable arguments are modified in place. Recursion: a function calling itself with a base case (factorial, Fibonacci). Docstrings. Modules and importing. Flow of execution. Advantages: reusability, modularity, readability, easy debugging.

📘

Defining and calling

  • Def add(a, b): return a + b
  • Call add(3, 4) gives 7
  • Default arguments must come after non-default ones: def greet(name, msg="Hello")
  • Keyword arguments: greet(msg="Hi", name="Ram")
Read the full explanation

def add(a, b): return a + b. Call add(3, 4) gives 7. Default arguments must come after non-default ones: def greet(name, msg="Hello"). Keyword arguments: greet(msg="Hi", name="Ram"). Returning multiple values: return a, b. A function without return returns None. Functions may call other functions. Docstring in triple quotes describes the function.

🧠

Scope and mutability

  • A variable defined inside a function is local
  • One defined outside is global
  • A local variable hides a global of the same name
  • To modify global use the global keyword
Read the full explanation

A variable defined inside a function is local; one defined outside is global. A local variable hides a global of the same name; to modify global use the global keyword. Lists passed to functions can be changed in place; integers cannot. Order of search: Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in.

🌟

Recursion and modules

  • Recursive factorial: def fact(n): if n == 0: return 1
  • Return n * fact(n-1)
  • Fibonacci recursion
  • Each call adds a frame to the stack
Read the full explanation

Recursive factorial: def fact(n): if n == 0: return 1; return n * fact(n-1). Fibonacci recursion. Each call adds a frame to the stack; missing base case causes RecursionError. Modules: math, random, statistics; user modules. from math import sqrt. Built-in functions: abs, round, max, min, sum, sorted, len, type, int, str.

🧮

DefaultPreset valuef(a, b=2)
LocalInside functionTemporary
GlobalOutsideWhole file
globalModify globalKeyword
🎯 Remember A recursive function must have a base case to stop the recursion.

lessons.title: Strings
yt: class 11 computer science python strings slicing methods

blocks.x: A string is an immutable sequence of Unicode characters in single, double or triple quotes. Indexing: forward 0 to n-1, backward -1 to -n. Slicing s[start:stop:step]; s[::-1] reverses. Operations: concatenation +, repetition *, membership in, comparison. Functions: len(), max(), min(). Methods: upper(), lower(), title(), capitalize(), swapcase(), strip(), lstrip(), rstrip(), find(), index(), count(), replace(), split(), join(), startswith(), endswith(), isalpha(), isdigit(), isalnum(), islower(), isupper(), isspace(), partition(). Traversal with for loop and index. Programs: palindrome, count vowels, reverse, capitalise words.
Deep dive: Indexing and slicing

s = "HELLO": s[0] = H, s[-1] = O, s[1:4] = ELL, s[:3] = HEL, s[2:] = LLO, s[::2] = HLO, s[::-1] = OLLEH. Strings are immutable: s[0] = "J" gives TypeError. Concatenation "Hi" + "There"; repetition "ab" * 3 = ababab. in: "ell" in s is True. Comparison uses Unicode values. ord("A") = 65, chr(97) = a.
Deep dive: String methods

"hello world".title() gives Hello World; "abc".upper() gives ABC; " hi ".strip() gives hi; "banana".count("a") gives 3; "banana".find("n") gives 2 (-1 if not found); index raises ValueError if absent; replace("a", "o"); "a,b,c".split(",") gives list; "-".join(["a","b"]) gives a-b; startswith, endswith; isalpha, isdigit; partition returns a 3-tuple.
Deep dive: Traversal and programs

for ch in s: print(ch); for i in range(len(s)): print(s[i]). Count vowels: if ch in "aeiouAEIOU". Palindrome: s == s[::-1]. Reverse words. Count uppercase letters with isupper(). Replace spaces. Word count with split(). Escape sequences in strings. Raw strings. Multi-line strings with triple quotes.
Hindi saransh
Python mein string: anuvartan, katan (slicing), vidhiyan. s[::-1] ulta karta hai. String achal (immutable) hota hai.

Visual lesson

Strings

A string is an immutable sequence of Unicode characters in single, double or triple quotes

🔑

Big idea

  • A string is an immutable sequence of Unicode characters in single, double or triple quotes
  • Indexing: forward 0 to n-1, backward -1 to -n
  • Slicing s[start:stop:step]
  • S[::-1] reverses
Read the full explanation

A string is an immutable sequence of Unicode characters in single, double or triple quotes. Indexing: forward 0 to n-1, backward -1 to -n. Slicing s[start:stop:step]; s[::-1] reverses. Operations: concatenation +, repetition *, membership in, comparison. Functions: len(), max(), min(). Methods: upper(), lower(), title(), capitalize(), swapcase(), strip(), lstrip(), rstrip(), find(), index(), count(), replace(), split(), join(), startswith(), endswith(), isalpha(), isdigit(), isalnum(), islower(), isupper(), isspace(), partition(). Traversal with for loop and index. Programs: palindrome, count vowels, reverse, capitalise words.

📌

Indexing and slicing

  • S = "HELLO": s[0] = H, s[-1] = O, s[1:4] = ELL, s[:3] = HEL, s[2:] = LLO, s[::2] = HLO, s[::-1] = OLLEH
  • Strings are immutable: s[0] = "J" gives TypeError
  • Concatenation "Hi" + "There"
  • Repetition "ab" * 3 = ababab
Read the full explanation

s = "HELLO": s[0] = H, s[-1] = O, s[1:4] = ELL, s[:3] = HEL, s[2:] = LLO, s[::2] = HLO, s[::-1] = OLLEH. Strings are immutable: s[0] = "J" gives TypeError. Concatenation "Hi" + "There"; repetition "ab" * 3 = ababab. in: "ell" in s is True. Comparison uses Unicode values. ord("A") = 65, chr(97) = a.

🔄

String methods

  • "hello world".title() gives Hello World
  • "abc".upper() gives ABC
  • " hi ".strip() gives hi
  • "banana".count("a") gives 3
Read the full explanation

"hello world".title() gives Hello World; "abc".upper() gives ABC; " hi ".strip() gives hi; "banana".count("a") gives 3; "banana".find("n") gives 2 (-1 if not found); index raises ValueError if absent; replace("a", "o"); "a,b,c".split(",") gives list; "-".join(["a","b"]) gives a-b; startswith, endswith; isalpha, isdigit; partition returns a 3-tuple.

🌟

Traversal and programs

  • For ch in s: print(ch)
  • For i in range(len(s)): print(s[i])
  • Count vowels: if ch in "aeiouAEIOU"
  • Palindrome: s == s[::-1]

for ch in s: print(ch); for i in range(len(s)): print(s[i]). Count vowels: if ch in "aeiouAEIOU". Palindrome: s == s[::-1]. Reverse words. Count uppercase letters with isupper(). Replace spaces. Word count with split(). Escape sequences in strings. Raw strings. Multi-line strings with triple quotes.

lessons.title: Lists
yt: class 11 computer science python lists methods sorting

blocks.x: A list is an ordered, mutable sequence of items in square brackets; items can be of different types. Indexing and slicing as in strings. Operations: concatenation, repetition, membership, comparison. Functions: len, max, min, sum, sorted, list(). Methods: append, extend, insert, remove, pop, clear, index, count, reverse, sort, copy. del statement. Nested lists. Traversal with for. Difference between sort (in place) and sorted (new list). Aliasing versus copy. Programs: sum, maximum, linear search, bubble sort, count even numbers, remove duplicates, merge lists, list comprehension.
Deep dive: Basics

L = [10, 20, 30, 40]: L[0] = 10, L[-1] = 40, L[1:3] = [20, 30]. Mutable: L[1] = 25. Creating lists: list("abc") gives [a, b, c]; list(range(5)). Concatenation [1,2] + [3]; repetition [0] * 3 = [0,0,0]. Nested list matrix M[1][2].
Deep dive: Methods

append(x) adds at the end; extend(iterable) adds many; insert(i, x) adds at a position; remove(x) deletes the first occurrence; pop(i) removes and returns the item (last by default); clear(); index(x); count(x); reverse(); sort() sorts in place (reverse=True for descending); sorted(L) returns a new list; copy() makes a shallow copy; del L[i]. Aliasing: M = L refers to the same list; M = L.copy() or L[:] creates a copy.
Deep dive: Programs

Sum: total = 0; for x in L: total += x. Maximum without max(). Linear search. Bubble sort with nested loops and swap L[j], L[j+1] = L[j+1], L[j]. Remove duplicates by checking membership. Count even numbers. Reverse list. Merge sorted lists. List comprehension: [x*x for x in range(1, 6)]. Statistics: mean, median.
Hindi saransh
Soochi (list) kramit aur parivartaniya hoti hai. append, extend, insert, remove, pop, sort. Copy aur alias mein antar.
sort() changes the list in place and returns None, while sorted() returns a new list.

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Lists

A list is an ordered, mutable sequence of items in square brackets

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Basics›3Methods›4Programs
L[1:3]Items 1 and 2
🔑

Big idea

  • A list is an ordered, mutable sequence of items in square brackets
  • Items can be of different types
  • Indexing and slicing as in strings
  • Operations: concatenation, repetition, membership, comparison
Read the full explanation

A list is an ordered, mutable sequence of items in square brackets; items can be of different types. Indexing and slicing as in strings. Operations: concatenation, repetition, membership, comparison. Functions: len, max, min, sum, sorted, list(). Methods: append, extend, insert, remove, pop, clear, index, count, reverse, sort, copy. del statement. Nested lists. Traversal with for. Difference between sort (in place) and sorted (new list). Aliasing versus copy. Programs: sum, maximum, linear search, bubble sort, count even numbers, remove duplicates, merge lists, list comprehension.

📘

Basics

  • L = [10, 20, 30, 40]: L[0] = 10, L[-1] = 40, L[1:3] = [20, 30]
  • Mutable: L[1] = 25
  • Creating lists: list("abc") gives [a, b, c]
  • List(range(5))
Read the full explanation

L = [10, 20, 30, 40]: L[0] = 10, L[-1] = 40, L[1:3] = [20, 30]. Mutable: L[1] = 25. Creating lists: list("abc") gives [a, b, c]; list(range(5)). Concatenation [1,2] + [3]; repetition [0] * 3 = [0,0,0]. Nested list matrix M[1][2].

🔄

Methods

  • Append(x) adds at the end
  • Extend(iterable) adds many
  • Insert(i, x) adds at a position
  • Remove(x) deletes the first occurrence
Read the full explanation

append(x) adds at the end; extend(iterable) adds many; insert(i, x) adds at a position; remove(x) deletes the first occurrence; pop(i) removes and returns the item (last by default); clear(); index(x); count(x); reverse(); sort() sorts in place (reverse=True for descending); sorted(L) returns a new list; copy() makes a shallow copy; del L[i]. Aliasing: M = L refers to the same list; M = L.copy() or L[:] creates a copy.

🌟

Programs

  • Sum: total = 0
  • For x in L: total += x
  • Maximum without max()
  • Linear search
Read the full explanation

Sum: total = 0; for x in L: total += x. Maximum without max(). Linear search. Bubble sort with nested loops and swap L[j], L[j+1] = L[j+1], L[j]. Remove duplicates by checking membership. Count even numbers. Reverse list. Merge sorted lists. List comprehension: [x*x for x in range(1, 6)]. Statistics: mean, median.

🧮

Formula tiles

appendAdd at endL.append(5)
insertAdd at indexL.insert(0, 5)
removeDelete valueL.remove(5)
popDelete indexL.pop()
sortIn placeL.sort()
reverseReverseL.reverse()
L[1:3]Items 1 and 2Stop excluded
L[::-1]ReverseStep -1
🎯 Remember sort() changes the list in place and returns None, while sorted() returns a new list.
🇮🇳

lessons.title: Tuples and Dictionaries
yt: class 11 computer science python tuples dictionaries methods

blocks.x: A tuple is an ordered immutable sequence in parentheses; a single-element tuple needs a trailing comma (5,). Operations: indexing, slicing, concatenation, repetition, membership; functions len, max, min, sum, sorted, tuple(); methods count and index. Tuple assignment and unpacking: a, b = b, a. Nested tuples. Dictionary: unordered (insertion-ordered since 3.7) mutable collection of key-value pairs in braces; keys are unique and immutable; values any type. Access d[key], get(key, default), keys(), values(), items(), update(), pop(), popitem(), del, clear(), len(), in checks keys. Traversal. Programs: count word frequency, student marks, phone book.
Deep dive: Tuples

t = (1, 2, 3); t[0] = 1; t cannot be changed (TypeError). Single element: t = (5,). Packing and unpacking: x, y, z = t. Return of multiple values from functions as a tuple. Why tuples: faster, safe, usable as dictionary keys. Sort a tuple with sorted() returns a list. tuple("abc") gives (a, b, c). Concatenation creates a new tuple.
Deep dive: Dictionaries

d = {"name": "Ria", "age": 16}. d["name"] returns Ria; d["city"] raises KeyError; d.get("city") returns None. Adding or updating d["city"] = "Delhi". Methods: keys(), values(), items(), update(other), pop(key), popitem(), del d[key], clear(), copy(). Membership "age" in d checks keys. Dictionary comprehension. len(d) counts pairs. Keys must be immutable (strings, numbers, tuples).
Deep dive: Programs

Word frequency: for w in words: d[w] = d.get(w, 0) + 1. Count characters. Student marks dictionary and find topper. Merge dictionaries with update. Invert a dictionary. Sort by key with sorted(d). Use items() in a for loop: for k, v in d.items(). Nested dictionary for records. Mean of values using sum(d.values()) / len(d).

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Tuples and Dictionaries

A tuple is an ordered immutable sequence in parentheses

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Tuples›3Dictionaries›4Programs
Single(5,)
🔑

Big idea

  • A tuple is an ordered immutable sequence in parentheses
  • A single-element tuple needs a trailing comma (5,)
  • Operations: indexing, slicing, concatenation, repetition, membership
  • Functions len, max, min, sum, sorted, tuple()
Read the full explanation

A tuple is an ordered immutable sequence in parentheses; a single-element tuple needs a trailing comma (5,). Operations: indexing, slicing, concatenation, repetition, membership; functions len, max, min, sum, sorted, tuple(); methods count and index. Tuple assignment and unpacking: a, b = b, a. Nested tuples. Dictionary: unordered (insertion-ordered since 3.7) mutable collection of key-value pairs in braces; keys are unique and immutable; values any type. Access d[key], get(key, default), keys(), values(), items(), update(), pop(), popitem(), del, clear(), len(), in checks keys. Traversal. Programs: count word frequency, student marks, phone book.

📌

Tuples

  • T = (1, 2, 3)
  • T cannot be changed (TypeError)
  • Single element: t = (5,)
  • Packing and unpacking: x, y, z = t
Read the full explanation

t = (1, 2, 3); t[0] = 1; t cannot be changed (TypeError). Single element: t = (5,). Packing and unpacking: x, y, z = t. Return of multiple values from functions as a tuple. Why tuples: faster, safe, usable as dictionary keys. Sort a tuple with sorted() returns a list. tuple("abc") gives (a, b, c). Concatenation creates a new tuple.

🧠

Dictionaries

  • D = {"name": "Ria", "age": 16}
  • D["name"] returns Ria
  • D["city"] raises KeyError
  • D.get("city") returns None
Read the full explanation

d = {"name": "Ria", "age": 16}. d["name"] returns Ria; d["city"] raises KeyError; d.get("city") returns None. Adding or updating d["city"] = "Delhi". Methods: keys(), values(), items(), update(other), pop(key), popitem(), del d[key], clear(), copy(). Membership "age" in d checks keys. Dictionary comprehension. len(d) counts pairs. Keys must be immutable (strings, numbers, tuples).

🌟

Programs

  • Word frequency: for w in words: d[w] = d.get(w, 0) + 1
  • Count characters
  • Student marks dictionary and find topper
  • Merge dictionaries with update
Read the full explanation

Word frequency: for w in words: d[w] = d.get(w, 0) + 1. Count characters. Student marks dictionary and find topper. Merge dictionaries with update. Invert a dictionary. Sort by key with sorted(d). Use items() in a for loop: for k, v in d.items(). Nested dictionary for records. Mean of values using sum(d.values()) / len(d).

lessons.title: Societal Impact
yt: class 11 computer science societal impact cyber safety digital footprint IPR e-waste

blocks.x: Digital footprint (active and passive). Netiquette. Cyber safety: protecting identity, passwords, secure websites (https), avoiding scams. Cyber crime: hacking, phishing, identity theft, cyber bullying, cyber stalking, ransomware, spam. Cyber law: IT Act 2000 (amended 2008). Intellectual property rights: copyright, patent, trademark; plagiarism; licensing (GPL, Creative Commons). Digital property. Open source and free software. E-waste management: reduce, reuse, recycle; hazardous substances. Technology and health: ergonomics, screen time, addiction. Digital society: e-governance (Digilocker, UPI), e-commerce, e-learning, e-banking. Technology and gender and accessibility; digital divide; net neutrality.
Deep dive: Digital footprint and cyber safety

Active footprint: posts, comments, forms you fill. Passive footprint: cookies, IP address, browsing history collected without your action. Strong password: 8+ characters with mixed letters, numbers, symbols; two-factor authentication; use https; avoid public Wi-Fi for banking; update software. Phishing and social engineering; cyber bullying (harassment through digital means); cyber grooming; reporting at cybercrime.gov.in.
Deep dive: IPR and law

Copyright protects original literary, artistic, musical works automatically; a patent protects inventions for 20 years; trademarks protect brand names and logos. Plagiarism is presenting others' work as one's own. Licences: GPL (copyleft), Creative Commons (attribution, share-alike, non-commercial). IT Act 2000 recognises electronic records and digital signatures and punishes hacking (Section 66), identity theft (66C), cyber terrorism (66F). Data protection and privacy.
Deep dive: E-waste, health, society

E-waste: discarded electronics with lead, mercury, cadmium. Management: reuse, recycle, buy-back schemes, authorised recyclers; E-Waste Management Rules. Ergonomics: posture, 20-20-20 rule. Digital addiction, screen time. E-governance services: Aadhaar, DigiLocker, UMANG, e-Hospital. Digital divide, assistive technology, inclusive design. Technology for gender equality.
Hindi saransh
Samajik prabhav: digital paadchinh, cyber suraksha, IPR, e-kachra. IT Adhiniyam 2000.

Digital footprint (active and passive). Netiquette. Cyber safety: protecting identity, passwords, secure websites (https), avoiding scams. Cyber crime: hacking, phishing, identity theft, cyber bullying, cyber stalking, ransomware, spam. Cyber law: IT Act 2000 (amended 2008). Intellectual property rights: copyright, patent, trademark; plagiarism; licensing (GPL, Creative Commons). Digital property. Open source and free software. E-waste management: reduce, reuse, recycle; hazardous substances. Technology and health: ergonomics, screen time, addiction. Digital society: e-governance (Digilocker, UPI), e-commerce, e-learning, e-banking. Technology and gender and accessibility; digital divide; net neutrality.

📌

Digital footprint and cyber safety

  • Active footprint: posts, comments, forms you fill
  • Passive footprint: cookies, IP address, browsing history collected without your action
  • Strong password: 8+ characters with mixed letters, numbers, symbols
  • Two-factor authentication
Read the full explanation

Active footprint: posts, comments, forms you fill. Passive footprint: cookies, IP address, browsing history collected without your action. Strong password: 8+ characters with mixed letters, numbers, symbols; two-factor authentication; use https; avoid public Wi-Fi for banking; update software. Phishing and social engineering; cyber bullying (harassment through digital means); cyber grooming; reporting at cybercrime.gov.in.

⚖️

IPR and law

  • Copyright protects original literary, artistic, musical works automatically
  • A patent protects inventions for 20 years
  • Trademarks protect brand names and logos
  • Plagiarism is presenting others' work as one's own
Read the full explanation

Copyright protects original literary, artistic, musical works automatically; a patent protects inventions for 20 years; trademarks protect brand names and logos. Plagiarism is presenting others' work as one's own. Licences: GPL (copyleft), Creative Commons (attribution, share-alike, non-commercial). IT Act 2000 recognises electronic records and digital signatures and punishes hacking (Section 66), identity theft (66C), cyber terrorism (66F). Data protection and privacy.

🌟

E-waste, health, society

  • E-waste: discarded electronics with lead, mercury, cadmium
  • Management: reuse, recycle, buy-back schemes, authorised recyclers
  • E-Waste Management Rules
  • Ergonomics: posture, 20-20-20 rule
Read the full explanation

E-waste: discarded electronics with lead, mercury, cadmium. Management: reuse, recycle, buy-back schemes, authorised recyclers; E-Waste Management Rules. Ergonomics: posture, 20-20-20 rule. Digital addiction, screen time. E-governance services: Aadhaar, DigiLocker, UMANG, e-Hospital. Digital divide, assistive technology, inclusive design. Technology for gender equality.

lessons.title: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
yt: class 11 economics indian economy on the eve of independence colonial rule

blocks.x: Under British rule (1757 to 1947) India was a raw material supplier and a market for British goods. Economic policies of the colonial government: drain of wealth, de-industrialisation (decline of handicrafts), commercialisation of agriculture, zamindari system, land revenue. Agricultural stagnation: low productivity (about 0.4 to 0.5 percent growth), little irrigation. Industrial sector: decline of handicrafts, limited modern industry (TISCO 1907, cotton and jute mills), capital goods industry absent. Foreign trade: net exporter of primary goods and importer of finished goods; Suez Canal (1869); drain of wealth. Demographic: birth rate 48 per thousand, death rate 40, infant mortality 218 per thousand, life expectancy 32 years, literacy 16 percent, female literacy 7 percent. Occupational structure: 70-75 percent in agriculture. Infrastructure: railways (1850), ports, post and telegraph. Per capita income stagnant. Dadabhai Naoroji (Poverty and Un-British Rule in India).
Deep dive: Colonial policies

Drain of wealth: surplus of exports over imports used to pay Home charges, administrative costs of the British, wars. Land revenue systems: Permanent Settlement (1793) of Lord Cornwallis, Ryotwari, Mahalwari. Commercialisation: indigo, cotton, jute instead of foodgrains. Decline of handicrafts: heavy duties on Indian goods, cheap British machine-made goods, tariffs; unemployment of artisans. Zamindars collected rent and did not invest in agriculture. Famines.
Deep dive: Sectors and trade

Agriculture: low productivity, no irrigation or fertilisers, partition effect on jute and cotton. Industry: TISCO set up 1907 at Jamshedpur; cotton textile mills in Bombay and Ahmedabad; jute in Bengal; no capital goods industry; public sector small. Trade: India exported raw cotton, jute, sugar, indigo, jute; imported finished goods; Britain held monopoly control; Suez Canal reduced cost of trade; no tariffs against British imports.
Deep dive: Demography, occupation and infrastructure

Birth rate 48 and death rate 40 per thousand; IMR 218; life expectancy 44 in 1951 (about 32 earlier); literacy 16 percent. Occupational structure: agriculture 72 percent, manufacturing 10, services 18. Regional disparity: Madras, Bombay and Bengal presidencies. Positive aspects: railways, ports, communication, introduction of modern administrative system, though railways served British interests. Poverty was widespread with no estimates of national income before Naoroji, V. K. R. V. Rao.
Hindi saransh
Svatantrata ke samay Bharatiya arthvyavastha: aupniveshik shoshan, dhan ka nishkasan, hastshilp ka patan. Permanent Settlement 1793.
The colonial government's policies turned India into a supplier of raw materials and a market for British goods.

🔑

Big idea

  • Under British rule (1757 to 1947) India was a raw material supplier and a market for British goods
  • Economic policies of the colonial government: drain of wealth, de-industrialisation (decline of handicrafts), commercialisation of agriculture…
  • Agricultural stagnation: low productivity (about 0.4 to 0.5 percent growth), little irrigation
  • Industrial sector: decline of handicrafts, limited modern industry (TISCO 1907, cotton and jute mills), capital goods industry absent
Read the full explanation

Under British rule (1757 to 1947) India was a raw material supplier and a market for British goods. Economic policies of the colonial government: drain of wealth, de-industrialisation (decline of handicrafts), commercialisation of agriculture, zamindari system, land revenue. Agricultural stagnation: low productivity (about 0.4 to 0.5 percent growth), little irrigation. Industrial sector: decline of handicrafts, limited modern industry (TISCO 1907, cotton and jute mills), capital goods industry absent. Foreign trade: net exporter of primary goods and importer of finished goods; Suez Canal (1869); drain of wealth. Demographic: birth rate 48 per thousand, death rate 40, infant mortality 218 per thousand, life expectancy 32 years, literacy 16 percent, female literacy 7 percent. Occupational structure: 70-75 percent in agriculture. Infrastructure: railways (1850), ports, post and telegraph. Per capita income stagnant. Dadabhai Naoroji (Poverty and Un-British Rule in India).

📌

Colonial policies

  • Drain of wealth: surplus of exports over imports used to pay Home charges, administrative costs of the British, wars
  • Land revenue systems: Permanent Settlement (1793) of Lord Cornwallis, Ryotwari, Mahalwari
  • Commercialisation: indigo, cotton, jute instead of foodgrains
  • Decline of handicrafts: heavy duties on Indian goods, cheap British machine-made goods, tariffs
Read the full explanation

Drain of wealth: surplus of exports over imports used to pay Home charges, administrative costs of the British, wars. Land revenue systems: Permanent Settlement (1793) of Lord Cornwallis, Ryotwari, Mahalwari. Commercialisation: indigo, cotton, jute instead of foodgrains. Decline of handicrafts: heavy duties on Indian goods, cheap British machine-made goods, tariffs; unemployment of artisans. Zamindars collected rent and did not invest in agriculture. Famines.

🧠

Sectors and trade

  • Agriculture: low productivity, no irrigation or fertilisers, partition effect on jute and cotton
  • Industry: TISCO set up 1907 at Jamshedpur
  • Cotton textile mills in Bombay and Ahmedabad
  • Jute in Bengal
Read the full explanation

Agriculture: low productivity, no irrigation or fertilisers, partition effect on jute and cotton. Industry: TISCO set up 1907 at Jamshedpur; cotton textile mills in Bombay and Ahmedabad; jute in Bengal; no capital goods industry; public sector small. Trade: India exported raw cotton, jute, sugar, indigo, jute; imported finished goods; Britain held monopoly control; Suez Canal reduced cost of trade; no tariffs against British imports.

🌟

Demography, occupation and infrastructure

  • Birth rate 48 and death rate 40 per thousand
  • Life expectancy 44 in 1951 (about 32 earlier)
  • Literacy 16 percent
  • Occupational structure: agriculture 72 percent, manufacturing 10, services 18
Read the full explanation

Birth rate 48 and death rate 40 per thousand; IMR 218; life expectancy 44 in 1951 (about 32 earlier); literacy 16 percent. Occupational structure: agriculture 72 percent, manufacturing 10, services 18. Regional disparity: Madras, Bombay and Bengal presidencies. Positive aspects: railways, ports, communication, introduction of modern administrative system, though railways served British interests. Poverty was widespread with no estimates of national income before Naoroji, V. K. R. V. Rao.

🎯 Remember The colonial government's policies turned India into a supplier of raw materials and a market for British goods.

lessons.title: Indian Economy 1950-1990
yt: class 11 economics indian economy 1950 1990 five year plans green revolution

blocks.x: Goals of planning: growth, modernisation, self-reliance, equity. Economic systems: capitalist, socialist, mixed. India adopted a mixed economy; Planning Commission (1950), Five Year Plans (First 1951-56 Harrod-Domar model, agriculture; Second 1956-61 Mahalanobis model, heavy industry). Agriculture: land reforms (abolition of intermediaries, tenancy regulation, ceiling on land holdings, consolidation), Green Revolution (HYV seeds, fertilisers, irrigation; wheat and rice; 1960s), subsidies and MSP. Industry: Industrial Policy Resolution 1956 (Schedule A, B, C), licensing, public sector, small scale industries reservation, MRTP Act 1969, FERA 1973. Trade policy: import substitution, protection (tariffs, quotas). Achievements: GDP growth about 3.5 percent (Hindu rate of growth), diversified industry, self-sufficiency in foodgrains. Limitations: inefficient public sector, licence raj, low growth, poverty. Economic reforms 1991 followed.
Deep dive: Planning and objectives

Planning Commission, headed by the Prime Minister, replaced by NITI Aayog in 2015. Plans: sector-wise priorities. Goals: growth in GDP, modernisation (technology, social outlook), self-reliance (reducing imports), equity (reducing inequality). Planning is a process of setting goals and allocating resources. Five Year Plans of 1951-90: first (agriculture, irrigation), second (heavy industry).
Deep dive: Agriculture and Green Revolution

Land reforms: abolition of zamindari (largely successful in removing intermediaries), tenancy reform, ceiling (limit on holding), consolidation. Green Revolution: HYV seeds, chemical fertilisers, irrigation, pesticides; wheat in Punjab, Haryana, west UP; rice in Andhra and Tamil Nadu; foodgrain output from 51 million tonnes (1950-51) to over 170 million tonnes. Marketable surplus rose. Risks: regional disparity, small farmers left out, risk of pest attacks. Subsidies: fertiliser, power; debate on subsidies and MSP.
Deep dive: Industry, trade and evaluation

IPR 1956: Schedule A (17 industries reserved for state), B (progressively state-owned), C (private). Industrial licensing under the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act 1951. Small scale industries for employment. Import substitution: protect domestic industries from foreign competition. Public sector: heavy industries, infrastructure. Criticism: delays, inefficiency, no competition. Achievements: diversified industrial base, self-reliant, growth about 4 percent. Failure: poverty, inefficiency, balance of payments crisis in 1991.
Hindi saransh
Bharatiya arthvyavastha 1950-1990: yojana, hari kranti, bhumi sudhar, audyogik neeti. Mishrit arthvyavastha.

🔑

Big idea

  • Goals of planning: growth, modernisation, self-reliance, equity
  • Economic systems: capitalist, socialist, mixed
  • India adopted a mixed economy
  • Planning Commission (1950), Five Year Plans (First 1951-56 Harrod-Domar model, agriculture
Read the full explanation

Goals of planning: growth, modernisation, self-reliance, equity. Economic systems: capitalist, socialist, mixed. India adopted a mixed economy; Planning Commission (1950), Five Year Plans (First 1951-56 Harrod-Domar model, agriculture; Second 1956-61 Mahalanobis model, heavy industry). Agriculture: land reforms (abolition of intermediaries, tenancy regulation, ceiling on land holdings, consolidation), Green Revolution (HYV seeds, fertilisers, irrigation; wheat and rice; 1960s), subsidies and MSP. Industry: Industrial Policy Resolution 1956 (Schedule A, B, C), licensing, public sector, small scale industries reservation, MRTP Act 1969, FERA 1973. Trade policy: import substitution, protection (tariffs, quotas). Achievements: GDP growth about 3.5 percent (Hindu rate of growth), diversified industry, self-sufficiency in foodgrains. Limitations: inefficient public sector, licence raj, low growth, poverty. Economic reforms 1991 followed.

📌

Planning and objectives

  • Planning Commission, headed by the Prime Minister, replaced by NITI Aayog in 2015
  • Plans: sector-wise priorities
  • Goals: growth in GDP, modernisation (technology, social outlook), self-reliance (reducing imports), equity (reducing inequality)
  • Planning is a process of setting goals and allocating resources
Read the full explanation

Planning Commission, headed by the Prime Minister, replaced by NITI Aayog in 2015. Plans: sector-wise priorities. Goals: growth in GDP, modernisation (technology, social outlook), self-reliance (reducing imports), equity (reducing inequality). Planning is a process of setting goals and allocating resources. Five Year Plans of 1951-90: first (agriculture, irrigation), second (heavy industry).

🕰️

Agriculture and Green Revolution

  • Land reforms: abolition of zamindari (largely successful in removing intermediaries), tenancy reform, ceiling (limit on holding), consolidation
  • Green Revolution: HYV seeds, chemical fertilisers, irrigation, pesticides
  • Wheat in Punjab, Haryana, west UP
  • Rice in Andhra and Tamil Nadu
Read the full explanation

Land reforms: abolition of zamindari (largely successful in removing intermediaries), tenancy reform, ceiling (limit on holding), consolidation. Green Revolution: HYV seeds, chemical fertilisers, irrigation, pesticides; wheat in Punjab, Haryana, west UP; rice in Andhra and Tamil Nadu; foodgrain output from 51 million tonnes (1950-51) to over 170 million tonnes. Marketable surplus rose. Risks: regional disparity, small farmers left out, risk of pest attacks. Subsidies: fertiliser, power; debate on subsidies and MSP.

🌟

Industry, trade and evaluation

  • IPR 1956: Schedule A (17 industries reserved for state), B (progressively state-owned), C (private)
  • Industrial licensing under the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act 1951
  • Small scale industries for employment
  • Import substitution: protect domestic industries from foreign competition
Read the full explanation

IPR 1956: Schedule A (17 industries reserved for state), B (progressively state-owned), C (private). Industrial licensing under the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act 1951. Small scale industries for employment. Import substitution: protect domestic industries from foreign competition. Public sector: heavy industries, infrastructure. Criticism: delays, inefficiency, no competition. Achievements: diversified industrial base, self-reliant, growth about 4 percent. Failure: poverty, inefficiency, balance of payments crisis in 1991.

🎯 Remember India adopted a mixed economy with both public and private sectors after independence.

Bharatiya arthvyavastha 1950-1990: yojana, hari kranti, bhumi sudhar, audyogik neeti. Mishrit arthvyavastha.

lessons.title: Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation: An Appraisal
yt: class 11 economics liberalisation privatisation globalisation LPG reforms 1991

blocks.x: Background of 1991 reforms: balance of payments crisis (foreign exchange reserves covering 2 weeks of imports), inflation, fiscal deficit, poor public sector performance, Gulf war. New Economic Policy: stabilisation (short-term) and structural reforms (long-term). Liberalisation: abolition of industrial licensing (except hazardous), deregulation of financial sector (RBI role from regulator to facilitator, bank branch freedom, interest rates), tax reforms (reduction in tax rates, VAT/GST later), foreign exchange reforms (devaluation of rupee by 18-19 percent in 1991, market determined exchange rate), trade and investment policy reforms (removal of quantitative restrictions, lower tariffs, FDI up to 51 percent initially). Privatisation: disinvestment and reduction of the public sector (navratna, maharatna). Globalisation: outsourcing, WTO (1995), BPO. Appraisal: GDP growth about 6-7 percent, service sector growth, poor agriculture growth, employment and inequality concerns.
Deep dive: Background and reforms

1991 crisis: forex reserves fell to cover about 2 weeks of imports; borrowing from IMF and World Bank with conditionality. LPG: stabilisation measures to maintain sufficient forex and control inflation; structural measures to improve efficiency by making Indian industry competitive. Industrial sector reforms: delicensing, reduction of public sector reservation (from 17 to 3 industries, later 2: atomic energy and railways), MRTP restrictions removed, freedom to import capital goods.
Deep dive: Components

Financial sector: private banks (HDFC, ICICI), FII allowed to invest, SEBI established (1992), RBI as facilitator. Tax: reduced income and corporate tax rates, simplification, GST (2017). Foreign exchange: rupee devalued, later market determined. Trade: removal of quantitative restrictions on imports, tariff reduction, no licensing for exports, export duties removed. Privatisation: disinvestment (sale of shares of PSUs), strategic sale. Globalisation: integration with the world economy, outsourcing (BPO), WTO membership since 1995.
Deep dive: Appraisal

Positives: GDP growth rose to about 7 percent, service sector emerged (contributing over 50 percent of GDP), forex reserves increased, FDI and FII inflows, exports rose, IT growth. Negatives: poor agricultural growth, industrial growth slowed, disinvestment criticism, jobless growth, inequality, reduction of agri subsidies, fiscal consolidation reducing social spending, lack of public investment, competition for small units. The reforms did not benefit all equally.

Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation: An Appraisal

Background of 1991 reforms: balance of payments crisis (foreign exchange reserves covering 2 weeks of imports), inflation, fiscal deficit, poor public sector…

🔑

Big idea

  • Background of 1991 reforms: balance of payments crisis (foreign exchange reserves covering 2 weeks of imports), inflation, fiscal deficit, poor…
  • New Economic Policy: stabilisation (short-term) and structural reforms (long-term)
  • Liberalisation: abolition of industrial licensing (except hazardous), deregulation of financial sector (RBI role from regulator to facilitator, bank…
  • Privatisation: disinvestment and reduction of the public sector (navratna, maharatna)
Read the full explanation

Background of 1991 reforms: balance of payments crisis (foreign exchange reserves covering 2 weeks of imports), inflation, fiscal deficit, poor public sector performance, Gulf war. New Economic Policy: stabilisation (short-term) and structural reforms (long-term). Liberalisation: abolition of industrial licensing (except hazardous), deregulation of financial sector (RBI role from regulator to facilitator, bank branch freedom, interest rates), tax reforms (reduction in tax rates, VAT/GST later), foreign exchange reforms (devaluation of rupee by 18-19 percent in 1991, market determined exchange rate), trade and investment policy reforms (removal of quantitative restrictions, lower tariffs, FDI up to 51 percent initially). Privatisation: disinvestment and reduction of the public sector (navratna, maharatna). Globalisation: outsourcing, WTO (1995), BPO. Appraisal: GDP growth about 6-7 percent, service sector growth, poor agriculture growth, employment and inequality concerns.

📌

Background and reforms

  • 1991 crisis: forex reserves fell to cover about 2 weeks of imports
  • Borrowing from IMF and World Bank with conditionality
  • LPG: stabilisation measures to maintain sufficient forex and control inflation
  • Structural measures to improve efficiency by making Indian industry competitive
Read the full explanation

1991 crisis: forex reserves fell to cover about 2 weeks of imports; borrowing from IMF and World Bank with conditionality. LPG: stabilisation measures to maintain sufficient forex and control inflation; structural measures to improve efficiency by making Indian industry competitive. Industrial sector reforms: delicensing, reduction of public sector reservation (from 17 to 3 industries, later 2: atomic energy and railways), MRTP restrictions removed, freedom to import capital goods.

🧠

Components

  • Financial sector: private banks (HDFC, ICICI), FII allowed to invest, SEBI established (1992), RBI as facilitator
  • Tax: reduced income and corporate tax rates, simplification, GST (2017)
  • Foreign exchange: rupee devalued, later market determined
  • Trade: removal of quantitative restrictions on imports, tariff reduction, no licensing for exports, export duties removed
Read the full explanation

Financial sector: private banks (HDFC, ICICI), FII allowed to invest, SEBI established (1992), RBI as facilitator. Tax: reduced income and corporate tax rates, simplification, GST (2017). Foreign exchange: rupee devalued, later market determined. Trade: removal of quantitative restrictions on imports, tariff reduction, no licensing for exports, export duties removed. Privatisation: disinvestment (sale of shares of PSUs), strategic sale. Globalisation: integration with the world economy, outsourcing (BPO), WTO membership since 1995.

🌟

Appraisal

  • Positives: GDP growth rose to about 7 percent, service sector emerged (contributing over 50 percent of GDP), forex reserves increased, FDI and FII…
  • Negatives: poor agricultural growth, industrial growth slowed, disinvestment criticism, jobless growth, inequality, reduction of agri subsidies…
  • The reforms did not benefit all equally
Read the full explanation

Positives: GDP growth rose to about 7 percent, service sector emerged (contributing over 50 percent of GDP), forex reserves increased, FDI and FII inflows, exports rose, IT growth. Negatives: poor agricultural growth, industrial growth slowed, disinvestment criticism, jobless growth, inequality, reduction of agri subsidies, fiscal consolidation reducing social spending, lack of public investment, competition for small units. The reforms did not benefit all equally.

🎯 Remember The 1991 economic reforms were triggered by a balance of payments crisis.

lessons.title: Poverty
yt: class 11 economics poverty line headcount ratio poverty alleviation MGNREGA

blocks.x: Poverty is the inability to meet basic needs. Absolute and relative poverty. Poverty line: minimum expenditure for basic needs; in India based on calorie norm (2400 kcal rural, 2100 kcal urban per person per day, earlier); Tendulkar committee (2009-10 Rs 27 per day rural, Rs 33 urban in 2011-12 estimates), Rangarajan committee. Head Count Ratio: percentage of poor. Poverty gap and poverty severity. Causes: colonial legacy, low growth, population pressure, unemployment, unequal land distribution, caste and gender, illiteracy. Poverty estimates: 1993-94 about 36 percent; 2011-12 about 22 percent (Tendulkar), 21.9 percent. Multidimensional Poverty Index (UNDP and OPHI) health, education, living standard. Anti-poverty programmes: MGNREGA (100 days wage employment), PMGSY, SGSY/NRLM, PMRY, SJSRY, PMAY, ICDS, PDS, National Food Security Act 2013, Mid-day meal, Jan Dhan. Two-pronged approach: growth and targeted programmes.
Deep dive: Measurement and causes

Poverty line is estimated on consumption expenditure; poverty is concentrated among scheduled castes, scheduled tribes, agricultural labourers, casual workers and in states such as Bihar, Odisha, Uttar Pradesh. Causes: low per capita income, population growth, unequal distribution of land and assets, unemployment and underemployment, social factors (customs, caste), colonial exploitation, lack of social security. Dimensions: income, health, education, vulnerability, social exclusion.
Deep dive: Poverty alleviation programmes

Growth-oriented approach (Green Revolution, industrialisation). Targeted: MGNREGA (2005) guarantees 100 days of wage employment to rural households; PMGSY for rural roads; NRLM for self-help groups; Swarnajayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana; PMAY for housing; PDS provides subsidised foodgrains; National Food Security Act 2013 covers about two-thirds of the population; Antyodaya Anna Yojana for the poorest. Evaluation: leakages, corruption, targeting errors, lack of awareness.
Deep dive: Multidimensional poverty and appraisal

MPI uses 10 indicators: nutrition, child mortality, years of schooling, school attendance, cooking fuel, sanitation, drinking water, electricity, housing, assets. India has reduced multidimensional poverty over the last decade. Challenges: regional inequality, urban poverty, vulnerability, quality of life, child malnutrition. Programmes should combine growth with human development (health, education), empower women and raise agricultural productivity.

Big idea

  • Absolute and relative poverty
  • Poverty line: minimum expenditure for basic needs
  • In India based on calorie norm (2400 kcal rural, 2100 kcal urban per person per day, earlier)
Read the full explanation

Poverty is the inability to meet basic needs. Absolute and relative poverty. Poverty line: minimum expenditure for basic needs; in India based on calorie norm (2400 kcal rural, 2100 kcal urban per person per day, earlier); Tendulkar committee (2009-10 Rs 27 per day rural, Rs 33 urban in 2011-12 estimates), Rangarajan committee. Head Count Ratio: percentage of poor. Poverty gap and poverty severity. Causes: colonial legacy, low growth, population pressure, unemployment, unequal land distribution, caste and gender, illiteracy. Poverty estimates: 1993-94 about 36 percent; 2011-12 about 22 percent (Tendulkar), 21.9 percent. Multidimensional Poverty Index (UNDP and OPHI) health, education, living standard. Anti-poverty programmes: MGNREGA (100 days wage employment), PMGSY, SGSY/NRLM, PMRY, SJSRY, PMAY, ICDS, PDS, National Food Security Act 2013, Mid-day meal, Jan Dhan. Two-pronged approach: growth and targeted programmes.

💡

Measurement and causes

  • Poverty line is estimated on consumption expenditure
  • Poverty is concentrated among scheduled castes, scheduled tribes, agricultural labourers, casual workers and in states such as Bihar, Odisha, Uttar…
  • Causes: low per capita income, population growth, unequal distribution of land and assets, unemployment and underemployment, social factors (customs…
  • Dimensions: income, health, education, vulnerability, social exclusion
Read the full explanation

Poverty line is estimated on consumption expenditure; poverty is concentrated among scheduled castes, scheduled tribes, agricultural labourers, casual workers and in states such as Bihar, Odisha, Uttar Pradesh. Causes: low per capita income, population growth, unequal distribution of land and assets, unemployment and underemployment, social factors (customs, caste), colonial exploitation, lack of social security. Dimensions: income, health, education, vulnerability, social exclusion.

🧠

Poverty alleviation programmes

  • Growth-oriented approach (Green Revolution, industrialisation)
  • Targeted: MGNREGA (2005) guarantees 100 days of wage employment to rural households
  • PMGSY for rural roads
  • NRLM for self-help groups
Read the full explanation

Growth-oriented approach (Green Revolution, industrialisation). Targeted: MGNREGA (2005) guarantees 100 days of wage employment to rural households; PMGSY for rural roads; NRLM for self-help groups; Swarnajayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana; PMAY for housing; PDS provides subsidised foodgrains; National Food Security Act 2013 covers about two-thirds of the population; Antyodaya Anna Yojana for the poorest. Evaluation: leakages, corruption, targeting errors, lack of awareness.

🌟

Multidimensional poverty and appraisal

  • MPI uses 10 indicators: nutrition, child mortality, years of schooling, school attendance, cooking fuel, sanitation, drinking water, electricity…
  • India has reduced multidimensional poverty over the last decade
  • Challenges: regional inequality, urban poverty, vulnerability, quality of life, child malnutrition
  • Programmes should combine growth with human development (health, education), empower women and raise agricultural productivity
Read the full explanation

MPI uses 10 indicators: nutrition, child mortality, years of schooling, school attendance, cooking fuel, sanitation, drinking water, electricity, housing, assets. India has reduced multidimensional poverty over the last decade. Challenges: regional inequality, urban poverty, vulnerability, quality of life, child malnutrition. Programmes should combine growth with human development (health, education), empower women and raise agricultural productivity.

lessons.title: Human Capital Formation in India
yt: class 11 economics human capital formation education health

blocks.x: Human capital is the stock of skills, knowledge, health and productive capacity embodied in people. Physical capital versus human capital. Human capital formation sources: expenditure on education, expenditure on health, on-the-job training, migration, information. Human capital and human development: human capital treats human beings as a means, human development treats them as ends. Education: literacy, enrolment, adult literacy; Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan, RTE Act 2009 (6-14 years), mid-day meal, National Education Policy 2020, higher education, vocational education. Education expenditure about 4.6 percent of GDP (target 6 percent). Problems: low female literacy, rural-urban gaps, brain drain, high dropout rates, quality, low public spending, unemployment of educated. Health: preventive and curative; NHM; Ayushman Bharat. Role of human capital in growth.
Deep dive: Concept and sources

Human capital improves labour productivity. Sources: education (increases efficiency and knowledge), health (improves ability to work: preventive medicine, curative medicine, social medicine, provision of clean drinking water and sanitation), on-the-job training (formal, informal), migration (for jobs with higher wages), information about labour market and education. Example: the difference between a skilled worker and an unskilled worker.
Deep dive: Education in India

Education expenditure by government and households; literacy rate 2011: 74 percent (male 82, female 65). Schemes: SSA, RTE, NPEGEL, Beti Bachao Beti Padhao, National Skill Development Mission. NEP 2020 recommends 5+3+3+4 structure and multi-disciplinary higher education; target gross enrolment ratio of 50 percent by 2035. Higher education: UGC, AICTE, central and state universities. Economic benefits: higher earnings, productivity, innovation. Problems: dropouts, gender gap, low quality, brain drain, spending below 6 percent of GDP.
Deep dive: Health and appraisal

Health indicators: life expectancy, IMR, MMR, nutrition. National Health Mission; Ayushman Bharat; immunisation. Public health spending about 2 percent of GDP. Private health care expansion. Appraisal: human capital formation enhances growth, but inequality in access, regional disparities and low public spending remain. Comparison with Kerala. Brain drain/brain gain. Role of NGOs and private sector.
Hindi saransh
Manav puunji nirman: shiksha, swasthya, prashikshan, pravasan. RTE 2009. Shiksha par saarvajanik vyay GDP ka 6% lakshya.
Human capital formation raises productivity through investment in education, health and training.

Visual lesson

Human Capital Formation in India

Human capital is the stock of skills, knowledge, health and productive capacity embodied in people

🔑

Big idea

  • Human capital is the stock of skills, knowledge, health and productive capacity embodied in people
  • Physical capital versus human capital
  • Human capital formation sources: expenditure on education, expenditure on health, on-the-job training, migration, information
  • Human capital and human development: human capital treats human beings as a means, human development treats them as ends
Read the full explanation

Human capital is the stock of skills, knowledge, health and productive capacity embodied in people. Physical capital versus human capital. Human capital formation sources: expenditure on education, expenditure on health, on-the-job training, migration, information. Human capital and human development: human capital treats human beings as a means, human development treats them as ends. Education: literacy, enrolment, adult literacy; Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan, RTE Act 2009 (6-14 years), mid-day meal, National Education Policy 2020, higher education, vocational education. Education expenditure about 4.6 percent of GDP (target 6 percent). Problems: low female literacy, rural-urban gaps, brain drain, high dropout rates, quality, low public spending, unemployment of educated. Health: preventive and curative; NHM; Ayushman Bharat. Role of human capital in growth.

📘

Concept and sources

  • Human capital improves labour productivity
  • Sources: education (increases efficiency and knowledge), health (improves ability to work: preventive medicine, curative medicine, social medicine…
  • Example: the difference between a skilled worker and an unskilled worker
Read the full explanation

Human capital improves labour productivity. Sources: education (increases efficiency and knowledge), health (improves ability to work: preventive medicine, curative medicine, social medicine, provision of clean drinking water and sanitation), on-the-job training (formal, informal), migration (for jobs with higher wages), information about labour market and education. Example: the difference between a skilled worker and an unskilled worker.

🧠

Education in India

  • Education expenditure by government and households
  • Literacy rate 2011: 74 percent (male 82, female 65)
  • Schemes: SSA, RTE, NPEGEL, Beti Bachao Beti Padhao, National Skill Development Mission
  • NEP 2020 recommends 5+3+3+4 structure and multi-disciplinary higher education
Read the full explanation

Education expenditure by government and households; literacy rate 2011: 74 percent (male 82, female 65). Schemes: SSA, RTE, NPEGEL, Beti Bachao Beti Padhao, National Skill Development Mission. NEP 2020 recommends 5+3+3+4 structure and multi-disciplinary higher education; target gross enrolment ratio of 50 percent by 2035. Higher education: UGC, AICTE, central and state universities. Economic benefits: higher earnings, productivity, innovation. Problems: dropouts, gender gap, low quality, brain drain, spending below 6 percent of GDP.

🌟

Health and appraisal

  • Health indicators: life expectancy, IMR, MMR, nutrition
  • National Health Mission
  • Ayushman Bharat
  • Public health spending about 2 percent of GDP
Read the full explanation

Health indicators: life expectancy, IMR, MMR, nutrition. National Health Mission; Ayushman Bharat; immunisation. Public health spending about 2 percent of GDP. Private health care expansion. Appraisal: human capital formation enhances growth, but inequality in access, regional disparities and low public spending remain. Comparison with Kerala. Brain drain/brain gain. Role of NGOs and private sector.

lessons.title: Rural Development
yt: class 11 economics rural development credit marketing diversification organic farming

blocks.x: Rural development is the action plan for the economic regeneration of villages. Key issues: credit, marketing, diversification of activities, productive employment, sustainable development. Rural credit: sources non-institutional (moneylenders, traders) and institutional (cooperatives, commercial banks, RRBs, NABARD, self-help groups, microfinance); NABARD set up in 1982; Kisan Credit Card. Agricultural marketing: regulated markets, cooperative marketing, e-NAM, minimum support price, warehouses, grading, standardisation; problems: middlemen, lack of storage. Diversification: crop and non-farm productive activities: animal husbandry (Operation Flood, White Revolution, Verghese Kurien, Amul), fisheries (Blue Revolution), horticulture (Golden Revolution), non-farm employment (agro-processing, handicrafts, tourism). Organic farming: no chemical inputs; benefits: health, soil fertility, export; problems: lower yields initially. Sustainable development of rural areas.
Deep dive: Rural credit

Rural indebtedness and need for credit for seeds, fertilisers, social functions. Non-institutional: moneylenders charging high interest, landlords. Institutional: Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS), commercial banks (nationalised in 1969), Regional Rural Banks (1975), NABARD (apex), SHGs (microcredit with 10-20 members), Kisan Credit Card. Problems: inadequate coverage, collateral requirement, farm loan waiver issues, regional disparity.
Deep dive: Marketing and diversification

Agricultural marketing: gathering, storage, grading, transport and sale. Government measures: regulated market (APMC), infrastructure (roads, storage), cooperative marketing societies, MSP, buffer stock, PDS, e-NAM. Alternative marketing channels: apni mandi (Punjab), hadaspar mandi (Pune), rythu bazars (Andhra), uzhavar sandies (Tamil Nadu). Diversification: change in cropping pattern; allied activities: animal husbandry (milk, meat, eggs), fisheries, horticulture; Operation Flood.
Deep dive: Organic farming and sustainability

Organic farming uses organic manures, biopesticides, crop rotation; benefits: higher price in export markets, healthy food, less pollution, employment; problems: lower yields, certification, awareness, small producer. Sustainable development: better infrastructure, education, health, women empowerment, rural industries, agro-based industries, tourism and IT. Role of cooperatives, SHGs, Sikkim as an organic state.
Hindi saransh
Gramin vikas: rin, vipanan, vividhikaran, jaivik kheti. NABARD 1982. Operation Flood se shwet kranti.
NABARD is the apex institution for rural credit in India, established in 1982.

Big idea

  • Rural development is the action plan for the economic regeneration of villages
  • Key issues: credit, marketing, diversification of activities, productive employment, sustainable development
  • Rural credit: sources non-institutional (moneylenders, traders) and institutional (cooperatives, commercial banks, RRBs, NABARD, self-help groups…

Read the full explanation

Rural development is the action plan for the economic regeneration of villages. Key issues: credit, marketing, diversification of activities, productive employment, sustainable development. Rural credit: sources non-institutional (moneylenders, traders) and institutional (cooperatives, commercial banks, RRBs, NABARD, self-help groups, microfinance); NABARD set up in 1982; Kisan Credit Card. Agricultural marketing: regulated markets, cooperative marketing, e-NAM, minimum support price, warehouses, grading, standardisation; problems: middlemen, lack of storage. Diversification: crop and non-farm productive activities: animal husbandry (Operation Flood, White Revolution, Verghese Kurien, Amul), fisheries (Blue Revolution), horticulture (Golden Revolution), non-farm employment (agro-processing, handicrafts, tourism). Organic farming: no chemical inputs; benefits: health, soil fertility, export; problems: lower yields initially. Sustainable development of rural areas.

📌

Rural credit

  • Rural indebtedness and need for credit for seeds, fertilisers, social functions
  • Non-institutional: moneylenders charging high interest, landlords
  • Institutional: Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS), commercial banks (nationalised in 1969), Regional Rural Banks (1975), NABARD (apex)…
  • Problems: inadequate coverage, collateral requirement, farm loan waiver issues, regional disparity
Read the full explanation

Rural indebtedness and need for credit for seeds, fertilisers, social functions. Non-institutional: moneylenders charging high interest, landlords. Institutional: Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS), commercial banks (nationalised in 1969), Regional Rural Banks (1975), NABARD (apex), SHGs (microcredit with 10-20 members), Kisan Credit Card. Problems: inadequate coverage, collateral requirement, farm loan waiver issues, regional disparity.

🧠

Marketing and diversification

  • Agricultural marketing: gathering, storage, grading, transport and sale
  • Government measures: regulated market (APMC), infrastructure (roads, storage), cooperative marketing societies, MSP, buffer stock, PDS, e-NAM
  • Alternative marketing channels: apni mandi (Punjab), hadaspar mandi (Pune), rythu bazars (Andhra), uzhavar sandies (Tamil Nadu)
  • Diversification: change in cropping pattern
Read the full explanation

Agricultural marketing: gathering, storage, grading, transport and sale. Government measures: regulated market (APMC), infrastructure (roads, storage), cooperative marketing societies, MSP, buffer stock, PDS, e-NAM. Alternative marketing channels: apni mandi (Punjab), hadaspar mandi (Pune), rythu bazars (Andhra), uzhavar sandies (Tamil Nadu). Diversification: change in cropping pattern; allied activities: animal husbandry (milk, meat, eggs), fisheries, horticulture; Operation Flood.

🧬

Organic farming and sustainability

  • Organic farming uses organic manures, biopesticides, crop rotation
  • Benefits: higher price in export markets, healthy food, less pollution, employment
  • Problems: lower yields, certification, awareness, small producer
  • Sustainable development: better infrastructure, education, health, women empowerment, rural industries, agro-based industries, tourism and IT
Read the full explanation

Organic farming uses organic manures, biopesticides, crop rotation; benefits: higher price in export markets, healthy food, less pollution, employment; problems: lower yields, certification, awareness, small producer. Sustainable development: better infrastructure, education, health, women empowerment, rural industries, agro-based industries, tourism and IT. Role of cooperatives, SHGs, Sikkim as an organic state.

lessons.title: Employment: Growth, Informalisation and Other Issues
yt: class 11 economics employment growth informalisation unemployment

blocks.x: Worker: a person who works to earn. Workforce participation rate (WPR) = (workers / population) x 100. Types of workers: self-employed, hired (regular salaried and casual wage labour). Employment in India: primary 45 percent, secondary 25, tertiary 30 (2018). Formal and informal sector: formal workers get social security; informal (unorganised) about 90 percent of workforce. Growth and employment: jobless growth; casualisation; informalisation. Unemployment: open, disguised (agriculture), seasonal, underemployment; educated unemployment; structural; cyclical. Government initiatives: MGNREGA, PMEGP, SGSY, NRLM, Skill India, Make in India, Start-up India. Employment generation. Rural, urban and female participation. Sector changes: agriculture workforce shifting to services.
Deep dive: Basic concepts

Gainful employment, WPR for males and females in rural and urban areas (urban lower). Self-employed form about 52 percent of workforce; regular salaried about 24 percent; casual labour 24 percent. Rural women WPR is higher because of poverty. Employment by status and sector. Employment by region: Himachal and Kerala differ. Informal sector workers are not protected by laws.
Deep dive: Growth, informalisation and unemployment

Jobless growth: GDP grows without matching jobs; informalisation: shift to informal work with poor conditions; casualisation. Unemployment types: disguised (more workers than needed), seasonal (agriculture off-season), open, educated, structural. Underemployment. Causes: population growth, low growth in manufacturing, rural-urban migration, mismatched skills. Consequences: poverty, wasted human resources, social unrest.
Deep dive: Government and issues

Government as an employer: public sector employs about 6 percent. Schemes: MGNREGA, PMEGP, SGSY. Policies for the informal sector: social security (e-Shram, PM-SYM). Issues: child labour, wage inequality, gender gap, insecure jobs, lack of skills. Remedies: labour-intensive industries, small and medium enterprises, skill development, education, rural infrastructure, agro-based industries.

Read the full explanation

Worker: a person who works to earn. Workforce participation rate (WPR) = (workers / population) x 100. Types of workers: self-employed, hired (regular salaried and casual wage labour). Employment in India: primary 45 percent, secondary 25, tertiary 30 (2018). Formal and informal sector: formal workers get social security; informal (unorganised) about 90 percent of workforce. Growth and employment: jobless growth; casualisation; informalisation. Unemployment: open, disguised (agriculture), seasonal, underemployment; educated unemployment; structural; cyclical. Government initiatives: MGNREGA, PMEGP, SGSY, NRLM, Skill India, Make in India, Start-up India. Employment generation. Rural, urban and female participation. Sector changes: agriculture workforce shifting to services.

📘

Basic concepts

  • Gainful employment, WPR for males and females in rural and urban areas (urban lower)
  • Self-employed form about 52 percent of workforce
  • Regular salaried about 24 percent
  • Casual labour 24 percent
Read the full explanation

Gainful employment, WPR for males and females in rural and urban areas (urban lower). Self-employed form about 52 percent of workforce; regular salaried about 24 percent; casual labour 24 percent. Rural women WPR is higher because of poverty. Employment by status and sector. Employment by region: Himachal and Kerala differ. Informal sector workers are not protected by laws.

🧠

Growth, informalisation and unemployment

  • Jobless growth: GDP grows without matching jobs
  • Informalisation: shift to informal work with poor conditions
  • Casualisation
  • Unemployment types: disguised (more workers than needed), seasonal (agriculture off-season), open, educated, structural
Read the full explanation

Jobless growth: GDP grows without matching jobs; informalisation: shift to informal work with poor conditions; casualisation. Unemployment types: disguised (more workers than needed), seasonal (agriculture off-season), open, educated, structural. Underemployment. Causes: population growth, low growth in manufacturing, rural-urban migration, mismatched skills. Consequences: poverty, wasted human resources, social unrest.

🏛️

Government and issues

  • Government as an employer: public sector employs about 6 percent
  • Schemes: MGNREGA, PMEGP, SGSY
  • Policies for the informal sector: social security (e-Shram, PM-SYM)
  • Issues: child labour, wage inequality, gender gap, insecure jobs, lack of skills
Read the full explanation

Government as an employer: public sector employs about 6 percent. Schemes: MGNREGA, PMEGP, SGSY. Policies for the informal sector: social security (e-Shram, PM-SYM). Issues: child labour, wage inequality, gender gap, insecure jobs, lack of skills. Remedies: labour-intensive industries, small and medium enterprises, skill development, education, rural infrastructure, agro-based industries.

lessons.title: Infrastructure
yt: class 11 economics infrastructure energy health transport

blocks.x: Infrastructure: facilities supporting economic activity and social life. Economic infrastructure: energy, transport, communication, banking. Social infrastructure: education, health, housing. Importance: raises productivity, contributes to growth, improves quality of life, attracts investment. Energy: commercial (coal, petroleum, electricity) and non-commercial (firewood, dung, agricultural waste); conventional (thermal, hydel, nuclear) and non-conventional (solar, wind, tidal, biogas); installed capacity; transmission and distribution losses; Rural energy: firewood dependence, LPG. Health: preventive and curative; hospitals (public and private); life expectancy; infant mortality; India's health expenditure low; traditional systems (AYUSH); problems. Challenges: low public spending, rural-urban gaps, power shortage, inefficiency. Public-private partnership (PPP). Infrastructure in Delhi, Kerala.
Deep dive: Energy

Commercial energy: coal (about 55 percent of commercial use), oil, gas, hydropower, nuclear. Electricity generation: thermal (about 60 percent), hydel, nuclear (about 2 percent), renewable. Per capita consumption low. T&D losses 20-25 percent. Non-conventional energy: solar (National Solar Mission), wind (Tamil Nadu, Gujarat), biogas. Problems: shortage of power, financial losses of SEBs, delay, pollution, price subsidies. Reforms: Electricity Act 2003, private participation, Ujjwala for LPG.
Deep dive: Transport and communication

Roads: National Highways (2 percent of roads but carry large traffic), PMGSY, railways (largest network), airports, ports. Communication: telecom, internet, post. Digital India. Infrastructure bottlenecks. Quality of life: housing, drinking water, sanitation (Swachh Bharat). Role of infrastructure in attracting FDI and enhancing exports.
Deep dive: Health infrastructure

Health indicators: life expectancy 69 years, IMR about 30, MMR. Health care: primary health centres, community centres, district hospitals, medical colleges. Public spending about 1.3 to 2 percent of GDP. Private sector dominates (about 70 percent of out-patient). Problems: shortage of doctors and beds, rural-urban gap, high out-of-pocket expenditure, malnutrition, communicable diseases. Initiatives: NHM, Ayushman Bharat, AYUSH (Ayurveda, Yoga, Unani, Siddha, Homeopathy), telemedicine.
Hindi saransh
Aadharbhoot sanrachna: urja, parivahan, swasthya. Gair-paramparik urja: saur, pavan. Vidyut vitran haani.
Energy, transport and communication are economic infrastructure; education and health are social infrastructure.

Big idea

  • Infrastructure: facilities supporting economic activity and social life
  • Economic infrastructure: energy, transport, communication, banking
  • Social infrastructure: education, health, housing
  • Importance: raises productivity, contributes to growth, improves quality of life, attracts investment
Read the full explanation

Infrastructure: facilities supporting economic activity and social life. Economic infrastructure: energy, transport, communication, banking. Social infrastructure: education, health, housing. Importance: raises productivity, contributes to growth, improves quality of life, attracts investment. Energy: commercial (coal, petroleum, electricity) and non-commercial (firewood, dung, agricultural waste); conventional (thermal, hydel, nuclear) and non-conventional (solar, wind, tidal, biogas); installed capacity; transmission and distribution losses; Rural energy: firewood dependence, LPG. Health: preventive and curative; hospitals (public and private); life expectancy; infant mortality; India's health expenditure low; traditional systems (AYUSH); problems. Challenges: low public spending, rural-urban gaps, power shortage, inefficiency. Public-private partnership (PPP). Infrastructure in Delhi, Kerala.

🚀

Energy

  • Commercial energy: coal (about 55 percent of commercial use), oil, gas, hydropower, nuclear
  • Electricity generation: thermal (about 60 percent), hydel, nuclear (about 2 percent), renewable
  • Per capita consumption low
  • T&D losses 20-25 percent
Read the full explanation

Commercial energy: coal (about 55 percent of commercial use), oil, gas, hydropower, nuclear. Electricity generation: thermal (about 60 percent), hydel, nuclear (about 2 percent), renewable. Per capita consumption low. T&D losses 20-25 percent. Non-conventional energy: solar (National Solar Mission), wind (Tamil Nadu, Gujarat), biogas. Problems: shortage of power, financial losses of SEBs, delay, pollution, price subsidies. Reforms: Electricity Act 2003, private participation, Ujjwala for LPG.

🧠

Transport and communication

  • Roads: National Highways (2 percent of roads but carry large traffic), PMGSY, railways (largest network), airports, ports
  • Communication: telecom, internet, post
  • Digital India
  • Infrastructure bottlenecks
Read the full explanation

Roads: National Highways (2 percent of roads but carry large traffic), PMGSY, railways (largest network), airports, ports. Communication: telecom, internet, post. Digital India. Infrastructure bottlenecks. Quality of life: housing, drinking water, sanitation (Swachh Bharat). Role of infrastructure in attracting FDI and enhancing exports.

🌟

Health infrastructure

  • Health indicators: life expectancy 69 years, IMR about 30, MMR
  • Health care: primary health centres, community centres, district hospitals, medical colleges
  • Public spending about 1.3 to 2 percent of GDP
  • Private sector dominates (about 70 percent of out-patient)
Read the full explanation

Health indicators: life expectancy 69 years, IMR about 30, MMR. Health care: primary health centres, community centres, district hospitals, medical colleges. Public spending about 1.3 to 2 percent of GDP. Private sector dominates (about 70 percent of out-patient). Problems: shortage of doctors and beds, rural-urban gap, high out-of-pocket expenditure, malnutrition, communicable diseases. Initiatives: NHM, Ayushman Bharat, AYUSH (Ayurveda, Yoga, Unani, Siddha, Homeopathy), telemedicine.
