lessons.title: Environment and Sustainable Development
yt: class 11 economics environment and sustainable development

blocks.x: Environment is the total planetary inheritance and the totality of resources. Functions: supplies resources, assimilates waste, sustains life, provides aesthetic services. Carrying capacity and absorptive capacity. Environmental issues: global warming, ozone depletion, biodiversity loss, land degradation, air and water pollution, waste. Causes in India: poverty, population, industrialisation, urbanisation, deforestation. Sustainable development (Brundtland Commission 1987): meeting present needs without compromising future generations. Strategies: use of non-conventional energy (solar, wind, hydro), LPG and gobar gas in rural areas, CNG in urban transport, mass transit, wind power, small hydro, traditional knowledge and practices, biocomposting, biopest control, organic farming. Sustainable development goals (17 SDGs, 2015). Ecological economics. Polluter pays, CPCB, Environment Protection Act 1986.
Deep dive: Environment and economy

Environment performs four vital functions: supplies resources (renewable and non-renewable), assimilates waste, sustains life by genetic and biodiversity, provides aesthetic services. Absorptive capacity: ability to absorb degradation. Carrying capacity: resource extraction should not exceed regeneration. Environmental crisis: when waste exceeds absorptive capacity and resource extraction exceeds regeneration. Opportunity cost of negative environmental impact.
Deep dive: Issues in India

Land degradation, biodiversity loss, global warming and climate change (greenhouse gases), ozone depletion (CFCs, Montreal Protocol), air pollution (Delhi, vehicles), water pollution (Ganga), urban waste, loss of forest cover; India's forest cover about 24 percent. Population pressure and poverty degrade land. Industrialisation and agriculture (intensive use of chemicals). Economic cost: health costs, loss of productivity. Environmental laws and institutions: Central Pollution Control Board (1974), Air Act 1981, Water Act 1974.
Deep dive: Sustainable development

Brundtland: meeting needs of the present without compromising the future. Herman Daly: harvesting rates no greater than regeneration, waste emission within assimilative capacity. Strategies: renewable energy, LPG and gobar gas in rural areas, CNG in cities, mass transport, wind power, solar photovoltaic, small hydro plants, traditional knowledge (Ayurveda, Yoga), biocomposting, biopest control, organic farming, waste recycling. Costs: change of mindset. SDGs: 17 goals including clean energy and climate action. Status: Rio Earth Summit, Paris Agreement.
Hindi saransh
Paryavaran aur satat vikas: Brundtland aayog. Dharaneeya vikas ke upay: saur urja, CNG, jaivik khad. 17 SDG.
Sustainable development means meeting present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs.

Read the full explanation

Environment is the total planetary inheritance and the totality of resources. Functions: supplies resources, assimilates waste, sustains life, provides aesthetic services. Carrying capacity and absorptive capacity. Environmental issues: global warming, ozone depletion, biodiversity loss, land degradation, air and water pollution, waste. Causes in India: poverty, population, industrialisation, urbanisation, deforestation. Sustainable development (Brundtland Commission 1987): meeting present needs without compromising future generations. Strategies: use of non-conventional energy (solar, wind, hydro), LPG and gobar gas in rural areas, CNG in urban transport, mass transit, wind power, small hydro, traditional knowledge and practices, biocomposting, biopest control, organic farming. Sustainable development goals (17 SDGs, 2015). Ecological economics. Polluter pays, CPCB, Environment Protection Act 1986.

🏛️

Environment and economy

  • Environment performs four vital functions: supplies resources (renewable and non-renewable), assimilates waste, sustains life by genetic and…
  • Absorptive capacity: ability to absorb degradation
  • Carrying capacity: resource extraction should not exceed regeneration
  • Environmental crisis: when waste exceeds absorptive capacity and resource extraction exceeds regeneration
Read the full explanation

Environment performs four vital functions: supplies resources (renewable and non-renewable), assimilates waste, sustains life by genetic and biodiversity, provides aesthetic services. Absorptive capacity: ability to absorb degradation. Carrying capacity: resource extraction should not exceed regeneration. Environmental crisis: when waste exceeds absorptive capacity and resource extraction exceeds regeneration. Opportunity cost of negative environmental impact.

🧠

Issues in India

  • Land degradation, biodiversity loss, global warming and climate change (greenhouse gases), ozone depletion (CFCs, Montreal Protocol), air pollution…
  • India's forest cover about 24 percent
  • Population pressure and poverty degrade land
  • Industrialisation and agriculture (intensive use of chemicals)
Read the full explanation

Land degradation, biodiversity loss, global warming and climate change (greenhouse gases), ozone depletion (CFCs, Montreal Protocol), air pollution (Delhi, vehicles), water pollution (Ganga), urban waste, loss of forest cover; India's forest cover about 24 percent. Population pressure and poverty degrade land. Industrialisation and agriculture (intensive use of chemicals). Economic cost: health costs, loss of productivity. Environmental laws and institutions: Central Pollution Control Board (1974), Air Act 1981, Water Act 1974.

🌟

Sustainable development

  • Brundtland: meeting needs of the present without compromising the future
  • Herman Daly: harvesting rates no greater than regeneration, waste emission within assimilative capacity
  • Strategies: renewable energy, LPG and gobar gas in rural areas, CNG in cities, mass transport, wind power, solar photovoltaic, small hydro plants…
  • Costs: change of mindset
Read the full explanation

Brundtland: meeting needs of the present without compromising the future. Herman Daly: harvesting rates no greater than regeneration, waste emission within assimilative capacity. Strategies: renewable energy, LPG and gobar gas in rural areas, CNG in cities, mass transport, wind power, solar photovoltaic, small hydro plants, traditional knowledge (Ayurveda, Yoga), biocomposting, biopest control, organic farming, waste recycling. Costs: change of mindset. SDGs: 17 goals including clean energy and climate action. Status: Rio Earth Summit, Paris Agreement.

🎯 Remember Sustainable development means meeting present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs.

lessons.title: Comparative Development Experiences of India and Its Neighbours
yt: class 11 economics comparative development India China Pakistan

blocks.x: India, China and Pakistan: common starting points in the late 1940s. China: 1949 revolution, Great Leap Forward (1958, industrialisation, communes), Cultural Revolution (1966-76), reforms of 1978 (Household Responsibility System, Township and Village Enterprises, Special Economic Zones, dual pricing). Pakistan: 1947; import substitution; Green Revolution in 1960s; reforms in the 1980s; economic problems; low investment in social sectors. Demographic indicators: population (China 1.4 billion, India 1.4 billion, Pakistan 0.2 billion); sex ratio; fertility; one-child policy (1979 to 2015). GDP growth: China about 9-10 percent (1978 on); India 6-7 percent; Pakistan 4-5 percent. Sectoral shares. Human development indicators: HDI rank, life expectancy, literacy, access to water and sanitation. Poverty. Lessons: India's democratic planning; China's manufacturing export-led growth; Pakistan's lack of diversification and dependence on remittances.
Deep dive: China and Pakistan's development strategies

China: land reforms, commune system, Great Leap Forward (rapid industrialisation), Proletarian Cultural Revolution (students to rural), 1978 reforms in stages: phase 1 agriculture (communes dismantled, household responsibility), phase 2 industry (TVEs, foreign investment, SEZs, dual pricing), open door policy. Pakistan: mixed economy, import substitution, Green Revolution, nationalisation 1970s, deregulation in 1988, remittances, borrowing; politically unstable; low savings.
Deep dive: Comparative indicators

Population: China 1.4 billion, growth rate 0.5 percent; India 1.4 billion, 1.0; Pakistan 0.2 billion, 2.0. Sex ratio: India 943 females per 1000 males (2011), China about 940, Pakistan about 940. Fertility rate: China 1.6, India 2.4, Pakistan 3.6. Urbanisation: China 60 percent. GDP growth in 1980s: China 10 percent; India 5.7 (1980-90). Sector shares: China manufacturing and services; India services share high; Pakistan agriculture. HDI 2018: China 85th, India 129th, Pakistan 150th (approx). Life expectancy: China 76, India 69, Pakistan 67.
Deep dive: Appraisal

Neighbours share colonial history. Lessons: India's growth is service-led; China's manufacturing-led with large investment in education and health; Pakistan had slower diversification. Democracy versus authoritarianism; role of the state; agriculture-to-industry shift; gender gaps; poverty. Common issues: unemployment, regional disparity and environmental costs. SAARC and regional cooperation.
Hindi saransh
Bharat, China aur Pakistan ka tulnatmak vikas. China ke 1978 ke sudhar, Pakistan mein vividhikaran ki kami.

Comparative Development Experiences of India and Its Neighbours

India, China and Pakistan: common starting points in the late 1940s

Big idea

  • India, China and Pakistan: common starting points in the late 1940s
  • China: 1949 revolution, Great Leap Forward (1958, industrialisation, communes), Cultural Revolution (1966-76), reforms of 1978 (Household…
  • Pakistan: 1947

Read the full explanation

India, China and Pakistan: common starting points in the late 1940s. China: 1949 revolution, Great Leap Forward (1958, industrialisation, communes), Cultural Revolution (1966-76), reforms of 1978 (Household Responsibility System, Township and Village Enterprises, Special Economic Zones, dual pricing). Pakistan: 1947; import substitution; Green Revolution in 1960s; reforms in the 1980s; economic problems; low investment in social sectors. Demographic indicators: population (China 1.4 billion, India 1.4 billion, Pakistan 0.2 billion); sex ratio; fertility; one-child policy (1979 to 2015). GDP growth: China about 9-10 percent (1978 on); India 6-7 percent; Pakistan 4-5 percent. Sectoral shares. Human development indicators: HDI rank, life expectancy, literacy, access to water and sanitation. Poverty. Lessons: India's democratic planning; China's manufacturing export-led growth; Pakistan's lack of diversification and dependence on remittances.

📌

China and Pakistan's development strategies

  • China: land reforms, commune system, Great Leap Forward (rapid industrialisation), Proletarian Cultural Revolution (students to rural), 1978 reforms…
  • Pakistan: mixed economy, import substitution, Green Revolution, nationalisation 1970s, deregulation in 1988, remittances, borrowing
  • Politically unstable
Read the full explanation

China: land reforms, commune system, Great Leap Forward (rapid industrialisation), Proletarian Cultural Revolution (students to rural), 1978 reforms in stages: phase 1 agriculture (communes dismantled, household responsibility), phase 2 industry (TVEs, foreign investment, SEZs, dual pricing), open door policy. Pakistan: mixed economy, import substitution, Green Revolution, nationalisation 1970s, deregulation in 1988, remittances, borrowing; politically unstable; low savings.

🧠

Comparative indicators

  • Population: China 1.4 billion, growth rate 0.5 percent
  • India 1.4 billion, 1.0
  • Pakistan 0.2 billion, 2.0
  • Sex ratio: India 943 females per 1000 males (2011), China about 940, Pakistan about 940
Read the full explanation

Population: China 1.4 billion, growth rate 0.5 percent; India 1.4 billion, 1.0; Pakistan 0.2 billion, 2.0. Sex ratio: India 943 females per 1000 males (2011), China about 940, Pakistan about 940. Fertility rate: China 1.6, India 2.4, Pakistan 3.6. Urbanisation: China 60 percent. GDP growth in 1980s: China 10 percent; India 5.7 (1980-90). Sector shares: China manufacturing and services; India services share high; Pakistan agriculture. HDI 2018: China 85th, India 129th, Pakistan 150th (approx). Life expectancy: China 76, India 69, Pakistan 67.

🌟

Appraisal

  • Neighbours share colonial history
  • Lessons: India's growth is service-led
  • China's manufacturing-led with large investment in education and health
  • Pakistan had slower diversification
Read the full explanation

Neighbours share colonial history. Lessons: India's growth is service-led; China's manufacturing-led with large investment in education and health; Pakistan had slower diversification. Democracy versus authoritarianism; role of the state; agriculture-to-industry shift; gender gaps; poverty. Common issues: unemployment, regional disparity and environmental costs. SAARC and regional cooperation.

lessons.title: Statistics: Introduction, Collection, Organisation and Presentation of Data
yt: class 11 economics statistics collection organisation presentation of data

blocks.x: Statistics: singular (methods) and plural (data). Functions: simplification, comparison, formulation of hypothesis. Limitations. Data: primary (collected by the investigator) and secondary (published or unpublished). Methods of collecting primary data: personal interview, questionnaire/schedule, telephone, observation; census versus sample survey; sampling: random (simple, stratified, systematic) and non-random (judgement, convenience, quota); errors: sampling and non-sampling. Organisation of data: raw data, array, frequency distribution (discrete, continuous; class interval, class limits, class mark, class width), exclusive and inclusive method, cumulative frequency (less than, more than), tally marks. Presentation: tables (title, number, head note, stub, caption, body, source), diagrams (bar, multiple bar, sub-divided bar, pie chart), graphs (histogram, frequency polygon, ogive, time series line graph, frequency curve). Sources: NSSO, Census, RBI.
Deep dive: Data collection

Census collects data from every unit (population census every 10 years); sample uses a part. Questionnaire: set of questions mailed; schedule filled by an enumerator. Sampling methods: simple random sampling (lottery, random number tables), stratified, systematic, cluster; purposive, convenience. Errors: sampling error (due to using a sample), non-sampling error (faulty design, non-response). Secondary sources: government publications, RBI bulletins, NSSO reports, Economic Survey. Pilot survey.
Deep dive: Organisation

Class interval, e.g., 10-20; class limits 10 and 20; class mark = (upper + lower)/2 = 15; class width = upper - lower = 10; Sturges: number of classes = 1 + 3.322 log N. Exclusive (upper limit excluded) vs inclusive method. Cumulative frequency: less than type adds up from the top; more than type adds from the bottom. Example: marks 0-10, 10-20, 20-30 with frequency 5, 8, 7. Relative frequency. Tally marks in groups of five.
Deep dive: Presentation

Table parts: table number, title, head note, caption (column heading), stub (row heading), body, footnote, source. Bar diagrams: simple, multiple, subdivided, percentage; pie chart: angle = (value/total) x 360. Histogram: bars touching; frequency polygon: joining mid-points; ogive: cumulative frequency curve (less than and more than; intersection gives the median). Time series graph. Merits of diagrams: attractive, easy to understand; demerits: only approximate.

Sankhyiki: aankdon ka sangrahan, vargikaran, prastuti. Varg madhya = (upari + nimn)/2. Pie chart kon = (maan/kul) x 360.

Visual lesson

Statistics: Introduction, Collection, Organisation and Presentation of Data

Statistics: singular (methods) and plural (data)

Classes1 + 3.322 log N
🔑

Big idea

  • Statistics: singular (methods) and plural (data)
  • Functions: simplification, comparison, formulation of hypothesis
  • Data: primary (collected by the investigator) and secondary (published or unpublished)
  • Methods of collecting primary data: personal interview, questionnaire/schedule, telephone, observation
Read the full explanation

Statistics: singular (methods) and plural (data). Functions: simplification, comparison, formulation of hypothesis. Limitations. Data: primary (collected by the investigator) and secondary (published or unpublished). Methods of collecting primary data: personal interview, questionnaire/schedule, telephone, observation; census versus sample survey; sampling: random (simple, stratified, systematic) and non-random (judgement, convenience, quota); errors: sampling and non-sampling. Organisation of data: raw data, array, frequency distribution (discrete, continuous; class interval, class limits, class mark, class width), exclusive and inclusive method, cumulative frequency (less than, more than), tally marks. Presentation: tables (title, number, head note, stub, caption, body, source), diagrams (bar, multiple bar, sub-divided bar, pie chart), graphs (histogram, frequency polygon, ogive, time series line graph, frequency curve). Sources: NSSO, Census, RBI.

📌

Data collection

  • Census collects data from every unit (population census every 10 years)
  • Sample uses a part
  • Questionnaire: set of questions mailed
  • Schedule filled by an enumerator
Read the full explanation

Census collects data from every unit (population census every 10 years); sample uses a part. Questionnaire: set of questions mailed; schedule filled by an enumerator. Sampling methods: simple random sampling (lottery, random number tables), stratified, systematic, cluster; purposive, convenience. Errors: sampling error (due to using a sample), non-sampling error (faulty design, non-response). Secondary sources: government publications, RBI bulletins, NSSO reports, Economic Survey. Pilot survey.

🧬

Organisation

  • Class interval, e.g., 10-20
  • Class limits 10 and 20
  • Class mark = (upper + lower)/2 = 15
  • Class width = upper - lower = 10
Read the full explanation

Class interval, e.g., 10-20; class limits 10 and 20; class mark = (upper + lower)/2 = 15; class width = upper - lower = 10; Sturges: number of classes = 1 + 3.322 log N. Exclusive (upper limit excluded) vs inclusive method. Cumulative frequency: less than type adds up from the top; more than type adds from the bottom. Example: marks 0-10, 10-20, 20-30 with frequency 5, 8, 7. Relative frequency. Tally marks in groups of five.

🌟

Presentation

  • Table parts: table number, title, head note, caption (column heading), stub (row heading), body, footnote, source
  • Bar diagrams: simple, multiple, subdivided, percentage
  • Pie chart: angle = (value/total) x 360
  • Histogram: bars touching
Read the full explanation

Table parts: table number, title, head note, caption (column heading), stub (row heading), body, footnote, source. Bar diagrams: simple, multiple, subdivided, percentage; pie chart: angle = (value/total) x 360. Histogram: bars touching; frequency polygon: joining mid-points; ogive: cumulative frequency curve (less than and more than; intersection gives the median). Time series graph. Merits of diagrams: attractive, easy to understand; demerits: only approximate.

lessons.title: Statistics: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
yt: class 11 economics measures of central tendency mean median mode dispersion standard deviation

blocks.x: Central tendency: arithmetic mean (simple, weighted, grouped: direct, short-cut, step deviation), median (middle value; for continuous series Median = l + ((N/2 - cf)/f) x h), mode (most frequent; Mode = l + ((f1 - f0)/(2f1 - f0 - f2)) x h), empirical relation Mode = 3 Median - 2 Mean. Properties of mean: sum of deviations is zero; affected by extreme values. Quartiles, deciles, percentiles. Dispersion: range, quartile deviation, mean deviation, standard deviation (sigma), variance, coefficient of variation = (sigma/mean) x 100, Lorenz curve. Absolute and relative measures. Example: mean of 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 is 30; standard deviation about 14.14. Grouped example: classes 0-10, 10-20, 20-30, 30-40 with frequencies 5, 8, 12, 5 give mean 20.67, median 21.67 and mode 23.64.
Deep dive: Mean, median and mode

Simple mean = sum x / n. Weighted mean = sum wx / sum w. Grouped mean = sum fx / sum f with class marks. Step deviation: mean = A + (sum fd / sum f) x h. Median: arrange in order; odd n median is the (n+1)/2 th; even is the average of two middle items. Worked grouped example: N = 30; cumulative frequencies 5, 13, 25, 30; N/2 = 15 lies in 20-30; median = 20 + (15 - 13)/12 x 10 = 21.67. Mode: highest frequency class 20-30 with f1 = 12, f0 = 8, f2 = 5; mode = 20 + (12 - 8)/(24 - 8 - 5) x 10 = 23.64. Mean = 620/30 = 20.67. Check: 3 median - 2 mean = 65 - 41.33 = 23.67, near the mode.
Deep dive: Dispersion

Range = L - S; coefficient of range = (L - S)/(L + S). Quartile deviation = (Q3 - Q1)/2; coefficient = (Q3 - Q1)/(Q3 + Q1). Mean deviation = sum |x - mean| / n. Standard deviation: sigma = sqrt( sum (x - mean)^2 / n ). For 10, 20, 30, 40, 50: deviations -20, -10, 0, 10, 20; squares 400, 100, 0, 100, 400 sum 1000; variance 200; sigma = 14.14; coefficient of variation = 14.14/30 x 100 = 47.1 percent. Lower CV means greater consistency. If every value is increased by a constant, mean changes but sigma does not; if multiplied by k, both multiply by k.
Deep dive: Uses and Lorenz curve

Mean for continuous variables, median for skewed data or open-ended classes, mode for the most common size (shoes). Merits and demerits of each. Lorenz curve shows income inequality: the line of equality is the diagonal; the farther the curve, the greater the inequality; Gini coefficient is the area ratio. Quartiles divide data into four equal parts. Comparison of two series with CV.

Visual lesson

Statistics: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion

Central tendency: arithmetic mean (simple, weighted, grouped: direct, short-cut, step deviation), median (middle value

Medianl + ((N/2 - cf)/f) h
SDsqrt(sum (x - mean)^2 / n)

🔑

Big idea

  • Central tendency: arithmetic mean (simple, weighted, grouped: direct, short-cut, step deviation), median (middle value
  • For continuous series Median = l + ((N/2 - cf)/f) x h), mode (most frequent
  • Mode = l + ((f1 - f0)/(2f1 - f0 - f2)) x h), empirical relation Mode = 3 Median - 2 Mean
  • Properties of mean: sum of deviations is zero
Read the full explanation

Central tendency: arithmetic mean (simple, weighted, grouped: direct, short-cut, step deviation), median (middle value; for continuous series Median = l + ((N/2 - cf)/f) x h), mode (most frequent; Mode = l + ((f1 - f0)/(2f1 - f0 - f2)) x h), empirical relation Mode = 3 Median - 2 Mean. Properties of mean: sum of deviations is zero; affected by extreme values. Quartiles, deciles, percentiles. Dispersion: range, quartile deviation, mean deviation, standard deviation (sigma), variance, coefficient of variation = (sigma/mean) x 100, Lorenz curve. Absolute and relative measures. Example: mean of 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 is 30; standard deviation about 14.14. Grouped example: classes 0-10, 10-20, 20-30, 30-40 with frequencies 5, 8, 12, 5 give mean 20.67, median 21.67 and mode 23.64.

📌

Mean, median and mode

  • Simple mean = sum x / n
  • Weighted mean = sum wx / sum w
  • Grouped mean = sum fx / sum f with class marks
  • Step deviation: mean = A + (sum fd / sum f) x h
Read the full explanation

Simple mean = sum x / n. Weighted mean = sum wx / sum w. Grouped mean = sum fx / sum f with class marks. Step deviation: mean = A + (sum fd / sum f) x h. Median: arrange in order; odd n median is the (n+1)/2 th; even is the average of two middle items. Worked grouped example: N = 30; cumulative frequencies 5, 13, 25, 30; N/2 = 15 lies in 20-30; median = 20 + (15 - 13)/12 x 10 = 21.67. Mode: highest frequency class 20-30 with f1 = 12, f0 = 8, f2 = 5; mode = 20 + (12 - 8)/(24 - 8 - 5) x 10 = 23.64. Mean = 620/30 = 20.67. Check: 3 median - 2 mean = 65 - 41.33 = 23.67, near the mode.

🧠

Dispersion

  • Range = L - S
  • Coefficient of range = (L - S)/(L + S)
  • Quartile deviation = (Q3 - Q1)/2
  • Coefficient = (Q3 - Q1)/(Q3 + Q1)
Read the full explanation

Range = L - S; coefficient of range = (L - S)/(L + S). Quartile deviation = (Q3 - Q1)/2; coefficient = (Q3 - Q1)/(Q3 + Q1). Mean deviation = sum |x - mean| / n. Standard deviation: sigma = sqrt( sum (x - mean)^2 / n ). For 10, 20, 30, 40, 50: deviations -20, -10, 0, 10, 20; squares 400, 100, 0, 100, 400 sum 1000; variance 200; sigma = 14.14; coefficient of variation = 14.14/30 x 100 = 47.1 percent. Lower CV means greater consistency. If every value is increased by a constant, mean changes but sigma does not; if multiplied by k, both multiply by k.

💡

Uses and Lorenz curve

  • Mean for continuous variables, median for skewed data or open-ended classes, mode for the most common size (shoes)
  • Merits and demerits of each
  • Lorenz curve shows income inequality: the line of equality is the diagonal
  • The farther the curve, the greater the inequality
Read the full explanation

Mean for continuous variables, median for skewed data or open-ended classes, mode for the most common size (shoes). Merits and demerits of each. Lorenz curve shows income inequality: the line of equality is the diagonal; the farther the curve, the greater the inequality; Gini coefficient is the area ratio. Quartiles divide data into four equal parts. Comparison of two series with CV.

lessons.title: Statistics: Correlation, Index Numbers and Use of Statistical Tools
yt: class 11 economics correlation index numbers laspeyres paasche CPI WPI

blocks.x: Correlation measures the degree and direction of the linear relationship between two variables. Types: positive, negative, no correlation, linear and non-linear. Scatter diagram. Karl Pearson coefficient r = (n sum xy - sum x sum y) / sqrt((n sum x^2 - (sum x)^2)(n sum y^2 - (sum y)^2)), range -1 to +1. Spearman rank correlation rs = 1 - 6 sum d^2 / (n (n^2 - 1)). Interpretation: r close to 1 is high positive; correlation does not imply causation. Example: x = 1 to 5 and y = 2, 4, 5, 4, 5 give r = 0.7746; ranks 1,2,3,4,5 and 2,1,4,3,5 give rs = 0.8. Index numbers: relative change in a variable over time; base year = 100. Price index: Laspeyres (base year quantities) = sum p1q0 / sum p0q0 x 100; Paasche (current quantities) = sum p1q1 / sum p0q1 x 100; Fisher = sqrt(L x P). Example: p0 = 10, 20; q0 = 5, 3; p1 = 12, 25; q1 = 6, 4 gives Laspeyres 122.73, Paasche 122.86, Fisher 122.79. Types: CPI, WPI, IIP, Sensex. Use of statistical tools, project work in economics.
Deep dive: Correlation

Scatter diagram: points rising show positive; falling show negative. Karl Pearson: example x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; y = 2, 4, 5, 4, 5; sum x = 15; sum y = 20; sum xy = 66; sum x^2 = 55; sum y^2 = 86; numerator = 5 x 66 - 15 x 20 = 30; denominator = sqrt((275 - 225)(430 - 400)) = sqrt(50 x 30) = 38.73; r = 0.7746. Properties: unit-free, between -1 and +1, unaffected by change of origin and scale. Spearman: d = -1, 1, -1, 1, 0; sum d^2 = 4; rs = 1 - 24/120 = 0.8. Correlation is not causation (spurious).
Deep dive: Index numbers

Index number measures changes in prices, quantities or values; weighted and unweighted. Construction: choose the base, items and prices. Simple aggregate: sum p1 / sum p0 x 100. Laspeyres uses base-year weights: sum p1q0 = 12 x 5 + 25 x 3 = 135; sum p0q0 = 50 + 60 = 110; index = 122.73. Paasche uses current-year weights: sum p1q1 = 72 + 100 = 172; sum p0q1 = 60 + 80 = 140; index = 122.86. Fisher is the geometric mean = 122.79. Consumer Price Index (CPI): cost of living; WPI: wholesale prices (in India with base 2011-12); IIP: industrial output; Sensex: 30 stocks of BSE. Inflation = (CPI_t - CPI_{t-1}) / CPI_{t-1} x 100.
Deep dive: Uses and cautions

Uses: measure inflation, adjust wages (DA), deflate GDP, policy making. Limitations: sampling errors, base year choice, changing consumption patterns. Real wages = money wages / CPI x 100. Statistical tools in project: collect data, present with tables and diagrams, compute averages, interpret and conclude. Ethics of using statistics: avoid misleading graphs.

Visual lesson

Statistics: Correlation, Index Numbers and Use of Statistical Tools

Correlation measures the degree and direction of the linear relationship between two variables

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Correlation›3Index numbers›4Uses and cautions
Spearman1 - 6 sum d^2 / n(n^2 - 1)
Laspeyressum p1q0 / sum p0q0 x 100
Paaschesum p1q1 / sum p0q1 x 100
Real wageMoney wage / CPI x 100
🔑

Big idea

  • Correlation measures the degree and direction of the linear relationship between two variables
  • Types: positive, negative, no correlation, linear and non-linear
  • Scatter diagram
  • Karl Pearson coefficient r = (n sum xy - sum x sum y) / sqrt((n sum x2 - (sum x)2)(n sum y2 - (sum y)2)), range -1 to +1
Read the full explanation

Correlation measures the degree and direction of the linear relationship between two variables. Types: positive, negative, no correlation, linear and non-linear. Scatter diagram. Karl Pearson coefficient r = (n sum xy - sum x sum y) / sqrt((n sum x^2 - (sum x)^2)(n sum y^2 - (sum y)^2)), range -1 to +1. Spearman rank correlation rs = 1 - 6 sum d^2 / (n (n^2 - 1)). Interpretation: r close to 1 is high positive; correlation does not imply causation. Example: x = 1 to 5 and y = 2, 4, 5, 4, 5 give r = 0.7746; ranks 1,2,3,4,5 and 2,1,4,3,5 give rs = 0.8. Index numbers: relative change in a variable over time; base year = 100. Price index: Laspeyres (base year quantities) = sum p1q0 / sum p0q0 x 100; Paasche (current quantities) = sum p1q1 / sum p0q1 x 100; Fisher = sqrt(L x P). Example: p0 = 10, 20; q0 = 5, 3; p1 = 12, 25; q1 = 6, 4 gives Laspeyres 122.73, Paasche 122.86, Fisher 122.79. Types: CPI, WPI, IIP, Sensex. Use of statistical tools, project work in economics.

📌

Correlation

  • Scatter diagram: points rising show positive
  • Falling show negative
  • Karl Pearson: example x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
  • Y = 2, 4, 5, 4, 5
Read the full explanation

Scatter diagram: points rising show positive; falling show negative. Karl Pearson: example x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; y = 2, 4, 5, 4, 5; sum x = 15; sum y = 20; sum xy = 66; sum x^2 = 55; sum y^2 = 86; numerator = 5 x 66 - 15 x 20 = 30; denominator = sqrt((275 - 225)(430 - 400)) = sqrt(50 x 30) = 38.73; r = 0.7746. Properties: unit-free, between -1 and +1, unaffected by change of origin and scale. Spearman: d = -1, 1, -1, 1, 0; sum d^2 = 4; rs = 1 - 24/120 = 0.8. Correlation is not causation (spurious).

🧠

Index numbers

  • Index number measures changes in prices, quantities or values
  • Weighted and unweighted
  • Construction: choose the base, items and prices
  • Simple aggregate: sum p1 / sum p0 x 100
Read the full explanation

Index number measures changes in prices, quantities or values; weighted and unweighted. Construction: choose the base, items and prices. Simple aggregate: sum p1 / sum p0 x 100. Laspeyres uses base-year weights: sum p1q0 = 12 x 5 + 25 x 3 = 135; sum p0q0 = 50 + 60 = 110; index = 122.73. Paasche uses current-year weights: sum p1q1 = 72 + 100 = 172; sum p0q1 = 60 + 80 = 140; index = 122.86. Fisher is the geometric mean = 122.79. Consumer Price Index (CPI): cost of living; WPI: wholesale prices (in India with base 2011-12); IIP: industrial output; Sensex: 30 stocks of BSE. Inflation = (CPI_t - CPI_{t-1}) / CPI_{t-1} x 100.

💡

Uses and cautions

  • Uses: measure inflation, adjust wages (DA), deflate GDP, policy making
  • Limitations: sampling errors, base year choice, changing consumption patterns
  • Real wages = money wages / CPI x 100
  • Statistical tools in project: collect data, present with tables and diagrams, compute averages, interpret and conclude
Read the full explanation

Uses: measure inflation, adjust wages (DA), deflate GDP, policy making. Limitations: sampling errors, base year choice, changing consumption patterns. Real wages = money wages / CPI x 100. Statistical tools in project: collect data, present with tables and diagrams, compute averages, interpret and conclude. Ethics of using statistics: avoid misleading graphs.

lessons.title: The Portrait of a Lady
yt: class 11 english hornbill the portrait of a lady khushwant singh summary

blocks.x: The Portrait of a Lady by Khushwant Singh is a memoir of the writer's grandmother. She was old, fair, wrinkled and walked with a hunched back, always in white, with her silver hair. In the village she took the boy to school, taught him the alphabet and the morning prayer, and spent her time at the temple. When the family moved to the city she lost her role as his teacher and spent time spinning, feeding the sparrows and sitting by the window. The boy went abroad for higher studies; she greeted him at the station and, for the first time, sang to the beat of a drum, a day or two before she died. The sparrows sat around her body in silence. The lesson: love and memory, ageing, the generation gap, and how simple loving goodness lingers.
Deep dive: Character of the grandmother

She is portrayed as a loving, religious, simple woman. She spent most of the day with prayer and with rosary. She walked the boy to school with a wooden slate and fed stray dogs with stale chapattis. In the city, the boy attended an English school and learned science, and the grandmother could not help. She did not complain. She sought companionship in feeding sparrows.
Deep dive: Themes and technique

The memoir uses simple, affectionate description and understatement. Themes: the generation gap, the changing relationship between the two as the boy grows, tradition versus modernity, death and the continuity of love. The contrast between her sorrow at his departure and the unusual joy at his return. The sparrows as a symbol of her compassion. The narrator is detached but warm.
Deep dive: Words and phrases to understand

Hunched, spartan, rosary, serene, quarrelsome, mundane, nostalgic. Simile: she looked like the winter landscape in the mountains. Comparisons: the white clad figure like a winter landscape. Irony and understatement in the description of the death scene.
Hindi saransh
Ek mahila ka chitra: lekhak ki dadi ka sneh, dharmikta aur mrityu. Gauraiyon ka shaant shok.
The grandmother is remembered with love: the story shows the unchanging love of a grandparent as the world around changes.

Visual lesson

The Portrait of a Lady

The Portrait of a Lady by Khushwant Singh is a memoir of the writer's grandmother

🔑

Big idea

  • The Portrait of a Lady by Khushwant Singh is a memoir of the writer's grandmother
  • She was old, fair, wrinkled and walked with a hunched back, always in white, with her silver hair
  • In the village she took the boy to school, taught him the alphabet and the morning prayer, and spent her time at the temple
  • When the family moved to the city she lost her role as his teacher and spent time spinning, feeding the sparrows and sitting by the window
Read the full explanation

The Portrait of a Lady by Khushwant Singh is a memoir of the writer's grandmother. She was old, fair, wrinkled and walked with a hunched back, always in white, with her silver hair. In the village she took the boy to school, taught him the alphabet and the morning prayer, and spent her time at the temple. When the family moved to the city she lost her role as his teacher and spent time spinning, feeding the sparrows and sitting by the window. The boy went abroad for higher studies; she greeted him at the station and, for the first time, sang to the beat of a drum, a day or two before she died. The sparrows sat around her body in silence. The lesson: love and memory, ageing, the generation gap, and how simple loving goodness lingers.

📌

Character of the grandmother

  • She is portrayed as a loving, religious, simple woman
  • She spent most of the day with prayer and with rosary
  • She walked the boy to school with a wooden slate and fed stray dogs with stale chapattis
  • In the city, the boy attended an English school and learned science, and the grandmother could not help
Read the full explanation

She is portrayed as a loving, religious, simple woman. She spent most of the day with prayer and with rosary. She walked the boy to school with a wooden slate and fed stray dogs with stale chapattis. In the city, the boy attended an English school and learned science, and the grandmother could not help. She did not complain. She sought companionship in feeding sparrows.

🧠

Themes and technique

  • The memoir uses simple, affectionate description and understatement
  • Themes: the generation gap, the changing relationship between the two as the boy grows, tradition versus modernity, death and the continuity of love
  • The contrast between her sorrow at his departure and the unusual joy at his return
  • The sparrows as a symbol of her compassion
Read the full explanation

The memoir uses simple, affectionate description and understatement. Themes: the generation gap, the changing relationship between the two as the boy grows, tradition versus modernity, death and the continuity of love. The contrast between her sorrow at his departure and the unusual joy at his return. The sparrows as a symbol of her compassion. The narrator is detached but warm.

✍️

Words and phrases to understand

  • Hunched, spartan, rosary, serene, quarrelsome, mundane, nostalgic
  • Simile: she looked like the winter landscape in the mountains
  • Comparisons: the white clad figure like a winter landscape
  • Irony and understatement in the description of the death scene

blocks.x: This is a true account of a family's round-the-world sailing voyage by Gordon Cook and Alan East. The Cook family sailed on the small boat Wavewalker with their young children, aiming to experience nature and teamwork. In the southern Indian Ocean, the family was hit by a terrible storm with huge waves. The boat was knocked about by gigantic waves; the family endured, using a drogue and careful sailing, and the boat survived. Their courage, unity and attitude: the family chose to face fear together rather than to be afraid of death. Themes: courage, family unity, the power of nature, human endurance, the importance of preparation and faith in each other.
Deep dive: The voyage

The family's adventure began as a long sea journey. Preparation included knowledge, training and support. They had a sailing boat Wavewalker, and the journey took them across oceans. The sea changed from calm to terrifying. Descriptions show the helplessness of humans before nature and the importance of keeping calm.
Deep dive: The storm and survival

The storm in the Indian Ocean produced waves as tall as a building and a very strong wind. The family tried different measures, used a drogue to slow the boat, and held together. They passed days of fear but the parents encouraged the children. Eventually the sea calmed and the family continued the journey with a deeper bond.
Deep dive: Lessons and style

Lessons: be prepared, stay together, do not lose hope, courage is not absence of fear but mastery of fear. The account uses first-person narration, vivid description and short sentences to create tension and suspense. The title expresses the strength drawn from togetherness.

Samudri yatra aur toofan: parivar ki ekta aur saahas. Prakriti ke samne manushya ki vivshta.
Courage is facing fear together, not the absence of fear.

Visual lesson

We’re Not Afraid to Die... if We Can All Be Together

This is a true account of a family's round-the-world sailing voyage by Gordon Cook and Alan East

🔑

Big idea

  • This is a true account of a family's round-the-world sailing voyage by Gordon Cook and Alan East
  • The Cook family sailed on the small boat Wavewalker with their young children, aiming to experience nature and teamwork
  • In the southern Indian Ocean, the family was hit by a terrible storm with huge waves
  • The boat was knocked about by gigantic waves
Read the full explanation

This is a true account of a family's round-the-world sailing voyage by Gordon Cook and Alan East. The Cook family sailed on the small boat Wavewalker with their young children, aiming to experience nature and teamwork. In the southern Indian Ocean, the family was hit by a terrible storm with huge waves. The boat was knocked about by gigantic waves; the family endured, using a drogue and careful sailing, and the boat survived. Their courage, unity and attitude: the family chose to face fear together rather than to be afraid of death. Themes: courage, family unity, the power of nature, human endurance, the importance of preparation and faith in each other.

📌

The voyage

  • The family's adventure began as a long sea journey
  • Preparation included knowledge, training and support
  • They had a sailing boat Wavewalker, and the journey took them across oceans
  • The sea changed from calm to terrifying
Read the full explanation

The family's adventure began as a long sea journey. Preparation included knowledge, training and support. They had a sailing boat Wavewalker, and the journey took them across oceans. The sea changed from calm to terrifying. Descriptions show the helplessness of humans before nature and the importance of keeping calm.

🧠

The storm and survival

  • The storm in the Indian Ocean produced waves as tall as a building and a very strong wind
  • The family tried different measures, used a drogue to slow the boat, and held together
  • They passed days of fear but the parents encouraged the children
  • Eventually the sea calmed and the family continued the journey with a deeper bond
🌟

Lessons and style

  • Lessons: be prepared, stay together, do not lose hope, courage is not absence of fear but mastery of fear
  • The account uses first-person narration, vivid description and short sentences to create tension and suspense
  • The title expresses the strength drawn from togetherness

lessons.title: Discovering Tut: the Saga Continues
yt: class 11 english hornbill discovering tut saga continues howard carter

blocks.x: Discovering Tut: the Saga Continues by A. R. Williams is about Tutankhamun, the boy pharaoh of Egypt (c. 1333 to 1323 BCE), who became king at about nine and died at about eighteen or nineteen. Howard Carter found his tomb in 1922 in the Valley of the Kings, with golden treasure. The mummy was examined by X-rays in 1968 and scanned by CT in 2005 under Zahi Hawass. Scientists debated the cause of death: the 1968 X-ray suggested a blow to the head and a bone fragment in the skull, indicating murder; the CT scan showed no sign of a blow, but a broken leg that may have become infected, suggesting an accident. Theories of the curse of the pharaohs. Mummification and Egyptian beliefs in afterlife; the discovery lets historians learn about royal life. The text also traces how modern science (forensic examination, 3-D reconstruction) is solving ancient mysteries.
Deep dive: The discovery

Howard Carter, a British archaeologist, spent years searching and discovered the tomb with steps in November 1922, funded by Lord Carnarvon. The tomb was found almost intact and contained thousands of objects, including the gold mask. Tutankhamun became pharaoh after the religious upheaval of his father Akhenaten; he restored the old gods.
Deep dive: Investigations of death

1968: Liverpool University team under R. G. Harrison X-rayed the mummy and found a thickening at the skull. 2005: Egyptian team led by Zahi Hawass used CT scanners and found no blow, but evidence of a broken leg possibly infected shortly before death. Modern DNA tests later suggested malaria and a bone disease. The mystery remains. Theories include murder by court officials such as Ay or Horemheb.
Deep dive: Themes and style

Themes: the persistence of history, scientific curiosity, how technology revises old ideas, the allure of mystery. The article is factual and journalistic, with names, dates and quotations; headings direct the reader. Words: pharaoh, tomb, mummy, artefact, forensic.

Read the full explanation

Discovering Tut: the Saga Continues by A. R. Williams is about Tutankhamun, the boy pharaoh of Egypt (c. 1333 to 1323 BCE), who became king at about nine and died at about eighteen or nineteen. Howard Carter found his tomb in 1922 in the Valley of the Kings, with golden treasure. The mummy was examined by X-rays in 1968 and scanned by CT in 2005 under Zahi Hawass. Scientists debated the cause of death: the 1968 X-ray suggested a blow to the head and a bone fragment in the skull, indicating murder; the CT scan showed no sign of a blow, but a broken leg that may have become infected, suggesting an accident. Theories of the curse of the pharaohs. Mummification and Egyptian beliefs in afterlife; the discovery lets historians learn about royal life. The text also traces how modern science (forensic examination, 3-D reconstruction) is solving ancient mysteries.

📌

The discovery

  • Howard Carter, a British archaeologist, spent years searching and discovered the tomb with steps in November 1922, funded by Lord Carnarvon
  • The tomb was found almost intact and contained thousands of objects, including the gold mask
  • Tutankhamun became pharaoh after the religious upheaval of his father Akhenaten
  • He restored the old gods
🧠

Investigations of death

  • 1968: Liverpool University team under R
  • Harrison X-rayed the mummy and found a thickening at the skull
  • 2005: Egyptian team led by Zahi Hawass used CT scanners and found no blow, but evidence of a broken leg possibly infected shortly before death
  • Modern DNA tests later suggested malaria and a bone disease
Read the full explanation

1968: Liverpool University team under R. G. Harrison X-rayed the mummy and found a thickening at the skull. 2005: Egyptian team led by Zahi Hawass used CT scanners and found no blow, but evidence of a broken leg possibly infected shortly before death. Modern DNA tests later suggested malaria and a bone disease. The mystery remains. Theories include murder by court officials such as Ay or Horemheb.

yt: class 11 english hornbill landscape of the soul nathalie trouveroy summary

blocks.x: Landscape of the Soul by Nathalie Trouveroy compares the Western and Chinese traditions of painting. In the West, painting is based on realism: art portrays the world accurately, using perspective and the 3-D effect; religion shaped early art; the focus was on human figure and action. In Chinese painting, artists look for harmony with nature: landscape (shan shui, mountains and water) is the main subject; the artist does not paint nature as it appears but its inner spirit; blank spaces, mist, and a few small human figures show the vastness of nature. The author contrasts the two traditions and mentions the legend of an old Chinese painter who vanished into his own painting, and the story of Taoist and Zen influence. Themes: the difference between East and West, art as a mirror of philosophy, spirituality in art.
Deep dive: Western art

The West: since the Renaissance, art emphasised realism, perspective, light, shadow, portraits and religious themes. The painter is the observer standing outside nature. Painting depicts what is seen: man at centre, with the figure in action. Oil paints, canvas. Famous traditions: Renaissance, Baroque.
Deep dive: Chinese art

Chinese painting uses ink and brush on silk and paper. Shan shui means mountain-water. Influence of Taoism, Confucianism and Buddhism: harmony of man and nature. The painter paints the spirit and the essence rather than appearance. Emptiness (blank space) is a part of the composition: the reader's imagination completes it. Human figures are tiny to show humility.
Deep dive: Themes and lessons

The cultural difference between mind and nature in East and West. The ideal of the Chinese painter: to become one with nature. The story of the legendary painter who walks into his own picture symbolises merging with art. The text teaches respect for different traditions and the idea that art reveals the philosophy of a civilisation.
Hindi saransh
Aatma ka drishya: Pashchimi aur Chini kala ki tulna. Chini chitrakala mein prakriti ke saath ekta.
Chinese painting seeks the inner spirit of nature, while Western painting traditionally seeks accurate depiction.

blocks.x: The Ailing Planet by Nani Palkhivala argues that the Earth is sick because of human activities and that the green movement is humanity's attempt to heal it. Early societies lived in harmony with nature; the Industrial Revolution and modern technology led to over-exploitation of resources. The essay speaks of population explosion, pollution, the greenhouse effect, depletion of the ozone layer, loss of forests and species. The green movement began when people recognised that economic growth was damaging the planet and that natural resources are limited. It calls for the idea of sustainable use and preserving the earth for future generations, underlining that the planet is not inherited from ancestors but borrowed from children. It stresses that nature has her limits; the Earth can be saved by individual action, stronger laws and international cooperation. Themes: environmental degradation, responsibility, hope and action.
Deep dive: Problem of the ailing planet

The earth is under stress from population growth, industrialisation, deforestation, depletion of fossil fuels, pollution of air and water and global warming. The author warns that if the damage continues, future generations will inherit a poorer world. Human greed and short-term gains are the root of the problem. Economic growth without ecological sense is harmful.
Deep dive: The green movement

The green movement is a worldwide movement that aims to protect the environment. It spread through scientists, writers, activists and common citizens. Its principles: respect for nature, sustainable development, reducing consumption and waste, conserving energy and protecting biodiversity. Recognition came with conferences such as the Earth Summit. Governments introduced laws. The movement connects ecology with economics and ethics.
Deep dive: Message and style

The essay argues persuasively, using facts, rhetorical statements and an urgent tone. It ends on hope: individuals can contribute through simple lifestyles and cooperation. Key words: ecology, sustainable, degradation, biodiversity, conservation. The idea of stewardship: humans are trustees of the earth.

lessons.title: The Browning Version
yt: class 11 english hornbill the browning version terence rattigan summary

blocks.x: The Browning Version is an extract from a play by Terence Rattigan. Mr Andrew Crocker-Harris, a Classics teacher, is retiring from a public school because of ill health. He is a strict, unpopular and lonely teacher, nicknamed the Crock, whose wife Millie is unkind and unfaithful. The young pupil Taplow comes to his room for extra work. Taplow gives him a parting gift: a second-hand copy of Browning's translation of the Agamemnon of Aeschylus, inscribed with a line from the play, God from afar looks graciously upon a gentle master. The kindness moves Crocker-Harris to tears, showing that he has feelings after all. Millie mocks him, saying Taplow wanted to get good marks. The scene reveals the contrast between the gentle pupil and the cold teacher, the hidden humanity in the harsh and the cruelty of the unthinking. Themes: appreciation, loneliness, emotional repression and kindness.
Deep dive: Characters

Andrew Crocker-Harris is a middle-aged Classics master, once an excellent scholar, now disliked by students for his rigid discipline. He hides his emotions. Taplow is a 15-year-old sensitive student who likes the teacher more than others do. Frobisher is a young science master who is cheerful and speaks frankly. Millie is Crocker-Harris's wife, who mocks him and has an affair. The headmaster is mentioned. John Taplow's act of kindness.
Deep dive: Story and symbols

The gift of a book symbolises respect and humanity. The Agamemnon is a play by Aeschylus, and the translation is by Robert Browning. The inscription shows the pupil's understanding. The tears shows the teacher's hidden emotional life. The contrast between Taplow's sincerity and Millie's cynicism. Humour and irony: Taplow tries to appear indifferent. The dramatic form uses stage directions and dialogue.
Deep dive: Themes

Kindness changes people; the gap between how others see us and who we are; the need for appreciation; loneliness in old age; the cruelty of mockery; the education system. Language: dialogue, stage directions, irony and understatement.
Hindi saransh
Natak ka ansh: shikshak aur shishya ka bhavnatmak sambandh. Taplow ka upahar Crocker-Harris ko dravit kar deta hai.
A small act of kindness can reveal and touch the hidden humanity in a harsh person.

The Browning Version

Big idea

  • The Browning Version is an extract from a play by Terence Rattigan
  • Mr Andrew Crocker-Harris, a Classics teacher, is retiring from a public school because of ill health
  • He is a strict, unpopular and lonely teacher, nicknamed the Crock, whose wife Millie is unkind and unfaithful
  • The young pupil Taplow comes to his room for extra work
Read the full explanation

The Browning Version is an extract from a play by Terence Rattigan. Mr Andrew Crocker-Harris, a Classics teacher, is retiring from a public school because of ill health. He is a strict, unpopular and lonely teacher, nicknamed the Crock, whose wife Millie is unkind and unfaithful. The young pupil Taplow comes to his room for extra work. Taplow gives him a parting gift: a second-hand copy of Browning's translation of the Agamemnon of Aeschylus, inscribed with a line from the play, God from afar looks graciously upon a gentle master. The kindness moves Crocker-Harris to tears, showing that he has feelings after all. Millie mocks him, saying Taplow wanted to get good marks. The scene reveals the contrast between the gentle pupil and the cold teacher, the hidden humanity in the harsh and the cruelty of the unthinking. Themes: appreciation, loneliness, emotional repression and kindness.

📌

Characters

  • Andrew Crocker-Harris is a middle-aged Classics master, once an excellent scholar, now disliked by students for his rigid discipline
  • He hides his emotions
  • Taplow is a 15-year-old sensitive student who likes the teacher more than others do
  • Frobisher is a young science master who is cheerful and speaks frankly

Andrew Crocker-Harris is a middle-aged Classics master, once an excellent scholar, now disliked by students for his rigid discipline. He hides his emotions. Taplow is a 15-year-old sensitive student who likes the teacher more than others do. Frobisher is a young science master who is cheerful and speaks frankly. Millie is Crocker-Harris's wife, who mocks him and has an affair. The headmaster is mentioned. John Taplow's act of kindness.

  • The gift of a book symbolises respect and humanity
  • The Agamemnon is a play by Aeschylus, and the translation is by Robert Browning
  • The inscription shows the pupil's understanding
  • The tears shows the teacher's hidden emotional life

The gift of a book symbolises respect and humanity. The Agamemnon is a play by Aeschylus, and the translation is by Robert Browning. The inscription shows the pupil's understanding. The tears shows the teacher's hidden emotional life. The contrast between Taplow's sincerity and Millie's cynicism. Humour and irony: Taplow tries to appear indifferent. The dramatic form uses stage directions and dialogue.

🌟

Themes

  • Kindness changes people
  • The gap between how others see us and who we are
  • The need for appreciation
  • Loneliness in old age

Kindness changes people; the gap between how others see us and who we are; the need for appreciation; loneliness in old age; the cruelty of mockery; the education system. Language: dialogue, stage directions, irony and understatement.

lessons.title: The Adventure
yt: class 11 english hornbill the adventure jayant narlikar summary

blocks.x: The Adventure by Jayant Narlikar is a science fiction story about parallel universes. Professor Gangadharpant Gaitonde, a historian, is travelling by train and is about to go to Pune. In a mix-up of time and space he finds himself in a world where the Marathas won the Battle of Panipat in 1761, and the British never ruled India. The world is different: the Maratha empire stretched across, the cities are not as he knew. In this alternate history he finds that the places bear different names. He returns to his familiar world and is unsure whether he dreamed it. The story explores the idea that the universe may split at critical events (the branching of history) and that a person can cross from one branch to another. Themes: history and chance, the many-world hypothesis, science fiction and identity.
Deep dive: Plot

Professor Gaitonde is a history teacher who enjoys discussing the effect of chance on history. He boards a train, has a strange experience when the train changes direction and he steps into a different Bombay in which Victoria Terminus is replaced by something else; Indian people have different names and the British are not present. The professor meets a friend and a policeman, then realises that he has crossed into a parallel world where history diverged at Panipat. After reading a newspaper he learns that the Marathas defeated the Afghan invaders.
Deep dive: Ideas

The story relates to quantum mechanics and the many-worlds idea: when an event has more than one outcome, the universe may branch. It shows that small events like a battle can change the entire future, making history contingent. The professor's curiosity and scientific reading of the situation drive the plot. Style: first-person narration within a frame of discussion; science explained simply.
Deep dive: Themes and evaluation

Themes: chance in history, the idea of parallel universes, the importance of imagination and science fiction as a genre. Humour: his reaction to the new world. The story introduces students to alternate history and to the work of Jayant Narlikar, a leading astrophysicist and writer.

Big idea

  • The Adventure by Jayant Narlikar is a science fiction story about parallel universes
  • Professor Gangadharpant Gaitonde, a historian, is travelling by train and is about to go to Pune
  • In a mix-up of time and space he finds himself in a world where the Marathas won the Battle of Panipat in 1761, and the British never ruled India
  • The world is different: the Maratha empire stretched across, the cities are not as he knew
Read the full explanation

The Adventure by Jayant Narlikar is a science fiction story about parallel universes. Professor Gangadharpant Gaitonde, a historian, is travelling by train and is about to go to Pune. In a mix-up of time and space he finds himself in a world where the Marathas won the Battle of Panipat in 1761, and the British never ruled India. The world is different: the Maratha empire stretched across, the cities are not as he knew. In this alternate history he finds that the places bear different names. He returns to his familiar world and is unsure whether he dreamed it. The story explores the idea that the universe may split at critical events (the branching of history) and that a person can cross from one branch to another. Themes: history and chance, the many-world hypothesis, science fiction and identity.

📌

Plot

  • Professor Gaitonde is a history teacher who enjoys discussing the effect of chance on history
  • He boards a train, has a strange experience when the train changes direction and he steps into a different Bombay in which Victoria Terminus is…
  • Indian people have different names and the British are not present
  • The professor meets a friend and a policeman, then realises that he has crossed into a parallel world where history diverged at Panipat
Read the full explanation

Professor Gaitonde is a history teacher who enjoys discussing the effect of chance on history. He boards a train, has a strange experience when the train changes direction and he steps into a different Bombay in which Victoria Terminus is replaced by something else; Indian people have different names and the British are not present. The professor meets a friend and a policeman, then realises that he has crossed into a parallel world where history diverged at Panipat. After reading a newspaper he learns that the Marathas defeated the Afghan invaders.

🧠

Ideas

  • The story relates to quantum mechanics and the many-worlds idea: when an event has more than one outcome, the universe may branch
  • It shows that small events like a battle can change the entire future, making history contingent
  • The professor's curiosity and scientific reading of the situation drive the plot
  • Style: first-person narration within a frame of discussion
Read the full explanation

The story relates to quantum mechanics and the many-worlds idea: when an event has more than one outcome, the universe may branch. It shows that small events like a battle can change the entire future, making history contingent. The professor's curiosity and scientific reading of the situation drive the plot. Style: first-person narration within a frame of discussion; science explained simply.

🌟

Themes and evaluation

  • Themes: chance in history, the idea of parallel universes, the importance of imagination and science fiction as a genre
  • Humour: his reaction to the new world
  • The story introduces students to alternate history and to the work of Jayant Narlikar, a leading astrophysicist and writer

lessons.title: Silk Road
yt: class 11 english hornbill silk road nick middleton mount kailash tibet

blocks.x: Silk Road by Nick Middleton is a travelogue of his journey in Tibet to Mount Kailash, the sacred mountain. Middleton travels with a driver, Tsetan, a guide and a cook, in a Land Cruiser across the Tibetan plateau, along an old branch of the ancient Silk Road, a trade route that carried silk and other goods between China and Europe. He suffers from altitude sickness and fatigue and the group faces rough terrain, rain, cold and difficulties with the vehicle. He meets locals, a nomad, passes small towns such as Zhongba and Darchen and sees that Tibetan pilgrims walk around the mountain in a circuit (kora) believing it cleanses sins. Mount Kailash is sacred to Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and Bon followers; Lake Manasarovar is nearby. Themes: adventure, human endurance, faith and the pull of the sacred.
Deep dive: The journey

The writer sets out with the aim to see Mount Kailash. The journey goes through remote high-altitude terrain at over 4000 metres. They face a snowstorm, a broken-down vehicle and rough roads. The writer has a headache and nausea because of altitude. The writer describes the people: nomads, shopkeepers, pilgrims. The mountain is a symbol of faith.
Deep dive: Silk Road and context

The Silk Road was a network of trade routes linking China to the Mediterranean, carrying silk, spices, ideas and religions. In the story the writer travels on a southern route through Tibet. The pilgrims believe that circling Kailash gives merit. The title links history with the present journey.
Deep dive: Themes and style

Travel writing combines description, humour and observation. The writer is an outsider who observes with curiosity. Themes: endurance, belief and the unity of cultures; nature's vastness; contrasts between modern vehicles and traditional pilgrim walkers. Vocabulary: pilgrimage, terrain, altitude, plateau, nomad.

Big idea

  • Silk Road by Nick Middleton is a travelogue of his journey in Tibet to Mount Kailash, the sacred mountain
  • Middleton travels with a driver, Tsetan, a guide and a cook, in a Land Cruiser across the Tibetan plateau, along an old branch of the ancient Silk…

Read the full explanation

Silk Road by Nick Middleton is a travelogue of his journey in Tibet to Mount Kailash, the sacred mountain. Middleton travels with a driver, Tsetan, a guide and a cook, in a Land Cruiser across the Tibetan plateau, along an old branch of the ancient Silk Road, a trade route that carried silk and other goods between China and Europe. He suffers from altitude sickness and fatigue and the group faces rough terrain, rain, cold and difficulties with the vehicle. He meets locals, a nomad, passes small towns such as Zhongba and Darchen and sees that Tibetan pilgrims walk around the mountain in a circuit (kora) believing it cleanses sins. Mount Kailash is sacred to Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and Bon followers; Lake Manasarovar is nearby. Themes: adventure, human endurance, faith and the pull of the sacred.

📌

The journey

  • The writer sets out with the aim to see Mount Kailash
  • The journey goes through remote high-altitude terrain at over 4000 metres
  • They face a snowstorm, a broken-down vehicle and rough roads
  • The writer has a headache and nausea because of altitude
Read the full explanation

The writer sets out with the aim to see Mount Kailash. The journey goes through remote high-altitude terrain at over 4000 metres. They face a snowstorm, a broken-down vehicle and rough roads. The writer has a headache and nausea because of altitude. The writer describes the people: nomads, shopkeepers, pilgrims. The mountain is a symbol of faith.

🧠

Silk Road and context

  • The Silk Road was a network of trade routes linking China to the Mediterranean, carrying silk, spices, ideas and religions
  • In the story the writer travels on a southern route through Tibet
  • The pilgrims believe that circling Kailash gives merit
  • The title links history with the present journey
🌟

Themes and style

  • Travel writing combines description, humour and observation
  • The writer is an outsider who observes with curiosity
  • Themes: endurance, belief and the unity of cultures
  • Nature's vastness
Read the full explanation

Travel writing combines description, humour and observation. The writer is an outsider who observes with curiosity. Themes: endurance, belief and the unity of cultures; nature's vastness; contrasts between modern vehicles and traditional pilgrim walkers. Vocabulary: pilgrimage, terrain, altitude, plateau, nomad.

lessons.title: A Photograph
yt: class 11 english hornbill poem a photograph shirley toulson summary

blocks.x: A Photograph by Shirley Toulson describes the poet looking at an old photograph of her mother as a young girl, at the seaside with two cousins, taken by an unknown relative. The photograph recalls a happy moment when the girl was laughing at the sea. Twenty years after the photograph, the poet recalls her mother's laughter; now the mother is dead and the picture remains, with the poet's silence. The poem shows how photographs preserve memory and how the passing of time and death leave a silent grief. Themes: memory, loss, change and the permanence of the photograph against the impermanence of life.
Deep dive: Stanzas

First: the photograph of the mother with cousins, a sunny day at the sea, with the paddling girls. Second: the sea and the mother's laughter in the picture; the poet remembers her mother's smile. Third: the poet in the present, the mother now dead; the photograph holds a moment of joy; the poet's unspoken grief. The poem has free verse and simple language.
Deep dive: Devices

Imagery of the sea; contrast between the carefree past and silent present; the tone is nostalgic and sorrowful. The photograph is a symbol of memory. Repetition of time ideas. Poetic effect: understatement of grief.
Deep dive: Themes
Time passes and takes loved ones; memory and photographs preserve the past; death and silence; family bonds across generations. The poet understands her mother's joy and life through the picture.
Hindi saransh
Ek photo: bachpan ki khushi aur maa ki yaad. Samay, mrityu aur maun dukh.
A photograph freezes a moment of joy even after the person has gone.

Read the full explanation

A Photograph by Shirley Toulson describes the poet looking at an old photograph of her mother as a young girl, at the seaside with two cousins, taken by an unknown relative. The photograph recalls a happy moment when the girl was laughing at the sea. Twenty years after the photograph, the poet recalls her mother's laughter; now the mother is dead and the picture remains, with the poet's silence. The poem shows how photographs preserve memory and how the passing of time and death leave a silent grief. Themes: memory, loss, change and the permanence of the photograph against the impermanence of life.

blocks.x: The Laburnum Top by Ted Hughes describes a laburnum tree in early spring, still and silent, until a goldfinch arrives. The bird enters the tree and the whole tree seems to come alive with a vibrant sound and activity as the bird calls and the chicks answer from the nest in the tree. The goldfinch moves quickly with its mate or chicks, and the tree seems to rattle with life and movement like a machine. When the bird flies away, the tree returns to quiet. The poem shows the vitality of nature and the way a living creature transforms the world around it. Themes: energy of nature, harmony between bird and tree, cycle of life and renewal.
Deep dive: Stages

The tree is quiet and still in the early part of the year. A goldfinch lands and the tree comes alive with a sharp, loud sound. The bird's mate or chicks respond from the nest, producing a lively chorus. The bird's sudden departure leaves the tree in stillness again. The poem is of four stanzas of free verse.
Deep dive: Imagery and devices

Metaphors comparing the tree to a machine, a source of electric sound and a being with a pulse; contrast of stillness and activity; sound imagery; personification of the tree. Movement and colour, with the bird's bright plumage and the laburnum's yellow flowers.
Deep dive: Themes
Nature's vitality; interdependence of tree and bird; sudden change from stillness to energy; the poet's keen observation of nature. Ted Hughes is known for his animal poetry.

lessons.title: The Voice of the Rain
yt: class 11 english hornbill poem the voice of the rain walt whitman summary

blocks.x: The Voice of the Rain by Walt Whitman is a conversation between the poet and the rain. The poet asks who the rain is. The rain answers that it is the poem of the earth, rising as vapour from the land and sea, ascending to the sky and then falling back to refresh the earth. The rain compares itself to a song that begins in the heart, goes into the air and returns to the heart that composed it. The poem shows the water cycle and compares it with the cycle of poetry. Themes: the cycle of nature, transformation, renewal and the relationship between nature and poetry.
Deep dive: Structure

The poet asks who the rain is. The rain describes itself as the endless cycle of water; it rises from earth as vapour, reaches the clouds, returns as rain and gives life to the earth. The poem ends with a comparison with a song: a song begins in the poet's heart and returns to the heart. It is written in free verse with a question-answer form.
Deep dive: Devices
Personification of the rain; dialogue; metaphor of the rain as the poem of the earth; imagery of rising and falling; simile of the rain to a song. The cyclic structure echoes the water cycle.
Deep dive: Themes

The unity of nature and art; the cycle of life; transformation in nature; renewal; the generosity of rain; the cycle of creation. Walt Whitman was an American poet known for free verse and Leaves of Grass.

1Big idea›2Structure›3Devices›4Themes
🔑

Big idea

  • The Voice of the Rain by Walt Whitman is a conversation between the poet and the rain
  • The poet asks who the rain is
  • The rain answers that it is the poem of the earth, rising as vapour from the land and sea, ascending to the sky and then falling back to refresh the…
  • The rain compares itself to a song that begins in the heart, goes into the air and returns to the heart that composed it
Read the full explanation

The Voice of the Rain by Walt Whitman is a conversation between the poet and the rain. The poet asks who the rain is. The rain answers that it is the poem of the earth, rising as vapour from the land and sea, ascending to the sky and then falling back to refresh the earth. The rain compares itself to a song that begins in the heart, goes into the air and returns to the heart that composed it. The poem shows the water cycle and compares it with the cycle of poetry. Themes: the cycle of nature, transformation, renewal and the relationship between nature and poetry.

📌

Structure

  • The poet asks who the rain is
  • The rain describes itself as the endless cycle of water
  • It rises from earth as vapour, reaches the clouds, returns as rain and gives life to the earth
  • The poem ends with a comparison with a song: a song begins in the poet's heart and returns to the heart
Read the full explanation

The poet asks who the rain is. The rain describes itself as the endless cycle of water; it rises from earth as vapour, reaches the clouds, returns as rain and gives life to the earth. The poem ends with a comparison with a song: a song begins in the poet's heart and returns to the heart. It is written in free verse with a question-answer form.

🧠

Devices

  • Personification of the rain
  • Metaphor of the rain as the poem of the earth
  • Imagery of rising and falling
  • Simile of the rain to a song
Read the full explanation

Personification of the rain; dialogue; metaphor of the rain as the poem of the earth; imagery of rising and falling; simile of the rain to a song. The cyclic structure echoes the water cycle.

🌟

Themes

  • The unity of nature and art
  • The cycle of life
  • Transformation in nature
  • The generosity of rain
Read the full explanation

The unity of nature and art; the cycle of life; transformation in nature; renewal; the generosity of rain; the cycle of creation. Walt Whitman was an American poet known for free verse and Leaves of Grass.

blocks.x: Childhood by Markus Natten reflects on the loss of childhood. The poet asks when his childhood went, whether it was when he found that Hell is not a place of fire but the cruelty and pain of the world, or when he realised that adults do not always mean what they say. He asks whether childhood was lost when he began to understand that thoughts and words are not the same, or when he started to imitate adults and hide his real self. The poet concludes that childhood has been replaced by adult cleverness. He wonders where his innocence went and suspects it is somewhere else, perhaps in a child. Themes: loss of innocence, growing up, hypocrisy of adults, the search for the lost self.
Deep dive: Content

The poem opens with a question: when did my childhood go. He recalls the time he first learned that Hell is not an actual place of fire but the suffering in the world. He realises that adults are often insincere. He thinks of the day he began to separate thought from speech and to imitate others. His innocence is replaced by cleverness. At the end he asks where childhood is now, perhaps in other children.
Deep dive: Devices

Rhetorical questions; contrast between innocence and experience; personal reflective tone; irony of adults' behaviour; simple language. The structure is a series of questions leading to an uncertain answer.
Deep dive: Themes
Loss of innocence; growing up; hypocrisy and artificiality of adult life; nostalgia for childhood; the search for identity. The poem speaks about the process of growing up as a gradual loss.

lessons.title: Father to Son
yt: class 11 english hornbill poem father to son elizabeth jennings summary

blocks.x: Father to Son by Elizabeth Jennings describes the gap between a father and his son. The father says he does not understand his son, and the son does not understand him; they live in the same house but there is a lack of communication. The father wants to reach out and bridge the distance, to walk with his son and share his life, but does not know how, and the son too is silent. The poem expresses regret, love and helplessness. It ends with the father's wish for the son to be near him, though he feels he cannot reach him. Themes: generation gap, communication, love and regret in family relations.
Deep dive: Content

The father says he cannot understand his son, who is a stranger even though he is of his blood. The son is not a stranger but not understood. The father recalls that the son once walked beside him and wishes to build the bond again. He feels that he has failed to communicate. The poem expresses a desire for reconciliation and shows the emotional distance in the family.
Deep dive: Devices

Plain, direct language; rhetorical question; contrast between the physical closeness and emotional distance; a reflective and sad tone; the father's voice as the speaker. The repetition of ideas of strangeness and the use of conversational rhythm.

Read the full explanation

Father to Son by Elizabeth Jennings describes the gap between a father and his son. The father says he does not understand his son, and the son does not understand him; they live in the same house but there is a lack of communication. The father wants to reach out and bridge the distance, to walk with his son and share his life, but does not know how, and the son too is silent. The poem expresses regret, love and helplessness. It ends with the father's wish for the son to be near him, though he feels he cannot reach him. Themes: generation gap, communication, love and regret in family relations.

  • The son is not a stranger but not understood
  • The father recalls that the son once walked beside him and wishes to build the bond again

The father says he cannot understand his son, who is a stranger even though he is of his blood. The son is not a stranger but not understood. The father recalls that the son once walked beside him and wishes to build the bond again. He feels that he has failed to communicate. The poem expresses a desire for reconciliation and shows the emotional distance in the family.
