lessons.title: The Summer of the Beautiful White Horse
yt: class 11 english snapshots summer of the beautiful white horse william saroyan

blocks.x: The Summer of the Beautiful White Horse by William Saroyan is told by Aram, a nine-year-old Armenian boy in California. His cousin Mourad, who is thirteen and considered mad in the family, wakes him early one morning with a beautiful white horse. Aram knows the family is poor and honest, and the horse must be stolen. He is afraid but loves riding. For about two weeks they ride the horse in secret, hiding it in a vineyard barn. Then they return it to its owner John Byro, who recognises that his horse looks better. The boys return the horse. Byro says that the horse was well kept and lets the matter go. Themes: honesty, innocence of childhood, poverty, family honour and the beauty of the horse.
Deep dive: Characters

Aram: narrator, nine, honest and innocent. Mourad: cousin, thirteen, adventurous and passionate about horses. Uncle Khosrove: a loud, impatient uncle who says do not mind; famous for his temper. John Byro: the owner of the horse, a farmer. The Garoghlanian family: known for honesty and poverty.
Deep dive: Plot and setting

The story is set in Fresno, California, among Armenian immigrants during the early twentieth century. Mourad brings a horse. Aram worries about the family's reputation. They keep the horse in a shed in the vineyard and ride in the early mornings. The horse becomes better with feeding. When they return the horse, Byro recognises it and says it is his, but accepts. The title suggests the beauty and the magic of the summer.
Deep dive: Themes
Honesty and family honour; the tension between poverty and pride; the joy of childhood adventure; Armenian cultural background; humour in the way the boys treat the horse; moral dilemma of the boys.

Safed ghode ki garmi: do cousin ghoda churate hain aur lautate hain. Imaandari aur bachpan.

blocks.x: The Address by Marga Minco is a story of a girl who survives the Second World War and returns to find her mother's belongings. During the war, her mother gave valuables to Mrs Dorling and gave the girl the address. After the war, the narrator visits the house and sees that Mrs Dorling has her mother's things. Mrs Dorling pretends not to know her and is cold; the narrator is taken round to see the objects but receives nothing. She is uneasy and leaves. Years later she visits again, but the sight of her mother's belongings in a stranger's house is painful. She feels that the things now belong to the past and abandons the search. Deep dive: Plot

The narrator's mother gave her the address of Mrs Dorling, an acquaintance with whom she left valuables. After the war the narrator finds the house and sees familiar items: a cloth, a bowl and other items. Mrs Dorling invites her in but behaves like a stranger. The narrator is uncomfortable, takes nothing and leaves. She later tries again but cannot go through with it.
Deep dive: Characters
The narrator is sensitive, quiet and mourns her mother. Mrs Dorling is guilty, selfish and uneasy. The mother is only remembered through objects. The girl in the house is Mrs Dorling's daughter.
Deep dive: Themes
The war's emotional damage; the power of objects to carry memory; the selfishness of people who took advantage; the narrator's inability to claim her mother's things; loss and survival.

blocks.x: Ranga's Marriage by Masti Venkatesha Iyengar is a humorous story set in the village of Hosahalli in Karnataka. Ranga, a young man, returns from Bangalore after studying and has become modern in his ways. Shyama Joyisa, the village astrologer and matchmaker, is determined to marry him to Ratna, a village girl. The astrologer predicts a marriage match and by clever manoeuvres involves Ranga and Ratna until they marry. The story is narrated by the writer, who is amused by the astrologer's plans. The tale highlights village life, the role of astrology and matchmaking and the playful trick that leads to marriage. Themes: tradition and modernity, village life, humour, marriage customs.
Deep dive: Characters

Ranga: educated, modern and well-mannered. Shyama Joyisa: the astrologer, shrewd and humorous. Ratna: the village girl, young and quiet. Rama Rao: the writer's friend or the narrator. The villagers: curious and traditional.
Deep dive: Plot

Ranga returns to Hosahalli. The astrologer sees him as a suitable match for Ratna. Without openly saying, he tells Ranga that Ratna is a good girl. He gradually brings them together through a visit and a mild trick. After a proposal, they marry. The story ends happily.
Deep dive: Themes
Village life; arranged marriage; humour and irony; tradition versus modern education; the matchmaker as a figure of village society; the charm of the story.
Hindi saransh
Ranga ka vivah: gaon ka jyotishi apni chaturai se Ranga aur Ratna ka vivah karata hai.
The astrologer's clever planning brings two people together, and the story is a humorous picture of village life.

yt: class 11 english snapshots albert einstein at school patrick pringle

blocks.x: Albert Einstein at School by Patrick Pringle describes the young Einstein's experience in a German school. Einstein was a thoughtful pupil who did not like the rote learning and harsh discipline of the Luitpold Gymnasium in Munich. His teachers thought him slow and the Greek teacher, who disliked his questioning attitude, told him that he would never be successful. A teacher told him that his mere presence spoiled the respect of the class. Einstein said he could not stay and left school, taking a certificate from a doctor to prove a need for rest. He left for Italy to join his family. Later he developed his ideas on relativity. Themes: rote learning versus questioning, creativity, authority and genius.
Deep dive: Episodes

Einstein, aged about fifteen, attends the Luitpold Gymnasium. He dislikes the teaching, which stresses memory. He asks questions that the teachers cannot answer. The Greek teacher tells him he will not make anything of his life. Einstein decides to leave the school with a medical certificate. He goes to Italy, and later studies in Zurich.
Deep dive: Characters

Einstein: thoughtful, independent and brilliant. The Greek teacher: strict and unhappy with questioning. The family doctor: understanding. Einstein's parents: moved to Italy and supported his talents.
Deep dive: Themes

The education system that stifles creativity; a questioning mind; the difference between knowledge and memory; the importance of freedom in learning; the later success of a boy who was told he would fail.
Hindi saransh
Einstein skool mein: ratne wali padhai se asantosh aur swatantra soch.
Einstein left a school that discouraged questions, and went on to change physics.

lessons.title: Mother’s Day
yt: class 11 english snapshots mothers day j b priestley

blocks.x: Mother's Day is a one-act comedy by J. B. Priestley. Mrs Annie Pearson is a mild woman who is taken for granted by her husband George and her children Doris and Cyril. Her friend Mrs Fitzgerald, a fortune-teller and neighbour, suggests that she should assert herself. Mrs Fitzgerald uses a magic spell to exchange their personalities, so that Mrs Pearson speaks like Mrs Fitzgerald. When the family comes home, Mrs Pearson (in Mrs Fitzgerald's manner) refuses to do their work and tells them to look after themselves. The family is shocked and begs her to return to normal. Finally the spell is reversed, but Mrs Pearson now speaks firmly, showing she has gained confidence. Themes: respect for the mother, the role of housewife, humour and assertion.
Deep dive: Characters

Mrs Pearson: gentle, passive and weak at the start; turns firm. Mrs Fitzgerald: strong, practical and outspoken. Doris and Cyril: self-centred, lazy, demanding. George Pearson: selfish and authoritarian. The play uses humour and contrast.
Deep dive: Plot

Mrs Pearson complains to Mrs Fitzgerald about her family's lack of respect. Mrs Fitzgerald says she should change her ways. They exchange personalities. Doris, Cyril and George arrive; they find Mrs Pearson (as Mrs Fitzgerald) unusual. She refuses to serve them, goes to play cards and leaves them to prepare supper. The family is in shock. Eventually the exchange is reversed.
Deep dive: Themes
The family should respect and share work with a mother; assertiveness; humour as social comment; gender roles in households; the title is ironic as the family does not honour mothers.
Hindi saransh
Maa ka din: Mrs Pearson ko parivar nazarandaz karta hai; vyaktitva badalne par ve dridh ho jati hain.
A mother deserves respect and shared household work, not to be taken for granted.

Read the full explanation

Mother's Day is a one-act comedy by J. B. Priestley. Mrs Annie Pearson is a mild woman who is taken for granted by her husband George and her children Doris and Cyril. Her friend Mrs Fitzgerald, a fortune-teller and neighbour, suggests that she should assert herself. Mrs Fitzgerald uses a magic spell to exchange their personalities, so that Mrs Pearson speaks like Mrs Fitzgerald. When the family comes home, Mrs Pearson (in Mrs Fitzgerald's manner) refuses to do their work and tells them to look after themselves. The family is shocked and begs her to return to normal. Finally the spell is reversed, but Mrs Pearson now speaks firmly, showing she has gained confidence. Themes: respect for the mother, the role of housewife, humour and assertion.

📌

Characters

  • Mrs Pearson: gentle, passive and weak at the start
  • Mrs Fitzgerald: strong, practical and outspoken
  • Doris and Cyril: self-centred, lazy, demanding
  • George Pearson: selfish and authoritarian

Mrs Pearson: gentle, passive and weak at the start; turns firm. Mrs Fitzgerald: strong, practical and outspoken. Doris and Cyril: self-centred, lazy, demanding. George Pearson: selfish and authoritarian. The play uses humour and contrast.

🧠

Plot

  • Mrs Pearson complains to Mrs Fitzgerald about her family's lack of respect
  • Mrs Fitzgerald says she should change her ways
  • They exchange personalities
  • Doris, Cyril and George arrive
Read the full explanation

Mrs Pearson complains to Mrs Fitzgerald about her family's lack of respect. Mrs Fitzgerald says she should change her ways. They exchange personalities. Doris, Cyril and George arrive; they find Mrs Pearson (as Mrs Fitzgerald) unusual. She refuses to serve them, goes to play cards and leaves them to prepare supper. The family is in shock. Eventually the exchange is reversed.

🌟

Themes

  • The family should respect and share work with a mother
  • Assertiveness
  • Humour as social comment

blocks.x: The Ghat of the Only World by Amitav Ghosh is a tribute to his friend, the Kashmiri-American poet Agha Shahid Ali, who died of brain cancer in December 2001. The essay recalls how the writer learned of the illness, the poet's courage in the face of death and his love of poetry, Kashmir, Delhi and Begum Akhtar's music. Shahid's poem about the Ganga, the ghat and the idea of a world in which one rests, gave the essay its title. The writer reflects on friendship, mortality and the way Shahid lived. Shahid wanted his ashes scattered in the Ganga and Kashmir. Themes: friendship, memory, death, poetry and exile.
Deep dive: Content

Ghosh recalls meeting Shahid in Delhi in the 1970s and later in America. When Shahid fell ill and underwent treatment, he kept writing. Shahid loved Kashmir, the Ganga and Begum Akhtar's music, and wrote in English with Urdu forms such as the ghazal. In the last days, friends gathered. Shahid died on 8 December 2001 at Amherst. The ghat of the only world is where Ganga flows and where the poet would have wished to be remembered.
Deep dive: Style
Personal essay, elegiac and reflective; mixes memories with poetic ideas. The writer is both friend and storyteller. Cultural references: Kashmiri culture, Hindustani music and Urdu poetry.
Deep dive: Themes
Friendship and loss; the dignity of the poet facing death; exile and belonging; poetry as a way of life; the cultural unity of India and Kashmir.
Hindi saransh
Ek dost ko shraddhanjali: Shahid Ali ki yaadein, kavita aur Kashmir.
The essay honours a friend whose love of poetry and homeland remained strong even in illness.

blocks.x: Birth by A. J. Cronin is an extract from The Citadel. Dr Andrew Manson, a young doctor in a Welsh mining town, attends a difficult delivery at the home of Susan Mutch, a poor woman. After a long labour he delivers the child, which appears stillborn. He gives priority to the mother, who is dangerously ill, and then hands the baby to the nurse, thinking it is dead. But he decides to make an effort to revive the child. He puts the baby alternately in hot and cold water, massages, and finally the baby gasps and cries. The mother survives too. The story shows the doctor's commitment, hope and the miracle of life. Themes: duty, perseverance, hope and the value of life.
Deep dive: Plot

Manson is called in the night to help Mrs Mutch. After a long wait, he delivers the baby, which is not breathing. Dr Hannah is not there. The mother is in danger. The nurse hands the baby to Manson who tries to revive it. He alternates between hot and cold water and rubs the child. After a long effort, the baby cries. The mother recovers.
Deep dive: Characters
Dr Andrew Manson: young, dedicated, thoughtful. Mrs Susan Mutch: young, brave mother. Hannah: the experienced doctor who later helps. The nurse: practical and caring. Mr Joe Mutch: father who waits.
Deep dive: Themes
Medical dedication; hope and persistence; the sanctity of life; the importance of not giving up; compassion.
Hindi saransh
Janm: ek doctor ki lagan se mrit samjhe gaye shishu ko jeevan milta hai.
The doctor's perseverance saved a baby that everyone thought was dead.

Birth by A. J. Cronin is an extract from The Citadel. Dr Andrew Manson, a young doctor in a Welsh mining town, attends a difficult delivery at the home of Susan Mutch, a poor woman. After a long labour he delivers the child, which appears stillborn. He gives priority to the mother, who is dangerously ill, and then hands the baby to the nurse, thinking it is dead. But he decides to make an effort to revive the child. He puts the baby alternately in hot and cold water, massages, and finally the baby gasps and cries. The mother survives too. The story shows the doctor's commitment, hope and the miracle of life. Themes: duty, perseverance, hope and the value of life.

lessons.title: The Tale of Melon City
yt: class 11 english snapshots the tale of melon city vikram seth

blocks.x: The Tale of Melon City by Vikram Seth is a humorous poem in a narrative form and a satire. A king builds an arch across a road. When the king passes under it, his crown is knocked off because the arch is too low. The king orders the chief builder to be hanged. The chief builder blames the workmen, who blame the architect, who blames the king himself. Finally the blame reaches the king, who is too proud to accept it. The wise men then say that the noose must hang whoever it fits, and since it fits only the king, he is spared by a trick: to avoid hanging, the king insists that the man who is hanged must be the one worthy of the throne. The ministers decide that the next person to pass by will be made king; the passer-by is an idiot who says he wants to be a melon, and the melon is crowned. The city is called Melon City. The poem satirises political folly and arbitrary rulers. Themes: absurdity of authority, satire, justice.
Deep dive: Plot

The king builds a royal arch. His crown is knocked off. He orders the chief builder to be hanged. Each person passes blame until it comes to the king. The courtiers say the noose fits the king. The king is made to realise that justice is blind; the king asks the wise men. The ministers decide to choose a king by chance: the next person to pass is an idiot. The idiot says that he wants a melon. The melon is crowned. The city is called Melon City.
Deep dive: Satire

The poem mocks absurd laws and the arbitrary power of rulers, the foolishness of officials and the way of passing blame. It shows an unjust system in comic form and that rulers can be as foolish as their subjects.
Deep dive: Style
Simple rhyming couplets, fable-like, humorous, an ironic tone; the language is light and the story builds to an absurd ending.

Kharbuje ke shahar ki kahani: vyangya, jahan raja ki jagah kharbooja shaasak banta hai.
The poem uses humour to satirise unjust and foolish rulers.

lessons.title: Writing Skills: Notice, Poster, Letter, Article, Speech and Debate
yt: class 11 english core writing skills notice poster letter article speech debate format

blocks.x: Writing skills in Class 11 English Core cover notices, posters, letters (to the editor, business and job application), articles, speeches and debates. Each format has its own layout, tone and length. A notice has the name of the issuing body, the word NOTICE, date, heading, body in 50 words, and the name and designation of the writer. A poster has a catchy heading, brief matter, visuals and details of the issuing authority. A formal letter has the sender address, date, receiver address, subject, salutation, body, complimentary close and signature. An article has a title, byline and body of introduction, development and conclusion. A speech opens by greeting the audience and closes with thanks. A debate presents the arguments for or against a motion with evidence and rebuttal.
Deep dive: Notices and posters

Notice: issuing body, NOTICE, date, heading, matter (who, what, when, where, contact), signature with name and designation. Poster: bold title, slogan, concise matter, contact details, a visual idea, and the issuing authority. Both must be brief and to the point.
Deep dive: Letters

Formal letter: sender address, date, receiver, subject line, salutation (Sir or Madam), body (introduction, details, request), close (Yours faithfully) and signature. Letters to the editor express opinion on public issues. Job application letters give qualifications and attach a resume. Business letters make orders or complaints.
Deep dive: Articles, speeches and debates

Article: title, byline, introduction, body, conclusion. Speech: greeting, topic, arguments, appeal, thanks. Debate: opening, points for or against, counter-arguments and conclusion. Use formal vocabulary, linking words and facts; keep to the word limit.
Hindi saransh
Lekhan kaushal: soochna, poster, patra, lekh, bhashan aur vaad-vivaad ke praroop.
Follow the format exactly: examiners award marks for layout, content, expression and accuracy.

Writing Skills: Notice, Poster, Letter, Article, Speech and Debate

Writing skills in Class 11 English Core cover notices, posters, letters (to the editor, business and job application), articles, speeches and debates

Flat concept map (2D)

🔑

Big idea

  • Writing skills in Class 11 English Core cover notices, posters, letters (to the editor, business and job application), articles, speeches and debates
  • Each format has its own layout, tone and length
  • A notice has the name of the issuing body, the word NOTICE, date, heading, body in 50 words, and the name and designation of the writer
  • A poster has a catchy heading, brief matter, visuals and details of the issuing authority
Read the full explanation

Writing skills in Class 11 English Core cover notices, posters, letters (to the editor, business and job application), articles, speeches and debates. Each format has its own layout, tone and length. A notice has the name of the issuing body, the word NOTICE, date, heading, body in 50 words, and the name and designation of the writer. A poster has a catchy heading, brief matter, visuals and details of the issuing authority. A formal letter has the sender address, date, receiver address, subject, salutation, body, complimentary close and signature. An article has a title, byline and body of introduction, development and conclusion. A speech opens by greeting the audience and closes with thanks. A debate presents the arguments for or against a motion with evidence and rebuttal.

📌

Notices and posters

  • Notice: issuing body, NOTICE, date, heading, matter (who, what, when, where, contact), signature with name and designation
  • Poster: bold title, slogan, concise matter, contact details, a visual idea, and the issuing authority
  • Both must be brief and to the point
🧠

Letters

  • Formal letter: sender address, date, receiver, subject line, salutation (Sir or Madam), body (introduction, details, request), close (Yours…
  • Letters to the editor express opinion on public issues
  • Job application letters give qualifications and attach a resume
  • Business letters make orders or complaints
🌟

Articles, speeches and debates

  • Article: title, byline, introduction, body, conclusion
  • Speech: greeting, topic, arguments, appeal, thanks
  • Debate: opening, points for or against, counter-arguments and conclusion
  • Use formal vocabulary, linking words and facts
Read the full explanation

Article: title, byline, introduction, body, conclusion. Speech: greeting, topic, arguments, appeal, thanks. Debate: opening, points for or against, counter-arguments and conclusion. Use formal vocabulary, linking words and facts; keep to the word limit.

🧮

SpeechGreeting, points, thanksAudience
🎯 Remember Follow the format exactly: examiners award marks for layout, content, expression and accuracy.

lessons.title: Grammar and Reading Comprehension
yt: class 11 english core grammar tenses modals determiners reported speech passive

blocks.x: Grammar and reading comprehension skills tested in Class 11 include determiners, tenses, modals, subject-verb agreement, reported speech, the active and passive voice, gap filling, editing and omission. Reading comprehension passages test understanding, inference, vocabulary and summarising. Rules: a singular subject takes a singular verb; modals such as can, could, may, might, must, should express ability, permission, possibility or obligation; reported speech shifts tense back and changes pronouns and time words; the passive voice uses the form of be plus the past participle. For reading, read the questions first, scan the passage, locate answers and use own words where required.
Deep dive: Tenses and agreement

Simple present for habits and facts; present continuous for ongoing actions; present perfect for results linked to now; simple past for finished actions; past perfect for an earlier past action. Subject-verb agreement: each, every, either, neither take a singular verb; a plural subject takes a plural verb; two subjects joined by and take a plural verb.
Deep dive: Modals and determiners

Can shows ability; may shows permission or possibility; must shows necessity; should shows advice; would shows a polite request. Determiners: a, an, the, some, any, much, many, few, little, each, every.
Deep dive: Reported speech and passive

Direct to indirect: say becomes said, present becomes past, here becomes there, today becomes that day, now becomes then. Passive: object becomes subject, be plus past participle, by the agent. Reading: skim, scan, infer.
Hindi saransh
Vyakaran aur gadyansh: tense, modals, reported speech, passive voice aur anuchhed samajh.
In editing, check each line for tense, agreement, preposition and article errors.

Grammar and reading comprehension skills tested in Class 11 include determiners, tenses, modals, subject-verb agreement, reported speech, the active and passive voice, gap filling, editing and omission. Reading comprehension passages test understanding, inference, vocabulary and summarising. Rules: a singular subject takes a singular verb; modals such as can, could, may, might, must, should express ability, permission, possibility or obligation; reported speech shifts tense back and changes pronouns and time words; the passive voice uses the form of be plus the past participle. For reading, read the questions first, scan the passage, locate answers and use own words where required.

📌

Tenses and agreement

  • Simple present for habits and facts
  • Present continuous for ongoing actions
  • Present perfect for results linked to now
  • Simple past for finished actions
Read the full explanation

Simple present for habits and facts; present continuous for ongoing actions; present perfect for results linked to now; simple past for finished actions; past perfect for an earlier past action. Subject-verb agreement: each, every, either, neither take a singular verb; a plural subject takes a plural verb; two subjects joined by and take a plural verb.

🧠

Modals and determiners

  • Can shows ability
  • May shows permission or possibility
  • Must shows necessity
  • Should shows advice
Read the full explanation

Can shows ability; may shows permission or possibility; must shows necessity; should shows advice; would shows a polite request. Determiners: a, an, the, some, any, much, many, few, little, each, every.

🌟

Reported speech and passive

  • Direct to indirect: say becomes said, present becomes past, here becomes there, today becomes that day, now becomes then
  • Passive: object becomes subject, be plus past participle, by the agent
  • Reading: skim, scan, infer

blocks.x: Geography is the study of the earth as the home of humankind. The word comes from the Greek geo (earth) and graphos (description). Eratosthenes first used the term and calculated the circumference of the earth. Geography studies the spatial distribution of phenomena, the relationships between humans and the environment, and the changes over time. It is an integrating discipline that draws from natural and social sciences. Its two main branches are physical geography and human geography. Physical geography includes geomorphology, climatology, hydrology and soil geography; human geography includes social, economic, population and settlement geography. Approaches include systematic and regional approaches, and the discipline uses maps, GIS and remote sensing. The dualisms of physical versus human, systematic versus regional and ideographic versus nomothetic have shaped the subject.
Deep dive: Scope and branches

Physical geography studies the natural environment: the lithosphere, atmosphere, hydrosphere and biosphere. Human geography studies people, cultures, economies and settlements. Biogeography links life to environment. Systematic geography studies a phenomenon across the world; regional geography studies all phenomena in one region.
Deep dive: Approaches and thinkers

Eratosthenes coined the word geography. Humboldt and Ritter founded modern geography in Germany. Ratzel proposed environmental determinism; Vidal de la Blache proposed possibilism; Griffith Taylor proposed neo-determinism or stop-and-go determinism. Geography is both a science and an art of description.
Deep dive: Tools and importance

Maps, globes, GIS, GPS and remote sensing are major tools. Geography helps in planning, resource management, disaster preparedness and understanding the environment. Career fields include cartography, planning, meteorology and environmental management.

lessons.title: The Origin and Evolution of the Earth
yt: class 11 geography origin and evolution of the earth big bang nebular hypothesis

blocks.x: Theories of the origin of the earth range from early ideas of Kant and Laplace's nebular hypothesis to the modern Big Bang theory. Kant proposed a cold, slowly rotating nebula; Laplace modified this into a hot, rotating nebula that threw off rings that condensed into planets. Chamberlin and Moulton proposed the planetesimal hypothesis, in which a passing star pulled material from the sun. Jeans and Jeffreys proposed the tidal hypothesis. Later, Otto Schmidt and Carl Weizsacker proposed a dust cloud around the sun. The modern theory is the Big Bang, proposed by Georges Lemaitre and supported by Edwin Hubble's expanding universe, in which the universe began about 13.7 billion years ago from a tiny, extremely dense point. Stars formed within galaxies from nebulae; planets formed by accretion within the solar nebula. The earth formed about 4.6 billion years ago, differentiated into core, mantle and crust, and its atmosphere evolved in three stages with the help of volcanic outgassing; life began about 3.8 billion years ago.
Deep dive: Early theories

Kant (1755) proposed a gaseous nebula. Laplace (1796) described a hot rotating nebula that shed rings. Chamberlin and Moulton proposed the planetesimal hypothesis. Jeans and Jeffreys proposed the tidal hypothesis. Schmidt, Weizsacker and Kuiper developed dust-cloud models. Hoyle proposed the steady-state hypothesis; Lemaitre proposed the primeval atom, and Hubble showed the galaxies were receding.
Deep dive: Big Bang and solar system

About 13.7 billion years ago the universe was in a single dense point; it expanded. Stars formed from clouds of hydrogen; within the solar nebula, planetesimals formed planets by accretion. The inner planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars) are terrestrial; the outer planets (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune) are Jovian. The moon is thought to have formed from a giant impact with a Mars-sized body.
Deep dive: Evolution of the earth

Earth became layered by density differentiation; heavier iron sank to the core. The early atmosphere of hydrogen and helium was lost; volcanic outgassing added water vapour, carbon dioxide, nitrogen and ammonia. Cooling led to rain and oceans. Life arose in the oceans; photosynthesis added oxygen.

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

The Origin and Evolution of the Earth

Theories of the origin of the earth range from early ideas of Kant and Laplace's nebular hypothesis to the modern Big Bang theory

Earth4.6 billion years
Life3.8 billion years
Hubble1920s
🔑

Big idea

  • Theories of the origin of the earth range from early ideas of Kant and Laplace's nebular hypothesis to the modern Big Bang theory
  • Kant proposed a cold, slowly rotating nebula
  • Laplace modified this into a hot, rotating nebula that threw off rings that condensed into planets
  • Chamberlin and Moulton proposed the planetesimal hypothesis, in which a passing star pulled material from the sun
Read the full explanation

Theories of the origin of the earth range from early ideas of Kant and Laplace's nebular hypothesis to the modern Big Bang theory. Kant proposed a cold, slowly rotating nebula; Laplace modified this into a hot, rotating nebula that threw off rings that condensed into planets. Chamberlin and Moulton proposed the planetesimal hypothesis, in which a passing star pulled material from the sun. Jeans and Jeffreys proposed the tidal hypothesis. Later, Otto Schmidt and Carl Weizsacker proposed a dust cloud around the sun. The modern theory is the Big Bang, proposed by Georges Lemaitre and supported by Edwin Hubble's expanding universe, in which the universe began about 13.7 billion years ago from a tiny, extremely dense point. Stars formed within galaxies from nebulae; planets formed by accretion within the solar nebula. The earth formed about 4.6 billion years ago, differentiated into core, mantle and crust, and its atmosphere evolved in three stages with the help of volcanic outgassing; life began about 3.8 billion years ago.

📌

Early theories

  • Kant (1755) proposed a gaseous nebula
  • Laplace (1796) described a hot rotating nebula that shed rings
  • Chamberlin and Moulton proposed the planetesimal hypothesis
  • Jeans and Jeffreys proposed the tidal hypothesis
Read the full explanation

Kant (1755) proposed a gaseous nebula. Laplace (1796) described a hot rotating nebula that shed rings. Chamberlin and Moulton proposed the planetesimal hypothesis. Jeans and Jeffreys proposed the tidal hypothesis. Schmidt, Weizsacker and Kuiper developed dust-cloud models. Hoyle proposed the steady-state hypothesis; Lemaitre proposed the primeval atom, and Hubble showed the galaxies were receding.

🧠

Big Bang and solar system

  • About 13.7 billion years ago the universe was in a single dense point
  • Stars formed from clouds of hydrogen
  • Within the solar nebula, planetesimals formed planets by accretion
  • The inner planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars) are terrestrial
Read the full explanation

About 13.7 billion years ago the universe was in a single dense point; it expanded. Stars formed from clouds of hydrogen; within the solar nebula, planetesimals formed planets by accretion. The inner planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars) are terrestrial; the outer planets (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune) are Jovian. The moon is thought to have formed from a giant impact with a Mars-sized body.

🌟

Evolution of the earth

  • Earth became layered by density differentiation
  • Heavier iron sank to the core
  • The early atmosphere of hydrogen and helium was lost
  • Volcanic outgassing added water vapour, carbon dioxide, nitrogen and ammonia
Read the full explanation

Earth became layered by density differentiation; heavier iron sank to the core. The early atmosphere of hydrogen and helium was lost; volcanic outgassing added water vapour, carbon dioxide, nitrogen and ammonia. Cooling led to rain and oceans. Life arose in the oceans; photosynthesis added oxygen.

lessons.title: Interior of the Earth
yt: class 11 geography interior of the earth seismic waves crust mantle core

blocks.x: The interior of the earth cannot be seen directly; it is studied through direct sources such as mining, drilling and volcanic eruptions, and indirect sources such as temperature, pressure and density with depth, meteorites, gravity, magnetic fields and, most importantly, seismic waves. Earthquakes produce body waves (P and S waves) and surface waves (L waves). P waves are primary or compressional waves that travel through solids, liquids and gases; S waves are secondary or shear waves that travel only through solids. The shadow zones of P and S waves show that the outer core is liquid. The earth has three layers: the crust (thin, up to about 35 km in the continents and 5 km in oceans), the mantle (up to 2900 km) and the core (from 2900 km to 6371 km, with a liquid outer core and a solid inner core). The Mohorovicic discontinuity separates the crust from the mantle, the Gutenberg discontinuity separates the mantle from the core and the Lehmann discontinuity separates the outer and inner core. Volcanoes arise from magma and are classified as shield, composite, caldera, flood basalt and mid-ocean ridge types.
Deep dive: Sources and waves

Direct: surface rocks, mines, deep drilling (Kola, Russia), volcanoes. Indirect: temperature rises with depth, pressure and density increase, meteorites and gravity anomalies. Seismic waves: P waves are faster and longitudinal; S waves are slower and transverse; L waves travel along the surface and cause the most damage. The earthquake focus is where energy is released; the epicentre is the point above it.
Deep dive: Layers

Crust: silica and alumina (sial) in continents; silica and magnesium (sima) in oceans; average density about 3 g per cubic cm. Mantle: upper and lower, containing the asthenosphere, rich in iron and magnesium silicates; density 3.4 to 5.6. Core: nife (nickel and iron), density 9.9 to 13; temperature up to about 6000 degrees Celsius.
Deep dive: Earthquakes and volcanoes

Earthquake causes: faulting, volcanic activity, plate movement, human activity. Measured by the Richter scale (magnitude) and the Mercalli scale (intensity). Volcanoes: active, dormant and extinct; shield volcanoes are gentle; composite volcanoes are explosive; Krakatoa is an example of a caldera.

Prithvi ka bhitari bhaag: bhookampiya tarange, parat, moho aur gutenberg asamanyata, bhookamp aur jwalamukhi.
P waves pass through all media; S waves cannot pass through liquids, which proves the outer core is liquid.

🔑

Big idea

  • The interior of the earth cannot be seen directly
  • It is studied through direct sources such as mining, drilling and volcanic eruptions, and indirect sources such as temperature, pressure and density…
  • Earthquakes produce body waves (P and S waves) and surface waves (L waves)
  • P waves are primary or compressional waves that travel through solids, liquids and gases
Read the full explanation

The interior of the earth cannot be seen directly; it is studied through direct sources such as mining, drilling and volcanic eruptions, and indirect sources such as temperature, pressure and density with depth, meteorites, gravity, magnetic fields and, most importantly, seismic waves. Earthquakes produce body waves (P and S waves) and surface waves (L waves). P waves are primary or compressional waves that travel through solids, liquids and gases; S waves are secondary or shear waves that travel only through solids. The shadow zones of P and S waves show that the outer core is liquid. The earth has three layers: the crust (thin, up to about 35 km in the continents and 5 km in oceans), the mantle (up to 2900 km) and the core (from 2900 km to 6371 km, with a liquid outer core and a solid inner core). The Mohorovicic discontinuity separates the crust from the mantle, the Gutenberg discontinuity separates the mantle from the core and the Lehmann discontinuity separates the outer and inner core. Volcanoes arise from magma and are classified as shield, composite, caldera, flood basalt and mid-ocean ridge types.

🌊

Sources and waves

  • Direct: surface rocks, mines, deep drilling (Kola, Russia), volcanoes
  • Indirect: temperature rises with depth, pressure and density increase, meteorites and gravity anomalies
  • Seismic waves: P waves are faster and longitudinal
  • S waves are slower and transverse
Read the full explanation

Direct: surface rocks, mines, deep drilling (Kola, Russia), volcanoes. Indirect: temperature rises with depth, pressure and density increase, meteorites and gravity anomalies. Seismic waves: P waves are faster and longitudinal; S waves are slower and transverse; L waves travel along the surface and cause the most damage. The earthquake focus is where energy is released; the epicentre is the point above it.

🧠

Layers

  • Crust: silica and alumina (sial) in continents
  • Silica and magnesium (sima) in oceans
  • Average density about 3 g per cubic cm
  • Mantle: upper and lower, containing the asthenosphere, rich in iron and magnesium silicates
Read the full explanation

Crust: silica and alumina (sial) in continents; silica and magnesium (sima) in oceans; average density about 3 g per cubic cm. Mantle: upper and lower, containing the asthenosphere, rich in iron and magnesium silicates; density 3.4 to 5.6. Core: nife (nickel and iron), density 9.9 to 13; temperature up to about 6000 degrees Celsius.

🌟

Earthquakes and volcanoes

  • Earthquake causes: faulting, volcanic activity, plate movement, human activity
  • Measured by the Richter scale (magnitude) and the Mercalli scale (intensity)
  • Volcanoes: active, dormant and extinct
  • Shield volcanoes are gentle
Read the full explanation

Earthquake causes: faulting, volcanic activity, plate movement, human activity. Measured by the Richter scale (magnitude) and the Mercalli scale (intensity). Volcanoes: active, dormant and extinct; shield volcanoes are gentle; composite volcanoes are explosive; Krakatoa is an example of a caldera.

lessons.title: Distribution of Oceans and Continents
yt: class 11 geography continental drift plate tectonics sea floor spreading

blocks.x: The distribution of oceans and continents is explained by the theory of continental drift, sea floor spreading and plate tectonics. Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift in 1912: all continents were once joined as a supercontinent called Pangaea, surrounded by the Panthalassa ocean, which broke up into Laurasia and Gondwanaland and then drifted. His evidence included the matching coastlines of Africa and South America, similar rock formations, fossils such as Mesosaurus and Glossopteris, placer deposits and glaciation. Wegener suggested pole-fleeing and tidal forces as the cause, which were rejected. Harry Hess proposed sea floor spreading in the 1960s, based on mid-ocean ridges, magnetic anomalies and the age of the sea floor. Plate tectonics, proposed by McKenzie, Parker and Morgan, divided the lithosphere into seven major plates and several minor ones. The movement is driven by convection currents in the mantle. Plates move at divergent, convergent and transform boundaries. The Indian plate moved north, collided with the Eurasian plate and formed the Himalayas.
Deep dive: Continental drift

Pangaea, Panthalassa, Laurasia, Gondwanaland. Evidences: jigsaw fit, rocks of similar age, fossils, tillite deposits and placer deposits (gold in Ghana). Gondwana rocks in India, Africa, South America, Australia and Antarctica. Forces: pole-fleeing and tidal force were criticised.
Deep dive: Sea floor spreading

Mid-ocean ridges are underwater mountains with a rift; lava rises and spreads. The rocks near the ridge are young and those far away are older. Magnetic reversals recorded in rocks are symmetrical on both sides of the ridge. The ocean floor is no older than about 200 million years.
Deep dive: Plate tectonics

Major plates: Pacific, North American, South American, Eurasian, African, Indo-Australian and Antarctic. Boundaries: divergent (plates move apart, new crust forms), convergent (plates collide, subduction or mountain building) and transform (plates slide past). The Indian plate has moved about 15 cm per year at times, and now about 5 cm.

🔑

Big idea

  • The distribution of oceans and continents is explained by the theory of continental drift, sea floor spreading and plate tectonics
  • Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift in 1912: all continents were once joined as a supercontinent called Pangaea, surrounded by the Panthalassa…
  • His evidence included the matching coastlines of Africa and South America, similar rock formations, fossils such as Mesosaurus and Glossopteris…
  • Wegener suggested pole-fleeing and tidal forces as the cause, which were rejected
Read the full explanation

The distribution of oceans and continents is explained by the theory of continental drift, sea floor spreading and plate tectonics. Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift in 1912: all continents were once joined as a supercontinent called Pangaea, surrounded by the Panthalassa ocean, which broke up into Laurasia and Gondwanaland and then drifted. His evidence included the matching coastlines of Africa and South America, similar rock formations, fossils such as Mesosaurus and Glossopteris, placer deposits and glaciation. Wegener suggested pole-fleeing and tidal forces as the cause, which were rejected. Harry Hess proposed sea floor spreading in the 1960s, based on mid-ocean ridges, magnetic anomalies and the age of the sea floor. Plate tectonics, proposed by McKenzie, Parker and Morgan, divided the lithosphere into seven major plates and several minor ones. The movement is driven by convection currents in the mantle. Plates move at divergent, convergent and transform boundaries. The Indian plate moved north, collided with the Eurasian plate and formed the Himalayas.

📌

Continental drift

  • Pangaea, Panthalassa, Laurasia, Gondwanaland
  • Evidences: jigsaw fit, rocks of similar age, fossils, tillite deposits and placer deposits (gold in Ghana)
  • Gondwana rocks in India, Africa, South America, Australia and Antarctica
  • Forces: pole-fleeing and tidal force were criticised
🧠

Sea floor spreading

  • Mid-ocean ridges are underwater mountains with a rift
  • Lava rises and spreads
  • The rocks near the ridge are young and those far away are older
  • Magnetic reversals recorded in rocks are symmetrical on both sides of the ridge
Read the full explanation

Mid-ocean ridges are underwater mountains with a rift; lava rises and spreads. The rocks near the ridge are young and those far away are older. Magnetic reversals recorded in rocks are symmetrical on both sides of the ridge. The ocean floor is no older than about 200 million years.

🌟

Plate tectonics

  • Major plates: Pacific, North American, South American, Eurasian, African, Indo-Australian and Antarctic
  • Boundaries: divergent (plates move apart, new crust forms), convergent (plates collide, subduction or mountain building) and transform (plates slide…
  • The Indian plate has moved about 15 cm per year at times, and now about 5 cm
🧮

lessons.title: Minerals and Rocks
yt: class 11 geography minerals and rocks igneous sedimentary metamorphic rock cycle

blocks.x: A mineral is a naturally occurring, inorganic substance with a definite chemical composition and physical properties. Rocks are aggregates of minerals. Eight elements make up most of the crust: oxygen, silicon, aluminium, iron, calcium, sodium, potassium and magnesium. Major minerals include feldspar (most abundant), quartz, pyroxene, amphibole, mica and olivine. Physical properties: crystal form, cleavage, fracture, lustre, colour, streak, transparency, structure, hardness (the Mohs scale) and specific gravity. Rocks are of three types: igneous (formed by cooling of magma), sedimentary (formed by deposition and compaction of sediments) and metamorphic (formed by changes due to heat and pressure). Igneous rocks are classified as intrusive (granite, gabbro) and extrusive (basalt). Sedimentary rocks include sandstone, limestone and shale. Metamorphic rocks include slate, marble, quartzite and gneiss. The rock cycle explains the transformation of one rock type into another.
Deep dive: Minerals

Silicates (quartz, feldspar, mica) are the most abundant; metallic minerals (ferrous, non-ferrous, precious) and non-metallic minerals. Properties: lustre, hardness, cleavage. Mohs scale from 1 (talc) to 10 (diamond).
Deep dive: Rocks

Igneous: primary rocks, no fossils, crystalline. Intrusive: granite (plutonic), dolerite. Extrusive: basalt. Sedimentary: layered, may contain fossils; mechanical (sandstone, conglomerate), organic (coal, limestone) and chemical (gypsum, rock salt). Metamorphic: changed by heat, pressure or fluids; shale to slate, limestone to marble, sandstone to quartzite, granite to gneiss, coal to graphite.
Deep dive: Rock cycle
Igneous rocks weather to sediments; sediments form sedimentary rocks; heat and pressure make metamorphic rocks; melting returns them to magma. The cycle is continuous and has no fixed start.

Khanij aur chattanein: aagneya, parteedaar aur roopantarit chattanein tatha chattan chakra.
Remember transformations: shale to slate, limestone to marble, sandstone to quartzite, granite to gneiss.

lessons.title: Geomorphic Processes and Landforms
yt: class 11 geography geomorphic processes weathering erosion deposition landforms

blocks.x: Geomorphic processes are the forces that shape the earth's surface. They are of two types: endogenic processes (from within the earth, such as diastrophism and volcanism) and exogenic processes (from outside, such as weathering, mass movement, erosion and deposition). Weathering is the in-situ breakdown of rocks by physical, chemical and biological means. Physical weathering includes frost action, exfoliation and thermal expansion; chemical weathering includes solution, carbonation, hydration, oxidation and reduction. Mass movements include creep, flow, slide and fall. Erosion and deposition are carried out by running water, groundwater, glaciers, waves and wind, which produce characteristic landforms. Running water forms V-shaped valleys, waterfalls, meanders, ox-bow lakes, floodplains and deltas. Glaciers produce cirques, U-shaped valleys, moraines and eskers. Groundwater forms karst topography with sinkholes, caves, stalactites and stalagmites. Waves create cliffs, beaches and sea stacks; winds create deflation hollows, mushroom rocks, barchans and loess.
Deep dive: Processes

Endogenic: diastrophism (folding, faulting), volcanism, earthquakes. Exogenic: weathering, mass wasting, erosion and transport, deposition. Gradation: degradation (lowering of relief) and aggradation (raising by deposition). Soil formation is a result of weathering; its factors are parent material, topography, climate, organisms and time.
Deep dive: Weathering and mass movement

Physical: frost wedging, salt weathering, exfoliation (onion skin), block disintegration. Chemical: carbonation of limestone, oxidation of iron. Biological: roots, burrowing animals. Mass movements: soil creep, mudflow, landslide, rockfall and slump, triggered by gravity and water.
Deep dive: Landforms

River: gorges, canyons, meanders, ox-bow lakes, levees, deltas. Glacier: cirques, arêtes, horns, hanging valleys, fjords, drumlins. Karst: sinkholes, uvalas, dolines, stalactites. Coast: stacks, arches, spits. Wind: barchans, seif dunes, yardangs.
Hindi saransh
Bhu-aakritik prakram aur sthalakritiyan: apakshay, apardan, nadi, himnad, bhumigat jal, tarang aur pavan.
Remember: endogenic forces build the relief, exogenic forces wear it down, and gradation levels it.

Geomorphic Processes and Landforms

Geomorphic processes are the forces that shape the earth's surface

🔑

Big idea

  • Geomorphic processes are the forces that shape the earth's surface
  • They are of two types: endogenic processes (from within the earth, such as diastrophism and volcanism) and exogenic processes (from outside, such as…
  • Weathering is the in-situ breakdown of rocks by physical, chemical and biological means
  • Physical weathering includes frost action, exfoliation and thermal expansion
Read the full explanation

Geomorphic processes are the forces that shape the earth's surface. They are of two types: endogenic processes (from within the earth, such as diastrophism and volcanism) and exogenic processes (from outside, such as weathering, mass movement, erosion and deposition). Weathering is the in-situ breakdown of rocks by physical, chemical and biological means. Physical weathering includes frost action, exfoliation and thermal expansion; chemical weathering includes solution, carbonation, hydration, oxidation and reduction. Mass movements include creep, flow, slide and fall. Erosion and deposition are carried out by running water, groundwater, glaciers, waves and wind, which produce characteristic landforms. Running water forms V-shaped valleys, waterfalls, meanders, ox-bow lakes, floodplains and deltas. Glaciers produce cirques, U-shaped valleys, moraines and eskers. Groundwater forms karst topography with sinkholes, caves, stalactites and stalagmites. Waves create cliffs, beaches and sea stacks; winds create deflation hollows, mushroom rocks, barchans and loess.

🔄

Processes

  • Endogenic: diastrophism (folding, faulting), volcanism, earthquakes
  • Exogenic: weathering, mass wasting, erosion and transport, deposition
  • Gradation: degradation (lowering of relief) and aggradation (raising by deposition)
  • Soil formation is a result of weathering
Read the full explanation

Endogenic: diastrophism (folding, faulting), volcanism, earthquakes. Exogenic: weathering, mass wasting, erosion and transport, deposition. Gradation: degradation (lowering of relief) and aggradation (raising by deposition). Soil formation is a result of weathering; its factors are parent material, topography, climate, organisms and time.

🕰️

Weathering and mass movement

  • Physical: frost wedging, salt weathering, exfoliation (onion skin), block disintegration
  • Chemical: carbonation of limestone, oxidation of iron
  • Biological: roots, burrowing animals
  • Mass movements: soil creep, mudflow, landslide, rockfall and slump, triggered by gravity and water
🌟

Landforms

  • River: gorges, canyons, meanders, ox-bow lakes, levees, deltas
  • Glacier: cirques, arêtes, horns, hanging valleys, fjords, drumlins
  • Karst: sinkholes, uvalas, dolines, stalactites
  • Coast: stacks, arches, spits
Read the full explanation

River: gorges, canyons, meanders, ox-bow lakes, levees, deltas. Glacier: cirques, arêtes, horns, hanging valleys, fjords, drumlins. Karst: sinkholes, uvalas, dolines, stalactites. Coast: stacks, arches, spits. Wind: barchans, seif dunes, yardangs.

lessons.title: Composition and Structure of the Atmosphere
yt: class 11 geography composition and structure of the atmosphere layers

blocks.x: The atmosphere is the envelope of gases around the earth held by gravity. By volume, dry air has about 78 percent nitrogen, 21 percent oxygen, 0.93 percent argon, 0.04 percent carbon dioxide and traces of neon, helium, ozone and hydrogen. Water vapour varies from 0 to 4 percent and dust particles act as hygroscopic nuclei. The atmosphere has five layers: the troposphere (average 13 km, up to 18 km at the equator and 8 km at the poles; temperature falls at 6.5 degrees Celsius per km, the layer of weather), the stratosphere (to about 50 km; contains the ozone layer, with temperature rising upward), the mesosphere (to about 80 km; coldest, up to minus 100 degrees Celsius), the thermosphere (80 to 400 km; ionosphere reflects radio waves; temperature rises up to 1000 degrees Celsius) and the exosphere (the uppermost layer merging into space). The tropopause, stratopause and mesopause are the boundaries between layers.
Deep dive: Composition

Gases: nitrogen 78.08, oxygen 20.95, argon 0.93, carbon dioxide 0.036. Oxygen supports respiration; nitrogen dilutes oxygen and is used in fixation; carbon dioxide absorbs heat and causes the greenhouse effect; ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation. Water vapour is the source of clouds and rain. Dust gives rise to scattering, red sunsets and condensation.
Deep dive: Layers

Troposphere: contains 90 percent of air, weather occurs, temperature falls with height. Stratosphere: ozone, stable, jet aeroplanes. Mesosphere: meteors burn. Thermosphere: aurora, satellites, ionosphere. Exosphere: lightest gases escape.
Deep dive: Importance

The atmosphere provides air for breathing, shields from ultraviolet rays, regulates temperature and supports the water cycle. Ozone depletion, caused by CFCs, makes the ozone hole over the Antarctic. The Montreal Protocol of 1987 phased out CFCs.
Hindi saransh
Vayumandal ki sanrachna aur sanghatan: tropospher, stratospher, mesospher, thermospher aur exospher.
Weather occurs only in the troposphere; the ozone layer is in the stratosphere.

The tropopause, stratopause and mesopause are the boundaries between layers.

  • Nitrogen dilutes oxygen and is used in fixation

blocks.x: The earth receives energy from the sun as short-wave radiation called insolation. The amount of insolation received at the top of the atmosphere is about 1.94 calories per square cm per minute, called the solar constant. Insolation varies with the angle of the sun's rays, the length of the day, the transparency of the atmosphere and the land's configuration. The earth is at perihelion (nearest, about 147 million km) on 3 January and at aphelion (farthest, 152 million km) on 4 July. Of 100 units of insolation, about 35 are reflected back (the albedo), 14 are absorbed by the atmosphere and 51 reach the earth's surface. The earth radiates 51 units as terrestrial radiation, and the heat budget is balanced. Heating takes place through conduction, convection, advection and radiation. The temperature decreases with height at the normal lapse rate of 6.5 C per km. Temperature inversion occurs when the temperature rises with height, such as on long winter nights with clear skies and calm air. Isotherms are lines joining places of equal temperature. The range of temperature, latitudes, altitude, ocean currents and distance from the sea control temperature.
Deep dive: Insolation

Solar constant 1.94 cal per cm2 per min. Latitude and the angle of the sun's rays decide the heat. Cloud cover, aerosols and land-sea contrast alter it. The albedo of the earth is 35 percent. The heat budget: 100 units in, 35 reflected, 14 absorbed in the air, 51 absorbed at the surface; then 51 radiated. Atmosphere radiates 48 in total and 34 comes from the surface; this leaves the earth neither warming nor cooling.
Deep dive: Heating and cooling

Conduction in contact; convection vertical; advection horizontal (the most important in mid-latitudes). Sunshine heats the land faster than the sea. Terrestrial radiation heats the atmosphere from below, which is why the temperature falls with height. The greenhouse effect traps outgoing radiation.
Deep dive: Temperature distribution

January and July isotherms bend over oceans and continents. Equator has high temperature and low range; continental interiors have high range. Cold and warm currents change coastal temperature. Temperature inversion produces fog and smog and is common in valleys.

lessons.title: Atmospheric Circulation and Weather Systems
yt: class 11 geography atmospheric circulation pressure belts winds monsoon cyclones

blocks.x: Atmospheric pressure is the weight of the column of air and is measured by a barometer in millibars. Pressure decreases with height. The pressure belts on the earth are the equatorial low, the subtropical highs, the subpolar lows and the polar highs. Winds blow from high to low pressure and are deflected by the Coriolis force (right in the northern hemisphere and left in the southern). The planetary winds are the trade winds (easterlies), the westerlies and the polar easterlies. Seasonal winds include monsoons; local winds include land and sea breezes, mountain and valley breezes, loo, foehn and chinook. General circulation has three cells: Hadley, Ferrel and Polar. Jet streams are narrow bands of fast winds in the upper troposphere. El Nino is the warming of the Pacific off Peru, which weakens the Southwest monsoon; La Nina is the opposite. Air masses (continental, maritime) meet at fronts. Cyclones are low-pressure systems; tropical cyclones form over warm seas and have eyes. Thunderstorms and tornadoes are localised systems.
Deep dive: Pressure and winds

Pressure gradient force, Coriolis force and friction determine wind direction. Geostrophic wind blows parallel to isobars. Trade winds blow from subtropical highs to the equator; westerlies from subtropical highs to subpolar lows; polar easterlies from polar highs. The Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone shifts with the sun.
Deep dive: Cells and jet streams

Hadley cell: 0 to 30 degrees; Ferrel cell: 30 to 60; Polar cell: 60 to 90. Subtropical jet stream and polar front jet stream. Jet streams affect the monsoon and western disturbances. Walker circulation links to El Nino and the Southern Oscillation.
Deep dive: Weather systems

Air masses: cP, cT, mP, mT. Fronts: cold front, warm front, occluded front. Temperate cyclones form at the polar front and travel west to east. Tropical cyclones have winds over 120 km per hour, a calm eye and torrential rain: hurricanes in the Atlantic, typhoons in the China Sea, cyclones in the Indian Ocean, willy-willies in Australia. Thunderstorms arise from convection, and tornadoes are narrow, violent funnels.

Vayumandalaya parisanchalan aur mausam tantra: dabav peti, pavan, jet dhara, vaat agra aur chakravaat.

Visual lesson

Atmospheric Circulation and Weather Systems

Atmospheric pressure is the weight of the column of air and is measured by a barometer in millibars

minutes

Q&A

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Pressure and winds›3Cells and jet streams›4Weather systems
🔑

Big idea

  • Atmospheric pressure is the weight of the column of air and is measured by a barometer in millibars
  • Pressure decreases with height
  • The pressure belts on the earth are the equatorial low, the subtropical highs, the subpolar lows and the polar highs
  • Winds blow from high to low pressure and are deflected by the Coriolis force (right in the northern hemisphere and left in the southern)
Read the full explanation

Atmospheric pressure is the weight of the column of air and is measured by a barometer in millibars. Pressure decreases with height. The pressure belts on the earth are the equatorial low, the subtropical highs, the subpolar lows and the polar highs. Winds blow from high to low pressure and are deflected by the Coriolis force (right in the northern hemisphere and left in the southern). The planetary winds are the trade winds (easterlies), the westerlies and the polar easterlies. Seasonal winds include monsoons; local winds include land and sea breezes, mountain and valley breezes, loo, foehn and chinook. General circulation has three cells: Hadley, Ferrel and Polar. Jet streams are narrow bands of fast winds in the upper troposphere. El Nino is the warming of the Pacific off Peru, which weakens the Southwest monsoon; La Nina is the opposite. Air masses (continental, maritime) meet at fronts. Cyclones are low-pressure systems; tropical cyclones form over warm seas and have eyes. Thunderstorms and tornadoes are localised systems.

📌

Pressure and winds

  • Pressure gradient force, Coriolis force and friction determine wind direction
  • Geostrophic wind blows parallel to isobars
  • Trade winds blow from subtropical highs to the equator
  • Westerlies from subtropical highs to subpolar lows
Read the full explanation

Pressure gradient force, Coriolis force and friction determine wind direction. Geostrophic wind blows parallel to isobars. Trade winds blow from subtropical highs to the equator; westerlies from subtropical highs to subpolar lows; polar easterlies from polar highs. The Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone shifts with the sun.

🧬

Cells and jet streams

  • Hadley cell: 0 to 30 degrees
  • Ferrel cell: 30 to 60
  • Polar cell: 60 to 90
  • Subtropical jet stream and polar front jet stream
Read the full explanation

Hadley cell: 0 to 30 degrees; Ferrel cell: 30 to 60; Polar cell: 60 to 90. Subtropical jet stream and polar front jet stream. Jet streams affect the monsoon and western disturbances. Walker circulation links to El Nino and the Southern Oscillation.

🌟

Weather systems

  • Air masses: cP, cT, mP, mT
  • Fronts: cold front, warm front, occluded front
  • Temperate cyclones form at the polar front and travel west to east
  • Tropical cyclones have winds over 120 km per hour, a calm eye and torrential rain: hurricanes in the Atlantic, typhoons in the China Sea, cyclones in…
Read the full explanation

Air masses: cP, cT, mP, mT. Fronts: cold front, warm front, occluded front. Temperate cyclones form at the polar front and travel west to east. Tropical cyclones have winds over 120 km per hour, a calm eye and torrential rain: hurricanes in the Atlantic, typhoons in the China Sea, cyclones in the Indian Ocean, willy-willies in Australia. Thunderstorms arise from convection, and tornadoes are narrow, violent funnels.

lessons.title: Water in the Atmosphere
yt: class 11 geography water in the atmosphere humidity clouds precipitation

blocks.x: Water vapour enters the atmosphere by evaporation, transpiration and sublimation. Humidity is the amount of water vapour in the air. Absolute humidity is the weight of water vapour per unit volume of air in grams per cubic metre; relative humidity is the percentage of moisture the air holds relative to its capacity at that temperature; specific humidity is the mass of vapour per kg of air. Saturation occurs when the air holds the maximum vapour; the temperature at which it occurs is the dew point. Condensation occurs when air cools to dew point. Forms of condensation include dew, frost, fog, mist and clouds. Clouds are classified as high clouds (cirrus, cirrostratus, cirrocumulus), middle clouds (altocumulus, altostratus), low clouds (stratus, stratocumulus, nimbostratus) and clouds of vertical development (cumulus and cumulonimbus). Precipitation takes the forms of rain, snow, sleet and hail. Types of rainfall are convectional, orographic and cyclonic or frontal. World rainfall is highest near the equator and on windward slopes, and low in the deserts.
Deep dive: Humidity

Absolute, specific and relative. Relative humidity = actual vapour divided by capacity times 100. Warm air holds more vapour. Evaporation depends on temperature, wind, humidity and the surface area. The dew point is the temperature at which air becomes saturated.
Deep dive: Condensation and clouds

Condensation needs cooling and nuclei. Dew forms on cool surfaces; frost when the dew point is below freezing; fog is a cloud at ground level, and mist is thinner. Clouds: cirrus (wispy), cumulus (puffy), stratus (layered), nimbus (rain-bearing).
Deep dive: Rainfall

Convectional: heated ground, rising air, daily afternoon rain in the equatorial belt. Orographic: moist wind forced up a mountain; the leeward side is a rain shadow. Cyclonic: along fronts. Distribution: Equatorial belt over 250 cm; windward coasts; deserts under 25 cm. Isohyets join equal rainfall.
Hindi saransh
Vayumandal mein jal: aardrata, vaashpikaran, badal, varshan ke prakar aur vishwa mein varsha ka vitaran.
Remember: relative humidity depends on temperature; warm air holds more moisture, so cooling raises relative humidity.

🔑

Big idea

  • Water vapour enters the atmosphere by evaporation, transpiration and sublimation
  • Humidity is the amount of water vapour in the air
  • Absolute humidity is the weight of water vapour per unit volume of air in grams per cubic metre
  • Relative humidity is the percentage of moisture the air holds relative to its capacity at that temperature
Read the full explanation

Water vapour enters the atmosphere by evaporation, transpiration and sublimation. Humidity is the amount of water vapour in the air. Absolute humidity is the weight of water vapour per unit volume of air in grams per cubic metre; relative humidity is the percentage of moisture the air holds relative to its capacity at that temperature; specific humidity is the mass of vapour per kg of air. Saturation occurs when the air holds the maximum vapour; the temperature at which it occurs is the dew point. Condensation occurs when air cools to dew point. Forms of condensation include dew, frost, fog, mist and clouds. Clouds are classified as high clouds (cirrus, cirrostratus, cirrocumulus), middle clouds (altocumulus, altostratus), low clouds (stratus, stratocumulus, nimbostratus) and clouds of vertical development (cumulus and cumulonimbus). Precipitation takes the forms of rain, snow, sleet and hail. Types of rainfall are convectional, orographic and cyclonic or frontal. World rainfall is highest near the equator and on windward slopes, and low in the deserts.

📌

Humidity

  • Absolute, specific and relative
  • Relative humidity = actual vapour divided by capacity times 100
  • Warm air holds more vapour
  • Evaporation depends on temperature, wind, humidity and the surface area
Read the full explanation

Absolute, specific and relative. Relative humidity = actual vapour divided by capacity times 100. Warm air holds more vapour. Evaporation depends on temperature, wind, humidity and the surface area. The dew point is the temperature at which air becomes saturated.

🧠

Condensation and clouds

  • Condensation needs cooling and nuclei
  • Dew forms on cool surfaces
  • Frost when the dew point is below freezing
  • Fog is a cloud at ground level, and mist is thinner
Read the full explanation

Condensation needs cooling and nuclei. Dew forms on cool surfaces; frost when the dew point is below freezing; fog is a cloud at ground level, and mist is thinner. Clouds: cirrus (wispy), cumulus (puffy), stratus (layered), nimbus (rain-bearing).

🌟

Rainfall

  • Convectional: heated ground, rising air, daily afternoon rain in the equatorial belt
  • Orographic: moist wind forced up a mountain
  • The leeward side is a rain shadow
  • Cyclonic: along fronts
Read the full explanation

Convectional: heated ground, rising air, daily afternoon rain in the equatorial belt. Orographic: moist wind forced up a mountain; the leeward side is a rain shadow. Cyclonic: along fronts. Distribution: Equatorial belt over 250 cm; windward coasts; deserts under 25 cm. Isohyets join equal rainfall.

blocks.x: Climate is the average weather over about 30 years. Climatic classification by Koppen (1918, modified 1931) uses letter codes: A for tropical humid, B for dry, C for warm temperate, D for cold snow forest, E for polar and H for highland. Koppen's subtypes use second and third letters: f (no dry season), m (monsoon), w (dry winter), s (dry summer), W (desert), S (steppe), T (tundra), F (ice cap). Thornthwaite proposed a classification based on precipitation effectiveness and potential evapotranspiration. The climatic groups include Af (tropical wet), Am (monsoon), Aw (savanna), BWh (hot desert), BSh (steppe), Cs (Mediterranean), Cfa (humid subtropical), Cfb (marine west coast), Dfc (taiga), ET (tundra) and EF (ice cap). Climate change has occurred through geological time: ice ages and interglacials, driven by astronomical (Milankovitch cycles), volcanic and solar variations. Present global warming is due to the enhanced greenhouse effect from burning fossil fuels, deforestation and agriculture. Greenhouse gases include carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, CFCs and water vapour. Effects: rise in temperature of about 1.1 degrees Celsius since the pre-industrial era, melting of glaciers, sea-level rise and extreme weather. International efforts include the Kyoto Protocol (1997), the Paris Agreement (2015), and the IPCC.
Deep dive: Koppen classification

A: all months above 18 C. B: evaporation exceeds rainfall. C: coldest month between minus 3 and 18 C. D: coldest below minus 3 C and warmest above 10 C. E: warmest month below 10 C. H: highlands. Examples: Af in the Amazon and Congo basins; Aw in African and Indian savannas; Cs in Mediterranean lands; Dfc in Siberia; ET in Arctic tundra.
Deep dive: Past change

Evidence: tree rings, ice cores, pollen, lake sediments and historical records. Glacial periods and interglacials. Causes: Milankovitch cycles (eccentricity, tilt, precession), solar output, volcanism, plate tectonics.
Deep dive: Global warming

Greenhouse effect is natural; enhancement is due to human activity. Carbon dioxide levels have risen from 280 to above 415 ppm. Mitigation: renewable energy, afforestation, efficiency and international accords like Paris Agreement with a 1.5 to 2 C target. Carbon credits.

lessons.title: Oceans and Ocean Water Movements
yt: class 11 geography oceans relief waves tides currents

blocks.x: The oceans cover about 71 percent of the earth. The ocean floor has four major divisions: the continental shelf, the continental slope, the deep sea plain and the oceanic deeps or trenches. Minor relief features include mid-oceanic ridges, seamounts, guyots, canyons and atolls. The Mariana Trench in the Pacific is the deepest, about 11,000 metres. The temperature of ocean water decreases with depth and with latitude, and the thermocline is the zone of rapid temperature change. Salinity is the amount of salt in grams per thousand grams of water; average ocean salinity is 35 parts per thousand. It is very high in landlocked water bodies such as the Dead Sea (about 340 ppt) and Lake Van, and in the subtropical oceans where evaporation is high. Movements of ocean water are of three types: waves, tides and currents. Waves are caused by the wind; their parts are the crest, trough, wave height, wavelength, period and frequency. Tides are the rise and fall of sea level caused by the moon and sun's gravitation. Spring tides occur at new and full moon; neap tides occur at the first and third quarter. The tidal range is highest in the Bay of Fundy. Ocean currents are large streams of water flowing in a definite direction; they may be warm or cold. Major currents include the Gulf Stream, North Atlantic Drift, Kuroshio, Labrador, Canary, Humboldt (Peru), Benguela, California and Oyashio.
Deep dive: Relief and temperature

Continental shelf: gentle slope up to 200 m depth, rich in fisheries and petroleum. Continental slope: steep. Deep sea plain: flat, 3000 to 6000 m. Trenches: deepest. Temperature: surface warm at the equator, falls to near 0 at the poles. Salinity: higher where evaporation is high and inflow is low (Red Sea, subtropics), lower near river mouths and poles.
Deep dive: Waves and tides

Wave height depends on wind speed. Tsunamis are seismic sea waves. Tides: diurnal, semi-diurnal and mixed. Spring tide: sun, moon and earth in line. Neap tide: at right angles. Tides help navigation and tidal power.
Deep dive: Currents

Currents are driven by wind, temperature and salinity differences, and the Coriolis force deflects them. Gyres rotate clockwise in the northern hemisphere and anticlockwise in the southern. Warm currents: Gulf Stream, Kuroshio, Brazil, Agulhas. Cold currents: Labrador, Canary, Humboldt, Benguela, California. Effects: temperature, fog, fisheries (Grand Banks where warm and cold meet).

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Oceans and Ocean Water Movements

The oceans cover about 71 percent of the earth

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Relief and temperature›3Waves and tides›4Currents
Ocean area71%
Salinity35 ppt
Shelf200 m
🔑

Big idea

  • The oceans cover about 71 percent of the earth
  • The ocean floor has four major divisions: the continental shelf, the continental slope, the deep sea plain and the oceanic deeps or trenches
  • Minor relief features include mid-oceanic ridges, seamounts, guyots, canyons and atolls
  • The Mariana Trench in the Pacific is the deepest, about 11,000 metres
Read the full explanation

The oceans cover about 71 percent of the earth. The ocean floor has four major divisions: the continental shelf, the continental slope, the deep sea plain and the oceanic deeps or trenches. Minor relief features include mid-oceanic ridges, seamounts, guyots, canyons and atolls. The Mariana Trench in the Pacific is the deepest, about 11,000 metres. The temperature of ocean water decreases with depth and with latitude, and the thermocline is the zone of rapid temperature change. Salinity is the amount of salt in grams per thousand grams of water; average ocean salinity is 35 parts per thousand. It is very high in landlocked water bodies such as the Dead Sea (about 340 ppt) and Lake Van, and in the subtropical oceans where evaporation is high. Movements of ocean water are of three types: waves, tides and currents. Waves are caused by the wind; their parts are the crest, trough, wave height, wavelength, period and frequency. Tides are the rise and fall of sea level caused by the moon and sun's gravitation. Spring tides occur at new and full moon; neap tides occur at the first and third quarter. The tidal range is highest in the Bay of Fundy. Ocean currents are large streams of water flowing in a definite direction; they may be warm or cold. Major currents include the Gulf Stream, North Atlantic Drift, Kuroshio, Labrador, Canary, Humboldt (Peru), Benguela, California and Oyashio.

🌡️

Relief and temperature

  • Continental shelf: gentle slope up to 200 m depth, rich in fisheries and petroleum
  • Continental slope: steep
  • Deep sea plain: flat, 3000 to 6000 m
  • Trenches: deepest
Read the full explanation

Continental shelf: gentle slope up to 200 m depth, rich in fisheries and petroleum. Continental slope: steep. Deep sea plain: flat, 3000 to 6000 m. Trenches: deepest. Temperature: surface warm at the equator, falls to near 0 at the poles. Salinity: higher where evaporation is high and inflow is low (Red Sea, subtropics), lower near river mouths and poles.

🌊

Waves and tides

  • Wave height depends on wind speed
  • Tsunamis are seismic sea waves
  • Tides: diurnal, semi-diurnal and mixed
  • Spring tide: sun, moon and earth in line
Read the full explanation

Wave height depends on wind speed. Tsunamis are seismic sea waves. Tides: diurnal, semi-diurnal and mixed. Spring tide: sun, moon and earth in line. Neap tide: at right angles. Tides help navigation and tidal power.

⚡

Currents

  • Currents are driven by wind, temperature and salinity differences, and the Coriolis force deflects them
  • Gyres rotate clockwise in the northern hemisphere and anticlockwise in the southern
  • Warm currents: Gulf Stream, Kuroshio, Brazil, Agulhas
  • Cold currents: Labrador, Canary, Humboldt, Benguela, California
Read the full explanation

Currents are driven by wind, temperature and salinity differences, and the Coriolis force deflects them. Gyres rotate clockwise in the northern hemisphere and anticlockwise in the southern. Warm currents: Gulf Stream, Kuroshio, Brazil, Agulhas. Cold currents: Labrador, Canary, Humboldt, Benguela, California. Effects: temperature, fog, fisheries (Grand Banks where warm and cold meet).

lessons.title: Life on the Earth and Biodiversity
yt: class 11 geography biosphere ecosystem biodiversity conservation

blocks.x: The biosphere is the zone of life on the earth, formed by the interaction of the lithosphere, atmosphere and hydrosphere. An ecosystem is a functional unit of living organisms and their environment. The components are abiotic (soil, water, air, sunlight) and biotic (producers, consumers and decomposers). Energy flows through food chains and food webs in trophic levels; the 10 percent law states that only about 10 percent of energy passes to the next level. Ecological pyramids show numbers, biomass or energy. Biogeochemical cycles include the carbon, nitrogen, water, oxygen and phosphorus cycles. Biomes are large ecological regions: forest, grassland, desert, tundra and aquatic. Biodiversity is the variety of life at the level of genes, species and ecosystems. About 1.7 million species are described, and tropical regions have the highest diversity. Hotspots are areas with high endemism and threat; India has four hotspots: the Himalaya, the Western Ghats, Indo-Burma and the Sundaland (Nicobar). Threats include habitat loss, over-exploitation, invasive species and climate change. Conservation can be in situ (national parks, sanctuaries, biosphere reserves) or ex situ (zoos, botanical gardens, seed banks). The IUCN Red List classifies species as extinct, critically endangered, endangered, vulnerable and so on. International efforts include the Convention on Biological Diversity (Rio, 1992), CITES and the Ramsar Convention.
Deep dive: Ecosystem

Producers are green plants; primary consumers are herbivores; secondary and tertiary consumers are carnivores; decomposers are bacteria and fungi. Food chains: grazing and detritus. Ecological pyramids are upright (grassland) or inverted (number in a tree ecosystem). Biomes: tropical rainforest, savanna, temperate grassland, taiga, tundra and desert.
Deep dive: Cycles

Carbon cycle: photosynthesis, respiration, combustion, decomposition. Nitrogen cycle: fixation by bacteria and lightning, nitrification, assimilation, denitrification. Water cycle. Phosphorus cycle is sedimentary.
Deep dive: Biodiversity and conservation

Genetic, species and ecosystem diversity. Hotspots, endemism, extinction. Protected areas: national parks, wildlife sanctuaries and biosphere reserves such as Nilgiri. Project Tiger (1973), Project Elephant. Conservation helps for ecological balance, resources and ethics.
