lessons.title: भारतीय गायिकाओं में बेजोड़: लता मंगेशकर
yt: class 11 hindi vitan lata mangeshkar kumar gandharva ganpan

blocks.x: भारतीय गायिकाओं में बेजोड़ : लता मंगेशकर कुमार गंधर्व द्वारा लिखा गया व्यक्तित्व-चित्रण है। प्रसिद्ध शास्त्रीय गायक कुमार गंधर्व लता मंगेशकर की गायकी की विशेषताओं का विश्लेषण करते हैं। वे बताते हैं कि लता की आवाज़ में सुरीलापन, निर्मलता, सहजता और कोमलता है, जो उनकी सबसे बड़ी विशेषता है। उनके अनुसार लता के गायन में गानपन है, अर्थात गाना सुनने वाले को मनुष्य के हृदय तक पहुँचाने वाला आत्मीय तत्त्व। लता ने चित्रपट संगीत को लोकप्रिय बनाया और उसे शास्त्रीय गायन के बराबर प्रतिष्ठा दिलाई। कुमार गंधर्व मानते हैं कि तीन-साढ़े तीन मिनट के गीत में वही रस पैदा कर देना, जो शास्त्रीय संगीत की तीन घंटे की महफ़िल में होता है, लता की असाधारण उपलब्धि है। लता के स्वर में कहीं कोई कृत्रिमता नहीं है और उनकी गायकी में निश्छलता और अद्भुत तैयारी दिखाई देती है।
गहन अध्ययन: गानपन
गानपन वह गुण है जो गीत को सुनते ही दिल को छू लेता है। लता के गाने में यह स्वाभाविक रूप से मौजूद है, जो उन्हें अन्य गायिकाओं से अलग करता है।
गहन अध्ययन: लता की गायकी
लता का स्वर सुरीला, पतला और निर्मल है। गले में मिठास, स्वर की स्थिरता, शब्दों का स्पष्ट उच्चारण और गीत के भाव की सही अभिव्यक्ति उनकी विशेषताएँ हैं। कठिन तानें भी वे सहज ढंग से लेती हैं।
गहन अध्ययन: सिनेमा संगीत का योगदान
लता ने चित्रपट संगीत को जनसामान्य तक पहुँचाया। उन्होंने साधारण श्रोताओं में संगीत के प्रति रुचि पैदा की और सुरों के प्रति संवेदनशीलता बढ़ाई। शास्त्रीय और सुगम संगीत के बीच की दूरी कम की।
Hindi saransh
कुमार गंधर्व के अनुसार लता मंगेशकर का गानपन, सुरीलापन और सहजता उन्हें बेजोड़ बनाते हैं।
गानपन = गीत में वह आत्मीय सहजता जो सीधे हृदय को छू लेती है।

भारतीय गायिकाओं में बेजोड़ : लता मंगेशकर कुमार गंधर्व द्वारा लिखा गया व्यक्तित्व-चित्रण है। प्रसिद्ध शास्त्रीय गायक कुमार गंधर्व लता मंगेशकर की गायकी की विशेषताओं का विश्लेषण करते हैं। वे बताते हैं कि लता की आवाज़ में सुरीलापन, निर्मलता, सहजता और कोमलता है, जो उनकी सबसे बड़ी विशेषता है। उनके अनुसार लता के गायन में गानपन है, अर्थात गाना सुनने वाले को मनुष्य के हृदय तक पहुँचाने वाला आत्मीय तत्त्व। लता ने चित्रपट संगीत को लोकप्रिय बनाया और उसे शास्त्रीय गायन के बराबर प्रतिष्ठा दिलाई। कुमार गंधर्व मानते हैं कि तीन-साढ़े तीन मिनट के गीत में वही रस पैदा कर देना, जो शास्त्रीय संगीत की तीन घंटे की महफ़िल में होता है, लता की असाधारण उपलब्धि है। लता के स्वर में कहीं कोई कृत्रिमता नहीं है और उनकी गायकी में निश्छलता और अद्भुत तैयारी दिखाई देती है।

lessons.title: राजस्थान की रजत बूँदें
yt: class 11 hindi vitan rajasthan ki rajat bunden anupam mishra kuin

blocks.x: राजस्थान की रजत बूँदें अनुपम मिश्र की पुस्तक का अंश है जिसमें राजस्थान के मरुस्थलीय क्षेत्रों में जल-संचय की पारंपरिक पद्धतियों का वर्णन है। राजस्थान में वर्षा बहुत कम होती है, इसलिए वहाँ के लोगों ने वर्षा की हर बूँद को संजोने की कला विकसित की। पाठ में कुईं (कुंई) का विशेष वर्णन है, जो छोटे व्यास की गहरी खुदाई होती है। इसकी खुदाई और चिनाई का काम चेजारो करते हैं। रेत के नीचे खड़िया पट्टी (जिप्सम की परत) होती है जो वर्षा-जल को नीचे जाने से रोकती है। वर्षा-जल रेत में समाता है और कुईं में रेजाणी पानी के रूप में एकत्र होता है, जो शुद्ध और मीठा होता है। पानी के तीन रूप हैं: पालर पानी (वर्षा का सीधे मिलने वाला), रेजाणी पानी (रेत में समाया हुआ) और पाताल पानी (भूमिगत)। यह पाठ पारंपरिक ज्ञान और सामुदायिक जल-प्रबंधन का महत्त्व दिखाता है।
गहन अध्ययन: कुईं का विज्ञान
कुईं का मुँह छोटा, लगभग चार-पाँच फुट, और गहराई कई फुट होती है। बनावट में खड़िया पट्टी तक खुदाई कर पत्थर या ईंटों से चिनाई की जाती है। वर्षा-जल धीरे-धीरे रेत में रिसकर कुईं के भीतर इकट्ठा होता है।
गहन अध्ययन: पानी के रूप
पालर पानी वर्षा से सीधे प्राप्त पानी है जिसे कुंडों में संजोया जाता है। रेजाणी पानी रेत की परतों के बीच नमी के रूप में रहता है और कुईं में मिलता है। पाताल पानी खारा और गहरे कुएँ का पानी है।
गहन अध्ययन: सामाजिक पक्ष
जल-संग्रह सामूहिक भागीदारी और परंपरागत कौशल का परिणाम है। चेजारो की कारीगरी और सम्मान, कुईं की मिल्कियत और समाज के नियम जल-संस्कृति को दर्शाते हैं।
Hindi saransh
राजस्थान की रजत बूँदें सिखाती हैं कि कम वर्षा वाले क्षेत्र में भी पारंपरिक ज्ञान से जल को सहेजा जा सकता है।
तीन पानी याद रखें: पालर, रेजाणी और पाताल।

राजस्थान की रजत बूँदें अनुपम मिश्र की पुस्तक का अंश है जिसमें राजस्थान के मरुस्थलीय क्षेत्रों में जल-संचय की पारंपरिक पद्धतियों का वर्णन है। राजस्थान में वर्षा बहुत कम होती है, इसलिए वहाँ के लोगों ने वर्षा की हर बूँद को संजोने की कला विकसित की। पाठ में कुईं (कुंई) का विशेष वर्णन है, जो छोटे व्यास की गहरी खुदाई होती है। इसकी खुदाई और चिनाई का काम चेजारो करते हैं। रेत के नीचे खड़िया पट्टी (जिप्सम की परत) होती है जो वर्षा-जल को नीचे जाने से रोकती है। वर्षा-जल रेत में समाता है और कुईं में रेजाणी पानी के रूप में एकत्र होता है, जो शुद्ध और मीठा होता है। पानी के तीन रूप हैं: पालर पानी (वर्षा का सीधे मिलने वाला), रेजाणी पानी (रेत में समाया हुआ) और पाताल पानी (भूमिगत)। यह पाठ पारंपरिक ज्ञान और सामुदायिक जल-प्रबंधन का महत्त्व दिखाता है।

blocks.x: आलो आँधारि बेबी हालदार की आत्मकथा है। मूल रूप से बांग्ला में लिखी गई इस पुस्तक का हिंदी अनुवाद प्रबोध कुमार ने किया है। आलो आँधारि का अर्थ है प्रकाश और अँधेरा। यह एक घरेलू नौकरानी के जीवन के संघर्ष, पीड़ा और आत्मसम्मान की कहानी है। बेबी का बचपन कठिनाइयों में बीता, माँ घर छोड़कर चली गई और पिता ने कम उम्र में उसका विवाह कर दिया। पति से मार-पीट और अत्याचार सहने के बाद वह अपने बच्चों के साथ अलग रहने का निर्णय लेती है और दिल्ली-गुड़गाँव में घरों में काम करती है। उसे एक विद्वान परिवार में काम मिला जहाँ मालिक प्रबोध कुमार, जिन्हें वह तातुश कहती है, ने उसे पढ़ने और लिखने के लिए प्रेरित किया। उनकी प्रेरणा से बेबी ने अपनी कहानी लिखी जो एक सशक्त आत्मकथा बनी। पाठ में स्त्री-संघर्ष, आत्मनिर्भरता और शिक्षा की शक्ति का संदेश है।
गहन अध्ययन: कथानक
बेबी हालदार परिवार की कठिनाइयों, पति के अत्याचार और घरेलू काम के संघर्ष के बीच जीती है। तातुश के घर में उसे किताबें पढ़ने और लिखने का अवसर मिला। यह आत्मकथा उसके लिए नई पहचान बनी।
गहन अध्ययन: पात्र
बेबी साहसी, संवेदनशील और परिश्रमी है। तातुश दयालु, विद्वान और प्रोत्साहन देने वाले हैं। बेबी के बच्चे उसके संघर्ष का कारण और प्रेरणा दोनों हैं।
गहन अध्ययन: संदेश
शिक्षा और अवसर मिलने पर साधारण स्त्री भी असाधारण कार्य कर सकती है। संवेदनशील समाज किसी की प्रतिभा को उभार सकता है।
Hindi saransh
आलो आँधारि में अँधेरे जीवन से प्रकाश की ओर बढ़ती एक स्त्री के संघर्ष और आत्मसम्मान का चित्रण है।
आत्मकथा में लेखक अपने जीवन के अनुभव प्रथम पुरुष में बताता है।

आलो आँधारि बेबी हालदार की आत्मकथा है। मूल रूप से बांग्ला में लिखी गई इस पुस्तक का हिंदी अनुवाद प्रबोध कुमार ने किया है। आलो आँधारि का अर्थ है प्रकाश और अँधेरा। यह एक घरेलू नौकरानी के जीवन के संघर्ष, पीड़ा और आत्मसम्मान की कहानी है। बेबी का बचपन कठिनाइयों में बीता, माँ घर छोड़कर चली गई और पिता ने कम उम्र में उसका विवाह कर दिया। पति से मार-पीट और अत्याचार सहने के बाद वह अपने बच्चों के साथ अलग रहने का निर्णय लेती है और दिल्ली-गुड़गाँव में घरों में काम करती है। उसे एक विद्वान परिवार में काम मिला जहाँ मालिक प्रबोध कुमार, जिन्हें वह तातुश कहती है, ने उसे पढ़ने और लिखने के लिए प्रेरित किया। उनकी प्रेरणा से बेबी ने अपनी कहानी लिखी जो एक सशक्त आत्मकथा बनी। पाठ में स्त्री-संघर्ष, आत्मनिर्भरता और शिक्षा की शक्ति का संदेश है।

गहन अध्ययन: संदेश

  • शिक्षा और अवसर मिलने पर साधारण स्त्री भी असाधारण कार्य कर सकती है। संवेदनशील समाज किसी की प्रतिभा को उभार सकता है।

lessons.title: शब्द-विचार, संधि और समास
yt: class 11 hindi vyakaran sangya sarvanam visheshan kriya sandhi samas upsarg pratyay

blocks.x: हिंदी व्याकरण में शब्द-भेद के आठ प्रकार हैं: संज्ञा, सर्वनाम, विशेषण, क्रिया, क्रिया-विशेषण, संबंधबोधक, समुच्चयबोधक और विस्मयादिबोधक। विकारी शब्द (संज्ञा, सर्वनाम, विशेषण, क्रिया) रूप बदलते हैं और अविकारी शब्द (क्रिया-विशेषण आदि) नहीं बदलते। संज्ञा तीन प्रकार की है: जातिवाचक, व्यक्तिवाचक और भाववाचक। सर्वनाम के छह भेद हैं: पुरुषवाचक, निश्चयवाचक, अनिश्चयवाचक, संबंधवाचक, प्रश्नवाचक और निजवाचक। कारक आठ हैं: कर्ता, कर्म, करण, संप्रदान, अपादान, संबंध, अधिकरण और संबोधन। संधि दो वर्णों के मेल से होने वाले विकार को कहते हैं और उसके तीन भेद हैं: स्वर संधि, व्यंजन संधि और विसर्ग संधि। स्वर संधि के भेद दीर्घ, गुण, वृद्धि, यण और अयादि हैं। समास के छह भेद हैं: अव्ययीभाव, तत्पुरुष, कर्मधारय, द्विगु, द्वंद्व और बहुव्रीहि। उपसर्ग शब्द से पहले और प्रत्यय शब्द के बाद जुड़ते हैं।
गहन अध्ययन: शब्द-भेद

संज्ञा नाम बताती है, सर्वनाम संज्ञा के स्थान पर आता है, विशेषण संज्ञा की विशेषता बताता है और क्रिया कार्य को दर्शाती है। लिंग (पुल्लिंग, स्त्रीलिंग), वचन (एकवचन, बहुवचन) और काल (भूत, वर्तमान, भविष्य) शब्द के रूप बदलते हैं।
गहन अध्ययन: संधि

दीर्घ संधि में समान स्वर मिलकर दीर्घ बनते हैं, जैसे विद्या + आलय = विद्यालय। गुण संधि में अ या आ के बाद इ, उ, ऋ आए तो ए, ओ, अर् बनते हैं, जैसे महा + इंद्र = महेंद्र। यण संधि में इ, उ, ऋ के बाद असमान स्वर आए तो य्, व्, र् बनते हैं, जैसे अति + अधिक = अत्यधिक। वृद्धि संधि में अ या आ के बाद ए, ऐ आए तो ऐ और ओ, औ आए तो औ बनता है, जैसे सदा + एव = सदैव।
गहन अध्ययन: समास

अव्ययीभाव में पहला पद अव्यय होता है, जैसे यथाशक्ति। तत्पुरुष में दूसरा पद प्रधान होता है, जैसे राजपुत्र। कर्मधारय में विशेषण-विशेष्य संबंध होता है, जैसे नीलकमल। द्विगु में पहला पद संख्या है, जैसे त्रिलोक। द्वंद्व में दोनों पद प्रधान हैं, जैसे माता-पिता। बहुव्रीहि में अन्य पद प्रधान होता है, जैसे दशानन।
Hindi saransh
हिंदी व्याकरण के शब्द-भेद, संधि और समास को उदाहरण सहित समझना भाषा-ज्ञान की नींव है।
संधि वर्णों का मेल है, समास शब्दों का संक्षेप; दोनों में अंतर याद रखें।

qa.q: संज्ञा क्या है?
qa.a: संज्ञा: किसी नाम का बोध कराने वाला शब्द।

qa.q: 'किसी नाम का बोध कराने वाला शब्द' किसे कहते हैं?
सर्वनाम क्या है?
qa.a: सर्वनाम: संज्ञा के स्थान पर आने वाला शब्द।

qa.q: 'संज्ञा के स्थान पर आने वाला शब्द' किसे कहते हैं?
विशेषण क्या है?
qa.a: विशेषण: संज्ञा या सर्वनाम की विशेषता बताने वाला शब्द।

qa.q: 'संज्ञा या सर्वनाम की विशेषता बताने वाला शब्द' किसे कहते हैं?
क्रिया क्या है?
'कार्य-व्यापार बताने वाला शब्द' किसे कहते हैं?
क्रिया-विशेषण क्या है?
qa.a: क्रिया-विशेषण: क्रिया की विशेषता बताने वाला शब्द।

qa.q: 'क्रिया की विशेषता बताने वाला शब्द' किसे कहते हैं?
संबंधबोधक क्या है?
qa.a: संबंधबोधक: संज्ञा का अन्य शब्दों से संबंध जोड़ने वाला शब्द।

qa.q: 'संज्ञा का अन्य शब्दों से संबंध जोड़ने वाला शब्द' किसे कहते हैं?
समुच्चयबोधक क्या है?
qa.a: समुच्चयबोधक: दो शब्दों या वाक्यों को जोड़ने वाला शब्द।

qa.q: 'दो शब्दों या वाक्यों को जोड़ने वाला शब्द' किसे कहते हैं?
विस्मयादिबोधक क्या है?
qa.a: विस्मयादिबोधक: हर्ष, शोक आदि भाव प्रकट करने वाला शब्द।

qa.q: 'हर्ष, शोक आदि भाव प्रकट करने वाला शब्द' किसे कहते हैं?
जातिवाचक संज्ञा क्या है?
qa.a: जातिवाचक संज्ञा: पूरी जाति का बोध कराने वाली संज्ञा।

qa.q: 'पूरी जाति का बोध कराने वाली संज्ञा' किसे कहते हैं?
व्यक्तिवाचक संज्ञा क्या है?
qa.a: व्यक्तिवाचक संज्ञा: किसी विशेष नाम की संज्ञा।

qa.q: 'किसी विशेष नाम की संज्ञा' किसे कहते हैं?
भाववाचक संज्ञा क्या है?
qa.a: भाववाचक संज्ञा: गुण, दशा या भाव की संज्ञा।

qa.q: 'गुण, दशा या भाव की संज्ञा' किसे कहते हैं?
पुरुषवाचक सर्वनाम क्या है?
qa.a: पुरुषवाचक सर्वनाम: मैं, तुम, वह जैसे सर्वनाम।

qa.q: 'मैं, तुम, वह जैसे सर्वनाम' किसे कहते हैं?
निजवाचक सर्वनाम क्या है?
qa.a: निजवाचक सर्वनाम: अपने आप का बोध कराने वाला सर्वनाम।

qa.q: 'अपने आप का बोध कराने वाला सर्वनाम' किसे कहते हैं?
कारक क्या है?
qa.a: कारक: संज्ञा का क्रिया से संबंध।

qa.q: 'संज्ञा का क्रिया से संबंध' किसे कहते हैं?
कर्ता कारक क्या है?
'काम करने वाला' किसे कहते हैं?
कर्म कारक क्या है?
qa.a: कर्म कारक: जिस पर क्रिया का फल पड़े।

qa.q: 'जिस पर क्रिया का फल पड़े' किसे कहते हैं?
करण कारक क्या है?
qa.a: करण कारक: साधन बताने वाला कारक।

qa.q: 'साधन बताने वाला कारक' किसे कहते हैं?
संप्रदान कारक क्या है?
qa.a: संप्रदान कारक: जिसके लिए कार्य हो।

qa.q: 'जिसके लिए कार्य हो' किसे कहते हैं?
अपादान कारक क्या है?
qa.a: अपादान कारक: अलगाव बताने वाला कारक।

qa.q: 'अलगाव बताने वाला कारक' किसे कहते हैं?
अधिकरण कारक क्या है?
qa.a: अधिकरण कारक: स्थान या समय बताने वाला कारक।

qa.q: 'स्थान या समय बताने वाला कारक' किसे कहते हैं?
संधि क्या है?
'दो वर्णों का मेल' किसे कहते हैं?
स्वर संधि क्या है?
qa.a: स्वर संधि: स्वर से स्वर का मेल।

qa.q: 'स्वर से स्वर का मेल' किसे कहते हैं?
व्यंजन संधि क्या है?
qa.a: व्यंजन संधि: व्यंजन का स्वर या व्यंजन से मेल।

qa.q: 'व्यंजन का स्वर या व्यंजन से मेल' किसे कहते हैं?
विसर्ग संधि क्या है?
qa.a: विसर्ग संधि: विसर्ग का स्वर या व्यंजन से मेल।

qa.q: 'विसर्ग का स्वर या व्यंजन से मेल' किसे कहते हैं?
दीर्घ संधि क्या है?
qa.a: दीर्घ संधि: समान स्वरों से दीर्घ स्वर बनना।

qa.q: 'समान स्वरों से दीर्घ स्वर बनना' किसे कहते हैं?
गुण संधि क्या है?
qa.a: गुण संधि: अ या आ के बाद इ, उ आदि से ए, ओ बनना।

qa.q: 'अ या आ के बाद इ, उ आदि से ए, ओ बनना' किसे कहते हैं?
वृद्धि संधि क्या है?
qa.a: वृद्धि संधि: अ या आ के बाद ए, ऐ से ऐ बनना।

qa.q: 'अ या आ के बाद ए, ऐ से ऐ बनना' किसे कहते हैं?
यण संधि क्या है?
qa.a: यण संधि: इ, उ के बाद असमान स्वर से य्, व् बनना।

qa.q: 'इ, उ के बाद असमान स्वर से य्, व् बनना' किसे कहते हैं?
अयादि संधि क्या है?
qa.a: अयादि संधि: ए, ऐ, ओ, औ के बाद स्वर से अय्, आय् आदि बनना।

qa.q: 'ए, ऐ, ओ, औ के बाद स्वर से अय्, आय् आदि बनना' किसे कहते हैं?
समास क्या है?
'संक्षेप में शब्द जोड़ना' किसे कहते हैं?
अव्ययीभाव समास क्या है?
qa.a: अव्ययीभाव समास: पहला पद अव्यय प्रधान।

qa.q: 'पहला पद अव्यय प्रधान' किसे कहते हैं?
तत्पुरुष समास क्या है?
'दूसरा पद प्रधान' किसे कहते हैं?
कर्मधारय समास क्या है?
'विशेषण-विशेष्य संबंध वाला' किसे कहते हैं?
द्विगु समास क्या है?
'पहला पद संख्यावाचक' किसे कहते हैं?
द्वंद्व समास क्या है?
'दोनों पद प्रधान' किसे कहते हैं?
बहुव्रीहि समास क्या है?
qa.a: बहुव्रीहि समास: अन्य पद की प्रधानता।

qa.q: 'अन्य पद की प्रधानता' किसे कहते हैं?
उपसर्ग क्या है?
qa.a: उपसर्ग: शब्द के आरंभ में जुड़ने वाला अंश।

qa.q: 'शब्द के आरंभ में जुड़ने वाला अंश' किसे कहते हैं?
प्रत्यय क्या है?
qa.a: प्रत्यय: शब्द के अंत में जुड़ने वाला अंश।

qa.q: 'शब्द के अंत में जुड़ने वाला अंश' किसे कहते हैं?
लिंग क्या है?
qa.a: लिंग: पुल्लिंग या स्त्रीलिंग का भेद।

qa.q: 'पुल्लिंग या स्त्रीलिंग का भेद' किसे कहते हैं?
वचन क्या है?
qa.a: वचन: एक या अनेक का बोध।

qa.q: 'एक या अनेक का बोध' किसे कहते हैं?
काल क्या है?
qa.a: काल: क्रिया के समय का बोध।

qa.q: 'क्रिया के समय का बोध' किसे कहते हैं?
भूतकाल क्या है?
'बीते समय की क्रिया' किसे कहते हैं?
वर्तमान काल क्या है?
qa.a: वर्तमान काल: चल रहे समय की क्रिया।

qa.q: 'चल रहे समय की क्रिया' किसे कहते हैं?
भविष्यत् काल क्या है?
qa.a: भविष्यत् काल: आने वाले समय की क्रिया।

qa.q: 'आने वाले समय की क्रिया' किसे कहते हैं?
विकारी शब्द क्या है?
qa.a: विकारी शब्द: रूप बदलने वाले शब्द।

qa.q: 'रूप बदलने वाले शब्द' किसे कहते हैं?
अविकारी शब्द क्या है?
qa.a: अविकारी शब्द: रूप न बदलने वाले शब्द।

qa.q: 'रूप न बदलने वाले शब्द' किसे कहते हैं?
विग्रह क्या है?
'समास को खोलकर लिखना' किसे कहते हैं?
संधि-विच्छेद क्या है?
qa.a: संधि-विच्छेद: मिले वर्णों को अलग करना।

qa.q: 'मिले वर्णों को अलग करना' किसे कहते हैं?
वाच्य क्या है?
qa.a: वाच्य: कर्ता, कर्म या भाव की प्रधानता।

qa.q: 'कर्ता, कर्म या भाव की प्रधानता' किसे कहते हैं?
अव्यय क्या है?
qa.a: अव्यय: रूप न बदलने वाला शब्द।

qa.q: 'रूप न बदलने वाला शब्द' किसे कहते हैं?
कारक कितने होते हैं?
समास के कितने भेद हैं?
संधि के कितने भेद हैं?
विद्या + आलय का संधि रूप क्या है?
महा + इंद्र का संधि रूप क्या है?
अति + अधिक का संधि रूप क्या है?
सदा + एव का संधि रूप क्या है?
माता-पिता में कौन-सा समास है?

quiz.q: 'किसी नाम का बोध कराने वाला शब्द' - यह किसका वर्णन है?
quiz.why: संज्ञा: किसी नाम का बोध कराने वाला शब्द।

हिंदी व्याकरण में शब्द-भेद के आठ प्रकार हैं: संज्ञा, सर्वनाम, विशेषण, क्रिया, क्रिया-विशेषण, संबंधबोधक, समुच्चयबोधक और विस्मयादिबोधक। विकारी शब्द (संज्ञा, सर्वनाम, विशेषण, क्रिया) रूप बदलते हैं और अविकारी शब्द (क्रिया-विशेषण आदि) नहीं बदलते। संज्ञा तीन प्रकार की है: जातिवाचक, व्यक्तिवाचक और भाववाचक। सर्वनाम के छह भेद हैं: पुरुषवाचक, निश्चयवाचक, अनिश्चयवाचक, संबंधवाचक, प्रश्नवाचक और निजवाचक। कारक आठ हैं: कर्ता, कर्म, करण, संप्रदान, अपादान, संबंध, अधिकरण और संबोधन। संधि दो वर्णों के मेल से होने वाले विकार को कहते हैं और उसके तीन भेद हैं: स्वर संधि, व्यंजन संधि और विसर्ग संधि। स्वर संधि के भेद दीर्घ, गुण, वृद्धि, यण और अयादि हैं। समास के छह भेद हैं: अव्ययीभाव, तत्पुरुष, कर्मधारय, द्विगु, द्वंद्व और बहुव्रीहि। उपसर्ग शब्द से पहले और प्रत्यय शब्द के बाद जुड़ते हैं।

📌

गहन अध्ययन: शब्द-भेद

  • संज्ञा नाम बताती है, सर्वनाम संज्ञा के स्थान पर आता है, विशेषण संज्ञा की विशेषता बताता है और क्रिया कार्य को दर्शाती है। लिंग (पुल्लिंग, स्त्रीलिंग)…
🧠

गहन अध्ययन: संधि

  • दीर्घ संधि में समान स्वर मिलकर दीर्घ बनते हैं, जैसे विद्या + आलय = विद्यालय। गुण संधि में अ या आ के बाद इ, उ, ऋ आए तो ए, ओ, अर् बनते हैं, जैसे महा +…
🌟

गहन अध्ययन: समास

  • अव्ययीभाव में पहला पद अव्यय होता है, जैसे यथाशक्ति। तत्पुरुष में दूसरा पद प्रधान होता है, जैसे राजपुत्र। कर्मधारय में विशेषण-विशेष्य संबंध होता है…
🧮

Formula tiles

संज्ञा के भेदतीनजाति, व्यक्ति, भाव
सर्वनाम के भेदछहपुरुष आदि
कारकआठकर्ता से संबोधन
संधितीनस्वर, व्यंजन, विसर्ग
समासछहअव्ययीभाव आदि
🎯 Remember संधि वर्णों का मेल है, समास शब्दों का संक्षेप; दोनों में अंतर याद रखें।
🇮🇳

हिंदी सार

हिंदी व्याकरण के शब्द-भेद, संधि और समास को उदाहरण सहित समझना भाषा-ज्ञान की नींव है।

lessons.title: अलंकार, रस, छंद, मुहावरे और लोकोक्तियाँ
yt: class 11 hindi vyakaran alankar ras chhand muhavare lokoktiyan paryayvachi vilom

blocks.x: काव्य की शोभा बढ़ाने वाले तत्त्वों को अलंकार कहते हैं। इनके दो भेद हैं: शब्दालंकार (अनुप्रास, यमक, श्लेष) और अर्थालंकार (उपमा, रूपक, उत्प्रेक्षा, अतिशयोक्ति, मानवीकरण)। काव्य से मिलने वाले आनंद को रस कहते हैं। रस के नौ भेद माने गए हैं: शृंगार, हास्य, करुण, रौद्र, वीर, भयानक, वीभत्स, अद्भुत और शांत। वात्सल्य और भक्ति को भी कुछ विद्वान रस मानते हैं। रस के चार अंग हैं: स्थायी भाव, विभाव, अनुभाव और संचारी भाव। छंद वर्णों या मात्राओं की गणना पर आधारित नियम हैं; मात्रिक छंदों में दोहा, चौपाई, सोरठा और रोला प्रमुख हैं। दोहे में 13 और 11 मात्राओं के चरण होते हैं। चौपाई में 16 मात्राएँ प्रत्येक चरण में होती हैं। मुहावरे विशेष अर्थ देने वाले वाक्यांश होते हैं, जैसे आँखों का तारा। लोकोक्तियाँ लोक में प्रचलित कहावतें हैं, जैसे अधजल गगरी छलकत जाए। पर्यायवाची समान अर्थ वाले और विलोम विपरीत अर्थ वाले शब्द होते हैं।
गहन अध्ययन: अलंकार

अनुप्रास में वर्णों की आवृत्ति होती है, यमक में एक शब्द अलग अर्थों में बार-बार आता है, श्लेष में एक शब्द के कई अर्थ होते हैं। उपमा में समान गुण से तुलना होती है, रूपक में उपमेय पर उपमान का आरोप होता है। उत्प्रेक्षा में संभावना की कल्पना होती है।
गहन अध्ययन: रस और स्थायी भाव
शृंगार का स्थायी भाव रति, हास्य का हास, करुण का शोक, रौद्र का क्रोध, वीर का उत्साह, भयानक का भय, वीभत्स का जुगुप्सा, अद्भुत का विस्मय और शांत का निर्वेद है। वात्सल्य का वत्सलता और भक्ति का अनुराग है।
गहन अध्ययन: छंद, मुहावरे और लोकोक्ति
दोहा अर्धसम मात्रिक छंद है। चौपाई सममात्रिक छंद है। मुहावरे का प्रयोग वाक्य में होता है और उसका लाक्षणिक अर्थ होता है। लोकोक्ति अपने आप में पूर्ण कथन है और अनुभव से उपजी होती है।

काव्य की शोभा बढ़ाने वाले तत्त्वों को अलंकार कहते हैं। इनके दो भेद हैं: शब्दालंकार (अनुप्रास, यमक, श्लेष) और अर्थालंकार (उपमा, रूपक, उत्प्रेक्षा, अतिशयोक्ति, मानवीकरण)। काव्य से मिलने वाले आनंद को रस कहते हैं। रस के नौ भेद माने गए हैं: शृंगार, हास्य, करुण, रौद्र, वीर, भयानक, वीभत्स, अद्भुत और शांत। वात्सल्य और भक्ति को भी कुछ विद्वान रस मानते हैं। रस के चार अंग हैं: स्थायी भाव, विभाव, अनुभाव और संचारी भाव। छंद वर्णों या मात्राओं की गणना पर आधारित नियम हैं; मात्रिक छंदों में दोहा, चौपाई, सोरठा और रोला प्रमुख हैं। दोहे में 13 और 11 मात्राओं के चरण होते हैं। चौपाई में 16 मात्राएँ प्रत्येक चरण में होती हैं। मुहावरे विशेष अर्थ देने वाले वाक्यांश होते हैं, जैसे आँखों का तारा। लोकोक्तियाँ लोक में प्रचलित कहावतें हैं, जैसे अधजल गगरी छलकत जाए। पर्यायवाची समान अर्थ वाले और विलोम विपरीत अर्थ वाले शब्द होते हैं।

lessons.title: From the Beginning of Time
yt: class 11 history from the beginning of time early humans evolution stone age

blocks.x: Human history begins in Africa, where the earliest hominids appeared about 5.6 million years ago. The main stages are the Australopithecines (about 5.6 to 2.5 million years ago), Homo habilis (about 2.5 to 2 million years ago), Homo erectus (about 1.8 million years ago) and Homo sapiens (modern humans, about 195,000 years ago). Charles Darwin's On the Origin of Species (1859) and The Descent of Man (1871) gave the theory of evolution by natural selection. Early humans were hunter-gatherers who made stone tools, learned to use fire, developed speech and later made cave paintings, as at Altamira in Spain and Lascaux and Chauvet in France. The Stone Age is divided into the Palaeolithic, Mesolithic and Neolithic periods. Around 10,000 to 12,000 years ago the last Ice Age ended, climates warmed, and people began to domesticate plants and animals, which led to agriculture, settled life and the first villages. Sources include fossils, tools, paintings and the study of living hunter-gatherer societies such as the Hadza.
Deep dive: Evolution of humans

Primates appeared about 36 million years ago, hominoids about 24 million and hominids about 5.6 million. Hominids walk on two legs, have larger brains and make tools. Australopithecus fossils such as Lucy were found in Ethiopia. Homo erectus used fire and spread out of Africa. Homo sapiens developed larger brains and complex language; the Neanderthals lived in Europe.
Deep dive: Ways of life

The Palaeolithic way of life was hunting and gathering in small mobile groups. Tools were made of stone, bone and wood. Fire was used for cooking, warmth and protection. Art, rituals and burials show symbolic thought. The Neolithic brought farming, pottery and permanent villages.
Deep dive: Sources and debates

Archaeologists use stone tools, bones, hearths and cave art. Scientists use radiocarbon and potassium-argon dating. Debates include the origin of language, the cause of Neanderthal extinction and the role of gender in hunting and gathering.

Visual lesson

From the Beginning of Time

Human history begins in Africa, where the earliest hominids appeared about 5.6 million years ago

Big idea

  • Human history begins in Africa, where the earliest hominids appeared about 5.6 million years ago
  • The main stages are the Australopithecines (about 5.6 to 2.5 million years ago), Homo habilis (about 2.5 to 2 million years ago), Homo erectus (about…
  • Charles Darwin's On the Origin of Species (1859) and The Descent of Man (1871) gave the theory of evolution by natural selection

Read the full explanation

Human history begins in Africa, where the earliest hominids appeared about 5.6 million years ago. The main stages are the Australopithecines (about 5.6 to 2.5 million years ago), Homo habilis (about 2.5 to 2 million years ago), Homo erectus (about 1.8 million years ago) and Homo sapiens (modern humans, about 195,000 years ago). Charles Darwin's On the Origin of Species (1859) and The Descent of Man (1871) gave the theory of evolution by natural selection. Early humans were hunter-gatherers who made stone tools, learned to use fire, developed speech and later made cave paintings, as at Altamira in Spain and Lascaux and Chauvet in France. The Stone Age is divided into the Palaeolithic, Mesolithic and Neolithic periods. Around 10,000 to 12,000 years ago the last Ice Age ended, climates warmed, and people began to domesticate plants and animals, which led to agriculture, settled life and the first villages. Sources include fossils, tools, paintings and the study of living hunter-gatherer societies such as the Hadza.

🧬

Evolution of humans

  • Primates appeared about 36 million years ago, hominoids about 24 million and hominids about 5.6 million
  • Hominids walk on two legs, have larger brains and make tools
  • Australopithecus fossils such as Lucy were found in Ethiopia
  • Homo erectus used fire and spread out of Africa
Read the full explanation

Primates appeared about 36 million years ago, hominoids about 24 million and hominids about 5.6 million. Hominids walk on two legs, have larger brains and make tools. Australopithecus fossils such as Lucy were found in Ethiopia. Homo erectus used fire and spread out of Africa. Homo sapiens developed larger brains and complex language; the Neanderthals lived in Europe.

🧠

Ways of life

  • The Palaeolithic way of life was hunting and gathering in small mobile groups
  • Tools were made of stone, bone and wood
  • Fire was used for cooking, warmth and protection
  • Art, rituals and burials show symbolic thought
Read the full explanation

The Palaeolithic way of life was hunting and gathering in small mobile groups. Tools were made of stone, bone and wood. Fire was used for cooking, warmth and protection. Art, rituals and burials show symbolic thought. The Neolithic brought farming, pottery and permanent villages.

🌟

Sources and debates

  • Archaeologists use stone tools, bones, hearths and cave art
  • Scientists use radiocarbon and potassium-argon dating
  • Debates include the origin of language, the cause of Neanderthal extinction and the role of gender in hunting and gathering
🎯 Remember Remember the order: Australopithecus, Homo habilis, Homo erectus, Homo sapiens.

lessons.title: Writing and City Life
yt: class 11 history writing and city life mesopotamia sumer uruk cuneiform

blocks.x: Mesopotamia means the land between rivers: the Tigris and the Euphrates in present-day Iraq. Here around 3000 BCE the first cities appeared in Sumer, such as Uruk, Ur and Nippur. The Sumerians invented cuneiform writing (wedge-shaped signs on clay tablets) around 3200 BCE for recording temple accounts. Cities grew because of agriculture on irrigated land, trade with distant lands like Dilmun (Bahrain), Magan (Oman) and Meluhha (the Indus region), and the organised power of temples. Temples (ziggurats) were centres of economy and religion. Kings such as Sargon of Akkad (about 2370 BCE) created the first empire. Hammurabi of Babylon (about 1792 to 1750 BCE) issued a famous law code. The Assyrian king Ashurbanipal built a library at Nineveh. Mesopotamians developed the wheel, the plough, bronze, a calendar and a sexagesimal (base 60) number system. The Epic of Gilgamesh is among the oldest literary works. Leonard Woolley excavated the royal tombs of Ur.
Deep dive: City life

Uruk was the earliest city, with temples, craftsmen and traders. Cities needed rulers, surplus food and specialists. Irrigation canals and flood control required co-operation. Urban society had priests, scribes, merchants, craftsmen, farmers and slaves.
Deep dive: Writing

Writing began as pictographs and became cuneiform on clay tablets with a reed stylus. Scribes were trained in schools called tablet houses. Writing helped record trade, law, astronomy and literature. Cuneiform was used for several languages across West Asia.
Deep dive: Empires and legacy

Akkadian, Babylonian and Assyrian empires followed. Hammurabi's code reflected social order and punishment. Mesopotamian science influenced later Greek learning. The 60-minute hour and 360-degree circle trace to Mesopotamia.

Read the full explanation

Mesopotamia means the land between rivers: the Tigris and the Euphrates in present-day Iraq. Here around 3000 BCE the first cities appeared in Sumer, such as Uruk, Ur and Nippur. The Sumerians invented cuneiform writing (wedge-shaped signs on clay tablets) around 3200 BCE for recording temple accounts. Cities grew because of agriculture on irrigated land, trade with distant lands like Dilmun (Bahrain), Magan (Oman) and Meluhha (the Indus region), and the organised power of temples. Temples (ziggurats) were centres of economy and religion. Kings such as Sargon of Akkad (about 2370 BCE) created the first empire. Hammurabi of Babylon (about 1792 to 1750 BCE) issued a famous law code. The Assyrian king Ashurbanipal built a library at Nineveh. Mesopotamians developed the wheel, the plough, bronze, a calendar and a sexagesimal (base 60) number system. The Epic of Gilgamesh is among the oldest literary works. Leonard Woolley excavated the royal tombs of Ur.

📌

City life

  • Uruk was the earliest city, with temples, craftsmen and traders
  • Cities needed rulers, surplus food and specialists
  • Irrigation canals and flood control required co-operation
  • Urban society had priests, scribes, merchants, craftsmen, farmers and slaves
✍️

Writing

  • Writing began as pictographs and became cuneiform on clay tablets with a reed stylus
  • Scribes were trained in schools called tablet houses
  • Writing helped record trade, law, astronomy and literature
  • Cuneiform was used for several languages across West Asia
🕰️

Empires and legacy

  • Akkadian, Babylonian and Assyrian empires followed
  • Hammurabi's code reflected social order and punishment
  • Mesopotamian science influenced later Greek learning
  • The 60-minute hour and 360-degree circle trace to Mesopotamia

lessons.title: An Empire Across Three Continents
yt: class 11 history roman empire augustus constantine republic

blocks.x: The Roman Empire stretched across Europe, North Africa and West Asia around the Mediterranean. Rome began as a city-state on the Tiber, ruled by kings, then became a Republic in 509 BCE governed by consuls, the Senate and assemblies. The Roman Republic expanded through wars, including the Punic Wars against Carthage. Julius Caesar conquered Gaul and was assassinated in 44 BCE. His grand-nephew Octavian became Augustus in 27 BCE and began the Principate, the first Roman emperor and founder of the Pax Romana. Later emperors included Trajan (the empire at its greatest extent, 117 CE), Hadrian, Marcus Aurelius and Diocletian, who reorganised the empire into a Tetrarchy. Constantine made Christianity legal by the Edict of Milan in 313 CE and founded Constantinople in 330 CE. In 476 CE the last Western emperor, Romulus Augustulus, was deposed by Odoacer, while the Eastern Roman or Byzantine Empire continued until 1453. Roman society had patricians and plebeians, slaves and coloni. Rome's achievements include roads, aqueducts, law, Latin and amphitheatres such as the Colosseum.
Deep dive: Republic to empire

The Republic had Senate, consuls and tribunes. Civil wars and the rise of generals like Pompey and Caesar ended it. Augustus kept republican forms but held real power through the army and the Senate. The empire was divided into provinces governed by governors.
Deep dive: Economy and society

Agriculture, trade across the Mediterranean, slavery and large estates (latifundia) supported the economy. Cities had forums, baths and amphitheatres. Roman women had limited rights. Slaves worked on farms and mines. Roman law developed ideas of citizenship and property.
Deep dive: Crisis and decline

The third century saw civil war, plague, inflation and barbarian invasions. Diocletian and Constantine restored order. The Western empire fell to Germanic tribes. The Eastern empire survived with Constantinople as the capital.

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

An Empire Across Three Continents

The Roman Empire stretched across Europe, North Africa and West Asia around the Mediterranean

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Republic to empire›3Economy and society›4Crisis and decline
Republic509 BCE
Caesar killed44 BCE
Augustus27 BCE
Edict of Milan313 CE
Western fall476 CE
🔑

Big idea

  • The Roman Empire stretched across Europe, North Africa and West Asia around the Mediterranean
  • Rome began as a city-state on the Tiber, ruled by kings, then became a Republic in 509 BCE governed by consuls, the Senate and assemblies
  • The Roman Republic expanded through wars, including the Punic Wars against Carthage
  • Julius Caesar conquered Gaul and was assassinated in 44 BCE
Read the full explanation

The Roman Empire stretched across Europe, North Africa and West Asia around the Mediterranean. Rome began as a city-state on the Tiber, ruled by kings, then became a Republic in 509 BCE governed by consuls, the Senate and assemblies. The Roman Republic expanded through wars, including the Punic Wars against Carthage. Julius Caesar conquered Gaul and was assassinated in 44 BCE. His grand-nephew Octavian became Augustus in 27 BCE and began the Principate, the first Roman emperor and founder of the Pax Romana. Later emperors included Trajan (the empire at its greatest extent, 117 CE), Hadrian, Marcus Aurelius and Diocletian, who reorganised the empire into a Tetrarchy. Constantine made Christianity legal by the Edict of Milan in 313 CE and founded Constantinople in 330 CE. In 476 CE the last Western emperor, Romulus Augustulus, was deposed by Odoacer, while the Eastern Roman or Byzantine Empire continued until 1453. Roman society had patricians and plebeians, slaves and coloni. Rome's achievements include roads, aqueducts, law, Latin and amphitheatres such as the Colosseum.

🕰️

Republic to empire

  • The Republic had Senate, consuls and tribunes
  • Civil wars and the rise of generals like Pompey and Caesar ended it
  • Augustus kept republican forms but held real power through the army and the Senate
  • The empire was divided into provinces governed by governors
🏛️

Economy and society

  • Agriculture, trade across the Mediterranean, slavery and large estates (latifundia) supported the economy
  • Cities had forums, baths and amphitheatres
  • Roman women had limited rights
  • Slaves worked on farms and mines
Read the full explanation

Agriculture, trade across the Mediterranean, slavery and large estates (latifundia) supported the economy. Cities had forums, baths and amphitheatres. Roman women had limited rights. Slaves worked on farms and mines. Roman law developed ideas of citizenship and property.

🌟

Crisis and decline

  • The third century saw civil war, plague, inflation and barbarian invasions
  • Diocletian and Constantine restored order
  • The Western empire fell to Germanic tribes
  • The Eastern empire survived with Constantinople as the capital
🎯 Remember Republic 509 BCE, Augustus 27 BCE, Constantinople 330 CE, fall of the West 476 CE.

blocks.x: Islam arose in Arabia in the seventh century CE through the Prophet Muhammad (570 to 632 CE). In 622 CE the Prophet migrated from Mecca to Medina (the Hijra), which marks the beginning of the Islamic calendar. After his death the community was led by the Rashidun caliphs: Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali. The Umayyad dynasty (661 to 750 CE), with its capital at Damascus, expanded the empire to Spain in the west and Sind in the east; the battle of Karbala in 680 CE, in which Husayn was killed, caused a lasting split between Sunni and Shia communities. The Abbasids (750 to 1258 CE) overthrew the Umayyads and built Baghdad as their capital. They patronised learning at the House of Wisdom, where Greek, Persian and Indian works were translated. Scholars like Al-Khwarizmi (algebra), Al-Razi (medicine), Ibn Sina (Avicenna), Ibn Rushd (Averroes), Ibn Khaldun (history) and Al-Biruni advanced knowledge. The Fatimids ruled Egypt, the Seljuq Turks took over Baghdad in 1055, and the Crusades (1095 to 1291) brought conflict with Christian Europe; Saladin retook Jerusalem in 1187. The Mongols under Hulagu destroyed Baghdad in 1258.
Deep dive: Early Islam and caliphate

The Prophet formed a community (umma) in Medina. The caliph was the successor and leader. Conquests spread Islam across West Asia and North Africa. The empire used Arabic as an administrative language and issued coins.
Deep dive: Dynasties

Umayyads: Arab aristocracy, Damascus, administrative reforms by Abd al-Malik. Abbasids: Persian influence, Baghdad, Al-Mamun and Harun al-Rashid. Fatimids: Shia dynasty in Cairo that founded Al-Azhar. Seljuqs: Turkish power. Mongols ended the Abbasid caliphate in 1258.
Deep dive: Culture and economy

Cities like Baghdad, Cordoba and Cairo became centres of learning. Mathematics, astronomy, medicine and philosophy flourished. Trade networks connected the Indian Ocean and the Mediterranean. Mosques, madrasas and libraries spread learning.

Big idea

  • Islam arose in Arabia in the seventh century CE through the Prophet Muhammad (570 to 632 CE)
  • In 622 CE the Prophet migrated from Mecca to Medina (the Hijra), which marks the beginning of the Islamic calendar
  • After his death the community was led by the Rashidun caliphs: Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali

Read the full explanation

Islam arose in Arabia in the seventh century CE through the Prophet Muhammad (570 to 632 CE). In 622 CE the Prophet migrated from Mecca to Medina (the Hijra), which marks the beginning of the Islamic calendar. After his death the community was led by the Rashidun caliphs: Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali. The Umayyad dynasty (661 to 750 CE), with its capital at Damascus, expanded the empire to Spain in the west and Sind in the east; the battle of Karbala in 680 CE, in which Husayn was killed, caused a lasting split between Sunni and Shia communities. The Abbasids (750 to 1258 CE) overthrew the Umayyads and built Baghdad as their capital. They patronised learning at the House of Wisdom, where Greek, Persian and Indian works were translated. Scholars like Al-Khwarizmi (algebra), Al-Razi (medicine), Ibn Sina (Avicenna), Ibn Rushd (Averroes), Ibn Khaldun (history) and Al-Biruni advanced knowledge. The Fatimids ruled Egypt, the Seljuq Turks took over Baghdad in 1055, and the Crusades (1095 to 1291) brought conflict with Christian Europe; Saladin retook Jerusalem in 1187. The Mongols under Hulagu destroyed Baghdad in 1258.

📌

Early Islam and caliphate

  • The Prophet formed a community (umma) in Medina
  • The caliph was the successor and leader
  • Conquests spread Islam across West Asia and North Africa
  • The empire used Arabic as an administrative language and issued coins
🧠

Dynasties

  • Umayyads: Arab aristocracy, Damascus, administrative reforms by Abd al-Malik
  • Abbasids: Persian influence, Baghdad, Al-Mamun and Harun al-Rashid
  • Fatimids: Shia dynasty in Cairo that founded Al-Azhar
  • Seljuqs: Turkish power
Read the full explanation

Umayyads: Arab aristocracy, Damascus, administrative reforms by Abd al-Malik. Abbasids: Persian influence, Baghdad, Al-Mamun and Harun al-Rashid. Fatimids: Shia dynasty in Cairo that founded Al-Azhar. Seljuqs: Turkish power. Mongols ended the Abbasid caliphate in 1258.

🏛️

Culture and economy

  • Cities like Baghdad, Cordoba and Cairo became centres of learning
  • Mathematics, astronomy, medicine and philosophy flourished
  • Trade networks connected the Indian Ocean and the Mediterranean
  • Mosques, madrasas and libraries spread learning
🎯 Remember Hijra 622 CE marks Year 1 of the Islamic calendar.

lessons.title: Nomadic Empires
yt: class 11 history nomadic empires mongols genghis khan

blocks.x: Nomadic empires were created by pastoral peoples of the Central Asian steppe. The best known are the Mongols. Temujin was born about 1162 and was proclaimed Genghis Khan (Chinggis Khan), the universal ruler, at a kuriltai in 1206. Mongol society was organised in clans and tribes bound by oaths of loyalty (the anda) and the yasa, a code of laws. Their army was disciplined and fast, based on horse archers and a decimal organisation of units of ten, a hundred, a thousand and ten thousand. Genghis Khan conquered northern China, Central Asia (Khwarezm), parts of Persia and Russia; he died in 1227. His sons and grandsons continued the conquests: Ogodei, Mongke and Kublai Khan, who founded the Yuan dynasty in China. Hulagu destroyed Baghdad in 1258. The empire was divided into khanates: the Golden Horde in Russia, the Il-Khanate in Persia and the Chagatai Khanate in Central Asia. The Mongols created the yam, a postal relay system, and protected trade along the Silk Road, the Pax Mongolica. Baghdad's fall and the destruction of Central Asian cities had enormous costs, but the Mongols also promoted trade and exchange of knowledge. Later Timur (Tamerlane) and the Mughal founder Babur claimed Mongol descent.
Deep dive: Society and army

Mongol society was pastoral nomadic. The army used speed, discipline and feigned retreats. Conquered skilled people were often used by the Mongols. Religious tolerance was usual. The yasa was the common law.
Deep dive: Conquests and rule

Genghis Khan united the tribes, defeated the Jin and Khwarezm, and attacked Persia. The empire was divided among his sons after his death. Kublai Khan became emperor of China as the Yuan dynasty. Mongols ruled Russia as the Golden Horde for about two centuries.
Deep dive: Effects

Destruction of cities such as Merv and Baghdad, but also trade, the yam post and movement of ideas. The Black Death travelled along these trade routes. Mongol rule left a lasting political and cultural legacy.

Nomadic Empires

Nomadic empires were created by pastoral peoples of the Central Asian steppe

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Society and army›3Conquests and rule›4Effects
🔑

Big idea

  • Nomadic empires were created by pastoral peoples of the Central Asian steppe
  • The best known are the Mongols
  • Temujin was born about 1162 and was proclaimed Genghis Khan (Chinggis Khan), the universal ruler, at a kuriltai in 1206
  • Mongol society was organised in clans and tribes bound by oaths of loyalty (the anda) and the yasa, a code of laws
Read the full explanation

Nomadic empires were created by pastoral peoples of the Central Asian steppe. The best known are the Mongols. Temujin was born about 1162 and was proclaimed Genghis Khan (Chinggis Khan), the universal ruler, at a kuriltai in 1206. Mongol society was organised in clans and tribes bound by oaths of loyalty (the anda) and the yasa, a code of laws. Their army was disciplined and fast, based on horse archers and a decimal organisation of units of ten, a hundred, a thousand and ten thousand. Genghis Khan conquered northern China, Central Asia (Khwarezm), parts of Persia and Russia; he died in 1227. His sons and grandsons continued the conquests: Ogodei, Mongke and Kublai Khan, who founded the Yuan dynasty in China. Hulagu destroyed Baghdad in 1258. The empire was divided into khanates: the Golden Horde in Russia, the Il-Khanate in Persia and the Chagatai Khanate in Central Asia. The Mongols created the yam, a postal relay system, and protected trade along the Silk Road, the Pax Mongolica. Baghdad's fall and the destruction of Central Asian cities had enormous costs, but the Mongols also promoted trade and exchange of knowledge. Later Timur (Tamerlane) and the Mughal founder Babur claimed Mongol descent.

📌

Society and army

  • Mongol society was pastoral nomadic
  • The army used speed, discipline and feigned retreats
  • Conquered skilled people were often used by the Mongols
  • Religious tolerance was usual
Read the full explanation

Mongol society was pastoral nomadic. The army used speed, discipline and feigned retreats. Conquered skilled people were often used by the Mongols. Religious tolerance was usual. The yasa was the common law.

⚖️

Conquests and rule

  • Genghis Khan united the tribes, defeated the Jin and Khwarezm, and attacked Persia
  • The empire was divided among his sons after his death
  • Kublai Khan became emperor of China as the Yuan dynasty
  • Mongols ruled Russia as the Golden Horde for about two centuries
🌟

Effects

  • Destruction of cities such as Merv and Baghdad, but also trade, the yam post and movement of ideas
  • The Black Death travelled along these trade routes
  • Mongol rule left a lasting political and cultural legacy

lessons.title: The Three Orders
yt: class 11 history three orders feudalism medieval europe

blocks.x: Between the ninth and sixteenth centuries Western Europe was organised in what the French called three orders: those who fought (the nobility), those who prayed (the clergy) and those who worked (the peasants). This was the feudal society. After the fall of Rome, Europe was fragmented; Charlemagne (crowned emperor by the Pope in 800 CE) united much of it. Feudalism developed in France and then England after the Norman conquest of 1066 under William, Duke of Normandy. Lords granted land (fiefs) to vassals in return for military service, and vassals swore homage. The manor was the lord's estate, with a manor house, a demesne and peasant holdings. Serfs were bound to the land and owed labour services (corvee) and dues, and paid the tithe to the Church. The Church was powerful: monasteries such as Benedictine (founded by St Benedict, 529) and Cistercian houses, and the Pope in Rome. In the eleventh century, population growth, new technology like the heavy plough and the three-field system, and trade led to the growth of towns. The fourteenth century saw the Black Death (1347 to 1350), the Hundred Years' War and the Jacquerie peasant revolt in France (1358) and the English Peasants' Revolt (1381), which weakened serfdom. Strong monarchies emerged in France, England and Spain.
Deep dive: Feudalism

Feudalism was a system of landholding and obligations between lords and vassals. The king gave land to great lords, who gave it to knights. Knights fought in return. Castles were the centres of power. The code of chivalry guided knights.
Deep dive: Manor and peasants

Peasants held land from the lord and worked on his demesne. Serfs could not leave the manor. The three-field system raised yields. Water mills and the heavy plough helped. Peasants paid taxes in labour, kind and money.
Deep dive: Church and towns

The Church owned land and collected the tithe. Monasteries were centres of learning. Towns grew with trade and craft guilds; the saying was that town air makes you free. Cathedrals such as Chartres show Gothic architecture.

The Three Orders

Big idea

  • Between the ninth and sixteenth centuries Western Europe was organised in what the French called three orders: those who fought (the nobility), those…
  • This was the feudal society
  • After the fall of Rome, Europe was fragmented
  • Charlemagne (crowned emperor by the Pope in 800 CE) united much of it
Read the full explanation

Between the ninth and sixteenth centuries Western Europe was organised in what the French called three orders: those who fought (the nobility), those who prayed (the clergy) and those who worked (the peasants). This was the feudal society. After the fall of Rome, Europe was fragmented; Charlemagne (crowned emperor by the Pope in 800 CE) united much of it. Feudalism developed in France and then England after the Norman conquest of 1066 under William, Duke of Normandy. Lords granted land (fiefs) to vassals in return for military service, and vassals swore homage. The manor was the lord's estate, with a manor house, a demesne and peasant holdings. Serfs were bound to the land and owed labour services (corvee) and dues, and paid the tithe to the Church. The Church was powerful: monasteries such as Benedictine (founded by St Benedict, 529) and Cistercian houses, and the Pope in Rome. In the eleventh century, population growth, new technology like the heavy plough and the three-field system, and trade led to the growth of towns. The fourteenth century saw the Black Death (1347 to 1350), the Hundred Years' War and the Jacquerie peasant revolt in France (1358) and the English Peasants' Revolt (1381), which weakened serfdom. Strong monarchies emerged in France, England and Spain.

📌

Feudalism

  • Feudalism was a system of landholding and obligations between lords and vassals
  • The king gave land to great lords, who gave it to knights
  • Knights fought in return
  • Castles were the centres of power
Read the full explanation

Feudalism was a system of landholding and obligations between lords and vassals. The king gave land to great lords, who gave it to knights. Knights fought in return. Castles were the centres of power. The code of chivalry guided knights.

🧠

Manor and peasants

  • Peasants held land from the lord and worked on his demesne
  • Serfs could not leave the manor
  • The three-field system raised yields
  • Water mills and the heavy plough helped
Read the full explanation

Peasants held land from the lord and worked on his demesne. Serfs could not leave the manor. The three-field system raised yields. Water mills and the heavy plough helped. Peasants paid taxes in labour, kind and money.

🌟

Church and towns

  • The Church owned land and collected the tithe
  • Monasteries were centres of learning
  • Towns grew with trade and craft guilds
  • The saying was that town air makes you free
Read the full explanation

The Church owned land and collected the tithe. Monasteries were centres of learning. Towns grew with trade and craft guilds; the saying was that town air makes you free. Cathedrals such as Chartres show Gothic architecture.

blocks.x: Between the fourteenth and seventeenth centuries Europe saw the Renaissance, a rebirth of interest in classical Greek and Roman learning, beginning in the Italian city-states such as Florence, Venice, Genoa, Milan and Rome. Wealthy merchants and patrons like the Medici family supported artists and scholars. Humanism, taught by thinkers such as Petrarch (the father of humanism), emphasised human potential and the study of the classics. Artists like Leonardo da Vinci (Mona Lisa, The Last Supper), Michelangelo (Sistine Chapel, David) and Raphael produced masterpieces, and Brunelleschi designed the dome of Florence cathedral. Literary figures included Dante and Machiavelli. The printing press of Johann Gutenberg (about 1450) spread ideas quickly. The Reformation began in 1517 when Martin Luther posted his 95 theses in Wittenberg against indulgences; John Calvin and Zwingli also led reforms, and Henry VIII founded the Church of England. The Catholic Counter-Reformation included the Society of Jesus (Jesuits) founded by Ignatius Loyola. The Scientific Revolution followed: Copernicus (1543) proposed a sun-centred universe, Galileo used the telescope and was condemned by the Church in 1633, Kepler described elliptical orbits, Vesalius studied anatomy, and Newton explained gravitation in 1687. Exploration also expanded horizons, with Columbus in 1492 and Vasco da Gama reaching India in 1498.
Deep dive: Renaissance

Italian cities were rich from trade and had links with the Byzantine and Islamic worlds. Humanists studied classical texts. Painters used perspective and realism. Architecture revived classical forms. Women such as Isabella d'Este patronised art.
Deep dive: Reformation

Luther challenged indulgences and the authority of the Pope. The Bible was translated into German. Protestant churches arose in Germany, Switzerland and England. Religious wars followed. The Catholic Church responded with reforms.
Deep dive: Scientific revolution

Observation and experiment replaced reliance on ancient authority. Copernicus, Galileo, Kepler and Newton changed astronomy and physics. Printing and universities spread new knowledge. These changes shaped the modern outlook.

Read the full explanation

Between the fourteenth and seventeenth centuries Europe saw the Renaissance, a rebirth of interest in classical Greek and Roman learning, beginning in the Italian city-states such as Florence, Venice, Genoa, Milan and Rome. Wealthy merchants and patrons like the Medici family supported artists and scholars. Humanism, taught by thinkers such as Petrarch (the father of humanism), emphasised human potential and the study of the classics. Artists like Leonardo da Vinci (Mona Lisa, The Last Supper), Michelangelo (Sistine Chapel, David) and Raphael produced masterpieces, and Brunelleschi designed the dome of Florence cathedral. Literary figures included Dante and Machiavelli. The printing press of Johann Gutenberg (about 1450) spread ideas quickly. The Reformation began in 1517 when Martin Luther posted his 95 theses in Wittenberg against indulgences; John Calvin and Zwingli also led reforms, and Henry VIII founded the Church of England. The Catholic Counter-Reformation included the Society of Jesus (Jesuits) founded by Ignatius Loyola. The Scientific Revolution followed: Copernicus (1543) proposed a sun-centred universe, Galileo used the telescope and was condemned by the Church in 1633, Kepler described elliptical orbits, Vesalius studied anatomy, and Newton explained gravitation in 1687. Exploration also expanded horizons, with Columbus in 1492 and Vasco da Gama reaching India in 1498.

📌

Renaissance

  • Italian cities were rich from trade and had links with the Byzantine and Islamic worlds
  • Humanists studied classical texts
  • Painters used perspective and realism
  • Architecture revived classical forms
Read the full explanation

Italian cities were rich from trade and had links with the Byzantine and Islamic worlds. Humanists studied classical texts. Painters used perspective and realism. Architecture revived classical forms. Women such as Isabella d'Este patronised art.

🧠

Reformation

  • Luther challenged indulgences and the authority of the Pope
  • The Bible was translated into German
  • Protestant churches arose in Germany, Switzerland and England
  • Religious wars followed
Read the full explanation

Luther challenged indulgences and the authority of the Pope. The Bible was translated into German. Protestant churches arose in Germany, Switzerland and England. Religious wars followed. The Catholic Church responded with reforms.

🕰️

Scientific revolution

  • Observation and experiment replaced reliance on ancient authority
  • Copernicus, Galileo, Kepler and Newton changed astronomy and physics
  • Printing and universities spread new knowledge
  • These changes shaped the modern outlook

blocks.x: In the late fifteenth century European voyages brought contact between Europe and the Americas, with devastating results for American peoples. Christopher Columbus, sailing for Spain, reached the Caribbean in 1492, thinking he had reached the Indies; the people he met were called Indians. Portugal, under Prince Henry the Navigator, explored the African coast, and Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498. Amerigo Vespucci showed that the land was a new continent, which was named America. Three great civilisations then existed. The Aztecs of Mexico, with the capital Tenochtitlan on Lake Texcoco, were conquered by Hernan Cortes in 1521. The Mayas of Central America built cities and temples and developed a calendar and writing. The Incas of Peru, with the capital Cuzco and a vast road network, were conquered by Francisco Pizarro in 1532. The Spanish and Portuguese came for gold, God and glory. Diseases such as smallpox killed millions of Native Americans. Spanish rule created the encomienda system of forced labour; African slaves were brought to work on plantations and mines, beginning the Atlantic slave trade. The Treaty of Tordesillas in 1494 divided the new lands between Spain and Portugal. Silver from Potosi flowed to Europe. Later the English settled in North America at Jamestown in 1607. The Columbian Exchange moved crops like potato, maize and tomato to Europe, and horses, sugar and diseases to the Americas.
Deep dive: Voyages

Advances in ships and navigation, the compass, and the desire for trade with Asia, wealth and spread of Christianity drove exploration. Spain and Portugal led. Portugal found the sea route to India. Spain funded Columbus.
Deep dive: American civilisations

The Aztecs, Mayas and Incas had advanced agriculture, cities and states. Aztecs practised human sacrifice and built causeways in Tenochtitlan. Mayas had a calendar and writing. Incas used quipu cords and terraced farming.
Deep dive: Consequences

Conquest, disease and forced labour destroyed native societies. The slave trade grew. Europe gained silver, gold and new foods. The world economy changed. Debates in Spain, such as by Las Casas, questioned the treatment of the Indians.

Visual lesson

Confrontation of Cultures

In the late fifteenth century European voyages brought contact between Europe and the Americas, with devastating results for American peoples

🔑

Big idea

  • In the late fifteenth century European voyages brought contact between Europe and the Americas, with devastating results for American peoples
  • Christopher Columbus, sailing for Spain, reached the Caribbean in 1492, thinking he had reached the Indies
  • The people he met were called Indians
  • Portugal, under Prince Henry the Navigator, explored the African coast, and Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498
Read the full explanation

In the late fifteenth century European voyages brought contact between Europe and the Americas, with devastating results for American peoples. Christopher Columbus, sailing for Spain, reached the Caribbean in 1492, thinking he had reached the Indies; the people he met were called Indians. Portugal, under Prince Henry the Navigator, explored the African coast, and Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498. Amerigo Vespucci showed that the land was a new continent, which was named America. Three great civilisations then existed. The Aztecs of Mexico, with the capital Tenochtitlan on Lake Texcoco, were conquered by Hernan Cortes in 1521. The Mayas of Central America built cities and temples and developed a calendar and writing. The Incas of Peru, with the capital Cuzco and a vast road network, were conquered by Francisco Pizarro in 1532. The Spanish and Portuguese came for gold, God and glory. Diseases such as smallpox killed millions of Native Americans. Spanish rule created the encomienda system of forced labour; African slaves were brought to work on plantations and mines, beginning the Atlantic slave trade. The Treaty of Tordesillas in 1494 divided the new lands between Spain and Portugal. Silver from Potosi flowed to Europe. Later the English settled in North America at Jamestown in 1607. The Columbian Exchange moved crops like potato, maize and tomato to Europe, and horses, sugar and diseases to the Americas.

📌

Voyages

  • Advances in ships and navigation, the compass, and the desire for trade with Asia, wealth and spread of Christianity drove exploration
  • Spain and Portugal led
  • Portugal found the sea route to India
  • Spain funded Columbus
🧠

American civilisations

  • The Aztecs, Mayas and Incas had advanced agriculture, cities and states
  • Aztecs practised human sacrifice and built causeways in Tenochtitlan
  • Mayas had a calendar and writing
  • Incas used quipu cords and terraced farming
🌟

Consequences

  • Conquest, disease and forced labour destroyed native societies
  • The slave trade grew
  • Europe gained silver, gold and new foods
  • The world economy changed
Read the full explanation

Conquest, disease and forced labour destroyed native societies. The slave trade grew. Europe gained silver, gold and new foods. The world economy changed. Debates in Spain, such as by Las Casas, questioned the treatment of the Indians.

🎯 Remember Columbus 1492, Cortes 1521, Pizarro 1532.

lessons.title: The Industrial Revolution
yt: class 11 history industrial revolution britain steam engine factories

blocks.x: The Industrial Revolution began in Britain from about 1760 and later spread to Europe, the United States and Japan. It changed production from handwork to machines and from homes to factories. Britain had advantages: coal and iron deposits, colonial markets and raw materials, capital, an agricultural revolution with enclosures, a growing population and good rivers and canals. Key inventions in textiles were John Kay's flying shuttle (1733), James Hargreaves' spinning jenny (1764), Richard Arkwright's water frame (1769), Samuel Crompton's mule and Edmund Cartwright's power loom (1785). Thomas Newcomen built an early steam engine; James Watt improved it in 1769, and Matthew Boulton helped to produce it. Abraham Darby used coke for iron smelting. George Stephenson's locomotive Rocket (1829) and the Liverpool and Manchester Railway (1830) began the railway age. Roads and canals improved transport. Factory towns like Manchester and Birmingham grew rapidly. Workers, including women and children, worked long hours in poor conditions; Factory Acts such as that of 1833 limited child labour. Humphry Davy invented the safety lamp for miners. Luddites broke machines between 1811 and 1817. The Chartist movement demanded political rights. Social thinkers such as Robert Owen and Karl Marx criticised industrial capitalism. Industrialisation also fuelled imperialism and, in India, harmed handloom industries.
Deep dive: Causes

Britain had capital from trade, coal and iron, new agricultural methods and colonies for markets. Inventors responded to demand for cloth. Cotton from India and America was the key raw material. Government policy favoured trade.
Deep dive: Technology
Textile machines, the steam engine, iron and coal and railways formed the base. Factories used power machines and division of labour. Steamships followed. These raised output and cut costs.
Deep dive: Social effects

Urbanisation brought slums, disease and pollution. Child labour was widespread. Trade unions, reform laws and later welfare followed. A new working class and industrial middle class emerged. Wealth grew, but unequally.

Visual lesson

The Industrial Revolution

The Industrial Revolution began in Britain from about 1760 and later spread to Europe, the United States and Japan

Factory Act1833
🔑

Big idea

  • The Industrial Revolution began in Britain from about 1760 and later spread to Europe, the United States and Japan
  • It changed production from handwork to machines and from homes to factories
  • Britain had advantages: coal and iron deposits, colonial markets and raw materials, capital, an agricultural revolution with enclosures, a growing…
  • Key inventions in textiles were John Kay's flying shuttle (1733), James Hargreaves' spinning jenny (1764), Richard Arkwright's water frame (1769)…
Read the full explanation

The Industrial Revolution began in Britain from about 1760 and later spread to Europe, the United States and Japan. It changed production from handwork to machines and from homes to factories. Britain had advantages: coal and iron deposits, colonial markets and raw materials, capital, an agricultural revolution with enclosures, a growing population and good rivers and canals. Key inventions in textiles were John Kay's flying shuttle (1733), James Hargreaves' spinning jenny (1764), Richard Arkwright's water frame (1769), Samuel Crompton's mule and Edmund Cartwright's power loom (1785). Thomas Newcomen built an early steam engine; James Watt improved it in 1769, and Matthew Boulton helped to produce it. Abraham Darby used coke for iron smelting. George Stephenson's locomotive Rocket (1829) and the Liverpool and Manchester Railway (1830) began the railway age. Roads and canals improved transport. Factory towns like Manchester and Birmingham grew rapidly. Workers, including women and children, worked long hours in poor conditions; Factory Acts such as that of 1833 limited child labour. Humphry Davy invented the safety lamp for miners. Luddites broke machines between 1811 and 1817. The Chartist movement demanded political rights. Social thinkers such as Robert Owen and Karl Marx criticised industrial capitalism. Industrialisation also fuelled imperialism and, in India, harmed handloom industries.

💡

Causes

  • Britain had capital from trade, coal and iron, new agricultural methods and colonies for markets
  • Inventors responded to demand for cloth
  • Cotton from India and America was the key raw material
  • Government policy favoured trade
🧠

Technology

  • Textile machines, the steam engine, iron and coal and railways formed the base
  • Factories used power machines and division of labour
  • Steamships followed
  • These raised output and cut costs
🌟

Social effects

  • Urbanisation brought slums, disease and pollution
  • Child labour was widespread
  • Trade unions, reform laws and later welfare followed
  • A new working class and industrial middle class emerged
Read the full explanation

Urbanisation brought slums, disease and pollution. Child labour was widespread. Trade unions, reform laws and later welfare followed. A new working class and industrial middle class emerged. Wealth grew, but unequally.

lessons.title: Displacing Indigenous Peoples
yt: class 11 history displacing indigenous peoples native americans australia aborigines

blocks.x: From the sixteenth century European settlers in North America and Australia displaced the native peoples. In North America, the Native Americans (called Red Indians by Europeans) lived in societies such as the Iroquois, Cherokee, Sioux and Apache. The British settled from Jamestown in 1607 and the Pilgrim Fathers reached New England in 1620 on the Mayflower. The Thirteen Colonies became the United States after the Declaration of Independence (1776). The nation expanded westwards; the Louisiana Purchase of 1803 doubled its size. Policies like the Indian Removal Act (1830) forced tribes onto reservations, and the Trail of Tears (1838) saw Cherokee marched west. The Homestead Act (1862) gave land to settlers, railways crossed the plains, buffalo were hunted nearly to extinction, and battles like Wounded Knee (1890) ended resistance. In Canada Europeans displaced native peoples too. In Australia, the Aboriginal people had lived for about 60,000 years before Captain James Cook claimed the east coast for Britain in 1770. The first British convict settlement was set up at Sydney in 1788. Settlers took land for sheep, farming and gold after 1851. Aboriginal people died through disease and violence, and children were removed from families in the policy of the Stolen Generations. Land rights were recognised only later, as in the Mabo decision of 1992. Europeans justified displacement through ideas of civilisation and progress, while indigenous peoples had different ideas of land as shared and sacred.
Deep dive: North America

Native societies were hunters and farmers with rich cultures and a deep link to land. European settlement brought conflict, disease and treaties often broken. The government pushed tribes west to reservations. Cattle ranching and mining spread.
Deep dive: Australia

Aboriginal people had complex clan systems and Dreaming stories. British settlers occupied land treating it as empty, a doctrine called terra nullius. Frontier violence and disease reduced the population. Protest and court cases later won rights.
Deep dive: Perspectives
Settlers saw frontier as opportunity; indigenous peoples saw loss. Museums and history writing were shaped by settlers. Modern debates include apologies, land return and recognition.

Displacing Indigenous Peoples

From the sixteenth century European settlers in North America and Australia displaced the native peoples

Big idea

  • From the sixteenth century European settlers in North America and Australia displaced the native peoples

Read the full explanation

From the sixteenth century European settlers in North America and Australia displaced the native peoples. In North America, the Native Americans (called Red Indians by Europeans) lived in societies such as the Iroquois, Cherokee, Sioux and Apache. The British settled from Jamestown in 1607 and the Pilgrim Fathers reached New England in 1620 on the Mayflower. The Thirteen Colonies became the United States after the Declaration of Independence (1776). The nation expanded westwards; the Louisiana Purchase of 1803 doubled its size. Policies like the Indian Removal Act (1830) forced tribes onto reservations, and the Trail of Tears (1838) saw Cherokee marched west. The Homestead Act (1862) gave land to settlers, railways crossed the plains, buffalo were hunted nearly to extinction, and battles like Wounded Knee (1890) ended resistance. In Canada Europeans displaced native peoples too. In Australia, the Aboriginal people had lived for about 60,000 years before Captain James Cook claimed the east coast for Britain in 1770. The first British convict settlement was set up at Sydney in 1788. Settlers took land for sheep, farming and gold after 1851. Aboriginal people died through disease and violence, and children were removed from families in the policy of the Stolen Generations. Land rights were recognised only later, as in the Mabo decision of 1992. Europeans justified displacement through ideas of civilisation and progress, while indigenous peoples had different ideas of land as shared and sacred.

📌

North America

  • Native societies were hunters and farmers with rich cultures and a deep link to land
  • European settlement brought conflict, disease and treaties often broken
  • The government pushed tribes west to reservations
  • Cattle ranching and mining spread
🧠

Australia

  • Aboriginal people had complex clan systems and Dreaming stories
  • British settlers occupied land treating it as empty, a doctrine called terra nullius
  • Frontier violence and disease reduced the population
  • Protest and court cases later won rights
🌟

Perspectives

  • Settlers saw frontier as opportunity
  • Indigenous peoples saw loss
  • Museums and history writing were shaped by settlers
  • Modern debates include apologies, land return and recognition
🎯 Remember Mayflower 1620, Indian Removal 1830, Cook 1770, Sydney 1788.

lessons.title: Paths to Modernisation
yt: class 11 history paths to modernisation china japan meiji restoration opium war

blocks.x: In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries Japan and China followed different paths to modernity. Japan was ruled by the Tokugawa shoguns from 1603, who followed a policy of isolation (sakoku), with the emperor in Kyoto. In 1853 the American Commodore Matthew Perry arrived with warships and the Treaty of Kanagawa in 1854 opened Japanese ports. The shogunate collapsed and in 1868 the Meiji Restoration restored power to the emperor Meiji, who moved the capital to Tokyo. Japan's slogan was Fukoku Kyohei, rich country, strong army. The Meiji government abolished the feudal domains, introduced conscription, a new education system, railways, factories and a constitution in 1889. Japan became the first Asian industrial power, defeated China in 1894 to 1895 and Russia in 1904 to 1905, and annexed Korea in 1910. Thinkers like Fukuzawa Yukichi urged learning from the West. In China, the Qing dynasty faced the Opium Wars: the First (1839 to 1842) ended with the Treaty of Nanjing, ceding Hong Kong; the Second (1856 to 1860) followed. The Taiping Rebellion (1850 to 1864) led by Hong Xiuquan killed millions. Reformers like Kang Youwei urged change in the Hundred Days Reform (1898), and the Boxer Uprising (1900) opposed foreigners. Sun Yat-sen led the Revolution of 1911, ending the empire; his Three Principles were nationalism, democracy and livelihood. The May Fourth Movement of 1919 stressed new culture. The Communist Party was founded in 1921, and under Mao Zedong won the civil war, founding the People's Republic of China in 1949, followed by the Great Leap Forward (1958) and Cultural Revolution (1966). Deng Xiaoping launched reforms from 1978.
Deep dive: Japan

Isolation under the shoguns ended with Perry. The Meiji leaders modernised the army, schools, economy and state. Japan became an imperial power. Zaibatsu firms such as Mitsubishi led industry. Militarism grew in the 1930s.
Deep dive: China

The Qing faced foreign powers and unequal treaties. Opium trade drained silver and led to war. Reform failed under the Qing. The 1911 Revolution ended the dynasty. The Nationalists (Kuomintang) and Communists later fought for power.
Deep dive: Comparison

Japan modernised from above under a strong state and avoided colonisation. China was weakened by foreign pressure and internal rebellion. Both searched for national strength, but with different results.

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Paths to Modernisation

In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries Japan and China followed different paths to modernity

🔑

Big idea

  • In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries Japan and China followed different paths to modernity
  • Japan was ruled by the Tokugawa shoguns from 1603, who followed a policy of isolation (sakoku), with the emperor in Kyoto
  • In 1853 the American Commodore Matthew Perry arrived with warships and the Treaty of Kanagawa in 1854 opened Japanese ports
  • The shogunate collapsed and in 1868 the Meiji Restoration restored power to the emperor Meiji, who moved the capital to Tokyo
Read the full explanation

In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries Japan and China followed different paths to modernity. Japan was ruled by the Tokugawa shoguns from 1603, who followed a policy of isolation (sakoku), with the emperor in Kyoto. In 1853 the American Commodore Matthew Perry arrived with warships and the Treaty of Kanagawa in 1854 opened Japanese ports. The shogunate collapsed and in 1868 the Meiji Restoration restored power to the emperor Meiji, who moved the capital to Tokyo. Japan's slogan was Fukoku Kyohei, rich country, strong army. The Meiji government abolished the feudal domains, introduced conscription, a new education system, railways, factories and a constitution in 1889. Japan became the first Asian industrial power, defeated China in 1894 to 1895 and Russia in 1904 to 1905, and annexed Korea in 1910. Thinkers like Fukuzawa Yukichi urged learning from the West. In China, the Qing dynasty faced the Opium Wars: the First (1839 to 1842) ended with the Treaty of Nanjing, ceding Hong Kong; the Second (1856 to 1860) followed. The Taiping Rebellion (1850 to 1864) led by Hong Xiuquan killed millions. Reformers like Kang Youwei urged change in the Hundred Days Reform (1898), and the Boxer Uprising (1900) opposed foreigners. Sun Yat-sen led the Revolution of 1911, ending the empire; his Three Principles were nationalism, democracy and livelihood. The May Fourth Movement of 1919 stressed new culture. The Communist Party was founded in 1921, and under Mao Zedong won the civil war, founding the People's Republic of China in 1949, followed by the Great Leap Forward (1958) and Cultural Revolution (1966). Deng Xiaoping launched reforms from 1978.

📌

Japan

  • Isolation under the shoguns ended with Perry
  • The Meiji leaders modernised the army, schools, economy and state
  • Japan became an imperial power
  • Zaibatsu firms such as Mitsubishi led industry
Read the full explanation

Isolation under the shoguns ended with Perry. The Meiji leaders modernised the army, schools, economy and state. Japan became an imperial power. Zaibatsu firms such as Mitsubishi led industry. Militarism grew in the 1930s.

🧠

China

  • The Qing faced foreign powers and unequal treaties
  • Opium trade drained silver and led to war
  • Reform failed under the Qing
  • The 1911 Revolution ended the dynasty
Read the full explanation

The Qing faced foreign powers and unequal treaties. Opium trade drained silver and led to war. Reform failed under the Qing. The 1911 Revolution ended the dynasty. The Nationalists (Kuomintang) and Communists later fought for power.

🌟

Comparison

  • Japan modernised from above under a strong state and avoided colonisation
  • China was weakened by foreign pressure and internal rebellion
  • Both searched for national strength, but with different results
🎯 Remember Perry 1853, Meiji 1868, Opium War 1839, Revolution 1911, PRC 1949.
🇮🇳

lessons.title: Computer System
yt: class 11 informatics practices computer system hardware software memory

blocks.x: A computer system is a combination of hardware and software that accepts data (input), processes it and produces results (output). The main hardware units are the input devices (keyboard, mouse, scanner), the Central Processing Unit or CPU with its Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU), Control Unit (CU) and registers, the memory and the output devices (monitor, printer). Memory is of two types: primary memory (RAM, which is volatile, and ROM, which is non-volatile) and secondary memory (hard disk, SSD, pen drive, CD/DVD). Units: 1 byte = 8 bits, 1 KB = 1024 bytes, 1 MB = 1024 KB, 1 GB = 1024 MB, 1 TB = 1024 GB. Software is of three types: system software (operating system such as Windows, Linux, Android; language processors; device drivers), application software (word processor, spreadsheet) and utility software (antivirus, disk cleaner). Language processors translate a program: an assembler converts assembly language to machine language, a compiler translates the whole program at once, and an interpreter translates and runs it line by line. Python uses an interpreter. Computers store everything in binary; number systems include decimal (base 10), binary (base 2), octal (base 8) and hexadecimal (base 16). Encoding schemes include ASCII (7 bits, 128 characters), ISCII for Indian scripts and Unicode, which covers all languages. The operating system manages memory, processes, files and devices; examples of types are single-user, multi-user and real-time. A computer has a bus system to carry data and the ports connect devices such as USB and HDMI.
Deep dive: Hardware

The CPU is the brain: ALU does arithmetic and logic, CU controls operations, registers hold data temporarily. Cache is a small fast memory between CPU and RAM. RAM holds running programs; ROM stores startup instructions. Secondary memory stores data permanently.
Deep dive: Software and translators

System software runs the machine; application software helps users. A compiler checks the entire code and gives errors together; an interpreter stops at the first error. Open source software can be modified, as with Linux and Python.
Deep dive: Number systems and encoding

Binary uses 0 and 1; octal uses 0-7; hexadecimal uses 0-9 and A-F. Conversions use repeated division or place values. ASCII gives each character a code, for example A is 65. Unicode (UTF-8) supports all scripts, including Devanagari.
Hindi saransh
Computer system: CPU, memory, input-output aur software milkar kaam karte hain; binary mein sab kuch store hota hai.
Remember: compiler = whole program, interpreter = line by line (Python).

Visual lesson

Computer System

A computer system is a combination of hardware and software that accepts data (input), processes it and produces results (output)

Flat concept map (2D)
