🔑

Big idea

  • A computer system is a combination of hardware and software that accepts data (input), processes it and produces results (output)
  • The main hardware units are the input devices (keyboard, mouse, scanner), the Central Processing Unit or CPU with its Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU)…
  • Memory is of two types: primary memory (RAM, which is volatile, and ROM, which is non-volatile) and secondary memory (hard disk, SSD, pen drive…
  • Units: 1 byte = 8 bits, 1 KB = 1024 bytes, 1 MB = 1024 KB, 1 GB = 1024 MB, 1 TB = 1024 GB
Read the full explanation

A computer system is a combination of hardware and software that accepts data (input), processes it and produces results (output). The main hardware units are the input devices (keyboard, mouse, scanner), the Central Processing Unit or CPU with its Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU), Control Unit (CU) and registers, the memory and the output devices (monitor, printer). Memory is of two types: primary memory (RAM, which is volatile, and ROM, which is non-volatile) and secondary memory (hard disk, SSD, pen drive, CD/DVD). Units: 1 byte = 8 bits, 1 KB = 1024 bytes, 1 MB = 1024 KB, 1 GB = 1024 MB, 1 TB = 1024 GB. Software is of three types: system software (operating system such as Windows, Linux, Android; language processors; device drivers), application software (word processor, spreadsheet) and utility software (antivirus, disk cleaner). Language processors translate a program: an assembler converts assembly language to machine language, a compiler translates the whole program at once, and an interpreter translates and runs it line by line. Python uses an interpreter. Computers store everything in binary; number systems include decimal (base 10), binary (base 2), octal (base 8) and hexadecimal (base 16). Encoding schemes include ASCII (7 bits, 128 characters), ISCII for Indian scripts and Unicode, which covers all languages. The operating system manages memory, processes, files and devices; examples of types are single-user, multi-user and real-time. A computer has a bus system to carry data and the ports connect devices such as USB and HDMI.

🕰️

Hardware

  • The CPU is the brain: ALU does arithmetic and logic, CU controls operations, registers hold data temporarily
  • Cache is a small fast memory between CPU and RAM
  • RAM holds running programs
  • ROM stores startup instructions
Read the full explanation

The CPU is the brain: ALU does arithmetic and logic, CU controls operations, registers hold data temporarily. Cache is a small fast memory between CPU and RAM. RAM holds running programs; ROM stores startup instructions. Secondary memory stores data permanently.

🕰️

Software and translators

  • System software runs the machine
  • Application software helps users
  • A compiler checks the entire code and gives errors together
  • An interpreter stops at the first error
Read the full explanation

System software runs the machine; application software helps users. A compiler checks the entire code and gives errors together; an interpreter stops at the first error. Open source software can be modified, as with Linux and Python.

🌟

Number systems and encoding

  • Binary uses 0 and 1
  • Octal uses 0-7
  • Hexadecimal uses 0-9 and A-F
  • Conversions use repeated division or place values
Read the full explanation

Binary uses 0 and 1; octal uses 0-7; hexadecimal uses 0-9 and A-F. Conversions use repeated division or place values. ASCII gives each character a code, for example A is 65. Unicode (UTF-8) supports all scripts, including Devanagari.

🧮

🎯 Remember compiler = whole program, interpreter = line by line (Python).

yt: class 11 informatics practices python basics variables data types operators

blocks.x: Python is a high-level, interpreted, general-purpose language created by Guido van Rossum and released in 1991. It is case sensitive, uses indentation to define blocks and is free and open source. A Python program can be run in interactive mode (the shell, with the >>> prompt) or script mode (a .py file). Tokens are the smallest units: keywords (such as if, else, while, for, def, True, False, None), identifiers (names given to variables and functions), literals, operators and punctuators. Identifier rules: they may contain letters, digits and underscore, cannot start with a digit and cannot be a keyword. A variable is a name referring to a value; Python is dynamically typed, so the type is decided by the value. Standard data types are int, float, complex, bool, str, list, tuple, dict and set; None is the null type. Mutable types (list, dict, set) can be changed after creation; immutable types (int, float, str, tuple) cannot. Operators: arithmetic (+, -, *, /, //, %, **), relational (<, >, <=, >=, ==, !=), logical (and, or, not), assignment (=, +=, -=), identity (is, is not) and membership (in, not in). Division / always gives a float, // gives floor division and % gives the remainder. Precedence: parentheses, then **, then unary minus, then *, /, //, %, then + and -, then comparison, not, and, or. The input() function reads a string, so int() or float() converts it; print() displays output with the sep and end parameters. Comments begin with #. type() shows the type and id() the memory address. Type conversion can be implicit or explicit.
Deep dive: Data types and variables

Numbers are int, float and complex. A string is a sequence of characters in quotes. The bool type has True and False, equal to 1 and 0. Assigning a = b = 5 gives both names the value 5. Multiple assignment a, b = 1, 2 is allowed. Variables can change type when reassigned.
Deep dive: Operators

** is exponentiation and is right associative. // floors the result, so -7 // 2 is -4. % gives the remainder, so 7 % 3 is 1. == compares values, while is compares identity. and returns the first false operand or the last value.
Deep dive: Input and output
input() always returns a string. For numbers write int(input()). print(a, b, sep="-", end="!") controls separators. Escape sequences include newline and tab. f-strings were added in Python 3.6.

Python ek saral, interpreted bhasha hai; variable, data type aur operator iski buniyaad hain.

Big idea

  • It is case sensitive, uses indentation to define blocks and is free and open source
  • A Python program can be run in interactive mode (the shell, with the >>> prompt) or script mode (a .py file)

Read the full explanation

Python is a high-level, interpreted, general-purpose language created by Guido van Rossum and released in 1991. It is case sensitive, uses indentation to define blocks and is free and open source. A Python program can be run in interactive mode (the shell, with the >>> prompt) or script mode (a .py file). Tokens are the smallest units: keywords (such as if, else, while, for, def, True, False, None), identifiers (names given to variables and functions), literals, operators and punctuators. Identifier rules: they may contain letters, digits and underscore, cannot start with a digit and cannot be a keyword. A variable is a name referring to a value; Python is dynamically typed, so the type is decided by the value. Standard data types are int, float, complex, bool, str, list, tuple, dict and set; None is the null type. Mutable types (list, dict, set) can be changed after creation; immutable types (int, float, str, tuple) cannot. Operators: arithmetic (+, -, *, /, //, %, ), relational (<, >, <=, >=, ==, !=), logical (and, or, not), assignment (=, +=, -=), identity (is, is not) and membership (in, not in). Division / always gives a float, // gives floor division and % gives the remainder. Precedence: parentheses, then , then unary minus, then *, /, //, %, then + and -, then comparison, not, and, or. The input() function reads a string, so int() or float() converts it; print() displays output with the sep and end parameters. Comments begin with #. type() shows the type and id() the memory address. Type conversion can be implicit or explicit.

📌

Data types and variables

  • Numbers are int, float and complex
  • A string is a sequence of characters in quotes
  • The bool type has True and False, equal to 1 and 0
  • Assigning a = b = 5 gives both names the value 5
Read the full explanation

Numbers are int, float and complex. A string is a sequence of characters in quotes. The bool type has True and False, equal to 1 and 0. Assigning a = b = 5 gives both names the value 5. Multiple assignment a, b = 1, 2 is allowed. Variables can change type when reassigned.

🧠

Operators

  • Is exponentiation and is right associative
  • // floors the result, so -7 // 2 is -4
  • % gives the remainder, so 7 % 3 is 1
  • == compares values, while is compares identity
Read the full explanation

is exponentiation and is right associative. // floors the result, so -7 // 2 is -4. % gives the remainder, so 7 % 3 is 1. == compares values, while is compares identity. and returns the first false operand or the last value.

🌟

Input and output

  • Input() always returns a string
  • For numbers write int(input())
  • Print(a, b, sep="-", end="!") controls separators
  • Escape sequences include newline and tab
Read the full explanation

input() always returns a string. For numbers write int(input()). print(a, b, sep="-", end="!") controls separators. Escape sequences include newline and tab. f-strings were added in Python 3.6.

lessons.title: Control Flow and Strings
yt: class 11 informatics practices python if else loops strings functions

blocks.x: Control flow decides the order of execution. Selection uses if, if-else and if-elif-else with a colon and indented block. Iteration uses for and while loops. The for loop works with range(start, stop, step), where stop is excluded; range(5) gives 0 to 4. The while loop repeats while a condition is true. break exits the loop, continue skips to the next iteration, and pass does nothing. A loop can have an else block that runs when the loop ends without break. Nested loops are used for patterns. A string is an immutable sequence of characters with indexing from 0 and negative indexing from -1. Slicing s[start:stop:step] gives a part of the string. Operations include concatenation (+), repetition (*), membership (in) and comparison. Functions: len(), upper(), lower(), title(), capitalize(), strip(), find(), index(), count(), replace(), split(), join(), isalpha(), isdigit(), isalnum(), startswith() and endswith(). A user-defined function is made with def, may take parameters and may return a value. Arguments can be positional, keyword or default. Variables inside a function have local scope; global variables are declared outside. Modules like math (sqrt, ceil, floor, pow, pi), random (random, randint, randrange) and statistics (mean, median, mode) are imported with import. Common programs: factorial, prime check, Fibonacci series, palindrome and sum of digits.
Deep dive: Selection and loops
The if-elif chain checks conditions in order. range(1, 10, 2) gives 1, 3, 5, 7, 9. A while loop needs a change in the variable to stop. break leaves the loop at once; continue goes to the next cycle.
Deep dive: Strings

Index 0 is the first character and -1 the last. A slice with step -1 reverses a string. Strings cannot be changed in place, so a new string is created. Methods return new strings. split() returns a list; join() builds a string from a list.
Deep dive: Functions and modules
A function without return gives None. Default parameters must come after non-default ones. Local variables hide global ones inside functions. The math and random modules are used often in programs.

Visual lesson

Control Flow and Strings

Control flow decides the order of execution

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Selection and loops›3Strings›4Functions and modules
range(5)0 to 4
🔑

Big idea

  • Control flow decides the order of execution
  • Selection uses if, if-else and if-elif-else with a colon and indented block
  • Iteration uses for and while loops
  • The for loop works with range(start, stop, step), where stop is excluded
Read the full explanation

Control flow decides the order of execution. Selection uses if, if-else and if-elif-else with a colon and indented block. Iteration uses for and while loops. The for loop works with range(start, stop, step), where stop is excluded; range(5) gives 0 to 4. The while loop repeats while a condition is true. break exits the loop, continue skips to the next iteration, and pass does nothing. A loop can have an else block that runs when the loop ends without break. Nested loops are used for patterns. A string is an immutable sequence of characters with indexing from 0 and negative indexing from -1. Slicing s[start:stop:step] gives a part of the string. Operations include concatenation (+), repetition (*), membership (in) and comparison. Functions: len(), upper(), lower(), title(), capitalize(), strip(), find(), index(), count(), replace(), split(), join(), isalpha(), isdigit(), isalnum(), startswith() and endswith(). A user-defined function is made with def, may take parameters and may return a value. Arguments can be positional, keyword or default. Variables inside a function have local scope; global variables are declared outside. Modules like math (sqrt, ceil, floor, pow, pi), random (random, randint, randrange) and statistics (mean, median, mode) are imported with import. Common programs: factorial, prime check, Fibonacci series, palindrome and sum of digits.

📌

Selection and loops

  • The if-elif chain checks conditions in order
  • Range(1, 10, 2) gives 1, 3, 5, 7, 9
  • A while loop needs a change in the variable to stop
  • Break leaves the loop at once
Read the full explanation

The if-elif chain checks conditions in order. range(1, 10, 2) gives 1, 3, 5, 7, 9. A while loop needs a change in the variable to stop. break leaves the loop at once; continue goes to the next cycle.

🧠

Strings

  • Index 0 is the first character and -1 the last
  • A slice with step -1 reverses a string
  • Strings cannot be changed in place, so a new string is created
  • Methods return new strings
Read the full explanation

Index 0 is the first character and -1 the last. A slice with step -1 reverses a string. Strings cannot be changed in place, so a new string is created. Methods return new strings. split() returns a list; join() builds a string from a list.

🌟

Functions and modules

  • A function without return gives None
  • Default parameters must come after non-default ones
  • Local variables hide global ones inside functions
  • The math and random modules are used often in programs
🧮

defFunctionKeyword
🎯 Remember range stop value is not included.

lessons.title: Lists and Tuples
yt: class 11 informatics practices lists tuples python data handling

blocks.x: A list is an ordered, mutable collection written in square brackets, for example [1, 2, "a", 3.5]. Elements can be of different types, indexed from 0, and sliced like strings. Operations: concatenation (+), repetition (*), membership (in), len(), min(), max(), sum(), sorted() and list(). Methods: append() adds one element at the end, extend() adds many, insert(i, x) adds at a position, remove(x) deletes the first occurrence, pop() removes and returns the last (or at index), del removes by index or slice, index() finds a position, count() counts occurrences, sort() orders in place, reverse() reverses in place and clear() empties the list. Lists can be nested (a list of lists), as in a matrix. Copying with b = a gives another name for the same list; b = a.copy() or list(a) makes a separate copy. A tuple is an ordered immutable collection written in parentheses, for example (1, 2, 3); a single-element tuple needs a comma, as (5,). Tuples support indexing, slicing, concatenation, repetition, count() and index(), but not append, remove or item assignment. Tuple packing and unpacking allow a, b = b, a to swap values. Tuples are faster and safer for fixed data. Traversal uses a for loop. Common programs: finding the largest number, linear search, reversing a list, counting frequency, and computing mean and median of a list. sorted() returns a new list while sort() changes the original. A tuple can contain a mutable list, and that inner list can still change.
Deep dive: Lists

Lists are mutable, so assignment to an index changes them. append adds a single item, even a list. extend adds each element of an iterable. pop(i) returns the removed item. Slicing creates a new list. Sorting needs comparable items.
Deep dive: Tuples

Tuples are immutable and hashable if elements are hashable. They are used for fixed records and as dictionary keys. Tuples can be returned from functions to give many values. Concatenation makes a new tuple.
Deep dive: Comparison and programs

Lists are for changing data; tuples for constant data. Linear search checks each element in turn. Bubble sort swaps adjacent elements. Mean is sum divided by count; median is the middle value of sorted data.
Hindi saransh
List badli ja sakti hai (mutable), tuple nahi; dono mein indexing aur slicing hoti hai.
Remember: a one-element tuple needs a comma, as (5,).

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Lists and Tuples

A list is an ordered, mutable collection written in square brackets, for example [1, 2, "a", 3.5]

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Lists›3Tuples›4Comparison and programs
🔑

Big idea

  • A list is an ordered, mutable collection written in square brackets, for example [1, 2, "a", 3.5]
  • Elements can be of different types, indexed from 0, and sliced like strings
  • Operations: concatenation (+), repetition (*), membership (in), len(), min(), max(), sum(), sorted() and list()
  • Methods: append() adds one element at the end, extend() adds many, insert(i, x) adds at a position, remove(x) deletes the first occurrence, pop()…
Read the full explanation

A list is an ordered, mutable collection written in square brackets, for example [1, 2, "a", 3.5]. Elements can be of different types, indexed from 0, and sliced like strings. Operations: concatenation (+), repetition (*), membership (in), len(), min(), max(), sum(), sorted() and list(). Methods: append() adds one element at the end, extend() adds many, insert(i, x) adds at a position, remove(x) deletes the first occurrence, pop() removes and returns the last (or at index), del removes by index or slice, index() finds a position, count() counts occurrences, sort() orders in place, reverse() reverses in place and clear() empties the list. Lists can be nested (a list of lists), as in a matrix. Copying with b = a gives another name for the same list; b = a.copy() or list(a) makes a separate copy. A tuple is an ordered immutable collection written in parentheses, for example (1, 2, 3); a single-element tuple needs a comma, as (5,). Tuples support indexing, slicing, concatenation, repetition, count() and index(), but not append, remove or item assignment. Tuple packing and unpacking allow a, b = b, a to swap values. Tuples are faster and safer for fixed data. Traversal uses a for loop. Common programs: finding the largest number, linear search, reversing a list, counting frequency, and computing mean and median of a list. sorted() returns a new list while sort() changes the original. A tuple can contain a mutable list, and that inner list can still change.

📌

Lists

  • Lists are mutable, so assignment to an index changes them
  • Append adds a single item, even a list
  • Extend adds each element of an iterable
  • Pop(i) returns the removed item
Read the full explanation

Lists are mutable, so assignment to an index changes them. append adds a single item, even a list. extend adds each element of an iterable. pop(i) returns the removed item. Slicing creates a new list. Sorting needs comparable items.

🧠

Tuples

  • Tuples are immutable and hashable if elements are hashable
  • They are used for fixed records and as dictionary keys
  • Tuples can be returned from functions to give many values
  • Concatenation makes a new tuple
🌟

Comparison and programs

  • Lists are for changing data
  • Tuples for constant data
  • Linear search checks each element in turn
  • Bubble sort swaps adjacent elements
Read the full explanation

Lists are for changing data; tuples for constant data. Linear search checks each element in turn. Bubble sort swaps adjacent elements. Mean is sum divided by count; median is the middle value of sorted data.

🧮

Formula tiles

Tuple( )Immutable
appendOne itemEnd
extendMany itemsEnd
popRemove lastReturns
🎯 Remember a one-element tuple needs a comma, as (5,).

lessons.title: Dictionaries
yt: class 11 informatics practices dictionary python key value

blocks.x: A dictionary is an unordered (insertion-ordered from Python 3.7) mutable collection of key-value pairs written in curly braces, for example d = {"name": "Asha", "age": 16}. Keys must be unique and immutable (numbers, strings, tuples); values can be of any type and may repeat. Items are accessed by key, as d["name"]; a missing key raises KeyError, while d.get("x") returns None or a default. Adding or changing a pair uses d[key] = value. Deleting uses del d[key], pop(key) or popitem(), and clear() empties it. Methods: keys() returns the keys, values() the values, items() the (key, value) pairs, update() merges another dictionary, copy() makes a copy, setdefault() inserts a key if absent, and fromkeys() creates a dictionary from keys. len() gives the number of pairs and the in operator tests for a key, not a value. Traversal uses for k in d, for k, v in d.items(). Dictionaries are built with dict() or from a list of pairs. Nested dictionaries hold dictionaries as values. Typical programs: counting character frequency, counting words, storing student records and finding the key with the maximum value. sorted(d) sorts the keys. Dictionaries use hashing, which makes lookup very fast. Unlike lists, they are accessed by key and not by position. json files resemble dictionaries.
Deep dive: Basics
Keys are unique; assigning a duplicate key overwrites the old value. Keys must be hashable, so lists cannot be keys but tuples can. Values may be lists or other dictionaries.
Deep dive: Methods

get avoids errors for missing keys. update adds or replaces many pairs. pop removes a key and returns its value. items gives pairs for unpacking in loops. keys and values give views of the dictionary.
Deep dive: Programs
Frequency counting: for ch in s: d[ch] = d.get(ch, 0) + 1. Student record: a dictionary of dictionaries. Searching by key is faster than searching a list.
Hindi saransh
Dictionary key-value jodiyon ka sangrah hai; key unique aur immutable honi chahiye.
Remember: in checks keys, not values.

Visual lesson

Dictionaries

A dictionary is an unordered (insertion-ordered from Python 3.7) mutable collection of key-value pairs written in curly braces, for example d = {"name": "Asha", "age":…

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Basics›3Methods›4Programs
🔑

Big idea

  • A dictionary is an unordered (insertion-ordered from Python 3.7) mutable collection of key-value pairs written in curly braces, for example d =…
  • Keys must be unique and immutable (numbers, strings, tuples)
  • Values can be of any type and may repeat
  • Items are accessed by key, as d["name"]
Read the full explanation

A dictionary is an unordered (insertion-ordered from Python 3.7) mutable collection of key-value pairs written in curly braces, for example d = {"name": "Asha", "age": 16}. Keys must be unique and immutable (numbers, strings, tuples); values can be of any type and may repeat. Items are accessed by key, as d["name"]; a missing key raises KeyError, while d.get("x") returns None or a default. Adding or changing a pair uses d[key] = value. Deleting uses del d[key], pop(key) or popitem(), and clear() empties it. Methods: keys() returns the keys, values() the values, items() the (key, value) pairs, update() merges another dictionary, copy() makes a copy, setdefault() inserts a key if absent, and fromkeys() creates a dictionary from keys. len() gives the number of pairs and the in operator tests for a key, not a value. Traversal uses for k in d, for k, v in d.items(). Dictionaries are built with dict() or from a list of pairs. Nested dictionaries hold dictionaries as values. Typical programs: counting character frequency, counting words, storing student records and finding the key with the maximum value. sorted(d) sorts the keys. Dictionaries use hashing, which makes lookup very fast. Unlike lists, they are accessed by key and not by position. json files resemble dictionaries.

📘

Basics

  • Keys are unique
  • Assigning a duplicate key overwrites the old value
  • Keys must be hashable, so lists cannot be keys but tuples can
  • Values may be lists or other dictionaries
🔄

Methods

  • Get avoids errors for missing keys
  • Update adds or replaces many pairs
  • Pop removes a key and returns its value
  • Items gives pairs for unpacking in loops
Read the full explanation

get avoids errors for missing keys. update adds or replaces many pairs. pop removes a key and returns its value. items gives pairs for unpacking in loops. keys and values give views of the dictionary.

🌟

Programs

  • Frequency counting: for ch in s: d[ch] = d.get(ch, 0) + 1
  • Student record: a dictionary of dictionaries
  • Searching by key is faster than searching a list

lessons.title: Introduction to NumPy
yt: class 11 informatics practices numpy array python

blocks.x: NumPy (Numerical Python) is a library for fast numerical computing with arrays, imported as import numpy as np. A NumPy array (ndarray) is a grid of values of the same type, indexed by non-negative integers. Arrays are faster and use less memory than lists and support vectorised operations without loops. Creation: np.array([1,2,3]), np.zeros(shape), np.ones(shape), np.arange(start, stop, step), np.linspace(start, stop, num), np.full(shape, value), np.eye(n) and np.random.random(). Attributes: ndim (number of dimensions), shape (rows, columns), size (total elements), dtype (data type) and itemsize. Arrays can be one-dimensional (a vector), two-dimensional (a matrix) or higher. Indexing and slicing work like lists: a[1:4], and a[1,2] or a[1][2] for 2D. Boolean indexing selects elements by a condition, such as a[a>5]. Operations are element-wise: +, -, *, / and ** work between arrays of the same shape, and a scalar is broadcast across the array. Functions: sum, mean, median, max, min, std, var, sqrt, sin and dot. Aggregations accept an axis argument: axis=0 works down columns, axis=1 across rows. reshape() changes shape without changing data, and flatten()/ravel() make 1D arrays. Joining uses concatenate, vstack and hstack, and splitting uses split. Sorting uses np.sort and argsort. Arrays can be read from text files using loadtxt and genfromtxt and saved with savetxt. The astype() method changes dtype, and arrays of different shapes can broadcast if dimensions are compatible.
Deep dive: Arrays
All elements share one dtype, so mixed input is converted. shape gives a tuple, for example (3, 4). arange excludes stop; linspace includes both ends. zeros and ones take a shape tuple.
Deep dive: Operations
Arithmetic is element-wise, so a * b is not matrix multiplication; use dot or matmul. Statistical functions with axis give row-wise or column-wise results. Boolean masks filter data.
Deep dive: Manipulation and files
reshape needs the same number of elements. vstack stacks arrays vertically; hstack stacks horizontally. loadtxt reads numbers from a file. Arrays work well with data science libraries.
Hindi saransh
NumPy array same type ke elementon ka fast grid hai; operations element-wise hote hain.
Remember: a * b is element-wise, not matrix multiplication.

Visual lesson

Introduction to NumPy

NumPy (Numerical Python) is a library for fast numerical computing with arrays, imported as import numpy as np

🔑

Big idea

  • NumPy (Numerical Python) is a library for fast numerical computing with arrays, imported as import numpy as np
  • A NumPy array (ndarray) is a grid of values of the same type, indexed by non-negative integers
  • Arrays are faster and use less memory than lists and support vectorised operations without loops
  • Creation: np.array([1,2,3]), np.zeros(shape), np.ones(shape), np.arange(start, stop, step), np.linspace(start, stop, num), np.full(shape, value)…
Read the full explanation

NumPy (Numerical Python) is a library for fast numerical computing with arrays, imported as import numpy as np. A NumPy array (ndarray) is a grid of values of the same type, indexed by non-negative integers. Arrays are faster and use less memory than lists and support vectorised operations without loops. Creation: np.array([1,2,3]), np.zeros(shape), np.ones(shape), np.arange(start, stop, step), np.linspace(start, stop, num), np.full(shape, value), np.eye(n) and np.random.random(). Attributes: ndim (number of dimensions), shape (rows, columns), size (total elements), dtype (data type) and itemsize. Arrays can be one-dimensional (a vector), two-dimensional (a matrix) or higher. Indexing and slicing work like lists: a[1:4], and a[1,2] or a[1][2] for 2D. Boolean indexing selects elements by a condition, such as a[a>5]. Operations are element-wise: +, -, *, / and work between arrays of the same shape, and a scalar is broadcast across the array. Functions: sum, mean, median, max, min, std, var, sqrt, sin and dot. Aggregations accept an axis argument: axis=0 works down columns, axis=1 across rows. reshape() changes shape without changing data, and flatten()/ravel() make 1D arrays. Joining uses concatenate, vstack and hstack, and splitting uses split. Sorting uses np.sort and argsort. Arrays can be read from text files using loadtxt and genfromtxt and saved with savetxt. The astype() method changes dtype, and arrays of different shapes can broadcast if dimensions are compatible.

🔦

Arrays

  • All elements share one dtype, so mixed input is converted
  • Shape gives a tuple, for example (3, 4)
  • Arange excludes stop
  • Linspace includes both ends
Read the full explanation

All elements share one dtype, so mixed input is converted. shape gives a tuple, for example (3, 4). arange excludes stop; linspace includes both ends. zeros and ones take a shape tuple.

🧠

Operations

  • Arithmetic is element-wise, so a * b is not matrix multiplication
  • Use dot or matmul
  • Statistical functions with axis give row-wise or column-wise results
  • Boolean masks filter data
🌟

Manipulation and files

  • Reshape needs the same number of elements
  • Vstack stacks arrays vertically
  • Hstack stacks horizontally
  • Loadtxt reads numbers from a file
Read the full explanation

reshape needs the same number of elements. vstack stacks arrays vertically; hstack stacks horizontally. loadtxt reads numbers from a file. Arrays work well with data science libraries.

lessons.title: Database Concepts
yt: class 11 informatics practices database concepts dbms relational keys

blocks.x: A database is an organised collection of related data, and a Database Management System (DBMS) is software to create, store, retrieve and manage it. Examples: MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, MS Access and SQLite. A file system stores data in separate files, which causes data redundancy, inconsistency, difficulty in access and poor security; a DBMS reduces these problems, controls access, supports backup and allows sharing. The relational model by E. F. Codd (1970) stores data in relations (tables) made of rows (tuples or records) and columns (attributes or fields). Terms: the degree is the number of attributes, the cardinality is the number of tuples, the domain is the set of possible values of an attribute, and a schema is the structure of the table. Keys: a candidate key is an attribute (or set) that can uniquely identify rows; the primary key is the candidate key chosen to identify rows and cannot be null or duplicate; alternate keys are the remaining candidate keys; a foreign key refers to the primary key of another table and links tables; a composite key uses more than one attribute. Relations have rows with no fixed order, unique rows and atomic values. Integrity constraints include NOT NULL, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY and CHECK. A DBMS has users such as database administrators, developers and end users. SQL, the Structured Query Language, is used to work with relational databases; it has DDL (CREATE, ALTER, DROP), DML (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE), DQL (SELECT) and DCL (GRANT, REVOKE). The data types are INT, FLOAT, CHAR(n), VARCHAR(n), DATE and DECIMAL.
Deep dive: Why DBMS
A DBMS reduces redundancy and inconsistency, enforces integrity, allows concurrent access and offers security. It separates data from programs. Examples are banks, railways and schools.
Deep dive: Relational model
A table has rows and columns with a unique name. The primary key identifies each row. Foreign keys maintain referential integrity between tables. Degree counts columns; cardinality counts rows.
Deep dive: SQL categories
DDL defines structure; DML changes data; DQL queries data; DCL controls permissions. MySQL is a popular open-source RDBMS.
Hindi saransh
Database mein data tables ki rows aur columns mein rakha jata hai; primary key har row ko alag pehchan deti hai.
Remember: degree = columns; cardinality = rows.

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Database Concepts

A database is an organised collection of related data, and a Database Management System (DBMS) is software to create, store, retrieve and manage it

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Why DBMS›3Relational model›4SQL categories
🔑

Big idea

  • A database is an organised collection of related data, and a Database Management System (DBMS) is software to create, store, retrieve and manage it
  • Examples: MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, MS Access and SQLite
  • A file system stores data in separate files, which causes data redundancy, inconsistency, difficulty in access and poor security
  • A DBMS reduces these problems, controls access, supports backup and allows sharing
Read the full explanation

A database is an organised collection of related data, and a Database Management System (DBMS) is software to create, store, retrieve and manage it. Examples: MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, MS Access and SQLite. A file system stores data in separate files, which causes data redundancy, inconsistency, difficulty in access and poor security; a DBMS reduces these problems, controls access, supports backup and allows sharing. The relational model by E. F. Codd (1970) stores data in relations (tables) made of rows (tuples or records) and columns (attributes or fields). Terms: the degree is the number of attributes, the cardinality is the number of tuples, the domain is the set of possible values of an attribute, and a schema is the structure of the table. Keys: a candidate key is an attribute (or set) that can uniquely identify rows; the primary key is the candidate key chosen to identify rows and cannot be null or duplicate; alternate keys are the remaining candidate keys; a foreign key refers to the primary key of another table and links tables; a composite key uses more than one attribute. Relations have rows with no fixed order, unique rows and atomic values. Integrity constraints include NOT NULL, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY and CHECK. A DBMS has users such as database administrators, developers and end users. SQL, the Structured Query Language, is used to work with relational databases; it has DDL (CREATE, ALTER, DROP), DML (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE), DQL (SELECT) and DCL (GRANT, REVOKE). The data types are INT, FLOAT, CHAR(n), VARCHAR(n), DATE and DECIMAL.

📌

Why DBMS

  • A DBMS reduces redundancy and inconsistency, enforces integrity, allows concurrent access and offers security
  • It separates data from programs
  • Examples are banks, railways and schools
🧠

Relational model

  • A table has rows and columns with a unique name
  • The primary key identifies each row
  • Foreign keys maintain referential integrity between tables
  • Degree counts columns
Read the full explanation

A table has rows and columns with a unique name. The primary key identifies each row. Foreign keys maintain referential integrity between tables. Degree counts columns; cardinality counts rows.

🌟

SQL categories

  • DDL defines structure
  • DML changes data
  • DQL queries data
  • DCL controls permissions
Read the full explanation

DDL defines structure; DML changes data; DQL queries data; DCL controls permissions. MySQL is a popular open-source RDBMS.

lessons.title: SQL Queries
yt: class 11 informatics practices sql select where group by aggregate functions

blocks.x: SQL commands are used in MySQL. CREATE DATABASE school; creates a database and USE school; selects it. CREATE TABLE student (rollno INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL, marks FLOAT, dob DATE); creates a table. DESC student (or DESCRIBE) shows its structure. ALTER TABLE adds, modifies or drops a column or constraint (ALTER TABLE student ADD city VARCHAR(20);). DROP TABLE removes the table. INSERT INTO student VALUES (1, "Ravi", 85.5, "2008-05-01"); adds a row. UPDATE student SET marks = 90 WHERE rollno = 1; changes data. DELETE FROM student WHERE rollno = 1; removes rows. SELECT * FROM student; shows all columns; SELECT name, marks FROM student; shows chosen columns. DISTINCT removes duplicates and AS gives an alias. WHERE filters rows with relational operators (=, <>, !=, <, >, <=, >=), logical operators (AND, OR, NOT), BETWEEN (inclusive), IN, LIKE with wildcards (% for any number of characters and _ for exactly one) and IS NULL. ORDER BY sorts ascending (ASC, default) or descending (DESC). Aggregate functions are COUNT(), SUM(), AVG(), MAX() and MIN(); COUNT(*) counts all rows while COUNT(column) ignores NULLs. GROUP BY groups rows with the same value and HAVING filters groups, whereas WHERE filters rows before grouping. Single-row functions include UPPER(), LOWER(), LENGTH(), ROUND(), MOD(), POWER(), NOW(), CURDATE(), SUBSTR() and LEFT(). LIMIT restricts the number of rows. A join combines tables; a Cartesian product pairs every row of one table with every row of the other, and a join with a condition on matching keys gives an equi-join.
Deep dive: DDL and DML

CREATE, ALTER and DROP change structure; INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE change data. Without WHERE, UPDATE and DELETE affect all rows. Text and dates are written in quotes. A primary key must be unique and not null.
Deep dive: SELECT queries

The order of clauses is SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY. LIKE "A%" matches names starting with A; LIKE "_a%" matches names with a as the second letter. BETWEEN 60 AND 80 includes 60 and 80.
Deep dive: Aggregates and joins

Aggregates summarise many rows into one value. GROUP BY with an aggregate gives one result per group. HAVING works on aggregate conditions. A Cartesian product has rows equal to the product of row counts; its degree is the sum of degrees.
Hindi saransh
SQL mein CREATE, INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE aur GROUP BY se database ka data sambhala jata hai.
Remember: WHERE filters rows; HAVING filters groups.

Visual lesson

SQL Queries

SQL commands are used in MySQL

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2DDL and DML›3SELECT queries›4Aggregates and joins
🔑

Big idea

  • SQL commands are used in MySQL
  • CREATE DATABASE school
  • Creates a database and USE school
  • CREATE TABLE student (rollno INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL, marks FLOAT, dob DATE)
Read the full explanation

SQL commands are used in MySQL. CREATE DATABASE school; creates a database and USE school; selects it. CREATE TABLE student (rollno INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL, marks FLOAT, dob DATE); creates a table. DESC student (or DESCRIBE) shows its structure. ALTER TABLE adds, modifies or drops a column or constraint (ALTER TABLE student ADD city VARCHAR(20);). DROP TABLE removes the table. INSERT INTO student VALUES (1, "Ravi", 85.5, "2008-05-01"); adds a row. UPDATE student SET marks = 90 WHERE rollno = 1; changes data. DELETE FROM student WHERE rollno = 1; removes rows. SELECT * FROM student; shows all columns; SELECT name, marks FROM student; shows chosen columns. DISTINCT removes duplicates and AS gives an alias. WHERE filters rows with relational operators (=, <>, !=, <, >, <=, >=), logical operators (AND, OR, NOT), BETWEEN (inclusive), IN, LIKE with wildcards (% for any number of characters and _ for exactly one) and IS NULL. ORDER BY sorts ascending (ASC, default) or descending (DESC). Aggregate functions are COUNT(), SUM(), AVG(), MAX() and MIN(); COUNT(*) counts all rows while COUNT(column) ignores NULLs. GROUP BY groups rows with the same value and HAVING filters groups, whereas WHERE filters rows before grouping. Single-row functions include UPPER(), LOWER(), LENGTH(), ROUND(), MOD(), POWER(), NOW(), CURDATE(), SUBSTR() and LEFT(). LIMIT restricts the number of rows. A join combines tables; a Cartesian product pairs every row of one table with every row of the other, and a join with a condition on matching keys gives an equi-join.

📌

DDL and DML

  • CREATE, ALTER and DROP change structure
  • INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE change data
  • Without WHERE, UPDATE and DELETE affect all rows
  • Text and dates are written in quotes
Read the full explanation

CREATE, ALTER and DROP change structure; INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE change data. Without WHERE, UPDATE and DELETE affect all rows. Text and dates are written in quotes. A primary key must be unique and not null.

🧠

SELECT queries

  • The order of clauses is SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY
  • LIKE "A%" matches names starting with A
  • LIKE "_a%" matches names with a as the second letter
  • BETWEEN 60 AND 80 includes 60 and 80
🌟

Aggregates and joins

  • Aggregates summarise many rows into one value
  • GROUP BY with an aggregate gives one result per group
  • HAVING works on aggregate conditions
  • A Cartesian product has rows equal to the product of row counts
Read the full explanation

Aggregates summarise many rows into one value. GROUP BY with an aggregate gives one result per group. HAVING works on aggregate conditions. A Cartesian product has rows equal to the product of row counts; its degree is the sum of degrees.

🧮

lessons.title: Societal Impacts
yt: class 11 informatics practices societal impacts digital footprint cyber safety ewaste

blocks.x: Information technology affects society in many ways, and responsible use matters. A digital footprint is the trail of data we leave online; an active footprint is data shared deliberately (posts, emails) and a passive footprint is data collected without our active input (browsing history, IP address, cookies). Net etiquette (netiquette) means polite behaviour online: be respectful, avoid sharing false news, respect privacy and copyright. Communication etiquette covers email, chat and social media. Cyberbullying is harassment online. Cyber crime includes hacking, phishing (fake messages to steal details), identity theft, ransomware, spam, trolling and cyberstalking. Malware includes viruses, worms, Trojan horses, spyware and ransomware; antivirus software, firewalls and updates protect systems. Safe practices include strong passwords, two-factor authentication, not clicking unknown links and using secure HTTPS websites. Intellectual property rights protect creations: copyright for creative works, patents for inventions and trademarks for brand names. Plagiarism is presenting another person's work as your own. Licences: open source and Creative Commons allow sharing with conditions; free and open source software (FOSS) is widely used. The Information Technology Act, 2000 is the main Indian law on cyber crime and electronic records, amended in 2008. Digital property, cyber law, privacy and data protection are key issues; India passed the Digital Personal Data Protection Act in 2023. E-waste is discarded electronic goods such as computers and phones; it contains toxic metals like lead and mercury, and should be recycled, reused or disposed of properly. Green computing reduces energy use. Technology also raises gender and disability issues, so assistive technologies and accessibility are important, and the digital divide is the gap between those with and without access. Health issues include eye strain, repetitive strain injury, poor posture and addiction. Indian initiatives include Digital India, DigiLocker, UPI and CERT-In.
Deep dive: Digital footprint and etiquette
Everything we post can be traced. Active footprints are deliberate; passive ones are collected silently. Privacy settings reduce exposure. Think before posting and respect others online.
Deep dive: Cyber crime and law

Phishing tricks people with fake sites. Hacking is unauthorised access. Identity theft misuses personal data. The IT Act, 2000 defines offences and penalties. Report cyber crime at cybercrime.gov.in or the national helpline 1930.
Deep dive: E-waste and health
E-waste contains harmful substances; recycling recovers metals. The 3 Rs are reduce, reuse and recycle. Good ergonomics and breaks protect health. Accessibility helps persons with disabilities.

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Societal Impacts

Information technology affects society in many ways, and responsible use matters

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Digital footprint and…›3Cyber crime and law›4E-waste and health
IT Act2000
🔑

Big idea

  • Information technology affects society in many ways, and responsible use matters
  • A digital footprint is the trail of data we leave online
  • An active footprint is data shared deliberately (posts, emails) and a passive footprint is data collected without our active input (browsing history…
  • Net etiquette (netiquette) means polite behaviour online: be respectful, avoid sharing false news, respect privacy and copyright
Read the full explanation

Information technology affects society in many ways, and responsible use matters. A digital footprint is the trail of data we leave online; an active footprint is data shared deliberately (posts, emails) and a passive footprint is data collected without our active input (browsing history, IP address, cookies). Net etiquette (netiquette) means polite behaviour online: be respectful, avoid sharing false news, respect privacy and copyright. Communication etiquette covers email, chat and social media. Cyberbullying is harassment online. Cyber crime includes hacking, phishing (fake messages to steal details), identity theft, ransomware, spam, trolling and cyberstalking. Malware includes viruses, worms, Trojan horses, spyware and ransomware; antivirus software, firewalls and updates protect systems. Safe practices include strong passwords, two-factor authentication, not clicking unknown links and using secure HTTPS websites. Intellectual property rights protect creations: copyright for creative works, patents for inventions and trademarks for brand names. Plagiarism is presenting another person's work as your own. Licences: open source and Creative Commons allow sharing with conditions; free and open source software (FOSS) is widely used. The Information Technology Act, 2000 is the main Indian law on cyber crime and electronic records, amended in 2008. Digital property, cyber law, privacy and data protection are key issues; India passed the Digital Personal Data Protection Act in 2023. E-waste is discarded electronic goods such as computers and phones; it contains toxic metals like lead and mercury, and should be recycled, reused or disposed of properly. Green computing reduces energy use. Technology also raises gender and disability issues, so assistive technologies and accessibility are important, and the digital divide is the gap between those with and without access. Health issues include eye strain, repetitive strain injury, poor posture and addiction. Indian initiatives include Digital India, DigiLocker, UPI and CERT-In.

📌

Digital footprint and etiquette

  • Everything we post can be traced
  • Active footprints are deliberate
  • Passive ones are collected silently
  • Privacy settings reduce exposure
Read the full explanation

Everything we post can be traced. Active footprints are deliberate; passive ones are collected silently. Privacy settings reduce exposure. Think before posting and respect others online.

⚖️

Cyber crime and law

  • Phishing tricks people with fake sites
  • Hacking is unauthorised access
  • Identity theft misuses personal data
  • The IT Act, 2000 defines offences and penalties
Read the full explanation

Phishing tricks people with fake sites. Hacking is unauthorised access. Identity theft misuses personal data. The IT Act, 2000 defines offences and penalties. Report cyber crime at cybercrime.gov.in or the national helpline 1930.

🌟

E-waste and health

  • E-waste contains harmful substances
  • Recycling recovers metals
  • The 3 Rs are reduce, reuse and recycle
  • Good ergonomics and breaks protect health
Read the full explanation

E-waste contains harmful substances; recycling recovers metals. The 3 Rs are reduce, reuse and recycle. Good ergonomics and breaks protect health. Accessibility helps persons with disabilities.

yt: class 11 complex numbers

blocks.x: A complex number is z = a + ib with i^2 = -1. Its modulus is |z| = sqrt(a^2 + b^2), its conjugate is a - ib, and its argument is the angle theta with tan theta = b/a (in the correct quadrant). The quadratic ax^2 + bx + c = 0 has roots (-b +- sqrt(b^2 - 4ac))/2a, which are complex when the discriminant is negative.
Deep dive: algebra of complex numbers

A complex number z = a + ib has real part a and imaginary part b. Two complex numbers are equal when their real and imaginary parts are equal. Addition and subtraction are done part by part; multiplication uses (a + ib)(c + id) = (ac - bd) + i(ad + bc). The powers of i repeat with period 4: i^1 = i, i^2 = -1, i^3 = -i, i^4 = 1, so i^n depends on n mod 4. The conjugate of z is z-bar = a - ib, and z x z-bar = a^2 + b^2 = |z|^2, which is how division is done: (a + ib)/(c + id) = (a + ib)(c - id)/(c^2 + d^2).
Deep dive: modulus, argument and the Argand plane

Each complex number is a point (a, b) on the Argand plane. The modulus |z| = sqrt (a^2 + b^2) is the distance from the origin; the argument is the angle the line from the origin makes with the positive real axis; the principal argument lies in (-pi, pi]. Polar form: z = r (cos theta + i sin theta). Properties: |z1 z2| = |z1||z2|, |z1/z2| = |z1|/|z2|, |z-bar| = |z|, z + z-bar = 2 Re(z), z - z-bar = 2i Im(z), |z1 + z2| <= |z1| + |z2| (triangle inequality). The square root of a complex number a + ib is found by assuming x + iy and equating squares.
Deep dive: quadratic equations with complex roots

For ax^2 + bx + c = 0 with real a, b, c the discriminant D = b^2 - 4ac decides the roots: D > 0 two distinct real roots, D = 0 two equal real roots, D < 0 two complex conjugate roots (-b +- i sqrt(-D))/2a. Sum of roots = -b/a and product = c/a hold for complex roots too. A quadratic with given roots p and q is x^2 - (p + q)x + pq = 0. The cube roots of unity are 1, w and w^2 where w = (-1 + i sqrt 3)/2, with 1 + w + w^2 = 0 and w^3 = 1. **Common mistakes:** taking i^2 as 1, forgetting to change the sign of the imaginary part for the conjugate, and reading the argument from the wrong quadrant.

Visual lesson

Complex numbers and quadratic equations

A complex number is z = a + ib with i^2 = -1

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Algebra of complex numbers›3Modulus, argument and the…›4Quadratic equations with…
Modulussqrt (a^2 + b^2)
🔑

Big idea

  • A complex number is z = a + ib with i2 = -1
  • Its modulus is |z| = sqrt(a2 + b2), its conjugate is a - ib, and its argument is the angle theta with tan theta = b/a (in the correct quadrant)
  • The quadratic ax2 + bx + c = 0 has roots (-b +- sqrt(b2 - 4ac))/2a, which are complex when the discriminant is negative
📌

Algebra of complex numbers

  • A complex number z = a + ib has real part a and imaginary part b
  • Two complex numbers are equal when their real and imaginary parts are equal
  • Addition and subtraction are done part by part
  • Multiplication uses (a + ib)(c + id) = (ac - bd) + i(ad + bc)
Read the full explanation

A complex number z = a + ib has real part a and imaginary part b. Two complex numbers are equal when their real and imaginary parts are equal. Addition and subtraction are done part by part; multiplication uses (a + ib)(c + id) = (ac - bd) + i(ad + bc). The powers of i repeat with period 4: i^1 = i, i^2 = -1, i^3 = -i, i^4 = 1, so i^n depends on n mod 4. The conjugate of z is z-bar = a - ib, and z x z-bar = a^2 + b^2 = |z|^2, which is how division is done: (a + ib)/(c + id) = (a + ib)(c - id)/(c^2 + d^2).

🧠

Modulus, argument and the Argand plane

  • Each complex number is a point (a, b) on the Argand plane
  • The modulus |z| = sqrt (a2 + b2) is the distance from the origin
  • The argument is the angle the line from the origin makes with the positive real axis
  • The principal argument lies in (-pi, pi]
Read the full explanation

Each complex number is a point (a, b) on the Argand plane. The modulus |z| = sqrt (a^2 + b^2) is the distance from the origin; the argument is the angle the line from the origin makes with the positive real axis; the principal argument lies in (-pi, pi]. Polar form: z = r (cos theta + i sin theta). Properties: |z1 z2| = |z1||z2|, |z1/z2| = |z1|/|z2|, |z-bar| = |z|, z + z-bar = 2 Re(z), z - z-bar = 2i Im(z), |z1 + z2| <= |z1| + |z2| (triangle inequality). The square root of a complex number a + ib is found by assuming x + iy and equating squares.

🧮

Quadratic equations with complex roots

  • For ax2 + bx + c = 0 with real a, b, c the discriminant D = b2 - 4ac decides the roots: D > 0 two distinct real roots, D = 0 two equal real roots…
  • Sum of roots = -b/a and product = c/a hold for complex roots too
  • A quadratic with given roots p and q is x2 - (p + q)x + pq = 0
  • The cube roots of unity are 1, w and w2 where w = (-1 + i sqrt 3)/2, with 1 + w + w2 = 0 and w3 = 1
Read the full explanation

For ax^2 + bx + c = 0 with real a, b, c the discriminant D = b^2 - 4ac decides the roots: D > 0 two distinct real roots, D = 0 two equal real roots, D < 0 two complex conjugate roots (-b +- i sqrt(-D))/2a. Sum of roots = -b/a and product = c/a hold for complex roots too. A quadratic with given roots p and q is x^2 - (p + q)x + pq = 0. The cube roots of unity are 1, w and w^2 where w = (-1 + i sqrt 3)/2, with 1 + w + w^2 = 0 and w^3 = 1. Common mistakes: taking i^2 as 1, forgetting to change the sign of the imaginary part for the conjugate, and reading the argument from the wrong quadrant.

lessons.title: Linear inequalities
yt: class 11 linear inequalities

blocks.x: An inequality compares two expressions with <, >, <= or >=. Adding or subtracting the same number keeps the sign; multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses it. Solutions are written as intervals; two-variable inequalities represent half-planes bounded by a line.
Deep dive: rules and intervals

Rules: (i) equal numbers can be added to or subtracted from both sides; (ii) both sides can be multiplied or divided by a positive number; (iii) multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the inequality sign. Solution sets are intervals: (a, b) open, [a, b] closed, [a, b) half-open; infinity is never included. For example x >= 2 is [2, infinity) and x < 5 is (-infinity, 5). Integer solutions: list the integers inside the interval. Natural number solutions begin at 1.
Deep dive: compound and modulus inequalities

A compound inequality a < x < b means x > a and x < b together (intersection). For |x| < a (a > 0): -a < x < a. For |x| > a: x < -a or x > a. For |x - c| <= d: c - d <= x <= c + d. Always check the endpoints against the original strict or non-strict sign.
Deep dive: graphical solution of two-variable inequalities

To graph ax + by <= c, draw the line ax + by = c (dashed for strict, solid for non-strict), test the origin (0, 0) and shade the side that satisfies the inequality; if the line passes through the origin test another point. The solution of a system is the common shaded region, which can be bounded or unbounded.

Big idea

  • An inequality compares two expressions with <, >, <= or >=
  • Adding or subtracting the same number keeps the sign
  • Multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses it
  • Solutions are written as intervals
Read the full explanation

An inequality compares two expressions with <, >, <= or >=. Adding or subtracting the same number keeps the sign; multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses it. Solutions are written as intervals; two-variable inequalities represent half-planes bounded by a line.

⚖️

Rules and intervals

  • Rules: (i) equal numbers can be added to or subtracted from both sides
  • (ii) both sides can be multiplied or divided by a positive number
  • (iii) multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the inequality sign
  • Solution sets are intervals: (a, b) open, [a, b] closed, [a, b) half-open
Read the full explanation

Rules: (i) equal numbers can be added to or subtracted from both sides; (ii) both sides can be multiplied or divided by a positive number; (iii) multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the inequality sign. Solution sets are intervals: (a, b) open, [a, b] closed, [a, b) half-open; infinity is never included. For example x >= 2 is [2, infinity) and x < 5 is (-infinity, 5). Integer solutions: list the integers inside the interval. Natural number solutions begin at 1.

🧠

Compound and modulus inequalities

  • A compound inequality a < x < b means x > a and x < b together (intersection)
  • For |x| < a (a > 0): -a < x < a
  • For |x| > a: x < -a or x > a
  • For |x - c| <= d: c - d <= x <= c + d
Read the full explanation

A compound inequality a < x < b means x > a and x < b together (intersection). For |x| < a (a > 0): -a < x < a. For |x| > a: x < -a or x > a. For |x - c| <= d: c - d <= x <= c + d. Always check the endpoints against the original strict or non-strict sign.

🧪

Graphical solution of two-variable inequalities

  • To graph ax + by <= c, draw the line ax + by = c (dashed for strict, solid for non-strict), test the origin (0, 0) and shade the side that satisfies…
  • If the line passes through the origin test another point
  • The solution of a system is the common shaded region, which can be bounded or unbounded

blocks.x: A set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects. Sets are written in roster form {1, 2, 3} or set-builder form {x : x is a natural number less than 4}. Standard sets: N (natural numbers), W (whole numbers), Z (integers), Q (rationals), R (reals). The empty set is written as {} and has no elements; a singleton has one element; a finite set has a countable number of elements. Two sets are equal if they have the same elements; equivalent sets have the same number of elements. A is a subset of B if every element of A is in B. The power set P(A) is the set of all subsets; if A has n elements, P(A) has 2^n elements and there are 2^n - 1 proper subsets. A proper subset is a subset that is not equal to the set. Intervals: open (a, b), closed [a, b], and half open [a, b) or (a, b]. Operations: union A U B (elements in A or B), intersection A n B (elements in both), difference A - B (in A but not B), complement A' = U - A and symmetric difference. Disjoint sets have empty intersection. Laws: commutative, associative, distributive A U (B n C) = (A U B) n (A U C), identity, idempotent, De Morgan (A U B)' = A' n B' and (A n B)' = A' U B'. Cardinality: n(A U B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A n B), and for three sets n(A U B U C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) - n(A n B) - n(B n C) - n(A n C) + n(A n B n C). n(A') = n(U) - n(A). Venn diagrams use circles in a rectangle to show sets, introduced by John Venn. The number of elements in A x B is n(A) times n(B).
Deep dive: Representation and types

Roster lists elements; set-builder gives a rule. Empty, singleton, finite, infinite, universal and equal sets are the main types. A set does not repeat elements. Notation: x in A means x belongs to A.
Deep dive: Operations and laws
Union combines, intersection shares, difference removes. De Morgan laws connect complements. Distributive laws are used to simplify expressions. A - B equals A n B'.
Deep dive: Counting with Venn diagrams
For word problems define sets, draw circles and fill the central region first. n(A U B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A n B). The number who like exactly one of A or B is n(A) + n(B) - 2n(A n B).

In Venn word problems always fill the innermost overlap first.

Visual lesson

Sets

A set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects

minutes
formulas

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Representation and types›3Operations and laws›4Counting with Venn diagrams
Subsets2^n
Proper subsets2^n - 1
🔑

Big idea

  • A set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects
  • Sets are written in roster form {1, 2, 3} or set-builder form {x : x is a natural number less than 4}
  • Standard sets: N (natural numbers), W (whole numbers), Z (integers), Q (rationals), R (reals)
  • The empty set is written as {} and has no elements
Read the full explanation

A set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects. Sets are written in roster form {1, 2, 3} or set-builder form {x : x is a natural number less than 4}. Standard sets: N (natural numbers), W (whole numbers), Z (integers), Q (rationals), R (reals). The empty set is written as {} and has no elements; a singleton has one element; a finite set has a countable number of elements. Two sets are equal if they have the same elements; equivalent sets have the same number of elements. A is a subset of B if every element of A is in B. The power set P(A) is the set of all subsets; if A has n elements, P(A) has 2^n elements and there are 2^n - 1 proper subsets. A proper subset is a subset that is not equal to the set. Intervals: open (a, b), closed [a, b], and half open [a, b) or (a, b]. Operations: union A U B (elements in A or B), intersection A n B (elements in both), difference A - B (in A but not B), complement A' = U - A and symmetric difference. Disjoint sets have empty intersection. Laws: commutative, associative, distributive A U (B n C) = (A U B) n (A U C), identity, idempotent, De Morgan (A U B)' = A' n B' and (A n B)' = A' U B'. Cardinality: n(A U B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A n B), and for three sets n(A U B U C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) - n(A n B) - n(B n C) - n(A n C) + n(A n B n C). n(A') = n(U) - n(A). Venn diagrams use circles in a rectangle to show sets, introduced by John Venn. The number of elements in A x B is n(A) times n(B).

📌

Representation and types

  • Roster lists elements
  • Set-builder gives a rule
  • Empty, singleton, finite, infinite, universal and equal sets are the main types
  • A set does not repeat elements
Read the full explanation

Roster lists elements; set-builder gives a rule. Empty, singleton, finite, infinite, universal and equal sets are the main types. A set does not repeat elements. Notation: x in A means x belongs to A.

⚖️

Operations and laws

  • Union combines, intersection shares, difference removes
  • De Morgan laws connect complements
  • Distributive laws are used to simplify expressions
  • A - B equals A n B'
🌟

Counting with Venn diagrams

  • For word problems define sets, draw circles and fill the central region first
  • N(A U B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A n B)
  • The number who like exactly one of A or B is n(A) + n(B) - 2n(A n B)

lessons.title: Relations and Functions
yt: class 11 maths relations and functions domain range types

blocks.x: The Cartesian product A x B is the set of all ordered pairs (a, b) with a in A and b in B; (a, b) = (c, d) only if a = c and b = d. A x B is not equal to B x A in general, and n(A x B) = n(A) n(B). A relation R from A to B is any subset of A x B. The domain is the set of first elements, the codomain is B and the range is the set of second elements actually used. The number of relations from A to B is 2^(mn) where m = n(A) and n = n(B). A function f from A to B assigns to each element of A exactly one element of B, written f: A -> B. Every function is a relation, but not every relation is a function. Domain is A, codomain is B and range is the set of images. Types of function: constant, identity f(x) = x, polynomial, rational, modulus f(x) = |x|, signum, greatest integer f(x) = [x], linear, quadratic. Real functions: the domain of 1/x is R - {0}; of sqrt(x) is x >= 0; of log x is x > 0. Graphs: f(x) = x^2 is a parabola, f(x) = |x| is a V shape, f(x) = [x] is a step graph, f(x) = 1/x is a hyperbola. Algebra of functions: (f + g)(x) = f(x) + g(x), (fg)(x) = f(x)g(x), (f/g)(x) = f(x)/g(x) with g(x) not 0 and (cf)(x) = c f(x). Counting: the number of functions from A to B is n^m; the number of one-one functions is nPm when n >= m. The vertical line test checks whether a graph is a function. The relation can be shown by an arrow diagram, a roster form or a table.
Deep dive: Relations
A relation can be described by a rule such as y = x + 2. Domain and range are found from the pairs. The inverse relation swaps the elements of the pairs. A relation on A has subsets of A x A.
Deep dive: Functions

For a function, each input has one output. In an arrow diagram no element of A is left without an arrow and none has two arrows. Range is a subset of codomain. Piecewise functions use different rules on different intervals.
Deep dive: Domain and graphs
For sqrt(f(x)) need f(x) >= 0. For 1/f(x) need f(x) not 0. For log f(x) need f(x) > 0. Modulus function is non-negative. Greatest integer function [x] gives the largest integer not greater than x.
Hindi saransh
Sambandh aur falan: A x B ke subset ko sambandh kehte hain; falan mein har input ka ek hi output hota hai.
Use the vertical line test: a vertical line must cut the graph at most once.

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Relations and Functions

The Cartesian product A x B is the set of all ordered pairs (a, b) with a in A and b in B

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Relations›3Functions›4Domain and graphs
Relations2^(mn)
🔑

Big idea

  • The Cartesian product A x B is the set of all ordered pairs (a, b) with a in A and b in B
  • (a, b) = (c, d) only if a = c and b = d
  • A x B is not equal to B x A in general, and n(A x B) = n(A) n(B)
  • A relation R from A to B is any subset of A x B
Read the full explanation

The Cartesian product A x B is the set of all ordered pairs (a, b) with a in A and b in B; (a, b) = (c, d) only if a = c and b = d. A x B is not equal to B x A in general, and n(A x B) = n(A) n(B). A relation R from A to B is any subset of A x B. The domain is the set of first elements, the codomain is B and the range is the set of second elements actually used. The number of relations from A to B is 2^(mn) where m = n(A) and n = n(B). A function f from A to B assigns to each element of A exactly one element of B, written f: A -> B. Every function is a relation, but not every relation is a function. Domain is A, codomain is B and range is the set of images. Types of function: constant, identity f(x) = x, polynomial, rational, modulus f(x) = |x|, signum, greatest integer f(x) = [x], linear, quadratic. Real functions: the domain of 1/x is R - {0}; of sqrt(x) is x >= 0; of log x is x > 0. Graphs: f(x) = x^2 is a parabola, f(x) = |x| is a V shape, f(x) = [x] is a step graph, f(x) = 1/x is a hyperbola. Algebra of functions: (f + g)(x) = f(x) + g(x), (fg)(x) = f(x)g(x), (f/g)(x) = f(x)/g(x) with g(x) not 0 and (cf)(x) = c f(x). Counting: the number of functions from A to B is n^m; the number of one-one functions is nPm when n >= m. The vertical line test checks whether a graph is a function. The relation can be shown by an arrow diagram, a roster form or a table.

📌

Relations

  • A relation can be described by a rule such as y = x + 2
  • Domain and range are found from the pairs
  • The inverse relation swaps the elements of the pairs
  • A relation on A has subsets of A x A
🧠

Functions

  • For a function, each input has one output
  • In an arrow diagram no element of A is left without an arrow and none has two arrows
  • Range is a subset of codomain
  • Piecewise functions use different rules on different intervals
🌟

Domain and graphs

  • For sqrt(f(x)) need f(x) >= 0
  • For 1/f(x) need f(x) not 0
  • For log f(x) need f(x) > 0
  • Modulus function is non-negative
Read the full explanation

For sqrt(f(x)) need f(x) >= 0. For 1/f(x) need f(x) not 0. For log f(x) need f(x) > 0. Modulus function is non-negative. Greatest integer function [x] gives the largest integer not greater than x.

blocks.x: An angle is measured in degrees or radians. 180 degrees = pi radians, so 1 radian is about 57.3 degrees; radian measure = degree measure x pi/180. For a circle of radius r, the arc length is s = r times theta (theta in radians). The trigonometric functions are sin, cos, tan, cosec, sec and cot. On the unit circle a point has coordinates (cos x, sin x). Signs by quadrant follow the rule All, Sin, Tan, Cos (ASTC): all positive in the first, sin in the second, tan in the third and cos in the fourth. Fundamental identities: sin^2 x + cos^2 x = 1, 1 + tan^2 x = sec^2 x, 1 + cot^2 x = cosec^2 x. Values: sin 0 = 0, sin 30 = 1/2, sin 45 = 1/sqrt 2, sin 60 = sqrt3/2, sin 90 = 1; cos is the reverse. tan 45 = 1. Domain and range: sin and cos have domain R and range [-1, 1]; tan has period pi and range R. Periods: sin, cos, cosec, sec have period 2 pi; tan and cot have pi. sin(-x) = -sin x (odd), cos(-x) = cos x (even). Compound angles: sin(A + B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B; cos(A + B) = cos A cos B - sin A sin B; tan(A + B) = (tan A + tan B)/(1 - tan A tan B). Double angle: sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A; cos 2A = cos^2 A - sin^2 A = 2cos^2 A - 1 = 1 - 2 sin^2 A; tan 2A = 2 tan A/(1 - tan^2 A). Triple angle: sin 3A = 3 sin A - 4 sin^3 A; cos 3A = 4 cos^3 A - 3 cos A. Product to sum: 2 sin A cos B = sin(A+B) + sin(A-B). Sum to product: sin C + sin D = 2 sin((C+D)/2) cos((C-D)/2). Equations: sin x = sin y gives x = n pi + (-1)^n y; cos x = cos y gives x = 2n pi plus or minus y; tan x = tan y gives x = n pi + y.
Deep dive: Angles and circle

Convert degrees to radians by multiplying by pi/180. Arc length s = r theta and sector area is half r^2 theta. A full turn is 2 pi radians. Angles in standard position are measured from the positive x-axis.
Deep dive: Functions and identities
Use ASTC for signs. Reduce angles with pi plus or minus x. sin(90 - x) = cos x and cos(90 - x) = sin x. Identities simplify and prove expressions.
Deep dive: Compound angles and equations
Formulas for A plus or minus B lead to double and triple angle formulas. Product and sum formulas help in transformations. General solutions use the integer n.

🔑

Big idea

  • An angle is measured in degrees or radians
  • 180 degrees = pi radians, so 1 radian is about 57.3 degrees
  • Radian measure = degree measure x pi/180
  • For a circle of radius r, the arc length is s = r times theta (theta in radians)
Read the full explanation

An angle is measured in degrees or radians. 180 degrees = pi radians, so 1 radian is about 57.3 degrees; radian measure = degree measure x pi/180. For a circle of radius r, the arc length is s = r times theta (theta in radians). The trigonometric functions are sin, cos, tan, cosec, sec and cot. On the unit circle a point has coordinates (cos x, sin x). Signs by quadrant follow the rule All, Sin, Tan, Cos (ASTC): all positive in the first, sin in the second, tan in the third and cos in the fourth. Fundamental identities: sin^2 x + cos^2 x = 1, 1 + tan^2 x = sec^2 x, 1 + cot^2 x = cosec^2 x. Values: sin 0 = 0, sin 30 = 1/2, sin 45 = 1/sqrt 2, sin 60 = sqrt3/2, sin 90 = 1; cos is the reverse. tan 45 = 1. Domain and range: sin and cos have domain R and range [-1, 1]; tan has period pi and range R. Periods: sin, cos, cosec, sec have period 2 pi; tan and cot have pi. sin(-x) = -sin x (odd), cos(-x) = cos x (even). Compound angles: sin(A + B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B; cos(A + B) = cos A cos B - sin A sin B; tan(A + B) = (tan A + tan B)/(1 - tan A tan B). Double angle: sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A; cos 2A = cos^2 A - sin^2 A = 2cos^2 A - 1 = 1 - 2 sin^2 A; tan 2A = 2 tan A/(1 - tan^2 A). Triple angle: sin 3A = 3 sin A - 4 sin^3 A; cos 3A = 4 cos^3 A - 3 cos A. Product to sum: 2 sin A cos B = sin(A+B) + sin(A-B). Sum to product: sin C + sin D = 2 sin((C+D)/2) cos((C-D)/2). Equations: sin x = sin y gives x = n pi + (-1)^n y; cos x = cos y gives x = 2n pi plus or minus y; tan x = tan y gives x = n pi + y.

📐

Angles and circle

  • Convert degrees to radians by multiplying by pi/180
  • Arc length s = r theta and sector area is half r2 theta
  • A full turn is 2 pi radians
  • Angles in standard position are measured from the positive x-axis
🧠

Functions and identities

  • Use ASTC for signs
  • Reduce angles with pi plus or minus x
  • Sin(90 - x) = cos x and cos(90 - x) = sin x
  • Identities simplify and prove expressions
🧮

Compound angles and equations

  • Formulas for A plus or minus B lead to double and triple angle formulas
  • Product and sum formulas help in transformations
  • General solutions use the integer n

lessons.title: Sequences and Series
yt: class 11 maths sequences and series ap gp means sums

blocks.x: A sequence is a list of numbers in a definite order; a series is the sum of the terms. In an Arithmetic Progression (AP) the difference d between consecutive terms is constant: a, a + d, a + 2d, ... The nth term is a_n = a + (n - 1)d and the sum of n terms is S_n = n/2 [2a + (n - 1)d] = n/2 (a + l), where l is the last term. Three numbers in AP can be taken as a - d, a, a + d. The arithmetic mean of a and b is (a + b)/2, and n arithmetic means between a and b are inserted using d = (b - a)/(n + 1). In a Geometric Progression (GP) the ratio r is constant: a, ar, ar^2, ... The nth term is a_n = a r^(n-1) and the sum is S_n = a (r^n - 1)/(r - 1) for r not 1 (or a(1 - r^n)/(1 - r)); for r = 1, S_n = na. The sum to infinity exists when |r| < 1 and equals a/(1 - r). The geometric mean of a and b is sqrt(ab), and n geometric means between a and b use r = (b/a)^(1/(n+1)). Relation between means: AM >= GM, with equality when the numbers are equal, and AM times HM = GM squared for two numbers. Special sums: sum of first n natural numbers = n(n + 1)/2, sum of squares = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6 and sum of cubes = [n(n + 1)/2]^2. Arithmetico-geometric series have terms (a + (k-1)d) r^(k-1). Applications include compound interest, population growth and recurring deposits. If a, b, c are in AP then 2b = a + c; if in GP then b^2 = ac.
Deep dive: AP

Common difference d = a_(n+1) - a_n. Middle term gives the average. Sum can also be written using the first and last terms. If the terms of an AP are all multiplied or increased by a constant it stays an AP.
Deep dive: GP
Common ratio r = a_(n+1)/a_n. The sum to infinity applies only for |r| < 1. A recurring decimal like 0.333... is the sum of a GP. Compound interest amounts form a GP.
Deep dive: Means and special sums
AM, GM and HM relate by AM >= GM >= HM for positive numbers. The sums of n, n squared and n cubed are standard. They are used to sum series by writing the nth term.
Hindi saransh
Shreni: AP mein a_n = a + (n-1)d aur GP mein a_n = ar^(n-1); anant GP ka yog a/(1-r) jab |r| < 1.
For infinite GP check |r| < 1 before using a/(1 - r).

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Sequences and Series

A sequence is a list of numbers in a definite order

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2AP›3GP›4Means and special sums
AP nth terma + (n-1)d
AP sumn/2 [2a + (n-1)d]
GP nth terma r^(n-1)
GP suma(r^n - 1)/(r - 1)
Infinite GPa/(1 - r)
🔑

Big idea

  • A sequence is a list of numbers in a definite order
  • A series is the sum of the terms
  • In an Arithmetic Progression (AP) the difference d between consecutive terms is constant: a, a + d, a + 2d,
  • The nth term is a_n = a + (n - 1)d and the sum of n terms is S_n = n/2 [2a + (n - 1)d] = n/2 (a + l), where l is the last term
Read the full explanation

A sequence is a list of numbers in a definite order; a series is the sum of the terms. In an Arithmetic Progression (AP) the difference d between consecutive terms is constant: a, a + d, a + 2d, ... The nth term is a_n = a + (n - 1)d and the sum of n terms is S_n = n/2 [2a + (n - 1)d] = n/2 (a + l), where l is the last term. Three numbers in AP can be taken as a - d, a, a + d. The arithmetic mean of a and b is (a + b)/2, and n arithmetic means between a and b are inserted using d = (b - a)/(n + 1). In a Geometric Progression (GP) the ratio r is constant: a, ar, ar^2, ... The nth term is a_n = a r^(n-1) and the sum is S_n = a (r^n - 1)/(r - 1) for r not 1 (or a(1 - r^n)/(1 - r)); for r = 1, S_n = na. The sum to infinity exists when |r| < 1 and equals a/(1 - r). The geometric mean of a and b is sqrt(ab), and n geometric means between a and b use r = (b/a)^(1/(n+1)). Relation between means: AM >= GM, with equality when the numbers are equal, and AM times HM = GM squared for two numbers. Special sums: sum of first n natural numbers = n(n + 1)/2, sum of squares = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6 and sum of cubes = [n(n + 1)/2]^2. Arithmetico-geometric series have terms (a + (k-1)d) r^(k-1). Applications include compound interest, population growth and recurring deposits. If a, b, c are in AP then 2b = a + c; if in GP then b^2 = ac.

📌

AP

  • Common difference d = a_(n+1) - a_n
  • Middle term gives the average
  • Sum can also be written using the first and last terms
  • If the terms of an AP are all multiplied or increased by a constant it stays an AP
🧠

GP

  • Common ratio r = a_(n+1)/a_n
  • The sum to infinity applies only for |r| < 1
  • A recurring decimal like 0.333
  • Is the sum of a GP
Read the full explanation

Common ratio r = a_(n+1)/a_n. The sum to infinity applies only for |r| < 1. A recurring decimal like 0.333... is the sum of a GP. Compound interest amounts form a GP.

🌟

Means and special sums

  • AM, GM and HM relate by AM >= GM >= HM for positive numbers
  • The sums of n, n squared and n cubed are standard
  • They are used to sum series by writing the nth term

GP nth terma r^(n-1)Geometric
GP suma(r^n - 1)/(r - 1)r not 1
Infinite GPa/(1 - r) | r | < 1
🎯 Remember For infinite GP check |r| < 1 before using a/(1 - r).
