  • Its aims are to understand how psychological factors affect performance, to teach mental skills, to handle stress and to enhance enjoyment
  • Personality is the sum of the characteristics that make a person unique
Read the full explanation

Psychology is the scientific study of behaviour and mental processes. Sports psychology applies psychological principles to sports to improve performance and well-being. Its aims are to understand how psychological factors affect performance, to teach mental skills, to handle stress and to enhance enjoyment. Personality is the sum of the characteristics that make a person unique. Carl Jung classified people as introverts (inward looking, quiet) and extroverts (outgoing, sociable); an ambivert has both. Sheldon's somatotypes link body build to temperament: endomorph (round, relaxed), mesomorph (muscular, energetic) and ectomorph (thin, introverted). The Big Five traits are openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism. Personality and sports: team sport players are often extroverts; individual sport players are often more introverted, and personality affects choice of sport. Motivation is the force that energises and directs behaviour toward a goal. Intrinsic motivation comes from within (enjoyment, satisfaction); extrinsic motivation comes from outside (rewards, medals, praise). Techniques to motivate: set clear goals, give feedback and rewards, use praise, create a positive environment, vary training and involve athletes in decisions. Achievement motivation is the drive to succeed. Exercise adherence is continuing a programme of exercise; factors that support it include enjoyment, social support, convenience, goal setting and seeing results; barriers include lack of time, injury and lack of facilities. Strategies to improve adherence: set realistic goals, choose enjoyable activities, exercise with friends, keep records and reward progress. Mental skills include goal setting, imagery, relaxation, self-talk and concentration. Anxiety and arousal affect performance; the inverted-U hypothesis says moderate arousal gives best performance. Aggression in sports can be hostile or instrumental. Team cohesion improves performance. Sportspersons should learn to handle pressure and failure and develop confidence.

📌

Personality

  • Personality is shaped by heredity and environment
  • Jung's types and Sheldon's body types are early theories
  • Traits are stable patterns
  • The Big Five model is widely used
🧠

Motivation

  • Intrinsic motivation is long lasting
  • Extrinsic can help but may reduce interest if overused
  • Goals should be specific, measurable and achievable
  • Coaches use feedback and encouragement
🌟

Exercise adherence

  • Many people stop exercise within months
  • Enjoyment, support and planning improve adherence
  • Time management and variety help
  • Health benefits motivate long-term participation

lessons.title: Training and Doping
yt: class 11 physical education sports training strength endurance speed doping wada nada

blocks.x: Sports training is a systematic process of preparing an athlete to improve performance through exercise. Principles: overload, specificity, progression, reversibility, individual differences and variety. Warm-up prepares the body and reduces injury; cool-down helps recovery. Strength is the ability to overcome resistance; types are maximum strength, explosive strength (power) and strength endurance. Methods include isometric (no change in length), isotonic (concentric and eccentric) and isokinetic (constant speed). Endurance is the ability to resist fatigue; aerobic endurance uses oxygen while anaerobic endurance works without enough oxygen. Methods: continuous running, interval training and fartlek (speed play, developed in Sweden). Speed is the ability to perform movement in the shortest time: reaction speed, movement speed and acceleration speed. Flexibility is the range of movement; it can be static or dynamic, active or passive, improved by stretching. Coordinative abilities include balance, rhythm, orientation, differentiation and reaction. Training load has intensity and volume. Periodisation divides training into preparatory, competition and transition periods. Doping is the use of banned substances or methods to improve performance unfairly. The World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) was formed in 1999 and has its headquarters at Montreal; the National Anti-Doping Agency (NADA) was set up in India in 2009. WADA publishes the Prohibited List annually. Classes of prohibited substances include anabolic steroids, stimulants, narcotics, diuretics and masking agents, peptide hormones and growth factors, and beta-2 agonists; prohibited methods include blood doping and gene doping. Reasons athletes use drugs: pressure to win, fame and money. Side effects: steroids cause liver damage, heart disease, hormonal imbalance and aggression; stimulants cause high blood pressure and addiction; diuretics cause dehydration; blood doping causes clotting and stroke. Consequences include disqualification, loss of medals and bans. Prevention: education, testing and strict penalties. The athlete is responsible for substances found in the body (strict liability). Dope tests use urine and blood samples taken in two bottles A and B.
Deep dive: Training

Overload means training harder than normal to adapt. Specificity means training the energy system and muscles used in the sport. Progression raises the load gradually. Reversibility means fitness is lost when training stops.
Deep dive: Training methods
Isometric exercises hold a position. Interval training alternates work and rest. Fartlek varies speed over distance. Stretching develops flexibility. Circuit training mixes exercises at stations.
Deep dive: Doping
Doping is unethical and unsafe. WADA and NADA test athletes. Penalties can end careers. Athletes should know the list and take only permitted medicines.

Visual lesson

Training and Doping

Sports training is a systematic process of preparing an athlete to improve performance through exercise

🔑

Big idea

  • Sports training is a systematic process of preparing an athlete to improve performance through exercise
  • Principles: overload, specificity, progression, reversibility, individual differences and variety
  • Warm-up prepares the body and reduces injury
  • Cool-down helps recovery
Read the full explanation

Sports training is a systematic process of preparing an athlete to improve performance through exercise. Principles: overload, specificity, progression, reversibility, individual differences and variety. Warm-up prepares the body and reduces injury; cool-down helps recovery. Strength is the ability to overcome resistance; types are maximum strength, explosive strength (power) and strength endurance. Methods include isometric (no change in length), isotonic (concentric and eccentric) and isokinetic (constant speed). Endurance is the ability to resist fatigue; aerobic endurance uses oxygen while anaerobic endurance works without enough oxygen. Methods: continuous running, interval training and fartlek (speed play, developed in Sweden). Speed is the ability to perform movement in the shortest time: reaction speed, movement speed and acceleration speed. Flexibility is the range of movement; it can be static or dynamic, active or passive, improved by stretching. Coordinative abilities include balance, rhythm, orientation, differentiation and reaction. Training load has intensity and volume. Periodisation divides training into preparatory, competition and transition periods. Doping is the use of banned substances or methods to improve performance unfairly. The World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) was formed in 1999 and has its headquarters at Montreal; the National Anti-Doping Agency (NADA) was set up in India in 2009. WADA publishes the Prohibited List annually. Classes of prohibited substances include anabolic steroids, stimulants, narcotics, diuretics and masking agents, peptide hormones and growth factors, and beta-2 agonists; prohibited methods include blood doping and gene doping. Reasons athletes use drugs: pressure to win, fame and money. Side effects: steroids cause liver damage, heart disease, hormonal imbalance and aggression; stimulants cause high blood pressure and addiction; diuretics cause dehydration; blood doping causes clotting and stroke. Consequences include disqualification, loss of medals and bans. Prevention: education, testing and strict penalties. The athlete is responsible for substances found in the body (strict liability). Dope tests use urine and blood samples taken in two bottles A and B.

📌

Training

  • Overload means training harder than normal to adapt
  • Specificity means training the energy system and muscles used in the sport
  • Progression raises the load gradually
  • Reversibility means fitness is lost when training stops
🔄

Training methods

  • Isometric exercises hold a position
  • Interval training alternates work and rest
  • Fartlek varies speed over distance
  • Stretching develops flexibility

Isometric exercises hold a position. Interval training alternates work and rest. Fartlek varies speed over distance. Stretching develops flexibility. Circuit training mixes exercises at stations.

Doping

  • Doping is unethical and unsafe
  • WADA and NADA test athletes
  • Penalties can end careers

lessons.title: Units and Measurements
yt: class 11 physics units and measurements si units dimensions significant figures errors

blocks.x: Physics is based on measurement. A physical quantity has a numerical value and a unit. Fundamental (base) quantities in the SI system are length (metre, m), mass (kilogram, kg), time (second, s), electric current (ampere, A), temperature (kelvin, K), amount of substance (mole, mol) and luminous intensity (candela, cd). Supplementary units are the radian (plane angle) and steradian (solid angle). Derived units come from base units, for example newton (kg m s^-2) and joule (kg m^2 s^-2). The SI system was adopted in 1971 and is based on seven base units. Dimensions are the powers of base quantities in a derived quantity: [M], [L], [T]. Examples: velocity [L T^-1], acceleration [L T^-2], force [M L T^-2], work and energy [M L^2 T^-2], power [M L^2 T^-3], pressure [M L^-1 T^-2]. Uses of dimensional analysis: checking the correctness of an equation, deriving relations between quantities and converting units. Limitations: it cannot find dimensionless constants and cannot handle trigonometric or exponential functions. The principle of homogeneity says every term in a correct equation has the same dimensions. Significant figures are the reliable digits in a measurement. Rules: all non-zero digits are significant; zeros between non-zero digits are significant; leading zeros are not; trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant. In multiplication or division the result has as many significant figures as the quantity with the fewest; in addition or subtraction it keeps the least number of decimal places. Errors: the absolute error is the difference between the measured and true value; mean absolute error is the average of absolute errors; relative error is the ratio of mean absolute error to the mean value; percentage error is relative error times 100. Systematic errors (instrumental, personal, environmental) shift all readings; random errors vary. Combination of errors: in addition and subtraction absolute errors add; in multiplication and division relative errors add; for x to the power n the relative error is n times that of x. Least count of a vernier caliper is 0.1 mm (1 main scale division minus 1 vernier division) and of a screw gauge is pitch divided by number of divisions on the circular scale, usually 0.01 mm. Accuracy refers to closeness to the true value and precision to closeness among measurements. Orders of magnitude: 1 light year = 9.46 x 10^15 m; 1 astronomical unit = 1.496 x 10^11 m; 1 parsec = 3.08 x 10^16 m; 1 atomic mass unit = 1.66 x 10^-27 kg.
Deep dive: Units and dimensions

SI is a coherent system. Dimensions help check formulas. For example the formula for time period T = 2 pi sqrt(l/g) has dimension [T] on both sides. Dimensional analysis gives only the form of a relation.
Deep dive: Significant figures
Counting significant figures shows precision. 0.00250 has three. 2.50 x 10^3 has three. Rounding follows standard rules: drop digits below 5 and raise if above 5.
Deep dive: Errors and instruments
Errors add differently for sums and products. Vernier calipers and screw gauges give precise readings using the least count. Zero error must be corrected.
Hindi saransh
Matrak aur mapan: SI ki 7 mool matrak, dimension ka upyog, sarthak ank aur truti ke niyam.
Remember: in products, relative errors add; in sums, absolute errors add.

Units and Measurements

🔑

Big idea

  • Physics is based on measurement
  • A physical quantity has a numerical value and a unit
  • Fundamental (base) quantities in the SI system are length (metre, m), mass (kilogram, kg), time (second, s), electric current (ampere, A)…
  • Supplementary units are the radian (plane angle) and steradian (solid angle)
Read the full explanation

Physics is based on measurement. A physical quantity has a numerical value and a unit. Fundamental (base) quantities in the SI system are length (metre, m), mass (kilogram, kg), time (second, s), electric current (ampere, A), temperature (kelvin, K), amount of substance (mole, mol) and luminous intensity (candela, cd). Supplementary units are the radian (plane angle) and steradian (solid angle). Derived units come from base units, for example newton (kg m s^-2) and joule (kg m^2 s^-2). The SI system was adopted in 1971 and is based on seven base units. Dimensions are the powers of base quantities in a derived quantity: [M], [L], [T]. Examples: velocity [L T^-1], acceleration [L T^-2], force [M L T^-2], work and energy [M L^2 T^-2], power [M L^2 T^-3], pressure [M L^-1 T^-2]. Uses of dimensional analysis: checking the correctness of an equation, deriving relations between quantities and converting units. Limitations: it cannot find dimensionless constants and cannot handle trigonometric or exponential functions. The principle of homogeneity says every term in a correct equation has the same dimensions. Significant figures are the reliable digits in a measurement. Rules: all non-zero digits are significant; zeros between non-zero digits are significant; leading zeros are not; trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant. In multiplication or division the result has as many significant figures as the quantity with the fewest; in addition or subtraction it keeps the least number of decimal places. Errors: the absolute error is the difference between the measured and true value; mean absolute error is the average of absolute errors; relative error is the ratio of mean absolute error to the mean value; percentage error is relative error times 100. Systematic errors (instrumental, personal, environmental) shift all readings; random errors vary. Combination of errors: in addition and subtraction absolute errors add; in multiplication and division relative errors add; for x to the power n the relative error is n times that of x. Least count of a vernier caliper is 0.1 mm (1 main scale division minus 1 vernier division) and of a screw gauge is pitch divided by number of divisions on the circular scale, usually 0.01 mm. Accuracy refers to closeness to the true value and precision to closeness among measurements. Orders of magnitude: 1 light year = 9.46 x 10^15 m; 1 astronomical unit = 1.496 x 10^11 m; 1 parsec = 3.08 x 10^16 m; 1 atomic mass unit = 1.66 x 10^-27 kg.

📌

Units and dimensions

  • SI is a coherent system
  • Dimensions help check formulas
  • For example the formula for time period T = 2 pi sqrt(l/g) has dimension [T] on both sides
  • Dimensional analysis gives only the form of a relation
🧠

Significant figures

  • Counting significant figures shows precision
  • 0.00250 has three
  • 2.50 x 103 has three
  • Rounding follows standard rules: drop digits below 5 and raise if above 5
🌟

Errors and instruments

  • Errors add differently for sums and products
  • Vernier calipers and screw gauges give precise readings using the least count
  • Zero error must be corrected
🧮

lessons.title: Motion in a Straight Line
yt: class 11 physics motion in a straight line kinematics equations graphs

blocks.x: Kinematics describes motion without considering its causes. An object is at rest or in motion relative to a frame of reference. Motion in one dimension is along a straight line. Distance is the total path length (scalar); displacement is the shortest change in position with direction (vector). Speed is distance divided by time (scalar); velocity is displacement divided by time (vector). Average speed = total distance/total time; average velocity = displacement/time. Instantaneous velocity is the limit of displacement per unit time as the time interval tends to zero, v = dx/dt. Acceleration a = dv/dt = change in velocity per unit time; retardation (deceleration) is negative acceleration. For uniform acceleration the equations of motion are v = u + at; s = ut + (1/2) a t^2; v^2 = u^2 + 2as; and the distance in the nth second s_n = u + a(2n - 1)/2. Free fall: an object released from rest falls with acceleration g = 9.8 m s^-2 (about 10) toward the earth if air resistance is neglected; for upward motion use a = -g. The time of ascent equals the time of descent, the maximum height is u^2/(2g) and the time of flight is 2u/g. Graphs: in a position-time graph the slope gives velocity; in a velocity-time graph the slope gives acceleration and the area under the graph gives displacement; in an acceleration-time graph the area gives change in velocity. A straight horizontal line in an x-t graph means rest; a straight inclined line means uniform velocity; a curve means acceleration. Relative velocity: velocity of A relative to B is v_AB = v_A - v_B; for objects moving in opposite directions speeds add. Stopping distance = v^2/(2a). Calculus form: v = dx/dt, a = dv/dt = v dv/dx; integrate to find x and v. Reaction time and braking distance are important in road safety.
Deep dive: Basic quantities
Position is relative to an origin. Distance is never negative; displacement may be zero for a round trip. Speed is the magnitude of velocity only for instantaneous values. Units: m/s and m/s^2.
Deep dive: Equations of motion
These apply only for constant acceleration. Choose the sign convention first. Pick the equation that does not contain the unknown you do not need. For free fall take upward as positive and a = -g.
Deep dive: Graphs
Slopes and areas on graphs give velocity, acceleration and displacement. A velocity-time graph with a negative slope shows deceleration. Area below the axis is negative displacement.

Motion in a Straight Line

Kinematics describes motion without considering its causes

🔑

Big idea

  • Kinematics describes motion without considering its causes
  • An object is at rest or in motion relative to a frame of reference
  • Motion in one dimension is along a straight line
  • Distance is the total path length (scalar)
Read the full explanation

Kinematics describes motion without considering its causes. An object is at rest or in motion relative to a frame of reference. Motion in one dimension is along a straight line. Distance is the total path length (scalar); displacement is the shortest change in position with direction (vector). Speed is distance divided by time (scalar); velocity is displacement divided by time (vector). Average speed = total distance/total time; average velocity = displacement/time. Instantaneous velocity is the limit of displacement per unit time as the time interval tends to zero, v = dx/dt. Acceleration a = dv/dt = change in velocity per unit time; retardation (deceleration) is negative acceleration. For uniform acceleration the equations of motion are v = u + at; s = ut + (1/2) a t^2; v^2 = u^2 + 2as; and the distance in the nth second s_n = u + a(2n - 1)/2. Free fall: an object released from rest falls with acceleration g = 9.8 m s^-2 (about 10) toward the earth if air resistance is neglected; for upward motion use a = -g. The time of ascent equals the time of descent, the maximum height is u^2/(2g) and the time of flight is 2u/g. Graphs: in a position-time graph the slope gives velocity; in a velocity-time graph the slope gives acceleration and the area under the graph gives displacement; in an acceleration-time graph the area gives change in velocity. A straight horizontal line in an x-t graph means rest; a straight inclined line means uniform velocity; a curve means acceleration. Relative velocity: velocity of A relative to B is v_AB = v_A - v_B; for objects moving in opposite directions speeds add. Stopping distance = v^2/(2a). Calculus form: v = dx/dt, a = dv/dt = v dv/dx; integrate to find x and v. Reaction time and braking distance are important in road safety.

📘

Basic quantities

  • Position is relative to an origin
  • Distance is never negative
  • Displacement may be zero for a round trip
  • Speed is the magnitude of velocity only for instantaneous values
Read the full explanation

Position is relative to an origin. Distance is never negative; displacement may be zero for a round trip. Speed is the magnitude of velocity only for instantaneous values. Units: m/s and m/s^2.

🧮

Equations of motion

  • These apply only for constant acceleration
  • Choose the sign convention first
  • Pick the equation that does not contain the unknown you do not need
  • For free fall take upward as positive and a = -g
🌟

Graphs

  • Slopes and areas on graphs give velocity, acceleration and displacement
  • A velocity-time graph with a negative slope shows deceleration
  • Area below the axis is negative displacement

lessons.title: Motion in a Plane
yt: class 11 physics motion in a plane vectors projectile motion circular motion

blocks.x: Scalars have magnitude only (mass, time, speed) and vectors have magnitude and direction (displacement, velocity, force). Vectors are added by the triangle law or parallelogram law. For two vectors A and B at angle theta, the magnitude of the resultant R = sqrt(A^2 + B^2 + 2AB cos theta) and the direction tan(alpha) = B sin theta/(A + B cos theta). Subtraction is addition of the negative vector. A vector can be resolved into rectangular components: A_x = A cos theta and A_y = A sin theta, with magnitude sqrt(A_x^2 + A_y^2). Unit vectors i, j, k point along x, y, z. The scalar (dot) product A.B = AB cos theta is a scalar, commutative; i.i = 1 and i.j = 0. The vector (cross) product A x B = AB sin theta n is a vector perpendicular to both; i x j = k and it is not commutative. Projectile motion: an object thrown at angle theta with speed u follows a parabola. Horizontal component u cos theta is constant; vertical component u sin theta changes with acceleration -g. Time of flight T = 2u sin theta/g; maximum height H = u^2 sin^2 theta/(2g); horizontal range R = u^2 sin 2 theta/g. Maximum range occurs at 45 degrees, equal ranges for angles theta and 90 - theta, and R = 4H/tan theta. The equation of the path is y = x tan theta - g x^2/(2u^2 cos^2 theta). For a horizontal projection from a height h, the time of fall is sqrt(2h/g). Uniform circular motion: speed is constant but velocity changes direction, so there is acceleration directed toward the centre, a_c = v^2/r = omega^2 r; the period T = 2 pi r/v, frequency f = 1/T, angular velocity omega = 2 pi/T = 2 pi f and v = r omega. Angular displacement is in radians. Centripetal force F = m v^2/r. Relative velocity in two dimensions uses vector subtraction, as in rain-man and river-boat problems.
Deep dive: Vectors
The parallelogram law finds the resultant. Component method is easier for many vectors. Dot product gives work; cross product gives torque. Zero vector has zero magnitude.
Deep dive: Projectile
Horizontal and vertical motions are independent. At the highest point the vertical velocity is zero but horizontal velocity remains. Range is symmetric about 45 degrees. Air resistance is ignored.
Deep dive: Circular motion
Centripetal acceleration points to the centre. Speed is constant in uniform circular motion. Angular speed omega = v/r. Examples: planets, stones whirled on strings.

Motion in a Plane

Scalars have magnitude only (mass, time, speed) and vectors have magnitude and direction (displacement, velocity, force)

🔑

Big idea

  • Scalars have magnitude only (mass, time, speed) and vectors have magnitude and direction (displacement, velocity, force)
  • Vectors are added by the triangle law or parallelogram law
  • For two vectors A and B at angle theta, the magnitude of the resultant R = sqrt(A2 + B2 + 2AB cos theta) and the direction tan(alpha) = B sin…
  • Subtraction is addition of the negative vector
Read the full explanation

Scalars have magnitude only (mass, time, speed) and vectors have magnitude and direction (displacement, velocity, force). Vectors are added by the triangle law or parallelogram law. For two vectors A and B at angle theta, the magnitude of the resultant R = sqrt(A^2 + B^2 + 2AB cos theta) and the direction tan(alpha) = B sin theta/(A + B cos theta). Subtraction is addition of the negative vector. A vector can be resolved into rectangular components: A_x = A cos theta and A_y = A sin theta, with magnitude sqrt(A_x^2 + A_y^2). Unit vectors i, j, k point along x, y, z. The scalar (dot) product A.B = AB cos theta is a scalar, commutative; i.i = 1 and i.j = 0. The vector (cross) product A x B = AB sin theta n is a vector perpendicular to both; i x j = k and it is not commutative. Projectile motion: an object thrown at angle theta with speed u follows a parabola. Horizontal component u cos theta is constant; vertical component u sin theta changes with acceleration -g. Time of flight T = 2u sin theta/g; maximum height H = u^2 sin^2 theta/(2g); horizontal range R = u^2 sin 2 theta/g. Maximum range occurs at 45 degrees, equal ranges for angles theta and 90 - theta, and R = 4H/tan theta. The equation of the path is y = x tan theta - g x^2/(2u^2 cos^2 theta). For a horizontal projection from a height h, the time of fall is sqrt(2h/g). Uniform circular motion: speed is constant but velocity changes direction, so there is acceleration directed toward the centre, a_c = v^2/r = omega^2 r; the period T = 2 pi r/v, frequency f = 1/T, angular velocity omega = 2 pi/T = 2 pi f and v = r omega. Angular displacement is in radians. Centripetal force F = m v^2/r. Relative velocity in two dimensions uses vector subtraction, as in rain-man and river-boat problems.

📌

Vectors

  • The parallelogram law finds the resultant
  • Component method is easier for many vectors
  • Dot product gives work
  • Cross product gives torque
Read the full explanation

The parallelogram law finds the resultant. Component method is easier for many vectors. Dot product gives work; cross product gives torque. Zero vector has zero magnitude.

🧠

Projectile

  • Horizontal and vertical motions are independent
  • At the highest point the vertical velocity is zero but horizontal velocity remains
  • Range is symmetric about 45 degrees
  • Air resistance is ignored
🚀

Circular motion

  • Centripetal acceleration points to the centre
  • Speed is constant in uniform circular motion
  • Angular speed omega = v/r
  • Examples: planets, stones whirled on strings

blocks.x: Newton's laws of motion explain the cause of motion. First law (law of inertia): a body remains at rest or in uniform motion in a straight line unless acted on by an unbalanced external force. Inertia is the property of resisting change in the state of motion; mass is its measure. Second law: the rate of change of momentum is proportional to the applied force, F = dp/dt = m a (for constant mass). Linear momentum p = m v with unit kg m s^-1. The SI unit of force is the newton: 1 N = 1 kg m s^-2. Third law: to every action there is an equal and opposite reaction; action and reaction act on different bodies. Impulse J = F x dt = change in momentum; the unit is N s. The law of conservation of linear momentum states that if no external force acts, total momentum remains constant, and it is applied in recoil of a gun, rocket propulsion and collisions. Equilibrium of concurrent forces needs the vector sum to be zero; Lami's theorem relates three forces. Friction opposes relative motion: static friction f_s <= mu_s N, kinetic friction f_k = mu_k N with mu_k less than mu_s, and rolling friction is smaller. The angle of friction is tan^-1 mu; the angle of repose equals the angle of friction. On an incline of angle theta the component along the plane is mg sin theta and perpendicular is mg cos theta; a body just slides when tan theta = mu. Circular motion needs a centripetal force F = m v^2/r provided by tension, friction or gravity; for a vehicle on a level road v_max = sqrt(mu r g); on a banked road v = sqrt(r g tan theta) with no friction; for a vertical circle the minimum speed at the lowest point is sqrt(5 g r) and at the top sqrt(g r). Weight is mg; apparent weight in a lift is m(g plus or minus a). Free body diagrams show all forces on a body. Tension in a string and normal reaction are contact forces. For two blocks connected by a string, acceleration a = (m1 - m2) g/(m1 + m2) in an Atwood machine. Pseudo force acts in non-inertial frames.
Deep dive: Newton's laws

The first law defines inertia and force. The second law gives the measure of force. The third law explains pairs of forces. Forces of action and reaction never cancel because they act on different bodies.
Deep dive: Momentum and impulse
Conservation of momentum holds in collisions and explosions. Impulse equals change in momentum. A cricketer draws the hands back to increase the time and lower the force.
Deep dive: Friction and circular motion

Friction depends on the nature of surfaces and normal reaction, not on area. Kinetic friction is less than limiting static friction. Banking reduces the need for friction. Free body diagrams make problems simple.

🔑

Big idea

  • Newton's laws of motion explain the cause of motion
  • First law (law of inertia): a body remains at rest or in uniform motion in a straight line unless acted on by an unbalanced external force
  • Inertia is the property of resisting change in the state of motion
  • Mass is its measure
Read the full explanation

Newton's laws of motion explain the cause of motion. First law (law of inertia): a body remains at rest or in uniform motion in a straight line unless acted on by an unbalanced external force. Inertia is the property of resisting change in the state of motion; mass is its measure. Second law: the rate of change of momentum is proportional to the applied force, F = dp/dt = m a (for constant mass). Linear momentum p = m v with unit kg m s^-1. The SI unit of force is the newton: 1 N = 1 kg m s^-2. Third law: to every action there is an equal and opposite reaction; action and reaction act on different bodies. Impulse J = F x dt = change in momentum; the unit is N s. The law of conservation of linear momentum states that if no external force acts, total momentum remains constant, and it is applied in recoil of a gun, rocket propulsion and collisions. Equilibrium of concurrent forces needs the vector sum to be zero; Lami's theorem relates three forces. Friction opposes relative motion: static friction f_s <= mu_s N, kinetic friction f_k = mu_k N with mu_k less than mu_s, and rolling friction is smaller. The angle of friction is tan^-1 mu; the angle of repose equals the angle of friction. On an incline of angle theta the component along the plane is mg sin theta and perpendicular is mg cos theta; a body just slides when tan theta = mu. Circular motion needs a centripetal force F = m v^2/r provided by tension, friction or gravity; for a vehicle on a level road v_max = sqrt(mu r g); on a banked road v = sqrt(r g tan theta) with no friction; for a vertical circle the minimum speed at the lowest point is sqrt(5 g r) and at the top sqrt(g r). Weight is mg; apparent weight in a lift is m(g plus or minus a). Free body diagrams show all forces on a body. Tension in a string and normal reaction are contact forces. For two blocks connected by a string, acceleration a = (m1 - m2) g/(m1 + m2) in an Atwood machine. Pseudo force acts in non-inertial frames.

Newton's laws

  • The first law defines inertia and force
  • The second law gives the measure of force
  • The third law explains pairs of forces
  • Forces of action and reaction never cancel because they act on different bodies

Momentum and impulse

  • Conservation of momentum holds in collisions and explosions
  • Impulse equals change in momentum
  • A cricketer draws the hands back to increase the time and lower the force
🚀

Friction and circular motion

  • Friction depends on the nature of surfaces and normal reaction, not on area
  • Kinetic friction is less than limiting static friction
  • Banking reduces the need for friction
  • Free body diagrams make problems simple

lessons.title: Work, Energy and Power
yt: class 11 physics work energy power conservation collisions

blocks.x: Work is done when a force produces displacement: W = F d cos theta = F.d (a scalar). Its unit is the joule (1 J = 1 N m). Work is positive when the force has a component along the displacement, negative when opposite (friction) and zero when perpendicular or when there is no displacement (carrying a load horizontally). Work done by a variable force is the area under the force-displacement graph, W = integral F dx. Energy is the capacity to do work; unit joule. Kinetic energy K = (1/2) m v^2 = p^2/(2m). Work-energy theorem: net work done equals the change in kinetic energy, W = K_f - K_i. Potential energy is the energy due to position or configuration: gravitational PE = m g h; spring PE = (1/2) k x^2. A force is conservative if the work done is independent of the path or zero in a closed path (gravity, spring); friction is non-conservative. Conservation of mechanical energy: for conservative forces K + U = constant. Hooke's law F = -k x, spring constant k in N/m. Power is the rate of doing work: P = W/t = F.v; unit watt (1 W = 1 J/s); 1 horsepower = 746 W; 1 kilowatt hour = 3.6 x 10^6 J. Efficiency = useful output/input x 100. Collisions: in an elastic collision both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved; in an inelastic collision only momentum is conserved; in a perfectly inelastic collision the bodies stick together. For an elastic head-on collision of masses m1 and m2: v1' = ((m1 - m2) v1 + 2 m2 v2)/(m1 + m2) and v2' = ((m2 - m1) v2 + 2 m1 v1)/(m1 + m2). For equal masses the velocities exchange. Coefficient of restitution e = relative speed of separation divided by relative speed of approach; e = 1 for elastic and 0 for perfectly inelastic. Rain, bouncing ball, pendulum and roller coaster illustrate energy changes. Mass-energy relation E = m c^2 by Einstein. Forms of energy include mechanical, heat, light, sound, chemical, nuclear and electrical. The loss of kinetic energy in perfectly inelastic collision is (1/2) mu v_rel^2 with reduced mass mu. A body dropped from height h has speed sqrt(2gh) at the ground.
Deep dive: Work and energy
Work depends on force, displacement and the angle between them. Kinetic energy depends on speed squared. Potential energy depends on position. The work-energy theorem applies to all forces.
Deep dive: Conservation
Mechanical energy is conserved if only conservative forces act. A swinging pendulum converts potential to kinetic energy and back. With friction, mechanical energy falls and becomes heat.
Deep dive: Power and collisions
Power tells how fast work is done. Elastic collisions conserve both momentum and kinetic energy. Inelastic collisions lose kinetic energy but momentum is conserved. e measures elasticity.

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Work, Energy and Power

Work is done when a force produces displacement: W = F d cos theta = F.d (a scalar)

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Work and energy›3Conservation›4Power and collisions
Kinetic energy1/2 m v^2
🔑

Big idea

  • Work is done when a force produces displacement: W = F d cos theta = F.d (a scalar)
  • Its unit is the joule (1 J = 1 N m)
  • Work is positive when the force has a component along the displacement, negative when opposite (friction) and zero when perpendicular or when there…
  • Work done by a variable force is the area under the force-displacement graph, W = integral F dx
Read the full explanation

Work is done when a force produces displacement: W = F d cos theta = F.d (a scalar). Its unit is the joule (1 J = 1 N m). Work is positive when the force has a component along the displacement, negative when opposite (friction) and zero when perpendicular or when there is no displacement (carrying a load horizontally). Work done by a variable force is the area under the force-displacement graph, W = integral F dx. Energy is the capacity to do work; unit joule. Kinetic energy K = (1/2) m v^2 = p^2/(2m). Work-energy theorem: net work done equals the change in kinetic energy, W = K_f - K_i. Potential energy is the energy due to position or configuration: gravitational PE = m g h; spring PE = (1/2) k x^2. A force is conservative if the work done is independent of the path or zero in a closed path (gravity, spring); friction is non-conservative. Conservation of mechanical energy: for conservative forces K + U = constant. Hooke's law F = -k x, spring constant k in N/m. Power is the rate of doing work: P = W/t = F.v; unit watt (1 W = 1 J/s); 1 horsepower = 746 W; 1 kilowatt hour = 3.6 x 10^6 J. Efficiency = useful output/input x 100. Collisions: in an elastic collision both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved; in an inelastic collision only momentum is conserved; in a perfectly inelastic collision the bodies stick together. For an elastic head-on collision of masses m1 and m2: v1' = ((m1 - m2) v1 + 2 m2 v2)/(m1 + m2) and v2' = ((m2 - m1) v2 + 2 m1 v1)/(m1 + m2). For equal masses the velocities exchange. Coefficient of restitution e = relative speed of separation divided by relative speed of approach; e = 1 for elastic and 0 for perfectly inelastic. Rain, bouncing ball, pendulum and roller coaster illustrate energy changes. Mass-energy relation E = m c^2 by Einstein. Forms of energy include mechanical, heat, light, sound, chemical, nuclear and electrical. The loss of kinetic energy in perfectly inelastic collision is (1/2) mu v_rel^2 with reduced mass mu. A body dropped from height h has speed sqrt(2gh) at the ground.

🚀

Work and energy

  • Work depends on force, displacement and the angle between them
  • Kinetic energy depends on speed squared
  • Potential energy depends on position
  • The work-energy theorem applies to all forces
🧠

Conservation

  • Mechanical energy is conserved if only conservative forces act
  • A swinging pendulum converts potential to kinetic energy and back
  • With friction, mechanical energy falls and becomes heat
🚀

Power and collisions

  • Power tells how fast work is done
  • Elastic collisions conserve both momentum and kinetic energy
  • Inelastic collisions lose kinetic energy but momentum is conserved
  • E measures elasticity
🧮

Formula tiles

🎯 Remember Momentum is conserved in all collisions; kinetic energy only in elastic ones.

lessons.title: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
yt: class 11 physics rotational motion centre of mass torque moment of inertia angular momentum

blocks.x: A rigid body is one in which the distance between any two particles remains constant. The centre of mass of a system of particles is x_cm = (m1 x1 + m2 x2 + ...)/(m1 + m2 + ...); the centre of mass of a uniform rod is at its midpoint, of a ring at its centre, and of a triangular lamina at its centroid. The motion of the centre of mass is as if all mass is concentrated there and all external forces act there; if no external force acts, the centre of mass moves with constant velocity. Rotational motion: angular displacement theta (radian), angular velocity omega = d theta/dt, angular acceleration alpha = d omega/dt, with v = r omega and a_t = r alpha. Equations of rotational motion are omega = omega_0 + alpha t; theta = omega_0 t + (1/2) alpha t^2; omega^2 = omega_0^2 + 2 alpha theta. Torque tau = r x F = r F sin theta is the turning effect of a force, with unit N m. Moment of inertia I = sum m r^2 is the rotational analogue of mass. Torque = I alpha. Rotational kinetic energy = (1/2) I omega^2. Angular momentum L = I omega = r x p; torque is the rate of change of angular momentum. Conservation of angular momentum: if net external torque is zero, L is constant (ice skater spinning faster by pulling arms in; diver). Moment of inertia of common bodies about the axis through the centre: ring M R^2; disc (1/2) M R^2; solid sphere (2/5) M R^2; hollow sphere (2/3) M R^2; rod about its centre (1/12) M L^2; rod about an end (1/3) M L^2; solid cylinder (1/2) M R^2. Radius of gyration k is given by I = M k^2. Theorem of parallel axes: I = I_cm + M d^2. Theorem of perpendicular axes (for planar bodies): I_z = I_x + I_y. Rolling motion without slipping has v = R omega, and the total kinetic energy = (1/2) M v^2 (1 + k^2/R^2). A body rolling down an incline has acceleration a = g sin theta/(1 + k^2/R^2). Equilibrium of a rigid body requires net force zero and net torque zero. Couple is a pair of equal and opposite forces with torque equal to force times perpendicular distance. Principle of moments: in equilibrium sum of clockwise moments equals sum of anticlockwise moments. Centre of gravity coincides with the centre of mass in a uniform field.
Deep dive: Centre of mass

Position is the mass-weighted average. It may lie outside the body (a ring). For two particles the centre of mass lies closer to the heavier one. Explosion in flight does not change centre of mass motion.
Deep dive: Rotation
Angular quantities mirror linear ones: omega like v, alpha like a, I like m, torque like F, L like p. Moment of inertia depends on mass distribution and the axis.
Deep dive: Angular momentum and rolling
Without external torque L is conserved. Rolling combines translation and rotation. At the point of contact the velocity is zero. A solid sphere reaches the bottom of an incline before a hollow one.

Ghurnan gati: dravyaman kendra, bal-aghurn, jadatva aghurn I = sum mr2 aur kon-sanvegh sanrakshan.
Remember: Torque = I alpha, like Force = m a.

Visual lesson

System of Particles and Rotational Motion

A rigid body is one in which the distance between any two particles remains constant

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Centre of mass›3Rotation›4Angular momentum and rolling
Rotational KE1/2 I omega^2
🔑

Big idea

  • A rigid body is one in which the distance between any two particles remains constant
  • The centre of mass of a system of particles is x_cm = (m1 x1 + m2 x2 + ...)/(m1 + m2 + ...)
  • The centre of mass of a uniform rod is at its midpoint, of a ring at its centre, and of a triangular lamina at its centroid
  • The motion of the centre of mass is as if all mass is concentrated there and all external forces act there
Read the full explanation

A rigid body is one in which the distance between any two particles remains constant. The centre of mass of a system of particles is x_cm = (m1 x1 + m2 x2 + ...)/(m1 + m2 + ...); the centre of mass of a uniform rod is at its midpoint, of a ring at its centre, and of a triangular lamina at its centroid. The motion of the centre of mass is as if all mass is concentrated there and all external forces act there; if no external force acts, the centre of mass moves with constant velocity. Rotational motion: angular displacement theta (radian), angular velocity omega = d theta/dt, angular acceleration alpha = d omega/dt, with v = r omega and a_t = r alpha. Equations of rotational motion are omega = omega_0 + alpha t; theta = omega_0 t + (1/2) alpha t^2; omega^2 = omega_0^2 + 2 alpha theta. Torque tau = r x F = r F sin theta is the turning effect of a force, with unit N m. Moment of inertia I = sum m r^2 is the rotational analogue of mass. Torque = I alpha. Rotational kinetic energy = (1/2) I omega^2. Angular momentum L = I omega = r x p; torque is the rate of change of angular momentum. Conservation of angular momentum: if net external torque is zero, L is constant (ice skater spinning faster by pulling arms in; diver). Moment of inertia of common bodies about the axis through the centre: ring M R^2; disc (1/2) M R^2; solid sphere (2/5) M R^2; hollow sphere (2/3) M R^2; rod about its centre (1/12) M L^2; rod about an end (1/3) M L^2; solid cylinder (1/2) M R^2. Radius of gyration k is given by I = M k^2. Theorem of parallel axes: I = I_cm + M d^2. Theorem of perpendicular axes (for planar bodies): I_z = I_x + I_y. Rolling motion without slipping has v = R omega, and the total kinetic energy = (1/2) M v^2 (1 + k^2/R^2). A body rolling down an incline has acceleration a = g sin theta/(1 + k^2/R^2). Equilibrium of a rigid body requires net force zero and net torque zero. Couple is a pair of equal and opposite forces with torque equal to force times perpendicular distance. Principle of moments: in equilibrium sum of clockwise moments equals sum of anticlockwise moments. Centre of gravity coincides with the centre of mass in a uniform field.

📌

Centre of mass

  • Position is the mass-weighted average
  • It may lie outside the body (a ring)
  • For two particles the centre of mass lies closer to the heavier one
  • Explosion in flight does not change centre of mass motion
🧠

Rotation

  • Angular quantities mirror linear ones: omega like v, alpha like a, I like m, torque like F, L like p
  • Moment of inertia depends on mass distribution and the axis
🌟

Angular momentum and rolling

  • Without external torque L is conserved
  • Rolling combines translation and rotation
  • At the point of contact the velocity is zero
  • A solid sphere reaches the bottom of an incline before a hollow one
🧮

lessons.title: Gravitation
yt: class 11 physics gravitation kepler laws escape velocity satellites g variation

blocks.x: Newton's law of universal gravitation: every particle attracts every other with a force F = G m1 m2/r^2, directed along the line joining them, where G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2 kg^-2 (found by Cavendish). Gravitation is always attractive, a central and conservative force, and G is a universal constant. Acceleration due to gravity at the surface g = G M/R^2 = 9.8 m s^-2. Variation of g: with height h, g' = g (1 - 2h/R) for small h and g' = g R^2/(R + h)^2 in general; with depth d, g' = g (1 - d/R), and g is zero at the centre; with latitude, g is minimum at the equator and maximum at the poles; due to rotation, g' = g - R omega^2 cos^2 (latitude). Kepler's laws: (1) planets move in elliptical orbits with the Sun at one focus; (2) the line joining a planet and the Sun sweeps equal areas in equal times (conservation of angular momentum); (3) T^2 is proportional to a^3 (T^2/a^3 = constant). Gravitational potential energy U = -G M m/r; gravitational potential V = -G M/r; potential energy near the surface = m g h. Escape velocity v_e = sqrt(2 G M/R) = sqrt(2 g R) = 11.2 km/s for the earth; it does not depend on the mass of the body. Orbital velocity of a satellite near the earth v_o = sqrt(g R) = 7.9 km/s, and v_e = sqrt(2) v_o. For a satellite at height h, v_o = sqrt(G M/(R + h)); time period T = 2 pi sqrt((R + h)^3/(G M)); about 84 minutes near the earth's surface. Energy of a satellite: kinetic energy = G M m/(2r), potential energy = -G M m/r, total = -G M m/(2r); the binding energy is G M m/(2r). A geostationary satellite orbits in the equatorial plane in the same direction as the earth rotates with a period of 24 hours at a height of about 36,000 km; it appears fixed in the sky and is used for communication. Polar satellites have low orbits passing over poles and are used for remote sensing. Weightlessness occurs in a satellite because both satellite and astronaut are in free fall. Gravitational field intensity E = F/m = G M/r^2 and has the same units as acceleration. Inside a hollow shell the field is zero. Mass of the earth M = g R^2/G = 6 x 10^24 kg.
Deep dive: Law of gravitation

Force varies inversely with the square of distance. Gravitational force is weakest of the four fundamental forces but acts over long distance. Mass determines the force; weight is the gravitational force on a body.
Deep dive: Kepler and orbits
Planets move faster near the Sun (perihelion) and slower far away (aphelion). Orbital period depends only on the semi-major axis. Satellites move in circles or ellipses under gravity.
Deep dive: Escape and satellites
Escape velocity is the minimum speed to leave the earth's gravity. It is independent of direction and mass. Satellites have negative total energy, meaning they are bound.

Visual lesson

Gravitation

Newton's law of universal gravitation: every particle attracts every other with a force F = G m1 m2/r^2, directed along the line joining them, where G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N…

🔑

Big idea

  • Newton's law of universal gravitation: every particle attracts every other with a force F = G m1 m2/r2, directed along the line joining them, where…
  • Gravitation is always attractive, a central and conservative force, and G is a universal constant
  • Acceleration due to gravity at the surface g = G M/R2 = 9.8 m s-2
  • Variation of g: with height h, g' = g (1 - 2h/R) for small h and g' = g R2/(R + h)2 in general
Read the full explanation

Newton's law of universal gravitation: every particle attracts every other with a force F = G m1 m2/r^2, directed along the line joining them, where G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2 kg^-2 (found by Cavendish). Gravitation is always attractive, a central and conservative force, and G is a universal constant. Acceleration due to gravity at the surface g = G M/R^2 = 9.8 m s^-2. Variation of g: with height h, g' = g (1 - 2h/R) for small h and g' = g R^2/(R + h)^2 in general; with depth d, g' = g (1 - d/R), and g is zero at the centre; with latitude, g is minimum at the equator and maximum at the poles; due to rotation, g' = g - R omega^2 cos^2 (latitude). Kepler's laws: (1) planets move in elliptical orbits with the Sun at one focus; (2) the line joining a planet and the Sun sweeps equal areas in equal times (conservation of angular momentum); (3) T^2 is proportional to a^3 (T^2/a^3 = constant). Gravitational potential energy U = -G M m/r; gravitational potential V = -G M/r; potential energy near the surface = m g h. Escape velocity v_e = sqrt(2 G M/R) = sqrt(2 g R) = 11.2 km/s for the earth; it does not depend on the mass of the body. Orbital velocity of a satellite near the earth v_o = sqrt(g R) = 7.9 km/s, and v_e = sqrt(2) v_o. For a satellite at height h, v_o = sqrt(G M/(R + h)); time period T = 2 pi sqrt((R + h)^3/(G M)); about 84 minutes near the earth's surface. Energy of a satellite: kinetic energy = G M m/(2r), potential energy = -G M m/r, total = -G M m/(2r); the binding energy is G M m/(2r). A geostationary satellite orbits in the equatorial plane in the same direction as the earth rotates with a period of 24 hours at a height of about 36,000 km; it appears fixed in the sky and is used for communication. Polar satellites have low orbits passing over poles and are used for remote sensing. Weightlessness occurs in a satellite because both satellite and astronaut are in free fall. Gravitational field intensity E = F/m = G M/r^2 and has the same units as acceleration. Inside a hollow shell the field is zero. Mass of the earth M = g R^2/G = 6 x 10^24 kg.

🧮

Law of gravitation

  • Force varies inversely with the square of distance
  • Gravitational force is weakest of the four fundamental forces but acts over long distance
  • Mass determines the force
  • Weight is the gravitational force on a body
🧠

Kepler and orbits

  • Planets move faster near the Sun (perihelion) and slower far away (aphelion)
  • Orbital period depends only on the semi-major axis
  • Satellites move in circles or ellipses under gravity
🌟

Escape and satellites

  • Escape velocity is the minimum speed to leave the earth's gravity
  • It is independent of direction and mass
  • Satellites have negative total energy, meaning they are bound
🧮

lessons.title: Mechanical properties of solids and fluids
yt: class 11 physics mechanical properties of fluids

blocks.x: Stress = force/area, strain = change/original, Young modulus Y = stress/strain. Fluid pressure P = P0 + rho g h; Pascal law transmits pressure equally; Archimedes: buoyant force = weight of fluid displaced. Continuity A1 v1 = A2 v2; Bernoulli P + (1/2) rho v^2 + rho g h = constant. Surface tension S = F/l, capillary rise h = 2 S cos theta/(rho g r), terminal velocity v = 2 r^2 (rho - sigma) g/(9 eta).
Deep dive: elasticity

When a deforming force acts on a body, internal restoring forces appear. Stress = restoring force per unit area (N/m^2 = Pa). Strain = fractional change: longitudinal (change in length/length), volumetric (change in volume/volume) or shear (angle of shear). Hooke law: within the elastic limit stress is proportional to strain. Young modulus Y = (F/A)/(DL/L), bulk modulus B = -P/(DV/V) with compressibility 1/B, shear modulus G = shear stress/shear strain. Poisson ratio = lateral strain/longitudinal strain, with a value between -1 and 0.5. Elastic energy per unit volume = (1/2) x stress x strain. Work done in stretching a wire = (1/2) F x DL = (1/2) Y A DL^2/L. Steel is more elastic than rubber because it has a higher modulus.
Deep dive: fluid statics and dynamics

Pressure P = F/A; in a fluid at rest P = P0 + rho g h and acts equally in all directions at a given depth. Pascal law: pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished (hydraulic lift F2/F1 = A2/A1). Archimedes principle: the upthrust equals the weight of fluid displaced; a body floats when its density is less than the fluid (fraction submerged = rho_body/rho_fluid). Steady (streamline) flow of an incompressible fluid satisfies the equation of continuity A1 v1 = A2 v2. Bernoulli theorem: P + (1/2) rho v^2 + rho g h = constant along a streamline; speed of efflux from a hole at depth h is v = sqrt (2 g h) (Torricelli). Applications: venturimeter, aerofoil lift, atomiser, Magnus effect.
Deep dive: viscosity and surface tension

Viscous force F = eta A (dv/dx); the SI unit of viscosity eta is Pa s (poise in CGS: 1 Pa s = 10 poise). Stokes law: F = 6 pi eta r v. Terminal velocity of a sphere falling in a fluid v_t = 2 r^2 (rho - sigma) g/(9 eta). Reynolds number Re = rho v d/eta decides laminar (< 1000) or turbulent (> 2000) flow. Surface tension S = F/l = energy per unit area; excess pressure inside a drop is 2S/R, inside a soap bubble 4S/R. Capillary rise h = 2 S cos theta/(r rho g). Angle of contact is acute for liquids that wet glass (water), obtuse for non-wetting liquids (mercury). Surface energy of a drop = S x area; work to form a bubble of radius R is 8 pi R^2 S.

Visual lesson

Mechanical properties of solids and fluids

Stress = force/area, strain = change/original, Young modulus Y = stress/strain

Excess pressure drop2S/R
Excess pressure bubble4S/R
🔑

Big idea

  • Stress = force/area, strain = change/original, Young modulus Y = stress/strain
  • Fluid pressure P = P0 + rho g h
  • Pascal law transmits pressure equally
  • Archimedes: buoyant force = weight of fluid displaced
Read the full explanation

Stress = force/area, strain = change/original, Young modulus Y = stress/strain. Fluid pressure P = P0 + rho g h; Pascal law transmits pressure equally; Archimedes: buoyant force = weight of fluid displaced. Continuity A1 v1 = A2 v2; Bernoulli P + (1/2) rho v^2 + rho g h = constant. Surface tension S = F/l, capillary rise h = 2 S cos theta/(rho g r), terminal velocity v = 2 r^2 (rho - sigma) g/(9 eta).

📌

Elasticity

  • When a deforming force acts on a body, internal restoring forces appear
  • Stress = restoring force per unit area (N/m2 = Pa)
  • Strain = fractional change: longitudinal (change in length/length), volumetric (change in volume/volume) or shear (angle of shear)
  • Hooke law: within the elastic limit stress is proportional to strain
Read the full explanation

When a deforming force acts on a body, internal restoring forces appear. Stress = restoring force per unit area (N/m^2 = Pa). Strain = fractional change: longitudinal (change in length/length), volumetric (change in volume/volume) or shear (angle of shear). Hooke law: within the elastic limit stress is proportional to strain. Young modulus Y = (F/A)/(DL/L), bulk modulus B = -P/(DV/V) with compressibility 1/B, shear modulus G = shear stress/shear strain. Poisson ratio = lateral strain/longitudinal strain, with a value between -1 and 0.5. Elastic energy per unit volume = (1/2) x stress x strain. Work done in stretching a wire = (1/2) F x DL = (1/2) Y A DL^2/L. Steel is more elastic than rubber because it has a higher modulus.

🧠

Fluid statics and dynamics

  • Pressure P = F/A
  • In a fluid at rest P = P0 + rho g h and acts equally in all directions at a given depth
  • Pascal law: pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished (hydraulic lift F2/F1 = A2/A1)
  • Archimedes principle: the upthrust equals the weight of fluid displaced
Read the full explanation

Pressure P = F/A; in a fluid at rest P = P0 + rho g h and acts equally in all directions at a given depth. Pascal law: pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished (hydraulic lift F2/F1 = A2/A1). Archimedes principle: the upthrust equals the weight of fluid displaced; a body floats when its density is less than the fluid (fraction submerged = rho_body/rho_fluid). Steady (streamline) flow of an incompressible fluid satisfies the equation of continuity A1 v1 = A2 v2. Bernoulli theorem: P + (1/2) rho v^2 + rho g h = constant along a streamline; speed of efflux from a hole at depth h is v = sqrt (2 g h) (Torricelli). Applications: venturimeter, aerofoil lift, atomiser, Magnus effect.

🌟

Viscosity and surface tension

  • Viscous force F = eta A (dv/dx)
  • The SI unit of viscosity eta is Pa s (poise in CGS: 1 Pa s = 10 poise)
  • Stokes law: F = 6 pi eta r v
  • Terminal velocity of a sphere falling in a fluid v_t = 2 r2 (rho - sigma) g/(9 eta)
Read the full explanation

Viscous force F = eta A (dv/dx); the SI unit of viscosity eta is Pa s (poise in CGS: 1 Pa s = 10 poise). Stokes law: F = 6 pi eta r v. Terminal velocity of a sphere falling in a fluid v_t = 2 r^2 (rho - sigma) g/(9 eta). Reynolds number Re = rho v d/eta decides laminar (< 1000) or turbulent (> 2000) flow. Surface tension S = F/l = energy per unit area; excess pressure inside a drop is 2S/R, inside a soap bubble 4S/R. Capillary rise h = 2 S cos theta/(r rho g). Angle of contact is acute for liquids that wet glass (water), obtuse for non-wetting liquids (mercury). Surface energy of a drop = S x area; work to form a bubble of radius R is 8 pi R^2 S.

lessons.title: Oscillations and waves
yt: class 11 physics oscillations and waves

blocks.x: Simple harmonic motion has acceleration a = -omega^2 x, period T = 2 pi/omega, displacement x = A sin (omega t + phi), speed v = omega sqrt(A^2 - x^2). For a spring T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k); for a simple pendulum T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g). A wave has speed v = f lambda; on a string v = sqrt(T/mu); in a gas v = sqrt(gamma P/rho); stationary waves, beats and the Doppler effect follow.
Deep dive: simple harmonic motion

In SHM the restoring force is proportional to displacement and directed towards the mean position: F = -k x, so a = -omega^2 x with omega^2 = k/m. Displacement x = A sin (omega t + phi); velocity v = A omega cos (omega t + phi) = omega sqrt (A^2 - x^2), maximum A omega at the mean position; maximum acceleration A omega^2 at the extremes. Time period T = 2 pi/omega, frequency f = 1/T, and omega = 2 pi f. Energy: kinetic (1/2) m omega^2 (A^2 - x^2), potential (1/2) m omega^2 x^2, total (1/2) m omega^2 A^2 = (1/2) k A^2, constant. Kinetic and potential energies each oscillate at twice the frequency of the motion; their time-average is half the total.
Deep dive: spring, pendulum and combinations

A mass m on a spring: T = 2 pi sqrt (m/k). Springs in series: 1/k = 1/k1 + 1/k2; in parallel: k = k1 + k2. Simple pendulum: T = 2 pi sqrt (L/g), independent of mass and amplitude (small angles); the seconds pendulum (T = 2 s) has length about 1 m. In an accelerating lift g becomes g +- a; on the Moon g is one-sixth so T is larger by sqrt 6. Physical pendulum: T = 2 pi sqrt (I/(m g d)). Damped oscillations lose amplitude exponentially; forced oscillations show resonance when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency.
Deep dive: wave motion

A progressive wave y = A sin (k x - omega t) has wave number k = 2 pi/lambda, speed v = omega/k = f lambda. Transverse waves (particles move perpendicular to propagation) travel in solids on strings; longitudinal waves (compressions and rarefactions) such as sound need a medium. Speed on a stretched string v = sqrt (T/mu); in a gas v = sqrt (gamma P/rho) = sqrt (gamma R T/M), increasing about 0.6 m/s per degree Celsius near 20 C. Stationary waves arise from superposition of two opposite waves: nodes (zero amplitude) and antinodes (maximum), adjacent nodes lambda/2 apart. A string fixed at both ends: f_n = n v/(2L); an open pipe: f_n = n v/(2L); a closed pipe: f_n = (2n - 1) v/(4L) (odd harmonics only). Beats: two close frequencies f1 and f2 give beat frequency |f1 - f2|. Doppler effect: f' = f (v +- v_o)/(v -+ v_s).

Visual lesson

Oscillations and waves

Simple harmonic motion has acceleration a = -omega^2 x, period T = 2 pi/omega, displacement x = A sin (omega t + phi), speed v = omega sqrt(A^2 - x^2)

🔑

Big idea

  • Simple harmonic motion has acceleration a = -omega2 x, period T = 2 pi/omega, displacement x = A sin (omega t + phi), speed v = omega sqrt(A2 - x2)
  • For a spring T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k)

Read the full explanation

Simple harmonic motion has acceleration a = -omega^2 x, period T = 2 pi/omega, displacement x = A sin (omega t + phi), speed v = omega sqrt(A^2 - x^2). For a spring T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k); for a simple pendulum T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g). A wave has speed v = f lambda; on a string v = sqrt(T/mu); in a gas v = sqrt(gamma P/rho); stationary waves, beats and the Doppler effect follow.

🚀

Simple harmonic motion

  • In SHM the restoring force is proportional to displacement and directed towards the mean position: F = -k x, so a = -omega2 x with omega2 = k/m
  • Displacement x = A sin (omega t + phi)
  • Velocity v = A omega cos (omega t + phi) = omega sqrt (A2 - x2), maximum A omega at the mean position
  • Maximum acceleration A omega2 at the extremes
Read the full explanation

In SHM the restoring force is proportional to displacement and directed towards the mean position: F = -k x, so a = -omega^2 x with omega^2 = k/m. Displacement x = A sin (omega t + phi); velocity v = A omega cos (omega t + phi) = omega sqrt (A^2 - x^2), maximum A omega at the mean position; maximum acceleration A omega^2 at the extremes. Time period T = 2 pi/omega, frequency f = 1/T, and omega = 2 pi f. Energy: kinetic (1/2) m omega^2 (A^2 - x^2), potential (1/2) m omega^2 x^2, total (1/2) m omega^2 A^2 = (1/2) k A^2, constant. Kinetic and potential energies each oscillate at twice the frequency of the motion; their time-average is half the total.

🧠

Spring, pendulum and combinations

  • A mass m on a spring: T = 2 pi sqrt (m/k)
  • Springs in series: 1/k = 1/k1 + 1/k2
  • In parallel: k = k1 + k2
  • Simple pendulum: T = 2 pi sqrt (L/g), independent of mass and amplitude (small angles)
Read the full explanation

A mass m on a spring: T = 2 pi sqrt (m/k). Springs in series: 1/k = 1/k1 + 1/k2; in parallel: k = k1 + k2. Simple pendulum: T = 2 pi sqrt (L/g), independent of mass and amplitude (small angles); the seconds pendulum (T = 2 s) has length about 1 m. In an accelerating lift g becomes g +- a; on the Moon g is one-sixth so T is larger by sqrt 6. Physical pendulum: T = 2 pi sqrt (I/(m g d)). Damped oscillations lose amplitude exponentially; forced oscillations show resonance when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency.

🌊

Wave motion

  • A progressive wave y = A sin (k x - omega t) has wave number k = 2 pi/lambda, speed v = omega/k = f lambda
  • Transverse waves (particles move perpendicular to propagation) travel in solids on strings
  • Longitudinal waves (compressions and rarefactions) such as sound need a medium
  • Speed on a stretched string v = sqrt (T/mu)
Read the full explanation

A progressive wave y = A sin (k x - omega t) has wave number k = 2 pi/lambda, speed v = omega/k = f lambda. Transverse waves (particles move perpendicular to propagation) travel in solids on strings; longitudinal waves (compressions and rarefactions) such as sound need a medium. Speed on a stretched string v = sqrt (T/mu); in a gas v = sqrt (gamma P/rho) = sqrt (gamma R T/M), increasing about 0.6 m/s per degree Celsius near 20 C. Stationary waves arise from superposition of two opposite waves: nodes (zero amplitude) and antinodes (maximum), adjacent nodes lambda/2 apart. A string fixed at both ends: f_n = n v/(2L); an open pipe: f_n = n v/(2L); a closed pipe: f_n = (2n - 1) v/(4L) (odd harmonics only). Beats: two close frequencies f1 and f2 give beat frequency |f1 - f2|. Doppler effect: f' = f (v +- v_o)/(v -+ v_s).

lessons.title: Heat, kinetic theory and thermodynamics
yt: class 11 physics thermodynamics

blocks.x: Heat Q = m c DT; PV = nRT; the kinetic energy per molecule is (3/2) k T and v_rms = sqrt(3RT/M). First law: Q = DU + W. Efficiency of a Carnot engine = 1 - T2/T1. Heat flow by conduction H = k A DT/L; Stefan law E = sigma T^4; Wien law lambda_m T = b.
Deep dive: temperature, heat and calorimetry

Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of molecules; heat is energy in transit due to a temperature difference. Scales: C/5 = (F - 32)/9 = (K - 273)/5. Heat required Q = m c DT; for a phase change Q = m L (latent heat of fusion for ice 336 kJ/kg, of vaporisation of water 2260 kJ/kg). Principle of calorimetry: heat lost = heat gained. Specific heat of water is 4200 J/(kg K). Thermal expansion: DL = alpha L DT, DA = 2 alpha A DT, DV = 3 alpha V DT. Water shows anomalous expansion between 0 and 4 C, with maximum density at 4 C.
Deep dive: kinetic theory of gases

Ideal gas equation PV = nRT = N k T with R = 8.31 J/(mol K) and k = 1.38 x 10^-23 J/K. Pressure P = (1/3) rho v_rms^2. Average kinetic energy per molecule (3/2) k T; v_rms = sqrt (3RT/M), v_avg = sqrt (8RT/(pi M)), v_mp = sqrt (2RT/M), with v_rms : v_avg : v_mp = sqrt 3 : sqrt (8/pi) : sqrt 2. Degrees of freedom f: energy per mole (f/2) R T; monatomic f = 3, diatomic f = 5 at room temperature. C_v = (f/2) R, C_p = C_v + R (Mayer), gamma = C_p/C_v = 1 + 2/f: 5/3 for monatomic, 7/5 for diatomic. Mean free path lambda = 1/(sqrt 2 pi d^2 n).
Deep dive: thermodynamics and transfer

First law: Q = DU + W where W = integral P dV. Isothermal: DU = 0, W = nRT ln (V2/V1), PV = constant. Adiabatic: Q = 0, P V^gamma = constant, W = (P1 V1 - P2 V2)/(gamma - 1). Isobaric: W = P DV. Isochoric: W = 0. Heat engine efficiency = W/Q1 = 1 - Q2/Q1; a Carnot engine between T1 and T2 has efficiency 1 - T2/T1 (maximum). Refrigerator coefficient of performance = T2/(T1 - T2). Second law: heat cannot flow by itself from cold to hot (Clausius); no engine converts all heat to work (Kelvin-Planck). Conduction H = k A (T1 - T2)/L; convection; radiation: a black body emits E = sigma T^4 per unit area (Stefan), with sigma = 5.67 x 10^-8 W/(m^2 K^4); Wien displacement lambda_m T = 2.9 x 10^-3 m K; Newton law of cooling: rate of cooling proportional to temperature difference.

Big idea

Read the full explanation

Heat Q = m c DT; PV = nRT; the kinetic energy per molecule is (3/2) k T and v_rms = sqrt(3RT/M). First law: Q = DU + W. Efficiency of a Carnot engine = 1 - T2/T1. Heat flow by conduction H = k A DT/L; Stefan law E = sigma T^4; Wien law lambda_m T = b.

🌡️

Temperature, heat and calorimetry

  • Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of molecules
  • Heat is energy in transit due to a temperature difference
  • Scales: C/5 = (F - 32)/9 = (K - 273)/5
  • Heat required Q = m c DT
Read the full explanation

Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of molecules; heat is energy in transit due to a temperature difference. Scales: C/5 = (F - 32)/9 = (K - 273)/5. Heat required Q = m c DT; for a phase change Q = m L (latent heat of fusion for ice 336 kJ/kg, of vaporisation of water 2260 kJ/kg). Principle of calorimetry: heat lost = heat gained. Specific heat of water is 4200 J/(kg K). Thermal expansion: DL = alpha L DT, DA = 2 alpha A DT, DV = 3 alpha V DT. Water shows anomalous expansion between 0 and 4 C, with maximum density at 4 C.

🧠

Kinetic theory of gases

  • Ideal gas equation PV = nRT = N k T with R = 8.31 J/(mol K) and k = 1.38 x 10-23 J/K
  • Pressure P = (1/3) rho v_rms2
  • Average kinetic energy per molecule (3/2) k T
  • V_rms = sqrt (3RT/M), v_avg = sqrt (8RT/(pi M)), v_mp = sqrt (2RT/M), with v_rms : v_avg : v_mp = sqrt 3 : sqrt (8/pi) : sqrt 2
Read the full explanation

Ideal gas equation PV = nRT = N k T with R = 8.31 J/(mol K) and k = 1.38 x 10^-23 J/K. Pressure P = (1/3) rho v_rms^2. Average kinetic energy per molecule (3/2) k T; v_rms = sqrt (3RT/M), v_avg = sqrt (8RT/(pi M)), v_mp = sqrt (2RT/M), with v_rms : v_avg : v_mp = sqrt 3 : sqrt (8/pi) : sqrt 2. Degrees of freedom f: energy per mole (f/2) R T; monatomic f = 3, diatomic f = 5 at room temperature. C_v = (f/2) R, C_p = C_v + R (Mayer), gamma = C_p/C_v = 1 + 2/f: 5/3 for monatomic, 7/5 for diatomic. Mean free path lambda = 1/(sqrt 2 pi d^2 n).

🌡️

Thermodynamics and transfer

  • First law: Q = DU + W where W = integral P dV
  • Isothermal: DU = 0, W = nRT ln (V2/V1), PV = constant
  • Adiabatic: Q = 0, P V^gamma = constant, W = (P1 V1 - P2 V2)/(gamma - 1)
  • Isobaric: W = P DV
Read the full explanation

First law: Q = DU + W where W = integral P dV. Isothermal: DU = 0, W = nRT ln (V2/V1), PV = constant. Adiabatic: Q = 0, P V^gamma = constant, W = (P1 V1 - P2 V2)/(gamma - 1). Isobaric: W = P DV. Isochoric: W = 0. Heat engine efficiency = W/Q1 = 1 - Q2/Q1; a Carnot engine between T1 and T2 has efficiency 1 - T2/T1 (maximum). Refrigerator coefficient of performance = T2/(T1 - T2). Second law: heat cannot flow by itself from cold to hot (Clausius); no engine converts all heat to work (Kelvin-Planck). Conduction H = k A (T1 - T2)/L; convection; radiation: a black body emits E = sigma T^4 per unit area (Stefan), with sigma = 5.67 x 10^-8 W/(m^2 K^4); Wien displacement lambda_m T = 2.9 x 10^-3 m K; Newton law of cooling: rate of cooling proportional to temperature difference.

lessons.title: Constitution: Why and How?
yt: class 11 political science constitution why and how constituent assembly

blocks.x: A constitution is a set of fundamental rules that decide how a country is governed. Its functions are to create trust and coordination among people, to specify how the government will be constituted and who has power to take decisions, to limit the power of government over citizens and to enable society to fulfil its aspirations. The Indian Constitution was made by the Constituent Assembly, formed in 1946 under the Cabinet Mission Plan. Its first meeting was held on 9 December 1946 with Sachchidananda Sinha as the temporary chairman, and Dr Rajendra Prasad was elected permanent president on 11 December 1946. The Assembly originally had 389 members, reduced to 299 after Partition. The Drafting Committee was set up on 29 August 1947 with Dr B R Ambedkar as chairman, and B N Rau was the constitutional adviser. The Objectives Resolution, moved by Jawaharlal Nehru on 13 December 1946 and adopted on 22 January 1947, laid down the philosophy. The Assembly took 2 years, 11 months and 18 days, held 11 sessions, and adopted the Constitution on 26 November 1949; it came into force on 26 January 1950. 26 January was chosen because the Purna Swaraj resolution was adopted at Lahore in 1929 and Independence Day was celebrated on that date in 1930. Constitution Day is celebrated on 26 November. The original Constitution had 395 articles, 22 parts and 8 schedules. Sources: the Government of India Act 1935 for the federal scheme and administration; Britain for parliamentary government; the USA for fundamental rights and judicial review; Ireland for Directive Principles; Canada for a strong Centre; Australia for the concurrent list; Germany (Weimar) for emergency provisions; the USSR for fundamental duties; and South Africa for the amendment procedure. The Preamble describes India as sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic and republic, with justice, liberty, equality and fraternity; the words socialist and secular were added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976. The Constitution is flexible and rigid, a living document. Ambedkar warned that constitutional morality must be cultivated.
Deep dive: Making of the constitution

The Constituent Assembly was not elected by universal franchise but represented all major groups. It debated in open sessions and drew on national movement ideals. Committees such as the Union Powers Committee and Fundamental Rights Committee prepared drafts.
Deep dive: Features and philosophy

The Constitution protects rights, limits government and provides for democracy. It balances liberty and social justice. The Preamble expresses its philosophy; the Constitution is the longest written constitution of any country.
Deep dive: Procedures and balance
It balances a strong Centre and states. It allows amendment but protects the basic structure. It accommodates diversity through special provisions.

Constitution: Why and How?

A constitution is a set of fundamental rules that decide how a country is governed

Big idea

Read the full explanation

A constitution is a set of fundamental rules that decide how a country is governed. Its functions are to create trust and coordination among people, to specify how the government will be constituted and who has power to take decisions, to limit the power of government over citizens and to enable society to fulfil its aspirations. The Indian Constitution was made by the Constituent Assembly, formed in 1946 under the Cabinet Mission Plan. Its first meeting was held on 9 December 1946 with Sachchidananda Sinha as the temporary chairman, and Dr Rajendra Prasad was elected permanent president on 11 December 1946. The Assembly originally had 389 members, reduced to 299 after Partition. The Drafting Committee was set up on 29 August 1947 with Dr B R Ambedkar as chairman, and B N Rau was the constitutional adviser. The Objectives Resolution, moved by Jawaharlal Nehru on 13 December 1946 and adopted on 22 January 1947, laid down the philosophy. The Assembly took 2 years, 11 months and 18 days, held 11 sessions, and adopted the Constitution on 26 November 1949; it came into force on 26 January 1950. 26 January was chosen because the Purna Swaraj resolution was adopted at Lahore in 1929 and Independence Day was celebrated on that date in 1930. Constitution Day is celebrated on 26 November. The original Constitution had 395 articles, 22 parts and 8 schedules. Sources: the Government of India Act 1935 for the federal scheme and administration; Britain for parliamentary government; the USA for fundamental rights and judicial review; Ireland for Directive Principles; Canada for a strong Centre; Australia for the concurrent list; Germany (Weimar) for emergency provisions; the USSR for fundamental duties; and South Africa for the amendment procedure. The Preamble describes India as sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic and republic, with justice, liberty, equality and fraternity; the words socialist and secular were added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976. The Constitution is flexible and rigid, a living document. Ambedkar warned that constitutional morality must be cultivated.

🏛️

Making of the constitution

  • The Constituent Assembly was not elected by universal franchise but represented all major groups
  • It debated in open sessions and drew on national movement ideals
  • Committees such as the Union Powers Committee and Fundamental Rights Committee prepared drafts
🧠

Features and philosophy

  • The Constitution protects rights, limits government and provides for democracy
  • It balances liberty and social justice
  • The Preamble expresses its philosophy
  • The Constitution is the longest written constitution of any country
🔄

Procedures and balance

  • It balances a strong Centre and states
  • It allows amendment but protects the basic structure
  • It accommodates diversity through special provisions
🎯 Remember adopted 26 Nov 1949; in force 26 Jan 1950.
