lessons.title: Rights in the Indian Constitution
yt: class 11 political science rights in the indian constitution fundamental rights dpsp duties

blocks.x: Fundamental Rights are in Part III (Articles 12 to 35) and are enforceable by courts. The six fundamental rights are: the Right to Equality (Articles 14 to 18), the Right to Freedom (Articles 19 to 22), the Right against Exploitation (Articles 23 and 24), the Right to Freedom of Religion (Articles 25 to 28), Cultural and Educational Rights (Articles 29 and 30) and the Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32). Article 14 guarantees equality before law and equal protection of laws; Article 15 prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth; Article 16 gives equality of opportunity in public employment; Article 17 abolishes untouchability; Article 18 abolishes titles. Article 19 gives six freedoms: speech and expression, assembly, association, movement, residence and profession. Article 20 protects against conviction for offences; Article 21 protects life and personal liberty; Article 21A (86th Amendment, 2002) makes education compulsory for children aged 6 to 14; Article 22 protects against arbitrary arrest. Article 23 prohibits trafficking and forced labour; Article 24 prohibits employment of children below 14 in hazardous work. Article 25 gives freedom of conscience and religion. Article 29 protects the interests of minorities and Article 30 gives minorities the right to establish educational institutions. Article 32, called by Ambedkar the heart and soul of the Constitution, lets a person move the Supreme Court; writs are habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto; High Courts issue writs under Article 226. The right to property was removed from fundamental rights by the 44th Amendment in 1978 and is now a legal right under Article 300A. Rights may be restricted by reasonable restrictions in public interest, and can be suspended in an emergency (except Articles 20 and 21). Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV, Articles 36 to 51) are guidelines for the state to build a welfare state; they are non-justiciable. Fundamental Duties (Part IV-A, Article 51A) were added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976 on the Swaran Singh Committee and number 11 after the 86th Amendment added a duty of parents to educate children. The Kesavananda Bharati case (1973) established the basic structure doctrine; Maneka Gandhi (1978) widened Article 21. The National Human Rights Commission was set up in 1993 under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993. The Right to Information Act, 2005 and the Right to Education Act, 2009 expanded rights.
Deep dive: Fundamental rights
Rights protect individuals against the state. Equality removes discrimination. Freedom includes speech but with reasonable limits. Remedies make rights effective.
Deep dive: Directive Principles and duties

DPSP aim at social and economic democracy, including equal pay, living wage, village panchayats and uniform civil code (Article 44). Duties remind citizens to respect the Constitution, protect the environment and promote harmony.
Deep dive: Interpretation
Courts have widened Article 21 to include privacy, education, health and livelihood. The Puttaswamy case (2017) held privacy a fundamental right. Writs protect rights quickly.

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Rights in the Indian Constitution

Fundamental Rights are in Part III (Articles 12 to 35) and are enforceable by courts

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Fundamental rights›3Directive Principles and…›4Interpretation
Equality14-18
Freedom19-22
Exploitation23-24
Religion25-28
Remedies32
🔑

Big idea

  • Fundamental Rights are in Part III (Articles 12 to 35) and are enforceable by courts
  • The six fundamental rights are: the Right to Equality (Articles 14 to 18), the Right to Freedom (Articles 19 to 22), the Right against Exploitation…
  • Article 14 guarantees equality before law and equal protection of laws
  • Article 15 prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth
Read the full explanation

Fundamental Rights are in Part III (Articles 12 to 35) and are enforceable by courts. The six fundamental rights are: the Right to Equality (Articles 14 to 18), the Right to Freedom (Articles 19 to 22), the Right against Exploitation (Articles 23 and 24), the Right to Freedom of Religion (Articles 25 to 28), Cultural and Educational Rights (Articles 29 and 30) and the Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32). Article 14 guarantees equality before law and equal protection of laws; Article 15 prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth; Article 16 gives equality of opportunity in public employment; Article 17 abolishes untouchability; Article 18 abolishes titles. Article 19 gives six freedoms: speech and expression, assembly, association, movement, residence and profession. Article 20 protects against conviction for offences; Article 21 protects life and personal liberty; Article 21A (86th Amendment, 2002) makes education compulsory for children aged 6 to 14; Article 22 protects against arbitrary arrest. Article 23 prohibits trafficking and forced labour; Article 24 prohibits employment of children below 14 in hazardous work. Article 25 gives freedom of conscience and religion. Article 29 protects the interests of minorities and Article 30 gives minorities the right to establish educational institutions. Article 32, called by Ambedkar the heart and soul of the Constitution, lets a person move the Supreme Court; writs are habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto; High Courts issue writs under Article 226. The right to property was removed from fundamental rights by the 44th Amendment in 1978 and is now a legal right under Article 300A. Rights may be restricted by reasonable restrictions in public interest, and can be suspended in an emergency (except Articles 20 and 21). Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV, Articles 36 to 51) are guidelines for the state to build a welfare state; they are non-justiciable. Fundamental Duties (Part IV-A, Article 51A) were added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976 on the Swaran Singh Committee and number 11 after the 86th Amendment added a duty of parents to educate children. The Kesavananda Bharati case (1973) established the basic structure doctrine; Maneka Gandhi (1978) widened Article 21. The National Human Rights Commission was set up in 1993 under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993. The Right to Information Act, 2005 and the Right to Education Act, 2009 expanded rights.

🏛️

Fundamental rights

  • Rights protect individuals against the state
  • Equality removes discrimination
  • Freedom includes speech but with reasonable limits
  • Remedies make rights effective
⚖️

Directive Principles and duties

  • DPSP aim at social and economic democracy, including equal pay, living wage, village panchayats and uniform civil code (Article 44)
  • Duties remind citizens to respect the Constitution, protect the environment and promote harmony
🌟

Interpretation

  • Courts have widened Article 21 to include privacy, education, health and livelihood
  • The Puttaswamy case (2017) held privacy a fundamental right
  • Writs protect rights quickly
🎯 Remember Remember six rights: Equality, Freedom, Against Exploitation, Religion, Cultural-Educational, Constitutional Remedies.
🇮🇳

हिंदी सार

Moolbhut adhikar Part III (Anuchhed 12-35) mein hain; Anuchhed 32 sanvaidhanik upchar ka adhikar hai; DPSP Part IV mein.

lessons.title: Election and Representation
yt: class 11 political science election and representation fptp pr election commission

blocks.x: Elections are the means of choosing representatives in a democracy. Two main systems exist: First Past the Post (FPTP), in which the candidate with the most votes in a constituency wins (used in India for Lok Sabha and state assemblies), and Proportional Representation (PR), in which parties get seats in proportion to their votes. India adopted FPTP because it is simple and gives stable governments. PR is used in India through the single transferable vote for elections to the Rajya Sabha, the President and the Vice President. Universal adult franchise is given by Article 326; the voting age was reduced from 21 to 18 by the 61st Amendment in 1988. The Election Commission of India (Article 324) is an independent body that supervises elections; it was set up on 25 January 1950 (observed as National Voters Day). It consists of the Chief Election Commissioner and other commissioners. Sukumar Sen was the first Chief Election Commissioner. The first general election was held in 1951-52. Electoral laws are the Representation of the People Acts of 1950 and 1951. The Model Code of Conduct guides parties and candidates during elections. Constituencies are demarcated by the Delimitation Commission; seats are reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. The Lok Sabha has 543 elected members; the Rajya Sabha has up to 250 members (238 elected by states and 12 nominated by the President). Anglo-Indian nomination was ended by the 104th Amendment (2019). Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs) were first used in Kerala in 1982 and in all of India from 2004; VVPAT slips give verification; NOTA (none of the above) was introduced after a 2013 Supreme Court order. Reforms: free and fair elections, curbing money power and criminalisation, disclosure of assets and criminal records, and the anti-defection law. The Women's Reservation Act (106th Amendment, 2023) reserves one-third of seats in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies for women, to take effect after delimitation. Representation means that elected members speak for the people; reservation ensures inclusion of weaker groups. Panchayati Raj institutions have one-third reservation for women (73rd and 74th Amendments).
Deep dive: FPTP and PR
FPTP is easy to understand and often gives clear winners but a candidate may win without a majority of votes. PR gives a fairer share of seats to parties but may lead to coalitions. India chose FPTP.
Deep dive: Election Commission
It prepares electoral rolls, schedules elections, enforces the code of conduct, recognises parties and allots symbols. It is independent of the government.
Deep dive: Reservation and reforms
Reserved seats ensure that disadvantaged groups are represented. Reforms deal with money power, criminals in politics and voter awareness.
Hindi saransh
Chunav aur pratinidhitva: India mein FPTP pranali hai; Nirvachan Aayog (Anuchhed 324) swatantra roop se chunav karata hai.
Remember: FPTP = most votes wins; PR = seats by vote share.

Big idea

  • Elections are the means of choosing representatives in a democracy
  • Two main systems exist: First Past the Post (FPTP), in which the candidate with the most votes in a constituency wins (used in India for Lok Sabha…
  • India adopted FPTP because it is simple and gives stable governments

Read the full explanation

Elections are the means of choosing representatives in a democracy. Two main systems exist: First Past the Post (FPTP), in which the candidate with the most votes in a constituency wins (used in India for Lok Sabha and state assemblies), and Proportional Representation (PR), in which parties get seats in proportion to their votes. India adopted FPTP because it is simple and gives stable governments. PR is used in India through the single transferable vote for elections to the Rajya Sabha, the President and the Vice President. Universal adult franchise is given by Article 326; the voting age was reduced from 21 to 18 by the 61st Amendment in 1988. The Election Commission of India (Article 324) is an independent body that supervises elections; it was set up on 25 January 1950 (observed as National Voters Day). It consists of the Chief Election Commissioner and other commissioners. Sukumar Sen was the first Chief Election Commissioner. The first general election was held in 1951-52. Electoral laws are the Representation of the People Acts of 1950 and 1951. The Model Code of Conduct guides parties and candidates during elections. Constituencies are demarcated by the Delimitation Commission; seats are reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. The Lok Sabha has 543 elected members; the Rajya Sabha has up to 250 members (238 elected by states and 12 nominated by the President). Anglo-Indian nomination was ended by the 104th Amendment (2019). Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs) were first used in Kerala in 1982 and in all of India from 2004; VVPAT slips give verification; NOTA (none of the above) was introduced after a 2013 Supreme Court order. Reforms: free and fair elections, curbing money power and criminalisation, disclosure of assets and criminal records, and the anti-defection law. The Women's Reservation Act (106th Amendment, 2023) reserves one-third of seats in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies for women, to take effect after delimitation. Representation means that elected members speak for the people; reservation ensures inclusion of weaker groups. Panchayati Raj institutions have one-third reservation for women (73rd and 74th Amendments).

📌

FPTP and PR

  • FPTP is easy to understand and often gives clear winners but a candidate may win without a majority of votes
  • PR gives a fairer share of seats to parties but may lead to coalitions
  • India chose FPTP
🧠

Election Commission

  • It prepares electoral rolls, schedules elections, enforces the code of conduct, recognises parties and allots symbols
  • It is independent of the government
🌟

Reservation and reforms

  • Reserved seats ensure that disadvantaged groups are represented
  • Reforms deal with money power, criminals in politics and voter awareness

lessons.title: The Executive
yt: class 11 political science the executive president prime minister council of ministers governor

blocks.x: The executive implements laws and runs the government. It has political executives (President, Prime Minister, ministers) and a permanent executive (civil servants). India has a parliamentary system in which the real executive power rests with the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers, while the President is the nominal head of the state. The President (Article 52) is elected by an Electoral College of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the elected members of the state legislative assemblies (Article 54) by proportional representation using the single transferable vote. Qualifications: citizen of India, at least 35 years old and qualified to be elected to the Lok Sabha. The term is five years and the President can be removed by impeachment (Article 61) for violating the Constitution. The Vice President (Article 63) is elected by members of both Houses and is the ex-officio chairman of the Rajya Sabha. Powers of the President: executive (appoints PM, ministers, governors, judges), legislative (summons and prorogues Parliament, dissolves the Lok Sabha, issues ordinances under Article 123), financial (money bills need recommendation), judicial (pardoning power under Article 72) and emergency powers (Articles 352, 356, 360). Veto powers: absolute, suspensive and pocket. By the 42nd and 44th Amendments the President must act on the advice of the Council of Ministers but may return it once for reconsideration. The Prime Minister (Article 74 and 75) is the leader of the majority in the Lok Sabha; the Council of Ministers has Cabinet ministers, ministers of state and deputy ministers and is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha (Article 75(3)). The 91st Amendment (2003) limits the size of the council to 15 percent of the Lok Sabha membership. The Cabinet is the core decision-making body. The Governor (Article 153) is appointed by the President and acts on the advice of the state council of ministers. The Chief Minister heads the state council. The permanent executive consists of civil servants recruited by the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) through all India services (IAS, IPS, IFS). Neutrality, anonymity and permanence are features of the civil service. Collective responsibility means that the council sinks or swims together; individual responsibility applies to each minister. The first President was Dr Rajendra Prasad. The Prime Minister Office (PMO) assists the PM.
Deep dive: President and Vice President
The President is the constitutional head. Election is indirect. Powers are mostly exercised on the advice of ministers. Situations such as a hung Parliament give the President real discretion.
Deep dive: Prime Minister and ministers
The PM chooses ministers and allocates portfolios. Cabinet takes policy decisions. The council is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha and can be removed by a no-confidence vote.
Deep dive: Governor and bureaucracy
The Governor is the nominal head of a state with some discretion. Civil servants advise ministers and implement policy. UPSC ensures merit-based recruitment.

The Executive

The executive implements laws and runs the government

Big idea

  • India has a parliamentary system in which the real executive power rests with the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers, while the President is the…

Read the full explanation

The executive implements laws and runs the government. It has political executives (President, Prime Minister, ministers) and a permanent executive (civil servants). India has a parliamentary system in which the real executive power rests with the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers, while the President is the nominal head of the state. The President (Article 52) is elected by an Electoral College of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the elected members of the state legislative assemblies (Article 54) by proportional representation using the single transferable vote. Qualifications: citizen of India, at least 35 years old and qualified to be elected to the Lok Sabha. The term is five years and the President can be removed by impeachment (Article 61) for violating the Constitution. The Vice President (Article 63) is elected by members of both Houses and is the ex-officio chairman of the Rajya Sabha. Powers of the President: executive (appoints PM, ministers, governors, judges), legislative (summons and prorogues Parliament, dissolves the Lok Sabha, issues ordinances under Article 123), financial (money bills need recommendation), judicial (pardoning power under Article 72) and emergency powers (Articles 352, 356, 360). Veto powers: absolute, suspensive and pocket. By the 42nd and 44th Amendments the President must act on the advice of the Council of Ministers but may return it once for reconsideration. The Prime Minister (Article 74 and 75) is the leader of the majority in the Lok Sabha; the Council of Ministers has Cabinet ministers, ministers of state and deputy ministers and is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha (Article 75(3)). The 91st Amendment (2003) limits the size of the council to 15 percent of the Lok Sabha membership. The Cabinet is the core decision-making body. The Governor (Article 153) is appointed by the President and acts on the advice of the state council of ministers. The Chief Minister heads the state council. The permanent executive consists of civil servants recruited by the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) through all India services (IAS, IPS, IFS). Neutrality, anonymity and permanence are features of the civil service. Collective responsibility means that the council sinks or swims together; individual responsibility applies to each minister. The first President was Dr Rajendra Prasad. The Prime Minister Office (PMO) assists the PM.

📌

President and Vice President

  • The President is the constitutional head
  • Election is indirect
  • Powers are mostly exercised on the advice of ministers
  • Situations such as a hung Parliament give the President real discretion
🧠

Prime Minister and ministers

  • The PM chooses ministers and allocates portfolios
  • Cabinet takes policy decisions
  • The council is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha and can be removed by a no-confidence vote
🌟

Governor and bureaucracy

  • The Governor is the nominal head of a state with some discretion
  • Civil servants advise ministers and implement policy
  • UPSC ensures merit-based recruitment

lessons.title: The Legislature
yt: class 11 political science the legislature parliament lok sabha rajya sabha

blocks.x: The legislature makes laws, controls the executive and approves the budget. India has a bicameral Parliament at the Union level, consisting of the President, the Lok Sabha (House of the People) and the Rajya Sabha (Council of States) (Article 79). The Lok Sabha has up to 552 members under the Constitution and currently 543 elected; its term is five years, and it can be dissolved earlier. The Speaker presides. The Rajya Sabha has a maximum of 250 members, of whom 238 are elected by the state legislatures and 12 are nominated by the President for expertise in literature, science, art and social service; it is a permanent house, with one-third of members retiring every two years, and each member has a six-year term. The Vice President is its chairman. Functions of Parliament: legislative, executive control, financial, representative, deliberative, judicial (impeachment) and constituent (amendment under Article 368). Bills are ordinary, money, financial or constitutional amendment bills. A Money Bill (Article 110) can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha on the recommendation of the President; the Rajya Sabha can only recommend changes within 14 days. A bill passes through three readings in each House, and then gets the President's assent. In a deadlock over an ordinary bill the President summons a joint sitting (Article 108), presided by the Speaker. Parliament controls the executive through question hour, zero hour, adjournment motions, calling attention motions, no-confidence motions and committees. Parliamentary committees include the Public Accounts Committee (PAC), Estimates Committee and Committee on Public Undertakings. The Budget is presented annually by the Finance Minister. The Anti-Defection law (52nd Amendment, 1985; Tenth Schedule) disqualifies members who defect from their party; the 91st Amendment removed the exemption for splits. The Lok Sabha Speaker decides disqualification. The quorum is one-tenth of the total members. Privileges protect freedom of speech inside the House. State legislatures have a Vidhan Sabha and in some states a Vidhan Parishad. Parliament amends the Constitution by special majority. The first Lok Sabha was constituted in 1952, and the first sitting of the Rajya Sabha was on 13 May 1952.
Deep dive: Houses
Lok Sabha represents the people; Rajya Sabha represents the states. Lok Sabha has more power over money and the council of ministers. Rajya Sabha has special powers over states (Article 249).
Deep dive: Law making
A bill is introduced, debated, voted, passed by both Houses and signed by the President. Money bills are special. Joint sittings resolve deadlocks except for money and constitutional amendment bills.
Deep dive: Control of executive
Parliament holds the executive accountable by questions, debates and committees. No-confidence vote can topple the government. Committees scrutinise spending and policies.

Big idea

  • The legislature makes laws, controls the executive and approves the budget
  • India has a bicameral Parliament at the Union level, consisting of the President, the Lok Sabha (House of the People) and the Rajya Sabha (Council of…
  • The Lok Sabha has up to 552 members under the Constitution and currently 543 elected
  • Its term is five years, and it can be dissolved earlier
Read the full explanation

The legislature makes laws, controls the executive and approves the budget. India has a bicameral Parliament at the Union level, consisting of the President, the Lok Sabha (House of the People) and the Rajya Sabha (Council of States) (Article 79). The Lok Sabha has up to 552 members under the Constitution and currently 543 elected; its term is five years, and it can be dissolved earlier. The Speaker presides. The Rajya Sabha has a maximum of 250 members, of whom 238 are elected by the state legislatures and 12 are nominated by the President for expertise in literature, science, art and social service; it is a permanent house, with one-third of members retiring every two years, and each member has a six-year term. The Vice President is its chairman. Functions of Parliament: legislative, executive control, financial, representative, deliberative, judicial (impeachment) and constituent (amendment under Article 368). Bills are ordinary, money, financial or constitutional amendment bills. A Money Bill (Article 110) can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha on the recommendation of the President; the Rajya Sabha can only recommend changes within 14 days. A bill passes through three readings in each House, and then gets the President's assent. In a deadlock over an ordinary bill the President summons a joint sitting (Article 108), presided by the Speaker. Parliament controls the executive through question hour, zero hour, adjournment motions, calling attention motions, no-confidence motions and committees. Parliamentary committees include the Public Accounts Committee (PAC), Estimates Committee and Committee on Public Undertakings. The Budget is presented annually by the Finance Minister. The Anti-Defection law (52nd Amendment, 1985; Tenth Schedule) disqualifies members who defect from their party; the 91st Amendment removed the exemption for splits. The Lok Sabha Speaker decides disqualification. The quorum is one-tenth of the total members. Privileges protect freedom of speech inside the House. State legislatures have a Vidhan Sabha and in some states a Vidhan Parishad. Parliament amends the Constitution by special majority. The first Lok Sabha was constituted in 1952, and the first sitting of the Rajya Sabha was on 13 May 1952.

💡

Houses

  • Lok Sabha represents the people
  • Rajya Sabha represents the states
  • Lok Sabha has more power over money and the council of ministers
  • Rajya Sabha has special powers over states (Article 249)
⚖️

Law making

  • A bill is introduced, debated, voted, passed by both Houses and signed by the President
  • Money bills are special
  • Joint sittings resolve deadlocks except for money and constitutional amendment bills
🌟

Control of executive

  • Parliament holds the executive accountable by questions, debates and committees
  • No-confidence vote can topple the government
  • Committees scrutinise spending and policies
🧮

lessons.title: The Judiciary
yt: class 11 political science the judiciary supreme court high court judicial review pil independence

blocks.x: The judiciary settles disputes, interprets the Constitution and protects rights. India has an integrated and independent judiciary with the Supreme Court at the top, High Courts in the states and subordinate courts below. Independence is secured by the method of appointment, security of tenure, fixed salaries charged to the Consolidated Fund, and the power to punish for contempt. Judges are appointed by the President in consultation with the Chief Justice of India; in practice the collegium system of senior judges recommends appointments (evolved through the Three Judges cases). A judge of the Supreme Court retires at 65 and a High Court judge at 62; judges can be removed only by impeachment on proven misbehaviour or incapacity by a special majority in Parliament (Article 124(4)). The Supreme Court was inaugurated on 28 January 1950; it has the Chief Justice and a maximum of 33 other judges (34 in total). Jurisdiction: original (disputes between the Union and states, and enforcement of fundamental rights under Article 32), appellate (civil, criminal and constitutional cases from High Courts), advisory (Article 143, opinion for the President) and writ jurisdiction. The Supreme Court is a court of record and the final interpreter of the Constitution, and its law binds all courts (Article 141). Judicial review is the power to examine the constitutionality of laws and executive actions and strike down those against the Constitution. The Kesavananda Bharati case (1973) held that Parliament cannot alter the basic structure. High Courts (Article 214) have original, appellate and supervisory jurisdiction, with 25 High Courts today. The first High Courts were set up in 1862 at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras. Subordinate courts include district courts, sessions courts and family courts; Lok Adalats and Nyaya Panchayats give speedy justice. Public Interest Litigation (PIL) began in the late 1970s with Justices P N Bhagwati and V R Krishna Iyer, allowing anyone to approach the court on behalf of the poor or for public causes. Judicial activism refers to an active role of courts in protecting rights; critics warn of judicial overreach. Concerns include pendency of cases and delays. The idea of separation of powers keeps the judiciary free from executive control. The Constitution also provides for a Supreme Court Collegium, National Judicial Appointments Commission (struck down in 2015 as unconstitutional).
Deep dive: Independence
Independent judiciary is essential for rule of law. Fixed tenure and salary protect judges. Parliament cannot discuss the conduct of a judge except during removal proceedings.
Deep dive: Powers
The Supreme Court protects fundamental rights through writs and settles federal disputes. Judicial review checks laws and actions. Advisory opinion helps the President on legal questions.
Deep dive: Access to justice
PIL, Lok Adalats and legal aid help the poor. Courts have extended rights on environment and gender. Delays and pendency remain challenges.

🔑

Big idea

  • The judiciary settles disputes, interprets the Constitution and protects rights
  • India has an integrated and independent judiciary with the Supreme Court at the top, High Courts in the states and subordinate courts below
  • Independence is secured by the method of appointment, security of tenure, fixed salaries charged to the Consolidated Fund, and the power to punish…
  • Judges are appointed by the President in consultation with the Chief Justice of India
Read the full explanation

The judiciary settles disputes, interprets the Constitution and protects rights. India has an integrated and independent judiciary with the Supreme Court at the top, High Courts in the states and subordinate courts below. Independence is secured by the method of appointment, security of tenure, fixed salaries charged to the Consolidated Fund, and the power to punish for contempt. Judges are appointed by the President in consultation with the Chief Justice of India; in practice the collegium system of senior judges recommends appointments (evolved through the Three Judges cases). A judge of the Supreme Court retires at 65 and a High Court judge at 62; judges can be removed only by impeachment on proven misbehaviour or incapacity by a special majority in Parliament (Article 124(4)). The Supreme Court was inaugurated on 28 January 1950; it has the Chief Justice and a maximum of 33 other judges (34 in total). Jurisdiction: original (disputes between the Union and states, and enforcement of fundamental rights under Article 32), appellate (civil, criminal and constitutional cases from High Courts), advisory (Article 143, opinion for the President) and writ jurisdiction. The Supreme Court is a court of record and the final interpreter of the Constitution, and its law binds all courts (Article 141). Judicial review is the power to examine the constitutionality of laws and executive actions and strike down those against the Constitution. The Kesavananda Bharati case (1973) held that Parliament cannot alter the basic structure. High Courts (Article 214) have original, appellate and supervisory jurisdiction, with 25 High Courts today. The first High Courts were set up in 1862 at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras. Subordinate courts include district courts, sessions courts and family courts; Lok Adalats and Nyaya Panchayats give speedy justice. Public Interest Litigation (PIL) began in the late 1970s with Justices P N Bhagwati and V R Krishna Iyer, allowing anyone to approach the court on behalf of the poor or for public causes. Judicial activism refers to an active role of courts in protecting rights; critics warn of judicial overreach. Concerns include pendency of cases and delays. The idea of separation of powers keeps the judiciary free from executive control. The Constitution also provides for a Supreme Court Collegium, National Judicial Appointments Commission (struck down in 2015 as unconstitutional).

📌

Independence

  • Independent judiciary is essential for rule of law
  • Fixed tenure and salary protect judges
  • Parliament cannot discuss the conduct of a judge except during removal proceedings
🚀

Powers

  • The Supreme Court protects fundamental rights through writs and settles federal disputes
  • Judicial review checks laws and actions
  • Advisory opinion helps the President on legal questions
🌟

Access to justice

  • PIL, Lok Adalats and legal aid help the poor
  • Courts have extended rights on environment and gender
  • Delays and pendency remain challenges

lessons.title: Federalism
yt: class 11 political science federalism union list state list concurrent list centre state relations

blocks.x: Federalism is a system of government in which power is divided between a central authority and constituent units, each with its own sphere. The Indian Constitution describes India as a Union of States (Article 1). It sets up a federation with a strong Centre, sometimes called quasi-federal. Features: a written constitution, two levels of government, division of powers, an independent judiciary and rigid amendment on federal matters. The Seventh Schedule has three lists: the Union List (defence, foreign affairs, currency, railways; originally 97 subjects, now 98), the State List (police, public order, agriculture, local government; now 59 subjects) and the Concurrent List (education, forests, marriage, criminal law; now 52 subjects). Residuary powers lie with the Union. In a conflict on the concurrent list, the Union law prevails. Unitary features: a strong Centre, single citizenship, an integrated judiciary, All India Services, Governors appointed by the Centre, emergency powers (Article 356, President's Rule) and the power of Parliament to reorganise states. Centre-state relations: legislative (Articles 245 to 255), administrative (Articles 256 to 263) and financial (Articles 268 to 293). The Finance Commission (Article 280) is set up every five years to recommend sharing of taxes. The Inter-State Council (Article 263) promotes coordination. Planning Commission was replaced by NITI Aayog in 2015. The Goods and Services Tax (101st Amendment, 2016) is governed by the GST Council. The Sarkaria Commission (1983) and the Punchhi Commission (2007) studied centre-state relations. States Reorganisation: linguistic reorganisation followed the Fazl Ali Commission (1953) and the States Reorganisation Act 1956; Andhra Pradesh was the first linguistic state in 1953; Telangana became the 29th state in 2014. Special provisions for some states under Article 371 and the Fifth and Sixth Schedules for tribal areas; Article 370 was abrogated in 2019 and Jammu and Kashmir was reorganised as Union Territories. Language policy: Hindi in Devanagari is the official language (Article 343) with English; the Eighth Schedule recognises 22 languages. Demands for autonomy and disputes over river waters (Cauvery) show tension. Cooperative federalism emphasises partnership.
Deep dive: Division of powers
The three lists divide subjects. States are supreme in the State List. Parliament may legislate on a State List subject in the national interest if the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution (Article 249).
Deep dive: Strong Centre
Emergency, financial dependence and Governor powers give the Centre strength. Asymmetric provisions accommodate diversity. Tensions arise over President's Rule and grants.
Deep dive: Linguistic states and diversity
Reorganisation on linguistic lines strengthened unity. Language and regional movements show diversity. Federalism accommodates multiple identities within one nation.

Visual lesson

Federalism

Federalism is a system of government in which power is divided between a central authority and constituent units, each with its own sphere

Read the full explanation

Federalism is a system of government in which power is divided between a central authority and constituent units, each with its own sphere. The Indian Constitution describes India as a Union of States (Article 1). It sets up a federation with a strong Centre, sometimes called quasi-federal. Features: a written constitution, two levels of government, division of powers, an independent judiciary and rigid amendment on federal matters. The Seventh Schedule has three lists: the Union List (defence, foreign affairs, currency, railways; originally 97 subjects, now 98), the State List (police, public order, agriculture, local government; now 59 subjects) and the Concurrent List (education, forests, marriage, criminal law; now 52 subjects). Residuary powers lie with the Union. In a conflict on the concurrent list, the Union law prevails. Unitary features: a strong Centre, single citizenship, an integrated judiciary, All India Services, Governors appointed by the Centre, emergency powers (Article 356, President's Rule) and the power of Parliament to reorganise states. Centre-state relations: legislative (Articles 245 to 255), administrative (Articles 256 to 263) and financial (Articles 268 to 293). The Finance Commission (Article 280) is set up every five years to recommend sharing of taxes. The Inter-State Council (Article 263) promotes coordination. Planning Commission was replaced by NITI Aayog in 2015. The Goods and Services Tax (101st Amendment, 2016) is governed by the GST Council. The Sarkaria Commission (1983) and the Punchhi Commission (2007) studied centre-state relations. States Reorganisation: linguistic reorganisation followed the Fazl Ali Commission (1953) and the States Reorganisation Act 1956; Andhra Pradesh was the first linguistic state in 1953; Telangana became the 29th state in 2014. Special provisions for some states under Article 371 and the Fifth and Sixth Schedules for tribal areas; Article 370 was abrogated in 2019 and Jammu and Kashmir was reorganised as Union Territories. Language policy: Hindi in Devanagari is the official language (Article 343) with English; the Eighth Schedule recognises 22 languages. Demands for autonomy and disputes over river waters (Cauvery) show tension. Cooperative federalism emphasises partnership.

🚀

Division of powers

  • The three lists divide subjects
  • States are supreme in the State List
  • Parliament may legislate on a State List subject in the national interest if the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution (Article 249)
🧠

Strong Centre

  • Emergency, financial dependence and Governor powers give the Centre strength
  • Asymmetric provisions accommodate diversity
  • Tensions arise over President's Rule and grants
🌟

Linguistic states and diversity

  • Reorganisation on linguistic lines strengthened unity
  • Language and regional movements show diversity
  • Federalism accommodates multiple identities within one nation

lessons.title: Local Governments
yt: class 11 political science local governments panchayati raj 73rd 74th amendment

blocks.x: Local self-government is the government of villages and towns by locally elected bodies. It brings democracy closer to people, promotes participation and ensures local problems are solved locally. Gandhi stressed gram swaraj. After Independence, the Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957) recommended a three-tier Panchayati Raj; the first Panchayati Raj was launched at Nagaur in Rajasthan on 2 October 1959. The Ashok Mehta Committee (1977) recommended a two-tier system. The 73rd Amendment (1992, in force from 24 April 1993; National Panchayati Raj Day) added Part IX of the Constitution (Articles 243 to 243O) and the Eleventh Schedule with 29 subjects. The 74th Amendment (1992, in force from 1 June 1993) added Part IX-A (Articles 243P to 243ZG) and the Twelfth Schedule with 18 subjects for urban local bodies. Structure of Panchayati Raj: Gram Panchayat at the village level, Panchayat Samiti at the block level and Zila Parishad at the district level. The Gram Sabha consists of all adult voters of a village and is the foundation. Members are directly elected for a five-year term; if a body is dissolved, elections must be held within six months. One-third of seats (and offices) are reserved for women, and seats are reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in proportion to their population; many states have raised women reservation to 50 percent. A State Election Commission conducts elections and a State Finance Commission reviews finances every five years. Urban local bodies are Nagar Panchayat (transitional areas), Municipal Council (smaller urban areas) and Municipal Corporation (large cities). Ward committees and the Mayor or Chairperson lead them. The Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act, PESA, was passed in 1996 for tribal areas. Challenges: inadequate funds, dependence on state governments, bureaucratic control, limited powers (the 3 Fs: functions, funds, functionaries) and proxy rule by relatives of elected women (sarpanch-pati). Benefits: participation, accountability, development and empowerment of women and weaker sections. Social audit and the MGNREGA scheme (2005) are linked to Gram Sabhas. Panchayat committee work: planning for economic development and social justice.
Deep dive: Why local governments
They bring government closer, solve local problems and train leaders. They enable participation by weaker sections. Local needs differ and are best known locally.
Deep dive: 73rd and 74th Amendments
They made local bodies constitutional institutions with regular elections, reserved seats, finance commissions and defined powers. State laws determine details.
Deep dive: Working and challenges
Funds and staff remain with states. Gram Sabha meetings may be poorly attended. Women reservation improved representation but needs real empowerment.

Visual lesson

Local Governments

Local self-government is the government of villages and towns by locally elected bodies

🔑

Big idea

  • Local self-government is the government of villages and towns by locally elected bodies
  • It brings democracy closer to people, promotes participation and ensures local problems are solved locally
  • Gandhi stressed gram swaraj
  • After Independence, the Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957) recommended a three-tier Panchayati Raj
Read the full explanation

Local self-government is the government of villages and towns by locally elected bodies. It brings democracy closer to people, promotes participation and ensures local problems are solved locally. Gandhi stressed gram swaraj. After Independence, the Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957) recommended a three-tier Panchayati Raj; the first Panchayati Raj was launched at Nagaur in Rajasthan on 2 October 1959. The Ashok Mehta Committee (1977) recommended a two-tier system. The 73rd Amendment (1992, in force from 24 April 1993; National Panchayati Raj Day) added Part IX of the Constitution (Articles 243 to 243O) and the Eleventh Schedule with 29 subjects. The 74th Amendment (1992, in force from 1 June 1993) added Part IX-A (Articles 243P to 243ZG) and the Twelfth Schedule with 18 subjects for urban local bodies. Structure of Panchayati Raj: Gram Panchayat at the village level, Panchayat Samiti at the block level and Zila Parishad at the district level. The Gram Sabha consists of all adult voters of a village and is the foundation. Members are directly elected for a five-year term; if a body is dissolved, elections must be held within six months. One-third of seats (and offices) are reserved for women, and seats are reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in proportion to their population; many states have raised women reservation to 50 percent. A State Election Commission conducts elections and a State Finance Commission reviews finances every five years. Urban local bodies are Nagar Panchayat (transitional areas), Municipal Council (smaller urban areas) and Municipal Corporation (large cities). Ward committees and the Mayor or Chairperson lead them. The Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act, PESA, was passed in 1996 for tribal areas. Challenges: inadequate funds, dependence on state governments, bureaucratic control, limited powers (the 3 Fs: functions, funds, functionaries) and proxy rule by relatives of elected women (sarpanch-pati). Benefits: participation, accountability, development and empowerment of women and weaker sections. Social audit and the MGNREGA scheme (2005) are linked to Gram Sabhas. Panchayat committee work: planning for economic development and social justice.

🏛️

Why local governments

  • They bring government closer, solve local problems and train leaders
  • They enable participation by weaker sections
  • Local needs differ and are best known locally
🧠

73rd and 74th Amendments

  • They made local bodies constitutional institutions with regular elections, reserved seats, finance commissions and defined powers
  • State laws determine details
🚀

Working and challenges

  • Funds and staff remain with states
  • Gram Sabha meetings may be poorly attended
  • Women reservation improved representation but needs real empowerment
🧮

🎯 Remember 73rd = rural (Part IX, 29 subjects); 74th = urban (Part IX-A, 18 subjects).

lessons.title: Constitution as a Living Document
yt: class 11 political science constitution as a living document amendment basic structure

blocks.x: A living document adapts to changing needs while preserving basic values. The Indian Constitution has provision for its own amendment under Article 368. There are three methods: some provisions can be amended by a simple majority of Parliament (such as the formation of new states, citizenship, Rajya Sabha seats); most provisions need a special majority, which is a majority of the total membership of each House and at least two-thirds of members present and voting; and federal provisions (election of the President, the Union-state distribution of powers, the Supreme Court and High Courts, representation of states in Parliament) need a special majority plus ratification by at least half of the state legislatures. The President must give assent to an amendment bill. The Constitution was amended for the first time in 1951 (First Amendment, adding the Ninth Schedule and restrictions on freedom of speech). Important amendments: 7th (1956, reorganisation of states); 24th and 25th (1971); 42nd (1976, mini-constitution: added socialist, secular, integrity, fundamental duties); 44th (1978, removed the right to property as fundamental right); 52nd (1985, anti-defection); 61st (1988, voting age 18); 73rd and 74th (1992, local government); 86th (2002, right to education); 91st (2003, size of the council of ministers); 101st (2016, GST); 103rd (2019, 10 percent reservation for the economically weaker sections); 104th (2019); 106th (2023, women reservation). The basic structure doctrine: in Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala (1973) the Supreme Court held that Parliament can amend any part but cannot destroy the basic structure; earlier in Golaknath (1967) it had said Parliament cannot amend fundamental rights; Minerva Mills (1980) reaffirmed the basic structure; S R Bommai (1994) held secularism part of the basic structure and limited the use of Article 356. Basic features include supremacy of the Constitution, republican and democratic government, secularism, separation of powers, federalism, judicial review, free and fair elections and the rule of law. Amendments reflect political consensus, judicial interpretation and social change. The Constitution has stood the test of time because it is flexible but protects core values; some amendments were criticised, such as the 42nd and the 39th. The Constitution is also altered by judicial interpretation and conventions.
Deep dive: Amendment procedure
Simple majority for minor matters, special majority for most and ratification for federal provisions. Unlike some countries, no referendum is needed. State legislatures cannot initiate an amendment.
Deep dive: Basic structure
The doctrine limits Parliament's power. It protects democracy, rights and the rule of law from being destroyed by temporary majorities. The court decides what constitutes basic structure.
Deep dive: Change by interpretation
Courts expand meaning, as with Article 21. Conventions such as the PM being the Lok Sabha leader develop. Political practice, coalitions and judicial review shape the working of the Constitution.

Visual lesson

Constitution as a Living Document

A living document adapts to changing needs while preserving basic values

AmendmentArticle 368
Kesavananda1973
42nd1976
🔑

Big idea

  • A living document adapts to changing needs while preserving basic values
  • The Indian Constitution has provision for its own amendment under Article 368
  • There are three methods: some provisions can be amended by a simple majority of Parliament (such as the formation of new states, citizenship, Rajya…
  • Most provisions need a special majority, which is a majority of the total membership of each House and at least two-thirds of members present and…
Read the full explanation

A living document adapts to changing needs while preserving basic values. The Indian Constitution has provision for its own amendment under Article 368. There are three methods: some provisions can be amended by a simple majority of Parliament (such as the formation of new states, citizenship, Rajya Sabha seats); most provisions need a special majority, which is a majority of the total membership of each House and at least two-thirds of members present and voting; and federal provisions (election of the President, the Union-state distribution of powers, the Supreme Court and High Courts, representation of states in Parliament) need a special majority plus ratification by at least half of the state legislatures. The President must give assent to an amendment bill. The Constitution was amended for the first time in 1951 (First Amendment, adding the Ninth Schedule and restrictions on freedom of speech). Important amendments: 7th (1956, reorganisation of states); 24th and 25th (1971); 42nd (1976, mini-constitution: added socialist, secular, integrity, fundamental duties); 44th (1978, removed the right to property as fundamental right); 52nd (1985, anti-defection); 61st (1988, voting age 18); 73rd and 74th (1992, local government); 86th (2002, right to education); 91st (2003, size of the council of ministers); 101st (2016, GST); 103rd (2019, 10 percent reservation for the economically weaker sections); 104th (2019); 106th (2023, women reservation). The basic structure doctrine: in Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala (1973) the Supreme Court held that Parliament can amend any part but cannot destroy the basic structure; earlier in Golaknath (1967) it had said Parliament cannot amend fundamental rights; Minerva Mills (1980) reaffirmed the basic structure; S R Bommai (1994) held secularism part of the basic structure and limited the use of Article 356. Basic features include supremacy of the Constitution, republican and democratic government, secularism, separation of powers, federalism, judicial review, free and fair elections and the rule of law. Amendments reflect political consensus, judicial interpretation and social change. The Constitution has stood the test of time because it is flexible but protects core values; some amendments were criticised, such as the 42nd and the 39th. The Constitution is also altered by judicial interpretation and conventions.

🔄

Amendment procedure

  • Simple majority for minor matters, special majority for most and ratification for federal provisions
  • Unlike some countries, no referendum is needed
  • State legislatures cannot initiate an amendment
📘

Basic structure

  • The doctrine limits Parliament's power
  • It protects democracy, rights and the rule of law from being destroyed by temporary majorities
  • The court decides what constitutes basic structure
🌟

Change by interpretation

  • Courts expand meaning, as with Article 21
  • Conventions such as the PM being the Lok Sabha leader develop
  • Political practice, coalitions and judicial review shape the working of the Constitution

lessons.title: The Philosophy of the Constitution
yt: class 11 political science philosophy of the constitution liberty equality secularism

blocks.x: The philosophy of the Constitution means the vision and values behind it. The framers wanted to end colonial and social oppression and create a democratic society. The Preamble, drawn from the Objectives Resolution of Jawaharlal Nehru, expresses this vision: justice (social, economic and political), liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship, equality of status and of opportunity, and fraternity assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the nation. Key features of the philosophy: commitment to individual freedom and rights; social justice and the protection of the weaker sections through reservations and special provisions (Articles 15, 16, 17); respect for diversity and group rights, including minority educational rights (Articles 29 and 30); the Indian model of secularism in which the state keeps principled distance from all religions and intervenes to reform them, as with abolition of untouchability, rather than strict separation; universal franchise, giving every adult one vote regardless of caste, gender or wealth; federalism with a strong Centre and asymmetric provisions; a national identity based on unity in diversity; and procedural achievements such as the commitment to parliamentary democracy and constitutional government. Ambedkar insisted that political democracy must lead to social and economic democracy and warned about contradictions: one person one vote but one person one value was denied. Gandhi's influence is seen in the Directive Principles (village panchayats, prohibition, cottage industries). Nehru's influence is seen in the welfare state and secularism. Criticisms: it is unwieldy and too long; unrepresentative, because the Assembly was not elected by universal suffrage; and alien, borrowed from the West. Replies: the Constitution adapted ideas to the Indian context; it was framed after wide debate; borrowing is not a defect; and continuity with national movement ideas such as the Nehru Report (1928) and the Karachi Resolution (1931) shows it grew from the freedom struggle. The Constitution is a means for self-government and a social revolution. Ideas of dignity, equality and non-discrimination guide it. Constitutional morality means loyalty to constitutional values. The philosophy is also expressed in the Fundamental Duties and the Directive Principles.
Deep dive: Core values
Liberty, equality, justice and fraternity are central. The state protects rights but also promotes social change. Secular state means neither a state religion nor hostility to religion.
Deep dive: Balance
The Constitution balances individual rights with community values and group rights. It balances a strong Centre with state autonomy and political rights with social justice.
Deep dive: Criticisms and replies
Critics say it is a borrowed document. Defenders say it was rooted in the national movement. It has been creatively used by citizens and courts.

Visual lesson

The Philosophy of the Constitution

The philosophy of the Constitution means the vision and values behind it

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Core values›3Balance›4Criticisms and replies
Karachi Resolution1931
Nehru Report1928
🔑

Big idea

  • The philosophy of the Constitution means the vision and values behind it
  • The framers wanted to end colonial and social oppression and create a democratic society
  • The Preamble, drawn from the Objectives Resolution of Jawaharlal Nehru, expresses this vision: justice (social, economic and political), liberty of…
  • Key features of the philosophy: commitment to individual freedom and rights
Read the full explanation

The philosophy of the Constitution means the vision and values behind it. The framers wanted to end colonial and social oppression and create a democratic society. The Preamble, drawn from the Objectives Resolution of Jawaharlal Nehru, expresses this vision: justice (social, economic and political), liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship, equality of status and of opportunity, and fraternity assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the nation. Key features of the philosophy: commitment to individual freedom and rights; social justice and the protection of the weaker sections through reservations and special provisions (Articles 15, 16, 17); respect for diversity and group rights, including minority educational rights (Articles 29 and 30); the Indian model of secularism in which the state keeps principled distance from all religions and intervenes to reform them, as with abolition of untouchability, rather than strict separation; universal franchise, giving every adult one vote regardless of caste, gender or wealth; federalism with a strong Centre and asymmetric provisions; a national identity based on unity in diversity; and procedural achievements such as the commitment to parliamentary democracy and constitutional government. Ambedkar insisted that political democracy must lead to social and economic democracy and warned about contradictions: one person one vote but one person one value was denied. Gandhi's influence is seen in the Directive Principles (village panchayats, prohibition, cottage industries). Nehru's influence is seen in the welfare state and secularism. Criticisms: it is unwieldy and too long; unrepresentative, because the Assembly was not elected by universal suffrage; and alien, borrowed from the West. Replies: the Constitution adapted ideas to the Indian context; it was framed after wide debate; borrowing is not a defect; and continuity with national movement ideas such as the Nehru Report (1928) and the Karachi Resolution (1931) shows it grew from the freedom struggle. The Constitution is a means for self-government and a social revolution. Ideas of dignity, equality and non-discrimination guide it. Constitutional morality means loyalty to constitutional values. The philosophy is also expressed in the Fundamental Duties and the Directive Principles.

📌

Core values

  • Liberty, equality, justice and fraternity are central
  • The state protects rights but also promotes social change
  • Secular state means neither a state religion nor hostility to religion
🧠

Balance

  • The Constitution balances individual rights with community values and group rights
  • It balances a strong Centre with state autonomy and political rights with social justice
🌟

Criticisms and replies

  • Critics say it is a borrowed document
  • Defenders say it was rooted in the national movement
  • It has been creatively used by citizens and courts

lessons.title: Political Theory: An Introduction
yt: class 11 political science political theory an introduction politics why study

blocks.x: Politics is concerned with the collective decisions that affect society: how power is gained, used and shared, and how a community lives together. Aristotle called man a political animal. Political theory systematically thinks about the ideas and principles that shape constitutions, governments and social life, such as freedom, equality, justice, rights, citizenship, nationalism and secularism. The word theory comes from the Greek theoria, meaning to see; political theory asks what should be, as well as what is. Political theory is distinct from political science, which empirically studies institutions. It deals with the meaning of concepts, their justification and the critique of existing arrangements. Political theorists examine how political ideas apply in real life: for example, what freedom means when people are poor. Ancient thinkers include Plato (The Republic), Aristotle (Politics), and Kautilya (Arthashastra); modern thinkers include Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau, Mill and Marx. Political theory is not only academic: it grew from practical problems in the Indian national movement, the French Revolution and other struggles. Gandhi, Ambedkar, Tagore and Nehru produced political thought. Why study political theory? It helps citizens to develop reasoning, to question ideas, to participate in debates, to resolve conflicts and to understand the world. Political concepts such as liberty and equality are contested: their meaning differs by context. The study of political theory helps us to see that we are all part of political life, to value freedom of thought, and to defend good arguments. Theory should be balanced with reality; abstract ideas should be tested against experience. Key ideas: sovereignty, state, government, law, power and authority. Political theory also includes debates between schools such as liberalism, socialism, conservatism and feminism. Political theorists discuss both ends (values) and means (institutions). Techniques include logical reasoning, clarity of language and examples. A democratic society needs citizens who can argue reasonably and with tolerance. Political theory promotes critical thinking, including about gender, caste and class. Empirical study looks at what is; normative study at what ought to be.
Deep dive: What is politics
Politics deals with power and public life, not only elections. It is present in families, schools and nations when decisions affect others. Gandhi saw politics as service.
Deep dive: Political theory
It clarifies concepts and defends values. It questions assumptions and connects ideas to real problems. It uses reasoning and evidence.
Deep dive: Why study it
Studying theory builds citizenship, tolerance and critical thinking. It prepares one to take part in democracy and to resolve disputes through argument.

Political Theory: An Introduction

Politics is concerned with the collective decisions that affect society: how power is gained, used and shared, and how a community lives together

🔑

Big idea

  • Politics is concerned with the collective decisions that affect society: how power is gained, used and shared, and how a community lives together
  • Aristotle called man a political animal
  • Political theory systematically thinks about the ideas and principles that shape constitutions, governments and social life, such as freedom…

Read the full explanation

Politics is concerned with the collective decisions that affect society: how power is gained, used and shared, and how a community lives together. Aristotle called man a political animal. Political theory systematically thinks about the ideas and principles that shape constitutions, governments and social life, such as freedom, equality, justice, rights, citizenship, nationalism and secularism. The word theory comes from the Greek theoria, meaning to see; political theory asks what should be, as well as what is. Political theory is distinct from political science, which empirically studies institutions. It deals with the meaning of concepts, their justification and the critique of existing arrangements. Political theorists examine how political ideas apply in real life: for example, what freedom means when people are poor. Ancient thinkers include Plato (The Republic), Aristotle (Politics), and Kautilya (Arthashastra); modern thinkers include Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau, Mill and Marx. Political theory is not only academic: it grew from practical problems in the Indian national movement, the French Revolution and other struggles. Gandhi, Ambedkar, Tagore and Nehru produced political thought. Why study political theory? It helps citizens to develop reasoning, to question ideas, to participate in debates, to resolve conflicts and to understand the world. Political concepts such as liberty and equality are contested: their meaning differs by context. The study of political theory helps us to see that we are all part of political life, to value freedom of thought, and to defend good arguments. Theory should be balanced with reality; abstract ideas should be tested against experience. Key ideas: sovereignty, state, government, law, power and authority. Political theory also includes debates between schools such as liberalism, socialism, conservatism and feminism. Political theorists discuss both ends (values) and means (institutions). Techniques include logical reasoning, clarity of language and examples. A democratic society needs citizens who can argue reasonably and with tolerance. Political theory promotes critical thinking, including about gender, caste and class. Empirical study looks at what is; normative study at what ought to be.

  • It is present in families, schools and nations when decisions affect others

  • It questions assumptions and connects ideas to real problems
  • It uses reasoning and evidence

  • Studying theory builds citizenship, tolerance and critical thinking
  • It prepares one to take part in democracy and to resolve disputes through argument

lessons.title: Freedom
yt: class 11 political science freedom liberty negative positive harm principle

blocks.x: Freedom (liberty) is the absence of constraints and the ability to make choices and develop one's potential. Ideal of freedom was central in the national movement: Gandhi's Hind Swaraj (1909) distinguished swaraj as self-rule and self-mastery, and Tilak said that swaraj is my birthright. Freedom has two aspects: the absence of external constraints and the presence of conditions that enable development. Constraints may come from external force, from laws, from social structures such as caste, from poverty and from internalised ideas. Isaiah Berlin in Two Concepts of Liberty (1958) separated negative liberty (freedom from interference, the area in which a person is left alone) and positive liberty (freedom to develop and act, which needs conditions such as education and resources). Negative liberty asks how much area is free of interference; positive liberty asks whether people can be masters of their own lives. Some constraints are necessary: law restricts some freedoms to protect others. John Stuart Mill in On Liberty (1859) proposed the harm principle: the only reason for interfering with an individual is to prevent harm to others. He distinguished self-regarding actions (affecting only oneself, where there should be no interference) from other-regarding actions (affecting others, which can be regulated). Mill defended freedom of thought and expression because truth emerges from debate. Freedom of expression has limits (reasonable restrictions on speech under Article 19(2)): incitement to violence, defamation, public order. Freedom and the state: the state protects freedom but may also threaten it. Freedom and social groups: customs and caste can restrict freedom; women have faced restrictions. Freedom from fear was emphasised by Aung San Suu Kyi. Freedom of belief; the right to dissent; the importance of pluralism. Freedom of the press is part of freedom of expression. Positive freedom is advanced by policies of education and health. The Constitution protects freedom through Article 19 (speech, assembly, association, movement, residence, profession), Article 21 (life and liberty) and Article 25. Debates include banning books, censorship, hate speech and the right to protest. Freedom has costs and responsibilities. Reasonable limits are placed by the state, but must be justified. Freedom and equality are linked.
Deep dive: Meaning of freedom
Freedom means freedom from constraint and freedom to act. Constraints may be external or social. A free society allows diverse ways of life.
Deep dive: Negative and positive liberty
Negative liberty protects the private space. Positive liberty empowers people. Both are needed: a poor person may be legally free but unable to use freedom.
Deep dive: Harm principle and expression
Mill allowed limits only to prevent harm to others. Free expression helps truth and democracy. Debates continue about hate speech and censorship.

Visual lesson

Freedom

Freedom (liberty) is the absence of constraints and the ability to make choices and develop one's potential

🔑

Big idea

  • Freedom (liberty) is the absence of constraints and the ability to make choices and develop one's potential
  • Ideal of freedom was central in the national movement: Gandhi's Hind Swaraj (1909) distinguished swaraj as self-rule and self-mastery, and Tilak said…

Read the full explanation

Freedom (liberty) is the absence of constraints and the ability to make choices and develop one's potential. Ideal of freedom was central in the national movement: Gandhi's Hind Swaraj (1909) distinguished swaraj as self-rule and self-mastery, and Tilak said that swaraj is my birthright. Freedom has two aspects: the absence of external constraints and the presence of conditions that enable development. Constraints may come from external force, from laws, from social structures such as caste, from poverty and from internalised ideas. Isaiah Berlin in Two Concepts of Liberty (1958) separated negative liberty (freedom from interference, the area in which a person is left alone) and positive liberty (freedom to develop and act, which needs conditions such as education and resources). Negative liberty asks how much area is free of interference; positive liberty asks whether people can be masters of their own lives. Some constraints are necessary: law restricts some freedoms to protect others. John Stuart Mill in On Liberty (1859) proposed the harm principle: the only reason for interfering with an individual is to prevent harm to others. He distinguished self-regarding actions (affecting only oneself, where there should be no interference) from other-regarding actions (affecting others, which can be regulated). Mill defended freedom of thought and expression because truth emerges from debate. Freedom of expression has limits (reasonable restrictions on speech under Article 19(2)): incitement to violence, defamation, public order. Freedom and the state: the state protects freedom but may also threaten it. Freedom and social groups: customs and caste can restrict freedom; women have faced restrictions. Freedom from fear was emphasised by Aung San Suu Kyi. Freedom of belief; the right to dissent; the importance of pluralism. Freedom of the press is part of freedom of expression. Positive freedom is advanced by policies of education and health. The Constitution protects freedom through Article 19 (speech, assembly, association, movement, residence, profession), Article 21 (life and liberty) and Article 25. Debates include banning books, censorship, hate speech and the right to protest. Freedom has costs and responsibilities. Reasonable limits are placed by the state, but must be justified. Freedom and equality are linked.

📘

Meaning of freedom

  • Freedom means freedom from constraint and freedom to act
  • Constraints may be external or social
  • A free society allows diverse ways of life
🧠

Negative and positive liberty

  • Negative liberty protects the private space
  • Positive liberty empowers people
  • Both are needed: a poor person may be legally free but unable to use freedom
⚖️

Harm principle and expression

  • Mill allowed limits only to prevent harm to others
  • Free expression helps truth and democracy
  • Debates continue about hate speech and censorship

blocks.x: Equality means that all human beings have equal worth and should have equal opportunities to develop. It does not mean sameness; it means treating people as equals and removing unjust barriers. Importance: equality is a powerful moral and political ideal in the struggles against slavery, apartheid, caste and gender discrimination, as in the French Revolution slogan of liberty, equality, fraternity. Dimensions: political equality (equal citizenship, one person one vote, right to contest elections, freedom of expression), social equality (equal opportunities and facilities, access to healthcare, education and basic needs, abolition of caste and untouchability) and economic equality (reduction of gaps in wealth and income, class inequality). Natural inequalities arise from differences in talent and ability; social inequalities arise from differences in opportunity and status created by society, such as caste, class and gender. Formal equality means equal rights before law (Article 14); substantive equality needs special measures to remove disadvantages. Equality of opportunity gives everyone a fair start; equality of outcome aims at equal results; these can conflict. Affirmative action or positive discrimination includes reservations for SC, ST and OBC in India (Articles 15(4), 16(4)) to correct historical injustice. The Indian Constitution guarantees equality before the law (Article 14), prohibits discrimination (Article 15), ensures equal opportunity in public employment (Article 16), abolishes untouchability (Article 17) and titles (Article 18); the Directive Principles require equal pay for equal work (Article 39). Perspectives: Liberals support equality of opportunity and a minimum standard of living; Marxists see class inequality arising from private ownership of the means of production and advocate economic equality (Marx and Engels); Feminists point to gender inequality and patriarchy (the private-public divide); Egalitarians such as Rousseau noted that inequality arises from society. Rawls argued that inequalities are acceptable only if they benefit the least advantaged. Ambedkar fought caste inequality. Universal adult franchise gave political equality in 1950. Issues: wealth concentration, wage gaps between men and women, access to education, and the debate over reservation. Equality and liberty complement each other. Social movements (Dalit, women, tribal) demand equality. Equality means equal respect for the dignity of all.
Deep dive: What equality means
Equality is about equal moral worth. It does not remove all differences. Unequal treatment may be justified only where it corrects disadvantage.
Deep dive: Dimensions and types
Political, social and economic equality interact. Formal equality is not enough where starting points differ. Affirmative action corrects past discrimination.
Deep dive: Perspectives
Liberals, Marxists and feminists approach equality differently. Rawls links equality to fairness. Debates concern how far the state should intervene.
Hindi saransh
Samanta: avsar ki samanta aur parinam ki samanta; rajnitik, samajik aur aarthik samanta; Anuchhed 14-18.

Equality means that all human beings have equal worth and should have equal opportunities to develop. It does not mean sameness; it means treating people as equals and removing unjust barriers. Importance: equality is a powerful moral and political ideal in the struggles against slavery, apartheid, caste and gender discrimination, as in the French Revolution slogan of liberty, equality, fraternity. Dimensions: political equality (equal citizenship, one person one vote, right to contest elections, freedom of expression), social equality (equal opportunities and facilities, access to healthcare, education and basic needs, abolition of caste and untouchability) and economic equality (reduction of gaps in wealth and income, class inequality). Natural inequalities arise from differences in talent and ability; social inequalities arise from differences in opportunity and status created by society, such as caste, class and gender. Formal equality means equal rights before law (Article 14); substantive equality needs special measures to remove disadvantages. Equality of opportunity gives everyone a fair start; equality of outcome aims at equal results; these can conflict. Affirmative action or positive discrimination includes reservations for SC, ST and OBC in India (Articles 15(4), 16(4)) to correct historical injustice. The Indian Constitution guarantees equality before the law (Article 14), prohibits discrimination (Article 15), ensures equal opportunity in public employment (Article 16), abolishes untouchability (Article 17) and titles (Article 18); the Directive Principles require equal pay for equal work (Article 39). Perspectives: Liberals support equality of opportunity and a minimum standard of living; Marxists see class inequality arising from private ownership of the means of production and advocate economic equality (Marx and Engels); Feminists point to gender inequality and patriarchy (the private-public divide); Egalitarians such as Rousseau noted that inequality arises from society. Rawls argued that inequalities are acceptable only if they benefit the least advantaged. Ambedkar fought caste inequality. Universal adult franchise gave political equality in 1950. Issues: wealth concentration, wage gaps between men and women, access to education, and the debate over reservation. Equality and liberty complement each other. Social movements (Dalit, women, tribal) demand equality. Equality means equal respect for the dignity of all.

📌

What equality means

  • Equality is about equal moral worth
  • It does not remove all differences
  • Unequal treatment may be justified only where it corrects disadvantage
🧠

Dimensions and types

  • Political, social and economic equality interact
  • Formal equality is not enough where starting points differ
  • Affirmative action corrects past discrimination
🌟

Perspectives

  • Liberals, Marxists and feminists approach equality differently
  • Rawls links equality to fairness
  • Debates concern how far the state should intervene
