  • Theories: instinct theory (behaviour driven by innate tendencies), drive-reduction theory (Clark Hull
Read the full explanation

Motivation is the force that energises and directs behaviour toward a goal. It involves needs (a lack or deficit), drives (internal states that push to satisfy needs) and incentives (external objects or goals that attract). Types of motives: biological motives (hunger, thirst, sleep, sex, avoidance of pain) and psychosocial motives (achievement, affiliation, power, curiosity). Theories: instinct theory (behaviour driven by innate tendencies), drive-reduction theory (Clark Hull; behaviour reduces tension), arousal theory (optimal level of arousal; Yerkes-Dodson law) and incentive theory. Maslow's hierarchy of needs places needs in a pyramid: physiological, safety, love and belongingness, esteem and self-actualisation; lower needs must be satisfied before higher ones; the first four are deficiency needs and self-actualisation is a growth need. Hunger: controlled by the hypothalamus (lateral hypothalamus starts eating; ventromedial hypothalamus stops it), blood glucose level and stomach contractions. Thirst is regulated by water balance. Achievement motivation (David McClelland): need for achievement (n-Ach) is the desire to excel; people with high n-Ach set moderately difficult goals, seek feedback and take personal responsibility. Affiliation and power are other needs. Intrinsic motivation (internal satisfaction) versus extrinsic motivation (rewards). Conflicts of motives: approach-approach, avoidance-avoidance and approach-avoidance. Emotion is a complex state with physiological arousal, subjective feeling and expressive behaviour. Components: cognitive, physiological and behavioural. Theories: James-Lange (bodily arousal comes first and the emotion follows), Cannon-Bard (arousal and emotion occur simultaneously through the thalamus), Schachter-Singer two-factor theory (arousal plus cognitive label) and Lazarus's cognitive appraisal theory. The limbic system, especially the amygdala, is central to emotions such as fear. Basic emotions (Paul Ekman): happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise and disgust, recognised universally through facial expressions. Cultural display rules govern how emotions are expressed. Emotional intelligence (Salovey and Mayer; popularised by Daniel Goleman) is the ability to perceive, understand and regulate emotions in oneself and others; it includes self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy and social skills. Managing negative emotions: relaxation, cognitive reappraisal, positive thinking, social support, exercise and yoga. Stress, anxiety and anger affect health. Positive emotions help well-being. Emotions and motivation are linked. Lie detectors (polygraph) measure physiological arousal.

📌

Motivation

  • Motives arise from needs and are directed by incentives
  • Biological motives support survival
  • Psychosocial motives are learned
  • Maslow's hierarchy arranges them by priority
🚀

Emotion

  • Emotions combine arousal, feeling and expression
  • The theories differ on the order of arousal and emotion
  • Culture shapes display rules
🚀

Emotional intelligence

  • Emotional intelligence helps in relationships and success
  • Skills can be developed
  • Managing negative emotions protects health

blocks.x: Sociology is the systematic study of human society and social behaviour. The word comes from the Latin socius (companion) and the Greek logos (study); it was coined by Auguste Comte in 1838. Sociology emerged in Europe from the Enlightenment, the Industrial Revolution and the French Revolution, which created questions about social order and change. Founders: Auguste Comte (the father of sociology, positivism), Emile Durkheim (suicide, division of labour, social facts), Karl Marx (class conflict) and Max Weber (verstehen, ideal types). C Wright Mills introduced the sociological imagination, the ability to link personal troubles with public issues and to see the interplay of biography and history. Personal troubles are private matters felt by the individual, whereas public issues are matters of social structure; for example, unemployment of one person is a personal trouble but mass unemployment is a public issue. Sociology and common sense differ: sociology uses systematic evidence and methods, whereas common sense is based on unexamined belief. Sociology differs from other social sciences: economics studies production and consumption, political science studies power and the state, psychology studies the individual mind, history studies the past, and anthropology studies cultures and early societies; sociology studies society as a whole and interactions between its parts. Scope of sociology: the study of institutions such as family, religion, education and economy, as well as groups, class and change. Sociology in India: it began in Bombay University in 1919 with Patrick Geddes, then Lucknow (G S Ghurye, D P Mukerji, A K Saran) and Delhi (M N Srinivas). Indian sociology was shaped by colonial rule, British social anthropology and nationalism. Key Indian terms: caste, family, village studies and tribe. Sociology applies to careers in social work, research, teaching, policy and administration. Sociology is a science of society but is not like natural science because human beings have consciousness and meanings. Perspectives: functionalism, conflict and interactionism. Micro sociology studies small-scale interaction and macro sociology studies large structures. Pure sociology builds knowledge while applied sociology solves problems. Sociology promotes critical and objective understanding, making the familiar strange.

Sociology emerged in Europe in response to rapid changes. Comte named it. Durkheim, Marx and Weber shaped its main traditions.
Deep dive: Sociological imagination
Mills asks us to connect private troubles with public issues. This lets us see that individual lives are shaped by social forces.
Deep dive: Sociology in India
Indian sociology developed from universities in Bombay, Lucknow and Delhi. Scholars studied caste, tribe, village and family.

blocks.x: Society is a system of social relationships; a web of interactions among individuals and groups. Sociology treats the individual and society as interlinked. Individuals are born into groups: a social group is a collection of people who interact regularly and share a sense of belonging. Types: primary groups (face-to-face, close and personal; family, friends; Charles Cooley) and secondary groups (large, impersonal, goal-oriented; school, office, political party); in-groups (we) and out-groups (they); reference groups (those whose standards we use to judge ourselves); peer groups. Quasi-groups are aggregates without structure, such as a crowd or a queue. Social stratification is the hierarchy of groups in society by power, prestige and wealth, as in caste, class, estate and slavery. Status is a socially defined position; ascribed status is assigned at birth (caste, sex, race) and achieved status is earned (doctor, teacher). A person holds many statuses (status set). Role is the behaviour expected of the person who holds a status; role conflict arises when roles of different statuses clash and role strain arises within one role. Social norms are rules of behaviour: folkways (customs), mores (strong moral norms) and laws. Values are shared ideas of what is good. Sanctions reward conformity (positive) or punish deviance (negative); formal and informal sanctions. Social control maintains order through agencies such as family, religion and law. Culture and social structure: structure refers to patterned relationships among the parts of society. Social interaction involves cooperation, competition and conflict. Cooperation is working together for a common goal; competition is striving for the same limited goal in a rule-bound way; conflict is a struggle to win or dominate and may involve violence; accommodation is a temporary adjustment; assimilation is merging of cultures. Social inequality takes forms of class, caste, gender and race. Karl Marx saw classes as groups defined by ownership of means of production (bourgeoisie and proletariat); Weber added status and party to class. Society and the individual: Durkheim stressed that social facts are external to and coercive of individuals. Social order and change. Types of society: hunting and gathering, pastoral, agrarian, industrial and post-industrial. The social contract, marketplace and community are older ideas. Groups can be formal (organised rules) or informal. Group size, membership and boundaries define groups.
Deep dive: Groups
Primary groups are small and intimate; secondary groups are large and goal-oriented. Reference groups shape aspirations. In-group and out-group distinctions create boundaries.
Deep dive: Status and role
Status is a position and role is the expected behaviour. Ascribed status is given; achieved status is earned. Role conflict and role strain create stress.
Deep dive: Interaction and inequality
Cooperation, competition and conflict are social processes. Stratification ranks groups. Marx and Weber explain class differently.

lessons.title: Social Institutions: Continuity and Change
yt: class 11 sociology social institutions family marriage kinship religion economy politics education

blocks.x: Social institutions are established and organised sets of norms and roles that meet basic social needs. Main institutions: family, marriage, kinship, economy, polity, education and religion. Family is a group of persons related by blood, marriage or adoption who live together and cooperate economically. Types by structure: nuclear (parents and children) and joint or extended (several generations). Types by authority: patriarchal (male authority) and matriarchal (female authority; as among the Khasis of Meghalaya). Types by residence: patrilocal (living with the husband's family), matrilocal (with the wife's) and neolocal. Types by descent: patrilineal and matrilineal. Changes in the family: industrialisation, urbanisation, education and women's employment lead to nuclear families, smaller size, and changing roles. Marriage is a socially approved union between two persons. Forms: monogamy (one spouse), polygamy (polygyny: many wives; polyandry: many husbands, as among the Todas). Endogamy is marriage within a group (caste) and exogamy is marriage outside a group (gotra). Hypergamy and hypogamy refer to marriage into a higher or lower group. Practices: dowry, child marriage, bride price. Kinship is the web of relationships through blood (consanguineal) and marriage (affinal). Descent groups and kin terms. Economy: types of economy: hunting-gathering, agricultural, industrial; capitalism, socialism and mixed economy. Karl Marx described modes of production. The jajmani system is a traditional exchange of goods and services between castes in villages. Globalisation and liberalisation have changed work. Gender division of labour. Politics: power is the ability to carry out one's will despite resistance (Weber); authority is legitimate power. Weber's types of authority: traditional, legal-rational and charismatic. State is a political institution with territory, government and sovereignty. Democracy, monarchy and dictatorship. Education: formal and informal; socialisation, selection and social mobility; the role of the school in transmitting culture. Inequalities in education by caste, class and gender; the Right to Education Act, 2009 provides free and compulsory education for ages 6 to 14. Religion: Durkheim defined religion as a unified system of beliefs and practices relative to sacred things; the sacred and the profane. Functions: social solidarity and meaning. Secularisation reduces the influence of religion. Communalism is use of religious identity for political aims. Religion in India is diverse. Continuity and change run together in institutions.
Deep dive: Family and marriage
Family forms vary by structure, authority, residence and descent. Marriage rules include endogamy and exogamy. Industrialisation and education have changed family patterns.
Deep dive: Economy and politics
Economy organises production and distribution. Politics concerns power and authority. Weber described three types of authority.
Deep dive: Education and religion
Education socialises and sorts. Religion creates solidarity and meaning. Secularisation and communalism are modern issues.

Visual lesson

Social Institutions: Continuity and Change

Social institutions are established and organised sets of norms and roles that meet basic social needs

formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Family and marriage›3Economy and politics›4Education and religion
Weber3 authority
RTE2009
🔑

Big idea

  • Social institutions are established and organised sets of norms and roles that meet basic social needs
  • Main institutions: family, marriage, kinship, economy, polity, education and religion
  • Family is a group of persons related by blood, marriage or adoption who live together and cooperate economically
  • Types by structure: nuclear (parents and children) and joint or extended (several generations)
Read the full explanation

Social institutions are established and organised sets of norms and roles that meet basic social needs. Main institutions: family, marriage, kinship, economy, polity, education and religion. Family is a group of persons related by blood, marriage or adoption who live together and cooperate economically. Types by structure: nuclear (parents and children) and joint or extended (several generations). Types by authority: patriarchal (male authority) and matriarchal (female authority; as among the Khasis of Meghalaya). Types by residence: patrilocal (living with the husband's family), matrilocal (with the wife's) and neolocal. Types by descent: patrilineal and matrilineal. Changes in the family: industrialisation, urbanisation, education and women's employment lead to nuclear families, smaller size, and changing roles. Marriage is a socially approved union between two persons. Forms: monogamy (one spouse), polygamy (polygyny: many wives; polyandry: many husbands, as among the Todas). Endogamy is marriage within a group (caste) and exogamy is marriage outside a group (gotra). Hypergamy and hypogamy refer to marriage into a higher or lower group. Practices: dowry, child marriage, bride price. Kinship is the web of relationships through blood (consanguineal) and marriage (affinal). Descent groups and kin terms. Economy: types of economy: hunting-gathering, agricultural, industrial; capitalism, socialism and mixed economy. Karl Marx described modes of production. The jajmani system is a traditional exchange of goods and services between castes in villages. Globalisation and liberalisation have changed work. Gender division of labour. Politics: power is the ability to carry out one's will despite resistance (Weber); authority is legitimate power. Weber's types of authority: traditional, legal-rational and charismatic. State is a political institution with territory, government and sovereignty. Democracy, monarchy and dictatorship. Education: formal and informal; socialisation, selection and social mobility; the role of the school in transmitting culture. Inequalities in education by caste, class and gender; the Right to Education Act, 2009 provides free and compulsory education for ages 6 to 14. Religion: Durkheim defined religion as a unified system of beliefs and practices relative to sacred things; the sacred and the profane. Functions: social solidarity and meaning. Secularisation reduces the influence of religion. Communalism is use of religious identity for political aims. Religion in India is diverse. Continuity and change run together in institutions.

📌

Family and marriage

  • Family forms vary by structure, authority, residence and descent
  • Marriage rules include endogamy and exogamy
  • Industrialisation and education have changed family patterns
🏛️

Economy and politics

  • Economy organises production and distribution
  • Politics concerns power and authority
  • Weber described three types of authority
🌟

Education and religion

  • Education socialises and sorts
  • Religion creates solidarity and meaning
  • Secularisation and communalism are modern issues

lessons.title: Culture and Socialisation
yt: class 11 sociology culture socialisation norms values agencies cooley mead

blocks.x: Culture is the whole way of life of a society: its knowledge, beliefs, art, morals, laws, customs and habits acquired by members as part of society (E B Tylor). Dimensions: the cognitive (knowledge and ideas), the normative (rules and values) and the material (tools, clothing, buildings). Material culture consists of physical objects; non-material culture consists of ideas, beliefs and values. Cultural lag (William Ogburn) refers to the delay of non-material culture in adjusting to changes in material culture. Cultural diversity: subcultures (youth culture, regional culture) and countercultures. Ethnocentrism is judging other cultures by the standards of one's own and considering them inferior; cultural relativism is understanding a culture in its own terms. Cosmopolitanism welcomes cultural difference. Cultural change occurs through innovation, diffusion and contact. Sanskritisation is a process by which lower castes imitate the practices of higher castes (M N Srinivas); Westernisation is the adoption of Western ways. Socialisation is the process by which individuals learn the culture, norms and values of society and develop a sense of self. Primary socialisation occurs in childhood within the family; secondary socialisation occurs later in school, peers and the workplace. Anticipatory socialisation prepares for future roles; resocialisation involves new norms (as in prison or army). Agents of socialisation: family, peer group, school, mass media, religion and workplace. Gender socialisation teaches gender roles. Theories of self: Charles Cooley's looking-glass self (we see ourselves as others see us), George Herbert Mead's stages of the self (preparatory, play, game stage; the I and the me; the generalised other) and Freud's id, ego and superego. Feral children such as Kamala and Amala show the importance of socialisation. Socialisation and individuality: both nature and nurture shape the person. Conformity and deviance. Sociologists view socialisation as a lifelong process. Mass media like television and the internet influence values. Culture and identity: language, symbols and rituals. Sociology studies how culture is transmitted across generations. Popular culture and consumer culture are modern forms. Cultural globalisation spreads global brands and ideas.
Deep dive: Culture
Culture includes knowledge, norms and material objects. Cultural lag appears when ideas lag behind technology. Sanskritisation and Westernisation are Indian processes of change.
Deep dive: Socialisation
Socialisation turns the child into a social being. The family is the main agent in childhood; peers, school and media follow.
Deep dive: Self
Cooley and Mead explain how the self develops through interaction with others. The generalised other represents society's expectations.

Visual lesson

Culture and Socialisation

Culture is the whole way of life of a society: its knowledge, beliefs, art, morals, laws, customs and habits acquired by members as part of society (E B Tylor)

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Culture›3Socialisation›4Self
🔑

Big idea

  • Culture is the whole way of life of a society: its knowledge, beliefs, art, morals, laws, customs and habits acquired by members as part of society…
  • Dimensions: the cognitive (knowledge and ideas), the normative (rules and values) and the material (tools, clothing, buildings)
  • Material culture consists of physical objects
  • Non-material culture consists of ideas, beliefs and values
Read the full explanation

Culture is the whole way of life of a society: its knowledge, beliefs, art, morals, laws, customs and habits acquired by members as part of society (E B Tylor). Dimensions: the cognitive (knowledge and ideas), the normative (rules and values) and the material (tools, clothing, buildings). Material culture consists of physical objects; non-material culture consists of ideas, beliefs and values. Cultural lag (William Ogburn) refers to the delay of non-material culture in adjusting to changes in material culture. Cultural diversity: subcultures (youth culture, regional culture) and countercultures. Ethnocentrism is judging other cultures by the standards of one's own and considering them inferior; cultural relativism is understanding a culture in its own terms. Cosmopolitanism welcomes cultural difference. Cultural change occurs through innovation, diffusion and contact. Sanskritisation is a process by which lower castes imitate the practices of higher castes (M N Srinivas); Westernisation is the adoption of Western ways. Socialisation is the process by which individuals learn the culture, norms and values of society and develop a sense of self. Primary socialisation occurs in childhood within the family; secondary socialisation occurs later in school, peers and the workplace. Anticipatory socialisation prepares for future roles; resocialisation involves new norms (as in prison or army). Agents of socialisation: family, peer group, school, mass media, religion and workplace. Gender socialisation teaches gender roles. Theories of self: Charles Cooley's looking-glass self (we see ourselves as others see us), George Herbert Mead's stages of the self (preparatory, play, game stage; the I and the me; the generalised other) and Freud's id, ego and superego. Feral children such as Kamala and Amala show the importance of socialisation. Socialisation and individuality: both nature and nurture shape the person. Conformity and deviance. Sociologists view socialisation as a lifelong process. Mass media like television and the internet influence values. Culture and identity: language, symbols and rituals. Sociology studies how culture is transmitted across generations. Popular culture and consumer culture are modern forms. Cultural globalisation spreads global brands and ideas.

📌

Culture

  • Culture includes knowledge, norms and material objects
  • Cultural lag appears when ideas lag behind technology
  • Sanskritisation and Westernisation are Indian processes of change
🧠

Socialisation

  • Socialisation turns the child into a social being
  • The family is the main agent in childhood
  • Peers, school and media follow
🌟

Self

  • Cooley and Mead explain how the self develops through interaction with others
  • The generalised other represents society's expectations

lessons.title: Doing Sociology: Research Methods
yt: class 11 sociology research methods survey observation interview objectivity

blocks.x: Sociological research uses systematic methods to study society. Research can be quantitative (numbers, statistics) or qualitative (meanings, descriptions). Challenges: subjectivity, objectivity and reflexivity. Objectivity means studying without personal bias; Max Weber said sociologists should be value-neutral but aware of values; Durkheim argued for studying social facts like things. Subjectivity involves personal views and beliefs. Reflexivity means reflecting on one's own role in research. Insider and outsider perspectives; participants may behave differently when observed. Methods: survey, interview, observation, case study and use of secondary sources. Survey: collects data from a large number of people, often by a questionnaire, from a sample drawn from the population. Sampling: random, stratified and quota sampling; a representative sample reflects the population. Interview: a face-to-face conversation; structured (fixed questions), unstructured and semi-structured; advantages are depth and flexibility, disadvantages include time and interviewer bias. Observation: participant observation (researcher joins the group; used by anthropologists and in village studies) and non-participant observation. Advantage: rich, in-depth information; disadvantage: time-consuming and subjective. Questionnaire: written set of questions, open or closed. Case study: intensive study of a single case. Use of secondary sources: census, official records, newspapers and documents. Steps of research: choosing a problem, framing hypotheses, selecting a method, collecting data, analysis and reporting. Triangulation combines methods. A pilot study tests the method before the main study. Ethics: informed consent, confidentiality and avoiding harm. Questions of Indian sociology: village studies by M N Srinivas (Rampura) used participant observation. Census of India is a large secondary source. Benefits and limits of each method: surveys are broad but shallow; observation is deep but limited. Choice of method depends on the research question. Sociological research can lead to policy, but needs care to avoid stereotypes. Reliability and validity apply. Measurement and variables: a variable is a characteristic that varies; a hypothesis is a testable statement; a universe is the whole population. Fieldwork is research in natural settings.
Deep dive: Objectivity
Sociologists strive to be objective but know values affect research. Reflexivity helps them see their own influence. Weber advised value neutrality.
Deep dive: Methods
Surveys give breadth; observation and interviews give depth. Sampling makes surveys feasible. Triangulation increases confidence.
Deep dive: Ethics
Researchers must protect participants through consent and confidentiality. Fieldwork requires sensitivity.
Hindi saransh
Samajshastriya anusandhan: sarvekshan, sakshatkar, nirikshan, nidarshan aur vastunishthata; Srinivas ka Rampura adhyayan.
Remember: participant observation = researcher joins the group.

Visual lesson

Doing Sociology: Research Methods

Sociological research uses systematic methods to study society

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Objectivity›3Methods›4Ethics
🔑

Big idea

  • Sociological research uses systematic methods to study society
  • Research can be quantitative (numbers, statistics) or qualitative (meanings, descriptions)
  • Challenges: subjectivity, objectivity and reflexivity
  • Objectivity means studying without personal bias
Read the full explanation

Sociological research uses systematic methods to study society. Research can be quantitative (numbers, statistics) or qualitative (meanings, descriptions). Challenges: subjectivity, objectivity and reflexivity. Objectivity means studying without personal bias; Max Weber said sociologists should be value-neutral but aware of values; Durkheim argued for studying social facts like things. Subjectivity involves personal views and beliefs. Reflexivity means reflecting on one's own role in research. Insider and outsider perspectives; participants may behave differently when observed. Methods: survey, interview, observation, case study and use of secondary sources. Survey: collects data from a large number of people, often by a questionnaire, from a sample drawn from the population. Sampling: random, stratified and quota sampling; a representative sample reflects the population. Interview: a face-to-face conversation; structured (fixed questions), unstructured and semi-structured; advantages are depth and flexibility, disadvantages include time and interviewer bias. Observation: participant observation (researcher joins the group; used by anthropologists and in village studies) and non-participant observation. Advantage: rich, in-depth information; disadvantage: time-consuming and subjective. Questionnaire: written set of questions, open or closed. Case study: intensive study of a single case. Use of secondary sources: census, official records, newspapers and documents. Steps of research: choosing a problem, framing hypotheses, selecting a method, collecting data, analysis and reporting. Triangulation combines methods. A pilot study tests the method before the main study. Ethics: informed consent, confidentiality and avoiding harm. Questions of Indian sociology: village studies by M N Srinivas (Rampura) used participant observation. Census of India is a large secondary source. Benefits and limits of each method: surveys are broad but shallow; observation is deep but limited. Choice of method depends on the research question. Sociological research can lead to policy, but needs care to avoid stereotypes. Reliability and validity apply. Measurement and variables: a variable is a characteristic that varies; a hypothesis is a testable statement; a universe is the whole population. Fieldwork is research in natural settings.

📌

Objectivity

  • Sociologists strive to be objective but know values affect research
  • Reflexivity helps them see their own influence
  • Weber advised value neutrality
🔄

Methods

  • Surveys give breadth
  • Observation and interviews give depth
  • Sampling makes surveys feasible
  • Triangulation increases confidence
🌟

Ethics

  • Researchers must protect participants through consent and confidentiality
  • Fieldwork requires sensitivity

lessons.title: Social Structure, Stratification and Social Processes
yt: class 11 sociology social structure stratification caste class gender social control

blocks.x: Social structure is the pattern of relationships among individuals, groups and institutions in society. Social stratification is the ranking of groups in a hierarchy of power, prestige and wealth. It is persistent over generations, universal but variable, social (not biological), and supported by ideas. Forms: slavery, estate, caste and class. Theories: functionalist (Davis and Moore: stratification is necessary to fill important roles), Marxist (class conflict) and Weberian (class, status and party). Caste: a hereditary, endogamous, occupation-based, ranked system in India; features include hierarchy, restrictions on food and social contact, purity and pollution, and rules of marriage; the four varnas are Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and Shudras, with Dalits (outcastes or Scheduled Castes) outside. Colonial rule changed caste through censuses. Caste today: sanskritisation, dominant caste, caste associations, politics and reservations. Untouchability was abolished by Article 17 of the Constitution. Class: groups based on economic position (Marx: owners and workers). Tribe: community linked to territory, with a common culture, often called Adivasi; tribal issues include land alienation and displacement. Gender: socially constructed roles of men and women, distinct from sex; patriarchy is male dominance; women's movement for equality; sex ratio and gender gaps. Social inequality in India includes disability and discrimination. Affirmative action: reservations for SC, ST and OBC (Mandal Commission, 1990 implementation) and for women in local bodies. Prejudice is a pre-formed negative attitude and discrimination is unfair action; stereotype is a fixed image. Social exclusion denies groups full participation. Social mobility: vertical (up or down) and horizontal; open and closed systems; intergenerational and intragenerational. Social control: formal (law, police, courts) and informal (family, religion, gossip) means. Deviance is behaviour violating norms; Durkheim and Merton (strain theory) explained it. Crime is deviance punished by law. Conformity versus deviance. Social order is maintained by control. Social processes: cooperation, competition, conflict. Karl Marx said conflict drives change. Social inequality is also found in race and religion. The Indian state works through laws such as the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 and the SC and ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989. Social movements for equality include those of B R Ambedkar, Jyotiba Phule and Periyar.
Deep dive: Stratification
Societies rank groups by power, prestige and wealth. Closed systems like caste limit mobility; open systems like class allow it. Theories explain it as necessary or as exploitative.
Deep dive: Caste, tribe and gender
Caste involves hierarchy, purity and endogamy. Tribes have faced displacement. Gender is socially constructed and patriarchy shapes inequality.
Deep dive: Control and deviance
Social control maintains order. Deviance breaks norms. Merton's strain theory links deviance to a gap between goals and means.
Hindi saransh
Samajik sanrachana aur starikaran: jati, varg, janjati, ling; samajik niyantran aur vichalan; Ambedkar, Phule aur Periyar ke andolan.
Remember: caste is ascribed and closed; class is achieved and open.

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Social Structure, Stratification and Social Processes

Social structure is the pattern of relationships among individuals, groups and institutions in society

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Stratification›3Caste, tribe and gender›4Control and deviance
PCR Act1955
🔑

Big idea

  • Social structure is the pattern of relationships among individuals, groups and institutions in society
  • Social stratification is the ranking of groups in a hierarchy of power, prestige and wealth
  • It is persistent over generations, universal but variable, social (not biological), and supported by ideas
  • Forms: slavery, estate, caste and class
Read the full explanation

Social structure is the pattern of relationships among individuals, groups and institutions in society. Social stratification is the ranking of groups in a hierarchy of power, prestige and wealth. It is persistent over generations, universal but variable, social (not biological), and supported by ideas. Forms: slavery, estate, caste and class. Theories: functionalist (Davis and Moore: stratification is necessary to fill important roles), Marxist (class conflict) and Weberian (class, status and party). Caste: a hereditary, endogamous, occupation-based, ranked system in India; features include hierarchy, restrictions on food and social contact, purity and pollution, and rules of marriage; the four varnas are Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and Shudras, with Dalits (outcastes or Scheduled Castes) outside. Colonial rule changed caste through censuses. Caste today: sanskritisation, dominant caste, caste associations, politics and reservations. Untouchability was abolished by Article 17 of the Constitution. Class: groups based on economic position (Marx: owners and workers). Tribe: community linked to territory, with a common culture, often called Adivasi; tribal issues include land alienation and displacement. Gender: socially constructed roles of men and women, distinct from sex; patriarchy is male dominance; women's movement for equality; sex ratio and gender gaps. Social inequality in India includes disability and discrimination. Affirmative action: reservations for SC, ST and OBC (Mandal Commission, 1990 implementation) and for women in local bodies. Prejudice is a pre-formed negative attitude and discrimination is unfair action; stereotype is a fixed image. Social exclusion denies groups full participation. Social mobility: vertical (up or down) and horizontal; open and closed systems; intergenerational and intragenerational. Social control: formal (law, police, courts) and informal (family, religion, gossip) means. Deviance is behaviour violating norms; Durkheim and Merton (strain theory) explained it. Crime is deviance punished by law. Conformity versus deviance. Social order is maintained by control. Social processes: cooperation, competition, conflict. Karl Marx said conflict drives change. Social inequality is also found in race and religion. The Indian state works through laws such as the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 and the SC and ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989. Social movements for equality include those of B R Ambedkar, Jyotiba Phule and Periyar.

📌

Stratification

  • Societies rank groups by power, prestige and wealth
  • Closed systems like caste limit mobility
  • Open systems like class allow it
  • Theories explain it as necessary or as exploitative
🧠

Caste, tribe and gender

  • Caste involves hierarchy, purity and endogamy
  • Tribes have faced displacement
  • Gender is socially constructed and patriarchy shapes inequality
🌟

Control and deviance

  • Social control maintains order
  • Deviance breaks norms
  • Merton's strain theory links deviance to a gap between goals and means
🧮

lessons.title: Social Change and Social Order in Rural and Urban Society
yt: class 11 sociology social change rural urban agrarian structure urbanisation migration

blocks.x: Social change is the alteration in social structure, institutions and relationships over time. Types: evolutionary and revolutionary; short-term and long-term. Causes: ecological, economic (Marx), political, cultural (Weber's Protestant ethic), technology and ideas. Social order is maintained by social control. Rural society: in India about 65 percent of the population lives in villages (2011 Census). Agrarian structure: land ownership, tenancy and labour. Rural classes: landlords, tenants, small farmers and landless labourers. Caste and land are linked. Land reforms: abolition of zamindari (intermediaries), tenancy reforms, land ceilings and consolidation. The Green Revolution (1960s) used high-yielding seeds, irrigation and fertilisers and raised food production but increased regional and class inequality. Other changes: mechanisation, commercialisation, migration, indebtedness and agrarian distress including farmers' suicides. Bonded labour (abolished by law in 1976), and migrant labour. Rural social change includes panchayati raj institutions (73rd Amendment, 1992). Globalisation affects agriculture through trade and contract farming. Urban society: urbanisation is the growth of towns and cities. In 2011, about 31 percent of Indians lived in urban areas. A town: population at least 5,000, density 400 per sq km and at least 75 percent of male working population in non-agricultural work (Census definition). Features of urban life: heterogeneity, anonymity, formal relations and division of labour. Urban problems: slums, housing shortage, pollution, traffic, crime and unemployment. Louis Wirth described urbanism as a way of life. Migration: push factors (poverty, unemployment) and pull factors (jobs, education). Industrialisation spurred urban growth in Mumbai, Kolkata, Delhi and Chennai. Cities in colonial India: Bombay, Calcutta and Madras as port cities. The idea of class in urban society and the role of the middle class. Urban planning and Smart Cities. Rural-urban differences: occupation, density, kinship ties and mobility. Rural-urban continuum. Social movements and change: tribal, women's and Dalit movements. Sociologists use ideas of modernisation. Factory work and trade unions in cities. Mahatma Gandhi emphasised village republics.
Deep dive: Social change
Change is continuous; some is gradual and some sudden. Many factors—economy, technology, ideas and politics—cause change. Social order and change coexist.
Deep dive: Rural change
Land reforms, the Green Revolution and panchayati raj reshaped villages. Inequality and distress remain. Migration links villages to cities.
Deep dive: Urban life
Cities are large, dense and diverse. Anonymity and division of labour mark urban life. Slums and pollution are challenges.

Visual lesson

Social Change and Social Order in Rural and Urban Society

Social change is the alteration in social structure, institutions and relationships over time

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Social change›3Rural change›4Urban life
Green Revolution1960s
73rd Amendment1992
Bonded labour1976
Census 201131% urban
🔑

Big idea

  • Social change is the alteration in social structure, institutions and relationships over time
  • Types: evolutionary and revolutionary
  • Short-term and long-term
  • Causes: ecological, economic (Marx), political, cultural (Weber's Protestant ethic), technology and ideas
Read the full explanation

Social change is the alteration in social structure, institutions and relationships over time. Types: evolutionary and revolutionary; short-term and long-term. Causes: ecological, economic (Marx), political, cultural (Weber's Protestant ethic), technology and ideas. Social order is maintained by social control. Rural society: in India about 65 percent of the population lives in villages (2011 Census). Agrarian structure: land ownership, tenancy and labour. Rural classes: landlords, tenants, small farmers and landless labourers. Caste and land are linked. Land reforms: abolition of zamindari (intermediaries), tenancy reforms, land ceilings and consolidation. The Green Revolution (1960s) used high-yielding seeds, irrigation and fertilisers and raised food production but increased regional and class inequality. Other changes: mechanisation, commercialisation, migration, indebtedness and agrarian distress including farmers' suicides. Bonded labour (abolished by law in 1976), and migrant labour. Rural social change includes panchayati raj institutions (73rd Amendment, 1992). Globalisation affects agriculture through trade and contract farming. Urban society: urbanisation is the growth of towns and cities. In 2011, about 31 percent of Indians lived in urban areas. A town: population at least 5,000, density 400 per sq km and at least 75 percent of male working population in non-agricultural work (Census definition). Features of urban life: heterogeneity, anonymity, formal relations and division of labour. Urban problems: slums, housing shortage, pollution, traffic, crime and unemployment. Louis Wirth described urbanism as a way of life. Migration: push factors (poverty, unemployment) and pull factors (jobs, education). Industrialisation spurred urban growth in Mumbai, Kolkata, Delhi and Chennai. Cities in colonial India: Bombay, Calcutta and Madras as port cities. The idea of class in urban society and the role of the middle class. Urban planning and Smart Cities. Rural-urban differences: occupation, density, kinship ties and mobility. Rural-urban continuum. Social movements and change: tribal, women's and Dalit movements. Sociologists use ideas of modernisation. Factory work and trade unions in cities. Mahatma Gandhi emphasised village republics.

📌

Social change

  • Change is continuous
  • Some is gradual and some sudden
  • Many factors—economy, technology, ideas and politics—cause change
  • Social order and change coexist
🧠

Rural change

  • Land reforms, the Green Revolution and panchayati raj reshaped villages
  • Inequality and distress remain
  • Migration links villages to cities
🌟

Urban life

  • Cities are large, dense and diverse
  • Anonymity and division of labour mark urban life
  • Slums and pollution are challenges
🧮

lessons.title: Environment and Society
yt: class 11 sociology environment ecology chipko silent valley sardar sarovar

blocks.x: Environment includes the physical and living surroundings of humans. Ecology is the study of relationships between organisms and their environment. Sociologists see environmental problems as social: they arise from social organisation, power and inequality. Social ecology studies how social structures shape environment use. Ecology and society: pre-modern societies lived close to nature; industrialisation intensified exploitation. Environmental problems: resource depletion (water, forests, minerals), pollution (air, water, soil, noise), climate change, loss of biodiversity, waste and disasters. Ecological degradation is unequal: the poor are often most affected. Resources are used unequally; environmental conflicts arise over access to land, forest and water. Examples: the Chipko movement (1973) in Uttarakhand, where villagers, many of them women, hugged trees to protect forests from commercial felling; leaders included Sunderlal Bahuguna and Chandi Prasad Bhatt. The Silent Valley movement in Kerala (1970s–80s) saved a rainforest from a hydroelectric project. The Narmada Bachao Andolan (Medha Patkar) opposed the Sardar Sarovar dam over displacement. The Bhopal gas tragedy (1984) was an industrial disaster at the Union Carbide plant that killed thousands. Disasters can be natural or human-made; the 2004 tsunami and the 2001 Bhuj earthquake are examples. Sociologists see disasters as social because vulnerability depends on poverty and policy. Environmental law and policy: the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, the Forest Rights Act, 2006, and the Water Act, 1974. Globalisation and consumption raise pressure. Sustainable development meets present needs without harming future generations (Brundtland Report, 1987). Ideas of environmental justice and the rights of the poor to natural resources. The Rio Earth Summit (1992), the Kyoto Protocol (1997) and the Paris Agreement (2015) address climate change. Water scarcity and privatisation of water. Role of communities in managing resources: community forest management. Environmental movements link livelihood with ecology. Ramachandra Guha described the environmentalism of the poor. Urban environmental issues: waste, slums and air quality. Individuals and governments share responsibility. Awareness and education help protect the environment.
Deep dive: Environment as social
Environmental problems arise from how societies organise production and consumption. Power and inequality decide who gains and who bears the cost.
Deep dive: Movements
Chipko, Silent Valley and Narmada are major movements. They link livelihood, ecology and rights.
Deep dive: Disasters and law
Disasters have social causes of vulnerability. Laws and international agreements seek protection and sustainable development.

🔑

Big idea

  • Environment includes the physical and living surroundings of humans
  • Ecology is the study of relationships between organisms and their environment
  • Sociologists see environmental problems as social: they arise from social organisation, power and inequality
  • Social ecology studies how social structures shape environment use
Read the full explanation

Environment includes the physical and living surroundings of humans. Ecology is the study of relationships between organisms and their environment. Sociologists see environmental problems as social: they arise from social organisation, power and inequality. Social ecology studies how social structures shape environment use. Ecology and society: pre-modern societies lived close to nature; industrialisation intensified exploitation. Environmental problems: resource depletion (water, forests, minerals), pollution (air, water, soil, noise), climate change, loss of biodiversity, waste and disasters. Ecological degradation is unequal: the poor are often most affected. Resources are used unequally; environmental conflicts arise over access to land, forest and water. Examples: the Chipko movement (1973) in Uttarakhand, where villagers, many of them women, hugged trees to protect forests from commercial felling; leaders included Sunderlal Bahuguna and Chandi Prasad Bhatt. The Silent Valley movement in Kerala (1970s–80s) saved a rainforest from a hydroelectric project. The Narmada Bachao Andolan (Medha Patkar) opposed the Sardar Sarovar dam over displacement. The Bhopal gas tragedy (1984) was an industrial disaster at the Union Carbide plant that killed thousands. Disasters can be natural or human-made; the 2004 tsunami and the 2001 Bhuj earthquake are examples. Sociologists see disasters as social because vulnerability depends on poverty and policy. Environmental law and policy: the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, the Forest Rights Act, 2006, and the Water Act, 1974. Globalisation and consumption raise pressure. Sustainable development meets present needs without harming future generations (Brundtland Report, 1987). Ideas of environmental justice and the rights of the poor to natural resources. The Rio Earth Summit (1992), the Kyoto Protocol (1997) and the Paris Agreement (2015) address climate change. Water scarcity and privatisation of water. Role of communities in managing resources: community forest management. Environmental movements link livelihood with ecology. Ramachandra Guha described the environmentalism of the poor. Urban environmental issues: waste, slums and air quality. Individuals and governments share responsibility. Awareness and education help protect the environment.

📌

Environment as social

  • Environmental problems arise from how societies organise production and consumption
  • Power and inequality decide who gains and who bears the cost
🕰️

Movements

  • Chipko, Silent Valley and Narmada are major movements
  • They link livelihood, ecology and rights
⚖️

Disasters and law

  • Disasters have social causes of vulnerability
  • Laws and international agreements seek protection and sustainable development

lessons.title: Introducing Western Sociologists
yt: class 11 sociology western sociologists comte durkheim marx weber

blocks.x: Early sociology developed in Europe in the nineteenth century amid industrialisation and revolution. Auguste Comte (1798–1857) coined sociology and proposed positivism; he described the law of three stages of human thought (theological, metaphysical and positive) and divided sociology into social statics and social dynamics. Herbert Spencer applied evolution to society (survival of the fittest). Emile Durkheim (1858–1917) established sociology as an academic discipline in France; he defined social facts as ways of acting, thinking and feeling that are external to the individual and exercise coercion. His works include The Division of Labour in Society (1893), Rules of Sociological Method (1895), Suicide (1897) and The Elementary Forms of Religious Life (1912). He distinguished mechanical solidarity (traditional societies, similarity) and organic solidarity (modern societies, interdependence). Types of suicide: egoistic, altruistic, anomic and fatalistic. Anomie is a state of normlessness. He stressed the collective conscience and the sacred–profane distinction in religion. Karl Marx (1818–1883) saw history as class struggle; with Friedrich Engels, he wrote The Communist Manifesto (1848); Das Kapital (1867) analysed capitalism. Historical materialism says that the economic base (forces and relations of production) shapes the superstructure (law, politics, religion). Modes of production: primitive communism, ancient (slave), feudal, capitalist and socialist. In capitalism, the bourgeoisie own capital and the proletariat sell labour; surplus value is extracted; alienation separates workers from their product, process, fellow workers and self. Class consciousness leads to revolution. Max Weber (1864–1920) emphasised interpretive understanding (verstehen) and social action. His types of social action: instrumentally rational, value rational, affective and traditional. The ideal type is an analytical construct. Bureaucracy is rational organisation with hierarchy, rules and expertise. Authority types: traditional, legal-rational and charismatic. In The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism (1905), he linked Calvinist values to the rise of capitalism. Class, status and party are dimensions of stratification. Comparison: Durkheim stressed social solidarity and order; Marx stressed conflict and change; Weber stressed meaning and rationalisation. Disenchantment of the world and the iron cage of rationality are Weberian ideas. Georg Simmel and Talcott Parsons are other thinkers. Positivism versus interpretivism.
Deep dive: Comte and Spencer
Comte named sociology and proposed the law of three stages. Spencer applied evolution to society.
Deep dive: Durkheim
Durkheim treated social facts as things. He explained suicide, division of labour and religion through social causes.
Deep dive: Marx and Weber
Marx saw class conflict and alienation under capitalism. Weber stressed meaning, authority and rationalisation.
Hindi saransh
Pashchimi samajshastri: Comte (sakaratmakta), Durkheim (samajik tathya, aatmahatya), Marx (varg sangharsh) aur Weber (verstehen, adarsh prarup).
Remember: Durkheim = social facts; Marx = class conflict; Weber = verstehen.

Historical materialism says that the economic base (forces and relations of production) shapes the superstructure (law, politics, religion). Modes of production: primitive communism, ancient (slave), feudal, capitalist and socialist. In capitalism, the bourgeoisie own capital and the proletariat sell labour; surplus value is extracted; alienation separates workers from their product, process, fellow workers and self. Class consciousness leads to revolution. Max Weber (1864–1920) emphasised interpretive understanding (verstehen) and social action. His types of social action: instrumentally rational, value rational, affective and traditional. The ideal type is an analytical construct. Bureaucracy is rational organisation with hierarchy, rules and expertise. Authority types: traditional, legal-rational and charismatic. In The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism (1905), he linked Calvinist values to the rise of capitalism. Class, status and party are dimensions of stratification. Comparison: Durkheim stressed social solidarity and order; Marx stressed conflict and change; Weber stressed meaning and rationalisation. Disenchantment of the world and the iron cage of rationality are Weberian ideas. Georg Simmel and Talcott Parsons are other thinkers. Positivism versus interpretivism.

📌

Comte and Spencer

  • Comte named sociology and proposed the law of three stages
  • Spencer applied evolution to society
🧠

Durkheim

  • Durkheim treated social facts as things
  • He explained suicide, division of labour and religion through social causes
🌟

Marx and Weber

  • Marx saw class conflict and alienation under capitalism
  • Weber stressed meaning, authority and rationalisation

lessons.title: Indian Sociologists

blocks.x: Indian sociology developed as scholars studied caste, tribe, village and family in the context of colonial rule and nationalism. G S Ghurye (1893–1983), regarded as the founder of institutionalised sociology in India, headed the Department of Sociology at Bombay University. He wrote Caste and Race in India (1932) and studied caste, tribes (calling them backward Hindus), religion and kinship. His six features of caste: segmental division of society, hierarchy, restrictions on feeding and social intercourse, civil and religious disabilities and privileges, lack of unrestricted choice of occupation, and restrictions on marriage. He took an Indological approach using texts, and supported integration of tribes. D P Mukerji (1894–1961) of Lucknow University advocated Marxist ideas applied to Indian traditions; he believed that Indian sociologists should know Indian traditions, yet be open to change, and he stressed the role of tradition, class conflict and the importance of the interplay of tradition, change and conflict. A R Desai (1915–1994) used a Marxist approach; he wrote Social Background of Indian Nationalism (1948); he argued that nationalism arose from material changes under colonial rule and criticised the modern state as a welfare state which worked for the rich. Radhakamal Mukerjee (1889–1968) was a sociologist-economist at Lucknow who studied social ecology, values and civilisation. M N Srinivas (1916–1999) did village studies, wrote The Remembered Village (1976) on Rampura, and coined Sanskritisation, dominant caste and Westernisation; he used fieldwork and the structural-functional approach; he established the Delhi School of Sociology and wrote on religion and society among the Coorgs (1952). A K Saran, a Lucknow sociologist, criticised Western approaches. Louis Dumont studied hierarchy in Homo Hierarchicus. Iravati Karve studied kinship. Comparisons: Ghurye (Indological), Mukerji (dialectical), Desai (Marxist), Srinivas (fieldwork). Indian sociologists tried to understand society through its own context. They contributed to understanding caste, tribe, village and nationalism. Later scholars: Andre Beteille studied Sripuram and caste, class and power; Yogendra Singh on modernisation of Indian tradition. Colonial influence on Indian sociology.
Deep dive: Ghurye and Srinivas
Ghurye used texts to study caste and tribes. Srinivas pioneered fieldwork and village studies. Both shaped Indian sociology.
Deep dive: D P Mukerji and A R Desai
Mukerji combined Marxism with Indian tradition. Desai analysed nationalism and the state in Marxist terms.
Deep dive: Other scholars
Karve studied kinship; Dumont, caste hierarchy; Beteille, caste and class. Indian sociology grew through debate with Western ideas.

Indian sociology developed as scholars studied caste, tribe, village and family in the context of colonial rule and nationalism. G S Ghurye (1893–1983), regarded as the founder of institutionalised sociology in India, headed the Department of Sociology at Bombay University. He wrote Caste and Race in India (1932) and studied caste, tribes (calling them backward Hindus), religion and kinship. His six features of caste: segmental division of society, hierarchy, restrictions on feeding and social intercourse, civil and religious disabilities and privileges, lack of unrestricted choice of occupation, and restrictions on marriage. He took an Indological approach using texts, and supported integration of tribes. D P Mukerji (1894–1961) of Lucknow University advocated Marxist ideas applied to Indian traditions; he believed that Indian sociologists should know Indian traditions, yet be open to change, and he stressed the role of tradition, class conflict and the importance of the interplay of tradition, change and conflict. A R Desai (1915–1994) used a Marxist approach; he wrote Social Background of Indian Nationalism (1948); he argued that nationalism arose from material changes under colonial rule and criticised the modern state as a welfare state which worked for the rich. Radhakamal Mukerjee (1889–1968) was a sociologist-economist at Lucknow who studied social ecology, values and civilisation. M N Srinivas (1916–1999) did village studies, wrote The Remembered Village (1976) on Rampura, and coined Sanskritisation, dominant caste and Westernisation; he used fieldwork and the structural-functional approach; he established the Delhi School of Sociology and wrote on religion and society among the Coorgs (1952). A K Saran, a Lucknow sociologist, criticised Western approaches. Louis Dumont studied hierarchy in Homo Hierarchicus. Iravati Karve studied kinship. Comparisons: Ghurye (Indological), Mukerji (dialectical), Desai (Marxist), Srinivas (fieldwork). Indian sociologists tried to understand society through its own context. They contributed to understanding caste, tribe, village and nationalism. Later scholars: Andre Beteille studied Sripuram and caste, class and power; Yogendra Singh on modernisation of Indian tradition. Colonial influence on Indian sociology.

📌

Ghurye and Srinivas

  • Ghurye used texts to study caste and tribes
  • Srinivas pioneered fieldwork and village studies
  • Both shaped Indian sociology
🧠

D P Mukerji and A R Desai

  • Mukerji combined Marxism with Indian tradition
  • Desai analysed nationalism and the state in Marxist terms
🌟

Other scholars

  • Karve studied kinship
  • Dumont, caste hierarchy
  • Beteille, caste and class
  • Indian sociology grew through debate with Western ideas

lessons.title: Accounting for Partnership Firms: Fundamentals
yt: class 12 accountancy partnership fundamentals deed capital accounts interest on drawings

blocks.x: A partnership is the relation between persons who have agreed to share the profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all (Indian Partnership Act, 1932, Section 4). Features: two or more persons (minimum 2; maximum 50 under the Companies Act 2013 and rules), agreement, business, profit sharing, mutual agency and unlimited liability. The partnership deed is the written agreement; it generally contains the firm's name, nature of business, capital contributions, profit sharing ratio, interest on capital and drawings, salary or commission to partners, interest on loans and rules for admission, retirement and settlement of accounts. If the deed is silent, the provisions of the Partnership Act apply under Section 13: no interest on capital; no salary or commission; profits shared equally; interest on a partner's loan at 6 percent per annum; and no interest on drawings. Fixed capital method: capital account remains unchanged except for additions or withdrawals of capital, and a separate current account records interest, salary, drawings and profit share. Fluctuating capital method: all adjustments are made directly in the capital account. Profit and Loss Appropriation Account shows the distribution of profit: it is debited with interest on capital, partner's salary, commission and transfer to reserve, and credited with net profit from the P&L account and interest on drawings. Interest on capital is calculated on opening capital (or on capital after adjustment as per the deed) at the agreed rate. Interest on drawings is a gain to the firm; its calculation depends on the date and amount of drawings. If drawings are made at the beginning of each month, the average period is 6.5 months; at the end of each month 5.5 months; in the middle of each month 6 months; and for equal amounts at the beginning of each quarter 7.5 months, at the end 4.5 months. Interest on drawings = total drawings x rate/100 x average months/12. Product method is used where amounts differ. Guarantee of minimum profit to a partner: the deficiency is borne by the other partners in a given ratio or by one partner. Past adjustments: where an omission is found after accounts are closed, a rectification entry through the Adjustment Account is passed rather than reopening the accounts; the net effect is shared among partners in the old ratio. Partner's loan is not capital, so interest on it is a charge against profit, not an appropriation. Interest on capital is an appropriation if the firm has profit; if there is a loss, no interest on capital is payable unless the deed so provides (and it is then a charge). Salary is an appropriation unless stated as a charge. Partners' capital accounts: debit side drawings, interest on drawings, losses; credit side opening balance, interest on capital, salary and profit share. Admission to the Act: the firm is not a separate legal entity from partners.
Deep dive: Partnership Act provisions
Section 4 defines partnership; Section 13 gives default rules. Equal sharing of profit, no interest on capital, 6 percent on loan. The deed overrides defaults.
Deep dive: Capital accounts
Fixed capital keeps capital constant with a current account for other items. Fluctuating capital adjusts everything in the capital account. Choose the method per the deed.
Deep dive: Appropriation account
It distributes profit among partners after interest, salary and reserve. Interest on drawings is credited. Past adjustments are passed through an adjustment account.

Sajhedari: Bhartiya Sajhedari Adhiniyam 1932; dhara 13 ke anusar byaj par koi byaj nahin, vetan nahin, laabh samaan, rin par 6% byaj.
Remember: if the deed is silent, profits are shared equally and loan interest is 6 percent.

problems.q: Drawings of Rs 12,000 made equally at the start of each month for a year at 10 percent. Compute interest.
problems.a: Total drawings 12 x 12000 = 1,44,000; average months 6.5; interest = 144000 x 10/100 x 6.5/12 = Rs 7,800.

problems.q: Distinguish between fixed and fluctuating capital methods.
problems.a: Fixed keeps capital unchanged with a current account; fluctuating records all items in the capital account.

Read the full explanation

A partnership is the relation between persons who have agreed to share the profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all (Indian Partnership Act, 1932, Section 4). Features: two or more persons (minimum 2; maximum 50 under the Companies Act 2013 and rules), agreement, business, profit sharing, mutual agency and unlimited liability. The partnership deed is the written agreement; it generally contains the firm's name, nature of business, capital contributions, profit sharing ratio, interest on capital and drawings, salary or commission to partners, interest on loans and rules for admission, retirement and settlement of accounts. If the deed is silent, the provisions of the Partnership Act apply under Section 13: no interest on capital; no salary or commission; profits shared equally; interest on a partner's loan at 6 percent per annum; and no interest on drawings. Fixed capital method: capital account remains unchanged except for additions or withdrawals of capital, and a separate current account records interest, salary, drawings and profit share. Fluctuating capital method: all adjustments are made directly in the capital account. Profit and Loss Appropriation Account shows the distribution of profit: it is debited with interest on capital, partner's salary, commission and transfer to reserve, and credited with net profit from the P&L account and interest on drawings. Interest on capital is calculated on opening capital (or on capital after adjustment as per the deed) at the agreed rate. Interest on drawings is a gain to the firm; its calculation depends on the date and amount of drawings. If drawings are made at the beginning of each month, the average period is 6.5 months; at the end of each month 5.5 months; in the middle of each month 6 months; and for equal amounts at the beginning of each quarter 7.5 months, at the end 4.5 months. Interest on drawings = total drawings x rate/100 x average months/12. Product method is used where amounts differ. Guarantee of minimum profit to a partner: the deficiency is borne by the other partners in a given ratio or by one partner. Past adjustments: where an omission is found after accounts are closed, a rectification entry through the Adjustment Account is passed rather than reopening the accounts; the net effect is shared among partners in the old ratio. Partner's loan is not capital, so interest on it is a charge against profit, not an appropriation. Interest on capital is an appropriation if the firm has profit; if there is a loss, no interest on capital is payable unless the deed so provides (and it is then a charge). Salary is an appropriation unless stated as a charge. Partners' capital accounts: debit side drawings, interest on drawings, losses; credit side opening balance, interest on capital, salary and profit share. Admission to the Act: the firm is not a separate legal entity from partners.

📌

Partnership Act provisions

  • Section 4 defines partnership
  • Section 13 gives default rules
  • Equal sharing of profit, no interest on capital, 6 percent on loan
  • The deed overrides defaults
🧠

Capital accounts

  • Fixed capital keeps capital constant with a current account for other items
  • Fluctuating capital adjusts everything in the capital account
  • Choose the method per the deed
🌟

Appropriation account

  • It distributes profit among partners after interest, salary and reserve
  • Interest on drawings is credited
  • Past adjustments are passed through an adjustment account
🎯 Remember if the deed is silent, profits are shared equally and loan interest is 6 percent.

lessons.title: Goodwill
yt: class 12 accountancy goodwill valuation average super profit capitalisation

blocks.x: Goodwill is the value of the reputation of a firm in respect of profits expected in future over and above the normal profits. It is an intangible asset but not a fictitious one, and is a non-current asset that cannot be seen or touched. Features: it is an intangible asset, helps to earn super profits, its value fluctuates and it cannot be separated from the business. Factors affecting goodwill: nature of business, location, efficiency of management, market situation, special advantages such as patents, and the risk involved. Need for valuation: change in profit sharing ratio, admission of a partner, retirement or death of a partner, dissolution when the business is sold as a going concern, and sale of the business. Methods: (1) Average Profit Method: Goodwill = Average profit x Number of years purchase. Average profit = total profit of past years / number of years. (2) Super Profit Method: Super profit = Average profit - Normal profit; Goodwill = Super profit x Number of years purchase. Normal profit = Capital employed x Normal rate of return / 100. Capital employed = Total assets (excluding goodwill and fictitious assets) - Outside liabilities, or equals the sum of partners' capital plus reserves. (3) Capitalisation of Average Profit: Capitalised value = Average profit x 100 / Normal rate of return; Goodwill = Capitalised value - Capital employed (net assets). (4) Capitalisation of Super Profit: Goodwill = Super profit x 100 / Normal rate of return. Adjustments before calculating average profit: abnormal gains or losses are removed; non-recurring items are adjusted; changes in the value of closing stock are adjusted; items like interest on investments and tax are adjusted as required; remuneration of partners is deducted if not already charged. Weighted average profit method gives weights to the years (such as 1, 2, 3) with the most recent year having the highest weight: Weighted average = Sum of (profit x weight) / Sum of weights. Treatment of goodwill in an existing business: purchased goodwill is shown in the balance sheet as an asset. Goodwill when a partner is admitted: premium brought by the new partner. Hidden goodwill: when the capital of a new partner is given with his share, goodwill is calculated as the difference between the total capital of the firm and the net assets. Accounting Standard 26 (AS 26) prohibits recognition of self-generated goodwill; only purchased goodwill is recorded. Normal rate of return is the rate expected in similar business. Number of years of purchase is a matter of agreement. Adjusted average profit may need adjustments for abnormal items, such as a loss by fire (added back). Super profit arises when the actual profit exceeds normal profit.
Deep dive: Concept and factors
Goodwill is the extra earning power due to reputation. Location, management, and market conditions affect it. It is recorded only when purchased.
Deep dive: Methods
Average profit multiplies average profit by years of purchase. Super profit methods use the excess of actual over normal profit. Capitalisation methods divide by the normal rate.
Deep dive: Adjustments
Profit must be adjusted for abnormal and non-recurring items and for partners' remuneration. Capital employed excludes goodwill.

Goodwill

Read the full explanation

Goodwill is the value of the reputation of a firm in respect of profits expected in future over and above the normal profits. It is an intangible asset but not a fictitious one, and is a non-current asset that cannot be seen or touched. Features: it is an intangible asset, helps to earn super profits, its value fluctuates and it cannot be separated from the business. Factors affecting goodwill: nature of business, location, efficiency of management, market situation, special advantages such as patents, and the risk involved. Need for valuation: change in profit sharing ratio, admission of a partner, retirement or death of a partner, dissolution when the business is sold as a going concern, and sale of the business. Methods: (1) Average Profit Method: Goodwill = Average profit x Number of years purchase. Average profit = total profit of past years / number of years. (2) Super Profit Method: Super profit = Average profit - Normal profit; Goodwill = Super profit x Number of years purchase. Normal profit = Capital employed x Normal rate of return / 100. Capital employed = Total assets (excluding goodwill and fictitious assets) - Outside liabilities, or equals the sum of partners' capital plus reserves. (3) Capitalisation of Average Profit: Capitalised value = Average profit x 100 / Normal rate of return; Goodwill = Capitalised value - Capital employed (net assets). (4) Capitalisation of Super Profit: Goodwill = Super profit x 100 / Normal rate of return. Adjustments before calculating average profit: abnormal gains or losses are removed; non-recurring items are adjusted; changes in the value of closing stock are adjusted; items like interest on investments and tax are adjusted as required; remuneration of partners is deducted if not already charged. Weighted average profit method gives weights to the years (such as 1, 2, 3) with the most recent year having the highest weight: Weighted average = Sum of (profit x weight) / Sum of weights. Treatment of goodwill in an existing business: purchased goodwill is shown in the balance sheet as an asset. Goodwill when a partner is admitted: premium brought by the new partner. Hidden goodwill: when the capital of a new partner is given with his share, goodwill is calculated as the difference between the total capital of the firm and the net assets. Accounting Standard 26 (AS 26) prohibits recognition of self-generated goodwill; only purchased goodwill is recorded. Normal rate of return is the rate expected in similar business. Number of years of purchase is a matter of agreement. Adjusted average profit may need adjustments for abnormal items, such as a loss by fire (added back). Super profit arises when the actual profit exceeds normal profit.

📘

Concept and factors

  • Goodwill is the extra earning power due to reputation
  • Location, management, and market conditions affect it
  • It is recorded only when purchased
🔄

Methods

  • Average profit multiplies average profit by years of purchase
  • Super profit methods use the excess of actual over normal profit
  • Capitalisation methods divide by the normal rate
🌟

Adjustments

  • Profit must be adjusted for abnormal and non-recurring items and for partners' remuneration
  • Capital employed excludes goodwill
🎯 Remember super profit = average profit minus normal profit.
🇮🇳

lessons.title: Change in Profit Sharing Ratio
yt: class 12 accountancy change in profit sharing ratio sacrificing gaining ratio reserves revaluation

blocks.x: A change in profit sharing ratio among existing partners amounts to the reconstitution of the firm; the old firm is deemed to be dissolved but the business continues. Some partners gain and some sacrifice in profit share. Sacrificing ratio = Old ratio - New ratio (for the partner who sacrifices). Gaining ratio = New ratio - Old ratio (for the partner who gains). The gaining partners compensate the sacrificing partners for the loss of future profits through goodwill. Treatment of goodwill: (1) if goodwill already appears in the books, it is written off to partners' capital accounts in the old ratio (Partners' Capital A/cs Dr; To Goodwill) and then a new valuation is raised in the new ratio; (2) a premium for goodwill is adjusted by debiting the gaining partners' capital accounts and crediting the sacrificing partners' capital accounts in the sacrificing ratio. Goodwill is distributed according to the ratio of gain and sacrifice: Gaining Partners' Capital A/c Dr; To Sacrificing Partners' Capital A/c. Accumulated profits and losses (general reserve, profit and loss account balance, reserve fund) belong to old partners and are distributed among them in the old ratio: General Reserve A/c Dr; To Partners' Capital A/cs. Accumulated losses (debit balance of P&L and deferred revenue expenditure) are written off in the old ratio. Reserves can be retained in the books if the partners agree, in which case no adjusting entry is passed (or a memorandum is prepared). Revaluation of assets and reassessment of liabilities: since the values may have changed, a Revaluation Account is prepared; increase in assets and decrease in liabilities are credited (gains); decrease in assets and increase in liabilities are debited (losses). The profit or loss on revaluation is transferred to partners' capital accounts in the old ratio. Adjustment of capitals: partners may agree to adjust capitals in the new profit sharing ratio. Steps: calculate the new capitals of the partners on the basis of the total capital of the firm; compare with existing capital to find shortage or surplus; adjust through cash or current account. Past adjustments. Memorandum Revaluation Account is used where assets and liabilities are to be shown at old values after the revaluation. The reconstituted firm's balance sheet is then prepared. The treatment of goodwill may also be hidden within the agreed capitals. Where the question gives that the change in the ratio happens with the entire goodwill at a given value, then each partner's share in the goodwill is credited in the old ratio and debited in the new ratio. Net effect: Credit old ratio share, debit new ratio share.
Deep dive: Sacrificing and gaining ratios
Compare old and new shares. The partner whose share falls sacrifices; the one whose share rises gains. The gainers compensate the sacrificers.
Deep dive: Goodwill and reserves
Existing goodwill is written off in the old ratio. New goodwill is adjusted in gaining and sacrificing ratio. Reserves go to old partners in the old ratio.
Deep dive: Revaluation
Revaluation updates assets and liabilities. Gain or loss goes to the old ratio. A memorandum account preserves book values.
