lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Change in Profit Sharing Ratio

A change in profit sharing ratio among existing partners amounts to the reconstitution of the firm

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Sacrificing and gaining…›3Goodwill and reserves›4Revaluation
🔑

Big idea

  • A change in profit sharing ratio among existing partners amounts to the reconstitution of the firm
  • The old firm is deemed to be dissolved but the business continues
  • Some partners gain and some sacrifice in profit share
  • Sacrificing ratio = Old ratio - New ratio (for the partner who sacrifices)
Read the full explanation

A change in profit sharing ratio among existing partners amounts to the reconstitution of the firm; the old firm is deemed to be dissolved but the business continues. Some partners gain and some sacrifice in profit share. Sacrificing ratio = Old ratio - New ratio (for the partner who sacrifices). Gaining ratio = New ratio - Old ratio (for the partner who gains). The gaining partners compensate the sacrificing partners for the loss of future profits through goodwill. Treatment of goodwill: (1) if goodwill already appears in the books, it is written off to partners' capital accounts in the old ratio (Partners' Capital A/cs Dr; To Goodwill) and then a new valuation is raised in the new ratio; (2) a premium for goodwill is adjusted by debiting the gaining partners' capital accounts and crediting the sacrificing partners' capital accounts in the sacrificing ratio. Goodwill is distributed according to the ratio of gain and sacrifice: Gaining Partners' Capital A/c Dr; To Sacrificing Partners' Capital A/c. Accumulated profits and losses (general reserve, profit and loss account balance, reserve fund) belong to old partners and are distributed among them in the old ratio: General Reserve A/c Dr; To Partners' Capital A/cs. Accumulated losses (debit balance of P&L and deferred revenue expenditure) are written off in the old ratio. Reserves can be retained in the books if the partners agree, in which case no adjusting entry is passed (or a memorandum is prepared). Revaluation of assets and reassessment of liabilities: since the values may have changed, a Revaluation Account is prepared; increase in assets and decrease in liabilities are credited (gains); decrease in assets and increase in liabilities are debited (losses). The profit or loss on revaluation is transferred to partners' capital accounts in the old ratio. Adjustment of capitals: partners may agree to adjust capitals in the new profit sharing ratio. Steps: calculate the new capitals of the partners on the basis of the total capital of the firm; compare with existing capital to find shortage or surplus; adjust through cash or current account. Past adjustments. Memorandum Revaluation Account is used where assets and liabilities are to be shown at old values after the revaluation. The reconstituted firm's balance sheet is then prepared. The treatment of goodwill may also be hidden within the agreed capitals. Where the question gives that the change in the ratio happens with the entire goodwill at a given value, then each partner's share in the goodwill is credited in the old ratio and debited in the new ratio. Net effect: Credit old ratio share, debit new ratio share.

📌

Sacrificing and gaining ratios

  • Compare old and new shares
  • The partner whose share falls sacrifices
  • The one whose share rises gains
  • The gainers compensate the sacrificers
🧠

Goodwill and reserves

  • Existing goodwill is written off in the old ratio
  • New goodwill is adjusted in gaining and sacrificing ratio
  • Reserves go to old partners in the old ratio
🌟

Revaluation

  • Revaluation updates assets and liabilities
  • Gain or loss goes to the old ratio
  • A memorandum account preserves book values
🎯 Remember sacrificing ratio = old minus new; gaining ratio = new minus old.
🇮🇳

lessons.title: Admission of a Partner
yt: class 12 accountancy admission of a partner new ratio sacrificing premium revaluation capital

blocks.x: Admission of a new partner reconstitutes the firm: the old firm is dissolved and a new one formed, with the business continuing. Under Section 31 of the Partnership Act, a person can be admitted only with the consent of all existing partners. The new partner acquires a right to share in future profits and in the assets. Adjustments required: (1) new profit sharing ratio, (2) sacrificing ratio, (3) goodwill, (4) revaluation of assets and liabilities, (5) treatment of reserves and accumulated profits and losses, (6) adjustment of capitals. New profit ratio: the new partner's share is acquired from old partners either in an agreed proportion or equally. If the new partner takes 1/5 share from all partners in their old ratio, the old partners' shares reduce proportionately: Sacrificing ratio = Old ratio when the share is taken in the old ratio. If the new partner gets his share from specific partners, the sacrificing ratio = Old share - New share. Goodwill: the new partner brings premium for goodwill in cash because he acquires a right to future super profits; the premium is shared by the sacrificing partners in the sacrificing ratio. Cash A/c Dr; To Premium for Goodwill A/c. Premium for Goodwill A/c Dr; To Sacrificing partners' Capital A/cs (in sacrificing ratio). If premium is not brought in cash (the goodwill is paid privately), no entry is passed. If the new partner is unable to bring the premium, current account is debited: New Partner's Current A/c Dr. Hidden goodwill: when the capital brought by the new partner is more or less than his proportionate share, the difference implies goodwill. Total capital of new firm = New partner's capital x Reciprocal of his share; Goodwill = Total capital of firm - Net assets (actual combined). Revaluation: Revaluation A/c is prepared and profit or loss is shared among old partners in the old ratio. Reserves and accumulated profits and losses are credited or debited to old partners in the old ratio. Adjustment of capitals: if the old partners' capitals are to be in the new profit ratio, new capital of old partners = Total capital x New share; excess or shortage is adjusted by cash or current account. Treatment of goodwill already in books: written off in the old ratio. Preparation of the balance sheet of the new firm shows capitals, reserves and revalued assets. Ledger accounts: Partners' Capital Accounts, Revaluation Account, and Balance Sheet. Capital of the new partner may be given in cash or kind. Journal entry for the capital: Cash A/c Dr; To New Partner's Capital A/c.
Deep dive: Reconstitution and ratios
Admission needs consent of all partners. The new partner acquires shares from old partners; sacrifice is computed as old share minus new share.
Deep dive: Goodwill
The new partner pays a premium for the right to future super profits. Sacrificing partners receive it. Hidden goodwill is derived from capital.
Deep dive: Revaluation and capital
Revaluation gain or loss goes to old partners. Reserves go to old partners. Capitals may be adjusted to the new ratio.
Hindi saransh
Naye bhagidar ka pravesh: puraani firm ka punargathan; sakhyati ka premium tyag anupat mein bantta hai; punarmulyankan ka laabh puraane anupat mein.
Remember: premium for goodwill is shared in the sacrificing ratio; revaluation and reserves go to the old ratio.

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Admission of a Partner

Admission of a new partner reconstitutes the firm: the old firm is dissolved and a new one formed, with the business continuing

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Reconstitution and ratios›3Goodwill›4Revaluation and capital
🔑

Big idea

  • Admission of a new partner reconstitutes the firm: the old firm is dissolved and a new one formed, with the business continuing
  • Under Section 31 of the Partnership Act, a person can be admitted only with the consent of all existing partners
  • The new partner acquires a right to share in future profits and in the assets
  • Adjustments required: (1) new profit sharing ratio, (2) sacrificing ratio, (3) goodwill, (4) revaluation of assets and liabilities, (5) treatment of…
Read the full explanation

Admission of a new partner reconstitutes the firm: the old firm is dissolved and a new one formed, with the business continuing. Under Section 31 of the Partnership Act, a person can be admitted only with the consent of all existing partners. The new partner acquires a right to share in future profits and in the assets. Adjustments required: (1) new profit sharing ratio, (2) sacrificing ratio, (3) goodwill, (4) revaluation of assets and liabilities, (5) treatment of reserves and accumulated profits and losses, (6) adjustment of capitals. New profit ratio: the new partner's share is acquired from old partners either in an agreed proportion or equally. If the new partner takes 1/5 share from all partners in their old ratio, the old partners' shares reduce proportionately: Sacrificing ratio = Old ratio when the share is taken in the old ratio. If the new partner gets his share from specific partners, the sacrificing ratio = Old share - New share. Goodwill: the new partner brings premium for goodwill in cash because he acquires a right to future super profits; the premium is shared by the sacrificing partners in the sacrificing ratio. Cash A/c Dr; To Premium for Goodwill A/c. Premium for Goodwill A/c Dr; To Sacrificing partners' Capital A/cs (in sacrificing ratio). If premium is not brought in cash (the goodwill is paid privately), no entry is passed. If the new partner is unable to bring the premium, current account is debited: New Partner's Current A/c Dr. Hidden goodwill: when the capital brought by the new partner is more or less than his proportionate share, the difference implies goodwill. Total capital of new firm = New partner's capital x Reciprocal of his share; Goodwill = Total capital of firm - Net assets (actual combined). Revaluation: Revaluation A/c is prepared and profit or loss is shared among old partners in the old ratio. Reserves and accumulated profits and losses are credited or debited to old partners in the old ratio. Adjustment of capitals: if the old partners' capitals are to be in the new profit ratio, new capital of old partners = Total capital x New share; excess or shortage is adjusted by cash or current account. Treatment of goodwill already in books: written off in the old ratio. Preparation of the balance sheet of the new firm shows capitals, reserves and revalued assets. Ledger accounts: Partners' Capital Accounts, Revaluation Account, and Balance Sheet. Capital of the new partner may be given in cash or kind. Journal entry for the capital: Cash A/c Dr; To New Partner's Capital A/c.

🏛️

Reconstitution and ratios

  • Admission needs consent of all partners
  • The new partner acquires shares from old partners
  • Sacrifice is computed as old share minus new share
🧠

Goodwill

  • The new partner pays a premium for the right to future super profits
  • Sacrificing partners receive it
  • Hidden goodwill is derived from capital
🌟

Revaluation and capital

  • Revaluation gain or loss goes to old partners
  • Reserves go to old partners
  • Capitals may be adjusted to the new ratio
🎯 Remember premium for goodwill is shared in the sacrificing ratio; revaluation and reserves go to the old ratio.
🇮🇳

lessons.title: Retirement and Death of a Partner
yt: class 12 accountancy retirement death partner gaining ratio settlement joint life policy

blocks.x: Retirement of a partner is withdrawal from the firm; under Section 32 a partner may retire with the consent of all partners, in accordance with an agreement or, in a partnership at will, by giving notice. On retirement the firm is reconstituted and the continuing partners continue the business. The retiring partner is entitled to his capital, share in reserves and accumulated profits, share in revaluation profit, share of goodwill, interest on capital and salary up to the date of retirement, and share of profit up to the date of retirement. Adjustments: (1) new profit sharing ratio, (2) gaining ratio = New ratio - Old ratio, (3) goodwill, (4) revaluation, (5) reserves, (6) joint life policy, (7) settlement of the amount due, (8) adjustment of capitals. New ratio: if not given, the retiring partner's share is divided among the continuing partners in the old ratio or as agreed (so new ratio is their old ratio), or equally, or in the specified proportion of acquisition. Gaining ratio: continuing partners gain and compensate the retiring partner for goodwill. Goodwill entry: Remaining partners' Capital A/cs Dr (in gaining ratio); To Retiring Partner's Capital A/c (for his share of goodwill). If goodwill already appears in the books it is written off in the old ratio. Revaluation Account: gain or loss shared by all partners (including the retiring partner) in the old ratio. Reserves and accumulated profits are credited to all partners in the old ratio. Joint life policy (JLP): the firm insures the lives of all partners; premium is charged to P&L; at retirement or death the policy is realised at its surrender value; the policy account is shown in the balance sheet at surrender value; if the policy is shown at surrender value, no extra entry, and if shown at premium paid, the policy is transferred to partners in the old ratio. When the death of a partner occurs, the firm receives the policy amount: Bank A/c Dr; To Joint Life Policy A/c; the policy reserve is transferred to partners' capital. Settlement of the amount due: (a) paid in lump sum in cash, (b) paid in instalments with interest on the unpaid balance, (c) transferred to loan account on which interest at 6 percent (or as agreed) per annum is payable (the retiring partner's loan); (d) part cash and part loan. If the deed says that the amount is to be paid in instalments with interest, the interest is calculated on the outstanding balance. Death of a partner: the legal representatives of the deceased are entitled to his capital, reserves, goodwill share, interest on capital and share of profit up to the date of death. Share of profit up to date of death is calculated on the basis of time (proportionate to the period) or sales (turnover basis), or last year's profits. Executor's Account is opened; the amount due is transferred to the Executor's A/c. Interest on drawings up to date of death is charged. Deceased partner's drawings are deducted. Capital adjustment: continuing partners' capitals may be adjusted in the new ratio. Deficit is brought in cash or the amount is paid. The profit and loss suspense account is used for profit up to date of death: Profit and Loss Suspense A/c Dr; To Deceased Partner's Capital A/c.
Deep dive: Retirement
The retiring partner is paid his capital, reserves, goodwill and revaluation share. Continuing partners gain the retiring share and compensate him.
Deep dive: Death
The legal representative receives the amount due. Profit up to death is computed on time or turnover basis. A suspense account may be used.
Deep dive: Settlement
The amount may be paid at once or in instalments, or converted to a loan with interest. A joint life policy provides funds for payment.

Visual lesson

Retirement and Death of a Partner

Retirement of a partner is withdrawal from the firm

Q&A

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Retirement›3Death›4Settlement
🔑

Big idea

  • Retirement of a partner is withdrawal from the firm
  • Under Section 32 a partner may retire with the consent of all partners, in accordance with an agreement or, in a partnership at will, by giving notice
  • On retirement the firm is reconstituted and the continuing partners continue the business
  • The retiring partner is entitled to his capital, share in reserves and accumulated profits, share in revaluation profit, share of goodwill, interest…
Read the full explanation

Retirement of a partner is withdrawal from the firm; under Section 32 a partner may retire with the consent of all partners, in accordance with an agreement or, in a partnership at will, by giving notice. On retirement the firm is reconstituted and the continuing partners continue the business. The retiring partner is entitled to his capital, share in reserves and accumulated profits, share in revaluation profit, share of goodwill, interest on capital and salary up to the date of retirement, and share of profit up to the date of retirement. Adjustments: (1) new profit sharing ratio, (2) gaining ratio = New ratio - Old ratio, (3) goodwill, (4) revaluation, (5) reserves, (6) joint life policy, (7) settlement of the amount due, (8) adjustment of capitals. New ratio: if not given, the retiring partner's share is divided among the continuing partners in the old ratio or as agreed (so new ratio is their old ratio), or equally, or in the specified proportion of acquisition. Gaining ratio: continuing partners gain and compensate the retiring partner for goodwill. Goodwill entry: Remaining partners' Capital A/cs Dr (in gaining ratio); To Retiring Partner's Capital A/c (for his share of goodwill). If goodwill already appears in the books it is written off in the old ratio. Revaluation Account: gain or loss shared by all partners (including the retiring partner) in the old ratio. Reserves and accumulated profits are credited to all partners in the old ratio. Joint life policy (JLP): the firm insures the lives of all partners; premium is charged to P&L; at retirement or death the policy is realised at its surrender value; the policy account is shown in the balance sheet at surrender value; if the policy is shown at surrender value, no extra entry, and if shown at premium paid, the policy is transferred to partners in the old ratio. When the death of a partner occurs, the firm receives the policy amount: Bank A/c Dr; To Joint Life Policy A/c; the policy reserve is transferred to partners' capital. Settlement of the amount due: (a) paid in lump sum in cash, (b) paid in instalments with interest on the unpaid balance, (c) transferred to loan account on which interest at 6 percent (or as agreed) per annum is payable (the retiring partner's loan); (d) part cash and part loan. If the deed says that the amount is to be paid in instalments with interest, the interest is calculated on the outstanding balance. Death of a partner: the legal representatives of the deceased are entitled to his capital, reserves, goodwill share, interest on capital and share of profit up to the date of death. Share of profit up to date of death is calculated on the basis of time (proportionate to the period) or sales (turnover basis), or last year's profits. Executor's Account is opened; the amount due is transferred to the Executor's A/c. Interest on drawings up to date of death is charged. Deceased partner's drawings are deducted. Capital adjustment: continuing partners' capitals may be adjusted in the new ratio. Deficit is brought in cash or the amount is paid. The profit and loss suspense account is used for profit up to date of death: Profit and Loss Suspense A/c Dr; To Deceased Partner's Capital A/c.

📌

Retirement

  • The retiring partner is paid his capital, reserves, goodwill and revaluation share
  • Continuing partners gain the retiring share and compensate him
🧠

Death

  • The legal representative receives the amount due
  • Profit up to death is computed on time or turnover basis
  • A suspense account may be used
🌟

Settlement

  • The amount may be paid at once or in instalments, or converted to a loan with interest
  • A joint life policy provides funds for payment
🎯 Remember gaining ratio = new ratio minus old ratio; the gainers pay the retiring partner for goodwill.
🇮🇳

lessons.title: Dissolution of a Partnership Firm
yt: class 12 accountancy dissolution realisation account order of payment insolvency

blocks.x: Dissolution of a partnership means the partnership between all partners ends; dissolution of the firm means the business is closed, its assets sold, liabilities paid and the surplus distributed. Section 39 of the Partnership Act defines dissolution of the firm as the dissolution of partnership between all partners. Modes of dissolution: by agreement (Section 40), compulsory dissolution (Section 41; when all partners or all but one become insolvent, or the business becomes unlawful), on the happening of certain contingencies (Section 42; expiry of term, completion of the venture, death of a partner, insolvency of a partner), by notice in a partnership at will (Section 43) and by the court (Section 44; for lunacy, permanent incapacity, misconduct, persistent breach, transfer of interest, continuous losses, or on just and equitable grounds). Settlement of accounts (Section 48): losses, including deficiency of capital, are paid first out of profits, next out of capital and lastly by the partners individually in their profit-sharing ratio. Assets, including any sum contributed by the partners to make up deficiencies of capital, are applied in this order: (1) in paying the debts of the firm to third parties; (2) in paying each partner proportionately what is due to him on account of advances as distinguished from capital; (3) in paying each partner proportionately what is due to him on account of capital; (4) the residue, if any, is divided among the partners in the profit sharing ratio. Realisation Account: prepared to record the sale of assets and settlement of liabilities and to find the profit or loss on realisation. Debit side: all assets (other than cash, bank and fictitious assets) at book values, liabilities paid, realisation expenses paid by the firm. Credit side: liabilities (external) at book values, amounts realised from assets, assets taken over by partners. Profit or loss on realisation is transferred to partners' capital accounts in the profit sharing ratio. Accounts not transferred to Realisation: Capital Accounts, Current Accounts, Partners' loan, Reserves and P&L balance and fictitious assets; these are settled through partners' accounts. Reserves and accumulated profits are transferred to partners' capital accounts in the profit sharing ratio. Partner's loan is paid before capital. Partner's loan is transferred to his capital account if adjusted so. A partner who takes an asset is debited with the value. If a partner agrees to pay a liability, his capital is debited. Expenses of realisation borne by a partner: the partner's capital is credited with the commission or expenses, and the firm is charged only if the deed says so. Unrecorded assets: if sold, credited in the Realisation Account. Unrecorded liabilities: if paid, debited. Deficiency of capital: a partner with a debit balance of capital must bring in cash. If a partner is insolvent, the loss is shared by the solvent partners in the capital ratio (Garner v Murray rule) — not the profit sharing ratio — and capital accounts are used. Garner v Murray applies in the absence of agreement, and the insolvent partner's deficiency is borne by the solvent partners in the ratio of their last agreed capitals (before dissolution, after adjusting for profits and losses). The cash book shows the final settlement.
Deep dive: Modes and law
Dissolution can be by agreement, compulsion, contingency, notice or court. Section 48 sets the order of payment. Losses come first from profit, then capital and then partners.
Deep dive: Realisation account
It records sales of assets and payment of liabilities. Its result is shared in the profit ratio. Partner accounts are closed afterward.
Deep dive: Insolvent partner
The Garner v Murray rule makes solvent partners share the deficiency in the capital ratio. It does not use the profit ratio.

Sajhedari firm ka visarjan: vasuli khata, dhara 48 ke anusar bhugtan ka kram aur Garner v Murray niyam.

Visual lesson

Dissolution of a Partnership Firm

Dissolution of a partnership means the partnership between all partners ends

formulas
Q&A

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Modes and law›3Realisation account›4Insolvent partner
🔑

Big idea

  • Dissolution of a partnership means the partnership between all partners ends
  • Dissolution of the firm means the business is closed, its assets sold, liabilities paid and the surplus distributed
  • Section 39 of the Partnership Act defines dissolution of the firm as the dissolution of partnership between all partners
  • Modes of dissolution: by agreement (Section 40), compulsory dissolution (Section 41
Read the full explanation

Dissolution of a partnership means the partnership between all partners ends; dissolution of the firm means the business is closed, its assets sold, liabilities paid and the surplus distributed. Section 39 of the Partnership Act defines dissolution of the firm as the dissolution of partnership between all partners. Modes of dissolution: by agreement (Section 40), compulsory dissolution (Section 41; when all partners or all but one become insolvent, or the business becomes unlawful), on the happening of certain contingencies (Section 42; expiry of term, completion of the venture, death of a partner, insolvency of a partner), by notice in a partnership at will (Section 43) and by the court (Section 44; for lunacy, permanent incapacity, misconduct, persistent breach, transfer of interest, continuous losses, or on just and equitable grounds). Settlement of accounts (Section 48): losses, including deficiency of capital, are paid first out of profits, next out of capital and lastly by the partners individually in their profit-sharing ratio. Assets, including any sum contributed by the partners to make up deficiencies of capital, are applied in this order: (1) in paying the debts of the firm to third parties; (2) in paying each partner proportionately what is due to him on account of advances as distinguished from capital; (3) in paying each partner proportionately what is due to him on account of capital; (4) the residue, if any, is divided among the partners in the profit sharing ratio. Realisation Account: prepared to record the sale of assets and settlement of liabilities and to find the profit or loss on realisation. Debit side: all assets (other than cash, bank and fictitious assets) at book values, liabilities paid, realisation expenses paid by the firm. Credit side: liabilities (external) at book values, amounts realised from assets, assets taken over by partners. Profit or loss on realisation is transferred to partners' capital accounts in the profit sharing ratio. Accounts not transferred to Realisation: Capital Accounts, Current Accounts, Partners' loan, Reserves and P&L balance and fictitious assets; these are settled through partners' accounts. Reserves and accumulated profits are transferred to partners' capital accounts in the profit sharing ratio. Partner's loan is paid before capital. Partner's loan is transferred to his capital account if adjusted so. A partner who takes an asset is debited with the value. If a partner agrees to pay a liability, his capital is debited. Expenses of realisation borne by a partner: the partner's capital is credited with the commission or expenses, and the firm is charged only if the deed says so. Unrecorded assets: if sold, credited in the Realisation Account. Unrecorded liabilities: if paid, debited. Deficiency of capital: a partner with a debit balance of capital must bring in cash. If a partner is insolvent, the loss is shared by the solvent partners in the capital ratio (Garner v Murray rule) — not the profit sharing ratio — and capital accounts are used. Garner v Murray applies in the absence of agreement, and the insolvent partner's deficiency is borne by the solvent partners in the ratio of their last agreed capitals (before dissolution, after adjusting for profits and losses). The cash book shows the final settlement.

⚖️

Modes and law

  • Dissolution can be by agreement, compulsion, contingency, notice or court
  • Section 48 sets the order of payment
  • Losses come first from profit, then capital and then partners
🧠

Realisation account

  • It records sales of assets and payment of liabilities
  • Its result is shared in the profit ratio
  • Partner accounts are closed afterward
🌟

Insolvent partner

  • The Garner v Murray rule makes solvent partners share the deficiency in the capital ratio
  • It does not use the profit ratio
🎯 Remember order of payment: outside debts, partner loans, partner capital, then surplus in profit ratio.
🇮🇳

हिंदी सार

Sajhedari firm ka visarjan: vasuli khata, dhara 48 ke anusar bhugtan ka kram aur Garner v Murray niyam.

lessons.title: Accounting for Share Capital
yt: class 12 accountancy share capital forfeiture reissue oversubscription premium discount

blocks.x: A company is an artificial person created by law with a separate legal entity, perpetual succession and limited liability. Share capital is the capital raised by issuing shares. Types of shares: equity shares (ordinary; carry voting rights and variable dividend) and preference shares (preferential right of dividend and repayment). Classes of share capital: Authorised capital (maximum capital as per the Memorandum of Association), Issued capital (offered to the public), Subscribed capital (taken up by the public), Called-up capital (the part of subscribed capital called by the company) and Paid-up capital (the part of called-up capital paid). Uncalled capital is the remaining and reserve capital is a part of uncalled capital that can be called only on winding up. Issue of shares: the share is issued by a prospectus; money is collected in stages as application, allotment and calls. Under Section 52 of the Companies Act 2013, securities premium is the amount received over the face value of shares; it can be used for issuing bonus shares, writing off preliminary expenses, issue expenses, premium on redemption of preference shares or debentures, and buying back shares. Minimum subscription is 90 percent of the issue (SEBI norms). Application money is the amount payable with the application; allotment is the acceptance of applications and the sum due on allotment; calls are the further demand. Journal entries: Bank A/c Dr; To Share Application A/c (on receipt). Share Application A/c Dr; To Share Capital A/c (on allotment); To Bank (refund). Share Allotment A/c Dr; To Share Capital; To Securities Premium. Bank A/c Dr; To Share Allotment A/c. Calls in arrears: the amount called but unpaid by a shareholder (a debit balance). Calls in advance: amount received before it is called (a credit balance; shown as a liability). Interest on calls in arrears per Table F is 10 percent (company may charge) and on calls in advance 12 percent. Over-subscription: when the applications received exceed the shares offered; the company may reject some applications and refund the money, allot shares in proportion (pro rata), or use a combination; the excess money is adjusted in allotment. Under-subscription: applications less than shares offered; allotment is made to all. Issue at par, at premium and at discount: shares can be issued at a discount only for sweat equity and not under normal conditions after the Companies Act 2013. Issue of shares for consideration other than cash: shares issued to vendors for purchase of assets; Sundry Assets A/c Dr; To Vendor; Vendor Dr; To Share Capital. Forfeiture of shares: cancellation of the shares for non-payment of calls. Share Capital A/c Dr (with called-up); To Calls in Arrears; To Share Forfeiture A/c (amount received). Securities premium unpaid is debited to the Securities Premium account when forfeited if the premium was not received. Reissue of forfeited shares: Bank Dr; Share Forfeiture Dr (loss); To Share Capital. The balance in the Share Forfeiture account after reissue (the gain) is transferred to Capital Reserve. The maximum discount on reissue is the amount credited to forfeited shares account for the shares reissued. Presentation in the balance sheet: Share capital under Shareholders' Funds, with details of authorised, issued, subscribed and paid-up capital.
Deep dive: Share capital
Authorised, issued, subscribed, called-up and paid-up capital describe stages of raising funds. Shares may be equity or preference.
Deep dive: Issue
Money is collected through application, allotment and calls. Securities premium arises above face value. Oversubscription needs pro rata allotment or refund.
Deep dive: Forfeiture
Shares are forfeited for non-payment. Reissue may be at a discount. The profit goes to capital reserve.
Hindi saransh
Anshpunji ka lekhankan: aavedan, bantan aur maang; pratibhuti premium, zabti aur punah-nirgaman; pratibhut paaripoorn.
Remember: forfeiture credits forfeited amount; reissue gain goes to capital reserve.

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Accounting for Share Capital

A company is an artificial person created by law with a separate legal entity, perpetual succession and limited liability

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Share capital›3Issue›4Forfeiture
🔑

Big idea

  • A company is an artificial person created by law with a separate legal entity, perpetual succession and limited liability
  • Share capital is the capital raised by issuing shares
  • Types of shares: equity shares (ordinary
  • Carry voting rights and variable dividend) and preference shares (preferential right of dividend and repayment)
Read the full explanation

A company is an artificial person created by law with a separate legal entity, perpetual succession and limited liability. Share capital is the capital raised by issuing shares. Types of shares: equity shares (ordinary; carry voting rights and variable dividend) and preference shares (preferential right of dividend and repayment). Classes of share capital: Authorised capital (maximum capital as per the Memorandum of Association), Issued capital (offered to the public), Subscribed capital (taken up by the public), Called-up capital (the part of subscribed capital called by the company) and Paid-up capital (the part of called-up capital paid). Uncalled capital is the remaining and reserve capital is a part of uncalled capital that can be called only on winding up. Issue of shares: the share is issued by a prospectus; money is collected in stages as application, allotment and calls. Under Section 52 of the Companies Act 2013, securities premium is the amount received over the face value of shares; it can be used for issuing bonus shares, writing off preliminary expenses, issue expenses, premium on redemption of preference shares or debentures, and buying back shares. Minimum subscription is 90 percent of the issue (SEBI norms). Application money is the amount payable with the application; allotment is the acceptance of applications and the sum due on allotment; calls are the further demand. Journal entries: Bank A/c Dr; To Share Application A/c (on receipt). Share Application A/c Dr; To Share Capital A/c (on allotment); To Bank (refund). Share Allotment A/c Dr; To Share Capital; To Securities Premium. Bank A/c Dr; To Share Allotment A/c. Calls in arrears: the amount called but unpaid by a shareholder (a debit balance). Calls in advance: amount received before it is called (a credit balance; shown as a liability). Interest on calls in arrears per Table F is 10 percent (company may charge) and on calls in advance 12 percent. Over-subscription: when the applications received exceed the shares offered; the company may reject some applications and refund the money, allot shares in proportion (pro rata), or use a combination; the excess money is adjusted in allotment. Under-subscription: applications less than shares offered; allotment is made to all. Issue at par, at premium and at discount: shares can be issued at a discount only for sweat equity and not under normal conditions after the Companies Act 2013. Issue of shares for consideration other than cash: shares issued to vendors for purchase of assets; Sundry Assets A/c Dr; To Vendor; Vendor Dr; To Share Capital. Forfeiture of shares: cancellation of the shares for non-payment of calls. Share Capital A/c Dr (with called-up); To Calls in Arrears; To Share Forfeiture A/c (amount received). Securities premium unpaid is debited to the Securities Premium account when forfeited if the premium was not received. Reissue of forfeited shares: Bank Dr; Share Forfeiture Dr (loss); To Share Capital. The balance in the Share Forfeiture account after reissue (the gain) is transferred to Capital Reserve. The maximum discount on reissue is the amount credited to forfeited shares account for the shares reissued. Presentation in the balance sheet: Share capital under Shareholders' Funds, with details of authorised, issued, subscribed and paid-up capital.

📌

Share capital

  • Authorised, issued, subscribed, called-up and paid-up capital describe stages of raising funds
  • Shares may be equity or preference
🧠

Issue

  • Money is collected through application, allotment and calls
  • Securities premium arises above face value
  • Oversubscription needs pro rata allotment or refund
🌟

Forfeiture

  • Shares are forfeited for non-payment
  • Reissue may be at a discount
  • The profit goes to capital reserve
🎯 Remember forfeiture credits forfeited amount; reissue gain goes to capital reserve.
🇮🇳

हिंदी सार

Anshpunji ka lekhankan: aavedan, bantan aur maang; pratibhuti premium, zabti aur punah-nirgaman; pratibhut paaripoorn.

lessons.title: Issue and Redemption of Debentures
yt: class 12 accountancy debentures issue redemption debenture redemption reserve sinking fund

blocks.x: A debenture is a written acknowledgement of a debt by a company, usually under its common seal, containing a promise to pay interest at a fixed rate and to repay the principal on a specified date. Debenture holders are creditors, not owners. Types: secured (mortgage) and unsecured (naked); redeemable and irredeemable; convertible and non-convertible; registered and bearer. Interest on debentures is a charge against profit, payable whether or not there is profit. Tax is deducted at source (TDS) on interest. Issue: debentures can be issued for cash, for consideration other than cash (to vendors) and as collateral security. Issue at par, at premium or at discount. Premium on issue is a capital profit credited to Securities Premium and is not a revenue profit. Discount on issue is a capital loss, debited to Discount on Issue of Debentures A/c and written off, usually in the year of issue from securities premium or the statement of profit and loss over the life of debentures. Redeemable at par, premium or discount. Premium on redemption is a loss, accounted at the time of issue by debiting Loss on Issue of Debentures A/c and crediting Premium on Redemption of Debentures A/c (a liability). Journal entries: Debenture Application and Allotment A/c Dr; To Debentures A/c; To Securities Premium. Debentures issued as collateral security: only a memorandum or a note, unless the loan is defaulted; Debentures Suspense A/c Dr; To Debentures A/c, and interest is not payable on collateral debentures; the balance sheet shows the loan with a note and the collateral security. Section 71 of the Companies Act, 2013: a company may issue debentures with the option to convert into shares. Debenture Redemption Reserve (DRR): a company issuing debentures must create DRR out of profits; as per Rule 18 of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014, listed companies are exempt, as are NBFCs and housing finance companies, and for others DRR is 10 percent of the value of outstanding debentures; investment in specified securities (called debenture redemption investment) of not less than 15 percent of debentures maturing in the year must be made by 30 April. Methods of redemption: (a) lump sum at maturity, (b) in instalments (annual drawings by lot), (c) purchase in the open market (own debentures; cancel or keep as investment), and (d) conversion into shares or new debentures. Redemption out of capital or profits. Sinking fund method: a fixed amount is set aside every year and invested outside; the amount grows with interest; Sinking Fund A/c, Sinking Fund Investment A/c. Own debentures purchased: Own Debentures A/c Dr; interest on own debentures is income. Gain or loss on cancellation transferred to Capital Reserve. Conversion: Debentures A/c Dr; To Share Capital A/c; To Securities Premium. Redemption entries: Debentures A/c Dr; To Debenture holders A/c; Debenture holders A/c Dr; To Bank A/c. DRR is transferred to General Reserve after redemption. Interest on debentures: Interest A/c Dr; To Debenture holders A/c; TDS Payable A/c.
Deep dive: Debentures
Debentures are a loan with fixed interest. Interest is payable regardless of profit. Debenture holders are creditors.
Deep dive: Issue
Debentures may be issued at par, premium or discount. Premium is a capital profit. Collateral issue is only a memorandum entry.
Deep dive: Redemption
Redemption can be lump sum, instalments, open market or conversion. DRR and investment requirements protect holders. Sinking fund accumulates money.
Hindi saransh
Rinpatra: nirgaman, byaj, mochan; rinpatra mochan sanchit kosh (DRR) aur sinking fund vidhi.
Remember: interest on debentures is a charge on profit; DRR is created out of profit.

Issue and Redemption of Debentures

🔑

Big idea

  • A debenture is a written acknowledgement of a debt by a company, usually under its common seal, containing a promise to pay interest at a fixed rate…
  • Debenture holders are creditors, not owners
  • Types: secured (mortgage) and unsecured (naked)
  • Redeemable and irredeemable
Read the full explanation

A debenture is a written acknowledgement of a debt by a company, usually under its common seal, containing a promise to pay interest at a fixed rate and to repay the principal on a specified date. Debenture holders are creditors, not owners. Types: secured (mortgage) and unsecured (naked); redeemable and irredeemable; convertible and non-convertible; registered and bearer. Interest on debentures is a charge against profit, payable whether or not there is profit. Tax is deducted at source (TDS) on interest. Issue: debentures can be issued for cash, for consideration other than cash (to vendors) and as collateral security. Issue at par, at premium or at discount. Premium on issue is a capital profit credited to Securities Premium and is not a revenue profit. Discount on issue is a capital loss, debited to Discount on Issue of Debentures A/c and written off, usually in the year of issue from securities premium or the statement of profit and loss over the life of debentures. Redeemable at par, premium or discount. Premium on redemption is a loss, accounted at the time of issue by debiting Loss on Issue of Debentures A/c and crediting Premium on Redemption of Debentures A/c (a liability). Journal entries: Debenture Application and Allotment A/c Dr; To Debentures A/c; To Securities Premium. Debentures issued as collateral security: only a memorandum or a note, unless the loan is defaulted; Debentures Suspense A/c Dr; To Debentures A/c, and interest is not payable on collateral debentures; the balance sheet shows the loan with a note and the collateral security. Section 71 of the Companies Act, 2013: a company may issue debentures with the option to convert into shares. Debenture Redemption Reserve (DRR): a company issuing debentures must create DRR out of profits; as per Rule 18 of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014, listed companies are exempt, as are NBFCs and housing finance companies, and for others DRR is 10 percent of the value of outstanding debentures; investment in specified securities (called debenture redemption investment) of not less than 15 percent of debentures maturing in the year must be made by 30 April. Methods of redemption: (a) lump sum at maturity, (b) in instalments (annual drawings by lot), (c) purchase in the open market (own debentures; cancel or keep as investment), and (d) conversion into shares or new debentures. Redemption out of capital or profits. Sinking fund method: a fixed amount is set aside every year and invested outside; the amount grows with interest; Sinking Fund A/c, Sinking Fund Investment A/c. Own debentures purchased: Own Debentures A/c Dr; interest on own debentures is income. Gain or loss on cancellation transferred to Capital Reserve. Conversion: Debentures A/c Dr; To Share Capital A/c; To Securities Premium. Redemption entries: Debentures A/c Dr; To Debenture holders A/c; Debenture holders A/c Dr; To Bank A/c. DRR is transferred to General Reserve after redemption. Interest on debentures: Interest A/c Dr; To Debenture holders A/c; TDS Payable A/c.

📌

Debentures

  • Debentures are a loan with fixed interest
  • Interest is payable regardless of profit
  • Debenture holders are creditors
🧠

Issue

  • Debentures may be issued at par, premium or discount
  • Premium is a capital profit
  • Collateral issue is only a memorandum entry
🌟

Redemption

  • Redemption can be lump sum, instalments, open market or conversion
  • DRR and investment requirements protect holders
  • Sinking fund accumulates money
🎯 Remember interest on debentures is a charge on profit; DRR is created out of profit.
🇮🇳

blocks.x: Financial statements are the final outcome of the accounting process, prepared to show the financial position and performance of a business. Under Section 129 of the Companies Act 2013, a company must prepare financial statements in the form given in Schedule III: the Balance Sheet, the Statement of Profit and Loss, the Cash Flow Statement (for companies other than certain small ones), the Statement of Changes in Equity and notes. Features of financial statements: they are historical, based on accounting concepts, show interim and final data and are prepared for stakeholders. Objectives: to provide information about financial position, performance and cash flows. The Balance Sheet shows assets, liabilities and equity at a point in time. Part I Equity and Liabilities: (1) Shareholders' funds: share capital, reserves and surplus (capital reserve, capital redemption reserve, securities premium, debenture redemption reserve, general reserve, surplus i.e. balance in the statement of profit and loss), and money received against share warrants; (2) Share application money pending allotment; (3) Non-current liabilities: long-term borrowings (debentures, bonds, term loans), deferred tax liabilities (net), other long-term liabilities (trade payables long-term), and long-term provisions (provision for employee benefits); (4) Current liabilities: short-term borrowings (bank overdraft, cash credit, loans repayable on demand), trade payables (creditors and bills payable), other current liabilities (current maturities of long-term debt, interest accrued, unpaid dividend, calls in advance, outstanding expenses) and short-term provisions (provision for tax, proposed dividend, provision for employee benefits). Part II Assets: (1) Non-current assets: property, plant and equipment and intangible assets (goodwill, patents, trademarks), capital work-in-progress, intangible assets under development, non-current investments, long-term loans and advances, deferred tax assets and other non-current assets (preliminary expenses to the extent not written off); (2) Current assets: current investments, inventories (raw material, work-in-progress, finished goods, stock-in-trade, stores and spares, loose tools), trade receivables (debtors and bills receivable), cash and cash equivalents (cash in hand, bank balance, cheques in hand, fixed deposits with maturity up to three months), short-term loans and advances (advance tax, prepaid expenses, loans to employees) and other current assets (accrued income, advances for supply of goods). Current means expected to be realised or settled within 12 months or the operating cycle. Statement of Profit and Loss: Revenue from operations (sale of products and services, other operating revenues, less excise duty), other income (interest, dividends, profit on sale of fixed assets), total revenue, expenses (cost of materials consumed, purchases of stock-in-trade, changes in inventories of finished goods, work-in-progress and stock-in-trade, employee benefit expenses, finance costs, depreciation and amortisation, other expenses), profit before tax, tax expense (current and deferred) and profit for the period. Earnings per share is disclosed. Notes to accounts give detail. Vertical or horizontal format; Schedule III uses a vertical format. Balance Sheet as at; Statement of Profit and Loss for the year ended. Contingent liabilities are disclosed in notes. Prior period items are shown separately. Format adds comparative figures for the previous year.
Deep dive: Statements
Schedule III prescribes the balance sheet and profit and loss format. The cash flow statement and notes complete the set.
Deep dive: Balance sheet
Equity and liabilities and assets are classified into current and non-current. Shareholders' funds include share capital and reserves.
Deep dive: Profit and loss
Revenue and other income are matched with expenses. Tax is deducted to find profit for the period.

Company ke vittiya vivaran: Schedule III ke anusar tulan patra aur laabh-haani vivaran; chalu aur ghair-chalu vargikaran.

Visual lesson

Financial Statements of a Company

Financial statements are the final outcome of the accounting process, prepared to show the financial position and performance of a business

🔑

Big idea

  • Financial statements are the final outcome of the accounting process, prepared to show the financial position and performance of a business
  • Under Section 129 of the Companies Act 2013, a company must prepare financial statements in the form given in Schedule III: the Balance Sheet, the…
  • Features of financial statements: they are historical, based on accounting concepts, show interim and final data and are prepared for stakeholders
  • Objectives: to provide information about financial position, performance and cash flows
Read the full explanation

Financial statements are the final outcome of the accounting process, prepared to show the financial position and performance of a business. Under Section 129 of the Companies Act 2013, a company must prepare financial statements in the form given in Schedule III: the Balance Sheet, the Statement of Profit and Loss, the Cash Flow Statement (for companies other than certain small ones), the Statement of Changes in Equity and notes. Features of financial statements: they are historical, based on accounting concepts, show interim and final data and are prepared for stakeholders. Objectives: to provide information about financial position, performance and cash flows. The Balance Sheet shows assets, liabilities and equity at a point in time. Part I Equity and Liabilities: (1) Shareholders' funds: share capital, reserves and surplus (capital reserve, capital redemption reserve, securities premium, debenture redemption reserve, general reserve, surplus i.e. balance in the statement of profit and loss), and money received against share warrants; (2) Share application money pending allotment; (3) Non-current liabilities: long-term borrowings (debentures, bonds, term loans), deferred tax liabilities (net), other long-term liabilities (trade payables long-term), and long-term provisions (provision for employee benefits); (4) Current liabilities: short-term borrowings (bank overdraft, cash credit, loans repayable on demand), trade payables (creditors and bills payable), other current liabilities (current maturities of long-term debt, interest accrued, unpaid dividend, calls in advance, outstanding expenses) and short-term provisions (provision for tax, proposed dividend, provision for employee benefits). Part II Assets: (1) Non-current assets: property, plant and equipment and intangible assets (goodwill, patents, trademarks), capital work-in-progress, intangible assets under development, non-current investments, long-term loans and advances, deferred tax assets and other non-current assets (preliminary expenses to the extent not written off); (2) Current assets: current investments, inventories (raw material, work-in-progress, finished goods, stock-in-trade, stores and spares, loose tools), trade receivables (debtors and bills receivable), cash and cash equivalents (cash in hand, bank balance, cheques in hand, fixed deposits with maturity up to three months), short-term loans and advances (advance tax, prepaid expenses, loans to employees) and other current assets (accrued income, advances for supply of goods). Current means expected to be realised or settled within 12 months or the operating cycle. Statement of Profit and Loss: Revenue from operations (sale of products and services, other operating revenues, less excise duty), other income (interest, dividends, profit on sale of fixed assets), total revenue, expenses (cost of materials consumed, purchases of stock-in-trade, changes in inventories of finished goods, work-in-progress and stock-in-trade, employee benefit expenses, finance costs, depreciation and amortisation, other expenses), profit before tax, tax expense (current and deferred) and profit for the period. Earnings per share is disclosed. Notes to accounts give detail. Vertical or horizontal format; Schedule III uses a vertical format. Balance Sheet as at; Statement of Profit and Loss for the year ended. Contingent liabilities are disclosed in notes. Prior period items are shown separately. Format adds comparative figures for the previous year.

📌

Statements

  • Schedule III prescribes the balance sheet and profit and loss format
  • The cash flow statement and notes complete the set
🧠

Balance sheet

  • Equity and liabilities and assets are classified into current and non-current
  • Shareholders' funds include share capital and reserves
🌟

Profit and loss

  • Revenue and other income are matched with expenses
  • Tax is deducted to find profit for the period
🎯 Remember current = realised or settled within 12 months or the operating cycle.

lessons.title: Analysis of Financial Statements
yt: class 12 accountancy analysis financial statements comparative common size tools

blocks.x: Analysis of financial statements is the process of identifying the financial strengths and weaknesses of a firm by establishing relationships between items of the balance sheet and the statement of profit and loss. Interpretation is explaining the meaning of the analysed data. Objectives: to assess profitability, liquidity, solvency and efficiency; to forecast and to compare. Users: management, investors, creditors, employees, government and researchers. Tools: (1) Comparative statements, (2) Common size statements, (3) Ratio analysis, (4) Cash flow analysis and (5) Trend analysis. Comparative statements show the figures of two or more years side by side, with absolute change (increase or decrease) and percentage change. Percentage change = (Absolute change / Base year amount) x 100. The earlier year is the base year. If the base is zero or negative, the percentage cannot be calculated. Comparative balance sheet and comparative statement of profit and loss. Common size statements express each item as a percentage of a common base: in the balance sheet the base is the total of assets (or total of equity and liabilities); in the statement of profit and loss the base is revenue from operations (net sales). Common size % = (Item / Base) x 100. Advantages: enables inter-firm and intra-firm comparison and shows structure. Trend analysis shows the direction of change using index numbers; Trend % = (Current year figure / Base year figure) x 100, with base year = 100. Limitations of financial analysis: based on historical data, ignores price level changes, ignores qualitative factors, accounting policies differ across firms, and a single year's data is not enough. Horizontal analysis compares data over time; vertical analysis compares items within a single year. Intra-firm comparison compares the firm over years; inter-firm comparison compares with other firms. Types of analysts: internal (management, using internal records) and external (outsiders, using published reports). Short-term and long-term analysis. Analysis for creditors focuses on solvency and liquidity; for investors, profitability and returns; for employees, stability. Financial statements are interim or annual. Importance of accuracy. The comparison of a company with the industry average, using benchmarks. Window dressing manipulates figures to look better. Steps in analysis: determine the purpose, collect the data, select the tool, compute and interpret. Examples: increase in revenue from Rs 10 lakh to Rs 12 lakh is an absolute change of Rs 2 lakh and a percentage change of 20 percent. Consistency in format aids comparison.
Deep dive: Tools
Comparative statements show change; common size shows structure; ratios show relationships; trend shows direction. Each needs a base.
Deep dive: Computation
Percentage change uses the earlier year as base. Common size uses total assets or revenue. Trend uses a base year of 100.
Deep dive: Limits
Analysis relies on past data and accounting policies. Qualitative factors and price changes are ignored.

Visual lesson

Analysis of Financial Statements

Analysis of financial statements is the process of identifying the financial strengths and weaknesses of a firm by establishing relationships between items of the…

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Tools›3Computation›4Limits
🔑

Big idea

  • Analysis of financial statements is the process of identifying the financial strengths and weaknesses of a firm by establishing relationships between…
  • Interpretation is explaining the meaning of the analysed data
  • Objectives: to assess profitability, liquidity, solvency and efficiency
  • To forecast and to compare
Read the full explanation

Analysis of financial statements is the process of identifying the financial strengths and weaknesses of a firm by establishing relationships between items of the balance sheet and the statement of profit and loss. Interpretation is explaining the meaning of the analysed data. Objectives: to assess profitability, liquidity, solvency and efficiency; to forecast and to compare. Users: management, investors, creditors, employees, government and researchers. Tools: (1) Comparative statements, (2) Common size statements, (3) Ratio analysis, (4) Cash flow analysis and (5) Trend analysis. Comparative statements show the figures of two or more years side by side, with absolute change (increase or decrease) and percentage change. Percentage change = (Absolute change / Base year amount) x 100. The earlier year is the base year. If the base is zero or negative, the percentage cannot be calculated. Comparative balance sheet and comparative statement of profit and loss. Common size statements express each item as a percentage of a common base: in the balance sheet the base is the total of assets (or total of equity and liabilities); in the statement of profit and loss the base is revenue from operations (net sales). Common size % = (Item / Base) x 100. Advantages: enables inter-firm and intra-firm comparison and shows structure. Trend analysis shows the direction of change using index numbers; Trend % = (Current year figure / Base year figure) x 100, with base year = 100. Limitations of financial analysis: based on historical data, ignores price level changes, ignores qualitative factors, accounting policies differ across firms, and a single year's data is not enough. Horizontal analysis compares data over time; vertical analysis compares items within a single year. Intra-firm comparison compares the firm over years; inter-firm comparison compares with other firms. Types of analysts: internal (management, using internal records) and external (outsiders, using published reports). Short-term and long-term analysis. Analysis for creditors focuses on solvency and liquidity; for investors, profitability and returns; for employees, stability. Financial statements are interim or annual. Importance of accuracy. The comparison of a company with the industry average, using benchmarks. Window dressing manipulates figures to look better. Steps in analysis: determine the purpose, collect the data, select the tool, compute and interpret. Examples: increase in revenue from Rs 10 lakh to Rs 12 lakh is an absolute change of Rs 2 lakh and a percentage change of 20 percent. Consistency in format aids comparison.

📌

Tools

  • Comparative statements show change
  • Common size shows structure
  • Ratios show relationships
  • Trend shows direction
Read the full explanation

Comparative statements show change; common size shows structure; ratios show relationships; trend shows direction. Each needs a base.

🧠

Computation

  • Percentage change uses the earlier year as base
  • Common size uses total assets or revenue
  • Trend uses a base year of 100
🌟

Limits

  • Analysis relies on past data and accounting policies
  • Qualitative factors and price changes are ignored
🎯 Remember percentage change = absolute change / base year x 100.
🇮🇳

lessons.title: Accounting Ratios
yt: class 12 accountancy accounting ratios liquidity solvency activity profitability

blocks.x: An accounting ratio expresses the relationship between two accounting figures. Ratio analysis helps in understanding liquidity, solvency, activity and profitability. Classification: (1) Liquidity ratios, (2) Solvency ratios, (3) Activity or turnover ratios and (4) Profitability ratios. Liquidity ratios: Current ratio = Current assets / Current liabilities (ideal 2:1); Quick or liquid ratio = Quick assets / Current liabilities (ideal 1:1), where quick assets = current assets - inventories - prepaid expenses. Solvency ratios: Debt-equity ratio = Long-term debt (or Debt) / Equity (Shareholders' funds) (ideal 2:1); Total assets to debt ratio = Total assets / Long-term debt; Proprietary ratio = Shareholders' funds / Total assets; Interest coverage ratio = Net profit before interest and tax / Interest on long-term debt. Activity ratios: Inventory turnover ratio = Cost of revenue from operations / Average inventory (times); average inventory = (Opening + closing) / 2; Trade receivables turnover ratio = Net credit revenue from operations / Average trade receivables (times); Trade payables turnover = Net credit purchases / Average trade payables; Working capital turnover = Revenue from operations / Working capital; Fixed assets turnover = Revenue from operations / Net fixed assets; Collection period = 365 / receivable turnover; Payment period = 365 / payables turnover. Profitability ratios: Gross profit ratio = (Gross profit / Revenue from operations) x 100; Operating ratio = (Operating cost / Revenue from operations) x 100, where operating cost = cost of revenue from operations + operating expenses; Operating profit ratio = 100 - Operating ratio; Net profit ratio = (Net profit / Revenue from operations) x 100; Return on investment (ROI) = (Profit before interest and tax / Capital employed) x 100; Return on equity; Earnings per share = (Net profit after tax - preference dividend) / Number of equity shares; Price-earning ratio = Market price per share / EPS; Dividend per share. Capital employed = Shareholders' funds + Non-current liabilities, or Net fixed assets + Working capital. Working capital = Current assets - Current liabilities. Cost of revenue from operations = Opening inventory + Purchases + Direct expenses - Closing inventory. Gross profit = Revenue from operations - Cost of revenue from operations. Interpretation: A high current ratio suggests liquidity but may signal idle assets; a high debt-equity ratio signals higher risk; a high inventory turnover shows efficient sales; a high receivables turnover shows quick collection. Effect of transactions on ratios: for example, if current assets and liabilities equal, issuing shares for cash raises the current ratio. Limitations: ratios are based on past data, different accounting policies, no qualitative factors, and need comparison with norms. Working capital positive indicates current assets exceed current liabilities. Net profit means profit before tax less tax as per the question. Quick assets exclude inventories and prepaid. Current liabilities include proposed dividend. Ratios can be expressed as a pure ratio, a percentage or in times. Return on investment uses PBIT. Net profit ratio uses profit after tax, as per the question.
Deep dive: Liquidity and solvency
Current and quick ratios show short-term ability. Debt-equity and proprietary ratios show long-term strength.
Deep dive: Activity
Turnover ratios show how fast inventory and receivables move. Higher turnover generally means efficiency.
Deep dive: Profitability
Gross, operating and net ratios use revenue as base. ROI uses capital employed. Interpretation needs comparison.

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Accounting Ratios

An accounting ratio expresses the relationship between two accounting figures

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Liquidity and solvency›3Activity›4Profitability
🔑

Big idea

  • An accounting ratio expresses the relationship between two accounting figures
  • Ratio analysis helps in understanding liquidity, solvency, activity and profitability
  • Classification: (1) Liquidity ratios, (2) Solvency ratios, (3) Activity or turnover ratios and (4) Profitability ratios
  • Liquidity ratios: Current ratio = Current assets / Current liabilities (ideal 2:1)
Read the full explanation

An accounting ratio expresses the relationship between two accounting figures. Ratio analysis helps in understanding liquidity, solvency, activity and profitability. Classification: (1) Liquidity ratios, (2) Solvency ratios, (3) Activity or turnover ratios and (4) Profitability ratios. Liquidity ratios: Current ratio = Current assets / Current liabilities (ideal 2:1); Quick or liquid ratio = Quick assets / Current liabilities (ideal 1:1), where quick assets = current assets - inventories - prepaid expenses. Solvency ratios: Debt-equity ratio = Long-term debt (or Debt) / Equity (Shareholders' funds) (ideal 2:1); Total assets to debt ratio = Total assets / Long-term debt; Proprietary ratio = Shareholders' funds / Total assets; Interest coverage ratio = Net profit before interest and tax / Interest on long-term debt. Activity ratios: Inventory turnover ratio = Cost of revenue from operations / Average inventory (times); average inventory = (Opening + closing) / 2; Trade receivables turnover ratio = Net credit revenue from operations / Average trade receivables (times); Trade payables turnover = Net credit purchases / Average trade payables; Working capital turnover = Revenue from operations / Working capital; Fixed assets turnover = Revenue from operations / Net fixed assets; Collection period = 365 / receivable turnover; Payment period = 365 / payables turnover. Profitability ratios: Gross profit ratio = (Gross profit / Revenue from operations) x 100; Operating ratio = (Operating cost / Revenue from operations) x 100, where operating cost = cost of revenue from operations + operating expenses; Operating profit ratio = 100 - Operating ratio; Net profit ratio = (Net profit / Revenue from operations) x 100; Return on investment (ROI) = (Profit before interest and tax / Capital employed) x 100; Return on equity; Earnings per share = (Net profit after tax - preference dividend) / Number of equity shares; Price-earning ratio = Market price per share / EPS; Dividend per share. Capital employed = Shareholders' funds + Non-current liabilities, or Net fixed assets + Working capital. Working capital = Current assets - Current liabilities. Cost of revenue from operations = Opening inventory + Purchases + Direct expenses - Closing inventory. Gross profit = Revenue from operations - Cost of revenue from operations. Interpretation: A high current ratio suggests liquidity but may signal idle assets; a high debt-equity ratio signals higher risk; a high inventory turnover shows efficient sales; a high receivables turnover shows quick collection. Effect of transactions on ratios: for example, if current assets and liabilities equal, issuing shares for cash raises the current ratio. Limitations: ratios are based on past data, different accounting policies, no qualitative factors, and need comparison with norms. Working capital positive indicates current assets exceed current liabilities. Net profit means profit before tax less tax as per the question. Quick assets exclude inventories and prepaid. Current liabilities include proposed dividend. Ratios can be expressed as a pure ratio, a percentage or in times. Return on investment uses PBIT. Net profit ratio uses profit after tax, as per the question.

📌

Liquidity and solvency

  • Current and quick ratios show short-term ability
  • Debt-equity and proprietary ratios show long-term strength
🧠

Activity

  • Turnover ratios show how fast inventory and receivables move
  • Higher turnover generally means efficiency
🌟

Profitability

  • Gross, operating and net ratios use revenue as base
  • ROI uses capital employed
  • Interpretation needs comparison
🎯 Remember current ratio ideal 2:1; quick ratio ideal 1:1; debt-equity ideal 2:1.
🇮🇳

lessons.title: Cash Flow Statement
yt: class 12 accountancy cash flow statement AS 3 operating investing financing

blocks.x: A cash flow statement shows the inflows and outflows of cash and cash equivalents during a period, classified into operating, investing and financing activities. It is prepared as per Accounting Standard 3 (AS 3). Cash includes cash in hand and demand deposits with banks; cash equivalents are short-term, highly liquid investments (maturity up to three months) readily convertible into known amounts of cash. Objectives: to show the sources and uses of cash, to assess the ability to generate cash and to plan. Operating activities are the principal revenue-producing activities of the enterprise and activities other than investing and financing. Examples of inflows: cash receipts from customers; outflows: payments to suppliers, employees, taxes. Investing activities are acquisition and disposal of long-term assets and investments not included in cash equivalents: purchase and sale of fixed assets, purchase and sale of investments, loans given and repaid, interest and dividends received. Financing activities change the size and composition of owners' capital and borrowings: issue of shares and debentures, redemption, buy-back, payment of dividends, repayment of loans, and interest paid. Under AS 3, interest and dividends received and paid for non-financial enterprises: interest paid is a financing activity, and interest and dividends received are investing activities; dividend paid is a financing activity. Income tax paid is shown under operating activities. Methods of reporting operating activities: direct method (gross cash receipts and payments) and indirect method (adjusting net profit before tax for non-cash and non-operating items). Indirect method steps: Net profit before tax and extraordinary items (net profit as per the statement of profit and loss + tax + transfer to reserve + proposed dividend, if applicable); add non-cash and non-operating expenses: depreciation, amortisation of intangible assets and preliminary expenses written off, interest on borrowings, loss on sale of fixed assets, provision for doubtful debts; subtract non-operating income: dividend and interest received, profit on sale of fixed assets or investments; this gives operating profit before working capital changes; then adjust for changes in current assets and current liabilities: increase in current assets (except cash and cash equivalents) is deducted; decrease is added; increase in current liabilities is added; decrease is deducted; this gives cash generated from operations; deduct income tax paid to get net cash from operating activities. Cash flow from investing activities: purchase of fixed assets (outflow), sale of fixed assets (inflow), purchase and sale of investments, interest and dividends received (inflow). Cash flow from financing activities: proceeds from issue of shares and debentures (inflow), redemption and repayment (outflow), interest paid and dividend paid (outflow). Net increase or decrease in cash = Operating + Investing + Financing. Opening balance + net change = closing balance of cash and cash equivalents. Transactions not involving cash flows: purchase of assets by issue of shares, bonus shares, conversion of debentures, depreciation, and transfer between cash and bank or cash equivalents. Extra-ordinary items are shown separately. Format: A Cash flows from operating activities; B investing; C financing; net increase; add opening; closing.
Deep dive: Classification
Cash flows are grouped into operating, investing and financing. AS 3 guides classification of interest and dividends.
Deep dive: Operating activities
The indirect method adjusts profit for non-cash and non-operating items and for working capital changes. Tax paid is deducted.
Deep dive: Investing and financing
Investing covers fixed assets and investments. Financing covers shares, debentures, loans, interest paid and dividends.
Hindi saransh
Rokad pravah vivaran (AS 3): sanchalan, nivesh aur vittiya gatividhiyan; apratyaksh vidhi mein laabh ko samayojit karte hain.
Remember: increase in current assets is deducted; increase in current liabilities is added.

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Cash Flow Statement

A cash flow statement shows the inflows and outflows of cash and cash equivalents during a period, classified into operating, investing and financing activities

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Classification›3Operating activities›4Investing and financing
🔑

Big idea

  • A cash flow statement shows the inflows and outflows of cash and cash equivalents during a period, classified into operating, investing and financing…
  • It is prepared as per Accounting Standard 3 (AS 3)
  • Cash includes cash in hand and demand deposits with banks
  • Cash equivalents are short-term, highly liquid investments (maturity up to three months) readily convertible into known amounts of cash
Read the full explanation

A cash flow statement shows the inflows and outflows of cash and cash equivalents during a period, classified into operating, investing and financing activities. It is prepared as per Accounting Standard 3 (AS 3). Cash includes cash in hand and demand deposits with banks; cash equivalents are short-term, highly liquid investments (maturity up to three months) readily convertible into known amounts of cash. Objectives: to show the sources and uses of cash, to assess the ability to generate cash and to plan. Operating activities are the principal revenue-producing activities of the enterprise and activities other than investing and financing. Examples of inflows: cash receipts from customers; outflows: payments to suppliers, employees, taxes. Investing activities are acquisition and disposal of long-term assets and investments not included in cash equivalents: purchase and sale of fixed assets, purchase and sale of investments, loans given and repaid, interest and dividends received. Financing activities change the size and composition of owners' capital and borrowings: issue of shares and debentures, redemption, buy-back, payment of dividends, repayment of loans, and interest paid. Under AS 3, interest and dividends received and paid for non-financial enterprises: interest paid is a financing activity, and interest and dividends received are investing activities; dividend paid is a financing activity. Income tax paid is shown under operating activities. Methods of reporting operating activities: direct method (gross cash receipts and payments) and indirect method (adjusting net profit before tax for non-cash and non-operating items). Indirect method steps: Net profit before tax and extraordinary items (net profit as per the statement of profit and loss + tax + transfer to reserve + proposed dividend, if applicable); add non-cash and non-operating expenses: depreciation, amortisation of intangible assets and preliminary expenses written off, interest on borrowings, loss on sale of fixed assets, provision for doubtful debts; subtract non-operating income: dividend and interest received, profit on sale of fixed assets or investments; this gives operating profit before working capital changes; then adjust for changes in current assets and current liabilities: increase in current assets (except cash and cash equivalents) is deducted; decrease is added; increase in current liabilities is added; decrease is deducted; this gives cash generated from operations; deduct income tax paid to get net cash from operating activities. Cash flow from investing activities: purchase of fixed assets (outflow), sale of fixed assets (inflow), purchase and sale of investments, interest and dividends received (inflow). Cash flow from financing activities: proceeds from issue of shares and debentures (inflow), redemption and repayment (outflow), interest paid and dividend paid (outflow). Net increase or decrease in cash = Operating + Investing + Financing. Opening balance + net change = closing balance of cash and cash equivalents. Transactions not involving cash flows: purchase of assets by issue of shares, bonus shares, conversion of debentures, depreciation, and transfer between cash and bank or cash equivalents. Extra-ordinary items are shown separately. Format: A Cash flows from operating activities; B investing; C financing; net increase; add opening; closing.

📌

Classification

  • Cash flows are grouped into operating, investing and financing
  • AS 3 guides classification of interest and dividends
🧠

Operating activities

  • The indirect method adjusts profit for non-cash and non-operating items and for working capital changes
  • Tax paid is deducted
🌟

Investing and financing

  • Investing covers fixed assets and investments
  • Financing covers shares, debentures, loans, interest paid and dividends
🎯 Remember increase in current assets is deducted; increase in current liabilities is added.
🇮🇳
