blocks.x: The flower is the reproductive organ of angiosperms. The stamen has an anther and filament; the anther is usually bilobed and dithecous (two lobes, four microsporangia). Microsporangium wall layers from outside: epidermis, endothecium, middle layers and tapetum; the tapetum nourishes the developing pollen grains. Microsporogenesis: pollen mother cells (2n) undergo meiosis to form tetrads of microspores (n). The pollen grain (male gametophyte) has a two-layered wall: the outer exine made of sporopollenin, one of the most resistant organic materials, with germ pores, and the inner intine of cellulose and pectin. A mature pollen grain has a vegetative cell and a generative cell which divides into two male gametes. The pistil (carpel) has stigma, style and ovary. The ovule has funicle, hilum, integuments, micropyle, nucellus and chalaza. Megasporogenesis: the megaspore mother cell (2n) undergoes meiosis to form four megaspores (n), of which three degenerate and one functional megaspore develops into the female gametophyte (embryo sac). The typical embryo sac is monosporic, 7-celled and 8-nucleate: the egg apparatus (an egg and two synergids with filiform apparatus), three antipodal cells and a central cell with two polar nuclei. Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma. Types: autogamy, geitonogamy (same plant, different flower; genetically like autogamy but ecologically cross-pollination) and xenogamy (genetically different plants). Agents: wind (anemophily), water (hydrophily), insects (entomophily), birds and bats. Outbreeding devices: dichogamy, herkogamy, self-incompatibility, dioecy and unisexual flowers. Cleistogamous flowers never open and are always autogamous. Pollen-pistil interaction: compatible pollen germinates to form a pollen tube. Double fertilisation is unique to angiosperms: one male gamete fuses with the egg (syngamy) to form the zygote, and the other fuses with the two polar nuclei (triple fusion) to form the primary endosperm nucleus (3n). Post-fertilisation: endosperm develops before the embryo; types include free-nuclear, cellular and helobial; coconut water is free-nuclear endosperm. Embryo development: zygote, proembryo, globular, heart-shaped and mature embryo. A dicot embryo has two cotyledons, epicotyl and hypocotyl; the monocot embryo has one cotyledon (scutellum in grasses), coleoptile and coleorhiza. Seed develops from ovule and fruit from ovary; ovule integuments become seed coat (testa and tegmen). Perisperm is the persistent nucellus (black pepper, beet). Albuminous seeds retain endosperm (wheat, castor); non-albuminous seeds do not (pea, groundnut). Apomixis is the formation of seeds without fertilisation; polyembryony is more than one embryo in a seed (citrus, mango). Parthenocarpy forms seedless fruit (banana). Pollen banks, emasculation and bagging are used in plant breeding. Pollen allergy comes from Parthenium. Pollen is rich in nutrients.
Deep dive: Male and female gametophytes
The anther produces pollen by microsporogenesis; the ovule produces the embryo sac by megasporogenesis. The embryo sac has seven cells and eight nuclei.
Deep dive: Pollination and fertilisation
Pollination transfers pollen to the stigma. Double fertilisation produces zygote and endosperm. Triple fusion gives the 3n endosperm.
Deep dive: Seed and fruit
The zygote forms the embryo, the ovule forms the seed and the ovary forms the fruit. Endosperm may persist or be consumed.

Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants

The flower is the reproductive organ of angiosperms

Embryo sac7 cells
Endosperm3n
🔑

Big idea

  • The flower is the reproductive organ of angiosperms
  • The stamen has an anther and filament
  • The anther is usually bilobed and dithecous (two lobes, four microsporangia)
  • Microsporangium wall layers from outside: epidermis, endothecium, middle layers and tapetum
Read the full explanation

The flower is the reproductive organ of angiosperms. The stamen has an anther and filament; the anther is usually bilobed and dithecous (two lobes, four microsporangia). Microsporangium wall layers from outside: epidermis, endothecium, middle layers and tapetum; the tapetum nourishes the developing pollen grains. Microsporogenesis: pollen mother cells (2n) undergo meiosis to form tetrads of microspores (n). The pollen grain (male gametophyte) has a two-layered wall: the outer exine made of sporopollenin, one of the most resistant organic materials, with germ pores, and the inner intine of cellulose and pectin. A mature pollen grain has a vegetative cell and a generative cell which divides into two male gametes. The pistil (carpel) has stigma, style and ovary. The ovule has funicle, hilum, integuments, micropyle, nucellus and chalaza. Megasporogenesis: the megaspore mother cell (2n) undergoes meiosis to form four megaspores (n), of which three degenerate and one functional megaspore develops into the female gametophyte (embryo sac). The typical embryo sac is monosporic, 7-celled and 8-nucleate: the egg apparatus (an egg and two synergids with filiform apparatus), three antipodal cells and a central cell with two polar nuclei. Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma. Types: autogamy, geitonogamy (same plant, different flower; genetically like autogamy but ecologically cross-pollination) and xenogamy (genetically different plants). Agents: wind (anemophily), water (hydrophily), insects (entomophily), birds and bats. Outbreeding devices: dichogamy, herkogamy, self-incompatibility, dioecy and unisexual flowers. Cleistogamous flowers never open and are always autogamous. Pollen-pistil interaction: compatible pollen germinates to form a pollen tube. Double fertilisation is unique to angiosperms: one male gamete fuses with the egg (syngamy) to form the zygote, and the other fuses with the two polar nuclei (triple fusion) to form the primary endosperm nucleus (3n). Post-fertilisation: endosperm develops before the embryo; types include free-nuclear, cellular and helobial; coconut water is free-nuclear endosperm. Embryo development: zygote, proembryo, globular, heart-shaped and mature embryo. A dicot embryo has two cotyledons, epicotyl and hypocotyl; the monocot embryo has one cotyledon (scutellum in grasses), coleoptile and coleorhiza. Seed develops from ovule and fruit from ovary; ovule integuments become seed coat (testa and tegmen). Perisperm is the persistent nucellus (black pepper, beet). Albuminous seeds retain endosperm (wheat, castor); non-albuminous seeds do not (pea, groundnut). Apomixis is the formation of seeds without fertilisation; polyembryony is more than one embryo in a seed (citrus, mango). Parthenocarpy forms seedless fruit (banana). Pollen banks, emasculation and bagging are used in plant breeding. Pollen allergy comes from Parthenium. Pollen is rich in nutrients.

📌

Male and female gametophytes

  • The anther produces pollen by microsporogenesis
  • The ovule produces the embryo sac by megasporogenesis
  • The embryo sac has seven cells and eight nuclei
🧠

Pollination and fertilisation

  • Pollination transfers pollen to the stigma
  • Double fertilisation produces zygote and endosperm
  • Triple fusion gives the 3n endosperm
🌟

Seed and fruit

  • The zygote forms the embryo, the ovule forms the seed and the ovary forms the fruit
  • Endosperm may persist or be consumed

lessons.title: Human Reproduction
yt: class 12 biology human reproduction gametogenesis menstrual cycle fertilisation implantation placenta

blocks.x: Humans are sexually reproducing and viviparous. The male reproductive system: a pair of testes in the scrotum (2 to 2.5 degrees Celsius lower than body temperature for spermatogenesis), epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct, urethra, penis and accessory glands (seminal vesicles, prostate and bulbourethral glands). Each testis has about 250 compartments called testicular lobules, each containing one to three seminiferous tubules lined with spermatogonia (male germ cells) and Sertoli cells (nourish sperm); Leydig (interstitial) cells outside the tubules produce androgens. Spermatogenesis: spermatogonia (2n) divide mitotically; primary spermatocyte (2n) undergoes meiosis I to form two secondary spermatocytes (n) and meiosis II to form four spermatids, which transform into sperms by spermiogenesis. GnRH from the hypothalamus stimulates the pituitary to release LH and FSH; LH acts on Leydig cells to secrete androgens (testosterone); FSH acts on Sertoli cells. A sperm has a head (with acrosome containing hydrolytic enzymes and nucleus), neck, middle piece (mitochondria) and tail. Semen is seminal plasma plus sperm; about 200 to 300 million sperm are released in one ejaculation, and at least 60 percent must be normal and motile for fertility. The female reproductive system: ovaries, oviducts (fallopian tubes: infundibulum, ampulla, isthmus), uterus (perimetrium, myometrium, endometrium), cervix, vagina, external genitalia, and mammary glands. Oogenesis begins during embryonic development; oogonia form primary oocytes that get arrested at prophase I; at puberty about 60,000 to 80,000 remain; a primary follicle becomes a secondary follicle, a tertiary follicle and then a mature Graafian follicle; the secondary oocyte (arrested at metaphase II) is released at ovulation; meiosis II is completed only after sperm entry, producing the ovum and a second polar body. The menstrual cycle lasts about 28 days; ovulation occurs on about day 14. Phases: menstrual (days 1 to 5), follicular or proliferative, ovulatory and luteal or secretory. LH surge triggers ovulation. The corpus luteum secretes progesterone; if no fertilisation, it degenerates and menstruation begins. Menarche is the first menstruation and menopause the cessation at 50 years. Fertilisation occurs in the ampulla; the sperm acrosomal enzymes (hyaluronidase) dissolve the zona pellucida; entry of a sperm induces the cortical reaction that blocks polyspermy. The zygote undergoes cleavage to form a morula (8 to 16 cells), then the blastocyst with trophoblast and inner cell mass; the trophoblast implants in the endometrium. Placenta is formed by chorionic villi and uterine tissue, and is connected to the embryo by the umbilical cord; it facilitates exchange of oxygen, nutrients and waste and acts as an endocrine tissue producing hCG, hPL, oestrogen and progesterone; relaxin is produced in later stages. The inner cell mass differentiates into the three germ layers: ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm. After one month of pregnancy the heart is formed; by the end of the second month limbs and digits develop; by the end of the first trimester most major organ systems are formed. Gestation is about nine months. Parturition is induced by a complex neuroendocrine mechanism involving cortisol, oestrogen and oxytocin. Lactation: colostrum, the first milk, contains antibodies (IgA) vital for the new-born's immunity.
Deep dive: Male and female systems
Testes make sperm and testosterone; ovaries make ova and hormones. Accessory glands and ducts support gamete transport.
Deep dive: Gametogenesis and cycle
Spermatogenesis yields four sperms per cell; oogenesis yields one ovum. The menstrual cycle is controlled by FSH, LH, oestrogen and progesterone.
Deep dive: Fertilisation to birth
Fertilisation in the ampulla is followed by cleavage and implantation. The placenta supports the foetus. Parturition is hormone controlled.

Human Reproduction

Humans are sexually reproducing and viviparous

🔑

Big idea

  • Humans are sexually reproducing and viviparous

Read the full explanation

Humans are sexually reproducing and viviparous. The male reproductive system: a pair of testes in the scrotum (2 to 2.5 degrees Celsius lower than body temperature for spermatogenesis), epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct, urethra, penis and accessory glands (seminal vesicles, prostate and bulbourethral glands). Each testis has about 250 compartments called testicular lobules, each containing one to three seminiferous tubules lined with spermatogonia (male germ cells) and Sertoli cells (nourish sperm); Leydig (interstitial) cells outside the tubules produce androgens. Spermatogenesis: spermatogonia (2n) divide mitotically; primary spermatocyte (2n) undergoes meiosis I to form two secondary spermatocytes (n) and meiosis II to form four spermatids, which transform into sperms by spermiogenesis. GnRH from the hypothalamus stimulates the pituitary to release LH and FSH; LH acts on Leydig cells to secrete androgens (testosterone); FSH acts on Sertoli cells. A sperm has a head (with acrosome containing hydrolytic enzymes and nucleus), neck, middle piece (mitochondria) and tail. Semen is seminal plasma plus sperm; about 200 to 300 million sperm are released in one ejaculation, and at least 60 percent must be normal and motile for fertility. The female reproductive system: ovaries, oviducts (fallopian tubes: infundibulum, ampulla, isthmus), uterus (perimetrium, myometrium, endometrium), cervix, vagina, external genitalia, and mammary glands. Oogenesis begins during embryonic development; oogonia form primary oocytes that get arrested at prophase I; at puberty about 60,000 to 80,000 remain; a primary follicle becomes a secondary follicle, a tertiary follicle and then a mature Graafian follicle; the secondary oocyte (arrested at metaphase II) is released at ovulation; meiosis II is completed only after sperm entry, producing the ovum and a second polar body. The menstrual cycle lasts about 28 days; ovulation occurs on about day 14. Phases: menstrual (days 1 to 5), follicular or proliferative, ovulatory and luteal or secretory. LH surge triggers ovulation. The corpus luteum secretes progesterone; if no fertilisation, it degenerates and menstruation begins. Menarche is the first menstruation and menopause the cessation at 50 years. Fertilisation occurs in the ampulla; the sperm acrosomal enzymes (hyaluronidase) dissolve the zona pellucida; entry of a sperm induces the cortical reaction that blocks polyspermy. The zygote undergoes cleavage to form a morula (8 to 16 cells), then the blastocyst with trophoblast and inner cell mass; the trophoblast implants in the endometrium. Placenta is formed by chorionic villi and uterine tissue, and is connected to the embryo by the umbilical cord; it facilitates exchange of oxygen, nutrients and waste and acts as an endocrine tissue producing hCG, hPL, oestrogen and progesterone; relaxin is produced in later stages. The inner cell mass differentiates into the three germ layers: ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm. After one month of pregnancy the heart is formed; by the end of the second month limbs and digits develop; by the end of the first trimester most major organ systems are formed. Gestation is about nine months. Parturition is induced by a complex neuroendocrine mechanism involving cortisol, oestrogen and oxytocin. Lactation: colostrum, the first milk, contains antibodies (IgA) vital for the new-born's immunity.

📌

Male and female systems

  • Testes make sperm and testosterone
  • Ovaries make ova and hormones
  • Accessory glands and ducts support gamete transport
🔄

Gametogenesis and cycle

  • Spermatogenesis yields four sperms per cell
  • Oogenesis yields one ovum
  • The menstrual cycle is controlled by FSH, LH, oestrogen and progesterone
🌟

Fertilisation to birth

  • Fertilisation in the ampulla is followed by cleavage and implantation
  • The placenta supports the foetus
  • Parturition is hormone controlled
🧮

lessons.title: Reproductive Health
yt: class 12 biology reproductive health contraception STDs infertility MTP ART IVF

blocks.x: Reproductive health means total well-being in all aspects of reproduction: physical, emotional, behavioural and social. India was among the first countries to initiate action plans and programmes at the national level to attain total reproductive health; the family planning programmes were initiated in 1951 and are now called the Reproductive and Child Health Care (RCH) programmes. Components: sex education in schools, awareness of problems related to adolescence and sex-related abuse, the use of contraception, awareness of STDs, antenatal and postnatal care, and prevention of infertility. Statutory bodies: Amniocentesis for sex determination is banned (the Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques Act, 1994) to check female foeticide, though it is permitted to detect genetic disorders. Population explosion: the population grew from about 350 million at independence to over 1.2 billion by 2011. Contraception: an ideal contraceptive should be user-friendly, easily available, effective and reversible, with no side-effects. Natural or traditional methods: periodic abstinence (avoiding coitus from day 10 to 17 of the cycle), withdrawal or coitus interruptus and lactational amenorrhoea (absence of menstruation during lactation, effective up to six months). Barrier methods: condoms (for male and female), diaphragms, cervical caps and vaults. Condoms also protect against STDs and AIDS. Intra-uterine devices (IUDs): non-medicated (Lippes loop), copper releasing (CuT, Cu7, Multiload 375) and hormone-releasing (Progestasert, LNG-20). Copper ions suppress sperm motility and fertilising capacity; hormone releasing IUDs make the uterus unsuitable for implantation. Oral contraceptives: pills such as Saheli (non-steroidal, once a week) and progestogen-oestrogen combinations; they inhibit ovulation and implantation and alter cervical mucus. Emergency contraception: administration of progestogens or IUDs within 72 hours of coitus. Surgical methods (sterilisation): vasectomy in males and tubectomy in females. Medical termination of pregnancy (MTP) was legalised in 1971; it is safe up to 12 weeks of pregnancy, and the MTP Amendment Act, 2021 extends the upper limit to 24 weeks for certain categories. Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) include gonorrhoea, syphilis, genital herpes, chlamydiasis, genital warts, trichomoniasis, hepatitis-B and HIV/AIDS. Hepatitis-B, genital herpes and HIV are viral; the first three, namely gonorrhoea, syphilis and chlamydiasis, are curable with antibiotics. Prevention: avoid sex with unknown or multiple partners, use condoms and seek early diagnosis. Infertility: inability to conceive despite unprotected intercourse for a year. Assisted reproductive technologies (ART): In vitro fertilisation (IVF) followed by embryo transfer (ET) in a laboratory with zygote or early embryos up to 8 blastomeres transferred into the fallopian tube (ZIFT) and embryos with more than 8 blastomeres into the uterus (IUT). Gamete intra-fallopian transfer (GIFT) transfers ova into the fallopian tube. Intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) injects a sperm directly into an ovum. Artificial insemination (AI) and IUI transfers semen into the vagina or uterus. Test tube baby: the first was Louise Brown in 1978; India's first was born in 1986. Adoption is another option.
Deep dive: Reproductive health
It includes physical, emotional and social well-being. Sex education, safe motherhood and STI awareness are key. RCH programmes address them.
Deep dive: Contraception
Methods include natural, barrier, IUD, pills and surgical. Each has merits and limits. Condoms protect against STIs.
Deep dive: MTP, STIs and ART
MTP is legal under limits. STIs are prevented by safe behaviour. ART such as IVF and ICSI help infertile couples.

Read the full explanation

Reproductive health means total well-being in all aspects of reproduction: physical, emotional, behavioural and social. India was among the first countries to initiate action plans and programmes at the national level to attain total reproductive health; the family planning programmes were initiated in 1951 and are now called the Reproductive and Child Health Care (RCH) programmes. Components: sex education in schools, awareness of problems related to adolescence and sex-related abuse, the use of contraception, awareness of STDs, antenatal and postnatal care, and prevention of infertility. Statutory bodies: Amniocentesis for sex determination is banned (the Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques Act, 1994) to check female foeticide, though it is permitted to detect genetic disorders. Population explosion: the population grew from about 350 million at independence to over 1.2 billion by 2011. Contraception: an ideal contraceptive should be user-friendly, easily available, effective and reversible, with no side-effects. Natural or traditional methods: periodic abstinence (avoiding coitus from day 10 to 17 of the cycle), withdrawal or coitus interruptus and lactational amenorrhoea (absence of menstruation during lactation, effective up to six months). Barrier methods: condoms (for male and female), diaphragms, cervical caps and vaults. Condoms also protect against STDs and AIDS. Intra-uterine devices (IUDs): non-medicated (Lippes loop), copper releasing (CuT, Cu7, Multiload 375) and hormone-releasing (Progestasert, LNG-20). Copper ions suppress sperm motility and fertilising capacity; hormone releasing IUDs make the uterus unsuitable for implantation. Oral contraceptives: pills such as Saheli (non-steroidal, once a week) and progestogen-oestrogen combinations; they inhibit ovulation and implantation and alter cervical mucus. Emergency contraception: administration of progestogens or IUDs within 72 hours of coitus. Surgical methods (sterilisation): vasectomy in males and tubectomy in females. Medical termination of pregnancy (MTP) was legalised in 1971; it is safe up to 12 weeks of pregnancy, and the MTP Amendment Act, 2021 extends the upper limit to 24 weeks for certain categories. Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) include gonorrhoea, syphilis, genital herpes, chlamydiasis, genital warts, trichomoniasis, hepatitis-B and HIV/AIDS. Hepatitis-B, genital herpes and HIV are viral; the first three, namely gonorrhoea, syphilis and chlamydiasis, are curable with antibiotics. Prevention: avoid sex with unknown or multiple partners, use condoms and seek early diagnosis. Infertility: inability to conceive despite unprotected intercourse for a year. Assisted reproductive technologies (ART): In vitro fertilisation (IVF) followed by embryo transfer (ET) in a laboratory with zygote or early embryos up to 8 blastomeres transferred into the fallopian tube (ZIFT) and embryos with more than 8 blastomeres into the uterus (IUT). Gamete intra-fallopian transfer (GIFT) transfers ova into the fallopian tube. Intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) injects a sperm directly into an ovum. Artificial insemination (AI) and IUI transfers semen into the vagina or uterus. Test tube baby: the first was Louise Brown in 1978; India's first was born in 1986. Adoption is another option.

📌

Reproductive health

  • It includes physical, emotional and social well-being
  • Sex education, safe motherhood and STI awareness are key
  • RCH programmes address them
🧠

Contraception

  • Methods include natural, barrier, IUD, pills and surgical
  • Each has merits and limits
  • Condoms protect against STIs
🌟

MTP, STIs and ART

  • MTP is legal under limits
  • STIs are prevented by safe behaviour
  • ART such as IVF and ICSI help infertile couples

lessons.title: Principles of Inheritance and Variation
yt: class 12 biology inheritance mendel linkage sex determination pedigree chromosomal disorders

blocks.x: Genetics is the study of inheritance and variation. Gregor Mendel (1822 to 1884) conducted hybridisation experiments on garden pea (Pisum sativum) for seven years and discovered the laws of inheritance; he studied seven pairs of contrasting characters (stem height, flower colour, flower position, pod shape, pod colour, seed shape and seed colour). Alleles are alternative forms of a gene. A monohybrid cross between pure tall (TT) and dwarf (tt) gives all tall F1 (Tt); selfing F1 gives F2 with a phenotypic ratio of 3:1 and genotypic ratio of 1:2:1. Law of dominance: characters are controlled by factors; where two dissimilar factors are present, only one dominant expresses. Law of segregation: alleles separate during gamete formation so that a gamete carries only one allele; this is the law of purity of gametes. Test cross: crossing F1 or an unknown dominant phenotype with a homozygous recessive parent, giving 1:1 if heterozygous. Back cross is crossing with either parent. Dihybrid cross: round yellow (RRYY) x wrinkled green (rryy) gives 9:3:3:1 in F2; Law of independent assortment: when two pairs of traits are combined, segregation of one pair is independent of the other. Chromosomal theory of inheritance (Sutton and Boveri, 1902): chromosomes are vehicles of genes. Deviations from Mendel: incomplete dominance (snapdragon or Antirrhinum, 1:2:1 phenotypic ratio), codominance (ABO blood group alleles IA and IB), multiple alleles (IA, IB, i; three alleles but an individual has any two), pleiotropy (one gene affecting multiple traits, such as phenylketonuria), polygenic inheritance (skin colour, height). Blood groups: IAIA or IAi: A; IBIB or IBi: B; IAIB: AB; ii: O. Sex determination: XX-XY in humans and Drosophila (male heterogametic); XX-XO in grasshopper; ZW-ZZ in birds (female heterogametic). In humans, sex is determined by the sperm. Linkage: genes on the same chromosome are inherited together; Morgan studied Drosophila (yellow-bodied, white-eyed female x brown-bodied, red-eyed male) and found linkage and recombination; strength of linkage depends on the distance; Alfred Sturtevant used recombination frequency to map genes. Mutation: sudden heritable change; point mutation includes sickle-cell anaemia (substitution of Glu by Val in beta globin at the sixth position, a GAG to GUG change). Mendelian disorders: autosomal recessive (sickle-cell anaemia, phenylketonuria, thalassaemia), X-linked recessive (haemophilia, red-green colour blindness) and autosomal dominant (Huntington's disease, myotonic dystrophy). Haemophilia: a heterozygous female is a carrier. Thalassaemia is a quantitative defect in globin chain synthesis (alpha in chromosome 16, beta in chromosome 11). Chromosomal disorders: Down syndrome (trisomy 21; 47 chromosomes), Klinefelter syndrome (XXY; 47), Turner syndrome (XO; 45). Pedigree analysis is used to trace traits in families. Pedigree symbols: square male, circle female, shaded affected. Variation arises from mutation, recombination and gene flow.
Deep dive: Mendel's laws
Dominance, segregation and independent assortment explain inheritance. Test cross reveals genotype. Dihybrid cross gives 9:3:3:1.
Deep dive: Beyond Mendel
Incomplete dominance, codominance, multiple alleles, pleiotropy and polygenic inheritance extend the laws. ABO blood groups show three of these.
Deep dive: Linkage, sex and disorders
Linked genes recombine less often. Sex is determined by chromosomes. Mendelian and chromosomal disorders can be traced by pedigrees.
Hindi saransh
Anuvanshikta ke siddhant: Mendel ke niyam, vyutkram, ling nirdharan, sahalagnata aur anuvanshik vikar.
Remember: monohybrid 3:1 and 1:2:1; dihybrid 9:3:3:1; test cross 1:1.

Visual lesson

Principles of Inheritance and Variation

Genetics is the study of inheritance and variation

🔑

Big idea

  • Genetics is the study of inheritance and variation
  • Gregor Mendel (1822 to 1884) conducted hybridisation experiments on garden pea (Pisum sativum) for seven years and discovered the laws of inheritance
  • He studied seven pairs of contrasting characters (stem height, flower colour, flower position, pod shape, pod colour, seed shape and seed colour)
  • Alleles are alternative forms of a gene
Read the full explanation

Genetics is the study of inheritance and variation. Gregor Mendel (1822 to 1884) conducted hybridisation experiments on garden pea (Pisum sativum) for seven years and discovered the laws of inheritance; he studied seven pairs of contrasting characters (stem height, flower colour, flower position, pod shape, pod colour, seed shape and seed colour). Alleles are alternative forms of a gene. A monohybrid cross between pure tall (TT) and dwarf (tt) gives all tall F1 (Tt); selfing F1 gives F2 with a phenotypic ratio of 3:1 and genotypic ratio of 1:2:1. Law of dominance: characters are controlled by factors; where two dissimilar factors are present, only one dominant expresses. Law of segregation: alleles separate during gamete formation so that a gamete carries only one allele; this is the law of purity of gametes. Test cross: crossing F1 or an unknown dominant phenotype with a homozygous recessive parent, giving 1:1 if heterozygous. Back cross is crossing with either parent. Dihybrid cross: round yellow (RRYY) x wrinkled green (rryy) gives 9:3:3:1 in F2; Law of independent assortment: when two pairs of traits are combined, segregation of one pair is independent of the other. Chromosomal theory of inheritance (Sutton and Boveri, 1902): chromosomes are vehicles of genes. Deviations from Mendel: incomplete dominance (snapdragon or Antirrhinum, 1:2:1 phenotypic ratio), codominance (ABO blood group alleles IA and IB), multiple alleles (IA, IB, i; three alleles but an individual has any two), pleiotropy (one gene affecting multiple traits, such as phenylketonuria), polygenic inheritance (skin colour, height). Blood groups: IAIA or IAi: A; IBIB or IBi: B; IAIB: AB; ii: O. Sex determination: XX-XY in humans and Drosophila (male heterogametic); XX-XO in grasshopper; ZW-ZZ in birds (female heterogametic). In humans, sex is determined by the sperm. Linkage: genes on the same chromosome are inherited together; Morgan studied Drosophila (yellow-bodied, white-eyed female x brown-bodied, red-eyed male) and found linkage and recombination; strength of linkage depends on the distance; Alfred Sturtevant used recombination frequency to map genes. Mutation: sudden heritable change; point mutation includes sickle-cell anaemia (substitution of Glu by Val in beta globin at the sixth position, a GAG to GUG change). Mendelian disorders: autosomal recessive (sickle-cell anaemia, phenylketonuria, thalassaemia), X-linked recessive (haemophilia, red-green colour blindness) and autosomal dominant (Huntington's disease, myotonic dystrophy). Haemophilia: a heterozygous female is a carrier. Thalassaemia is a quantitative defect in globin chain synthesis (alpha in chromosome 16, beta in chromosome 11). Chromosomal disorders: Down syndrome (trisomy 21; 47 chromosomes), Klinefelter syndrome (XXY; 47), Turner syndrome (XO; 45). Pedigree analysis is used to trace traits in families. Pedigree symbols: square male, circle female, shaded affected. Variation arises from mutation, recombination and gene flow.

⚖️

Mendel's laws

  • Dominance, segregation and independent assortment explain inheritance
  • Test cross reveals genotype
  • Dihybrid cross gives 9:3:3:1
🧠

Beyond Mendel

  • Incomplete dominance, codominance, multiple alleles, pleiotropy and polygenic inheritance extend the laws
  • ABO blood groups show three of these
🌟

Linkage, sex and disorders

  • Linked genes recombine less often
  • Sex is determined by chromosomes
  • Mendelian and chromosomal disorders can be traced by pedigrees

yt: class 12 biology molecular basis inheritance DNA replication transcription translation lac operon HGP

blocks.x: DNA is a long polymer of deoxyribonucleotides; each nucleotide has a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar (deoxyribose) and a phosphate group. Purines are adenine and guanine; pyrimidines are cytosine, thymine (in DNA) and uracil (in RNA). Chargaff's rule: A = T and G = C so that purines equal pyrimidines. Watson and Crick (1953) proposed the double-helix model, based on X-ray diffraction data from Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins: two antiparallel polynucleotide chains held by hydrogen bonds (A-T two bonds; G-C three bonds); the helix has a pitch of 3.4 nm with 10 base pairs per turn and the distance between base pairs is 0.34 nm. Nucleosome: DNA wrapped around a histone octamer (H2A, H2B, H3, H4, each twice), about 200 bp; histones are positively charged basic proteins; euchromatin is loosely packed and active, heterochromatin is densely packed and inactive. Griffith (1928) discovered transformation in Streptococcus pneumoniae; Avery, MacLeod and McCarty showed that DNA is the transforming principle; Hershey and Chase (1952) used radioactive 32P and 35S in bacteriophages to prove that DNA is the genetic material. Meselson and Stahl (1958) used 15N and E. coli to prove semiconservative replication of DNA. Replication begins at the origin of replication; helicase unwinds the helix; DNA polymerase adds nucleotides only in the 5' to 3' direction; the leading strand is continuous and the lagging strand is discontinuous (Okazaki fragments) joined by DNA ligase. RNA types: mRNA, tRNA (adapter, cloverleaf) and rRNA (structural and catalytic). Transcription: DNA-dependent RNA polymerase synthesises RNA from the template strand (3' to 5') in the 5' to 3' direction using a promoter and terminator; in bacteria one RNA polymerase; in eukaryotes RNA polymerase I (rRNA), II (mRNA) and III (tRNA, 5S rRNA). In eukaryotes, hnRNA undergoes splicing (introns removed, exons joined), capping (methyl guanosine triphosphate at the 5' end) and tailing (polyadenylation at the 3' end). Genetic code: triplet; 64 codons; 61 code for amino acids; AUG is the start codon (methionine); UAA, UAG and UGA are stop codons; the code is degenerate, unambiguous, universal and non-overlapping; Nirenberg, Khorana and Matthaei deciphered it. Translation: ribosome (30S and 50S in prokaryotes forming 70S) uses mRNA to make a polypeptide; aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase charges tRNA; peptide bonds form between amino acids. Regulation of gene expression: Jacob and Monod proposed the lac operon in E. coli (1961): structural genes lacZ, lacY, lacA; promoter, operator and the regulatory gene lacI that codes for a repressor; lactose (inducer) binds the repressor, allowing transcription — it is an inducible system under negative regulation. Human Genome Project (1990 to 2003): about 3 billion base pairs; around 30,000 genes (later estimates about 20,000 to 25,000); chromosome 1 has the most genes (2968) and Y the fewest (231); only about 1.5 percent of the genome codes for proteins; over 99.9 percent of bases are the same in all humans; SNPs (single nucleotide polymorphisms) number about 1.4 million; Methods: ESTs and sequence annotation. DNA fingerprinting (Alec Jeffreys) uses VNTRs (variable number of tandem repeats) and Southern blotting; uses include forensics and paternity tests.
Deep dive: Structure of DNA
Two antiparallel chains with A-T and G-C pairing form a double helix. Histones package DNA into nucleosomes. Experiments proved DNA is the genetic material.
Deep dive: Central dogma
DNA replicates semiconservatively, is transcribed to RNA and translated into protein. The genetic code is triplet and degenerate.
Deep dive: Regulation and genome
The lac operon shows negative regulation. The Human Genome Project mapped about 3 billion base pairs. DNA fingerprinting uses VNTRs.

Big idea

  • DNA is a long polymer of deoxyribonucleotides
  • Each nucleotide has a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar (deoxyribose) and a phosphate group
  • Purines are adenine and guanine
  • Pyrimidines are cytosine, thymine (in DNA) and uracil (in RNA)
Read the full explanation

DNA is a long polymer of deoxyribonucleotides; each nucleotide has a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar (deoxyribose) and a phosphate group. Purines are adenine and guanine; pyrimidines are cytosine, thymine (in DNA) and uracil (in RNA). Chargaff's rule: A = T and G = C so that purines equal pyrimidines. Watson and Crick (1953) proposed the double-helix model, based on X-ray diffraction data from Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins: two antiparallel polynucleotide chains held by hydrogen bonds (A-T two bonds; G-C three bonds); the helix has a pitch of 3.4 nm with 10 base pairs per turn and the distance between base pairs is 0.34 nm. Nucleosome: DNA wrapped around a histone octamer (H2A, H2B, H3, H4, each twice), about 200 bp; histones are positively charged basic proteins; euchromatin is loosely packed and active, heterochromatin is densely packed and inactive. Griffith (1928) discovered transformation in Streptococcus pneumoniae; Avery, MacLeod and McCarty showed that DNA is the transforming principle; Hershey and Chase (1952) used radioactive 32P and 35S in bacteriophages to prove that DNA is the genetic material. Meselson and Stahl (1958) used 15N and E. coli to prove semiconservative replication of DNA. Replication begins at the origin of replication; helicase unwinds the helix; DNA polymerase adds nucleotides only in the 5' to 3' direction; the leading strand is continuous and the lagging strand is discontinuous (Okazaki fragments) joined by DNA ligase. RNA types: mRNA, tRNA (adapter, cloverleaf) and rRNA (structural and catalytic). Transcription: DNA-dependent RNA polymerase synthesises RNA from the template strand (3' to 5') in the 5' to 3' direction using a promoter and terminator; in bacteria one RNA polymerase; in eukaryotes RNA polymerase I (rRNA), II (mRNA) and III (tRNA, 5S rRNA). In eukaryotes, hnRNA undergoes splicing (introns removed, exons joined), capping (methyl guanosine triphosphate at the 5' end) and tailing (polyadenylation at the 3' end). Genetic code: triplet; 64 codons; 61 code for amino acids; AUG is the start codon (methionine); UAA, UAG and UGA are stop codons; the code is degenerate, unambiguous, universal and non-overlapping; Nirenberg, Khorana and Matthaei deciphered it. Translation: ribosome (30S and 50S in prokaryotes forming 70S) uses mRNA to make a polypeptide; aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase charges tRNA; peptide bonds form between amino acids. Regulation of gene expression: Jacob and Monod proposed the lac operon in E. coli (1961): structural genes lacZ, lacY, lacA; promoter, operator and the regulatory gene lacI that codes for a repressor; lactose (inducer) binds the repressor, allowing transcription — it is an inducible system under negative regulation. Human Genome Project (1990 to 2003): about 3 billion base pairs; around 30,000 genes (later estimates about 20,000 to 25,000); chromosome 1 has the most genes (2968) and Y the fewest (231); only about 1.5 percent of the genome codes for proteins; over 99.9 percent of bases are the same in all humans; SNPs (single nucleotide polymorphisms) number about 1.4 million; Methods: ESTs and sequence annotation. DNA fingerprinting (Alec Jeffreys) uses VNTRs (variable number of tandem repeats) and Southern blotting; uses include forensics and paternity tests.

📌

Structure of DNA

  • Two antiparallel chains with A-T and G-C pairing form a double helix
  • Histones package DNA into nucleosomes
  • Experiments proved DNA is the genetic material
🧠

Central dogma

  • DNA replicates semiconservatively, is transcribed to RNA and translated into protein
  • The genetic code is triplet and degenerate
🌟

Regulation and genome

  • The lac operon shows negative regulation
  • The Human Genome Project mapped about 3 billion base pairs
  • DNA fingerprinting uses VNTRs

lessons.title: Evolution
yt: class 12 biology evolution origin of life darwin natural selection hardy weinberg speciation

blocks.x: Origin of life: the universe is about 20 billion years old and Earth about 4.5 billion years. Big Bang theory. Oparin and Haldane proposed that the first form of life could have come from pre-existing non-living organic molecules (chemical evolution). Stanley Miller (1953) simulated early earth conditions (CH4, H2, NH3 and water vapour at 800 degrees Celsius) in a closed flask and formed amino acids, supporting chemical evolution. The first non-cellular forms may have been RNA, and the first cellular forms anaerobic heterotrophs. Louis Pasteur disproved spontaneous generation. Evidences of evolution: fossils (study is palaeontology; the age of fossils is known by radioactive dating), comparative anatomy and morphology: homologous organs (similar structure, different function; forelimbs of whale, bat, cheetah and human; divergent evolution) and analogous organs (different structure, same function; wings of butterfly and bird; convergent evolution); vestigial organs; biochemical similarities; adaptive radiation: Darwin's finches in the Galapagos islands, and Australian marsupials; convergent evolution: Australian marsupials and placental mammals. Adaptive radiation is evolution of different species in a geographical area starting from a point. Lamarck proposed the theory of use and disuse of organs and inheritance of acquired characters (giraffe neck). Darwin's theory (On the Origin of Species, 1859, after the voyage of HMS Beagle): branching descent and natural selection; the observations are that populations produce more offspring than survive, variations exist, and the fittest survive (differential reproduction). Alfred Wallace independently reached similar conclusions based on the Malay Archipelago. Industrial melanism: in England, the proportion of dark-coloured peppered moths (Biston betularia) rose after industrialisation because soot-covered tree trunks favoured dark moths. Mutation theory: Hugo de Vries proposed that mutations (large, discontinuous variations) cause speciation (saltation). Hardy-Weinberg principle: allelic frequencies in a population are stable and constant from generation to generation; p + q = 1; p2 + 2pq + q2 = 1; the gene pool remains constant (genetic equilibrium). Factors that disturb equilibrium: gene migration or gene flow, genetic drift, mutation, genetic recombination and natural selection. Genetic drift is a change in allele frequency by chance; founder effect is when drift occurs in a small group of colonisers. Natural selection can be stabilising, directional or disruptive. Speciation involves reproductive isolation. Origin of man: Dryopithecus and Ramapithecus were hairy and walked like gorillas and chimpanzees; Australopithecus (about 2 mya) ate fruit; Homo habilis (about 2 mya; brain capacity 650 to 800 cc; probably did not eat meat); Homo erectus (about 1.5 mya; brain 900 cc; ate meat); Neanderthal man (brain 1400 cc; lived 100,000 to 40,000 years ago; used hides to protect their body and buried their dead); Homo sapiens arose in Africa about 75,000 to 10,000 years ago; modern Homo sapiens arose in the Middle East about 34,000 years ago. Cave art developed about 18,000 years ago; agriculture about 10,000 years ago.
Deep dive: Origin of life
Chemical evolution preceded biological evolution. The Miller experiment formed amino acids from simple gases. First cells were anaerobic heterotrophs.
Deep dive: Evidence and mechanism
Fossils, homology, analogy and biogeography support evolution. Natural selection acts on variation. Industrial melanism is a field example.
Deep dive: Population genetics and humans
Hardy-Weinberg describes equilibrium; drift, flow, mutation and selection disturb it. Human evolution proceeded from Australopithecus to Homo sapiens.

Visual lesson

Evolution

Origin of life: the universe is about 20 billion years old and Earth about 4.5 billion years

Origin of Species1859
🔑

Big idea

  • Origin of life: the universe is about 20 billion years old and Earth about 4.5 billion years
  • Big Bang theory
  • Oparin and Haldane proposed that the first form of life could have come from pre-existing non-living organic molecules (chemical evolution)
  • Stanley Miller (1953) simulated early earth conditions (CH4, H2, NH3 and water vapour at 800 degrees Celsius) in a closed flask and formed amino…
Read the full explanation

Origin of life: the universe is about 20 billion years old and Earth about 4.5 billion years. Big Bang theory. Oparin and Haldane proposed that the first form of life could have come from pre-existing non-living organic molecules (chemical evolution). Stanley Miller (1953) simulated early earth conditions (CH4, H2, NH3 and water vapour at 800 degrees Celsius) in a closed flask and formed amino acids, supporting chemical evolution. The first non-cellular forms may have been RNA, and the first cellular forms anaerobic heterotrophs. Louis Pasteur disproved spontaneous generation. Evidences of evolution: fossils (study is palaeontology; the age of fossils is known by radioactive dating), comparative anatomy and morphology: homologous organs (similar structure, different function; forelimbs of whale, bat, cheetah and human; divergent evolution) and analogous organs (different structure, same function; wings of butterfly and bird; convergent evolution); vestigial organs; biochemical similarities; adaptive radiation: Darwin's finches in the Galapagos islands, and Australian marsupials; convergent evolution: Australian marsupials and placental mammals. Adaptive radiation is evolution of different species in a geographical area starting from a point. Lamarck proposed the theory of use and disuse of organs and inheritance of acquired characters (giraffe neck). Darwin's theory (On the Origin of Species, 1859, after the voyage of HMS Beagle): branching descent and natural selection; the observations are that populations produce more offspring than survive, variations exist, and the fittest survive (differential reproduction). Alfred Wallace independently reached similar conclusions based on the Malay Archipelago. Industrial melanism: in England, the proportion of dark-coloured peppered moths (Biston betularia) rose after industrialisation because soot-covered tree trunks favoured dark moths. Mutation theory: Hugo de Vries proposed that mutations (large, discontinuous variations) cause speciation (saltation). Hardy-Weinberg principle: allelic frequencies in a population are stable and constant from generation to generation; p + q = 1; p2 + 2pq + q2 = 1; the gene pool remains constant (genetic equilibrium). Factors that disturb equilibrium: gene migration or gene flow, genetic drift, mutation, genetic recombination and natural selection. Genetic drift is a change in allele frequency by chance; founder effect is when drift occurs in a small group of colonisers. Natural selection can be stabilising, directional or disruptive. Speciation involves reproductive isolation. Origin of man: Dryopithecus and Ramapithecus were hairy and walked like gorillas and chimpanzees; Australopithecus (about 2 mya) ate fruit; Homo habilis (about 2 mya; brain capacity 650 to 800 cc; probably did not eat meat); Homo erectus (about 1.5 mya; brain 900 cc; ate meat); Neanderthal man (brain 1400 cc; lived 100,000 to 40,000 years ago; used hides to protect their body and buried their dead); Homo sapiens arose in Africa about 75,000 to 10,000 years ago; modern Homo sapiens arose in the Middle East about 34,000 years ago. Cave art developed about 18,000 years ago; agriculture about 10,000 years ago.

📌

Origin of life

  • Chemical evolution preceded biological evolution
  • The Miller experiment formed amino acids from simple gases
  • First cells were anaerobic heterotrophs
🧠

Evidence and mechanism

  • Fossils, homology, analogy and biogeography support evolution
  • Natural selection acts on variation
  • Industrial melanism is a field example
🧬

Population genetics and humans

  • Hardy-Weinberg describes equilibrium
  • Drift, flow, mutation and selection disturb it
  • Human evolution proceeded from Australopithecus to Homo sapiens

lessons.title: Human Health and Disease
yt: class 12 biology human health disease immunity AIDS cancer drugs vaccination

blocks.x: Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being. Disease types: infectious (communicable) and non-infectious. Common diseases: typhoid (Salmonella typhi; Widal test), pneumonia (Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae), common cold (rhino viruses), malaria (Plasmodium; female Anopheles mosquito; Plasmodium falciparum causes malignant malaria; haemozoin released on rupture of RBCs causes fever and chill), amoebiasis (Entamoeba histolytica), ascariasis (Ascaris), filariasis (Wuchereria; elephantiasis), ringworm (Microsporum, Trichophyton, Epidermophyton) and dengue and chikungunya (Aedes mosquitoes). Immunity: innate immunity (barriers: physical, physiological, cellular and cytokine barriers) and acquired immunity (specific; primary and secondary responses; memory). Cells: B-lymphocytes produce antibodies (humoral immunity); T-lymphocytes mediate cell-mediated immunity. An antibody (immunoglobulin) has four peptide chains: two light and two heavy (H2L2); types are IgA, IgM, IgE, IgG. Active immunity is produced when the host is exposed to antigens (infection or vaccine) and takes time; passive immunity is by readymade antibodies (colostrum IgA; tetanus antitoxin). Vaccination uses weakened or inactivated pathogens, creating memory; Edward Jenner introduced vaccination for smallpox. Recombinant DNA technology has produced a hepatitis B vaccine from yeast. Allergy is an exaggerated response to allergens; IgE, histamine and serotonin are released from mast cells; antihistamine and adrenaline treat. Autoimmunity: the body attacks self cells (rheumatoid arthritis). The lymphoid organs: primary (bone marrow and thymus) and secondary (spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, Peyer's patches, MALT). Organ transplant rejection occurs due to the immune system. AIDS (Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome) is caused by HIV, a retrovirus with RNA genome. Transmission: sexual contact, contaminated blood and needles, and from infected mother to child; not by touch or sharing food. HIV infects helper T-cells (CD4 cells); in the macrophages the viral RNA gets converted to DNA by reverse transcriptase; the immunity falls and opportunistic infections such as tuberculosis occur. Diagnosis by ELISA. Treatment: anti-retroviral therapy, which is not a cure. NACO and NGOs spread awareness; National AIDS Control Organisation. Cancer: uncontrolled cell division; contact inhibition is lost; normal cells are checked by contact inhibition; benign tumours remain localised, while malignant tumours spread by metastasis. Carcinogens: physical (X-rays, gamma rays, UV), chemical (tobacco smoke) and biological (oncogenic viruses with cellular oncogenes or proto-oncogenes). Detection: biopsy, radiography, CT, MRI and antibodies against cancer-specific antigens. Treatment: surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy and immunotherapy with biological response modifiers such as alpha-interferon. Drugs and alcohol abuse: opioids (heroin or smack from morphine of Papaver somniferum, binds to opioid receptors), cannabinoids (marijuana, hashish, charas, ganja from Cannabis sativa), coca alkaloids (cocaine from Erythroxylum coca), and atropine and datura. Adolescence and drug abuse: peer pressure, curiosity and stress. Prevention: education, counselling and professional help.
Deep dive: Pathogens and diseases
Bacteria, viruses, protozoa, helminths and fungi cause disease. Vectors transmit malaria and dengue. Hygiene and vector control prevent them.
Deep dive: Immunity
Innate barriers and acquired B and T cell responses protect us. Vaccines build memory. Allergy and autoimmunity are errors of immunity.
Deep dive: AIDS, cancer and drugs
HIV destroys helper T cells. Cancer arises from uncontrolled growth and metastasis. Drug abuse harms health and needs prevention and counselling.
Hindi saransh
Manav swasthya aur rog: pratirakshan, tika, AIDS, kainsar aur nasha; HIV CD4 T-koshikaon par aakraman karta hai.
Remember: HIV is a retrovirus that infects helper T cells.

Human Health and Disease

Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being

Big idea

  • Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being

Read the full explanation

Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being. Disease types: infectious (communicable) and non-infectious. Common diseases: typhoid (Salmonella typhi; Widal test), pneumonia (Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae), common cold (rhino viruses), malaria (Plasmodium; female Anopheles mosquito; Plasmodium falciparum causes malignant malaria; haemozoin released on rupture of RBCs causes fever and chill), amoebiasis (Entamoeba histolytica), ascariasis (Ascaris), filariasis (Wuchereria; elephantiasis), ringworm (Microsporum, Trichophyton, Epidermophyton) and dengue and chikungunya (Aedes mosquitoes). Immunity: innate immunity (barriers: physical, physiological, cellular and cytokine barriers) and acquired immunity (specific; primary and secondary responses; memory). Cells: B-lymphocytes produce antibodies (humoral immunity); T-lymphocytes mediate cell-mediated immunity. An antibody (immunoglobulin) has four peptide chains: two light and two heavy (H2L2); types are IgA, IgM, IgE, IgG. Active immunity is produced when the host is exposed to antigens (infection or vaccine) and takes time; passive immunity is by readymade antibodies (colostrum IgA; tetanus antitoxin). Vaccination uses weakened or inactivated pathogens, creating memory; Edward Jenner introduced vaccination for smallpox. Recombinant DNA technology has produced a hepatitis B vaccine from yeast. Allergy is an exaggerated response to allergens; IgE, histamine and serotonin are released from mast cells; antihistamine and adrenaline treat. Autoimmunity: the body attacks self cells (rheumatoid arthritis). The lymphoid organs: primary (bone marrow and thymus) and secondary (spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, Peyer's patches, MALT). Organ transplant rejection occurs due to the immune system. AIDS (Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome) is caused by HIV, a retrovirus with RNA genome. Transmission: sexual contact, contaminated blood and needles, and from infected mother to child; not by touch or sharing food. HIV infects helper T-cells (CD4 cells); in the macrophages the viral RNA gets converted to DNA by reverse transcriptase; the immunity falls and opportunistic infections such as tuberculosis occur. Diagnosis by ELISA. Treatment: anti-retroviral therapy, which is not a cure. NACO and NGOs spread awareness; National AIDS Control Organisation. Cancer: uncontrolled cell division; contact inhibition is lost; normal cells are checked by contact inhibition; benign tumours remain localised, while malignant tumours spread by metastasis. Carcinogens: physical (X-rays, gamma rays, UV), chemical (tobacco smoke) and biological (oncogenic viruses with cellular oncogenes or proto-oncogenes). Detection: biopsy, radiography, CT, MRI and antibodies against cancer-specific antigens. Treatment: surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy and immunotherapy with biological response modifiers such as alpha-interferon. Drugs and alcohol abuse: opioids (heroin or smack from morphine of Papaver somniferum, binds to opioid receptors), cannabinoids (marijuana, hashish, charas, ganja from Cannabis sativa), coca alkaloids (cocaine from Erythroxylum coca), and atropine and datura. Adolescence and drug abuse: peer pressure, curiosity and stress. Prevention: education, counselling and professional help.

📌

Pathogens and diseases

  • Bacteria, viruses, protozoa, helminths and fungi cause disease
  • Vectors transmit malaria and dengue
  • Hygiene and vector control prevent them
🧠

Immunity

  • Innate barriers and acquired B and T cell responses protect us
  • Vaccines build memory
  • Allergy and autoimmunity are errors of immunity
🌟

AIDS, cancer and drugs

  • HIV destroys helper T cells
  • Cancer arises from uncontrolled growth and metastasis
  • Drug abuse harms health and needs prevention and counselling

lessons.title: Microbes in Human Welfare
yt: class 12 biology microbes human welfare fermentation sewage biogas biofertiliser

blocks.x: Microbes are present everywhere and are beneficial in household products, industrial products, sewage treatment, energy generation and as biocontrol agents and biofertilisers. Household: Lactobacillus (lactic acid bacteria, LAB) converts milk to curd; it increases vitamin B12 and checks disease-causing microbes in the stomach. Dough for idli and dosa is fermented by bacteria; the puffed-up appearance of bread is due to CO2 produced by the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae (baker's yeast). Toddy is made by fermentation of sap from palms. Cheese: Swiss cheese has large holes due to a large amount of CO2 produced by the bacterium Propionibacterium sharmanii; Roquefort cheese is ripened by growing a specific fungus (Penicillium roqueforti). Industrial products: fermentors (bioreactors) in industry. Beverages: Saccharomyces cerevisiae is used for fermenting malted cereals and fruit juices to produce wine, beer, whisky, brandy and rum (distillation gives whisky, brandy and rum; wine and beer are not distilled). Antibiotics: Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin from Penicillium notatum in 1928; Ernest Chain and Howard Florey established its effectiveness and the three got the Nobel Prize in 1945. Organic acids: Aspergillus niger (citric acid), Acetobacter aceti (acetic acid), Clostridium butylicum (butyric acid) and Lactobacillus (lactic acid). Enzymes: lipases in detergents, pectinases and proteases to clarify bottled juices, streptokinase produced by Streptococcus (clot buster, used to remove clots in the blood vessels of patients with myocardial infarction). Bioactive molecules: cyclosporin A (immunosuppressive agent in organ transplants; from the fungus Trichoderma polysporum), statins (blood cholesterol lowering agent; Monascus purpureus). Sewage treatment: primary treatment (physical removal of floating debris and grit by sedimentation, producing primary sludge and effluent) and secondary or biological treatment (the primary effluent is passed into aeration tanks where aerobic microbes form flocs; BOD (biochemical oxygen demand) reduces; the effluent is then passed into a settling tank where bacterial flocs sediment as activated sludge; part is used as inoculum and the remaining is passed into anaerobic sludge digesters, where anaerobic bacteria produce biogas (methane, hydrogen sulphide and carbon dioxide)). BOD measures organic matter; the greater the BOD, the more polluted the water. The Ganga Action Plan and Yamuna Action Plan. Biogas: methanogens (Methanobacterium) in the rumen of cattle and in anaerobic sludge produce methane; the starting material is cattle dung (gobar); the biogas plant has a digester and a gas holder; the technology was developed in India by IARI and KVIC. Biocontrol agents: Ladybird for aphids, dragonflies for mosquitoes, Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) for butterfly caterpillars, Trichoderma for plant pathogens, and Baculoviruses (Nucleopolyhedrovirus) for insects. Biofertilisers: bacteria (Rhizobium symbiotic with legume roots, Azospirillum and Azotobacter free-living nitrogen fixers), fungi (mycorrhiza such as Glomus, which absorb phosphorus), and cyanobacteria (Anabaena, Nostoc, Oscillatoria in paddy fields; Azolla with Anabaena).
Deep dive: Household and industrial
Microbes make curd, bread, cheese, wine and antibiotics. Fermentors scale production. Enzymes and bioactive molecules have medical uses.
Deep dive: Sewage and biogas
Primary and secondary treatment lower BOD. Methanogens in sludge digesters make biogas.
Deep dive: Biocontrol and biofertilisers
Microbial agents replace chemicals for pests and fertilisers. Rhizobium, mycorrhiza and cyanobacteria improve soil fertility.

Big idea

Read the full explanation

Microbes are present everywhere and are beneficial in household products, industrial products, sewage treatment, energy generation and as biocontrol agents and biofertilisers. Household: Lactobacillus (lactic acid bacteria, LAB) converts milk to curd; it increases vitamin B12 and checks disease-causing microbes in the stomach. Dough for idli and dosa is fermented by bacteria; the puffed-up appearance of bread is due to CO2 produced by the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae (baker's yeast). Toddy is made by fermentation of sap from palms. Cheese: Swiss cheese has large holes due to a large amount of CO2 produced by the bacterium Propionibacterium sharmanii; Roquefort cheese is ripened by growing a specific fungus (Penicillium roqueforti). Industrial products: fermentors (bioreactors) in industry. Beverages: Saccharomyces cerevisiae is used for fermenting malted cereals and fruit juices to produce wine, beer, whisky, brandy and rum (distillation gives whisky, brandy and rum; wine and beer are not distilled). Antibiotics: Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin from Penicillium notatum in 1928; Ernest Chain and Howard Florey established its effectiveness and the three got the Nobel Prize in 1945. Organic acids: Aspergillus niger (citric acid), Acetobacter aceti (acetic acid), Clostridium butylicum (butyric acid) and Lactobacillus (lactic acid). Enzymes: lipases in detergents, pectinases and proteases to clarify bottled juices, streptokinase produced by Streptococcus (clot buster, used to remove clots in the blood vessels of patients with myocardial infarction). Bioactive molecules: cyclosporin A (immunosuppressive agent in organ transplants; from the fungus Trichoderma polysporum), statins (blood cholesterol lowering agent; Monascus purpureus). Sewage treatment: primary treatment (physical removal of floating debris and grit by sedimentation, producing primary sludge and effluent) and secondary or biological treatment (the primary effluent is passed into aeration tanks where aerobic microbes form flocs; BOD (biochemical oxygen demand) reduces; the effluent is then passed into a settling tank where bacterial flocs sediment as activated sludge; part is used as inoculum and the remaining is passed into anaerobic sludge digesters, where anaerobic bacteria produce biogas (methane, hydrogen sulphide and carbon dioxide)). BOD measures organic matter; the greater the BOD, the more polluted the water. The Ganga Action Plan and Yamuna Action Plan. Biogas: methanogens (Methanobacterium) in the rumen of cattle and in anaerobic sludge produce methane; the starting material is cattle dung (gobar); the biogas plant has a digester and a gas holder; the technology was developed in India by IARI and KVIC. Biocontrol agents: Ladybird for aphids, dragonflies for mosquitoes, Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) for butterfly caterpillars, Trichoderma for plant pathogens, and Baculoviruses (Nucleopolyhedrovirus) for insects. Biofertilisers: bacteria (Rhizobium symbiotic with legume roots, Azospirillum and Azotobacter free-living nitrogen fixers), fungi (mycorrhiza such as Glomus, which absorb phosphorus), and cyanobacteria (Anabaena, Nostoc, Oscillatoria in paddy fields; Azolla with Anabaena).

💡

Household and industrial

  • Microbes make curd, bread, cheese, wine and antibiotics
  • Fermentors scale production
  • Enzymes and bioactive molecules have medical uses
🧠

Sewage and biogas

  • Primary and secondary treatment lower BOD
  • Methanogens in sludge digesters make biogas
🌟

Biocontrol and biofertilisers

  • Microbial agents replace chemicals for pests and fertilisers
  • Rhizobium, mycorrhiza and cyanobacteria improve soil fertility

lessons.title: Biotechnology: Principles and Processes
yt: class 12 biology biotechnology principles processes recombinant DNA restriction enzymes PCR vectors

blocks.x: Biotechnology is the use of living organisms or their products for human welfare. The European Federation of Biotechnology (EFB) defines it as the integration of natural science and organisms, cells, parts thereof and molecular analogues for products and services. The two core techniques are genetic engineering (altering the genetic material of organisms) and bioprocess engineering (maintenance of sterile conditions to allow growth of the desired microbe/eukaryotic cell in large quantities). Stanley Cohen and Herbert Boyer (1972) constructed the first recombinant DNA by linking an antibiotic resistance gene with a native plasmid of Salmonella typhimurium. Tools of rDNA technology: (1) Restriction enzymes: molecular scissors; Hind II was the first restriction endonuclease (isolated by Smith and Wilcox); EcoRI (from Escherichia coli RY 13) recognises the palindromic sequence GAATTC and cuts between G and A, creating sticky ends. Exonucleases remove nucleotides from the ends; endonucleases cut at specific positions within the DNA. Restriction enzymes were discovered by Arber; Werner Arber, Hamilton Smith and Daniel Nathans got the Nobel Prize. Palindromes read the same on both strands in the 5' to 3' direction. DNA ligase joins the cut fragments. (2) Cloning vectors: plasmids (circular extrachromosomal DNA), bacteriophages and Ti plasmid of Agrobacterium. Features of a vector: origin of replication (ori), selectable marker, cloning sites and small size. pBR322 was the first vector: ori, antibiotic resistance genes ampR and tetR, rop gene and unique cloning sites: BamHI, SalI, PstI, EcoRI, ClaI and HindIII. Selectable markers: ampicillin, chloramphenicol, tetracycline or kanamycin resistance. Insertional inactivation: in the pUC vectors, insertion of foreign DNA into the lacZ gene (beta-galactosidase) inactivates it; recombinant colonies are white and non-recombinants are blue in the presence of a chromogenic substrate. (3) Competent host: DNA is a hydrophilic molecule and cannot pass through membranes; the bacterial cells are made competent by treating with a specific concentration of divalent cations such as calcium, followed by heat shock at 42 degrees Celsius. Other methods: microinjection, biolistics (gene gun, using gold or tungsten particles) and disarmed pathogen vectors. Processes: isolation of DNA (lysozyme for bacteria, cellulase for plants, chitinase for fungus; RNase removes RNA, protease removes proteins; the DNA precipitates in chilled ethanol as fine threads), cutting by restriction enzymes, gel electrophoresis (agarose gel; DNA is negatively charged and moves towards the anode; ethidium bromide staining under UV light shows orange bands), elution, amplification by PCR (Kary Mullis; steps: denaturation at 94 degrees C, annealing with primers, and extension by Taq polymerase from Thermus aquaticus, which is thermostable), insertion into the vector, transformation, selection and expression. Bioreactors: stirred-tank reactors with an agitator system, an oxygen delivery system, foam control, temperature and pH control, and sampling ports; sparged stirred tank bioreactor. Downstream processing: separation and purification of the product, formulation with preservatives and clinical trials.
Deep dive: Tools
Restriction enzymes cut at palindromic sites and ligase joins fragments. Vectors carry the gene and have ori and selectable markers.
Deep dive: Process
DNA is isolated, cut, run on gels, ligated into a vector and transformed into competent cells. PCR amplifies DNA with Taq polymerase.
Deep dive: Scale-up
Bioreactors provide controlled conditions. Downstream processing purifies the product.

Read the full explanation

Biotechnology is the use of living organisms or their products for human welfare. The European Federation of Biotechnology (EFB) defines it as the integration of natural science and organisms, cells, parts thereof and molecular analogues for products and services. The two core techniques are genetic engineering (altering the genetic material of organisms) and bioprocess engineering (maintenance of sterile conditions to allow growth of the desired microbe/eukaryotic cell in large quantities). Stanley Cohen and Herbert Boyer (1972) constructed the first recombinant DNA by linking an antibiotic resistance gene with a native plasmid of Salmonella typhimurium. Tools of rDNA technology: (1) Restriction enzymes: molecular scissors; Hind II was the first restriction endonuclease (isolated by Smith and Wilcox); EcoRI (from Escherichia coli RY 13) recognises the palindromic sequence GAATTC and cuts between G and A, creating sticky ends. Exonucleases remove nucleotides from the ends; endonucleases cut at specific positions within the DNA. Restriction enzymes were discovered by Arber; Werner Arber, Hamilton Smith and Daniel Nathans got the Nobel Prize. Palindromes read the same on both strands in the 5' to 3' direction. DNA ligase joins the cut fragments. (2) Cloning vectors: plasmids (circular extrachromosomal DNA), bacteriophages and Ti plasmid of Agrobacterium. Features of a vector: origin of replication (ori), selectable marker, cloning sites and small size. pBR322 was the first vector: ori, antibiotic resistance genes ampR and tetR, rop gene and unique cloning sites: BamHI, SalI, PstI, EcoRI, ClaI and HindIII. Selectable markers: ampicillin, chloramphenicol, tetracycline or kanamycin resistance. Insertional inactivation: in the pUC vectors, insertion of foreign DNA into the lacZ gene (beta-galactosidase) inactivates it; recombinant colonies are white and non-recombinants are blue in the presence of a chromogenic substrate. (3) Competent host: DNA is a hydrophilic molecule and cannot pass through membranes; the bacterial cells are made competent by treating with a specific concentration of divalent cations such as calcium, followed by heat shock at 42 degrees Celsius. Other methods: microinjection, biolistics (gene gun, using gold or tungsten particles) and disarmed pathogen vectors. Processes: isolation of DNA (lysozyme for bacteria, cellulase for plants, chitinase for fungus; RNase removes RNA, protease removes proteins; the DNA precipitates in chilled ethanol as fine threads), cutting by restriction enzymes, gel electrophoresis (agarose gel; DNA is negatively charged and moves towards the anode; ethidium bromide staining under UV light shows orange bands), elution, amplification by PCR (Kary Mullis; steps: denaturation at 94 degrees C, annealing with primers, and extension by Taq polymerase from Thermus aquaticus, which is thermostable), insertion into the vector, transformation, selection and expression. Bioreactors: stirred-tank reactors with an agitator system, an oxygen delivery system, foam control, temperature and pH control, and sampling ports; sparged stirred tank bioreactor. Downstream processing: separation and purification of the product, formulation with preservatives and clinical trials.

📌

Tools

  • Restriction enzymes cut at palindromic sites and ligase joins fragments
  • Vectors carry the gene and have ori and selectable markers
🔄

Process

  • DNA is isolated, cut, run on gels, ligated into a vector and transformed into competent cells
  • PCR amplifies DNA with Taq polymerase
🌟

Scale-up

  • Bioreactors provide controlled conditions
  • Downstream processing purifies the product

lessons.title: Biotechnology and its Applications
yt: class 12 biology biotechnology applications Bt cotton insulin gene therapy transgenic RNAi biopiracy

blocks.x: Applications of biotechnology are in agriculture, medicine, environment and industry. Agriculture: GM (genetically modified) crops are produced to make crops more tolerant to abiotic stresses (cold, drought, salt, heat), reduce reliance on chemical pesticides (pest-resistant crops), reduce post-harvest losses, increase efficiency of mineral usage and enhance the nutritional value (Golden Rice, rich in Vitamin A). Bt toxin is produced by Bacillus thuringiensis; cry genes code for proteins that kill certain insects: cryIAc and cryIIAb control cotton bollworms, and cryIAb controls corn borer. The Bt toxin is present as an inactive protoxin; in the insect gut, the alkaline pH solubilises it and it binds to midgut epithelial cells creating pores that cause swelling and lysis, killing the insect. Bt cotton is a GM crop in India. RNA interference (RNAi): silencing of a specific mRNA due to a complementary dsRNA molecule that binds to and prevents translation; used against the nematode Meloidogyne incognita infecting tobacco roots, by producing sense and antisense RNA in the host to form dsRNA. Medicine: genetically engineered insulin: insulin consists of two short polypeptide chains, A and B (21 and 30 amino acids), linked by disulphide bridges; in humans it is synthesised as pro-insulin with a C peptide that is removed on maturation. In 1983, Eli Lilly produced two DNA sequences corresponding to A and B chains of human insulin and introduced them in E. coli to produce them separately, then combined by disulphide bonds (Humulin). Gene therapy: the first clinical gene therapy was given in 1990 to a four-year-old girl with adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency, which is caused by deletion of the ADA gene; lymphocytes from the patient's blood are grown in culture, a functional ADA cDNA (using a retroviral vector) is introduced and returned to the patient; permanent cure requires introducing genes from marrow cells. Molecular diagnosis: PCR to detect HIV, ELISA (antigen-antibody interaction) and DNA or RNA probe labelled with radioactive molecule (autoradiography) detect mutations. Transgenic animals: animals whose DNA has been manipulated to possess and express a foreign gene; mice, rats, rabbits, pigs, sheep, cows and fish are made. Uses: normal physiology and development, study of disease, biological products (alpha-1-antitrypsin for emphysema; the first transgenic cow Rosie (1997) produced human alpha-lactalbumin-enriched milk; 2.4 grams per litre), vaccine safety (polio vaccine tested in transgenic mice) and chemical safety testing (toxicity). Ethical issues: GEAC (Genetic Engineering Approval Committee) makes decisions regarding the validity of GM research and safety of introducing GM organisms for public services. Biopiracy: the use of bio-resources by multinational companies and other organisations without proper authorisation from the countries and people concerned; examples are patents on basmati rice, turmeric and neem; India has passed the Indian Patents Bill. Cry genes. Bioremediation. Biowar.
Deep dive: Agriculture
GM crops resist pests and stress. Bt cotton uses cry genes. RNAi silences genes in pests.
Deep dive: Medicine
Recombinant insulin and gene therapy treat disease. PCR and ELISA diagnose it. Transgenic animals make biological products.
Deep dive: Ethics
GEAC regulates GM organisms. Biopiracy raises concerns about patents on traditional resources.

🔑

Big idea

  • Applications of biotechnology are in agriculture, medicine, environment and industry
  • Agriculture: GM (genetically modified) crops are produced to make crops more tolerant to abiotic stresses (cold, drought, salt, heat), reduce…
  • Bt toxin is produced by Bacillus thuringiensis
  • Cry genes code for proteins that kill certain insects: cryIAc and cryIIAb control cotton bollworms, and cryIAb controls corn borer
Read the full explanation

Applications of biotechnology are in agriculture, medicine, environment and industry. Agriculture: GM (genetically modified) crops are produced to make crops more tolerant to abiotic stresses (cold, drought, salt, heat), reduce reliance on chemical pesticides (pest-resistant crops), reduce post-harvest losses, increase efficiency of mineral usage and enhance the nutritional value (Golden Rice, rich in Vitamin A). Bt toxin is produced by Bacillus thuringiensis; cry genes code for proteins that kill certain insects: cryIAc and cryIIAb control cotton bollworms, and cryIAb controls corn borer. The Bt toxin is present as an inactive protoxin; in the insect gut, the alkaline pH solubilises it and it binds to midgut epithelial cells creating pores that cause swelling and lysis, killing the insect. Bt cotton is a GM crop in India. RNA interference (RNAi): silencing of a specific mRNA due to a complementary dsRNA molecule that binds to and prevents translation; used against the nematode Meloidogyne incognita infecting tobacco roots, by producing sense and antisense RNA in the host to form dsRNA. Medicine: genetically engineered insulin: insulin consists of two short polypeptide chains, A and B (21 and 30 amino acids), linked by disulphide bridges; in humans it is synthesised as pro-insulin with a C peptide that is removed on maturation. In 1983, Eli Lilly produced two DNA sequences corresponding to A and B chains of human insulin and introduced them in E. coli to produce them separately, then combined by disulphide bonds (Humulin). Gene therapy: the first clinical gene therapy was given in 1990 to a four-year-old girl with adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency, which is caused by deletion of the ADA gene; lymphocytes from the patient's blood are grown in culture, a functional ADA cDNA (using a retroviral vector) is introduced and returned to the patient; permanent cure requires introducing genes from marrow cells. Molecular diagnosis: PCR to detect HIV, ELISA (antigen-antibody interaction) and DNA or RNA probe labelled with radioactive molecule (autoradiography) detect mutations. Transgenic animals: animals whose DNA has been manipulated to possess and express a foreign gene; mice, rats, rabbits, pigs, sheep, cows and fish are made. Uses: normal physiology and development, study of disease, biological products (alpha-1-antitrypsin for emphysema; the first transgenic cow Rosie (1997) produced human alpha-lactalbumin-enriched milk; 2.4 grams per litre), vaccine safety (polio vaccine tested in transgenic mice) and chemical safety testing (toxicity). Ethical issues: GEAC (Genetic Engineering Approval Committee) makes decisions regarding the validity of GM research and safety of introducing GM organisms for public services. Biopiracy: the use of bio-resources by multinational companies and other organisations without proper authorisation from the countries and people concerned; examples are patents on basmati rice, turmeric and neem; India has passed the Indian Patents Bill. Cry genes. Bioremediation. Biowar.

📌

Agriculture

  • GM crops resist pests and stress
  • Bt cotton uses cry genes
  • RNAi silences genes in pests
🧠

Medicine

  • Recombinant insulin and gene therapy treat disease
  • PCR and ELISA diagnose it
  • Transgenic animals make biological products
🌟

Ethics

  • GEAC regulates GM organisms
  • Biopiracy raises concerns about patents on traditional resources
