lessons.title: Organisms and Populations
yt: class 12 biology organisms populations adaptation population interactions growth curve

blocks.x: Ecology is the study of interactions among organisms and between the organism and its physical (abiotic) environment. Levels of biological organisation: organisms, populations, communities, ecosystems, biomes and the biosphere. Major abiotic factors are temperature, water, light and soil. Responses to abiotic factors: regulate (thermoregulation and osmoregulation: birds and mammals), conform (most animals and plants), migrate (Siberian cranes to Keoladeo National Park, Bharatpur) and suspend (hibernation, aestivation, diapause, spores and seeds). Adaptations: kangaroo rat in North American deserts meets its water needs by internal fat oxidation and concentrates its urine; desert plants have a thick cuticle and sunken stomata, and CAM photosynthesis; Opuntia has no leaves and spines instead; mammals from colder climates have shorter ears and limbs to minimise heat loss (Allen's rule); in the polar seas aquatic mammals have a thick layer of fat (blubber). Many fish thrive in Antarctic waters at sub-zero temperature. Organisms in high altitudes face altitude sickness (low atmospheric pressure, body response includes increased red blood cell production, decreased binding capacity of haemoglobin and increased breathing rate). Water: stenothermal organisms tolerate a narrow range of temperature; eurythermal tolerate a wide range; stenohaline tolerate a narrow range of salinity; euryhaline a wide one. Behaviour: desert lizards bask in the sun and move into shade. Population attributes: birth rate (natality), death rate (mortality), sex ratio, age distribution (pre-reproductive, reproductive and post-reproductive; age pyramids may be expanding, stable or declining) and population density. Population size is measured by the number, biomass or percent cover; Pt+1 = Pt + [(N + I) - (M + E)], where N is natality, M is mortality, I is immigration and E is emigration. Growth models: exponential (J-shaped) growth: dN/dt = rN; N(t) = N0 e^rt; where r is the intrinsic rate of natural increase. Logistic (S-shaped) growth with limited resources: dN/dt = rN (K - N)/K; K is the carrying capacity. Life history variation: organisms evolve to maximise their reproductive fitness (r-selected and K-selected). Population interactions: mutualism (+ +; lichens, mycorrhiza, fig and wasp, orchid Ophrys and bee through sexual deceit), competition (- -; Gause's competitive exclusion principle: two closely related species competing for the same resources cannot coexist indefinitely; resource partitioning enables coexistence, as with MacArthur's warblers), predation (+ -; keeps prey populations in check; cactus Opuntia controlled by the cactus-feeding predator Cactoblastis in Australia), parasitism (+ -; ectoparasites and endoparasites, brood parasitism of koel and crow), commensalism (+ 0; epiphytes on mango, barnacles on whales, cattle egret and cattle) and amensalism (- 0; Penicillium and bacteria). Prey defences: camouflage, toxic chemicals (Monarch butterfly), thorns and spines. Plant defences: nicotine, caffeine, quinine, strychnine and opium; Calotropis produces poisonous cardiac glycosides.
Deep dive: Responses and adaptations
Organisms regulate, conform, migrate or suspend. Adaptations suit deserts, cold and altitude.
Deep dive: Population attributes
Birth, death, immigration and emigration change population size. Age pyramids show structure.
Deep dive: Growth and interactions
Exponential and logistic growth models describe growth. Species interactions include mutualism, competition, predation and parasitism.
Hindi saransh
Jeev aur jansankhya: anukoolan, jansankhya vriddhi (J aur S vakra), vahan kshamta aur jeev-jeev antarkriyayen.

Read the full explanation

Ecology is the study of interactions among organisms and between the organism and its physical (abiotic) environment. Levels of biological organisation: organisms, populations, communities, ecosystems, biomes and the biosphere. Major abiotic factors are temperature, water, light and soil. Responses to abiotic factors: regulate (thermoregulation and osmoregulation: birds and mammals), conform (most animals and plants), migrate (Siberian cranes to Keoladeo National Park, Bharatpur) and suspend (hibernation, aestivation, diapause, spores and seeds). Adaptations: kangaroo rat in North American deserts meets its water needs by internal fat oxidation and concentrates its urine; desert plants have a thick cuticle and sunken stomata, and CAM photosynthesis; Opuntia has no leaves and spines instead; mammals from colder climates have shorter ears and limbs to minimise heat loss (Allen's rule); in the polar seas aquatic mammals have a thick layer of fat (blubber). Many fish thrive in Antarctic waters at sub-zero temperature. Organisms in high altitudes face altitude sickness (low atmospheric pressure, body response includes increased red blood cell production, decreased binding capacity of haemoglobin and increased breathing rate). Water: stenothermal organisms tolerate a narrow range of temperature; eurythermal tolerate a wide range; stenohaline tolerate a narrow range of salinity; euryhaline a wide one. Behaviour: desert lizards bask in the sun and move into shade. Population attributes: birth rate (natality), death rate (mortality), sex ratio, age distribution (pre-reproductive, reproductive and post-reproductive; age pyramids may be expanding, stable or declining) and population density. Population size is measured by the number, biomass or percent cover; Pt+1 = Pt + [(N + I) - (M + E)], where N is natality, M is mortality, I is immigration and E is emigration. Growth models: exponential (J-shaped) growth: dN/dt = rN; N(t) = N0 e^rt; where r is the intrinsic rate of natural increase. Logistic (S-shaped) growth with limited resources: dN/dt = rN (K - N)/K; K is the carrying capacity. Life history variation: organisms evolve to maximise their reproductive fitness (r-selected and K-selected). Population interactions: mutualism (+ +; lichens, mycorrhiza, fig and wasp, orchid Ophrys and bee through sexual deceit), competition (- -; Gause's competitive exclusion principle: two closely related species competing for the same resources cannot coexist indefinitely; resource partitioning enables coexistence, as with MacArthur's warblers), predation (+ -; keeps prey populations in check; cactus Opuntia controlled by the cactus-feeding predator Cactoblastis in Australia), parasitism (+ -; ectoparasites and endoparasites, brood parasitism of koel and crow), commensalism (+ 0; epiphytes on mango, barnacles on whales, cattle egret and cattle) and amensalism (- 0; Penicillium and bacteria). Prey defences: camouflage, toxic chemicals (Monarch butterfly), thorns and spines. Plant defences: nicotine, caffeine, quinine, strychnine and opium; Calotropis produces poisonous cardiac glycosides.

📌

Responses and adaptations

  • Organisms regulate, conform, migrate or suspend
  • Adaptations suit deserts, cold and altitude
🧠

Population attributes

  • Birth, death, immigration and emigration change population size
  • Age pyramids show structure
🌟

Growth and interactions

  • Exponential and logistic growth models describe growth
  • Species interactions include mutualism, competition, predation and parasitism
🎯 Remember exponential growth is J-shaped; logistic is S-shaped with carrying capacity K.

yt: class 12 biology ecosystem productivity decomposition energy flow nutrient cycling succession

blocks.x: An ecosystem is a functional unit of nature where living organisms interact among themselves and with the surrounding physical environment. Ecosystem categories: terrestrial (forest, grassland, desert) and aquatic (pond, wetland, lake, river, estuary). Structure: species composition and stratification (vertical distribution of different species occupying different levels, such as trees on top, shrubs, herbs). Pond ecosystem: abiotic components (water, light, temperature, inorganic and organic substances), producers (phytoplankton, algae, macrophytes), consumers (zooplankton, fish) and decomposers (bacteria, fungi). Productivity: primary production is the amount of biomass or organic matter produced per unit area over a time period by plants during photosynthesis. Gross primary productivity (GPP) is the rate of production of organic matter during photosynthesis; net primary productivity (NPP) = GPP - R (respiration losses). Secondary productivity is the rate of formation of new organic matter by consumers. Primary productivity depends on the plant species, environmental factors and nutrient availability. Annual NPP of the whole biosphere is about 170 billion tons (dry weight) of organic matter; the productivity of oceans is only 55 billion tons though they cover 70 percent of the area, because of limited light penetration. Decomposition: fragmentation by detritivores (earthworm), leaching, catabolism by bacterial and fungal enzymes, humification (accumulation of humus, a dark amorphous substance resistant to microbial action, acting as a reservoir of nutrients) and mineralisation. Decomposition is oxygen-requiring; rate is controlled by chemical composition of detritus (lignin and chitin slow; nitrogen and sugars fast) and climatic factors (temperature and soil moisture; warm and moist environment favours it, low temperature and anaerobiosis inhibit it). Energy flow: the sun is the source; only 2 to 10 percent of the PAR (photosynthetically active radiation, 50 percent of incident solar radiation) is captured by plants. Producers, primary consumers (herbivores), secondary consumers (carnivores) and tertiary consumers form trophic levels. Food chains: the grazing food chain (GFC) begins with producers and the detritus food chain (DFC) begins with dead organic matter; in aquatic ecosystems the GFC is the major conduit of energy flow, whereas in terrestrial ecosystems the DFC is. The 10 percent law (Lindeman): only about 10 percent of energy is transferred from one trophic level to the next. Food web is a network of interconnecting food chains. Ecological pyramids: pyramid of numbers, biomass and energy; the pyramid of energy is always upright; the pyramid of numbers and biomass can be inverted (biomass pyramid inverted in the sea; numbers pyramid inverted in a tree ecosystem). Limitations: it does not account for the same species at two trophic levels and saprophytes. Ecological succession: gradual and fairly predictable change in the species composition of a given area. Primary succession starts on a barren area (bare rock) with pioneer species; the pioneer in a lithosere is lichens; the seral stages lead to a climax community. Hydrarch succession takes place in wetter areas, and xerarch in dry areas. Secondary succession begins in areas where natural biotic communities have been destroyed, such as abandoned farm lands, burned or cut forests; faster. Nutrient cycling: carbon cycle (about 71 percent of carbon is dissolved in oceans; atmosphere has 1 percent; fossil fuels; the human activities add CO2), phosphorus cycle (no gaseous exchange; rocks are the reservoir), and nutrient cycling is gaseous or sedimentary. Ecosystem services: purification of air and water, mitigation of droughts and floods, nutrient cycling, pollination; Robert Costanza and colleagues estimated their value at US$33 trillion a year.
Deep dive: Productivity and decomposition
GPP minus respiration gives NPP. Decomposition recycles nutrients through fragmentation, leaching, catabolism, humification and mineralisation.
Deep dive: Energy flow
Energy flows one way through trophic levels with 10 percent transfer. Grazing and detritus food chains form food webs. Pyramids show the structure.
Deep dive: Succession and cycles
Succession leads to a climax community. Carbon and phosphorus cycle through reservoirs. Ecosystem services have great value.

Read the full explanation

An ecosystem is a functional unit of nature where living organisms interact among themselves and with the surrounding physical environment. Ecosystem categories: terrestrial (forest, grassland, desert) and aquatic (pond, wetland, lake, river, estuary). Structure: species composition and stratification (vertical distribution of different species occupying different levels, such as trees on top, shrubs, herbs). Pond ecosystem: abiotic components (water, light, temperature, inorganic and organic substances), producers (phytoplankton, algae, macrophytes), consumers (zooplankton, fish) and decomposers (bacteria, fungi). Productivity: primary production is the amount of biomass or organic matter produced per unit area over a time period by plants during photosynthesis. Gross primary productivity (GPP) is the rate of production of organic matter during photosynthesis; net primary productivity (NPP) = GPP - R (respiration losses). Secondary productivity is the rate of formation of new organic matter by consumers. Primary productivity depends on the plant species, environmental factors and nutrient availability. Annual NPP of the whole biosphere is about 170 billion tons (dry weight) of organic matter; the productivity of oceans is only 55 billion tons though they cover 70 percent of the area, because of limited light penetration. Decomposition: fragmentation by detritivores (earthworm), leaching, catabolism by bacterial and fungal enzymes, humification (accumulation of humus, a dark amorphous substance resistant to microbial action, acting as a reservoir of nutrients) and mineralisation. Decomposition is oxygen-requiring; rate is controlled by chemical composition of detritus (lignin and chitin slow; nitrogen and sugars fast) and climatic factors (temperature and soil moisture; warm and moist environment favours it, low temperature and anaerobiosis inhibit it). Energy flow: the sun is the source; only 2 to 10 percent of the PAR (photosynthetically active radiation, 50 percent of incident solar radiation) is captured by plants. Producers, primary consumers (herbivores), secondary consumers (carnivores) and tertiary consumers form trophic levels. Food chains: the grazing food chain (GFC) begins with producers and the detritus food chain (DFC) begins with dead organic matter; in aquatic ecosystems the GFC is the major conduit of energy flow, whereas in terrestrial ecosystems the DFC is. The 10 percent law (Lindeman): only about 10 percent of energy is transferred from one trophic level to the next. Food web is a network of interconnecting food chains. Ecological pyramids: pyramid of numbers, biomass and energy; the pyramid of energy is always upright; the pyramid of numbers and biomass can be inverted (biomass pyramid inverted in the sea; numbers pyramid inverted in a tree ecosystem). Limitations: it does not account for the same species at two trophic levels and saprophytes. Ecological succession: gradual and fairly predictable change in the species composition of a given area. Primary succession starts on a barren area (bare rock) with pioneer species; the pioneer in a lithosere is lichens; the seral stages lead to a climax community. Hydrarch succession takes place in wetter areas, and xerarch in dry areas. Secondary succession begins in areas where natural biotic communities have been destroyed, such as abandoned farm lands, burned or cut forests; faster. Nutrient cycling: carbon cycle (about 71 percent of carbon is dissolved in oceans; atmosphere has 1 percent; fossil fuels; the human activities add CO2), phosphorus cycle (no gaseous exchange; rocks are the reservoir), and nutrient cycling is gaseous or sedimentary. Ecosystem services: purification of air and water, mitigation of droughts and floods, nutrient cycling, pollination; Robert Costanza and colleagues estimated their value at US$33 trillion a year.

📌

Productivity and decomposition

  • GPP minus respiration gives NPP
  • Decomposition recycles nutrients through fragmentation, leaching, catabolism, humification and mineralisation
🔄

Energy flow

  • Energy flows one way through trophic levels with 10 percent transfer
  • Grazing and detritus food chains form food webs
  • Pyramids show the structure
🔄

Succession and cycles

  • Succession leads to a climax community
  • Carbon and phosphorus cycle through reservoirs
  • Ecosystem services have great value

lessons.title: Biodiversity and Conservation
yt: class 12 biology biodiversity conservation hotspots extinction patterns in situ ex situ

blocks.x: Biodiversity is the variety of life on Earth; Edward Wilson popularised the term. Levels: genetic diversity (a species with variation in genes; India has more than 50,000 genetically different strains of rice and 1,000 varieties of mango), species diversity (Western Ghats have more amphibian species than the Eastern Ghats) and ecological diversity (India has deserts, rain forests, mangroves, coral reefs, wetlands, estuaries and alpine meadows, hence a greater ecosystem diversity than Norway). Globally about 1.5 million species have been described; Robert May estimated 7 million; more than 70 percent of the species recorded are animals, of which insects are more than 70 percent; plants (including algae, fungi, bryophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms) constitute no more than 22 percent. India has 2.4 percent of the world's land area but 8.1 percent of global species diversity; it is one of the 12 mega-diversity countries. Patterns of biodiversity: latitudinal gradient (species diversity decreases from equator to poles; Colombia has 1,400 bird species, New York 105 and Greenland 56; India has 1,200). Reasons: the tropics have been undisturbed for millions of years (more time for species diversification), stable and predictable climate promotes niche specialisation, and more solar energy produces higher productivity. Species-area relationship (Alexander von Humboldt): within a region, species richness increases with increasing explored area but only up to a limit; log S = log C + Z log A, where S is species richness, A is area, Z is the slope of the line (regression coefficient), and C is the Y-intercept; the value of Z lies between 0.1 and 0.2 irrespective of the taxonomic group or region; for very large areas such as continents, the slope is steeper (0.6 to 1.2). Importance: the loss of biodiversity leads to decline in plant production, lowered resistance to environmental perturbations and increased variability in ecosystem processes. Stability: David Tilman showed that plots with more species showed less year-to-year variation in total biomass. Paul Ehrlich's rivet popper hypothesis. Loss of biodiversity: 784 extinctions (359 invertebrates, 338 vertebrates and 87 plants) in the last 500 years (the Dodo, quagga, thylacine, Steller's sea cow, three subspecies of tiger: Bali, Javan and Caspian). The Amazon rainforest is called the lungs of the planet. The Sixth Extinction is in progress. Causes of loss, the evil quartet: habitat loss and fragmentation (the most important cause), over-exploitation, alien species invasions (Nile perch in Lake Victoria; water hyacinth; Parthenium; African catfish Clarias gariepinus) and co-extinctions. Conservation: in situ (on site): national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, biosphere reserves, sacred groves and biodiversity hotspots. Hotspots are regions with very high levels of species richness and high endemism; there are 34 hotspots in the world; three in India: Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma and the Himalaya. Ex situ (off site): zoological parks, botanical gardens, wildlife safari parks, cryopreservation (gene banks) and seed banks. The Convention on Biological Diversity (Rio de Janeiro Earth Summit 1992), the World Summit on Sustainable Development (Johannesburg, 2002) and the Biological Diversity Act (India, 2002).
Deep dive: Levels and patterns
Genetic, species and ecological diversity make up biodiversity. Diversity is highest in the tropics and rises with area.
Deep dive: Loss
Habitat loss, over-exploitation, alien species and co-extinctions drive extinction.
Deep dive: Conservation
In situ methods protect habitats; ex situ methods protect species outside. Hotspots set conservation priorities.
Hindi saransh
Jaiv vividhta aur sanrakshan: sthaniya aur bahari sanrakshan, garm sthal (hotspot), vilupti ke karan (evil quartet).
Remember: evil quartet = habitat loss, over-exploitation, alien invasions, co-extinctions.

Visual lesson

Biodiversity and Conservation

Biodiversity is the variety of life on Earth

Flat concept map (2D)

Hotspots34 world
Species described1.5 million
India2.4% land
🔑

Big idea

  • Biodiversity is the variety of life on Earth
  • Edward Wilson popularised the term
  • Levels: genetic diversity (a species with variation in genes
  • India has more than 50,000 genetically different strains of rice and 1,000 varieties of mango), species diversity (Western Ghats have more amphibian…
Read the full explanation

Biodiversity is the variety of life on Earth; Edward Wilson popularised the term. Levels: genetic diversity (a species with variation in genes; India has more than 50,000 genetically different strains of rice and 1,000 varieties of mango), species diversity (Western Ghats have more amphibian species than the Eastern Ghats) and ecological diversity (India has deserts, rain forests, mangroves, coral reefs, wetlands, estuaries and alpine meadows, hence a greater ecosystem diversity than Norway). Globally about 1.5 million species have been described; Robert May estimated 7 million; more than 70 percent of the species recorded are animals, of which insects are more than 70 percent; plants (including algae, fungi, bryophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms) constitute no more than 22 percent. India has 2.4 percent of the world's land area but 8.1 percent of global species diversity; it is one of the 12 mega-diversity countries. Patterns of biodiversity: latitudinal gradient (species diversity decreases from equator to poles; Colombia has 1,400 bird species, New York 105 and Greenland 56; India has 1,200). Reasons: the tropics have been undisturbed for millions of years (more time for species diversification), stable and predictable climate promotes niche specialisation, and more solar energy produces higher productivity. Species-area relationship (Alexander von Humboldt): within a region, species richness increases with increasing explored area but only up to a limit; log S = log C + Z log A, where S is species richness, A is area, Z is the slope of the line (regression coefficient), and C is the Y-intercept; the value of Z lies between 0.1 and 0.2 irrespective of the taxonomic group or region; for very large areas such as continents, the slope is steeper (0.6 to 1.2). Importance: the loss of biodiversity leads to decline in plant production, lowered resistance to environmental perturbations and increased variability in ecosystem processes. Stability: David Tilman showed that plots with more species showed less year-to-year variation in total biomass. Paul Ehrlich's rivet popper hypothesis. Loss of biodiversity: 784 extinctions (359 invertebrates, 338 vertebrates and 87 plants) in the last 500 years (the Dodo, quagga, thylacine, Steller's sea cow, three subspecies of tiger: Bali, Javan and Caspian). The Amazon rainforest is called the lungs of the planet. The Sixth Extinction is in progress. Causes of loss, the evil quartet: habitat loss and fragmentation (the most important cause), over-exploitation, alien species invasions (Nile perch in Lake Victoria; water hyacinth; Parthenium; African catfish Clarias gariepinus) and co-extinctions. Conservation: in situ (on site): national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, biosphere reserves, sacred groves and biodiversity hotspots. Hotspots are regions with very high levels of species richness and high endemism; there are 34 hotspots in the world; three in India: Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma and the Himalaya. Ex situ (off site): zoological parks, botanical gardens, wildlife safari parks, cryopreservation (gene banks) and seed banks. The Convention on Biological Diversity (Rio de Janeiro Earth Summit 1992), the World Summit on Sustainable Development (Johannesburg, 2002) and the Biological Diversity Act (India, 2002).

📌

Levels and patterns

  • Genetic, species and ecological diversity make up biodiversity
  • Diversity is highest in the tropics and rises with area
🧠

Loss

  • Habitat loss, over-exploitation, alien species and co-extinctions drive extinction
🌟

Conservation

  • In situ methods protect habitats
  • Ex situ methods protect species outside
  • Hotspots set conservation priorities
🎯 Remember evil quartet = habitat loss, over-exploitation, alien invasions, co-extinctions.

blocks.x: Management is the process of working with and through others to achieve organisational objectives efficiently and effectively. Effectiveness means completing the task on time (doing the right thing); efficiency means doing the task correctly with minimum cost (doing things right). Characteristics: management is a goal-oriented process, pervasive, multidimensional, a continuous process, a group activity and a dynamic function; it is intangible. Objectives: organisational (survival, profit, growth), social (benefit to society, use of eco-friendly methods, creating employment) and personal (needs of employees: financial benefits, social recognition, personal growth). Importance: achieving group goals, increasing efficiency, creating a dynamic organisation, achieving personal objectives and development of society. Management as science: systematised body of knowledge, principles based on repeated experimentation, but principles lack universal validity; management as art: theoretical knowledge, personalised application, creativity, based on practice and creativity; management as profession: well-defined body of knowledge, restricted entry, professional association (such as AIMA, All India Management Association) and ethical code, service motive; management is not yet a full profession. Levels of management: top level (board of directors, CEO; determine objectives and policies, integrate and coordinate), middle level (departmental heads, divisional managers; interpret policies and coordinate between top and lower levels) and supervisory or operational level (foremen, supervisors; direct workers' efforts). Functions of management: planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling. Planning: deciding in advance what to do; organising: assigning duties, grouping tasks; staffing: filling positions with the right people; directing: motivating, leading, communicating and supervising; controlling: comparing actual performance with standards and correcting deviations. Coordination is the force that binds all functions; it is the essence of management. Features of coordination: integrates group efforts, ensures unity of action, a continuous process, an all-pervasive function, is the responsibility of all managers and a deliberate function. It is needed due to the size and complexity of the organisation. Importance of coordination: growth in size, functional differentiation, specialisation. Henri Fayol is regarded as the father of general management theory. Peter Drucker said that management is a multi-purpose organ that manages business, managers and workers. Key terms: management as an activity, as a group of people and as a discipline. Management and administration: administration is the determination of objectives and policies at top level, while management implements them; however, the two are used interchangeably. Managers in the modern context handle change and technology.
Deep dive: Concept
Management gets work done through others. Efficiency and effectiveness together make it successful. It is goal oriented, pervasive and continuous.
Deep dive: Nature
Management has aspects of science, art and profession. Levels are top, middle and operational. Functions are planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling.
Deep dive: Coordination
Coordination integrates the efforts of different departments. It is the essence of management and the responsibility of all managers.

Importance: achieving group goals, increasing efficiency, creating a dynamic organisation, achieving personal objectives and development of society. Management as science: systematised body of knowledge, principles based on repeated experimentation, but principles lack universal validity; management as art: theoretical knowledge, personalised application, creativity, based on practice and creativity; management as profession: well-defined body of knowledge, restricted entry, professional association (such as AIMA, All India Management Association) and ethical code, service motive; management is not yet a full profession. Levels of management: top level (board of directors, CEO; determine objectives and policies, integrate and coordinate), middle level (departmental heads, divisional managers; interpret policies and coordinate between top and lower levels) and supervisory or operational level (foremen, supervisors; direct workers' efforts). Functions of management: planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling. Planning: deciding in advance what to do; organising: assigning duties, grouping tasks; staffing: filling positions with the right people; directing: motivating, leading, communicating and supervising; controlling: comparing actual performance with standards and correcting deviations. Coordination is the force that binds all functions; it is the essence of management. Features of coordination: integrates group efforts, ensures unity of action, a continuous process, an all-pervasive function, is the responsibility of all managers and a deliberate function. It is needed due to the size and complexity of the organisation. Importance of coordination: growth in size, functional differentiation, specialisation. Henri Fayol is regarded as the father of general management theory. Peter Drucker said that management is a multi-purpose organ that manages business, managers and workers. Key terms: management as an activity, as a group of people and as a discipline. Management and administration: administration is the determination of objectives and policies at top level, while management implements them; however, the two are used interchangeably. Managers in the modern context handle change and technology.

📘

Concept

  • Management gets work done through others
  • Efficiency and effectiveness together make it successful
  • It is goal oriented, pervasive and continuous
🧠

Nature

  • Management has aspects of science, art and profession
  • Levels are top, middle and operational
  • Functions are planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling
🌟

Coordination

  • Coordination integrates the efforts of different departments
  • It is the essence of management and the responsibility of all managers

lessons.title: Principles of Management
yt: class 12 business studies principles of management fayol taylor scientific management

blocks.x: Principles of management are broad and general guidelines for decision making and behaviour. Features: universal applicability, general guidelines, formed by practice and experimentation, flexible, mainly behavioural, cause-effect relationship and contingent. Significance: providing managers with useful insights into reality, optimum utilisation of resources and effective administration, scientific decisions, meeting changing environment requirements, fulfilling social responsibility and management training and research. Henri Fayol (1841 to 1925) was a French mining engineer; his book is General and Industrial Management (1916); he identified fourteen principles: (1) Division of work (specialisation), (2) Authority and responsibility (authority is the right to give orders; responsibility the obligation; they go together), (3) Discipline (obedience to rules), (4) Unity of command (one boss for one subordinate), (5) Unity of direction (one head and one plan for a group of activities with the same objective), (6) Subordination of individual interest to general interest, (7) Remuneration of employees (fair), (8) Centralisation and decentralisation, (9) Scalar chain (formal lines of authority from highest to lowest; Gang plank is the shortcut or direct contact in emergencies), (10) Order (right place for people and things), (11) Equity (fairness; kindness and justice), (12) Stability of personnel, (13) Initiative and (14) Esprit de corps (union is strength; teamwork). Fayol's principles are flexible; his five functions are forecasting, planning, organising, commanding and controlling, and he divided business activities into technical, commercial, financial, security, accounting and managerial. F.W. Taylor (1856 to 1915), the father of scientific management, wrote The Principles of Scientific Management (1911). His principles: (1) Science, not rule of thumb, (2) Harmony, not discord, (3) Cooperation, not individualism, (4) Development of each and every person to his or her greatest efficiency and prosperity. Techniques of scientific management: (a) Functional foremanship: eight specialists, four in the planning department (route clerk, instruction card clerk, time and cost clerk, disciplinarian) and four in the production department (speed boss, gang boss, repair boss, inspector); (b) Standardisation and simplification of work (standardisation of processes, raw materials, product, machines and working conditions; simplification eliminates unnecessary diversity); (c) Method study (one best way); (d) Motion study (movements of workers; unnecessary movements eliminated); (e) Time study (standard time for each task) and (f) Fatigue study (rest intervals); (g) Differential piece wage system (higher rate for efficient workers; for example, Rs 10 per piece for 100 pieces or more and Rs 5 for fewer). Taylor's mental revolution means a change in attitude of workers and management towards each other: both should focus on increasing the surplus. Taylor and Fayol compared: Fayol gave general management at top level and is a practitioner; Taylor focused on shop floor and was a scientist; Fayol's principles apply universally, Taylor's are specific. Both complement each other.
Deep dive: Principles
Management principles are universal, flexible guidelines. They help in decisions, resource use and social responsibility.
Deep dive: Fayol
Fayol gave fourteen principles for general management such as unity of command, scalar chain and esprit de corps.
Deep dive: Taylor
Taylor proposed scientific management based on science, harmony, cooperation and development. His techniques include time and motion study.

Prabandhan ke siddhant: Fayol ke 14 siddhant aur Taylor ka vaigyanik prabandhan; mansik kranti.

🔑

Big idea

  • Principles of management are broad and general guidelines for decision making and behaviour
  • Features: universal applicability, general guidelines, formed by practice and experimentation, flexible, mainly behavioural, cause-effect…
  • Significance: providing managers with useful insights into reality, optimum utilisation of resources and effective administration, scientific…

Read the full explanation

Principles of management are broad and general guidelines for decision making and behaviour. Features: universal applicability, general guidelines, formed by practice and experimentation, flexible, mainly behavioural, cause-effect relationship and contingent. Significance: providing managers with useful insights into reality, optimum utilisation of resources and effective administration, scientific decisions, meeting changing environment requirements, fulfilling social responsibility and management training and research. Henri Fayol (1841 to 1925) was a French mining engineer; his book is General and Industrial Management (1916); he identified fourteen principles: (1) Division of work (specialisation), (2) Authority and responsibility (authority is the right to give orders; responsibility the obligation; they go together), (3) Discipline (obedience to rules), (4) Unity of command (one boss for one subordinate), (5) Unity of direction (one head and one plan for a group of activities with the same objective), (6) Subordination of individual interest to general interest, (7) Remuneration of employees (fair), (8) Centralisation and decentralisation, (9) Scalar chain (formal lines of authority from highest to lowest; Gang plank is the shortcut or direct contact in emergencies), (10) Order (right place for people and things), (11) Equity (fairness; kindness and justice), (12) Stability of personnel, (13) Initiative and (14) Esprit de corps (union is strength; teamwork). Fayol's principles are flexible; his five functions are forecasting, planning, organising, commanding and controlling, and he divided business activities into technical, commercial, financial, security, accounting and managerial. F.W. Taylor (1856 to 1915), the father of scientific management, wrote The Principles of Scientific Management (1911). His principles: (1) Science, not rule of thumb, (2) Harmony, not discord, (3) Cooperation, not individualism, (4) Development of each and every person to his or her greatest efficiency and prosperity. Techniques of scientific management: (a) Functional foremanship: eight specialists, four in the planning department (route clerk, instruction card clerk, time and cost clerk, disciplinarian) and four in the production department (speed boss, gang boss, repair boss, inspector); (b) Standardisation and simplification of work (standardisation of processes, raw materials, product, machines and working conditions; simplification eliminates unnecessary diversity); (c) Method study (one best way); (d) Motion study (movements of workers; unnecessary movements eliminated); (e) Time study (standard time for each task) and (f) Fatigue study (rest intervals); (g) Differential piece wage system (higher rate for efficient workers; for example, Rs 10 per piece for 100 pieces or more and Rs 5 for fewer). Taylor's mental revolution means a change in attitude of workers and management towards each other: both should focus on increasing the surplus. Taylor and Fayol compared: Fayol gave general management at top level and is a practitioner; Taylor focused on shop floor and was a scientist; Fayol's principles apply universally, Taylor's are specific. Both complement each other.

  • Management principles are universal, flexible guidelines
  • They help in decisions, resource use and social responsibility

  • Fayol gave fourteen principles for general management such as unity of command, scalar chain and esprit de corps

lessons.title: Business Environment
yt: class 12 business studies business environment economic political legal social technological demonetisation LPG

blocks.x: Business environment is the sum total of all individuals, institutions and other forces that are outside the control of a business enterprise but may affect its performance. Features: totality of external forces, specific and general forces, inter-relatedness, dynamic, uncertainty, relativity and complexity. Importance: identification of opportunities and getting first mover advantage, identification of threats and early warning signals, tapping useful resources, coping with rapid changes, assisting in planning and policy formulation, improving performance and image building. Dimensions: economic, social, technological, political and legal. Economic environment: economic conditions, policies and system, such as interest rates, inflation, fiscal and monetary policy, the Planning Commission (replaced by NITI Aayog in 2015). Social: customs, values, expectations of society; Technological: innovations, scientific improvements; Political: political stability, government attitudes and policies; Legal: laws such as the Consumer Protection Act, the Companies Act, and the Competition Act. Economic reforms in India since 1991: the New Industrial Policy 1991 (LPG: liberalisation, privatisation, globalisation). Liberalisation: end of licence-permit raj, freedom to import and export, abolition of licensing for most industries, increase in the number of industries open to private sector, reduced tariffs and the freedom to fix prices. Privatisation: transfer of ownership of public sector enterprises to private; disinvestment (selling a part of the equity), and the Department of Disinvestment was set up. Globalisation: integration of the Indian economy with the world economy; outsourcing of services; the World Trade Organisation (WTO; successor to GATT in 1995). Impact of government policy changes on business and industry: increasing competition, more demanding customers, rapidly changing technological environment, necessity for change, need for developing human resources, market orientation and loss of budgetary support to the public sector. Demonetisation: on 8 November 2016, the Government of India declared that Rs 500 and Rs 1000 notes were no longer legal tender to curb black money, corruption and counterfeit currency; the new Rs 500 and Rs 2000 notes were issued. Impact: digital payments increased and the cash dependence reduced. SWOT and PESTLE analysis help in assessing the environment. Environmental scanning is the process of monitoring. Business environment includes micro environment (customers, suppliers, competitors, intermediaries) and macro environment (general forces). Make in India, Digital India and GST (Goods and Services Tax, introduced from 1 July 2017) are recent reforms.
Deep dive: Concept and importance
Business environment includes external forces beyond control. It helps identify opportunities and threats and improve planning.
Deep dive: Dimensions
Economic, social, technological, political and legal factors shape business. Each affects decisions differently.
Deep dive: Reforms
Liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation changed Indian business. Demonetisation and GST are later changes.
Hindi saransh
Vyapar paryavaran: arthik, samajik, praudyogik, rajnitik aur vidhik; 1991 ki LPG neeti, notebandi (2016) aur GST (2017).
Remember: LPG reforms began in 1991; demonetisation on 8 November 2016.

  • Features: totality of external forces, specific and general forces, inter-relatedness, dynamic, uncertainty, relativity and complexity

Read the full explanation

Business environment is the sum total of all individuals, institutions and other forces that are outside the control of a business enterprise but may affect its performance. Features: totality of external forces, specific and general forces, inter-relatedness, dynamic, uncertainty, relativity and complexity. Importance: identification of opportunities and getting first mover advantage, identification of threats and early warning signals, tapping useful resources, coping with rapid changes, assisting in planning and policy formulation, improving performance and image building. Dimensions: economic, social, technological, political and legal. Economic environment: economic conditions, policies and system, such as interest rates, inflation, fiscal and monetary policy, the Planning Commission (replaced by NITI Aayog in 2015). Social: customs, values, expectations of society; Technological: innovations, scientific improvements; Political: political stability, government attitudes and policies; Legal: laws such as the Consumer Protection Act, the Companies Act, and the Competition Act. Economic reforms in India since 1991: the New Industrial Policy 1991 (LPG: liberalisation, privatisation, globalisation). Liberalisation: end of licence-permit raj, freedom to import and export, abolition of licensing for most industries, increase in the number of industries open to private sector, reduced tariffs and the freedom to fix prices. Privatisation: transfer of ownership of public sector enterprises to private; disinvestment (selling a part of the equity), and the Department of Disinvestment was set up. Globalisation: integration of the Indian economy with the world economy; outsourcing of services; the World Trade Organisation (WTO; successor to GATT in 1995). Impact of government policy changes on business and industry: increasing competition, more demanding customers, rapidly changing technological environment, necessity for change, need for developing human resources, market orientation and loss of budgetary support to the public sector. Demonetisation: on 8 November 2016, the Government of India declared that Rs 500 and Rs 1000 notes were no longer legal tender to curb black money, corruption and counterfeit currency; the new Rs 500 and Rs 2000 notes were issued. Impact: digital payments increased and the cash dependence reduced. SWOT and PESTLE analysis help in assessing the environment. Environmental scanning is the process of monitoring. Business environment includes micro environment (customers, suppliers, competitors, intermediaries) and macro environment (general forces). Make in India, Digital India and GST (Goods and Services Tax, introduced from 1 July 2017) are recent reforms.

📘

Concept and importance

  • Business environment includes external forces beyond control
  • It helps identify opportunities and threats and improve planning
🧠

Dimensions

  • Economic, social, technological, political and legal factors shape business
  • Each affects decisions differently
🌟

Reforms

  • Liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation changed Indian business
  • Demonetisation and GST are later changes
🎯 Remember LPG reforms began in 1991; demonetisation on 8 November 2016.
🇮🇳

Vyapar paryavaran: arthik, samajik, praudyogik, rajnitik aur vidhik; 1991 ki LPG neeti, notebandi (2016) aur GST (2017).

lessons.title: Planning
yt: class 12 business studies planning importance limitations steps types of plans

blocks.x: Planning is deciding in advance what to do, when to do it, how to do it and who is to do it. It bridges the gap between where we are and where we want to go. Features: planning focuses on achieving objectives, is a primary function, is pervasive, is continuous, is futuristic, involves decision making and is a mental exercise. Importance: planning provides direction, reduces the risk of uncertainty, reduces overlapping and wasteful activities, promotes innovative ideas, facilitates decision making and establishes standards for controlling. Limitations: planning leads to rigidity, may not work in a dynamic environment, reduces creativity, involves huge costs, is a time-consuming process and does not guarantee success. Planning process: (1) setting objectives, (2) developing premises (assumptions about the future: internal or external; tangible or intangible), (3) identifying alternative courses of action, (4) evaluating alternative courses, (5) selecting an alternative, (6) implementing the plan and (7) follow-up action. Types of plans (single-use and standing): Objectives (end results), Strategy (comprehensive plan for achieving organisational objectives; three dimensions: determining long-term objectives, adopting a course of action and allocating resources; includes the environment), Policy (general statements guiding thinking and action in decision making; a standing plan that provides the framework within which action takes place), Procedure (the chronological sequence of steps to be taken to perform a task; standing plan), Method (the way in which a task has to be performed; the prescribed way), Rule (specific statement that tells what is to be done; no discretion), Programme (a detailed statement about a project covering objectives, policies, procedures, rules, tasks, human and physical resources), Budget (statement of expected results expressed in numerical terms). Difference: a policy gives direction for thinking, a rule is rigid and must be followed; a procedure is a sequence of steps whereas a method is a single way of performing one step. Plans are made at all levels; planning is done by managers at all levels but top management sets strategy. Planning premises affect the quality of plans. Single-use plans are programmes, budgets and projects; standing plans are policies, procedures, methods and rules. Planning and controlling are inseparable: planning without control is meaningless and control without planning is blind. Planning is a primary function because other functions follow it. Planning is based on forecasting.
Deep dive: Concept and importance
Planning provides direction and reduces risk. It sets standards for control. It is a continuous and pervasive function.
Deep dive: Process
The planning process runs from objectives to follow-up. Premises and alternatives are key steps.
Deep dive: Types of plans
Objectives, strategy, policy, procedure, method, rule, programme and budget differ in scope and rigidity.
Hindi saransh
Niyojan: bhavishya ke baare mein purva nirdharan; uddeshya, vyuharachna, niti, prakriya, paddhati, niyam, karyakram aur bajat.

🔑

Big idea

  • Planning is deciding in advance what to do, when to do it, how to do it and who is to do it
  • It bridges the gap between where we are and where we want to go
  • Features: planning focuses on achieving objectives, is a primary function, is pervasive, is continuous, is futuristic, involves decision making and…
  • Importance: planning provides direction, reduces the risk of uncertainty, reduces overlapping and wasteful activities, promotes innovative ideas…
Read the full explanation

Planning is deciding in advance what to do, when to do it, how to do it and who is to do it. It bridges the gap between where we are and where we want to go. Features: planning focuses on achieving objectives, is a primary function, is pervasive, is continuous, is futuristic, involves decision making and is a mental exercise. Importance: planning provides direction, reduces the risk of uncertainty, reduces overlapping and wasteful activities, promotes innovative ideas, facilitates decision making and establishes standards for controlling. Limitations: planning leads to rigidity, may not work in a dynamic environment, reduces creativity, involves huge costs, is a time-consuming process and does not guarantee success. Planning process: (1) setting objectives, (2) developing premises (assumptions about the future: internal or external; tangible or intangible), (3) identifying alternative courses of action, (4) evaluating alternative courses, (5) selecting an alternative, (6) implementing the plan and (7) follow-up action. Types of plans (single-use and standing): Objectives (end results), Strategy (comprehensive plan for achieving organisational objectives; three dimensions: determining long-term objectives, adopting a course of action and allocating resources; includes the environment), Policy (general statements guiding thinking and action in decision making; a standing plan that provides the framework within which action takes place), Procedure (the chronological sequence of steps to be taken to perform a task; standing plan), Method (the way in which a task has to be performed; the prescribed way), Rule (specific statement that tells what is to be done; no discretion), Programme (a detailed statement about a project covering objectives, policies, procedures, rules, tasks, human and physical resources), Budget (statement of expected results expressed in numerical terms). Difference: a policy gives direction for thinking, a rule is rigid and must be followed; a procedure is a sequence of steps whereas a method is a single way of performing one step. Plans are made at all levels; planning is done by managers at all levels but top management sets strategy. Planning premises affect the quality of plans. Single-use plans are programmes, budgets and projects; standing plans are policies, procedures, methods and rules. Planning and controlling are inseparable: planning without control is meaningless and control without planning is blind. Planning is a primary function because other functions follow it. Planning is based on forecasting.

📘

Concept and importance

  • Planning provides direction and reduces risk
  • It sets standards for control
  • It is a continuous and pervasive function
🔄

Process

  • The planning process runs from objectives to follow-up
  • Premises and alternatives are key steps
🌟

Types of plans

  • Objectives, strategy, policy, procedure, method, rule, programme and budget differ in scope and rigidity

lessons.title: Organising
yt: class 12 business studies organising structure functional divisional delegation decentralisation formal informal

blocks.x: Organising is the process of defining and grouping activities and establishing authority relationships among them. Steps: (1) identification and division of work, (2) departmentalisation (grouping of jobs into departments on the basis of functions or products), (3) assignment of duties and (4) establishing reporting relationships. Importance: specialisation, clarity in working relationships, optimum utilisation of resources, adaptation to change, effective administration, development of personnel and expansion and growth. Organisation structure is the framework within which managerial and operating tasks are performed. Functional structure: grouping of jobs of similar nature under a department (production, marketing, finance). Advantages: specialisation, control over functions, efficiency, training is easier and reduced duplication. Disadvantages: functional objectives may be overemphasised, difficult to coordinate, and conflict among departments. Suitable for large firms with diverse activities but a single product line. Divisional structure: grouping on the basis of products or markets such as the Reliance divisions. Advantages: performance can be assessed, quick decision making, facilitates expansion and gives a chance for development of managers; disadvantages: conflict over allocation of funds, duplication of activities and increased cost, and competition among divisions. Formal organisation: the structure of well-defined jobs, each bearing a measure of authority and responsibility; it follows the rules, is created by top management and has a clear chain; the advantages: fixing of responsibility, unity of command and the certainty of tasks; disadvantages: delay in action due to formality, limited scope for personal initiative and ignores human relations. Informal organisation: a network of social relationships arising spontaneously due to personal interactions among employees; it has no written rules, it is not deliberately created and develops within the formal structure. Advantages: fast spread of information, fulfils social needs and supports formal structure; disadvantages: spread of rumours, resistance to change and pressure for conformity. Delegation of authority: the downward transfer of authority from a superior to a subordinate. Elements: authority (the right to give orders), responsibility (the obligation to perform; it cannot be delegated, because it flows upward) and accountability (answerability for the final outcome; it cannot be delegated). Authority flows downward and responsibility flows upward. Importance: effective management, employee development, motivation, facilitation of growth, better coordination and quicker decisions. Decentralisation: systematic delegation of authority at all levels of management; centralisation is concentration of decision-making at the top. Difference: delegation is a process of sharing authority between a superior and a subordinate, while decentralisation is a policy decision to share authority at all levels; delegation is compulsory in the process, while decentralisation is optional; the two are complementary: decentralisation is the extension of delegation to the lowest level. Importance of decentralisation: develops initiative among subordinates, develops managerial talent, quick decision-making, relief to top management, facilitates growth and better control. Span of management is the number of subordinates reporting to one superior.
Deep dive: Process and structure
Organising divides work and sets authority relations. Functional and divisional structures suit different firms.
Deep dive: Formal and informal
The formal structure is deliberate; the informal arises spontaneously. Both coexist and support each other.
Deep dive: Delegation
Authority is delegated, but responsibility and accountability remain with the superior. Decentralisation extends delegation systematically.

Sangathan: karya vibhajan, vibhagikaran, karya-sauncna; karyatmak aur vibhagiya sanrachna, prattyayojan aur vikendrikaran.

🔑

Big idea

  • Organising is the process of defining and grouping activities and establishing authority relationships among them
  • Steps: (1) identification and division of work, (2) departmentalisation (grouping of jobs into departments on the basis of functions or products)…
  • Importance: specialisation, clarity in working relationships, optimum utilisation of resources, adaptation to change, effective administration…

Read the full explanation

Organising is the process of defining and grouping activities and establishing authority relationships among them. Steps: (1) identification and division of work, (2) departmentalisation (grouping of jobs into departments on the basis of functions or products), (3) assignment of duties and (4) establishing reporting relationships. Importance: specialisation, clarity in working relationships, optimum utilisation of resources, adaptation to change, effective administration, development of personnel and expansion and growth. Organisation structure is the framework within which managerial and operating tasks are performed. Functional structure: grouping of jobs of similar nature under a department (production, marketing, finance). Advantages: specialisation, control over functions, efficiency, training is easier and reduced duplication. Disadvantages: functional objectives may be overemphasised, difficult to coordinate, and conflict among departments. Suitable for large firms with diverse activities but a single product line. Divisional structure: grouping on the basis of products or markets such as the Reliance divisions. Advantages: performance can be assessed, quick decision making, facilitates expansion and gives a chance for development of managers; disadvantages: conflict over allocation of funds, duplication of activities and increased cost, and competition among divisions. Formal organisation: the structure of well-defined jobs, each bearing a measure of authority and responsibility; it follows the rules, is created by top management and has a clear chain; the advantages: fixing of responsibility, unity of command and the certainty of tasks; disadvantages: delay in action due to formality, limited scope for personal initiative and ignores human relations. Informal organisation: a network of social relationships arising spontaneously due to personal interactions among employees; it has no written rules, it is not deliberately created and develops within the formal structure. Advantages: fast spread of information, fulfils social needs and supports formal structure; disadvantages: spread of rumours, resistance to change and pressure for conformity. Delegation of authority: the downward transfer of authority from a superior to a subordinate. Elements: authority (the right to give orders), responsibility (the obligation to perform; it cannot be delegated, because it flows upward) and accountability (answerability for the final outcome; it cannot be delegated). Authority flows downward and responsibility flows upward. Importance: effective management, employee development, motivation, facilitation of growth, better coordination and quicker decisions. Decentralisation: systematic delegation of authority at all levels of management; centralisation is concentration of decision-making at the top. Difference: delegation is a process of sharing authority between a superior and a subordinate, while decentralisation is a policy decision to share authority at all levels; delegation is compulsory in the process, while decentralisation is optional; the two are complementary: decentralisation is the extension of delegation to the lowest level. Importance of decentralisation: develops initiative among subordinates, develops managerial talent, quick decision-making, relief to top management, facilitates growth and better control. Span of management is the number of subordinates reporting to one superior.

🔄

Process and structure

  • Organising divides work and sets authority relations
  • Functional and divisional structures suit different firms
🧠

Formal and informal

  • The formal structure is deliberate
  • The informal arises spontaneously
  • Both coexist and support each other
🌟

Delegation

  • Authority is delegated, but responsibility and accountability remain with the superior
  • Decentralisation extends delegation systematically

lessons.title: Staffing
yt: class 12 business studies staffing recruitment selection training human resource management

blocks.x: Staffing is the process of finding the right people for the right job: it includes recruitment, selection, placement, training, development, appraisal and compensation of personnel. Human resource management is the broader term; it covers staffing. Importance: obtaining competent personnel, higher performance, continuous survival and growth, optimum utilisation of human resources, job satisfaction and morale. Staffing is a function of all managers, and a part of the human resource department in large organisations. The Staffing process: (1) estimating manpower requirements (workload analysis and workforce analysis), (2) recruitment, (3) selection, (4) placement and orientation (induction), (5) training and development, (6) performance appraisal and (7) promotion and career planning and compensation. Recruitment is the process of searching for prospective employees and stimulating them to apply for jobs. Sources: internal (transfers, promotions) and external (direct recruitment, casual callers, advertisement, employment exchanges, placement agencies and management consultants, campus recruitment, recommendations of employees, labour contractors, web publishing and e-recruitment). Internal sources: transfer (shifting an employee from one job to another without change in status or pay) and promotion (shifting to a higher position with higher pay, status and responsibilities). Merits of internal recruitment: motivation, simple, economical, stability. Demerits: no new talent, limits the choice and may lead to rivalry. External sources: fresh talent, wider choice, competitive spirit; demerits: expensive, time consuming and demoralising for existing staff. Selection is the process of choosing from the pool of applicants the right candidate; steps: preliminary screening, selection tests (intelligence, aptitude, personality, trade or proficiency and interest tests), employment interview (structured and unstructured), reference and background checks, selection decision, medical examination, job offer and contract of employment. Recruitment is positive (attracting), while selection is negative (rejecting unsuitable). Training is the process of increasing the knowledge and skills of an employee for doing a particular job; development is the growth of an employee in all respects, concerned with the overall growth of managers. Training is job-oriented and short term; development is career oriented, long term. Importance of training: benefits to the organisation (systematic learning, higher productivity and less wastage) and employees (better career opportunities, higher earnings and more satisfaction). Methods: on-the-job (apprenticeship programmes, coaching, job rotation, internship training) and off-the-job (classroom lectures/conferences, films, case studies, computer modelling, vestibule training and programmed instruction). Induction is the introduction of a new employee to the organisation. Vestibule training provides training in a duplicate workplace. Internship training is a joint programme with educational institutions. Apprenticeship programmes provide both theoretical and practical training.
Deep dive: Staffing process
Staffing runs from manpower planning to compensation. Recruitment and selection fill positions with suitable people.
Deep dive: Recruitment and selection
Recruitment attracts applicants from internal and external sources. Selection filters by tests, interviews and checks.
Deep dive: Training
Training improves skills for a job; development builds overall growth. On-the-job and off-the-job methods are used.
Hindi saransh
Karmachari-vyavastha: bharti, chayan, prashikshan aur vikas; aantarik aur bahari strot.
Remember: recruitment is positive; selection is negative; training is job oriented; development is career oriented.

Big idea

Read the full explanation

Staffing is the process of finding the right people for the right job: it includes recruitment, selection, placement, training, development, appraisal and compensation of personnel. Human resource management is the broader term; it covers staffing. Importance: obtaining competent personnel, higher performance, continuous survival and growth, optimum utilisation of human resources, job satisfaction and morale. Staffing is a function of all managers, and a part of the human resource department in large organisations. The Staffing process: (1) estimating manpower requirements (workload analysis and workforce analysis), (2) recruitment, (3) selection, (4) placement and orientation (induction), (5) training and development, (6) performance appraisal and (7) promotion and career planning and compensation. Recruitment is the process of searching for prospective employees and stimulating them to apply for jobs. Sources: internal (transfers, promotions) and external (direct recruitment, casual callers, advertisement, employment exchanges, placement agencies and management consultants, campus recruitment, recommendations of employees, labour contractors, web publishing and e-recruitment). Internal sources: transfer (shifting an employee from one job to another without change in status or pay) and promotion (shifting to a higher position with higher pay, status and responsibilities). Merits of internal recruitment: motivation, simple, economical, stability. Demerits: no new talent, limits the choice and may lead to rivalry. External sources: fresh talent, wider choice, competitive spirit; demerits: expensive, time consuming and demoralising for existing staff. Selection is the process of choosing from the pool of applicants the right candidate; steps: preliminary screening, selection tests (intelligence, aptitude, personality, trade or proficiency and interest tests), employment interview (structured and unstructured), reference and background checks, selection decision, medical examination, job offer and contract of employment. Recruitment is positive (attracting), while selection is negative (rejecting unsuitable). Training is the process of increasing the knowledge and skills of an employee for doing a particular job; development is the growth of an employee in all respects, concerned with the overall growth of managers. Training is job-oriented and short term; development is career oriented, long term. Importance of training: benefits to the organisation (systematic learning, higher productivity and less wastage) and employees (better career opportunities, higher earnings and more satisfaction). Methods: on-the-job (apprenticeship programmes, coaching, job rotation, internship training) and off-the-job (classroom lectures/conferences, films, case studies, computer modelling, vestibule training and programmed instruction). Induction is the introduction of a new employee to the organisation. Vestibule training provides training in a duplicate workplace. Internship training is a joint programme with educational institutions. Apprenticeship programmes provide both theoretical and practical training.

🔄

Staffing process

  • Staffing runs from manpower planning to compensation
  • Recruitment and selection fill positions with suitable people
🧠

Recruitment and selection

  • Recruitment attracts applicants from internal and external sources
  • Selection filters by tests, interviews and checks
🌟

Training

  • Training improves skills for a job
  • Development builds overall growth
  • On-the-job and off-the-job methods are used

blocks.x: Directing is the function of instructing, guiding, counselling, motivating and leading people in an organisation to achieve its objectives. Features: it initiates action, takes place at every level, is a continuous activity and flows from top to bottom. Importance: initiates action, integrates efforts, means of motivation, provides stability and balance, and facilitates change. Elements of directing: supervision, motivation, leadership and communication. Supervision is the function of overseeing the work of subordinates; the supervisor is the link between workers and management and is a factor in discipline, morale and training. Motivation is the process of stimulating people to action to accomplish desired goals. A motive is an inner state that energises behaviour; a motivator is a stimulus. Features: an internal feeling, a goal-directed behaviour, can be positive or negative and a complex process. Maslow's need hierarchy theory: physiological needs (food, shelter), safety/security needs (job security), affiliation/belonging needs (friendship), esteem needs (status, recognition) and self-actualisation needs (realising one's potential); a satisfied need no longer motivates; assumptions: people's behaviour is based on their needs. Herzberg's two-factor theory: hygiene factors (salary, working conditions, job security, supervision) prevent dissatisfaction but do not motivate; motivators (achievement, recognition, responsibility, growth) motivate. Financial incentives: pay and allowances, productivity linked wage incentives, bonus, profit sharing, co-partnership/stock option, retirement benefits and perquisites; non-financial: status, organisational climate, career advancement opportunity, job enrichment, employee recognition programmes, job security and employee participation. Leadership is the process of influencing the behaviour of people to strive willingly for group goals. Features: influence, followers, common goal, a continuous process and situational. Importance: induces action, provides guidance, creates confidence, builds morale and coordinates. Styles: autocratic (authoritarian, all decisions by leader), democratic (participative, consults subordinates) and laissez-faire (free rein, leader gives minimum direction). Qualities: physical features, knowledge, integrity, initiative, communication skills, motivation, self-confidence, decisiveness, social skills. Communication is the process of exchange of ideas, views, facts, feelings between two or more persons to create common understanding. Elements: sender, message, encoding, media, decoding, receiver, feedback and noise. Formal communication follows the official channel: vertical (downward and upward) and horizontal; informal communication or grapevine includes single strand, gossip, probability and cluster chains. Barriers: semantic (words and symbols), psychological (premature evaluation, lack of attention, loss by transmission and poor retention, distrust), organisational (organisational policy, rules, status, complexity in organisational structure, organisational facilities) and personal barriers (fear of challenge to authority, lack of confidence of superiors in their subordinates, unwillingness to communicate, lack of proper incentive). Improving communication: clarify the ideas, communicate according to the needs of the receiver, consult others, be aware of the language, tone and content, convey things of help and value, ensure proper feedback and communicate for the present as well as the future and be a good listener.
Deep dive: Motivation
Maslow and Herzberg explain what motivates people. Financial and non-financial incentives work together.
Deep dive: Leadership
Leaders influence people toward goals. Autocratic, democratic and laissez-faire styles fit different situations.
Deep dive: Communication
Communication needs a sender, message, medium, receiver and feedback. Barriers can be semantic, psychological, organisational or personal.
Hindi saransh
Nirdeshan: paryavekshan, abhiprerna (Maslow ke 5 star), netritva shaili aur sampreshan ke baadhaen.
Remember: Maslow top need is self-actualisation; hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction but do not motivate.

Read the full explanation

Directing is the function of instructing, guiding, counselling, motivating and leading people in an organisation to achieve its objectives. Features: it initiates action, takes place at every level, is a continuous activity and flows from top to bottom. Importance: initiates action, integrates efforts, means of motivation, provides stability and balance, and facilitates change. Elements of directing: supervision, motivation, leadership and communication. Supervision is the function of overseeing the work of subordinates; the supervisor is the link between workers and management and is a factor in discipline, morale and training. Motivation is the process of stimulating people to action to accomplish desired goals. A motive is an inner state that energises behaviour; a motivator is a stimulus. Features: an internal feeling, a goal-directed behaviour, can be positive or negative and a complex process. Maslow's need hierarchy theory: physiological needs (food, shelter), safety/security needs (job security), affiliation/belonging needs (friendship), esteem needs (status, recognition) and self-actualisation needs (realising one's potential); a satisfied need no longer motivates; assumptions: people's behaviour is based on their needs. Herzberg's two-factor theory: hygiene factors (salary, working conditions, job security, supervision) prevent dissatisfaction but do not motivate; motivators (achievement, recognition, responsibility, growth) motivate. Financial incentives: pay and allowances, productivity linked wage incentives, bonus, profit sharing, co-partnership/stock option, retirement benefits and perquisites; non-financial: status, organisational climate, career advancement opportunity, job enrichment, employee recognition programmes, job security and employee participation. Leadership is the process of influencing the behaviour of people to strive willingly for group goals. Features: influence, followers, common goal, a continuous process and situational. Importance: induces action, provides guidance, creates confidence, builds morale and coordinates. Styles: autocratic (authoritarian, all decisions by leader), democratic (participative, consults subordinates) and laissez-faire (free rein, leader gives minimum direction). Qualities: physical features, knowledge, integrity, initiative, communication skills, motivation, self-confidence, decisiveness, social skills. Communication is the process of exchange of ideas, views, facts, feelings between two or more persons to create common understanding. Elements: sender, message, encoding, media, decoding, receiver, feedback and noise. Formal communication follows the official channel: vertical (downward and upward) and horizontal; informal communication or grapevine includes single strand, gossip, probability and cluster chains. Barriers: semantic (words and symbols), psychological (premature evaluation, lack of attention, loss by transmission and poor retention, distrust), organisational (organisational policy, rules, status, complexity in organisational structure, organisational facilities) and personal barriers (fear of challenge to authority, lack of confidence of superiors in their subordinates, unwillingness to communicate, lack of proper incentive). Improving communication: clarify the ideas, communicate according to the needs of the receiver, consult others, be aware of the language, tone and content, convey things of help and value, ensure proper feedback and communicate for the present as well as the future and be a good listener.

📌

Motivation

  • Maslow and Herzberg explain what motivates people
  • Financial and non-financial incentives work together

  • Autocratic, democratic and laissez-faire styles fit different situations
