lessons.title: Controlling
yt: class 12 business studies controlling importance process techniques budgetary control ROI PERT CPM

blocks.x: Controlling is the management function of ensuring that activities are performed as per plans by comparing actual performance with standards and taking corrective action where deviations are found. It involves setting standards, measuring performance, comparing actual with standard, analysing deviations and taking corrective action. Features: controlling is an end function, a pervasive function, a forward-looking function, a continuous activity and has a close relation with planning (planning without controlling is meaningless and controlling without planning is blind). Importance: accomplishing organisational goals, judging accuracy of standards, making efficient use of resources, improving employee motivation, ensuring order and discipline and facilitating coordination in action. Limitations: difficulty in setting quantitative standards, little control on external factors, resistance from employees (for example, to surveillance by cameras) and costly affair. Process of controlling: (1) setting performance standards (quantitative or qualitative), (2) measurement of actual performance (personal observation, sample checking, performance reports), (3) comparing actual performance with standards, (4) analysing deviations (critical point control: the focus on key result areas, which are critical to the success; management by exception: attention only to significant deviations; the range of deviation is accepted) and (5) taking corrective action. Techniques of managerial control: Traditional techniques: personal observation; statistical reports; breakeven analysis (the level of output at which there is no profit or loss; BEP = Fixed cost / (Selling price per unit - Variable cost per unit)) and budgetary control (a technique of managerial control in which all operations are planned in advance in the form of budgets and actual results are compared with budgetary standards; budgets are of types: sales, production, cash, material, capital expenditure and research and development). Modern techniques: return on investment (ROI = Net income / Total investment; a useful technique to measure the overall performance of a business and its units), ratio analysis (liquidity, solvency, profitability and turnover ratios), responsibility accounting (a system of accounting in which different sections, divisions and departments of an organisation are set up as responsibility centres: cost centre, revenue centre, profit centre and investment centre), management audit (systematic appraisal of the overall performance of the management), PERT (Programme Evaluation and Review Technique) and CPM (Critical Path Method) — network techniques used for planning, scheduling and controlling large projects: steps are to define activities, develop the network, estimate time, identify the critical path (the longest path), and revise. PERT uses three time estimates (optimistic, pessimistic and most likely), suitable for projects where time estimates are uncertain; CPM uses a single time estimate, suitable for projects where activities are routine and where cost is also a factor. Management information system (MIS) is a computer-based information system that provides information and support for effective decision making. Controlling and planning: planning is the base. Standards should be flexible and quantifiable.
Deep dive: Concept and process
Controlling compares actual with standards and corrects deviations. Critical point control and management by exception focus attention.
Deep dive: Techniques
Traditional techniques include observation, reports, breakeven analysis and budgets. Modern techniques include ROI, ratio analysis, responsibility accounting, PERT and CPM.
Deep dive: Planning and control
They are inseparable. Plans give standards; control checks results.
Hindi saransh
Niyantran: manak nirdharan, mapan, tulna, vichalan vishleshan aur sudharatmak karyavahi; bajtiya niyantran, ROI, PERT aur CPM.

Big idea

Read the full explanation

Controlling is the management function of ensuring that activities are performed as per plans by comparing actual performance with standards and taking corrective action where deviations are found. It involves setting standards, measuring performance, comparing actual with standard, analysing deviations and taking corrective action. Features: controlling is an end function, a pervasive function, a forward-looking function, a continuous activity and has a close relation with planning (planning without controlling is meaningless and controlling without planning is blind). Importance: accomplishing organisational goals, judging accuracy of standards, making efficient use of resources, improving employee motivation, ensuring order and discipline and facilitating coordination in action. Limitations: difficulty in setting quantitative standards, little control on external factors, resistance from employees (for example, to surveillance by cameras) and costly affair. Process of controlling: (1) setting performance standards (quantitative or qualitative), (2) measurement of actual performance (personal observation, sample checking, performance reports), (3) comparing actual performance with standards, (4) analysing deviations (critical point control: the focus on key result areas, which are critical to the success; management by exception: attention only to significant deviations; the range of deviation is accepted) and (5) taking corrective action. Techniques of managerial control: Traditional techniques: personal observation; statistical reports; breakeven analysis (the level of output at which there is no profit or loss; BEP = Fixed cost / (Selling price per unit - Variable cost per unit)) and budgetary control (a technique of managerial control in which all operations are planned in advance in the form of budgets and actual results are compared with budgetary standards; budgets are of types: sales, production, cash, material, capital expenditure and research and development). Modern techniques: return on investment (ROI = Net income / Total investment; a useful technique to measure the overall performance of a business and its units), ratio analysis (liquidity, solvency, profitability and turnover ratios), responsibility accounting (a system of accounting in which different sections, divisions and departments of an organisation are set up as responsibility centres: cost centre, revenue centre, profit centre and investment centre), management audit (systematic appraisal of the overall performance of the management), PERT (Programme Evaluation and Review Technique) and CPM (Critical Path Method) — network techniques used for planning, scheduling and controlling large projects: steps are to define activities, develop the network, estimate time, identify the critical path (the longest path), and revise. PERT uses three time estimates (optimistic, pessimistic and most likely), suitable for projects where time estimates are uncertain; CPM uses a single time estimate, suitable for projects where activities are routine and where cost is also a factor. Management information system (MIS) is a computer-based information system that provides information and support for effective decision making. Controlling and planning: planning is the base. Standards should be flexible and quantifiable.

📘

Concept and process

  • Controlling compares actual with standards and corrects deviations
  • Critical point control and management by exception focus attention
🧠

Techniques

  • Traditional techniques include observation, reports, breakeven analysis and budgets
  • Modern techniques include ROI, ratio analysis, responsibility accounting, PERT and CPM
🌟

Planning and control

  • They are inseparable
  • Plans give standards
  • Control checks results
🎯 Remember planning without controlling is meaningless; controlling without planning is blind.
🇮🇳

yt: class 12 business studies financial management capital structure fixed capital working capital dividend

blocks.x: Financial management is concerned with the optimal procurement as well as the usage of finance. Role: financial planning, financing, investment and control; it helps in determining financial needs, ensuring adequate funds at the least cost, maximising shareholders' wealth and managing risk. Objectives: wealth maximisation (maximise the market value of shares) is preferred over profit maximisation because it considers risk, time value of money and the interest of shareholders. Three decisions: investment decision, financing decision and dividend decision. Investment decision (capital budgeting) is the decision on how the firm's funds are invested in different assets; long-term capital budgeting decisions are about fixed assets, with factors affecting: cash flows of the project, the rate of return, the investment criteria involved and risk. Short-term investment decision is working capital management. Financing decision: the decision about the proportion of debt and equity; it depends on the cost of funds, risk and flotation cost. Factors affecting financing decisions: cost, risk, floatation cost, cash flow position, control considerations, state of capital markets, fixed operating cost and the tax rate. Dividend decision: how much of profit is distributed as dividends and how much is retained. Factors affecting dividend decision: amount of earnings, stability of earnings, stability of dividends, growth opportunities, cash flow position, shareholders' preference, taxation policy, stock market reaction, access to capital market and legal constraints. Financial planning is the preparation of a financial blueprint of an organisation's future operations; its objectives are to ensure availability of funds and to avoid excess funds; importance: ensures adequate funds, helps in avoiding business shocks and surprises, helps in co-ordinating various business functions, reduces waste, duplication of efforts and gaps in planning, and links present with future. Capital structure is the mix of owners' funds (equity share capital, preference share capital, retained earnings) and borrowed funds (debentures, loans). Financial leverage or trading on equity is the use of fixed-cost debt in the capital structure to increase the return to equity shareholders; when ROI exceeds the cost of debt, the earning per share rises. Debt-equity ratio = Debt / Equity. Factors affecting capital structure: cash flow position, interest coverage ratio (ICR = EBIT / Interest), debt service coverage ratio, return on investment, cost of debt, tax rate, cost of equity, floatation costs, risk consideration, flexibility, control, regulatory framework, stock market conditions, capital structure of companies in the same industry. Fixed capital is the investment in long-term assets; factors affecting the choice: nature of business, scale of operations, choice of technique, technology upgradation, growth prospects, diversification, financing alternatives and level of collaboration. Working capital is the capital required for day-to-day operations: Gross working capital = Total current assets; Net working capital = Current assets - Current liabilities. Factors affecting working capital requirements: nature of business, scale of operations, business cycle, seasonal factors, production cycle, credit allowed, credit availability, operating efficiency and the level of competition. Cost of capital and risk are important in decision making.
Deep dive: Decisions
Investment, financing and dividend decisions aim to maximise shareholders' wealth. Each depends on cost, risk and returns.
Deep dive: Capital structure
The mix of debt and equity affects risk and returns. Trading on equity raises EPS when ROI exceeds interest cost.
Deep dive: Fixed and working capital
Fixed capital funds long-term assets; working capital funds day-to-day operations. Many factors decide requirements.
Hindi saransh
Vittiya prabandhan: nivesh, vittiya aur laabhansh nirnay; poonji sanrachna, sthayi poonji aur karyashil poonji.
Remember: wealth maximisation is preferred to profit maximisation.

Read the full explanation

Financial management is concerned with the optimal procurement as well as the usage of finance. Role: financial planning, financing, investment and control; it helps in determining financial needs, ensuring adequate funds at the least cost, maximising shareholders' wealth and managing risk. Objectives: wealth maximisation (maximise the market value of shares) is preferred over profit maximisation because it considers risk, time value of money and the interest of shareholders. Three decisions: investment decision, financing decision and dividend decision. Investment decision (capital budgeting) is the decision on how the firm's funds are invested in different assets; long-term capital budgeting decisions are about fixed assets, with factors affecting: cash flows of the project, the rate of return, the investment criteria involved and risk. Short-term investment decision is working capital management. Financing decision: the decision about the proportion of debt and equity; it depends on the cost of funds, risk and flotation cost. Factors affecting financing decisions: cost, risk, floatation cost, cash flow position, control considerations, state of capital markets, fixed operating cost and the tax rate. Dividend decision: how much of profit is distributed as dividends and how much is retained. Factors affecting dividend decision: amount of earnings, stability of earnings, stability of dividends, growth opportunities, cash flow position, shareholders' preference, taxation policy, stock market reaction, access to capital market and legal constraints. Financial planning is the preparation of a financial blueprint of an organisation's future operations; its objectives are to ensure availability of funds and to avoid excess funds; importance: ensures adequate funds, helps in avoiding business shocks and surprises, helps in co-ordinating various business functions, reduces waste, duplication of efforts and gaps in planning, and links present with future. Capital structure is the mix of owners' funds (equity share capital, preference share capital, retained earnings) and borrowed funds (debentures, loans). Financial leverage or trading on equity is the use of fixed-cost debt in the capital structure to increase the return to equity shareholders; when ROI exceeds the cost of debt, the earning per share rises. Debt-equity ratio = Debt / Equity. Factors affecting capital structure: cash flow position, interest coverage ratio (ICR = EBIT / Interest), debt service coverage ratio, return on investment, cost of debt, tax rate, cost of equity, floatation costs, risk consideration, flexibility, control, regulatory framework, stock market conditions, capital structure of companies in the same industry. Fixed capital is the investment in long-term assets; factors affecting the choice: nature of business, scale of operations, choice of technique, technology upgradation, growth prospects, diversification, financing alternatives and level of collaboration. Working capital is the capital required for day-to-day operations: Gross working capital = Total current assets; Net working capital = Current assets - Current liabilities. Factors affecting working capital requirements: nature of business, scale of operations, business cycle, seasonal factors, production cycle, credit allowed, credit availability, operating efficiency and the level of competition. Cost of capital and risk are important in decision making.

📌

Decisions

  • Investment, financing and dividend decisions aim to maximise shareholders' wealth
  • Each depends on cost, risk and returns
🧠

Capital structure

  • The mix of debt and equity affects risk and returns
  • Trading on equity raises EPS when ROI exceeds interest cost
🚀

Fixed and working capital

  • Fixed capital funds long-term assets
  • Working capital funds day-to-day operations
  • Many factors decide requirements

blocks.x: A financial market is a market for the creation and exchange of financial assets. Functions: mobilisation of savings and channelling them into the most productive uses, facilitating price discovery, providing liquidity to financial assets and reducing the cost of transactions. Types: money market and capital market. Money market is a market for short-term funds (up to one year), with the Reserve Bank of India as the regulator and no physical location; instruments: Treasury bills (T-bills; issued by the RBI on behalf of the Government of India, zero coupon, in denominations of Rs 25,000 with maturities of 14, 91, 182 and 364 days), Commercial paper (CP; introduced in 1990; unsecured promissory note issued by large, creditworthy companies with maturity from 15 days to one year), Call money (for one day; notice money 2 to 14 days; the interest rate is called the call rate), Certificate of deposit (CD; unsecured negotiable short-term instruments issued by commercial banks and financial institutions; introduced in 1989), and Commercial bill (a bill of exchange used to finance the working capital needs of business firms). Capital market is a market for long-term funds with the SEBI as the regulator; it consists of primary market and secondary market. Primary market (new issues market): deals with the issue of new securities for the first time; methods of floating new issues: public issue through prospectus (IPO and FPO), offer for sale (shares offered to the public by existing owners through intermediaries such as issuing houses or stockbrokers), private placement (allotment of securities to institutional investors and selected individuals), rights issue (the existing shareholders have the right to subscribe in proportion), and e-IPO (online through the stock exchange). Secondary market (stock exchange): where existing securities are bought and sold; functions: providing liquidity and marketability, pricing of securities, safety of transactions, contributing to economic growth, spreading of equity cult and providing scope for speculation. Stock exchange is an institution which provides a platform for buying and selling of existing securities. Stock exchanges in India: the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE; 1875; oldest in Asia) and the National Stock Exchange (NSE; 1992; recognised as a stock exchange in 1993; started trading in 1994; the first demutualised electronic exchange). OTCEI (Over the Counter Exchange of India; 1992) and the Interconnected Stock Exchange of India. Trading procedure: select a broker; open a demat account with a depository (NSDL and CDSL) and a trading account; placing an order; executing the order; settlement (T+1 now; originally rolling settlement of T+2). Demat: dematerialisation (conversion of physical shares into electronic form), depository (an institution holding securities in electronic form; NSDL (1996) and CDSL (1999)). Depository participant (DP) is an agent of the depository. SEBI (Securities and Exchange Board of India) was established on 12 April 1992 under the SEBI Act 1992; objectives: to regulate stock exchanges and the securities industry to promote their orderly functioning, to protect the rights and interests of investors and to prevent trading malpractices. Functions: regulatory (registration of brokers, regulation of stock exchanges, prohibition of insider trading and fraudulent practices), development (investor education, training of intermediaries) and protective. Sensex is the index of the BSE of 30 companies; Nifty is the index of NSE of 50 companies.
Deep dive: Money market
It deals in short-term instruments such as T-bills, commercial paper, call money and CDs under RBI regulation.
Deep dive: Capital market
The primary market issues new securities; the secondary market trades existing ones. SEBI regulates it.
Deep dive: Trading
Trading needs a broker, demat and trading accounts. NSDL and CDSL are depositories. Sensex and Nifty are indices.
Hindi saransh
Vittiya bazar: mudra bazar (T-bill, CP, CD), poonji bazar (prathmik aur dwitiyak), SEBI (1992), demat khata, Sensex aur Nifty.
Remember: SEBI was established on 12 April 1992; Sensex has 30 companies and Nifty 50.

Big idea

Read the full explanation

A financial market is a market for the creation and exchange of financial assets. Functions: mobilisation of savings and channelling them into the most productive uses, facilitating price discovery, providing liquidity to financial assets and reducing the cost of transactions. Types: money market and capital market. Money market is a market for short-term funds (up to one year), with the Reserve Bank of India as the regulator and no physical location; instruments: Treasury bills (T-bills; issued by the RBI on behalf of the Government of India, zero coupon, in denominations of Rs 25,000 with maturities of 14, 91, 182 and 364 days), Commercial paper (CP; introduced in 1990; unsecured promissory note issued by large, creditworthy companies with maturity from 15 days to one year), Call money (for one day; notice money 2 to 14 days; the interest rate is called the call rate), Certificate of deposit (CD; unsecured negotiable short-term instruments issued by commercial banks and financial institutions; introduced in 1989), and Commercial bill (a bill of exchange used to finance the working capital needs of business firms). Capital market is a market for long-term funds with the SEBI as the regulator; it consists of primary market and secondary market. Primary market (new issues market): deals with the issue of new securities for the first time; methods of floating new issues: public issue through prospectus (IPO and FPO), offer for sale (shares offered to the public by existing owners through intermediaries such as issuing houses or stockbrokers), private placement (allotment of securities to institutional investors and selected individuals), rights issue (the existing shareholders have the right to subscribe in proportion), and e-IPO (online through the stock exchange). Secondary market (stock exchange): where existing securities are bought and sold; functions: providing liquidity and marketability, pricing of securities, safety of transactions, contributing to economic growth, spreading of equity cult and providing scope for speculation. Stock exchange is an institution which provides a platform for buying and selling of existing securities. Stock exchanges in India: the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE; 1875; oldest in Asia) and the National Stock Exchange (NSE; 1992; recognised as a stock exchange in 1993; started trading in 1994; the first demutualised electronic exchange). OTCEI (Over the Counter Exchange of India; 1992) and the Interconnected Stock Exchange of India. Trading procedure: select a broker; open a demat account with a depository (NSDL and CDSL) and a trading account; placing an order; executing the order; settlement (T+1 now; originally rolling settlement of T+2). Demat: dematerialisation (conversion of physical shares into electronic form), depository (an institution holding securities in electronic form; NSDL (1996) and CDSL (1999)). Depository participant (DP) is an agent of the depository. SEBI (Securities and Exchange Board of India) was established on 12 April 1992 under the SEBI Act 1992; objectives: to regulate stock exchanges and the securities industry to promote their orderly functioning, to protect the rights and interests of investors and to prevent trading malpractices. Functions: regulatory (registration of brokers, regulation of stock exchanges, prohibition of insider trading and fraudulent practices), development (investor education, training of intermediaries) and protective. Sensex is the index of the BSE of 30 companies; Nifty is the index of NSE of 50 companies.

📌

Money market

  • It deals in short-term instruments such as T-bills, commercial paper, call money and CDs under RBI regulation
🧠

Capital market

  • The primary market issues new securities
  • The secondary market trades existing ones
  • SEBI regulates it
🌟

Trading

  • Trading needs a broker, demat and trading accounts
  • NSDL and CDSL are depositories
  • Sensex and Nifty are indices

lessons.title: Marketing Management
yt: class 12 business studies marketing management marketing mix product branding pricing promotion

blocks.x: Marketing is a social and managerial process by which individuals and groups obtain what they need and want through creating, offering and exchanging products of value with others. Marketing involves the creation of exchange, satisfaction of needs and wants, and profit. Features: needs and wants, creating a market offering, customer value, exchange mechanism. Marketing management is the planning, organising, directing and controlling of marketing activities. Philosophies: production concept, product concept, selling concept, marketing concept and societal marketing concept. Marketing vs selling: marketing focuses on customer needs and satisfaction with profit through satisfaction, selling focuses on the product and profit through sales volume. Marketing mix: the set of marketing tools used to pursue marketing objectives: product, price, place and promotion (the 4 Ps). Product is a bundle of benefits, a good, service or idea; classification: consumer goods (convenience: staples, impulse and emergency; shopping; specialty) and industrial goods (raw materials, installations, supplies and services). Branding: the process of giving a name, term, sign or symbol; brand name, trade mark (a brand or part of it that is legally registered). Benefits of branding to the customer: helps in identification of products, ensures quality, helps in status; to the marketer: differentiation, advertising and promotion programme, price differential, and goodwill building. Features of a good brand name: short and simple, easy to spell, pronounce and recognise, suggestive of the product's benefits, distinctive and adaptable, capable of being registered and protected legally. Packaging: the activity of designing and producing a container or wrapper; levels: primary (immediate container), secondary (additional layer), transportation packaging. Functions: product identification, product protection, convenience, promotion. Labelling: the display of information on or with the package; functions: describes the product and specifies its contents, identification of the product or brand, grading of products, helps in promotion of products and provides information required by law. Price: the amount of money paid for a product; factors affecting price determination: product cost, utility and demand, extent of competition in the market, government and legal regulations, pricing objectives and marketing methods used. Pricing objectives: obtaining market share leadership, surviving in a competitive market, attaining product quality leadership, maximising current profit. Physical distribution and place: channels of distribution: direct (zero level), one-level (retailer), two-level (wholesaler and retailer) and three-level (agent). Role of channels: to bridge the gap between producer and consumer. Functions of the middlemen. Components of physical distribution: order processing, transportation, warehousing, inventory control and packaging. Promotion mix: advertising (paid, impersonal communication through mass media), personal selling (oral presentation to prospective buyers), sales promotion (short-term incentives to encourage purchase, such as rebates, discounts, refunds, product combinations, quantity gift, instant draw and scratch card, full finance @ 0%, sampling, contests) and publicity (non-paid; part of public relations), and public relations. Advertising objections: adds to cost, undermines social values, confuses buyers, encourages the sale of inferior products, and some advertisements are in bad taste. Advantages: reach and builds the brand image. AIDA model. Personal selling: personal interaction. Difference: advertising is impersonal, personal selling is face to face. Marketing mix also influences consumer behaviour.
Deep dive: Marketing and mix
Marketing meets customer needs through the mix of product, price, place and promotion. Marketing focuses on satisfaction while selling focuses on volume.
Deep dive: Product
Branding, packaging and labelling support the product. Good brand names are simple and legally protectable.
Deep dive: Price, place and promotion
Price depends on cost, demand and competition. Channels deliver goods; promotion informs and persuades.
Hindi saransh
Vipanan prabandhan: vipanan mishran (4P), brand, pariveshtan, label, mulya, vitran vahika aur sanvardhan.
Remember: 4 Ps = product, price, place and promotion.

Read the full explanation

Marketing is a social and managerial process by which individuals and groups obtain what they need and want through creating, offering and exchanging products of value with others. Marketing involves the creation of exchange, satisfaction of needs and wants, and profit. Features: needs and wants, creating a market offering, customer value, exchange mechanism. Marketing management is the planning, organising, directing and controlling of marketing activities. Philosophies: production concept, product concept, selling concept, marketing concept and societal marketing concept. Marketing vs selling: marketing focuses on customer needs and satisfaction with profit through satisfaction, selling focuses on the product and profit through sales volume. Marketing mix: the set of marketing tools used to pursue marketing objectives: product, price, place and promotion (the 4 Ps). Product is a bundle of benefits, a good, service or idea; classification: consumer goods (convenience: staples, impulse and emergency; shopping; specialty) and industrial goods (raw materials, installations, supplies and services). Branding: the process of giving a name, term, sign or symbol; brand name, trade mark (a brand or part of it that is legally registered). Benefits of branding to the customer: helps in identification of products, ensures quality, helps in status; to the marketer: differentiation, advertising and promotion programme, price differential, and goodwill building. Features of a good brand name: short and simple, easy to spell, pronounce and recognise, suggestive of the product's benefits, distinctive and adaptable, capable of being registered and protected legally. Packaging: the activity of designing and producing a container or wrapper; levels: primary (immediate container), secondary (additional layer), transportation packaging. Functions: product identification, product protection, convenience, promotion. Labelling: the display of information on or with the package; functions: describes the product and specifies its contents, identification of the product or brand, grading of products, helps in promotion of products and provides information required by law. Price: the amount of money paid for a product; factors affecting price determination: product cost, utility and demand, extent of competition in the market, government and legal regulations, pricing objectives and marketing methods used. Pricing objectives: obtaining market share leadership, surviving in a competitive market, attaining product quality leadership, maximising current profit. Physical distribution and place: channels of distribution: direct (zero level), one-level (retailer), two-level (wholesaler and retailer) and three-level (agent). Role of channels: to bridge the gap between producer and consumer. Functions of the middlemen. Components of physical distribution: order processing, transportation, warehousing, inventory control and packaging. Promotion mix: advertising (paid, impersonal communication through mass media), personal selling (oral presentation to prospective buyers), sales promotion (short-term incentives to encourage purchase, such as rebates, discounts, refunds, product combinations, quantity gift, instant draw and scratch card, full finance @ 0%, sampling, contests) and publicity (non-paid; part of public relations), and public relations. Advertising objections: adds to cost, undermines social values, confuses buyers, encourages the sale of inferior products, and some advertisements are in bad taste. Advantages: reach and builds the brand image. AIDA model. Personal selling: personal interaction. Difference: advertising is impersonal, personal selling is face to face. Marketing mix also influences consumer behaviour.

  • Marketing focuses on satisfaction while selling focuses on volume

  • Branding, packaging and labelling support the product
  • Good brand names are simple and legally protectable

  • Channels deliver goods
  • Promotion informs and persuades

lessons.title: Consumer Protection
yt: class 12 business studies consumer protection act 2019 rights responsibilities redressal

blocks.x: A consumer is a person who buys goods or avails any service for a consideration for personal use. The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 replaced the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 and came into effect in July 2020. Importance of consumer protection: from the consumer's point of view (consumer ignorance, unorganised consumers, widespread exploitation) and from the business point of view (long-term interest, social responsibility, moral justification, government intervention, survival and growth). Ways and means of consumer protection: efforts of business (self-regulation, chambers of commerce, business associations), consumer awareness, consumer organisations and non-governmental organisations (voluntary consumer associations; Consumer Guidance Society of India) and government (legislation). Legal framework: Consumer Protection Act (CPA), Sale of Goods Act 1930, Indian Contract Act 1872, Essential Commodities Act 1955, Agricultural Produce (Grading and Marketing) Act 1937, Prevention of Food Adulteration Act 1954 (now Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006), Standards of Weights and Measures Act 1976, Trade Marks Act 1999, Competition Act 2002, and the Bureau of Indian Standards Act 2016 (BIS; ISI mark for industrial products; Agmark for agricultural products; Hallmark for jewellery). Consumer rights (CPA 2019, Section 2(9)): (1) right to safety, (2) right to be informed, (3) right to choose, (4) right to be heard, (5) right to seek redressal and (6) right to consumer awareness. Consumer responsibilities: be aware of various goods and services, buy only standardised goods, learn about the risks associated with products, read labels carefully, assert yourself to ensure a fair deal, be honest in your dealings, ask for a cash memo, use the product as per instructions, be conscious of your rights and file a complaint in an appropriate consumer forum, and protect the environment. Who can file a complaint: a consumer, any recognised consumer association, one or more consumers with the same interest, the Central or State Government, the Central Consumer Protection Authority, or legal heir or representative of a deceased consumer. Redressal: Consumer Disputes Redressal Agencies: District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (up to Rs 1 crore), State Commission (above Rs 1 crore up to Rs 10 crore) and National Commission (above Rs 10 crore). Appeals: from District to State, from State to National and from National to the Supreme Court (within 30 days). Reliefs available to the consumer: to remove the defect in goods, replace the goods, refund the price, pay compensation for loss or injury, discontinue unfair trade practices, withdraw hazardous goods, issue corrective advertisement, and pay punitive damages and cost of the litigation. Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) regulates matters relating to violation of consumer rights, unfair trade practices and false or misleading advertisements. Product liability: the liability of the manufacturer, service provider or seller for harm caused by a defective product. E-commerce is covered; mediation cells are set up. National Consumer Day is observed on 24 December (the date the CPA 1986 was enacted) and World Consumer Rights Day on 15 March. Fee: the complaints to be filed in writing with the registered post; for claims up to Rs 5 lakh there is no fee. Consumer protection and unfair trade practices.
Deep dive: Rights and responsibilities
Consumers have six rights and corresponding responsibilities. Awareness and assertiveness are essential.
Deep dive: Redressal
District, State and National commissions handle disputes by value. Reliefs include repair, replacement, refund and compensation.
Deep dive: Law
The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 created the CCPA and covers product liability and e-commerce. Other laws protect consumers too.

Visual lesson

Consumer Protection

A consumer is a person who buys goods or avails any service for a consideration for personal use

🔑

Big idea

  • A consumer is a person who buys goods or avails any service for a consideration for personal use

Read the full explanation

A consumer is a person who buys goods or avails any service for a consideration for personal use. The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 replaced the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 and came into effect in July 2020. Importance of consumer protection: from the consumer's point of view (consumer ignorance, unorganised consumers, widespread exploitation) and from the business point of view (long-term interest, social responsibility, moral justification, government intervention, survival and growth). Ways and means of consumer protection: efforts of business (self-regulation, chambers of commerce, business associations), consumer awareness, consumer organisations and non-governmental organisations (voluntary consumer associations; Consumer Guidance Society of India) and government (legislation). Legal framework: Consumer Protection Act (CPA), Sale of Goods Act 1930, Indian Contract Act 1872, Essential Commodities Act 1955, Agricultural Produce (Grading and Marketing) Act 1937, Prevention of Food Adulteration Act 1954 (now Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006), Standards of Weights and Measures Act 1976, Trade Marks Act 1999, Competition Act 2002, and the Bureau of Indian Standards Act 2016 (BIS; ISI mark for industrial products; Agmark for agricultural products; Hallmark for jewellery). Consumer rights (CPA 2019, Section 2(9)): (1) right to safety, (2) right to be informed, (3) right to choose, (4) right to be heard, (5) right to seek redressal and (6) right to consumer awareness. Consumer responsibilities: be aware of various goods and services, buy only standardised goods, learn about the risks associated with products, read labels carefully, assert yourself to ensure a fair deal, be honest in your dealings, ask for a cash memo, use the product as per instructions, be conscious of your rights and file a complaint in an appropriate consumer forum, and protect the environment. Who can file a complaint: a consumer, any recognised consumer association, one or more consumers with the same interest, the Central or State Government, the Central Consumer Protection Authority, or legal heir or representative of a deceased consumer. Redressal: Consumer Disputes Redressal Agencies: District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (up to Rs 1 crore), State Commission (above Rs 1 crore up to Rs 10 crore) and National Commission (above Rs 10 crore). Appeals: from District to State, from State to National and from National to the Supreme Court (within 30 days). Reliefs available to the consumer: to remove the defect in goods, replace the goods, refund the price, pay compensation for loss or injury, discontinue unfair trade practices, withdraw hazardous goods, issue corrective advertisement, and pay punitive damages and cost of the litigation. Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) regulates matters relating to violation of consumer rights, unfair trade practices and false or misleading advertisements. Product liability: the liability of the manufacturer, service provider or seller for harm caused by a defective product. E-commerce is covered; mediation cells are set up. National Consumer Day is observed on 24 December (the date the CPA 1986 was enacted) and World Consumer Rights Day on 15 March. Fee: the complaints to be filed in writing with the registered post; for claims up to Rs 5 lakh there is no fee. Consumer protection and unfair trade practices.

🏛️

Rights and responsibilities

  • Consumers have six rights and corresponding responsibilities
  • Awareness and assertiveness are essential
🧠

Redressal

  • District, State and National commissions handle disputes by value
  • Reliefs include repair, replacement, refund and compensation
⚖️

Law

  • The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 created the CCPA and covers product liability and e-commerce
  • Other laws protect consumers too

lessons.title: Solutions
yt: class 12 chemistry solutions colligative properties raoult law osmotic pressure van t hoff

blocks.x: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of two or more components. The component present in the largest amount is the solvent and the other is the solute. Concentration terms: mass percentage = (mass of component / total mass) x 100; volume percentage; mass by volume percentage; parts per million (ppm) = (number of parts of component / total parts) x 10^6; mole fraction x_A = n_A / (n_A + n_B), and the sum of mole fractions is 1; molarity M = moles of solute / volume of solution in litres (depends on temperature); molality m = moles of solute / mass of solvent in kg (independent of temperature). Solubility: the maximum amount of solute that dissolves in a given amount of solvent at a given temperature; like dissolves like. Henry's law: the partial pressure of a gas in the vapour phase is proportional to its mole fraction in the solution: p = K_H x. Higher K_H means lower solubility; K_H increases with temperature, so gas solubility decreases as temperature rises. Applications: soda water bottles are sealed under high pressure; scuba divers suffer from bends (use helium-diluted air); anoxia at high altitude. Vapour pressure of a liquid solution; Raoult's law: the partial vapour pressure of each volatile component is directly proportional to its mole fraction: p_A = p_A^0 x_A, and total pressure p = p_A^0 x_A + p_B^0 x_B. For a solution of a non-volatile solute, the relative lowering of vapour pressure (p^0 - p)/p^0 = x_B (mole fraction of solute). Ideal solutions obey Raoult's law over the entire range; enthalpy of mixing is zero and volume change is zero (n-hexane and n-heptane; bromoethane and chloroethane). Non-ideal solutions show positive deviation (A-B interactions weaker than A-A and B-B; ethanol and acetone; Delta H mixing positive; Delta V positive) or negative deviation (A-B interactions stronger; chloroform and acetone; nitric acid and water; Delta H negative). Azeotropes are binary mixtures having the same composition in liquid and vapour phase and boiling at constant temperature: minimum boiling azeotropes (positive deviation; ethanol-water 95.5% ethanol) and maximum boiling azeotropes (negative deviation; nitric acid 68% and water). Colligative properties depend on the number of solute particles and not on their nature: (1) relative lowering of vapour pressure, (2) elevation of boiling point: Delta T_b = K_b m, where K_b is the molal elevation constant (K_b water = 0.52 K kg/mol), (3) depression of freezing point: Delta T_f = K_f m (K_f water = 1.86 K kg/mol) and (4) osmotic pressure. Molar mass from them: M_B = K_b x 1000 x w_B / (Delta T_b x w_A) for boiling point and similarly. Osmosis: the flow of solvent through a semipermeable membrane from pure solvent to solution (or lower to higher concentration). Osmotic pressure Pi = C R T = (n/V) R T; the molar mass M = w R T / (Pi V). Isotonic solutions have the same osmotic pressure (0.9% NaCl is isotonic with blood); hypertonic and hypotonic solutions cause shrinking or swelling of cells. Reverse osmosis occurs when a pressure larger than osmotic pressure is applied to the solution side and is used in desalination. Abnormal molar masses: association (e.g. ethanoic acid dimerises in benzene) decreases colligative effect, dissociation (KCl in water) increases it. van't Hoff factor i = normal molar mass / abnormal molar mass = observed colligative property / calculated; i = 1 + (n-1) alpha for dissociation; modified: Delta T_b = i K_b m, Delta T_f = i K_f m, Pi = i C R T. Examples: i for NaCl = 2, K2SO4 = 3, glucose = 1.
Deep dive: Concentration and Henry's law
Molality is temperature independent; molarity is not. Gas solubility rises with pressure and falls with temperature.
Deep dive: Raoult's law
Ideal solutions obey Raoult's law; non-ideal ones deviate positively or negatively. Azeotropes cannot be separated by fractional distillation.
Deep dive: Colligative properties
They depend on number of particles. The van't Hoff factor corrects for association and dissociation.
Hindi saransh
Vilayan: sandrata ke pad, Henry aur Raoult ke niyam, sahgunatmak gun, parasaran dab aur van't Hoff gunank.
Remember: molality is independent of temperature; colligative properties depend on number of particles.

A solution is a homogeneous mixture of two or more components

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Concentration and Henry's…›3Raoult's law›4Colligative properties
🔑

Big idea

  • A solution is a homogeneous mixture of two or more components
  • The component present in the largest amount is the solvent and the other is the solute
  • Concentration terms: mass percentage = (mass of component / total mass) x 100
  • Volume percentage
Read the full explanation

A solution is a homogeneous mixture of two or more components. The component present in the largest amount is the solvent and the other is the solute. Concentration terms: mass percentage = (mass of component / total mass) x 100; volume percentage; mass by volume percentage; parts per million (ppm) = (number of parts of component / total parts) x 10^6; mole fraction x_A = n_A / (n_A + n_B), and the sum of mole fractions is 1; molarity M = moles of solute / volume of solution in litres (depends on temperature); molality m = moles of solute / mass of solvent in kg (independent of temperature). Solubility: the maximum amount of solute that dissolves in a given amount of solvent at a given temperature; like dissolves like. Henry's law: the partial pressure of a gas in the vapour phase is proportional to its mole fraction in the solution: p = K_H x. Higher K_H means lower solubility; K_H increases with temperature, so gas solubility decreases as temperature rises. Applications: soda water bottles are sealed under high pressure; scuba divers suffer from bends (use helium-diluted air); anoxia at high altitude. Vapour pressure of a liquid solution; Raoult's law: the partial vapour pressure of each volatile component is directly proportional to its mole fraction: p_A = p_A^0 x_A, and total pressure p = p_A^0 x_A + p_B^0 x_B. For a solution of a non-volatile solute, the relative lowering of vapour pressure (p^0 - p)/p^0 = x_B (mole fraction of solute). Ideal solutions obey Raoult's law over the entire range; enthalpy of mixing is zero and volume change is zero (n-hexane and n-heptane; bromoethane and chloroethane). Non-ideal solutions show positive deviation (A-B interactions weaker than A-A and B-B; ethanol and acetone; Delta H mixing positive; Delta V positive) or negative deviation (A-B interactions stronger; chloroform and acetone; nitric acid and water; Delta H negative). Azeotropes are binary mixtures having the same composition in liquid and vapour phase and boiling at constant temperature: minimum boiling azeotropes (positive deviation; ethanol-water 95.5% ethanol) and maximum boiling azeotropes (negative deviation; nitric acid 68% and water). Colligative properties depend on the number of solute particles and not on their nature: (1) relative lowering of vapour pressure, (2) elevation of boiling point: Delta T_b = K_b m, where K_b is the molal elevation constant (K_b water = 0.52 K kg/mol), (3) depression of freezing point: Delta T_f = K_f m (K_f water = 1.86 K kg/mol) and (4) osmotic pressure. Molar mass from them: M_B = K_b x 1000 x w_B / (Delta T_b x w_A) for boiling point and similarly. Osmosis: the flow of solvent through a semipermeable membrane from pure solvent to solution (or lower to higher concentration). Osmotic pressure Pi = C R T = (n/V) R T; the molar mass M = w R T / (Pi V). Isotonic solutions have the same osmotic pressure (0.9% NaCl is isotonic with blood); hypertonic and hypotonic solutions cause shrinking or swelling of cells. Reverse osmosis occurs when a pressure larger than osmotic pressure is applied to the solution side and is used in desalination. Abnormal molar masses: association (e.g. ethanoic acid dimerises in benzene) decreases colligative effect, dissociation (KCl in water) increases it. van't Hoff factor i = normal molar mass / abnormal molar mass = observed colligative property / calculated; i = 1 + (n-1) alpha for dissociation; modified: Delta T_b = i K_b m, Delta T_f = i K_f m, Pi = i C R T. Examples: i for NaCl = 2, K2SO4 = 3, glucose = 1.

⚖️

Concentration and Henry's law

  • Molality is temperature independent
  • Molarity is not
  • Gas solubility rises with pressure and falls with temperature
⚖️

Raoult's law

  • Ideal solutions obey Raoult's law
  • Non-ideal ones deviate positively or negatively
  • Azeotropes cannot be separated by fractional distillation
🌟

Colligative properties

  • They depend on number of particles
  • The van't Hoff factor corrects for association and dissociation
🎯 Remember molality is independent of temperature; colligative properties depend on number of particles.
🇮🇳

lessons.title: Electrochemistry
yt: class 12 chemistry electrochemistry nernst equation conductance kohlrausch faraday cells corrosion

blocks.x: Electrochemistry studies the relationship between electrical energy and chemical reactions. A galvanic (voltaic) cell converts chemical energy into electrical energy through a spontaneous redox reaction: the Daniell cell has Zn|Zn2+ || Cu2+|Cu; the zinc anode undergoes oxidation, and the copper cathode undergoes reduction; a salt bridge (KCl or KNO3 in agar) maintains electrical neutrality. The cell is represented as Zn(s)|Zn2+(aq) || Cu2+(aq)|Cu(s). Electrode potential is measured against the standard hydrogen electrode (SHE), which is assigned 0.00 V. E cell = E cathode - E anode. Standard electrode potentials: Zn2+/Zn = -0.76 V; Cu2+/Cu = +0.34 V; so E cell of Daniell cell = 1.10 V. A more positive reduction potential means a stronger oxidising agent; a lower value means stronger reducing agent. The Nernst equation: E cell = E0 cell - (RT/nF) ln Q; at 298 K, E cell = E0 - (0.0591/n) log Q. At equilibrium E cell = 0 and E0 = (0.0591/n) log Kc. Gibbs energy: Delta G0 = -nF E0 cell; Delta G0 = -RT ln K. Faraday constant F = 96,500 C/mol (96487). Conductance G = 1/R (siemens); resistivity rho, conductivity kappa = 1/rho = G (l/A) = G G*, where G* is the cell constant (l/A). Molar conductivity Lambda_m = kappa x 1000 / C (S cm2 mol-1) where C is in mol/L. Strong electrolytes: Lambda_m increases slowly with dilution: Debye-Huckel-Onsager equation Lambda_m = Lambda_m0 - A sqrt(C). Weak electrolytes: Lambda_m rises steeply on dilution because the degree of dissociation increases and cannot be extrapolated to zero concentration. Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions: Lambda_m0 = lambda+0 + lambda-0 (the limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte is the sum of the contributions of its cation and anion). Degree of dissociation alpha = Lambda_m / Lambda_m0 and K_a = C alpha^2 / (1 - alpha). Electrolysis: Faraday's first law: the mass deposited m = Z I t; the amount of substance deposited is proportional to the quantity of charge passed; second law: masses deposited by the same charge are proportional to their equivalent weights. 1 mole of electrons = 1 faraday = 96500 C. Products of electrolysis depend on the nature of the electrolyte, electrode, and overpotential: electrolysis of molten NaCl gives Na and Cl2; aqueous NaCl gives H2 at the cathode and Cl2 at the anode with NaOH formed. Batteries: primary (Dry cell/Leclanche cell: Zn anode, graphite cathode with MnO2 and NH4Cl, EMF 1.5 V; mercury cell used in watches, hearing aids; constant 1.35 V) and secondary (lead storage battery: Pb anode and PbO2 cathode in 38% H2SO4, 12 V, discharge gives PbSO4 and water; nickel-cadmium cell). Fuel cells convert the energy of combustion of fuels such as hydrogen directly into electricity: H2-O2 fuel cell with an alkaline KOH electrolyte, used in Apollo space programme, efficiency about 70%, pollution-free; anode: 2H2 + 4OH- -> 4H2O + 4e-; cathode: O2 + 2H2O + 4e- -> 4OH-. Corrosion is an electrochemical phenomenon: rusting of iron; at the anode Fe -> Fe2+ + 2e-; at the cathode O2 + 4H+ + 4e- -> 2H2O; Fe2+ oxidised to Fe3+ forms Fe2O3.xH2O (rust). Prevention: barrier protection by painting, galvanisation (zinc coating) and cathodic protection with a more reactive metal such as Mg.
Deep dive: Galvanic cells and Nernst equation
A spontaneous redox reaction generates EMF. The Nernst equation links potential to concentration. Delta G = -nFE.
Deep dive: Conductance
Molar conductivity rises on dilution. Kohlrausch law gives limiting molar conductivities of weak electrolytes.
Deep dive: Electrolysis, batteries, corrosion
Faraday's laws quantify electrolysis. Batteries and fuel cells give practical power. Corrosion is an electrochemical process.

Electrochemistry

Electrochemistry studies the relationship between electrical energy and chemical reactions

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Galvanic cells and Nernst…›3Conductance›4Electrolysis, batteries…
🔑

Big idea

  • Electrochemistry studies the relationship between electrical energy and chemical reactions
  • A galvanic (voltaic) cell converts chemical energy into electrical energy through a spontaneous redox reaction: the Daniell cell has Zn|Zn2+ ||…
  • The zinc anode undergoes oxidation, and the copper cathode undergoes reduction
  • A salt bridge (KCl or KNO3 in agar) maintains electrical neutrality
Read the full explanation

Electrochemistry studies the relationship between electrical energy and chemical reactions. A galvanic (voltaic) cell converts chemical energy into electrical energy through a spontaneous redox reaction: the Daniell cell has Zn|Zn2+ || Cu2+|Cu; the zinc anode undergoes oxidation, and the copper cathode undergoes reduction; a salt bridge (KCl or KNO3 in agar) maintains electrical neutrality. The cell is represented as Zn(s)|Zn2+(aq) || Cu2+(aq)|Cu(s). Electrode potential is measured against the standard hydrogen electrode (SHE), which is assigned 0.00 V. E cell = E cathode - E anode. Standard electrode potentials: Zn2+/Zn = -0.76 V; Cu2+/Cu = +0.34 V; so E cell of Daniell cell = 1.10 V. A more positive reduction potential means a stronger oxidising agent; a lower value means stronger reducing agent. The Nernst equation: E cell = E0 cell - (RT/nF) ln Q; at 298 K, E cell = E0 - (0.0591/n) log Q. At equilibrium E cell = 0 and E0 = (0.0591/n) log Kc. Gibbs energy: Delta G0 = -nF E0 cell; Delta G0 = -RT ln K. Faraday constant F = 96,500 C/mol (96487). Conductance G = 1/R (siemens); resistivity rho, conductivity kappa = 1/rho = G (l/A) = G G*, where G* is the cell constant (l/A). Molar conductivity Lambda_m = kappa x 1000 / C (S cm2 mol-1) where C is in mol/L. Strong electrolytes: Lambda_m increases slowly with dilution: Debye-Huckel-Onsager equation Lambda_m = Lambda_m0 - A sqrt(C). Weak electrolytes: Lambda_m rises steeply on dilution because the degree of dissociation increases and cannot be extrapolated to zero concentration. Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions: Lambda_m0 = lambda+0 + lambda-0 (the limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte is the sum of the contributions of its cation and anion). Degree of dissociation alpha = Lambda_m / Lambda_m0 and K_a = C alpha^2 / (1 - alpha). Electrolysis: Faraday's first law: the mass deposited m = Z I t; the amount of substance deposited is proportional to the quantity of charge passed; second law: masses deposited by the same charge are proportional to their equivalent weights. 1 mole of electrons = 1 faraday = 96500 C. Products of electrolysis depend on the nature of the electrolyte, electrode, and overpotential: electrolysis of molten NaCl gives Na and Cl2; aqueous NaCl gives H2 at the cathode and Cl2 at the anode with NaOH formed. Batteries: primary (Dry cell/Leclanche cell: Zn anode, graphite cathode with MnO2 and NH4Cl, EMF 1.5 V; mercury cell used in watches, hearing aids; constant 1.35 V) and secondary (lead storage battery: Pb anode and PbO2 cathode in 38% H2SO4, 12 V, discharge gives PbSO4 and water; nickel-cadmium cell). Fuel cells convert the energy of combustion of fuels such as hydrogen directly into electricity: H2-O2 fuel cell with an alkaline KOH electrolyte, used in Apollo space programme, efficiency about 70%, pollution-free; anode: 2H2 + 4OH- -> 4H2O + 4e-; cathode: O2 + 2H2O + 4e- -> 4OH-. Corrosion is an electrochemical phenomenon: rusting of iron; at the anode Fe -> Fe2+ + 2e-; at the cathode O2 + 4H+ + 4e- -> 2H2O; Fe2+ oxidised to Fe3+ forms Fe2O3.xH2O (rust). Prevention: barrier protection by painting, galvanisation (zinc coating) and cathodic protection with a more reactive metal such as Mg.

🧮

Galvanic cells and Nernst equation

  • A spontaneous redox reaction generates EMF
  • The Nernst equation links potential to concentration
  • Delta G = -nFE
🧠

Conductance

  • Molar conductivity rises on dilution
  • Kohlrausch law gives limiting molar conductivities of weak electrolytes
🌟

Electrolysis, batteries, corrosion

  • Faraday's laws quantify electrolysis
  • Batteries and fuel cells give practical power
  • Corrosion is an electrochemical process
🎯 Remember E cell = E cathode minus E anode; Delta G = -nFE.
🇮🇳

lessons.title: Chemical Kinetics
yt: class 12 chemistry chemical kinetics rate law order half life arrhenius activation energy

blocks.x: Chemical kinetics is the study of rates of chemical reactions and the factors affecting them and the mechanism. The rate of a reaction is the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time: for R -> P, average rate = -Delta[R]/Delta t = +Delta[P]/Delta t; instantaneous rate is dx/dt. For aA + bB -> cC + dD, rate = -(1/a) d[A]/dt = -(1/b) d[B]/dt = (1/c) d[C]/dt. Units of rate: mol L-1 s-1. Factors affecting rate: concentration of reactants, temperature, catalyst, surface area and nature of reactants, and radiation. Rate law: rate = k [A]^x [B]^y, where x and y are determined experimentally; k is the rate constant. Order of reaction is the sum of the exponents x + y, determined experimentally and can be zero, fractional or whole. Molecularity is the number of reacting species colliding simultaneously in an elementary step; it is always a whole number (1, 2, 3) and cannot be zero or fractional; it applies only to elementary reactions. Units of k: for order n, (mol L-1)^(1-n) s-1. Zero order: rate = k, [A] = [A]0 - kt; units of k are mol L-1 s-1; t1/2 = [A]0/2k. First order: rate = k[A]; integrated: ln([A]0/[A]) = kt, or k = (2.303/t) log([A]0/[A]); units s-1; t1/2 = 0.693/k, independent of initial concentration. Examples of first-order reactions: decomposition of N2O5, radioactive decay, hydrogenation of ethene; pseudo first order reactions: hydrolysis of ethyl acetate (acid catalysed), inversion of cane sugar; these seem first order since one reactant is in large excess. Determination of order: initial rate method, integrated rate method, graphical (plot of log[A] vs t is a straight line with slope = -k/2.303 for first order). Temperature dependence: the rate generally doubles for every 10 degrees rise (temperature coefficient 2 to 3). The Arrhenius equation: k = A e^(-Ea/RT); where A is the Arrhenius (frequency or pre-exponential) factor and Ea is the activation energy: ln k = ln A - Ea/RT; log k = log A - Ea/(2.303 RT); a plot of ln k vs 1/T is a straight line with slope -Ea/R; log(k2/k1) = (Ea/(2.303 R)) ((T2 - T1)/(T1 T2)). Activation energy is the minimum extra energy that reactants must have to form the activated complex (threshold energy - average energy of reactants); lower activation energy gives faster reactions. The fraction of molecules with energy equal to or greater than Ea is e^(-Ea/RT). Collision theory: reaction requires collisions with proper orientation and energy greater than the threshold: rate = P Z_AB e^(-Ea/RT), where P is the steric (probability) factor. A catalyst provides an alternate pathway of lower activation energy; it does not change Delta H or the equilibrium constant. Mechanism: complex reactions occur in steps; the slowest step is the rate-determining step; the order depends on the slowest step. Example: 2NO2 + F2 -> 2NO2F: rate = k[NO2][F2]. Radioactive decay is first order.
Deep dive: Rate and order
Rate laws are determined experimentally. Order is not equal to stoichiometry. Molecularity applies to elementary steps.
Deep dive: Integrated rate laws
Zero and first-order reactions have distinct plots and half-lives. First order half-life is constant.
Deep dive: Temperature and catalyst
The Arrhenius equation gives activation energy. Catalysts lower Ea without changing equilibrium.

Visual lesson

Chemical Kinetics

Chemical kinetics is the study of rates of chemical reactions and the factors affecting them and the mechanism

formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Rate and order›3Integrated rate laws›4Temperature and catalyst
🔑

Big idea

  • Chemical kinetics is the study of rates of chemical reactions and the factors affecting them and the mechanism
  • The rate of a reaction is the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time: for R -> P, average rate = -Delta[R]/Delta t =…
  • Instantaneous rate is dx/dt
  • For aA + bB -> cC + dD, rate = -(1/a) d[A]/dt = -(1/b) d[B]/dt = (1/c) d[C]/dt
Read the full explanation

Chemical kinetics is the study of rates of chemical reactions and the factors affecting them and the mechanism. The rate of a reaction is the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time: for R -> P, average rate = -Delta[R]/Delta t = +Delta[P]/Delta t; instantaneous rate is dx/dt. For aA + bB -> cC + dD, rate = -(1/a) d[A]/dt = -(1/b) d[B]/dt = (1/c) d[C]/dt. Units of rate: mol L-1 s-1. Factors affecting rate: concentration of reactants, temperature, catalyst, surface area and nature of reactants, and radiation. Rate law: rate = k [A]^x [B]^y, where x and y are determined experimentally; k is the rate constant. Order of reaction is the sum of the exponents x + y, determined experimentally and can be zero, fractional or whole. Molecularity is the number of reacting species colliding simultaneously in an elementary step; it is always a whole number (1, 2, 3) and cannot be zero or fractional; it applies only to elementary reactions. Units of k: for order n, (mol L-1)^(1-n) s-1. Zero order: rate = k, [A] = [A]0 - kt; units of k are mol L-1 s-1; t1/2 = [A]0/2k. First order: rate = k[A]; integrated: ln([A]0/[A]) = kt, or k = (2.303/t) log([A]0/[A]); units s-1; t1/2 = 0.693/k, independent of initial concentration. Examples of first-order reactions: decomposition of N2O5, radioactive decay, hydrogenation of ethene; pseudo first order reactions: hydrolysis of ethyl acetate (acid catalysed), inversion of cane sugar; these seem first order since one reactant is in large excess. Determination of order: initial rate method, integrated rate method, graphical (plot of log[A] vs t is a straight line with slope = -k/2.303 for first order). Temperature dependence: the rate generally doubles for every 10 degrees rise (temperature coefficient 2 to 3). The Arrhenius equation: k = A e^(-Ea/RT); where A is the Arrhenius (frequency or pre-exponential) factor and Ea is the activation energy: ln k = ln A - Ea/RT; log k = log A - Ea/(2.303 RT); a plot of ln k vs 1/T is a straight line with slope -Ea/R; log(k2/k1) = (Ea/(2.303 R)) ((T2 - T1)/(T1 T2)). Activation energy is the minimum extra energy that reactants must have to form the activated complex (threshold energy - average energy of reactants); lower activation energy gives faster reactions. The fraction of molecules with energy equal to or greater than Ea is e^(-Ea/RT). Collision theory: reaction requires collisions with proper orientation and energy greater than the threshold: rate = P Z_AB e^(-Ea/RT), where P is the steric (probability) factor. A catalyst provides an alternate pathway of lower activation energy; it does not change Delta H or the equilibrium constant. Mechanism: complex reactions occur in steps; the slowest step is the rate-determining step; the order depends on the slowest step. Example: 2NO2 + F2 -> 2NO2F: rate = k[NO2][F2]. Radioactive decay is first order.

📌

Rate and order

  • Rate laws are determined experimentally
  • Order is not equal to stoichiometry
  • Molecularity applies to elementary steps
⚖️

Integrated rate laws

  • Zero and first-order reactions have distinct plots and half-lives
  • First order half-life is constant
🌡️

Temperature and catalyst

  • The Arrhenius equation gives activation energy
  • Catalysts lower Ea without changing equilibrium
🎯 Remember first order t1/2 = 0.693/k; zero order t1/2 = [A]0/2k.
🇮🇳

lessons.title: The d- and f-Block Elements
yt: class 12 chemistry d block f block transition elements lanthanoids actinoids KMnO4 K2Cr2O7

blocks.x: The d-block elements are those in which the last electron enters the d-orbital; they occupy groups 3 to 12 and include the 3d, 4d, 5d and 6d series. Transition elements have partly filled d-orbitals in their atoms or ions; zinc, cadmium and mercury (group 12) are not considered transition elements because they have fully filled d10 configuration in the atom and ions. General electronic configuration (n-1)d1-10 ns1-2. Properties: metallic, high melting points (except Zn, Cd and Hg, which are low), because of strong metallic bonding by unpaired d-electrons; high enthalpies of atomisation; the melting points rise to a maximum at about d5 (Cr, Mo, W) and then fall; atomic radii decrease along a series then remain nearly constant owing to the d-electron shielding; lanthanoid contraction makes 4d and 5d radii of the second and third series similar (Zr and Hf). Ionisation enthalpies increase along the series. Variable oxidation states because (n-1)d and ns electrons have comparable energies; Mn shows +2 to +7. Stability of higher oxidation states in oxides and fluorides; lower oxidation states in ionic compounds. Standard electrode potentials: E0 Cu2+/Cu is positive (+0.34) as the sum of enthalpy of atomisation, ionisation and hydration is unfavourable. Magnetic properties: paramagnetism due to unpaired electrons; magnetic moment mu = sqrt(n(n+2)) BM where n is the number of unpaired electrons. Coloured ions due to d-d transitions: Ti3+, Cu2+ (blue) and Ni2+ (green); Sc3+, Zn2+ and Ti4+ are colourless as they have empty or fully filled d orbitals. Complex formation is due to small size, high charge and availability of vacant d orbitals. Catalytic properties: Fe in Haber process, V2O5 in the contact process, Ni in hydrogenation. Interstitial compounds (TiC, Fe3H) are hard and high-melting. Alloys: brass (Cu-Zn), bronze (Cu-Sn) and steel. Important compounds: potassium dichromate K2Cr2O7 prepared from chromite ore FeCr2O4 by fusion with sodium carbonate in air to form sodium chromate (yellow), acidified to sodium dichromate (orange), then treated with KCl; in acidic solution it is a strong oxidising agent: Cr2O7^2- + 14H+ + 6e- -> 2Cr3+ + 7H2O; chromate-dichromate equilibrium depends on pH: yellow CrO4^2- in basic and orange Cr2O7^2- in acidic medium. Potassium permanganate KMnO4 is prepared from pyrolusite MnO2 by fusion with KOH in air to give green K2MnO4, which is oxidised electrolytically or by disproportionation in acid to purple KMnO4. In acid: MnO4- + 8H+ + 5e- -> Mn2+ + 4H2O (equivalent weight M/5); in neutral or faintly alkaline: MnO4- + 2H2O + 3e- -> MnO2 + 4OH-. Oxidises Fe2+ to Fe3+, oxalate to CO2, SO2 and H2S. The f-block elements: lanthanoids (4f series, atomic numbers 58 to 71; Ce to Lu) and actinoids (5f series, 90 to 103; Th to Lr). Lanthanoids: general configuration [Xe]4f1-14 5d0-1 6s2; common oxidation state +3 (Ce +4, Eu +2); lanthanoid contraction is the steady decrease in atomic and ionic radii with increasing atomic number due to poor shielding by 4f electrons; consequences: similarity of 4d and 5d elements, difficulty in separation of lanthanoids, and decrease in basicity of hydroxides. Misch metal (lanthanoid 95% with iron 5%, traces of S, C, Ca, Al) is used for making flints for lighters. Actinoids are radioactive, with a wide range of oxidation states (+3 to +7); less shielding by 5f electrons. Uses: Mg-Ce alloys.
Deep dive: General properties
Transition metals show variable oxidation states, coloured ions, magnetism, catalysis and complex formation. Lanthanoid contraction affects the third series.
Deep dive: K2Cr2O7 and KMnO4
Both are strong oxidising agents in acid. Their preparations and half reactions are important.
Deep dive: f-block
Lanthanoids mostly show +3 state and contraction; actinoids are radioactive with many oxidation states.

Visual lesson

The d- and f-Block Elements

The d-block elements are those in which the last electron enters the d-orbital

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2General properties›3K2Cr2O7 and KMnO4›4F-block
Lanthanoids58-71

Misch metal95% lanthanoid + 5% Fe
🔑

Big idea

  • The d-block elements are those in which the last electron enters the d-orbital
  • They occupy groups 3 to 12 and include the 3d, 4d, 5d and 6d series
  • Transition elements have partly filled d-orbitals in their atoms or ions
  • Zinc, cadmium and mercury (group 12) are not considered transition elements because they have fully filled d10 configuration in the atom and ions
Read the full explanation

The d-block elements are those in which the last electron enters the d-orbital; they occupy groups 3 to 12 and include the 3d, 4d, 5d and 6d series. Transition elements have partly filled d-orbitals in their atoms or ions; zinc, cadmium and mercury (group 12) are not considered transition elements because they have fully filled d10 configuration in the atom and ions. General electronic configuration (n-1)d1-10 ns1-2. Properties: metallic, high melting points (except Zn, Cd and Hg, which are low), because of strong metallic bonding by unpaired d-electrons; high enthalpies of atomisation; the melting points rise to a maximum at about d5 (Cr, Mo, W) and then fall; atomic radii decrease along a series then remain nearly constant owing to the d-electron shielding; lanthanoid contraction makes 4d and 5d radii of the second and third series similar (Zr and Hf). Ionisation enthalpies increase along the series. Variable oxidation states because (n-1)d and ns electrons have comparable energies; Mn shows +2 to +7. Stability of higher oxidation states in oxides and fluorides; lower oxidation states in ionic compounds. Standard electrode potentials: E0 Cu2+/Cu is positive (+0.34) as the sum of enthalpy of atomisation, ionisation and hydration is unfavourable. Magnetic properties: paramagnetism due to unpaired electrons; magnetic moment mu = sqrt(n(n+2)) BM where n is the number of unpaired electrons. Coloured ions due to d-d transitions: Ti3+, Cu2+ (blue) and Ni2+ (green); Sc3+, Zn2+ and Ti4+ are colourless as they have empty or fully filled d orbitals. Complex formation is due to small size, high charge and availability of vacant d orbitals. Catalytic properties: Fe in Haber process, V2O5 in the contact process, Ni in hydrogenation. Interstitial compounds (TiC, Fe3H) are hard and high-melting. Alloys: brass (Cu-Zn), bronze (Cu-Sn) and steel. Important compounds: potassium dichromate K2Cr2O7 prepared from chromite ore FeCr2O4 by fusion with sodium carbonate in air to form sodium chromate (yellow), acidified to sodium dichromate (orange), then treated with KCl; in acidic solution it is a strong oxidising agent: Cr2O7^2- + 14H+ + 6e- -> 2Cr3+ + 7H2O; chromate-dichromate equilibrium depends on pH: yellow CrO4^2- in basic and orange Cr2O7^2- in acidic medium. Potassium permanganate KMnO4 is prepared from pyrolusite MnO2 by fusion with KOH in air to give green K2MnO4, which is oxidised electrolytically or by disproportionation in acid to purple KMnO4. In acid: MnO4- + 8H+ + 5e- -> Mn2+ + 4H2O (equivalent weight M/5); in neutral or faintly alkaline: MnO4- + 2H2O + 3e- -> MnO2 + 4OH-. Oxidises Fe2+ to Fe3+, oxalate to CO2, SO2 and H2S. The f-block elements: lanthanoids (4f series, atomic numbers 58 to 71; Ce to Lu) and actinoids (5f series, 90 to 103; Th to Lr). Lanthanoids: general configuration [Xe]4f1-14 5d0-1 6s2; common oxidation state +3 (Ce +4, Eu +2); lanthanoid contraction is the steady decrease in atomic and ionic radii with increasing atomic number due to poor shielding by 4f electrons; consequences: similarity of 4d and 5d elements, difficulty in separation of lanthanoids, and decrease in basicity of hydroxides. Misch metal (lanthanoid 95% with iron 5%, traces of S, C, Ca, Al) is used for making flints for lighters. Actinoids are radioactive, with a wide range of oxidation states (+3 to +7); less shielding by 5f electrons. Uses: Mg-Ce alloys.

General properties

  • Transition metals show variable oxidation states, coloured ions, magnetism, catalysis and complex formation
  • Lanthanoid contraction affects the third series
🧠

K2Cr2O7 and KMnO4

  • Both are strong oxidising agents in acid
  • Their preparations and half reactions are important
🌟

F-block

  • Lanthanoids mostly show +3 state and contraction
  • Actinoids are radioactive with many oxidation states
🎯 Remember lanthanoid contraction makes Zr and Hf nearly the same size.

blocks.x: Coordination compounds contain a central metal atom or ion bonded to a fixed number of ligands (ions or molecules) by coordinate bonds; examples K4[Fe(CN)6], [Cu(NH3)4]SO4, [Ni(CO)4]. Double salts such as Mohr's salt (FeSO4.(NH4)2SO4.6H2O), carnallite and potash alum dissociate completely into simple ions in water, but complexes do not lose identity. Werner's theory (1893, Nobel Prize 1913): metals show two types of valence: primary valence (oxidation state; ionisable; satisfied by negative ions) and secondary valence (coordination number; non-ionisable; satisfied by neutral molecules or negative ions); secondary valences have a fixed spatial arrangement: octahedral (CN 6), tetrahedral and square planar (CN 4). Terms: coordination entity (the central atom plus ligands in square brackets), central atom/ion, ligands (monodentate: Cl-, NH3, H2O, CN-; bidentate: ethane-1,2-diamine (en), oxalate; polydentate: EDTA, which is hexadentate; ambidentate: NO2- (nitro N or nitrito O) and SCN- (thiocyanato S or isothiocyanato N)), coordination number (the number of ligand donor atoms bonded to the metal), coordination sphere, counter ions, oxidation number and homoleptic (only one kind of donor group) and heteroleptic complexes. Chelate: a ligand binding through two or more donor atoms to form ring structures; chelates are more stable. Nomenclature (IUPAC): cation named first; ligands named in alphabetical order before the metal; anionic ligands end in -o (chlorido, cyanido, oxalato), neutral ligands retain names except aqua (H2O), ammine (NH3), carbonyl (CO) and nitrosyl (NO); prefixes di, tri, tetra for simple ligands and bis, tris for complex ones; the oxidation state of the metal is in Roman numerals in brackets; for anionic complexes the metal name ends in -ate (ferrate, cuprate, argentate, aurate, plumbate, stannate). Example: [Co(NH3)6]Cl3 is hexaamminecobalt(III) chloride. K3[Fe(CN)6] is potassium hexacyanidoferrate(III). Isomerism: structural (linkage, coordination, ionisation, hydrate, solvate) and stereoisomerism (geometrical: cis-trans in [Pt(NH3)2Cl2] square planar and in [Co(NH3)4Cl2]+ octahedral; fac-mer in MA3B3; optical isomerism in octahedral complexes such as [Co(en)3]3+ and cis-[CoCl2(en)2]). Square planar MA4 and tetrahedral complexes do not show geometrical isomerism. Bonding: Valence bond theory (VBT) uses hybridisation: octahedral d2sp3 (inner orbital, low spin, strong field ligands) or sp3d2 (outer orbital, high spin, weak field ligands); tetrahedral sp3; square planar dsp2. [Ni(CO)4] is tetrahedral and diamagnetic (Ni(0) d10 sp3); [Ni(CN)4]2- is square planar and diamagnetic (dsp2); [NiCl4]2- is tetrahedral and paramagnetic; [Fe(CN)6]4- is diamagnetic d2sp3; [FeF6]3- is paramagnetic sp3d2. Crystal field theory (CFT): ligands are point charges that split the d orbitals; in octahedral fields, the t2g (lower; dxy, dyz, dzx) and eg (higher; dx2-y2, dz2) sets are separated by Delta_o; strong field ligands (large Delta_o > P, the pairing energy) give low spin; weak field gives high spin. The spectrochemical series: I- < Br- < SCN- < Cl- < F- < OH- < C2O4^2- < H2O < NCS- < edta4- < NH3 < en < CN- < CO. In tetrahedral complexes, Delta_t = (4/9) Delta_o, so they are always high spin. Colour comes from d-d transitions of the complementary colour absorbed. Importance: haemoglobin (Fe), chlorophyll (Mg), vitamin B12 (Co), cisplatin (anticancer), EDTA in hardness estimation, extraction of silver and gold by cyanide complexes, Ni purified by Mond process, and qualitative analysis (Ni-DMG red precipitate).
Deep dive: Werner and nomenclature
Primary and secondary valences give oxidation state and coordination number. IUPAC naming lists ligands alphabetically and states the oxidation number.
Deep dive: Isomerism and bonding
Geometrical and optical isomerism arise in octahedral and square planar complexes. VBT uses hybridisation; CFT uses d-orbital splitting.
Deep dive: Importance
Complexes occur in biology, medicine, extraction and analysis.

Big idea
