Read the full explanation

Coordination compounds contain a central metal atom or ion bonded to a fixed number of ligands (ions or molecules) by coordinate bonds; examples K4[Fe(CN)6], [Cu(NH3)4]SO4, [Ni(CO)4]. Double salts such as Mohr's salt (FeSO4.(NH4)2SO4.6H2O), carnallite and potash alum dissociate completely into simple ions in water, but complexes do not lose identity. Werner's theory (1893, Nobel Prize 1913): metals show two types of valence: primary valence (oxidation state; ionisable; satisfied by negative ions) and secondary valence (coordination number; non-ionisable; satisfied by neutral molecules or negative ions); secondary valences have a fixed spatial arrangement: octahedral (CN 6), tetrahedral and square planar (CN 4). Terms: coordination entity (the central atom plus ligands in square brackets), central atom/ion, ligands (monodentate: Cl-, NH3, H2O, CN-; bidentate: ethane-1,2-diamine (en), oxalate; polydentate: EDTA, which is hexadentate; ambidentate: NO2- (nitro N or nitrito O) and SCN- (thiocyanato S or isothiocyanato N)), coordination number (the number of ligand donor atoms bonded to the metal), coordination sphere, counter ions, oxidation number and homoleptic (only one kind of donor group) and heteroleptic complexes. Chelate: a ligand binding through two or more donor atoms to form ring structures; chelates are more stable. Nomenclature (IUPAC): cation named first; ligands named in alphabetical order before the metal; anionic ligands end in -o (chlorido, cyanido, oxalato), neutral ligands retain names except aqua (H2O), ammine (NH3), carbonyl (CO) and nitrosyl (NO); prefixes di, tri, tetra for simple ligands and bis, tris for complex ones; the oxidation state of the metal is in Roman numerals in brackets; for anionic complexes the metal name ends in -ate (ferrate, cuprate, argentate, aurate, plumbate, stannate). Example: [Co(NH3)6]Cl3 is hexaamminecobalt(III) chloride. K3[Fe(CN)6] is potassium hexacyanidoferrate(III). Isomerism: structural (linkage, coordination, ionisation, hydrate, solvate) and stereoisomerism (geometrical: cis-trans in [Pt(NH3)2Cl2] square planar and in [Co(NH3)4Cl2]+ octahedral; fac-mer in MA3B3; optical isomerism in octahedral complexes such as [Co(en)3]3+ and cis-[CoCl2(en)2]). Square planar MA4 and tetrahedral complexes do not show geometrical isomerism. Bonding: Valence bond theory (VBT) uses hybridisation: octahedral d2sp3 (inner orbital, low spin, strong field ligands) or sp3d2 (outer orbital, high spin, weak field ligands); tetrahedral sp3; square planar dsp2. [Ni(CO)4] is tetrahedral and diamagnetic (Ni(0) d10 sp3); [Ni(CN)4]2- is square planar and diamagnetic (dsp2); [NiCl4]2- is tetrahedral and paramagnetic; [Fe(CN)6]4- is diamagnetic d2sp3; [FeF6]3- is paramagnetic sp3d2. Crystal field theory (CFT): ligands are point charges that split the d orbitals; in octahedral fields, the t2g (lower; dxy, dyz, dzx) and eg (higher; dx2-y2, dz2) sets are separated by Delta_o; strong field ligands (large Delta_o > P, the pairing energy) give low spin; weak field gives high spin. The spectrochemical series: I- < Br- < SCN- < Cl- < F- < OH- < C2O4^2- < H2O < NCS- < edta4- < NH3 < en < CN- < CO. In tetrahedral complexes, Delta_t = (4/9) Delta_o, so they are always high spin. Colour comes from d-d transitions of the complementary colour absorbed. Importance: haemoglobin (Fe), chlorophyll (Mg), vitamin B12 (Co), cisplatin (anticancer), EDTA in hardness estimation, extraction of silver and gold by cyanide complexes, Ni purified by Mond process, and qualitative analysis (Ni-DMG red precipitate).

📌

Werner and nomenclature

  • Primary and secondary valences give oxidation state and coordination number
  • IUPAC naming lists ligands alphabetically and states the oxidation number
⚗️

Isomerism and bonding

  • Geometrical and optical isomerism arise in octahedral and square planar complexes
  • VBT uses hybridisation
  • CFT uses d-orbital splitting
🌟

Importance

  • Complexes occur in biology, medicine, extraction and analysis

lessons.title: Haloalkanes and Haloarenes
yt: class 12 chemistry haloalkanes haloarenes SN1 SN2 nucleophilic substitution chirality freons DDT

blocks.x: Haloalkanes contain a halogen attached to an sp3 carbon; haloarenes contain halogen on an sp2 carbon of an aromatic ring. Classification: mono, di, polyhalogen compounds; alkyl (primary, secondary, tertiary), allylic, benzylic, vinylic and aryl halides. Nomenclature: IUPAC names; e.g. CH3CH2Br is bromoethane. Nature of C-X bond: polar; bond length increases and bond enthalpy decreases from C-F to C-I. Preparation of haloalkanes: from alcohols with HX/ZnCl2 (Lucas reagent), PCl5, PCl3 or SOCl2 (best method as the by-products are gases); from hydrocarbons by free radical halogenation (gives mixtures); addition of HX to alkenes (Markovnikov's rule) and halogens; halogen exchange: Finkelstein reaction (alkyl chloride or bromide with NaI in dry acetone gives alkyl iodide) and Swarts reaction (alkyl chloride/bromide with AgF, Hg2F2, CoF2 or SbF3 gives alkyl fluoride). Haloarenes: electrophilic substitution with halogens in presence of Lewis acid; Sandmeyer reaction (diazonium salt with CuCl/HCl or CuBr/HBr); Gattermann reaction (Cu powder). Physical properties: boiling points are higher than hydrocarbons of comparable mass; they increase with mass of the halogen; branching lowers; insoluble in water; denser than water (chloro derivatives, bromo, iodo). Chemical reactions: nucleophilic substitution (SN) is the main reaction. SN2 (substitution nucleophilic bimolecular): single step, rate = k[RX][Nu], inversion of configuration (Walden inversion), favoured by primary alkyl halides and polar aprotic solvents; order of reactivity: methyl > primary > secondary > tertiary. SN1 (unimolecular): two steps; first slow step forms a carbocation; rate = k[RX]; racemisation (retention and inversion) with chiral substrates; favoured by tertiary, allylic and benzylic halides in polar protic solvents: tertiary > secondary > primary. Reactivity of halides: RI > RBr > RCl > RF. Chirality: a carbon with four different groups is a chiral (asymmetric) centre; enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images, optically active; a racemic mixture (50:50) is optically inactive, called (+/-). Dextrorotatory (d or +) rotates the plane of polarised light to the right and laevorotatory (l or -) to the left. Elimination reactions: dehydrohalogenation with alcoholic KOH follows Saytzeff (Zaitsev) rule: the more substituted alkene is the major product. Reaction with aqueous KOH gives alcohols; alcoholic KOH gives alkenes. With metals: Grignard reagent RMgX is formed with Mg in dry ether; Wurtz reaction gives alkanes with sodium in dry ether (2RX + 2Na -> R-R + 2NaX); Wurtz-Fittig reaction gives alkylarenes. Haloarenes are less reactive towards nucleophilic substitution due to resonance (partial double bond character), sp2 hybridised carbon (shorter C-X bond) and instability of phenyl cation; they undergo nucleophilic substitution with strongly electron withdrawing groups at ortho or para positions (2,4-dinitrochlorobenzene reacts readily). Electrophilic substitution in haloarenes: halogens are deactivating but ortho-para directing. Fittig reaction gives biaryls. Polyhalogen compounds: dichloromethane (solvent; paint remover; harms the central nervous system), trichloromethane (chloroform; anaesthetic earlier; oxidised by air to poisonous phosgene so stored in dark bottles filled completely), triiodomethane (iodoform; antiseptic; yellow solid), tetrachloromethane (carbon tetrachloride; fire extinguisher; damages the liver and contributes to ozone depletion), freons (CFCs; refrigerants; ozone depletion) and DDT (dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane; first chlorinated organic insecticide; non-biodegradable and toxic to fish; banned in many countries).
Deep dive: Substitution
SN2 gives inversion in one step; SN1 gives racemisation via a carbocation. Reactivity depends on structure and solvent.
Deep dive: Preparation and elimination
Alkyl halides are made from alcohols or alkenes. Alcoholic KOH gives alkenes following Saytzeff rule.
Deep dive: Haloarenes and polyhalogens
Haloarenes resist nucleophilic substitution unless activated. Freons and DDT cause environmental problems.
Hindi saransh
Halo-alkane aur halo-arene: SN1, SN2, Saytzeff niyam, Grignard abhikarak, freon aur DDT.
Remember: SN2 inverts; SN1 racemises; reactivity RI > RBr > RCl > RF.

Visual lesson

Haloalkanes and Haloarenes

Haloalkanes contain a halogen attached to an sp3 carbon

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Substitution›3Preparation and elimination›4Haloarenes and polyhalogens
🔑

Big idea

  • Haloalkanes contain a halogen attached to an sp3 carbon
  • Haloarenes contain halogen on an sp2 carbon of an aromatic ring
  • Classification: mono, di, polyhalogen compounds
  • Alkyl (primary, secondary, tertiary), allylic, benzylic, vinylic and aryl halides
Read the full explanation

Haloalkanes contain a halogen attached to an sp3 carbon; haloarenes contain halogen on an sp2 carbon of an aromatic ring. Classification: mono, di, polyhalogen compounds; alkyl (primary, secondary, tertiary), allylic, benzylic, vinylic and aryl halides. Nomenclature: IUPAC names; e.g. CH3CH2Br is bromoethane. Nature of C-X bond: polar; bond length increases and bond enthalpy decreases from C-F to C-I. Preparation of haloalkanes: from alcohols with HX/ZnCl2 (Lucas reagent), PCl5, PCl3 or SOCl2 (best method as the by-products are gases); from hydrocarbons by free radical halogenation (gives mixtures); addition of HX to alkenes (Markovnikov's rule) and halogens; halogen exchange: Finkelstein reaction (alkyl chloride or bromide with NaI in dry acetone gives alkyl iodide) and Swarts reaction (alkyl chloride/bromide with AgF, Hg2F2, CoF2 or SbF3 gives alkyl fluoride). Haloarenes: electrophilic substitution with halogens in presence of Lewis acid; Sandmeyer reaction (diazonium salt with CuCl/HCl or CuBr/HBr); Gattermann reaction (Cu powder). Physical properties: boiling points are higher than hydrocarbons of comparable mass; they increase with mass of the halogen; branching lowers; insoluble in water; denser than water (chloro derivatives, bromo, iodo). Chemical reactions: nucleophilic substitution (SN) is the main reaction. SN2 (substitution nucleophilic bimolecular): single step, rate = k[RX][Nu], inversion of configuration (Walden inversion), favoured by primary alkyl halides and polar aprotic solvents; order of reactivity: methyl > primary > secondary > tertiary. SN1 (unimolecular): two steps; first slow step forms a carbocation; rate = k[RX]; racemisation (retention and inversion) with chiral substrates; favoured by tertiary, allylic and benzylic halides in polar protic solvents: tertiary > secondary > primary. Reactivity of halides: RI > RBr > RCl > RF. Chirality: a carbon with four different groups is a chiral (asymmetric) centre; enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images, optically active; a racemic mixture (50:50) is optically inactive, called (+/-). Dextrorotatory (d or +) rotates the plane of polarised light to the right and laevorotatory (l or -) to the left. Elimination reactions: dehydrohalogenation with alcoholic KOH follows Saytzeff (Zaitsev) rule: the more substituted alkene is the major product. Reaction with aqueous KOH gives alcohols; alcoholic KOH gives alkenes. With metals: Grignard reagent RMgX is formed with Mg in dry ether; Wurtz reaction gives alkanes with sodium in dry ether (2RX + 2Na -> R-R + 2NaX); Wurtz-Fittig reaction gives alkylarenes. Haloarenes are less reactive towards nucleophilic substitution due to resonance (partial double bond character), sp2 hybridised carbon (shorter C-X bond) and instability of phenyl cation; they undergo nucleophilic substitution with strongly electron withdrawing groups at ortho or para positions (2,4-dinitrochlorobenzene reacts readily). Electrophilic substitution in haloarenes: halogens are deactivating but ortho-para directing. Fittig reaction gives biaryls. Polyhalogen compounds: dichloromethane (solvent; paint remover; harms the central nervous system), trichloromethane (chloroform; anaesthetic earlier; oxidised by air to poisonous phosgene so stored in dark bottles filled completely), triiodomethane (iodoform; antiseptic; yellow solid), tetrachloromethane (carbon tetrachloride; fire extinguisher; damages the liver and contributes to ozone depletion), freons (CFCs; refrigerants; ozone depletion) and DDT (dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane; first chlorinated organic insecticide; non-biodegradable and toxic to fish; banned in many countries).

📌

Substitution

  • SN2 gives inversion in one step
  • SN1 gives racemisation via a carbocation
  • Reactivity depends on structure and solvent
🧠

Preparation and elimination

  • Alkyl halides are made from alcohols or alkenes
  • Alcoholic KOH gives alkenes following Saytzeff rule
🌟

Haloarenes and polyhalogens

  • Haloarenes resist nucleophilic substitution unless activated
  • Freons and DDT cause environmental problems
🧮

lessons.title: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
yt: class 12 chemistry alcohols phenols ethers lucas test kolbe reimer tiemann williamson

blocks.x: Alcohols contain an -OH on an sp3 carbon; phenols contain -OH on an sp2 carbon of benzene; ethers have an oxygen bonded to two carbons (R-O-R). Classification of alcohols: primary, secondary and tertiary; monohydric, dihydric (glycol), trihydric (glycerol). Preparation of alcohols: hydration of alkenes (acid catalysed, Markovnikov), hydroboration-oxidation (anti-Markovnikov), reduction of aldehydes and ketones using NaBH4 or LiAlH4 (also catalytic H2), carboxylic acids and esters with LiAlH4, and Grignard reagents with carbonyl compounds (HCHO gives primary alcohols, other aldehydes give secondary, ketones give tertiary alcohols). Manufacture of ethanol: fermentation of sugar by zymase of yeast; invertase converts sucrose to glucose and fructose. Methanol is made from water gas (CO + 2H2 at 200-300 atm, 573 K with ZnO-Cr2O3 catalyst). Physical properties: higher boiling points than comparable hydrocarbons and ethers due to hydrogen bonding; solubility decreases with alkyl chain; boiling point order primary > secondary > tertiary. Chemical reactions: (a) acidity of alcohols: weaker than water; order methanol > primary > secondary > tertiary; react with sodium to give alkoxide and hydrogen; (b) reaction with HX (Lucas test: HCl/ZnCl2: tertiary gives turbidity immediately, secondary in 5 minutes, primary on heating); (c) dehydration with conc. H2SO4: at 443 K gives ethene (alkene), at 413 K gives ethoxyethane (ether); (d) oxidation: primary alcohols give aldehydes with PCC and carboxylic acids with KMnO4 or K2Cr2O7; secondary give ketones; tertiary resist oxidation; (e) esterification with acids. Phenols: preparation from haloarenes (Dow process), benzenesulphonic acid, diazonium salts and cumene (cumene process: cumene oxidation to cumene hydroperoxide and treatment with dilute acid gives phenol and acetone). Phenol is more acidic than alcohols because of resonance stabilisation of the phenoxide ion; electron-withdrawing groups (nitro) increase acidity (2,4,6-trinitrophenol or picric acid is strongly acidic), electron-donating groups decrease it. Reactions of phenols: electrophilic substitution (OH is ortho-para directing and activating): nitration (dilute HNO3 gives o- and p-nitrophenol; conc. gives picric acid), halogenation (bromine water gives 2,4,6-tribromophenol white precipitate), Kolbe's reaction (sodium phenoxide with CO2 at 400 K, 4-7 atm gives salicylic acid, the starting material for aspirin), Reimer-Tiemann reaction (phenol, CHCl3 and NaOH gives salicylaldehyde), reaction with zinc dust gives benzene; oxidation of phenol with chromic acid gives benzoquinone; coupling; FeCl3 test (violet colour). Ethers: preparation by dehydration of alcohols and Williamson synthesis (alkyl halide + sodium alkoxide; SN2; primary alkyl halides are best as tertiary give alkenes). Properties: lower boiling points than alcohols as no hydrogen bonding; cleavage by HI (excess hot) gives alkyl iodides; with an unsymmetrical ether the smaller alkyl group gives the alkyl iodide (SN2) unless a tertiary group gives SN1; anisole undergoes Friedel-Crafts reactions (ortho-para directing). Uses: methanol as a solvent and fuel; ethanol in medicine; denatured alcohol; phenol in antiseptics and Bakelite; diethyl ether as an anaesthetic.
Deep dive: Alcohols
Prepared by hydration, reduction and Grignard reactions. They show hydrogen bonding, acidity and oxidation behaviour depending on class. Lucas test distinguishes them.
Deep dive: Phenols
More acidic than alcohols; ring is activated for electrophilic substitution. Kolbe and Reimer-Tiemann reactions are key.
Deep dive: Ethers
Williamson synthesis uses SN2. Ethers are cleaved by HI.

Visual lesson

Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers

Alcohols contain an -OH on an sp3 carbon

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Alcohols›3Phenols›4Ethers
Dehydration443 K alkene
🔑

Big idea

  • Alcohols contain an -OH on an sp3 carbon
  • Phenols contain -OH on an sp2 carbon of benzene
  • Ethers have an oxygen bonded to two carbons (R-O-R)
  • Classification of alcohols: primary, secondary and tertiary
Read the full explanation

Alcohols contain an -OH on an sp3 carbon; phenols contain -OH on an sp2 carbon of benzene; ethers have an oxygen bonded to two carbons (R-O-R). Classification of alcohols: primary, secondary and tertiary; monohydric, dihydric (glycol), trihydric (glycerol). Preparation of alcohols: hydration of alkenes (acid catalysed, Markovnikov), hydroboration-oxidation (anti-Markovnikov), reduction of aldehydes and ketones using NaBH4 or LiAlH4 (also catalytic H2), carboxylic acids and esters with LiAlH4, and Grignard reagents with carbonyl compounds (HCHO gives primary alcohols, other aldehydes give secondary, ketones give tertiary alcohols). Manufacture of ethanol: fermentation of sugar by zymase of yeast; invertase converts sucrose to glucose and fructose. Methanol is made from water gas (CO + 2H2 at 200-300 atm, 573 K with ZnO-Cr2O3 catalyst). Physical properties: higher boiling points than comparable hydrocarbons and ethers due to hydrogen bonding; solubility decreases with alkyl chain; boiling point order primary > secondary > tertiary. Chemical reactions: (a) acidity of alcohols: weaker than water; order methanol > primary > secondary > tertiary; react with sodium to give alkoxide and hydrogen; (b) reaction with HX (Lucas test: HCl/ZnCl2: tertiary gives turbidity immediately, secondary in 5 minutes, primary on heating); (c) dehydration with conc. H2SO4: at 443 K gives ethene (alkene), at 413 K gives ethoxyethane (ether); (d) oxidation: primary alcohols give aldehydes with PCC and carboxylic acids with KMnO4 or K2Cr2O7; secondary give ketones; tertiary resist oxidation; (e) esterification with acids. Phenols: preparation from haloarenes (Dow process), benzenesulphonic acid, diazonium salts and cumene (cumene process: cumene oxidation to cumene hydroperoxide and treatment with dilute acid gives phenol and acetone). Phenol is more acidic than alcohols because of resonance stabilisation of the phenoxide ion; electron-withdrawing groups (nitro) increase acidity (2,4,6-trinitrophenol or picric acid is strongly acidic), electron-donating groups decrease it. Reactions of phenols: electrophilic substitution (OH is ortho-para directing and activating): nitration (dilute HNO3 gives o- and p-nitrophenol; conc. gives picric acid), halogenation (bromine water gives 2,4,6-tribromophenol white precipitate), Kolbe's reaction (sodium phenoxide with CO2 at 400 K, 4-7 atm gives salicylic acid, the starting material for aspirin), Reimer-Tiemann reaction (phenol, CHCl3 and NaOH gives salicylaldehyde), reaction with zinc dust gives benzene; oxidation of phenol with chromic acid gives benzoquinone; coupling; FeCl3 test (violet colour). Ethers: preparation by dehydration of alcohols and Williamson synthesis (alkyl halide + sodium alkoxide; SN2; primary alkyl halides are best as tertiary give alkenes). Properties: lower boiling points than alcohols as no hydrogen bonding; cleavage by HI (excess hot) gives alkyl iodides; with an unsymmetrical ether the smaller alkyl group gives the alkyl iodide (SN2) unless a tertiary group gives SN1; anisole undergoes Friedel-Crafts reactions (ortho-para directing). Uses: methanol as a solvent and fuel; ethanol in medicine; denatured alcohol; phenol in antiseptics and Bakelite; diethyl ether as an anaesthetic.

📌

Alcohols

  • Prepared by hydration, reduction and Grignard reactions
  • They show hydrogen bonding, acidity and oxidation behaviour depending on class
  • Lucas test distinguishes them
🧠

Phenols

  • More acidic than alcohols
  • Ring is activated for electrophilic substitution
  • Kolbe and Reimer-Tiemann reactions are key
🌟

Ethers

  • Williamson synthesis uses SN2
  • Ethers are cleaved by HI
🧮

lessons.title: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids
yt: class 12 chemistry aldehydes ketones carboxylic acids aldol cannizzaro tollens

blocks.x: Aldehydes (RCHO) and ketones (RCOR') contain the carbonyl group C=O; carboxylic acids contain -COOH. The carbonyl carbon is sp2 hybridised and trigonal planar; the C=O bond is polar and carbon is electrophilic. IUPAC: aldehyde suffix -al, ketone -one, acid -oic acid; common names formaldehyde (methanal), acetaldehyde (ethanal), acetone (propanone), formic (methanoic) and acetic (ethanoic) acid. Preparation of aldehydes and ketones: oxidation of primary and secondary alcohols; dehydrogenation of alcohols with Cu at 573 K; ozonolysis of alkenes; hydration of alkynes (ethyne gives ethanal; other alkynes give ketones); from acyl chlorides by Rosenmund reduction (H2, Pd-BaSO4, gives aldehydes), from nitriles by Stephen reaction (SnCl2/HCl then hydrolysis gives aldehydes) and with DIBAL-H; ketones from acyl chlorides with dialkylcadmium and by Friedel-Crafts acylation; aromatic aldehydes from toluene by oxidation with CrO3 in acetic anhydride (Etard reaction with CrO2Cl2) and by Gattermann-Koch reaction (benzene, CO, HCl, anhydrous AlCl3/CuCl). Properties: boiling points are higher than hydrocarbons and ethers but lower than alcohols (no hydrogen bonding between molecules); lower members are soluble in water. Nucleophilic addition: the mechanism where Nu attacks the carbonyl carbon; aldehydes are more reactive than ketones due to less steric hindrance and greater electrophilicity. Reactions: addition of HCN forms cyanohydrins; NaHSO3 forms bisulphite addition product; alcohols form hemiacetals and acetals (dry HCl); ammonia derivatives (NH2-Z) such as hydroxylamine, hydrazine, 2,4-DNP, semicarbazide give oximes, hydrazones, 2,4-DNP derivatives (orange/yellow precipitate used to detect the carbonyl) and semicarbazones. Reduction to alcohols (NaBH4, LiAlH4), to alkanes by Clemmensen reduction (Zn-Hg/conc. HCl) or Wolff-Kishner reduction (N2H4 then KOH/ethylene glycol). Oxidation: aldehydes are easily oxidised by mild oxidants: Tollens' test (ammoniacal silver nitrate; silver mirror), Fehling's test (alkaline copper(II) tartrate gives reddish brown Cu2O; aromatic aldehydes do not respond) and Benedict's test; ketones are not oxidised easily. Haloform reaction: methyl ketones (and ethanol, ethanal) with NaOX give the haloform (iodoform yellow ppt) and a carboxylate. Aldol condensation: aldehydes and ketones having alpha hydrogen undergo reaction in the presence of dilute alkali to form beta-hydroxy aldehydes (aldols) or ketones, which dehydrate on heating to give alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyls. Cross aldol. Cannizzaro reaction: aldehydes with no alpha hydrogen (HCHO, benzaldehyde) undergo disproportionation in conc. alkali to give an alcohol and the salt of a carboxylic acid. Electrophilic substitution in benzaldehyde occurs at the meta position. Uses: formaldehyde (formalin, 40% solution) for preservation; Bakelite; acetone as solvent; vanillin and benzaldehyde in perfumes. Carboxylic acids: prepared by oxidation of alcohols and aldehydes, hydrolysis of nitriles and amides, Grignard reagent with CO2, and oxidation of alkylbenzenes. Properties: high boiling points due to dimer formation through hydrogen bonding. Acidity: Ka; electron-withdrawing groups increase acidity (ClCH2COOH > CH3COOH); benzoic acid is stronger than acetic acid; formic acid (Ka 1.77 x 10^-4) is stronger than acetic acid. Reactions: formation of esters (Fischer esterification with alcohol and conc. H2SO4), acid chlorides (SOCl2, PCl5), anhydrides, amides; reduction with LiAlH4 to alcohols; decarboxylation (soda lime gives alkane; Kolbe electrolysis); Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky reaction (alpha halogenation with Cl2/Br2 and red phosphorus); ring substitution in benzoic acid occurs at meta position. Test: carboxylic acids liberate CO2 with sodium bicarbonate. Uses: acetic acid in vinegar (5-8%), benzoic acid as a preservative, soaps from higher fatty acids and nylon-6,6 from adipic acid.
Deep dive: Aldehydes and ketones
Nucleophilic addition is the characteristic reaction. Tollens' and Fehling's tests distinguish aldehydes; the iodoform test detects methyl ketones.
Deep dive: Name reactions
Aldol needs alpha hydrogen; Cannizzaro needs none. Clemmensen and Wolff-Kishner reduce C=O to CH2.
Deep dive: Carboxylic acids
Acids are strongly hydrogen bonded and acidic; electron-withdrawing groups increase acidity. Esterification and HVZ reaction are key.

Visual lesson

Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids

Aldehydes (RCHO) and ketones (RCOR') contain the carbonyl group C=O

🔑

Big idea

  • Aldehydes (RCHO) and ketones (RCOR') contain the carbonyl group C=O
  • Carboxylic acids contain -COOH
  • The carbonyl carbon is sp2 hybridised and trigonal planar
  • The C=O bond is polar and carbon is electrophilic
Read the full explanation

Aldehydes (RCHO) and ketones (RCOR') contain the carbonyl group C=O; carboxylic acids contain -COOH. The carbonyl carbon is sp2 hybridised and trigonal planar; the C=O bond is polar and carbon is electrophilic. IUPAC: aldehyde suffix -al, ketone -one, acid -oic acid; common names formaldehyde (methanal), acetaldehyde (ethanal), acetone (propanone), formic (methanoic) and acetic (ethanoic) acid. Preparation of aldehydes and ketones: oxidation of primary and secondary alcohols; dehydrogenation of alcohols with Cu at 573 K; ozonolysis of alkenes; hydration of alkynes (ethyne gives ethanal; other alkynes give ketones); from acyl chlorides by Rosenmund reduction (H2, Pd-BaSO4, gives aldehydes), from nitriles by Stephen reaction (SnCl2/HCl then hydrolysis gives aldehydes) and with DIBAL-H; ketones from acyl chlorides with dialkylcadmium and by Friedel-Crafts acylation; aromatic aldehydes from toluene by oxidation with CrO3 in acetic anhydride (Etard reaction with CrO2Cl2) and by Gattermann-Koch reaction (benzene, CO, HCl, anhydrous AlCl3/CuCl). Properties: boiling points are higher than hydrocarbons and ethers but lower than alcohols (no hydrogen bonding between molecules); lower members are soluble in water. Nucleophilic addition: the mechanism where Nu attacks the carbonyl carbon; aldehydes are more reactive than ketones due to less steric hindrance and greater electrophilicity. Reactions: addition of HCN forms cyanohydrins; NaHSO3 forms bisulphite addition product; alcohols form hemiacetals and acetals (dry HCl); ammonia derivatives (NH2-Z) such as hydroxylamine, hydrazine, 2,4-DNP, semicarbazide give oximes, hydrazones, 2,4-DNP derivatives (orange/yellow precipitate used to detect the carbonyl) and semicarbazones. Reduction to alcohols (NaBH4, LiAlH4), to alkanes by Clemmensen reduction (Zn-Hg/conc. HCl) or Wolff-Kishner reduction (N2H4 then KOH/ethylene glycol). Oxidation: aldehydes are easily oxidised by mild oxidants: Tollens' test (ammoniacal silver nitrate; silver mirror), Fehling's test (alkaline copper(II) tartrate gives reddish brown Cu2O; aromatic aldehydes do not respond) and Benedict's test; ketones are not oxidised easily. Haloform reaction: methyl ketones (and ethanol, ethanal) with NaOX give the haloform (iodoform yellow ppt) and a carboxylate. Aldol condensation: aldehydes and ketones having alpha hydrogen undergo reaction in the presence of dilute alkali to form beta-hydroxy aldehydes (aldols) or ketones, which dehydrate on heating to give alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyls. Cross aldol. Cannizzaro reaction: aldehydes with no alpha hydrogen (HCHO, benzaldehyde) undergo disproportionation in conc. alkali to give an alcohol and the salt of a carboxylic acid. Electrophilic substitution in benzaldehyde occurs at the meta position. Uses: formaldehyde (formalin, 40% solution) for preservation; Bakelite; acetone as solvent; vanillin and benzaldehyde in perfumes. Carboxylic acids: prepared by oxidation of alcohols and aldehydes, hydrolysis of nitriles and amides, Grignard reagent with CO2, and oxidation of alkylbenzenes. Properties: high boiling points due to dimer formation through hydrogen bonding. Acidity: Ka; electron-withdrawing groups increase acidity (ClCH2COOH > CH3COOH); benzoic acid is stronger than acetic acid; formic acid (Ka 1.77 x 10^-4) is stronger than acetic acid. Reactions: formation of esters (Fischer esterification with alcohol and conc. H2SO4), acid chlorides (SOCl2, PCl5), anhydrides, amides; reduction with LiAlH4 to alcohols; decarboxylation (soda lime gives alkane; Kolbe electrolysis); Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky reaction (alpha halogenation with Cl2/Br2 and red phosphorus); ring substitution in benzoic acid occurs at meta position. Test: carboxylic acids liberate CO2 with sodium bicarbonate. Uses: acetic acid in vinegar (5-8%), benzoic acid as a preservative, soaps from higher fatty acids and nylon-6,6 from adipic acid.

📌

Aldehydes and ketones

  • Nucleophilic addition is the characteristic reaction
  • Tollens' and Fehling's tests distinguish aldehydes
  • The iodoform test detects methyl ketones
⚗️

Name reactions

  • Aldol needs alpha hydrogen
  • Cannizzaro needs none
  • Clemmensen and Wolff-Kishner reduce C=O to CH2
⚗️

Carboxylic acids

  • Acids are strongly hydrogen bonded and acidic
  • Electron-withdrawing groups increase acidity
  • Esterification and HVZ reaction are key

lessons.title: Amines
yt: class 12 chemistry amines basicity hinsberg diazonium sandmeyer gabriel hofmann

blocks.x: Amines are derivatives of ammonia in which one, two or three hydrogens are replaced by alkyl or aryl groups, giving primary (1 degree), secondary (2 degree) and tertiary (3 degree) amines. The nitrogen is sp3 hybridised with a lone pair; the C-N-C angle in trimethylamine is about 108 degrees. Nomenclature: alkanamine (CH3NH2 methanamine), N-methylmethanamine, aniline (benzenamine). Preparation: reduction of nitro compounds (Sn/HCl, Fe/HCl, or H2/Pd) gives primary amines (iron with HCl is preferred industrially since FeCl2 formed is hydrolysed, so only a small amount of HCl is needed); ammonolysis of alkyl halides gives a mixture of 1, 2, 3 amines and quaternary salt; reduction of nitriles (LiAlH4 or H2/Ni) and amides (LiAlH4); Gabriel phthalimide synthesis (phthalimide with ethanolic KOH forms potassium phthalimide, which reacts with alkyl halide and is hydrolysed with alkali to give pure primary aliphatic amines; aromatic primary amines cannot be made because aryl halides do not undergo nucleophilic substitution); Hofmann bromamide degradation (amide with Br2 and NaOH gives a primary amine with one carbon atom less). Physical properties: lower amines are gases with fishy odour; primary and secondary amines form hydrogen bonds so have higher boiling points than hydrocarbons but lower than alcohols; tertiary amines cannot form intermolecular hydrogen bonds; boiling point order 1 > 2 > 3; lower amines are soluble in water; aniline is a colourless liquid turning brown on exposure to air. Basicity: amines are basic because of the lone pair on nitrogen; in aqueous solution the order for methyl amines is (CH3)2NH > CH3NH2 > (CH3)3N > NH3 due to the combined inductive, solvation and steric effects; for ethyl amines (C2H5)2NH > (C2H5)3N > C2H5NH2 > NH3; aniline is a weaker base than aliphatic amines because the lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring by resonance; electron-donating groups on the ring increase basicity and electron-withdrawing groups decrease it. Chemical reactions: alkylation; acylation (with acid chlorides, anhydrides in presence of a base like pyridine to give amides; used to protect the amino group); carbylamine reaction (isocyanide test): aliphatic and aromatic primary amines with chloroform and alcoholic KOH give foul-smelling isocyanides; reaction with nitrous acid: aliphatic primary amines give alcohols with N2 evolution, while aromatic primary amines give diazonium salts at 273-278 K (diazotisation). Hinsberg test: benzenesulphonyl chloride reacts with primary amines to give a product soluble in alkali, with secondary amines to give an insoluble product, and tertiary amines do not react. Aniline: electrophilic substitution is strongly activated and ortho-para directing: bromine water gives 2,4,6-tribromoaniline immediately; nitration directly gives a mixture including meta product because anilinium ion formed in acid is meta directing, so protection by acetylation is used; sulphonation gives sulphanilic acid (zwitterion); Friedel-Crafts reaction fails with aniline as it forms a salt with AlCl3. Diazonium salts (ArN2+X-): benzene diazonium chloride is stable only at 273-278 K; the stability of aromatic diazonium salts arises from resonance; reactions with loss of nitrogen: Sandmeyer reaction (CuCl/HCl, CuBr/HBr, CuCN/KCN), Gattermann reaction (Cu/HX), replacement by iodide (KI), by fluoride (HBF4 then heat: Balz-Schiemann), by H (hypophosphorous acid H3PO2, or ethanol), by OH (warming with water; phenol) and reactions retaining nitrogen: coupling reactions to form azo dyes (with phenol in mild alkaline medium gives p-hydroxyazobenzene, orange dye; with aniline in mild acidic medium gives p-aminoazobenzene, yellow dye). Importance: diazonium salts are important for synthesising aryl fluorides, iodides, cyanides and azo dyes; amines in drugs, dyes and nylon intermediates (hexamethylenediamine).
Deep dive: Basicity
Lone pair on nitrogen makes amines basic. Aliphatic amines are stronger than ammonia; aniline is weaker due to resonance.
Deep dive: Preparation and tests
Gabriel gives pure primary amines. Hofmann degradation shortens the chain by one carbon. Carbylamine and Hinsberg tests identify classes.
Deep dive: Diazonium salts
Diazonium salts give a range of aryl compounds by Sandmeyer and related reactions, and azo dyes by coupling.

🔑

Big idea

  • Amines are derivatives of ammonia in which one, two or three hydrogens are replaced by alkyl or aryl groups, giving primary (1 degree), secondary (2…
  • The nitrogen is sp3 hybridised with a lone pair

Read the full explanation

Amines are derivatives of ammonia in which one, two or three hydrogens are replaced by alkyl or aryl groups, giving primary (1 degree), secondary (2 degree) and tertiary (3 degree) amines. The nitrogen is sp3 hybridised with a lone pair; the C-N-C angle in trimethylamine is about 108 degrees. Nomenclature: alkanamine (CH3NH2 methanamine), N-methylmethanamine, aniline (benzenamine). Preparation: reduction of nitro compounds (Sn/HCl, Fe/HCl, or H2/Pd) gives primary amines (iron with HCl is preferred industrially since FeCl2 formed is hydrolysed, so only a small amount of HCl is needed); ammonolysis of alkyl halides gives a mixture of 1, 2, 3 amines and quaternary salt; reduction of nitriles (LiAlH4 or H2/Ni) and amides (LiAlH4); Gabriel phthalimide synthesis (phthalimide with ethanolic KOH forms potassium phthalimide, which reacts with alkyl halide and is hydrolysed with alkali to give pure primary aliphatic amines; aromatic primary amines cannot be made because aryl halides do not undergo nucleophilic substitution); Hofmann bromamide degradation (amide with Br2 and NaOH gives a primary amine with one carbon atom less). Physical properties: lower amines are gases with fishy odour; primary and secondary amines form hydrogen bonds so have higher boiling points than hydrocarbons but lower than alcohols; tertiary amines cannot form intermolecular hydrogen bonds; boiling point order 1 > 2 > 3; lower amines are soluble in water; aniline is a colourless liquid turning brown on exposure to air. Basicity: amines are basic because of the lone pair on nitrogen; in aqueous solution the order for methyl amines is (CH3)2NH > CH3NH2 > (CH3)3N > NH3 due to the combined inductive, solvation and steric effects; for ethyl amines (C2H5)2NH > (C2H5)3N > C2H5NH2 > NH3; aniline is a weaker base than aliphatic amines because the lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring by resonance; electron-donating groups on the ring increase basicity and electron-withdrawing groups decrease it. Chemical reactions: alkylation; acylation (with acid chlorides, anhydrides in presence of a base like pyridine to give amides; used to protect the amino group); carbylamine reaction (isocyanide test): aliphatic and aromatic primary amines with chloroform and alcoholic KOH give foul-smelling isocyanides; reaction with nitrous acid: aliphatic primary amines give alcohols with N2 evolution, while aromatic primary amines give diazonium salts at 273-278 K (diazotisation). Hinsberg test: benzenesulphonyl chloride reacts with primary amines to give a product soluble in alkali, with secondary amines to give an insoluble product, and tertiary amines do not react. Aniline: electrophilic substitution is strongly activated and ortho-para directing: bromine water gives 2,4,6-tribromoaniline immediately; nitration directly gives a mixture including meta product because anilinium ion formed in acid is meta directing, so protection by acetylation is used; sulphonation gives sulphanilic acid (zwitterion); Friedel-Crafts reaction fails with aniline as it forms a salt with AlCl3. Diazonium salts (ArN2+X-): benzene diazonium chloride is stable only at 273-278 K; the stability of aromatic diazonium salts arises from resonance; reactions with loss of nitrogen: Sandmeyer reaction (CuCl/HCl, CuBr/HBr, CuCN/KCN), Gattermann reaction (Cu/HX), replacement by iodide (KI), by fluoride (HBF4 then heat: Balz-Schiemann), by H (hypophosphorous acid H3PO2, or ethanol), by OH (warming with water; phenol) and reactions retaining nitrogen: coupling reactions to form azo dyes (with phenol in mild alkaline medium gives p-hydroxyazobenzene, orange dye; with aniline in mild acidic medium gives p-aminoazobenzene, yellow dye). Importance: diazonium salts are important for synthesising aryl fluorides, iodides, cyanides and azo dyes; amines in drugs, dyes and nylon intermediates (hexamethylenediamine).

📘

Basicity

  • Lone pair on nitrogen makes amines basic
  • Aliphatic amines are stronger than ammonia
  • Aniline is weaker due to resonance
🧠

Preparation and tests

  • Gabriel gives pure primary amines
  • Hofmann degradation shortens the chain by one carbon
  • Carbylamine and Hinsberg tests identify classes
⚗️

Diazonium salts

  • Diazonium salts give a range of aryl compounds by Sandmeyer and related reactions, and azo dyes by coupling

blocks.x: Biomolecules are the organic compounds that build and run living systems: carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, vitamins, hormones and enzymes. Carbohydrates are optically active polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones, or compounds that give these on hydrolysis; classified as monosaccharides (glucose, fructose, galactose; cannot be hydrolysed), oligosaccharides (disaccharides: sucrose, maltose, lactose) and polysaccharides (starch, cellulose, glycogen). Sugars are reducing (free aldehyde or ketone group, give Tollens and Fehling tests) or non-reducing (sucrose). Glucose C6H12O6 is an aldohexose; structure established by its reactions: acetylation with acetic anhydride shows five OH groups; oxidation with HNO3 gives saccharic acid (so it has a primary alcohol), with bromine water gives gluconic acid (so it has an aldehyde); HI gives n-hexane (straight chain of six carbons); HCN gives a cyanohydrin. It does not give Schiff's test and does not form a bisulphite addition product; the pentaacetate does not react with hydroxylamine; and glucose exists in two cyclic hemiacetal forms, alpha and beta anomers, differing at C-1 (the anomeric carbon); pyranose ring (six-membered) is formed by the C-1 aldehyde and C-5 OH. Mutarotation is the change in optical rotation on standing to a constant value of +52.5 degrees (alpha +111, beta +19.2). Glucose is D-(+)-glucose; the D and L descriptors refer to the configuration of the OH on the penultimate carbon relative to glyceraldehyde. Fructose is a ketohexose (D-(-)-fructose, furanose ring of five members). Sucrose is made of alpha-D-glucose and beta-D-fructose joined by a C1-C2 glycosidic link, hence non-reducing; it is dextrorotatory (+66.5), but on hydrolysis gives an equimolar mixture of glucose (+52.5) and fructose (-92.4), which is laevorotatory, hence the mixture is called invert sugar. Maltose has two alpha-D-glucose units joined by C1-C4 link (reducing). Lactose has beta-D-galactose and beta-D-glucose by a C1-C4 link (reducing, milk sugar). Starch has amylose (20 percent, water soluble, unbranched, alpha 1,4 links) and amylopectin (80 percent, insoluble, branched with alpha 1,4 and alpha 1,6 links). Cellulose is a straight chain of beta-D-glucose units with beta 1,4 links; humans cannot digest it. Glycogen is the animal starch stored in liver and muscles. Importance: energy source, cellulose in cell walls and paper, starch in food. Proteins are polymers of alpha-amino acids joined by peptide bonds (amide linkages). There are 20 standard amino acids; essential ones (valine, leucine, isoleucine, lysine, threonine, methionine, phenylalanine, tryptophan; histidine and arginine in children) cannot be made by the body; non-essential ones can. Amino acids exist as zwitterions (dipolar ions) in solution, are amphoteric, and have an isoelectric point where the net charge is zero and solubility is minimum. Glycine is the only optically inactive amino acid. Structures: primary (sequence of amino acids), secondary (alpha helix and beta pleated sheet held by hydrogen bonds), tertiary (folding by disulphide bridges, hydrogen bonds, ionic and van der Waals interactions) and quaternary (assembly of subunits, as in haemoglobin). Fibrous proteins (keratin, myosin) are insoluble; globular proteins (insulin, albumin) are soluble. Denaturation disrupts the secondary and tertiary structures but the primary structure remains, as in coagulation of egg white on boiling. Enzymes are biocatalysts, mostly globular proteins, specific and working at optimum temperature (about 310 K) and pH; they follow the lock-and-key model; examples are invertase, maltase, zymase, urease and pepsin; enzyme inhibitors compete for the active site. Vitamins are organic compounds required in small amounts: fat-soluble (A, D, E, K; stored in the body) and water-soluble (B group and C; need regular supply; excreted). Deficiency diseases: A (xerophthalmia, night blindness), B1 (beriberi), B2 (cheilosis), B6 (convulsions), B12 (pernicious anaemia), C (scurvy), D (rickets and osteomalacia), E (fragility of red blood cells), K (increased blood clotting time). Nucleic acids: DNA and RNA are polymers of nucleotides; a nucleotide has a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar and a phosphate group; a nucleoside is base plus sugar. DNA has 2-deoxyribose and bases A, G, C, T; RNA has ribose and A, G, C, U. DNA is a double helix with A pairing with T by two hydrogen bonds and G with C by three. RNA is single stranded: mRNA, rRNA and tRNA. DNA carries heredity and replication; RNA performs protein synthesis. Hormones: insulin (peptide; lowers blood sugar), thyroxine (iodinated), steroid hormones (testosterone, oestrogen, cortisone), adrenaline.
Deep dive: Carbohydrates
Glucose is an aldohexose with open and cyclic forms; sucrose is non-reducing and gives invert sugar. Starch is amylose plus amylopectin; cellulose has beta links.
Deep dive: Proteins and enzymes
Amino acids link by peptide bonds. Proteins have four levels of structure; denaturation destroys secondary and tertiary structure. Enzymes are specific protein catalysts.
Deep dive: Vitamins and nucleic acids
Vitamin deficiencies cause characteristic diseases. DNA and RNA differ in sugar and bases, and DNA pairs A-T and G-C.

🔑

Big idea

  • Biomolecules are the organic compounds that build and run living systems: carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, vitamins, hormones and…
  • Carbohydrates are optically active polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones, or compounds that give these on hydrolysis
  • Classified as monosaccharides (glucose, fructose, galactose
  • Cannot be hydrolysed), oligosaccharides (disaccharides: sucrose, maltose, lactose) and polysaccharides (starch, cellulose, glycogen)
Read the full explanation

Biomolecules are the organic compounds that build and run living systems: carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, vitamins, hormones and enzymes. Carbohydrates are optically active polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones, or compounds that give these on hydrolysis; classified as monosaccharides (glucose, fructose, galactose; cannot be hydrolysed), oligosaccharides (disaccharides: sucrose, maltose, lactose) and polysaccharides (starch, cellulose, glycogen). Sugars are reducing (free aldehyde or ketone group, give Tollens and Fehling tests) or non-reducing (sucrose). Glucose C6H12O6 is an aldohexose; structure established by its reactions: acetylation with acetic anhydride shows five OH groups; oxidation with HNO3 gives saccharic acid (so it has a primary alcohol), with bromine water gives gluconic acid (so it has an aldehyde); HI gives n-hexane (straight chain of six carbons); HCN gives a cyanohydrin. It does not give Schiff's test and does not form a bisulphite addition product; the pentaacetate does not react with hydroxylamine; and glucose exists in two cyclic hemiacetal forms, alpha and beta anomers, differing at C-1 (the anomeric carbon); pyranose ring (six-membered) is formed by the C-1 aldehyde and C-5 OH. Mutarotation is the change in optical rotation on standing to a constant value of +52.5 degrees (alpha +111, beta +19.2). Glucose is D-(+)-glucose; the D and L descriptors refer to the configuration of the OH on the penultimate carbon relative to glyceraldehyde. Fructose is a ketohexose (D-(-)-fructose, furanose ring of five members). Sucrose is made of alpha-D-glucose and beta-D-fructose joined by a C1-C2 glycosidic link, hence non-reducing; it is dextrorotatory (+66.5), but on hydrolysis gives an equimolar mixture of glucose (+52.5) and fructose (-92.4), which is laevorotatory, hence the mixture is called invert sugar. Maltose has two alpha-D-glucose units joined by C1-C4 link (reducing). Lactose has beta-D-galactose and beta-D-glucose by a C1-C4 link (reducing, milk sugar). Starch has amylose (20 percent, water soluble, unbranched, alpha 1,4 links) and amylopectin (80 percent, insoluble, branched with alpha 1,4 and alpha 1,6 links). Cellulose is a straight chain of beta-D-glucose units with beta 1,4 links; humans cannot digest it. Glycogen is the animal starch stored in liver and muscles. Importance: energy source, cellulose in cell walls and paper, starch in food. Proteins are polymers of alpha-amino acids joined by peptide bonds (amide linkages). There are 20 standard amino acids; essential ones (valine, leucine, isoleucine, lysine, threonine, methionine, phenylalanine, tryptophan; histidine and arginine in children) cannot be made by the body; non-essential ones can. Amino acids exist as zwitterions (dipolar ions) in solution, are amphoteric, and have an isoelectric point where the net charge is zero and solubility is minimum. Glycine is the only optically inactive amino acid. Structures: primary (sequence of amino acids), secondary (alpha helix and beta pleated sheet held by hydrogen bonds), tertiary (folding by disulphide bridges, hydrogen bonds, ionic and van der Waals interactions) and quaternary (assembly of subunits, as in haemoglobin). Fibrous proteins (keratin, myosin) are insoluble; globular proteins (insulin, albumin) are soluble. Denaturation disrupts the secondary and tertiary structures but the primary structure remains, as in coagulation of egg white on boiling. Enzymes are biocatalysts, mostly globular proteins, specific and working at optimum temperature (about 310 K) and pH; they follow the lock-and-key model; examples are invertase, maltase, zymase, urease and pepsin; enzyme inhibitors compete for the active site. Vitamins are organic compounds required in small amounts: fat-soluble (A, D, E, K; stored in the body) and water-soluble (B group and C; need regular supply; excreted). Deficiency diseases: A (xerophthalmia, night blindness), B1 (beriberi), B2 (cheilosis), B6 (convulsions), B12 (pernicious anaemia), C (scurvy), D (rickets and osteomalacia), E (fragility of red blood cells), K (increased blood clotting time). Nucleic acids: DNA and RNA are polymers of nucleotides; a nucleotide has a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar and a phosphate group; a nucleoside is base plus sugar. DNA has 2-deoxyribose and bases A, G, C, T; RNA has ribose and A, G, C, U. DNA is a double helix with A pairing with T by two hydrogen bonds and G with C by three. RNA is single stranded: mRNA, rRNA and tRNA. DNA carries heredity and replication; RNA performs protein synthesis. Hormones: insulin (peptide; lowers blood sugar), thyroxine (iodinated), steroid hormones (testosterone, oestrogen, cortisone), adrenaline.

📌

Carbohydrates

  • Glucose is an aldohexose with open and cyclic forms
  • Sucrose is non-reducing and gives invert sugar
  • Starch is amylose plus amylopectin
  • Cellulose has beta links
🧠

Proteins and enzymes

  • Amino acids link by peptide bonds
  • Proteins have four levels of structure
  • Denaturation destroys secondary and tertiary structure
  • Enzymes are specific protein catalysts
⚗️

Vitamins and nucleic acids

  • Vitamin deficiencies cause characteristic diseases
  • DNA and RNA differ in sugar and bases, and DNA pairs A-T and G-C

yt: class 12 computer science python revision data types operators control flow strings lists tuples dictionaries

blocks.x: Python is a high-level, interpreted, dynamically typed language created by Guido van Rossum. A program is made of tokens: keywords (if, else, while, for, def, return, True, False, None), identifiers, literals, operators and punctuators. Identifiers start with a letter or underscore and are case sensitive. Data types: int, float, complex, bool, str, list, tuple, dict, set and NoneType. Mutable types (list, dict, set) can be changed in place; immutable types (int, float, str, tuple) cannot. Operators: arithmetic (+ - * / // % **), relational (== != < > <= >=), logical (and or not), assignment, identity (is, is not) and membership (in, not in). Precedence: parentheses, **, unary, * / // %, + -, comparison, not, and, or. Type conversion is implicit or explicit using int(), float(), str(), list(). Input is read with input() as a string. Output uses print() with sep and end. Control flow: if-elif-else, for loops with range(start, stop, step) and while loops, with break and continue; the else clause of a loop runs if the loop was not broken. Strings are immutable sequences with indexing from 0 and negative indexing from -1, slicing s[a:b:c], and methods such as upper, lower, title, strip, split, join, find, count, replace, startswith, isalpha, isdigit. Lists are mutable ordered sequences with append, extend, insert, remove, pop, index, count, sort, reverse and the built-ins len, min, max, sum, sorted. Tuples are immutable and a single-element tuple needs a trailing comma. Dictionaries hold key-value pairs with unique immutable keys; methods get, keys, values, items, update, pop, del; dict lookup is by key. Nested lists form matrices. List comprehension builds lists compactly. Modules math, random and statistics are imported with import; random.randint(a,b) includes both ends, random.random() gives a float in [0,1). Common errors: SyntaxError, NameError, TypeError, IndexError, KeyError, ValueError, ZeroDivisionError.
Deep dive: Types and mutability
Lists, dicts and sets are mutable; strings, tuples and numbers are immutable. This affects assignment, passing to functions and use as dictionary keys.
Deep dive: Control flow
for iterates over a sequence, while repeats on a condition. break exits, continue skips, and loop else runs when no break happened.
Deep dive: Sequences
Indexing and slicing work across strings, lists and tuples. Methods differ: lists change in place while string methods return new strings.
Hindi saransh
Python punarvriti: data prakar, sanchalak, niyantran pravah, string, list, tuple aur dictionary.
Remember: range(a,b) excludes b; a single element tuple needs a comma.

Revision of Python

🔑

Big idea

  • Python is a high-level, interpreted, dynamically typed language created by Guido van Rossum
  • A program is made of tokens: keywords (if, else, while, for, def, return, True, False, None), identifiers, literals, operators and punctuators

Read the full explanation

Python is a high-level, interpreted, dynamically typed language created by Guido van Rossum. A program is made of tokens: keywords (if, else, while, for, def, return, True, False, None), identifiers, literals, operators and punctuators. Identifiers start with a letter or underscore and are case sensitive. Data types: int, float, complex, bool, str, list, tuple, dict, set and NoneType. Mutable types (list, dict, set) can be changed in place; immutable types (int, float, str, tuple) cannot. Operators: arithmetic (+ - * / // % ), relational (== != < > <= >=), logical (and or not), assignment, identity (is, is not) and membership (in, not in). Precedence: parentheses, , unary, * / // %, + -, comparison, not, and, or. Type conversion is implicit or explicit using int(), float(), str(), list(). Input is read with input() as a string. Output uses print() with sep and end. Control flow: if-elif-else, for loops with range(start, stop, step) and while loops, with break and continue; the else clause of a loop runs if the loop was not broken. Strings are immutable sequences with indexing from 0 and negative indexing from -1, slicing s[a:b:c], and methods such as upper, lower, title, strip, split, join, find, count, replace, startswith, isalpha, isdigit. Lists are mutable ordered sequences with append, extend, insert, remove, pop, index, count, sort, reverse and the built-ins len, min, max, sum, sorted. Tuples are immutable and a single-element tuple needs a trailing comma. Dictionaries hold key-value pairs with unique immutable keys; methods get, keys, values, items, update, pop, del; dict lookup is by key. Nested lists form matrices. List comprehension builds lists compactly. Modules math, random and statistics are imported with import; random.randint(a,b) includes both ends, random.random() gives a float in [0,1). Common errors: SyntaxError, NameError, TypeError, IndexError, KeyError, ValueError, ZeroDivisionError.

📌

Types and mutability

  • Lists, dicts and sets are mutable
  • Strings, tuples and numbers are immutable
  • This affects assignment, passing to functions and use as dictionary keys
🔄

Control flow

  • For iterates over a sequence, while repeats on a condition
  • Break exits, continue skips, and loop else runs when no break happened
🌟

Sequences

  • Indexing and slicing work across strings, lists and tuples
  • Methods differ: lists change in place while string methods return new strings

blocks.x: A function is a named block of reusable code defined with def and called by name. Benefits: modularity, reuse, readability and easier debugging. Syntax: def name(parameters): body, with return to send back a value; a function without return gives None. Parameters appear in the definition; arguments are the values passed in a call. Types of arguments: positional (matched by order), keyword (matched by name), default (parameter with a default value, which must come after non-default parameters) and variable length (*args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple, **kwargs collects keywords into a dictionary). A function can return multiple values as a tuple. Scope and the LEGB rule: Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in. A variable assigned inside a function is local; to modify a global variable inside a function the global keyword is needed. Mutable arguments such as lists are changed in place, while immutable arguments like integers and strings are not changed outside. Python passes object references, often called pass by object reference. Built-in functions: len, type, range, sum, min, max, abs, round, input, print, sorted. Module functions: math.sqrt, math.ceil, math.floor, math.pow, math.fabs, random.randint, random.randrange, statistics.mean, median, mode. User-defined modules are imported with import or from module import name. Recursion is a function calling itself with a base case and a recursive case; examples are factorial and Fibonacci; recursion uses stack frames and can raise RecursionError if the base case is missing. Lambda is an anonymous single-expression function: lambda x: x*x. Docstrings document a function. Functions are first-class objects: they can be passed as arguments or stored in variables.
Deep dive: Arguments
Positional, keyword, default and variable length arguments give flexible calls. Default parameters must follow non-default ones.
Deep dive: Scope
LEGB rule decides name lookup. Assignment in a function creates a local name unless declared global.
Deep dive: Recursion
A recursive function needs a base case and moves toward it. Each call adds a frame to the call stack.
Hindi saransh
Function: def se paribhashit, argument ke prakar, scope ka LEGB niyam, recursion aur lambda.

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Functions

A function is a named block of reusable code defined with def and called by name

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Arguments›3Scope›4Recursion
🔑

Big idea

  • A function is a named block of reusable code defined with def and called by name
  • Benefits: modularity, reuse, readability and easier debugging
  • Syntax: def name(parameters): body, with return to send back a value
  • A function without return gives None
Read the full explanation

A function is a named block of reusable code defined with def and called by name. Benefits: modularity, reuse, readability and easier debugging. Syntax: def name(parameters): body, with return to send back a value; a function without return gives None. Parameters appear in the definition; arguments are the values passed in a call. Types of arguments: positional (matched by order), keyword (matched by name), default (parameter with a default value, which must come after non-default parameters) and variable length (*args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple, kwargs collects keywords into a dictionary). A function can return multiple values as a tuple. Scope and the LEGB rule: Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in. A variable assigned inside a function is local; to modify a global variable inside a function the global keyword is needed. Mutable arguments such as lists are changed in place, while immutable arguments like integers and strings are not changed outside. Python passes object references, often called pass by object reference. Built-in functions: len, type, range, sum, min, max, abs, round, input, print, sorted. Module functions: math.sqrt, math.ceil, math.floor, math.pow, math.fabs, random.randint, random.randrange, statistics.mean, median, mode. User-defined modules are imported with import or from module import name. Recursion is a function calling itself with a base case and a recursive case; examples are factorial and Fibonacci; recursion uses stack frames and can raise RecursionError if the base case is missing. Lambda is an anonymous single-expression function: lambda x: x*x. Docstrings document a function. Functions are first-class objects: they can be passed as arguments or stored in variables.

📌

Arguments

  • Positional, keyword, default and variable length arguments give flexible calls
  • Default parameters must follow non-default ones
🧠

Scope

  • LEGB rule decides name lookup
  • Assignment in a function creates a local name unless declared global
🌟

Recursion

  • A recursive function needs a base case and moves toward it
  • Each call adds a frame to the call stack
🧮

Formula tiles

returnSends back value
*argsTuple of extras
**kwargsDictionary of keywords
LEGBLocal Enclosing Global Built-in
🎯 Remember a function with no return statement returns None.

lessons.title: Exception Handling
yt: class 12 computer science python exception handling try except finally raise assert

blocks.x: Errors are of three kinds: syntax errors (detected before running), runtime errors or exceptions (raised during execution) and logical errors (wrong output, no error message). An exception is an event that disrupts normal flow; if unhandled the program terminates with a traceback. Common built-in exceptions: SyntaxError, NameError, TypeError, ValueError, IndexError, KeyError, ZeroDivisionError, FileNotFoundError, ImportError, IOError, OverflowError, AttributeError and EOFError. Handling uses try, except, else and finally. The try block holds risky code; except catches a specific exception (or several, or a bare except for all); else runs if no exception occurred; finally always runs, used for cleanup such as closing files. Multiple except blocks are tested in order; the first match runs. The as keyword binds the exception object: except ValueError as e. The raise statement throws an exception deliberately: raise ValueError("message"). The assert statement checks a condition and raises AssertionError if false, useful for debugging. Exceptions can be user defined by subclassing Exception. Handling keeps programs robust and gives friendly messages. Debugging techniques: reading the traceback from the last line, using print statements, a debugger with breakpoints, and testing with sample inputs.
Deep dive: try-except flow
Risky code goes in try. A matching except handles the error, else runs if none occurred, and finally always runs.
Deep dive: raise and assert
raise creates an exception on purpose; assert checks a condition during development.
Deep dive: Error kinds
Syntax errors stop compilation, runtime errors raise exceptions, and logical errors give wrong answers silently.
Hindi saransh
Apvad prabandhan: try, except, else, finally, raise aur assert.
Remember: finally runs whether or not an exception occurred.

Read the full explanation

Errors are of three kinds: syntax errors (detected before running), runtime errors or exceptions (raised during execution) and logical errors (wrong output, no error message). An exception is an event that disrupts normal flow; if unhandled the program terminates with a traceback. Common built-in exceptions: SyntaxError, NameError, TypeError, ValueError, IndexError, KeyError, ZeroDivisionError, FileNotFoundError, ImportError, IOError, OverflowError, AttributeError and EOFError. Handling uses try, except, else and finally. The try block holds risky code; except catches a specific exception (or several, or a bare except for all); else runs if no exception occurred; finally always runs, used for cleanup such as closing files. Multiple except blocks are tested in order; the first match runs. The as keyword binds the exception object: except ValueError as e. The raise statement throws an exception deliberately: raise ValueError("message"). The assert statement checks a condition and raises AssertionError if false, useful for debugging. Exceptions can be user defined by subclassing Exception. Handling keeps programs robust and gives friendly messages. Debugging techniques: reading the traceback from the last line, using print statements, a debugger with breakpoints, and testing with sample inputs.

🔄

Try-except flow

  • Risky code goes in try
  • A matching except handles the error, else runs if none occurred, and finally always runs
🧠

Raise and assert

  • Raise creates an exception on purpose
  • Assert checks a condition during development
🌟

Error kinds

  • Syntax errors stop compilation, runtime errors raise exceptions, and logical errors give wrong answers silently

🎯 Remember finally runs whether or not an exception occurred.

lessons.title: File Handling
yt: class 12 computer science python file handling text binary csv pickle seek tell

blocks.x: Files store data permanently on secondary storage. Python handles text files (lines of characters ending with newline), binary files (bytes, such as images and pickled objects) and CSV files (comma separated values). open(filename, mode) returns a file object. Text modes: r (read, error if missing), w (write, creates or truncates), a (append), r+ (read and write), w+ and a+. Add b for binary: rb, wb, ab. The with statement closes the file automatically. Methods: read(n) reads n characters or the whole file, readline() reads one line, readlines() returns a list of lines, write(string), writelines(list) and close(). Newline characters must be added manually in write. File pointer: tell() returns the current position and seek(offset, whence) moves it; whence 0 is start, 1 current and 2 end. Binary files use the pickle module: pickle.dump(obj, file) writes and pickle.load(file) reads, raising EOFError at the end; the file must be opened in binary mode. Updating a binary record means reading all, modifying and writing back, or seeking to the record position. CSV uses the csv module: csv.reader(file) iterates rows as lists; csv.writer(file) with writerow and writerows; the newline="" argument avoids blank lines on Windows; delimiter can be changed. Absolute path starts at the root; relative path is from the current directory. Using os.path functions such as exists and getsize helps. Text files translate end-of-line characters, binary do not. Typical tasks: counting words, lines, vowels, copying selected lines, searching a record, and updating a record.
Deep dive: Modes
r, w, a and r+ differ in whether the file must exist and whether content is erased. Add b for binary.
Deep dive: Pointer
tell() reports and seek() moves the file pointer, enabling random access.
Deep dive: Binary and CSV
pickle stores Python objects as bytes; csv reads and writes rows of text.
Hindi saransh
Fail sanchalan: text, binary aur CSV file, open ke mode, seek aur tell, pickle.
Remember: mode w erases an existing file; mode a keeps it and adds at the end.

File Handling

🔑

Big idea

  • Files store data permanently on secondary storage
  • Python handles text files (lines of characters ending with newline), binary files (bytes, such as images and pickled objects) and CSV files (comma…
  • Open(filename, mode) returns a file object
  • Text modes: r (read, error if missing), w (write, creates or truncates), a (append), r+ (read and write), w+ and a+
Read the full explanation

Files store data permanently on secondary storage. Python handles text files (lines of characters ending with newline), binary files (bytes, such as images and pickled objects) and CSV files (comma separated values). open(filename, mode) returns a file object. Text modes: r (read, error if missing), w (write, creates or truncates), a (append), r+ (read and write), w+ and a+. Add b for binary: rb, wb, ab. The with statement closes the file automatically. Methods: read(n) reads n characters or the whole file, readline() reads one line, readlines() returns a list of lines, write(string), writelines(list) and close(). Newline characters must be added manually in write. File pointer: tell() returns the current position and seek(offset, whence) moves it; whence 0 is start, 1 current and 2 end. Binary files use the pickle module: pickle.dump(obj, file) writes and pickle.load(file) reads, raising EOFError at the end; the file must be opened in binary mode. Updating a binary record means reading all, modifying and writing back, or seeking to the record position. CSV uses the csv module: csv.reader(file) iterates rows as lists; csv.writer(file) with writerow and writerows; the newline="" argument avoids blank lines on Windows; delimiter can be changed. Absolute path starts at the root; relative path is from the current directory. Using os.path functions such as exists and getsize helps. Text files translate end-of-line characters, binary do not. Typical tasks: counting words, lines, vowels, copying selected lines, searching a record, and updating a record.

📌

Modes

  • R, w, a and r+ differ in whether the file must exist and whether content is erased
  • Add b for binary
🧠

Pointer

  • Tell() reports and seek() moves the file pointer, enabling random access
🌟

Binary and CSV

  • Pickle stores Python objects as bytes
  • Csv reads and writes rows of text
🧮

aAppendEnd
tellPosition
seekMove pointer
🎯 Remember mode w erases an existing file; mode a keeps it and adds at the end.

lessons.title: Stack
yt: class 12 computer science stack lifo push pop peek python list application infix postfix

blocks.x: A stack is a linear data structure in which insertion and deletion happen at one end called the top; it follows LIFO (Last In First Out). Operations: push (insert at the top), pop (remove from the top), peek or top (view the top without removing), isEmpty and size. Overflow occurs when pushing into a full stack (bounded implementation) and underflow when popping an empty stack. In Python a list serves as a stack: append() for push and pop() for pop; peek is s[-1]; empty check is len(s)==0. Applications: reversing a string or list, undo and redo in editors, back button of a browser, function call stack and recursion, balanced parenthesis checking, conversion of infix to postfix and evaluation of postfix expressions, and backtracking such as maze solving. Expression forms: infix (A+B, operator between operands), prefix (+AB) and postfix (AB+). Postfix evaluation: scan left to right; push operands; on an operator pop two, apply, and push the result; the last item is the answer. Infix to postfix: scan; operands go to output; operators are held on a stack according to precedence; ( is pushed and ) pops until (. Precedence: ^ then * / then + -. Push and pop each take constant time O(1).
Deep dive: LIFO
The most recently added item is removed first, like a pile of plates.
Deep dive: Python implementation
append for push and pop for pop on a list. Always check emptiness before popping.
Deep dive: Applications
Reversal, undo, bracket matching, function calls and postfix evaluation all rely on a stack.
Hindi saransh
Stack: LIFO sanrachna, push, pop, peek aur uske upyog.
Remember: pop on an empty stack is an underflow; guard it with an emptiness check.

🔑

Big idea

  • A stack is a linear data structure in which insertion and deletion happen at one end called the top
  • It follows LIFO (Last In First Out)
  • Operations: push (insert at the top), pop (remove from the top), peek or top (view the top without removing), isEmpty and size

Read the full explanation

A stack is a linear data structure in which insertion and deletion happen at one end called the top; it follows LIFO (Last In First Out). Operations: push (insert at the top), pop (remove from the top), peek or top (view the top without removing), isEmpty and size. Overflow occurs when pushing into a full stack (bounded implementation) and underflow when popping an empty stack. In Python a list serves as a stack: append() for push and pop() for pop; peek is s[-1]; empty check is len(s)==0. Applications: reversing a string or list, undo and redo in editors, back button of a browser, function call stack and recursion, balanced parenthesis checking, conversion of infix to postfix and evaluation of postfix expressions, and backtracking such as maze solving. Expression forms: infix (A+B, operator between operands), prefix (+AB) and postfix (AB+). Postfix evaluation: scan left to right; push operands; on an operator pop two, apply, and push the result; the last item is the answer. Infix to postfix: scan; operands go to output; operators are held on a stack according to precedence; ( is pushed and ) pops until (. Precedence: ^ then * / then + -. Push and pop each take constant time O(1).

📌

LIFO

  • The most recently added item is removed first, like a pile of plates
🧠

Python implementation

  • Append for push and pop for pop on a list
  • Always check emptiness before popping
💡

Applications

  • Reversal, undo, bracket matching, function calls and postfix evaluation all rely on a stack

lessons.title: Queue
yt: class 12 computer science queue fifo enqueue dequeue deque circular priority python

blocks.x: A queue is a linear data structure that follows FIFO (First In First Out): insertion happens at the rear and deletion at the front. Operations: enqueue (add at rear), dequeue (remove from front), front or peek, isEmpty and size. Underflow happens when dequeuing from an empty queue; overflow when enqueuing into a full bounded queue. In Python a list can be a queue using append() for enqueue and pop(0) for dequeue, though pop(0) shifts all elements and takes O(n); collections.deque gives O(1) at both ends. A deque (double ended queue) allows insertion and deletion at both front and rear, so it works as a stack or a queue. A circular queue reuses vacated space by wrapping the rear to the start using modulo arithmetic: rear = (rear+1) % size. A priority queue removes the element with the highest priority first rather than the oldest. Applications: CPU scheduling and job scheduling, printer spooling, call centre waiting lines, buffering in streaming, keyboard buffer, breadth first search and handling requests on servers. Stack versus queue: stack has one open end and LIFO order, queue has two ends and FIFO order.
Deep dive: FIFO
The first item inserted is the first removed, like people waiting in a line.
Deep dive: Variants
A deque works at both ends, a circular queue reuses space with modulo, and a priority queue serves the most important item first.
Deep dive: Python
append and pop(0) on a list work but pop(0) is O(n); deque offers O(1) operations at both ends.

🔑

Big idea

  • A queue is a linear data structure that follows FIFO (First In First Out): insertion happens at the rear and deletion at the front
  • Operations: enqueue (add at rear), dequeue (remove from front), front or peek, isEmpty and size
  • Underflow happens when dequeuing from an empty queue

Read the full explanation

A queue is a linear data structure that follows FIFO (First In First Out): insertion happens at the rear and deletion at the front. Operations: enqueue (add at rear), dequeue (remove from front), front or peek, isEmpty and size. Underflow happens when dequeuing from an empty queue; overflow when enqueuing into a full bounded queue. In Python a list can be a queue using append() for enqueue and pop(0) for dequeue, though pop(0) shifts all elements and takes O(n); collections.deque gives O(1) at both ends. A deque (double ended queue) allows insertion and deletion at both front and rear, so it works as a stack or a queue. A circular queue reuses vacated space by wrapping the rear to the start using modulo arithmetic: rear = (rear+1) % size. A priority queue removes the element with the highest priority first rather than the oldest. Applications: CPU scheduling and job scheduling, printer spooling, call centre waiting lines, buffering in streaming, keyboard buffer, breadth first search and handling requests on servers. Stack versus queue: stack has one open end and LIFO order, queue has two ends and FIFO order.

📌

FIFO

  • The first item inserted is the first removed, like people waiting in a line
🧠

Variants

  • A deque works at both ends, a circular queue reuses space with modulo, and a priority queue serves the most important item first
🌟

Python

  • Append and pop(0) on a list work but pop(0) is O(n)
  • Deque offers O(1) operations at both ends

blocks.x: Sorting arranges data in ascending or descending order, which speeds up searching and makes data easier to read. Bubble sort repeatedly compares adjacent elements and swaps them if out of order; after each pass the largest element settles at the end; n-1 passes; best case O(n) with an early-exit flag, average and worst O(n squared); stable and in place. Selection sort finds the minimum of the unsorted part and swaps it into position; always O(n squared) comparisons but at most n-1 swaps; not stable in the usual form; in place. Insertion sort builds a sorted portion by inserting each new element into its correct place by shifting larger elements; best case O(n) for already sorted data, worst O(n squared); stable; efficient for small or nearly sorted data and online data. Python offers list.sort() which sorts in place and sorted() which returns a new list, with reverse=True and key arguments; Python uses Timsort, O(n log n). Terms: pass (one scan through data), swap, comparison, stable sort (equal elements keep their original order), in place (needs O(1) extra memory). Example: sorting [5,2,4] by insertion: 2,5,4 then 2,4,5. Merge sort and quick sort are faster divide and conquer methods with O(n log n) average time, beyond the syllabus. Choose algorithm by size, partial order and memory.
Deep dive: Bubble sort
Adjacent swaps push the largest value to the end each pass. Add a swapped flag to stop early.
Deep dive: Selection and insertion
Selection picks the minimum each pass; insertion shifts larger elements to place the new one.
Deep dive: Complexity
All three are O(n squared) in the worst case; insertion and bubble reach O(n) when data is already sorted.

Bubble sort repeatedly compares adjacent elements and swaps them if out of order; after each pass the largest element settles at the end; n-1 passes; best case O(n) with an early-exit flag, average and worst O(n squared); stable and in place. Selection sort finds the minimum of the unsorted part and swaps it into position; always O(n squared) comparisons but at most n-1 swaps; not stable in the usual form; in place. Insertion sort builds a sorted portion by inserting each new element into its correct place by shifting larger elements; best case O(n) for already sorted data, worst O(n squared); stable; efficient for small or nearly sorted data and online data. Python offers list.sort() which sorts in place and sorted() which returns a new list, with reverse=True and key arguments; Python uses Timsort, O(n log n). Terms: pass (one scan through data), swap, comparison, stable sort (equal elements keep their original order), in place (needs O(1) extra memory). Example: sorting [5,2,4] by insertion: 2,5,4 then 2,4,5. Merge sort and quick sort are faster divide and conquer methods with O(n log n) average time, beyond the syllabus. Choose algorithm by size, partial order and memory.

📌

Bubble sort

  • Adjacent swaps push the largest value to the end each pass
  • Add a swapped flag to stop early
🧠

Selection and insertion

  • Selection picks the minimum each pass
  • Insertion shifts larger elements to place the new one
🌟

Complexity

  • All three are O(n squared) in the worst case
  • Insertion and bubble reach O(n) when data is already sorted
🧮
