lessons.title: Searching
yt: class 12 computer science searching linear binary hashing complexity

blocks.x: Searching finds the position of a target value in a collection. Linear search checks each element in turn until the target is found or the list ends; works on unsorted data; best case O(1), average and worst O(n). Binary search works only on sorted data: compare the target with the middle element; if equal, done; if the target is smaller, search the left half; otherwise the right half; repeat until found or the range is empty; each step halves the range, so time is O(log n); iterative version uses low, high and mid = (low+high)//2. Example: finding 23 in [2,5,8,12,16,23,38]: mid 12, then right half mid 23. Maximum comparisons for n elements is about log2(n) + 1; for 1000 items, about 10. Binary search needs random access, so it works well on lists. Hashing maps a key to an index using a hash function, e.g. key % table size, giving near O(1) average search; a collision occurs when two keys map to the same index and is resolved by chaining or open addressing (linear probing); a good hash function distributes keys uniformly; Python dictionaries and sets use hashing. Choose linear for small or unsorted data and binary for large sorted data; sorting costs O(n log n), worth it for many searches. Python also offers the in operator, index() and count().
Deep dive: Linear search
Scans elements one by one; simple and works on any list but slow for large data.
Deep dive: Binary search
Needs sorted data and halves the range each step, giving logarithmic time.
Deep dive: Hashing
A hash function jumps straight to an index; collisions are handled by chaining or probing.
Hindi saransh
Khoj: linear khoj, binary khoj aur hashing, unki jatilata.
Remember: binary search requires sorted data; linear search does not.

Searching finds the position of a target value in a collection. Linear search checks each element in turn until the target is found or the list ends; works on unsorted data; best case O(1), average and worst O(n). Binary search works only on sorted data: compare the target with the middle element; if equal, done; if the target is smaller, search the left half; otherwise the right half; repeat until found or the range is empty; each step halves the range, so time is O(log n); iterative version uses low, high and mid = (low+high)//2. Example: finding 23 in [2,5,8,12,16,23,38]: mid 12, then right half mid 23. Maximum comparisons for n elements is about log2(n) + 1; for 1000 items, about 10. Binary search needs random access, so it works well on lists. Hashing maps a key to an index using a hash function, e.g. key % table size, giving near O(1) average search; a collision occurs when two keys map to the same index and is resolved by chaining or open addressing (linear probing); a good hash function distributes keys uniformly; Python dictionaries and sets use hashing. Choose linear for small or unsorted data and binary for large sorted data; sorting costs O(n log n), worth it for many searches. Python also offers the in operator, index() and count().

📌

Linear search

  • Scans elements one by one
  • Simple and works on any list but slow for large data
🧠

Binary search

  • Needs sorted data and halves the range each step, giving logarithmic time
🌟

Hashing

  • A hash function jumps straight to an index
  • Collisions are handled by chaining or probing
🧮

lessons.title: Structured Query Language (SQL)
yt: class 12 computer science SQL create select where group by join aggregate functions

blocks.x: SQL is the standard language for relational databases. DDL (Data Definition Language): CREATE, ALTER, DROP. DML (Data Manipulation Language): INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, SELECT. Creating: CREATE DATABASE school; USE school; CREATE TABLE student (rollno INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL, marks FLOAT, dob DATE). Constraints: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, DEFAULT, CHECK. ALTER TABLE adds a column (ADD), changes a type (MODIFY) or removes a column (DROP COLUMN). DROP TABLE removes the table entirely. INSERT INTO student VALUES (1,"Asha",85.5,"2008-05-01"). UPDATE student SET marks=90 WHERE rollno=1. DELETE FROM student WHERE rollno=1; without WHERE all rows are deleted. SELECT: SELECT column list FROM table WHERE condition ORDER BY column ASC|DESC; SELECT * selects all columns; DISTINCT removes duplicates; AS gives an alias. WHERE conditions use relational operators, AND, OR, NOT, BETWEEN low AND high (inclusive), IN (list), LIKE with wildcards % (any string) and _ (a single character), IS NULL and IS NOT NULL (never = NULL). ORDER BY sorts, ascending by default. Aggregate functions: COUNT(*), COUNT(column) which ignores NULLs, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX. GROUP BY groups rows sharing a value so aggregates apply per group; HAVING filters groups after grouping, while WHERE filters rows before grouping; order of clauses: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY. Single row (scalar) functions: UCASE, LCASE, LENGTH, LEFT, RIGHT, MID, TRIM, INSTR, ROUND, MOD, POWER, NOW, DATE, MONTH, YEAR, DAYNAME. Joins combine rows from two tables: Cartesian product has degree d1+d2 and cardinality c1*c2; equi join uses equality on common columns; natural join removes the duplicate column; typically WHERE a.id = b.id. Aggregate with join and group by gives summaries.
Deep dive: DDL and DML
CREATE, ALTER and DROP define structure; INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and SELECT work with data.
Deep dive: SELECT clauses
WHERE filters rows, GROUP BY groups, HAVING filters groups and ORDER BY sorts.
Deep dive: Joins
Cartesian product multiplies cardinalities; an equi join filters it on equal key columns.
Hindi saransh
SQL: DDL, DML, SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING aur join.
Remember: WHERE filters rows; HAVING filters groups.

Visual lesson

Structured Query Language (SQL)

SQL is the standard language for relational databases

🔑

Big idea

  • SQL is the standard language for relational databases
  • DDL (Data Definition Language): CREATE, ALTER, DROP
  • DML (Data Manipulation Language): INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, SELECT
  • Creating: CREATE DATABASE school
Read the full explanation

SQL is the standard language for relational databases. DDL (Data Definition Language): CREATE, ALTER, DROP. DML (Data Manipulation Language): INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, SELECT. Creating: CREATE DATABASE school; USE school; CREATE TABLE student (rollno INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL, marks FLOAT, dob DATE). Constraints: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, DEFAULT, CHECK. ALTER TABLE adds a column (ADD), changes a type (MODIFY) or removes a column (DROP COLUMN). DROP TABLE removes the table entirely. INSERT INTO student VALUES (1,"Asha",85.5,"2008-05-01"). UPDATE student SET marks=90 WHERE rollno=1. DELETE FROM student WHERE rollno=1; without WHERE all rows are deleted. SELECT: SELECT column list FROM table WHERE condition ORDER BY column ASC|DESC; SELECT * selects all columns; DISTINCT removes duplicates; AS gives an alias. WHERE conditions use relational operators, AND, OR, NOT, BETWEEN low AND high (inclusive), IN (list), LIKE with wildcards % (any string) and _ (a single character), IS NULL and IS NOT NULL (never = NULL). ORDER BY sorts, ascending by default. Aggregate functions: COUNT(*), COUNT(column) which ignores NULLs, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX. GROUP BY groups rows sharing a value so aggregates apply per group; HAVING filters groups after grouping, while WHERE filters rows before grouping; order of clauses: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY. Single row (scalar) functions: UCASE, LCASE, LENGTH, LEFT, RIGHT, MID, TRIM, INSTR, ROUND, MOD, POWER, NOW, DATE, MONTH, YEAR, DAYNAME. Joins combine rows from two tables: Cartesian product has degree d1+d2 and cardinality c1*c2; equi join uses equality on common columns; natural join removes the duplicate column; typically WHERE a.id = b.id. Aggregate with join and group by gives summaries.

📌

DDL and DML

  • CREATE, ALTER and DROP define structure
  • INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and SELECT work with data
💡

SELECT clauses

  • WHERE filters rows, GROUP BY groups, HAVING filters groups and ORDER BY sorts
🌟

Joins

  • Cartesian product multiplies cardinalities
  • An equi join filters it on equal key columns

lessons.title: Python and SQL Connectivity
yt: class 12 computer science python mysql connector cursor execute fetchall commit parameterised query

blocks.x: Python programs can store and retrieve data in a MySQL database using a connector library such as mysql.connector (install with pip install mysql-connector-python). Steps: (1) import mysql.connector; (2) create a connection with mysql.connector.connect(host="localhost", user="root", passwd="...", database="school"); check is_connected(); (3) create a cursor object with con.cursor(), which executes queries and holds results; (4) run SQL with cur.execute(query); (5) for SELECT, fetch results using fetchone() (next row as a tuple, None if no more), fetchmany(n) (n rows) or fetchall() (all remaining rows as a list of tuples); rowcount gives the number of rows affected or fetched; (6) for INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE call con.commit() to save the changes, or con.rollback() to undo them; (7) close the cursor and connection with cur.close() and con.close(). Parameterised queries use placeholders: cur.execute("INSERT INTO student VALUES (%s,%s,%s)", (1,"Asha",85)); formatting a string with % or format() directly is risky because of SQL injection, where malicious input alters the query; placeholders let the driver escape values safely. Error handling uses try-except with mysql.connector.Error. The cursor position moves forward after each fetch. Common tasks: creating tables, inserting multiple rows with executemany, displaying records, searching by key, updating marks and deleting records. Data types map: INT to int, FLOAT to float, VARCHAR to str and DATE to datetime.date. A connection must be closed to free resources. Other connectors include sqlite3 which is built into Python.
Deep dive: Workflow
Connect, create cursor, execute, fetch or commit, then close.
Deep dive: Fetching
fetchone returns a single row, fetchmany a set number and fetchall every remaining row.
Deep dive: Safety
Use placeholders to prevent SQL injection and always commit changes made by INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE.
Hindi saransh
Python-SQL sanyojan: connector, cursor, execute, fetch, commit aur surakshit query.
Remember: without commit, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE are not saved.

Visual lesson

Python and SQL Connectivity

Python programs can store and retrieve data in a MySQL database using a connector library such as mysql.connector (install with pip install mysql-connector-python)

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Workflow›3Fetching›4Safety
🔑

Big idea

  • Python programs can store and retrieve data in a MySQL database using a connector library such as mysql.connector (install with pip install…
  • Steps: (1) import mysql.connector
  • (2) create a connection with mysql.connector.connect(host="localhost", user="root", passwd="...", database="school")
  • Check is_connected()
Read the full explanation

Python programs can store and retrieve data in a MySQL database using a connector library such as mysql.connector (install with pip install mysql-connector-python). Steps: (1) import mysql.connector; (2) create a connection with mysql.connector.connect(host="localhost", user="root", passwd="...", database="school"); check is_connected(); (3) create a cursor object with con.cursor(), which executes queries and holds results; (4) run SQL with cur.execute(query); (5) for SELECT, fetch results using fetchone() (next row as a tuple, None if no more), fetchmany(n) (n rows) or fetchall() (all remaining rows as a list of tuples); rowcount gives the number of rows affected or fetched; (6) for INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE call con.commit() to save the changes, or con.rollback() to undo them; (7) close the cursor and connection with cur.close() and con.close(). Parameterised queries use placeholders: cur.execute("INSERT INTO student VALUES (%s,%s,%s)", (1,"Asha",85)); formatting a string with % or format() directly is risky because of SQL injection, where malicious input alters the query; placeholders let the driver escape values safely. Error handling uses try-except with mysql.connector.Error. The cursor position moves forward after each fetch. Common tasks: creating tables, inserting multiple rows with executemany, displaying records, searching by key, updating marks and deleting records. Data types map: INT to int, FLOAT to float, VARCHAR to str and DATE to datetime.date. A connection must be closed to free resources. Other connectors include sqlite3 which is built into Python.

🔄

Workflow

  • Connect, create cursor, execute, fetch or commit, then close
🧠

Fetching

  • Fetchone returns a single row, fetchmany a set number and fetchall every remaining row
🌟

Safety

  • Use placeholders to prevent SQL injection and always commit changes made by INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE
🧮

Formula tiles

connectOpen connection
cursorRun queries
fetchallAll rows
commitSave changes
%sPlaceholder
🎯 Remember without commit, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE are not saved.

lessons.title: Computer Networks
yt: class 12 computer science networks lan wan topology switch router ip dns url protocol

blocks.x: A computer network is a set of interconnected devices that share resources and data. Types by size: PAN (personal area), LAN (local area, within a building), MAN (metropolitan, a city) and WAN (wide area, countries; the Internet is the largest WAN). Network devices: NIC (network interface card, with a unique MAC address), hub (broadcasts to all ports), switch (forwards to the intended port using MAC addresses), repeater (regenerates signals), bridge (connects two LANs), router (connects different networks and forwards packets using IP addresses), gateway (connects networks with different protocols) and modem (modulates and demodulates signals between digital and analogue). Topologies: bus (single backbone cable; cheap but a break fails the network), star (central hub or switch; easy to manage, but the centre is a point of failure), ring (each node connected to two others), mesh (every node connected to every other; reliable but costly) and tree (hierarchy of stars). Network types by architecture: client-server and peer-to-peer. Identification: IP address (IPv4 32 bits, like 192.168.1.1; IPv6 128 bits), MAC address (48 bits, burned into the NIC), domain name and URL. DNS (Domain Name System) translates domain names to IP addresses. Protocols are rules for communication: TCP/IP (reliable delivery, the Internet suite), HTTP and HTTPS (web), FTP (file transfer), SMTP, POP3 and IMAP (email), Telnet and SSH (remote login), VoIP (voice over IP), PPP. The web: a web page is a document; a website is a collection of pages; a browser such as Chrome displays them; a web server hosts them; URL: protocol://domain/path. Cloud computing offers services over the Internet: IaaS, PaaS and SaaS. Internet of Things connects smart devices. Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and NFC are wireless technologies; cellular generations are 2G to 5G.
Deep dive: Types and topologies
LAN, MAN and WAN differ by area; bus, star, ring, mesh and tree differ in layout and fault tolerance.
Deep dive: Devices
A switch uses MAC addresses within a LAN; a router uses IP addresses between networks; a gateway translates protocols.
Deep dive: Addressing
IP addresses identify hosts on a network, MAC addresses identify hardware and DNS maps names to IP.

Read the full explanation

A computer network is a set of interconnected devices that share resources and data. Types by size: PAN (personal area), LAN (local area, within a building), MAN (metropolitan, a city) and WAN (wide area, countries; the Internet is the largest WAN). Network devices: NIC (network interface card, with a unique MAC address), hub (broadcasts to all ports), switch (forwards to the intended port using MAC addresses), repeater (regenerates signals), bridge (connects two LANs), router (connects different networks and forwards packets using IP addresses), gateway (connects networks with different protocols) and modem (modulates and demodulates signals between digital and analogue). Topologies: bus (single backbone cable; cheap but a break fails the network), star (central hub or switch; easy to manage, but the centre is a point of failure), ring (each node connected to two others), mesh (every node connected to every other; reliable but costly) and tree (hierarchy of stars). Network types by architecture: client-server and peer-to-peer. Identification: IP address (IPv4 32 bits, like 192.168.1.1; IPv6 128 bits), MAC address (48 bits, burned into the NIC), domain name and URL. DNS (Domain Name System) translates domain names to IP addresses. Protocols are rules for communication: TCP/IP (reliable delivery, the Internet suite), HTTP and HTTPS (web), FTP (file transfer), SMTP, POP3 and IMAP (email), Telnet and SSH (remote login), VoIP (voice over IP), PPP. The web: a web page is a document; a website is a collection of pages; a browser such as Chrome displays them; a web server hosts them; URL: protocol://domain/path. Cloud computing offers services over the Internet: IaaS, PaaS and SaaS. Internet of Things connects smart devices. Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and NFC are wireless technologies; cellular generations are 2G to 5G.

📌

Types and topologies

  • LAN, MAN and WAN differ by area
  • Bus, star, ring, mesh and tree differ in layout and fault tolerance
🧠

Devices

  • A switch uses MAC addresses within a LAN
  • A router uses IP addresses between networks
  • A gateway translates protocols
🌟

Addressing

  • IP addresses identify hosts on a network, MAC addresses identify hardware and DNS maps names to IP

lessons.title: Data Communication
yt: class 12 computer science data communication bandwidth transmission media modes switching

blocks.x: Data communication is the exchange of data between two devices through a transmission medium. Components: sender, receiver, message, transmission medium and protocol. Measures: bandwidth (range of frequencies, measured in Hz for analogue and bits per second for digital), data transfer rate (bps, Kbps, Mbps, Gbps), throughput (actual rate), latency and noise. Units: 1 byte = 8 bits; 1 KB = 1024 bytes. Transmission modes: simplex (one direction, such as a keyboard or radio), half duplex (both directions but one at a time, like a walkie-talkie) and full duplex (both simultaneously, like a telephone). Transmission media: guided (wired): twisted pair (UTP, STP; cheap, used in LANs), coaxial cable (used in cable TV, higher bandwidth), optical fibre (light signals; very high speed, no electromagnetic interference, expensive and secure); unguided (wireless): radio waves, microwaves (line of sight, satellite), infrared (short range, remote controls) and Bluetooth. Switching techniques: circuit switching (dedicated path set up before communication, as in telephone networks; constant delay) and packet switching (data divided into packets that travel independently and are reassembled; efficient use of the links, used by the Internet). Message switching stores and forwards the whole message. Each packet has a header with source and destination addresses, sequence number and error check data. Errors in transmission are detected by parity, checksum or CRC. Analogue signals vary continuously; digital signals are discrete 0 and 1. Multiplexing combines several signals over one link. Communication needs encoding, transmission and decoding. Wi-Fi uses radio waves in the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands.
Deep dive: Modes
Simplex is one way, half duplex alternates and full duplex is two way at once.
Deep dive: Media
Twisted pair, coaxial and fibre are guided; radio, microwave and infrared are unguided. Fibre is fastest and immune to interference.
Deep dive: Switching
Circuit switching reserves a path; packet switching splits data into independently routed packets.
Hindi saransh
Data sanchar: bandwidth, sanchar madhyam, simplex/duplex aur switching.
Remember: the Internet uses packet switching; the telephone network used circuit switching.

🔑

Big idea

  • Data communication is the exchange of data between two devices through a transmission medium
  • Components: sender, receiver, message, transmission medium and protocol
  • Measures: bandwidth (range of frequencies, measured in Hz for analogue and bits per second for digital), data transfer rate (bps, Kbps, Mbps, Gbps)…

Read the full explanation

Data communication is the exchange of data between two devices through a transmission medium. Components: sender, receiver, message, transmission medium and protocol. Measures: bandwidth (range of frequencies, measured in Hz for analogue and bits per second for digital), data transfer rate (bps, Kbps, Mbps, Gbps), throughput (actual rate), latency and noise. Units: 1 byte = 8 bits; 1 KB = 1024 bytes. Transmission modes: simplex (one direction, such as a keyboard or radio), half duplex (both directions but one at a time, like a walkie-talkie) and full duplex (both simultaneously, like a telephone). Transmission media: guided (wired): twisted pair (UTP, STP; cheap, used in LANs), coaxial cable (used in cable TV, higher bandwidth), optical fibre (light signals; very high speed, no electromagnetic interference, expensive and secure); unguided (wireless): radio waves, microwaves (line of sight, satellite), infrared (short range, remote controls) and Bluetooth. Switching techniques: circuit switching (dedicated path set up before communication, as in telephone networks; constant delay) and packet switching (data divided into packets that travel independently and are reassembled; efficient use of the links, used by the Internet). Message switching stores and forwards the whole message. Each packet has a header with source and destination addresses, sequence number and error check data. Errors in transmission are detected by parity, checksum or CRC. Analogue signals vary continuously; digital signals are discrete 0 and 1. Multiplexing combines several signals over one link. Communication needs encoding, transmission and decoding. Wi-Fi uses radio waves in the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands.

📌

Modes

  • Simplex is one way, half duplex alternates and full duplex is two way at once
🧠

Media

  • Twisted pair, coaxial and fibre are guided
  • Radio, microwave and infrared are unguided
  • Fibre is fastest and immune to interference
🌟

Switching

  • Circuit switching reserves a path
  • Packet switching splits data into independently routed packets
🧮

🎯 Remember the Internet uses packet switching; the telephone network used circuit switching.

blocks.x: Cyber security protects systems, networks and data from attack. Threats: malware (malicious software): virus (attaches to files and needs a host program to spread), worm (self replicating over networks without a host), trojan (looks useful but hides harm), ransomware (encrypts files and demands payment), spyware (secretly collects information), adware (shows unwanted adverts), keylogger (records keystrokes) and botnets. Attacks: phishing (fake emails or sites to steal credentials), pharming (redirecting to fake sites), spoofing, eavesdropping or sniffing, man in the middle, denial of service (DoS) and distributed DoS (DDoS) flooding a server, SQL injection, brute force and password guessing, and social engineering. Protection: antivirus software, firewall (filters incoming and outgoing traffic by rules), HTTPS with SSL/TLS, strong passwords (long, mixed characters, unique), two factor authentication, regular updates and patches, backups, cautious clicking, and not installing pirated software. Cryptography: encryption converts plaintext to ciphertext and decryption reverses it; symmetric encryption uses one shared key (AES); asymmetric encryption uses a public and a private key (RSA); digital signature verifies sender and integrity. Cookies are small files that store site data. Intellectual property rights: copyright, patent, trademark; plagiarism is presenting others' work as your own; open source and free software, licences such as GPL and Creative Commons. Cyber crime and law: hacking (white hat, black hat, grey hat), identity theft, cyber bullying and online fraud are offences; the IT Act 2000 (amended 2008) is India's cyber law and it recognises digital signatures and electronic records; Section 66 deals with computer related offences. E-waste: discarded electronics should be recycled, reused or disposed of through authorised channels. Digital footprint: the trail of data left online. Netiquette: good online behaviour. Health: ergonomics and screen time.
Deep dive: Malware
Virus needs a host, worm spreads alone, trojan disguises, ransomware encrypts and spyware spies.
Deep dive: Defence
Layered defence uses firewall, antivirus, updates, strong passwords, two factor authentication and encryption.
Deep dive: Law and ethics
IT Act 2000 covers cyber crime; copyright, patents and trademarks protect intellectual property.

lessons.title: Introduction to Microeconomics
yt: class 12 economics microeconomics scarcity opportunity cost production possibility curve central problems

blocks.x: Economics studies how individuals, firms and governments choose to use scarce resources having alternative uses to satisfy unlimited wants. Microeconomics studies individual units (consumers, firms, markets); macroeconomics studies aggregates such as national income, inflation and unemployment. Scarcity arises because resources are limited while wants are unlimited, so choice is unavoidable. Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up. Economic activities: production, consumption and distribution. Positive economics describes what is; normative economics says what ought to be. Central problems of an economy: what to produce, how to produce and for whom to produce. What to produce concerns the choice and quantity of goods (consumer goods or capital goods); how to produce concerns the technique (labour intensive or capital intensive); for whom concerns distribution of income. lessons.title: Theory of Consumer Behaviour
yt: class 12 economics consumer equilibrium utility indifference curve budget line demand elasticity

blocks.x: Utility is the want satisfying power of a commodity. Total utility (TU) is the sum of utility from all units; marginal utility (MU) is the addition to TU from one more unit: MU = change in TU / change in quantity, or MUn = TUn - TUn-1. Law of diminishing marginal utility: as consumption of a good increases, MU from each additional unit falls, other things equal; TU rises at a decreasing rate while MU is positive, is maximum when MU is zero and falls when MU is negative. Consumer equilibrium in the one commodity case: MU of the good (in money terms) equals the price: MUx/Px = MU of money. In the two commodity case: MUx/Px = MUy/Py. Indifference curve approach: an indifference curve shows combinations of two goods that give equal satisfaction; an indifference map is a set of curves, with higher curves indicating more satisfaction. Properties: slope downward, convex to the origin (diminishing marginal rate of substitution, MRS), do not intersect, higher curve gives higher utility. MRS is the amount of one good the consumer gives up for one more unit of the other. Budget set: all bundles affordable with income M at prices P1 and P2: P1x1 + P2x2 <= M. The budget line P1x1 + P2x2 = M has slope -P1/P2 (the price ratio); a rise in income shifts it parallel outward; a price change rotates it. Consumer equilibrium (IC approach): where the budget line is tangent to the highest attainable indifference curve; MRS = P1/P2, and the IC is convex at that point. Demand: the quantity a consumer is willing and able to buy at a price in a given time. Law of demand: other things equal, price and quantity demanded are inversely related. Demand curve slopes downward due to the substitution effect, income effect and diminishing marginal utility. Determinants: price, income, prices of related goods (substitutes and complements), tastes and expectations. Normal goods: demand rises with income; inferior goods: demand falls with income. Movement along the curve is a change in quantity demanded (price changes); shift of the curve is a change in demand (other factors). Price elasticity of demand Ed = (percentage change in quantity demanded) / (percentage change in price); percentage method; total expenditure method: if price falls and expenditure rises, Ed>1; if unchanged, Ed=1; if it falls, Ed<1. Types: perfectly elastic (infinite), perfectly inelastic (zero), unitary, greater and less than one. Determinants: availability of substitutes, nature of the good (necessity versus luxury), proportion of income spent, time period and number of uses.
Deep dive: Utility
Diminishing marginal utility explains the downward sloping demand curve. A consumer is in equilibrium when MUx/Px = MUy/Py.
Deep dive: Indifference curves
Equilibrium is the tangency of the budget line and an indifference curve, where MRS equals the price ratio.
Deep dive: Demand and elasticity
Demand falls as price rises; elasticity measures responsiveness, measured by percentage or total expenditure method.

Visual lesson

Theory of Consumer Behaviour

Utility is the want satisfying power of a commodity

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Utility›3Indifference curves›4Demand and elasticity
MUTUn - TUn-1
Budget line slope-P1/P2
🔑

Big idea

  • Utility is the want satisfying power of a commodity
  • Total utility (TU) is the sum of utility from all units
  • Marginal utility (MU) is the addition to TU from one more unit: MU = change in TU / change in quantity, or MUn = TUn - TUn-1
  • Law of diminishing marginal utility: as consumption of a good increases, MU from each additional unit falls, other things equal
Read the full explanation

Utility is the want satisfying power of a commodity. Total utility (TU) is the sum of utility from all units; marginal utility (MU) is the addition to TU from one more unit: MU = change in TU / change in quantity, or MUn = TUn - TUn-1. Law of diminishing marginal utility: as consumption of a good increases, MU from each additional unit falls, other things equal; TU rises at a decreasing rate while MU is positive, is maximum when MU is zero and falls when MU is negative. Consumer equilibrium in the one commodity case: MU of the good (in money terms) equals the price: MUx/Px = MU of money. In the two commodity case: MUx/Px = MUy/Py. Indifference curve approach: an indifference curve shows combinations of two goods that give equal satisfaction; an indifference map is a set of curves, with higher curves indicating more satisfaction. Properties: slope downward, convex to the origin (diminishing marginal rate of substitution, MRS), do not intersect, higher curve gives higher utility. MRS is the amount of one good the consumer gives up for one more unit of the other. Budget set: all bundles affordable with income M at prices P1 and P2: P1x1 + P2x2 <= M. The budget line P1x1 + P2x2 = M has slope -P1/P2 (the price ratio); a rise in income shifts it parallel outward; a price change rotates it. Consumer equilibrium (IC approach): where the budget line is tangent to the highest attainable indifference curve; MRS = P1/P2, and the IC is convex at that point. Demand: the quantity a consumer is willing and able to buy at a price in a given time. Law of demand: other things equal, price and quantity demanded are inversely related. Demand curve slopes downward due to the substitution effect, income effect and diminishing marginal utility. Determinants: price, income, prices of related goods (substitutes and complements), tastes and expectations. Normal goods: demand rises with income; inferior goods: demand falls with income. Movement along the curve is a change in quantity demanded (price changes); shift of the curve is a change in demand (other factors). Price elasticity of demand Ed = (percentage change in quantity demanded) / (percentage change in price); percentage method; total expenditure method: if price falls and expenditure rises, Ed>1; if unchanged, Ed=1; if it falls, Ed<1. Types: perfectly elastic (infinite), perfectly inelastic (zero), unitary, greater and less than one. Determinants: availability of substitutes, nature of the good (necessity versus luxury), proportion of income spent, time period and number of uses.

📌

Utility

  • Diminishing marginal utility explains the downward sloping demand curve
  • A consumer is in equilibrium when MUx/Px = MUy/Py
🧠

Indifference curves

  • Equilibrium is the tangency of the budget line and an indifference curve, where MRS equals the price ratio
🌟

Demand and elasticity

  • Demand falls as price rises
  • Elasticity measures responsiveness, measured by percentage or total expenditure method

lessons.title: Production and Costs
yt: class 12 economics production function law of variable proportions returns to scale cost curves revenue

blocks.x: Production is the transformation of inputs into output. The production function expresses the maximum output from given inputs: Q = f(L, K). Short run: at least one factor is fixed; long run: all factors are variable. Total product (TP), average product (AP = TP/L) and marginal product (MP = change in TP / change in L, or TPn - TPn-1). Law of variable proportions (law of diminishing returns to a factor): when more units of a variable factor are combined with fixed factors, TP first rises at an increasing rate, then at a decreasing rate, reaches a maximum and falls. Stages: Stage I (increasing returns, MP rises up to its peak, AP rises till it equals MP); Stage II (diminishing returns, MP falls but is positive, TP rises at a decreasing rate until MP is zero; the rational stage); Stage III (negative returns, MP negative, TP falls). MP cuts AP at the maximum of AP; AP rises when MP is above AP. Returns to scale (long run): increasing, constant and decreasing returns when all inputs change in the same proportion. Costs: fixed cost (TFC; does not change with output), variable cost (TVC; changes with output), total cost TC = TFC + TVC. Average costs: AFC = TFC/Q (falls continuously; rectangular hyperbola), AVC = TVC/Q (U shaped), ATC or AC = TC/Q = AFC + AVC (U shaped), marginal cost MC = change in TC / change in Q = TCn - TCn-1 (equals the change in TVC; U shaped, cuts AVC and ATC at their minimum points from below). U shape arises from the law of variable proportions. Opportunity cost, explicit and implicit costs, sunk cost. Revenue: TR = P x Q; AR = TR/Q = price; MR = change in TR / change in Q. Under perfect competition AR = MR = price (horizontal). Under imperfect competition AR slopes downward and MR lies below AR. Profit = TR - TC. Break even: TR = TC. Shut down point: price equals minimum AVC. Supply: the quantity a seller is willing to offer at a price; law of supply: price and quantity supplied are directly related. Determinants: price of the good, input prices, technology, taxes and subsidies, goals and number of firms. Elasticity of supply: percentage change in quantity supplied / percentage change in price; a straight line supply curve through the origin has unit elasticity. Producer equilibrium: MC = MR and MC cuts MR from below (MC rising).
Deep dive: Short run production
TP, AP and MP follow the law of variable proportions: MP rises, falls, then turns negative. Stage II is the rational stage.
Deep dive: Costs
TC = TFC + TVC. MC is U shaped and cuts AVC and ATC at their minima. AFC falls throughout.
Deep dive: Revenue and equilibrium
Under perfect competition AR = MR = price. A producer is in equilibrium where MC = MR with MC rising.
Hindi saransh
Utpadan aur lagat: utpadan falan, parivartansheel anupat niyam, lagat vakra, aay aur utpadak santulan.

Production and Costs

Production is the transformation of inputs into output

🔑

Big idea

  • Production is the transformation of inputs into output
  • The production function expresses the maximum output from given inputs: Q = f(L, K)
  • Short run: at least one factor is fixed
  • Long run: all factors are variable
Read the full explanation

Production is the transformation of inputs into output. The production function expresses the maximum output from given inputs: Q = f(L, K). Short run: at least one factor is fixed; long run: all factors are variable. Total product (TP), average product (AP = TP/L) and marginal product (MP = change in TP / change in L, or TPn - TPn-1). Law of variable proportions (law of diminishing returns to a factor): when more units of a variable factor are combined with fixed factors, TP first rises at an increasing rate, then at a decreasing rate, reaches a maximum and falls. Stages: Stage I (increasing returns, MP rises up to its peak, AP rises till it equals MP); Stage II (diminishing returns, MP falls but is positive, TP rises at a decreasing rate until MP is zero; the rational stage); Stage III (negative returns, MP negative, TP falls). MP cuts AP at the maximum of AP; AP rises when MP is above AP. Returns to scale (long run): increasing, constant and decreasing returns when all inputs change in the same proportion. Costs: fixed cost (TFC; does not change with output), variable cost (TVC; changes with output), total cost TC = TFC + TVC. Average costs: AFC = TFC/Q (falls continuously; rectangular hyperbola), AVC = TVC/Q (U shaped), ATC or AC = TC/Q = AFC + AVC (U shaped), marginal cost MC = change in TC / change in Q = TCn - TCn-1 (equals the change in TVC; U shaped, cuts AVC and ATC at their minimum points from below). U shape arises from the law of variable proportions. Opportunity cost, explicit and implicit costs, sunk cost. Revenue: TR = P x Q; AR = TR/Q = price; MR = change in TR / change in Q. Under perfect competition AR = MR = price (horizontal). Under imperfect competition AR slopes downward and MR lies below AR. Profit = TR - TC. Break even: TR = TC. Shut down point: price equals minimum AVC. Supply: the quantity a seller is willing to offer at a price; law of supply: price and quantity supplied are directly related. Determinants: price of the good, input prices, technology, taxes and subsidies, goals and number of firms. Elasticity of supply: percentage change in quantity supplied / percentage change in price; a straight line supply curve through the origin has unit elasticity. Producer equilibrium: MC = MR and MC cuts MR from below (MC rising).

📌

Short run production

  • TP, AP and MP follow the law of variable proportions: MP rises, falls, then turns negative
  • Stage II is the rational stage
🧠

Costs

  • TC = TFC + TVC
  • MC is U shaped and cuts AVC and ATC at their minima
  • AFC falls throughout
🌟

Revenue and equilibrium

  • Under perfect competition AR = MR = price
  • A producer is in equilibrium where MC = MR with MC rising

lessons.title: Theory of the Firm under Perfect Competition
yt: class 12 economics perfect competition firm equilibrium supply curve price taker

blocks.x: Market forms are classified by the number of firms, nature of the product, entry and exit and information. Perfect competition features: a large number of buyers and sellers, homogeneous products, free entry and exit, perfect knowledge, perfect mobility of factors and no government intervention. Each firm is a price taker and the industry is the price maker; the demand curve facing a firm is perfectly elastic (horizontal) at the market price; AR = MR = price. Profit maximisation: a firm maximises profit where MC = MR and MC is rising (cuts MR from below), i.e. MC slope greater than MR slope. The firm earns supernormal profit if P > AC, normal profit if P = AC and incurs a loss if P < AC; in the short run a firm continues if P >= AVC (covers variable cost); it shuts down if P < minimum AVC. Short run supply curve of a firm: the rising portion of the MC curve above the minimum AVC. Long run: free entry and exit eliminate supernormal profit and losses, so firms earn normal profit at minimum AC where P = MC = AC. Industry supply is the horizontal sum of the supply curves of all firms. Elasticity of supply Es = (percentage change in quantity supplied) / (percentage change in price) = (dQ/dP) x (P/Q). Determinants: nature of the good, cost of production, time period and technology. Types: elastic, inelastic, unitary, perfectly elastic, perfectly inelastic. Geometric method: a straight line supply curve meeting the quantity axis has Es<1, meeting the price axis has Es>1, and passing through the origin has Es = 1. Price ceilings (maximum price, e.g. rent control) cause shortages; price floors (minimum price, e.g. minimum support price, minimum wage) cause surpluses. Normal profit is the minimum reward to the entrepreneur, included in cost.
Deep dive: Features
Many small firms, identical products, free entry and exit and perfect knowledge make the firm a price taker.
Deep dive: Equilibrium
The firm produces where MC = MR with MC rising; the short run supply curve is the MC curve above minimum AVC.
Deep dive: Long run
Free entry and exit lead to normal profit where P = MC = minimum AC.

Poorn pratispardha: farm ka santulan, MC = MR, lagbhag aur dirghkal mein samaan labh.

Big idea

  • Market forms are classified by the number of firms, nature of the product, entry and exit and information

  • Each firm is a price taker and the industry is the price maker

Read the full explanation

Market forms are classified by the number of firms, nature of the product, entry and exit and information. Perfect competition features: a large number of buyers and sellers, homogeneous products, free entry and exit, perfect knowledge, perfect mobility of factors and no government intervention. Each firm is a price taker and the industry is the price maker; the demand curve facing a firm is perfectly elastic (horizontal) at the market price; AR = MR = price. Profit maximisation: a firm maximises profit where MC = MR and MC is rising (cuts MR from below), i.e. MC slope greater than MR slope. The firm earns supernormal profit if P > AC, normal profit if P = AC and incurs a loss if P < AC; in the short run a firm continues if P >= AVC (covers variable cost); it shuts down if P < minimum AVC. Short run supply curve of a firm: the rising portion of the MC curve above the minimum AVC. Long run: free entry and exit eliminate supernormal profit and losses, so firms earn normal profit at minimum AC where P = MC = AC. Industry supply is the horizontal sum of the supply curves of all firms. Elasticity of supply Es = (percentage change in quantity supplied) / (percentage change in price) = (dQ/dP) x (P/Q). Determinants: nature of the good, cost of production, time period and technology. Types: elastic, inelastic, unitary, perfectly elastic, perfectly inelastic. Geometric method: a straight line supply curve meeting the quantity axis has Es<1, meeting the price axis has Es>1, and passing through the origin has Es = 1. Price ceilings (maximum price, e.g. rent control) cause shortages; price floors (minimum price, e.g. minimum support price, minimum wage) cause surpluses. Normal profit is the minimum reward to the entrepreneur, included in cost.

📌

Features

  • Many small firms, identical products, free entry and exit and perfect knowledge make the firm a price taker
🧠

Equilibrium

  • The firm produces where MC = MR with MC rising
  • The short run supply curve is the MC curve above minimum AVC
🌟

Long run

  • Free entry and exit lead to normal profit where P = MC = minimum AC

lessons.title: Market Equilibrium
yt: class 12 economics market equilibrium demand supply shift excess demand excess supply

blocks.x: Market equilibrium occurs when quantity demanded equals quantity supplied at a price called the equilibrium price; the quantity is the equilibrium quantity. At a price above equilibrium there is excess supply (surplus), which pushes the price down; at a price below there is excess demand (shortage), which pushes the price up. The market clears at equilibrium. Effects of shifts in demand with fixed supply: an increase in demand raises both the equilibrium price and quantity; a decrease lowers both. Shifts in supply with fixed demand: an increase in supply lowers the price and raises the quantity; a decrease raises the price and lowers the quantity. Simultaneous shifts: both demand and supply increase: the quantity rises, price may rise, fall or stay depending on relative changes; demand increases and supply decreases: price rises, quantity uncertain, and so on. Numerical problems: solve Qd = a - bP and Qs = c + dP by equating. For the firm with a fixed number of firms, equilibrium is determined by market forces; with free entry and exit the number of firms changes in the long run. Price ceiling at below equilibrium creates shortage; floor above equilibrium creates surplus. Applications: minimum support price in agriculture creates surplus stocks, rent control reduces housing supply. Consumer surplus is the difference between what a consumer is willing to pay and the price paid; producer surplus is the difference between the price received and the minimum acceptable price. Efficiency: equilibrium maximises total surplus. Other things equal (ceteris paribus), a change in price causes a movement along the curve, not a shift. Demand and supply schedules, curves and the market clearing mechanism show the invisible hand of Adam Smith.
Deep dive: Equilibrium
Equilibrium price equates demand and supply. Excess supply pushes price down; excess demand pushes it up.
Deep dive: Shifts
Demand rightwards raises price and quantity; supply rightwards lowers price but raises quantity.
Deep dive: Control
A binding ceiling creates shortage; a binding floor creates surplus.

Visual lesson

Market Equilibrium

Market equilibrium occurs when quantity demanded equals quantity supplied at a price called the equilibrium price

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Equilibrium›3Shifts›4Control
🔑

Big idea

  • Market equilibrium occurs when quantity demanded equals quantity supplied at a price called the equilibrium price
  • The quantity is the equilibrium quantity
  • At a price above equilibrium there is excess supply (surplus), which pushes the price down
  • At a price below there is excess demand (shortage), which pushes the price up
Read the full explanation

Market equilibrium occurs when quantity demanded equals quantity supplied at a price called the equilibrium price; the quantity is the equilibrium quantity. At a price above equilibrium there is excess supply (surplus), which pushes the price down; at a price below there is excess demand (shortage), which pushes the price up. The market clears at equilibrium. Effects of shifts in demand with fixed supply: an increase in demand raises both the equilibrium price and quantity; a decrease lowers both. Shifts in supply with fixed demand: an increase in supply lowers the price and raises the quantity; a decrease raises the price and lowers the quantity. Simultaneous shifts: both demand and supply increase: the quantity rises, price may rise, fall or stay depending on relative changes; demand increases and supply decreases: price rises, quantity uncertain, and so on. Numerical problems: solve Qd = a - bP and Qs = c + dP by equating. For the firm with a fixed number of firms, equilibrium is determined by market forces; with free entry and exit the number of firms changes in the long run. Price ceiling at below equilibrium creates shortage; floor above equilibrium creates surplus. Applications: minimum support price in agriculture creates surplus stocks, rent control reduces housing supply. Consumer surplus is the difference between what a consumer is willing to pay and the price paid; producer surplus is the difference between the price received and the minimum acceptable price. Efficiency: equilibrium maximises total surplus. Other things equal (ceteris paribus), a change in price causes a movement along the curve, not a shift. Demand and supply schedules, curves and the market clearing mechanism show the invisible hand of Adam Smith.

📌

Equilibrium

  • Equilibrium price equates demand and supply
  • Excess supply pushes price down
  • Excess demand pushes it up
🧠

Shifts

  • Demand rightwards raises price and quantity
  • Supply rightwards lowers price but raises quantity
🌟

Control

  • A binding ceiling creates shortage
  • A binding floor creates surplus
🧮

Supply upP down Q up

lessons.title: Non-competitive Markets
yt: class 12 economics monopoly monopolistic competition oligopoly price discrimination collusion

blocks.x: Non competitive (imperfect) markets include monopoly, monopolistic competition and oligopoly. Monopoly: a single seller, no close substitutes and barriers to entry (patents, legal licence, control over resources, economies of scale). The monopolist is a price maker. Its demand (AR) curve slopes downward and MR lies below AR; MR is twice as steep as AR for a straight line. Equilibrium: MC = MR with MC cutting MR from below; the firm can earn supernormal profit even in the long run because of barriers. Price discrimination is charging different prices for the same good to different buyers (first, second, third degree). Natural monopoly occurs where economies of scale make one firm cheapest; public utilities. Monopolistic competition: a large number of sellers, differentiated products (brands), free entry and exit, selling costs (advertising), and each firm has some control over price; the demand curve is downward sloping and relatively elastic; short run supernormal profit or loss; long run normal profit through entry and exit, with price equal to AC but above MC and output below the minimum AC point (excess capacity). Examples: toothpaste, soaps, restaurants, clothes. Oligopoly: a few large firms, interdependence in decisions, barriers to entry, product homogeneous or differentiated, price rigidity (kinked demand curve) and non-price competition. Collusion: firms agree on price or output, as a cartel (e.g. OPEC); collusion is illegal in many countries; non-collusive oligopoly leads to price wars. Duopoly: two sellers. Comparison: perfect competition has P=MC and efficient allocation, monopoly has P>MC and deadweight loss, and monopolistic competition has excess capacity. Features compared in the table: number of firms, product, entry, price control, selling cost and demand elasticity. Government regulation: competition law and the Competition Commission of India (CCI) prevent anti-competitive practices.
Deep dive: Monopoly
One seller with barriers to entry faces a downward sloping demand curve and maximises profit at MC = MR.
Deep dive: Monopolistic competition
Many firms sell differentiated products; advertising matters and long run profit is normal.
Deep dive: Oligopoly
A few interdependent firms; kinked demand explains rigid prices; collusion forms cartels.

Visual lesson

Non-competitive Markets

Non competitive (imperfect) markets include monopoly, monopolistic competition and oligopoly

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Monopoly›3Monopolistic competition›4Oligopoly
🔑

Big idea

  • Non competitive (imperfect) markets include monopoly, monopolistic competition and oligopoly
  • Monopoly: a single seller, no close substitutes and barriers to entry (patents, legal licence, control over resources, economies of scale)
  • The monopolist is a price maker
  • Its demand (AR) curve slopes downward and MR lies below AR
Read the full explanation

Non competitive (imperfect) markets include monopoly, monopolistic competition and oligopoly. Monopoly: a single seller, no close substitutes and barriers to entry (patents, legal licence, control over resources, economies of scale). The monopolist is a price maker. Its demand (AR) curve slopes downward and MR lies below AR; MR is twice as steep as AR for a straight line. Equilibrium: MC = MR with MC cutting MR from below; the firm can earn supernormal profit even in the long run because of barriers. Price discrimination is charging different prices for the same good to different buyers (first, second, third degree). Natural monopoly occurs where economies of scale make one firm cheapest; public utilities. Monopolistic competition: a large number of sellers, differentiated products (brands), free entry and exit, selling costs (advertising), and each firm has some control over price; the demand curve is downward sloping and relatively elastic; short run supernormal profit or loss; long run normal profit through entry and exit, with price equal to AC but above MC and output below the minimum AC point (excess capacity). Examples: toothpaste, soaps, restaurants, clothes. Oligopoly: a few large firms, interdependence in decisions, barriers to entry, product homogeneous or differentiated, price rigidity (kinked demand curve) and non-price competition. Collusion: firms agree on price or output, as a cartel (e.g. OPEC); collusion is illegal in many countries; non-collusive oligopoly leads to price wars. Duopoly: two sellers. Comparison: perfect competition has P=MC and efficient allocation, monopoly has P>MC and deadweight loss, and monopolistic competition has excess capacity. Features compared in the table: number of firms, product, entry, price control, selling cost and demand elasticity. Government regulation: competition law and the Competition Commission of India (CCI) prevent anti-competitive practices.

📌

Monopoly

  • One seller with barriers to entry faces a downward sloping demand curve and maximises profit at MC = MR
🧠

Monopolistic competition

  • Many firms sell differentiated products
  • Advertising matters and long run profit is normal
🌟

Oligopoly

  • A few interdependent firms
  • Kinked demand explains rigid prices
  • Collusion forms cartels
🧮

lessons.title: National Income Accounting
yt: class 12 economics national income GDP GNP NNP circular flow methods real nominal GDP deflator

blocks.x: Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole: output, income, employment and prices. Circular flow of income: households supply factors to firms and receive factor payments; firms supply goods and receive spending; leakages (savings, taxes, imports) and injections (investment, government spending, exports). Basic concepts: consumption goods and capital goods; final and intermediate goods (only final goods are counted to avoid double counting); stocks and flows (capital, wealth are stocks; investment, income are flows); gross and net investment; depreciation (consumption of fixed capital); GDP is the market value of all final goods and services produced within the domestic territory in a year; GNP = GDP + net factor income from abroad (NFIA); NDP = GDP - depreciation; NNP = GNP - depreciation. At market price versus factor cost: GDP at factor cost = GDP at market price - indirect taxes + subsidies; NNP at factor cost = National Income (NI). Personal income and personal disposable income. Methods: (1) Production or value added method: GVA = value of output - intermediate consumption; sum of value added by all sectors; GDP at market price = GVA at basic prices + net product taxes. (2) Income method: compensation of employees + operating surplus (rent, interest, profit) + mixed income + net factor income from abroad = NNP at factor cost. (3) Expenditure method: GDP = C + I + G + (X - M). NNP at factor cost = GDP at MP - depreciation + NFIA - NIT (net indirect taxes). Nominal GDP is at current prices; real GDP at constant (base year) prices: Real GDP = Nominal GDP / Price index x 100. GDP deflator = (Nominal GDP / Real GDP) x 100. GDP and welfare: limitations include non-monetary transactions, externalities, distribution of income, unpaid household work and underground economy; GDP does not measure well being fully. Green GDP. Real income and price level. Exclusions from national income: second-hand sales, financial transfers, pensions, scholarships, windfall gains. Precautions to avoid double counting. Per capita income = National income / population.
Deep dive: Circular flow
Households and firms exchange factors and goods; savings, taxes and imports are leakages while investment, government spending and exports are injections.
Deep dive: Three methods
Value added, income and expenditure methods all give the same GDP in principle.
Deep dive: Real and nominal
Real GDP removes price effects; the deflator is nominal over real times 100. GDP is an imperfect measure of welfare.
Hindi saransh
Rashtriya aay lekha: GDP, GNP, NNP, teen vidhiyan, vastavik aur mudra GDP.

Visual lesson

National Income Accounting

Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole: output, income, employment and prices

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Circular flow›3Three methods›4Real and nominal
DeflatorNom/Real x 100
🔑

Big idea

  • Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole: output, income, employment and prices
  • Circular flow of income: households supply factors to firms and receive factor payments
  • Firms supply goods and receive spending
  • Leakages (savings, taxes, imports) and injections (investment, government spending, exports)
Read the full explanation

Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole: output, income, employment and prices. Circular flow of income: households supply factors to firms and receive factor payments; firms supply goods and receive spending; leakages (savings, taxes, imports) and injections (investment, government spending, exports). Basic concepts: consumption goods and capital goods; final and intermediate goods (only final goods are counted to avoid double counting); stocks and flows (capital, wealth are stocks; investment, income are flows); gross and net investment; depreciation (consumption of fixed capital); GDP is the market value of all final goods and services produced within the domestic territory in a year; GNP = GDP + net factor income from abroad (NFIA); NDP = GDP - depreciation; NNP = GNP - depreciation. At market price versus factor cost: GDP at factor cost = GDP at market price - indirect taxes + subsidies; NNP at factor cost = National Income (NI). Personal income and personal disposable income. Methods: (1) Production or value added method: GVA = value of output - intermediate consumption; sum of value added by all sectors; GDP at market price = GVA at basic prices + net product taxes. (2) Income method: compensation of employees + operating surplus (rent, interest, profit) + mixed income + net factor income from abroad = NNP at factor cost. (3) Expenditure method: GDP = C + I + G + (X - M). NNP at factor cost = GDP at MP - depreciation + NFIA - NIT (net indirect taxes). Nominal GDP is at current prices; real GDP at constant (base year) prices: Real GDP = Nominal GDP / Price index x 100. GDP deflator = (Nominal GDP / Real GDP) x 100. GDP and welfare: limitations include non-monetary transactions, externalities, distribution of income, unpaid household work and underground economy; GDP does not measure well being fully. Green GDP. Real income and price level. Exclusions from national income: second-hand sales, financial transfers, pensions, scholarships, windfall gains. Precautions to avoid double counting. Per capita income = National income / population.

🔄

Circular flow

  • Households and firms exchange factors and goods
  • Savings, taxes and imports are leakages while investment, government spending and exports are injections
🔄

Three methods

  • Value added, income and expenditure methods all give the same GDP in principle
🌟

Real and nominal

  • Real GDP removes price effects
  • The deflator is nominal over real times 100
  • GDP is an imperfect measure of welfare
🧮

Formula tiles

GDPC + I + G + (X-M)
GNPGDP + NFIA
NDPGDP - Dep
FCMP - NIT
DeflatorNom/Real x 100
🎯 Remember GNP = GDP + net factor income from abroad.

lessons.title: Money and Banking
yt: class 12 economics money functions supply RBI credit creation CRR SLR repo monetary policy

blocks.x: Barter: exchange of goods for goods; its drawback is the lack of double coincidence of wants. Money is anything generally accepted as a medium of exchange. Functions: primary: medium of exchange and unit of account; secondary: store of value and standard of deferred payments; contingent: transfer of value. Money supply: M1 = currency with the public + demand deposits with banks + other deposits with RBI; broader aggregates M2, M3 and M4. Demand for money: transactions demand and speculative demand (inversely related to interest rate). Commercial banks accept deposits, give loans and create credit. Money creation: money multiplier = 1 / LRR, where LRR (legal reserve ratio) is the cash reserve ratio. Credit creation: initial deposit x money multiplier; banks create demand deposits when loans are given. Example: initial deposit 1000 and reserve ratio 20 percent gives multiplier 5 and total deposits 5000. Central bank (Reserve Bank of India, set up in 1935 and nationalised in 1949): issues currency (notes except one rupee), banker to government, banker's bank, controller of credit and custodian of foreign exchange. Quantitative tools of monetary policy: bank rate; repo rate (rate at which RBI lends to banks against securities; an increase reduces borrowing and tightens credit); reverse repo rate (rate at which RBI borrows from banks); CRR (cash reserve ratio: share of deposits held as cash with RBI); SLR (statutory liquidity ratio: share held in liquid assets such as gold and government securities); open market operations (buying/selling government securities; buying injects money, selling withdraws it); margin requirements. Qualitative tools: moral suasion, selective credit control. Monetary policy fights inflation by tightening and recession by easing. Fiat money is legal tender by decree; commodity money has intrinsic value. Legal tender: limited and unlimited. Demonetisation. Digital payments: UPI, cards and wallets. Banks: scheduled, commercial, cooperative, regional rural. Credit creation limited by the reserve ratio.
Deep dive: Money
Money solves the double coincidence problem; it is a medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value and standard of deferred payment.
Deep dive: Credit creation
Banks lend a part of deposits and so create money; the multiplier is the reciprocal of the reserve ratio.
Deep dive: Monetary policy
RBI uses repo, reverse repo, CRR, SLR and open market operations to control credit and inflation.
Hindi saransh
Mudra aur banking: mudra ke karya, saakh srijan, RBI aur mudra niti ke upkaran.
Remember: money multiplier = 1 / reserve ratio.

Big idea

  • Barter: exchange of goods for goods
  • Its drawback is the lack of double coincidence of wants
  • Money is anything generally accepted as a medium of exchange
  • Functions: primary: medium of exchange and unit of account
Read the full explanation

Barter: exchange of goods for goods; its drawback is the lack of double coincidence of wants. Money is anything generally accepted as a medium of exchange. Functions: primary: medium of exchange and unit of account; secondary: store of value and standard of deferred payments; contingent: transfer of value. Money supply: M1 = currency with the public + demand deposits with banks + other deposits with RBI; broader aggregates M2, M3 and M4. Demand for money: transactions demand and speculative demand (inversely related to interest rate). Commercial banks accept deposits, give loans and create credit. Money creation: money multiplier = 1 / LRR, where LRR (legal reserve ratio) is the cash reserve ratio. Credit creation: initial deposit x money multiplier; banks create demand deposits when loans are given. Example: initial deposit 1000 and reserve ratio 20 percent gives multiplier 5 and total deposits 5000. Central bank (Reserve Bank of India, set up in 1935 and nationalised in 1949): issues currency (notes except one rupee), banker to government, banker's bank, controller of credit and custodian of foreign exchange. Quantitative tools of monetary policy: bank rate; repo rate (rate at which RBI lends to banks against securities; an increase reduces borrowing and tightens credit); reverse repo rate (rate at which RBI borrows from banks); CRR (cash reserve ratio: share of deposits held as cash with RBI); SLR (statutory liquidity ratio: share held in liquid assets such as gold and government securities); open market operations (buying/selling government securities; buying injects money, selling withdraws it); margin requirements. Qualitative tools: moral suasion, selective credit control. Monetary policy fights inflation by tightening and recession by easing. Fiat money is legal tender by decree; commodity money has intrinsic value. Legal tender: limited and unlimited. Demonetisation. Digital payments: UPI, cards and wallets. Banks: scheduled, commercial, cooperative, regional rural. Credit creation limited by the reserve ratio.

📌

Money

  • Money solves the double coincidence problem
  • It is a medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value and standard of deferred payment
🧠

Credit creation

  • Banks lend a part of deposits and so create money
  • The multiplier is the reciprocal of the reserve ratio
🌟

Monetary policy

  • RBI uses repo, reverse repo, CRR, SLR and open market operations to control credit and inflation

lessons.title: Determination of Income and Employment
yt: class 12 economics aggregate demand multiplier consumption function MPC investment inflationary deflationary gap

blocks.x: Keynes: in the short run, income and employment are determined by effective demand, i.e. aggregate demand (AD) equal to aggregate supply (AS). Ex ante and ex post. Aggregate demand AD = C + I + G + (X - M); in a simple two sector model AD = C + I. Consumption function C = a + bY, where a is autonomous consumption and b is the marginal propensity to consume (MPC); APC = C/Y; MPC = change in C / change in Y; APS = S/Y; MPS = change in S / change in Y; APC + APS = 1; MPC + MPS = 1. Saving function S = -a + (1 - b)Y. Break-even point where C = Y, S = 0. Investment: autonomous investment is independent of income; induced investment depends on income. Equilibrium income: Y = C + I, or S = I (saving equals investment); at income above equilibrium, S > I and output falls (unplanned inventory accumulation); below equilibrium, S < I and output rises. Y* = (a + I)/(1 - b). Investment multiplier k = change in Y / change in I = 1/(1 - MPC) = 1/MPS. Larger MPC means a bigger multiplier. The multiplier works both ways (forward and backward). Full employment: employment of all who are willing and able to work at the prevailing wage rate; involuntary unemployment exists below full employment; Keynes rejected the classical idea that supply creates its own demand (Say's law). Excess demand (inflationary gap): AD exceeds the AD needed for full employment equilibrium, so the price level rises. Deficient demand (deflationary gap): AD falls short of the AD needed for full employment; output and employment fall. Measures to correct excess demand: fiscal (reduce government expenditure, raise taxes), monetary (raise CRR, repo rate, SLR, sell securities, tighter credit); to correct deficient demand: the opposite (more government spending, lower taxes, lower interest rates, buy securities). Unemployment types: frictional, structural, cyclical, disguised. Paradox of thrift: if everyone saves more, aggregate income falls so total savings may not increase.
Deep dive: Equilibrium
Income is at equilibrium where AD = AS or planned saving equals planned investment.
Deep dive: Multiplier
k = 1/(1 - MPC) = 1/MPS; a rise in investment raises income by a multiple.
Deep dive: Gaps
Excess demand causes an inflationary gap; deficient demand a deflationary gap. Fiscal and monetary tools correct them.
Hindi saransh
Aay aur rozgar nirdharan: samagra mang, upbhog falan, gunak, mudrasphiti aur mandi ki khai.
Remember: MPC + MPS = 1 and multiplier = 1 / MPS.

Visual lesson

Determination of Income and Employment

Keynes: in the short run, income and employment are determined by effective demand, i.e. aggregate demand (AD) equal to aggregate supply (AS)

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Equilibrium›3Multiplier›4Gaps
MPC + MPS1
Multiplier1 / (1-MPC)
Y(a+I)/(1-b)
🔑

Big idea

  • Keynes: in the short run, income and employment are determined by effective demand, i.e. aggregate demand (AD) equal to aggregate supply (AS)
  • Ex ante and ex post
  • Aggregate demand AD = C + I + G + (X - M)
  • In a simple two sector model AD = C + I
Read the full explanation

Keynes: in the short run, income and employment are determined by effective demand, i.e. aggregate demand (AD) equal to aggregate supply (AS). Ex ante and ex post. Aggregate demand AD = C + I + G + (X - M); in a simple two sector model AD = C + I. Consumption function C = a + bY, where a is autonomous consumption and b is the marginal propensity to consume (MPC); APC = C/Y; MPC = change in C / change in Y; APS = S/Y; MPS = change in S / change in Y; APC + APS = 1; MPC + MPS = 1. Saving function S = -a + (1 - b)Y. Break-even point where C = Y, S = 0. Investment: autonomous investment is independent of income; induced investment depends on income. Equilibrium income: Y = C + I, or S = I (saving equals investment); at income above equilibrium, S > I and output falls (unplanned inventory accumulation); below equilibrium, S < I and output rises. Y* = (a + I)/(1 - b). Investment multiplier k = change in Y / change in I = 1/(1 - MPC) = 1/MPS. Larger MPC means a bigger multiplier. The multiplier works both ways (forward and backward). Full employment: employment of all who are willing and able to work at the prevailing wage rate; involuntary unemployment exists below full employment; Keynes rejected the classical idea that supply creates its own demand (Say's law). Excess demand (inflationary gap): AD exceeds the AD needed for full employment equilibrium, so the price level rises. Deficient demand (deflationary gap): AD falls short of the AD needed for full employment; output and employment fall. Measures to correct excess demand: fiscal (reduce government expenditure, raise taxes), monetary (raise CRR, repo rate, SLR, sell securities, tighter credit); to correct deficient demand: the opposite (more government spending, lower taxes, lower interest rates, buy securities). Unemployment types: frictional, structural, cyclical, disguised. Paradox of thrift: if everyone saves more, aggregate income falls so total savings may not increase.

📌

Equilibrium

  • Income is at equilibrium where AD = AS or planned saving equals planned investment
🎯

Multiplier

  • K = 1/(1 - MPC) = 1/MPS
  • A rise in investment raises income by a multiple
🌟

Gaps

  • Excess demand causes an inflationary gap
  • Deficient demand a deflationary gap
  • Fiscal and monetary tools correct them
🧮

Formula tiles

EquilibriumAD = AS or S = I

🎯 Remember MPC + MPS = 1 and multiplier = 1 / MPS.

lessons.title: Government Budget and the Economy
yt: class 12 economics government budget revenue expenditure fiscal deficit primary deficit taxes

blocks.x: The government budget is an annual statement of estimated receipts and expenditure of the government for a financial year (April 1 to March 31), presented under Article 112 of the Constitution; the Union Budget is presented by the Finance Minister. Objectives: reallocation of resources, redistribution of income and wealth, economic stability and growth, and management of public enterprises. Components: revenue account and capital account. Revenue receipts neither create a liability nor reduce assets: tax revenue (direct taxes such as income tax and corporation tax, indirect taxes such as GST and customs) and non-tax revenue (interest, dividends, fees, fines). Capital receipts create a liability or reduce assets: borrowings, recovery of loans and disinvestment (sale of shares of public sector enterprises). Revenue expenditure does not create assets (salaries, interest payments, subsidies, grants); capital expenditure creates assets or reduces liabilities (roads, buildings, loans given, repayment of debt). Planned and non-planned expenditure (older classification); developmental and non-developmental. Balanced budget: receipts = expenditure; surplus: receipts > expenditure; deficit: expenditure > receipts. Revenue deficit = revenue expenditure - revenue receipts. Fiscal deficit = total expenditure - total receipts excluding borrowing = borrowings; it shows the borrowing requirement. Primary deficit = fiscal deficit - interest payments; it shows the borrowing needed for expenditure other than interest. Effective revenue deficit. Measures of deficit: a high revenue deficit means the government is dissaving. Deficit financing: borrowing, printing money; consequences: inflation, debt burden and crowding out. Fiscal policy: taxation, expenditure and public debt. Taxes: direct (burden cannot be shifted) versus indirect (burden can be shifted); progressive, proportional and regressive taxes. GST replaced many indirect taxes in 2017. The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act 2003 targets deficit reduction. Subsidy, public goods (non-rival and non-excludable), merit goods and externalities justify government spending. Debt: internal and external; debt service. Budget multiplier.
Deep dive: Receipts and expenditure
Revenue items do not alter assets or liabilities; capital items do. Both receipts and expenditure are split this way.
Deep dive: Deficits
Revenue deficit, fiscal deficit and primary deficit measure different gaps; fiscal deficit equals borrowing.
Deep dive: Fiscal policy
The government uses taxes, spending and borrowing to allocate resources, redistribute income and stabilise the economy.
Hindi saransh
Sarkari bajat: rajasva aur poonji, rajasva ghata, rajkoshiya ghata, praathmik ghata aur kar.
Remember: fiscal deficit = borrowing; primary deficit = fiscal deficit - interest.

Revenue receipts neither create a liability nor reduce assets: tax revenue (direct taxes such as income tax and corporation tax, indirect taxes such as GST and customs) and non-tax revenue (interest, dividends, fees, fines). Capital receipts create a liability or reduce assets: borrowings, recovery of loans and disinvestment (sale of shares of public sector enterprises). Revenue expenditure does not create assets (salaries, interest payments, subsidies, grants); capital expenditure creates assets or reduces liabilities (roads, buildings, loans given, repayment of debt). Planned and non-planned expenditure (older classification); developmental and non-developmental. Balanced budget: receipts = expenditure; surplus: receipts > expenditure; deficit: expenditure > receipts. Revenue deficit = revenue expenditure - revenue receipts. Fiscal deficit = total expenditure - total receipts excluding borrowing = borrowings; it shows the borrowing requirement. Primary deficit = fiscal deficit - interest payments; it shows the borrowing needed for expenditure other than interest. Effective revenue deficit. Measures of deficit: a high revenue deficit means the government is dissaving. Deficit financing: borrowing, printing money; consequences: inflation, debt burden and crowding out. Fiscal policy: taxation, expenditure and public debt. Taxes: direct (burden cannot be shifted) versus indirect (burden can be shifted); progressive, proportional and regressive taxes. GST replaced many indirect taxes in 2017. The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act 2003 targets deficit reduction. Subsidy, public goods (non-rival and non-excludable), merit goods and externalities justify government spending. Debt: internal and external; debt service. Budget multiplier.

📌

Receipts and expenditure

  • Revenue items do not alter assets or liabilities
  • Capital items do
  • Both receipts and expenditure are split this way
🧠

Deficits

  • Revenue deficit, fiscal deficit and primary deficit measure different gaps
  • Fiscal deficit equals borrowing
🌟

Fiscal policy

  • The government uses taxes, spending and borrowing to allocate resources, redistribute income and stabilise the economy
🧮

Fiscal deficitBorrowing
Primary deficitFD - interest
🎯 Remember fiscal deficit = borrowing; primary deficit = fiscal deficit - interest.

blocks.x: An open economy trades goods, services and assets with other countries. Balance of payments (BoP) is a systematic record of all economic transactions between residents of a country and the rest of the world in a year. Components: the current account records trade in goods (visible items, balance of trade), trade in services (invisible items), income and transfers; the capital account records capital flows: foreign direct investment (FDI), foreign portfolio investment (FPI), external borrowing and assistance, and changes in reserves. Balance of trade (BOT) = exports of goods - imports of goods; a surplus is favourable and a deficit unfavourable. Current account deficit shows excess of imports (including invisibles) over exports. BoP always balances in accounting terms because of double entry book keeping; autonomous items (taken for profit, independent of BoP position) versus accommodating items (taken to settle a deficit); BoP deficit = autonomous receipts less than payments, financed by selling foreign exchange reserves or borrowing. Foreign exchange: foreign currencies; the exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another. Systems: fixed exchange rate (the government fixes the rate, the Bretton Woods system until 1971; devaluation and revaluation), flexible or floating (determined by demand and supply in the foreign exchange market; appreciation and depreciation), and managed floating (the central bank intervenes; the system India uses). Determination: the demand for foreign exchange comes from imports, foreign travel, gifts and investment abroad and slopes downward; supply comes from exports, foreign investment inflows and remittances and slopes upward; equilibrium where they meet. A rise in the exchange rate (more rupees per dollar) is a depreciation of the rupee, making exports cheaper and imports dearer; appreciation does the opposite. Nominal exchange rate versus real exchange rate = e x P*/P. Purchasing power parity. Foreign exchange reserves held by the RBI. Devaluation is a deliberate lowering of the rate in a fixed system. Merits of flexible rate: automatic adjustment; demerits: instability. Speculation. Spot and forward markets.
Deep dive: Balance of payments
The current account holds trade, services, income and transfers; the capital account holds investment and borrowing.
Deep dive: Exchange rate
The rate is determined by demand and supply of foreign exchange; depreciation makes exports cheaper and imports costlier.
Deep dive: Systems
Fixed, flexible and managed float differ in central bank intervention; India follows managed floating.

An open economy trades goods, services and assets with other countries. Balance of payments (BoP) is a systematic record of all economic transactions between residents of a country and the rest of the world in a year. Components: the current account records trade in goods (visible items, balance of trade), trade in services (invisible items), income and transfers; the capital account records capital flows: foreign direct investment (FDI), foreign portfolio investment (FPI), external borrowing and assistance, and changes in reserves. Balance of trade (BOT) = exports of goods - imports of goods; a surplus is favourable and a deficit unfavourable. Current account deficit shows excess of imports (including invisibles) over exports.
