Foreign exchange: foreign currencies; the exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another. Systems: fixed exchange rate (the government fixes the rate, the Bretton Woods system until 1971; devaluation and revaluation), flexible or floating (determined by demand and supply in the foreign exchange market; appreciation and depreciation), and managed floating (the central bank intervenes; the system India uses). Determination: the demand for foreign exchange comes from imports, foreign travel, gifts and investment abroad and slopes downward; supply comes from exports, foreign investment inflows and remittances and slopes upward; equilibrium where they meet. A rise in the exchange rate (more rupees per dollar) is a depreciation of the rupee, making exports cheaper and imports dearer; appreciation does the opposite. Nominal exchange rate versus real exchange rate = e x P*/P. Purchasing power parity. Foreign exchange reserves held by the RBI. Devaluation is a deliberate lowering of the rate in a fixed system. Merits of flexible rate: automatic adjustment; demerits: instability. Speculation. Spot and forward markets.

lessons.title: The Last Lesson
yt: class 12 english flamingo the last lesson alphonse daudet summary franz m hamel

blocks.x: The Last Lesson by Alphonse Daudet is set in Alsace, a French region that Prussia had taken after the Franco-Prussian War of 1870-71. The narrator, a schoolboy named Franz, is late for school and tempted to skip it and play outside on a bright, warm morning. On his way he passes the town hall, where a crowd reads the bulletin board that has carried bad news for two years. The blacksmith Wachter tells him not to hurry because he will get to school in time. At school, instead of the usual noise, there is silence. M. Hamel wears his best green coat, a frilled shirt and a black silk cap, which he wore only on inspection days and prize days. The back benches are occupied by village elders including old Hauser with his three-cornered hat, the former mayor and the postmaster. M. Hamel announces that an order from Berlin says only German will be taught in the schools of Alsace and Lorraine, and that this is his last French lesson. Franz is shocked and regrets that he had neglected his lessons; he realises he can hardly write French and that his books, which seemed a nuisance, are now like old friends. M. Hamel tells the class that the blame lies with everyone, parents who preferred to send children to work and himself who sent them to water his flowers and gave them a holiday to go fishing. He says that French is the most beautiful, clearest and most logical language, and that when a people are enslaved, as long as they hold fast to their language it is as if they had the key to their prison. The lesson on grammar is followed by reading, writing (copy slips reading France, Alsace), and a lesson in history. The old Hauser spells out the letters with the children, weeping. At the church clock striking twelve and the Prussian trumpets sounding, M. Hamel stands pale, tries to speak but chokes, takes chalk and writes in large letters Vive la France, then makes a gesture that school is dismissed. Themes: linguistic imperialism, patriotism, regret over lost opportunities and the value of education and mother tongue. Style: simple first person narrative, symbolism (the bulletin board, the green coat), irony (the pigeons that may be made to coo in German). Teacher and student relationship changes from fear to respect.
Deep dive: Language and freedom
The story shows that language is bound to identity; losing it means losing freedom. M. Hamel calls it the key to the prison.
Deep dive: Characters
Franz changes from a careless boy to a repentant learner; M. Hamel from stern teacher to an emotional patriot.
Deep dive: Symbols
The bulletin board, the formal dress of M. Hamel and the Vive la France message symbolise loss, respect and resistance.
Hindi saransh
Antim paath: Alsace mein French ki jagah German thopi gayi; M. Hamel ka antim paath mattrbhasha aur deshprem ka sandesh deta hai.
Remember: the story is set in Alsace after the Franco-Prussian War.

On his way he passes the town hall, where a crowd reads the bulletin board that has carried bad news for two years. The blacksmith Wachter tells him not to hurry because he will get to school in time. At school, instead of the usual noise, there is silence. M. Hamel wears his best green coat, a frilled shirt and a black silk cap, which he wore only on inspection days and prize days. The back benches are occupied by village elders including old Hauser with his three-cornered hat, the former mayor and the postmaster. M. Hamel announces that an order from Berlin says only German will be taught in the schools of Alsace and Lorraine, and that this is his last French lesson. Franz is shocked and regrets that he had neglected his lessons; he realises he can hardly write French and that his books, which seemed a nuisance, are now like old friends. M. Hamel tells the class that the blame lies with everyone, parents who preferred to send children to work and himself who sent them to water his flowers and gave them a holiday to go fishing. He says that French is the most beautiful, clearest and most logical language, and that when a people are enslaved, as long as they hold fast to their language it is as if they had the key to their prison. The lesson on grammar is followed by reading, writing (copy slips reading France, Alsace), and a lesson in history. The old Hauser spells out the letters with the children, weeping. At the church clock striking twelve and the Prussian trumpets sounding, M. Hamel stands pale, tries to speak but chokes, takes chalk and writes in large letters Vive la France, then makes a gesture that school is dismissed. Themes: linguistic imperialism, patriotism, regret over lost opportunities and the value of education and mother tongue. Style: simple first person narrative, symbolism (the bulletin board, the green coat), irony (the pigeons that may be made to coo in German). Teacher and student relationship changes from fear to respect.

📌

Language and freedom

  • The story shows that language is bound to identity
  • Losing it means losing freedom
  • Hamel calls it the key to the prison
🧠

Characters

  • Franz changes from a careless boy to a repentant learner
  • Hamel from stern teacher to an emotional patriot
🌟

Symbols

  • The bulletin board, the formal dress of M
  • Hamel and the Vive la France message symbolise loss, respect and resistance

blocks.x: Lost Spring: Stories of Stolen Childhood by Anees Jung has two parts. Part I: Sometimes I find a Gold Coin describes Saheb-e-Alam, a ragpicker boy from Dhaka whose family left their home when storms swept away their fields and homes. He lives in Seemapuri, on the outskirts of Delhi, in a squatters settlement with about 10,000 ragpickers who came from Bangladesh in 1971, with no identity other than ration cards for food. For them, garbage is gold: it is a means of survival and for children it is wrapped in wonder (sometimes finding a rupee or even a ten rupee note in the heap). Saheb wears discarded tennis shoes and walks barefoot though he dreams of playing tennis, as the narrator remarks that she likes to see him play at the club. The writer offers to start a school, and he asks eagerly whether she will; the promise remains unkept. Saheb later finds work at a tea stall for 800 rupees and all the meals, but loses his carefree freedom: the steel canister he carries is heavier than the plastic bag he used to carry, and he is no longer his own master. Part II: I want to Drive a Motor Car describes Mukesh in Firozabad, the centre of the glass-blowing industry, where families have worked on bangles for generations. Children and parents work in dark hutments with high temperatures, unsafe furnaces, and poor ventilation, losing their eyesight. The caste system and the exploitation by middlemen, policemen, bureaucrats and politicians keep them trapped; the bangle makers say it is their karma (destiny) to be bangle makers. A girl named Savita is described as one who sits with her mother welding pieces of coloured glass into circles, and she is unaware that the bangles symbolise an Indian woman's suhaag. Mukesh insists on being his own master and dreams of becoming a motor mechanic, saying he will go to the garage which is a distance away from his home; the writer comments that dreams are in his eyes though bangle makers are afraid to dream. The theme: poverty, child labour, exploitation, lost childhood, the burden of tradition and the denial of the right to education. The title Lost Spring signifies the childhood that is stolen. Anees Jung's style is journalistic, reportage with description, irony and compassion. Related law: the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009 and the prohibition of child labour.
Deep dive: Saheb
His life shows the poverty of migrant ragpickers; garbage is both survival and a dream, and employment ends his freedom.
Deep dive: Mukesh and Firozabad
Generations of glass bangle makers are trapped by tradition, caste and middlemen, yet Mukesh dares to dream.
Deep dive: Theme
Childhood is stolen by poverty and exploitation, and the state and society fail to protect it.

Lost Spring: Stories of Stolen Childhood by Anees Jung has two parts. Part I: Sometimes I find a Gold Coin describes Saheb-e-Alam, a ragpicker boy from Dhaka whose family left their home when storms swept away their fields and homes. He lives in Seemapuri, on the outskirts of Delhi, in a squatters settlement with about 10,000 ragpickers who came from Bangladesh in 1971, with no identity other than ration cards for food. For them, garbage is gold: it is a means of survival and for children it is wrapped in wonder (sometimes finding a rupee or even a ten rupee note in the heap). Saheb wears discarded tennis shoes and walks barefoot though he dreams of playing tennis, as the narrator remarks that she likes to see him play at the club. The writer offers to start a school, and he asks eagerly whether she will; the promise remains unkept. Saheb later finds work at a tea stall for 800 rupees and all the meals, but loses his carefree freedom: the steel canister he carries is heavier than the plastic bag he used to carry, and he is no longer his own master. Part II: I want to Drive a Motor Car describes Mukesh in Firozabad, the centre of the glass-blowing industry, where families have worked on bangles for generations. Children and parents work in dark hutments with high temperatures, unsafe furnaces, and poor ventilation, losing their eyesight. The caste system and the exploitation by middlemen, policemen, bureaucrats and politicians keep them trapped; the bangle makers say it is their karma (destiny) to be bangle makers. A girl named Savita is described as one who sits with her mother welding pieces of coloured glass into circles, and she is unaware that the bangles symbolise an Indian woman's suhaag. Mukesh insists on being his own master and dreams of becoming a motor mechanic, saying he will go to the garage which is a distance away from his home; the writer comments that dreams are in his eyes though bangle makers are afraid to dream. The theme: poverty, child labour, exploitation, lost childhood, the burden of tradition and the denial of the right to education. The title Lost Spring signifies the childhood that is stolen. Anees Jung's style is journalistic, reportage with description, irony and compassion. Related law: the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009 and the prohibition of child labour.

blocks.x: Deep Water is an extract from Of Men and Mountains by William Douglas, a US Supreme Court Justice. It describes his fear of water and how he overcame it. As a child of about three or four, he went with his father to the beach in California; the waves knocked him down and he was frightened by the experience; he felt choked, terrified and watched his world fade. This childhood experience left him with an abiding fear of water. At the age of ten or eleven, he decided to learn to swim at the Yakima YMCA pool. One day he went alone, and a big boy, thinking it a joke, threw him into the deep end. He sank to the bottom, struggled, and decided to spring upward from the bottom to the surface; he planned to jump with a surge and use the strength of his legs, but he came up with water in his mouth and could not move forward. He was panicked, he swallowed water, lost consciousness, then woke to find the boy and lifeguard had pulled him out. The experience left him with a terrifying fear of water; it kept him away from canoeing, fishing and swimming, and made him feel that he had missed out on the pleasure of camping and the outdoors. At first he thought of a way out and hired an instructor who trained him over several months: the instructor held a belt around his waist and a rope through a pulley, and asked him to put his face in the water, blow bubbles, kick and stretch his legs. Gradually he learned to swim in the pool using the instructor's training, overcoming his fear bit by bit; but still the terror returned when he swam alone in the lake, until he conquered it fully in Lake Wentworth, New Hampshire. At Lake Wentworth, he swam across the lake and felt the terror return in the middle but he screamed to himself, told his legs to swim and finally reached the shore; he realised that I had conquered fear; he learned that the only thing to fear is fear itself, a line of Roosevelt which he recalls. The theme: fear, determination, will power, perseverance and the training required to overcome it. Style: autobiographical, vivid descriptions of panic, suspense, short sentences in moments of danger.
Deep dive: The fear
A near drowning at the YMCA pool created an enduring terror of water that reached into adult life.
Deep dive: The training
A patient instructor used a rope and belt, with drills in breathing, kicking and floating, building confidence step by step.
Deep dive: The lesson
Will power and practice overcome fear; the only thing to fear is fear itself.

Deep Water is an extract from Of Men and Mountains by William Douglas, a US Supreme Court Justice. It describes his fear of water and how he overcame it. As a child of about three or four, he went with his father to the beach in California; the waves knocked him down and he was frightened by the experience; he felt choked, terrified and watched his world fade. This childhood experience left him with an abiding fear of water. At the age of ten or eleven, he decided to learn to swim at the Yakima YMCA pool. One day he went alone, and a big boy, thinking it a joke, threw him into the deep end. He sank to the bottom, struggled, and decided to spring upward from the bottom to the surface; he planned to jump with a surge and use the strength of his legs, but he came up with water in his mouth and could not move forward. He was panicked, he swallowed water, lost consciousness, then woke to find the boy and lifeguard had pulled him out. The experience left him with a terrifying fear of water; it kept him away from canoeing, fishing and swimming, and made him feel that he had missed out on the pleasure of camping and the outdoors. At first he thought of a way out and hired an instructor who trained him over several months: the instructor held a belt around his waist and a rope through a pulley, and asked him to put his face in the water, blow bubbles, kick and stretch his legs. Gradually he learned to swim in the pool using the instructor's training, overcoming his fear bit by bit; but still the terror returned when he swam alone in the lake, until he conquered it fully in Lake Wentworth, New Hampshire. At Lake Wentworth, he swam across the lake and felt the terror return in the middle but he screamed to himself, told his legs to swim and finally reached the shore; he realised that I had conquered fear; he learned that the only thing to fear is fear itself, a line of Roosevelt which he recalls. The theme: fear, determination, will power, perseverance and the training required to overcome it. lessons.title: The Rattrap
yt: class 12 english flamingo the rattrap selma lagerlof summary edla willmansson ironmaster

blocks.x: The Rattrap by Selma Lagerlof (Swedish Nobel laureate) tells of a peddler who made and sold small rattraps of wire. As his business did not support him, he also begged and stole to survive. One day he thought that the whole world was a rattrap: it offers riches, joy, shelter and food as bait, and once someone is tempted to touch the bait, it closes in and everything ends. A kindly old crofter gives him shelter for the night and entertains him with stories and a game of cards; he mentions the 30 kronor he received from the creamery for his cow's milk and shows the peddler the money. In the morning when the crofter left for work, the peddler stole the money from the leather pouch hanging on the window frame, believing himself clever. Fleeing, he went into the forest, lost his way, and realised that he was caught in a rattrap himself, like a rat, wandering round and round. In the evening he heard hammering from an ironworks, found a blacksmith who allowed him to sleep by the furnace, and met the ironmaster, who mistook him for an old regimental comrade, Captain von Stahle. He invited him home, but the peddler refused. The ironmaster's daughter Edla Willmansson persuaded him to come for Christmas; the peddler, who feared being arrested, was warmly welcomed; Edla treated him with kindness, even when the ironmaster discovered that he was not the captain. When the ironmaster threatened to call the sheriff, Edla insisted he be allowed to stay for Christmas, saying that we should extend a kindness in the holiday season. The peddler left, taking a gift of Christmas present: a suit of clothes. Later Edla received a rattrap in a package from the peddler with 30 kronor and a letter in which he wrote that he had been raised from a rat to a captain by her kindness, and returned what he had stolen. He signed himself as Captain von Stahle. Themes: human goodness, kindness and trust transform a person; the world is a rattrap of temptation; Christmas spirit and compassion; individuals can reform; the distinction between appearance and reality. Style: allegory, irony, symbolism, third person narrative, humour.
Deep dive: The rattrap metaphor
The world is a rattrap: baits of riches, shelter and food lure people to their ruin; the peddler himself is caught.
Deep dive: Edla
Her kindness, understanding and trust draw out the peddler's goodness; she is unlike her pragmatic father.
Deep dive: Transformation
The peddler returns the stolen money and signs as Captain von Stahle; kindness reforms.

Read the full explanation

The Rattrap by Selma Lagerlof (Swedish Nobel laureate) tells of a peddler who made and sold small rattraps of wire. As his business did not support him, he also begged and stole to survive. One day he thought that the whole world was a rattrap: it offers riches, joy, shelter and food as bait, and once someone is tempted to touch the bait, it closes in and everything ends. A kindly old crofter gives him shelter for the night and entertains him with stories and a game of cards; he mentions the 30 kronor he received from the creamery for his cow's milk and shows the peddler the money. In the morning when the crofter left for work, the peddler stole the money from the leather pouch hanging on the window frame, believing himself clever. Fleeing, he went into the forest, lost his way, and realised that he was caught in a rattrap himself, like a rat, wandering round and round. In the evening he heard hammering from an ironworks, found a blacksmith who allowed him to sleep by the furnace, and met the ironmaster, who mistook him for an old regimental comrade, Captain von Stahle. He invited him home, but the peddler refused. The ironmaster's daughter Edla Willmansson persuaded him to come for Christmas; the peddler, who feared being arrested, was warmly welcomed; Edla treated him with kindness, even when the ironmaster discovered that he was not the captain. When the ironmaster threatened to call the sheriff, Edla insisted he be allowed to stay for Christmas, saying that we should extend a kindness in the holiday season. The peddler left, taking a gift of Christmas present: a suit of clothes. Later Edla received a rattrap in a package from the peddler with 30 kronor and a letter in which he wrote that he had been raised from a rat to a captain by her kindness, and returned what he had stolen. He signed himself as Captain von Stahle. Themes: human goodness, kindness and trust transform a person; the world is a rattrap of temptation; Christmas spirit and compassion; individuals can reform; the distinction between appearance and reality. Style: allegory, irony, symbolism, third person narrative, humour.

📌

The rattrap metaphor

  • The world is a rattrap: baits of riches, shelter and food lure people to their ruin
  • The peddler himself is caught
🧠

Edla

  • Her kindness, understanding and trust draw out the peddler's goodness
  • She is unlike her pragmatic father
🌟

Transformation

  • The peddler returns the stolen money and signs as Captain von Stahle
  • Kindness reforms
🧮

lessons.title: Indigo
yt: class 12 english flamingo indigo louis fischer gandhi champaran rajkumar shukla

blocks.x: Indigo by Louis Fischer, from his book The Life of Mahatma Gandhi, describes Gandhi's first satyagraha in India, in Champaran, Bihar, in 1917. At the Congress session in Lucknow in December 1916, a poor peasant named Rajkumar Shukla from Champaran asked Gandhi to come to his district, where peasants were forced under the tinkathia system to grow indigo on three twentieths (3/20) of their land for their British landlords. When the Germans invented synthetic indigo, the landlords demanded compensation from peasants to release them from the contract, and the peasants now wanted their money back. Shukla followed Gandhi to Cawnpore, Ahmedabad and Calcutta, and finally Gandhi went with him to Patna, where he was received at the house of Rajendra Prasad, whose servants took him for a peasant. In Muzaffarpur, Gandhi met Professor J. B. Kripalani and lawyers who explained the situation, and then proceeded to Motihari. The commissioner, Morehead, ordered him to leave Tirhut; Gandhi refused and was summoned to appear in court. Thousands of peasants gathered around the courthouse; the government was baffled. Gandhi pleaded guilty, saying he disobeyed out of a higher duty, the voice of conscience; the judge postponed the sentence, and finally the case against Gandhi was withdrawn. Gandhi, assisted by lawyers including Rajendra Prasad, Brij Kishore, Mazharul Haq and others, collected the evidence from thousands of peasants. The Lieutenant Governor invited him and set up an inquiry commission with Gandhi as a member. Gandhi agreed to a settlement in which the landlords refunded only 25 percent of the money they had illegally extracted; he accepted it, saying the amount was not important but that the landlords had surrendered part of their prestige. Within a few years the British planters left, and indigo cultivation vanished. Gandhi also engaged in social work: schools, health work, and he insisted that people be self-reliant; he told C. F. Andrews not to stay, saying that the battle should be fought by Indians themselves, so that the peasants would learn courage and self-reliance. Themes: civil disobedience, non-violence, courage, self-reliance, leadership, justice for the poor. The title refers to the dye plant and the colonial exploitation tied to it.
Deep dive: Champaran
The tinkathia system forced peasants to grow indigo; Gandhi investigated, was ordered to leave, defied the order and won an inquiry.
Deep dive: Methods
Non-violent civil disobedience, collecting evidence and winning public support made the government yield.
Deep dive: Self-reliance
Gandhi told Andrews to leave because freedom must be earned by Indians; this freed the peasants from fear.
Hindi saransh
Indigo: Champaran mein Gandhi ka pehla satyagraha, neel kisanon ko nyay aur nirbhayta ka path.
Remember: the planters refunded 25 percent; the lasting gain was freedom from fear.

Read the full explanation

Indigo by Louis Fischer, from his book The Life of Mahatma Gandhi, describes Gandhi's first satyagraha in India, in Champaran, Bihar, in 1917. At the Congress session in Lucknow in December 1916, a poor peasant named Rajkumar Shukla from Champaran asked Gandhi to come to his district, where peasants were forced under the tinkathia system to grow indigo on three twentieths (3/20) of their land for their British landlords. When the Germans invented synthetic indigo, the landlords demanded compensation from peasants to release them from the contract, and the peasants now wanted their money back. Shukla followed Gandhi to Cawnpore, Ahmedabad and Calcutta, and finally Gandhi went with him to Patna, where he was received at the house of Rajendra Prasad, whose servants took him for a peasant. In Muzaffarpur, Gandhi met Professor J. B. Kripalani and lawyers who explained the situation, and then proceeded to Motihari. The commissioner, Morehead, ordered him to leave Tirhut; Gandhi refused and was summoned to appear in court. Thousands of peasants gathered around the courthouse; the government was baffled. Gandhi pleaded guilty, saying he disobeyed out of a higher duty, the voice of conscience; the judge postponed the sentence, and finally the case against Gandhi was withdrawn. Gandhi, assisted by lawyers including Rajendra Prasad, Brij Kishore, Mazharul Haq and others, collected the evidence from thousands of peasants. The Lieutenant Governor invited him and set up an inquiry commission with Gandhi as a member. Gandhi agreed to a settlement in which the landlords refunded only 25 percent of the money they had illegally extracted; he accepted it, saying the amount was not important but that the landlords had surrendered part of their prestige. Within a few years the British planters left, and indigo cultivation vanished. Gandhi also engaged in social work: schools, health work, and he insisted that people be self-reliant; he told C. F. Andrews not to stay, saying that the battle should be fought by Indians themselves, so that the peasants would learn courage and self-reliance. Themes: civil disobedience, non-violence, courage, self-reliance, leadership, justice for the poor. The title refers to the dye plant and the colonial exploitation tied to it.

📌

Champaran

  • The tinkathia system forced peasants to grow indigo
  • Gandhi investigated, was ordered to leave, defied the order and won an inquiry
🔄

Methods

  • Non-violent civil disobedience, collecting evidence and winning public support made the government yield
🌟

Self-reliance

  • Gandhi told Andrews to leave because freedom must be earned by Indians
  • This freed the peasants from fear

lessons.title: Poets and Pancakes
yt: class 12 english flamingo poets and pancakes asokamitran gemini studios

blocks.x: Poets and Pancakes is an extract from the memoir My Years with Boss by Asokamitran, who worked at Gemini Studios in Madras (now Chennai), a leading Indian film studio of the 1940s and 1950s, owned by S. S. Vasan, whom the staff called the Boss. The title joins two ideas: Pancake, a brand of make-up used in huge quantities in the studio's make-up department, and the poets who were drawn to the studio. The make-up department was crowded with people from different regions, and the narrator describes them with gentle satire. The emblem of Gemini was a pair of twins blowing bugles, and the studio's gate carried it. The narrator describes several characters: the Legal Adviser, a lawyer in a khadi dhoti who seldom had any real legal work; and Kothamangalam Subbu, Vasan's talented right-hand man, called Number Two, a poet who headed the story department and wrote verse. The story department was a group of writers who looked after the scripts. The studio had visitors: a group from the Moral Re-Armament (MRA) movement staged shows there, and later the English poet Stephen Spender, editor of the magazine Encounter, visited; the studio staff did not know who he was, and the narrator, who was an ordinary employee, had to explain English poetry to the staff. The extract is a humorous account of how the film world, busy with commerce, treated art, poets and writers. Themes: art versus commerce, the gap between creative people and the film industry, and humour. Style: anecdotal, ironic first person narration with satire.
Deep dive: Gemini Studios
A busy film studio whose departments and staff are described with gentle satire.
Deep dive: The Boy and the Legal Adviser
Characters like the Boy (Subbu) and the Legal Adviser show the odd mix of art and bureaucracy in the studio.
Deep dive: Poets and film
The visits of MRA and of a poet show how little the film world understood poetry.

Read the full explanation

Poets and Pancakes is an extract from the memoir My Years with Boss by Asokamitran, who worked at Gemini Studios in Madras (now Chennai), a leading Indian film studio of the 1940s and 1950s, owned by S. S. Vasan, whom the staff called the Boss. The title joins two ideas: Pancake, a brand of make-up used in huge quantities in the studio's make-up department, and the poets who were drawn to the studio. The make-up department was crowded with people from different regions, and the narrator describes them with gentle satire. The emblem of Gemini was a pair of twins blowing bugles, and the studio's gate carried it. The narrator describes several characters: the Legal Adviser, a lawyer in a khadi dhoti who seldom had any real legal work; and Kothamangalam Subbu, Vasan's talented right-hand man, called Number Two, a poet who headed the story department and wrote verse. The story department was a group of writers who looked after the scripts. The studio had visitors: a group from the Moral Re-Armament (MRA) movement staged shows there, and later the English poet Stephen Spender, editor of the magazine Encounter, visited; the studio staff did not know who he was, and the narrator, who was an ordinary employee, had to explain English poetry to the staff. The extract is a humorous account of how the film world, busy with commerce, treated art, poets and writers. Themes: art versus commerce, the gap between creative people and the film industry, and humour. Style: anecdotal, ironic first person narration with satire.

📌

Gemini Studios

  • A busy film studio whose departments and staff are described with gentle satire
🧠

The Boy and the Legal Adviser

  • Characters like the Boy (Subbu) and the Legal Adviser show the odd mix of art and bureaucracy in the studio
🌟

Poets and film

  • The visits of MRA and of a poet show how little the film world understood poetry

lessons.title: The Interview
yt: class 12 english flamingo the interview christopher silvester umberto eco mukund padmanabhan

blocks.x: The Interview has two parts: an essay by Christopher Silvester from The Penguin Book of Interviews on the art and role of the interview, and an interview of the Italian scholar and novelist Umberto Eco by Mukund Padmanabhan of The Hindu. Part I: The interview is a major source of communication in modern society and has a central place in journalism. The first interview was published in 1859, by Horace Greeley of the New York Tribune with Brigham Young. Many famous people disliked it: Rudyard Kipling called it a crime and an offence against the rights of the individual, H. G. Wells described it as an ordeal, Saul Bellow compared it to having your fingerprints taken, Lewis Carroll refused to meet journalists, and V. S. Naipaul said that some people are wounded by interviews and that a little of the soul is taken away. Supporters say it is a supremely serviceable medium of communication and, in the hands of a skilled interviewer, a creative art that brings a person alive. Part II: Umberto Eco is a professor at the University of Bologna, a scholar of semiotics, and a bestselling novelist whose first novel was The Name of the Rose. In the interview Padmanabhan asks how he manages to write so much; Eco says he uses the empty spaces of life, those small gaps of time in waiting or travelling, to write, and that he does not have a fixed pattern. He is humorous and modest, and the interview shows the mind of a scholar who is also a novelist. Themes: the role and ethics of the interview, creativity, and the interplay of scholarship and fiction.
Deep dive: The interview as a form
It dates from 1859; some great writers loathed it as an intrusion, others praised it as an art.
Deep dive: Eco
Scholar and novelist; he uses the empty spaces of life to write; The Name of the Rose is his famous novel.
Deep dive: Contrasting views
The essay balances attack and defence, the interview shows an example of a good interview.
Hindi saransh
The Interview: interview ki kala par nibandh aur Umberto Eco se vartalaap.

Read the full explanation

The Interview has two parts: an essay by Christopher Silvester from The Penguin Book of Interviews on the art and role of the interview, and an interview of the Italian scholar and novelist Umberto Eco by Mukund Padmanabhan of The Hindu. Part I: The interview is a major source of communication in modern society and has a central place in journalism. The first interview was published in 1859, by Horace Greeley of the New York Tribune with Brigham Young. Many famous people disliked it: Rudyard Kipling called it a crime and an offence against the rights of the individual, H. G. Wells described it as an ordeal, Saul Bellow compared it to having your fingerprints taken, Lewis Carroll refused to meet journalists, and V. S. Naipaul said that some people are wounded by interviews and that a little of the soul is taken away. Supporters say it is a supremely serviceable medium of communication and, in the hands of a skilled interviewer, a creative art that brings a person alive. Part II: Umberto Eco is a professor at the University of Bologna, a scholar of semiotics, and a bestselling novelist whose first novel was The Name of the Rose. In the interview Padmanabhan asks how he manages to write so much; Eco says he uses the empty spaces of life, those small gaps of time in waiting or travelling, to write, and that he does not have a fixed pattern. He is humorous and modest, and the interview shows the mind of a scholar who is also a novelist. Themes: the role and ethics of the interview, creativity, and the interplay of scholarship and fiction.

📌

The interview as a form

  • It dates from 1859
  • Some great writers loathed it as an intrusion, others praised it as an art
🧠

Eco

  • Scholar and novelist
  • He uses the empty spaces of life to write
  • The Name of the Rose is his famous novel
🌟

Contrasting views

  • The essay balances attack and defence, the interview shows an example of a good interview

blocks.x: Going Places by A. R. Barton is a short story about the dreams of a teenage girl and the gap between fantasy and reality. Sophie and her friend Jansie are two schoolgirls. Sophie is imaginative and ambitious: she dreams of becoming an actress, then of owning a boutique and becoming a famous fashion designer, and she is fascinated by Danny Casey, a famous footballer whom she imagines meeting. She builds a fantasy in which Danny Casey would come to her boutique. Jansie, who is practical and cautious, doubts Sophie's stories and tells her to be sensible. Sophie lives in a modest home with parents and an elder brother, Geoff; the family life is plain and Sophie dreams of escaping it. She talks about her dreams to Jansie, and in her imagination she goes to meet Danny Casey. In the end the reality is that Danny does not come; she is left with her hope. Themes: dream and reality, adolescent imagination, desire to escape an ordinary life, the pressure of a modest background, and hope. Style: simple narrative with dialogue; contrast between Sophie's romantic outlook and Jansie's practical one. Moral: dreams give hope and direction but must be balanced with a sense of reality.
Deep dive: Sophie
Imaginative, ambitious and dissatisfied; she builds a fantasy around Danny Casey to escape a dull life.
Deep dive: Jansie
Practical and realistic; she sees Sophie's fantasy as impossible.
Deep dive: Theme
The story contrasts fantasy and reality and shows how dreams sustain young people from modest backgrounds.

lessons.title: My Mother at Sixty-six
yt: class 12 english flamingo poem my mother at sixty six kamala das analysis

blocks.x: My Mother at Sixty-six is a poem by Kamala Das (also known as Madhavikutty and Kamala Surayya), a major Indian poet writing in English and Malayalam. The speaker is driving from her parents' home in Cochin to the Cochin airport to catch a flight to Delhi. Her mother sits beside her, sleeping or dozing with her mouth open. The speaker looks at her mother's face, which is pale and ashen like that of a corpse, and the sight makes her heart ache with the thought of losing her. To escape the painful thought she looks outside the car: she sees young trees which seem to be sprinting and merry children spilling out of their homes, contrasting with her mother's old age, that is, the vitality of youth against the decay of age. After the security check at the airport, she stands a few yards away from her mother and looks again at her face, which is pale, wan, like a late winter's moon. She feels the same old familiar ache and childhood fear of losing her mother. She puts on a smile and says goodbye with the words see you soon, Amma, hiding her pain, hoping that her mother will be fine. Themes: ageing, the fear of separation and death, mother daughter love, the contrast between old age and youth, helplessness. Poetic devices: simile (ashen like that of a corpse; pale as a late winter's moon), metaphor, personification (sprinting trees), imagery (visual), contrast, enjambment, repetition of the word smile. The poem is written in free verse with a conversational tone. The pale moon of winter stands for waning life and the smile conceals the pain.
Deep dive: The scene
The car journey and airport parting set the poet's fear of losing her ageing mother against the energy of nature and children.
Deep dive: Images
The corpse-like face and the late winter moon show age; sprinting trees and children show life.
Deep dive: The smile
The poet's forced smile and goodbye hide her pain and hope for another meeting.
Hindi saransh
My Mother at Sixty-six: Kamala Das ki vridh maa ko khone ke dar ki kavita.
Remember: the poem contrasts ageing mother with sprinting trees and merry children.

Read the full explanation

My Mother at Sixty-six is a poem by Kamala Das (also known as Madhavikutty and Kamala Surayya), a major Indian poet writing in English and Malayalam. The speaker is driving from her parents' home in Cochin to the Cochin airport to catch a flight to Delhi. Her mother sits beside her, sleeping or dozing with her mouth open. The speaker looks at her mother's face, which is pale and ashen like that of a corpse, and the sight makes her heart ache with the thought of losing her. To escape the painful thought she looks outside the car: she sees young trees which seem to be sprinting and merry children spilling out of their homes, contrasting with her mother's old age, that is, the vitality of youth against the decay of age. After the security check at the airport, she stands a few yards away from her mother and looks again at her face, which is pale, wan, like a late winter's moon. She feels the same old familiar ache and childhood fear of losing her mother. She puts on a smile and says goodbye with the words see you soon, Amma, hiding her pain, hoping that her mother will be fine. Themes: ageing, the fear of separation and death, mother daughter love, the contrast between old age and youth, helplessness. Poetic devices: simile (ashen like that of a corpse; pale as a late winter's moon), metaphor, personification (sprinting trees), imagery (visual), contrast, enjambment, repetition of the word smile. The poem is written in free verse with a conversational tone. The pale moon of winter stands for waning life and the smile conceals the pain.

📌

The scene

  • The car journey and airport parting set the poet's fear of losing her ageing mother against the energy of nature and children
🧠

Images

  • The corpse-like face and the late winter moon show age
  • Sprinting trees and children show life
🌟

The smile

  • The poet's forced smile and goodbye hide her pain and hope for another meeting

yt: class 12 english flamingo poem keeping quiet pablo neruda analysis

blocks.x: Keeping Quiet is a poem by the Chilean poet Pablo Neruda (translated into English), a Nobel laureate for Literature in 1971. The poet asks us to count up to twelve and then keep still. For once on earth, let us not speak in any language and not move our arms so much. It would be an exotic moment without rush, without engines, when all of us would be together in a sudden strangeness. The fishermen in the cold sea would not harm the whales, and the man gathering salt would look at his hurt hands. People who prepare green wars, wars with gas and fire, victories with no survivors, would put on clean clothes and walk about with their brothers in the shade, doing nothing. What the poet wants is not total inactivity: life is what it is about; he does not want to deal with death. He says that if we were not so single-minded in pursuing our aims and for once did nothing, a huge silence might interrupt this sadness of never understanding ourselves and of threatening ourselves with death. Perhaps the earth can teach us as when everything seems dead and later proves to be alive. Now the poet will count up to twelve and the reader should keep quiet while he goes. Themes: introspection, peace, brotherhood, the futility of war, the destruction of nature, the need for self-examination. Devices: repetition of counting, imagery of fishermen and whales (conservation), personification, irony (people can be at peace by doing nothing), contrast between activity and stillness, free verse, direct address in plural form (let us). Tone: persuasive, calm and yet urgent.
Deep dive: Stillness
A moment of stillness will help humans recognise their unity and rethink war, greed and harm to nature.
Deep dive: Not death
The silence he asks for is not death or inaction; it is a pause for introspection that leads to renewal, as in the earth in winter.
Deep dive: Images
The whales, salt gatherer and war makers show harm to nature and fellow humans.
Hindi saransh
Keeping Quiet: Pablo Neruda ka maun ka sandesh, shanti, bhaichare aur aatmchintan ka aagrah.
Remember: keeping quiet is not death; it is silence for self-examination.

Keeping Quiet

Keeping Quiet is a poem by the Chilean poet Pablo Neruda (translated into English), a Nobel laureate for Literature in 1971

🔑

Big idea

  • Keeping Quiet is a poem by the Chilean poet Pablo Neruda (translated into English), a Nobel laureate for Literature in 1971
  • The poet asks us to count up to twelve and then keep still
  • For once on earth, let us not speak in any language and not move our arms so much
  • It would be an exotic moment without rush, without engines, when all of us would be together in a sudden strangeness
Read the full explanation

Keeping Quiet is a poem by the Chilean poet Pablo Neruda (translated into English), a Nobel laureate for Literature in 1971. The poet asks us to count up to twelve and then keep still. For once on earth, let us not speak in any language and not move our arms so much. It would be an exotic moment without rush, without engines, when all of us would be together in a sudden strangeness. The fishermen in the cold sea would not harm the whales, and the man gathering salt would look at his hurt hands. People who prepare green wars, wars with gas and fire, victories with no survivors, would put on clean clothes and walk about with their brothers in the shade, doing nothing. What the poet wants is not total inactivity: life is what it is about; he does not want to deal with death. He says that if we were not so single-minded in pursuing our aims and for once did nothing, a huge silence might interrupt this sadness of never understanding ourselves and of threatening ourselves with death. Perhaps the earth can teach us as when everything seems dead and later proves to be alive. Now the poet will count up to twelve and the reader should keep quiet while he goes. Themes: introspection, peace, brotherhood, the futility of war, the destruction of nature, the need for self-examination. Devices: repetition of counting, imagery of fishermen and whales (conservation), personification, irony (people can be at peace by doing nothing), contrast between activity and stillness, free verse, direct address in plural form (let us). Tone: persuasive, calm and yet urgent.

📌

Stillness

  • A moment of stillness will help humans recognise their unity and rethink war, greed and harm to nature
🧠

Not death

  • The silence he asks for is not death or inaction
  • It is a pause for introspection that leads to renewal, as in the earth in winter
🌟

Images

  • The whales, salt gatherer and war makers show harm to nature and fellow humans
🧮

NotDeath
ThemePeace
🎯 Remember keeping quiet is not death; it is silence for self-examination.

lessons.title: A Thing of Beauty
yt: class 12 english flamingo poem a thing of beauty keats endymion analysis

blocks.x: A Thing of Beauty is an extract from the long poem Endymion (1818) by the English Romantic poet John Keats. The poem begins with the idea that a thing of beauty is a joy for ever: its loveliness increases and never passes into nothingness; it will keep a bower of quiet for us and a sleep full of sweet dreams, health and quiet breathing. Therefore, every morning we are wreathing a flowery band to bind us to the earth, in spite of despondence, of the inhuman dearth of noble natures and of the gloomy days, all the unhealthy and dark ways that are cut for our search. Yet some shape of beauty moves away the pall from our dark spirits. Such are the sun, the moon, trees old and young, sprouting a shady boon for simple sheep, and daffodils in the green world they live in; and clear rills that for themselves make a cooling covert against the summer's heat; the mid-forest brake rich with a sprinkling of fair musk-rose blooms. Also there is the grandeur of the dooms we have imagined for the mighty dead; all lovely tales that we have heard or read: an endless fountain of immortal drink, pouring unto us from the heaven's brink. The poet says that beauty is our companion and a source of consolation in a world of suffering, and its power is not limited to the moment but also lives on in memory. Nature, tales of heroes and imagination feed the human spirit. Themes: the lasting power of beauty, nature as a healer, imagination and consolation in a troubled world. Devices: metaphor (flowery band; endless fountain of immortal drink), alliteration (sweet dreams, health and quiet breathing), personification (spirits), imagery of nature, rhyming couplets (heroic couplets) in iambic pentameter, rich diction. Tone: lyrical and celebratory. Keats also believed that beauty is truth.
Deep dive: Beauty lasts
Beauty never fades into nothingness; it gives lasting joy, peaceful sleep and sweet dreams.
Deep dive: Consolation
Nature, heroic stories and imagination are bonds to the earth that console us amid sorrow and dark days.
Deep dive: Images
Sun, moon, trees, daffodils, rills and musk-rose blooms show the beauty of nature that heals.
Hindi saransh
A Thing of Beauty: Keats ki kavita - sundar vastu sada aanand deti hai aur prakriti hamara sambal hai.

Read the full explanation

A Thing of Beauty is an extract from the long poem Endymion (1818) by the English Romantic poet John Keats. The poem begins with the idea that a thing of beauty is a joy for ever: its loveliness increases and never passes into nothingness; it will keep a bower of quiet for us and a sleep full of sweet dreams, health and quiet breathing. Therefore, every morning we are wreathing a flowery band to bind us to the earth, in spite of despondence, of the inhuman dearth of noble natures and of the gloomy days, all the unhealthy and dark ways that are cut for our search. Yet some shape of beauty moves away the pall from our dark spirits. Such are the sun, the moon, trees old and young, sprouting a shady boon for simple sheep, and daffodils in the green world they live in; and clear rills that for themselves make a cooling covert against the summer's heat; the mid-forest brake rich with a sprinkling of fair musk-rose blooms. Also there is the grandeur of the dooms we have imagined for the mighty dead; all lovely tales that we have heard or read: an endless fountain of immortal drink, pouring unto us from the heaven's brink. The poet says that beauty is our companion and a source of consolation in a world of suffering, and its power is not limited to the moment but also lives on in memory. Nature, tales of heroes and imagination feed the human spirit. Themes: the lasting power of beauty, nature as a healer, imagination and consolation in a troubled world. Devices: metaphor (flowery band; endless fountain of immortal drink), alliteration (sweet dreams, health and quiet breathing), personification (spirits), imagery of nature, rhyming couplets (heroic couplets) in iambic pentameter, rich diction. Tone: lyrical and celebratory. Keats also believed that beauty is truth.

blocks.x: A Roadside Stand is a poem by the American poet Robert Frost (1874-1963). It describes a small, poor roadside stand built by farmers on a country highway, a little pine-board stand that appeals to city motorists to stop and buy their produce. The poet empathises with these poor country people who have set up a stand to sell fruits, vegetables and other produce, hoping for a better life through the passing traffic. The poem begins with the stand put up with painted signs begging passersby to stop; but the cars passed by quickly, the drivers wanted to go faster and did not stop for the rural poor; few stopped, and the poet feels the hope of the sellers is ignored. The poet feels deeply for the rural poor who dream of getting money to meet their needs but are ignored; the farmers, he says, are tired of waiting for kindness. He is also critical of the city people, and of the government, whose plan for the rural poor is to create new towns and extend help but only in a slow way, leaving rural poverty unattended. The poet says that he wishes some kind of help could come, and how bitter it is that those who do the nation's hard work receive nothing; his heart aches that they have been cheated by the "greedy" city; the poet suspects that real help, which he calls selfless generosity, will not come. Themes: rural poverty versus urban indifference, the failure of social welfare, the false promise of progress, the cruelty of modern economic systems, empathy. Devices: irony, personification (the polished traffic), imagery, contrast (country vs city), rhyme scheme, tone of sympathy and anger. The poem reflects the Great Depression era in America, where farmers suffered.

Deep dive: The indifference

Deep dive: The poet

yt: class 12 english flamingo poem aunt jennifers tigers adrienne rich analysis

blocks.x: Aunt Jennifer's Tigers is a poem by the American poet and feminist Adrienne Rich (1929-2012), written in 1951. It is a poem of three stanzas, written in rhyming couplets. Aunt Jennifer embroiders tigers on a panel: they prance across the screen, bright topaz denizens of a world of green. They do not fear the men beneath the tree; they pace in sleek chivalric certainty. The tigers are bold, confident, free and fearless, in sharp contrast to Aunt Jennifer, who is timid, fearful and tired, and whose fingers flutter through her wool as she works. She finds it hard to pull the ivory needle because her wedding ring sits heavily on her finger, the massive weight of Uncle's wedding band, which stands for the burden of marriage and male domination. When Aunt Jennifer is dead, her terrified hands will lie still, still ringed with ordeals she was mastered by, but the tigers she made will go on prancing, proud and unafraid. Themes: the oppression of women in marriage and patriarchy, the longing for freedom, the power of art and creativity as an escape and a legacy, contrast between the real and the imagined. Symbols: tigers (freedom, strength, courage, the free self she cannot be), the wedding band (oppression, male dominance), the needle (her creative effort). Devices: contrast, symbolism, imagery, metaphor, enjambment, rhymed couplets (aabb), irony in the tigers' fearlessness. Tone: sympathetic and critical. Message: women's creativity and the desire for freedom survive their suppression.
Deep dive: Aunt Jennifer
Timid and burdened by marriage; she makes tigers that she can never be.
Deep dive: Tigers
Symbols of freedom, strength and fearlessness; they remain proud after she dies.
Deep dive: Ring
The wedding band symbolises male domination and the weight of marriage.

Big idea

  • Aunt Jennifer's Tigers is a poem by the American poet and feminist Adrienne Rich (1929-2012), written in 1951
  • It is a poem of three stanzas, written in rhyming couplets

Read the full explanation

Aunt Jennifer's Tigers is a poem by the American poet and feminist Adrienne Rich (1929-2012), written in 1951. It is a poem of three stanzas, written in rhyming couplets. Aunt Jennifer embroiders tigers on a panel: they prance across the screen, bright topaz denizens of a world of green. They do not fear the men beneath the tree; they pace in sleek chivalric certainty. The tigers are bold, confident, free and fearless, in sharp contrast to Aunt Jennifer, who is timid, fearful and tired, and whose fingers flutter through her wool as she works. She finds it hard to pull the ivory needle because her wedding ring sits heavily on her finger, the massive weight of Uncle's wedding band, which stands for the burden of marriage and male domination. When Aunt Jennifer is dead, her terrified hands will lie still, still ringed with ordeals she was mastered by, but the tigers she made will go on prancing, proud and unafraid. Themes: the oppression of women in marriage and patriarchy, the longing for freedom, the power of art and creativity as an escape and a legacy, contrast between the real and the imagined. Symbols: tigers (freedom, strength, courage, the free self she cannot be), the wedding band (oppression, male dominance), the needle (her creative effort). Devices: contrast, symbolism, imagery, metaphor, enjambment, rhymed couplets (aabb), irony in the tigers' fearlessness. Tone: sympathetic and critical. Message: women's creativity and the desire for freedom survive their suppression.

yt: class 12 english vistas the third level jack finney grand central station charley sam

blocks.x: The Third Level by Jack Finney is a fantasy about a man who finds a hidden level at Grand Central Station in New York that leads into the past. The narrator, Charley, tells his psychiatrist friend Sam Weiner that Grand Central has a third level in addition to the two that everybody knows. One night, taking a wrong turn, he found himself on a level with old fashioned gas lamps, wooden ticket windows and men and women in clothes of the 1890s: it was the year 1894. He tried to buy tickets for Galesburg, Illinois, the quiet town of his childhood, to escape the world of worry and tension, but the clerk refused his modern money, which was larger than the notes then in use. Charley rushed out to exchange his money for old currency, but the amount he could manage was too little, and when he returned he could not find the third level again. Sam, the psychiatrist, called it a waking dream, a wish fulfilment of a man who wants to escape modern life. Charley's wife Louisa was worried by his search, but Sam later began to believe him. Charley and Sam both collected old currency, and Sam, a stamp collector, vanished. Later Charley found among his stamp collection a first day cover dated July 18, 1894, posted from Galesburg, Illinois, and addressed to him. It was a letter from Sam, saying he had found the third level, bought a ticket with old money, and settled in Galesburg, a pleasant, quiet place, and urged Charley and Louisa to join him. Themes: escape from the stress and insecurity of modern life, nostalgia for a peaceful past, fantasy and reality. Style: first person narration, conversational tone.
Deep dive: The third level
An imaginary level of Grand Central leading to the year 1894 offers escape from modern stress.
Deep dive: Sam and Charley
Sam first explains the third level as wishful dreaming, but then goes to the past himself, leaving a letter.
Deep dive: Theme
The story is about escape from war, tension and insecurity to a quiet past.
Hindi saransh
The Third Level: Grand Central ka teesra star - 1894 ke Galesburg ki or palayan ki kalpana.
Remember: Charley seeks Galesburg, 1894; Sam finds a way and sends a letter.

yt: class 12 english vistas the tiger king kalki maharaja jung jung bahadur pratibandapuram

blocks.x: The Tiger King by Kalki (R. Krishnamurthy) is a satire on the vanity and arrogance of rulers and on blind belief in prophecy. The Maharaja of Pratibandapuram, Jung Jung Bahadur, was given the title the Tiger King after astrologers predicted, when he was only ten days old, that he would die by a tiger. The infant Maharaja himself declared that he would kill a hundred tigers to prove the astrologers wrong. When he became king, he began to hunt tigers; the Dewan and other officials praised him and made arrangements. He killed seventy tigers, and the state ran short of tigers; the Maharaja threatened officials who failed him. Read the full explanation

The Tiger King by Kalki (R. Krishnamurthy) is a satire on the vanity and arrogance of rulers and on blind belief in prophecy. The Maharaja of Pratibandapuram, Jung Jung Bahadur, was given the title the Tiger King after astrologers predicted, when he was only ten days old, that he would die by a tiger. The infant Maharaja himself declared that he would kill a hundred tigers to prove the astrologers wrong. When he became king, he began to hunt tigers; the Dewan and other officials praised him and made arrangements. He killed seventy tigers, and the state ran short of tigers; the Maharaja threatened officials who failed him. To meet his target he married into a princess's family that was famed for its tigers, and he continued until he had killed ninety nine. The hundredth tiger was hard to find; when at last an old, weak tiger was found, the Maharaja shot at it and missed, but the tiger fell dead from fright, and the Maharaja thought he had killed the hundredth tiger. His court celebrated, but a tiger in the story turned out to be the cause of his end: a wooden toy tiger bought for the Maharaja's three year old son as a birthday gift had a splinter that pierced his hand; the wound turned septic and the Maharaja died. The prophecy had come true in an unexpected way. Themes: the irony of fate, arrogance of power, absurdity of blind faith, cruelty to wildlife. Style: satire, exaggeration, humour and dramatic irony.

yt: class 12 english vistas journey to the end of the earth tishani doshi antarctica

blocks.x: Journey to the End of the Earth is a travelogue by Tishani Doshi about her journey to Antarctica, the southernmost continent, on a student expedition organised by Students on Ice. The writer sailed from Argentina and crossed the rough Drake Passage to reach Antarctica. She explains that the continent holds the key to the earth's past, present and future. Its layers of ice hold records of climate, with ice cores that give information about hundreds of thousands of years. Millions of years ago, Antarctica was joined with India, Africa, South America and Australia in the supercontinent Gondwana, about 650 million years ago in the writer's account. Antarctica is the coldest, driest and windiest continent, and is protected by the Antarctic Treaty of 1959 for peace and science. India has research stations there. The writer saw icebergs, penguins and other wildlife and realised how fragile the ecosystem is. She cautions about global warming, melting ice and the ozone hole, first detected over Antarctica in 1985, and about the need for human beings to act responsibly. The visit made her think about time, the age of the earth and the smallness of humans. Themes: environmental awareness, global warming, unity of the earth, adventure and curiosity. Style: travel writing, vivid description, scientific facts and personal reflection.
Deep dive: Antarctica
The continent holds a record of the earth's climate in its ice and shows how connected the earth's continents once were.
Deep dive: Warning
Melting ice, global warming and the ozone hole warn of environmental danger.
Deep dive: Personal view
The journey makes the writer reflect on human smallness and responsibility to the planet.

  • Journey to the End of the Earth is a travelogue by Tishani Doshi about her journey to Antarctica, the southernmost continent, on a student expedition…
  • The writer sailed from Argentina and crossed the rough Drake Passage to reach Antarctica

Read the full explanation

Journey to the End of the Earth is a travelogue by Tishani Doshi about her journey to Antarctica, the southernmost continent, on a student expedition organised by Students on Ice. The writer sailed from Argentina and crossed the rough Drake Passage to reach Antarctica. She explains that the continent holds the key to the earth's past, present and future. Its layers of ice hold records of climate, with ice cores that give information about hundreds of thousands of years. Millions of years ago, Antarctica was joined with India, Africa, South America and Australia in the supercontinent Gondwana, about 650 million years ago in the writer's account. Antarctica is the coldest, driest and windiest continent, and is protected by the Antarctic Treaty of 1959 for peace and science. India has research stations there. The writer saw icebergs, penguins and other wildlife and realised how fragile the ecosystem is. She cautions about global warming, melting ice and the ozone hole, first detected over Antarctica in 1985, and about the need for human beings to act responsibly. The visit made her think about time, the age of the earth and the smallness of humans. Themes: environmental awareness, global warming, unity of the earth, adventure and curiosity. Style: travel writing, vivid description, scientific facts and personal reflection.

📌

Antarctica

  • The continent holds a record of the earth's climate in its ice and shows how connected the earth's continents once were
🕰️

Warning

  • Melting ice, global warming and the ozone hole warn of environmental danger
🌟

Personal view

  • The journey makes the writer reflect on human smallness and responsibility to the planet

yt: class 12 english vistas the enemy pearl s buck sadao hana prisoner of war

blocks.x: The Enemy by Pearl S. Buck is set in Japan during the Second World War. Dr Sadao Hoki, a Japanese surgeon who studied in America under Dr Harley, lives by the sea with his wife Hana. One day they find a wounded American soldier washed ashore, a prisoner of war who has escaped. Sadao decides to treat him though it is risky to shelter an enemy; Hana is reluctant at first but helps him. Sadao operates on the man at home. The servants, shocked that an enemy is being cared for, leave. Sadao is torn between his duty as a doctor and as a patriot. He is the personal doctor of the General, who is old and ill, and he finally informs the General. The General promises to send assassins to kill the prisoner quietly, but they never come: the General has forgotten the matter. Fearing the man will be discovered, Sadao helps the prisoner escape in a boat to a nearby island with food, water and a torch, and tells him to signal to a Korean fishing boat. The soldier escapes. Themes: humanity beyond nationality, duty of a doctor, conflict between patriotism and compassion, prejudice in war. Characters: Sadao is humane and professional, Hana is brave and caring, the General is self centred, the servants are loyal but prejudiced. Style: third person narration with irony and suspense.
Deep dive: Conflict
Sadao is caught between his duty to his country and his duty to save life.
Deep dive: Humanity
The doctor's compassion overcomes national hatred; Hana joins him in helping the enemy.
Deep dive: General
The General's selfishness lets Sadao off; he forgets the plan because he needs the doctor.

yt: class 12 english vistas on the face of it susan hill mr lamb derry garden

blocks.x: On the Face of It by Susan Hill is a one-act play about the meeting of two lonely people: Mr Lamb, an old man with a tin leg who lives alone in a garden, and Derry, a teenage boy whose face is badly scarred by acid burns on one side. Derry is bitter and ashamed because people shun him; he thinks no one will ever accept him. One day he climbs the wall of Mr Lamb's garden. Mr Lamb, a kind and cheerful man, welcomes him, offers him apples and tells him of the pleasures of the garden, the bees, the flowers and the smell of the earth. On the Face of It by Susan Hill is a one-act play about the meeting of two lonely people: Mr Lamb, an old man with a tin leg who lives alone in a garden, and Derry, a teenage boy whose face is badly scarred by acid burns on one side. Derry is bitter and ashamed because people shun him; he thinks no one will ever accept him. One day he climbs the wall of Mr Lamb's garden. Mr Lamb, a kind and cheerful man, welcomes him, offers him apples and tells him of the pleasures of the garden, the bees, the flowers and the smell of the earth. He tells Derry that the garden is open to all and that he should not hide from the world. Derry slowly begins to trust him. Mr Lamb says that the face is only the surface and that he should go out and meet people. At the end of the play, Mr Lamb dies in an accident while picking apples, but Derry goes on with the lesson Mr Lamb taught him. Themes: loneliness, physical difference, prejudice, acceptance, friendship and human contact. Symbols: the garden (life and acceptance), the wall (isolation), the gate (welcome), the tin leg (disability), the apple (friendship). Style: play, mostly dialogue, symbolic.

lessons.title: Memories of Childhood
yt: class 12 english vistas memories of childhood zitkala sa bama cutting of my long hair we too are human beings

blocks.x: Memories of Childhood has two autobiographical accounts of discrimination. Part I: The Cutting of My Long Hair by Zitkala-Sa (Gertrude Simmons Bonnin), a Native American (Sioux) woman, describes her experience at the white missionary boarding school (Carlisle Indian School) in the United States, where she is forced to give up her tribal ways. She is excited about a trip to the East but finds the school harsh: she is woken by a bell, made to follow rules, and at the dining hall must bow and eat with knives and forks. When she learns that her long hair will be cut, she is horrified, for in her tribe only cowards and mourners had their hair cut and shingled; her mother had told her that only cowards had their hair shingled. She hides under a bed upstairs, but is found and dragged out, tied to a chair and her hair cut. She cries and feels that she has lost her individuality; she feels like a little animal driven by a herder. She is helpless against the cruelty and the loss of her tribe's culture. Part II: We Too Are Human Beings by Bama (Faustina Mary Fatima Rani), a Dalit writer from Tamil Nadu, describes how, as a child of the third class, she walks back from school and sees an elderly Dalit man carrying a packet of food by a string, without touching it, to a landlord of the upper caste. She finds this funny but her elder brother explains that it is not funny but a case of untouchability: the upper castes think Dalits are polluted. She is shocked and determined to excel; her brother advises her to study hard to get respect and wealth: if you study, you will have the respect denied to us; we must study with all our might, become the first in the class. She works hard and stands first in her class; many people become her friends. Themes: discrimination (racial and caste), loss of identity, the power of education to overcome oppression, resistance, dignity. Style: first person autobiographical narration, simple language, striking imagery.
Deep dive: Zitkala-Sa
A Native American child is forcibly assimilated; the cutting of her hair is a symbol of lost identity.
Deep dive: Bama
Untouchability shocks the child; her brother's advice to study hard becomes her route to dignity.
Deep dive: Common ground
Both texts show discrimination and how a child learns to resist it; Bama turns to education while Zitkala-Sa mourns lost heritage.
Hindi saransh
Bachpan ki yaadein: Zitkala-Sa aur Bama dwara bhedbhav ke anubhav, shiksha se mukti ka sandesh.
Remember: Zitkala-Sa faces racial assimilation; Bama faces caste discrimination.

Memories of Childhood has two autobiographical accounts of discrimination

🔑

Big idea

  • Memories of Childhood has two autobiographical accounts of discrimination
  • Part I: The Cutting of My Long Hair by Zitkala-Sa (Gertrude Simmons Bonnin), a Native American (Sioux) woman, describes her experience at the white…
  • She is excited about a trip to the East but finds the school harsh: she is woken by a bell, made to follow rules, and at the dining hall must bow and…
  • When she learns that her long hair will be cut, she is horrified, for in her tribe only cowards and mourners had their hair cut and shingled
Read the full explanation

Memories of Childhood has two autobiographical accounts of discrimination. Part I: The Cutting of My Long Hair by Zitkala-Sa (Gertrude Simmons Bonnin), a Native American (Sioux) woman, describes her experience at the white missionary boarding school (Carlisle Indian School) in the United States, where she is forced to give up her tribal ways. She is excited about a trip to the East but finds the school harsh: she is woken by a bell, made to follow rules, and at the dining hall must bow and eat with knives and forks. When she learns that her long hair will be cut, she is horrified, for in her tribe only cowards and mourners had their hair cut and shingled; her mother had told her that only cowards had their hair shingled. She hides under a bed upstairs, but is found and dragged out, tied to a chair and her hair cut. She cries and feels that she has lost her individuality; she feels like a little animal driven by a herder. She is helpless against the cruelty and the loss of her tribe's culture. Part II: We Too Are Human Beings by Bama (Faustina Mary Fatima Rani), a Dalit writer from Tamil Nadu, describes how, as a child of the third class, she walks back from school and sees an elderly Dalit man carrying a packet of food by a string, without touching it, to a landlord of the upper caste. She finds this funny but her elder brother explains that it is not funny but a case of untouchability: the upper castes think Dalits are polluted. She is shocked and determined to excel; her brother advises her to study hard to get respect and wealth: if you study, you will have the respect denied to us; we must study with all our might, become the first in the class. She works hard and stands first in her class; many people become her friends. Themes: discrimination (racial and caste), loss of identity, the power of education to overcome oppression, resistance, dignity. Style: first person autobiographical narration, simple language, striking imagery.

📌

Zitkala-Sa

  • A Native American child is forcibly assimilated
  • The cutting of her hair is a symbol of lost identity
🧠

Bama

  • Untouchability shocks the child
  • Her brother's advice to study hard becomes her route to dignity
🌟

Common ground

  • Both texts show discrimination and how a child learns to resist it
  • Bama turns to education while Zitkala-Sa mourns lost heritage

lessons.title: Writing Skills
yt: class 12 english core writing skills notice invitation reply letter article report speech advertisement format

blocks.x: The Class 12 English Core writing section tests short and long compositions in set formats. Notice: a short formal announcement written in a box with the heading NOTICE, the name of the issuing organisation, the date, a title, the body (event, date, time, venue, contact) and the writer's name and designation; the limit is about 50 words; use passive voice and impersonal style. Poster and advertisement: a catchy slogan, key details, contact information, and an eye-catching layout; classified advertisements are compact and use abbreviations. Invitation and reply: formal invitations are in the third person with an impersonal style, giving host, occasion, date, time, venue and RSVP; replies accept or decline in the same third person style; informal invitations are in the first person. Letters: formal letters have sender's address, date, receiver's address, subject line, salutation (Sir or Madam), body, and complimentary close (Yours faithfully for Sir or Madam; Yours sincerely when a name is known) and signature. Types: letter to the editor (on a social problem or public issue; the writer addresses the editor, gives a heading, states the problem with facts and suggests solutions), job application with a CV or bio-data (covering letter and resume with career objective, education, experience, skills, references), business letters (letter of enquiry, order, complaint, reply to complaint), and letters seeking information from institutions. Article: 150-200 words with a title, a byline, an introduction, a body of two to three paragraphs and a conclusion; types: descriptive, argumentative and informative. Report: a factual account of an event with a title, reporter name and place and date line; it is written in the past tense and the passive voice, in a formal style; types: event reports and newspaper reports. Speech: begin with a salutation to the audience, introduce the topic, give arguments, appeal and end with thanks; use spoken style, rhetorical questions. Debate: for or against motion. Tips: plan and revise, follow word limits, use paragraphs, avoid slang and errors, and use cohesive devices such as therefore, moreover and however. Marking: format, content, expression and accuracy.
Deep dive: Formats
Each form has its own layout and style; marks are given for format, content, fluency and accuracy.
Deep dive: Letters
Formal letters need the sender's address, date, receiver's address, subject, salutation, body and complimentary close.
Deep dive: Articles and reports
Articles have a headline, byline and structured paragraphs; reports use the past tense and passive voice.
Hindi saransh
Lekhan kaushal: soochna, patra, lekh, report aur bhashan ke prarup.
Remember: a notice is brief and impersonal; a report is in the past tense and passive.

  • The Class 12 English Core writing section tests short and long compositions in set formats
  • Notice: a short formal announcement written in a box with the heading NOTICE, the name of the issuing organisation, the date, a title, the body…
  • The limit is about 50 words
  • Use passive voice and impersonal style
Read the full explanation

The Class 12 English Core writing section tests short and long compositions in set formats. Notice: a short formal announcement written in a box with the heading NOTICE, the name of the issuing organisation, the date, a title, the body (event, date, time, venue, contact) and the writer's name and designation; the limit is about 50 words; use passive voice and impersonal style. Poster and advertisement: a catchy slogan, key details, contact information, and an eye-catching layout; classified advertisements are compact and use abbreviations. Invitation and reply: formal invitations are in the third person with an impersonal style, giving host, occasion, date, time, venue and RSVP; replies accept or decline in the same third person style; informal invitations are in the first person. Letters: formal letters have sender's address, date, receiver's address, subject line, salutation (Sir or Madam), body, and complimentary close (Yours faithfully for Sir or Madam; Yours sincerely when a name is known) and signature. Types: letter to the editor (on a social problem or public issue; the writer addresses the editor, gives a heading, states the problem with facts and suggests solutions), job application with a CV or bio-data (covering letter and resume with career objective, education, experience, skills, references), business letters (letter of enquiry, order, complaint, reply to complaint), and letters seeking information from institutions. Article: 150-200 words with a title, a byline, an introduction, a body of two to three paragraphs and a conclusion; types: descriptive, argumentative and informative. Report: a factual account of an event with a title, reporter name and place and date line; it is written in the past tense and the passive voice, in a formal style; types: event reports and newspaper reports. Speech: begin with a salutation to the audience, introduce the topic, give arguments, appeal and end with thanks; use spoken style, rhetorical questions. Debate: for or against motion. Tips: plan and revise, follow word limits, use paragraphs, avoid slang and errors, and use cohesive devices such as therefore, moreover and however. Marking: format, content, expression and accuracy.

📌

Formats

  • Each form has its own layout and style
  • Marks are given for format, content, fluency and accuracy
🧠

Letters

  • Formal letters need the sender's address, date, receiver's address, subject, salutation, body and complimentary close
🌟

Articles and reports

  • Articles have a headline, byline and structured paragraphs
  • Reports use the past tense and passive voice
