lessons.title: Grammar and Reading Comprehension
yt: class 12 english core grammar reading comprehension tenses modals determiners reported speech editing gap filling

blocks.x: The Class 12 English Core language section tests reading comprehension and grammar through gap filling, editing, omission and sentence reordering. Reading comprehension: read the passage quickly for the main idea, then closely; look for the answer in the text, infer meanings of words from context, identify tone and the writer's purpose, and write brief answers in your own words; note-making and summarising use headings, abbreviations and a title. Tenses: simple present (habits), present continuous (now), present perfect (past action with present result), simple past, past continuous, past perfect (earlier of two past actions), simple future; the sequence of tenses requires agreement between main and subordinate clauses. Subject verb agreement: a singular subject takes a singular verb; collective nouns act as singular; either or and neither nor agree with the nearer subject; each, every, one and everyone are singular; none can be either. Determiners: articles a, an, the; quantifiers some, any, much, many, few, a few, little, a little; demonstratives this, that, these, those; each, every, either, neither. Prepositions show relation of time, place and direction: in, on, at, by, with, for, since, during. Modals: can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would, must, ought to and need; they express ability, permission, possibility, obligation and advice. Reported speech: change pronouns, tenses (present becomes past), time and place words (now becomes then, today that day, tomorrow the next day, here there), and use say, tell, ask or order; questions use if or whether for yes or no questions and keep the wh word for others, with statement word order. Voice: active to passive uses the past participle of the verb with be in the right tense. Conditionals: type 1 (real: if present, will), type 2 (unreal present: if past, would), type 3 (unreal past: if had, would have). Editing: errors in tense, articles, prepositions, agreement and spelling. Omission: find the missing word. Gap filling: choose the correct word using context. Reordering: arrange words into a meaningful sentence. Linkers and connectors: and, but, so, because, although, however, therefore. Punctuation and spelling.
Deep dive: Reading
Skim for gist, scan for details, use context for vocabulary and answer in your own words.
Deep dive: Core grammar
Tenses, agreement, determiners, prepositions and modals form most of the grammar questions.
Deep dive: Transformations
Reported speech, voice and conditionals transform sentences while keeping meaning.
Hindi saransh
Vyakaran aur pathan: tense, agreement, modal, reported speech aur gap filling.
Remember: in reported speech the tense moves back and the pronouns, time and place change.

Reading comprehension: read the passage quickly for the main idea, then closely; look for the answer in the text, infer meanings of words from context, identify tone and the writer's purpose, and write brief answers in your own words; note-making and summarising use headings, abbreviations and a title. Tenses: simple present (habits), present continuous (now), present perfect (past action with present result), simple past, past continuous, past perfect (earlier of two past actions), simple future; the sequence of tenses requires agreement between main and subordinate clauses. Subject verb agreement: a singular subject takes a singular verb; collective nouns act as singular; either or and neither nor agree with the nearer subject; each, every, one and everyone are singular; none can be either. Determiners: articles a, an, the; quantifiers some, any, much, many, few, a few, little, a little; demonstratives this, that, these, those; each, every, either, neither. Prepositions show relation of time, place and direction: in, on, at, by, with, for, since, during. Modals: can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would, must, ought to and need; they express ability, permission, possibility, obligation and advice. Reported speech: change pronouns, tenses (present becomes past), time and place words (now becomes then, today that day, tomorrow the next day, here there), and use say, tell, ask or order; questions use if or whether for yes or no questions and keep the wh word for others, with statement word order. Voice: active to passive uses the past participle of the verb with be in the right tense. Conditionals: type 1 (real: if present, will), type 2 (unreal present: if past, would), type 3 (unreal past: if had, would have). Editing: errors in tense, articles, prepositions, agreement and spelling. Omission: find the missing word. Gap filling: choose the correct word using context. Reordering: arrange words into a meaningful sentence. Linkers and connectors: and, but, so, because, although, however, therefore. Punctuation and spelling.

lessons.title: Human Geography: Nature and Scope
yt: class 12 geography human geography nature scope determinism possibilism neo determinism ratzel semple vidal

blocks.x: Human geography studies the relationship between humans and the physical environment, the spatial distribution of human phenomena, and the way people and places interact. Definitions: Friedrich Ratzel defined it as the synthesis of physical geography and the study of human societies; Ellen C. Semple defined it as the study of the changing relationship between the unresting man and the unstable earth; Paul Vidal de la Blache defined it as the study of the relationship between the earth and the human beings it supports, a conception resulting from a more synthetic knowledge of the earth and its inhabitants. Nature: it studies the interrelationship between physical environment and socio-cultural environment made by humans. Naturalisation of humans: early humans were slaves of nature and adapted to it, worshipping its forces. Humanisation of nature: with technology, humans modified nature and created the cultural landscape. Environmental determinism (Ratzel and the Greek scholars) held that nature controls human activities; possibilism (Vidal de la Blache, Febvre) held that nature gives possibilities and humans choose among them; neo-determinism or stop-and-go determinism (Griffith Taylor) is a middle path: neither red lights (absolute determinism) nor green lights (absolute possibilism), but humans should follow the signals of nature and proceed with caution. Time-space compression has reduced distances through transport and communication technology. Fields and sub-fields: social geography, urban geography, political geography, population geography, settlement geography, economic geography (resource, agriculture, industry, marketing, tourism, international trade), historical geography, cultural geography, behavioural geography, medical geography and gender geography. Approaches in the growth of the discipline: early exploration and description, regional analysis, areal differentiation, spatial organisation (quantitative revolution, 1950s-60s), humanistic, radical and behavioural approaches (1970s), and post-modernism in the 1990s. Human geography is related to other social sciences such as sociology, economics, anthropology and political science. Scope: study of population, resources, development, settlements, activities and their location.
Deep dive: Definitions
Ratzel, Semple and Vidal de la Blache each stressed the relationship between humans and the earth.
Deep dive: Determinism and possibilism
Nature controls (determinism) versus humans choose (possibilism); neo-determinism is the middle path.
Deep dive: Fields
Human geography has many sub-fields, from social and urban to medical and behavioural geography.

lessons.title: The World Population
yt: class 12 geography world population distribution density growth demographic transition composition

blocks.x: The study of population is the study of the number, distribution, growth and composition of people. Distribution: the world population is unevenly distributed; about 90 percent lives on about 10 percent of the land. Density of population is the number of persons per square kilometre. Arithmetic density is total population divided by total area; physiological density is population divided by net cultivable area; agricultural density is the number of agricultural workers per unit of cultivated land. Factors influencing distribution: (1) geographical factors: availability of water, landforms (plains attract settlement, mountains do not), climate (extreme climates repel), and soils (fertile alluvial soils attract); (2) economic factors: minerals, urbanisation and industrialisation; (3) social and cultural factors: religious or cultural importance, and political factors such as government policy. Population growth is the change in the number of people over time; growth rate is expressed as a percentage. Natural increase = births - deaths; actual growth = births - deaths + in-migration - out-migration. Positive growth occurs when births exceed deaths or when people migrate in; negative growth when deaths exceed births or people migrate out. Components of change: fertility (birth rate), mortality (death rate) and migration. Doubling time is the number of years a population takes to double. Trends: the world population was about 1 billion around 1804 and has risen rapidly since the Industrial Revolution and advances in medicine. Read the full explanation

The study of population is the study of the number, distribution, growth and composition of people. Distribution: the world population is unevenly distributed; about 90 percent lives on about 10 percent of the land. Density of population is the number of persons per square kilometre. Arithmetic density is total population divided by total area; physiological density is population divided by net cultivable area; agricultural density is the number of agricultural workers per unit of cultivated land. Factors influencing distribution: (1) geographical factors: availability of water, landforms (plains attract settlement, mountains do not), climate (extreme climates repel), and soils (fertile alluvial soils attract); (2) economic factors: minerals, urbanisation and industrialisation; (3) social and cultural factors: religious or cultural importance, and political factors such as government policy. Population growth is the change in the number of people over time; growth rate is expressed as a percentage. Natural increase = births - deaths; actual growth = births - deaths + in-migration - out-migration. Positive growth occurs when births exceed deaths or when people migrate in; negative growth when deaths exceed births or people migrate out. Components of change: fertility (birth rate), mortality (death rate) and migration. Doubling time is the number of years a population takes to double. Trends: the world population was about 1 billion around 1804 and has risen rapidly since the Industrial Revolution and advances in medicine. Demographic transition theory describes three stages: Stage 1 high fertility and high mortality, slow growth; Stage 2 high fertility with declining mortality, rapid growth; Stage 3 low fertility and low mortality, slow or zero growth. Population control: family planning, awareness, education and health care. Population composition covers age-sex structure (shown by age-sex pyramids), sex ratio, literacy, occupational structure, and rural urban composition. Sex ratio is the number of females per 1000 males. Age groups: children (0-14), working age (15-59) and aged (60+). Dependency ratio. Malthus argued that population grows faster than food supply.

lessons.title: Human Development
yt: class 12 geography human development HDI mahbub ul haq amartya sen equity sustainability productivity empowerment

blocks.x: Human development is the process of enlarging people's choices and building human capabilities. The concept was introduced by Dr Mahbub ul Haq (Pakistani economist) and Amartya Sen (Indian economist, Nobel laureate), with the UNDP publishing its first Human Development Report in 1990. Growth versus development: growth is a quantitative change in output (such as GDP) while development is a qualitative change that improves well-being. Four pillars of human development: equity (equal access to opportunities), sustainability (continuity of opportunities for present and future generations), productivity (human labour productivity through investment in people) and empowerment (power to make choices). Approaches: income approach (human development is linked to income), welfare approach (humans as beneficiaries), basic needs approach (health, education, food, water, shelter) and capability approach (Amartya Sen: building capabilities in health, education and access to resources). Human Development Index (HDI): a composite index with three dimensions: a long and healthy life (life expectancy at birth), knowledge (mean years of schooling and expected years of schooling) and a decent standard of living (gross national income per capita in PPP dollars); each dimension ranges between 0 and 1. HDI is classified as very high, high, medium and low. Other indices: Human Poverty Index (HPI), Gender Development Index (GDI), Gender Inequality Index (GII), and Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI). Countries with high HDI are Norway, Switzerland and others; low HDI countries are often in Sub-Saharan Africa. International comparisons: size of the country does not decide HDI; small countries such as Sri Lanka and Costa Rica have done well in human development relative to income; Kerala has high human development in India. Indicators of human development: literacy, life expectancy, infant mortality, access to safe drinking water, and nutrition. Factors that influence: political commitment, governance, public spending on health and education, and equity. HDI is a relative measure. The 2010 Human Development Report introduced inequality-adjusted HDI.
Deep dive: Concept
Human development enlarges choices and capabilities; Mahbub ul Haq and Amartya Sen developed it.
Deep dive: Pillars
Equity, sustainability, productivity and empowerment are the four pillars.
Deep dive: HDI
HDI combines life expectancy, schooling and income per capita into a single index between 0 and 1.

Read the full explanation

Human development is the process of enlarging people's choices and building human capabilities. The concept was introduced by Dr Mahbub ul Haq (Pakistani economist) and Amartya Sen (Indian economist, Nobel laureate), with the UNDP publishing its first Human Development Report in 1990. Growth versus development: growth is a quantitative change in output (such as GDP) while development is a qualitative change that improves well-being. Four pillars of human development: equity (equal access to opportunities), sustainability (continuity of opportunities for present and future generations), productivity (human labour productivity through investment in people) and empowerment (power to make choices). Approaches: income approach (human development is linked to income), welfare approach (humans as beneficiaries), basic needs approach (health, education, food, water, shelter) and capability approach (Amartya Sen: building capabilities in health, education and access to resources). Human Development Index (HDI): a composite index with three dimensions: a long and healthy life (life expectancy at birth), knowledge (mean years of schooling and expected years of schooling) and a decent standard of living (gross national income per capita in PPP dollars); each dimension ranges between 0 and 1. HDI is classified as very high, high, medium and low. Other indices: Human Poverty Index (HPI), Gender Development Index (GDI), Gender Inequality Index (GII), and Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI). Countries with high HDI are Norway, Switzerland and others; low HDI countries are often in Sub-Saharan Africa. International comparisons: size of the country does not decide HDI; small countries such as Sri Lanka and Costa Rica have done well in human development relative to income; Kerala has high human development in India. Indicators of human development: literacy, life expectancy, infant mortality, access to safe drinking water, and nutrition. Factors that influence: political commitment, governance, public spending on health and education, and equity. HDI is a relative measure. The 2010 Human Development Report introduced inequality-adjusted HDI.

lessons.title: Primary Activities
yt: class 12 geography primary activities hunting gathering pastoralism agriculture mining plantation shifting cultivation

blocks.x: Primary activities are those that depend on the use of earth's resources such as land, water, vegetation, building materials and minerals: hunting, gathering, pastoral activities, fishing, forestry, mining and quarrying, and agriculture. People who work in them are called red-collar workers because of their outdoor, rural work. Hunting and gathering: the oldest economic activity. Gathering is practised in the cold high latitudes (northern Canada, northern Eurasia, southern Chile) and in low latitudes (Amazon basin, tropical Africa, northern Australia and the interior of Southeast Asia); it requires little capital and low technology and gives low yield per person. Pastoralism: nomadic herding is the rearing of animals by moving from place to place for fodder, e.g. in Sahara, Central Asia, Tibet, and the Arctic; transhumance is seasonal movement between pastures at different altitudes or latitudes, e.g. the Gujjars and Bakarwals of the Himalayas; commercial livestock rearing is ranching in the temperate grasslands. Agriculture: subsistence agriculture (crops are mostly consumed by the farmer's family) includes primitive subsistence farming (shifting cultivation or slash and burn, known as jhumming in northeast India, milpa in Central America, ladang in Malaysia and Indonesia, roça in Brazil; and nomadic herding), and intensive subsistence agriculture (wet rice cultivation dominant in monsoon Asia, and dry crop cultivation where rainfall is low). Commercial agriculture: extensive commercial grain cultivation (wheat in the prairies of North America, Pampas of Argentina, Steppes of Eurasia), mixed farming (Europe), dairy farming (Denmark, New Zealand), Mediterranean agriculture (citrus fruits, grapes, olives), market gardening and horticulture (Netherlands), plantation agriculture (tea, coffee, cocoa, rubber, sugarcane, bananas) and co-operative and collective farming. Mining: factors affecting mining: size and grade of deposit, accessibility, and technology and capital; methods are surface or open-cast mining (cheap, quick) and underground or shaft mining (for deep deposits, more risky). Fishing: major fishing grounds are the continental shelf areas (Grand Banks off Newfoundland, North Sea and the Northwest Pacific); Japan, China and Peru are leading countries. Forestry. Red collar workers.
Deep dive: Hunting and herding
Gathering and nomadic herding are low technology activities; transhumance is seasonal vertical movement.
Deep dive: Agriculture
Subsistence farming includes shifting cultivation and intensive farming; commercial farming includes plantations, grain and dairy farming.
Deep dive: Mining and fishing
Open-cast and shaft mining depend on deposit depth; the continental shelf has rich fishing grounds.

Read the full explanation

Primary activities are those that depend on the use of earth's resources such as land, water, vegetation, building materials and minerals: hunting, gathering, pastoral activities, fishing, forestry, mining and quarrying, and agriculture. People who work in them are called red-collar workers because of their outdoor, rural work. Hunting and gathering: the oldest economic activity. Gathering is practised in the cold high latitudes (northern Canada, northern Eurasia, southern Chile) and in low latitudes (Amazon basin, tropical Africa, northern Australia and the interior of Southeast Asia); it requires little capital and low technology and gives low yield per person. Pastoralism: nomadic herding is the rearing of animals by moving from place to place for fodder, e.g. in Sahara, Central Asia, Tibet, and the Arctic; transhumance is seasonal movement between pastures at different altitudes or latitudes, e.g. the Gujjars and Bakarwals of the Himalayas; commercial livestock rearing is ranching in the temperate grasslands. Agriculture: subsistence agriculture (crops are mostly consumed by the farmer's family) includes primitive subsistence farming (shifting cultivation or slash and burn, known as jhumming in northeast India, milpa in Central America, ladang in Malaysia and Indonesia, roça in Brazil; and nomadic herding), and intensive subsistence agriculture (wet rice cultivation dominant in monsoon Asia, and dry crop cultivation where rainfall is low). Commercial agriculture: extensive commercial grain cultivation (wheat in the prairies of North America, Pampas of Argentina, Steppes of Eurasia), mixed farming (Europe), dairy farming (Denmark, New Zealand), Mediterranean agriculture (citrus fruits, grapes, olives), market gardening and horticulture (Netherlands), plantation agriculture (tea, coffee, cocoa, rubber, sugarcane, bananas) and co-operative and collective farming. Mining: factors affecting mining: size and grade of deposit, accessibility, and technology and capital; methods are surface or open-cast mining (cheap, quick) and underground or shaft mining (for deep deposits, more risky). Fishing: major fishing grounds are the continental shelf areas (Grand Banks off Newfoundland, North Sea and the Northwest Pacific); Japan, China and Peru are leading countries. Forestry. Red collar workers.

📌

Hunting and herding

  • Gathering and nomadic herding are low technology activities
  • Transhumance is seasonal vertical movement
🧠

Agriculture

  • Subsistence farming includes shifting cultivation and intensive farming
  • Commercial farming includes plantations, grain and dairy farming
🌟

Mining and fishing

  • Open-cast and shaft mining depend on deposit depth
  • The continental shelf has rich fishing grounds

lessons.title: Secondary Activities
yt: class 12 geography secondary activities manufacturing industries location weber classification high technology

blocks.x: Secondary activities change raw materials into more valuable products: manufacturing, processing and construction. People who work in them are called blue-collar workers. Manufacturing is the production of goods through processing of raw materials; it is the backbone of economic development and reduces dependence on agriculture. Factors affecting location: market, raw materials, labour supply, sources of energy, transport and communication, government policy, agglomeration economies and cost of land. Weber's least cost theory: industries are located where the total cost of production is minimum, considering transport cost, labour cost and agglomeration. Classification by size: household or cottage industries, small scale industries, large scale industries. By inputs or raw materials: agro-based (cotton, woollen, jute, silk, rubber, sugar, tea, coffee, edible oil), mineral-based (iron and steel, cement, aluminium, machine tools, petrochemicals), chemical-based (petrochemical, salt, fertilisers, plastic), forest-based (pulp and paper, furniture, lac), and animal-based (leather, woollen). By output: basic or key industries (iron and steel) and consumer industries (sugar, soap). By ownership: public sector (e.g. SAIL, BHEL), private sector (TISCO, Reliance), joint sector (Oil India), cooperative sector. Footloose industries are not tied to raw materials or markets, e.g. IT industry and diamond cutting. Industrial regions: Ruhr in Germany, Great Lakes in the USA, Mumbai-Pune and Hugli in India. High technology industry is characterised by research and development, a highly skilled workforce, and automation; examples are Silicon Valley (California) and Silicon Plateau (Bengaluru). Technopolis. Industrial pollution and conservation. Manufacturing in world regions: Europe, North America, East Asia. Cotton textile, iron and steel, and fertilisers are major examples. Agglomeration economies are benefits of locating near other firms. Industrial landscape and urbanisation.
Deep dive: Location
Raw materials, market, labour, power and transport decide where industries locate; Weber stressed least cost.
Deep dive: Classification
Industries are classified by size, raw material, output and ownership.
Deep dive: High technology
High-tech and footloose industries depend on skills and research rather than raw materials.

🔑

Big idea

  • Secondary activities change raw materials into more valuable products: manufacturing, processing and construction
  • People who work in them are called blue-collar workers
  • Manufacturing is the production of goods through processing of raw materials
  • It is the backbone of economic development and reduces dependence on agriculture
Read the full explanation

Secondary activities change raw materials into more valuable products: manufacturing, processing and construction. People who work in them are called blue-collar workers. Manufacturing is the production of goods through processing of raw materials; it is the backbone of economic development and reduces dependence on agriculture. Factors affecting location: market, raw materials, labour supply, sources of energy, transport and communication, government policy, agglomeration economies and cost of land. Weber's least cost theory: industries are located where the total cost of production is minimum, considering transport cost, labour cost and agglomeration. Classification by size: household or cottage industries, small scale industries, large scale industries. By inputs or raw materials: agro-based (cotton, woollen, jute, silk, rubber, sugar, tea, coffee, edible oil), mineral-based (iron and steel, cement, aluminium, machine tools, petrochemicals), chemical-based (petrochemical, salt, fertilisers, plastic), forest-based (pulp and paper, furniture, lac), and animal-based (leather, woollen). By output: basic or key industries (iron and steel) and consumer industries (sugar, soap). By ownership: public sector (e.g. SAIL, BHEL), private sector (TISCO, Reliance), joint sector (Oil India), cooperative sector. Footloose industries are not tied to raw materials or markets, e.g. IT industry and diamond cutting. Industrial regions: Ruhr in Germany, Great Lakes in the USA, Mumbai-Pune and Hugli in India. High technology industry is characterised by research and development, a highly skilled workforce, and automation; examples are Silicon Valley (California) and Silicon Plateau (Bengaluru). Technopolis. Industrial pollution and conservation. Manufacturing in world regions: Europe, North America, East Asia. Cotton textile, iron and steel, and fertilisers are major examples. Agglomeration economies are benefits of locating near other firms. Industrial landscape and urbanisation.

📌

Location

  • Raw materials, market, labour, power and transport decide where industries locate
  • Weber stressed least cost
🧠

Classification

  • Industries are classified by size, raw material, output and ownership
🌟

High technology

  • High-tech and footloose industries depend on skills and research rather than raw materials

lessons.title: Tertiary and Quaternary Activities
yt: class 12 geography tertiary quaternary quinary activities services trade tourism outsourcing

blocks.x: Tertiary activities involve the sale and exchange of goods and services: trade, transport, communication and services. People engaged in them are called white-collar workers. Services include professional and personal services such as teaching, medicine, law, banking and entertainment, and they are provided by people who have skills. Types: retail trading (sale of goods to the consumer), wholesale trading (sale in bulk to retailers), transport, communication, professional services (doctors, lawyers, teachers), personal services (barbers, domestic helpers), and tourism. Trade and commerce: trading centres include rural marketing centres, urban marketing centres, and periodic markets (weekly haats); retail trading is carried out in shops, supermarkets and malls, and door to door; wholesale trading by merchants. Tourism is a major service; tourist regions: the Mediterranean, the Alps, the Himalayas, coastal Southeast Asia; factors: climate, landscape, accessibility, heritage and facilities; medical tourism is growing in India. Quaternary activities are specialised tertiary activities involving knowledge: information gathering, research and development, and data processing; they are connected to outsourcing, where work is contracted out to another firm or country (BPO, KPO), in places with a lower cost of labour such as India. The digital divide arises because of unequal access to computers and the Internet. Quinary activities are the highest level of decision making: top executives, government officials, senior scientists, financial and legal consultants, and intellectual services. They are seen as a separate class of the service sector. Information and communication technology (ICT) and the growth of the service economy. Employment in the tertiary sector increases with economic development. Data entry and call centres in India are examples of outsourcing. Examples: Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Gurgaon, Noida as IT hubs. Medical and legal services.
Deep dive: Tertiary
Trade, transport, communication and services are the activities that exchange goods and provide skills.
Deep dive: Quaternary
Knowledge-based work such as research, data processing and outsourcing forms the quaternary sector.
Deep dive: Quinary
The highest-level decision makers and thinkers form the quinary sector.

Visual lesson

Tertiary and Quaternary Activities

Tertiary activities involve the sale and exchange of goods and services: trade, transport, communication and services

1Big idea›2Tertiary›3Quaternary›4Quinary
🔑

Big idea

  • Tertiary activities involve the sale and exchange of goods and services: trade, transport, communication and services
  • People engaged in them are called white-collar workers
  • Services include professional and personal services such as teaching, medicine, law, banking and entertainment, and they are provided by people who…
  • Types: retail trading (sale of goods to the consumer), wholesale trading (sale in bulk to retailers), transport, communication, professional services…
Read the full explanation

Tertiary activities involve the sale and exchange of goods and services: trade, transport, communication and services. People engaged in them are called white-collar workers. Services include professional and personal services such as teaching, medicine, law, banking and entertainment, and they are provided by people who have skills. Types: retail trading (sale of goods to the consumer), wholesale trading (sale in bulk to retailers), transport, communication, professional services (doctors, lawyers, teachers), personal services (barbers, domestic helpers), and tourism. Trade and commerce: trading centres include rural marketing centres, urban marketing centres, and periodic markets (weekly haats); retail trading is carried out in shops, supermarkets and malls, and door to door; wholesale trading by merchants. Tourism is a major service; tourist regions: the Mediterranean, the Alps, the Himalayas, coastal Southeast Asia; factors: climate, landscape, accessibility, heritage and facilities; medical tourism is growing in India. Quaternary activities are specialised tertiary activities involving knowledge: information gathering, research and development, and data processing; they are connected to outsourcing, where work is contracted out to another firm or country (BPO, KPO), in places with a lower cost of labour such as India. The digital divide arises because of unequal access to computers and the Internet. Quinary activities are the highest level of decision making: top executives, government officials, senior scientists, financial and legal consultants, and intellectual services. They are seen as a separate class of the service sector. Information and communication technology (ICT) and the growth of the service economy. Employment in the tertiary sector increases with economic development. Data entry and call centres in India are examples of outsourcing. Examples: Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Gurgaon, Noida as IT hubs. Medical and legal services.

📌

Tertiary

  • Trade, transport, communication and services are the activities that exchange goods and provide skills
🧠

Quaternary

  • Knowledge-based work such as research, data processing and outsourcing forms the quaternary sector
🌟

Quinary

  • The highest-level decision makers and thinkers form the quinary sector
🧮

yt: class 12 geography transport communication roads railways waterways pipelines suez panama trans siberian internet

blocks.x: Transport is the movement of people, goods and services from one place to another; communication is the transfer of information. Modes of transport: land (roads, railways, pipelines), water (inland waterways, sea routes and oceanic routes) and air. Roads are the most used for short and medium distances: metalled and unmetalled; the density of roads varies; the major national road networks are in North America and Europe; the Trans-Canada Highway (the longest national highway, 7821 km), the Pan-American Highway (connects Alaska to Chile) and the Trans-Siberian highway. Railways are suited for long distances and bulk goods: the Trans-Siberian Railway (Moscow to Vladivostok, about 9,332 km, the longest double-tracked electrified railway), the Canadian Pacific Railway (Vancouver to Montreal, 1886), the Union Pacific railway, and the Trans-Australian railway. Pipelines carry liquids and gases such as crude oil, natural gas and water; they have low running cost; the world has pipelines connecting oil fields to refineries and ports. Water transport has the cheapest cost for heavy goods: inland waterways: the Great Lakes-St Lawrence Seaway, the Rhine and Danube waterways, the Mississippi, and the Ganga in India. Sea routes: the Suez Canal (opened 1869 by Ferdinand de Lesseps, linking the Mediterranean Sea at Port Said with the Red Sea at Suez; shortens the Europe-Asia route) and the Panama Canal (opened 1914, linking the Atlantic Ocean with the Pacific Ocean; saves distance between the east and west coast of USA). Major ocean routes: the North Atlantic route (busiest), Mediterranean-Indian Ocean route, Cape of Good Hope route, South Atlantic route and North Pacific route. Air transport is the fastest and most costly; Europe, North America and Asia have dense air traffic; the busiest air route is the North Atlantic; global hubs include London, New York, Singapore. Communication: from early couriers and telegraph to telephone, radio, television, satellites, mobile phones and the Internet; satellite communication allows global links; the Internet and e-commerce have revolutionised communication and trade. Cyberspace. Time space convergence. Gateways and ports.
Deep dive: Modes
Roads, railways, pipelines, waterways and airways each suit different goods and distances.
Deep dive: Canals
The Suez and Panama canals shortened sea routes dramatically.
Deep dive: Communication
Satellites, mobile phones and the Internet connect the world instantly and reshape trade.

Parivahan aur sanchar: sadak, rel, jal, vayu, pipeline, Suez aur Panama nahar aur internet.
Remember: Suez links the Mediterranean and Red Sea; Panama links the Atlantic and Pacific.

lessons.title: Human Settlements
yt: class 12 geography human settlements rural urban patterns functional classification megacity conurbation

blocks.x: A human settlement is a cluster of dwellings of any type or size where people live; it may be permanent or temporary. Settlements are classified as rural or urban on the basis of size, occupation and functions: rural settlements are small and depend largely on primary activities like agriculture; urban settlements are larger and have secondary and tertiary activities. Rural-urban differences also include density and way of life. Patterns of rural settlements: compact or nucleated (houses built close together, e.g. in fertile plains), dispersed or isolated (scattered houses in hilly or forest areas), and sub-types by shape: linear (along a road, railway or river), rectangular, circular, star-like (roads converging), T-shaped, Y-shaped, cross-shaped, double village. Factors: water supply, terrain, climate, defence, culture. Rural settlements have problems of inadequate infrastructure, poor sanitation and water. Urban settlements are classified by size: town (a small urban settlement), city (a larger urban centre of at least one lakh people in Indian usage), million city (one million), conurbation (a continuous urban area formed by the merging of towns and cities, a term coined by Patrick Geddes), megalopolis (a super metropolitan region, term used by Jean Gottman for the northeastern urban region of the USA), and megacity (over 10 million). Functional classification of towns: administrative (capital cities like Delhi, Washington D.C., Canberra), trading and commercial centres, industrial (Pittsburgh, Jamshedpur), mining (Broken Hill, Dhanbad), military or garrison (cantonment towns), cultural or religious (Varanasi, Jerusalem, Mecca), residential, transport hubs (ports like Rotterdam), recreational and tourist (Miami, Shimla). Urban pattern and structure; urbanisation is the rise of the share of population living in towns; world urban population is growing and exceeding rural; problems: overcrowding, slums, pollution, traffic and shortage of water; solutions include planning, smart growth. Rural-urban continuum and rurban areas. Primate city. Satellite towns. The first city with a million people was London around 1800. Cities such as Tokyo and Delhi are among the most populous.
Deep dive: Rural patterns
Compact, dispersed, linear, rectangular, star-like and other patterns arise from site and cultural factors.
Deep dive: Urban size
Towns, cities, million cities, conurbations, megalopolises and megacities rank settlements by size.
Deep dive: Functions
Towns may be administrative, industrial, mining, cultural, transport or tourist centres.
Hindi saransh
Manav bastiyan: gramin aur nagariya bastiyon ke prakar, pratiman aur karyatmak vargikaran.
Remember: megacity means over 10 million; conurbation was coined by Patrick Geddes.

Visual lesson

Human Settlements

A human settlement is a cluster of dwellings of any type or size where people live

Megacity10 million
🔑

Big idea

  • A human settlement is a cluster of dwellings of any type or size where people live
  • It may be permanent or temporary
  • Settlements are classified as rural or urban on the basis of size, occupation and functions: rural settlements are small and depend largely on…
  • Urban settlements are larger and have secondary and tertiary activities
Read the full explanation

A human settlement is a cluster of dwellings of any type or size where people live; it may be permanent or temporary. Settlements are classified as rural or urban on the basis of size, occupation and functions: rural settlements are small and depend largely on primary activities like agriculture; urban settlements are larger and have secondary and tertiary activities. Rural-urban differences also include density and way of life. Patterns of rural settlements: compact or nucleated (houses built close together, e.g. in fertile plains), dispersed or isolated (scattered houses in hilly or forest areas), and sub-types by shape: linear (along a road, railway or river), rectangular, circular, star-like (roads converging), T-shaped, Y-shaped, cross-shaped, double village. Factors: water supply, terrain, climate, defence, culture. Rural settlements have problems of inadequate infrastructure, poor sanitation and water. Urban settlements are classified by size: town (a small urban settlement), city (a larger urban centre of at least one lakh people in Indian usage), million city (one million), conurbation (a continuous urban area formed by the merging of towns and cities, a term coined by Patrick Geddes), megalopolis (a super metropolitan region, term used by Jean Gottman for the northeastern urban region of the USA), and megacity (over 10 million). Functional classification of towns: administrative (capital cities like Delhi, Washington D.C., Canberra), trading and commercial centres, industrial (Pittsburgh, Jamshedpur), mining (Broken Hill, Dhanbad), military or garrison (cantonment towns), cultural or religious (Varanasi, Jerusalem, Mecca), residential, transport hubs (ports like Rotterdam), recreational and tourist (Miami, Shimla). Urban pattern and structure; urbanisation is the rise of the share of population living in towns; world urban population is growing and exceeding rural; problems: overcrowding, slums, pollution, traffic and shortage of water; solutions include planning, smart growth. Rural-urban continuum and rurban areas. Primate city. Satellite towns. The first city with a million people was London around 1800. Cities such as Tokyo and Delhi are among the most populous.

📌

Rural patterns

  • Compact, dispersed, linear, rectangular, star-like and other patterns arise from site and cultural factors
🧠

Urban size

  • Towns, cities, million cities, conurbations, megalopolises and megacities rank settlements by size
🌟

Functions

  • Towns may be administrative, industrial, mining, cultural, transport or tourist centres

lessons.title: India: Population and Migration
yt: class 12 geography india population census 2011 density sex ratio literacy migration push pull

blocks.x: According to Census 2011, the population of India was 1,210.9 million (about 17.5 percent of the world population), with a density of 382 persons per sq km. Uttar Pradesh is the most populous state; Sikkim and Lakshadweep have the smallest populations among states and UTs; Bihar has the highest density among states (1106 per sq km) while Arunachal Pradesh has the lowest (17); among UTs, NCT of Delhi has the highest density. The decadal growth rate during 2001-2011 was 17.7 percent (slowest since 1951-61). Growth rate was highest in Dadra and Nagar Haveli among UTs and Meghalaya among states; Kerala and Nagaland recorded low growth. Sex ratio is the number of females per 1000 males: India's sex ratio in 2011 was 943; Kerala had the highest (1084) and Haryana the lowest among states (879); Daman and Diu had the lowest among UTs. Child sex ratio (0-6 years) was 919. Literacy: 74.04 percent in 2011 (male 82.14, female 65.46); Kerala had the highest literacy (93.91 percent) and Bihar the lowest (63.82 percent). Age composition: children 0-14, working age 15-59, aged 60 and above; India has a young population with a large working age share. Rural-urban composition: about 68.8 percent rural and 31.2 percent urban in 2011. Occupational structure: primary (agriculture and mining), secondary and tertiary; a high share depends on agriculture. Adolescents (10-19 years) form about 21 percent. Population problems: high birth rate, poverty, low literacy. Population policy: Family Planning started in 1952; the National Population Policy 2000 aims to bring down the total fertility rate to replacement level and achieve stable population; Adolescents as targets. Migration is the movement of people from one place to another. Types: internal (within the country) and international (outside); interstate and intrastate. Streams: rural-rural (mostly women migrate after marriage), rural-urban, urban-urban, urban-rural. Causes: push factors (poverty, unemployment, natural disasters, poor living conditions) and pull factors (better employment, education, health and services). Consequences: economic (remittances), demographic (age and sex selectivity), social (cultural change, integration) and environmental (slums, pressure on cities, depletion of resources). Remittances from abroad are a big source of foreign exchange.
Deep dive: Census 2011
Population of 1210.9 million, density 382, sex ratio 943, literacy 74.04 percent.
Deep dive: Composition
Young age structure, mostly rural, with high dependence on agriculture.
Deep dive: Migration
Push and pull factors drive rural-rural, rural-urban and other streams, with economic and social consequences.

Big idea

  • According to Census 2011, the population of India was 1,210.9 million (about 17.5 percent of the world population), with a density of 382 persons per…
  • Uttar Pradesh is the most populous state
  • Sikkim and Lakshadweep have the smallest populations among states and UTs

Read the full explanation

According to Census 2011, the population of India was 1,210.9 million (about 17.5 percent of the world population), with a density of 382 persons per sq km. Uttar Pradesh is the most populous state; Sikkim and Lakshadweep have the smallest populations among states and UTs; Bihar has the highest density among states (1106 per sq km) while Arunachal Pradesh has the lowest (17); among UTs, NCT of Delhi has the highest density. The decadal growth rate during 2001-2011 was 17.7 percent (slowest since 1951-61). Growth rate was highest in Dadra and Nagar Haveli among UTs and Meghalaya among states; Kerala and Nagaland recorded low growth. Sex ratio is the number of females per 1000 males: India's sex ratio in 2011 was 943; Kerala had the highest (1084) and Haryana the lowest among states (879); Daman and Diu had the lowest among UTs. Child sex ratio (0-6 years) was 919. Literacy: 74.04 percent in 2011 (male 82.14, female 65.46); Kerala had the highest literacy (93.91 percent) and Bihar the lowest (63.82 percent). Age composition: children 0-14, working age 15-59, aged 60 and above; India has a young population with a large working age share. Rural-urban composition: about 68.8 percent rural and 31.2 percent urban in 2011. Occupational structure: primary (agriculture and mining), secondary and tertiary; a high share depends on agriculture. Adolescents (10-19 years) form about 21 percent. Population problems: high birth rate, poverty, low literacy. Population policy: Family Planning started in 1952; the National Population Policy 2000 aims to bring down the total fertility rate to replacement level and achieve stable population; Adolescents as targets. Migration is the movement of people from one place to another. Types: internal (within the country) and international (outside); interstate and intrastate. Streams: rural-rural (mostly women migrate after marriage), rural-urban, urban-urban, urban-rural. Causes: push factors (poverty, unemployment, natural disasters, poor living conditions) and pull factors (better employment, education, health and services). Consequences: economic (remittances), demographic (age and sex selectivity), social (cultural change, integration) and environmental (slums, pressure on cities, depletion of resources). Remittances from abroad are a big source of foreign exchange.

📌

🧠

  • Young age structure, mostly rural, with high dependence on agriculture

lessons.title: India: Human Settlements
yt: class 12 geography india human settlements rural clustered dispersed urban towns metropolitan functional classification

blocks.x: In India, settlements are classified as rural or urban. Rural settlements are found in villages. Types of rural settlements: clustered settlements (compact, closely built houses, in the fertile plains of north India, Ganga plain and the fertile alluvial tracts), semi-clustered settlements (partly clustered, found in Gujarat plains and parts of Rajasthan), hamleted settlements (the settlement is divided into several units physically separated but with a common name, found in Ganga plain, Chhattisgarh and lower valleys of the Himalayas), and dispersed or isolated settlements (small hamlets or single houses on hill slopes, in the Himalayan, northeastern, Western Ghats and dry areas such as Rajasthan). Factors for rural settlement patterns: water availability, relief, defence and culture. Urban settlements: the Census defines urban places as all places with a municipality, corporation, cantonment board or notified town area committee (statutory towns) and all other places which satisfy these criteria: a minimum population of 5000, at least 75 percent male working population in non-agricultural pursuits and a density of at least 400 persons per sq km (census towns). Urban centres are grouped by population into six classes: Class I (1,00,000 and above), II (50,000-99,999), III (20,000-49,999), IV (10,000-19,999), V (5,000-9,999) and VI (below 5,000). A million city has over 1 million, and a megacity has more than 10 million. Evolution of towns: ancient (Varanasi, Prayag, Pataliputra, Madurai), medieval (Delhi, Hyderabad, Jaipur, Lucknow: forts and temples), modern (British: Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata as colonial ports and Chandigarh as a planned city). Functional classification: administrative towns and cities (Chandigarh, New Delhi, Bhopal), industrial towns (Mumbai, Salem, Coimbatore, Bhilai), transport cities (Kandla, Kochi, Visakhapatnam), commercial towns (Kolkata, Satna), mining towns (Raniganj, Jharia, Ankleshwar), garrison cantonment towns (Ambala, Jalandhar, Mhow, Babina), educational towns (Roorkee, Pilani, Varanasi), religious and cultural towns (Varanasi, Madurai, Puri, Amritsar, Ajmer), tourist towns (Nainital, Udhagamandalam, Mount Abu). Problems of urban settlements: overcrowding, slums, water shortage, lack of electricity, transport, sewerage, pollution and crime. Rural settlements face problems of poor infrastructure and sanitation. Population by size; The 2011 census shows 31.16 percent urban.
Deep dive: Rural types
Clustered, semi-clustered, hamleted and dispersed settlements relate to terrain and water.
Deep dive: Urban definition
Statutory towns have municipalities; census towns satisfy 5000, 75 percent non-agri male workers and 400 density.
Deep dive: Functions and problems
Towns serve administrative, industrial, transport, mining, military and religious functions and face crowding and slums.

Big idea

Read the full explanation

In India, settlements are classified as rural or urban. Rural settlements are found in villages. Types of rural settlements: clustered settlements (compact, closely built houses, in the fertile plains of north India, Ganga plain and the fertile alluvial tracts), semi-clustered settlements (partly clustered, found in Gujarat plains and parts of Rajasthan), hamleted settlements (the settlement is divided into several units physically separated but with a common name, found in Ganga plain, Chhattisgarh and lower valleys of the Himalayas), and dispersed or isolated settlements (small hamlets or single houses on hill slopes, in the Himalayan, northeastern, Western Ghats and dry areas such as Rajasthan). Factors for rural settlement patterns: water availability, relief, defence and culture. Urban settlements: the Census defines urban places as all places with a municipality, corporation, cantonment board or notified town area committee (statutory towns) and all other places which satisfy these criteria: a minimum population of 5000, at least 75 percent male working population in non-agricultural pursuits and a density of at least 400 persons per sq km (census towns). Urban centres are grouped by population into six classes: Class I (1,00,000 and above), II (50,000-99,999), III (20,000-49,999), IV (10,000-19,999), V (5,000-9,999) and VI (below 5,000). A million city has over 1 million, and a megacity has more than 10 million. Evolution of towns: ancient (Varanasi, Prayag, Pataliputra, Madurai), medieval (Delhi, Hyderabad, Jaipur, Lucknow: forts and temples), modern (British: Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata as colonial ports and Chandigarh as a planned city). Functional classification: administrative towns and cities (Chandigarh, New Delhi, Bhopal), industrial towns (Mumbai, Salem, Coimbatore, Bhilai), transport cities (Kandla, Kochi, Visakhapatnam), commercial towns (Kolkata, Satna), mining towns (Raniganj, Jharia, Ankleshwar), garrison cantonment towns (Ambala, Jalandhar, Mhow, Babina), educational towns (Roorkee, Pilani, Varanasi), religious and cultural towns (Varanasi, Madurai, Puri, Amritsar, Ajmer), tourist towns (Nainital, Udhagamandalam, Mount Abu). Problems of urban settlements: overcrowding, slums, water shortage, lack of electricity, transport, sewerage, pollution and crime. Rural settlements face problems of poor infrastructure and sanitation. Population by size; The 2011 census shows 31.16 percent urban.

  • Census towns satisfy 5000, 75 percent non-agri male workers and 400 density
🌟

  • Towns serve administrative, industrial, transport, mining, military and religious functions and face crowding and slums

blocks.x: Land is a natural resource of prime importance. India's land use categories: forests, land put to non-agricultural uses, barren and wasteland, permanent pastures and grazing land, miscellaneous tree crops, culturable wasteland, current fallow, other than current fallow and net sown area. Net sown area is about 46 percent of the reporting area; forest cover is below the 33 percent target of the National Forest Policy 1952. Common property resources (CPRs) such as community forests, pastures and village ponds are owned by the community. Land degradation is caused by deforestation, overgrazing, mining and salinisation; wastelands need reclamation. Agriculture is the main occupation of about half of the population. Cropping seasons: Kharif (June to September; rice, maize, jowar, bajra, tur, moong, urad, cotton, jute, groundnut, soyabean), Rabi (October to March; wheat, barley, peas, gram, mustard, linseed) and Zaid (summer; watermelon, cucumber, vegetables and fodder). Types of farming: primitive subsistence, intensive subsistence, commercial and plantation. Major crops: rice (staple of the east and south; needs high temperature, above 25 C, and rainfall above 100 cm; West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Andhra Pradesh lead); wheat (second most important cereal; rabi crop; cool growing season and warm ripening; 50-75 cm rainfall; Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh); millets (jowar, bajra, ragi) are coarse grains; maize; pulses (gram, tur); oilseeds (groundnut, mustard, soyabean); sugarcane (tropical crop; Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Karnataka); tea (Assam, West Bengal, Tamil Nadu, Kerala), coffee (Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu), cotton (black soil; Maharashtra, Gujarat), jute (Bengal, golden fibre) and rubber (Kerala). Green Revolution (1960s) increased yields of wheat and rice with HYV seeds, fertilisers and irrigation in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh. Problems: dependence on monsoon, small holdings, fragmentation, inadequate irrigation, soil degradation, and lack of credit. Government measures: land reforms, minimum support price, crop insurance, Kisan Credit Card and irrigation projects. Organic farming. Food security.

Nine categories describe land use; net sown area is the main agricultural area.
Deep dive: Seasons and crops
Kharif, rabi and zaid seasons sustain different crops; rice and wheat are the principal cereals.

The Green Revolution raised output but regional gaps, small holdings and degradation remain.

lessons.title: Water and Mineral Resources
yt: class 12 geography india water resources groundwater irrigation rainwater harvesting minerals iron ore coal energy

blocks.x: India has about 4 percent of the world's freshwater but 16 percent of its population. Water resources: surface water (rivers, lakes, ponds, tanks) and groundwater; the annual precipitation is about 4000 cubic km. Irrigation is needed because of uneven monsoons: sources are wells and tube wells (the main source in northern plains), canals (in plains of north India, Punjab, UP, Haryana), tanks (in the peninsular plateau, Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh). Multipurpose river valley projects: Bhakra Nangal, Hirakud, Damodar Valley, Tungabhadra. Water scarcity and quality problems; groundwater depletion in Punjab and Haryana; pollution. Conservation: rainwater harvesting, watershed management and recycling. The Indira Gandhi Canal. Minerals: ferrous (iron ore, manganese, chromite), non-ferrous (bauxite, copper, lead, zinc, gold) and non-metallic (mica, limestone, salt, potash). India has abundant iron ore in Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Karnataka; manganese in Odisha and Madhya Pradesh; bauxite in Odisha; copper in Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan; mica in Jharkhand, Andhra Pradesh and Rajasthan; limestone in cement. Energy resources: conventional: coal (Gondwana coalfields hold the bulk of the reserves; Jharia, Raniganj, Bokaro; lignite at Neyveli), petroleum (Mumbai High, Gujarat, Assam), natural gas (Krishna-Godavari basin, Mumbai High), hydroelectricity and thermal power, nuclear energy (uranium, thorium: Tarapur, Kota, Kalpakkam, Narora, Kakrapar); non-conventional: solar, wind (Tamil Nadu, Gujarat), biogas, tidal and geothermal energy (Manikaran, Puga), and biomass. Gondwana coal has about 98 percent of the reserves and 99 percent of production. Conservation of minerals: recycling, substitutes, efficient use. Energy efficiency. Mineral belts: north-eastern plateau, central, southern and western belts. Sustainable development.
Deep dive: Water
India has limited per capita water; wells, canals and tanks irrigate; rainwater harvesting and watershed management conserve it.
Deep dive: Minerals
Ferrous, non-ferrous and non-metallic minerals are concentrated in the peninsular plateau.
Deep dive: Energy
Coal, oil and gas lead; nuclear and renewable sources are growing.

Read the full explanation

India has about 4 percent of the world's freshwater but 16 percent of its population. Water resources: surface water (rivers, lakes, ponds, tanks) and groundwater; the annual precipitation is about 4000 cubic km. Irrigation is needed because of uneven monsoons: sources are wells and tube wells (the main source in northern plains), canals (in plains of north India, Punjab, UP, Haryana), tanks (in the peninsular plateau, Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh). Multipurpose river valley projects: Bhakra Nangal, Hirakud, Damodar Valley, Tungabhadra. Water scarcity and quality problems; groundwater depletion in Punjab and Haryana; pollution. Conservation: rainwater harvesting, watershed management and recycling. The Indira Gandhi Canal. Minerals: ferrous (iron ore, manganese, chromite), non-ferrous (bauxite, copper, lead, zinc, gold) and non-metallic (mica, limestone, salt, potash). India has abundant iron ore in Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Karnataka; manganese in Odisha and Madhya Pradesh; bauxite in Odisha; copper in Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan; mica in Jharkhand, Andhra Pradesh and Rajasthan; limestone in cement. Energy resources: conventional: coal (Gondwana coalfields hold the bulk of the reserves; Jharia, Raniganj, Bokaro; lignite at Neyveli), petroleum (Mumbai High, Gujarat, Assam), natural gas (Krishna-Godavari basin, Mumbai High), hydroelectricity and thermal power, nuclear energy (uranium, thorium: Tarapur, Kota, Kalpakkam, Narora, Kakrapar); non-conventional: solar, wind (Tamil Nadu, Gujarat), biogas, tidal and geothermal energy (Manikaran, Puga), and biomass. Gondwana coal has about 98 percent of the reserves and 99 percent of production. Conservation of minerals: recycling, substitutes, efficient use. Energy efficiency. Mineral belts: north-eastern plateau, central, southern and western belts. Sustainable development.

lessons.title: Manufacturing Industries
yt: class 12 geography india manufacturing industries cotton textile iron steel fertiliser cement it industrial regions

blocks.x: Manufacturing is the backbone of development: it reduces dependence on agriculture, creates jobs, earns foreign exchange and removes regional disparities. The contribution of manufacturing to GDP in India is about 17 percent (2011-12), well below the 25 percent target in the National Manufacturing Policy 2011. Location factors: raw material, labour, capital, power, market, transport and government policy. Industries are classified by raw material (agro-based, mineral-based), role (basic and consumer), capital investment (small scale: investment up to a limit), ownership (public, private, joint, cooperative) and bulk and weight of raw material and finished goods. Agro-based industries: cotton textiles (Mumbai, Ahmedabad; first mill at Fort Gloster near Kolkata in 1818, and the first successful mill at Mumbai in 1854; Mumbai was called the Cottonopolis of India; India is a large exporter of yarn), jute textiles (West Bengal, along the Hugli; the first mill in 1855 at Rishra), sugar (shifting from north India to Maharashtra and Karnataka due to higher sucrose content and a longer crushing period; cooperative mills), silk and woollen. Mineral-based industries: iron and steel (the basic industry; first successful plant at Jamshedpur by TISCO in 1907; others: IISCO at Burnpur, Bhilai, Rourkela, Durgapur, Bokaro, Visakhapatnam, Salem, Bhadravati; the plants are near raw materials, mostly Chotanagpur plateau), aluminium (bauxite; Odisha, Kerala, Uttar Pradesh), cement (limestone, silica, gypsum and coal; the first plant in Chennai in 1904), and chemical industries such as fertilisers (nitrogenous, phosphatic and potash; Green Revolution demand), petrochemicals and pharmaceuticals. Knowledge-based industries: information technology (Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Noida, Pune, Chennai), electronics and software parks. Industrial regions: Mumbai-Pune, Hugli, Bengaluru-Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, Chotanagpur, Vishakhapatnam-Guntur, Gurugram-Delhi-Meerut, Kollam-Thiruvananthapuram. Industrial pollution: air, water, noise; control measures include treating effluents, filters and recycling of water, use of cleaner fuels. Special Economic Zones (SEZs). Make in India (2014).
Deep dive: Importance
Manufacturing creates jobs, adds value and promotes growth.
Deep dive: Major industries
Cotton textiles, jute, sugar, iron and steel, fertilisers, cement and IT are key industries.
Deep dive: Regions and pollution
Clusters concentrate in industrial regions; effluent control is vital.

Read the full explanation

Manufacturing is the backbone of development: it reduces dependence on agriculture, creates jobs, earns foreign exchange and removes regional disparities. The contribution of manufacturing to GDP in India is about 17 percent (2011-12), well below the 25 percent target in the National Manufacturing Policy 2011. Location factors: raw material, labour, capital, power, market, transport and government policy. Industries are classified by raw material (agro-based, mineral-based), role (basic and consumer), capital investment (small scale: investment up to a limit), ownership (public, private, joint, cooperative) and bulk and weight of raw material and finished goods. Agro-based industries: cotton textiles (Mumbai, Ahmedabad; first mill at Fort Gloster near Kolkata in 1818, and the first successful mill at Mumbai in 1854; Mumbai was called the Cottonopolis of India; India is a large exporter of yarn), jute textiles (West Bengal, along the Hugli; the first mill in 1855 at Rishra), sugar (shifting from north India to Maharashtra and Karnataka due to higher sucrose content and a longer crushing period; cooperative mills), silk and woollen. Mineral-based industries: iron and steel (the basic industry; first successful plant at Jamshedpur by TISCO in 1907; others: IISCO at Burnpur, Bhilai, Rourkela, Durgapur, Bokaro, Visakhapatnam, Salem, Bhadravati; the plants are near raw materials, mostly Chotanagpur plateau), aluminium (bauxite; Odisha, Kerala, Uttar Pradesh), cement (limestone, silica, gypsum and coal; the first plant in Chennai in 1904), and chemical industries such as fertilisers (nitrogenous, phosphatic and potash; Green Revolution demand), petrochemicals and pharmaceuticals. Knowledge-based industries: information technology (Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Noida, Pune, Chennai), electronics and software parks. Industrial regions: Mumbai-Pune, Hugli, Bengaluru-Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, Chotanagpur, Vishakhapatnam-Guntur, Gurugram-Delhi-Meerut, Kollam-Thiruvananthapuram. Industrial pollution: air, water, noise; control measures include treating effluents, filters and recycling of water, use of cleaner fuels. Special Economic Zones (SEZs). Make in India (2014).

📌

Importance

  • Manufacturing creates jobs, adds value and promotes growth
🧠

Major industries

  • Cotton textiles, jute, sugar, iron and steel, fertilisers, cement and IT are key industries
🌟

Regions and pollution

  • Clusters concentrate in industrial regions
  • Effluent control is vital

lessons.title: Planning and Sustainable Development
yt: class 12 geography planning sustainable development target area hill area indira gandhi canal bharmaur niti aayog brundtland

blocks.x: Planning is the process of deciding how to use resources to achieve development goals. Types: sectoral planning (for sectors like agriculture, industry), and regional or spatial planning (for areas that lag behind). India began planning in 1951 through five-year plans by the Planning Commission, which was replaced by the NITI Aayog in 2015. Target area planning: concentrates on backward areas, e.g. Command Area Development, Drought Prone Area Programme (DPAP) and Hill Area Development Programme. Hill area development programme started in the Fifth Five Year Plan (1974) for 15 districts of Uttar Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh, Assam, West Bengal and Tamil Nadu; the Western Ghats Development programme (1981) and the Tribal sub-plan (1974) are also notable. Drought prone area programme covers semi-arid regions, with watershed development and afforestation. Bharmaur region of Himachal Pradesh: an example of tribal area development; Gaddis, a tribal community, live here; its Integrated Tribal Development Project started in 1974; it improved literacy and increased female literacy; roads, schools and health were developed. Sustainable development, as defined by the Brundtland Commission in Our Common Future (1987), is development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. It involves economic, social and environmental dimensions. Indira Gandhi Canal Command Area (earlier known as the Rajasthan Canal) is among the largest canal projects, with water from the Sutlej-Beas (Harike barrage) flowing to western Rajasthan; two stages; Stage I is in Ganganagar, Hanumangarh and Bikaner (northern part) and Stage II covers Bikaner, Jaisalmer, Barmer and Jodhpur; its Command Area Development includes land levelling, afforestation, shelter belts and pasture development, and cropping pattern reform; problems include waterlogging and salinity due to excess irrigation; recommended sustainability measures: proper use of water, afforestation and pasture development, eco-friendly farming and crop diversification. Concepts: economic disparities, balanced regional development.
Deep dive: Planning
Sectoral and regional planning aim to reduce disparities; target area planning focuses on backward areas.
Deep dive: Case studies
The Indira Gandhi Canal and Bharmaur show planning in a desert and in a tribal hill region.
Deep dive: Sustainability
Sustainable development meets present needs without harming future generations.

Niyojan aur satat vikas: lakshya kshetra niyojan, Indira Gandhi nahar, Bharmaur aur satat vikas ki avdharna.

Read the full explanation

Planning is the process of deciding how to use resources to achieve development goals. Types: sectoral planning (for sectors like agriculture, industry), and regional or spatial planning (for areas that lag behind). India began planning in 1951 through five-year plans by the Planning Commission, which was replaced by the NITI Aayog in 2015. Target area planning: concentrates on backward areas, e.g. Command Area Development, Drought Prone Area Programme (DPAP) and Hill Area Development Programme. Hill area development programme started in the Fifth Five Year Plan (1974) for 15 districts of Uttar Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh, Assam, West Bengal and Tamil Nadu; the Western Ghats Development programme (1981) and the Tribal sub-plan (1974) are also notable. Drought prone area programme covers semi-arid regions, with watershed development and afforestation. Bharmaur region of Himachal Pradesh: an example of tribal area development; Gaddis, a tribal community, live here; its Integrated Tribal Development Project started in 1974; it improved literacy and increased female literacy; roads, schools and health were developed. Sustainable development, as defined by the Brundtland Commission in Our Common Future (1987), is development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. It involves economic, social and environmental dimensions. Indira Gandhi Canal Command Area (earlier known as the Rajasthan Canal) is among the largest canal projects, with water from the Sutlej-Beas (Harike barrage) flowing to western Rajasthan; two stages; Stage I is in Ganganagar, Hanumangarh and Bikaner (northern part) and Stage II covers Bikaner, Jaisalmer, Barmer and Jodhpur; its Command Area Development includes land levelling, afforestation, shelter belts and pasture development, and cropping pattern reform; problems include waterlogging and salinity due to excess irrigation; recommended sustainability measures: proper use of water, afforestation and pasture development, eco-friendly farming and crop diversification. Concepts: economic disparities, balanced regional development.

📌

Planning

  • Sectoral and regional planning aim to reduce disparities
  • Target area planning focuses on backward areas
🧠

Case studies

  • The Indira Gandhi Canal and Bharmaur show planning in a desert and in a tribal hill region
🌟

Sustainability

  • Sustainable development meets present needs without harming future generations

lessons.title: India: Transport, Communication and International Trade
yt: class 12 geography india roads railways waterways airways pipelines ports communication international trade

blocks.x: India has one of the largest road networks in the world. Roads: National Highways (NHAI, established 1988), State Highways, district roads, rural roads, border roads (BRO set up 1960), and expressways. The Golden Quadrilateral Super Highway connects Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata; the North-South Corridor links Srinagar and Kanyakumari; the East-West Corridor links Silchar and Porbandar. Railways: the first train ran in 1853 between Mumbai and Thane; the Indian railways network is among the largest in the world, with 16 zones; broad gauge is 1.676 m; the Konkan Railway (1998) links Mumbai and Mangalore; Metro rail in cities. Pipelines: carry crude oil and natural gas from oil fields to refineries and ports (Naharkatiya to Barauni; Salaya to Mathura; Hazira-Vijaipur-Jagdishpur gas pipeline). Waterways: Inland National Waterways: NW-1 (Allahabad to Haldia on the Ganga-Bhagirathi-Hugli), NW-2 (Sadiya to Dhubri on the Brahmaputra) and NW-3 (West Coast Canal, Kottapuram to Kollam). Major ports: Kandla, Mumbai, Jawaharlal Nehru Port (Nhava Sheva), Marmagao, New Mangalore, Kochi, Tuticorin, Chennai, Visakhapatnam, Paradip, Kolkata (with Haldia). Airways: Airports Authority of India; Air India is the national carrier; international airports at Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata and others. Communication: postal services (the largest network), telecom (landline, mobile, broadband), radio, television, newspapers and the Internet; satellites such as INSAT help communication. International trade: India's exports include gems and jewellery, engineering goods, petroleum products, textiles, chemicals and agricultural goods; imports include petroleum, electronic goods, gold and machinery. Major trading partners: USA, China, UAE and Saudi Arabia. Trade is influenced by the shift to a liberal economy after 1991. Ports act as gateways. India has a trade deficit usually. Information technology is a major service export. Tourism. Balanced trade.
Deep dive: Roads and rails
Golden Quadrilateral and the corridors form the highway backbone; Indian Railways began in 1853.
Deep dive: Ports and waterways
Major ports handle foreign trade; National Waterways use rivers and canals.
Deep dive: Trade
Gems, engineering goods and petroleum products lead exports; crude oil leads imports.

Read the full explanation

India has one of the largest road networks in the world. Roads: National Highways (NHAI, established 1988), State Highways, district roads, rural roads, border roads (BRO set up 1960), and expressways. The Golden Quadrilateral Super Highway connects Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata; the North-South Corridor links Srinagar and Kanyakumari; the East-West Corridor links Silchar and Porbandar. Railways: the first train ran in 1853 between Mumbai and Thane; the Indian railways network is among the largest in the world, with 16 zones; broad gauge is 1.676 m; the Konkan Railway (1998) links Mumbai and Mangalore; Metro rail in cities. Pipelines: carry crude oil and natural gas from oil fields to refineries and ports (Naharkatiya to Barauni; Salaya to Mathura; Hazira-Vijaipur-Jagdishpur gas pipeline). Waterways: Inland National Waterways: NW-1 (Allahabad to Haldia on the Ganga-Bhagirathi-Hugli), NW-2 (Sadiya to Dhubri on the Brahmaputra) and NW-3 (West Coast Canal, Kottapuram to Kollam). Major ports: Kandla, Mumbai, Jawaharlal Nehru Port (Nhava Sheva), Marmagao, New Mangalore, Kochi, Tuticorin, Chennai, Visakhapatnam, Paradip, Kolkata (with Haldia). Airways: Airports Authority of India; Air India is the national carrier; international airports at Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata and others. Communication: postal services (the largest network), telecom (landline, mobile, broadband), radio, television, newspapers and the Internet; satellites such as INSAT help communication. International trade: India's exports include gems and jewellery, engineering goods, petroleum products, textiles, chemicals and agricultural goods; imports include petroleum, electronic goods, gold and machinery. Major trading partners: USA, China, UAE and Saudi Arabia. Trade is influenced by the shift to a liberal economy after 1991. Ports act as gateways. India has a trade deficit usually. Information technology is a major service export. Tourism. Balanced trade.

yt: class 12 geography environmental pollution urban waste slums land degradation delhi yamuna

blocks.x: This chapter looks at four major problems from a geographical perspective: environmental pollution, urban waste disposal, urbanisation and slums, and land degradation. Environmental pollution is the contamination of the environment by harmful substances. Types: air pollution (from vehicles, industries, burning of fuels; affects health and causes acid rain, global warming and ozone depletion), water pollution (from industrial effluents, sewage and agricultural run-off; affects rivers like the Ganga and Yamuna), soil pollution, noise pollution and solid waste. Causes include rapid urbanisation, industrialisation and population growth. Control: cleaner fuels such as CNG, emission standards, treatment plants, afforestation, public awareness. Ganga Action Plan was started in 1985 to clean the river; the Yamuna Action Plan followed. The Namami Gange programme is a more recent mission. Pollutants from industry and cities flow to rivers. Urban waste disposal: solid waste from households, commercial establishments and industries (municipal solid waste); growing amounts due to consumption; problems: unscientific disposal in open dumps, health hazards, groundwater contamination by leachate, and air pollution from burning. Solutions: segregation at source, recycling, composting, waste to energy and sanitary landfills; the three Rs reduce, reuse and recycle. Urbanisation and slums: the rapid growth of cities leads to slums, unauthorised colonies and informal settlements for the urban poor; slums are densely crowded areas with poor housing, inadequate water and sanitation, and are located near factories, railway lines and open drains. Problems of slums: health, crime, exploitation of residents, substance abuse and child labour. Government approaches: slum improvement, Jawaharlal Nehru National Urban Renewal Mission, housing for all and in-situ rehabilitation. Land degradation: deterioration of land quality due to soil erosion, waterlogging, salinisation, deforestation, overgrazing and mining; areas such as Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan face waterlogging and salinisation; wastelands need reclamation. Remedies: afforestation, check dams, contour ploughing, shelter belts, crop rotation, organic manure. Sustainable use of land. Education, awareness, and policy.
Deep dive: Pollution
Urban and industrial growth pollute air, water and soil; clean fuels and treatment plants help.
Deep dive: Waste and slums
Solid waste and slums grow with urbanisation; segregation, recycling and housing improvement are solutions.
Deep dive: Land degradation
Erosion, waterlogging and salinity degrade land; afforestation and soil conservation restore it.
Hindi saransh
Chuninda mudde: pradushan, shahri kachra, jhuggi-jhopdi aur bhoomi apardan ke bhaugolik pahlu.
Remember: reduce, reuse and recycle manage urban waste; Ganga Action Plan began in 1985.

Government approaches: slum improvement, Jawaharlal Nehru National Urban Renewal Mission, housing for all and in-situ rehabilitation. Land degradation: deterioration of land quality due to soil erosion, waterlogging, salinisation, deforestation, overgrazing and mining; areas such as Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan face waterlogging and salinisation; wastelands need reclamation. Remedies: afforestation, check dams, contour ploughing, shelter belts, crop rotation, organic manure. Sustainable use of land. Education, awareness, and policy.
