lessons.title: मुहावरे, लोकोक्तियाँ और वाक्य-शुद्धि
yt: class 12 hindi vyakaran muhavare lokoktiyan vakya shuddhi vartani

blocks.x: भाषा को प्रभावी बनाने के लिए मुहावरे और लोकोक्तियों का प्रयोग होता है। मुहावरा ऐसा वाक्यांश है जो अपने सामान्य अर्थ को छोड़कर विशेष अर्थ देता है और वाक्य में प्रयोग होने पर ही सार्थक होता है। जैसे आँखों का तारा होना का अर्थ बहुत प्रिय होना है। लोकोक्ति पूरा कथन है, जो लोक के अनुभव से बना है और स्वतंत्र वाक्य की तरह चलता है, जैसे नाच न जाने आँगन टेढ़ा। मुहावरे का रूप वाक्य में काल, वचन और लिंग के अनुसार बदलता है, जबकि लोकोक्ति प्रायः अपरिवर्तित रहती है। वाक्य-शुद्धि में वर्तनी, लिंग, वचन, कारक, काल और शब्द-क्रम की शुद्धता देखी जाती है। अशुद्ध वाक्यों के सामान्य कारण हैं: लिंग-वचन की भूल, अनावश्यक शब्द, ग़लत शब्द-क्रम और विराम-चिह्नों की चूक। शब्द-शुद्धि में अशुद्ध वर्तनी जैसे आशीर्वाद को आर्शीवाद लिखना ग़लत है। पर्यायवाची, विलोम और अनेकार्थी शब्द भी भाषा-बोध में पूछे जाते हैं। इन सबके अभ्यास से भाषा में शुद्धता और सौंदर्य दोनों आते हैं।
गहन अध्ययन: मुहावरा
मुहावरा विशेष अर्थ देने वाला वाक्यांश है और वाक्य में काल-लिंग-वचन के अनुसार बदलता है।
गहन अध्ययन: लोकोक्ति
लोकोक्ति लोक-अनुभव से उपजा पूरा कथन है और प्रायः बिना बदले प्रयुक्त होती है।
गहन अध्ययन: वाक्य-शुद्धि
लिंग, वचन, कारक, काल, वर्तनी और शब्द-क्रम की भूलें सुधारना वाक्य-शुद्धि है।
Hindi saransh
मुहावरा वाक्यांश है और लोकोक्ति पूरा कथन; दोनों का सही प्रयोग भाषा को प्रभावशाली बनाता है।
मुहावरे का प्रयोग वाक्य में करने पर काल, वचन और लिंग का ध्यान रखें।

qa.q: मुहावरा क्या है?
qa.a: मुहावरा: विशेष अर्थ देने वाला वाक्यांश।

qa.q: 'विशेष अर्थ देने वाला वाक्यांश' किसे कहते हैं?
लोकोक्ति क्या है?
qa.a: लोकोक्ति: लोक-अनुभव से बना पूरा कथन।

qa.q: 'लोक-अनुभव से बना पूरा कथन' किसे कहते हैं?
मुहावरे का रूप क्या है?
qa.a: मुहावरे का रूप: वाक्य के अनुसार बदलता है।

qa.q: 'वाक्य के अनुसार बदलता है' किसे कहते हैं?
लोकोक्ति का रूप क्या है?
qa.a: लोकोक्ति का रूप: प्रायः अपरिवर्तित रहता है।

qa.q: 'प्रायः अपरिवर्तित रहता है' किसे कहते हैं?
मुहावरे का अर्थ क्या है?
qa.a: मुहावरे का अर्थ: लाक्षणिक होता है।

qa.q: 'लाक्षणिक होता है' किसे कहते हैं?
लोकोक्ति का आधार क्या है?
qa.a: लोकोक्ति का आधार: लोक का अनुभव।

qa.q: 'लोक का अनुभव' किसे कहते हैं?
कहावत क्या है?
'लोकोक्ति का दूसरा नाम' किसे कहते हैं?
अर्थ-विस्तार क्या है?
qa.a: अर्थ-विस्तार: मुहावरे से भाषा में आता है।

qa.q: 'मुहावरे से भाषा में आता है' किसे कहते हैं?
आँखों का तारा क्या है?
qa.a: आँखों का तारा: बहुत प्रिय व्यक्ति।

qa.q: 'बहुत प्रिय व्यक्ति' किसे कहते हैं?
आसमान सिर पर उठाना क्या है?
qa.a: आसमान सिर पर उठाना: बहुत शोर मचाना।

qa.q: 'बहुत शोर मचाना' किसे कहते हैं?
हाथ मलना क्या है?
'पछताना' किसे कहते हैं?
दाँतों तले उँगली दबाना क्या है?
qa.a: दाँतों तले उँगली दबाना: आश्चर्यचकित होना।

qa.q: 'आश्चर्यचकित होना' किसे कहते हैं?
ऊँट के मुँह में जीरा क्या है?
qa.a: ऊँट के मुँह में जीरा: ज़रूरत से बहुत कम।

qa.q: 'ज़रूरत से बहुत कम' किसे कहते हैं?
नौ दो ग्यारह होना क्या है?
qa.a: नौ दो ग्यारह होना: भाग जाना।

qa.q: 'भाग जाना' किसे कहते हैं?
अँगूठा दिखाना क्या है?
'साफ़ इनकार करना' किसे कहते हैं?
आँखें खुलना क्या है?
qa.a: आँखें खुलना: सच्चाई का बोध होना।

qa.q: 'सच्चाई का बोध होना' किसे कहते हैं?
कान भरना क्या है?
'चुगली करके भड़काना' किसे कहते हैं?
पानी-पानी होना क्या है?
'लज्जित होना' किसे कहते हैं?
नाच न जाने आँगन टेढ़ा क्या है?
qa.a: नाच न जाने आँगन टेढ़ा: अपनी कमी दूसरों पर थोपना।

qa.q: 'अपनी कमी दूसरों पर थोपना' किसे कहते हैं?
अधजल गगरी छलकत जाए क्या है?
qa.a: अधजल गगरी छलकत जाए: कम ज्ञान वाला अधिक दिखावा करता है।

qa.q: 'कम ज्ञान वाला अधिक दिखावा करता है' किसे कहते हैं?
ऊँची दुकान फीका पकवान क्या है?
qa.a: ऊँची दुकान फीका पकवान: बाहरी दिखावा पर गुणवत्ता कम।

qa.q: 'बाहरी दिखावा पर गुणवत्ता कम' किसे कहते हैं?
एक अनार सौ बीमार क्या है?
qa.a: एक अनार सौ बीमार: वस्तु कम और चाहने वाले अधिक।

qa.q: 'वस्तु कम और चाहने वाले अधिक' किसे कहते हैं?
जैसी करनी वैसी भरनी क्या है?
qa.a: जैसी करनी वैसी भरनी: कर्म के अनुसार फल।

qa.q: 'कर्म के अनुसार फल' किसे कहते हैं?
न नौ मन तेल होगा न राधा नाचेगी क्या है?
qa.a: न नौ मन तेल होगा न राधा नाचेगी: असंभव शर्त रखकर टालना।

qa.q: 'असंभव शर्त रखकर टालना' किसे कहते हैं?
qa.a: न नौ मन तेल होगा न राधा नाचेगी।

qa.q: थोथा चना बाजे घना क्या है?
qa.a: थोथा चना बाजे घना: कम गुणवान अधिक शोर करता है।

qa.q: 'कम गुणवान अधिक शोर करता है' किसे कहते हैं?
दूध का जला छाछ भी फूँक-फूँककर पीता है क्या है?
qa.a: दूध का जला छाछ भी फूँक-फूँककर पीता है: एक बार धोखा खाया सावधान रहता है।

qa.q: 'एक बार धोखा खाया सावधान रहता है' किसे कहते हैं?
qa.a: दूध का जला छाछ भी फूँक-फूँककर पीता है।

qa.q: लिंग-दोष क्या है?
'पुल्लिंग-स्त्रीलिंग की भूल' किसे कहते हैं?
वचन-दोष क्या है?
'एकवचन-बहुवचन की भूल' किसे कहते हैं?
कारक-दोष क्या है?
'विभक्ति-चिह्न की भूल' किसे कहते हैं?
काल-दोष क्या है?
qa.a: काल-दोष: क्रिया के समय की भूल।

qa.q: 'क्रिया के समय की भूल' किसे कहते हैं?
वर्तनी-दोष क्या है?
'अक्षरों की त्रुटि' किसे कहते हैं?
शब्द-क्रम-दोष क्या है?
'शब्दों का ग़लत क्रम' किसे कहते हैं?
पुनरुक्ति क्या है?
'अनावश्यक दोहराव' किसे कहते हैं?
अनावश्यक शब्द क्या है?
qa.a: अनावश्यक शब्द: वाक्य को बोझिल बनाते हैं।

qa.q: 'वाक्य को बोझिल बनाते हैं' किसे कहते हैं?
विराम-चिह्न क्या है?
qa.a: विराम-चिह्न: पूर्ण विराम और अल्प विराम सहित।

qa.q: 'पूर्ण विराम और अल्प विराम सहित' किसे कहते हैं?
प्रयोग-दोष क्या है?
'ग़लत शब्द का चयन' किसे कहते हैं?
उज्ज्वल क्या है?
'चमकदार का शुद्ध रूप' किसे कहते हैं?
श्रीमती क्या है?
qa.a: श्रीमती: विवाहित स्त्री के लिए सम्मानसूचक।

qa.q: 'विवाहित स्त्री के लिए सम्मानसूचक' किसे कहते हैं?
प्रतीक्षा क्या है?
'इंतज़ार का शुद्ध रूप' किसे कहते हैं?
परीक्षा क्या है?
'इम्तिहान का शुद्ध रूप' किसे कहते हैं?
कृपया क्या है?
'अनुरोध का शुद्ध रूप' किसे कहते हैं?
द्वितीय क्या है?
'दूसरे का शुद्ध रूप' किसे कहते हैं?
अनुस्वार क्या है?
qa.a: अनुस्वार: बिंदु से लिखा जाने वाला वर्ण।

qa.q: 'बिंदु से लिखा जाने वाला वर्ण' किसे कहते हैं?
अनुनासिक क्या है?
qa.a: अनुनासिक: चंद्रबिंदु से लिखा जाने वाला वर्ण।

qa.q: 'चंद्रबिंदु से लिखा जाने वाला वर्ण' किसे कहते हैं?
पर्यायवाची क्या है?
'समान अर्थ वाले शब्द' किसे कहते हैं?
विलोम क्या है?
'विपरीत अर्थ वाले शब्द' किसे कहते हैं?
अनेकार्थी क्या है?
'कई अर्थ वाले शब्द' किसे कहते हैं?
समश्रुत भिन्नार्थक क्या है?
qa.a: समश्रुत भिन्नार्थक: देखने-सुनने में मिलते पर अलग अर्थ वाले।

qa.q: 'देखने-सुनने में मिलते पर अलग अर्थ वाले' किसे कहते हैं?
वाक्यांश के लिए एक शब्द क्या है?
qa.a: वाक्यांश के लिए एक शब्द: वाक्यांश का संक्षिप्त रूप।

qa.q: 'वाक्यांश का संक्षिप्त रूप' किसे कहते हैं?
तत्सम क्या है?
qa.a: तत्सम: संस्कृत से ज्यों के त्यों आए शब्द।

qa.q: 'संस्कृत से ज्यों के त्यों आए शब्द' किसे कहते हैं?
तद्भव क्या है?
qa.a: तद्भव: संस्कृत से बिगड़कर आए शब्द।

qa.q: 'संस्कृत से बिगड़कर आए शब्द' किसे कहते हैं?

भाषा को प्रभावी बनाने के लिए मुहावरे और लोकोक्तियों का प्रयोग होता है। मुहावरा ऐसा वाक्यांश है जो अपने सामान्य अर्थ को छोड़कर विशेष अर्थ देता है और वाक्य में प्रयोग होने पर ही सार्थक होता है। जैसे आँखों का तारा होना का अर्थ बहुत प्रिय होना है। लोकोक्ति पूरा कथन है, जो लोक के अनुभव से बना है और स्वतंत्र वाक्य की तरह चलता है, जैसे नाच न जाने आँगन टेढ़ा। मुहावरे का रूप वाक्य में काल, वचन और लिंग के अनुसार बदलता है, जबकि लोकोक्ति प्रायः अपरिवर्तित रहती है। वाक्य-शुद्धि में वर्तनी, लिंग, वचन, कारक, काल और शब्द-क्रम की शुद्धता देखी जाती है। अशुद्ध वाक्यों के सामान्य कारण हैं: लिंग-वचन की भूल, अनावश्यक शब्द, ग़लत शब्द-क्रम और विराम-चिह्नों की चूक। शब्द-शुद्धि में अशुद्ध वर्तनी जैसे आशीर्वाद को आर्शीवाद लिखना ग़लत है। पर्यायवाची, विलोम और अनेकार्थी शब्द भी भाषा-बोध में पूछे जाते हैं। इन सबके अभ्यास से भाषा में शुद्धता और सौंदर्य दोनों आते हैं।

📌

गहन अध्ययन: मुहावरा

  • मुहावरा विशेष अर्थ देने वाला वाक्यांश है और वाक्य में काल-लिंग-वचन के अनुसार बदलता है।
🧠

गहन अध्ययन: लोकोक्ति

  • लोकोक्ति लोक-अनुभव से उपजा पूरा कथन है और प्रायः बिना बदले प्रयुक्त होती है।
🌟

गहन अध्ययन: वाक्य-शुद्धि

  • लिंग, वचन, कारक, काल, वर्तनी और शब्द-क्रम की भूलें सुधारना वाक्य-शुद्धि है।

lessons.title: रस, छंद और अलंकार: पुनरावृत्ति
yt: class 12 hindi vyakaran ras chhand alankar doha chaupai upma rupak

blocks.x: काव्य की सुंदरता और प्रभाव के तीन आधार हैं: रस, छंद और अलंकार। रस काव्य से मिलने वाला आनंद है और इसके चार अंग हैं: स्थायी भाव, विभाव, अनुभाव और संचारी भाव। रस नौ माने गए हैं: शृंगार, हास्य, करुण, रौद्र, वीर, भयानक, वीभत्स, अद्भुत और शांत। इनके स्थायी भाव क्रमशः रति, हास, शोक, क्रोध, उत्साह, भय, जुगुप्सा, विस्मय और निर्वेद हैं। छंद मात्रा या वर्णों की गणना पर आधारित नियमबद्ध रचना है। मात्रिक छंदों में दोहा, चौपाई और सोरठा आते हैं; दोहे में पहले और तीसरे चरण में 13-13 तथा दूसरे और चौथे चरण में 11-11 मात्राएँ होती हैं। चौपाई के प्रत्येक चरण में 16 मात्राएँ होती हैं। अलंकार काव्य की शोभा बढ़ाते हैं। शब्दालंकारों में अनुप्रास, यमक और श्लेष तथा अर्थालंकारों में उपमा, रूपक, उत्प्रेक्षा और अतिशयोक्ति आते हैं। उपमा में दो वस्तुओं की समानता वाचक शब्द से बताई जाती है और रूपक में उपमेय पर उपमान का आरोप होता है। इन तीनों की पहचान से अपठित काव्यांश हल करना आसान होता है।
गहन अध्ययन: रस
रस के चार अंग और नौ भेद हैं, जिनके अपने स्थायी भाव होते हैं।
गहन अध्ययन: छंद
दोहा और चौपाई प्रमुख मात्रिक छंद हैं; दोहे में 13-11 और चौपाई में प्रति चरण 16 मात्राएँ होती हैं।
गहन अध्ययन: अलंकार
अनुप्रास, यमक, श्लेष, उपमा और रूपक जैसे अलंकार काव्य की शोभा बढ़ाते हैं।
Hindi saransh
रस आनंद देता है, छंद लय देता है और अलंकार शोभा बढ़ाते हैं; तीनों को पहचानना काव्य-बोध की कुंजी है।
रस की पहचान के लिए स्थायी भाव देखें; अलंकार की पहचान के लिए समानता, आवृत्ति या आरोप।

qa.q: रस क्या है?
qa.a: रस: काव्य से मिलने वाला आनंद।

qa.q: 'काव्य से मिलने वाला आनंद' किसे कहते हैं?
रस के अंग क्या है?
'चार' किसे कहते हैं?
रस के भेद क्या है?
'नौ' किसे कहते हैं?
स्थायी भाव क्या है?
qa.a: स्थायी भाव: रस का मूल मनोभाव।

Read the full explanation

काव्य की सुंदरता और प्रभाव के तीन आधार हैं: रस, छंद और अलंकार। रस काव्य से मिलने वाला आनंद है और इसके चार अंग हैं: स्थायी भाव, विभाव, अनुभाव और संचारी भाव। रस नौ माने गए हैं: शृंगार, हास्य, करुण, रौद्र, वीर, भयानक, वीभत्स, अद्भुत और शांत। इनके स्थायी भाव क्रमशः रति, हास, शोक, क्रोध, उत्साह, भय, जुगुप्सा, विस्मय और निर्वेद हैं। छंद मात्रा या वर्णों की गणना पर आधारित नियमबद्ध रचना है। मात्रिक छंदों में दोहा, चौपाई और सोरठा आते हैं; दोहे में पहले और तीसरे चरण में 13-13 तथा दूसरे और चौथे चरण में 11-11 मात्राएँ होती हैं। चौपाई के प्रत्येक चरण में 16 मात्राएँ होती हैं। अलंकार काव्य की शोभा बढ़ाते हैं। शब्दालंकारों में अनुप्रास, यमक और श्लेष तथा अर्थालंकारों में उपमा, रूपक, उत्प्रेक्षा और अतिशयोक्ति आते हैं। उपमा में दो वस्तुओं की समानता वाचक शब्द से बताई जाती है और रूपक में उपमेय पर उपमान का आरोप होता है। इन तीनों की पहचान से अपठित काव्यांश हल करना आसान होता है।

📌

गहन अध्ययन: रस

  • रस के चार अंग और नौ भेद हैं, जिनके अपने स्थायी भाव होते हैं।
🧠

गहन अध्ययन: छंद

  • दोहा और चौपाई प्रमुख मात्रिक छंद हैं
  • दोहे में 13-11 और चौपाई में प्रति चरण 16 मात्राएँ होती हैं।
🌟

गहन अध्ययन: अलंकार

  • अनुप्रास, यमक, श्लेष, उपमा और रूपक जैसे अलंकार काव्य की शोभा बढ़ाते हैं।
🧮

lessons.title: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation
yt: class 12 history theme 1 bricks beads and bones harappan civilisation mohenjodaro great bath

blocks.x: The Harappan or Indus Valley Civilisation flourished in the north-west of the subcontinent. Its Mature phase is dated roughly 2600 to 1900 BCE, preceded by Early Harappan cultures and followed by Late Harappan ones. Harappa, in modern Pakistan, was first noticed by Charles Masson in the 1820s; its systematic excavation began in 1921 under Daya Ram Sahni, while Mohenjodaro was excavated from 1922 under Rakhal Das Banerji. Alexander Cunningham, the first Director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India, had earlier visited Harappa; John Marshall, Director-General from 1902, publicised the discovery in 1924. Mortimer Wheeler later introduced stratigraphic methods. Major sites include Harappa, Mohenjodaro, Chanhudaro, Kalibangan, Lothal, Banawali, Rakhigarhi and Dholavira. Many settlements were divided into a smaller, higher citadel and a larger, lower town. Mohenjodaro had the Great Bath, a large tank made of baked bricks lined with bitumen. Drains were covered, and houses were built around courtyards. Bricks followed a standard ratio of 1:2:4. Granaries, standard weights made of chert, seals of steatite with an undeciphered script, and beads of carnelian show organised production and trade. Copper came from Khetri in Rajasthan, lapis lazuli from Shortughai in Afghanistan, and shell from Nageshwar and Balakot. Contacts with Mesopotamia, which called the region Meluhha, are attested; Dilmun (Bahrain) and Magan (Oman) were intermediaries. Craft production involved bead-making at Chanhudaro and Lothal. Farmers grew wheat, barley, pulses, peas, sesame and cotton; ploughs are shown by terracotta models and a field furrow at Kalibangan. Social differences are debated: burials show few differences, but some goods were rare. Archaeologists infer religion from seals, figurines and structures; the so-called Pashupati seal and the Mother Goddess figurines are interpreted with caution. The civilisation declined around 1900 BCE, with proposed causes including climate change, river shifts and deforestation.
Deep dive: Planning and architecture
Citadel and lower town, covered drains, baked-brick houses and the Great Bath point to strong civic planning.
Deep dive: Trade and craft
Seals, weights, beads, copper and lapis lazuli show long-distance trade with Mesopotamia and Central Asia.
Deep dive: Sources and interpretation
Archaeologists interpret seals, burials, figurines and structures, but the script is undeciphered, so conclusions stay tentative.

The Harappan or Indus Valley Civilisation flourished in the north-west of the subcontinent

🔑

Big idea

  • Its Mature phase is dated roughly 2600 to 1900 BCE, preceded by Early Harappan cultures and followed by Late Harappan ones

Read the full explanation

The Harappan or Indus Valley Civilisation flourished in the north-west of the subcontinent. Its Mature phase is dated roughly 2600 to 1900 BCE, preceded by Early Harappan cultures and followed by Late Harappan ones. Harappa, in modern Pakistan, was first noticed by Charles Masson in the 1820s; its systematic excavation began in 1921 under Daya Ram Sahni, while Mohenjodaro was excavated from 1922 under Rakhal Das Banerji. Alexander Cunningham, the first Director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India, had earlier visited Harappa; John Marshall, Director-General from 1902, publicised the discovery in 1924. Mortimer Wheeler later introduced stratigraphic methods. Major sites include Harappa, Mohenjodaro, Chanhudaro, Kalibangan, Lothal, Banawali, Rakhigarhi and Dholavira. Many settlements were divided into a smaller, higher citadel and a larger, lower town. Mohenjodaro had the Great Bath, a large tank made of baked bricks lined with bitumen. Drains were covered, and houses were built around courtyards. Bricks followed a standard ratio of 1:2:4. Granaries, standard weights made of chert, seals of steatite with an undeciphered script, and beads of carnelian show organised production and trade. Copper came from Khetri in Rajasthan, lapis lazuli from Shortughai in Afghanistan, and shell from Nageshwar and Balakot. Contacts with Mesopotamia, which called the region Meluhha, are attested; Dilmun (Bahrain) and Magan (Oman) were intermediaries. Craft production involved bead-making at Chanhudaro and Lothal. Farmers grew wheat, barley, pulses, peas, sesame and cotton; ploughs are shown by terracotta models and a field furrow at Kalibangan. Social differences are debated: burials show few differences, but some goods were rare. Archaeologists infer religion from seals, figurines and structures; the so-called Pashupati seal and the Mother Goddess figurines are interpreted with caution. The civilisation declined around 1900 BCE, with proposed causes including climate change, river shifts and deforestation.

📌

Planning and architecture

  • Citadel and lower town, covered drains, baked-brick houses and the Great Bath point to strong civic planning
🧠

Trade and craft

  • Seals, weights, beads, copper and lapis lazuli show long-distance trade with Mesopotamia and Central Asia
🌟

Sources and interpretation

  • Archaeologists interpret seals, burials, figurines and structures, but the script is undeciphered, so conclusions stay tentative
🧮

lessons.title: Kings, Farmers and Towns: Early States and Economies
yt: class 12 history theme 2 kings farmers and towns mahajanapadas mauryas ashoka inscriptions

blocks.x: Around the sixth century BCE, early states emerged in the Ganga plains. Sixteen Mahajanapadas were recorded, among them Magadha, Kosala, Vajji, Kuru, Panchala, Avanti and Gandhara. Magadha grew powerful through iron tools, fertile land, elephants and rivers; its capitals included Rajagriha and later Pataliputra. Rulers such as Bimbisara, Ajatashatru and Mahapadma Nanda expanded it. The Mauryan empire was founded by Chandragupta Maurya about 321 BCE and reached its peak under Ashoka. Sources include the Arthashastra, the Indica of the Greek ambassador Megasthenes, and inscriptions. Ashoka, after the Kalinga war about 261 BCE, adopted dhamma and appointed dhamma mahamattas. His edicts in Brahmi and Kharosthi were deciphered by James Prinsep in 1838. Administration at the centre involved the king, provincial governors and officials. Later states included the Satavahanas, Guptas and Pandyas. Prashastis such as the Prayaga Prashasti, composed by Harishena for Samudragupta, praised rulers, while the Junagadh inscription records the work of Rudradaman. Agricultural expansion used iron ploughs, irrigation and transplantation of paddy. Land grants to Brahmans and officials spread in the early centuries CE. Towns grew as centres of trade, crafts and administration. Mathura, Ujjayini, Arikamedu and Pataliputra were important. Punch-marked silver coins and later gold coins show an expanding money economy. Guilds or shrenis organised craftspeople. Roman trade brought gold to south India, as at Arikamedu.
Deep dive: Mahajanapadas and Magadha
Magadha rose through resources, strong rulers and strategic capitals; the Mauryas then built an empire.
Deep dive: Ashoka and dhamma
After Kalinga, Ashoka promoted dhamma through edicts and special officials, aiming at social harmony.
Deep dive: Towns and trade
Coins, guilds, crafts and trade networks, including Roman links, supported urban growth.
Hindi saransh
Mahajanapad, Magadh ka uday, Maurya samrajya, Ashoka ka dhamma, shilalekh, nagar aur vyapar.
Remember: Prinsep deciphered Brahmi in 1838; Ashoka and Kalinga c. 261 BCE.

Big idea

  • Sixteen Mahajanapadas were recorded, among them Magadha, Kosala, Vajji, Kuru, Panchala, Avanti and Gandhara

Read the full explanation

Around the sixth century BCE, early states emerged in the Ganga plains. Sixteen Mahajanapadas were recorded, among them Magadha, Kosala, Vajji, Kuru, Panchala, Avanti and Gandhara. Magadha grew powerful through iron tools, fertile land, elephants and rivers; its capitals included Rajagriha and later Pataliputra. Rulers such as Bimbisara, Ajatashatru and Mahapadma Nanda expanded it. The Mauryan empire was founded by Chandragupta Maurya about 321 BCE and reached its peak under Ashoka. Sources include the Arthashastra, the Indica of the Greek ambassador Megasthenes, and inscriptions. Ashoka, after the Kalinga war about 261 BCE, adopted dhamma and appointed dhamma mahamattas. His edicts in Brahmi and Kharosthi were deciphered by James Prinsep in 1838. Administration at the centre involved the king, provincial governors and officials. Later states included the Satavahanas, Guptas and Pandyas. Prashastis such as the Prayaga Prashasti, composed by Harishena for Samudragupta, praised rulers, while the Junagadh inscription records the work of Rudradaman. Agricultural expansion used iron ploughs, irrigation and transplantation of paddy. Land grants to Brahmans and officials spread in the early centuries CE. Towns grew as centres of trade, crafts and administration. Mathura, Ujjayini, Arikamedu and Pataliputra were important. Punch-marked silver coins and later gold coins show an expanding money economy. Guilds or shrenis organised craftspeople. Roman trade brought gold to south India, as at Arikamedu.

📌

Mahajanapadas and Magadha

  • Magadha rose through resources, strong rulers and strategic capitals
  • The Mauryas then built an empire
🧠

Ashoka and dhamma

  • After Kalinga, Ashoka promoted dhamma through edicts and special officials, aiming at social harmony
🌟

Towns and trade

  • Coins, guilds, crafts and trade networks, including Roman links, supported urban growth

lessons.title: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
yt: class 12 history theme 3 kinship caste and class mahabharata critical edition varna jati manusmriti

blocks.x: This theme examines social norms and the Mahabharata. The Mahabharata, traditionally ascribed to Vyasa, was composed over centuries from about 500 BCE and attained about 100,000 verses. A critical edition was prepared at the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute, Pune, under V.S. Sukthankar between 1919 and 1966. It narrates a conflict between the Kauravas and Pandavas over the kingdom of Hastinapura. Kinship rules in Brahmanical texts favoured patriliny, with property passing from father to sons. Women were expected to marry outside their gotra (exogamy), which was assigned from about 1000 BCE. The Dharmasutras and Dharmashastras, including the Manusmriti, laid down norms of marriage and eight forms of marriage were listed. Endogamy within the jati and polygyny were practised, and rare polyandry appears in the case of Draupadi. Inscriptions of the Satavahanas show names that include the mother, a matronymic, as in Gotami-putra. The varna order placed Brahmanas, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and Shudras in sequence and assigned duties to each, with those outside called untouchables or Chandalas. Texts such as the Manusmriti described these rules, and the Buddhist tradition challenged birth-based claims. Historians study the Mahabharata using many methods, noting later interpolations and changes. Characters such as Ekalavya and Hidimba illustrate attitudes towards forest peoples and outsiders. Gift-giving, dana, and different rules for property of women (stridhana) show ideals. The Chinese Buddhist pilgrim Fa-Hsien noted the lives of Chandalas.
Deep dive: Mahabharata as a source
The epic grew over centuries, so historians separate its layers and treat it as a source for ideals more than events.
Deep dive: Kinship and marriage
Patriliny, exogamy within gotras and eight forms of marriage shaped Brahmanical norms.
Deep dive: Varna and jati
Texts such as the Manusmriti ranked society by varna and marginalised Chandalas; Buddhist ideas questioned this.
Hindi saransh
Mahabharat ka critical edition, sambandh, gotra, varna aur jati ki vyavastha aur samajik viShamta.

Read the full explanation

This theme examines social norms and the Mahabharata. The Mahabharata, traditionally ascribed to Vyasa, was composed over centuries from about 500 BCE and attained about 100,000 verses. A critical edition was prepared at the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute, Pune, under V.S. Sukthankar between 1919 and 1966. It narrates a conflict between the Kauravas and Pandavas over the kingdom of Hastinapura. Kinship rules in Brahmanical texts favoured patriliny, with property passing from father to sons. Women were expected to marry outside their gotra (exogamy), which was assigned from about 1000 BCE. The Dharmasutras and Dharmashastras, including the Manusmriti, laid down norms of marriage and eight forms of marriage were listed. Endogamy within the jati and polygyny were practised, and rare polyandry appears in the case of Draupadi. Inscriptions of the Satavahanas show names that include the mother, a matronymic, as in Gotami-putra. The varna order placed Brahmanas, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and Shudras in sequence and assigned duties to each, with those outside called untouchables or Chandalas. Texts such as the Manusmriti described these rules, and the Buddhist tradition challenged birth-based claims. Historians study the Mahabharata using many methods, noting later interpolations and changes. Characters such as Ekalavya and Hidimba illustrate attitudes towards forest peoples and outsiders. Gift-giving, dana, and different rules for property of women (stridhana) show ideals. The Chinese Buddhist pilgrim Fa-Hsien noted the lives of Chandalas.

📌

Mahabharata as a source

  • The epic grew over centuries, so historians separate its layers and treat it as a source for ideals more than events
🧠

Kinship and marriage

  • Patriliny, exogamy within gotras and eight forms of marriage shaped Brahmanical norms
🌟

Varna and jati

  • Texts such as the Manusmriti ranked society by varna and marginalised Chandalas
  • Buddhist ideas questioned this

lessons.title: Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings: Cultural Developments
yt: class 12 history theme 4 thinkers beliefs and buildings sanchi stupa buddhism jainism

blocks.x: The Great Stupa at Sanchi in Madhya Pradesh survived because it escaped the attention of treasure hunters and was protected by the begums of Bhopal, Shah Jehan Begum and her successor Sultan Jehan Begum, who funded its preservation. John Marshall wrote its major study. The stupa, associated with the emperor Ashoka in the third century BCE, enshrines relics of the Buddha. It was a mound of earth later covered with bricks and stone, with a railing, gateways (toranas) and sculptures narrating Jataka stories. The period around the sixth century BCE saw new thinkers. Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, was born at Lumbini, attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya, gave his first sermon at Sarnath and died at Kushinagar. His teaching rests on the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path leading to nirvana, and he rejected the idea of a permanent soul. Mahavira, the twenty-fourth Tirthankara of Jainism, stressed ahimsa. The Ajivikas were another school. Upanishadic thinkers debated the atman and Brahman. Buddhism later split into Theravada and Mahayana; the latter celebrated the Bodhisattva and image worship. Monasteries, viharas, and chaitya halls were built. Alongside, devotional Hinduism grew with worship of Vishnu and Shiva. Vishnu was believed to take avatars, and temples with a garbhagriha emerged; examples include the Dashavatara Temple at Deogarh from the Gupta period and the rock-cut Kailashnatha Temple at Ellora. Historians use sculpture, inscriptions and texts, but must understand local traditions to read them correctly.
Deep dive: Sanchi and preservation
Sanchi survived through luck and care by the begums of Bhopal; its gateways narrate Jataka stories.
Deep dive: Buddhism and Jainism
Buddhist teachings stress the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path; Jainism stresses ahimsa.
Deep dive: Temples and devotion
Devotional worship of Vishnu and Shiva led to temple building with a sanctum, garbhagriha.

Read the full explanation

The Great Stupa at Sanchi in Madhya Pradesh survived because it escaped the attention of treasure hunters and was protected by the begums of Bhopal, Shah Jehan Begum and her successor Sultan Jehan Begum, who funded its preservation. John Marshall wrote its major study. The stupa, associated with the emperor Ashoka in the third century BCE, enshrines relics of the Buddha. It was a mound of earth later covered with bricks and stone, with a railing, gateways (toranas) and sculptures narrating Jataka stories. The period around the sixth century BCE saw new thinkers. Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, was born at Lumbini, attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya, gave his first sermon at Sarnath and died at Kushinagar. His teaching rests on the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path leading to nirvana, and he rejected the idea of a permanent soul. Mahavira, the twenty-fourth Tirthankara of Jainism, stressed ahimsa. The Ajivikas were another school. Upanishadic thinkers debated the atman and Brahman. Buddhism later split into Theravada and Mahayana; the latter celebrated the Bodhisattva and image worship. Monasteries, viharas, and chaitya halls were built. Alongside, devotional Hinduism grew with worship of Vishnu and Shiva. Vishnu was believed to take avatars, and temples with a garbhagriha emerged; examples include the Dashavatara Temple at Deogarh from the Gupta period and the rock-cut Kailashnatha Temple at Ellora. Historians use sculpture, inscriptions and texts, but must understand local traditions to read them correctly.

📌

Sanchi and preservation

  • Sanchi survived through luck and care by the begums of Bhopal
  • Its gateways narrate Jataka stories
🧠

Buddhism and Jainism

  • Buddhist teachings stress the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path
  • Jainism stresses ahimsa
🌟

Temples and devotion

  • Devotional worship of Vishnu and Shiva led to temple building with a sanctum, garbhagriha

lessons.title: Through the Eyes of Travellers: Perceptions of Society
yt: class 12 history theme 5 through the eyes of travellers al biruni ibn battuta bernier kitab ul hind

blocks.x: Travellers left accounts of the subcontinent that historians use with care. Al-Biruni, born in Khwarizm in Central Asia, came to India with the army of Mahmud of Ghazni, and wrote the Kitab-ul-Hind in Arabic around the eleventh century. He learned Sanskrit, studied texts such as Patanjali, and was critical of the caste system, comparing it with social divisions elsewhere. He wrote about astronomy, religion, and customs. Ibn Battuta, from Tangier in Morocco, travelled widely and reached India in 1333. He served as a qazi at the court of Muhammad bin Tughlaq in Delhi. His account, the Rihla, written in Arabic and compiled around 1355, describes cities, the postal system (the horse post uluq and the foot post dawa), and practices like sati. He found Indian cities thriving and the agrarian economy productive. Francois Bernier, a French physician, lived in India between 1656 and 1668 and was associated with Dara Shikoh and later a Mughal noble. His Travels in the Mogul Empire compared India with Europe and argued that the absence of private property in land harmed Mughal agriculture, a view modern historians question. Other travellers include Abd al-Razzaq, who visited Vijayanagara, and Peter Mundy, Jean-Baptiste Tavernier and Niccolao Manucci. Travellers observed trade, cities, crafts, women and slavery, but wrote from their own backgrounds, so their accounts reflect biases. Historians cross-check with other sources.
Deep dive: Al-Biruni
Al-Biruni used Sanskrit sources to write the Kitab-ul-Hind and criticised the caste system.
Deep dive: Ibn Battuta
Ibn Battuta described Delhi, cities and the postal system in the Rihla after serving the Tughlaq court.
Deep dive: Bernier
Bernier compared India with Europe and argued crown ownership of land caused decline, a claim historians dispute.

Big idea

  • Travellers left accounts of the subcontinent that historians use with care
  • Al-Biruni, born in Khwarizm in Central Asia, came to India with the army of Mahmud of Ghazni, and wrote the Kitab-ul-Hind in Arabic around the…

  • He wrote about astronomy, religion, and customs
Read the full explanation

Travellers left accounts of the subcontinent that historians use with care. Al-Biruni, born in Khwarizm in Central Asia, came to India with the army of Mahmud of Ghazni, and wrote the Kitab-ul-Hind in Arabic around the eleventh century. He learned Sanskrit, studied texts such as Patanjali, and was critical of the caste system, comparing it with social divisions elsewhere. He wrote about astronomy, religion, and customs. Ibn Battuta, from Tangier in Morocco, travelled widely and reached India in 1333. He served as a qazi at the court of Muhammad bin Tughlaq in Delhi. His account, the Rihla, written in Arabic and compiled around 1355, describes cities, the postal system (the horse post uluq and the foot post dawa), and practices like sati. He found Indian cities thriving and the agrarian economy productive. Francois Bernier, a French physician, lived in India between 1656 and 1668 and was associated with Dara Shikoh and later a Mughal noble. His Travels in the Mogul Empire compared India with Europe and argued that the absence of private property in land harmed Mughal agriculture, a view modern historians question. Other travellers include Abd al-Razzaq, who visited Vijayanagara, and Peter Mundy, Jean-Baptiste Tavernier and Niccolao Manucci. Travellers observed trade, cities, crafts, women and slavery, but wrote from their own backgrounds, so their accounts reflect biases. Historians cross-check with other sources.

📌

Al-Biruni

  • Al-Biruni used Sanskrit sources to write the Kitab-ul-Hind and criticised the caste system
🧠

Ibn Battuta

  • Ibn Battuta described Delhi, cities and the postal system in the Rihla after serving the Tughlaq court
🌟

Bernier

  • Bernier compared India with Europe and argued crown ownership of land caused decline, a claim historians dispute

lessons.title: Bhakti-Sufi Traditions: Changes in Religious Beliefs and Devotional Texts
yt: class 12 history theme 6 bhakti sufi traditions kabir nanak mirabai chishti

blocks.x: Between roughly the eighth and eighteenth centuries, devotional movements spread across the subcontinent. In the Tamil region, the Alvars devoted to Vishnu and the Nayanars devoted to Shiva composed hymns; women like Andal and Karaikkal Ammaiyar were among them. Basavanna founded the Virashaiva or Lingayat tradition in Karnataka in the twelfth century, rejecting caste and ritual pollution. Saguna bhakti worshipped deities with form, as in the Ramcharitmanas of Tulsidas and the songs of Mirabai and Surdas, while nirguna bhakti, as taught by Kabir, saw the divine as formless. Kabir, a weaver associated with Banaras, criticised ritual and sectarian divisions; his verses are compiled in the Bijak and the Kabir Granthavali. Guru Nanak, born in 1469 at Talwandi, founded Sikhism, taught one God, and set up a community at Kartarpur. The Adi Granth was compiled by Guru Arjan in 1604, and Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa in 1699. In western India, Namdev and Tukaram sang of Vithoba. Sufism, the mystical tradition of Islam, spread through silsilas or orders such as the Chishti and Suhrawardi. Sufis lived in khanqahs, and their tombs, dargahs, became centres of pilgrimage. Moinuddin Chishti at Ajmer, Nizamuddin Auliya at Delhi and Baba Farid are notable. Sufi poetry, qawwali and local languages helped spread ideas. Historians study these movements through hagiographies, poetry and inscriptions, noticing exchange between traditions rather than a simple division.
Deep dive: Bhakti movements
Alvars, Nayanars, Basavanna, Kabir, Nanak and Mirabai show diverse forms of devotion across regions.
Deep dive: Sufi silsilas
Sufi orders such as the Chishti created khanqahs and dargahs that became centres of devotion.
Deep dive: Exchange of ideas
Bhakti and Sufi traditions influenced each other through poetry, language and shared saint worship.

Visual lesson

Bhakti-Sufi Traditions: Changes in Religious Beliefs and Devotional Texts

Between roughly the eighth and eighteenth centuries, devotional movements spread across the subcontinent

🔑

Big idea

  • Between roughly the eighth and eighteenth centuries, devotional movements spread across the subcontinent
  • In the Tamil region, the Alvars devoted to Vishnu and the Nayanars devoted to Shiva composed hymns
  • Women like Andal and Karaikkal Ammaiyar were among them
  • Basavanna founded the Virashaiva or Lingayat tradition in Karnataka in the twelfth century, rejecting caste and ritual pollution
Read the full explanation

Between roughly the eighth and eighteenth centuries, devotional movements spread across the subcontinent. In the Tamil region, the Alvars devoted to Vishnu and the Nayanars devoted to Shiva composed hymns; women like Andal and Karaikkal Ammaiyar were among them. Basavanna founded the Virashaiva or Lingayat tradition in Karnataka in the twelfth century, rejecting caste and ritual pollution. Saguna bhakti worshipped deities with form, as in the Ramcharitmanas of Tulsidas and the songs of Mirabai and Surdas, while nirguna bhakti, as taught by Kabir, saw the divine as formless. Kabir, a weaver associated with Banaras, criticised ritual and sectarian divisions; his verses are compiled in the Bijak and the Kabir Granthavali. Guru Nanak, born in 1469 at Talwandi, founded Sikhism, taught one God, and set up a community at Kartarpur. The Adi Granth was compiled by Guru Arjan in 1604, and Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa in 1699. In western India, Namdev and Tukaram sang of Vithoba. Sufism, the mystical tradition of Islam, spread through silsilas or orders such as the Chishti and Suhrawardi. Sufis lived in khanqahs, and their tombs, dargahs, became centres of pilgrimage. Moinuddin Chishti at Ajmer, Nizamuddin Auliya at Delhi and Baba Farid are notable. Sufi poetry, qawwali and local languages helped spread ideas. Historians study these movements through hagiographies, poetry and inscriptions, noticing exchange between traditions rather than a simple division.

🕰️

Bhakti movements

  • Alvars, Nayanars, Basavanna, Kabir, Nanak and Mirabai show diverse forms of devotion across regions
🧠

Sufi silsilas

  • Sufi orders such as the Chishti created khanqahs and dargahs that became centres of devotion
🌟

Exchange of ideas

  • Bhakti and Sufi traditions influenced each other through poetry, language and shared saint worship

lessons.title: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
yt: class 12 history theme 7 vijayanagara hampi krishnadeva raya amara nayaka mahanavami dibba

blocks.x: Vijayanagara, meaning city of victory, was the capital of an empire founded in 1336 by Harihara and Bukka of the Sangama dynasty on the Tungabhadra river in Karnataka. Its ruins at Hampi were brought to attention in 1800 by Colin Mackenzie, a British engineer and antiquarian, who prepared the first survey map. Hampi was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986. The empire reached its peak under Krishnadeva Raya of the Tuluva dynasty, who ruled from 1509 to 1529. Rulers called themselves raya and shared power with the amara-nayakas, military chiefs who held land (amaram) in return for troops and tribute. The empire was defeated at the Battle of Talikota in 1565 by the combined forces of the Deccan sultanates, after which the capital declined. The city was spread over a sacred centre along the river and a royal centre in the south-west. The royal centre contained about sixty temples and palaces, including the Lotus Mahal, the Mahanavami Dibba, the Hazara Rama Temple and elephant stables. The Virupaksha temple and Vitthala temple, with its stone chariot, are major religious structures. Water was managed through tanks and canals, and fortification walls enclosed cultivated land. Foreign visitors, including Abd al-Razzaq from Persia, Domingo Paes and Duarte Barbosa from Portugal, and Fernao Nuniz, described the city, its markets and festivals such as Mahanavami. Rulers depended on trade in horses and spices through ports on the west coast.
Deep dive: Rise and fall
Founded in 1336, Vijayanagara peaked under Krishnadeva Raya and fell after Talikota in 1565.
Deep dive: Amara-nayaka system
Military chiefs held land in return for troops and tribute, strengthening and also straining the empire.
Deep dive: Capital city
The sacred and royal centres, temples, tanks and fortifications show planning and royal ritual.

Read the full explanation

Vijayanagara, meaning city of victory, was the capital of an empire founded in 1336 by Harihara and Bukka of the Sangama dynasty on the Tungabhadra river in Karnataka. Its ruins at Hampi were brought to attention in 1800 by Colin Mackenzie, a British engineer and antiquarian, who prepared the first survey map. Hampi was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986. The empire reached its peak under Krishnadeva Raya of the Tuluva dynasty, who ruled from 1509 to 1529. Rulers called themselves raya and shared power with the amara-nayakas, military chiefs who held land (amaram) in return for troops and tribute. The empire was defeated at the Battle of Talikota in 1565 by the combined forces of the Deccan sultanates, after which the capital declined. The city was spread over a sacred centre along the river and a royal centre in the south-west. The royal centre contained about sixty temples and palaces, including the Lotus Mahal, the Mahanavami Dibba, the Hazara Rama Temple and elephant stables. The Virupaksha temple and Vitthala temple, with its stone chariot, are major religious structures. Water was managed through tanks and canals, and fortification walls enclosed cultivated land. Foreign visitors, including Abd al-Razzaq from Persia, Domingo Paes and Duarte Barbosa from Portugal, and Fernao Nuniz, described the city, its markets and festivals such as Mahanavami. Rulers depended on trade in horses and spices through ports on the west coast.

  • Founded in 1336, Vijayanagara peaked under Krishnadeva Raya and fell after Talikota in 1565

  • Military chiefs held land in return for troops and tribute, strengthening and also straining the empire

lessons.title: Peasants, Zamindars and the State: Agrarian Society and the Mughal Empire
yt: class 12 history theme 8 peasants zamindars and the state ain i akbari abul fazl mughal land revenue

blocks.x: In the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, about 85 percent of the population lived in villages. The chief source for agrarian history is the Ain-i-Akbari, compiled by Abul Fazl in 1598 as part of the Akbarnama. It records revenue, crops, and social groups. Peasants were called raiyat or muzarian. There were khud-kashta peasants, who cultivated in their own village, and pahi-kashta, who cultivated land elsewhere. Land was abundant and labour scarce, and cultivation expanded with new crops from the Americas such as maize, chilli and tobacco, alongside jins-i-kamil or perfect crops like cotton and sugarcane. Villages had panchayats headed by the muqaddam or mandal, and jati panchayats regulated caste. The jajmani relationship tied artisans to peasants through service. Zamindars held hereditary rights and collected revenue; they often had forts and armed retainers and were intermediaries between peasants and the state. The land revenue system aimed at assessment (jama) and collection (hasil). Todar Mal, Akbar’s revenue minister, introduced the dahsala system based on average yields and prices over ten years. Measurement (zabt) was used in many regions; Akbar’s revenue was often one-third of the produce. Silver flowed into India through trade, supporting the money economy. Officials such as the amin, patwari and qanungo recorded land, and jagirdars held revenue assignments tied to their mansabs. Pastoralists and forest peoples like the Bhils also interacted with the state. Peasants sometimes resisted through flight and revolt.
Deep dive: Village society
Peasants, panchayats and the jajmani system shaped village life under Mughal rule.
Deep dive: Zamindars and revenue
Zamindars collected revenue as intermediaries, while the state assessed and collected it through officials.
Deep dive: Sources
The Ain-i-Akbari gives statistics, but it reflects the view of the imperial court.

Visual lesson

Peasants, Zamindars and the State: Agrarian Society and the Mughal Empire

In the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, about 85 percent of the population lived in villages

Ain-i-Akbari1598
🔑

Big idea

  • In the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, about 85 percent of the population lived in villages
  • The chief source for agrarian history is the Ain-i-Akbari, compiled by Abul Fazl in 1598 as part of the Akbarnama
  • It records revenue, crops, and social groups
  • Peasants were called raiyat or muzarian
Read the full explanation

In the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, about 85 percent of the population lived in villages. The chief source for agrarian history is the Ain-i-Akbari, compiled by Abul Fazl in 1598 as part of the Akbarnama. It records revenue, crops, and social groups. Peasants were called raiyat or muzarian. There were khud-kashta peasants, who cultivated in their own village, and pahi-kashta, who cultivated land elsewhere. Land was abundant and labour scarce, and cultivation expanded with new crops from the Americas such as maize, chilli and tobacco, alongside jins-i-kamil or perfect crops like cotton and sugarcane. Villages had panchayats headed by the muqaddam or mandal, and jati panchayats regulated caste. The jajmani relationship tied artisans to peasants through service. Zamindars held hereditary rights and collected revenue; they often had forts and armed retainers and were intermediaries between peasants and the state. The land revenue system aimed at assessment (jama) and collection (hasil). Todar Mal, Akbar’s revenue minister, introduced the dahsala system based on average yields and prices over ten years. Measurement (zabt) was used in many regions; Akbar’s revenue was often one-third of the produce. Silver flowed into India through trade, supporting the money economy. Officials such as the amin, patwari and qanungo recorded land, and jagirdars held revenue assignments tied to their mansabs. Pastoralists and forest peoples like the Bhils also interacted with the state. Peasants sometimes resisted through flight and revolt.

📌

Village society

  • Peasants, panchayats and the jajmani system shaped village life under Mughal rule
🧠

Zamindars and revenue

  • Zamindars collected revenue as intermediaries, while the state assessed and collected it through officials
🌟

Sources

  • The Ain-i-Akbari gives statistics, but it reflects the view of the imperial court

lessons.title: Kings and Chronicles: The Mughal Courts
yt: class 12 history theme 9 kings and chronicles mughal courts akbarnama baburnama sulh i kul

blocks.x: The Mughal empire was founded after Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat in 1526. His successors were Humayun, Akbar (from 1556), Jahangir (1605), Shah Jahan (1628) and Aurangzeb (1658). Mughal rulers claimed descent from Timur on the father’s side and from Genghis Khan on the mother’s side, and their court culture used Persian as the language of administration. Chronicles were written to glorify the emperor. Key texts include the Baburnama, Akbarnama and Ain-i-Akbari by Abul Fazl, the Badshahnama by Abdul Hamid Lahori, the Jahangirnama, and the Humayunnama by Gulbadan Begum. Illustrated manuscripts were made in the taswir khana or painting workshop, with painters and calligraphers, using the nastaliq style. The court at Fatehpur Sikri, Agra and Shahjahanabad organised daily ritual: jharokha darshan, taslim, kornish and sijda. The emperor was seen as a source of light, as per Abul Fazl’s idea of divine kingship. Akbar followed the policy of sulh-i-kul or universal peace, held religious discussions at the Ibadat Khana from 1575, and brought nobles from varied backgrounds into the mansabdari system, where rank was marked by zat and sawar. Nobles included Iranis, Turanis, Rajputs and Indian Muslims. Imperial women, such as Nur Jahan, Jahanara and Gulbadan Begum, played roles in politics and patronage. Provincial administration used subas under subedars, with officials such as diwan, bakhshi and qazi. Shah Jahan built the Red Fort and Taj Mahal, and Aurangzeb introduced the jizya in 1679. Diplomacy included embassies like that of Sir Thomas Roe at Jahangir’s court.
Deep dive: Chronicles and court
Persian chronicles and paintings projected an ideal image of rulers; historians read them critically.
Deep dive: Akbar’s policies
Sulh-i-kul, the Ibadat Khana and the mansabdari system aimed to integrate diverse nobles and communities.
Deep dive: Court life
Ceremonies like jharokha darshan and taslim showed imperial authority and accessibility.

Kings and Chronicles: The Mughal Courts

The Mughal empire was founded after Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat in 1526

🔑

Big idea

Read the full explanation

The Mughal empire was founded after Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat in 1526. His successors were Humayun, Akbar (from 1556), Jahangir (1605), Shah Jahan (1628) and Aurangzeb (1658). Mughal rulers claimed descent from Timur on the father’s side and from Genghis Khan on the mother’s side, and their court culture used Persian as the language of administration. Chronicles were written to glorify the emperor. Key texts include the Baburnama, Akbarnama and Ain-i-Akbari by Abul Fazl, the Badshahnama by Abdul Hamid Lahori, the Jahangirnama, and the Humayunnama by Gulbadan Begum. Illustrated manuscripts were made in the taswir khana or painting workshop, with painters and calligraphers, using the nastaliq style. The court at Fatehpur Sikri, Agra and Shahjahanabad organised daily ritual: jharokha darshan, taslim, kornish and sijda. The emperor was seen as a source of light, as per Abul Fazl’s idea of divine kingship. Akbar followed the policy of sulh-i-kul or universal peace, held religious discussions at the Ibadat Khana from 1575, and brought nobles from varied backgrounds into the mansabdari system, where rank was marked by zat and sawar. Nobles included Iranis, Turanis, Rajputs and Indian Muslims. Imperial women, such as Nur Jahan, Jahanara and Gulbadan Begum, played roles in politics and patronage. Provincial administration used subas under subedars, with officials such as diwan, bakhshi and qazi. Shah Jahan built the Red Fort and Taj Mahal, and Aurangzeb introduced the jizya in 1679. Diplomacy included embassies like that of Sir Thomas Roe at Jahangir’s court.

📌

Chronicles and court

  • Persian chronicles and paintings projected an ideal image of rulers
  • Historians read them critically
🧠

Akbar’s policies

  • Sulh-i-kul, the Ibadat Khana and the mansabdari system aimed to integrate diverse nobles and communities
🌟

Court life

  • Ceremonies like jharokha darshan and taslim showed imperial authority and accessibility

lessons.title: Colonialism and the Countryside: Exploring Official Archives
yt: class 12 history theme 10 colonialism and the countryside permanent settlement ryotwari santhals deccan riots

blocks.x: After the Battle of Plassey in 1757 and the grant of diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa in 1765, the East India Company sought a regular revenue. The Permanent Settlement of 1793, introduced by Lord Cornwallis in Bengal, fixed the revenue to be paid by zamindars permanently. Zamindars who failed to pay on time lost their estates under the sunset law, so many estates were auctioned. Jotedars, rich peasants, gained influence in villages. The Company expanded cultivation into hill areas. The Paharias of the Rajmahal hills lived by shifting cultivation and hunting, and were disturbed by settlers; Santhals, who came as cultivators, were settled in the Damin-i-Koh area in 1832, but were exploited by moneylenders and revolted in 1855-56 under Sido and Kanhu. In western India, the Ryotwari system, introduced by Thomas Munro in Madras and also in Bombay, settled revenue directly with the cultivator, with periodic revision. In north India, the Mahalwari system, devised by Holt Mackenzie in 1822, settled revenue with village communities. The American Civil War (1861-65) cut cotton supplies to Britain and caused a cotton boom in the Deccan, followed by a crash and heavy debt. In 1875 peasants in Poona and Ahmednagar attacked sahukars, an event called the Deccan Riots. The Deccan Riots Commission and the Deccan Agriculturists Relief Act of 1879 followed. Official archives such as revenue records, survey reports and Buchanan’s surveys are used by historians, but must be read for official bias.
Deep dive: Revenue settlements
Permanent Settlement, Ryotwari and Mahalwari systems differed in who paid revenue and how often it was revised.
Deep dive: Tribal and peasant revolts
Paharias, Santhals and Deccan peasants resisted exploitation by settlers, zamindars and moneylenders.
Deep dive: Archives
Official records are useful but reflect the colonial viewpoint, so historians read them with care.

Big idea

  • After the Battle of Plassey in 1757 and the grant of diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa in 1765, the East India Company sought a regular revenue
  • The Permanent Settlement of 1793, introduced by Lord Cornwallis in Bengal, fixed the revenue to be paid by zamindars permanently

  • Jotedars, rich peasants, gained influence in villages
Read the full explanation

After the Battle of Plassey in 1757 and the grant of diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa in 1765, the East India Company sought a regular revenue. The Permanent Settlement of 1793, introduced by Lord Cornwallis in Bengal, fixed the revenue to be paid by zamindars permanently. Zamindars who failed to pay on time lost their estates under the sunset law, so many estates were auctioned. Jotedars, rich peasants, gained influence in villages. The Company expanded cultivation into hill areas. The Paharias of the Rajmahal hills lived by shifting cultivation and hunting, and were disturbed by settlers; Santhals, who came as cultivators, were settled in the Damin-i-Koh area in 1832, but were exploited by moneylenders and revolted in 1855-56 under Sido and Kanhu. In western India, the Ryotwari system, introduced by Thomas Munro in Madras and also in Bombay, settled revenue directly with the cultivator, with periodic revision. In north India, the Mahalwari system, devised by Holt Mackenzie in 1822, settled revenue with village communities. The American Civil War (1861-65) cut cotton supplies to Britain and caused a cotton boom in the Deccan, followed by a crash and heavy debt. In 1875 peasants in Poona and Ahmednagar attacked sahukars, an event called the Deccan Riots. The Deccan Riots Commission and the Deccan Agriculturists Relief Act of 1879 followed. Official archives such as revenue records, survey reports and Buchanan’s surveys are used by historians, but must be read for official bias.

📌

Revenue settlements

  • Permanent Settlement, Ryotwari and Mahalwari systems differed in who paid revenue and how often it was revised
🧠

Tribal and peasant revolts

  • Paharias, Santhals and Deccan peasants resisted exploitation by settlers, zamindars and moneylenders
🌟

Archives

  • Official records are useful but reflect the colonial viewpoint, so historians read them with care

lessons.title: Rebels and the Raj: The Revolt of 1857
yt: class 12 history theme 11 rebels and the raj revolt of 1857 mangal pandey rani lakshmibai bahadur shah zafar

blocks.x: The Revolt of 1857 began at Meerut on 10 May 1857 when sepoys rose against their officers, marched to Delhi and proclaimed the Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar as their leader. It spread through north and central India, including Lucknow, Kanpur, Jhansi and Bihar. Causes included the British policy of annexation: the Doctrine of Lapse devised by Lord Dalhousie annexed states such as Satara and Jhansi, and Awadh was annexed in 1856 on grounds of misgovernment, deposing Nawab Wajid Ali Shah. The Subsidiary Alliance by Wellesley had earlier weakened states. Economic and social discontent included heavy revenue, loss of zamindari rights, and interference with customs. The immediate trigger was the introduction of the Enfield rifle with greased cartridges, rumoured to contain cow and pig fat, which offended Hindu and Muslim sepoys. Mangal Pandey of Barrackpore had acted in March 1857. Leaders included Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi, Nana Sahib at Kanpur, Begum Hazrat Mahal at Lucknow, Kunwar Singh in Bihar and Tatya Tope. The rebels used rumours, prophecies and symbols such as the chapati. The British under Governor-General Canning suppressed the revolt; Delhi was recaptured in September 1857, and Bahadur Shah was exiled to Rangoon. The Government of India Act of 1858 transferred power from the Company to the Crown, and Queen Victoria’s proclamation promised respect for rights and religions. Historians use official reports, rebel proclamations, letters, paintings and memoirs, which carry different perspectives.
Deep dive: Causes
Annexation, the Doctrine of Lapse, revenue pressures and the greased cartridge combined to cause the revolt.
Deep dive: Leaders and spread
Bahadur Shah, Rani Lakshmibai, Nana Sahib, Begum Hazrat Mahal and Kunwar Singh led resistance in different regions.
Deep dive: Aftermath
The Company’s rule ended in 1858; the Crown took over and promised religious non-interference.

Big idea

  • It spread through north and central India, including Lucknow, Kanpur, Jhansi and Bihar

Read the full explanation

The Revolt of 1857 began at Meerut on 10 May 1857 when sepoys rose against their officers, marched to Delhi and proclaimed the Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar as their leader. It spread through north and central India, including Lucknow, Kanpur, Jhansi and Bihar. Causes included the British policy of annexation: the Doctrine of Lapse devised by Lord Dalhousie annexed states such as Satara and Jhansi, and Awadh was annexed in 1856 on grounds of misgovernment, deposing Nawab Wajid Ali Shah. The Subsidiary Alliance by Wellesley had earlier weakened states. Economic and social discontent included heavy revenue, loss of zamindari rights, and interference with customs. The immediate trigger was the introduction of the Enfield rifle with greased cartridges, rumoured to contain cow and pig fat, which offended Hindu and Muslim sepoys. Mangal Pandey of Barrackpore had acted in March 1857. Leaders included Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi, Nana Sahib at Kanpur, Begum Hazrat Mahal at Lucknow, Kunwar Singh in Bihar and Tatya Tope. The rebels used rumours, prophecies and symbols such as the chapati. The British under Governor-General Canning suppressed the revolt; Delhi was recaptured in September 1857, and Bahadur Shah was exiled to Rangoon. The Government of India Act of 1858 transferred power from the Company to the Crown, and Queen Victoria’s proclamation promised respect for rights and religions. Historians use official reports, rebel proclamations, letters, paintings and memoirs, which carry different perspectives.

💡

Causes

  • Annexation, the Doctrine of Lapse, revenue pressures and the greased cartridge combined to cause the revolt
🧠

Leaders and spread

  • Bahadur Shah, Rani Lakshmibai, Nana Sahib, Begum Hazrat Mahal and Kunwar Singh led resistance in different regions
🌟

Aftermath

  • The Company’s rule ended in 1858
  • The Crown took over and promised religious non-interference

lessons.title: Colonial Cities: Urbanisation, Planning and Architecture
yt: class 12 history theme 12 colonial cities calcutta bombay madras new delhi lutyens baker

blocks.x: Colonial cities grew out of trade settlements and administrative needs. Madras developed around Fort St George from 1639, Bombay from the seven islands given to Charles II as dowry by Portugal in 1661 and leased to the East India Company in 1668, and Calcutta from the village sites of Sutanuti, Kalikata and Govindpur, where Job Charnock settled in 1690 and Fort William was built. These three became Presidency capitals. Cities had a White Town and a Black Town, with the former built around forts. Calcutta’s Lottery Committee of 1817 planned drainage and roads, and Lord Wellesley built Government House. The railways, beginning with the Mumbai-Thane line in 1853, linked ports to hinterlands. Bombay grew as a cotton and shipping centre, housing mill workers in chawls, and the Bombay Improvement Trust was set up in 1898 after the plague of 1896. Census operations began, with the first all-India census in 1872 and regular decennial census from 1881, creating data on population. Hill stations such as Shimla and cantonments were created for British health and security. Public buildings in Gothic, neo-classical and Indo-Saracenic styles, such as the Victoria Terminus and Gateway of India, expressed imperial power. In 1911 at the Delhi Durbar, King George V announced the shift of the capital from Calcutta to Delhi. Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker designed New Delhi, which was inaugurated in 1931. Historians use maps, photographs, census records and municipal reports to study cities.
Deep dive: Presidency cities
Madras, Bombay and Calcutta grew from trading posts into administrative and commercial centres.
Deep dive: Urban planning
Drainage, municipalities, improvement trusts and segregation shaped colonial cities.
Deep dive: Architecture and power
Gothic, neo-classical and Indo-Saracenic buildings, and New Delhi, displayed imperial authority.

Big idea

  • Madras developed around Fort St George from 1639, Bombay from the seven islands given to Charles II as dowry by Portugal in 1661 and leased to the…

Read the full explanation

Colonial cities grew out of trade settlements and administrative needs. Madras developed around Fort St George from 1639, Bombay from the seven islands given to Charles II as dowry by Portugal in 1661 and leased to the East India Company in 1668, and Calcutta from the village sites of Sutanuti, Kalikata and Govindpur, where Job Charnock settled in 1690 and Fort William was built. These three became Presidency capitals. Cities had a White Town and a Black Town, with the former built around forts. Calcutta’s Lottery Committee of 1817 planned drainage and roads, and Lord Wellesley built Government House. The railways, beginning with the Mumbai-Thane line in 1853, linked ports to hinterlands. Bombay grew as a cotton and shipping centre, housing mill workers in chawls, and the Bombay Improvement Trust was set up in 1898 after the plague of 1896. Census operations began, with the first all-India census in 1872 and regular decennial census from 1881, creating data on population. Hill stations such as Shimla and cantonments were created for British health and security. Public buildings in Gothic, neo-classical and Indo-Saracenic styles, such as the Victoria Terminus and Gateway of India, expressed imperial power. In 1911 at the Delhi Durbar, King George V announced the shift of the capital from Calcutta to Delhi. Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker designed New Delhi, which was inaugurated in 1931. Historians use maps, photographs, census records and municipal reports to study cities.

📌

  • Madras, Bombay and Calcutta grew from trading posts into administrative and commercial centres
🧠

Urban planning

  • Drainage, municipalities, improvement trusts and segregation shaped colonial cities
🚀

Architecture and power

  • Gothic, neo-classical and Indo-Saracenic buildings, and New Delhi, displayed imperial authority

lessons.title: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond
yt: class 12 history theme 13 mahatma gandhi nationalist movement champaran non cooperation dandi quit india

blocks.x: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi returned from South Africa in 1915 and was guided by Gopal Krishna Gokhale. In 1916 he spoke at the Banaras Hindu University opening. His early satyagrahas were at Champaran in 1917 for indigo peasants, at Ahmedabad in 1918 for mill workers, with Anasuya Sarabhai, and at Kheda in 1918 for peasants hit by crop failure. The Rowlatt Act of 1919 allowed detention without trial, and Gandhi called a nationwide hartal. On 13 April 1919 General Dyer fired on a crowd at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar. Gandhi linked the Khilafat cause with swaraj and launched the Non-Cooperation Movement in 1920, calling for boycott of courts, schools, councils and foreign cloth. After a mob burned a police station at Chauri Chaura in February 1922, he withdrew the movement. The Lahore session of 1929 under Jawaharlal Nehru adopted the goal of Purna Swaraj, and 26 January 1930 was observed as Independence Day. The Salt Satyagraha began with the Dandi March on 12 March 1930 from Sabarmati to Dandi, where he broke the salt law on 6 April; it began the Civil Disobedience Movement. The Gandhi-Irwin Pact of 1931 led Gandhi to the Second Round Table Conference. The Poona Pact of 1932 between Gandhi and B.R. Ambedkar settled on reserved seats instead of separate electorates for the depressed classes. The Government of India Act 1935 led to provincial elections in 1937. The Cripps Mission of 1942 failed, and the Quit India Movement was launched on 8 August 1942 with the call Do or Die. Historians use Gandhi’s writings, newspaper reports, police records and private letters to study the movement.
Deep dive: Early satyagrahas
Champaran, Ahmedabad and Kheda established Gandhi as a mass leader before 1920.
Deep dive: Mass movements
Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience and Quit India mobilised diverse groups across India.
Deep dive: Compromises
The Gandhi-Irwin Pact and Poona Pact show negotiation alongside protest.

Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond

Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi returned from South Africa in 1915 and was guided by Gopal Krishna Gokhale

🔑

Big idea

  • Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi returned from South Africa in 1915 and was guided by Gopal Krishna Gokhale
  • In 1916 he spoke at the Banaras Hindu University opening
  • His early satyagrahas were at Champaran in 1917 for indigo peasants, at Ahmedabad in 1918 for mill workers, with Anasuya Sarabhai, and at Kheda in…
  • The Rowlatt Act of 1919 allowed detention without trial, and Gandhi called a nationwide hartal
Read the full explanation

Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi returned from South Africa in 1915 and was guided by Gopal Krishna Gokhale. In 1916 he spoke at the Banaras Hindu University opening. His early satyagrahas were at Champaran in 1917 for indigo peasants, at Ahmedabad in 1918 for mill workers, with Anasuya Sarabhai, and at Kheda in 1918 for peasants hit by crop failure. The Rowlatt Act of 1919 allowed detention without trial, and Gandhi called a nationwide hartal. On 13 April 1919 General Dyer fired on a crowd at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar. Gandhi linked the Khilafat cause with swaraj and launched the Non-Cooperation Movement in 1920, calling for boycott of courts, schools, councils and foreign cloth. After a mob burned a police station at Chauri Chaura in February 1922, he withdrew the movement. The Lahore session of 1929 under Jawaharlal Nehru adopted the goal of Purna Swaraj, and 26 January 1930 was observed as Independence Day. The Salt Satyagraha began with the Dandi March on 12 March 1930 from Sabarmati to Dandi, where he broke the salt law on 6 April; it began the Civil Disobedience Movement. The Gandhi-Irwin Pact of 1931 led Gandhi to the Second Round Table Conference. The Poona Pact of 1932 between Gandhi and B.R. Ambedkar settled on reserved seats instead of separate electorates for the depressed classes. The Government of India Act 1935 led to provincial elections in 1937. The Cripps Mission of 1942 failed, and the Quit India Movement was launched on 8 August 1942 with the call Do or Die. Historians use Gandhi’s writings, newspaper reports, police records and private letters to study the movement.

📌

Early satyagrahas

  • Champaran, Ahmedabad and Kheda established Gandhi as a mass leader before 1920
🕰️

Mass movements

  • Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience and Quit India mobilised diverse groups across India
🌟

Compromises

  • The Gandhi-Irwin Pact and Poona Pact show negotiation alongside protest
🎯 Remember Dandi March 12 March 1930; Quit India 8 August 1942.

lessons.title: Understanding Partition: Politics, Memories, Experiences
yt: class 12 history theme 14 understanding partition muslim league lahore resolution direct action day radcliffe oral history

blocks.x: The Partition of India in 1947 was a result of long-term and short-term developments. The Muslim League was founded in 1906. The idea of a separate state was articulated by Muhammad Iqbal in 1930, and the name Pakistan was coined by Choudhary Rahmat Ali in 1933. The two-nation theory was endorsed by the Lahore Resolution of 23 March 1940. The provincial elections of 1937 were a turning point: the Congress formed ministries in most provinces, and the League’s refusal of a coalition in the United Provinces deepened distrust. In the 1945-46 elections, the Congress won general seats and the League won most Muslim seats. The Cabinet Mission of 1946 proposed a loose federation, which was not accepted. The League called Direct Action Day on 16 August 1946, leading to violence in Calcutta. Violence also spread to Noakhali, Bihar and Punjab, and Gandhi went to Noakhali. Lord Mountbatten arrived as viceroy in March 1947, and the 3 June 1947 plan announced the division. The Indian Independence Act was passed on 18 July 1947. The boundaries were drawn by Cyril Radcliffe in a few weeks, and Punjab and Bengal were divided. Pakistan came into being on 14 August and India on 15 August. About fifteen million people were displaced and perhaps a million died. Women suffered abduction, and later recovery operations were controversial. Historians use oral history, letters, diaries, memoirs and fiction such as Saadat Hasan Manto’s stories alongside government records to study Partition. Oral testimony captures ordinary experiences but depends on memory.
Deep dive: Causes
Communal politics, the 1937 elections, the Lahore Resolution and the failure of the Cabinet Mission led to division.
Deep dive: Violence and displacement
Direct Action Day began a cycle of violence, and millions migrated across new borders.
Deep dive: Sources
Oral histories, memoirs and fiction complement official records in understanding Partition.

Understanding Partition: Politics, Memories, Experiences

The Partition of India in 1947 was a result of long-term and short-term developments

🔑

Big idea

  • The Partition of India in 1947 was a result of long-term and short-term developments
  • The Muslim League was founded in 1906
  • The idea of a separate state was articulated by Muhammad Iqbal in 1930, and the name Pakistan was coined by Choudhary Rahmat Ali in 1933

Read the full explanation

The Partition of India in 1947 was a result of long-term and short-term developments. The Muslim League was founded in 1906. The idea of a separate state was articulated by Muhammad Iqbal in 1930, and the name Pakistan was coined by Choudhary Rahmat Ali in 1933. The two-nation theory was endorsed by the Lahore Resolution of 23 March 1940. The provincial elections of 1937 were a turning point: the Congress formed ministries in most provinces, and the League’s refusal of a coalition in the United Provinces deepened distrust. In the 1945-46 elections, the Congress won general seats and the League won most Muslim seats. The Cabinet Mission of 1946 proposed a loose federation, which was not accepted. The League called Direct Action Day on 16 August 1946, leading to violence in Calcutta. Violence also spread to Noakhali, Bihar and Punjab, and Gandhi went to Noakhali. Lord Mountbatten arrived as viceroy in March 1947, and the 3 June 1947 plan announced the division. The Indian Independence Act was passed on 18 July 1947. The boundaries were drawn by Cyril Radcliffe in a few weeks, and Punjab and Bengal were divided. Pakistan came into being on 14 August and India on 15 August. About fifteen million people were displaced and perhaps a million died. Women suffered abduction, and later recovery operations were controversial. Historians use oral history, letters, diaries, memoirs and fiction such as Saadat Hasan Manto’s stories alongside government records to study Partition. Oral testimony captures ordinary experiences but depends on memory.

💡

Causes

  • Communal politics, the 1937 elections, the Lahore Resolution and the failure of the Cabinet Mission led to division
🧠

Violence and displacement

  • Direct Action Day began a cycle of violence, and millions migrated across new borders
🌟

Sources

  • Oral histories, memoirs and fiction complement official records in understanding Partition
🎯 Remember Lahore Resolution 1940; Direct Action Day 16 Aug 1946; Radcliffe drew boundaries.

lessons.title: Framing the Constitution: The Beginning of a New Era
yt: class 12 history theme 15 framing the constitution constituent assembly ambedkar objectives resolution

blocks.x: The Constituent Assembly was formed in 1946 under the Cabinet Mission plan, with members elected indirectly by provincial assemblies, and met first on 9 December 1946. Rajendra Prasad was elected its president. The Assembly at first had about 300 members; after Partition it was reduced to about 299. The Muslim League members from areas that became Pakistan left, and Dr. B.R. Ambedkar was elected chairman of the Drafting Committee in August 1947. B.N. Rau served as the constitutional adviser. Jawaharlal Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution on 13 December 1946, which declared India an independent sovereign republic and promised justice, equality and freedom; it was adopted on 22 January 1947. The Assembly took two years, eleven months and eighteen days, with eleven sessions. The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into effect on 26 January 1950. Members debated key issues: separate electorates, which were opposed by many members after Partition; the powers of the Centre and states, with a strong Centre favoured; language, with the Munshi-Ayyangar formula settling on Hindi in Devanagari script as the official language with English continuing for fifteen years; and fundamental rights, which Sardar Patel and others discussed in committees. Women members included Hansa Mehta and Durgabai Deshmukh, and Jaipal Singh spoke for adivasis. The Assembly drew on the Government of India Act 1935 and models from other countries. Historians use Constituent Assembly Debates to understand the thinking behind the Constitution.
Deep dive: Making of the Assembly
Elected indirectly in 1946, the Assembly met on 9 December 1946 with Rajendra Prasad as president.
Deep dive: Key debates
Separate electorates, federalism, language and rights were hotly debated before compromises were reached.
Deep dive: Outcome
The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950.

Big idea

Read the full explanation

The Constituent Assembly was formed in 1946 under the Cabinet Mission plan, with members elected indirectly by provincial assemblies, and met first on 9 December 1946. Rajendra Prasad was elected its president. The Assembly at first had about 300 members; after Partition it was reduced to about 299. The Muslim League members from areas that became Pakistan left, and Dr. B.R. Ambedkar was elected chairman of the Drafting Committee in August 1947. B.N. Rau served as the constitutional adviser. Jawaharlal Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution on 13 December 1946, which declared India an independent sovereign republic and promised justice, equality and freedom; it was adopted on 22 January 1947. The Assembly took two years, eleven months and eighteen days, with eleven sessions. The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into effect on 26 January 1950. Members debated key issues: separate electorates, which were opposed by many members after Partition; the powers of the Centre and states, with a strong Centre favoured; language, with the Munshi-Ayyangar formula settling on Hindi in Devanagari script as the official language with English continuing for fifteen years; and fundamental rights, which Sardar Patel and others discussed in committees. Women members included Hansa Mehta and Durgabai Deshmukh, and Jaipal Singh spoke for adivasis. The Assembly drew on the Government of India Act 1935 and models from other countries. Historians use Constituent Assembly Debates to understand the thinking behind the Constitution.

📌

Making of the Assembly

  • Elected indirectly in 1946, the Assembly met on 9 December 1946 with Rajendra Prasad as president
🧠

Key debates

  • Separate electorates, federalism, language and rights were hotly debated before compromises were reached
🌟

Outcome

  • The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950

lessons.title: Data Handling using Pandas: Series
yt: class 12 informatics practices pandas series creation indexing slicing attributes methods

blocks.x: Pandas is a Python library for data analysis, imported as import pandas as pd. A Series is a one-dimensional labelled array that can hold any data type. A Series has an index (labels) and values; the default index is 0, 1, 2 and so on. A Series is created with pd.Series(data, index=...) from a list, a dictionary, a NumPy array or a scalar. If created from a dictionary, the keys become the index. If a scalar is given, an index must be supplied and the value is repeated. A Series has attributes such as index, values, dtype, shape, size, nbytes, ndim, hasnans, empty and name. Elements are accessed by label using s[label] or s.loc[label], and by position using s.iloc[position]. Slicing by position excludes the end, as in s[1:3], whereas slicing with labels includes the end. Boolean indexing selects values by a condition. Methods include head(n), tail(n), count(), and the arithmetic operations, which are aligned on the index; if labels do not match, the result is NaN. NaN stands for not a number and marks missing data. Series can be modified by assignment, and elements can be deleted using drop(). Vector operations apply to the whole Series, such as s * 2. Common functions include sum(), mean(), min(), max() and describe(), and a name can be given to the Series using the name attribute. The mean ignores NaN values by default.
Deep dive: Creating Series
A Series can be created from a list, dictionary, array or scalar, with an optional custom index.
Deep dive: Accessing data
Use labels with loc, positions with iloc, and conditions for boolean selection; positional slices exclude the end.
Deep dive: Operations
Arithmetic aligns by index and produces NaN for unmatched labels; head and tail view the ends.

Pandas Series: ek-aayami labelled array; index, values, attributes, slicing aur arithmetic.
Remember: positional slice excludes the end; label slice includes it.
