Visual lesson

Data Handling using Pandas: Series

Pandas is a Python library for data analysis, imported as import pandas as pd

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Creating Series›3Accessing data›4Operations
🔑

Big idea

  • Pandas is a Python library for data analysis, imported as import pandas as pd
  • A Series is a one-dimensional labelled array that can hold any data type
  • A Series has an index (labels) and values
  • The default index is 0, 1, 2 and so on
Read the full explanation

Pandas is a Python library for data analysis, imported as import pandas as pd. A Series is a one-dimensional labelled array that can hold any data type. A Series has an index (labels) and values; the default index is 0, 1, 2 and so on. A Series is created with pd.Series(data, index=...) from a list, a dictionary, a NumPy array or a scalar. If created from a dictionary, the keys become the index. If a scalar is given, an index must be supplied and the value is repeated. A Series has attributes such as index, values, dtype, shape, size, nbytes, ndim, hasnans, empty and name. Elements are accessed by label using s[label] or s.loc[label], and by position using s.iloc[position]. Slicing by position excludes the end, as in s[1:3], whereas slicing with labels includes the end. Boolean indexing selects values by a condition. Methods include head(n), tail(n), count(), and the arithmetic operations, which are aligned on the index; if labels do not match, the result is NaN. NaN stands for not a number and marks missing data. Series can be modified by assignment, and elements can be deleted using drop(). Vector operations apply to the whole Series, such as s * 2. Common functions include sum(), mean(), min(), max() and describe(), and a name can be given to the Series using the name attribute. The mean ignores NaN values by default.

📌

Creating Series

  • A Series can be created from a list, dictionary, array or scalar, with an optional custom index
🧠

Accessing data

  • Use labels with loc, positions with iloc, and conditions for boolean selection
  • Positional slices exclude the end
🌟

Operations

  • Arithmetic aligns by index and produces NaN for unmatched labels
  • Head and tail view the ends
🧮

blocks.x: A DataFrame is a two-dimensional labelled data structure with rows and columns, like a table. Each column is a Series, columns can hold different types, and both rows and columns can be labelled. A DataFrame is created with pd.DataFrame(data, index=..., columns=...) from a dictionary of lists, a list of dictionaries, a list of lists, a dictionary of Series or a NumPy array. Dictionary keys become column names, and with a list of dictionaries, missing keys become NaN. Attributes include index, columns, axes, dtypes, shape, size, values, ndim, T (transpose), empty and head/tail methods. A column is selected by df['col'] or df.col, and several columns with a list df[['a','b']]. Rows and cells are selected with loc by label and iloc by position. df.loc[row, col] selects a cell, df.loc[:, 'col'] selects a column, and df.iloc[0:2] selects the first two rows by position. A new column is added by assignment, df['new'] = values, while a new row is added with loc, for example df.loc['r'] = [..]. Rows and columns are deleted using drop with axis 0 for rows and 1 for columns. A column can be renamed with rename(columns={...}). Boolean indexing filters rows, as in df[df['marks'] > 80]. Data is read from CSV with pd.read_csv('file.csv') and written with to_csv('file.csv'), where index=False omits the index. The shape attribute gives (rows, columns). Iteration over rows is done with iterrows or itertuples, and over columns with iteritems or items.
Deep dive: Creating DataFrames
A dictionary of lists or Series, a list of dictionaries and arrays can create a DataFrame.
Deep dive: Selecting and changing
Use column names, loc and iloc to select; assignment adds columns; drop deletes rows or columns.
Deep dive: CSV files
read_csv loads data from a CSV file and to_csv saves a DataFrame, optionally without the index.

Visual lesson

Data Handling using Pandas: DataFrame

A DataFrame is a two-dimensional labelled data structure with rows and columns, like a table

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Creating DataFrames›3Selecting and changing›4CSV files
🔑

Big idea

  • A DataFrame is a two-dimensional labelled data structure with rows and columns, like a table
  • Each column is a Series, columns can hold different types, and both rows and columns can be labelled
  • A DataFrame is created with pd.DataFrame(data, index=..., columns=...) from a dictionary of lists, a list of dictionaries, a list of lists, a…
  • Dictionary keys become column names, and with a list of dictionaries, missing keys become NaN
Read the full explanation

A DataFrame is a two-dimensional labelled data structure with rows and columns, like a table. Each column is a Series, columns can hold different types, and both rows and columns can be labelled. A DataFrame is created with pd.DataFrame(data, index=..., columns=...) from a dictionary of lists, a list of dictionaries, a list of lists, a dictionary of Series or a NumPy array. Dictionary keys become column names, and with a list of dictionaries, missing keys become NaN. Attributes include index, columns, axes, dtypes, shape, size, values, ndim, T (transpose), empty and head/tail methods. A column is selected by df['col'] or df.col, and several columns with a list df[['a','b']]. Rows and cells are selected with loc by label and iloc by position. df.loc[row, col] selects a cell, df.loc[:, 'col'] selects a column, and df.iloc[0:2] selects the first two rows by position. A new column is added by assignment, df['new'] = values, while a new row is added with loc, for example df.loc['r'] = [..]. Rows and columns are deleted using drop with axis 0 for rows and 1 for columns. A column can be renamed with rename(columns={...}). Boolean indexing filters rows, as in df[df['marks'] > 80]. Data is read from CSV with pd.read_csv('file.csv') and written with to_csv('file.csv'), where index=False omits the index. The shape attribute gives (rows, columns). Iteration over rows is done with iterrows or itertuples, and over columns with iteritems or items.

📌

Creating DataFrames

  • A dictionary of lists or Series, a list of dictionaries and arrays can create a DataFrame
🧠

Selecting and changing

  • Use column names, loc and iloc to select
  • Assignment adds columns
  • Drop deletes rows or columns
🌟

CSV files

  • Read_csv loads data from a CSV file and to_csv saves a DataFrame, optionally without the index
🧮

lessons.title: Data Handling using Pandas: Analysis, Statistics and Aggregation
yt: class 12 informatics practices pandas statistics groupby aggregate sort descriptive pivot missing values

blocks.x: Pandas supports data analysis using statistical functions. Descriptive statistics include sum, mean, median, mode, min, max, std, var, count and quantile. describe() gives count, mean, std, min, quartiles and max for numeric columns. Most functions take axis, where axis=0 works down columns and axis=1 across rows, and skipna=True ignores NaN by default. Sorting uses sort_values(by=..., ascending=...) and sort_index(). Missing data is handled with isnull(), notnull(), dropna() and fillna(value). Duplicates are managed with duplicated() and drop_duplicates(). The groupby() method splits data into groups by a column, then applies an aggregate such as sum, mean or count, as in df.groupby('class')['marks'].mean(). The agg() method applies several functions. Pivot tables summarise data by index and columns with a function. The apply() method applies a function along an axis, and map or applymap apply functions to elements. Data can be merged with merge() on a common column, and concatenated with pd.concat() along rows or columns. Selection by conditions can combine tests with & and |, each condition in brackets. The unique() and nunique() functions find distinct values, and value_counts() counts them. Rank, cumsum and cumprod give cumulative measures. Indexing tools like set_index and reset_index change the index. Reading and cleaning data is a key step before analysis.
Deep dive: Descriptive statistics
sum, mean, median, std, min, max and describe summarise numeric columns; axis picks direction.
Deep dive: Cleaning
isnull, dropna, fillna and drop_duplicates prepare data for analysis.
Deep dive: Grouping and combining
groupby with aggregates summarises data by category; merge and concat combine DataFrames.
Hindi saransh
Pandas ke statistical function, sorting, missing values, groupby, merge aur concat se data vishleshan.
Remember: use & and | with brackets for multiple conditions.

Visual lesson

Data Handling using Pandas: Analysis, Statistics and Aggregation

Pandas supports data analysis using statistical functions

🔑

Big idea

  • Pandas supports data analysis using statistical functions
  • Descriptive statistics include sum, mean, median, mode, min, max, std, var, count and quantile
  • Describe() gives count, mean, std, min, quartiles and max for numeric columns
  • Most functions take axis, where axis=0 works down columns and axis=1 across rows, and skipna=True ignores NaN by default
Read the full explanation

Pandas supports data analysis using statistical functions. Descriptive statistics include sum, mean, median, mode, min, max, std, var, count and quantile. describe() gives count, mean, std, min, quartiles and max for numeric columns. Most functions take axis, where axis=0 works down columns and axis=1 across rows, and skipna=True ignores NaN by default. Sorting uses sort_values(by=..., ascending=...) and sort_index(). Missing data is handled with isnull(), notnull(), dropna() and fillna(value). Duplicates are managed with duplicated() and drop_duplicates(). The groupby() method splits data into groups by a column, then applies an aggregate such as sum, mean or count, as in df.groupby('class')['marks'].mean(). The agg() method applies several functions. Pivot tables summarise data by index and columns with a function. The apply() method applies a function along an axis, and map or applymap apply functions to elements. Data can be merged with merge() on a common column, and concatenated with pd.concat() along rows or columns. Selection by conditions can combine tests with & and |, each condition in brackets. The unique() and nunique() functions find distinct values, and value_counts() counts them. Rank, cumsum and cumprod give cumulative measures. Indexing tools like set_index and reset_index change the index. Reading and cleaning data is a key step before analysis.

📌

Descriptive statistics

  • Sum, mean, median, std, min, max and describe summarise numeric columns
  • Axis picks direction
🧠

Cleaning

  • Isnull, dropna, fillna and drop_duplicates prepare data for analysis
🌟

Grouping and combining

  • Groupby with aggregates summarises data by category
  • Merge and concat combine DataFrames

lessons.title: Data Visualisation using Matplotlib
yt: class 12 informatics practices matplotlib pyplot line bar histogram plot labels legend savefig

blocks.x: Data visualisation presents data graphically so that patterns can be seen. Matplotlib is a Python library, and pyplot is its module imported as import matplotlib.pyplot as plt. A line chart is drawn by plt.plot(x, y) and is used for trends over time. A bar chart is drawn by plt.bar(x, height) for comparing categories, and plt.barh draws horizontal bars. A histogram, drawn by plt.hist(data, bins=...), shows the frequency distribution of continuous data in intervals. A scatter plot uses plt.scatter, and a pie chart uses plt.pie. Labels and titles are added with plt.xlabel, plt.ylabel and plt.title. A legend is added with plt.legend and needs a label argument in each plot. Grid lines are shown with plt.grid. The figure is displayed with plt.show and saved with plt.savefig(filename). The format of lines can be changed with colour, linewidth, linestyle and marker arguments, such as plt.plot(x, y, color='r', linestyle='--', marker='o'). Axis limits are set with plt.xlim and plt.ylim, and ticks with plt.xticks and plt.yticks. Several plots can be drawn on the same axes, and the figure size can be set with plt.figure(figsize=(w, h)). Bar width is set with the width argument, and histogram types include bar and step. A DataFrame can also be plotted using df.plot(kind=...). Choosing the right chart type depends on the data, as line charts suit change over time while bar charts suit comparison.
Deep dive: Chart types
Line charts show trends, bar charts compare categories, histograms show distributions, and pie charts show parts of a whole.
Deep dive: Customising plots
Titles, axis labels, legends, colours, markers and grid lines make a chart clear and informative.
Deep dive: Saving
plt.show displays a chart, and plt.savefig saves it to a file.
Hindi saransh
Matplotlib: line, bar, histogram, scatter, pie; title, label, legend aur savefig.
Remember: call plt.savefig before plt.show to save a full figure.

Visual lesson

Data Visualisation using Matplotlib

Data visualisation presents data graphically so that patterns can be seen

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Chart types›3Customising plots›4Saving
🔑

Big idea

  • Data visualisation presents data graphically so that patterns can be seen
  • Matplotlib is a Python library, and pyplot is its module imported as import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
  • A line chart is drawn by plt.plot(x, y) and is used for trends over time
  • A bar chart is drawn by plt.bar(x, height) for comparing categories, and plt.barh draws horizontal bars
Read the full explanation

Data visualisation presents data graphically so that patterns can be seen. Matplotlib is a Python library, and pyplot is its module imported as import matplotlib.pyplot as plt. A line chart is drawn by plt.plot(x, y) and is used for trends over time. A bar chart is drawn by plt.bar(x, height) for comparing categories, and plt.barh draws horizontal bars. A histogram, drawn by plt.hist(data, bins=...), shows the frequency distribution of continuous data in intervals. A scatter plot uses plt.scatter, and a pie chart uses plt.pie. Labels and titles are added with plt.xlabel, plt.ylabel and plt.title. A legend is added with plt.legend and needs a label argument in each plot. Grid lines are shown with plt.grid. The figure is displayed with plt.show and saved with plt.savefig(filename). The format of lines can be changed with colour, linewidth, linestyle and marker arguments, such as plt.plot(x, y, color='r', linestyle='--', marker='o'). Axis limits are set with plt.xlim and plt.ylim, and ticks with plt.xticks and plt.yticks. Several plots can be drawn on the same axes, and the figure size can be set with plt.figure(figsize=(w, h)). Bar width is set with the width argument, and histogram types include bar and step. A DataFrame can also be plotted using df.plot(kind=...). Choosing the right chart type depends on the data, as line charts suit change over time while bar charts suit comparison.

📌

Chart types

  • Line charts show trends, bar charts compare categories, histograms show distributions, and pie charts show parts of a whole
🧠

Customising plots

  • Titles, axis labels, legends, colours, markers and grid lines make a chart clear and informative
🌟

Saving

  • Plt.show displays a chart, and plt.savefig saves it to a file
🧮

Formula tiles

Importimport matplotlib.pyplot as plt
Lineplt.plot(x, y)
Barplt.bar(x, h)
Histogramplt.hist(d, bins=n)
Saveplt.savefig('a.png')
🎯 Remember call plt.savefig before plt.show to save a full figure.

lessons.title: SQL: Database Concepts, DDL and DML
yt: class 12 informatics practices sql create table insert select update delete where constraints

blocks.x: A database is an organised collection of data, and a relational database stores data in tables or relations made of rows (tuples) and columns (attributes). A Database Management System, such as MySQL, manages it. SQL, Structured Query Language, is used to define and manipulate data. Data Definition Language (DDL) commands create and alter structure: CREATE DATABASE, USE, CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE and DROP TABLE. Data Manipulation Language (DML) commands include INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and SELECT. Common data types are INT, DECIMAL, CHAR, VARCHAR, DATE and FLOAT. Constraints include PRIMARY KEY, which uniquely identifies a row and cannot be null, NOT NULL, UNIQUE, DEFAULT and FOREIGN KEY. A candidate key can be a primary key, and an alternate key is a candidate key not chosen. A foreign key refers to the primary key of another table and maintains referential integrity. The degree of a table is the number of columns and the cardinality is the number of rows. The SELECT statement retrieves rows: SELECT * FROM student; SELECT name, marks FROM student WHERE marks > 80;. The WHERE clause uses relational operators, logical operators AND, OR, NOT, and BETWEEN, IN and LIKE. LIKE uses % for any number of characters and _ for exactly one. IS NULL checks for missing values. ORDER BY sorts results in ASC or DESC order, and DISTINCT removes duplicates. INSERT INTO table VALUES (...) adds a row, UPDATE table SET col = value WHERE condition changes data, and DELETE FROM table WHERE condition removes rows. ALTER TABLE can add a column or change a data type.
Deep dive: DDL and DML
DDL defines structure with CREATE, ALTER and DROP; DML handles data with INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and SELECT.
Deep dive: Keys and constraints
Primary key, foreign key, unique and not null constraints keep data correct and linked.
Deep dive: Querying
SELECT with WHERE, LIKE, BETWEEN, IN, ORDER BY and DISTINCT retrieves exactly the needed rows.

Visual lesson

SQL: Database Concepts, DDL and DML

A database is an organised collection of data, and a relational database stores data in tables or relations made of rows (tuples) and columns (attributes)

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2DDL and DML›3Keys and constraints›4Querying
🔑

Big idea

  • A database is an organised collection of data, and a relational database stores data in tables or relations made of rows (tuples) and columns…
  • A Database Management System, such as MySQL, manages it
  • SQL, Structured Query Language, is used to define and manipulate data
  • Data Definition Language (DDL) commands create and alter structure: CREATE DATABASE, USE, CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE and DROP TABLE
Read the full explanation

A database is an organised collection of data, and a relational database stores data in tables or relations made of rows (tuples) and columns (attributes). A Database Management System, such as MySQL, manages it. SQL, Structured Query Language, is used to define and manipulate data. Data Definition Language (DDL) commands create and alter structure: CREATE DATABASE, USE, CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE and DROP TABLE. Data Manipulation Language (DML) commands include INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and SELECT. Common data types are INT, DECIMAL, CHAR, VARCHAR, DATE and FLOAT. Constraints include PRIMARY KEY, which uniquely identifies a row and cannot be null, NOT NULL, UNIQUE, DEFAULT and FOREIGN KEY. A candidate key can be a primary key, and an alternate key is a candidate key not chosen. A foreign key refers to the primary key of another table and maintains referential integrity. The degree of a table is the number of columns and the cardinality is the number of rows. The SELECT statement retrieves rows: SELECT * FROM student; SELECT name, marks FROM student WHERE marks > 80;. The WHERE clause uses relational operators, logical operators AND, OR, NOT, and BETWEEN, IN and LIKE. LIKE uses % for any number of characters and _ for exactly one. IS NULL checks for missing values. ORDER BY sorts results in ASC or DESC order, and DISTINCT removes duplicates. INSERT INTO table VALUES (...) adds a row, UPDATE table SET col = value WHERE condition changes data, and DELETE FROM table WHERE condition removes rows. ALTER TABLE can add a column or change a data type.

📌

DDL and DML

  • DDL defines structure with CREATE, ALTER and DROP
  • DML handles data with INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and SELECT
🧠

Keys and constraints

  • Primary key, foreign key, unique and not null constraints keep data correct and linked
🌟

Querying

  • SELECT with WHERE, LIKE, BETWEEN, IN, ORDER BY and DISTINCT retrieves exactly the needed rows
🧮

Formula tiles

InsertINSERT INTO t VALUES (...);
UpdateUPDATE t SET c=v WHERE cond;
DeleteDELETE FROM t WHERE cond;
SortORDER BY col DESC;
🎯 Remember % matches any number of characters; _ matches exactly one.

lessons.title: SQL: Functions, GROUP BY, HAVING and Joins
yt: class 12 informatics practices sql functions aggregate group by having join cartesian product

blocks.x: SQL has single-row functions and multi-row (aggregate) functions. Single-row functions include numeric ones like POWER, ROUND and MOD, text ones like UPPER, LOWER, LENGTH, LEFT, RIGHT, MID, INSTR, LTRIM, RTRIM and TRIM, and date functions like NOW, DATE, MONTH, YEAR, DAYNAME and DAYOFMONTH. Aggregate functions work on a set of rows and return one value: MAX, MIN, AVG, SUM and COUNT; COUNT(*) counts all rows while COUNT(column) ignores NULL. The GROUP BY clause groups rows with the same value in a column, and aggregate functions are applied to each group. The HAVING clause filters groups after aggregation, whereas WHERE filters rows before grouping. For example, SELECT dept, AVG(salary) FROM emp GROUP BY dept HAVING AVG(salary) > 50000; The ORDER BY clause comes after GROUP BY and HAVING. A join combines rows from two or more tables. A Cartesian product pairs every row of one table with every row of another, giving cardinality m x n and degree a + b. An equi-join combines tables on equality of a column, using WHERE t1.col = t2.col or JOIN ... ON. A natural join joins tables on common columns and removes duplicate columns. Table aliases shorten queries. The usual order of clauses is SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING and ORDER BY. NULL values are ignored by aggregates except COUNT(*).
Deep dive: Functions
Single-row functions work on each value; aggregate functions return one value per group.
Deep dive: Grouping
GROUP BY forms groups; HAVING filters groups, WHERE filters rows.
Deep dive: Joins
Cartesian product pairs all rows; equi-join and natural join combine tables on matching columns.

Visual lesson

SQL: Functions, GROUP BY, HAVING and Joins

SQL has single-row functions and multi-row (aggregate) functions

Flat concept map (2D)

Group filterHAVING COUNT(*) > 2
🔑

Big idea

  • SQL has single-row functions and multi-row (aggregate) functions
  • Single-row functions include numeric ones like POWER, ROUND and MOD, text ones like UPPER, LOWER, LENGTH, LEFT, RIGHT, MID, INSTR, LTRIM, RTRIM and…
  • Aggregate functions work on a set of rows and return one value: MAX, MIN, AVG, SUM and COUNT
  • COUNT(*) counts all rows while COUNT(column) ignores NULL
Read the full explanation

SQL has single-row functions and multi-row (aggregate) functions. Single-row functions include numeric ones like POWER, ROUND and MOD, text ones like UPPER, LOWER, LENGTH, LEFT, RIGHT, MID, INSTR, LTRIM, RTRIM and TRIM, and date functions like NOW, DATE, MONTH, YEAR, DAYNAME and DAYOFMONTH. Aggregate functions work on a set of rows and return one value: MAX, MIN, AVG, SUM and COUNT; COUNT(*) counts all rows while COUNT(column) ignores NULL. The GROUP BY clause groups rows with the same value in a column, and aggregate functions are applied to each group. The HAVING clause filters groups after aggregation, whereas WHERE filters rows before grouping. For example, SELECT dept, AVG(salary) FROM emp GROUP BY dept HAVING AVG(salary) > 50000; The ORDER BY clause comes after GROUP BY and HAVING. A join combines rows from two or more tables. A Cartesian product pairs every row of one table with every row of another, giving cardinality m x n and degree a + b. An equi-join combines tables on equality of a column, using WHERE t1.col = t2.col or JOIN ... ON. A natural join joins tables on common columns and removes duplicate columns. Table aliases shorten queries. The usual order of clauses is SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING and ORDER BY. NULL values are ignored by aggregates except COUNT(*).

📌

Functions

  • Single-row functions work on each value
  • Aggregate functions return one value per group
🧠

Grouping

  • GROUP BY forms groups
  • HAVING filters groups, WHERE filters rows
🌟

Joins

  • Cartesian product pairs all rows
  • Equi-join and natural join combine tables on matching columns

lessons.title: Introduction to Computer Networks
yt: class 12 informatics practices computer networks lan wan topology router switch ip address dns protocols

blocks.x: A computer network is a set of interconnected devices that share data and resources. ARPANET, started in 1969, was the first major network and led to the Internet. Networks are classified by size: PAN covers a person’s devices, LAN a building or campus, MAN a city and WAN a large area such as a country; the Internet is a network of networks. Topology is the arrangement of nodes: bus uses a single backbone cable, star connects nodes to a central hub or switch, ring connects nodes in a loop, tree is a hierarchy of stars, and mesh connects nodes to many others. Star is common because a failure of one node does not affect others, but the central device is a single point of failure. Devices include the modem, which converts digital to analogue signals and back, hub, which broadcasts to all ports, switch, which forwards to the intended port, router, which connects networks and routes packets, repeater, which regenerates signals, and gateway, which connects different network types. Media may be wired (twisted pair, coaxial, optical fibre) or wireless (radio waves, microwave, infrared, satellite, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth). Every device has a 48-bit MAC address. An IP address identifies a device on a network: IPv4 is 32 bits and IPv6 is 128 bits. The Domain Name System (DNS) translates domain names to IP addresses. A URL is the address of a web resource. Protocols are rules for communication: HTTP and HTTPS for web pages, FTP for file transfer, SMTP, POP3 and IMAP for email, TCP/IP for the Internet, and VoIP for voice. The World Wide Web, invented by Tim Berners-Lee, is a service on the Internet. Bandwidth is the data capacity of a link, measured in bits per second. Cloud computing and the Internet of Things are modern trends.
Deep dive: Types and topologies
PAN, LAN, MAN and WAN differ by size; bus, star, ring, tree and mesh differ by layout.
Deep dive: Devices and media
Modems, hubs, switches, routers, repeaters and gateways connect devices over wired or wireless media.
Deep dive: Addresses and protocols
IP and MAC addresses identify devices, DNS maps names, and protocols like HTTP, SMTP and FTP define communication.

Read the full explanation

A computer network is a set of interconnected devices that share data and resources. ARPANET, started in 1969, was the first major network and led to the Internet. Networks are classified by size: PAN covers a person’s devices, LAN a building or campus, MAN a city and WAN a large area such as a country; the Internet is a network of networks. Topology is the arrangement of nodes: bus uses a single backbone cable, star connects nodes to a central hub or switch, ring connects nodes in a loop, tree is a hierarchy of stars, and mesh connects nodes to many others. Star is common because a failure of one node does not affect others, but the central device is a single point of failure. Devices include the modem, which converts digital to analogue signals and back, hub, which broadcasts to all ports, switch, which forwards to the intended port, router, which connects networks and routes packets, repeater, which regenerates signals, and gateway, which connects different network types. Media may be wired (twisted pair, coaxial, optical fibre) or wireless (radio waves, microwave, infrared, satellite, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth). Every device has a 48-bit MAC address. An IP address identifies a device on a network: IPv4 is 32 bits and IPv6 is 128 bits. The Domain Name System (DNS) translates domain names to IP addresses. A URL is the address of a web resource. Protocols are rules for communication: HTTP and HTTPS for web pages, FTP for file transfer, SMTP, POP3 and IMAP for email, TCP/IP for the Internet, and VoIP for voice. The World Wide Web, invented by Tim Berners-Lee, is a service on the Internet. Bandwidth is the data capacity of a link, measured in bits per second. Cloud computing and the Internet of Things are modern trends.

📌

Types and topologies

  • PAN, LAN, MAN and WAN differ by size
  • Bus, star, ring, tree and mesh differ by layout
🧠

Devices and media

  • Modems, hubs, switches, routers, repeaters and gateways connect devices over wired or wireless media
🌟

Addresses and protocols

  • IP and MAC addresses identify devices, DNS maps names, and protocols like HTTP, SMTP and FTP define communication

lessons.title: Societal Impacts: Digital Footprint, Cyber Safety, IPR and E-waste
yt: class 12 informatics practices societal impacts digital footprint cyber crime it act ipr plagiarism e waste

blocks.x: Digital technology has social and ethical impacts. A digital footprint is the trail of data left by online activity. An active footprint is data given deliberately, like posts or forms, while a passive footprint is collected without the user acting, like cookies or IP logs. Netiquette is courteous online behaviour. Cyberbullying is harassment online. Cyber crime includes hacking, phishing (fraudulent emails or sites to steal data), identity theft, ransomware, spam and eavesdropping. Safety measures include strong passwords, two-factor authentication, firewalls, antivirus and caution with links. The Information Technology Act, 2000, amended in 2008, is the main cyber law of India, recognising electronic records and digital signatures and defining cyber offences. Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) protect creations of the mind: copyright covers original literary, artistic and software works; patents protect inventions; trademarks protect brand identifiers. Plagiarism is presenting someone else’s work as one’s own. Software licences include proprietary and Free and Open Source Software (FOSS); the GNU General Public License and Creative Commons licences allow sharing under conditions. Electronic waste, e-waste, is discarded electronic devices, and it contains hazardous materials such as lead and mercury; the 3Rs of reduce, reuse and recycle apply. The digital divide is the gap between those with and without access to technology. E-governance delivers government services online, with examples like Aadhaar and DigiLocker. Health issues include eye strain and repetitive strain injury, and ergonomics helps. Data protection and privacy are growing concerns.
Deep dive: Digital footprint and safety
Active and passive footprints persist; strong passwords and caution protect users.
Deep dive: Cyber law and IPR
The IT Act 2000 defines cyber offences, and copyright, patents and trademarks protect creations.
Deep dive: E-waste and divide
E-waste needs safe disposal, and the digital divide shows unequal access to technology.

Societal Impacts: Digital Footprint, Cyber Safety, IPR and E-waste

Digital technology has social and ethical impacts

🔑

Big idea

  • Digital technology has social and ethical impacts
  • A digital footprint is the trail of data left by online activity
  • An active footprint is data given deliberately, like posts or forms, while a passive footprint is collected without the user acting, like cookies or…
  • Netiquette is courteous online behaviour
Read the full explanation

Digital technology has social and ethical impacts. A digital footprint is the trail of data left by online activity. An active footprint is data given deliberately, like posts or forms, while a passive footprint is collected without the user acting, like cookies or IP logs. Netiquette is courteous online behaviour. Cyberbullying is harassment online. Cyber crime includes hacking, phishing (fraudulent emails or sites to steal data), identity theft, ransomware, spam and eavesdropping. Safety measures include strong passwords, two-factor authentication, firewalls, antivirus and caution with links. The Information Technology Act, 2000, amended in 2008, is the main cyber law of India, recognising electronic records and digital signatures and defining cyber offences. Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) protect creations of the mind: copyright covers original literary, artistic and software works; patents protect inventions; trademarks protect brand identifiers. Plagiarism is presenting someone else’s work as one’s own. Software licences include proprietary and Free and Open Source Software (FOSS); the GNU General Public License and Creative Commons licences allow sharing under conditions. Electronic waste, e-waste, is discarded electronic devices, and it contains hazardous materials such as lead and mercury; the 3Rs of reduce, reuse and recycle apply. The digital divide is the gap between those with and without access to technology. E-governance delivers government services online, with examples like Aadhaar and DigiLocker. Health issues include eye strain and repetitive strain injury, and ergonomics helps. Data protection and privacy are growing concerns.

📌

Digital footprint and safety

  • Active and passive footprints persist
  • Strong passwords and caution protect users
⚖️

Cyber law and IPR

  • The IT Act 2000 defines cyber offences, and copyright, patents and trademarks protect creations
🌟

  • E-waste needs safe disposal, and the digital divide shows unequal access to technology

lessons.title: Project Work: Planning, Development and Viva
yt: class 12 informatics practices project work data analysis python pandas matplotlib mysql report viva

blocks.x: The Informatics Practices project applies skills learned in the course to a real problem. A good project follows stages: identify a problem, collect or choose a dataset, plan the design, develop the solution, test it and document the work. Typical project themes include analysis of student marks, sales data, weather records or health statistics. The data may be stored in a CSV file or MySQL database. Using Python, data is loaded into a Pandas DataFrame, cleaned by handling missing values and duplicates, and analysed using statistics, sorting, filtering and groupby. Results are visualised using Matplotlib charts such as line, bar and histogram, with titles, labels and legends. A database-based project uses SQL for queries, with tables and keys properly designed. The software development life cycle includes analysis, design, coding, testing, deployment and maintenance. The project report generally contains a title page, certificate, acknowledgement, index, introduction, objectives, system requirements, hardware and software used, source code with comments, sample output, conclusion, future scope and bibliography. Good coding practice involves meaningful variable names, comments, functions and modular design. Testing checks that the program gives correct results for normal and boundary inputs. During the viva, students are asked about the problem, dataset, libraries used, functions, queries and results. Honest citation of data sources and avoiding plagiarism are essential. Team projects need clear division of work and version control helps manage code. A project should be original, relevant and well documented.
Deep dive: Project stages
Identify a problem, choose data, design, code, test and document the work step by step.
Deep dive: Technical content
Use Pandas for cleaning and analysis, Matplotlib for charts and SQL for database queries.
Deep dive: Report and viva
The report documents the work; viva questions test understanding of data, code and results.
Hindi saransh
Project: samasya chunna, data, Pandas, Matplotlib, SQL, report aur viva ki taiyari.
Remember: be ready to explain every line of your code in the viva.

Read the full explanation

The Informatics Practices project applies skills learned in the course to a real problem. A good project follows stages: identify a problem, collect or choose a dataset, plan the design, develop the solution, test it and document the work. Typical project themes include analysis of student marks, sales data, weather records or health statistics. The data may be stored in a CSV file or MySQL database. Using Python, data is loaded into a Pandas DataFrame, cleaned by handling missing values and duplicates, and analysed using statistics, sorting, filtering and groupby. Results are visualised using Matplotlib charts such as line, bar and histogram, with titles, labels and legends. A database-based project uses SQL for queries, with tables and keys properly designed. The software development life cycle includes analysis, design, coding, testing, deployment and maintenance. The project report generally contains a title page, certificate, acknowledgement, index, introduction, objectives, system requirements, hardware and software used, source code with comments, sample output, conclusion, future scope and bibliography. Good coding practice involves meaningful variable names, comments, functions and modular design. Testing checks that the program gives correct results for normal and boundary inputs. During the viva, students are asked about the problem, dataset, libraries used, functions, queries and results. Honest citation of data sources and avoiding plagiarism are essential. Team projects need clear division of work and version control helps manage code. A project should be original, relevant and well documented.

lessons.title: Relations and Functions
yt: class 12 maths relations and functions equivalence relation one one onto bijective composition invertible

blocks.x: A relation R from a set A to a set B is a subset of the Cartesian product A x B. A relation on A is a subset of A x A. The empty relation has no pair and the universal relation contains all pairs. A relation R on A is reflexive if (a, a) is in R for every a, symmetric if (a, b) in R implies (b, a) in R, and transitive if (a, b) and (b, c) in R imply (a, c) in R. A relation that is reflexive, symmetric and transitive is an equivalence relation, and it partitions the set into disjoint equivalence classes. A function f from A to B assigns to each element of A exactly one element of B; A is the domain, B the codomain and the set of images is the range. A function is one-one (injective) if different elements have different images, and onto (surjective) if every element of B is an image. A function that is both is bijective. For finite sets, a function from A to A is one-one if and only if it is onto. If A has m elements and B has n elements, the number of functions is n^m, the number of relations is 2^(mn), and the number of one-one functions is nPm when n is at least m. The number of bijections from a set of n elements to itself is n factorial. The composition of f: A to B and g: B to C is gof(x) = g(f(x)). Composition is associative but not commutative. A function is invertible if and only if it is bijective, and then fog = I and gof = I for its inverse. The inverse of a bijection is also a bijection, and (gof) inverse equals f inverse o g inverse. A binary operation on a set A is a function from A x A to A. It is commutative if a * b = b * a and associative if (a * b) * c = a * (b * c). An identity element e satisfies a * e = e * a = a, and an inverse of a satisfies a * b = e. Examples to verify are the relation of congruence modulo and the relation of being in the same line.
Deep dive: Types of relations
Reflexive, symmetric and transitive properties combine to define equivalence relations, which partition a set.
Deep dive: Types of functions
One-one, onto and bijective functions decide invertibility; counting rules give the number of functions.
Deep dive: Composition and operations
Composition is associative, the inverse of gof is f inverse o g inverse, and binary operations may have identity and inverse.
Hindi saransh
Sambandh aur falan: reflexive, symmetric, transitive, equivalence relation, one-one, onto, inverse aur binary operation.
Remember: a function is invertible if and only if it is one-one and onto.

Visual lesson

Relations and Functions

Number of relations2^(mn)
🔑

Big idea

  • A relation R from a set A to a set B is a subset of the Cartesian product A x B
  • A relation on A is a subset of A x A
  • The empty relation has no pair and the universal relation contains all pairs
  • A relation R on A is reflexive if (a, a) is in R for every a, symmetric if (a, b) in R implies (b, a) in R, and transitive if (a, b) and (b, c) in R…
Read the full explanation

A relation R from a set A to a set B is a subset of the Cartesian product A x B. A relation on A is a subset of A x A. The empty relation has no pair and the universal relation contains all pairs. A relation R on A is reflexive if (a, a) is in R for every a, symmetric if (a, b) in R implies (b, a) in R, and transitive if (a, b) and (b, c) in R imply (a, c) in R. A relation that is reflexive, symmetric and transitive is an equivalence relation, and it partitions the set into disjoint equivalence classes. A function f from A to B assigns to each element of A exactly one element of B; A is the domain, B the codomain and the set of images is the range. A function is one-one (injective) if different elements have different images, and onto (surjective) if every element of B is an image. A function that is both is bijective. For finite sets, a function from A to A is one-one if and only if it is onto. If A has m elements and B has n elements, the number of functions is n^m, the number of relations is 2^(mn), and the number of one-one functions is nPm when n is at least m. The number of bijections from a set of n elements to itself is n factorial. The composition of f: A to B and g: B to C is gof(x) = g(f(x)). Composition is associative but not commutative. A function is invertible if and only if it is bijective, and then fog = I and gof = I for its inverse. The inverse of a bijection is also a bijection, and (gof) inverse equals f inverse o g inverse. A binary operation on a set A is a function from A x A to A. It is commutative if a * b = b * a and associative if (a * b) * c = a * (b * c). An identity element e satisfies a * e = e * a = a, and an inverse of a satisfies a * b = e. Examples to verify are the relation of congruence modulo and the relation of being in the same line.

📌

Types of relations

  • Reflexive, symmetric and transitive properties combine to define equivalence relations, which partition a set
🧠

Types of functions

  • One-one, onto and bijective functions decide invertibility
  • Counting rules give the number of functions
🌟

Composition and operations

  • Composition is associative, the inverse of gof is f inverse o g inverse, and binary operations may have identity and inverse

lessons.title: Inverse Trigonometric Functions
yt: class 12 maths inverse trigonometric functions principal value domain range properties

blocks.x: Trigonometric functions are not one-one over their full domains, so their inverses are defined by restricting the domain to an interval where they are bijective. The principal value branches are: sin inverse x has domain [-1, 1] and range [-pi/2, pi/2]; cos inverse x has domain [-1, 1] and range [0, pi]; tan inverse x has domain R and range (-pi/2, pi/2); cot inverse x has domain R and range (0, pi); sec inverse x has domain R minus (-1, 1) and range [0, pi] minus {pi/2}; cosec inverse x has domain R minus (-1, 1) and range [-pi/2, pi/2] minus {0}. The graph of an inverse function is the reflection of the original graph in the line y = x. Important identities: sin inverse(sin x) = x for x in [-pi/2, pi/2], and sin(sin inverse x) = x for x in [-1, 1]; sin inverse(-x) = - sin inverse x, cos inverse(-x) = pi - cos inverse x, tan inverse(-x) = - tan inverse x; sin inverse x + cos inverse x = pi/2 for x in [-1, 1]; tan inverse x + cot inverse x = pi/2 for real x; sec inverse x + cosec inverse x = pi/2 for modulus of x at least 1. Further, sin inverse(1/x) = cosec inverse x, cos inverse(1/x) = sec inverse x and tan inverse(1/x) = cot inverse x for suitable x. Sum and difference: tan inverse x + tan inverse y = tan inverse((x + y)/(1 - xy)) when xy < 1, and tan inverse x - tan inverse y = tan inverse((x - y)/(1 + xy)) when xy > -1. Also 2 tan inverse x = sin inverse(2x/(1 + x^2)) for modulus of x at most 1, 2 tan inverse x = cos inverse((1 - x^2)/(1 + x^2)) for x at least 0, and 2 tan inverse x = tan inverse(2x/(1 - x^2)) for modulus of x less than 1. Values to remember: sin inverse(1/2) = pi/6, cos inverse(1/2) = pi/3, tan inverse(1) = pi/4, and cos inverse(-1/2) = 2 pi/3. The principal value is the value of the function within the chosen range.
Deep dive: Branches
Each inverse trigonometric function is defined on a restricted interval known as its principal value branch.
Deep dive: Identities
Complementary and negative-argument identities simplify many problems.
Deep dive: Sum and double angle forms
tan inverse sum and 2 tan inverse x formulas convert expressions into simpler forms.

🔑

Big idea

  • Trigonometric functions are not one-one over their full domains, so their inverses are defined by restricting the domain to an interval where they…
  • The principal value branches are: sin inverse x has domain [-1, 1] and range [-pi/2, pi/2]
  • Cos inverse x has domain [-1, 1] and range [0, pi]
  • Tan inverse x has domain R and range (-pi/2, pi/2)
Read the full explanation

Trigonometric functions are not one-one over their full domains, so their inverses are defined by restricting the domain to an interval where they are bijective. The principal value branches are: sin inverse x has domain [-1, 1] and range [-pi/2, pi/2]; cos inverse x has domain [-1, 1] and range [0, pi]; tan inverse x has domain R and range (-pi/2, pi/2); cot inverse x has domain R and range (0, pi); sec inverse x has domain R minus (-1, 1) and range [0, pi] minus {pi/2}; cosec inverse x has domain R minus (-1, 1) and range [-pi/2, pi/2] minus {0}. The graph of an inverse function is the reflection of the original graph in the line y = x. Important identities: sin inverse(sin x) = x for x in [-pi/2, pi/2], and sin(sin inverse x) = x for x in [-1, 1]; sin inverse(-x) = - sin inverse x, cos inverse(-x) = pi - cos inverse x, tan inverse(-x) = - tan inverse x; sin inverse x + cos inverse x = pi/2 for x in [-1, 1]; tan inverse x + cot inverse x = pi/2 for real x; sec inverse x + cosec inverse x = pi/2 for modulus of x at least 1. Further, sin inverse(1/x) = cosec inverse x, cos inverse(1/x) = sec inverse x and tan inverse(1/x) = cot inverse x for suitable x. Sum and difference: tan inverse x + tan inverse y = tan inverse((x + y)/(1 - xy)) when xy < 1, and tan inverse x - tan inverse y = tan inverse((x - y)/(1 + xy)) when xy > -1. Also 2 tan inverse x = sin inverse(2x/(1 + x^2)) for modulus of x at most 1, 2 tan inverse x = cos inverse((1 - x^2)/(1 + x^2)) for x at least 0, and 2 tan inverse x = tan inverse(2x/(1 - x^2)) for modulus of x less than 1. Values to remember: sin inverse(1/2) = pi/6, cos inverse(1/2) = pi/3, tan inverse(1) = pi/4, and cos inverse(-1/2) = 2 pi/3. The principal value is the value of the function within the chosen range.

📌

  • Each inverse trigonometric function is defined on a restricted interval known as its principal value branch
🧠

  • Complementary and negative-argument identities simplify many problems
📐

blocks.x: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers arranged in rows and columns. A matrix with m rows and n columns has order m x n and has mn elements. Types include row matrix (1 x n), column matrix (m x 1), square matrix (m = n), diagonal matrix (non-diagonal elements zero), scalar matrix (equal diagonal elements), identity matrix I (diagonal elements one), zero matrix and triangular matrices. Two matrices are equal if they have the same order and equal corresponding elements. Addition and subtraction are defined for matrices of the same order and are done element by element. Addition is commutative and associative, the zero matrix is the additive identity, and every matrix A has an additive inverse -A. Scalar multiplication multiplies every element by the scalar k. The product AB of A (m x n) and B (n x p) is defined only if the number of columns of A equals the number of rows of B, and the product has order m x p, with element (i, j) found by multiplying row i of A with column j of B. Matrix multiplication is associative, distributive over addition, but not commutative in general; AB = 0 does not imply A = 0 or B = 0. The identity satisfies AI = IA = A. The transpose A′ of A interchanges rows and columns; (A′)′ = A, (A + B)′ = A′ + B′, (kA)′ = kA′ and (AB)′ = B′A′. A square matrix is symmetric if A′ = A and skew-symmetric if A′ = -A. In a skew-symmetric matrix all diagonal elements are zero. Every square matrix can be written as the sum of a symmetric matrix P = (A + A′)/2 and a skew-symmetric matrix Q = (A - A′)/2. An invertible matrix A has a matrix B with AB = BA = I, and the inverse is unique; (AB) inverse = B inverse A inverse. Elementary row and column operations are interchange of rows, multiplication of a row by a nonzero constant, and adding a multiple of a row to another, and they are used to find the inverse. Matrices have uses in solving linear equations and in computer graphics.
Deep dive: Operations
Addition needs equal order, multiplication needs columns of the first equal to rows of the second, and multiplication is not commutative.
Deep dive: Transpose and symmetry
(AB)′ = B′A′; every square matrix splits into symmetric and skew-symmetric parts.
Deep dive: Inverse
The inverse is unique and reverses the order in a product; elementary operations can find it.

🔑

Big idea

  • A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers arranged in rows and columns
  • A matrix with m rows and n columns has order m x n and has mn elements
  • Types include row matrix (1 x n), column matrix (m x 1), square matrix (m = n), diagonal matrix (non-diagonal elements zero), scalar matrix (equal…
  • Two matrices are equal if they have the same order and equal corresponding elements
Read the full explanation

A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers arranged in rows and columns. A matrix with m rows and n columns has order m x n and has mn elements. Types include row matrix (1 x n), column matrix (m x 1), square matrix (m = n), diagonal matrix (non-diagonal elements zero), scalar matrix (equal diagonal elements), identity matrix I (diagonal elements one), zero matrix and triangular matrices. Two matrices are equal if they have the same order and equal corresponding elements. Addition and subtraction are defined for matrices of the same order and are done element by element. Addition is commutative and associative, the zero matrix is the additive identity, and every matrix A has an additive inverse -A. Scalar multiplication multiplies every element by the scalar k. The product AB of A (m x n) and B (n x p) is defined only if the number of columns of A equals the number of rows of B, and the product has order m x p, with element (i, j) found by multiplying row i of A with column j of B. Matrix multiplication is associative, distributive over addition, but not commutative in general; AB = 0 does not imply A = 0 or B = 0. The identity satisfies AI = IA = A. The transpose A′ of A interchanges rows and columns; (A′)′ = A, (A + B)′ = A′ + B′, (kA)′ = kA′ and (AB)′ = B′A′. A square matrix is symmetric if A′ = A and skew-symmetric if A′ = -A. In a skew-symmetric matrix all diagonal elements are zero. Every square matrix can be written as the sum of a symmetric matrix P = (A + A′)/2 and a skew-symmetric matrix Q = (A - A′)/2. An invertible matrix A has a matrix B with AB = BA = I, and the inverse is unique; (AB) inverse = B inverse A inverse. Elementary row and column operations are interchange of rows, multiplication of a row by a nonzero constant, and adding a multiple of a row to another, and they are used to find the inverse. Matrices have uses in solving linear equations and in computer graphics.

📌

Operations

  • Addition needs equal order, multiplication needs columns of the first equal to rows of the second, and multiplication is not commutative
🧠

Transpose and symmetry

  • Every square matrix splits into symmetric and skew-symmetric parts
🌟

Inverse

  • The inverse is unique and reverses the order in a product
  • Elementary operations can find it
🧮

yt: class 12 determinants

blocks.x: The determinant of a square matrix is a single number: for [[a, b], [c, d]] it is ad - bc. A matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is non-zero, and then A^-1 = adj(A)/|A|. Cramer-style solutions use A^-1 B for the system AX = B. The area of a triangle with vertices (x1, y1), (x2, y2), (x3, y3) is half the absolute value of a determinant.
Deep dive: determinants and their properties

For a 2 x 2 matrix the determinant is ad - bc; for a 3 x 3 matrix expand along any row or column using minors and cofactors with the sign pattern (+ - +, - + -, + - +). Properties: swapping two rows changes the sign; a row of zeros or two identical (or proportional) rows gives 0; multiplying one row by k multiplies the determinant by k; adding a multiple of a row to another does not change the value; |A^T| = |A|; |AB| = |A||B|; |kA| = k^n |A| for an n x n matrix; the determinant of a triangular matrix is the product of the diagonal entries.
Deep dive: adjoint and inverse

The minor M_ij is the determinant left after deleting row i and column j; the cofactor is C_ij = (-1)^(i + j) M_ij. The adjoint adj A is the transpose of the cofactor matrix. Then A (adj A) = (adj A) A = |A| I, so A^-1 = adj A / |A| exists only if A is non-singular (|A| != 0). Properties: (AB)^-1 = B^-1 A^-1, (A^-1)^-1 = A, |adj A| = |A|^(n - 1), |A^-1| = 1/|A|.
Deep dive: solving equations and areas

For AX = B with |A| != 0 the unique solution is X = A^-1 B. If |A| = 0 and (adj A) B is non-zero the system is inconsistent; if (adj A) B = 0 it has infinitely many solutions (or none, check). Area of a triangle with vertices (x1, y1), (x2, y2), (x3, y3) = (1/2) |det [[x1, y1, 1], [x2, y2, 1], [x3, y3, 1]]|; three points are collinear when this determinant is 0.

Determinants and inverse of a matrix

The determinant of a square matrix is a single number: for [[a, b], [c, d]] it is ad - bc

1Big idea›2Determinants and their…›3Adjoint and inverse›4Solving equations and areas
Triangle area(1/2)
🔑

Big idea

  • The determinant of a square matrix is a single number: for [[a, b], [c, d]] it is ad - bc
  • A matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is non-zero, and then A-1 = adj(A)/|A|
  • Cramer-style solutions use A-1 B for the system AX = B
  • The area of a triangle with vertices (x1, y1), (x2, y2), (x3, y3) is half the absolute value of a determinant
📌

Determinants and their properties

  • For a 2 x 2 matrix the determinant is ad - bc
  • For a 3 x 3 matrix expand along any row or column using minors and cofactors with the sign pattern (+ - +, - + -, + - +)
  • Properties: swapping two rows changes the sign
  • A row of zeros or two identical (or proportional) rows gives 0
Read the full explanation

For a 2 x 2 matrix the determinant is ad - bc; for a 3 x 3 matrix expand along any row or column using minors and cofactors with the sign pattern (+ - +, - + -, + - +). Properties: swapping two rows changes the sign; a row of zeros or two identical (or proportional) rows gives 0; multiplying one row by k multiplies the determinant by k; adding a multiple of a row to another does not change the value; |A^T| = |A|; |AB| = |A||B|; |kA| = k^n |A| for an n x n matrix; the determinant of a triangular matrix is the product of the diagonal entries.

🧠

Adjoint and inverse

  • The minor M_ij is the determinant left after deleting row i and column j
  • The cofactor is C_ij = (-1)^(i + j) M_ij
  • The adjoint adj A is the transpose of the cofactor matrix
  • Then A (adj A) = (adj A) A = |A| I, so A-1 = adj A / |A| exists only if A is non-singular (|A| != 0)
Read the full explanation

The minor M_ij is the determinant left after deleting row i and column j; the cofactor is C_ij = (-1)^(i + j) M_ij. The adjoint adj A is the transpose of the cofactor matrix. Then A (adj A) = (adj A) A = |A| I, so A^-1 = adj A / |A| exists only if A is non-singular (|A| != 0). Properties: (AB)^-1 = B^-1 A^-1, (A^-1)^-1 = A, |adj A| = |A|^(n - 1), |A^-1| = 1/|A|.

🧮

Solving equations and areas

  • For AX = B with |A| != 0 the unique solution is X = A-1 B
  • If |A| = 0 and (adj A) B is non-zero the system is inconsistent
  • If (adj A) B = 0 it has infinitely many solutions (or none, check)
  • Area of a triangle with vertices (x1, y1), (x2, y2), (x3, y3) = (1/2) |det [[x1, y1, 1], [x2, y2, 1], [x3, y3, 1]]|
Read the full explanation

For AX = B with |A| != 0 the unique solution is X = A^-1 B. If |A| = 0 and (adj A) B is non-zero the system is inconsistent; if (adj A) B = 0 it has infinitely many solutions (or none, check). lessons.title: Continuity and differentiability
yt: class 12 continuity and differentiability

blocks.x: A function f is continuous at x = a if the limit as x tends to a equals f(a). It is differentiable at a if the derivative exists there; differentiable implies continuous but not conversely. Standard derivatives: d/dx x^n = n x^(n-1), sin x -> cos x, cos x -> -sin x, e^x -> e^x, log x -> 1/x. Rules: sum, product, quotient and chain rules.
Deep dive: continuity

f is continuous at x = a if lim (x -> a-) f(x) = lim (x -> a+) f(x) = f(a). A function is continuous on an interval if it is continuous at every point of it. Polynomials, sin x, cos x and e^x are continuous everywhere; rational functions are continuous except where the denominator is zero; |x| is continuous everywhere. Sums, differences, products and compositions of continuous functions are continuous, and so are quotients where the denominator is non-zero. To make a piecewise function continuous, equate the left and right limits at the join and solve for the unknown constant.
Deep dive: differentiability and rules

f is differentiable at a if the left and right derivatives exist and are equal. Differentiability implies continuity, but |x| is continuous and not differentiable at 0. Rules: (u + v)' = u' + v'; (uv)' = u'v + uv'; (u/v)' = (u'v - uv')/v^2; chain rule (f(g(x)))' = f'(g(x)) g'(x). Standard results: (x^n)' = n x^(n-1), (sin x)' = cos x, (cos x)' = -sin x, (tan x)' = sec^2 x, (e^x)' = e^x, (a^x)' = a^x log a, (log x)' = 1/x, (sin^-1 x)' = 1/sqrt (1 - x^2), (tan^-1 x)' = 1/(1 + x^2).
Deep dive: special techniques

Implicit differentiation: differentiate both sides with respect to x and treat y as a function of x (use dy/dx). Logarithmic differentiation is used for y = f(x)^g(x) and long products: take log first. Parametric form: dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt). Second derivative d^2y/dx^2 is the derivative of dy/dx. Rolle's theorem and the mean value theorem: if f is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b) then some c satisfies f'(c) = (f(b) - f(a))/(b - a).
Hindi saransh
Continuous: LHL = RHL = f(a). Differentiable => continuous.
Chain rule: d/dx f(g(x)) = f'(g(x)) g'(x).

lessons.title: Applications of Derivatives
yt: class 12 maths applications of derivatives rate of change increasing decreasing tangent normal maxima minima approximation

blocks.x: The derivative dy/dx measures the rate of change of y with respect to x. If a quantity y varies with time t, dy/dt is its rate of change; by the chain rule dy/dt = (dy/dx)(dx/dt). Examples include the rate of change of the area of a circle, A = pi r^2, giving dA/dt = 2 pi r dr/dt, and of the volume of a sphere, V = (4/3) pi r^3, giving dV/dt = 4 pi r^2 dr/dt. A function f is increasing on an interval if f′(x) > 0 and decreasing if f′(x) < 0 on the interval; it is strictly increasing if x1 < x2 gives f(x1) < f(x2). The slope of the tangent to y = f(x) at (x0, y0) is f′(x0), so the tangent is y - y0 = f′(x0)(x - x0). The normal is perpendicular to the tangent with slope -1/f′(x0), so its equation is y - y0 = (-1/f′(x0))(x - x0). Tangent and normal are parallel to the x-axis when the slope is zero or vertical, and the angle between a curve and a line can be found from slopes. Approximations use differentials: dy = f′(x) dx, and f(x + delta x) is approximately f(x) + f′(x) delta x. Maxima and minima: a point c is a critical point if f′(c) = 0 or f′(c) does not exist. The first derivative test says that if f′ changes sign from positive to negative at c, c is a local maximum, and from negative to positive a local minimum; if no sign change, it is a point of inflexion. The second derivative test says that if f′(c) = 0 and f″(c) < 0, then c is a local maximum, if f″(c) > 0 a local minimum, and if f″(c) = 0 the test fails. The absolute maximum and minimum of a continuous function on a closed interval [a, b] occur at critical points or at the end points. Word problems on optimisation include the maximum area of a rectangle of given perimeter, which is a square, the maximum volume of an open box formed from a square sheet, and the closed cylinder of fixed volume with minimum surface area, which has height equal to the diameter.
Deep dive: Rate and monotonicity
Rate of change uses the chain rule; the sign of f′ shows increasing or decreasing behaviour.
Deep dive: Tangent, normal and approximation
The tangent has slope f′(x0); differentials estimate small changes.
Deep dive: Maxima and minima
Use first or second derivative tests, and check endpoints for absolute extrema on closed intervals.

Visual lesson

Applications of Derivatives

The derivative dy/dx measures the rate of change of y with respect to x

minutes

Q&A

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Rate and monotonicity›3Tangent, normal and…›4Maxima and minima
Normal slope-1/f′(x0)
Second testf″ < 0 means max
🔑

Big idea

  • The derivative dy/dx measures the rate of change of y with respect to x
  • If a quantity y varies with time t, dy/dt is its rate of change
  • By the chain rule dy/dt = (dy/dx)(dx/dt)
  • Examples include the rate of change of the area of a circle, A = pi r2, giving dA/dt = 2 pi r dr/dt, and of the volume of a sphere, V = (4/3) pi…
Read the full explanation

The derivative dy/dx measures the rate of change of y with respect to x. If a quantity y varies with time t, dy/dt is its rate of change; by the chain rule dy/dt = (dy/dx)(dx/dt). Examples include the rate of change of the area of a circle, A = pi r^2, giving dA/dt = 2 pi r dr/dt, and of the volume of a sphere, V = (4/3) pi r^3, giving dV/dt = 4 pi r^2 dr/dt. A function f is increasing on an interval if f′(x) > 0 and decreasing if f′(x) < 0 on the interval; it is strictly increasing if x1 < x2 gives f(x1) < f(x2). The slope of the tangent to y = f(x) at (x0, y0) is f′(x0), so the tangent is y - y0 = f′(x0)(x - x0). The normal is perpendicular to the tangent with slope -1/f′(x0), so its equation is y - y0 = (-1/f′(x0))(x - x0). Tangent and normal are parallel to the x-axis when the slope is zero or vertical, and the angle between a curve and a line can be found from slopes. Approximations use differentials: dy = f′(x) dx, and f(x + delta x) is approximately f(x) + f′(x) delta x. Maxima and minima: a point c is a critical point if f′(c) = 0 or f′(c) does not exist. The first derivative test says that if f′ changes sign from positive to negative at c, c is a local maximum, and from negative to positive a local minimum; if no sign change, it is a point of inflexion. The second derivative test says that if f′(c) = 0 and f″(c) < 0, then c is a local maximum, if f″(c) > 0 a local minimum, and if f″(c) = 0 the test fails. The absolute maximum and minimum of a continuous function on a closed interval [a, b] occur at critical points or at the end points. Word problems on optimisation include the maximum area of a rectangle of given perimeter, which is a square, the maximum volume of an open box formed from a square sheet, and the closed cylinder of fixed volume with minimum surface area, which has height equal to the diameter.

📌

Rate and monotonicity

  • Rate of change uses the chain rule
  • The sign of f′ shows increasing or decreasing behaviour
🧠

Tangent, normal and approximation

  • The tangent has slope f′(x0)
  • Differentials estimate small changes
🌟

Maxima and minima

  • Use first or second derivative tests, and check endpoints for absolute extrema on closed intervals
🧮

Formula tiles

Tangenty - y0 = f′(x0)(x - x0)
Normal slope-1/f′(x0)
Approximationf(x+dx) = f(x) + f′(x) dx
Second testf″ < 0 means max
🎯 Remember f′(c) = 0 and f″(c) < 0 gives a local maximum.

lessons.title: Integrals
yt: class 12 maths integrals indefinite definite integration by parts partial fractions substitution properties fundamental theorem

blocks.x: Integration is the inverse of differentiation. If d/dx F(x) = f(x), then the indefinite integral of f is F(x) + C, where C is the constant of integration. Standard integrals: x^n integrates to x^(n+1)/(n+1) + C for n not equal to -1; 1/x integrates to ln of modulus x + C; e^x to e^x; a^x to a^x/ln a; sin x to -cos x; cos x to sin x; sec^2 x to tan x; cosec^2 x to -cot x; sec x tan x to sec x; cosec x cot x to -cosec x; 1/(1 + x^2) to tan inverse x; 1/sqrt(1 - x^2) to sin inverse x; 1/(x sqrt(x^2 - 1)) to sec inverse x. Further: tan x integrates to ln of modulus sec x, cot x to ln of modulus sin x, sec x to ln of modulus (sec x + tan x), cosec x to ln of modulus (cosec x - cot x). Standard forms: 1/(x^2 - a^2) gives (1/2a) ln of modulus((x - a)/(x + a)), 1/(a^2 - x^2) gives (1/2a) ln of modulus((a + x)/(a - x)), 1/(x^2 + a^2) gives (1/a) tan inverse(x/a), and 1/sqrt(a^2 - x^2) gives sin inverse(x/a). Methods include substitution, integration by parts, and partial fractions. Integration by parts: integral of u v dx = u times integral of v dx minus integral of (u′ times integral of v dx) dx; choose u by ILATE (inverse, logarithmic, algebraic, trigonometric, exponential). The special result: integral of e^x (f(x) + f′(x)) dx = e^x f(x) + C. Partial fractions are used for rational functions by splitting into simpler fractions. The definite integral from a to b of f(x) dx is the limit of a sum and equals F(b) - F(a), the second fundamental theorem. The first fundamental theorem says d/dx of the integral from a to x of f(t) dt equals f(x). Properties: the integral from a to b equals minus the integral from b to a; the integral from a to b equals the sum of integrals over [a, c] and [c, b]; the integral from a to b of f(x) dx equals the integral from a to b of f(a + b - x) dx; the integral from 0 to a of f(x) dx equals the integral from 0 to a of f(a - x) dx; the integral from -a to a of f(x) dx is 2 times the integral from 0 to a for even f and 0 for odd f. Substitution changes limits for definite integrals.
Deep dive: Indefinite integrals
Standard forms, substitution, parts (ILATE) and partial fractions give antiderivatives.
Deep dive: Definite integrals
The fundamental theorem gives F(b) - F(a); properties simplify integrals.
Deep dive: Symmetry
Even functions double the half-interval integral and odd functions give zero over symmetric limits.
Hindi saransh
Samakalan: aniyat aur niyat samakal, sthapan, bhagon dwara, aanshik bhinn aur kalan ke mool pramey.
Remember: ILATE order for parts; even f doubles, odd f gives zero on [-a, a].

🔑

Big idea

  • Integration is the inverse of differentiation
  • If d/dx F(x) = f(x), then the indefinite integral of f is F(x) + C, where C is the constant of integration
  • Standard integrals: x^n integrates to x^(n+1)/(n+1) + C for n not equal to -1
  • 1/x integrates to ln of modulus x + C
Read the full explanation

Integration is the inverse of differentiation. If d/dx F(x) = f(x), then the indefinite integral of f is F(x) + C, where C is the constant of integration. Standard integrals: x^n integrates to x^(n+1)/(n+1) + C for n not equal to -1; 1/x integrates to ln of modulus x + C; e^x to e^x; a^x to a^x/ln a; sin x to -cos x; cos x to sin x; sec^2 x to tan x; cosec^2 x to -cot x; sec x tan x to sec x; cosec x cot x to -cosec x; 1/(1 + x^2) to tan inverse x; 1/sqrt(1 - x^2) to sin inverse x; 1/(x sqrt(x^2 - 1)) to sec inverse x. Further: tan x integrates to ln of modulus sec x, cot x to ln of modulus sin x, sec x to ln of modulus (sec x + tan x), cosec x to ln of modulus (cosec x - cot x). Standard forms: 1/(x^2 - a^2) gives (1/2a) ln of modulus((x - a)/(x + a)), 1/(a^2 - x^2) gives (1/2a) ln of modulus((a + x)/(a - x)), 1/(x^2 + a^2) gives (1/a) tan inverse(x/a), and 1/sqrt(a^2 - x^2) gives sin inverse(x/a). Methods include substitution, integration by parts, and partial fractions. Integration by parts: integral of u v dx = u times integral of v dx minus integral of (u′ times integral of v dx) dx; choose u by ILATE (inverse, logarithmic, algebraic, trigonometric, exponential). The special result: integral of e^x (f(x) + f′(x)) dx = e^x f(x) + C. Partial fractions are used for rational functions by splitting into simpler fractions. The definite integral from a to b of f(x) dx is the limit of a sum and equals F(b) - F(a), the second fundamental theorem. The first fundamental theorem says d/dx of the integral from a to x of f(t) dt equals f(x). Properties: the integral from a to b equals minus the integral from b to a; the integral from a to b equals the sum of integrals over [a, c] and [c, b]; the integral from a to b of f(x) dx equals the integral from a to b of f(a + b - x) dx; the integral from 0 to a of f(x) dx equals the integral from 0 to a of f(a - x) dx; the integral from -a to a of f(x) dx is 2 times the integral from 0 to a for even f and 0 for odd f. Substitution changes limits for definite integrals.

📘

Indefinite integrals

  • Standard forms, substitution, parts (ILATE) and partial fractions give antiderivatives
📘

Definite integrals

  • The fundamental theorem gives F(b) - F(a)
  • Properties simplify integrals
🌟

Symmetry

  • Even functions double the half-interval integral and odd functions give zero over symmetric limits

lessons.title: Applications of Integrals
yt: class 12 maths application of integrals area under curves between curves ellipse circle parabola

blocks.x: A definite integral gives the area under a curve. The area bounded by the curve y = f(x), the x-axis and the lines x = a and x = b is the integral from a to b of y dx, provided f is positive; where the curve lies below the axis the integral is negative and the area is its absolute value. Similarly the area bounded by x = g(y), the y-axis and the lines y = c and y = d is the integral from c to d of x dy. The area between two curves y = f(x) and y = g(x) from x = a to x = b, where f is above g, is the integral from a to b of (f(x) - g(x)) dx. When the curves intersect, find intersection points by solving equations and split the region if the upper curve changes. Standard results: the area of a circle x^2 + y^2 = a^2 is pi a^2; the area of the ellipse x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 = 1 is pi a b; the area of the region enclosed by the parabola y^2 = 4ax and its latus rectum is 8a^2/3; the area between the parabola y^2 = 4ax and the line y = mx is 8a^2/(3 m^3); the area of the triangle with vertices on a line can be found by integrating line equations. The area bounded by y = x and y = x^2 is 1/6. The area of one arch of sine curve between 0 and pi is 2. The steps are: draw a rough sketch, identify limits by solving intersection points, choose vertical or horizontal strips, set up the integral and evaluate. The use of symmetry halves the work: for symmetric regions, compute one quadrant and multiply. Applications include finding areas of land plots, regions under velocity-time graphs (distance), and probability distributions. Area under a curve between 0 and a for modulus function can be found by splitting.
Deep dive: Area under a curve
Area is a definite integral; below the axis, take the absolute value.
Deep dive: Area between curves
Integrate upper minus lower between intersection limits, splitting when needed.
Deep dive: Standard areas
Circle pi a^2, ellipse pi a b and parabola with latus rectum 8a^2/3 are key results.

Applications of Integrals

A definite integral gives the area under a curve

🔑

Big idea

  • A definite integral gives the area under a curve
  • The area bounded by the curve y = f(x), the x-axis and the lines x = a and x = b is the integral from a to b of y dx, provided f is positive
  • Where the curve lies below the axis the integral is negative and the area is its absolute value
  • Similarly the area bounded by x = g(y), the y-axis and the lines y = c and y = d is the integral from c to d of x dy
Read the full explanation

A definite integral gives the area under a curve. The area bounded by the curve y = f(x), the x-axis and the lines x = a and x = b is the integral from a to b of y dx, provided f is positive; where the curve lies below the axis the integral is negative and the area is its absolute value. Similarly the area bounded by x = g(y), the y-axis and the lines y = c and y = d is the integral from c to d of x dy. The area between two curves y = f(x) and y = g(x) from x = a to x = b, where f is above g, is the integral from a to b of (f(x) - g(x)) dx. When the curves intersect, find intersection points by solving equations and split the region if the upper curve changes. Standard results: the area of a circle x^2 + y^2 = a^2 is pi a^2; the area of the ellipse x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 = 1 is pi a b; the area of the region enclosed by the parabola y^2 = 4ax and its latus rectum is 8a^2/3; the area between the parabola y^2 = 4ax and the line y = mx is 8a^2/(3 m^3); the area of the triangle with vertices on a line can be found by integrating line equations. The area bounded by y = x and y = x^2 is 1/6. The area of one arch of sine curve between 0 and pi is 2. The steps are: draw a rough sketch, identify limits by solving intersection points, choose vertical or horizontal strips, set up the integral and evaluate. The use of symmetry halves the work: for symmetric regions, compute one quadrant and multiply. Applications include finding areas of land plots, regions under velocity-time graphs (distance), and probability distributions. Area under a curve between 0 and a for modulus function can be found by splitting.

📐

Area under a curve

  • Area is a definite integral
  • Below the axis, take the absolute value
📐

Area between curves

  • Integrate upper minus lower between intersection limits, splitting when needed
📐

Standard areas

  • Circle pi a2, ellipse pi a b and parabola with latus rectum 8a2/3 are key results

lessons.title: Differential Equations
yt: class 12 maths differential equations order degree variable separable homogeneous linear integrating factor

blocks.x: A differential equation contains an independent variable, a dependent variable and derivatives. The order is the order of the highest derivative, and the degree is the power of the highest-order derivative after the equation is made free of radicals and fractions in the derivatives, defined only if it is a polynomial in the derivatives. For example, (d2y/dx2) + (dy/dx)^3 = 0 has order 2 and degree 1. A general solution contains arbitrary constants equal in number to the order, and a particular solution is obtained by giving values to the constants using initial conditions. To form a differential equation from a family of curves with n arbitrary constants, differentiate n times and eliminate the constants. Methods of solving first order, first degree equations: variable separable form dy/dx = f(x) g(y), solved by separating variables and integrating, i.e. integral of dy/g(y) = integral of f(x) dx + C. A homogeneous equation dy/dx = F(y/x) is solved by the substitution y = vx, so dy/dx = v + x dv/dx, which separates variables. A function f(x, y) is homogeneous of degree n if f(kx, ky) = k^n f(x, y). A linear first order equation has the form dy/dx + P y = Q, where P and Q are functions of x only. Its integrating factor is IF = e^(integral of P dx), and the solution is y (IF) = integral of Q (IF) dx + C. Another form is dx/dy + P1 x = Q1 with P1 and Q1 functions of y, with IF = e^(integral of P1 dy). Examples: dy/dx + y = e^(-x) has IF e^x. Population growth dP/dt = kP gives P = P0 e^(kt), radioactive decay and Newton’s law of cooling follow similar forms. Always check the order, degree and type before choosing a method.
Deep dive: Order and degree
Order is the highest derivative order; degree is its power when the equation is polynomial in derivatives.
Deep dive: Solving methods
Variable separable, homogeneous (y = vx) and linear (integrating factor) forms cover first-order equations.
Deep dive: Applications
Growth, decay and cooling problems lead to simple first-order equations.
Hindi saransh
Avkal samikaran: kram, ghaat, charon ka pruthakkaran, samaghat aur ranik samikaran, samakalan gunak.

Differential Equations

A differential equation contains an independent variable, a dependent variable and derivatives

🔑

Big idea

  • A differential equation contains an independent variable, a dependent variable and derivatives
  • The order is the order of the highest derivative, and the degree is the power of the highest-order derivative after the equation is made free of…
  • For example, (d2y/dx2) + (dy/dx)3 = 0 has order 2 and degree 1
  • A general solution contains arbitrary constants equal in number to the order, and a particular solution is obtained by giving values to the constants…
Read the full explanation

A differential equation contains an independent variable, a dependent variable and derivatives. The order is the order of the highest derivative, and the degree is the power of the highest-order derivative after the equation is made free of radicals and fractions in the derivatives, defined only if it is a polynomial in the derivatives. For example, (d2y/dx2) + (dy/dx)^3 = 0 has order 2 and degree 1. A general solution contains arbitrary constants equal in number to the order, and a particular solution is obtained by giving values to the constants using initial conditions. To form a differential equation from a family of curves with n arbitrary constants, differentiate n times and eliminate the constants. Methods of solving first order, first degree equations: variable separable form dy/dx = f(x) g(y), solved by separating variables and integrating, i.e. integral of dy/g(y) = integral of f(x) dx + C. A homogeneous equation dy/dx = F(y/x) is solved by the substitution y = vx, so dy/dx = v + x dv/dx, which separates variables. A function f(x, y) is homogeneous of degree n if f(kx, ky) = k^n f(x, y). A linear first order equation has the form dy/dx + P y = Q, where P and Q are functions of x only. Its integrating factor is IF = e^(integral of P dx), and the solution is y (IF) = integral of Q (IF) dx + C. Another form is dx/dy + P1 x = Q1 with P1 and Q1 functions of y, with IF = e^(integral of P1 dy). Examples: dy/dx + y = e^(-x) has IF e^x. Population growth dP/dt = kP gives P = P0 e^(kt), radioactive decay and Newton’s law of cooling follow similar forms. Always check the order, degree and type before choosing a method.

📌

Order and degree

  • Order is the highest derivative order
  • Degree is its power when the equation is polynomial in derivatives
🔄

Solving methods

  • Variable separable, homogeneous (y = vx) and linear (integrating factor) forms cover first-order equations
💡

Applications

  • Growth, decay and cooling problems lead to simple first-order equations
