lessons.title: Vector Algebra
yt: class 12 maths vector algebra dot product cross product position vector direction cosines section formula

blocks.x: A vector has magnitude and direction, whereas a scalar has only magnitude. The position vector of a point P(x, y, z) is OP = xi + yj + zk, with magnitude sqrt(x^2 + y^2 + z^2). The vector AB from A to B is the position vector of B minus that of A. A unit vector has magnitude 1 and the unit vector along a is a/|a|. Types include zero, unit, coinitial, collinear, equal and negative vectors. Direction ratios of a vector are its components a, b, c and the direction cosines are l = cos alpha = a/|a|, m = b/|a|, n = c/|a| with l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1. Addition follows the triangle law and parallelogram law; the section formula for a point dividing AB internally in ratio m:n is (m b + n a)/(m + n), and the midpoint is (a + b)/2. The scalar (dot) product a . b = |a||b| cos theta, and in components a1b1 + a2b2 + a3b3. It is commutative and distributive, is zero for perpendicular vectors, and a . a = |a|^2. The projection of a on b is (a . b)/|b|. The vector (cross) product a x b = |a||b| sin theta n, where n is a unit vector perpendicular to both given by the right-hand rule. It is anti-commutative, a x b = - b x a, zero for parallel vectors, and its magnitude equals the area of the parallelogram with sides a and b. In components it is the determinant with rows i j k, a1 a2 a3 and b1 b2 b3. The area of a triangle with sides a and b is half the magnitude of a x b. The scalar triple product [a b c] = a . (b x c) gives the volume of a parallelepiped, and three vectors are coplanar if it is zero. Also i x j = k, j x k = i, k x i = j, and i.i = 1, i.j = 0. The angle between two vectors satisfies cos theta = (a . b)/(|a||b|), and |a + b|^2 = |a|^2 + |b|^2 + 2 a . b.
Deep dive: Basics
Position vectors, magnitude, unit vectors and direction cosines describe vectors in space.
Deep dive: Products
The dot product gives a scalar and angle; the cross product gives a perpendicular vector and area.
Deep dive: Triple product
The scalar triple product gives volume and tests coplanarity.

Visual lesson

Vector Algebra

A vector has magnitude and direction, whereas a scalar has only magnitude

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Basics›3Products›4Triple product
🔑

Big idea

  • A vector has magnitude and direction, whereas a scalar has only magnitude
  • The position vector of a point P(x, y, z) is OP = xi + yj + zk, with magnitude sqrt(x2 + y2 + z2)
  • The vector AB from A to B is the position vector of B minus that of A
  • A unit vector has magnitude 1 and the unit vector along a is a/|a|
Read the full explanation

A vector has magnitude and direction, whereas a scalar has only magnitude. The position vector of a point P(x, y, z) is OP = xi + yj + zk, with magnitude sqrt(x^2 + y^2 + z^2). The vector AB from A to B is the position vector of B minus that of A. A unit vector has magnitude 1 and the unit vector along a is a/|a|. Types include zero, unit, coinitial, collinear, equal and negative vectors. Direction ratios of a vector are its components a, b, c and the direction cosines are l = cos alpha = a/|a|, m = b/|a|, n = c/|a| with l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1. Addition follows the triangle law and parallelogram law; the section formula for a point dividing AB internally in ratio m:n is (m b + n a)/(m + n), and the midpoint is (a + b)/2. The scalar (dot) product a . b = |a||b| cos theta, and in components a1b1 + a2b2 + a3b3. It is commutative and distributive, is zero for perpendicular vectors, and a . a = |a|^2. The projection of a on b is (a . b)/|b|. The vector (cross) product a x b = |a||b| sin theta n, where n is a unit vector perpendicular to both given by the right-hand rule. It is anti-commutative, a x b = - b x a, zero for parallel vectors, and its magnitude equals the area of the parallelogram with sides a and b. In components it is the determinant with rows i j k, a1 a2 a3 and b1 b2 b3. The area of a triangle with sides a and b is half the magnitude of a x b. The scalar triple product [a b c] = a . (b x c) gives the volume of a parallelepiped, and three vectors are coplanar if it is zero. Also i x j = k, j x k = i, k x i = j, and i.i = 1, i.j = 0. The angle between two vectors satisfies cos theta = (a . b)/(|a||b|), and |a + b|^2 = |a|^2 + |b|^2 + 2 a . b.

📘

Basics

  • Position vectors, magnitude, unit vectors and direction cosines describe vectors in space
🧠

Products

  • The dot product gives a scalar and angle
  • The cross product gives a perpendicular vector and area
🌟

Triple product

  • The scalar triple product gives volume and tests coplanarity
🧮

blocks.x: Direction ratios (a, b, c) of a line are any numbers proportional to its direction cosines l, m, n, where l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1. The line through (x1, y1, z1) with direction ratios (a, b, c) is (x - x1)/a = (y - y1)/b = (z - z1)/c. The plane ax + by + cz + d = 0 has normal (a, b, c); the distance of (x1, y1, z1) from it is |a x1 + b y1 + c z1 + d|/sqrt(a^2 + b^2 + c^2).
Deep dive: direction cosines and direction ratios

If a line makes angles alpha, beta, gamma with the axes, then l = cos alpha, m = cos beta, n = cos gamma are its direction cosines, with l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1. Direction ratios a, b, c are proportional to l, m, n, so l = a/sqrt (a^2 + b^2 + c^2) and so on. For the points P (x1, y1, z1) and Q (x2, y2, z2) the direction ratios of PQ are (x2 - x1, y2 - y1, z2 - z1). The angle theta between two lines with direction ratios (a1, b1, c1) and (a2, b2, c2) satisfies cos theta = |a1 a2 + b1 b2 + c1 c2| / (sqrt (a1^2 + b1^2 + c1^2) sqrt (a2^2 + b2^2 + c2^2)). Lines are perpendicular if a1 a2 + b1 b2 + c1 c2 = 0 and parallel if a1/a2 = b1/b2 = c1/c2.
Deep dive: equations of a line in space

Cartesian form through (x1, y1, z1) with direction ratios (a, b, c): (x - x1)/a = (y - y1)/b = (z - z1)/c. Vector form r = a + t b. Through two points the direction ratios are the differences of coordinates. The shortest distance between skew lines r = a1 + t b1 and r = a2 + s b2 is |(a2 - a1) . (b1 x b2)| / |b1 x b2|; for parallel lines it is |(a2 - a1) x b| / |b|. Skew lines are non-parallel, non-intersecting lines.
Deep dive: planes

The plane with unit normal n at distance d from the origin: r . n = d; Cartesian form lx + my + nz = d. General form ax + by + cz + d = 0 with normal (a, b, c). Plane through (x1, y1, z1) with normal (a, b, c): a (x - x1) + b (y - y1) + c (z - z1) = 0. Plane through three points: use the determinant of coordinates. The distance from (x1, y1, z1) to the plane is |a x1 + b y1 + c z1 + d| / sqrt (a^2 + b^2 + c^2). The angle between two planes equals the angle between their normals. Angle between a line and a plane: sin theta = |a l + b m + c n| / (|normal| |direction|).

If a line makes angles alpha, beta, gamma with the axes, then l = cos alpha, m = cos beta, n = cos gamma are its direction cosines, with l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1. Direction ratios a, b, c are proportional to l, m, n, so l = a/sqrt (a^2 + b^2 + c^2) and so on. For the points P (x1, y1, z1) and Q (x2, y2, z2) the direction ratios of PQ are (x2 - x1, y2 - y1, z2 - z1). The angle theta between two lines with direction ratios (a1, b1, c1) and (a2, b2, c2) satisfies cos theta = |a1 a2 + b1 b2 + c1 c2| / (sqrt (a1^2 + b1^2 + c1^2) sqrt (a2^2 + b2^2 + c2^2)). Lines are perpendicular if a1 a2 + b1 b2 + c1 c2 = 0 and parallel if a1/a2 = b1/b2 = c1/c2.

  • Vector form r = a + t b
  • Through two points the direction ratios are the differences of coordinates
  • The shortest distance between skew lines r = a1 + t b1 and r = a2 + s b2 is |(a2 - a1)

lessons.title: Linear Programming
yt: class 12 maths linear programming objective function constraints feasible region corner point method

blocks.x: Linear programming deals with optimising a linear objective function subject to linear inequalities called constraints. The objective function Z = ax + by is to be maximised or minimised, the variables x and y are called decision variables, and non-negativity restrictions x >= 0, y >= 0 apply. The feasible region is the common region determined by all constraints, including non-negativity. Points inside the region are feasible solutions; points outside are infeasible. A feasible solution that optimises the objective function is an optimal solution. The corner point theorem says that if the feasible region is bounded, the objective function has both a maximum and minimum at corner points. If the region is unbounded, a maximum or minimum may not exist; if the maximum (or minimum) exists it occurs at a corner point. For an unbounded region, draw the half-plane ax + by > M (for maximum) or < m (for minimum) and see if it has points in common with the feasible region; if not, M (or m) is the value. The corner point method has steps: formulate the problem mathematically, graph constraints, identify the feasible region, find corner points by solving boundary equations, compute Z at each corner and select the largest or smallest. If two corner points give the same optimal value, every point on the line segment joining them is also optimal, so there are infinitely many solutions. Typical problems include diet problems, which minimise cost subject to nutrient requirements, manufacturing problems that maximise profit under limited machine time and raw material, and transportation problems. The graph of a linear inequality is a half-plane, determined by testing a point such as the origin. A bounded region is enclosed within a circle, while an unbounded region extends indefinitely. An empty feasible region means there is no solution.
Deep dive: Formulation
Define variables, write the objective function and list the constraints with non-negativity conditions.
Deep dive: Corner point method
Graph the feasible region, find corner points and evaluate Z at each to find the optimum.
Deep dive: Special cases
Unbounded regions need extra checks, and two optimal corners give infinitely many optimal solutions.
Hindi saransh
Rekhik prograaman: uddeshya falan, simayen, sambhav kshetra aur kona-bindu vidhi.
Remember: optimal values of Z occur at corner points of the feasible region.

Visual lesson

Linear Programming

Linear programming deals with optimising a linear objective function subject to linear inequalities called constraints

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Formulation›3Corner point method›4Special cases
🔑

Big idea

  • Linear programming deals with optimising a linear objective function subject to linear inequalities called constraints
  • The objective function Z = ax + by is to be maximised or minimised, the variables x and y are called decision variables, and non-negativity…
  • The feasible region is the common region determined by all constraints, including non-negativity
  • Points inside the region are feasible solutions
Read the full explanation

Linear programming deals with optimising a linear objective function subject to linear inequalities called constraints. The objective function Z = ax + by is to be maximised or minimised, the variables x and y are called decision variables, and non-negativity restrictions x >= 0, y >= 0 apply. The feasible region is the common region determined by all constraints, including non-negativity. Points inside the region are feasible solutions; points outside are infeasible. A feasible solution that optimises the objective function is an optimal solution. The corner point theorem says that if the feasible region is bounded, the objective function has both a maximum and minimum at corner points. If the region is unbounded, a maximum or minimum may not exist; if the maximum (or minimum) exists it occurs at a corner point. For an unbounded region, draw the half-plane ax + by > M (for maximum) or < m (for minimum) and see if it has points in common with the feasible region; if not, M (or m) is the value. The corner point method has steps: formulate the problem mathematically, graph constraints, identify the feasible region, find corner points by solving boundary equations, compute Z at each corner and select the largest or smallest. If two corner points give the same optimal value, every point on the line segment joining them is also optimal, so there are infinitely many solutions. Typical problems include diet problems, which minimise cost subject to nutrient requirements, manufacturing problems that maximise profit under limited machine time and raw material, and transportation problems. The graph of a linear inequality is a half-plane, determined by testing a point such as the origin. A bounded region is enclosed within a circle, while an unbounded region extends indefinitely. An empty feasible region means there is no solution.

🧮

Formulation

  • Define variables, write the objective function and list the constraints with non-negativity conditions
🔄

Corner point method

  • Graph the feasible region, find corner points and evaluate Z at each to find the optimum
🌟

Special cases

  • Unbounded regions need extra checks, and two optimal corners give infinitely many optimal solutions

lessons.title: Probability
yt: class 12 maths probability conditional probability bayes theorem independent events random variable binomial distribution mean variance

blocks.x: Probability measures the likelihood of an event. The conditional probability of E given F, with P(F) not zero, is P(E|F) = P(E intersection F)/P(F). Properties: 0 <= P(E|F) <= 1, P(S|F) = P(F|F) = 1, and P((E union G)|F) = P(E|F) + P(G|F) - P((E intersection G)|F). The multiplication theorem says P(E intersection F) = P(E) P(F|E) = P(F) P(E|F). Events E and F are independent if P(E intersection F) = P(E) P(F); independence is different from mutual exclusion. If E and F are independent, so are E and F complement, and E complement and F complement. Three events are mutually independent if they are pairwise independent and P(A intersection B intersection C) = P(A)P(B)P(C). A partition of a sample space is a set of mutually exclusive, exhaustive events with positive probability. The theorem of total probability says P(A) = sum of P(Ei) P(A|Ei). Bayes’ theorem says P(Ei|A) = P(Ei) P(A|Ei) / sum of P(Ej) P(A|Ej); P(Ei) are priors and P(Ei|A) are posteriors. A random variable is a real-valued function defined on the sample space. The probability distribution lists values and probabilities, with sum of probabilities equal to 1. The mean or expectation is E(X) = sum of xi pi and the variance is Var(X) = sum of xi^2 pi minus (E(X))^2, with standard deviation the square root of variance. A Bernoulli trial has two outcomes, success and failure. The binomial distribution B(n, p) gives P(X = r) = nCr p^r q^(n - r) with q = 1 - p, and mean np and variance npq. Conditions are a fixed number n of independent trials with the same probability p. Problems include drawing cards or balls with and without replacement, the probability of at least one success is 1 minus q^n, and the use of tree diagrams.
Deep dive: Conditional probability
P(E|F) = P(E and F)/P(F); the multiplication rule follows directly.
Deep dive: Independence and Bayes
Independent events satisfy P(E and F) = P(E)P(F); Bayes’ theorem reverses conditioning using total probability.
Deep dive: Distributions
Random variables have mean and variance; the binomial distribution has mean np and variance npq.

Probability

Probability measures the likelihood of an event

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Conditional probability›3Independence and Bayes›4Distributions
🔑

Big idea

  • Probability measures the likelihood of an event
  • The conditional probability of E given F, with P(F) not zero, is P(E|F) = P(E intersection F)/P(F)
  • Properties: 0 <= P(E|F) <= 1, P(S|F) = P(F|F) = 1, and P((E union G)|F) = P(E|F) + P(G|F) - P((E intersection G)|F)
  • The multiplication theorem says P(E intersection F) = P(E) P(F|E) = P(F) P(E|F)
Read the full explanation

Probability measures the likelihood of an event. The conditional probability of E given F, with P(F) not zero, is P(E|F) = P(E intersection F)/P(F). Properties: 0 <= P(E|F) <= 1, P(S|F) = P(F|F) = 1, and P((E union G)|F) = P(E|F) + P(G|F) - P((E intersection G)|F). The multiplication theorem says P(E intersection F) = P(E) P(F|E) = P(F) P(E|F). Events E and F are independent if P(E intersection F) = P(E) P(F); independence is different from mutual exclusion. If E and F are independent, so are E and F complement, and E complement and F complement. Three events are mutually independent if they are pairwise independent and P(A intersection B intersection C) = P(A)P(B)P(C). A partition of a sample space is a set of mutually exclusive, exhaustive events with positive probability. The theorem of total probability says P(A) = sum of P(Ei) P(A|Ei). Bayes’ theorem says P(Ei|A) = P(Ei) P(A|Ei) / sum of P(Ej) P(A|Ej); P(Ei) are priors and P(Ei|A) are posteriors. A random variable is a real-valued function defined on the sample space. The probability distribution lists values and probabilities, with sum of probabilities equal to 1. The mean or expectation is E(X) = sum of xi pi and the variance is Var(X) = sum of xi^2 pi minus (E(X))^2, with standard deviation the square root of variance. A Bernoulli trial has two outcomes, success and failure. The binomial distribution B(n, p) gives P(X = r) = nCr p^r q^(n - r) with q = 1 - p, and mean np and variance npq. Conditions are a fixed number n of independent trials with the same probability p. Problems include drawing cards or balls with and without replacement, the probability of at least one success is 1 minus q^n, and the use of tree diagrams.

📌

Conditional probability

  • P(E|F) = P(E and F)/P(F)
  • The multiplication rule follows directly
🧠

Independence and Bayes

  • Independent events satisfy P(E and F) = P(E)P(F)
  • Bayes’ theorem reverses conditioning using total probability
🌟

Distributions

  • Random variables have mean and variance
  • The binomial distribution has mean np and variance npq

lessons.title: Management of Sporting Events
yt: class 12 physical education management of sporting events fixtures knockout league tournament committees marathon

blocks.x: Sports event management is the planning, organising, directing and controlling of a sports event. Its functions follow the managerial pattern: planning (goals, resources, schedule), organising (committees and duties), staffing (officials and volunteers), directing (leadership and coordination) and controlling (monitoring and evaluation). Committees are formed before, during and after an event: pre-event committees handle publicity, finance, ground and equipment, transport, accommodation, food, medical and technical matters; during-event committees look after the conduct and supervision; post-event committees handle results, thanks and evaluation. Intramural competitions are held within one institution, while extramural competitions involve teams from different institutions. A tournament has formats. In a knockout tournament, a team that loses is out; the number of matches equals N - 1 for N teams; if N is not a power of 2, byes equal the next power of 2 minus N, and byes are distributed in upper and lower halves with seeding to keep strong teams apart. In a league or round robin tournament, every team plays every other team once; the number of matches is N(N - 1)/2 and rounds are N - 1 for an even N and N for an odd N. In a cyclic fixture, teams are arranged in rotation. A combination tournament mixes knockout and league stages. Special events include Marathon (42.195 km), Run for Fun and Run for Specific Cause such as health or awareness, and community sports events for participation. Planning a run involves route, safety, hydration, volunteers, medical teams and clearance. A sports meet needs a schedule, officials, scoring and records.
Deep dive: Event management
Planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling are applied to sports events through committees.
Deep dive: Fixtures
Knockout, league and combination fixtures use formulas for the number of matches, rounds and byes.
Deep dive: Run events
Marathons and awareness runs need route planning, safety, hydration and medical arrangements.
Hindi saransh
Khel aayojan prabandhan: samitiyan, knockout aur league fixture, marathon aur Run for Fun.
Remember: knockout matches = N - 1; league matches = N(N - 1)/2.

Read the full explanation

Sports event management is the planning, organising, directing and controlling of a sports event. Its functions follow the managerial pattern: planning (goals, resources, schedule), organising (committees and duties), staffing (officials and volunteers), directing (leadership and coordination) and controlling (monitoring and evaluation). Committees are formed before, during and after an event: pre-event committees handle publicity, finance, ground and equipment, transport, accommodation, food, medical and technical matters; during-event committees look after the conduct and supervision; post-event committees handle results, thanks and evaluation. Intramural competitions are held within one institution, while extramural competitions involve teams from different institutions. A tournament has formats. In a knockout tournament, a team that loses is out; the number of matches equals N - 1 for N teams; if N is not a power of 2, byes equal the next power of 2 minus N, and byes are distributed in upper and lower halves with seeding to keep strong teams apart. In a league or round robin tournament, every team plays every other team once; the number of matches is N(N - 1)/2 and rounds are N - 1 for an even N and N for an odd N. In a cyclic fixture, teams are arranged in rotation. A combination tournament mixes knockout and league stages. Special events include Marathon (42.195 km), Run for Fun and Run for Specific Cause such as health or awareness, and community sports events for participation. Planning a run involves route, safety, hydration, volunteers, medical teams and clearance. A sports meet needs a schedule, officials, scoring and records.

  • Planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling are applied to sports events through committees
🧠

  • Knockout, league and combination fixtures use formulas for the number of matches, rounds and byes

  • Marathons and awareness runs need route planning, safety, hydration and medical arrangements

lessons.title: Children and Women in Sports
yt: class 12 physical education children and women in sports motor development postural deformities female athlete triad

blocks.x: Children go through physical, motor, mental and social development. Motor development is the progressive change in movement skills, and it depends on age, nutrition, heredity, environment and practice. Exercise guidelines for children recommend at least 60 minutes of moderate to vigorous physical activity daily, with strengthening activities three days a week. Regular activity improves growth, fitness, bone health, posture, concentration and confidence, while a sedentary lifestyle causes obesity and diabetes. Postural deformities include knock knees (the knees touch while the ankles are apart), bow legs (the knees are apart while the ankles touch), flat foot (the arch of the foot is flattened), round shoulders, kyphosis (excess forward curve of the upper back), lordosis (excess inward curve of the lower back) and scoliosis (sideways curve of the spine). Corrective exercises include stretching, strengthening, yoga and, where needed, medical advice. Women face special concerns in sports. Female athlete triad refers to the combination of disordered eating, amenorrhoea (missed menstrual cycles) and osteoporosis (weak bones). Causes include low energy intake and heavy training; prevention includes balanced diet, adequate calcium and iron, rest and counselling. Menstrual dysfunction and iron deficiency anaemia are common. Women’s participation is influenced by social attitudes, safety, facilities, lack of role models and family support. Measures to promote it include equal opportunity, women coaches, scholarships, safe facilities and media coverage. Pregnancy and post-pregnancy exercise should follow medical advice.
Deep dive: Children’s activity
Sixty minutes of daily activity supports growth and fitness and prevents lifestyle disease.
Deep dive: Postural deformities
Knock knees, bow legs, flat foot, kyphosis, lordosis and scoliosis are corrected by exercises and care.
Deep dive: Women in sports
The female athlete triad and social barriers need nutrition, counselling and supportive policies.

Bachche aur mahilayein: motor vikas, mudra vikriti, female athlete triad aur mahilaon ki bhagidari.

lessons.title: Yoga as Preventive Measure for Lifestyle Disease
yt: class 12 physical education yoga lifestyle disease obesity diabetes asthma hypertension back pain asanas pranayama

blocks.x: Lifestyle diseases arise from daily habits such as a sedentary lifestyle, poor diet, stress and lack of sleep. Common examples are obesity, diabetes, hypertension, asthma and back pain. Yoga is a preventive and corrective measure because asanas, pranayama and meditation improve circulation, digestion, flexibility and mental calm. Obesity is excess body fat; beneficial asanas include Tadasana, Katichakrasana, Pavanmuktasana, Matsyasana, Halasana, Pashchimottanasana, Ardha Matsyendrasana, Dhanurasana and Ustrasana. Diabetes is a condition in which the body cannot control blood sugar; helpful asanas include Katichakrasana, Pavanmuktasana, Bhujangasana, Shalabhasana, Dhanurasana, Pashchimottanasana and Ardha Matsyendrasana. Asthma is a respiratory disorder; helpful asanas include Sukhasana, Chakrasana, Gomukhasana, Parvatasana, Bhujangasana and Matsyasana, with pranayama such as Anulom Vilom. Hypertension is persistently high blood pressure; helpful asanas include Tadasana, Vajrasana, Ardha Chakrasana, Pavanmuktasana and Bhujangasana with relaxation like Shavasana. Back pain is treated with Tadasana, Ardha Chakrasana, Vakrasana, Bhujangasana and Shalabhasana. Pranayama such as Anulom Vilom, Kapalbhati, Bhramari and Ujjayi aid breathing and calm. Shatkarmas are cleansing techniques: Neti, Dhauti, Nauli, Basti, Trataka and Kapalbhati. Practice precautions include empty stomach, a clean airy place, supervision, and avoiding force. Contra-indications must be known: a person with a heart problem should not do vigorous practices. Surya Namaskar is a series of twelve postures.
Deep dive: Lifestyle diseases
Poor habits cause obesity, diabetes, hypertension, asthma and back pain, which yoga helps prevent.
Deep dive: Asanas
Different asanas are recommended for each condition, along with pranayama and relaxation.
Deep dive: Precautions
Practise on an empty stomach under guidance and follow contra-indications.
Hindi saransh
Yoga aur jeevan-shaili rog: motapa, madhumeh, ucch raktchaap, dama aur kamar dard ke liye asan.
Remember: Shavasana relaxes; Kapalbhati is also a shatkarma.

Visual lesson

Yoga as Preventive Measure for Lifestyle Disease

Lifestyle diseases arise from daily habits such as a sedentary lifestyle, poor diet, stress and lack of sleep

🔑

Big idea

  • Lifestyle diseases arise from daily habits such as a sedentary lifestyle, poor diet, stress and lack of sleep

Read the full explanation

Lifestyle diseases arise from daily habits such as a sedentary lifestyle, poor diet, stress and lack of sleep. Common examples are obesity, diabetes, hypertension, asthma and back pain. Yoga is a preventive and corrective measure because asanas, pranayama and meditation improve circulation, digestion, flexibility and mental calm. Obesity is excess body fat; beneficial asanas include Tadasana, Katichakrasana, Pavanmuktasana, Matsyasana, Halasana, Pashchimottanasana, Ardha Matsyendrasana, Dhanurasana and Ustrasana. Diabetes is a condition in which the body cannot control blood sugar; helpful asanas include Katichakrasana, Pavanmuktasana, Bhujangasana, Shalabhasana, Dhanurasana, Pashchimottanasana and Ardha Matsyendrasana. Asthma is a respiratory disorder; helpful asanas include Sukhasana, Chakrasana, Gomukhasana, Parvatasana, Bhujangasana and Matsyasana, with pranayama such as Anulom Vilom. Hypertension is persistently high blood pressure; helpful asanas include Tadasana, Vajrasana, Ardha Chakrasana, Pavanmuktasana and Bhujangasana with relaxation like Shavasana. Back pain is treated with Tadasana, Ardha Chakrasana, Vakrasana, Bhujangasana and Shalabhasana. Pranayama such as Anulom Vilom, Kapalbhati, Bhramari and Ujjayi aid breathing and calm. Shatkarmas are cleansing techniques: Neti, Dhauti, Nauli, Basti, Trataka and Kapalbhati. Practice precautions include empty stomach, a clean airy place, supervision, and avoiding force. Contra-indications must be known: a person with a heart problem should not do vigorous practices. Surya Namaskar is a series of twelve postures.

📌

Lifestyle diseases

  • Poor habits cause obesity, diabetes, hypertension, asthma and back pain, which yoga helps prevent
🧠

Asanas

  • Different asanas are recommended for each condition, along with pranayama and relaxation
🌟

Precautions

  • Practise on an empty stomach under guidance and follow contra-indications
🧮

🎯 Remember Shavasana relaxes; Kapalbhati is also a shatkarma.

lessons.title: Physical Education and Sports for CWSN
yt: class 12 physical education children with special needs disability disorder autism ADHD paralympics special olympics deaflympics

blocks.x: CWSN means Children With Special Needs. A disorder is a disturbance in the normal functioning of body or mind, while a disability is a physical or mental condition that limits movement, senses or activities. Disability is described as cognitive, physical and sensory. Cognitive disabilities include intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and specific learning disability (SLD) such as dyslexia (reading), dysgraphia (writing) and dyscalculia (mathematics). Physical disabilities include locomotor disability (difficulty in movement), visual impairment and hearing impairment. Physical activity gives CWSN better health, social inclusion, self-confidence, independence and motor skills. Strategies to make activities accessible include adapting rules, equipment and the environment, giving clear demonstration, keeping groups small, using teaching aids, ensuring safety and rewarding effort. Inclusive education and inclusive sports mean learning and playing together. Disability etiquette means people-first language and respect, for example saying a person with a disability, not a disabled person, asking before helping and speaking directly to the person. Organisations and events matter. The Paralympic Games grew from the work of Ludwig Guttmann at Stoke Mandeville, and the first Paralympic Games were held in Rome in 1960. Special Olympics was founded by Eunice Kennedy Shriver in 1968 for people with intellectual disability and its oath says Let me win, but if I cannot win, let me be brave in the attempt. Special Olympics Bharat is the Indian programme. The Deaflympics are for deaf athletes, first held in Paris in 1924. Counsellors, coaches, special educators and parents form the support team.
Deep dive: Disability and disorder
A disorder disturbs functioning; a disability limits activity. Types include cognitive, physical and sensory.
Deep dive: Inclusion
Adapted rules, equipment and attitudes let CWSN take part, gain confidence and become independent.
Deep dive: Events
Paralympics, Special Olympics and Deaflympics give CWSN a competitive platform.
Hindi saransh
CWSN ke liye khel: viklangta ke prakar, samaveshi khel, Paralympics, Special Olympics aur Deaflympics.
Remember: Special Olympics is for intellectual disability; Deaflympics is for deaf athletes.

Read the full explanation

CWSN means Children With Special Needs. A disorder is a disturbance in the normal functioning of body or mind, while a disability is a physical or mental condition that limits movement, senses or activities. Disability is described as cognitive, physical and sensory. Cognitive disabilities include intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and specific learning disability (SLD) such as dyslexia (reading), dysgraphia (writing) and dyscalculia (mathematics). Physical disabilities include locomotor disability (difficulty in movement), visual impairment and hearing impairment. Physical activity gives CWSN better health, social inclusion, self-confidence, independence and motor skills. Strategies to make activities accessible include adapting rules, equipment and the environment, giving clear demonstration, keeping groups small, using teaching aids, ensuring safety and rewarding effort. Inclusive education and inclusive sports mean learning and playing together. Disability etiquette means people-first language and respect, for example saying a person with a disability, not a disabled person, asking before helping and speaking directly to the person. Organisations and events matter. The Paralympic Games grew from the work of Ludwig Guttmann at Stoke Mandeville, and the first Paralympic Games were held in Rome in 1960. Special Olympics was founded by Eunice Kennedy Shriver in 1968 for people with intellectual disability and its oath says Let me win, but if I cannot win, let me be brave in the attempt. Special Olympics Bharat is the Indian programme. The Deaflympics are for deaf athletes, first held in Paris in 1924. Counsellors, coaches, special educators and parents form the support team.

📌

Disability and disorder

  • A disorder disturbs functioning
  • A disability limits activity
  • Types include cognitive, physical and sensory
🧠

Inclusion

  • Adapted rules, equipment and attitudes let CWSN take part, gain confidence and become independent
🌟

Events

  • Paralympics, Special Olympics and Deaflympics give CWSN a competitive platform

lessons.title: Sports and Nutrition
yt: class 12 physical education sports and nutrition balanced diet macro micro nutrients carbohydrates proteins fats vitamins pre competition diet

blocks.x: Nutrition is the process by which the body takes in and uses food. A balanced diet gives all nutrients in the right proportion to meet the needs of the body. Macronutrients are needed in large amounts: carbohydrates (4 kcal per gram, the main fuel), proteins (4 kcal per gram, for growth and repair) and fats (9 kcal per gram, concentrated energy). Micronutrients are needed in small amounts: vitamins and minerals. Vitamins A, D, E and K are fat soluble; vitamins B complex and C are water soluble. Deficiency diseases include night blindness (vitamin A), rickets (vitamin D), scurvy (vitamin C), beriberi (vitamin B1), goitre (iodine) and anaemia (iron). Calcium builds bones and teeth, iron forms haemoglobin, and sodium and potassium keep fluid balance. Water, about 60 per cent of body weight, regulates temperature and carries nutrients. Fibre or roughage is a non-nutritive component that aids digestion. Nutritive components give energy and growth; non-nutritive components such as fibre, water and colour agents do not give energy. Food intake and energy balance affect weight: healthy weight is judged by BMI, which equals weight in kg divided by height in metres squared. Pre-competition meals should be light, easy to digest and eaten about three to four hours before, with carbohydrates. During competition fluids and quick energy such as glucose are useful. After competition, carbohydrates and proteins restore glycogen and repair muscle. Eating disorders such as anorexia and bulimia harm athletes. Myths include that more protein always means more muscle, and that supplements replace food. Food intolerance and allergy need care.
Deep dive: Nutrients
Carbohydrates and fats give energy, proteins build and repair, vitamins and minerals protect and regulate.
Deep dive: Balanced diet
The right amounts of all nutrients support growth, performance and healthy weight measured by BMI.
Deep dive: Sports meals
Pre-competition meals are light with carbohydrates; post-competition meals restore glycogen and repair tissue.
Hindi saransh
Khel aur poshan: santulit aahar, poshak tatva, vitamin, khanij aur pratiyogita se pehle ka bhojan.

Read the full explanation

Nutrition is the process by which the body takes in and uses food. A balanced diet gives all nutrients in the right proportion to meet the needs of the body. Macronutrients are needed in large amounts: carbohydrates (4 kcal per gram, the main fuel), proteins (4 kcal per gram, for growth and repair) and fats (9 kcal per gram, concentrated energy). Micronutrients are needed in small amounts: vitamins and minerals. Vitamins A, D, E and K are fat soluble; vitamins B complex and C are water soluble. Deficiency diseases include night blindness (vitamin A), rickets (vitamin D), scurvy (vitamin C), beriberi (vitamin B1), goitre (iodine) and anaemia (iron). Calcium builds bones and teeth, iron forms haemoglobin, and sodium and potassium keep fluid balance. Water, about 60 per cent of body weight, regulates temperature and carries nutrients. Fibre or roughage is a non-nutritive component that aids digestion. Nutritive components give energy and growth; non-nutritive components such as fibre, water and colour agents do not give energy. Food intake and energy balance affect weight: healthy weight is judged by BMI, which equals weight in kg divided by height in metres squared. Pre-competition meals should be light, easy to digest and eaten about three to four hours before, with carbohydrates. During competition fluids and quick energy such as glucose are useful. After competition, carbohydrates and proteins restore glycogen and repair muscle. Eating disorders such as anorexia and bulimia harm athletes. Myths include that more protein always means more muscle, and that supplements replace food. Food intolerance and allergy need care.

📌

Nutrients

  • Carbohydrates and fats give energy, proteins build and repair, vitamins and minerals protect and regulate
🧠

Balanced diet

  • The right amounts of all nutrients support growth, performance and healthy weight measured by BMI
🌟

Sports meals

  • Pre-competition meals are light with carbohydrates
  • Post-competition meals restore glycogen and repair tissue

lessons.title: Test and Measurement in Sports
yt: class 12 physical education test and measurement rikli jones harvard step test 50 m dash sit and reach motor fitness

blocks.x: Measurement is the process of assigning numbers to a performance, while evaluation judges its quality against a standard. A test is a tool for measurement. Tests are used to assess fitness, select players, plan training and monitor progress. The Rikli and Jones Senior Citizen Fitness Test is for adults aged 60 and above and has seven items: chair stand test (lower body strength, 30 seconds), arm curl test (upper body strength, 30 seconds; 5 pound weight for women and 8 pound for men), chair sit and reach (lower body flexibility), back scratch (upper body flexibility), eight-foot up and go (agility and dynamic balance), and the six-minute walk or the two-minute step test (aerobic endurance). Motor fitness tests include the 50 m dash for speed, the 600 m run or walk for endurance, the standing broad jump for explosive leg strength, the medicine ball throw for arm strength and the sit and reach for flexibility. The Harvard Step Test measures cardiovascular fitness. The bench is 20 inches high for men and 18 inches for women, the stepping rate is 30 steps per minute for up to five minutes, and the pulse is counted from 1 to 1.5 minutes after exercise. The Physical Fitness Index is duration of exercise in seconds multiplied by 100, divided by 5.5 times the pulse count. A score above 90 is excellent, 80 to 89 good, 65 to 79 high average, 55 to 64 low average and below 55 poor. Measuring general motor fitness uses speed, strength, endurance and flexibility items together. Good tests are valid, reliable, objective and standardised.
Deep dive: Measurement and evaluation
Measurement gives numbers; evaluation judges them against a standard for selection and planning.
Deep dive: Rikli and Jones
A seven item test for older adults covering strength, flexibility, agility and endurance.
Deep dive: Harvard Step Test

Read the full explanation

Measurement is the process of assigning numbers to a performance, while evaluation judges its quality against a standard. A test is a tool for measurement. Tests are used to assess fitness, select players, plan training and monitor progress. The Rikli and Jones Senior Citizen Fitness Test is for adults aged 60 and above and has seven items: chair stand test (lower body strength, 30 seconds), arm curl test (upper body strength, 30 seconds; 5 pound weight for women and 8 pound for men), chair sit and reach (lower body flexibility), back scratch (upper body flexibility), eight-foot up and go (agility and dynamic balance), and the six-minute walk or the two-minute step test (aerobic endurance). Motor fitness tests include the 50 m dash for speed, the 600 m run or walk for endurance, the standing broad jump for explosive leg strength, the medicine ball throw for arm strength and the sit and reach for flexibility. The Harvard Step Test measures cardiovascular fitness. The bench is 20 inches high for men and 18 inches for women, the stepping rate is 30 steps per minute for up to five minutes, and the pulse is counted from 1 to 1.5 minutes after exercise. The Physical Fitness Index is duration of exercise in seconds multiplied by 100, divided by 5.5 times the pulse count. A score above 90 is excellent, 80 to 89 good, 65 to 79 high average, 55 to 64 low average and below 55 poor. Measuring general motor fitness uses speed, strength, endurance and flexibility items together. Good tests are valid, reliable, objective and standardised.

📌

Measurement and evaluation

  • Measurement gives numbers
  • Evaluation judges them against a standard for selection and planning

lessons.title: Physiology and Injuries in Sports
yt: class 12 physical education physiology injuries fracture sprain strain PRICER strength endurance speed flexibility fast twitch

blocks.x: Physiological factors determine each motor quality. Strength depends on muscle cross-section, muscle fibre type, age, gender, nervous coordination and hormones. Endurance depends on aerobic capacity (VO2 max), anaerobic threshold, muscle fuel stores, heart and lung efficiency and tolerance of lactic acid. Speed depends on reaction ability, muscle fibre composition (fast twitch), strength and flexibility. Flexibility depends on joint structure, muscle elasticity, tendons and ligaments, age, gender, temperature and warm-up. Coordination depends on the central nervous system and sense organs. Exercise improves heart size and stroke volume, lowers resting heart rate, raises lung capacity and strengthens muscles and bones. With ageing, muscle mass, bone density and flexibility decline. Gender differences include greater muscle mass and haemoglobin in males and more body fat in females. Sports injuries are classified as soft tissue, bone and joint injuries. Soft tissue injuries include abrasion (scrape), contusion (bruise), laceration (irregular cut), incision (clean cut), sprain (ligament tear) and strain (muscle or tendon tear). Bone injuries are fractures: simple, compound (open), greenstick (partial, in children), comminuted (broken into pieces), transverse, oblique and impacted. A dislocation is displacement of a bone from its joint. Causes include poor warm-up, faulty technique, fatigue, bad equipment and ground, and overtraining. Prevention includes proper warm-up, conditioning, protective equipment and rest. First aid for soft tissue injury follows PRICER: Protection, Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation and Rehabilitation. Cramps are painful involuntary muscle contractions treated with stretching and fluids.
Deep dive: Physiological factors
Strength, endurance, speed, flexibility and coordination depend on fibre type, aerobic capacity, nervous control and joint structure.
Deep dive: Injuries
Soft tissue, bone and joint injuries arise from poor warm-up, fatigue, faulty technique and bad equipment.
Deep dive: First aid
PRICER guides care: protection, rest, ice, compression, elevation and rehabilitation.

Khel mein sharir kriya aur chotein: shakti, sahansheelta, gati, lachilapan, fracture, sprain aur PRICER.
Remember: sprain is a ligament tear, strain is a muscle or tendon tear.

Visual lesson

Physiology and Injuries in Sports

Physiological factors determine each motor quality

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Physiological factors›3Injuries›4First aid
🔑

Big idea

  • Physiological factors determine each motor quality
  • Strength depends on muscle cross-section, muscle fibre type, age, gender, nervous coordination and hormones
  • Endurance depends on aerobic capacity (VO2 max), anaerobic threshold, muscle fuel stores, heart and lung efficiency and tolerance of lactic acid
  • Speed depends on reaction ability, muscle fibre composition (fast twitch), strength and flexibility
Read the full explanation

Physiological factors determine each motor quality. Strength depends on muscle cross-section, muscle fibre type, age, gender, nervous coordination and hormones. Endurance depends on aerobic capacity (VO2 max), anaerobic threshold, muscle fuel stores, heart and lung efficiency and tolerance of lactic acid. Speed depends on reaction ability, muscle fibre composition (fast twitch), strength and flexibility. Flexibility depends on joint structure, muscle elasticity, tendons and ligaments, age, gender, temperature and warm-up. Coordination depends on the central nervous system and sense organs. Exercise improves heart size and stroke volume, lowers resting heart rate, raises lung capacity and strengthens muscles and bones. With ageing, muscle mass, bone density and flexibility decline. Gender differences include greater muscle mass and haemoglobin in males and more body fat in females. Sports injuries are classified as soft tissue, bone and joint injuries. Soft tissue injuries include abrasion (scrape), contusion (bruise), laceration (irregular cut), incision (clean cut), sprain (ligament tear) and strain (muscle or tendon tear). Bone injuries are fractures: simple, compound (open), greenstick (partial, in children), comminuted (broken into pieces), transverse, oblique and impacted. A dislocation is displacement of a bone from its joint. Causes include poor warm-up, faulty technique, fatigue, bad equipment and ground, and overtraining. Prevention includes proper warm-up, conditioning, protective equipment and rest. First aid for soft tissue injury follows PRICER: Protection, Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation and Rehabilitation. Cramps are painful involuntary muscle contractions treated with stretching and fluids.

📌

Physiological factors

  • Strength, endurance, speed, flexibility and coordination depend on fibre type, aerobic capacity, nervous control and joint structure
🧠

Injuries

  • Soft tissue, bone and joint injuries arise from poor warm-up, fatigue, faulty technique and bad equipment
🌟

First aid

  • PRICER guides care: protection, rest, ice, compression, elevation and rehabilitation

lessons.title: Biomechanics and Sports
yt: class 12 physical education biomechanics newton laws levers equilibrium friction projectile axes planes

blocks.x: Biomechanics applies the laws of mechanics to living bodies and sport. Newton’s first law, the law of inertia, says a body stays at rest or in uniform motion unless acted on by a force; a footballer sliding after stopping and a runner continuing after the finish line show it. The second law says force equals mass times acceleration, F = ma; a harder kick gives a bigger acceleration. The third law says every action has an equal and opposite reaction; a sprinter pushes the ground back and the ground pushes forward. Levers have an effort, a load and a fulcrum. In a first class lever the fulcrum lies between effort and load, as in nodding the head; in a second class lever the load lies between fulcrum and effort, as in raising the heels; in a third class lever the effort lies between fulcrum and load, as in the biceps curl, the most common type in the body. Equilibrium is a state of balance: static when at rest and dynamic when moving. It is stable, unstable or neutral. Stability increases with a lower centre of gravity, a larger base of support, a heavier body and a line of gravity falling within the base. Friction opposes motion; static, sliding and rolling friction matter, and spikes and grip raise useful friction while lubrication reduces harmful friction. A projectile follows a curved path under gravity; the optimum angle of release for maximum range at the same height is 45 degrees. Planes divide the body: sagittal (left and right), frontal (front and back) and transverse (upper and lower), and movements occur around axes. Movement terms include flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, rotation and circumduction.
Deep dive: Newton’s laws
Inertia, F = ma and action reaction explain starts, kicks, throws and landings.
Deep dive: Levers
First, second and third class levers differ in the position of the fulcrum, load and effort.
Deep dive: Equilibrium and projectiles
A low centre of gravity and wide base add stability; 45 degrees gives the maximum range.
Hindi saransh
Khel ki jaiv-yantriki: Newton ke niyam, bhuja, santulan, gharshan aur prakshepya.
Remember: F = ma; biceps curl is a third class lever.

Big idea

  • Biomechanics applies the laws of mechanics to living bodies and sport
  • Newton’s first law, the law of inertia, says a body stays at rest or in uniform motion unless acted on by a force
  • A footballer sliding after stopping and a runner continuing after the finish line show it

Read the full explanation

Biomechanics applies the laws of mechanics to living bodies and sport. Newton’s first law, the law of inertia, says a body stays at rest or in uniform motion unless acted on by a force; a footballer sliding after stopping and a runner continuing after the finish line show it. The second law says force equals mass times acceleration, F = ma; a harder kick gives a bigger acceleration. The third law says every action has an equal and opposite reaction; a sprinter pushes the ground back and the ground pushes forward. Levers have an effort, a load and a fulcrum. In a first class lever the fulcrum lies between effort and load, as in nodding the head; in a second class lever the load lies between fulcrum and effort, as in raising the heels; in a third class lever the effort lies between fulcrum and load, as in the biceps curl, the most common type in the body. Equilibrium is a state of balance: static when at rest and dynamic when moving. It is stable, unstable or neutral. Stability increases with a lower centre of gravity, a larger base of support, a heavier body and a line of gravity falling within the base. Friction opposes motion; static, sliding and rolling friction matter, and spikes and grip raise useful friction while lubrication reduces harmful friction. A projectile follows a curved path under gravity; the optimum angle of release for maximum range at the same height is 45 degrees. Planes divide the body: sagittal (left and right), frontal (front and back) and transverse (upper and lower), and movements occur around axes. Movement terms include flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, rotation and circumduction.

⚖️

Newton’s laws

  • Inertia, F = ma and action reaction explain starts, kicks, throws and landings
🧠

Levers

  • First, second and third class levers differ in the position of the fulcrum, load and effort
🌟

Equilibrium and projectiles

  • A low centre of gravity and wide base add stability
  • 45 degrees gives the maximum range

lessons.title: Psychology and Sports
yt: class 12 physical education psychology and sports personality Jung Sheldon Big Five motivation aggression goal setting imagery

blocks.x: Sports psychology studies the mind of athletes and its effect on performance. Personality is the sum of the characteristics that make a person unique. Carl Jung classified people as introverts and extroverts; introverts are shy and inward looking, extroverts are outgoing and sociable. Sheldon’s body type theory links body build and temperament: endomorphic (round, soft; relaxed and sociable), mesomorphic (muscular; energetic and assertive) and ectomorphic (thin; reserved and thoughtful). The Big Five traits are openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism. Motivation is the inner drive that directs behaviour; intrinsic motivation comes from within, for enjoyment, and extrinsic motivation comes from rewards and recognition. Techniques to raise motivation include goal setting, rewards, praise, varied training and a good coach. Exercise adherence means sticking to a regular exercise programme; it improves with enjoyment, social support, convenient time and place, and realistic goals, and falls with injury, lack of time and boredom. Aggression is behaviour intended to harm. Hostile aggression aims to hurt another, while instrumental aggression is used to achieve a goal, and assertive behaviour is firm but within the rules. Psychological attributes include self-esteem (how one values oneself), mental imagery (rehearsing performance in the mind, internal or external), self-talk (positive statements to oneself) and goal setting. SMART goals are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic and Time bound. Relaxation and concentration help control anxiety.
Deep dive: Personality
Jung’s introvert and extrovert, Sheldon’s body types and the Big Five describe personality.
Deep dive: Motivation and adherence
Intrinsic and extrinsic motives, goals and support keep athletes training.
Deep dive: Mental skills
Self-esteem, imagery, self-talk and SMART goals improve performance and control aggression.

Visual lesson

Psychology and Sports

Sports psychology studies the mind of athletes and its effect on performance

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Personality›3Motivation and adherence›4Mental skills
🔑

Big idea

  • Sports psychology studies the mind of athletes and its effect on performance
  • Personality is the sum of the characteristics that make a person unique
  • Carl Jung classified people as introverts and extroverts
  • Introverts are shy and inward looking, extroverts are outgoing and sociable
Read the full explanation

Sports psychology studies the mind of athletes and its effect on performance. Personality is the sum of the characteristics that make a person unique. Carl Jung classified people as introverts and extroverts; introverts are shy and inward looking, extroverts are outgoing and sociable. Sheldon’s body type theory links body build and temperament: endomorphic (round, soft; relaxed and sociable), mesomorphic (muscular; energetic and assertive) and ectomorphic (thin; reserved and thoughtful). The Big Five traits are openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism. Motivation is the inner drive that directs behaviour; intrinsic motivation comes from within, for enjoyment, and extrinsic motivation comes from rewards and recognition. Techniques to raise motivation include goal setting, rewards, praise, varied training and a good coach. Exercise adherence means sticking to a regular exercise programme; it improves with enjoyment, social support, convenient time and place, and realistic goals, and falls with injury, lack of time and boredom. Aggression is behaviour intended to harm. Hostile aggression aims to hurt another, while instrumental aggression is used to achieve a goal, and assertive behaviour is firm but within the rules. Psychological attributes include self-esteem (how one values oneself), mental imagery (rehearsing performance in the mind, internal or external), self-talk (positive statements to oneself) and goal setting. SMART goals are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic and Time bound. Relaxation and concentration help control anxiety.

🧠

Motivation and adherence

  • Intrinsic and extrinsic motives, goals and support keep athletes training
🌟

  • Self-esteem, imagery, self-talk and SMART goals improve performance and control aggression

lessons.title: Training in Sports
yt: class 12 physical education training in sports strength endurance speed flexibility coordination circuit training fartlek interval

blocks.x: Sports training is a planned, systematic process to improve performance. Its aim is the development of motor qualities through load, overload and recovery. Strength is of three kinds: maximum strength (the greatest force in one effort), explosive strength (fast force, or power) and strength endurance (repeated force over time). Methods are isometric (muscle length does not change), isotonic (muscle length changes) and isokinetic (constant speed). Endurance is aerobic (with oxygen) or anaerobic (without enough oxygen), and its methods are continuous running, interval training (work and recovery intervals) and fartlek (speed play, a Swedish method with varying pace over natural ground). Speed has reaction, movement and acceleration abilities; acceleration runs and pace runs develop it. Flexibility is active (using own muscles) or passive (with outside help), and methods include static stretching, ballistic stretching and PNF (proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation). Coordinative abilities are orientation, differentiation, adaptation, rhythm, reaction, balance and coupling. Circuit training uses a series of stations done in turn, developed by Morgan and Adamson at the University of Leeds in 1953. Principles of training include overload, progression, specificity, individuality, reversibility and variety. Adaptation occurs during recovery, and supercompensation is the rise above the previous level. A warm-up prepares the body and a cool-down helps recovery. Periodisation divides the year into preparatory, competitive and transition periods.
Deep dive: Motor qualities
Strength, endurance, speed, flexibility and coordination are developed by specific methods.
Deep dive: Methods
Isometric, isotonic and isokinetic exercises; continuous, interval and fartlek runs; static, ballistic and PNF stretches.
Deep dive: Planning
Overload, progression, recovery and periodisation turn load into adaptation and peak form.

Read the full explanation

Sports training is a planned, systematic process to improve performance. Its aim is the development of motor qualities through load, overload and recovery. Strength is of three kinds: maximum strength (the greatest force in one effort), explosive strength (fast force, or power) and strength endurance (repeated force over time). Methods are isometric (muscle length does not change), isotonic (muscle length changes) and isokinetic (constant speed). Endurance is aerobic (with oxygen) or anaerobic (without enough oxygen), and its methods are continuous running, interval training (work and recovery intervals) and fartlek (speed play, a Swedish method with varying pace over natural ground). Speed has reaction, movement and acceleration abilities; acceleration runs and pace runs develop it. Flexibility is active (using own muscles) or passive (with outside help), and methods include static stretching, ballistic stretching and PNF (proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation). Coordinative abilities are orientation, differentiation, adaptation, rhythm, reaction, balance and coupling. Circuit training uses a series of stations done in turn, developed by Morgan and Adamson at the University of Leeds in 1953. Principles of training include overload, progression, specificity, individuality, reversibility and variety. Adaptation occurs during recovery, and supercompensation is the rise above the previous level. A warm-up prepares the body and a cool-down helps recovery. Periodisation divides the year into preparatory, competitive and transition periods.

📌

Motor qualities

  • Strength, endurance, speed, flexibility and coordination are developed by specific methods
🔄

Methods

  • Isometric, isotonic and isokinetic exercises
  • Continuous, interval and fartlek runs
  • Static, ballistic and PNF stretches
🌟

Planning

  • Overload, progression, recovery and periodisation turn load into adaptation and peak form

lessons.title: Electric Charges and Fields
yt: class 12 physics electric charges and fields coulomb law electric field dipole gauss law flux

blocks.x: Electric charge is a basic property of matter and is of two kinds, positive and negative. Like charges repel and unlike charges attract. Charge is conserved (it can neither be created nor destroyed in an isolated system), quantised (q = ne, with e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C) and additive. Bodies can be charged by friction, conduction and induction. Coulomb’s law gives the force between two point charges: F = k q1 q2 / r^2, with k = 1/(4 pi epsilon0) = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2, where epsilon0 = 8.85 x 10^-12 C^2 N^-1 m^-2. The force acts along the line joining the charges and obeys superposition. The electric field is the force per unit positive test charge, E = F/q, with unit N/C or V/m; for a point charge E = kq/r^2. Field lines begin on positive and end on negative charges, never cross, and are closer where the field is stronger. An electric dipole is a pair of equal and opposite charges separated by 2a, with dipole moment p = q x 2a pointing from negative to positive. On the axis, E = 2kp/r^3 (for r much greater than a) along p; on the equatorial line, E = kp/r^3 opposite to p. In a uniform field a dipole feels torque tau = pE sin theta and has potential energy U = -pE cos theta. Electric flux is phi = E A cos theta, in N m^2/C. Gauss’s law states that the total flux through a closed surface equals q enclosed divided by epsilon0. Applications: an infinite line charge gives E = lambda/(2 pi epsilon0 r); an infinite plane sheet gives E = sigma/(2 epsilon0); near a charged conductor E = sigma/epsilon0; a thin spherical shell gives E = kq/r^2 outside and zero inside. Charge on a conductor lies on its outer surface, and the field inside a conductor is zero.
Deep dive: Coulomb’s law and field
F = kq1q2/r^2 and E = kq/r^2 describe forces and fields of point charges and obey superposition.
Deep dive: Dipole
Dipole moment p = 2aq; axial field 2kp/r^3, equatorial field kp/r^3; torque pE sin theta.
Deep dive: Gauss’s law
Flux through a closed surface equals q enclosed / epsilon0, giving fields of lines, sheets and shells.
Hindi saransh
Vidyut aaveshan aur kshetra: Coulomb ka niyam, vidyut kshetra, dwidhruv aur Gauss ka niyam.
Remember: inside a charged conducting shell the field is zero; outside it acts like a point charge.

Electric Charges and Fields

Electric charge is a basic property of matter and is of two kinds, positive and negative

formulas

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Coulomb’s law and field›3Dipole›4Gauss’s law
🔑

Big idea

  • Electric charge is a basic property of matter and is of two kinds, positive and negative
  • Like charges repel and unlike charges attract
  • Charge is conserved (it can neither be created nor destroyed in an isolated system), quantised (q = ne, with e = 1.6 x 10-19 C) and additive
  • Bodies can be charged by friction, conduction and induction
Read the full explanation

Electric charge is a basic property of matter and is of two kinds, positive and negative. Like charges repel and unlike charges attract. Charge is conserved (it can neither be created nor destroyed in an isolated system), quantised (q = ne, with e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C) and additive. Bodies can be charged by friction, conduction and induction. Coulomb’s law gives the force between two point charges: F = k q1 q2 / r^2, with k = 1/(4 pi epsilon0) = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2, where epsilon0 = 8.85 x 10^-12 C^2 N^-1 m^-2. The force acts along the line joining the charges and obeys superposition. The electric field is the force per unit positive test charge, E = F/q, with unit N/C or V/m; for a point charge E = kq/r^2. Field lines begin on positive and end on negative charges, never cross, and are closer where the field is stronger. An electric dipole is a pair of equal and opposite charges separated by 2a, with dipole moment p = q x 2a pointing from negative to positive. On the axis, E = 2kp/r^3 (for r much greater than a) along p; on the equatorial line, E = kp/r^3 opposite to p. In a uniform field a dipole feels torque tau = pE sin theta and has potential energy U = -pE cos theta. Electric flux is phi = E A cos theta, in N m^2/C. Gauss’s law states that the total flux through a closed surface equals q enclosed divided by epsilon0. Applications: an infinite line charge gives E = lambda/(2 pi epsilon0 r); an infinite plane sheet gives E = sigma/(2 epsilon0); near a charged conductor E = sigma/epsilon0; a thin spherical shell gives E = kq/r^2 outside and zero inside. Charge on a conductor lies on its outer surface, and the field inside a conductor is zero.

⚖️

Coulomb’s law and field

  • F = kq1q2/r2 and E = kq/r2 describe forces and fields of point charges and obey superposition
🧠

Dipole

  • Dipole moment p = 2aq
  • Axial field 2kp/r3, equatorial field kp/r3
  • Torque pE sin theta
⚖️

Gauss’s law

  • Flux through a closed surface equals q enclosed / epsilon0, giving fields of lines, sheets and shells
🧮

Formula tiles

Coulomb forceF = q1 q2 / (4 pi epsilon0 r^2)
Field of point chargeE = kq / r^2

lessons.title: Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance
yt: class 12 physics electrostatic potential capacitance capacitor dielectric equipotential energy stored combination

blocks.x: Electrostatic potential at a point is the work done per unit positive charge in bringing it from infinity to that point, V = W/q, in volts (J/C). For a point charge V = kq/r; for a dipole on the axis V = kp/r^2 and on the equatorial line V = 0. Potential is a scalar and obeys superposition. The potential difference between two points is the work per unit charge, and the relation E = -dV/dr links field and potential. The potential energy of two point charges is U = k q1 q2 / r. An equipotential surface has the same potential everywhere; no work is done in moving a charge along it, field lines are perpendicular to it, and for a point charge these surfaces are concentric spheres. A conductor is an equipotential body. A capacitor stores charge and energy, with capacitance C = Q/V, in farad. For a parallel plate capacitor in air C = epsilon0 A/d. A dielectric of constant K raises capacitance to K epsilon0 A/d because polarisation reduces the field. In series, 1/C = 1/C1 + 1/C2 and charge is the same; in parallel, C = C1 + C2 and voltage is the same. Energy stored is U = (1/2) CV^2 = Q^2/(2C) = (1/2) QV, and energy density is (1/2) epsilon0 E^2. When a battery stays connected, V is constant; when it is disconnected, Q is constant. A dielectric slab of thickness t between plates gives C = epsilon0 A / (d - t + t/K). Sharing of charge between two connected capacitors conserves charge and loses energy as heat. Van de Graaff generators accumulate high voltages on a hollow sphere.
Deep dive: Potential
V = kq/r is a scalar; E = -dV/dr; equipotential surfaces are perpendicular to field lines.
Deep dive: Capacitance
C = Q/V; parallel plates give C = epsilon0 A/d and a dielectric multiplies it by K.
Deep dive: Energy and combinations
U = (1/2)CV^2; series 1/C adds, parallel C adds.
Hindi saransh
Vidyut vibhav aur dhaarita: vibhav, samvibhav tal, sandharit, dielectric aur sanchit urja.
Remember: series 1/C adds; parallel C adds; energy = half C V squared.

Electrostatic potential at a point is the work done per unit positive charge in bringing it from infinity to that point, V = W/q, in volts (J/C). For a point charge V = kq/r; for a dipole on the axis V = kp/r^2 and on the equatorial line V = 0. Potential is a scalar and obeys superposition. The potential difference between two points is the work per unit charge, and the relation E = -dV/dr links field and potential. The potential energy of two point charges is U = k q1 q2 / r. An equipotential surface has the same potential everywhere; no work is done in moving a charge along it, field lines are perpendicular to it, and for a point charge these surfaces are concentric spheres. A conductor is an equipotential body. A capacitor stores charge and energy, with capacitance C = Q/V, in farad. For a parallel plate capacitor in air C = epsilon0 A/d. A dielectric of constant K raises capacitance to K epsilon0 A/d because polarisation reduces the field. In series, 1/C = 1/C1 + 1/C2 and charge is the same; in parallel, C = C1 + C2 and voltage is the same. Energy stored is U = (1/2) CV^2 = Q^2/(2C) = (1/2) QV, and energy density is (1/2) epsilon0 E^2. When a battery stays connected, V is constant; when it is disconnected, Q is constant. A dielectric slab of thickness t between plates gives C = epsilon0 A / (d - t + t/K). Sharing of charge between two connected capacitors conserves charge and loses energy as heat. Van de Graaff generators accumulate high voltages on a hollow sphere.

📌

Potential

  • V = kq/r is a scalar
  • Equipotential surfaces are perpendicular to field lines
🧠

Capacitance

  • Parallel plates give C = epsilon0 A/d and a dielectric multiplies it by K
🚀

Energy and combinations

  • U = (1/2)CV2
  • Series 1/C adds, parallel C adds

lessons.title: Current Electricity
yt: class 12 physics current electricity ohm law drift velocity resistivity kirchhoff wheatstone potentiometer cells

blocks.x: Electric current is the rate of flow of charge, I = Q/t, in ampere. In a conductor, free electrons drift with drift velocity v_d = eE tau/m, and I = n e A v_d. Ohm’s law says V = IR for a conductor at constant temperature. Resistance R = rho L / A, where resistivity rho depends on the material and temperature, not on size. For metals resistivity rises with temperature (alpha positive), for semiconductors it falls, and alloys like manganin and constantan have a very small temperature coefficient. Conductivity sigma = 1/rho, and mobility mu = v_d/E. Resistors in series add, R = R1 + R2; in parallel 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2. A cell has emf E and internal resistance r; terminal voltage V = E - Ir, and the current is I = E/(R + r). Cells in series add emf and internal resistance; identical cells in parallel keep emf and reduce internal resistance. Kirchhoff’s laws: the junction rule (sum of currents at a node is zero, conservation of charge) and the loop rule (sum of potential changes around a loop is zero, conservation of energy). A Wheatstone bridge is balanced when P/Q = R/S, with no galvanometer current. The metre bridge applies this principle. A potentiometer measures emf without drawing current from the cell, and compares emfs by balance lengths: E1/E2 = l1/l2. Electrical power P = VI = I^2 R = V^2/R, and energy is Pt; the kilowatt hour is 3.6 x 10^6 J. Heating effect is H = I^2 R t. Colour code gives resistor values.

Deep dive: Potentiometer and power
The potentiometer compares emfs by balance length; P = VI = I^2R.

Visual lesson

Current Electricity

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Drift and Ohm›3Cells and circuits›4Potentiometer and power
🔑

Big idea

  • Electric current is the rate of flow of charge, I = Q/t, in ampere
  • In a conductor, free electrons drift with drift velocity v_d = eE tau/m, and I = n e A v_d
  • Ohm’s law says V = IR for a conductor at constant temperature
  • Resistance R = rho L / A, where resistivity rho depends on the material and temperature, not on size
Read the full explanation

Electric current is the rate of flow of charge, I = Q/t, in ampere. In a conductor, free electrons drift with drift velocity v_d = eE tau/m, and I = n e A v_d. Ohm’s law says V = IR for a conductor at constant temperature. Resistance R = rho L / A, where resistivity rho depends on the material and temperature, not on size. For metals resistivity rises with temperature (alpha positive), for semiconductors it falls, and alloys like manganin and constantan have a very small temperature coefficient. Conductivity sigma = 1/rho, and mobility mu = v_d/E. Resistors in series add, R = R1 + R2; in parallel 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2. A cell has emf E and internal resistance r; terminal voltage V = E - Ir, and the current is I = E/(R + r). Cells in series add emf and internal resistance; identical cells in parallel keep emf and reduce internal resistance. Kirchhoff’s laws: the junction rule (sum of currents at a node is zero, conservation of charge) and the loop rule (sum of potential changes around a loop is zero, conservation of energy). A Wheatstone bridge is balanced when P/Q = R/S, with no galvanometer current. The metre bridge applies this principle. A potentiometer measures emf without drawing current from the cell, and compares emfs by balance lengths: E1/E2 = l1/l2. Electrical power P = VI = I^2 R = V^2/R, and energy is Pt; the kilowatt hour is 3.6 x 10^6 J. Heating effect is H = I^2 R t. Colour code gives resistor values.

📌

⚡

Cells and circuits

  • Kirchhoff’s laws and the Wheatstone bridge solve networks
🚀

Potentiometer and power

  • The potentiometer compares emfs by balance length
  • P = VI = I2R

lessons.title: Electromagnetic Waves
yt: class 12 physics electromagnetic waves displacement current maxwell equations spectrum radio microwave X-ray gamma

blocks.x: Maxwell found that a changing electric field also produces a magnetic field and introduced the displacement current Id = epsilon0 d(phi_E)/dt, which makes Ampere’s law consistent. Maxwell’s four equations are Gauss’s law for electricity, Gauss’s law for magnetism, Faraday’s law and the Ampere-Maxwell law. They predict electromagnetic waves, whose speed in vacuum is c = 1/sqrt(mu0 epsilon0) = 3 x 10^8 m/s, equal to the speed of light, so light is electromagnetic. Hertz produced and detected the waves in 1887. EM waves are transverse: E and B are perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel, in phase, with E0/B0 = c. They need no medium, carry energy and momentum, and exert radiation pressure. In a medium, v = 1/sqrt(mu epsilon) and n = c/v. The energy density is shared equally between E and B, and the intensity is I = (1/2) epsilon0 E0^2 c. The spectrum in order of decreasing wavelength is radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays. Radio waves are used in communication and are produced by oscillating circuits. Microwaves are used in radar and microwave ovens (water molecules resonate near 2.45 GHz) and are produced by klystrons and magnetrons. Infrared waves come from hot bodies, are used in remote controls, physiotherapy and the greenhouse effect, and are called heat waves. Visible light spans about 400 nm to 700 nm. Ultraviolet waves come from the Sun and are used in sterilisation and LASIK, and the ozone layer absorbs most of them. X-rays, discovered by Roentgen in 1895, are produced when fast electrons strike a metal target and are used in medicine and security. Gamma rays come from nuclei and are used in cancer treatment.
Deep dive: Displacement current
A changing electric field acts like a current Id = epsilon0 dphi_E/dt and generates a magnetic field.
Deep dive: Wave properties
Transverse, in phase, E/B = c, carrying energy and momentum; speed 1/sqrt(mu0 epsilon0).
Deep dive: Spectrum
Radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray and gamma rays differ in wavelength, source and use.

Visual lesson

Electromagnetic Waves

Big idea

  • Maxwell found that a changing electric field also produces a magnetic field and introduced the displacement current Id = epsilon0 d(phi_E)/dt, which…
  • Maxwell’s four equations are Gauss’s law for electricity, Gauss’s law for magnetism, Faraday’s law and the Ampere-Maxwell law

  • Hertz produced and detected the waves in 1887
Read the full explanation

Maxwell found that a changing electric field also produces a magnetic field and introduced the displacement current Id = epsilon0 d(phi_E)/dt, which makes Ampere’s law consistent. Maxwell’s four equations are Gauss’s law for electricity, Gauss’s law for magnetism, Faraday’s law and the Ampere-Maxwell law. They predict electromagnetic waves, whose speed in vacuum is c = 1/sqrt(mu0 epsilon0) = 3 x 10^8 m/s, equal to the speed of light, so light is electromagnetic. Hertz produced and detected the waves in 1887. EM waves are transverse: E and B are perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel, in phase, with E0/B0 = c. They need no medium, carry energy and momentum, and exert radiation pressure. In a medium, v = 1/sqrt(mu epsilon) and n = c/v. The energy density is shared equally between E and B, and the intensity is I = (1/2) epsilon0 E0^2 c. The spectrum in order of decreasing wavelength is radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays. Radio waves are used in communication and are produced by oscillating circuits. Microwaves are used in radar and microwave ovens (water molecules resonate near 2.45 GHz) and are produced by klystrons and magnetrons. Infrared waves come from hot bodies, are used in remote controls, physiotherapy and the greenhouse effect, and are called heat waves. Visible light spans about 400 nm to 700 nm. Ultraviolet waves come from the Sun and are used in sterilisation and LASIK, and the ozone layer absorbs most of them. X-rays, discovered by Roentgen in 1895, are produced when fast electrons strike a metal target and are used in medicine and security. Gamma rays come from nuclei and are used in cancer treatment.

⚡

Displacement current

  • A changing electric field acts like a current Id = epsilon0 dphi_E/dt and generates a magnetic field
🌊

Wave properties

  • Transverse, in phase, E/B = c, carrying energy and momentum
  • Speed 1/sqrt(mu0 epsilon0)
🌟

Spectrum

  • Radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray and gamma rays differ in wavelength, source and use
🧮

Formula tiles

Displacement currentId = epsilon0 d(phi_E)/dt
Speed of EM wavesc = 1 / sqrt(mu0 epsilon0)
Wave speedc = f lambda
Field ratioE0 / B0 = c
IntensityI = 1/2 epsilon0 E0^2 c
Momentump = U / c
Refractive indexn = c / v
Speed in mediumv = 1 / sqrt(mu epsilon)
🎯 Remember order of increasing frequency is radio, micro, infrared, visible, UV, X, gamma.
