lessons.title: Ray Optics and Optical Instruments
yt: class 12 physics ray optics mirror lens refraction total internal reflection prism microscope telescope eye

blocks.x: Ray optics treats light as straight rays. For spherical mirrors, 1/v + 1/u = 1/f with f = R/2 and magnification m = -v/u, using the Cartesian sign convention. Refraction obeys Snell’s law, n1 sin i = n2 sin r, with refractive index n = c/v. Total internal reflection needs light going from a denser to a rarer medium at an angle above the critical angle C, where sin C = 1/n; it is used in optical fibres, prisms in binoculars and the sparkle of diamond, and causes mirages. Refraction at a spherical surface gives n2/v - n1/u = (n2 - n1)/R. For a thin lens, 1/v - 1/u = 1/f and the lens maker’s formula is 1/f = (n - 1)(1/R1 - 1/R2); magnification m = v/u. Power P = 1/f in dioptre, and thin lenses in contact give P = P1 + P2. A prism deviates light; for a thin prism delta = (n - 1)A, and for a prism n = sin((A + Dm)/2)/sin(A/2) at minimum deviation. Dispersion splits white light because n depends on wavelength; red bends least and violet most. The blue sky is due to Rayleigh scattering, proportional to 1/lambda^4, and red sunsets occur as blue is scattered away. A simple microscope gives m = 1 + D/f with D = 25 cm. A compound microscope gives m = (L/fo)(1 + D/fe) approximately (L is tube length). An astronomical telescope in normal adjustment has m = fo/fe and length fo + fe. Reflecting telescopes avoid chromatic aberration and allow large mirrors. In the eye, myopia is corrected by a concave lens, hypermetropia by a convex lens, presbyopia by bifocals and astigmatism by cylindrical lenses.
Deep dive: Mirrors and lenses
1/v + 1/u = 1/f for mirrors; 1/v - 1/u = 1/f for lenses; lens maker 1/f = (n-1)(1/R1 - 1/R2).
Deep dive: Total internal reflection
Dense to rare above the critical angle with sin C = 1/n gives fibre optics and diamond sparkle.
Deep dive: Instruments
Microscope and telescope magnifications and eye defects with corrective lenses.
Hindi saransh
Kiran prakashiki: darpan, lens, apvartan, poorn aantarik paravartan, prism, sookshmadarshi, doordarshi aur netra dosh.
Remember: sin C = 1/n; myopia needs a concave lens.

Ray Optics and Optical Instruments

Ray optics treats light as straight rays

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Mirrors and lenses›3Total internal reflection›4Instruments
🔑

Big idea

  • Ray optics treats light as straight rays
  • For spherical mirrors, 1/v + 1/u = 1/f with f = R/2 and magnification m = -v/u, using the Cartesian sign convention
  • Refraction obeys Snell’s law, n1 sin i = n2 sin r, with refractive index n = c/v
  • Total internal reflection needs light going from a denser to a rarer medium at an angle above the critical angle C, where sin C = 1/n
Read the full explanation

Ray optics treats light as straight rays. For spherical mirrors, 1/v + 1/u = 1/f with f = R/2 and magnification m = -v/u, using the Cartesian sign convention. Refraction obeys Snell’s law, n1 sin i = n2 sin r, with refractive index n = c/v. Total internal reflection needs light going from a denser to a rarer medium at an angle above the critical angle C, where sin C = 1/n; it is used in optical fibres, prisms in binoculars and the sparkle of diamond, and causes mirages. Refraction at a spherical surface gives n2/v - n1/u = (n2 - n1)/R. For a thin lens, 1/v - 1/u = 1/f and the lens maker’s formula is 1/f = (n - 1)(1/R1 - 1/R2); magnification m = v/u. Power P = 1/f in dioptre, and thin lenses in contact give P = P1 + P2. A prism deviates light; for a thin prism delta = (n - 1)A, and for a prism n = sin((A + Dm)/2)/sin(A/2) at minimum deviation. Dispersion splits white light because n depends on wavelength; red bends least and violet most. The blue sky is due to Rayleigh scattering, proportional to 1/lambda^4, and red sunsets occur as blue is scattered away. A simple microscope gives m = 1 + D/f with D = 25 cm. A compound microscope gives m = (L/fo)(1 + D/fe) approximately (L is tube length). An astronomical telescope in normal adjustment has m = fo/fe and length fo + fe. Reflecting telescopes avoid chromatic aberration and allow large mirrors. In the eye, myopia is corrected by a concave lens, hypermetropia by a convex lens, presbyopia by bifocals and astigmatism by cylindrical lenses.

🔦

Mirrors and lenses

  • 1/v + 1/u = 1/f for mirrors
  • 1/v - 1/u = 1/f for lenses
  • Lens maker 1/f = (n-1)(1/R1 - 1/R2)
🧠

Total internal reflection

  • Dense to rare above the critical angle with sin C = 1/n gives fibre optics and diamond sparkle
🌟

Instruments

  • Microscope and telescope magnifications and eye defects with corrective lenses
🧮

lessons.title: Wave Optics
yt: class 12 physics wave optics huygens interference young double slit diffraction polarisation brewster malus

blocks.x: Wave optics treats light as a wave. A wavefront is the locus of points in the same phase. Huygens’s principle says every point on a wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets, and the new wavefront is the envelope; it explains reflection and refraction. Interference is the superposition of two coherent waves. Constructive interference occurs for path difference n lambda and destructive for (n + 1/2) lambda. Young’s double slit experiment (1801) gives fringes of equal width beta = lambda D/d on a screen at distance D with slit separation d. The intensity is I = 4 I0 cos^2(phi/2). For amplitudes a1 and a2, Imax/Imin = ((a1 + a2)/(a1 - a2))^2. Sources must be coherent: constant phase difference from the same source. Diffraction is bending of light around obstacles or through narrow openings of size comparable to the wavelength. In single slit diffraction, minima occur at a sin theta = n lambda, the central maximum has angular width 2 lambda/a and is the brightest and widest, and its linear width is 2 lambda D/a. The Fresnel distance is a^2/lambda. Polarisation shows that light is a transverse wave. Unpolarised light passing a polaroid is reduced to half intensity. Malus’s law states I = I0 cos^2 theta for polarised light through an analyser. Brewster’s law gives the polarising angle with tan i_B = n, at which reflected and refracted rays are at 90 degrees. Polaroids reduce glare and are used in sunglasses, cameras and 3D glasses. Longitudinal waves such as sound cannot be polarised.
Deep dive: Huygens and interference
Secondary wavelets explain reflection and refraction; coherent waves interfere with beta = lambda D/d.
Deep dive: Diffraction
Single slit minima at a sin theta = n lambda; the central maximum is widest and brightest.
Deep dive: Polarisation
Malus I = I0 cos^2 theta and Brewster tan i_B = n show light is transverse.

Visual lesson

Wave Optics

Wave optics treats light as a wave

Flat concept map (2D)

Fresnel distancea^2 / lambda
🔑

Big idea

  • Wave optics treats light as a wave
  • A wavefront is the locus of points in the same phase
  • Huygens’s principle says every point on a wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets, and the new wavefront is the envelope
  • It explains reflection and refraction
Read the full explanation

Wave optics treats light as a wave. A wavefront is the locus of points in the same phase. Huygens’s principle says every point on a wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets, and the new wavefront is the envelope; it explains reflection and refraction. Interference is the superposition of two coherent waves. Constructive interference occurs for path difference n lambda and destructive for (n + 1/2) lambda. Young’s double slit experiment (1801) gives fringes of equal width beta = lambda D/d on a screen at distance D with slit separation d. The intensity is I = 4 I0 cos^2(phi/2). For amplitudes a1 and a2, Imax/Imin = ((a1 + a2)/(a1 - a2))^2. Sources must be coherent: constant phase difference from the same source. Diffraction is bending of light around obstacles or through narrow openings of size comparable to the wavelength. In single slit diffraction, minima occur at a sin theta = n lambda, the central maximum has angular width 2 lambda/a and is the brightest and widest, and its linear width is 2 lambda D/a. The Fresnel distance is a^2/lambda. Polarisation shows that light is a transverse wave. Unpolarised light passing a polaroid is reduced to half intensity. Malus’s law states I = I0 cos^2 theta for polarised light through an analyser. Brewster’s law gives the polarising angle with tan i_B = n, at which reflected and refracted rays are at 90 degrees. Polaroids reduce glare and are used in sunglasses, cameras and 3D glasses. Longitudinal waves such as sound cannot be polarised.

📌

Huygens and interference

  • Secondary wavelets explain reflection and refraction
  • Coherent waves interfere with beta = lambda D/d
🧠

Diffraction

  • Single slit minima at a sin theta = n lambda
  • The central maximum is widest and brightest
🌟

Polarisation

  • Malus I = I0 cos2 theta and Brewster tan i_B = n show light is transverse

lessons.title: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
yt: class 12 physics dual nature photoelectric effect einstein equation de broglie davisson germer work function stopping potential

blocks.x: The photoelectric effect is the emission of electrons from a metal surface when light of sufficient frequency falls on it. Hertz and Hallwachs observed it and Lenard studied it. The experimental facts: for a given frequency, the photocurrent is proportional to intensity; there is a threshold frequency nu0 below which no emission occurs, however intense the light; the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons depends on frequency, not intensity; and emission is instantaneous. The stopping potential V0 is the reverse voltage that stops the fastest electrons, so eV0 = KEmax. Classical wave theory failed to explain threshold, intensity independence and instant emission. Einstein (1905) proposed that light consists of quanta (photons), with E = h nu = hc/lambda, where h = 6.63 x 10^-34 J s; hc = 1240 eV nm. Einstein’s photoelectric equation is KEmax = h nu - phi0, where phi0 = h nu0 is the work function. A graph of V0 against nu is a straight line of slope h/e, with intercept on the frequency axis equal to nu0. Millikan verified it in 1916. A photon has momentum p = h/lambda and energy but zero rest mass. De Broglie (1924) proposed that matter has wave nature: lambda = h/p = h/mv. For an electron accelerated through V volts, lambda = 12.27/sqrt V angstrom. For a particle of kinetic energy K, lambda = h/sqrt(2mK). Davisson and Germer (1927) confirmed electron diffraction from a nickel crystal. Matter waves are not electromagnetic. The Heisenberg principle limits simultaneous knowledge of position and momentum. Photocells are used in alarms, automatic doors and light meters.
Deep dive: Photoelectric effect
Threshold frequency, intensity-proportional current, instantaneous emission and KE depending on frequency.
Deep dive: Einstein’s equation
KEmax = h nu - phi0 and eV0 = h nu - phi0; the V0 versus nu graph has slope h/e.
Deep dive: Matter waves

🔑

Big idea

  • The photoelectric effect is the emission of electrons from a metal surface when light of sufficient frequency falls on it
  • Hertz and Hallwachs observed it and Lenard studied it
  • The experimental facts: for a given frequency, the photocurrent is proportional to intensity
  • There is a threshold frequency nu0 below which no emission occurs, however intense the light
Read the full explanation

The photoelectric effect is the emission of electrons from a metal surface when light of sufficient frequency falls on it. Hertz and Hallwachs observed it and Lenard studied it. The experimental facts: for a given frequency, the photocurrent is proportional to intensity; there is a threshold frequency nu0 below which no emission occurs, however intense the light; the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons depends on frequency, not intensity; and emission is instantaneous. The stopping potential V0 is the reverse voltage that stops the fastest electrons, so eV0 = KEmax. Classical wave theory failed to explain threshold, intensity independence and instant emission. Einstein (1905) proposed that light consists of quanta (photons), with E = h nu = hc/lambda, where h = 6.63 x 10^-34 J s; hc = 1240 eV nm. Einstein’s photoelectric equation is KEmax = h nu - phi0, where phi0 = h nu0 is the work function. A graph of V0 against nu is a straight line of slope h/e, with intercept on the frequency axis equal to nu0. Millikan verified it in 1916. A photon has momentum p = h/lambda and energy but zero rest mass. De Broglie (1924) proposed that matter has wave nature: lambda = h/p = h/mv. For an electron accelerated through V volts, lambda = 12.27/sqrt V angstrom. For a particle of kinetic energy K, lambda = h/sqrt(2mK). Davisson and Germer (1927) confirmed electron diffraction from a nickel crystal. Matter waves are not electromagnetic. The Heisenberg principle limits simultaneous knowledge of position and momentum. Photocells are used in alarms, automatic doors and light meters.

lessons.title: Atoms
yt: class 12 physics atoms thomson rutherford scattering bohr model hydrogen spectrum lyman balmer paschen

blocks.x: Thomson’s plum pudding model pictured the atom as a positive sphere with electrons embedded in it. Geiger and Marsden, under Rutherford, scattered alpha particles from thin gold foil. Most passed straight through, a few were deflected through large angles and about one in 8000 turned back, so the positive charge and nearly all the mass lie in a tiny nucleus of size about 10^-15 m, compared with the atom’s 10^-10 m. Rutherford proposed the nuclear atom in 1911. The distance of closest approach for an alpha particle of kinetic energy K is r0 = (1/4 pi epsilon0) 2Ze^2/K. Rutherford’s model could not explain stability (an orbiting electron should radiate and spiral in) or the line spectra. Bohr’s model (1913) assumes stationary orbits with no radiation, quantised angular momentum mvr = nh/2 pi, and emission or absorption of a photon when an electron jumps, h nu = Ei - Ef. For hydrogen-like atoms, r_n = n^2 a0/Z with a0 = 0.529 angstrom, and E_n = -13.6 Z^2/n^2 eV. The ground state is -13.6 eV, so the ionisation energy is 13.6 eV; the first excited state is -3.4 eV. Kinetic energy is +13.6/n^2 eV and potential energy is -27.2/n^2 eV. Speed v_n is proportional to Z/n (about 2.19 x 10^6 m/s for n = 1) and time period grows as n^3. The Rydberg formula is 1/lambda = R(1/n1^2 - 1/n2^2) with R = 1.097 x 10^7 per metre. The spectral series are Lyman (n1 = 1, ultraviolet), Balmer (n1 = 2, visible), Paschen (n1 = 3, infrared), Brackett (n1 = 4) and Pfund (n1 = 5). De Broglie explained Bohr’s rule by standing waves, 2 pi r = n lambda. Bohr’s theory fails for multi-electron atoms and does not explain fine structure or intensities.
Deep dive: Rutherford model
Alpha scattering gave a tiny, dense, positive nucleus; the model could not explain stability or spectra.
Deep dive: Bohr model
Quantised orbits mvr = nh/2 pi, r_n = n^2 a0, E_n = -13.6/n^2 eV, and photon h nu = Ei - Ef.
Deep dive: Spectral series
Lyman, Balmer, Paschen, Brackett and Pfund correspond to final levels 1 to 5.

Visual lesson

Atoms

Thomson’s plum pudding model pictured the atom as a positive sphere with electrons embedded in it

🔑

Big idea

  • Thomson’s plum pudding model pictured the atom as a positive sphere with electrons embedded in it
  • Geiger and Marsden, under Rutherford, scattered alpha particles from thin gold foil
  • Most passed straight through, a few were deflected through large angles and about one in 8000 turned back, so the positive charge and nearly all the…
  • Rutherford proposed the nuclear atom in 1911
Read the full explanation

Thomson’s plum pudding model pictured the atom as a positive sphere with electrons embedded in it. Geiger and Marsden, under Rutherford, scattered alpha particles from thin gold foil. Most passed straight through, a few were deflected through large angles and about one in 8000 turned back, so the positive charge and nearly all the mass lie in a tiny nucleus of size about 10^-15 m, compared with the atom’s 10^-10 m. Rutherford proposed the nuclear atom in 1911. The distance of closest approach for an alpha particle of kinetic energy K is r0 = (1/4 pi epsilon0) 2Ze^2/K. Rutherford’s model could not explain stability (an orbiting electron should radiate and spiral in) or the line spectra. Bohr’s model (1913) assumes stationary orbits with no radiation, quantised angular momentum mvr = nh/2 pi, and emission or absorption of a photon when an electron jumps, h nu = Ei - Ef. For hydrogen-like atoms, r_n = n^2 a0/Z with a0 = 0.529 angstrom, and E_n = -13.6 Z^2/n^2 eV. The ground state is -13.6 eV, so the ionisation energy is 13.6 eV; the first excited state is -3.4 eV. Kinetic energy is +13.6/n^2 eV and potential energy is -27.2/n^2 eV. Speed v_n is proportional to Z/n (about 2.19 x 10^6 m/s for n = 1) and time period grows as n^3. The Rydberg formula is 1/lambda = R(1/n1^2 - 1/n2^2) with R = 1.097 x 10^7 per metre. The spectral series are Lyman (n1 = 1, ultraviolet), Balmer (n1 = 2, visible), Paschen (n1 = 3, infrared), Brackett (n1 = 4) and Pfund (n1 = 5). De Broglie explained Bohr’s rule by standing waves, 2 pi r = n lambda. Bohr’s theory fails for multi-electron atoms and does not explain fine structure or intensities.

📌

Rutherford model

  • Alpha scattering gave a tiny, dense, positive nucleus
  • The model could not explain stability or spectra
🧠

Bohr model

  • Quantised orbits mvr = nh/2 pi, r_n = n2 a0, E_n = -13.6/n2 eV, and photon h nu = Ei - Ef
🌟

Spectral series

  • Lyman, Balmer, Paschen, Brackett and Pfund correspond to final levels 1 to 5
🧮

Formula tiles

Closest approachr0 = 2Ze^2 / (4 pi epsilon0 K)
Bohr quantisationmvr = n h / 2 pi
Orbit radiusr_n = n^2 a0 / Z
Bohr radiusa0 = 0.529 angstrom
EnergyE_n = -13.6 Z^2 / n^2 eV
Photon from jumph nu = Ei - Ef
Rydberg1/lambda = R (1/n1^2 - 1/n2^2)
Rydberg constantR = 1.097e7 per metre
Kinetic energyK = -E_n
Potential energyU = 2 E_n
Speedv_n = 2.19e6 x Z / n m/s
🎯 Remember Lyman is UV (n=1); Balmer is visible (n=2).

lessons.title: Nuclei
yt: class 12 physics nuclei nuclear size mass defect binding energy radioactivity fission fusion half life

blocks.x: The nucleus consists of protons and neutrons (nucleons); the neutron was discovered by Chadwick in 1932. Atomic number Z is the number of protons, mass number A is the number of nucleons and neutron number is N = A - Z. Isotopes have the same Z but different A, isobars have the same A, and isotones have the same N. The atomic mass unit is 1 u = 1.66 x 10^-27 kg = 931.5 MeV/c^2. Nuclear radius R = R0 A^(1/3) with R0 = 1.2 fm, so nuclear density is about 2.3 x 10^17 kg/m^3 and independent of A. Mass defect is the difference between the sum of nucleon masses and the nuclear mass, and binding energy is mass defect times c^2. The binding energy per nucleon rises to a maximum of about 8.75 MeV near iron (A about 56) and then falls, so fusion of light nuclei and fission of heavy nuclei both release energy. Nuclear force is short range, strong, charge independent and saturated. Radioactivity was discovered by Becquerel in 1896. Alpha particles are helium nuclei, beta particles are electrons or positrons, gamma rays are photons. The decay law is N = N0 e^(-lambda t); half life T = 0.693/lambda; mean life is 1/lambda = 1.44 T. Activity R = lambda N, in becquerel (one decay per second); one curie is 3.7 x 10^10 Bq. In alpha decay Z falls by 2 and A by 4; in beta minus decay a neutron changes to a proton with an antineutrino; in beta plus decay a proton changes to a neutron with a neutrino. Fission, discovered by Hahn and Strassmann in 1938, splits a heavy nucleus like U-235 into two with about 200 MeV energy and neutrons that sustain a chain reaction; reactors use moderators and control rods. Fusion powers the Sun and needs very high temperature.
Deep dive: Nuclear structure
R = R0 A^(1/3); constant density; mass defect gives binding energy E = delta m c^2.
Deep dive: Radioactivity
N = N0 e^(-lambda t); half life 0.693/lambda; activity lambda N.
Deep dive: Fission and fusion
Binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron; fission and fusion each release energy.

🔑

Big idea

  • The nucleus consists of protons and neutrons (nucleons)
  • The neutron was discovered by Chadwick in 1932
  • Atomic number Z is the number of protons, mass number A is the number of nucleons and neutron number is N = A - Z
  • Isotopes have the same Z but different A, isobars have the same A, and isotones have the same N
Read the full explanation

The nucleus consists of protons and neutrons (nucleons); the neutron was discovered by Chadwick in 1932. Atomic number Z is the number of protons, mass number A is the number of nucleons and neutron number is N = A - Z. Isotopes have the same Z but different A, isobars have the same A, and isotones have the same N. The atomic mass unit is 1 u = 1.66 x 10^-27 kg = 931.5 MeV/c^2. Nuclear radius R = R0 A^(1/3) with R0 = 1.2 fm, so nuclear density is about 2.3 x 10^17 kg/m^3 and independent of A. Mass defect is the difference between the sum of nucleon masses and the nuclear mass, and binding energy is mass defect times c^2. The binding energy per nucleon rises to a maximum of about 8.75 MeV near iron (A about 56) and then falls, so fusion of light nuclei and fission of heavy nuclei both release energy. Nuclear force is short range, strong, charge independent and saturated. Radioactivity was discovered by Becquerel in 1896. Alpha particles are helium nuclei, beta particles are electrons or positrons, gamma rays are photons. The decay law is N = N0 e^(-lambda t); half life T = 0.693/lambda; mean life is 1/lambda = 1.44 T. Activity R = lambda N, in becquerel (one decay per second); one curie is 3.7 x 10^10 Bq. In alpha decay Z falls by 2 and A by 4; in beta minus decay a neutron changes to a proton with an antineutrino; in beta plus decay a proton changes to a neutron with a neutrino. Fission, discovered by Hahn and Strassmann in 1938, splits a heavy nucleus like U-235 into two with about 200 MeV energy and neutrons that sustain a chain reaction; reactors use moderators and control rods. Fusion powers the Sun and needs very high temperature.

⚛️

Nuclear structure

  • R = R0 A^(1/3)
  • Constant density
  • Mass defect gives binding energy E = delta m c2
🧠

Radioactivity

  • N = N0 e^(-lambda t)
  • Half life 0.693/lambda
  • Activity lambda N
🌟

Fission and fusion

  • Binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron
  • Fission and fusion each release energy
🧮

Mass defectdelta m = Z mp + (A - Z) mn - M
Binding energyE = delta m x 931.5 MeV
Decay lawN = N0 e^(-lambda t)

Mean lifetau = 1 / lambda = 1.44 T
ActivityR = lambda N
Remaining fractionN/N0 = (1/2)^(t/T)

🎯 Remember half life = 0.693 / decay constant.

lessons.title: Semiconductor Electronics
yt: class 12 physics semiconductor electronics p-n junction diode rectifier zener LED transistor logic gates

blocks.x: In solids, energy bands form: valence band, conduction band and a forbidden gap Eg. Conductors have overlapping or no gap, insulators have Eg greater than about 3 eV, and semiconductors have Eg below 3 eV; silicon has 1.1 eV and germanium 0.67 eV. Pure semiconductors are intrinsic, with equal electrons and holes. Doping makes them extrinsic. An n-type semiconductor is doped with pentavalent atoms such as phosphorus, arsenic or antimony (donors); electrons are the majority carriers. A p-type semiconductor is doped with trivalent atoms such as boron, aluminium, gallium or indium (acceptors); holes are the majority carriers. In both, n_e n_h = n_i^2. A p-n junction forms a depletion region and a barrier potential of about 0.7 V for silicon and 0.3 V for germanium. In forward bias the barrier lowers and current flows; in reverse bias the barrier rises and only a tiny leakage current flows. A half-wave rectifier uses one diode and its ripple frequency equals the input; a full-wave rectifier gives ripple of twice the input frequency; a capacitor filter smooths the output. A Zener diode, operated in reverse breakdown, regulates voltage. An LED is forward biased and emits light of colour set by the band gap. A photodiode works in reverse bias and detects light; a solar cell generates voltage from light. A transistor has emitter (heavily doped), base (thin, lightly doped) and collector (larger); it was invented in 1947 at Bell Labs by Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley. In a common emitter, current gain beta = Ic/Ib, alpha = Ic/Ie and beta = alpha/(1 - alpha). A common emitter amplifier reverses phase by 180 degrees. As a switch, the transistor is off in cut-off and on in saturation. Logic gates are OR, AND, NOT, NAND, NOR and XOR; NAND and NOR are universal gates.
Deep dive: Bands and doping
Eg decides conductor, semiconductor or insulator; n-type has donors, p-type has acceptors.
Deep dive: Diodes
Forward bias conducts, reverse blocks; rectifiers, Zener regulation, LED and photodiode.
Deep dive: Transistors and gates
beta = Ic/Ib; CE amplifier inverts; NAND and NOR are universal gates.

problems.q: Draw the truth table of a NAND gate and show why it is universal.

Big idea

Read the full explanation

In solids, energy bands form: valence band, conduction band and a forbidden gap Eg. Conductors have overlapping or no gap, insulators have Eg greater than about 3 eV, and semiconductors have Eg below 3 eV; silicon has 1.1 eV and germanium 0.67 eV. Pure semiconductors are intrinsic, with equal electrons and holes. Doping makes them extrinsic. An n-type semiconductor is doped with pentavalent atoms such as phosphorus, arsenic or antimony (donors); electrons are the majority carriers. A p-type semiconductor is doped with trivalent atoms such as boron, aluminium, gallium or indium (acceptors); holes are the majority carriers. In both, n_e n_h = n_i^2. A p-n junction forms a depletion region and a barrier potential of about 0.7 V for silicon and 0.3 V for germanium. In forward bias the barrier lowers and current flows; in reverse bias the barrier rises and only a tiny leakage current flows. A half-wave rectifier uses one diode and its ripple frequency equals the input; a full-wave rectifier gives ripple of twice the input frequency; a capacitor filter smooths the output. A Zener diode, operated in reverse breakdown, regulates voltage. An LED is forward biased and emits light of colour set by the band gap. A photodiode works in reverse bias and detects light; a solar cell generates voltage from light. A transistor has emitter (heavily doped), base (thin, lightly doped) and collector (larger); it was invented in 1947 at Bell Labs by Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley. In a common emitter, current gain beta = Ic/Ib, alpha = Ic/Ie and beta = alpha/(1 - alpha). A common emitter amplifier reverses phase by 180 degrees. As a switch, the transistor is off in cut-off and on in saturation. Logic gates are OR, AND, NOT, NAND, NOR and XOR; NAND and NOR are universal gates.

lessons.title: Magnetism and Matter
yt: class 12 physics magnetism and matter bar magnet earth magnetism dip declination para dia ferro hysteresis

blocks.x: A bar magnet has two poles of equal strength, and isolated magnetic poles (monopoles) do not exist. A freely suspended magnet points north-south. Magnetic field lines form closed loops, run from north to south outside the magnet and south to north inside, never cross, and are closer where the field is stronger. A current loop behaves as a magnetic dipole with moment m = NIA in A m^2. For a bar magnet, the axial field is B = (mu0/4pi) 2m/r^3 and the equatorial field is B = (mu0/4pi) m/r^3, opposite to m. In a uniform field the torque is mB sin theta and the potential energy is -mB cos theta. Gauss’s law for magnetism says the net flux through any closed surface is zero. Earth’s magnetism is described by three elements: declination (angle between magnetic and geographic meridians), dip or inclination (angle of the total field with the horizontal) and the horizontal component B_H. B_H = B cos delta, B_V = B sin delta and tan delta = B_V/B_H. At the magnetic equator the dip is zero; at the poles it is 90 degrees. Magnetisation M is magnetic moment per unit volume, H is magnetising field, B = mu0 (H + M), susceptibility chi = M/H and relative permeability mu_r = 1 + chi. Diamagnetic substances have small negative chi and are weakly repelled; paramagnetic substances have small positive chi, obey Curie’s law chi = C/T and are weakly attracted; ferromagnetic substances have large positive chi because of domains and lose ferromagnetism above the Curie temperature. Superconductors are perfectly diamagnetic. Hysteresis is the lag of B behind H; the loop gives retentivity and coercivity. Soft iron has low retentivity and coercivity, suiting electromagnets and transformer cores; steel has high values, suiting permanent magnets.
Deep dive: Bar magnet
Field lines are closed loops; axial field 2m mu0/4pi r^3 and equatorial half as large and opposite.
Deep dive: Earth’s magnetism
Declination, dip and horizontal component describe the field; tan dip = B_V/B_H.
Deep dive: Magnetic materials
Dia, para and ferromagnets differ in susceptibility; hysteresis guides material choice.
Hindi saransh
Chumbakatva aur padarth: chumbak, prithvi ka chumbakatva, dia para ferro padarth aur hysteresis.
Remember: diamagnetic chi is negative; ferromagnetic chi is large and positive.

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Magnetism and Matter

A bar magnet has two poles of equal strength, and isolated magnetic poles (monopoles) do not exist

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Bar magnet›3Earth’s magnetism›4Magnetic materials
🔑

Big idea

  • A bar magnet has two poles of equal strength, and isolated magnetic poles (monopoles) do not exist
  • A freely suspended magnet points north-south
  • Magnetic field lines form closed loops, run from north to south outside the magnet and south to north inside, never cross, and are closer where the…
  • A current loop behaves as a magnetic dipole with moment m = NIA in A m2
Read the full explanation

A bar magnet has two poles of equal strength, and isolated magnetic poles (monopoles) do not exist. A freely suspended magnet points north-south. Magnetic field lines form closed loops, run from north to south outside the magnet and south to north inside, never cross, and are closer where the field is stronger. A current loop behaves as a magnetic dipole with moment m = NIA in A m^2. For a bar magnet, the axial field is B = (mu0/4pi) 2m/r^3 and the equatorial field is B = (mu0/4pi) m/r^3, opposite to m. In a uniform field the torque is mB sin theta and the potential energy is -mB cos theta. Gauss’s law for magnetism says the net flux through any closed surface is zero. Earth’s magnetism is described by three elements: declination (angle between magnetic and geographic meridians), dip or inclination (angle of the total field with the horizontal) and the horizontal component B_H. B_H = B cos delta, B_V = B sin delta and tan delta = B_V/B_H. At the magnetic equator the dip is zero; at the poles it is 90 degrees. Magnetisation M is magnetic moment per unit volume, H is magnetising field, B = mu0 (H + M), susceptibility chi = M/H and relative permeability mu_r = 1 + chi. Diamagnetic substances have small negative chi and are weakly repelled; paramagnetic substances have small positive chi, obey Curie’s law chi = C/T and are weakly attracted; ferromagnetic substances have large positive chi because of domains and lose ferromagnetism above the Curie temperature. Superconductors are perfectly diamagnetic. Hysteresis is the lag of B behind H; the loop gives retentivity and coercivity. Soft iron has low retentivity and coercivity, suiting electromagnets and transformer cores; steel has high values, suiting permanent magnets.

⚡

Bar magnet

  • Field lines are closed loops
  • Axial field 2m mu0/4pi r3 and equatorial half as large and opposite
⚡

Earth’s magnetism

  • Declination, dip and horizontal component describe the field
  • Tan dip = B_V/B_H
⚡

Magnetic materials

  • Dia, para and ferromagnets differ in susceptibility
  • Hysteresis guides material choice
🧮

Formula tiles

Dipole momentm = N I A
Axial fieldB = mu0 2m / (4 pi r^3)
Equatorial fieldB = mu0 m / (4 pi r^3)
Torquetau = m B sin theta
EnergyU = -m B cos theta
Horizontal componentB_H = B cos delta
Vertical componentB_V = B sin delta
Diptan delta = B_V / B_H
Total fieldB = sqrt(B_H^2 + B_V^2)
MagnetisationB = mu0 (H + M)
Susceptibilitychi = M / H
Permeabilitymu_r = 1 + chi

All 13 are in the Formulas tab.

🎯 Remember diamagnetic chi is negative; ferromagnetic chi is large and positive.

lessons.title: Moving charges and magnetism
yt: class 12 physics moving charges and magnetism

blocks.x: A charge q moving with velocity v in field B feels F = q v B sin theta. Biot-Savart gives B = (mu0/4 pi) I dl x r / r^3; a long straight wire gives B = mu0 I/(2 pi r), a circular loop centre B = mu0 I/(2R), a solenoid B = mu0 n I. A current-carrying wire in a field feels F = B I L sin theta; a loop has torque tau = N I A B sin theta.
Deep dive: force on charges and currents

The magnetic force on a charge is F = q (v x B), magnitude q v B sin theta, perpendicular to both v and B, so it does no work. In a uniform field a charge moves in a circle when v is perpendicular to B: radius r = m v/(q B), period T = 2 pi m/(q B) (independent of speed), frequency f = qB/(2 pi m) (cyclotron frequency). If v has a component along B the path is a helix with pitch p = v cos theta T. With both E and B (velocity selector) the charge moves straight when q E = q v B, i.e. v = E/B. A straight wire of length L carrying current I in field B feels F = B I L sin theta; two parallel wires carrying currents I1 and I2 at distance d attract (same direction) or repel with force per unit length mu0 I1 I2/(2 pi d), which defines the ampere.
Deep dive: field due to currents

Biot-Savart law: dB = (mu0/4 pi) I dl sin theta / r^2. Long straight wire: B = mu0 I/(2 pi r). Centre of a circular loop of radius R: B = mu0 I/(2R); N turns: mu0 N I/(2R). On the axis of a loop: B = mu0 I R^2/(2 (R^2 + x^2)^(3/2)). Ampere circuital law: closed integral of B . dl = mu0 I_enclosed. Solenoid: B = mu0 n I inside (n turns per metre), almost zero outside; toroid: B = mu0 N I/(2 pi r). Semicircular arc of radius R at its centre: B = mu0 I/(4R).
Deep dive: torque, galvanometer and magnetic materials

A rectangular loop of N turns, area A, current I in field B has torque tau = N I A B sin theta = m x B where m = N I A is the magnetic dipole moment; potential energy U = -m . B. The moving-coil galvanometer has deflection proportional to current: N I A B = k phi, so current sensitivity phi/I = N A B/k. A galvanometer converts to an ammeter with a small shunt S = G Ig/(I - Ig) in parallel, and to a voltmeter by a large series resistance R = V/Ig - G. Materials: diamagnetic (weakly repelled, chi negative), paramagnetic (weakly attracted, chi small positive, Curie law chi proportional to 1/T), ferromagnetic (strongly attracted, hysteresis, Curie temperature). Bar magnet: B on the axis = (mu0/4 pi) 2m/r^3 and on the equator (mu0/4 pi) m/r^3 for r >> length. Earth field: horizontal component BH = B cos delta, vertical component B sin delta.

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Moving charges and magnetism

A charge q moving with velocity v in field B feels F = q v B sin theta

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Force on charges and…›3Field due to currents›4Torque, galvanometer and…
🔑

Big idea

  • A charge q moving with velocity v in field B feels F = q v B sin theta
  • Biot-Savart gives B = (mu0/4 pi) I dl x r / r3
  • A long straight wire gives B = mu0 I/(2 pi r), a circular loop centre B = mu0 I/(2R), a solenoid B = mu0 n I
  • A current-carrying wire in a field feels F = B I L sin theta
Read the full explanation

A charge q moving with velocity v in field B feels F = q v B sin theta. Biot-Savart gives B = (mu0/4 pi) I dl x r / r^3; a long straight wire gives B = mu0 I/(2 pi r), a circular loop centre B = mu0 I/(2R), a solenoid B = mu0 n I. A current-carrying wire in a field feels F = B I L sin theta; a loop has torque tau = N I A B sin theta.

⚡

Force on charges and currents

  • The magnetic force on a charge is F = q (v x B), magnitude q v B sin theta, perpendicular to both v and B, so it does no work
  • In a uniform field a charge moves in a circle when v is perpendicular to B: radius r = m v/(q B), period T = 2 pi m/(q B) (independent of speed)…
  • If v has a component along B the path is a helix with pitch p = v cos theta T
  • With both E and B (velocity selector) the charge moves straight when q E = q v B, i.e. v = E/B
Read the full explanation

The magnetic force on a charge is F = q (v x B), magnitude q v B sin theta, perpendicular to both v and B, so it does no work. In a uniform field a charge moves in a circle when v is perpendicular to B: radius r = m v/(q B), period T = 2 pi m/(q B) (independent of speed), frequency f = qB/(2 pi m) (cyclotron frequency). If v has a component along B the path is a helix with pitch p = v cos theta T. With both E and B (velocity selector) the charge moves straight when q E = q v B, i.e. v = E/B. A straight wire of length L carrying current I in field B feels F = B I L sin theta; two parallel wires carrying currents I1 and I2 at distance d attract (same direction) or repel with force per unit length mu0 I1 I2/(2 pi d), which defines the ampere.

⚡

Field due to currents

  • Biot-Savart law: dB = (mu0/4 pi) I dl sin theta / r2
  • Long straight wire: B = mu0 I/(2 pi r)
  • Centre of a circular loop of radius R: B = mu0 I/(2R)
  • N turns: mu0 N I/(2R)
Read the full explanation

Biot-Savart law: dB = (mu0/4 pi) I dl sin theta / r^2. Long straight wire: B = mu0 I/(2 pi r). Centre of a circular loop of radius R: B = mu0 I/(2R); N turns: mu0 N I/(2R). On the axis of a loop: B = mu0 I R^2/(2 (R^2 + x^2)^(3/2)). Ampere circuital law: closed integral of B . dl = mu0 I_enclosed. Solenoid: B = mu0 n I inside (n turns per metre), almost zero outside; toroid: B = mu0 N I/(2 pi r). Semicircular arc of radius R at its centre: B = mu0 I/(4R).

⚡

Torque, galvanometer and magnetic materials

  • A rectangular loop of N turns, area A, current I in field B has torque tau = N I A B sin theta = m x B where m = N I A is the magnetic dipole moment
  • Potential energy U = -m
  • The moving-coil galvanometer has deflection proportional to current: N I A B = k phi, so current sensitivity phi/I = N A B/k
  • A galvanometer converts to an ammeter with a small shunt S = G Ig/(I - Ig) in parallel, and to a voltmeter by a large series resistance R = V/Ig - G
Read the full explanation

A rectangular loop of N turns, area A, current I in field B has torque tau = N I A B sin theta = m x B where m = N I A is the magnetic dipole moment; potential energy U = -m . B. The moving-coil galvanometer has deflection proportional to current: N I A B = k phi, so current sensitivity phi/I = N A B/k. A galvanometer converts to an ammeter with a small shunt S = G Ig/(I - Ig) in parallel, and to a voltmeter by a large series resistance R = V/Ig - G. Materials: diamagnetic (weakly repelled, chi negative), paramagnetic (weakly attracted, chi small positive, Curie law chi proportional to 1/T), ferromagnetic (strongly attracted, hysteresis, Curie temperature). Bar magnet: B on the axis = (mu0/4 pi) 2m/r^3 and on the equator (mu0/4 pi) m/r^3 for r >> length. Earth field: horizontal component BH = B cos delta, vertical component B sin delta.

lessons.title: Electromagnetic induction and alternating current
yt: class 12 physics electromagnetic induction and ac

blocks.x: Faraday law: induced emf = -N d(phi)/dt; motional emf = B l v; self-inductance L gives emf = -L dI/dt and energy (1/2) L I^2. In an AC circuit with series L, C and R the impedance is Z = sqrt(R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2), X_L = omega L, X_C = 1/(omega C); resonance at omega = 1/sqrt(LC); average power P = V_rms I_rms cos phi; transformer Vs/Vp = Ns/Np.
Deep dive: induction laws

Magnetic flux phi = B A cos theta (unit weber). Faraday laws: an emf is induced whenever the flux through a circuit changes; its magnitude is e = -N d(phi)/dt. Lenz law gives the minus sign: the induced current opposes the change in flux (conservation of energy). Motional emf in a rod of length l moving with speed v perpendicular to B is e = B l v; a rod rotating about one end with angular speed omega gives e = (1/2) B omega l^2. Eddy currents are induced in bulk conductors and cause heating (used in induction furnaces and electromagnetic braking, reduced by laminating cores). Charge flowing in a coil q = N Dphi/R, independent of time.
Deep dive: inductance

Self-inductance L is defined by phi = L I; induced emf = -L dI/dt; energy stored U = (1/2) L I^2; for a long solenoid L = mu0 n^2 A l. Mutual inductance M gives emf in coil 2 = -M dI1/dt, with M = mu0 N1 N2 A/l for two coaxial solenoids. Time constant of an LR circuit is L/R; the current grows as I = I0 (1 - e^(-t R/L)). Inductors in series add; in parallel combine like resistors if there is no mutual coupling.
Deep dive: alternating current

An AC source V = V0 sin omega t has rms values V_rms = V0/sqrt 2 = 0.707 V0 and average value over a half cycle 0.637 V0. Reactances: X_L = omega L (current lags voltage by 90 degrees), X_C = 1/(omega C) (current leads by 90 degrees). Series LCR: Z = sqrt (R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2), tan phi = (X_L - X_C)/R, I_rms = V_rms/Z. Resonance at omega_0 = 1/sqrt (LC) where Z = R is minimum and current maximum; quality factor Q = omega_0 L/R = (1/R) sqrt (L/C). Average power P = V_rms I_rms cos phi, where cos phi = R/Z is the power factor (zero for a pure L or C: wattless current). A transformer works by mutual induction: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np = Ip/Is for an ideal one; step-up if Ns > Np. Losses: copper, iron (eddy and hysteresis), flux leakage, humming.

emf = -N dphi/dt. Z = sqrt(R^2 + (XL - XC)^2). Resonance f = 1/(2 pi sqrt(LC)).

qa.q: State Faraday's law of induction.
qa.a: The induced emf equals the negative rate of change of magnetic flux linked with the circuit.

qa.q: State Lenz's law.
qa.a: The induced current flows so as to oppose the change in flux that produces it.

qa.q: What is the SI unit of magnetic flux?
What is motional emf?
qa.a: The emf induced in a conductor moving across a magnetic field, e = B l v.

qa.q: What are eddy currents?
qa.a: Circulating currents induced in a bulk conductor by changing flux.

qa.q: How are eddy currents reduced?
What is self-inductance?
qa.a: The property of a coil by which it opposes a change in its own current.

qa.q: What is the SI unit of inductance?
What is the energy stored in an inductor?
What is mutual inductance?
qa.a: The emf induced in one coil due to a changing current in a neighbouring coil.

qa.q: What is the rms value of an alternating current?
Does a pure inductor consume power?
qa.a: No, the average power is zero.

qa.q: What is the phase difference between voltage and current in a pure inductor?

What is resonance in an LCR circuit?
qa.a: The condition X_L = X_C at which the impedance is minimum and the current is maximum.

qa.q: What is the resonant frequency?
What is the power factor?
What is wattless current?
qa.a: Current in a circuit with zero power factor, so no average power is consumed.

qa.q: What is a transformer?
qa.a: A device that changes AC voltage using mutual induction.

qa.q: What is a step-up transformer?
qa.a: A transformer with more secondary turns than primary turns.

qa.q: What are the losses in a transformer?
qa.a: Copper loss, iron loss, flux leakage and humming.

qa.q: What is the quality factor?
qa.a: A measure of the sharpness of resonance, omega_0 L/R.

qa.q: What is an AC generator?
qa.a: A device that converts mechanical energy into alternating current using induction.

qa.q: Why is AC preferred for power transmission?
qa.a: Its voltage can be changed easily by transformers, reducing losses.

Visual lesson

Electromagnetic induction and alternating current

Faraday law: induced emf = -N d(phi)/dt

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Induction laws›3Inductance›4Alternating current
🔑

Big idea

  • Faraday law: induced emf = -N d(phi)/dt
  • Motional emf = B l v
  • Self-inductance L gives emf = -L dI/dt and energy (1/2) L I2
  • In an AC circuit with series L, C and R the impedance is Z = sqrt(R2 + (X_L - X_C)2), X_L = omega L, X_C = 1/(omega C)
Read the full explanation

Faraday law: induced emf = -N d(phi)/dt; motional emf = B l v; self-inductance L gives emf = -L dI/dt and energy (1/2) L I^2. In an AC circuit with series L, C and R the impedance is Z = sqrt(R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2), X_L = omega L, X_C = 1/(omega C); resonance at omega = 1/sqrt(LC); average power P = V_rms I_rms cos phi; transformer Vs/Vp = Ns/Np.

⚖️

Induction laws

  • Magnetic flux phi = B A cos theta (unit weber)
  • Faraday laws: an emf is induced whenever the flux through a circuit changes
  • Its magnitude is e = -N d(phi)/dt
  • Lenz law gives the minus sign: the induced current opposes the change in flux (conservation of energy)
Read the full explanation

Magnetic flux phi = B A cos theta (unit weber). Faraday laws: an emf is induced whenever the flux through a circuit changes; its magnitude is e = -N d(phi)/dt. Lenz law gives the minus sign: the induced current opposes the change in flux (conservation of energy). Motional emf in a rod of length l moving with speed v perpendicular to B is e = B l v; a rod rotating about one end with angular speed omega gives e = (1/2) B omega l^2. Eddy currents are induced in bulk conductors and cause heating (used in induction furnaces and electromagnetic braking, reduced by laminating cores). Charge flowing in a coil q = N Dphi/R, independent of time.

🧠

Inductance

  • Self-inductance L is defined by phi = L I
  • Induced emf = -L dI/dt
  • Energy stored U = (1/2) L I2
  • For a long solenoid L = mu0 n2 A l
Read the full explanation

Self-inductance L is defined by phi = L I; induced emf = -L dI/dt; energy stored U = (1/2) L I^2; for a long solenoid L = mu0 n^2 A l. Mutual inductance M gives emf in coil 2 = -M dI1/dt, with M = mu0 N1 N2 A/l for two coaxial solenoids. Time constant of an LR circuit is L/R; the current grows as I = I0 (1 - e^(-t R/L)). Inductors in series add; in parallel combine like resistors if there is no mutual coupling.

⚡

Alternating current

  • An AC source V = V0 sin omega t has rms values V_rms = V0/sqrt 2 = 0.707 V0 and average value over a half cycle 0.637 V0
  • Reactances: X_L = omega L (current lags voltage by 90 degrees), X_C = 1/(omega C) (current leads by 90 degrees)
  • Series LCR: Z = sqrt (R2 + (X_L - X_C)2), tan phi = (X_L - X_C)/R, I_rms = V_rms/Z
  • Resonance at omega_0 = 1/sqrt (LC) where Z = R is minimum and current maximum
Read the full explanation

An AC source V = V0 sin omega t has rms values V_rms = V0/sqrt 2 = 0.707 V0 and average value over a half cycle 0.637 V0. Reactances: X_L = omega L (current lags voltage by 90 degrees), X_C = 1/(omega C) (current leads by 90 degrees). Series LCR: Z = sqrt (R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2), tan phi = (X_L - X_C)/R, I_rms = V_rms/Z. Resonance at omega_0 = 1/sqrt (LC) where Z = R is minimum and current maximum; quality factor Q = omega_0 L/R = (1/R) sqrt (L/C). Average power P = V_rms I_rms cos phi, where cos phi = R/Z is the power factor (zero for a pure L or C: wattless current). A transformer works by mutual induction: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np = Ip/Is for an ideal one; step-up if Ns > Np. Losses: copper, iron (eddy and hysteresis), flux leakage, humming.

lessons.title: Alternating Current
yt: class 12 physics alternating current rms reactance impedance resonance power factor transformer LC oscillations

blocks.x: An alternating voltage or current varies sinusoidally, v = v0 sin omega t and i = i0 sin omega t, with omega = 2 pi f. The average over a full cycle is zero; the root mean square value is i_rms = i0/sqrt 2 = 0.707 i0, and mains in India is about 230 V at 50 Hz. A resistor: voltage and current are in phase. An inductor: X_L = omega L and current lags voltage by 90 degrees. A capacitor: X_C = 1/(omega C) and current leads voltage by 90 degrees. In a series LCR circuit, the impedance is Z = sqrt(R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2) and the phase angle is tan phi = (X_L - X_C)/R. Resonance occurs when X_L = X_C, at omega0 = 1/sqrt(LC); impedance is minimum (Z = R) and current is maximum. The quality factor Q = omega0 L/R = (1/R) sqrt(L/C) measures sharpness, and the bandwidth is R/L in angular terms. Average power is P = V_rms I_rms cos phi, where cos phi = R/Z is the power factor. In a pure inductor or capacitor power factor is zero and the current is wattless. A choke coil reduces current with little power loss. LC oscillations have natural angular frequency 1/sqrt(LC), with energy exchanged between electric and magnetic forms. A transformer works on mutual induction: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np = Ip/Is for an ideal case. A step-up transformer has Ns greater than Np. Energy losses are copper loss, eddy current loss, hysteresis, flux leakage and humming, and a laminated soft iron core reduces them. An AC generator converts mechanical to electrical energy through electromagnetic induction.
Deep dive: Phasors and reactance
Resistor in phase, inductor lags and capacitor leads by 90 degrees; X_L = omega L, X_C = 1/omega C.
Deep dive: Resonance
At omega0 = 1/sqrt(LC), impedance equals R and current is maximum; Q = omega0 L / R.
Deep dive: Power and transformer
P = VI cos phi; transformer ratio Vs/Vp = Ns/Np with core losses minimised by lamination.

Visual lesson

Alternating Current

An alternating voltage or current varies sinusoidally, v = v0 sin omega t and i = i0 sin omega t, with omega = 2 pi f

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Phasors and reactance›3Resonance›4Power and transformer
🔑

Big idea

  • An alternating voltage or current varies sinusoidally, v = v0 sin omega t and i = i0 sin omega t, with omega = 2 pi f
  • The average over a full cycle is zero
  • The root mean square value is i_rms = i0/sqrt 2 = 0.707 i0, and mains in India is about 230 V at 50 Hz
  • A resistor: voltage and current are in phase
Read the full explanation

An alternating voltage or current varies sinusoidally, v = v0 sin omega t and i = i0 sin omega t, with omega = 2 pi f. The average over a full cycle is zero; the root mean square value is i_rms = i0/sqrt 2 = 0.707 i0, and mains in India is about 230 V at 50 Hz. A resistor: voltage and current are in phase. An inductor: X_L = omega L and current lags voltage by 90 degrees. A capacitor: X_C = 1/(omega C) and current leads voltage by 90 degrees. In a series LCR circuit, the impedance is Z = sqrt(R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2) and the phase angle is tan phi = (X_L - X_C)/R. Resonance occurs when X_L = X_C, at omega0 = 1/sqrt(LC); impedance is minimum (Z = R) and current is maximum. The quality factor Q = omega0 L/R = (1/R) sqrt(L/C) measures sharpness, and the bandwidth is R/L in angular terms. Average power is P = V_rms I_rms cos phi, where cos phi = R/Z is the power factor. In a pure inductor or capacitor power factor is zero and the current is wattless. A choke coil reduces current with little power loss. LC oscillations have natural angular frequency 1/sqrt(LC), with energy exchanged between electric and magnetic forms. A transformer works on mutual induction: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np = Ip/Is for an ideal case. A step-up transformer has Ns greater than Np. Energy losses are copper loss, eddy current loss, hysteresis, flux leakage and humming, and a laminated soft iron core reduces them. An AC generator converts mechanical to electrical energy through electromagnetic induction.

📌

Phasors and reactance

  • Resistor in phase, inductor lags and capacitor leads by 90 degrees
  • X_L = omega L, X_C = 1/omega C
🧠

Resonance

  • At omega0 = 1/sqrt(LC), impedance equals R and current is maximum
  • Q = omega0 L / R
🚀

Power and transformer

  • P = VI cos phi
  • Transformer ratio Vs/Vp = Ns/Np with core losses minimised by lamination
🧮

Formula tiles

RMS valueI_rms = I0 / sqrt 2
Inductive reactanceX_L = omega L
Capacitive reactanceX_C = 1 / (omega C)
ImpedanceZ = sqrt(R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2)
Phase angletan phi = (X_L - X_C) / R
Resonant frequencyomega0 = 1 / sqrt(LC)
Quality factorQ = omega0 L / R
Average powerP = V_rms I_rms cos phi
Power factorcos phi = R / Z

lessons.title: The Cold War Era
yt: class 12 political science the cold war era cuban missile crisis NATO warsaw pact non aligned movement NIEO

blocks.x: The Cold War was the rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union and their allies after the Second World War, fought through ideology, alliances, arms races and proxy wars rather than direct war between the superpowers. It followed the atomic bombing of Hiroshima on 6 August 1945 and Nagasaki on 9 August 1945. The world was bipolar: the capitalist, democratic Western bloc led by the US and the communist Eastern bloc led by the USSR. The Western bloc built NATO (1949), SEATO (1954) and CENTO (1955); the Soviet bloc formed the Warsaw Pact (1955) and Comecon (1949). The US launched the Truman Doctrine and Marshall Plan in 1947. The Berlin blockade of 1948-49 and the Berlin Wall of 1961 symbolised the division of Germany. Wars in Korea (1950-53) and Vietnam showed the Cold War turned hot in the Third World. The Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962, when the USSR placed missiles in Cuba under Fidel Castro and John F. Kennedy responded with a naval quarantine, was the closest the world came to nuclear war and ended with Khrushchev’s withdrawal of missiles. Arms control followed: the Partial Test Ban Treaty (1963), the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (1968), SALT I (1972) and the ABM Treaty (1972). Third World nations formed the Non-Aligned Movement: Nehru, Tito and Nasser led it with Sukarno and Nkrumah, and the first summit was at Belgrade in 1961. Non-alignment did not mean neutrality or isolation but independent judgement on each issue. Developing countries demanded a New International Economic Order, supported by UNCTAD’s 1972 report on trade. India followed non-alignment as an independent foreign policy.
Deep dive: Superpower rivalry
The US and USSR formed NATO and the Warsaw Pact and fought proxy wars without direct war.
Deep dive: Cuban Missile Crisis
October 1962 was the peak of nuclear danger and led to arms control talks.
Deep dive: Non-alignment
NAM chose independent policy, not neutrality; its first summit was in Belgrade in 1961.

problems.q: Distinguish non-alignment from neutrality.

problems.q: Evaluate the role of NAM in the Cold War.
problems.a: NAM gave newly independent states a voice, reduced bloc pressure, supported decolonisation and pushed for a NIEO, but it lacked unity and economic strength.

Big idea

  • The Cold War was the rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union and their allies after the Second World War, fought through ideology…
  • It followed the atomic bombing of Hiroshima on 6 August 1945 and Nagasaki on 9 August 1945

Read the full explanation

The Cold War was the rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union and their allies after the Second World War, fought through ideology, alliances, arms races and proxy wars rather than direct war between the superpowers. It followed the atomic bombing of Hiroshima on 6 August 1945 and Nagasaki on 9 August 1945. The world was bipolar: the capitalist, democratic Western bloc led by the US and the communist Eastern bloc led by the USSR. The Western bloc built NATO (1949), SEATO (1954) and CENTO (1955); the Soviet bloc formed the Warsaw Pact (1955) and Comecon (1949). The US launched the Truman Doctrine and Marshall Plan in 1947. The Berlin blockade of 1948-49 and the Berlin Wall of 1961 symbolised the division of Germany. Wars in Korea (1950-53) and Vietnam showed the Cold War turned hot in the Third World. The Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962, when the USSR placed missiles in Cuba under Fidel Castro and John F. Kennedy responded with a naval quarantine, was the closest the world came to nuclear war and ended with Khrushchev’s withdrawal of missiles. Arms control followed: the Partial Test Ban Treaty (1963), the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (1968), SALT I (1972) and the ABM Treaty (1972). Third World nations formed the Non-Aligned Movement: Nehru, Tito and Nasser led it with Sukarno and Nkrumah, and the first summit was at Belgrade in 1961. Non-alignment did not mean neutrality or isolation but independent judgement on each issue. Developing countries demanded a New International Economic Order, supported by UNCTAD’s 1972 report on trade. India followed non-alignment as an independent foreign policy.

Superpower rivalry

  • The US and USSR formed NATO and the Warsaw Pact and fought proxy wars without direct war
🧠

Cuban Missile Crisis

  • October 1962 was the peak of nuclear danger and led to arms control talks
🌟

Non-alignment

  • NAM chose independent policy, not neutrality
  • Its first summit was in Belgrade in 1961

lessons.title: The End of Bipolarity
yt: class 12 political science end of bipolarity soviet disintegration gorbachev glasnost perestroika shock therapy CIS

blocks.x: The Soviet Union emerged from the Russian Revolution of 1917 and formally came into being in 1922 as a federation of 15 republics. It was a one-party, state-controlled socialist system and a superpower with a huge military and nuclear arsenal. By the 1980s the system was weakened by stagnation under Brezhnev, bureaucracy, lack of freedom, a failing economy, the Afghanistan war after 1979 and the burden of the arms race. Mikhail Gorbachev became leader in 1985 and introduced reforms: perestroika (restructuring) and glasnost (openness). Reform raised demands for freedom in Eastern Europe, where the Berlin Wall fell in November 1989 and Germany reunified in October 1990. The Chernobyl disaster of 1986 exposed the system’s weaknesses. In August 1991 hardliners attempted a coup against Gorbachev and failed. The Baltic states Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania declared independence and Boris Yeltsin led Russia. In December 1991 Russia, Ukraine and Belarus formed the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), and the USSR ceased to exist on 25 December 1991, when Gorbachev resigned. The Warsaw Pact dissolved in 1991. Russia became the successor state, with the Soviet seat in the UN Security Council and the nuclear arsenal. Russia then adopted shock therapy under IMF and World Bank advice, a rapid shift to capitalism, which led to collapse of industries, inflation, unemployment and inequality, and a decline in the economy. The consequences were the end of the Cold War, the US becoming the sole superpower, the end of the socialist ideological bloc, rise of new states, and conflicts in Chechnya, Tajikistan, and the Balkans. Czechoslovakia split peacefully in 1993. India’s relations with Russia continued to be strong in defence, space and energy.
Deep dive: Soviet system
A one party socialist system with 15 republics that weakened through stagnation and war.
Deep dive: Gorbachev reforms
Perestroika and glasnost opened the system and led to demands for freedom.
Deep dive: Aftermath
The USSR dissolved in 1991; Russia adopted shock therapy; the US became the sole superpower.

Read the full explanation

The Soviet Union emerged from the Russian Revolution of 1917 and formally came into being in 1922 as a federation of 15 republics. It was a one-party, state-controlled socialist system and a superpower with a huge military and nuclear arsenal. By the 1980s the system was weakened by stagnation under Brezhnev, bureaucracy, lack of freedom, a failing economy, the Afghanistan war after 1979 and the burden of the arms race. Mikhail Gorbachev became leader in 1985 and introduced reforms: perestroika (restructuring) and glasnost (openness). Reform raised demands for freedom in Eastern Europe, where the Berlin Wall fell in November 1989 and Germany reunified in October 1990. The Chernobyl disaster of 1986 exposed the system’s weaknesses. In August 1991 hardliners attempted a coup against Gorbachev and failed. The Baltic states Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania declared independence and Boris Yeltsin led Russia. In December 1991 Russia, Ukraine and Belarus formed the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), and the USSR ceased to exist on 25 December 1991, when Gorbachev resigned. The Warsaw Pact dissolved in 1991. Russia became the successor state, with the Soviet seat in the UN Security Council and the nuclear arsenal. Russia then adopted shock therapy under IMF and World Bank advice, a rapid shift to capitalism, which led to collapse of industries, inflation, unemployment and inequality, and a decline in the economy. The consequences were the end of the Cold War, the US becoming the sole superpower, the end of the socialist ideological bloc, rise of new states, and conflicts in Chechnya, Tajikistan, and the Balkans. Czechoslovakia split peacefully in 1993. India’s relations with Russia continued to be strong in defence, space and energy.

lessons.title: US Hegemony in World Politics
yt: class 12 political science US hegemony gulf war 9/11 iraq war soft power hard power structural power

blocks.x: Hegemony means leadership or dominance. After the Soviet collapse in 1991 the United States became the sole superpower, and the world was called unipolar. Hegemony can be hard power (military), structural power (shaping the global economic order, as with Bretton Woods institutions and sea lanes) and soft power (ideas and culture, a term coined by Joseph Nye). The US military budget is larger than those of many nations together, and its economy and universities, Hollywood and the internet support its soft power. Key events were the Gulf War. Iraq under Saddam Hussein invaded Kuwait in August 1990; a US-led coalition under a UN mandate launched Operation Desert Storm in January 1991, and President George H. W. Bush spoke of a New World Order. The Clinton years emphasised economic and humanitarian action, including Kosovo and the missile strikes after the 1998 embassy bombings. On 11 September 2001 al-Qaeda attacked the World Trade Center and the Pentagon, and George W. Bush started the War on Terror: Operation Enduring Freedom in Afghanistan against the Taliban (2001) and Operation Iraqi Freedom in Iraq (2003) on the claim of weapons of mass destruction, none of which were found. The US prison at Guantanamo Bay drew criticism for human rights. The constraints on hegemony are the US’s own institutional architecture (separation of powers, a free press), the open nature of American society, and NATO, which may not always support it. India’s options towards the US are bandwagoning, hiding or resisting; India has chosen to engage on shared interests while keeping its strategic autonomy. Huntington’s clash of civilisations and Fukuyama’s end of history are debated interpretations. The US also stayed out of the Kyoto Protocol (2001) and the International Criminal Court.
Deep dive: Types of hegemony
Hard power is military, structural power shapes the economy, soft power is cultural attraction.
Deep dive: Events
The Gulf War in 1991, 9/11 in 2001, Afghanistan 2001 and Iraq 2003 define US unipolar action.
Deep dive: Limits and strategy
Domestic institutions and allies constrain hegemony; states can bandwagon, hide or resist.

problems.q: What is hegemony?
problems.a: Leadership or dominance of one power over the international system.

problems.q: Distinguish hard, structural and soft power.
problems.a: Hard power is military might, structural power shapes the global economic order, and soft power is attraction through culture and ideas.

problems.q: Evaluate the constraints on US hegemony.
problems.a: Domestic institutions, open public debate, allies such as NATO, economic rivals and anti-American sentiment constrain it.

Read the full explanation

Hegemony means leadership or dominance. After the Soviet collapse in 1991 the United States became the sole superpower, and the world was called unipolar. Hegemony can be hard power (military), structural power (shaping the global economic order, as with Bretton Woods institutions and sea lanes) and soft power (ideas and culture, a term coined by Joseph Nye). The US military budget is larger than those of many nations together, and its economy and universities, Hollywood and the internet support its soft power. Key events were the Gulf War. Iraq under Saddam Hussein invaded Kuwait in August 1990; a US-led coalition under a UN mandate launched Operation Desert Storm in January 1991, and President George H. W. Bush spoke of a New World Order. The Clinton years emphasised economic and humanitarian action, including Kosovo and the missile strikes after the 1998 embassy bombings. On 11 September 2001 al-Qaeda attacked the World Trade Center and the Pentagon, and George W. Bush started the War on Terror: Operation Enduring Freedom in Afghanistan against the Taliban (2001) and Operation Iraqi Freedom in Iraq (2003) on the claim of weapons of mass destruction, none of which were found. The US prison at Guantanamo Bay drew criticism for human rights. The constraints on hegemony are the US’s own institutional architecture (separation of powers, a free press), the open nature of American society, and NATO, which may not always support it. India’s options towards the US are bandwagoning, hiding or resisting; India has chosen to engage on shared interests while keeping its strategic autonomy. Huntington’s clash of civilisations and Fukuyama’s end of history are debated interpretations. The US also stayed out of the Kyoto Protocol (2001) and the International Criminal Court.

📌

Types of hegemony

  • Hard power is military, structural power shapes the economy, soft power is cultural attraction
🧠

Events

  • The Gulf War in 1991, 9/11 in 2001, Afghanistan 2001 and Iraq 2003 define US unipolar action
🌟

Limits and strategy

  • Domestic institutions and allies constrain hegemony
  • States can bandwagon, hide or resist

lessons.title: Alternative Centres of Power
yt: class 12 political science alternative centres of power european union ASEAN china economic reforms

blocks.x: After the Cold War several regions emerged as alternative centres of power to the United States. The European Union grew out of the Second World War destruction. The European Coal and Steel Community of 1951 (from the Schuman Plan of 1950) led to the European Economic Community under the Treaty of Rome in 1957, and the Maastricht Treaty of 1992 created the European Union (in force 1993). It has a common currency, the euro, introduced in 2002 for notes and coins, a European Parliament, a Council and a Commission, a flag, anthem and passports, and the Schengen area for open borders. The EU has the world’s large economy, but some members, like the UK, did not adopt the euro, and the UK voted to leave in 2016 (Brexit). ASEAN, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, was founded in Bangkok in 1967 by Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand; later Brunei, Vietnam, Laos, Myanmar and Cambodia joined, making ten members. The ASEAN Way means informal, non-confrontational and cooperative behaviour. ASEAN Vision 2020 (1997) led to the ASEAN Community with three pillars: the ASEAN Security Community, the ASEAN Economic Community and the ASEAN Socio-Cultural Community. The ASEAN Regional Forum (1994) handles security dialogue. Its secretariat is in Jakarta. China has been a rising economic power since Deng Xiaoping’s reforms of 1978 under the open door policy, creating Special Economic Zones and agricultural decollectivisation; it joined the WTO in 2001. China followed One Country, Two Systems for Hong Kong (1997) and Macau (1999). India and China fought a war in 1962, and relations were normalised after Rajiv Gandhi’s 1988 visit.
Deep dive: European Union
From ECSC 1951 and Treaty of Rome 1957 to Maastricht 1992, with a common currency and shared institutions.
Deep dive: ASEAN
Formed in 1967 with five members; the ASEAN Way and three community pillars guide it.
Deep dive: China
Deng Xiaoping’s 1978 reforms and SEZs made China a global economic power.

Visual lesson

Alternative Centres of Power

After the Cold War several regions emerged as alternative centres of power to the United States

Big idea

  • After the Cold War several regions emerged as alternative centres of power to the United States
  • The European Union grew out of the Second World War destruction
  • The European Coal and Steel Community of 1951 (from the Schuman Plan of 1950) led to the European Economic Community under the Treaty of Rome in…
  • It has a common currency, the euro, introduced in 2002 for notes and coins, a European Parliament, a Council and a Commission, a flag, anthem and…
Read the full explanation

After the Cold War several regions emerged as alternative centres of power to the United States. The European Union grew out of the Second World War destruction. The European Coal and Steel Community of 1951 (from the Schuman Plan of 1950) led to the European Economic Community under the Treaty of Rome in 1957, and the Maastricht Treaty of 1992 created the European Union (in force 1993). It has a common currency, the euro, introduced in 2002 for notes and coins, a European Parliament, a Council and a Commission, a flag, anthem and passports, and the Schengen area for open borders. The EU has the world’s large economy, but some members, like the UK, did not adopt the euro, and the UK voted to leave in 2016 (Brexit). ASEAN, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, was founded in Bangkok in 1967 by Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand; later Brunei, Vietnam, Laos, Myanmar and Cambodia joined, making ten members. The ASEAN Way means informal, non-confrontational and cooperative behaviour. ASEAN Vision 2020 (1997) led to the ASEAN Community with three pillars: the ASEAN Security Community, the ASEAN Economic Community and the ASEAN Socio-Cultural Community. The ASEAN Regional Forum (1994) handles security dialogue. Its secretariat is in Jakarta. China has been a rising economic power since Deng Xiaoping’s reforms of 1978 under the open door policy, creating Special Economic Zones and agricultural decollectivisation; it joined the WTO in 2001. China followed One Country, Two Systems for Hong Kong (1997) and Macau (1999). India and China fought a war in 1962, and relations were normalised after Rajiv Gandhi’s 1988 visit.

  • Formed in 1967 with five members
  • The ASEAN Way and three community pillars guide it

  • Deng Xiaoping’s 1978 reforms and SEZs made China a global economic power

yt: class 12 political science contemporary south asia SAARC pakistan bangladesh nepal sri lanka bhutan india relations

blocks.x: South Asia includes Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka. The region has diverse political systems. Pakistan has alternated between civilian and military rule: Ayub Khan took power in 1958, Yahya Khan in 1969, Zia-ul-Haq in 1977 and Pervez Musharraf in 1999. Bangladesh emerged in 1971 after the language and autonomy movement of East Pakistan led by Sheikh Mujibur Rahman and the war in which India helped. Nepal was a monarchy that became a federal democratic republic; the monarchy was abolished in 2008 and the new constitution adopted in 2015. Bhutan moved to constitutional monarchy, with its constitution in 2008. Sri Lanka had a civil war between the government and the Tamil group LTTE that ended in 2009; the Indo-Sri Lanka Accord of 1987 brought an Indian Peace Keeping Force. The Maldives became a republic in 1968. India is the largest democracy. Conflicts include India and Pakistan over Kashmir, wars in 1947-48, 1965, 1971 and 1999 (Kargil), the Tashkent Agreement of 1966 and the Shimla Agreement of 1972. The Indus Waters Treaty of 1960 shared the Indus rivers; the Ganga Water Treaty with Bangladesh was signed in 1996; the Indo-Nepal Treaty of Peace and Friendship dates from 1950; India’s treaty with Bhutan was revised in 2007. SAARC was founded at Dhaka in December 1985 with seven members, and Afghanistan joined in 2007; its headquarters is in Kathmandu. SAFTA was signed in 2004 and came into force in 2006. India’s role in the region is that of the largest economy, which creates both cooperation and mistrust. External powers such as the US and China have also increased involvement.
Deep dive: Political systems
Pakistan swung between military and civilian rule; Nepal, Bhutan and Bangladesh changed governance.
Deep dive: Conflicts and treaties
Kashmir, Kargil, Indus Waters, Ganga Waters and the 1950 Nepal treaty shape relations.
Deep dive: SAARC
Founded 1985 at Dhaka; SAFTA 2004; cooperation limited by political tension.

Big idea

  • The region has diverse political systems
  • Pakistan has alternated between civilian and military rule: Ayub Khan took power in 1958, Yahya Khan in 1969, Zia-ul-Haq in 1977 and Pervez Musharraf…

Read the full explanation

South Asia includes Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka. The region has diverse political systems. Pakistan has alternated between civilian and military rule: Ayub Khan took power in 1958, Yahya Khan in 1969, Zia-ul-Haq in 1977 and Pervez Musharraf in 1999. Bangladesh emerged in 1971 after the language and autonomy movement of East Pakistan led by Sheikh Mujibur Rahman and the war in which India helped. Nepal was a monarchy that became a federal democratic republic; the monarchy was abolished in 2008 and the new constitution adopted in 2015. Bhutan moved to constitutional monarchy, with its constitution in 2008. Sri Lanka had a civil war between the government and the Tamil group LTTE that ended in 2009; the Indo-Sri Lanka Accord of 1987 brought an Indian Peace Keeping Force. The Maldives became a republic in 1968. India is the largest democracy. Conflicts include India and Pakistan over Kashmir, wars in 1947-48, 1965, 1971 and 1999 (Kargil), the Tashkent Agreement of 1966 and the Shimla Agreement of 1972. The Indus Waters Treaty of 1960 shared the Indus rivers; the Ganga Water Treaty with Bangladesh was signed in 1996; the Indo-Nepal Treaty of Peace and Friendship dates from 1950; India’s treaty with Bhutan was revised in 2007. SAARC was founded at Dhaka in December 1985 with seven members, and Afghanistan joined in 2007; its headquarters is in Kathmandu. SAFTA was signed in 2004 and came into force in 2006. India’s role in the region is that of the largest economy, which creates both cooperation and mistrust. External powers such as the US and China have also increased involvement.

yt: class 12 political science international organisations united nations security council reform IMF world bank WTO

blocks.x: International organisations are needed to resolve conflicts, promote cooperation and manage global issues. The League of Nations was formed in 1920 but failed to prevent the Second World War. The United Nations was established on 24 October 1945, with its Charter signed at San Francisco in June 1945, and its headquarters is in New York. It has six principal organs: the General Assembly (all members, one country one vote), the Security Council, the Secretariat headed by the Secretary General, the Economic and Social Council, the International Court of Justice at The Hague and the Trusteeship Council (suspended since 1994). The Security Council has 15 members: five permanent (the US, UK, France, Russia and China) with veto power, and ten non-permanent members elected for two-year terms. Resolutions on substantive matters need nine votes and no veto. The ICJ has 15 judges elected for nine-year terms. The Secretary General is appointed for five years. UN specialised agencies include WHO, UNESCO, FAO, ILO and UNICEF; the IMF and World Bank (from Bretton Woods in 1944) handle finance, and the WTO (1995, successor to GATT of 1947) governs trade. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted on 10 December 1948. UN peacekeeping missions have been important. Reform is demanded: the Security Council has not been expanded since 1965, when non-permanent seats rose from six to ten, and the composition reflects 1945. India, Brazil, Germany and Japan (the G4) seek permanent seats, and India supports a more representative and democratic UN. India has been a major troop contributor to peacekeeping and a founding member of the UN. Reform of the UN includes structural, procedural and financial reforms.
Deep dive: United Nations
Six organs including the General Assembly, Security Council and ICJ; formed 1945.
Deep dive: Security Council
Five permanent members with veto and ten elected for two years; reform demanded by India and the G4.
Deep dive: Economic bodies
The IMF, World Bank and WTO regulate finance and trade.

Read the full explanation

International organisations are needed to resolve conflicts, promote cooperation and manage global issues. The League of Nations was formed in 1920 but failed to prevent the Second World War. The United Nations was established on 24 October 1945, with its Charter signed at San Francisco in June 1945, and its headquarters is in New York. It has six principal organs: the General Assembly (all members, one country one vote), the Security Council, the Secretariat headed by the Secretary General, the Economic and Social Council, the International Court of Justice at The Hague and the Trusteeship Council (suspended since 1994). The Security Council has 15 members: five permanent (the US, UK, France, Russia and China) with veto power, and ten non-permanent members elected for two-year terms. Resolutions on substantive matters need nine votes and no veto. The ICJ has 15 judges elected for nine-year terms. The Secretary General is appointed for five years. UN specialised agencies include WHO, UNESCO, FAO, ILO and UNICEF; the IMF and World Bank (from Bretton Woods in 1944) handle finance, and the WTO (1995, successor to GATT of 1947) governs trade. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted on 10 December 1948. UN peacekeeping missions have been important. Reform is demanded: the Security Council has not been expanded since 1965, when non-permanent seats rose from six to ten, and the composition reflects 1945. India, Brazil, Germany and Japan (the G4) seek permanent seats, and India supports a more representative and democratic UN. India has been a major troop contributor to peacekeeping and a founding member of the UN. Reform of the UN includes structural, procedural and financial reforms.

📌

  • Six organs including the General Assembly, Security Council and ICJ
🧠

Security Council

  • Five permanent members with veto and ten elected for two years
  • Reform demanded by India and the G4
🏛️

Economic bodies

  • The IMF, World Bank and WTO regulate finance and trade
