blocks.x: Security means freedom from threats. Traditional security concerns military threats to a state’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and independence, mostly from other states. Its responses are building military strength, alliances, deterrence, balance of power, disarmament, arms control and confidence building measures. Disarmament means giving up certain weapons, as in the Biological Weapons Convention (1972) and Chemical Weapons Convention (1992); arms control regulates their acquisition, as in the Partial Test Ban Treaty (1963), the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (1968), SALT and the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty (1972), START and the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty (1996). Confidence building measures include exchanging information and prior notice of exercises. Non-traditional security covers threats to human beings and not just states: environmental degradation, global poverty, health epidemics such as HIV/AIDS, bird flu, SARS and Ebola, terrorism, human rights violations and migration. Human security puts the individual at the centre and includes freedom from fear and freedom from want. Cooperative security stresses cooperation through international institutions. India’s security strategy has four components: strengthening military capability, strengthening international norms and institutions, meeting internal security challenges, and developing the economy. India conducted nuclear tests in 1974 (Pokhran-I) and in May 1998 (Pokhran-II) and follows a no first use doctrine, with a minimum credible deterrent. India has not signed the NPT and CTBT, calling them discriminatory. Terrorism, as on 9/11 and in India on 26/11 (Mumbai 2008), is a major non-traditional threat. Refugees and internally displaced persons are another concern.
Deep dive: Traditional security
Military threats between states answered by deterrence, alliances, arms control and disarmament.
Deep dive: Non-traditional security
Poverty, epidemics, terrorism, environment and migration threaten people; human security is the individual’s freedom from fear and want.
Deep dive: India’s approach
Military strength, norms, internal security and development; nuclear tests 1974 and 1998; no first use.

🔑

Big idea

  • Security means freedom from threats
  • Traditional security concerns military threats to a state’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and independence, mostly from other states
  • Its responses are building military strength, alliances, deterrence, balance of power, disarmament, arms control and confidence building measures
  • Disarmament means giving up certain weapons, as in the Biological Weapons Convention (1972) and Chemical Weapons Convention (1992)
Read the full explanation

Security means freedom from threats. Traditional security concerns military threats to a state’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and independence, mostly from other states. Its responses are building military strength, alliances, deterrence, balance of power, disarmament, arms control and confidence building measures. Disarmament means giving up certain weapons, as in the Biological Weapons Convention (1972) and Chemical Weapons Convention (1992); arms control regulates their acquisition, as in the Partial Test Ban Treaty (1963), the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (1968), SALT and the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty (1972), START and the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty (1996). Confidence building measures include exchanging information and prior notice of exercises. Non-traditional security covers threats to human beings and not just states: environmental degradation, global poverty, health epidemics such as HIV/AIDS, bird flu, SARS and Ebola, terrorism, human rights violations and migration. Human security puts the individual at the centre and includes freedom from fear and freedom from want. Cooperative security stresses cooperation through international institutions. India’s security strategy has four components: strengthening military capability, strengthening international norms and institutions, meeting internal security challenges, and developing the economy. India conducted nuclear tests in 1974 (Pokhran-I) and in May 1998 (Pokhran-II) and follows a no first use doctrine, with a minimum credible deterrent. India has not signed the NPT and CTBT, calling them discriminatory. Terrorism, as on 9/11 and in India on 26/11 (Mumbai 2008), is a major non-traditional threat. Refugees and internally displaced persons are another concern.

📌

Traditional security

  • Military threats between states answered by deterrence, alliances, arms control and disarmament
🧠

Non-traditional security

  • Poverty, epidemics, terrorism, environment and migration threaten people
  • Human security is the individual’s freedom from fear and want
🌟

India’s approach

  • Military strength, norms, internal security and development
  • Nuclear tests 1974 and 1998

blocks.x: Environmental concerns became a global political issue because of climate change, ozone depletion, loss of biodiversity, depletion of fresh water and degradation of land. The 1972 Stockholm Conference on the Human Environment began global debate. The 1987 Brundtland Report, Our Common Future, introduced sustainable development: meeting present needs without compromising future generations. The 1992 United Nations Conference on Environment and Development at Rio de Janeiro (the Earth Summit) produced the Rio Declaration, Agenda 21, the Convention on Biological Diversity and the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). Its principle of common but differentiated responsibilities says developed countries, which caused most emissions, must bear more of the burden. The Montreal Protocol (1987) controlled ozone-depleting substances. The Kyoto Protocol (1997, in force 2005) set binding emission cuts for developed countries, while India and China had no binding targets. The Paris Agreement (2015) aims to limit warming to well below 2 degrees C and pursue 1.5 degrees C, using nationally determined contributions. Global commons are areas outside any state’s sovereignty: the atmosphere, Antarctica, the ocean floor and outer space. The Antarctic Treaty of 1959 and the Madrid Protocol of 1991 protect Antarctica from mining. Resource politics includes oil and water; West Asia has half of oil reserves, and water conflicts arise over shared rivers. Indigenous peoples have special claims over resources and lifestyles. India supports common but differentiated responsibility, has a national climate plan, and argues that per capita emissions matter. Environmental movements in India include Chipko and the Narmada movement. The Global Environment Facility and Agenda 21 helped finance efforts.
Deep dive: Global agreements
Stockholm 1972, Brundtland 1987, Rio 1992, Kyoto 1997 and Paris 2015 shaped environmental politics.
Deep dive: Common but differentiated responsibility
Developed countries caused more emissions and must do more, a principle India defends.
Deep dive: Global commons
Antarctica, atmosphere, oceans and outer space belong to no one and need common protection.
Hindi saransh
Paryavaran aur prakritik sansadhan: Rio sammelan, Kyoto protocol, Paris samjhauta aur vaishvik sajhi sampatti.

Read the full explanation

Environmental concerns became a global political issue because of climate change, ozone depletion, loss of biodiversity, depletion of fresh water and degradation of land. The 1972 Stockholm Conference on the Human Environment began global debate. The 1987 Brundtland Report, Our Common Future, introduced sustainable development: meeting present needs without compromising future generations. The 1992 United Nations Conference on Environment and Development at Rio de Janeiro (the Earth Summit) produced the Rio Declaration, Agenda 21, the Convention on Biological Diversity and the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). Its principle of common but differentiated responsibilities says developed countries, which caused most emissions, must bear more of the burden. The Montreal Protocol (1987) controlled ozone-depleting substances. The Kyoto Protocol (1997, in force 2005) set binding emission cuts for developed countries, while India and China had no binding targets. The Paris Agreement (2015) aims to limit warming to well below 2 degrees C and pursue 1.5 degrees C, using nationally determined contributions. Global commons are areas outside any state’s sovereignty: the atmosphere, Antarctica, the ocean floor and outer space. The Antarctic Treaty of 1959 and the Madrid Protocol of 1991 protect Antarctica from mining. Resource politics includes oil and water; West Asia has half of oil reserves, and water conflicts arise over shared rivers. Indigenous peoples have special claims over resources and lifestyles. India supports common but differentiated responsibility, has a national climate plan, and argues that per capita emissions matter. Environmental movements in India include Chipko and the Narmada movement. The Global Environment Facility and Agenda 21 helped finance efforts.

📌

Global agreements

  • Stockholm 1972, Brundtland 1987, Rio 1992, Kyoto 1997 and Paris 2015 shaped environmental politics
🧠

Common but differentiated responsibility

  • Developed countries caused more emissions and must do more, a principle India defends
🌟

Global commons

  • Antarctica, atmosphere, oceans and outer space belong to no one and need common protection
🎯 Remember CBDR = common but differentiated responsibilities.

lessons.title: Globalisation
yt: class 12 political science globalisation economic cultural political dimensions IMF WTO impact india anti globalisation

blocks.x: Globalisation is the widening and deepening of flows of ideas, capital, commodities and people across the world. It is not new: trade along the Silk Route and colonial trade linked regions long ago. Its present phase is driven by technology (telecommunications, the internet, container shipping) and by policies of liberalisation. Its dimensions are economic (trade, finance, outsourcing), political (a changing role of the state) and cultural (spread of ideas, food, films and brands). Causes include the transport and communication revolution, trade liberalisation, and the role of the IMF, World Bank and WTO. The WTO (1995) replaced GATT (1947). The impact is mixed. Economic gains include higher trade, growth, cheaper goods, jobs in services such as call centres, and spread of technology; losses include unequal gains, job insecurity, farm distress and pressure on welfare and small producers. Politically, the state has retreated from welfare, but state capacity has not vanished, and some states have become stronger with technology. Culturally, globalisation spreads global culture and McDonaldisation, but it can also produce cultural homogenisation and, in reaction, cultural hybridisation, such as Indian food and films abroad. Critics include the Left, who see exploitation, and the Right, who see threats to culture. The World Social Forum, first held at Porto Alegre in Brazil in 2001, brought together anti-globalisation movements. India began economic reforms in 1991 under Narasimha Rao and Manmohan Singh, with liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation, and has grown in IT and services. Globalisation also raises migration, brain drain, labour mobility and issues of global trade rules.
Deep dive: Dimensions
Economic flows, political changes in the state and cultural exchange define globalisation.
Deep dive: Impact
Growth, jobs and technology on one side; inequality, insecurity and cultural homogenisation on the other.
Deep dive: Resistance and India
The World Social Forum opposes it; India liberalised its economy in 1991.

Read the full explanation

Globalisation is the widening and deepening of flows of ideas, capital, commodities and people across the world. It is not new: trade along the Silk Route and colonial trade linked regions long ago. Its present phase is driven by technology (telecommunications, the internet, container shipping) and by policies of liberalisation. Its dimensions are economic (trade, finance, outsourcing), political (a changing role of the state) and cultural (spread of ideas, food, films and brands). Causes include the transport and communication revolution, trade liberalisation, and the role of the IMF, World Bank and WTO. The WTO (1995) replaced GATT (1947). The impact is mixed. Economic gains include higher trade, growth, cheaper goods, jobs in services such as call centres, and spread of technology; losses include unequal gains, job insecurity, farm distress and pressure on welfare and small producers. Politically, the state has retreated from welfare, but state capacity has not vanished, and some states have become stronger with technology. Culturally, globalisation spreads global culture and McDonaldisation, but it can also produce cultural homogenisation and, in reaction, cultural hybridisation, such as Indian food and films abroad. Critics include the Left, who see exploitation, and the Right, who see threats to culture. The World Social Forum, first held at Porto Alegre in Brazil in 2001, brought together anti-globalisation movements. India began economic reforms in 1991 under Narasimha Rao and Manmohan Singh, with liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation, and has grown in IT and services. Globalisation also raises migration, brain drain, labour mobility and issues of global trade rules.

📌

Dimensions

  • Economic flows, political changes in the state and cultural exchange define globalisation
🧠

Impact

  • Growth, jobs and technology on one side
  • Inequality, insecurity and cultural homogenisation on the other
🌟

Resistance and India

  • The World Social Forum opposes it
  • India liberalised its economy in 1991

lessons.title: Challenges of Nation Building
yt: class 12 political science challenges of nation building partition princely states integration states reorganisation language

blocks.x: Independent India faced three challenges: to build a united nation respecting diversity, to establish a democratic constitutional order, and to ensure development and welfare of all. Independence on 15 August 1947 came with Partition on the basis of the two-nation theory, with the Radcliffe Line dividing Punjab and Bengal, and caused mass migration, violence and the deaths of many. The Constituent Assembly, with Dr Rajendra Prasad as president and B. R. Ambedkar as chairman of the drafting committee, framed the Constitution adopted on 26 November 1949 and in force on 26 January 1950. Nehru’s ‘tryst with destiny’ speech marked independence. Mahatma Gandhi was assassinated on 30 January 1948. Integration of about 565 princely states was led by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, as Deputy Prime Minister and Home Minister, with V. P. Menon, using Instruments of Accession by the 1947 Indian Independence Act option. Most states acceded peacefully; Junagadh joined after a plebiscite, Hyderabad was integrated after the police action of September 1948, and Manipur merged in 1949. Kashmir’s Maharaja Hari Singh signed the Instrument of Accession on 26 October 1947 after tribal raiders attacked. Reorganisation of states on linguistic lines followed: Potti Sriramulu’s fast unto death in 1952 led to Andhra State in 1953; the States Reorganisation Commission (1953) under Fazl Ali with K. M. Panikkar and H. N. Kunzru led to the States Reorganisation Act of 1956, creating 14 states and 6 union territories. Later, Maharashtra and Gujarat were formed in 1960, Punjab and Haryana in 1966, and Goa became a state in 1987. Linguistic reorganisation strengthened democracy and unity. Hindi as the official language and English as an associate language, the three language formula, and the Official Languages Act addressed language issues.
Deep dive: Partition and violence
1947 Partition on the two-nation theory caused mass migration and violence.
Deep dive: Integration
Patel and V. P. Menon integrated about 565 princely states by accession, with special cases at Junagadh, Hyderabad and Kashmir.
Deep dive: Linguistic states
Potti Sriramulu’s fast led to Andhra in 1953 and the 1956 States Reorganisation Act.

Read the full explanation

Independent India faced three challenges: to build a united nation respecting diversity, to establish a democratic constitutional order, and to ensure development and welfare of all. Independence on 15 August 1947 came with Partition on the basis of the two-nation theory, with the Radcliffe Line dividing Punjab and Bengal, and caused mass migration, violence and the deaths of many. The Constituent Assembly, with Dr Rajendra Prasad as president and B. R. Ambedkar as chairman of the drafting committee, framed the Constitution adopted on 26 November 1949 and in force on 26 January 1950. Nehru’s ‘tryst with destiny’ speech marked independence. Mahatma Gandhi was assassinated on 30 January 1948. Integration of about 565 princely states was led by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, as Deputy Prime Minister and Home Minister, with V. P. Menon, using Instruments of Accession by the 1947 Indian Independence Act option. Most states acceded peacefully; Junagadh joined after a plebiscite, Hyderabad was integrated after the police action of September 1948, and Manipur merged in 1949. Kashmir’s Maharaja Hari Singh signed the Instrument of Accession on 26 October 1947 after tribal raiders attacked. Reorganisation of states on linguistic lines followed: Potti Sriramulu’s fast unto death in 1952 led to Andhra State in 1953; the States Reorganisation Commission (1953) under Fazl Ali with K. M. Panikkar and H. N. Kunzru led to the States Reorganisation Act of 1956, creating 14 states and 6 union territories. Later, Maharashtra and Gujarat were formed in 1960, Punjab and Haryana in 1966, and Goa became a state in 1987. Linguistic reorganisation strengthened democracy and unity. Hindi as the official language and English as an associate language, the three language formula, and the Official Languages Act addressed language issues.

lessons.title: Era of One-Party Dominance
yt: class 12 political science one party dominance first general election congress system opposition parties kerala 1957

blocks.x: The Constituent Assembly chose democracy and universal adult franchise from the beginning. The Election Commission was set up in January 1950 with Sukumar Sen as the first Chief Election Commissioner. The first general elections were held in 1951-52, with about 17 crore voters, and the Congress won 364 of 489 Lok Sabha seats, with the Communist Party of India as the largest opposition party with 16 seats. Congress also won in most states. The elections were seen as a success of democracy, with voting by symbols for illiterate voters and polling in many phases. In 1957 and 1962 the Congress won again. India had a one-party dominant system but, unlike authoritarian one-party regimes, competition was free. The Congress was a rainbow coalition and an umbrella party, inherited the freedom movement legacy since 1885, and had social and ideological diversity. The Congress Socialist faction and others kept internal debate. Opposition parties included the Communist Party of India (1925), the Socialist Party (1948, later Praja Socialist Party), the Bharatiya Jana Sangh (1951, Syama Prasad Mookerjee), the Swatantra Party (1959, C. Rajagopalachari) and the Bharatiya Kranti Dal later. They were small but acted as a check. The Communists formed the first elected communist government in the world at the state level in Kerala in 1957 under E. M. S. Namboodiripad, which the Centre dismissed in 1959 under Article 356. Nehru dominated the Congress; opposition leaders such as Ram Manohar Lohia and Jayaprakash Narayan criticised it. Dominance of the Congress ended gradually in the 1967 elections.
Deep dive: First elections
1951-52 elections under Sukumar Sen gave Congress 364 of 489 seats.
Deep dive: Congress system
A broad umbrella with internal factions and a freedom movement legacy.
Deep dive: Opposition
CPI, Socialists, Jana Sangh and Swatantra Party acted as a check; Kerala 1957 was the first communist government.

problems.q: When and under whom were the first general elections held?
problems.a: In 1951-52 under Chief Election Commissioner Sukumar Sen.

problems.q: Why was Congress called an umbrella party?
problems.a: It included diverse social groups, ideologies and factions, so it worked like a coalition.

problems.q: How did one-party dominance in India differ from other countries?
problems.a: Other countries had one-party rule through force, while in India Congress won repeatedly in free and fair competitive elections.

Read the full explanation

The Constituent Assembly chose democracy and universal adult franchise from the beginning. The Election Commission was set up in January 1950 with Sukumar Sen as the first Chief Election Commissioner. The first general elections were held in 1951-52, with about 17 crore voters, and the Congress won 364 of 489 Lok Sabha seats, with the Communist Party of India as the largest opposition party with 16 seats. Congress also won in most states. The elections were seen as a success of democracy, with voting by symbols for illiterate voters and polling in many phases. In 1957 and 1962 the Congress won again. India had a one-party dominant system but, unlike authoritarian one-party regimes, competition was free. The Congress was a rainbow coalition and an umbrella party, inherited the freedom movement legacy since 1885, and had social and ideological diversity. The Congress Socialist faction and others kept internal debate. Opposition parties included the Communist Party of India (1925), the Socialist Party (1948, later Praja Socialist Party), the Bharatiya Jana Sangh (1951, Syama Prasad Mookerjee), the Swatantra Party (1959, C. Rajagopalachari) and the Bharatiya Kranti Dal later. They were small but acted as a check. The Communists formed the first elected communist government in the world at the state level in Kerala in 1957 under E. M. S. Namboodiripad, which the Centre dismissed in 1959 under Article 356. Nehru dominated the Congress; opposition leaders such as Ram Manohar Lohia and Jayaprakash Narayan criticised it. Dominance of the Congress ended gradually in the 1967 elections.

lessons.title: Politics of Planned Development
yt: class 12 political science planned development planning commission five year plans green revolution white revolution land reforms mixed economy

blocks.x: India chose planned development with a mixed economy: a strong public sector alongside private enterprise, to remove poverty and build industry after independence. The Bombay Plan of 1944 by industrialists favoured state involvement. The Planning Commission was established in 1950 with the Prime Minister as chairman, and the National Development Council in 1952 for state participation. The First Five Year Plan (1951-56) stressed agriculture, irrigation and dams like Bhakra Nangal and followed the Harrod-Domar model, with K. N. Raj as an architect. The Second Plan (1956-61), under P. C. Mahalanobis, stressed heavy industry and the public sector, setting up steel plants at Bhilai, Rourkela and Durgapur, and was backed by the Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956. The Third Plan (1961-66) was hit by wars with China (1962) and Pakistan (1965) and drought, leading to plan holidays from 1966 to 1969. Land reforms abolished zamindari, introduced tenancy reform, ceilings and consolidation, but with uneven success. The food crisis led to the Green Revolution in the 1960s with high-yield variety seeds, fertiliser and irrigation, supported by M. S. Swaminathan and Norman Borlaug, benefiting Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh but increasing regional and class inequalities. The White Revolution (Operation Flood) by Verghese Kurien, with Amul, made India a milk-surplus nation. Critics said the model gave too much power to the bureaucracy and slowed growth. The economic crisis of 1991 led to liberalisation. The Planning Commission was replaced by NITI Aayog on 1 January 2015. Kerala showed a model of human development.
Deep dive: Planning machinery
The Planning Commission (1950) and NDC (1952) guided Five Year Plans in a mixed economy.
Deep dive: Plans
The First Plan stressed agriculture; the Second Plan, Mahalanobis, stressed heavy industry and the public sector.
Deep dive: Rural change
Land reforms, the Green Revolution and Operation Flood changed agriculture with uneven benefits.

Politics of Planned Development

India chose planned development with a mixed economy: a strong public sector alongside private enterprise, to remove poverty and build industry after independence

Read the full explanation

India chose planned development with a mixed economy: a strong public sector alongside private enterprise, to remove poverty and build industry after independence. The Bombay Plan of 1944 by industrialists favoured state involvement. The Planning Commission was established in 1950 with the Prime Minister as chairman, and the National Development Council in 1952 for state participation. The First Five Year Plan (1951-56) stressed agriculture, irrigation and dams like Bhakra Nangal and followed the Harrod-Domar model, with K. N. Raj as an architect. The Second Plan (1956-61), under P. C. Mahalanobis, stressed heavy industry and the public sector, setting up steel plants at Bhilai, Rourkela and Durgapur, and was backed by the Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956. The Third Plan (1961-66) was hit by wars with China (1962) and Pakistan (1965) and drought, leading to plan holidays from 1966 to 1969. Land reforms abolished zamindari, introduced tenancy reform, ceilings and consolidation, but with uneven success. The food crisis led to the Green Revolution in the 1960s with high-yield variety seeds, fertiliser and irrigation, supported by M. S. Swaminathan and Norman Borlaug, benefiting Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh but increasing regional and class inequalities. The White Revolution (Operation Flood) by Verghese Kurien, with Amul, made India a milk-surplus nation. Critics said the model gave too much power to the bureaucracy and slowed growth. The economic crisis of 1991 led to liberalisation. The Planning Commission was replaced by NITI Aayog on 1 January 2015. Kerala showed a model of human development.

lessons.title: India’s External Relations
yt: class 12 political science india external relations non alignment china war 1962 pakistan wars 1965 1971 nuclear policy

blocks.x: India’s foreign policy aims to protect territorial integrity, sovereignty and economic development, and flows from the freedom movement, the Constitution (Article 51) and the Cold War context. Jawaharlal Nehru shaped early policy: non-alignment, peace and cooperation with all, anti-colonialism and the five principles of Panchsheel, signed with China in 1954. India supported decolonisation, hosted the Asian Relations Conference of 1947, supported Indonesia’s independence, took part in the Bandung Conference of 1955, and opposed apartheid. Relations with China began warmly: India recognised the People’s Republic in 1949-50, and Panchsheel was signed in 1954. Tibet became a point of tension, and after the 1959 revolt the Dalai Lama sought asylum in India. The border dispute led to the Sino-Indian war of October-November 1962, which was a setback for India; the defence budget rose and Nehru’s image suffered. With Pakistan, Kashmir led to the 1947-48 war. The 1965 war ended in the Tashkent Agreement of 1966 between Lal Bahadur Shastri and Ayub Khan, after which Shastri died at Tashkent. The 1971 crisis in East Pakistan created ten million refugees; the Indo-Soviet Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation of August 1971 was signed, and war in December 1971 led to Bangladesh and the Shimla Agreement of 1972. India tested a nuclear device in 1974 (Pokhran-I) and conducted five tests in 1998 (Pokhran-II). The Kargil conflict took place in 1999. India refused to sign the NPT and CTBT. After 1991, with the end of the Soviet Union, India adopted the Look East policy and improved relations with the US, signing a civil nuclear agreement in 2008. India’s Goa liberation took place in 1961.
Deep dive: Early policy
Non-alignment, Panchsheel and anti-colonialism shaped Nehru’s foreign policy.
Deep dive: Wars
1947-48 and 1965 and 1971 with Pakistan and 1962 with China shaped security policy.
Deep dive: Nuclear and post-1991 policy
Tests in 1974 and 1998, no first use, Look East and engagement with the US.

Read the full explanation

India’s foreign policy aims to protect territorial integrity, sovereignty and economic development, and flows from the freedom movement, the Constitution (Article 51) and the Cold War context. Jawaharlal Nehru shaped early policy: non-alignment, peace and cooperation with all, anti-colonialism and the five principles of Panchsheel, signed with China in 1954. India supported decolonisation, hosted the Asian Relations Conference of 1947, supported Indonesia’s independence, took part in the Bandung Conference of 1955, and opposed apartheid. Relations with China began warmly: India recognised the People’s Republic in 1949-50, and Panchsheel was signed in 1954. Tibet became a point of tension, and after the 1959 revolt the Dalai Lama sought asylum in India. The border dispute led to the Sino-Indian war of October-November 1962, which was a setback for India; the defence budget rose and Nehru’s image suffered. With Pakistan, Kashmir led to the 1947-48 war. The 1965 war ended in the Tashkent Agreement of 1966 between Lal Bahadur Shastri and Ayub Khan, after which Shastri died at Tashkent. The 1971 crisis in East Pakistan created ten million refugees; the Indo-Soviet Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation of August 1971 was signed, and war in December 1971 led to Bangladesh and the Shimla Agreement of 1972. India tested a nuclear device in 1974 (Pokhran-I) and conducted five tests in 1998 (Pokhran-II). The Kargil conflict took place in 1999. India refused to sign the NPT and CTBT. After 1991, with the end of the Soviet Union, India adopted the Look East policy and improved relations with the US, signing a civil nuclear agreement in 2008. India’s Goa liberation took place in 1961.

lessons.title: Challenges to the Congress System
yt: class 12 political science challenges to congress system 1967 elections syndicate congress split bank nationalisation garibi hatao

blocks.x: After Nehru’s death in May 1964 Lal Bahadur Shastri became Prime Minister; he promoted the slogan Jai Jawan Jai Kisan and led during the 1965 war, and died at Tashkent in January 1966. The Congress Syndicate, a group of regional leaders including K. Kamaraj, S. Nijalingappa and Atulya Ghosh, then chose Indira Gandhi as Prime Minister in January 1966, expecting she would be dependent on them. She faced drought, devaluation of the rupee in 1966 under US pressure and high prices. In the 1967 elections the Congress won a reduced majority in the Lok Sabha and lost power in several states: opposition parties formed coalitions called Samyukta Vidhayak Dal (SVD) governments, and the DMK under C. N. Annadurai won in Madras (Tamil Nadu). The era saw defections, the phrase ‘Aaya Ram Gaya Ram’ coming from Haryana, and political instability. Naxalbari uprising of 1967 began the Naxalite movement. The split came in 1969: after Zakir Husain died, the Syndicate named Sanjiva Reddy for President, Indira Gandhi supported V. V. Giri, who won, and the Congress split into Congress (O) and Congress (R). Indira Gandhi nationalised 14 major banks in July 1969, abolished the privy purses of former princes through the 26th Amendment in 1971, and took a left-leaning course. In 1971 she called early Lok Sabha elections, with the slogan Garibi Hatao against the Grand Alliance of opposition parties slogan Indira Hatao; Congress (R) won 352 seats. After the Bangladesh war of 1971 her position became dominant. The anti-defection law came much later in 1985. The new Congress was more personalised and centralised, with a direct appeal to voters.
Deep dive: 1967 elections
Congress lost many states; SVD coalitions and defections began a new phase.
Deep dive: 1969 split
Syndicate versus Indira Gandhi led to Congress (O) and Congress (R) after the presidential contest.
Deep dive: 1971 mandate
Bank nationalisation, privy purse abolition and Garibi Hatao won Congress (R) 352 seats.

Big idea

Read the full explanation

After Nehru’s death in May 1964 Lal Bahadur Shastri became Prime Minister; he promoted the slogan Jai Jawan Jai Kisan and led during the 1965 war, and died at Tashkent in January 1966. The Congress Syndicate, a group of regional leaders including K. Kamaraj, S. Nijalingappa and Atulya Ghosh, then chose Indira Gandhi as Prime Minister in January 1966, expecting she would be dependent on them. She faced drought, devaluation of the rupee in 1966 under US pressure and high prices. In the 1967 elections the Congress won a reduced majority in the Lok Sabha and lost power in several states: opposition parties formed coalitions called Samyukta Vidhayak Dal (SVD) governments, and the DMK under C. N. Annadurai won in Madras (Tamil Nadu). The era saw defections, the phrase ‘Aaya Ram Gaya Ram’ coming from Haryana, and political instability. Naxalbari uprising of 1967 began the Naxalite movement. The split came in 1969: after Zakir Husain died, the Syndicate named Sanjiva Reddy for President, Indira Gandhi supported V. V. Giri, who won, and the Congress split into Congress (O) and Congress (R). Indira Gandhi nationalised 14 major banks in July 1969, abolished the privy purses of former princes through the 26th Amendment in 1971, and took a left-leaning course. In 1971 she called early Lok Sabha elections, with the slogan Garibi Hatao against the Grand Alliance of opposition parties slogan Indira Hatao; Congress (R) won 352 seats. After the Bangladesh war of 1971 her position became dominant. The anti-defection law came much later in 1985. The new Congress was more personalised and centralised, with a direct appeal to voters.

  • Congress lost many states
  • SVD coalitions and defections began a new phase

  • Syndicate versus Indira Gandhi led to Congress (O) and Congress (R) after the presidential contest
🌟

1971 mandate

  • Bank nationalisation, privy purse abolition and Garibi Hatao won Congress (R) 352 seats

lessons.title: Crisis of the Democratic Order
yt: class 12 political science crisis of democratic order emergency 1975 JP movement allahabad verdict shah commission janata party

blocks.x: The early 1970s saw growing discontent over inflation, unemployment and corruption. The Navnirman movement in Gujarat (1974) and the Bihar movement led by Jayaprakash Narayan (JP) in 1974 called for Total Revolution; the railway strike of 1974 under George Fernandes paralysed services. Tension grew between the executive and judiciary: in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) the Supreme Court held that Parliament cannot change the basic structure of the Constitution, and the appointment of Chief Justice A. N. Ray superseded three senior judges. On 12 June 1975 the Allahabad High Court (Justice Jagmohanlal Sinha) found Indira Gandhi guilty of electoral malpractice in the case brought by Raj Narain, and set aside her election. The Supreme Court granted a conditional stay. On 25 June 1975 JP called for mass protest, and that night Emergency was declared under Article 352 on the ground of internal disturbance, and remained until 21 March 1977. Fundamental rights were suspended; press censorship was imposed; preventive detention under MISA jailed thousands including opposition leaders; some organisations like the RSS and Jamaat-e-Islami were banned. The 42nd Amendment of 1976 curtailed judicial review and extended the Lok Sabha term to six years. The Supreme Court in ADM Jabalpur (1976) held that fundamental rights could be suspended in the Emergency. Sanjay Gandhi’s extra-constitutional role, forced sterilisation and slum demolitions drew criticism. Elections in March 1977 saw Congress lose, and the Janata Party formed the first non-Congress government at the Centre with Morarji Desai as Prime Minister. The Shah Commission investigated Emergency excesses. The 44th Amendment (1978) made it harder to impose an Emergency, limiting grounds to armed rebellion. The Janata government fell in 1979, and Congress returned in 1980.
Deep dive: Movements and tension
Gujarat and Bihar movements, JP’s Total Revolution, the railway strike and clashes with the judiciary built the crisis.
Deep dive: The Emergency
Declared on 25 June 1975 under Article 352; rights, press and opposition were suppressed until March 1977.
Deep dive: Aftermath
The 1977 elections brought the Janata government; the 44th Amendment restricted future Emergencies.

Read the full explanation

The early 1970s saw growing discontent over inflation, unemployment and corruption. The Navnirman movement in Gujarat (1974) and the Bihar movement led by Jayaprakash Narayan (JP) in 1974 called for Total Revolution; the railway strike of 1974 under George Fernandes paralysed services. Tension grew between the executive and judiciary: in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) the Supreme Court held that Parliament cannot change the basic structure of the Constitution, and the appointment of Chief Justice A. N. Ray superseded three senior judges. On 12 June 1975 the Allahabad High Court (Justice Jagmohanlal Sinha) found Indira Gandhi guilty of electoral malpractice in the case brought by Raj Narain, and set aside her election. The Supreme Court granted a conditional stay. On 25 June 1975 JP called for mass protest, and that night Emergency was declared under Article 352 on the ground of internal disturbance, and remained until 21 March 1977. Fundamental rights were suspended; press censorship was imposed; preventive detention under MISA jailed thousands including opposition leaders; some organisations like the RSS and Jamaat-e-Islami were banned. The 42nd Amendment of 1976 curtailed judicial review and extended the Lok Sabha term to six years. The Supreme Court in ADM Jabalpur (1976) held that fundamental rights could be suspended in the Emergency. Sanjay Gandhi’s extra-constitutional role, forced sterilisation and slum demolitions drew criticism. Elections in March 1977 saw Congress lose, and the Janata Party formed the first non-Congress government at the Centre with Morarji Desai as Prime Minister. The Shah Commission investigated Emergency excesses. The 44th Amendment (1978) made it harder to impose an Emergency, limiting grounds to armed rebellion. The Janata government fell in 1979, and Congress returned in 1980.

🕰️

Movements and tension

  • Gujarat and Bihar movements, JP’s Total Revolution, the railway strike and clashes with the judiciary built the crisis
🧠

The Emergency

  • Declared on 25 June 1975 under Article 352
  • Rights, press and opposition were suppressed until March 1977
🌟

Aftermath

  • The 1977 elections brought the Janata government
  • The 44th Amendment restricted future Emergencies

lessons.title: Rise of Popular Movements
yt: class 12 political science rise of popular movements chipko dalit panthers bharatiya kisan union narmada bachao andolan RTI SEWA

blocks.x: Popular movements are collective actions by people outside the party system to press for demands. After the Emergency and the decline of the Congress system, many non-party movements arose, because parties did not address all issues. The Chipko movement began in 1973 in Uttarakhand (then Uttar Pradesh), when villagers, many of them women led by Gaura Devi, hugged trees to stop commercial felling; Sunderlal Bahuguna and Chandi Prasad Bhatt were its leaders; it stressed ecology and livelihood and is called a movement for protecting the forest and women’s participation. The Dalit Panthers was formed in 1972 in Maharashtra by Namdeo Dhasal and J. V. Pawar to fight caste atrocities and untouchability, inspired by Ambedkar and the Black Panthers. The Bharatiya Kisan Union (BKU) in western Uttar Pradesh under Mahendra Singh Tikait demanded better prices and electricity rates in the 1980s, with a large Delhi rally in 1988. The anti-arrack movement in Andhra Pradesh was led by rural women against alcohol. Self-Employed Women’s Association (SEWA), founded by Ela Bhatt in 1972, organised poor women workers. The Narmada Bachao Andolan (NBA) from 1985, led by Medha Patkar and Baba Amte, opposed the Sardar Sarovar dam on displacement and environment grounds. The Right to Information movement started in Rajasthan with the Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan (MKSS) in the 1990s and led to the RTI Act of 2005. The Mandal Commission (1980) recommended 27 per cent reservation for OBCs, which the V. P. Singh government implemented in 1990, leading to protests. The National Fishworkers’ Forum protested against trawlers. These movements show that popular movements are a part of democratic politics, using petitions, rallies and satyagraha, and they raised the demand of the marginalised, but some were limited by lack of resources.
Deep dive: Environment and livelihood
Chipko 1973 and Narmada Bachao Andolan 1985 linked ecology to people’s livelihoods.
Deep dive: Social movements
Dalit Panthers, BKU, SEWA and anti-arrack movement represented marginalised groups.
Deep dive: Rights movements
The RTI movement led to the 2005 Act and the Mandal Commission opened OBC reservation.

Big idea

Read the full explanation

Popular movements are collective actions by people outside the party system to press for demands. After the Emergency and the decline of the Congress system, many non-party movements arose, because parties did not address all issues. The Chipko movement began in 1973 in Uttarakhand (then Uttar Pradesh), when villagers, many of them women led by Gaura Devi, hugged trees to stop commercial felling; Sunderlal Bahuguna and Chandi Prasad Bhatt were its leaders; it stressed ecology and livelihood and is called a movement for protecting the forest and women’s participation. The Dalit Panthers was formed in 1972 in Maharashtra by Namdeo Dhasal and J. V. Pawar to fight caste atrocities and untouchability, inspired by Ambedkar and the Black Panthers. The Bharatiya Kisan Union (BKU) in western Uttar Pradesh under Mahendra Singh Tikait demanded better prices and electricity rates in the 1980s, with a large Delhi rally in 1988. The anti-arrack movement in Andhra Pradesh was led by rural women against alcohol. Self-Employed Women’s Association (SEWA), founded by Ela Bhatt in 1972, organised poor women workers. The Narmada Bachao Andolan (NBA) from 1985, led by Medha Patkar and Baba Amte, opposed the Sardar Sarovar dam on displacement and environment grounds. The Right to Information movement started in Rajasthan with the Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan (MKSS) in the 1990s and led to the RTI Act of 2005. The Mandal Commission (1980) recommended 27 per cent reservation for OBCs, which the V. P. Singh government implemented in 1990, leading to protests. The National Fishworkers’ Forum protested against trawlers. These movements show that popular movements are a part of democratic politics, using petitions, rallies and satyagraha, and they raised the demand of the marginalised, but some were limited by lack of resources.

📌

Environment and livelihood

  • Chipko 1973 and Narmada Bachao Andolan 1985 linked ecology to people’s livelihoods
🕰️

Social movements

  • Dalit Panthers, BKU, SEWA and anti-arrack movement represented marginalised groups
🕰️

Rights movements

  • The RTI movement led to the 2005 Act and the Mandal Commission opened OBC reservation

lessons.title: Regional Aspirations
yt: class 12 political science regional aspirations jammu kashmir punjab northeast assam mizoram nagaland sikkim goa

blocks.x: Regional aspirations are demands for autonomy, identity or statehood within a democratic framework. India accepts diversity, and accommodation of regional demands has strengthened unity. In Jammu and Kashmir, Article 370 gave special status; the autonomy debate, the 1953 dismissal of Sheikh Abdullah, militancy from the 1980s, and the 1996 return of elections shaped politics; Article 370 was revoked in August 2019 and the state split into two union territories. In Punjab, the Akali Dal’s Anandpur Sahib Resolution of 1973 demanded autonomy; militancy led to Operation Blue Star in June 1984 at the Golden Temple, the assassination of Indira Gandhi on 31 October 1984, and the Rajiv Gandhi-Longowal Accord of July 1985; peace and elections returned by the 1990s. The Northeast saw demands for autonomy: in Assam the movement against illegal migrants, led by the All Assam Students Union (AASU) from 1979, ended with the Assam Accord of 1985; in Mizoram, the Mizo National Front under Laldenga rebelled, and the Mizoram Accord of 1986 led to statehood in 1987; in Nagaland, the Naga National Council under Phizo sought independence, and Nagaland became a state in 1963; Manipur and Tripura have their own issues. Sikkim merged with India in 1975 as the 22nd state, and Goa achieved statehood in 1987 after liberation in 1961. In Tamil Nadu, the Dravidian movement and DMK, formed in 1949 by C. N. Annadurai, opposed Hindi imposition. The Gorkhaland demand arose in Darjeeling. In 2000 Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand and Jharkhand were created, and Telangana in 2014. The lessons are that regional aspirations are part of democratic politics, and that federalism, power sharing and respect for diversity solve conflicts.
Deep dive: Kashmir and Punjab
Autonomy, militancy and accords shaped Jammu and Kashmir and Punjab.
Deep dive: Northeast
Assam, Mizoram and Nagaland saw movements settled through accords and statehood.
Deep dive: Accommodation
Federalism, accords and new states such as Sikkim, Goa and Telangana accommodate aspirations.

Big idea

  • Regional aspirations are demands for autonomy, identity or statehood within a democratic framework
  • India accepts diversity, and accommodation of regional demands has strengthened unity
  • In Jammu and Kashmir, Article 370 gave special status
  • The autonomy debate, the 1953 dismissal of Sheikh Abdullah, militancy from the 1980s, and the 1996 return of elections shaped politics
Read the full explanation

Regional aspirations are demands for autonomy, identity or statehood within a democratic framework. India accepts diversity, and accommodation of regional demands has strengthened unity. In Jammu and Kashmir, Article 370 gave special status; the autonomy debate, the 1953 dismissal of Sheikh Abdullah, militancy from the 1980s, and the 1996 return of elections shaped politics; Article 370 was revoked in August 2019 and the state split into two union territories. In Punjab, the Akali Dal’s Anandpur Sahib Resolution of 1973 demanded autonomy; militancy led to Operation Blue Star in June 1984 at the Golden Temple, the assassination of Indira Gandhi on 31 October 1984, and the Rajiv Gandhi-Longowal Accord of July 1985; peace and elections returned by the 1990s. The Northeast saw demands for autonomy: in Assam the movement against illegal migrants, led by the All Assam Students Union (AASU) from 1979, ended with the Assam Accord of 1985; in Mizoram, the Mizo National Front under Laldenga rebelled, and the Mizoram Accord of 1986 led to statehood in 1987; in Nagaland, the Naga National Council under Phizo sought independence, and Nagaland became a state in 1963; Manipur and Tripura have their own issues. Sikkim merged with India in 1975 as the 22nd state, and Goa achieved statehood in 1987 after liberation in 1961. In Tamil Nadu, the Dravidian movement and DMK, formed in 1949 by C. N. Annadurai, opposed Hindi imposition. The Gorkhaland demand arose in Darjeeling. In 2000 Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand and Jharkhand were created, and Telangana in 2014. The lessons are that regional aspirations are part of democratic politics, and that federalism, power sharing and respect for diversity solve conflicts.

lessons.title: Recent Developments in Indian Politics
yt: class 12 political science recent developments indian politics coalition era mandal mandir 1991 reforms NDA UPA 2014 2019

blocks.x: The 1990s marked a new phase of Indian politics. The Congress system gave way to the era of coalitions: from 1989 no single party won a majority for several elections, and regional parties became important. Three factors shaped politics. Mandal: the 1990 implementation of the Mandal Commission by the V. P. Singh National Front government, giving 27 per cent reservation to OBCs in central jobs, brought backward castes into politics, and the Supreme Court upheld it in the Indra Sawhney case of 1992 with a creamy layer rule. Mandir (Ayodhya): the Ram Janmabhoomi movement led to the demolition of the Babri Masjid on 6 December 1992 and communal riots; the Supreme Court gave its verdict on the dispute in November 2019. Market: the economic reforms of 1991 under P. V. Narasimha Rao and Manmohan Singh began liberalisation. Rajiv Gandhi was assassinated in May 1991. Coalition governments followed: the National Front (1989), the United Front (1996), the BJP-led National Democratic Alliance under Atal Bihari Vajpayee (1998-2004), and the Congress-led United Progressive Alliance under Manmohan Singh (2004-2014). In 2014 the BJP under Narendra Modi won a single-party majority of 282 seats, the first in 30 years, and in 2019 it won 303 seats. Features of the new era include OBC and Dalit parties, regional parties, alliance politics, stability through the 91st Amendment of 2003 limiting the size of the council of ministers to 15 per cent, and the rise of identity politics. Other trends include the Election Commission’s role strengthened under T. N. Seshan, higher voter turnout, and debates on caste and secularism.
Deep dive: Three Ms
Mandal, Mandir and Market shaped the 1990s.
Deep dive: Coalitions
NDA and UPA coalitions governed from 1998 until 2014.
Deep dive: New majority
The BJP won a single-party majority in 2014 (282) and 2019 (303).

Bharatiya rajneeti ke haal ke vikas: gathbandhan ka daur, Mandal Mandir Market aur 2014 ke chunav.

  • Three factors shaped politics
  • Mandal: the 1990 implementation of the Mandal Commission by the V
Read the full explanation

The 1990s marked a new phase of Indian politics. The Congress system gave way to the era of coalitions: from 1989 no single party won a majority for several elections, and regional parties became important. Three factors shaped politics. Mandal: the 1990 implementation of the Mandal Commission by the V. P. Singh National Front government, giving 27 per cent reservation to OBCs in central jobs, brought backward castes into politics, and the Supreme Court upheld it in the Indra Sawhney case of 1992 with a creamy layer rule. Mandir (Ayodhya): the Ram Janmabhoomi movement led to the demolition of the Babri Masjid on 6 December 1992 and communal riots; the Supreme Court gave its verdict on the dispute in November 2019. Market: the economic reforms of 1991 under P. V. Narasimha Rao and Manmohan Singh began liberalisation. Rajiv Gandhi was assassinated in May 1991. Coalition governments followed: the National Front (1989), the United Front (1996), the BJP-led National Democratic Alliance under Atal Bihari Vajpayee (1998-2004), and the Congress-led United Progressive Alliance under Manmohan Singh (2004-2014). In 2014 the BJP under Narendra Modi won a single-party majority of 282 seats, the first in 30 years, and in 2019 it won 303 seats. Features of the new era include OBC and Dalit parties, regional parties, alliance politics, stability through the 91st Amendment of 2003 limiting the size of the council of ministers to 15 per cent, and the rise of identity politics. Other trends include the Election Commission’s role strengthened under T. N. Seshan, higher voter turnout, and debates on caste and secularism.

lessons.title: Variations in Psychological Attributes
yt: class 12 psychology variations in psychological attributes intelligence theories IQ gardner sternberg emotional intelligence creativity

blocks.x: Individual differences are the ways in which people differ from one another in traits and abilities. Intelligence is the global capacity to act purposefully, think rationally and deal effectively with the environment, in Wechsler’s definition. Intelligence tests began with Binet and Simon in 1905; the mental age (MA) is the level of mental development and the intelligence quotient is IQ = (MA / CA) x 100, where CA is chronological age. Terman revised the test as the Stanford-Binet in 1916, and Wechsler developed scales such as WAIS and WISC, which use deviation IQ. IQ scores follow a normal curve with mean 100 and standard deviation 15; about 2 per cent score above 130 (gifted) and below 70 (intellectual disability). Intellectual disability is graded mild (50-69), moderate (35-49), severe (20-34) and profound (below 20). Theories of intelligence include Spearman’s two-factor theory (general factor g and specific factors s), Thurstone’s seven primary mental abilities, Guilford’s structure of intellect (operations, contents, products), Gardner’s multiple intelligences (linguistic, logical-mathematical, spatial, musical, bodily-kinaesthetic, interpersonal, intrapersonal and naturalistic), Sternberg’s triarchic theory (componential or analytical, experiential or creative, contextual or practical) and the PASS model of Das, Kirby and Jarman (planning, attention-arousal, simultaneous and successive processing). Emotional intelligence, proposed by Salovey and Mayer in 1990 and popularised by Goleman, is the ability to perceive, understand, manage and use emotions. Aptitude is potential to acquire a skill. Creativity is producing novel and appropriate ideas; Guilford separated divergent thinking (fluency, flexibility, originality, elaboration) from convergent thinking, and the stages of creativity are preparation, incubation, illumination and verification. Psychological tests must be reliable, valid, standardised, and have norms; they may be verbal, non-verbal or performance tests, such as Raven’s Progressive Matrices and Kohs Block Design. Culture shapes intelligence, so tests should be as culture-fair as possible.
Deep dive: Intelligence and IQ
IQ = MA/CA x 100; scores form a normal curve with mean 100 and SD 15.
Deep dive: Theories
Spearman g, Thurstone, Guilford, Gardner’s eight intelligences, Sternberg’s triarchic and PASS.
Deep dive: Creativity and testing
Divergent thinking and four stages; tests must be reliable, valid and standardised.

Big idea

Read the full explanation

Individual differences are the ways in which people differ from one another in traits and abilities. Intelligence is the global capacity to act purposefully, think rationally and deal effectively with the environment, in Wechsler’s definition. Intelligence tests began with Binet and Simon in 1905; the mental age (MA) is the level of mental development and the intelligence quotient is IQ = (MA / CA) x 100, where CA is chronological age. Terman revised the test as the Stanford-Binet in 1916, and Wechsler developed scales such as WAIS and WISC, which use deviation IQ. IQ scores follow a normal curve with mean 100 and standard deviation 15; about 2 per cent score above 130 (gifted) and below 70 (intellectual disability). Intellectual disability is graded mild (50-69), moderate (35-49), severe (20-34) and profound (below 20). Theories of intelligence include Spearman’s two-factor theory (general factor g and specific factors s), Thurstone’s seven primary mental abilities, Guilford’s structure of intellect (operations, contents, products), Gardner’s multiple intelligences (linguistic, logical-mathematical, spatial, musical, bodily-kinaesthetic, interpersonal, intrapersonal and naturalistic), Sternberg’s triarchic theory (componential or analytical, experiential or creative, contextual or practical) and the PASS model of Das, Kirby and Jarman (planning, attention-arousal, simultaneous and successive processing). Emotional intelligence, proposed by Salovey and Mayer in 1990 and popularised by Goleman, is the ability to perceive, understand, manage and use emotions. Aptitude is potential to acquire a skill. Creativity is producing novel and appropriate ideas; Guilford separated divergent thinking (fluency, flexibility, originality, elaboration) from convergent thinking, and the stages of creativity are preparation, incubation, illumination and verification. Psychological tests must be reliable, valid, standardised, and have norms; they may be verbal, non-verbal or performance tests, such as Raven’s Progressive Matrices and Kohs Block Design. Culture shapes intelligence, so tests should be as culture-fair as possible.

lessons.title: Self and Personality
yt: class 12 psychology self and personality self concept self esteem self efficacy type trait freud rogers projective tests

blocks.x: The self is a person’s awareness of their own existence and identity. William James separated the I (the knower) from the Me (the known), and Cooley proposed the looking-glass self. Self-concept is the organised set of beliefs about oneself, self-esteem is the evaluation of one’s worth, and Bandura’s self-efficacy is belief in one’s ability to succeed in a task. Self-regulation is controlling one’s behaviour. In the Indian view the self is atman, the true inner self, beyond the body and mind. Personality is the relatively stable pattern of characteristics that makes a person unique; Allport defined it as the dynamic organisation within the individual of psychophysical systems that determine unique adjustment. Type approaches classify people into categories: Hippocrates’s four humours (sanguine, phlegmatic, choleric, melancholic), Sheldon’s somatotypes, Jung’s introvert and extrovert, Friedman and Rosenman’s Type A, B and C, and the Indian vata, pitta and kapha and the gunas sattva, rajas and tamas. Trait approaches describe personality through traits: Allport’s cardinal, central and secondary traits, Cattell’s 16 source traits (16PF), Eysenck’s extraversion, neuroticism and psychoticism, and the Big Five of Costa and McCrae (openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism). Freud’s psychodynamic theory has the id (pleasure principle), the ego (reality principle) and the superego (morality), with psychosexual stages oral, anal, phallic, latency and genital, and defence mechanisms such as repression, denial, projection, displacement, rationalisation, reaction formation, sublimation and regression. Jung proposed the collective unconscious and Adler the inferiority complex. Behaviourists like Skinner see personality as learned responses. Humanistic theorists: Rogers stressed the self, unconditional positive regard and the fully functioning person; Maslow stressed self-actualisation. Assessment uses self-report inventories, projective techniques such as the Rorschach inkblot test (ten cards), the Thematic Apperception Test of Murray and Morgan (pictures and a blank card), and the sentence completion test, plus behavioural analysis, interview and observation.
Deep dive: Self
James’s I and Me, self-concept, self-esteem and Bandura’s self-efficacy.
Deep dive: Theories of personality
Type, trait, psychodynamic, behavioural and humanistic approaches.
Deep dive: Assessment
Self-report inventories and projective tests like the Rorschach and TAT.
Hindi saransh
Svayam aur vyaktitva: aatma-dharna, vyaktitva ke sampraday, Freud, Rogers aur pariksha vidhiyan.
Remember: id pleasure; ego reality; superego morality.

Visual lesson

Self and Personality

The self is a person’s awareness of their own existence and identity

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Self›3Theories of personality›4Assessment
Rorschach10 cards
Hippocrates4 humours
🔑

Big idea

  • The self is a person’s awareness of their own existence and identity
  • William James separated the I (the knower) from the Me (the known), and Cooley proposed the looking-glass self
  • Self-concept is the organised set of beliefs about oneself, self-esteem is the evaluation of one’s worth, and Bandura’s self-efficacy is belief in…
  • Self-regulation is controlling one’s behaviour
Read the full explanation

The self is a person’s awareness of their own existence and identity. William James separated the I (the knower) from the Me (the known), and Cooley proposed the looking-glass self. Self-concept is the organised set of beliefs about oneself, self-esteem is the evaluation of one’s worth, and Bandura’s self-efficacy is belief in one’s ability to succeed in a task. Self-regulation is controlling one’s behaviour. In the Indian view the self is atman, the true inner self, beyond the body and mind. Personality is the relatively stable pattern of characteristics that makes a person unique; Allport defined it as the dynamic organisation within the individual of psychophysical systems that determine unique adjustment. Type approaches classify people into categories: Hippocrates’s four humours (sanguine, phlegmatic, choleric, melancholic), Sheldon’s somatotypes, Jung’s introvert and extrovert, Friedman and Rosenman’s Type A, B and C, and the Indian vata, pitta and kapha and the gunas sattva, rajas and tamas. Trait approaches describe personality through traits: Allport’s cardinal, central and secondary traits, Cattell’s 16 source traits (16PF), Eysenck’s extraversion, neuroticism and psychoticism, and the Big Five of Costa and McCrae (openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism). Freud’s psychodynamic theory has the id (pleasure principle), the ego (reality principle) and the superego (morality), with psychosexual stages oral, anal, phallic, latency and genital, and defence mechanisms such as repression, denial, projection, displacement, rationalisation, reaction formation, sublimation and regression. Jung proposed the collective unconscious and Adler the inferiority complex. Behaviourists like Skinner see personality as learned responses. Humanistic theorists: Rogers stressed the self, unconditional positive regard and the fully functioning person; Maslow stressed self-actualisation. Assessment uses self-report inventories, projective techniques such as the Rorschach inkblot test (ten cards), the Thematic Apperception Test of Murray and Morgan (pictures and a blank card), and the sentence completion test, plus behavioural analysis, interview and observation.

lessons.title: Meeting Life Challenges
yt: class 12 psychology meeting life challenges stress general adaptation syndrome coping life skills hardiness stress management

blocks.x: Stress is a pattern of responses to stimulus events (stressors) that disturb equilibrium and exceed coping ability. Lazarus and Folkman describe stress as a transaction between the person and environment, with primary appraisal (is it a threat?) and secondary appraisal (can I cope?). Hans Selye (1936) described the General Adaptation Syndrome in three stages: alarm reaction, resistance and exhaustion. Eustress is positive, motivating stress; distress is harmful. Sources of stress include life events (the Holmes and Rahe Social Readjustment Rating Scale, 1967), daily hassles, traumatic events, physical, psychological and social stressors. Effects include physiological (adrenaline and cortisol release, raised heart rate, illness), emotional (anxiety, depression), cognitive (poor concentration) and behavioural effects, and burnout, a state of physical, emotional and mental exhaustion. Learned helplessness (Seligman) and locus of control (Rotter) relate to stress. Coping is the effort to manage demands: Endler and Parker describe task-oriented coping (problem-focused), emotion-oriented coping and avoidance-oriented coping. Stress management techniques include relaxation such as Jacobson’s progressive muscle relaxation, meditation and yoga, biofeedback, creative visualisation, cognitive behavioural techniques including Meichenbaum’s stress inoculation training, and exercise. Stress-resistant factors include hardiness (Kobasa: commitment, control and challenge), positive attitude, social support and assertiveness. Positive health is more than absence of disease; WHO defines health as complete physical, mental and social well-being. Life skills, defined by WHO as abilities for adaptive and positive behaviour, number ten: self-awareness, empathy, critical thinking, creative thinking, decision making, problem solving, effective communication, interpersonal relationships, coping with stress and coping with emotions. Healthy lifestyle includes balanced diet, regular exercise, adequate sleep and avoiding smoking and alcohol.

Deep dive: Coping and management
Task, emotion and avoidance coping; relaxation, meditation, biofeedback and stress inoculation help.

Read the full explanation

Stress is a pattern of responses to stimulus events (stressors) that disturb equilibrium and exceed coping ability. Lazarus and Folkman describe stress as a transaction between the person and environment, with primary appraisal (is it a threat?) and secondary appraisal (can I cope?). Hans Selye (1936) described the General Adaptation Syndrome in three stages: alarm reaction, resistance and exhaustion. Eustress is positive, motivating stress; distress is harmful. Sources of stress include life events (the Holmes and Rahe Social Readjustment Rating Scale, 1967), daily hassles, traumatic events, physical, psychological and social stressors. Effects include physiological (adrenaline and cortisol release, raised heart rate, illness), emotional (anxiety, depression), cognitive (poor concentration) and behavioural effects, and burnout, a state of physical, emotional and mental exhaustion. Learned helplessness (Seligman) and locus of control (Rotter) relate to stress. Coping is the effort to manage demands: Endler and Parker describe task-oriented coping (problem-focused), emotion-oriented coping and avoidance-oriented coping. Stress management techniques include relaxation such as Jacobson’s progressive muscle relaxation, meditation and yoga, biofeedback, creative visualisation, cognitive behavioural techniques including Meichenbaum’s stress inoculation training, and exercise. Stress-resistant factors include hardiness (Kobasa: commitment, control and challenge), positive attitude, social support and assertiveness. Positive health is more than absence of disease; WHO defines health as complete physical, mental and social well-being. Life skills, defined by WHO as abilities for adaptive and positive behaviour, number ten: self-awareness, empathy, critical thinking, creative thinking, decision making, problem solving, effective communication, interpersonal relationships, coping with stress and coping with emotions. Healthy lifestyle includes balanced diet, regular exercise, adequate sleep and avoiding smoking and alcohol.

lessons.title: Psychological Disorders
yt: class 12 psychology psychological disorders anxiety OCD PTSD depression bipolar schizophrenia dissociative somatic DSM ICD

blocks.x: Abnormal behaviour is judged by several criteria: deviation from social norms, statistical infrequency, personal distress, maladaptive behaviour and danger to self or others, often summarised as the four Ds (deviance, distress, dysfunction, danger). Explanatory models include biological, psychodynamic, behavioural, cognitive, humanistic-existential and the diathesis-stress model, in which a vulnerability combines with stress. Classification systems are the DSM of the American Psychiatric Association and the ICD of the World Health Organization. Anxiety disorders include generalised anxiety disorder (persistent worry), panic disorder (sudden intense attacks), phobias (irrational fear of an object or situation, such as specific phobia, social phobia and agoraphobia), obsessive-compulsive disorder (recurring obsessions and compulsions) and post-traumatic stress disorder (flashbacks and hyperarousal after trauma). Somatic symptom disorders involve physical complaints with psychological causes, such as conversion disorder and illness anxiety (hypochondriasis). Dissociative disorders involve a break in memory or identity: dissociative amnesia, dissociative fugue and dissociative identity disorder, along with depersonalisation. Mood disorders include major depressive disorder (low mood, loss of interest, sleep and appetite change, fatigue, guilt) and bipolar disorder (alternating mania and depression); mania features elevated, irritable mood and high energy. Schizophrenia is a severe disorder with positive symptoms (delusions, which are false beliefs, hallucinations, which are perceptions without stimuli, and disorganised speech), negative symptoms (flat affect, avolition, alogia) and psychomotor symptoms. Substance-related disorders involve dependence with tolerance and withdrawal. Behavioural and developmental disorders include ADHD, oppositional defiant disorder and conduct disorder, and autism spectrum disorder. Eating disorders include anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa and binge eating disorder. Mental illness should be met with empathy, as stigma delays help seeking; mental health professionals include psychiatrists and clinical psychologists.
Deep dive: Concept of abnormality
Deviance, distress, dysfunction and danger; models include the diathesis-stress approach.
Deep dive: Major disorders
Anxiety, somatic, dissociative, mood, schizophrenia, substance and developmental disorders.
Deep dive: Stigma
Stigma delays help; understanding and professional treatment help recovery.

problems.q: Differentiate delusion and hallucination.
problems.a: A delusion is a false belief held despite evidence; a hallucination is a perception without any external stimulus.

problems.q: What are obsessions and compulsions?
problems.a: Obsessions are intrusive recurring thoughts; compulsions are repetitive behaviours performed to reduce the anxiety they cause.

problems.q: Explain the diathesis-stress model.
problems.a: A disorder arises when a biological or psychological vulnerability (diathesis) combines with environmental stress.

Read the full explanation

Abnormal behaviour is judged by several criteria: deviation from social norms, statistical infrequency, personal distress, maladaptive behaviour and danger to self or others, often summarised as the four Ds (deviance, distress, dysfunction, danger). Explanatory models include biological, psychodynamic, behavioural, cognitive, humanistic-existential and the diathesis-stress model, in which a vulnerability combines with stress. Classification systems are the DSM of the American Psychiatric Association and the ICD of the World Health Organization. Anxiety disorders include generalised anxiety disorder (persistent worry), panic disorder (sudden intense attacks), phobias (irrational fear of an object or situation, such as specific phobia, social phobia and agoraphobia), obsessive-compulsive disorder (recurring obsessions and compulsions) and post-traumatic stress disorder (flashbacks and hyperarousal after trauma). Somatic symptom disorders involve physical complaints with psychological causes, such as conversion disorder and illness anxiety (hypochondriasis). Dissociative disorders involve a break in memory or identity: dissociative amnesia, dissociative fugue and dissociative identity disorder, along with depersonalisation. Mood disorders include major depressive disorder (low mood, loss of interest, sleep and appetite change, fatigue, guilt) and bipolar disorder (alternating mania and depression); mania features elevated, irritable mood and high energy. Schizophrenia is a severe disorder with positive symptoms (delusions, which are false beliefs, hallucinations, which are perceptions without stimuli, and disorganised speech), negative symptoms (flat affect, avolition, alogia) and psychomotor symptoms. Substance-related disorders involve dependence with tolerance and withdrawal. Behavioural and developmental disorders include ADHD, oppositional defiant disorder and conduct disorder, and autism spectrum disorder. Eating disorders include anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa and binge eating disorder. Mental illness should be met with empathy, as stigma delays help seeking; mental health professionals include psychiatrists and clinical psychologists.

lessons.title: Therapeutic Approaches
yt: class 12 psychology therapeutic approaches psychotherapy behaviour therapy cognitive therapy beck ellis rogers biomedical ECT rehabilitation

blocks.x: Psychotherapy is a voluntary, systematic interaction between a client and a trained therapist to relieve distress and improve functioning. The therapeutic relationship, built on trust, empathy and confidentiality, is central. Psychodynamic therapy by Freud uses free association, dream analysis, interpretation, transference (feelings towards the therapist) and resistance, with the aim of catharsis and insight. Behaviour therapy applies learning principles. Joseph Wolpe’s systematic desensitisation uses reciprocal inhibition: the client learns relaxation, builds an anxiety hierarchy and faces feared stimuli step by step; flooding exposes the client at once; aversion therapy pairs an unwanted behaviour with an unpleasant stimulus; a token economy rewards desirable behaviour with tokens; modelling teaches by observation. Cognitive therapies change faulty thinking: Aaron Beck’s cognitive therapy corrects negative automatic thoughts in depression, and Albert Ellis’s rational emotive behaviour therapy uses the ABC model (Activating event, Belief, Consequence), disputing irrational beliefs; cognitive behaviour therapy combines both. Humanistic-existential therapies include Carl Rogers’s client-centred therapy, which uses unconditional positive regard, empathy and genuineness; Fritz Perls’s Gestalt therapy; and Viktor Frankl’s logotherapy, which seeks meaning. Biomedical therapies include drug therapy (antipsychotics, antidepressants, antianxiety drugs and mood stabilisers such as lithium), electroconvulsive therapy (introduced by Cerletti and Bini in 1938, used mainly for severe depression) and, rarely, psychosurgery. Group, family and couples therapy treat relationships. Alternative approaches include yoga, meditation and Vipassana. Rehabilitation helps people with mental illness live in the community through occupational therapy, social skills training and vocational training. The Rehabilitation Council of India regulates professionals, and the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 protects the rights of persons with mental illness. A psychiatrist is a medical doctor who can prescribe drugs; a clinical psychologist gives psychotherapy.
Deep dive: Psychotherapies
Psychodynamic, behavioural, cognitive and humanistic therapies target different problems.
Deep dive: Biomedical therapy
Drugs and ECT treat severe disorders alongside psychological help.
Deep dive: Rehabilitation
Occupational, social and vocational training restore community life; the 2017 Act protects rights.

Big idea

Read the full explanation

Psychotherapy is a voluntary, systematic interaction between a client and a trained therapist to relieve distress and improve functioning. The therapeutic relationship, built on trust, empathy and confidentiality, is central. Psychodynamic therapy by Freud uses free association, dream analysis, interpretation, transference (feelings towards the therapist) and resistance, with the aim of catharsis and insight. Behaviour therapy applies learning principles. Joseph Wolpe’s systematic desensitisation uses reciprocal inhibition: the client learns relaxation, builds an anxiety hierarchy and faces feared stimuli step by step; flooding exposes the client at once; aversion therapy pairs an unwanted behaviour with an unpleasant stimulus; a token economy rewards desirable behaviour with tokens; modelling teaches by observation. Cognitive therapies change faulty thinking: Aaron Beck’s cognitive therapy corrects negative automatic thoughts in depression, and Albert Ellis’s rational emotive behaviour therapy uses the ABC model (Activating event, Belief, Consequence), disputing irrational beliefs; cognitive behaviour therapy combines both. Humanistic-existential therapies include Carl Rogers’s client-centred therapy, which uses unconditional positive regard, empathy and genuineness; Fritz Perls’s Gestalt therapy; and Viktor Frankl’s logotherapy, which seeks meaning. Biomedical therapies include drug therapy (antipsychotics, antidepressants, antianxiety drugs and mood stabilisers such as lithium), electroconvulsive therapy (introduced by Cerletti and Bini in 1938, used mainly for severe depression) and, rarely, psychosurgery. Group, family and couples therapy treat relationships. Alternative approaches include yoga, meditation and Vipassana. Rehabilitation helps people with mental illness live in the community through occupational therapy, social skills training and vocational training. The Rehabilitation Council of India regulates professionals, and the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 protects the rights of persons with mental illness. A psychiatrist is a medical doctor who can prescribe drugs; a clinical psychologist gives psychotherapy.
