lessons.title: Attitude and Social Cognition
yt: class 12 psychology attitude social cognition cognitive dissonance prejudice stereotype attribution schema helping behaviour

blocks.x: An attitude is a state of mind with evaluative feelings about a person, object or idea. It has three components: affective (feelings), behavioural (action tendency) and cognitive (beliefs), the ABC components. Attitudes are formed by learning: association, reinforcement and modelling, through family and school, reference groups, personal experience and the media. Attitude change depends on source, message and target. Festinger’s cognitive dissonance theory (1957) says inconsistency among beliefs or between attitude and behaviour creates discomfort that motivates change; Heider’s balance theory describes harmony among a person, other and object. Persuasion is stronger when the source is credible and attractive. Attitudes can be measured by Likert’s scale (1932), Thurstone’s scale, the semantic differential and Bogardus’s social distance scale. A stereotype is a generalised belief about a group, prejudice is a preconceived negative attitude towards a group, and discrimination is unfair behaviour. Prejudice is reduced by intergroup contact (Allport’s contact hypothesis), superordinate goals (Sherif) and education, and by challenging stereotypes. Social cognition is how we process information about the social world. Schemas are mental frameworks that organise knowledge. Impression formation: Asch (1946) showed that central traits like warm and cold shape impressions. Attribution is explaining behaviour: internal (dispositional) or external (situational); Kelley’s covariation model uses consensus, distinctiveness and consistency. Biases include the fundamental attribution error (overestimating dispositional causes), the actor-observer effect and the self-serving bias. Presence of others affects behaviour: social facilitation (Triplett, 1898; Zajonc) improves performance on simple tasks, and social loafing (Ringelmann) reduces effort in groups. Pro-social behaviour includes helping and altruism; the bystander effect (Latane and Darley) shows that more onlookers reduce helping because of diffusion of responsibility. Aggression has been explained by the frustration-aggression hypothesis and social learning.
Deep dive: Attitude
ABC components; formed by learning; changed by source, message and target; dissonance motivates change.
Deep dive: Prejudice
Stereotype, prejudice and discrimination; contact and superordinate goals reduce them.
Deep dive: Social cognition
Schemas, attribution and biases explain how we judge others; bystander effect and social loafing in groups.

Big idea

  • An attitude is a state of mind with evaluative feelings about a person, object or idea
  • It has three components: affective (feelings), behavioural (action tendency) and cognitive (beliefs), the ABC components
  • Attitudes are formed by learning: association, reinforcement and modelling, through family and school, reference groups, personal experience and the…
  • Attitude change depends on source, message and target
Read the full explanation

An attitude is a state of mind with evaluative feelings about a person, object or idea. It has three components: affective (feelings), behavioural (action tendency) and cognitive (beliefs), the ABC components. Attitudes are formed by learning: association, reinforcement and modelling, through family and school, reference groups, personal experience and the media. Attitude change depends on source, message and target. Festinger’s cognitive dissonance theory (1957) says inconsistency among beliefs or between attitude and behaviour creates discomfort that motivates change; Heider’s balance theory describes harmony among a person, other and object. Persuasion is stronger when the source is credible and attractive. Attitudes can be measured by Likert’s scale (1932), Thurstone’s scale, the semantic differential and Bogardus’s social distance scale. A stereotype is a generalised belief about a group, prejudice is a preconceived negative attitude towards a group, and discrimination is unfair behaviour. Prejudice is reduced by intergroup contact (Allport’s contact hypothesis), superordinate goals (Sherif) and education, and by challenging stereotypes. Social cognition is how we process information about the social world. Schemas are mental frameworks that organise knowledge. Impression formation: Asch (1946) showed that central traits like warm and cold shape impressions. Attribution is explaining behaviour: internal (dispositional) or external (situational); Kelley’s covariation model uses consensus, distinctiveness and consistency. Biases include the fundamental attribution error (overestimating dispositional causes), the actor-observer effect and the self-serving bias. Presence of others affects behaviour: social facilitation (Triplett, 1898; Zajonc) improves performance on simple tasks, and social loafing (Ringelmann) reduces effort in groups. Pro-social behaviour includes helping and altruism; the bystander effect (Latane and Darley) shows that more onlookers reduce helping because of diffusion of responsibility. Aggression has been explained by the frustration-aggression hypothesis and social learning.

📌

  • ABC components
  • Formed by learning
  • Changed by source, message and target
  • Dissonance motivates change
🧠

Prejudice

  • Stereotype, prejudice and discrimination
  • Contact and superordinate goals reduce them
🌟

Social cognition

  • Schemas, attribution and biases explain how we judge others
  • Bystander effect and social loafing in groups

lessons.title: Social Influence and Group Processes
yt: class 12 psychology social influence group processes conformity obedience milgram asch groupthink leadership conflict

blocks.x: A group is two or more people who interact, share goals, norms and a sense of belonging. Groups form to satisfy needs for security, status, affiliation, goals and identity. Characteristics include norms (expected behaviour), roles, status, cohesiveness and shared goals. Types are primary or secondary, formal or informal, in-groups and out-groups. Tuckman’s stages of group formation are forming, storming, norming, performing and adjourning. Social influence includes conformity (changing behaviour to match the group), compliance (yielding to a request) and obedience (following orders). Asch’s 1951 line judgement experiment showed conformity to a unanimous majority. Milgram’s 1963 obedience experiment, in which participants gave what they thought were electric shocks up to 450 volts, found that about 65 per cent went to the maximum, showing the power of authority. Group polarisation is the strengthening of the average group view after discussion; groupthink (Janis) is poor decision making due to pressure for consensus. Social loafing and social facilitation affect performance. Leadership is influencing others towards goals; Lewin identified autocratic, democratic and laissez-faire styles in 1939; trait theories say leaders have certain qualities; Fiedler’s contingency model says effectiveness depends on fit between style and situation; transformational leaders inspire change. Crowds are temporary collections; a mob is an emotional, violent crowd, and deindividuation (Zimbardo) is loss of self-awareness in groups. Intergroup conflict can arise from competition: Sherif’s Robbers Cave experiment (1954) showed that competition created hostility and superordinate goals reduced it. Social identity theory of Tajfel explains in-group favouritism and out-group bias. Conflict resolution methods include contact, superordinate goals, negotiation, mediation and the GRIT (graduated reciprocation) approach. Cooperation and competition are the two basic orientations.
Deep dive: Group basics
Norms, roles, status and cohesiveness; Tuckman’s stages from forming to adjourning.
Deep dive: Social influence
Conformity (Asch), obedience (Milgram), polarisation and groupthink.
Deep dive: Leadership and conflict
Lewin’s styles, Fiedler’s model; Sherif’s Robbers Cave shows how superordinate goals reduce conflict.

Read the full explanation

A group is two or more people who interact, share goals, norms and a sense of belonging. Groups form to satisfy needs for security, status, affiliation, goals and identity. Characteristics include norms (expected behaviour), roles, status, cohesiveness and shared goals. Types are primary or secondary, formal or informal, in-groups and out-groups. Tuckman’s stages of group formation are forming, storming, norming, performing and adjourning. Social influence includes conformity (changing behaviour to match the group), compliance (yielding to a request) and obedience (following orders). Asch’s 1951 line judgement experiment showed conformity to a unanimous majority. Milgram’s 1963 obedience experiment, in which participants gave what they thought were electric shocks up to 450 volts, found that about 65 per cent went to the maximum, showing the power of authority. Group polarisation is the strengthening of the average group view after discussion; groupthink (Janis) is poor decision making due to pressure for consensus. Social loafing and social facilitation affect performance. Leadership is influencing others towards goals; Lewin identified autocratic, democratic and laissez-faire styles in 1939; trait theories say leaders have certain qualities; Fiedler’s contingency model says effectiveness depends on fit between style and situation; transformational leaders inspire change. Crowds are temporary collections; a mob is an emotional, violent crowd, and deindividuation (Zimbardo) is loss of self-awareness in groups. Intergroup conflict can arise from competition: Sherif’s Robbers Cave experiment (1954) showed that competition created hostility and superordinate goals reduced it. Social identity theory of Tajfel explains in-group favouritism and out-group bias. Conflict resolution methods include contact, superordinate goals, negotiation, mediation and the GRIT (graduated reciprocation) approach. Cooperation and competition are the two basic orientations.

lessons.title: Introducing Indian Society
yt: class 12 sociology introducing indian society colonialism nationalism social reform unity in diversity AR Desai Srinivas

blocks.x: Indian society is studied through its history, especially the colonial period, which shaped modern India’s economy, institutions and identity. Colonialism was a system of political and economic domination by Britain; it changed land revenue systems (the Permanent Settlement of 1793 under Cornwallis, the Ryotwari system and the Mahalwari system), ruined traditional handicrafts, and built railways (first run in 1853 from Bombay to Thane), the telegraph, post and modern education. It also created new classes: an English-educated middle class that became the base of nationalism. The colonial state conducted the census, and the first systematic census was in 1881, which classified people by caste and religion and affected identities. Nationalism emerged as a response to colonial rule; A. R. Desai’s Social Background of Indian Nationalism (1948) is a Marxist analysis that sees nationalism as arising from the material conditions created by colonialism, such as new communications, education, press and capitalism. The Indian National Congress was founded in 1885. Social reform movements such as those of Raja Rammohan Roy (who campaigned against sati, abolished in 1829), Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar (widow remarriage), Jyotiba Phule and Dr B. R. Ambedkar questioned social evils. Communalism developed as the use of religious identity for political ends, linked to colonial policies of divide and rule and to the 1947 Partition. Indian sociology grew with scholars such as G. S. Ghurye (Caste and Race in India), D. P. Mukerji, A. R. Desai and M. N. Srinivas (Sanskritisation, dominant caste, village studies). Nehru’s Discovery of India (1946) described unity in diversity, the idea that India’s many languages, religions and regions share a common cultural fabric. Sociology also studies how modern ideas such as secularism, democracy and citizenship were absorbed.
Deep dive: Colonialism
Land revenue changes, railways, education and a new middle class remade Indian society.
Deep dive: Nationalism and reform
A. R. Desai explained nationalism through material conditions; reformers challenged caste and gender evils.
Deep dive: Unity in diversity
Nehru’s Discovery of India describes a shared cultural fabric across diverse communities.

Read the full explanation

Indian society is studied through its history, especially the colonial period, which shaped modern India’s economy, institutions and identity. Colonialism was a system of political and economic domination by Britain; it changed land revenue systems (the Permanent Settlement of 1793 under Cornwallis, the Ryotwari system and the Mahalwari system), ruined traditional handicrafts, and built railways (first run in 1853 from Bombay to Thane), the telegraph, post and modern education. It also created new classes: an English-educated middle class that became the base of nationalism. The colonial state conducted the census, and the first systematic census was in 1881, which classified people by caste and religion and affected identities. Nationalism emerged as a response to colonial rule; A. R. Desai’s Social Background of Indian Nationalism (1948) is a Marxist analysis that sees nationalism as arising from the material conditions created by colonialism, such as new communications, education, press and capitalism. The Indian National Congress was founded in 1885. Social reform movements such as those of Raja Rammohan Roy (who campaigned against sati, abolished in 1829), Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar (widow remarriage), Jyotiba Phule and Dr B. R. Ambedkar questioned social evils. Communalism developed as the use of religious identity for political ends, linked to colonial policies of divide and rule and to the 1947 Partition. Indian sociology grew with scholars such as G. S. Ghurye (Caste and Race in India), D. P. Mukerji, A. R. Desai and M. N. Srinivas (Sanskritisation, dominant caste, village studies). Nehru’s Discovery of India (1946) described unity in diversity, the idea that India’s many languages, religions and regions share a common cultural fabric. Sociology also studies how modern ideas such as secularism, democracy and citizenship were absorbed.

📌

Colonialism

  • Land revenue changes, railways, education and a new middle class remade Indian society
🧠

Nationalism and reform

  • Desai explained nationalism through material conditions
  • Reformers challenged caste and gender evils
🌟

Unity in diversity

  • Nehru’s Discovery of India describes a shared cultural fabric across diverse communities

lessons.title: The Demographic Structure of Indian Society
yt: class 12 sociology demographic structure malthus demographic transition census 2011 sex ratio age structure literacy population policy

blocks.x: Demography is the systematic study of population: its size, growth, composition and distribution. Thomas Malthus, in his 1798 Essay on the Principle of Population, argued that population grows geometrically while food grows arithmetically, so checks such as famine and disease limit growth. Karl Marx and others disagreed, blaming social organisation. The theory of demographic transition says societies move from high birth and death rates to low birth and death rates through stages, with a period of rapid growth in between. Key concepts are birth rate, death rate, rate of natural increase, fertility rate, infant mortality rate, maternal mortality ratio, life expectancy and sex ratio (females per 1000 males). The Census of India is conducted every ten years; the first complete synchronous census was in 1881, and the 2011 Census was the 15th. India’s population in 2011 was about 121 crore (1.21 billion), the second largest in the world; the sex ratio was 943, and the child sex ratio (0-6) fell to 919; the literacy rate was about 74 per cent; and the decadal growth was about 17.6 per cent. Kerala has the highest sex ratio and literacy, while Haryana has the lowest child sex ratio. Uttar Pradesh is the most populous state. The age structure of India is young, and the working age group of 15-59 years offers a demographic dividend, while the dependency ratio compares dependents to workers. Declining child sex ratio reflects son preference, sex-selective abortion and neglect of girls; the PCPNDT Act of 1994 bans prenatal sex determination. India launched the first official family planning programme in 1952, the National Population Policy in 2000 and emphasises health, education and women’s empowerment. Urbanisation has risen, with about 31 per cent living in towns in 2011. Population issues also include ageing, migration and regional variation.

Malthus: geometric versus arithmetic growth; demographic transition in stages.

Read the full explanation

Demography is the systematic study of population: its size, growth, composition and distribution. Thomas Malthus, in his 1798 Essay on the Principle of Population, argued that population grows geometrically while food grows arithmetically, so checks such as famine and disease limit growth. Karl Marx and others disagreed, blaming social organisation. The theory of demographic transition says societies move from high birth and death rates to low birth and death rates through stages, with a period of rapid growth in between. Key concepts are birth rate, death rate, rate of natural increase, fertility rate, infant mortality rate, maternal mortality ratio, life expectancy and sex ratio (females per 1000 males). The Census of India is conducted every ten years; the first complete synchronous census was in 1881, and the 2011 Census was the 15th. India’s population in 2011 was about 121 crore (1.21 billion), the second largest in the world; the sex ratio was 943, and the child sex ratio (0-6) fell to 919; the literacy rate was about 74 per cent; and the decadal growth was about 17.6 per cent. Kerala has the highest sex ratio and literacy, while Haryana has the lowest child sex ratio. Uttar Pradesh is the most populous state. The age structure of India is young, and the working age group of 15-59 years offers a demographic dividend, while the dependency ratio compares dependents to workers. Declining child sex ratio reflects son preference, sex-selective abortion and neglect of girls; the PCPNDT Act of 1994 bans prenatal sex determination. India launched the first official family planning programme in 1952, the National Population Policy in 2000 and emphasises health, education and women’s empowerment. Urbanisation has risen, with about 31 per cent living in towns in 2011. Population issues also include ageing, migration and regional variation.

lessons.title: Social Institutions: Continuity and Change
yt: class 12 sociology social institutions caste family marriage kinship tribe sanskritisation jajmani

blocks.x: Social institutions are established ways of organising social life, including caste, tribe, family, marriage and kinship. Caste is a system of hierarchical, hereditary groups. Ghurye listed six features: segmental division, hierarchy, restrictions on feeding and social intercourse, civil and religious disabilities and privileges, lack of unrestricted choice of occupation and restrictions on marriage (endogamy). Varna is the fourfold classification (Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra) and jati is the actual local caste group. Concepts of purity and pollution (Dumont) underlie hierarchy. Colonialism altered caste through the census, land revenue and law. Post-independence, Article 17 abolished untouchability, but caste has changed rather than disappeared: M. N. Srinivas developed the concepts of Sanskritisation (a lower caste adopting upper caste rituals to rise in status, in his study of the Coorgs, 1952), westernisation and the dominant caste (numerically strong, owning land, with high political power). The jajmani system bound service castes to landowners in hereditary exchange. Caste is now linked with politics, and Beteille noted the weakening of caste in some areas of life. A tribe is a community with a common territory, language and culture, usually without a stratified caste structure; Scheduled Tribes are listed under Article 342, forming about 8.6 per cent of the population in 2011. Tribes are classified by their location, language and livelihood, and Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups need special care. The family is the basic unit; types include nuclear and joint families, patriarchal and matriarchal, patrilineal and matrilineal (the Khasi and Nair were matrilineal). Marriage forms: monogamy, polygamy (polygyny and polyandry), endogamy (marriage within a group), exogamy (outside it), hypergamy (marrying upwards) and hypogamy. Kinship ties are of blood (consanguineal) and marriage (affinal). Changes are shown by laws: the Hindu Marriage Act 1955, the Special Marriage Act 1954, the Dowry Prohibition Act 1961, the Child Marriage Restraint Act 1929 and the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act 2006.
Deep dive: Caste
Hierarchical hereditary groups; Ghurye’s six features; Srinivas’s Sanskritisation and dominant caste.
Deep dive: Tribe
A community of common territory, language and culture; Scheduled Tribes listed under Article 342.
Deep dive: Family and marriage
Nuclear and joint, patrilineal and matrilineal; endogamy, exogamy, hypergamy and laws of reform.

Samajik sansthayein: jati, janjati, parivar, vivah aur natedari; Sanskritikaran aur prabal jati.

Social institutions are established ways of organising social life, including caste, tribe, family, marriage and kinship

🔑

Big idea

  • Social institutions are established ways of organising social life, including caste, tribe, family, marriage and kinship
  • Caste is a system of hierarchical, hereditary groups
  • Ghurye listed six features: segmental division, hierarchy, restrictions on feeding and social intercourse, civil and religious disabilities and…
  • Varna is the fourfold classification (Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra) and jati is the actual local caste group
Read the full explanation

Social institutions are established ways of organising social life, including caste, tribe, family, marriage and kinship. Caste is a system of hierarchical, hereditary groups. Ghurye listed six features: segmental division, hierarchy, restrictions on feeding and social intercourse, civil and religious disabilities and privileges, lack of unrestricted choice of occupation and restrictions on marriage (endogamy). Varna is the fourfold classification (Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra) and jati is the actual local caste group. Concepts of purity and pollution (Dumont) underlie hierarchy. Colonialism altered caste through the census, land revenue and law. Post-independence, Article 17 abolished untouchability, but caste has changed rather than disappeared: M. N. Srinivas developed the concepts of Sanskritisation (a lower caste adopting upper caste rituals to rise in status, in his study of the Coorgs, 1952), westernisation and the dominant caste (numerically strong, owning land, with high political power). The jajmani system bound service castes to landowners in hereditary exchange. Caste is now linked with politics, and Beteille noted the weakening of caste in some areas of life. A tribe is a community with a common territory, language and culture, usually without a stratified caste structure; Scheduled Tribes are listed under Article 342, forming about 8.6 per cent of the population in 2011. Tribes are classified by their location, language and livelihood, and Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups need special care. The family is the basic unit; types include nuclear and joint families, patriarchal and matriarchal, patrilineal and matrilineal (the Khasi and Nair were matrilineal). Marriage forms: monogamy, polygamy (polygyny and polyandry), endogamy (marriage within a group), exogamy (outside it), hypergamy (marrying upwards) and hypogamy. Kinship ties are of blood (consanguineal) and marriage (affinal). Changes are shown by laws: the Hindu Marriage Act 1955, the Special Marriage Act 1954, the Dowry Prohibition Act 1961, the Child Marriage Restraint Act 1929 and the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act 2006.

lessons.title: The Market as a Social Institution
yt: class 12 sociology market social institution adam smith marx commodification weekly haat traditional trading communities consumption

blocks.x: Sociologists see the market not only as an economic mechanism but as a social institution embedded in culture, caste, kinship and power. Adam Smith (The Wealth of Nations, 1776) described the market as guided by an invisible hand of self-interest, with the division of labour and free competition. Karl Marx saw capitalism as a social system in which workers sell labour power for wages, with the owner appropriating surplus value, and described commodity fetishism, the way social relations between people appear as relations between things. Weber and others studied how culture shapes economic life. Markets existed in traditional forms: the weekly haat or periodic tribal market is a social meeting place as well as a trading point. Caste and trade were linked: communities such as the Marwaris, the Nakarattar Chettiars and the Gujarati Banias were traditional trading castes who used kinship networks, trust and credit; the Marwaris rose in the colonial period in Calcutta. Gift exchange studied by Malinowski (the Kula ring of the Trobriand Islands) and Mauss shows that non-market exchange builds social bonds. Colonialism transformed markets: it integrated India in the world economy, as an exporter of raw cotton, opium and indigo and importer of manufactured goods, and caused the decline of handicrafts. Commodification means that things like labour, land and even culture become things for sale. After 1991 liberalisation, the market expanded with malls, brands and consumer credit. Consumption is socially significant: Bourdieu argued that tastes mark social class and form cultural capital, and the culture of consumption creates status through goods. Globalisation links local markets to global ones, and the informal sector and street vendors continue. The sociological view shows that the market is not neutral and that economic action depends on social relations.
Deep dive: Perspectives
Smith’s invisible hand, Marx’s capitalism and surplus value, and the sociological idea that markets are embedded in society.
Deep dive: Traditional markets
Weekly haats and trading castes like the Marwaris and Chettiars show social bases of exchange.
Deep dive: Change
Colonialism, liberalisation and consumer culture transformed markets and commodified more of life.

Visual lesson

The Market as a Social Institution

Sociologists see the market not only as an economic mechanism but as a social institution embedded in culture, caste, kinship and power

🔑

Big idea

  • Adam Smith (The Wealth of Nations, 1776) described the market as guided by an invisible hand of self-interest, with the division of labour and free…

  • Weber and others studied how culture shapes economic life
Read the full explanation

Sociologists see the market not only as an economic mechanism but as a social institution embedded in culture, caste, kinship and power. Adam Smith (The Wealth of Nations, 1776) described the market as guided by an invisible hand of self-interest, with the division of labour and free competition. Karl Marx saw capitalism as a social system in which workers sell labour power for wages, with the owner appropriating surplus value, and described commodity fetishism, the way social relations between people appear as relations between things. Weber and others studied how culture shapes economic life. Markets existed in traditional forms: the weekly haat or periodic tribal market is a social meeting place as well as a trading point. Caste and trade were linked: communities such as the Marwaris, the Nakarattar Chettiars and the Gujarati Banias were traditional trading castes who used kinship networks, trust and credit; the Marwaris rose in the colonial period in Calcutta. Gift exchange studied by Malinowski (the Kula ring of the Trobriand Islands) and Mauss shows that non-market exchange builds social bonds. Colonialism transformed markets: it integrated India in the world economy, as an exporter of raw cotton, opium and indigo and importer of manufactured goods, and caused the decline of handicrafts. Commodification means that things like labour, land and even culture become things for sale. After 1991 liberalisation, the market expanded with malls, brands and consumer credit. Consumption is socially significant: Bourdieu argued that tastes mark social class and form cultural capital, and the culture of consumption creates status through goods. Globalisation links local markets to global ones, and the informal sector and street vendors continue. The sociological view shows that the market is not neutral and that economic action depends on social relations.

📌

Perspectives

  • Smith’s invisible hand, Marx’s capitalism and surplus value, and the sociological idea that markets are embedded in society
🧠

Traditional markets

  • Weekly haats and trading castes like the Marwaris and Chettiars show social bases of exchange
🌟

Change

  • Colonialism, liberalisation and consumer culture transformed markets and commodified more of life

lessons.title: Patterns of Social Inequality and Exclusion
yt: class 12 sociology social inequality exclusion untouchability dalit adivasi OBC women disability atrocities act reservation

blocks.x: Social inequality is the unequal distribution of resources and opportunities among groups, and social exclusion is the denial of full participation in society. Caste-based discrimination appears in untouchability, with segregation, humiliation, exploitation and violence. Scheduled Castes (Dalits) are listed under Article 341. Constitutional safeguards include Article 15 (no discrimination), Article 16(4) (reservation in jobs), Article 17 (abolition of untouchability), reservation in education and legislatures, and laws such as the Untouchability (Offences) Act 1955, renamed the Protection of Civil Rights Act in 1976, and the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act 1989. Reformers fought caste: Jyotiba Phule (Gulamgiri 1873, Satyashodhak Samaj 1873), B. R. Ambedkar (Annihilation of Caste 1936, Mahad Satyagraha 1927, the Poona Pact 1932), Periyar and Gandhi (who used the term Harijan). Adivasis or Scheduled Tribes, notified under Article 342, suffer displacement due to mining and dams, loss of forests and poverty; the Fifth and Sixth Schedules protect their areas, and the Forest Rights Act 2006 recognises forest rights. Other Backward Classes (OBCs) were studied by the Kaka Kalelkar Commission (1953) and the Mandal Commission (1980), which recommended 27 per cent reservation, implemented in 1990. Women face inequality through patriarchy in work, wages, property and safety; laws include the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act 2005 and the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005. Persons with disabilities are excluded by attitudes and lack of access; the Persons with Disabilities Act 1995 was replaced by the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016. Manual scavenging was prohibited by law. Inequality and exclusion are social not natural, and combine caste, class and gender.
Deep dive: Caste and untouchability
Article 17, the Protection of Civil Rights Act and the Atrocities Act 1989 fight untouchability.
Deep dive: Adivasis and OBCs
Adivasis face displacement and forest loss; Mandal Commission recommended 27 per cent OBC reservation.
Deep dive: Gender and disability
Patriarchy and inaccessibility exclude women and persons with disabilities; laws protect their rights.

Visual lesson

Patterns of Social Inequality and Exclusion

Social inequality is the unequal distribution of resources and opportunities among groups, and social exclusion is the denial of full participation in society

🔑

Big idea

  • Social inequality is the unequal distribution of resources and opportunities among groups, and social exclusion is the denial of full participation…
  • Caste-based discrimination appears in untouchability, with segregation, humiliation, exploitation and violence
  • Scheduled Castes (Dalits) are listed under Article 341
  • Constitutional safeguards include Article 15 (no discrimination), Article 16(4) (reservation in jobs), Article 17 (abolition of untouchability)…
Read the full explanation

Social inequality is the unequal distribution of resources and opportunities among groups, and social exclusion is the denial of full participation in society. Caste-based discrimination appears in untouchability, with segregation, humiliation, exploitation and violence. Scheduled Castes (Dalits) are listed under Article 341. Constitutional safeguards include Article 15 (no discrimination), Article 16(4) (reservation in jobs), Article 17 (abolition of untouchability), reservation in education and legislatures, and laws such as the Untouchability (Offences) Act 1955, renamed the Protection of Civil Rights Act in 1976, and the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act 1989. Reformers fought caste: Jyotiba Phule (Gulamgiri 1873, Satyashodhak Samaj 1873), B. R. Ambedkar (Annihilation of Caste 1936, Mahad Satyagraha 1927, the Poona Pact 1932), Periyar and Gandhi (who used the term Harijan). Adivasis or Scheduled Tribes, notified under Article 342, suffer displacement due to mining and dams, loss of forests and poverty; the Fifth and Sixth Schedules protect their areas, and the Forest Rights Act 2006 recognises forest rights. Other Backward Classes (OBCs) were studied by the Kaka Kalelkar Commission (1953) and the Mandal Commission (1980), which recommended 27 per cent reservation, implemented in 1990. Women face inequality through patriarchy in work, wages, property and safety; laws include the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act 2005 and the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005. Persons with disabilities are excluded by attitudes and lack of access; the Persons with Disabilities Act 1995 was replaced by the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016. Manual scavenging was prohibited by law. Inequality and exclusion are social not natural, and combine caste, class and gender.

  • Adivasis face displacement and forest loss
  • Mandal Commission recommended 27 per cent OBC reservation

lessons.title: The Challenges of Cultural Diversity
yt: class 12 sociology challenges of cultural diversity communalism secularism linguistic states national integration minority rights

blocks.x: India has great cultural diversity: many languages, religions, castes, tribes and regions. Diversity is a source of strength but also poses challenges such as regionalism, communalism, ethnic conflict and the integration of minorities. The Indian ideal of unity in diversity needs the state to balance recognition of identity with national unity. Community, nation and state are distinct: a nation is a large community with a sense of unity, a state is a political and legal body, and India is a nation-state with a plural society. Language is a key identity; the Eighth Schedule recognises 22 languages after the 2003 amendment, and the States Reorganisation Act of 1956 formed states on linguistic lines, after the 1953 Andhra movement, which proved that linguistic identity was compatible with national unity. The three-language formula and Hindi as official language with English as associate language remain debated. The census of 2011 showed the religious composition: about 79.8 per cent Hindus, 14.2 per cent Muslims, 2.3 per cent Christians, 1.7 per cent Sikhs, 0.7 per cent Buddhists and 0.4 per cent Jains. Minority rights are protected by Articles 29 and 30, which protect minorities’ culture and right to run educational institutions. Communalism is an ideology that uses religious identity for political mobilisation and sees other religious groups as opposed; it has produced riots, as in the Partition of 1947, the anti-Sikh violence of 1984, the Babri Masjid demolition and riots in 1992-93, and Gujarat in 2002. Secularism in India means equal respect for all religions by the state, not a strict separation as in the West. Ethnic and regional conflicts such as Kashmir, Punjab and the Northeast were addressed by accords and statehood. Role of the state includes protecting minority rights, ensuring equal treatment and promoting dialogue. National integration is promoted by shared symbols, education and constitutional values. A diverse society needs a sense of citizenship above narrower identities.
Deep dive: Diversity and language
Linguistic states and the Eighth Schedule recognised language identity without breaking unity.
Deep dive: Communalism and secularism
Communalism politicises religion; Indian secularism means equal respect for all faiths.
Deep dive: Minority rights
Articles 29 and 30 protect minority culture and educational institutions.

Read the full explanation

India has great cultural diversity: many languages, religions, castes, tribes and regions. Diversity is a source of strength but also poses challenges such as regionalism, communalism, ethnic conflict and the integration of minorities. The Indian ideal of unity in diversity needs the state to balance recognition of identity with national unity. Community, nation and state are distinct: a nation is a large community with a sense of unity, a state is a political and legal body, and India is a nation-state with a plural society. Language is a key identity; the Eighth Schedule recognises 22 languages after the 2003 amendment, and the States Reorganisation Act of 1956 formed states on linguistic lines, after the 1953 Andhra movement, which proved that linguistic identity was compatible with national unity. The three-language formula and Hindi as official language with English as associate language remain debated. The census of 2011 showed the religious composition: about 79.8 per cent Hindus, 14.2 per cent Muslims, 2.3 per cent Christians, 1.7 per cent Sikhs, 0.7 per cent Buddhists and 0.4 per cent Jains. Minority rights are protected by Articles 29 and 30, which protect minorities’ culture and right to run educational institutions. Communalism is an ideology that uses religious identity for political mobilisation and sees other religious groups as opposed; it has produced riots, as in the Partition of 1947, the anti-Sikh violence of 1984, the Babri Masjid demolition and riots in 1992-93, and Gujarat in 2002. Secularism in India means equal respect for all religions by the state, not a strict separation as in the West. Ethnic and regional conflicts such as Kashmir, Punjab and the Northeast were addressed by accords and statehood. Role of the state includes protecting minority rights, ensuring equal treatment and promoting dialogue. National integration is promoted by shared symbols, education and constitutional values. A diverse society needs a sense of citizenship above narrower identities.

blocks.x: Social change is the alteration of social structure and culture over time. Changes can be evolutionary (gradual) or revolutionary (rapid), and may be structural (affecting institutions such as the family and economy) or cultural. Causes include environmental, technological, economic, political and cultural factors. The Industrial Revolution in England in the late eighteenth century, with the steam engine of James Watt, the spinning jenny and the factory system, was a structural change that created industrial capitalism, wage labour and cities. The French Revolution of 1789 was a political revolution that spread ideas of liberty, equality and fraternity. Sociologists theorised the new society. Karl Marx saw capitalism as based on class conflict between bourgeoisie and proletariat, driven by the economy. Max Weber stressed rationalisation, bureaucracy and the role of ideas such as the Protestant ethic. Emile Durkheim analysed the division of labour and the shift from mechanical solidarity to organic solidarity, and warned of anomie. Urbanisation is the growth of towns and cities, with migration, slums, anonymity and diversity; sociologists like Weber and Simmel studied city life. In colonial India, the East India Company and later the Crown established new institutions: the railways (1853), telegraph, postal system, modern education and the factory, bringing urbanisation in port cities like Bombay, Madras and Calcutta, a market economy, and new classes. Colonial rule changed agrarian structures through the Permanent Settlement (1793), commercialised agriculture and dismantled handicrafts. After independence, planned development, public sector industry, land reforms and the Green Revolution transformed India. Technology such as the printing press and telegraph, and now the internet, speeds up change. Structural change in India includes industrialisation, urbanisation and the growth of a middle class, while many traditional institutions persist.

lessons.title: Cultural Change
yt: class 12 sociology cultural change sanskritisation westernisation modernisation secularisation reform movements brahmo samaj arya samaj aligarh

blocks.x: Cultural change refers to changes in values, beliefs, rituals and practices. In India it is seen through Sanskritisation, westernisation, modernisation and secularisation. M. N. Srinivas introduced Sanskritisation (the adoption of upper caste customs by lower castes) and westernisation (change in lifestyle, dress, food and ideas under British influence). Modernisation is the broader process of adopting modern ideas and institutions such as science, rationality, democracy and equality. Secularisation is the decline in the influence of religion on public life, though in India religion is also visible in public life. The nineteenth century saw social reform movements that questioned social evils and tried to reinterpret tradition. The Brahmo Samaj (1828, Raja Rammohan Roy) opposed sati, idol worship and supported women’s education; sati was banned in 1829 by Lord William Bentinck. The Prarthana Samaj (1867) worked in Maharashtra. The Arya Samaj (1875, Dayanand Saraswati) used the slogan Back to the Vedas and promoted education and widow remarriage. The Ramakrishna Mission (1897, Vivekananda) combined spirituality and service. The Aligarh Movement of Sir Syed Ahmad Khan (the Mohammedan Anglo-Oriental College, 1875) promoted modern education among Muslims. The Singh Sabha (1873) renewed Sikh identity. Jyotiba Phule’s Satyashodhak Samaj (1873) fought the caste order, Sri Narayana Guru’s SNDP (1903) uplifted the Ezhavas in Kerala, and Periyar’s Self-Respect Movement (1925) challenged Brahmin dominance in Tamil Nadu. Legislative reforms included the Widow Remarriage Act (1856) and the Age of Consent Act (1891). Reformers used print, schools and associations, and debated tradition and modernity. Reform movements had common features: they were responses to colonial modernity, valued rational thinking, were mostly led by the educated middle class, and often reinterpreted tradition. Their limitation was that their reach was often limited to the urban middle class. Media and education continue cultural change today.
Deep dive: Concepts
Sanskritisation, westernisation, modernisation and secularisation describe cultural change in India.
Deep dive: Reform movements
Brahmo Samaj, Arya Samaj, Aligarh, Singh Sabha, Satyashodhak Samaj, SNDP and Self-Respect Movement.
Deep dive: Laws and features
Sati ban 1829, Widow Remarriage Act 1856; reforms reinterpreted tradition and used modern means.

Big idea

Read the full explanation

Cultural change refers to changes in values, beliefs, rituals and practices. In India it is seen through Sanskritisation, westernisation, modernisation and secularisation. M. N. Srinivas introduced Sanskritisation (the adoption of upper caste customs by lower castes) and westernisation (change in lifestyle, dress, food and ideas under British influence). Modernisation is the broader process of adopting modern ideas and institutions such as science, rationality, democracy and equality. Secularisation is the decline in the influence of religion on public life, though in India religion is also visible in public life. The nineteenth century saw social reform movements that questioned social evils and tried to reinterpret tradition. The Brahmo Samaj (1828, Raja Rammohan Roy) opposed sati, idol worship and supported women’s education; sati was banned in 1829 by Lord William Bentinck. The Prarthana Samaj (1867) worked in Maharashtra. The Arya Samaj (1875, Dayanand Saraswati) used the slogan Back to the Vedas and promoted education and widow remarriage. The Ramakrishna Mission (1897, Vivekananda) combined spirituality and service. The Aligarh Movement of Sir Syed Ahmad Khan (the Mohammedan Anglo-Oriental College, 1875) promoted modern education among Muslims. The Singh Sabha (1873) renewed Sikh identity. Jyotiba Phule’s Satyashodhak Samaj (1873) fought the caste order, Sri Narayana Guru’s SNDP (1903) uplifted the Ezhavas in Kerala, and Periyar’s Self-Respect Movement (1925) challenged Brahmin dominance in Tamil Nadu. Legislative reforms included the Widow Remarriage Act (1856) and the Age of Consent Act (1891). Reformers used print, schools and associations, and debated tradition and modernity. Reform movements had common features: they were responses to colonial modernity, valued rational thinking, were mostly led by the educated middle class, and often reinterpreted tradition. Their limitation was that their reach was often limited to the urban middle class. Media and education continue cultural change today.

📘

Concepts

  • Sanskritisation, westernisation, modernisation and secularisation describe cultural change in India
🕰️

Reform movements

  • Brahmo Samaj, Arya Samaj, Aligarh, Singh Sabha, Satyashodhak Samaj, SNDP and Self-Respect Movement
⚖️

Laws and features

lessons.title: The Story of Indian Democracy
yt: class 12 sociology story of indian democracy constitution preamble fundamental rights panchayati raj 73rd amendment judicial review

blocks.x: India chose democracy through the Constitution, drafted by the Constituent Assembly (1946-49) in 2 years, 11 months and 18 days, with Dr B. R. Ambedkar as chairman of the drafting committee and Dr Rajendra Prasad as president; it was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950. The Preamble declares India a sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic, with justice, liberty, equality and fraternity; the words socialist and secular were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976). The Constitution gives Fundamental Rights (enforceable) and Directive Principles (guidelines), and Fundamental Duties were added in 1976. Universal adult franchise was granted at the start, as a bold step in a poor, unequal society; the first elections were held in 1951-52. India has a parliamentary system and a federal structure with a strong centre, an independent judiciary and judicial review, and public interest litigation (PIL) widened access to justice. Ambedkar warned that political democracy needs social and economic democracy. The Constitution also focuses on social justice by reservation for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, and later OBCs. Panchayati Raj, rooted in Gandhi’s ideal of Gram Swaraj, was strengthened by the 73rd Constitutional Amendment (1992, in force 1993), giving a three-tier structure (village, block, district), regular elections, Gram Sabhas, and reservation of at least one-third of seats for women (many states use 50 per cent), and for SCs and STs. The 74th Amendment did the same for urban local bodies. Social movements, civil society and an active press deepen democracy. Challenges include corruption, criminalisation, communalism, caste mobilisation and inequality. The Emergency of 1975-77 tested democracy, but elections in 1977 showed its resilience. Democracy in India is a continuing process involving participation of diverse groups.
Deep dive: Constitution
Drafted 1946-49, adopted 26 November 1949, in force 26 January 1950; Preamble with justice, liberty, equality, fraternity.
Deep dive: Institutions
Parliamentary federal democracy with universal franchise, independent judiciary and PIL.
Deep dive: Local democracy
73rd Amendment 1992 created three-tier Panchayati Raj with women’s reservation.

Bharatiya loktantra ki kahani: Samvidhan, Prastavana, maulik adhikar aur Panchayati Raj ka 73va sanshodhan.

India chose democracy through the Constitution, drafted by the Constituent Assembly (1946-49) in 2 years, 11 months and 18 days, with Dr B. R. Ambedkar as chairman of the drafting committee and Dr Rajendra Prasad as president; it was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950. The Preamble declares India a sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic, with justice, liberty, equality and fraternity; the words socialist and secular were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976). The Constitution gives Fundamental Rights (enforceable) and Directive Principles (guidelines), and Fundamental Duties were added in 1976. Universal adult franchise was granted at the start, as a bold step in a poor, unequal society; the first elections were held in 1951-52. India has a parliamentary system and a federal structure with a strong centre, an independent judiciary and judicial review, and public interest litigation (PIL) widened access to justice. Ambedkar warned that political democracy needs social and economic democracy. The Constitution also focuses on social justice by reservation for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, and later OBCs. Panchayati Raj, rooted in Gandhi’s ideal of Gram Swaraj, was strengthened by the 73rd Constitutional Amendment (1992, in force 1993), giving a three-tier structure (village, block, district), regular elections, Gram Sabhas, and reservation of at least one-third of seats for women (many states use 50 per cent), and for SCs and STs. The 74th Amendment did the same for urban local bodies. Social movements, civil society and an active press deepen democracy. Challenges include corruption, criminalisation, communalism, caste mobilisation and inequality. The Emergency of 1975-77 tested democracy, but elections in 1977 showed its resilience. Democracy in India is a continuing process involving participation of diverse groups.

lessons.title: Change and Development in Rural Society
yt: class 12 sociology rural society agrarian structure land reforms green revolution zamindari MGNREGA bonded labour migration

blocks.x: About two-thirds of Indians live in rural areas and depend on agriculture, which is the main source of livelihood. The agrarian structure includes landowners, tenants, sharecroppers and agricultural labourers, linked to caste: upper and dominant castes usually own land, while Dalits and landless castes work as labourers. Under the British, the Permanent Settlement (1793) made zamindars owners, the Ryotwari and Mahalwari systems taxed cultivators, high land revenue and commercialisation led to indebtedness. Village society had the jajmani system and rural indebtedness to moneylenders. After independence, land reforms aimed at equity and productivity: abolition of zamindari and intermediaries in the 1950s, tenancy reforms, ceilings on landholding and consolidation of holdings. Success was uneven, with better results in Kerala and West Bengal, while land ceiling surplus was small. Vinoba Bhave’s Bhoodan movement (1951) sought voluntary land gifts. The Green Revolution of the 1960s used high yielding variety seeds, fertilisers and irrigation, increased wheat and rice output in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh, but widened regional and class inequalities and caused ecological costs like falling water tables. Rural labour changed: the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act of 1976 outlawed bondage; the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act 2005 guarantees 100 days of wage employment. Commercialisation, mechanisation, contract farming and migration to cities and the Gulf have altered rural life; women do much farm work but own little land. Globalisation and market liberalisation exposed farmers to price fluctuations and input costs, and indebtedness and distress have been linked with farmers’ suicides. Rural-urban linkages, non-farm employment and remittances shape villages. The state tried to support rural development through the Public Distribution System, Minimum Support Price and credit.
Deep dive: Agrarian structure
Landowners, tenants and labourers linked to caste; colonial settlements brought indebtedness.
Deep dive: Reforms
Zamindari abolition, tenancy reform, land ceilings, Bhoodan, the Green Revolution and MGNREGA.
Deep dive: Contemporary change
Commercialisation, migration, distress and non-farm work reshape villages.

Read the full explanation

About two-thirds of Indians live in rural areas and depend on agriculture, which is the main source of livelihood. The agrarian structure includes landowners, tenants, sharecroppers and agricultural labourers, linked to caste: upper and dominant castes usually own land, while Dalits and landless castes work as labourers. Under the British, the Permanent Settlement (1793) made zamindars owners, the Ryotwari and Mahalwari systems taxed cultivators, high land revenue and commercialisation led to indebtedness. Village society had the jajmani system and rural indebtedness to moneylenders. After independence, land reforms aimed at equity and productivity: abolition of zamindari and intermediaries in the 1950s, tenancy reforms, ceilings on landholding and consolidation of holdings. Success was uneven, with better results in Kerala and West Bengal, while land ceiling surplus was small. Vinoba Bhave’s Bhoodan movement (1951) sought voluntary land gifts. The Green Revolution of the 1960s used high yielding variety seeds, fertilisers and irrigation, increased wheat and rice output in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh, but widened regional and class inequalities and caused ecological costs like falling water tables. Rural labour changed: the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act of 1976 outlawed bondage; the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act 2005 guarantees 100 days of wage employment. Commercialisation, mechanisation, contract farming and migration to cities and the Gulf have altered rural life; women do much farm work but own little land. Globalisation and market liberalisation exposed farmers to price fluctuations and input costs, and indebtedness and distress have been linked with farmers’ suicides. Rural-urban linkages, non-farm employment and remittances shape villages. The state tried to support rural development through the Public Distribution System, Minimum Support Price and credit.

lessons.title: Change and Development in Industrial Society
yt: class 12 sociology industrial society industrialisation trade unions informal sector liberalisation labour public sector tata steel

blocks.x: Industrialisation means the shift to factory production, mechanised work and wage labour. In colonial India industries developed unevenly: cotton textile mills in Bombay and Ahmedabad, jute mills in Calcutta, and the Tata Iron and Steel Company set up in 1907 at Sakchi (later Jamshedpur) by Jamsetji Tata’s family as a swadeshi enterprise. After independence the state led industrialisation through planning, public sector enterprises in steel, power and heavy industry, and the Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 under a mixed economy, with licences, import substitution and protection. Industrial policy changed after the 1991 reforms, which reduced licensing, opened up to foreign investment and liberalised imports. Industrial workers are in the organised (formal) sector with job security and benefits, and in the larger unorganised or informal sector, which employs about 90 per cent of the workforce, with low wages and no security. Women work in industries like textiles and garments, often at lower pay. Contract labour and casualisation have grown. Workers organised into trade unions: the Trade Unions Act 1926 recognised unions, and the All India Trade Union Congress (1920) was the first central union. Strikes such as the Bombay textile strike of 1982-83 led by Datta Samant showed workers’ militancy and the decline of mills. The Industrial Disputes Act 1947 and the Factories Act 1948 regulate relations and conditions. Small-scale and cottage industries are important in employment, and many reserved items were de-reserved after 1991. Migration brought workers to industrial cities, where chawls and slums housed them. Industrial development raises issues of pollution and safety, as in the Bhopal gas tragedy of December 1984, and of child labour, regulated by the Child Labour Act of 1986. Special Economic Zones were created under the Act of 2005. Globalisation increased outsourcing and flexible labour and weakened unions. Industrial society also changes family life, class and work culture.

Big idea

  • Industrialisation means the shift to factory production, mechanised work and wage labour
  • In colonial India industries developed unevenly: cotton textile mills in Bombay and Ahmedabad, jute mills in Calcutta, and the Tata Iron and Steel…
  • After independence the state led industrialisation through planning, public sector enterprises in steel, power and heavy industry, and the Industrial…

Read the full explanation

Industrialisation means the shift to factory production, mechanised work and wage labour. In colonial India industries developed unevenly: cotton textile mills in Bombay and Ahmedabad, jute mills in Calcutta, and the Tata Iron and Steel Company set up in 1907 at Sakchi (later Jamshedpur) by Jamsetji Tata’s family as a swadeshi enterprise. After independence the state led industrialisation through planning, public sector enterprises in steel, power and heavy industry, and the Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 under a mixed economy, with licences, import substitution and protection. Industrial policy changed after the 1991 reforms, which reduced licensing, opened up to foreign investment and liberalised imports. Industrial workers are in the organised (formal) sector with job security and benefits, and in the larger unorganised or informal sector, which employs about 90 per cent of the workforce, with low wages and no security. Women work in industries like textiles and garments, often at lower pay. Contract labour and casualisation have grown. Workers organised into trade unions: the Trade Unions Act 1926 recognised unions, and the All India Trade Union Congress (1920) was the first central union. Strikes such as the Bombay textile strike of 1982-83 led by Datta Samant showed workers’ militancy and the decline of mills. The Industrial Disputes Act 1947 and the Factories Act 1948 regulate relations and conditions. Small-scale and cottage industries are important in employment, and many reserved items were de-reserved after 1991. Migration brought workers to industrial cities, where chawls and slums housed them. Industrial development raises issues of pollution and safety, as in the Bhopal gas tragedy of December 1984, and of child labour, regulated by the Child Labour Act of 1986. Special Economic Zones were created under the Act of 2005. Globalisation increased outsourcing and flexible labour and weakened unions. Industrial society also changes family life, class and work culture.

lessons.title: Globalisation and Social Change
yt: class 12 sociology globalisation social change outsourcing BPO glocalisation global village transnational corporations consumption culture

blocks.x: Globalisation is the growing interconnection of economies, cultures and societies across the world. It is not new, but the present phase after 1991 is faster, based on information technology, communication and capital flows. Economic globalisation includes trade liberalisation, the role of the WTO (1995), transnational corporations (TNCs), global finance, outsourcing and business process outsourcing (BPO), as in call centres in Bangalore and Gurgaon. India’s reforms of 1991 (liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation) opened the economy, and the IT industry, services and exports grew. Global communication includes mobile phones, satellite television and the internet, which compress time and space (David Harvey), making the world a global village (Marshall McLuhan). Cultural change takes two forms: homogenisation, the spread of a uniform global culture of fast food, brands and music, and glocalisation (Roland Robertson), where global products adapt to local cultures, as with McDonald’s offering vegetarian items in India. Globalisation also affects work: employment in services grew, flexible and contract work spread, and women entered new jobs such as call centres, though under night shifts. Consumption patterns changed with malls, brands and credit. Farmers face competition and volatile world prices; small producers and artisans have lost, while some export crops have gained. Migration and remittances link families across nations. Media and the internet spread new ideas, and social media connect people. Critics point to inequality, job insecurity, cultural homogenisation and dominance of TNCs. Supporters point to growth, jobs, technology and wider choices. In sociological terms globalisation affects class, caste, gender and the state. The state’s role has changed from regulator to facilitator, but it has not disappeared. Globalisation, hence, brings change that is uneven and contested.
Deep dive: Economic globalisation
Liberalisation, WTO, TNCs, outsourcing and BPO changed India’s economy after 1991.
Deep dive: Culture
Homogenisation and glocalisation; global village and time-space compression.
Deep dive: Impacts
Growth and jobs alongside inequality, insecurity and pressure on farmers and artisans.

Read the full explanation

Globalisation is the growing interconnection of economies, cultures and societies across the world. It is not new, but the present phase after 1991 is faster, based on information technology, communication and capital flows. Economic globalisation includes trade liberalisation, the role of the WTO (1995), transnational corporations (TNCs), global finance, outsourcing and business process outsourcing (BPO), as in call centres in Bangalore and Gurgaon. India’s reforms of 1991 (liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation) opened the economy, and the IT industry, services and exports grew. Global communication includes mobile phones, satellite television and the internet, which compress time and space (David Harvey), making the world a global village (Marshall McLuhan). Cultural change takes two forms: homogenisation, the spread of a uniform global culture of fast food, brands and music, and glocalisation (Roland Robertson), where global products adapt to local cultures, as with McDonald’s offering vegetarian items in India. Globalisation also affects work: employment in services grew, flexible and contract work spread, and women entered new jobs such as call centres, though under night shifts. Consumption patterns changed with malls, brands and credit. Farmers face competition and volatile world prices; small producers and artisans have lost, while some export crops have gained. Migration and remittances link families across nations. Media and the internet spread new ideas, and social media connect people. Critics point to inequality, job insecurity, cultural homogenisation and dominance of TNCs. Supporters point to growth, jobs, technology and wider choices. In sociological terms globalisation affects class, caste, gender and the state. The state’s role has changed from regulator to facilitator, but it has not disappeared. Globalisation, hence, brings change that is uneven and contested.

lessons.title: Mass Media and Communications
yt: class 12 sociology mass media communications print press radio television internet social media doordarshan prasar bharati vernacular press

blocks.x: Mass media are means of communication that reach large audiences: print (newspapers, magazines), electronic (radio, television, cinema) and digital (internet and social media). They are one-way or interactive, have wide reach and shape opinion, culture and politics. The printing press, associated with Gutenberg around 1440, spread ideas and literacy. In India, the first newspaper, Hicky’s Bengal Gazette, began in 1780; Raja Rammohan Roy launched Sambad Kaumudi in 1821; the press became a tool of nationalism with leaders such as Tilak (Kesari and Mahratta), Gandhi (Young India, Harijan) and Ambedkar (Mooknayak, 1920). The colonial state used the Vernacular Press Act of 1878 under Lytton to restrict Indian language papers, and it was repealed in 1882. Radio began with the Indian Broadcasting Company in 1927 and was named All India Radio in 1936; private FM radio began from 1999 onwards. Television began in India as an experimental service in Delhi on 15 September 1959, Doordarshan expanded after 1975 with the SITE experiment and colour came in 1982 with the Asian Games. Satellite and cable television arrived after 1991 with Star TV and CNN, ending the state monopoly. Prasar Bharati, the public broadcaster, was set up under the Prasar Bharati Act 1990 and became operational in 1997. The first Indian feature film was Raja Harishchandra (1913) by Dadasaheb Phalke, and the first talkie was Alam Ara (1931). The internet and smartphones created social media and citizen journalism. Freedom of the press flows from Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution, subject to reasonable restrictions. Media influence democracy by informing citizens, but issues such as paid news, ownership concentration, sensationalism and TRP competition affect quality. Media convergence blurs boundaries among platforms. The digital divide means that access is unequal. Media are also shaped by market forces and advertising, and shape consumption and culture.
Deep dive: Media growth
From the 1780 press to radio, television, satellite channels and social media.
Deep dive: Press and nationalism
Newspapers spread nationalism; the Vernacular Press Act of 1878 tried to curb them.
Deep dive: Media and democracy
Article 19(1)(a) protects the press; paid news, ownership and the digital divide are concerns.

Read the full explanation

Mass media are means of communication that reach large audiences: print (newspapers, magazines), electronic (radio, television, cinema) and digital (internet and social media). They are one-way or interactive, have wide reach and shape opinion, culture and politics. The printing press, associated with Gutenberg around 1440, spread ideas and literacy. In India, the first newspaper, Hicky’s Bengal Gazette, began in 1780; Raja Rammohan Roy launched Sambad Kaumudi in 1821; the press became a tool of nationalism with leaders such as Tilak (Kesari and Mahratta), Gandhi (Young India, Harijan) and Ambedkar (Mooknayak, 1920). The colonial state used the Vernacular Press Act of 1878 under Lytton to restrict Indian language papers, and it was repealed in 1882. Radio began with the Indian Broadcasting Company in 1927 and was named All India Radio in 1936; private FM radio began from 1999 onwards. Television began in India as an experimental service in Delhi on 15 September 1959, Doordarshan expanded after 1975 with the SITE experiment and colour came in 1982 with the Asian Games. Satellite and cable television arrived after 1991 with Star TV and CNN, ending the state monopoly. Prasar Bharati, the public broadcaster, was set up under the Prasar Bharati Act 1990 and became operational in 1997. The first Indian feature film was Raja Harishchandra (1913) by Dadasaheb Phalke, and the first talkie was Alam Ara (1931). The internet and smartphones created social media and citizen journalism. Freedom of the press flows from Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution, subject to reasonable restrictions. Media influence democracy by informing citizens, but issues such as paid news, ownership concentration, sensationalism and TRP competition affect quality. Media convergence blurs boundaries among platforms. The digital divide means that access is unequal. Media are also shaped by market forces and advertising, and shape consumption and culture.

lessons.title: Social Movements
yt: class 12 sociology social movements peasant tribal dalit women environmental chipko narmada bardoli telangana old and new movements

blocks.x: A social movement is a sustained collective effort to bring about or resist social change, using organisation, ideology and leadership, often outside formal politics. Features include collective action, an organised leadership, a common ideology and a continuing effort. Theories include relative deprivation (frustration from a gap between expectation and reality) and resource mobilisation (the role of organisation and resources). Movements are classified as redemptive (changing individuals), reformative (changing structures gradually) and revolutionary (overthrowing the social order). Old social movements, such as the workers’ and peasant movements, focus on class and economic demands and are linked to parties; new social movements, such as environmental, women’s and Dalit movements, are about identity, ecology and rights. Peasant movements include the Champaran Satyagraha (1917), Kheda (1918), the Bardoli Satyagraha (1928) led by Vallabhbhai Patel, the Tebhaga movement in Bengal (1946-47), the Telangana movement (1946-51) and the Naxalbari uprising of 1967; the All India Kisan Sabha was formed in 1936 under Swami Sahajanand Saraswati. Tribal movements demand land, forest and identity; the Jharkhand movement led to the state in 2000. Dalit movements include the Mahad Satyagraha, Ambedkar’s conversion to Buddhism in 1956, and the Dalit Panthers (1972). Women’s movements began with reform in the nineteenth century and in modern times campaigned against dowry, rape (the Mathura case of 1972 and amendments of 1983), domestic violence, and for property rights; the Vishakha guidelines of 1997 led to the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act 2013, the Domestic Violence Act 2005 and the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act 2005; the Criminal Law Amendment of 2013 followed the Delhi protests of 2012, and the Women’s Reservation Act 2023 reserved one-third of seats in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies. Environmental movements include Chipko (1973), Narmada Bachao Andolan (1985) and Silent Valley in Kerala (1970s-80s). Movements shape law, policy and public opinion, but face repression, co-option and internal division. Social movements are essential to democracy because they voice marginalised concerns.
Deep dive: Concepts
Collective, organised, ideological efforts; relative deprivation and resource mobilisation; redemptive, reformative and revolutionary types.
Deep dive: Movements
Peasant, tribal, Dalit, women’s and environmental movements shaped India’s politics and laws.
Deep dive: Impact
Movements led to laws such as the 2013 harassment Act and 2005 property rights, and to states like Jharkhand.

problems.q: What is a social movement?
problems.a: A sustained collective effort, usually organised, to bring about or resist social change.

problems.q: Distinguish old and new social movements.
problems.a: Old movements, such as workers’ and peasant movements, focus on class and economic demands, while new ones, such as environmental and women’s movements, focus on identity, ecology and rights.

problems.q: Explain the contribution of the women’s movement to law.
problems.a: Campaigns led to anti-rape law changes in 1983 and 2013, the Domestic Violence Act 2005, the Hindu Succession Amendment 2005 and the 2013 workplace harassment Act after Vishakha guidelines.

Read the full explanation

A social movement is a sustained collective effort to bring about or resist social change, using organisation, ideology and leadership, often outside formal politics. Features include collective action, an organised leadership, a common ideology and a continuing effort. Theories include relative deprivation (frustration from a gap between expectation and reality) and resource mobilisation (the role of organisation and resources). Movements are classified as redemptive (changing individuals), reformative (changing structures gradually) and revolutionary (overthrowing the social order). Old social movements, such as the workers’ and peasant movements, focus on class and economic demands and are linked to parties; new social movements, such as environmental, women’s and Dalit movements, are about identity, ecology and rights. Peasant movements include the Champaran Satyagraha (1917), Kheda (1918), the Bardoli Satyagraha (1928) led by Vallabhbhai Patel, the Tebhaga movement in Bengal (1946-47), the Telangana movement (1946-51) and the Naxalbari uprising of 1967; the All India Kisan Sabha was formed in 1936 under Swami Sahajanand Saraswati. Tribal movements demand land, forest and identity; the Jharkhand movement led to the state in 2000. Dalit movements include the Mahad Satyagraha, Ambedkar’s conversion to Buddhism in 1956, and the Dalit Panthers (1972). Women’s movements began with reform in the nineteenth century and in modern times campaigned against dowry, rape (the Mathura case of 1972 and amendments of 1983), domestic violence, and for property rights; the Vishakha guidelines of 1997 led to the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act 2013, the Domestic Violence Act 2005 and the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act 2005; the Criminal Law Amendment of 2013 followed the Delhi protests of 2012, and the Women’s Reservation Act 2023 reserved one-third of seats in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies. Environmental movements include Chipko (1973), Narmada Bachao Andolan (1985) and Silent Valley in Kerala (1970s-80s). Movements shape law, policy and public opinion, but face repression, co-option and internal division. Social movements are essential to democracy because they voice marginalised concerns.

📘

Concepts

  • Collective, organised, ideological efforts
  • Relative deprivation and resource mobilisation
  • Redemptive, reformative and revolutionary types
🕰️

Movements

  • Peasant, tribal, Dalit, women’s and environmental movements shaped India’s politics and laws
🌟

Impact

  • Movements led to laws such as the 2013 harassment Act and 2005 property rights, and to states like Jharkhand
